title: HIV Ireland quit HSE programme due to ‘slagging’ and claims of corruption, WRC told
description: Charity defends complaint of whistleblower penalisation brought by veteran manager accused of bullying
content:
HIV Ireland pulled out of the launch of the HSE ’s You, Me and HIV programme last year because of online “slagging” and claims by the campaign’s ambassadors that there was “corruption” at the charity, its chief executive has said.
Stephen O’Hare was under cross-examination on Monday at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) , where the charity is defending a complaint of whistleblower penalisation brought by veteran manager Erin Nugent.
Nugent, who has worked at the charity since 1995, is facing disciplinary action, currently on hold, after being accused of bullying and harassment toward colleagues and insubordination towards O’Hare.
Her trade union, Fórsa , says this is to “punish” her for voicing concerns about HIV Ireland’s financial governance, and alleged discontent with the charity among the community of people living with HIV.
In addition to the disciplinary action, which the charity said was on “pause” pending the outcome of the Protected Disclosures Act 2014 complaint, Nugent maintains she has been “disappeared” as the public face of HIV Ireland at conferences and in the press as penalisation for whistleblowing.
Counsel for the charity Aoife McMahon said Nugent was only prevented from attending one related event: the launch of a HSE programme to combat stigma and misinformation about HIV, in January 2025 called You, Me and HIV.
The organisation disputes Nugent’s claim that she has been “disappeared” as the public face of HIV Ireland at conferences and in the press as penalisation for whistleblowing.
O’Hare’s evidence was that following World Aids Day on December 1st, 2024, the charity was subject to “commentary” from a number of members of the public and activists.
“They were alleging corruption, misappropriation of funds, alleging fraud at the organisation, and the people doing that were the people who were engaged by the HSE in their own publicity campaign, You, Me and HIV,” O’Hare said.
The comments were “very nasty” and “bordering on personally offensive”, he said.
HIV Ireland staff, including Nugent, were due to participate in a launch event for the HSE campaign on January 15th, 2025, he said.
O’Hare decided HIV Ireland would not participate in the HSE campaign in view of the fact its ambassadors were “openly slagging” his staff and organisation, he said.
He said he told the HSE the day before the launch: “Your ambassadors for your campaign are currently on social media saying defamatory things about HIV Ireland; they shouldn’t be doing that.” The HSE was “unhappy” with HIV Ireland’s stance, he added.
O’Hare’s evidence was that in late 2024, other HIV Ireland staff had come to him about interactions they had with Nugent where financial matters were discussed.
He had earlier in the year urged the charity’s board to take disciplinary action against Nugent, writing in a letter that he believed her to be engaged in “borderline insubordination” and “bullying behaviour”, the tribunal heard.
Cross-examining O’Hare, Louise O’Hara of Fórsa, for Nugent, said: “You essentially presided over the decline of relations and functions and used it to bring disciplinary action against a whistleblower… you massively overstepped to punish Dr Nugent.”
“No, none of what you said there is correct,” the chief executive said.
Adjudication officer Breiffni O’Neill has concluded hearings on the case and told the parties he intends to issue his decision in January.

title: VRT change to push up prices for nine of the top 10 bestselling new cars
description: The VRT increase will hit regular hybrids, but plug-in hybrids and EVs avoid the rise
content:
The decision to increase most Vehicle Registration Tax (VRT) rates by 1 per cent will affect prices for nine of the 10 bestselling models in the Irish new car market.
Cars with CO2 emissions over 80g/km will see a 1 per cent increase in VRT from January 1st next year, impacting tax bands three to 20. That emissions level means most regular hybrids will be hit with the tax rise, but most plug-in hybrid (PHEV) versions and all EVs will avoid the increase.
The change will see VRT increases on prices for the Toyota Yaris Cross, the current bestselling new car, along with the regular Yaris hybrid model.
The second most popular model on the market, Hyundai ’s Tucson, will also face a tax rise, though its plug-in hybrid version (PHEV), with emissions of up to 73g/km, avoids the increase.
[ Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income Opens in new window ]
Other models facing price increases to regular and hybrid cars include the Skoda Octavia, Kia Sportage, Skoda Kodiaq and Toyota Corolla.
Of the 128,268 new cars sold up to the end of September, 58 per cent fall into VRT tax bands that will see a 1 per cent increase. The Government estimates the change will generate €37 million in extra tax revenue in 2027.
[ Budget 2027 main points: €10 increase in pension and welfare rates; 20 cent per ml tax on vapes Opens in new window ]
The Minister for Finance, Simon Harris , also extended the current VRT relief on EVs until the end of 2028. The relief provides up to €5,000 off the calculated VRT due on electric cars.
While the industry expects EV and PHEV sales to equate to nearly 50 per cent of the new car market next year, Brian Cooke of the Society of the Irish Motor Industry said the VRT increase was unnecessary.
“The majority of people in the new year will buy a new car in the affected bands, and you are adding an unnecessary expense to people already facing increasing fuel costs and rising costs of living,” Cooke said. However, he welcomed the extension of the VRT relief on EVs.

title: Olivia Divilly, Síofra O’Shea and Aimee Mackin on shortlist for player of the year
description: Divilly played a central role in Galway’s All-Ireland triumph during the summer, scoring three points in the final
content:
Galway forward Olivia Divilly has once again made the shortlist for the TG4 Ladies Football Players’ Player of the Year.
Divilly, Kerry’s Síofra O’Shea – the top scorer in this year’s championship – and Armagh’s Aimee Mackin are the three nominees for the senior accolade.
In 2025, Divilly was shortlisted alongside Dublin’s Hannah Tyrrell and Kate Sullivan. Tyrrell ultimately won the award.
Divilly played a central role in Galway’s All-Ireland triumph during the summer, scoring three points in the final against Kerry and registering 2-27 over the course of the entire championship.
O’Shea scored five points in the decider and her overall haul in the championship was 3-30.
Armagh’s season ended at the semi-final stage, but Mackin was superb throughout and during the All-Ireland series she chalked up 5-12.
The winners will be revealed at the 2026 TG4 All-Star Awards banquet at The Bonnington Dublin Hotel on Saturday, November 14th.
TG4 Senior Players’ Player of the Year Award Nominees
Aimee Mackin (Armagh); Olivia Divilly (Galway); Síofra O’Shea (Kerry).
TG4 Intermediate Players’ Player of the Year Award Nominees
Eimear Smyth (Fermanagh); Saoirse Wynne (Roscommon); Anna Jones (Westmeath).
TG4 Junior Players’ Player of the Year Award Nominees
Maria O’Neill (Antrim); Róisín Bailey (Carlow); Sara Doyle (Carlow).

title: New mandatory register for Airbnb and other short-term lettings to open in December
description: Growth of often controversial sector and difficulty contacting hosts key reasons for new legislation
content:
A new register for people who rent out properties for short-term lets on online platforms such as Airbnb is to open on December 1st.
Regulation of short-term letting has proved controversial in Ireland and other countries, and the Government will attempt to bring clarity to the sector in a forthcoming Bill.
Minister for Tourism Peter Burke announced the publication of the Short Term Letting and Tourism Bill on Tuesday.
It will establish a new regulatory framework for short-term accommodation, in line with EU regulations.
The Bill will designate Fáilte Ireland as the competent authority responsible for implementing the new framework, including the establishment and operation of a national register of short-term lettings covering stays of up to 21 nights for the first time.
The Government cited the growth of short-term lettings and the difficulty in contacting hosts as key reasons for the new legislation.
“By establishing the register, we will improve the quality of data on tourist accommodation and strengthen transparency across the sector,” said Burke.
“The framework will provide greater clarity for hosts and platforms while helping public authorities better understand accommodation supply and support the sustainable development of tourism throughout the country, while also ensuring that long-term rental accommodation is also being prioritised, particularly in urban areas.”
The Bill will now proceed through the legislative process in the Oireachtas, with the register due to open on December 1st.
Hosts offering short-term accommodation rental services will be required to obtain and maintain a valid registration number and display it on all advertisements and listings.
Online short-term rental platforms will be required to display registration numbers, conduct random checks on listings, submit specified data on short-term rental activity and remove or disable access to non-compliant listings where required.
The legislation will also give Fáilte Ireland powers to monitor compliance, including the appointment of registration officers and authorised personnel to carry out inspections and investigations.
It also requires the production of information and records.
The Bill introduces a range of enforcement measures, including fixed payment notices and summary offences. In cases involving serious breaches by online short-term rental platforms, financial sanctions will apply.
These may include fines of up to 2 per cent of annual worldwide turnover.
All hosts must confirm they are compliant with planning rules to register, with provision in the Bill for hosts in locations with a population under 20,000 having two years to regularise their planning.

title: South Africa in running to stage Africa’s first Olympics as 2036 race hots up
description: Qatar widely regarded as frontrunners ahead of bids from India and Hungary
content:
South Africa is in the hunt to stage Africa’s first Olympics after it was named as one of seven countries that will formally present its case to host the 2036 Games in November.
However its bid, which would likely be spread across Cape Town, Johannesburg and Durban, is seen as a distinct outsider, with Qatar widely regarded as the frontrunners ahead of India and Hungary.
Turkey, Germany and the Republic of Korea make up the remaining countries that have been asked to present to the International Olympic Committee’s future bid committee next month, marking the first stage of a process that will end with a vote in 2029.
Qatar’s position at the top of the pecking order is partly down to the perceived strength of the bid and the fact that Asia will have not hosted a Games since Tokyo 2020. However a Doha Olympics would have to be moved from the Games’ traditional July-August slot due to the heat.
India is seen as the closest challenger, although its bid to host in Ahmedabad is seen to have slipped back during the past 18 months.
The Indian bid was given a wake-up call when it visited Lausanne in the summer of 2025, with concerns raised about mismanagement and governance issues at the Indian Olympic Association, the lack of detail in the bid, and the country’s dismal performance in the Paris Games.
If there is to be another strong challenger to Qatar, it could come from Hungary. Its bid, which is said to include not only Budapest but the Austrian capital Vienna and the Slovakian capital Bratislava, is very well regarded. However, it is unclear whether the new government in Hungary cares as much about hosting the Olympics as the previous prime minister, Viktor Orbán.
At this stage most of the other bids are being seen as placeholders for the 2040 Olympics. That includes Germany, given the potentially tricky optics surrounding a centenary Games.
In a handbook published on Tuesday, the IOC said the bids would be based on a number of technical factors – including the venues and athlete experience, political and public support, and the ability to deliver a great Games and a long-term legacy – as well as their vision for the Olympics.
“I was fortunate to compete at five Olympic Games, across four continents. Each had their own character,” said the IOC president Kirsty Coventry. “Each host brought something unique through its people, its culture and the way it chose to stage the Games. But wherever the Games take place, one thing must never change: athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do.
“As an athlete, you spend years working to make your Olympic dream come true. The experience you have when you finally reach the Olympic Games stays with you for the rest of your life. That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point.”
Other countries interested in bidding for 2036 have until the end of October to confirm their interest before nominations close. The IOC said that it would conduct feasibility assessments by March 2027 and in December 2028 its executive board would open a “targeted dialogue with a select number of preferred hosts”. In the summer of 2029 a vote will then be taken to select who will stage the 2036 Games. – Guardian

title: Capital gains tax cut will cost exchequer €186m a year in Budget 2027’s most expensive measure
description: Changes to R&D tax-credit scheme include 20% increase in first-year refunds
content:
The Government’s decision to reduce the standard rate of capital gains tax (CGT) will cost the exchequer an estimated €186 million in a full year, making it the single most expensive measure announced in Budget 2027 outside the personal income tax package.
Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris said the reduction in the CGT rate from 33 per cent to 31 per cent would “reward risk and facilitate the scaling-up of home-grown Irish firms”.
The new 31 per cent rate, which applies to profits from the sale or gifting of an asset, will not apply to sales of development land, which will continue to be taxed at 33 per cent, the Department of Finance said. It will apply to disposals made on or after October 7th.
The measure will cost the exchequer €46.5 million next year and €186 million in a full year, according to the Department of Finance ’s estimates, published with the budget on Tuesday.
Úna Ryan, tax partner at Grant Thornton Ireland, said the reduction, while modest, is “very much welcomed”.
However, she said it is “unlikely to materially change investment decisions, encourage significantly greater levels of entrepreneurship or meaningfully accelerate the recycling of capital into the Irish economy”, and a larger cut would have been better in that regard.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
Separately, Harris announced several changes to the research and development (R&D) tax-credit regime. The relief allows businesses undertaking research to claim back a percentage of the total costs of their activities in cash or against their corporation tax bill in annual instalments.
Currently, companies can claim back up to €87,500 in the first year. This threshold will now increase by 20 per cent to €105,000, to provide cash flow support to smaller R&D projects, Harris said in his budget speech.
It comes after his predecessor, Paschal Donohoe, increased the amount of relief available to businesses under the scheme from 30 per cent to 35 per cent of qualifying expenditure in Budget 2026.
[ Budget 2027 main points: Minimum wage to rise 79 cent; €12,000 per year limit for investment scheme Opens in new window ]
At the time, the Coalition also increased the threshold for first-year refunds under the scheme to €87,500 from €75,000 to support smaller projects.
On Tuesday, Harris said the upcoming finance bill will increase the existing limits for work subcontracted to third-level institutions and third-party companies to 20 per cent or €200,000, whichever is greater.
At the moment, companies can claim back subcontracted R&D costs of 15 per cent, up to a maximum of €100,000, against their total qualifying in-house R&D expenditure.
The so-called angel investor relief, which offers reduced rates of CGT to qualifying individuals and partnerships, has also been extended.
[ All inheritance tax free thresholds rise in the budget but no other reforms Opens in new window ]
The changes will cost an estimated €58.6 million next year and €118.3 million in a full year.
Commenting on the budget announcement, Ian Collins, tax partner and head of innovation incentives at EY Ireland, said businesses were not expecting movement on the headline rate after the changes announced last year.
“However, they have been looking for continued progress in modernising and broadening the R&D regime to make it more fit for purpose,” he added.
Separately, the Government announced a commitment to invest €1 billion in the scaling-up of indigenous Irish companies through the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF).
“This is ISIF’s biggest ever investment in scaling, and it will be a three-year programme running up to 2030,” Harris said.

title: Carlos Alcaraz takes first title since February with victory in Japan Open final
description: Playing just his third tournament since returning from injury, the Spaniard recovered from a shaky start to defeat Jiri Lehecka
content:
Carlos Alcaraz defeated Jiri Lehecka in the final of the Japan Open to win his first individual title since February.
Playing just his third tournament since returning from four-and-a-half months out with a wrist injury, Alcaraz recovered from a shaky start to defeat Czech Lehecka 7-6 (4) 6-4.
It is a second title in a row in the Japanese capital for Alcaraz, who showed patchy form at times but finished with a strong performance.
The Spaniard told Sky Sports: “I’m really happy to be able to lift a trophy again. It’s been a while and obviously it’s extra special after my injury.
“It was a tough week that I didn’t find my best tennis, my best level, but I did find the good solutions and I think that’s what matters in the end.
“I would say today was the best match of the week, or at least more consistent the level that I played, so I’m just really, really happy.”
Lehecka, ranked 19th, was sharper at the start and led 3-1 but Alcaraz hit back to level at 3-3 and showed his full repertoire of crowd-pleasing shots in the tie-break, winning five points in a row from 2-4.
He made his move in the seventh game of the second set with a break to lead 4-3 and looked delighted after clinching victory.
Alcaraz began the season by winning his seventh major title to complete the career Grand Slam at the Australian Open and also lifted the trophy in his next tournament in Doha before his injury lay-off.

title: Russia tells WHO there are no plague cases in Siberian city
description: Laboratory worker at plague research institute died last week
content:
Russian authorities told the World Health Organisation (WHO) on ‌Tuesday that it has no cases of plague in the city of ​Irkutsk in Siberia, where a laboratory worker at a plague research institute died last week , according to a spokesperson for the ​UN health agency.
Moscow, which is required under global health rules ⁠to respond to WHO requests within 24 hours, previously ‌told ‌the ​WHO authorities were investigating whether pneumonic plague caused the death of Daria Shipilova (28).
“No case of this dangerous ⁠disease has been ​recorded in the city of ​Irkutsk, Russian Federation,” Russian authorities said in an official ‌response to a WHO ​request, read out by WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier at ⁠a Geneva press briefing.
They ⁠also ​told the UN agency they have identified the people in contact with Shipilova and that test results for dangerous infectious pathogens were negative.
Reuters could not immediately establish if this meant that they had also tested Shipilova ‌and whether they could ⁠rule out plague in her case. The Russian diplomatic mission to the UN in Geneva ‌did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The WHO has ​previously said that the risk of ​plague to the general population appeared to be low. – Reuters

title: Carla Ward urges Ireland to thrive as favourites in World Cup playoff against Kazakhstan
description: Stephen Neligan joins as assistant before two-legged qualifying play-off
content:
It’s unlikely a trip from Sydney to Astana was on Stephen Neligan’s bingo card last week, but for a man who once worked in a sewage treatment plant and ended up as assistant manager of Everton’s women’s team, career swerves are nothing new.
The Australian has joined Carla Ward ’s Republic of Ireland set-up in advance of the World Cup qualifying playoff against Kazakhstan, the first leg of which takes place in Astana on Friday (12pm Irish time) before Páirc Uí Chaoimh hosts the return leg next Tuesday (7.30pm).
Technically, Neligan becomes Ward’s fourth assistant in just over a year, although Brian Sorensen, whom she chose as a replacement for Gary Cronin, had to withdraw before ever getting to fill the role when he was appointed interim manager of Aston Villa’s women last week. Neligan had been Sorensen’s assistant at Everton.
“Stephen was in the WSL for five years with Everton,” said Ward. “Previous to that he worked at Fortuna Hjorring in Denmark and before that in Australia. So he’s familiar to a lot of the players, he’s also familiar to myself, he’s someone I’ve known for a while.”
“He actually is somebody I tried to talk to seven or eight months ago about [joining] the process, but he was very much embedded in his job at Everton. It was very last-minute, but we’re delighted we got him on a flight from Sydney. He’s here and we’re delighted to have him. He’s with us for the next two windows, and then we’ll see from there.”
Since Villa sacked their manager, Natalia Arroyo, last week, there has been speculation about the club attempting to lure Ward back to where managed for three seasons.
[ Ireland v Kazakhstan World Cup playoff: Team news, kick-off time, where to watch Opens in new window ]
“I’m really happy where I am, to be honest,” she said. “I’ve said it very loudly, very clearly: I love my job here. Hopefully the organisation love what I do too. But, for me, there’s only one process in my mind, and that’s me being really honest. I wouldn’t entertain anything other than conversations about the next four games. That is as clear as I can be with anything.”
Ward and the squad travelled to Astana on Monday on a chartered flight, the journey, which included a refuelling stop in Turkey, taking close to 11 hours. They’ve been joined by the FAI’s communications manager Kieran Crowley, who will hope for a slightly less eventful window than the one he just endured with the men’s team.
They were greeted by temperatures close to zero, with snow forecast, but, to their relief, it’s due to warm up through the week. They will expect to book their place in the final qualifying playoff against Belgium or Poland, with Kazakhstan a lowly 98 in the Fifa rankings – 77 places below Ireland.
But a few factors will make Ireland cautious enough going into these games, notably the absence of their two most important players, captain Katie McCabe (suspended) and Denise O’Sullivan . Both will return for the second leg, O’Sullivan’s recent injury problems prompting Ward to spare her this trip. Add in the absence of Ruesha Littlejohn, who is still without a club, and that’s a significant loss of leadership.
“But I think we have a lot of leaders who emerged in the last campaign, and I think they’ll continue to do so,” ward said. “These moments are always opportunities for people to really step up. Naturally, Katie, Denise and Ruesha are big losses, but I have full belief in my squad. I believe in every single one of them. “
Another factor is that the first leg will be played on an artificial pitch – “and let me tell you, players don’t like playing on 3G”, Ward said.
“But that happens, so we’ll be ready, we believe it’s going to be okay. The ball will certainly move quickly, and that might work for us, but it’s the same for both teams.”
“We’ve got four cup finals,” Ward continued, adding in that likely two-legged affair against Belgium or Poland, where the prize for the winners will be a place in next summer’s World Cup in Brazil.
“There will be absolutely no complacency. We have used the underdog mentality as fuel before, and Kazakhstan will do exactly the same.
“When you look at the billboards around the place, you look at the TV stations here, everyone’s talking about the game. This is their World Cup final, essentially. It’s the biggest game for them in a very, very long time. We’ve thrived with the underdog tag before, let’s make sure that we don’t allow anyone else to thrive on it against us.”

title: Could Zuckerberg’s Waterford GAA club donations be a new wave of philanthropy in Ireland?
description: Ireland is entering an unprecedented transfer of wealth, but experts say more could be done to encourage charitable giving
content:
Before the arrival of the modern welfare state, there was philanthropy.
In the absence of a proper system of income tax to put a safety net under society, it was left to wealthy individuals to plug the gaps in society with some of their riches.
In Ireland, the legacy of the Scottish-American industrialist Andrew Carnegie can still be seen in many public libraries he funded the building of in the early 20th century.
Carnegie was famously driven by a semi-religious notion that the mega-rich should give away their surplus before they die and in the end he donated the equivalent of $6.9 billion (€6.2 billion) to charitable causes.
He lived at a time comparable to our own, where capitalism allowed individuals to amass huge fortunes.
Whether Mark Zuckerberg , founder and chief executive of Facebook’s parent group Meta, will be remembered like Carnegie is open to question but his recent charitable donation of €150,000 to three GAA clubs in Waterford has brought the practice back into focus.
Zuckerberg chose the three clubs closest to Strancally Castle near Youghal, which he purchased in August, and it is thought to be his first philanthropic act in Ireland.
Along with his wife Priscilla Chan, he said: “The GAA is at the heart of communities across Ireland. As new members of the Waterford community, we’re proud to support these local clubs and the important role they play.”
Zuckerberg is not the first high-profile businessperson to make a donation to the GAA.
[ Mark Zuckerberg’s few coins thrown to the GAA should not fool us Opens in new window ]
After giving millions of euros to Limerick GAA down through the years, in 2023 the racing magnate JP McManus gave €1 million to every county board in the country.
He had previously donated €100,000 to each in 2018.
But, according to those who advise on philanthropic work, there is now more scope for philanthropy in Ireland than ever before.
“There is €1.43 trillion in household wealth here,” says Éilis Murray, chief executive of Philanthropy Ireland.
“The wealth is there. Now that does not necessarily mean it is going to translate into philanthropy but for the first time we are having a conversation about it.”
Murray says Ireland is going through an unprecedented transfer of intergenerational wealth at the moment, and she and others are advocating that people consider using some of this money for charitable causes.
“In the United States and the UK they have a lot of inherited wealth and philanthropy is part of the DNA there. It is only beginning to emerge in Ireland,” she says.
This is not to say that, outside of inherited wealth, philanthropy has not already played a significant role here, she adds.
“One of the things most of us don’t realise is the amount of philanthropy that is being done and the impact that has on communities the length and breadth of the country,” says Murray.
“The Children’s Rights Alliance was a project initially funded through philanthropy. The legislation that followed all came from that movement and that area of support – by funding the research – it helped identify the issue that needed addressing.
“The same with marriage equality – funding went into identifying ‘what is the issue’?”
Philanthropy Ireland has been working with businesses too. Last month it helped Dublin-based investment firm Broadlake launch its charitable trust, the Broadlake Foundation.
Its ‘head of impact’ Daragh Anglim says the company believed it could help not-for-profit organisations expand by lending them some business expertise.
“We work with businesses that are in a stage of their development where they’re ready to grow,” he says.
“We thought about how we could match the skills and expertise of our people ... to help them deliver on their mission”.
Anglim says the company has committed €1 million along with 2,000 hours of support.
There are not the same tax incentives associated with philanthropy in Ireland as there might be in other parts of the world. In the case of Zuckerberg and McManus there is no obvious financial incentive behind their contributions here.
In the US, Zuckerberg has had to defend his charitable foundation from claims that the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative could enable him to avoid paying tax.
It was structured upon launch as a limited liability company as opposed to a typical charity or foundation. He transferred 99 per cent of his Facebook shares worth around $45 billion to it in 2015. It was also pointed out at the time that such a structure allowed for greater flexibility when it came to political lobbying.
The Facebook boss has said he and his wife will face capital gains tax on any sale of their shares, and he has foregone tax reliefs available through the traditional US philanthropic models.
At present in Ireland, tax relief on philanthropic donations works to the benefit of the recipient organisations.
This is designed to boost the overall contributions, allowing an approved charity or body to go to Revenue and claim back 31 per cent relief on top of a donation. The individual making the donation cannot avail of the relief.
This means a donation of €1,000 would be topped up with an additional €449 in relief by Revenue.
Niall O’Sullivan runs an independent service called The Philanthropy Adviser. It helps high net-worth individuals and companies consider their charitable options.
He is also a trustee of a group called ‘My Legacy’, which encourages people to leave a charitable gift behind in their will.
He believes there is more that could be done to tap into some of the vast money that now exists here – and there may be a reason why so many large donations – like those of JP McManus and Broadlake – top out at €1 million.
“There are a couple of things that inhibit philanthropy,” he says.
“There’s a cap of €1 million in any given year [in tax relief]. It sounds like a lot, but if you have a net worth of €50 million or €100 million and have made a decision to move into philanthropy, you might give more if there was a better tax incentive in place”.
O’Sullivan says there is lobbying of the Government going on around this at the moment.
“There is a lot of talk about all these wealth managers and estate planners. But when it comes to philanthropy they don’t have a lot to talk about [with clients]. They don’t have many financial instruments to discuss,” he says.
He says that, in the US, philanthropy is much more part of the “psyche” and there are many more options open to wealthy people who want to make donations.
“You wouldn’t need tax breaks in an ideal world, but we do need incentives. Especially now in Ireland where there is such a transfer of generational wealth. We have a real opportunity to embed philanthropy in Ireland.”
[ Mark Zuckerberg donates €150,000 to Waterford GAA clubs after buying castle in the area Opens in new window ]

title: All inheritance tax-free thresholds rise in the budget but no wider reforms
description: Thresholds rise to €44,000 for close relatives and €22,000 for non-relatives with children able to get €420,000 from parents
content:
People will be able to receive greater amounts in gifts or inheritance without paying tax under changes announced in the budget .
However, the Government has stopped short of wider reforms called for by a number of interest groups and analysts.
Minister for Finance Simon Harris confirmed that each of the three capital acquisitions tax (CAT) categories will be increased.
Category A, which mostly relates to children inheriting from their parents, will increase to €420,000 from €400,000 currently.
The tax exemption under category B, covering inheritances from a close blood relative – a grandparent, great-grandparent, sibling, aunt or uncle – will jump to €44,000 from €40,000.
All other inheritances and gifts are covered by category C, which moves from €20,000 currently to €22,000.
Those thresholds apply equally to gifts received in excess of the €3,000 annual small gift exemption.
Mary Moran, tax director at Baker Tilly Ireland, described the increases in thresholds as “modest”, adding “but the reality is that continued inflation will erode a substantial portion of the benefits from the changes”.
The Government collected €1.1 billion in CAT in 2025, with tax on gifts accounting for just 15 per cent of that, according to a report on inheritance tax in Ireland published last week by the Parliamentary Budget Office.
While the tax accounted for just 1 per cent of exchequer receipts, the amount it has raised has risen sharply, especially in recent years, with increases in excess of 30 per cent in each of the past two years. The €1.1 billion collected last year compares with €391 million back in 2007, just before the financial crash.
Category B beneficiaries account for the largest share of that sum, €449 million, followed by those in category A (€398.9 million). Dublin residents account for just over half of all CAT collected.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
The Government has come under pressure from a growing lobby who argue that people with no children are discriminated against under current rules because their beneficiaries can benefit by no more than €40,000 before tax kicks in, just one-tenth of the figure for children inheriting from their parents.
However, in advance of the budget, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers had ruled out any significant move in this direction. Speaking at the Dublin Economics Workshop, he said: “The cost of equalising inheritance tax between category A and B is hundreds of millions of euro, far outside of what’s available in our tax package.
“The tax expenditure cost of every €5,000-€10,000 [change to the thresholds] is very significant, so we have to be honest about what’s available when we’re prioritising income tax [in the budget],” he said.
The Government has focused over many years on trying to ensure that children should not be forced to sell a home inherited from a parent to meet a tax bill. However, that target has come under pressure in recent years, especially in Dublin, given the rise in the price of even average homes.
There have also been calls to lower the 33 per cent rate at which inheritance tax is charged on sums above the exemption thresholds.
Dave O’Brien, the head of tax at business advisory group Xeinadin Ireland, said before the budget announcement that lowering the rate at which the tax is charged at to 20 per cent – where it was for several years up to the financial crash – would encourage greater transfer of wealth between generations.
Another measure the Government should consider, he said, was the seven-year gifting rule that exists in the UK, under which any lifetime transfers are free of tax as long as the donor survives for seven years.

title: Never flippant or headline-grabbing, our restaurant critic Corinna Hardgrave always kept the reader in mind
description: Corinna Hardgrave, who has died, would cut to a restaurant’s essence with a lightness of touch but behind it was a serious integrity
content:
Corinna Hardgrave , restaurant critic at The Irish Times, died after an illness earlier this week . She was 64. As Corinna’s most recent editor at The Irish Times, I was lucky enough to accompany her on a couple of her trips into the wild as she conducted restaurant reviews. One was the notoriously hard to book Chubbys in Clontarf, Dublin 3 , where she wrote of hijacking my family’s reservation in pursuit of her professional goal. In reality, the evening was a pure pleasure, as everything was with Corinna – planning with her, reading her work, and sitting at the same table while she merrily but always professionally pursued her reviewing alchemy.
My daughter, with us in Chubbys that evening, recalls now how while I was admonishing her for having her elbows on the table, Corinna – who had perfect manners – told her never to worry about how she ate, just about enjoying her food. Enjoyment was the premise by which she lived and kindness to those around her was the natural byproduct of that.
[ Corinna Hardgrave, restaurant critic of The Irish Times, dies Opens in new window ]
For you, the reader, this kindness came in the form of always engaging and entertaining restaurant reviews and other work upon which you could rely fully and without question. Corinna carried her rare and immense skill for getting to a restaurant’s essence within a few hundred words with a characteristic lightness but never without seriousness. Her responsibility to be correct, fair and democratic was always woven through her work in a thread of integrity obvious even to those whose restaurants may have attracted negative reviews.
And there have certainly been those, containing zingers such as: “It is, without a doubt, the worst battered fish I’ve ever had. Anywhere. Ever.” and “It’s a revenue stream with a menu”. Once, there were oysters described as “four steamed lumps, swollen like they have spent too long in a sauna” and pasta “thick enough to give your jaw a workout”.
There was never flippancy in words such as this, and there was never an attempt to grab headlines with snappy dismissals of a hospitality team’s hard work – the motivation was always fairness backed by a service to readers who are seeking a positive experience worth their time and money when they eat out.
This desire could also be seen in Corinna’s longer pieces of writing in The Irish Times, such as where she highlighted poor staff conditions or unfairness in the hospitality sector. One example featured former workers in a restaurant reporting feeling “humiliated” and recalling habitually being called unpleasant names by an authority figure.
She was a fierce champion of Irish produce too, always seeking detailed information on a restaurant’s provenance policies before filing a review and calling them out when she was not satisfied – Polish chicken and smoked salmon from Scotland on a Dublin menu were among her most recent shocks .
When the Michelin Guide Ceremony for Britain and Ireland was being held in Dublin earlier this year, she was hugely critical of what she saw as a missed Irish opportunity to use a ready-made platform to promote domestic food and restaurant culture. “And the response? Very little,” she wrote. Improvement on this, and on restaurant provenance, would be a fitting legacy.
If there was a notable chink in Corinna’s fairness armour, it related to truffle oil – “People often ask me what I like to eat, and the answer is, just about everything, as long as it doesn’t come with truffle oil,” she once wrote, restating the position several times over her six years as restaurant critic for The Irish Times. “Dining etiquette should start with one basic law: no more truffle oil, anywhere, ever,” made it very clear, again, late last year .
Five-star reviews were rare across her career – which spanned several Irish titles – demonstrating the care she took in reflecting a restaurant’s whole picture. Two provide fitting bookends for her work in The Irish Times – one from soon after she began here and one from a couple of weeks ago.
“The very first spoonful, a tiny tomato that ruptures into a stream of joy in my mouth is as playful as it is exquisite. It looks like a cherry tomato, but it yields with a bit of pressure, the membrane cracking to release a gazpacho broth so pure, that I am worried that this menu may have peaked too soon,” she wrote at the start of her 2021 review of Chapter One by Mickael Viljanen in Dublin 1 . “This lunch is faultless and the level of precision is exceptional,” she concluded, predicting that Viljanen’s cooking would in time attract a third Michelin star.
Early last month, she reviewed Ómós, Cúán Greene’s much-admired restaurant and guest house in Abbeyleix , Co Laois. Again, she found “faultless” cooking.
“What you’re getting at Ómós is the confidence that comes with maturity, an understanding of what to leave out, both in the design of the restaurant and the menu. Some dishes are delicate, others quite robust – the 12 courses paced to balance one another. There’s a signature here, a chef’s imprint with original dishes you won’t find anywhere else,” she wrote. “I’d expect Ómós to go in at one star in the next Michelin Guide but, believe me, it is already cooking at two-star level.”
The huge care that went into writing these reviews was obvious, just as it was across all of Corinna’s insightful canon of articles. Those of us who travelled with her along the way enjoyed every element of the experience, just as much as her thousands of loyal readers did.

title: Calls for ban on rickshaws in Dublin following death of young mother
description: Galway city introduced bylaws in 2013 preventing use of rickshaws
content:
Councillors have called for a ban on rickshaws following the death of a young mother in an incident in Dublin city centre.
Danielle O’Keane (37) from Saval, Newry, Co Down, was seriously injured when she was struck by a car after falling from the rickshaw in which she was travelling on Saturday, September 26th. The mother of two was returning from a Westlife concert in the 3Arena with friends when the incident happened on North Wall Quay.
Her sister-in-law Aisling O’Keane told Newstalk last week that doctors said she had suffered a “life-ending brain injury”.
She was brought by ambulance to the Mater Misericordiae University Hospital for treatment but died five days later.
“Danielle doesn’t go out, so this was a rare occasion for her to try to go out and let her hair down”, he sister in-law said, adding that Danielle and her friends wore matching Westlife T-shirts to the concert.
Danielle’s children are aged two and five.
Fine Gael councillor Danny Byrne told both Newstalk Breakfast and RTÉ radio’s Today show with David McCullagh that the regulation of rickshaws was necessary to prevent further deaths.
“Anyone getting on a rickshaw around Dublin would have a legitimate expectation that that would be a safe mode of transport. I do not believe it’s a safe mode of transport,” he said.
“There’s legislation sitting there for almost 10 years that was supposed to regulate rickshaws, and it hasn’t been commenced. So, I’m calling on the Government to immediately commence that legislation.”
All motorised rickshaws need to be licensed and insured like cars and motorbikes, he added.
When asked whether these extra costs could put some rickshaw drivers out of business, Byrne said he did not care.
“To be honest, their costs are not my concern. My concerns are the safety of the citizens of Dublin,” he said.
Byrne said he was not a fan of rickshaws or other “dangerous modes of transport” such as e-scooters .
“I just don’t think they’re safe, they’re also probably being used for other reasons rather than carrying passengers.”
Concerns about rickshaws have existed for years, but the Government had failed to resolve the regulatory situation. Any mode of transport that was motorised should be properly licensed, insured and regulated, he said.
“At the moment it’s a wild-west situation. Anybody can go out there and grab a rickshaw and off they go. I’m just not sure of the value of them.”
Michael Crowe, Fianna Fáil councillor on Galway City Council, pointed out that there have been no rickshaws on the streets of Galway since 2013, when the introduction of bylaws ended that mode of transport there. Rickshaws had been crossing pedestrianised areas at speed, so it was “very foreseeable that some form of accident was going to take place”, Crowe said.
Gardaí are appealing to anyone who witnessed the collision to come forward.
Garda technical specialists examined the scene.
No other injuries were reported, gardaí said.
Road users who may have camera footage, including dashcam, and were travelling in the vicinity of North Wall Quay on Saturday, September 26th, between 10:30pm and 11:15pm, are asked to make this available to investigating gardaí.
Anyone with information is asked to contact Store Street Garda station on 01 666 8000, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111 or any Garda station.

title: Armed gardaí shot XL Bully dog four times after it attacked and killed owner, inquest told
description: Gardaí reviewed CCTV footage of the attack and the Director of Public Prosecutions ruled no criminal prosecution would follow
content:
Armed gardaí shot an XL Bully dog four times after it attacked and killed its owner in Co Limerick, an inquest has heard.
Evidence of the shots fired by gardaí to subdue and kill the dog was heard at the inquest into the death of Limerick woman Nicole Morey. Morey was killed by her pet dogs at her rented home, at Fedamore, Co Limerick, on June 4th, 2024.
The fatal attack occurred when Morey arrived home after celebrating her 23rd birthday with family and friends.
Following her death, laws were introduced making it illegal, from February 2025, to own XL Bully dogs without a certificate of exemption.
Limerick Coroner’s Court, sitting in Kilmallock, heard emergency services received a 999 call at 11.35pm on the night about a woman being attacked by a dog in the driveway of her home.
Gardaí told the inquest that armed officers arrived at the address at 11.50pm and observed two aggressive dogs at the scene “with blood on their faces”.
Paramedics were unable to access the property until the dogs were subdued.
Members of the Armed Support Unit, attached to An Garda Síochána, had to shoot the adult XL Bully four times before it eventually died, the inquest was told.
Morey, originally from Crossagalla in Limerick city, had been living at the property by herself; however, the dog attack was witnessed remotely by her former partner who had access to footage of CCTV cameras that were recording at the property.
Pathologist Dr Marcell Szasz gave evidence that Morey’s injuries were “consistent with a dog attack”.
Szasz said she suffered multiple puncture wounds and “very extensive trauma” in the mauling and that she died from haemorrhage and shock.
Limerick coroner John McNamara noted that following an “extensive investigation” by gardaí, which included reviewing CCTV footage of the attack, the Director of Public Prosecutions ruled no criminal prosecution would follow.
Addressing her family, McNamara said her death was “untimely and tragic”.
“I’m sure it’s etched in your memories forever; she was obviously a dog lover,” he said.
Returning a verdict of “misadventure”, the coroner ruled that her death could not be classified as an accident, and that it was the result of an unintended outcome of an intentional act by the dog.
Speaking afterwards, her father Patrick thanked the emergency services for their response and valiant efforts on the night.
“Nicole was always happy, she loved her family and her brothers and sisters and was very close to them,” he said.
He added that his late daughter “had such a good heart”.
“We can get on with missing her now,” he added.
The coroner, along with Garda Sgt David Delahunty expressed their sympathies and condolences to her family.

title: Asos shares slump after hack messages
description: Customers received unverified text message warning ‘Snowflake instance’ has been ‘fully compromised’
content:
Asos shares slumped the most in a year after users of its shopping app received a notification indicating its systems were hacked.
The notification, widely reported on social media , appeared to refer to the British online shopping platform’s data protection officer, as well as the Snowflake online data platform.
“Dear Asos DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance,” the notification said, alongside a link to a Telegram chat. “Engage with us, or we will leak it.”
A spokesperson for Asos had no immediate comment, while Snowflake didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Asos had 16.4 million active customers in more than 100 markets as of the end of its 2026 fiscal year. Its stock fell as much as 13 per cent in London, the largest intraday since September 2025, before paring the drop. Snowflake shares fell as much as 3.2 per cent in premarket trading in New York.
Hacking is proliferating, aided by artificial intelligence tools and sophisticated cybercrime groups, such as ShinyHunters, that target large organisations to steal data. A number of UK businesses have been affected recently.
Marks & Spencer endured months of disruption after an attack last year forced it to pause online clothing and home orders. The retailer was one of several targeted by hackers at around the same time, including rival co-op and luxury department store Harrods.
Jaguar Land Rover was also hit by a major cyberattack last year that led to the automaker shutting down factories around the world. – Bloomberg

title: Court of Appeal upholds Lisa Smith’s conviction for Islamic State membership
description: Former soldier travelled to Syria in 2015 to join terrorist group, Special Criminal Court found in 2022
content:
The Court of Appeal has upheld former soldier Lisa Smith’s conviction for membership of the terrorist group Islamic State .
Delivering judgment on Tuesday morning on behalf of the three-judge court, Judge John Edwards said there was no doubt the circumstances of Smith’s voluntary travel to Islamic State-controlled territory were “properly to be regarded as being capable of constituting sufficient acts of participation”.
“The establishment of membership did not require proof of combat, military activity or operational acts such as fundraising, training or dissemination of propaganda,” he said.
The court rejected all grounds raised by Smith and her appeal was therefore dismissed.
In 2022, Smith (44) became the first person to be convicted in an Irish court of an Islamic terrorist offence committed abroad when the three-judge, non-jury Special Criminal Court found she joined Islamic State, also known as Isis, when she travelled to Syria in 2015.
Smith, from Dundalk, Co Louth, had pleaded not guilty to membership of the unlawful terrorist group between October 28th, 2015, and December 1st, 2019.
Smith appealed her conviction after her bid to overturn her 15-month sentence was rejected by the Court of Appeal in 2023.
At her conviction appeal hearing last year, her senior counsel, Michael O’Higgins, argued Smith had travelled to Syria through “a religious obligation” and had not carried out any acts as a member of Islamic State.

title: Stripe UK employees paid average salary of £180,800 in 2025
description: New accounts reveal 60% jump in after-tax profits at British entity to £25.6 million
content:
Staff at Stripe’s UK arm were paid an average salary of £180,800 (€213,000) last year and an average total compensation of £325,000 (€382,920) when share-based payments and pension contributions are included, new company filings have revealed.
Stripe Payments UK, which employed an average of 340 people in 2025, mostly in sales, booked more than £1.12 billion in revenue, up almost 26 per cent from 2024.
After tax, the entity generated profits of more than £25.6 million, up by about 60 per cent from the previous year, according to the accounts filed with Companies House in the UK recently.
The payments giant increased its UK headcount in the year by about 18 per cent.
Consequently, total staff costs – including wages, salaries, social insurance costs, share-based payments and pensions – jumped by 12.3 per cent to more than £100.5 million.
It meant that a Stripe employee in the UK earned total average compensation of £325,000, up from £310,705 in 2024. In wages and salaries alone, the entity paid out almost £61.5 million, meaning the average salary at the company was £180,800, up from £167,531.
[ Budget 2027 main points: income tax cuts; cigarette price hike - what we know so far Opens in new window ]
In their report attached to the filings, the directors of Stripe Payments UK said the increase in turnover in the year was related to a jump in “processing-related activity”.
The company, which is an authorised electronic-money institution, is regulated by the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority.
However, the online payments company shifted payment processing for the majority of the group’s European customers away from the UK business to its Irish-regulated entity in 2020 due to Brexit.
[ Stripe to add 200 jobs at Dublin headquarters in endorsement of ‘Irish talent’ Opens in new window ]
Separate accounts filed in Dublin by the group’s main Irish entity last month revealed a more than 400 per cent increase in pretax profits last year to $445.5 million (€390.9 million).
It was also disclosed that the firm paid dividends of $467.2 million to its US parent, Stripe Laboratories, in May of this year. The $467.2 million dividend compares with a dividend of $9 million paid in 2025.
Earlier this year, Forbes estimated that Patrick and John Collison each had a net worth of $17.5 billion – up from $10.1 billion one year ago.
In February, the group was valued at $159 billion, up from $91.5 billion in 2025.
Stripe announced last week it would create 200 jobs at its Dublin HQ in engineering and human resources. The move marks a further expansion of Stripe’s Dublin headquarters, which was opened in 2013 and serves as the hub for Europe , the Middle East and Africa. The company employs more than 1,000 people in Ireland, with its headcount rising by more than 35 per cent since the start of the year.

title: Republic must acknowledge forgetting northern nationalists, Leo Varadkar says
description: Former taoiseach says reconciliation process required to ‘say sorry for the fact that happened’
content:
People in the Republic will one day need to offer apologies to northern nationalists for forgetting about them “for a very long time” after partition, former taoiseach Leo Varadkar has said.
Speaking in Dungannon, Co Tyrone, on Monday night, Varadkar said reconciliation was usually spoken about as if “it’s just about the two main communities of Northern Ireland becoming reconciled with each other”.
However, Varadkar told a conference organised by Mid-Ulster District Council that “we need to talk about the totality of reconciliation” required in any debate on constitutional change.
The South “went off and built our State and largely forgot about what happened up here for a very long time, certainly for decades. There’s a reconciliation process [needed], where we, to a certain extent, say sorry for the fact that that happened.”
During the Brexit years, he said, he had only truly understood the depth of feeling on the issue when he told “the nationalist people of Northern Ireland that they wouldn’t be left behind again.
“It was only after I said that and people contacted me that I really understood how deeply that’s felt by hundreds of thousands of people north of the Border, that they were pretty much left behind,” he said.
However, Varadkar warned pro-unification campaigners that a unity referendum should not be rushed because it could set the process back by 30 years if it were held too quickly and defeated.
Saying he was “reluctant” to set a date, he added: “I don’t think we’re ready. Not at the moment, anyway. I would have a concern that if we go into a Border poll too quickly, that it would not just be divisive, but be defeated.”
Pointing to the defeat of the 1999 referendum about making Australia a republic, he said the issue there had been rushed: “Everyone thought Australia would be a republic by now. It’s not happening anytime soon. If you get it wrong, you lose it.”
[ When is the time to trigger a Border poll? Opens in new window ]
A strong majority of people in the Republic have voiced support for Garvaghy Road residents facing an Orange Order march , but “there’s always two sides to that story”, he told his Dungannon audience.
“A lot of people south of the Border don’t really understand Northern Ireland, don’t come here often enough. What they see on display kind of makes them afraid and makes them worried,” he said.
“It makes them wonder about whether we’re ready for a united Ireland,” Varadkar said, adding that should be borne in mind “when it comes to a resolution to this”.
The South “didn’t have a choice” about partition, and it could not have been avoided, he said: “But [for the Republic] to actually make a decision to reject a united Ireland when there would be a majority for it in the North would be a very different thing.”
Drumcree “isn’t reflective of Northern Ireland”, where “hundreds of marches, orange, black, and green, happen without too much trouble”, he said, adding it must not damage the legacy left by this year’s Belfast Fleadh.
[ The Irish Times view on the Fleadh in Belfast: the unifying power of music Opens in new window ]
Taoiseach Micheál Martin’s call for clearer rules on calling a Border poll did “not get enough attention”, he said, adding that the Belfast Agreement was understandably “vague because it had to be”.
Many questions need answers, he said, including whether it would be called on the back of election results, opinion polls or a mix of both, or whether long-term residents who were not Irish or British citizens could vote.
[ Fintan O'Toole: Drumcree is theatre of the absurd, straight from Monty Python’s Ministry of Silly Walks Opens in new window ]
Supporting a trigger mechanism, Varadkar said the Irish Government should be able formally to urge London to call a Border poll if it “felt they were dragging their heels” on calling one that would pass.

title: Almost half of young adults cite cost issue in seeking mental health support, says survey
description: Mental Health Ireland says people are turning to exercise, time with family and friends, and nature
content:
More than four in 10 young adults aged 25-34 (44 per cent), cited cost as an issue when looking for mental health support, according to new research.
That compared to 12 per cent of those aged 65 and older who said affordability was an issue, according to a study from Mental Health Ireland.
Across all age groups, 31 per cent cited cost as a barrier to supporting their mental health, up from 26 per cent in 2025.
Other barriers to supporting personal mental health included not prioritising it (26 per cent), being unsure of how to access support (22 per cent) and lack of time (19 per cent). The survey also found only 39 per cent of 18– to 24-year-olds were “very open” to discussing mental health, compared with 63 per cent of 55– to 64-year-olds.
The findings were released in advance of World Mental Health Day on October 10th. October is also World Mental Health Month.
As to what would make it easier to ask for support, 44 per cent of people identified affordable support, 24 per cent said access to relevant information and 22 per cent identified support available in their community.
The annual survey also found that 81 per cent reported openness to talking about their mental health. However, one in three people (33 per cent) feared they would make things worse if they tried to support someone else, while 28 per cent were not confident they would make a difference.
The most common barrier to supporting someone else was uncertainty about whether they wanted help (35 per cent). A further 23 per cent said they did not feel informed enough about mental health, while 19 per cent were unfamiliar with the signs that someone needed support.
The survey showed that money management was the biggest stressor (66 per cent), followed by health and wellbeing (64 per cent) and work-related stress (50 per cent).
Spending time with friends and family (58 per cent) and exercise (57.5 per cent) were found to be the leading activities people regularly used to manage stress, followed by healthy habits including sleep and diet.
Spending time with friends and family rose from 56.7 per cent in 2025 to 58 per cent in 2026.
Mindfulness was used regularly to manage stress by 17.9 per cent of respondents, while 11.6 per cent sought therapy.
The research highlighted the role that spending time outdoors can play in how people look after their mental health. Some four in ten (41 per cent) said they regularly spent time in nature to manage their stress.
When asked about barriers to spending time in nature to improve their mental health, 43 per cent said nothing prevented them, 23 per cent said they did not have time and 17 per cent said they did not feel safe.
Dubliners were particularly likely to report being time poor, with 29 per cent citing time as a barrier compared with 23 per cent overall.
Mental Health Ireland chief executive Dr Lisa Cuthbert said: “This research tells us that people want to look after their mental health and are already taking practical steps to do that whether that’s exercising, spending time with family and friends or getting out into nature.
“However, it also shows us what can get in the way of good mental health. Cost matters, especially for younger people, and time matters.”

title: Irish commercial debt judgments fall by a quarter as financial distress eases
description: Start-up activity reaches new record, according to CRIFVision-Net data
content:
A sharp decline in the number and value of commercial debt judgments in the first nine months of the year suggests companies are under less financial pressure than they were a year ago, according to new data.
The figures, published by credit risk analyst CRIFVision-net, show that the value of commercial debt judgments against Irish companies fell by 21 per cent to €31 million in the nine months to the end of September.
Commercial judgment volumes also fell by 24 per cent year on year.
The data presents an “encouraging picture” of the trading environment, CRIFVision-net said in a statement. It “provides an important indicator of financial pressure and the ability of businesses and consumers to meet their obligations”.
It also suggests the level of financial distress that is captured through the data has eased compared with last year, the company said.
Meanwhile, some 21,921 companies were incorporated in the State over the same period, a new record and up 8 per cent from 2025.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
The information technology (IT) sector recorded the strongest growth, with new company formation increasing by 54 per cent year on year. This reflected “continued activity within Ireland’s technology and digital economy”, CRIFVision-net said.
“The motor sector also saw significant growth, with start-ups increasing by 23 per cent, while construction recorded a 15 per cent increase and manufacturing rose by 11 per cent,” it added.
Christine Cullen, managing director of CRIFVision-net, said the increase in start-up volumes illustrated “the resilience of the Irish business landscape”.
“Importantly, this growth was not confined to the main urban centres, with increased start-up activity recorded across the entire country,” she said.
[ Budget 2027 main points: income tax cuts; cigarette price hike - what we know so far Opens in new window ]
Overall, 18 counties experienced an increase in start-up activity, led by Sligo, which was up 21 per cent, Kilkenny, up 20 per cent, and Laois, up 19 per cent.
Most indicators suggest that the Irish domestic economy remains in robust health at the outset of the fourth quarter of 2026.
Last week, PwC said the Irish corporate insolvency rate remained “remarkably consistent”, running “well below the long-term average” in the first nine months of 2026.
There were 204 business failures in the third quarter of the year, bringing the total for the first nine months to 648, broadly in line with 633 over the same period last year.
Insolvency volumes also remain below the long-term average of about 250 per quarter since 2005, the firm said.
By the end of September, the insolvency rate per 10,000 businesses operating in the Republic was 27, well below the 21-year average of 49 per 10,000 businesses.
However, the headline data masked large increases in the rate of corporate insolvency in the retail and construction sector. PwC said the increases in those sectors were probably due to structural issues around changing consumer patterns as well as short-term cost pressures arising from soaring prices.

title: Police fire tear gas and charge at demonstrators as French school protests escalate
description: Demonstrators demand the government tackle understaffed and dilapidated classrooms
content:
Hundreds of schools shut, demonstrations filled the streets and there were running battles between hardline protesters and police in a nationwide “Black Tuesday” of protest called by French high school students demanding more funding and better conditions.
A march through Paris by students and teachers’ unions was estimated by organisers to number 100,000 people. A further 350,000 marched elsewhere in France, though estimates by the interior ministry were more modest.
The main bulk of the crowd was peaceful, with marchers young and old carrying home-made banners with messages like “the youth are furious”, “they don’t care about us” and “general strike”.
However, the protest was accompanied by groups of people dressed in black, many wearing ski-goggles and masks, who overturned recycling bins and threw glass bottles at police.
A group of people wearing fluorescent jackets and with their faces covered set fire to street debris and wheelie bins in the centre of the major Paris thoroughfare Boulevard Voltaire.
[ Naomi O'Leary: Inside the school protests in France that have spiralled into arson and street violence Opens in new window ]
Many shops along the route of the march had drawn down their shutters and brought stock inside in anticipation of potential disorder.
Young people holding flags could be seen fleeing from clouds of tear gas, with some protesters kicking the gas canisters back towards the lines of police.
As the march made its way through Paris, a furious debate was under way in the national parliament.
“Extreme violence has knocked on the door of high schools, it must be condemned unconditionally. In a functioning democracy, we cannot allow a space for the tolerance of violence,” French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu told the chamber.
“Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings. Attacking a teacher does not increase the number of substitute teachers.”
He accused the left-wing of promoting chaos as a strategy in advance of a presidential election due in spring and described the accusation that the government had ordered police repression against protesters as “a lie”.
Left-wing leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon joined the march, shaking the hands of protesters and urging them to take care.
The right-wing party of poll leader Marine Le Pen blamed the violence that has accompanied the protest movement on immigration.
“Teachers lynched, one of them doused with gasoline in La Ciotat: there are barbarians on our soil who seek to attack all symbols of French authority,” party president Jordan Bardella wrote on social media.
“If the State does not severely punish these unspeakable acts, if we do not quickly regain control of our immigration policy, France will definitively descend into chaos.”
There were clashes between protesters and police in Strasbourg and Lyon. The protests shut down classes at almost 900 of France’s 3,700 high schools, according to the education ministry, while multiple universities were shut or moved classes online.
At rallies in front of their high schools, some students made barricades out of bins and stood on them holding their protest signs.
Since the protests began, 215 pupils have been injured, along with 85 members of teaching staff, and 715 members police officers according to the government.
Injuries to the high school students, including damage to eyes from rubber bullets and an incident in which a police stun grenade reportedly destroyed a teenager’s hand, have horrified many.
Some politicians, including the leader of France’s green party, called on parents and teachers to join the demonstrating high-schoolers to protect them from police violence.
“Do we need children to lose their sight?” read a home-made sign held by an older lady marching in Paris.
While the government announced that classes would be suspended in high schools until the end of the week to allow for “internal democracy” to sort out issues between students and staff, the student organisers announced another day of nationwide protests on Thursday.

title: Doctors object to ‘self-healing’ coach who said cancer was curable with bicarbonate of soda
description: Barbara O’Neill, who is due to speak in Ireland next week, poses ‘sometimes life-threatening risks’ through her advice, experts warn
content:
Doctors, medical experts and charities have raised concerns about events by a controversial “self-healing” coach taking place in Ireland and the UK, saying her commentary poses “tangible and sometimes life-threatening risks to patients”.
Barbara O’Neill is a self-described naturopath and nutritionist who has written books on health and nutrition, shares videos on social media and lectures internationally about self-healing and natural remedies.
She previously told vulnerable patients their cancer was a fungus that could be cured with bicarbonate of soda rather than through conventional medical treatment, and discouraged vaccination and antibiotics.
In 2019, Australia’s New South Wales Health Care Complaints Commission banned her for life from providing any health services either voluntarily or in a paid capacity, including giving lectures in her native country.
The commission’s investigation found O’Neill never held any membership with any accredited professional health organisation and had failed to obtain any relevant health-related degrees or diplomas.
According to the investigation she also failed to keep records of consultations with clients, falsely claimed to be able to cure cancer, did not treat clients in a safe or ethical manner and posed a risk to the health and safety of members of the public.
She has a large audience on social media, with 3.6 million Instagram followers and 356,000 subscribers on YouTube .
O’Neill is due to speak at City North Hotel and Conference Centre in Gormanstown, Co Meath , next week. Tickets for her event, which is taking place over three days, range from €70 for one day, to €195 for a three-day ticket. “Premium” tickets cost up to €115 per day, or €320 for the three-day bundle.
According to the agenda, the event will discuss depression, cancer, natural treatments, and DNA and the “true cause of disease”.
“Our mission is rooted in the restorative power of God’s love and the healing teachings of Scripture,” the event page states.
“We are committed to nurturing the body, mind and soul, guiding individuals on a path to comprehensive well-being in alignment with God’s intended design for health and wholeness.”
In a letter to the Irish and UK venues that are hosting her tour, doctors, heads of charities and medical professionals raised concerns about the risk these events could pose to vulnerable individuals.
“As part of an international speaking tour, O’Neill is due to speak to your venue in October 2026, something she is explicitly banned from doing in her home state. At the event, she will spread dangerous health fictions to a susceptible audience, leeching off an illusion of legitimacy afforded to her by the surrounds of your respectable establishment,” the letter said.
“There is ample evidence that such misinformation can and will harm patients, and O’Neill has demonstrated a remarkable callousness about these harms. We appreciate that this is something with which you would likely want no association.”
It added: “We strongly feel, however, that this information should help in reaching an informed course of action, and are happy to provide supporting evidence and further information if required. While ultimately the choice whether to host such an event or not is down to yourselves, we hope that this missive is helpful in elucidating why medical science and healthcare professionals have justified concerns, and the tangible and sometimes life-threatening risks to patients that exposure to such toxic fictions pose.”
The letter was co-ordinated by David Robert Grimes, a science communicator and adjunct associate professor in biostatistics at Trinity College Dublin , who has authored a book on misinformation.
[ Influencers and nutrition misinformation: ‘There’s no accountability here, and it’s a massive problem’ Opens in new window ]
Among the signatories are Orla Dolan, chief executive of Breakthrough Cancer Research; Colin Doherty, head of the school of medicine at Trinity College Dublin; Derek Power, consultant medical oncologist in Cork; Jennifer Feighan, chief executive of the Irish Nutrition and Dietetics Institute; and Susan Smith, professor of general practice in Trinity College, among others.
The conference centre was contacted for comment. O’Neill was also contacted for comment.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo’s delusions about his fading ability have led to a sad end to his Portugal career
description: Once he was the best player in the world, but for years the former Manchester United and Real Madrid star has been deluded about his own fading ability
content:
If this is to be the end for Cristiano Ronaldo at international level, at least it can be said he left the stage as he bestrode it: with monumental self-regard. Ronaldo has always been a preening, self-absorbed player, but for a time, when he was one of the best in the world, it could be tolerated. For the past four years, though, he has actively and obviously held Portugal back. There is a great generation of technical talent here weighed down by the monstrous albatross of his ego.
To recap the basic details of the past couple of weeks. Ronaldo played 67 minutes of Portugal’s scratchy 1-0 win over Wales. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, who replaced Roberto Martínez after the World Cup, said he had a verbal agreement with Ronaldo that he would not start the following game against Norway but would perhaps come off the bench. Early in the second half, Ronaldo went to warm up – although whether that was on his own initiative or because Jesus had told him to is unclear. The game was tight, Portugal ultimately winning 2-1, and Jesus did not bring Ronaldo on.
To Ronaldo and his army of apologists, Jesus was guilty of an unacceptable provocation. Jesus’s view was that winning the game took priority over the extremely delicate feelings of a 41-year-old forward. Ronaldo walked out on the squad, and perhaps on his international career, although only three days later, seemingly after Jesus had refused to pay penance for his blasphemy. Which is sad, although perhaps not quite in the way Ronaldo thinks it is.
It’s possible Jesus, who also coached Ronaldo at Al Nassr, could have handled the situation differently. He is not, it’s fair to say, a diplomat. After Martínez’s soft-pedalling, that is, though, perhaps exactly what was needed. Jesus is 72. His vision of management is old-school, which is to say he is a dictator and he takes orders only from the club president, and then only if he feels like it. His career has been characterised by rifts with players who have resisted him. In a sense the only surprise is his falling out with Ronaldo took until the second game of his reign.
Others might have been cowed in the face of Ronaldo’s sulk, the online backlash and criticism from some of the Portuguese press, certain elements of which Ronaldo owns, but not Jesus. He is a man of great eloquence and is always quotable but, even by his standards, his response to the furore has been remarkable as he has insisted on the primacy of the team over any individual.
“I can say to any player that you’re starting on the bench: if I need you for 30 minutes you’re going to play, if I don’t need you, you’re not going to play,” he said. “The way I was reading the game he didn’t come on. Because it’s not Cristiano, just like it will never be any player, that will change my ideas as the coach. Never! Not him, not anyone in football. Not him, not anyone, not any president. Never! Zero!”
His hardline approach might have backfired had Portugal then lost to Denmark, but they won 4-2, playing superbly. Gonçalo Ramos, who might have thought he had already settled this argument by replacing Ronaldo at the 2022 World Cup for the last-16 game against Switzerland and scoring a hat-trick in a 6-1 win, set up the first and scored another against the Danes, having already scored the winner against Norway.
“The new manager is a great help,” Ramos said. “We have clearer ideas; we know exactly where each team-mate is, both in defence and attack. We’re improving day by day, and it’s all part of a process. We’re very happy with the win, once again against a good team.”
Ramos was on target on Sunday as Portugal came from behind to beat Norway at home, making it four wins out of four in this window.
[ Ken Early: Cristiano Ronaldo’s decline leaves Portugal paying the price against Colombia Opens in new window ]
The tendency until now has been for the other Portugal players to back Ronaldo, to insist he was an icon and that they didn’t mind his superannuated lumbering. Bruno Fernandes has been notably diplomatic, but others are starting to break cover.
Ramos’s former Paris Saint-Germain team-mate Vitinha, for instance, who has seen at club level how beneficial a purge of egos can be, observed that Portugal’s improvement has been “the work of the coach ... I think beyond the win, the content of our game was great”.
Jesus has offered Ronaldo another meeting to try to resolve the situation, but the Portuguese football federation seems already to have accepted how the affair will end, beginning plans for a farewell game for the country’s record scorer. Both Jesus and Ronaldo have indicated they will say more this week.
But the truth is that this is a break that should have happened long ago. For three tournaments, Ronaldo has undermined an extremely talented Portugal. This is a sad story. It is sad Ronaldo’s career should have ended this way.
