But the saddest element is that a great player could be so deluded about his own fading ability that a national team’s hopes and dreams should have been sacrificed to his quest to break goalscoring records. – Guardian

title: A5 ruling a ‘relief’ for bereaved families, All-Ireland winner who lost two siblings says
description: €2 billion upgrade would be Northern Ireland’s largest ever road project
content:
An All-Ireland winning footballer who lost his brother and sister in separate accidents on the same road has welcomed a court ruling which will allow the upgrade of the A5 in Northern Ireland to proceed.
On Tuesday, the Court of Appeal in Belfast quashed a previous ruling that blocked the long-stalled £1.7 billion (€2 billion) project to rebuild one of the most dangerous roads in Ireland.
Former Tyrone player Kevin Hughes, who backed a high-profile campaign to upgrade the A5 between Derry and Aughnacloy in Co Tyrone , said the verdict will bring “large relief” to bereaved families.
“It really is great to hear and not before time,” he said.
His brother, Paul (22), was killed in a crash on the adjoining A4 in 1997.
Four years later, his sister Helen (24) died close to the same spot near Ballygawley, Co Tyrone.
“For it to happen a second time on the same stretch of road possibly only half a mile apart, and a mile for our own house, was just devastating.
“Both were taken down in the prime of their lives.
“I’m the youngest and Paul was a huge figure for me to look up to in football. He always wanted to give back.
“When Helen passed away, I was 21. Me and her were probably the closest. She was a fantastic girl.”
There have been more than 50 fatalities on the A5 since 2006, with 10 dying in one year alone.
It is part of the main route between Dublin and the northwest.
Construction work on the new road should begin as soon as possible, Stormont Infrastructure minister Liz Kimmins told reporters outside court on Tuesday.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin said the €600 million investment from the Shared Island initiative pledged two years ago towards the project “remains in place”.
[ Appeal for prevention of more A5 road deaths following court order quashing upgrade Opens in new window ]
“Road safety is a key concern, and too many lives have been lost in tragic circumstances along the A5 over the years,” he said
“An upgraded road to the northwest will not only improve road safety but also bring economic and social benefits to people living along its route in Tyrone and Derry and in connecting counties such as Monaghan, and Donegal in particular.”
Approved by the Stormont Executive almost 20 years ago, the scheme has been mired in legal challenges and delays.
Campaign group Enough is Enough was set up in Co Tyrone three years to lobby Stormont to deliver on it.
Hughes became a prominent voice in the group, comparing the dramatic drop in fatalities on the A4 following its upgrade with the number of deaths on the A5.
People were “almost living in fear of going to your local school, going to your local shop, going to work” due to the treacherous stretch of road, he said.
“The facts speak for themselves. Since the new A4 bypass was completed, there’s only been two deaths in nearly 20 years,” he added.
“You compare that with the A5 over that same period. Even in the last week, there were three accidents three days in a row.
“From my own point of view, today’s ruling will bring large relief for families, and more so for families who don’t know what could have been around the corner.
“There were six of us in our family. As bad as it is for siblings, I can’t imagine what was like for my parents. I’m a father of four and the thought of losing two of them is unbearable.”
Campaigners were in court on Tuesday when a panel of Appeal Court judges, led by the Lady Chief Justice (LCJ) Siobhan Keegan, quashed a previous ruling.
The 58-mile (94 kms) proposal will be the North’s largest ever road project.
Last year, the High Court found the Department for Infrastructure’s plans did not comply with climate change targets, following a legal challenge from a group including residents, farmers and landowners.
The department then appealed against that ruling.
Describing the legal history of the project as “long and torturous”, Keegan ruled on four main grounds including human rights and climate change.
The judge who delivered the High Court ruling was “wrong in his approach and the outcomes he reached in relation to the issues”, she said.
Speaking outside court, Niall McKenna from Enough is Enough said it was “not a time for celebration”.
“Our campaign was all about saving lives. It was not to win court cases,” he said.
“My most pride is for the people who stand behind me, the families of victims of the A5, almost 60 in the 20 years since this road was supposed to have been delivered.
“It is too late for those people. Their loved ones are already gone.
“They have campaigned tirelessly to make sure that no other families have to suffer the pain that they have went through.”
A solicitor for the Alternative A5 Alliance – an umbrella body of landowners, farmers and supporters opposed to the road – said his clients will “carefully consider today’s judgment”. – Additional reporting by PA

title: Ardagh weighs selling African glass unit
description: Bondholders took control of Ardagh, which had been built up by Irishman Paul Coulson, last year
content:
Ardagh Group’s new owners are mulling the potential sale of its African glass business as they look to break up the packaging conglomerate to monetise its assets.
Conversations over a possible sale of Ardagh’s Africa business are still largely internal and at an early stage, and there is no guarantee a process will formally kick off, according to people familiar with the matter.
Paul Coulson , who started by taking control of the long-defunct Irish Glass Bottle Company in Ringsend, Dublin, built Ardagh over 25 years into an international glass and metal packaging giant with more than $9 billion (€8 billion) of annual sales, on the back of a series of debt-fuelled deals in so-called junk-bond markets.
That debt became unsustainable when earnings were hit after the Covid-19 pandemic by inflation, soaring interest rates and soft consumer demand on both sides of the Atlantic.
[ Ardagh looks to sell $3.14bn metal containers business Opens in new window ]
Late last year, bondholders who were owed $4.2 billion took control of the group with legacy equity holders, including Coulson, being paid $300 million.
Ardagh’s assets are expected to be sold over time rather than through a single transaction, with the various segments probably being marketed to different pools of buyers, the people said, asking not to be identified as they were not authorised to speak publicly.
Ardagh’s glass packaging business also spans Europe and the US, but the African unit is likely to be the first one to be lined up for a sale, the people added.
The African asset is viewed as a high-quality and growth asset, with about 90 per cent of the business coming from South Africa and the rest from Ethiopia, Nigeria and Kenya.
Ardagh was barred from selling its metal-packaging business by a district court in Luxembourg last month, potentially complicating the new owners’ efforts to capitalise on one of the group’s most valuable assets.
The order followed an application from a group of minority creditors who had challenged last year’s restructuring deal. In response, Ardagh had said it was “vigorously challenging the order and has made an application for it to be withdrawn”.
The combined glass packaging businesses in Europe and Africa posted $1.34 billion of revenue in the first six months of 2026, a 7.5 per cent jump year-over-year, according to Ardagh’s most recent report to investors. Adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation stood at $214 million, a 1.4 per cent decline from the same period last year. – Bloomberg

title: Niamh O’Brien, Irish dancer and wife of Michael Flatley, dies aged 52
description: Michael Flatley: ‘She was the most loving mother, wife and person, and our lives will never be the same without her’
content:
Niamh O’Brien, the Lord of the Dance lead performer who later married fellow Irish dancer Michael Flatley , has died aged 52.
She passed away peacefully at the Beacon Hospital in south Dublin, “following a period of illness”, a representative said.
Niamh O’Brien suffered from a long-standing lung condition, which deteriorated in the last year. She was due to fly to the United States to receive a lung transplant but died before it could be carried out.
Flatley said in a statement: “My heart is broken. I have lost my beautiful wife, Niamh, and my best friend. My gorgeous bride of 20 years has gone to the Lord in Heaven.
“She was the most loving mother, wife and person, and our lives will never be the same without her,” Flatley said.
“Thank you for all the love and kindness you have shown us. Please keep Niamh, Michael St James, and out family in your thoughts and prayers.”
Alongside the statement posted online, Flatley shared photos of his wife dancing, their wedding photo and a photo with their son, Michael St James.
“The Flatley and O’Brien families are devastated by Niamh’s sudden passing and have asked that their privacy be respected as they come to terms with this heartbreaking loss,” the representative continued.
“They express their sincere gratitude to the doctors, nurses and staff at Beacon Hospital who cared for Niamh over the past few weeks, and to everyone who has offered their kindness and support to the family,” she continued.
The couple married in October 2006 , in a Fermoy, Co Cork, church only 3km from the 18th-century Castlehyde estate, the Palladian-style ancestral home of first president of Ireland Douglas Hyde that Flatley bought in 1999 and later restored.
The couple have one child, Michael St James, who was born in 2007. Flatley himself was diagnosed with cancer in the past, and has spoken of his family’s support throughout those experiences.
Around Christmas in 2022, having been told of his cancer diagnosis by his doctor over the phone, Flatley later said in an interview: “I turned and there was Niamh ... She hugged me and everything seemed a little better.”
Niamh O’Brien, originally from Co Meath, competed as an Irish dancer at an elite level throughout her teenage years, placing fourth in the world championships when she was 17 years old.
After leaving the competition world to enter professional performances, she appeared in Riverdance , Lord of the Dance, Feet of Flames and Celtic Tiger – all live shows produced by Flatley that toured around the world.
In his autobiography published in 2007, Flatley recalled how he had known Niamh O’Brien for years as a friend and decided on New Year’s Eve 2006 that he was in love with her. They married 10 months later.
“It was Niamh I was looking for and she’d been right next to me on stage for all these years,” he wrote.
“Perfect partners on stage, I knew we could be perfect partners in life. There’s no way to explain how you know it’s the right person. You just do. And you know precisely at that second. I give thanks every day that she felt the same way.”
In an interview published in The Irish Times last year, he said: “I cannot remember us having bad words ... Of all the things I’ve got out of my dance career, my wife takes first place.”
Funeral arrangements for Niamh O’Brien will be announced in due course.

title: Social welfare, Help-to-Buy, tax changes and childcare costs: Everything we know about Budget 2027 so far
description: Spending of €7 billion planned with €1.5 billion in tax reductions
content:
B udget 2027 , to be presented on October 6th, is due to involve a package of €8.5 billion, with €7 billion in additional spending and €1.65 billion in tax reductions. The cost-of-living issue will be a key focus across the whole package.
While the €7 billion figure is large, an increase of about 6 per cent on this year, much of this money is already effectively allocated to various budgets to keep pace with inflation.
There will be key decisions announced in areas such as health – which is already running well above budget for this year – and education and in what to allocate for a new public sector pay deal. And, of course, in welfare, one of the mainstays of any budget package.
The €1.65 billion package - increased late in the day from €1.5 billion - leaves some for manoeuvre.
[ Budget 2027: ‘Specific consideration’ for measures to tackle rising heating oil costs Opens in new window ]
The big move will be a larger than flagged income tax package.
Minister for Finance Simon Harris has suggested that some money could be raised in tax increases, but these will be limited. packet of cigarettes is set to move to €20, though extra tax revenue here will be limited. The bank levy, raising €200 million, is expected to be renewed for another year.
ministers will also have to find money to make some adjustment on inheritance tax and on some new business measures. And to pay the full year cost of the 9 per cent VAT rate for hospitality, announced last year.
How much will be allocated to social protection – or welfare – will be a key issue. After some coming and going a general increase of €10 a week has been decided on, the same as the last budget.
The main welfare rates and pensions will be increased by this amount, though the main child benefit rate may stay where it is.
Promises to address child poverty are likely to see additional payments for people on welfare with children – known as child support payments –which are likely to rise by €6 a week. There may also be a further expansion of the Working Family Payment, which is paid to lower-income families on lower earnings.
The much-discussed second tier of child benefit payments which would be paid to all lower income families is not, however, expected to happen this year.
Eligibility for the carers’ allowance is due to be extended, allowing people who have somewhat higher incomes to qualify.
An increase in the level at which the higher 40 per cent income tax rate kicks is on the way. The current rate is €44,000 for a single person and €53,000 for a married couple.
An increase of €2,000 had been speculated. However the figure will be €2,500. This means the cut off point for entry to the higher 40 per cent income tax rate rises to €46,500 for a single person and €55,500 for a single earning married couple.
Harris will also indicate that the Government intends to increase the level at which the higher tax rate applies in successive budgets for the rest of its term.
The other big gain from the income tax changes will be from an increase in tax credits. The two main tax credits - the personal and PAYE credit - are both likely to rise by €125. The earned income credit ,which self employed people get instead of the PAYE credit, is expected to increase by the same amount. These would benefit all income tax payers, but give the highest proportional gain to the lower earners.
In broad terms, the standard rate band increase will be worth €500 a year to a single person earning over €46,000. The tax credit rises will add another €250, bringing the total to €750.
The budget will confirm the Government’s decision on an increase in the minimum wage. The Low Pay Commission recommended increasing it by 79 cent per hour, bringing the adult rate from €14.15 to €14.94 per hour from next January and it appears this has been accepted.
There will be a tweak in the entry level for the 3 per cent USC rate to make sure no one on the new minimum wage pays at this level.
A small increase in PRSI, which came into effect at the start of this month, will pull back the total increase in pay packages which workers feel a little when comparing this year with next year.
[ Income tax change is coming in Budget 2027. Here’s what it means for you Opens in new window ]
[ People who get up early were left disappointed by Varadkar. Harris is ready to try again Opens in new window ]
All things energy are hugely politically sensitive and will be central to the package. There will be three key elements – the carbon tax, excise taxes and cash supports to households.
A key focus will be additional supports for those struggling with energy bills through channels such as the fuel allowance scheme or household benefits packages, which help lower-income families meet daily bills.
The Government has resisted the return of energy credits – once-off cash payments to households to lower bills – saying it favoured more targeted, permanent measures.
A big issue will be excise taxes on fuel. These were reduced in two steps earlier this year and the first step to the return of normal rates had been due to take place in November. The Coalition will push the date when this will happen through the winter to March 1st. It will be interesting to see whether Harris hints at further possible extensions if wholesale energy prices remain high.
A Government taskforce has been looking at the area of permanent supports to help households deal with energy costs. As part of this, the budget is likely to have something to say on supports for encouraging retrofitting in older homes and there will also be a scrappage scheme for old boilers, which has already been announced. Grants of €600 are also coming for those installing storage batteries as part of a solar panels investment. This is in addition to grants of up to €1,800 already available for solar PV installations.
The fuel allowances, paid to 470,000 households during the colder months, looks set to increase by €5 a week to €43. There will be an extension of the fuel support scheme for hauliers and farmers. There will also be a fertiliser support package for farmers.
Annual carbon tax increases had been due to be given the go-ahead, as part of a planned series of increases up to 2030. But a big shake-up here is likely and all the increases look set to be put on hold.
The Coalition has indicated that there will be measures to actually reduce the price of home heating oil. The expected route would be to reduce the existing rate of carbon tax on the fuel. The Coalition will also rule out further carbon tax increases on home heating for the rest of its term.
Delaying planned carbon tax increases or reducing existing ones raises questions for spending, as revenue from this tax pays for areas such as SSIA grants for retrofitting – which the Government is trying to speed up – certain fuel-related welfare supports and some climate friendly programmes for farmers..
The Programme for Government commits to a permanent cost-of-disability payment to reflect the higher costs disabled people face in their daily lives. Minister for Social Protection Dara Calleary had a public consultation on it earlier this year.
A move is on the cards in the budget, but it will be less than campaigners are looking for. Social Justice Ireland has said a €20-a-week payment would cost €242 million in a year.
A new disability support payment will be announced, but on a lesser scale, involving one lump sum payments of €500, paid next January. There will be a commitment to look at how this support evolves in future.
First time buyers will be able to access up to €35,000 towards the deposit on their first home, under the Help-to-Buy scheme, after agreement was reached by party leaders. This increases the limit by €5,000.
There also looks set to be an increase in the rent tax credit, which is worth up to €1,000 per year to a single renter and €2,000 to a couple. A rise of €150 for single people and €300 for a couple if on the cards.
With interest rates on the up, there will be a focus on whether the mortgage tax credit will be renewed. This year it was worth 50 per cent of the increase in mortgage interest paid in 2026 versus 2022, capped at a maximum tax credit of €625.
An improvement in the rent-a-room tax allowances, which allows homeowners to earn up to €14,000 a year from renting out a room to a long-term renter (staying for at least 28 days) is expected.
There have been hints from all sides of Government that there would be some move here. Pre-budget documents drawn up by civil servants warned of the high cost of fundamental reform of the tax, such as aligning the tax relief for wider groups inheriting to the levels which currently apply to children.
So it appears there will be modest increases in the three thresholds. The Category A threshold of €400,000 is paid by children inheriting from parents and looks set to rise to €420,000. The Category B threshold of €40,000 applies – generally – to siblings, nieces, nephews, grandchildren and grandparents who get inheritances. The Category C threshold of €20,000, applies in most other cases.
Senior Ministers have also referred to the possibility of capital gains tax moves, and Harris has said that the 33 per cent rate is “objectively too high”. The budget will announce a 2 per cent cut.
There could be an extension of some CGT reliefs, such as those available to entrepreneurs and a commitment to look at the whole capital tax system, particularly as it relates to investment. The rate of the so-called deemed disposal tax, which put a charge on profits from investments in exchange traded funds every eight years, may be cut.
The Minister for Finance is due to announce key details of his savings scheme. The outline shape has already been revealed – it will offer tax-free investment options for households in stocks and shares subject to certain limits. The key question is what these will be. The budget will reveal three key things.
The first is a limit capping what individuals can put in each year - which is €12,000. This looks set to . The second is the total level of a savings fund that will remain free of all taxes. This is €50,000. The third is the level of a new special tax rate that will apply to the assets in the fund above this limit – which is 1 per cent.
As part of its cost-of-living package, the Government has promised further help for parents. Its programme promises to cap monthly costs at €200 per child, with progress made over the term of the Coalition. Higher investment to providers under the so-called core funding scheme was already announced to apply from September2026, together with weekly fee caps for parents.
This budget is set to announce a headline reduction of some €1,000 a year for parents of children in full-time care ( 45 hours a week) up to senior infants age. The weekly fees cap will fall to €55.
This will be achieved through an increased subsidy under the National Childcare Scheme - paid to providers and deducted from bills - and a cut in the cap on fees. Earlier reports had suggested these changes could come into effect in January, though the suggestion now is next September. There will also be measures to support the earnings of people working in the sector.
Harris has also hinted at increased tax relief for those minding a child or children in their home. At the moment a minder can earn up to €15,000 tax free per year for minding a maximum of three children – not counting their own. This could rise to €20,000.
It is expected that there will be an across-the-board €150 cut to student fees. A proposal to cut student fees by €250 a year was reportedly under discussion in late negotiations, but hopes for this had expired by Monday morning. Across the course of the day, however, the idea re-emerged, albeit at a lesser amount, with indications on Monday evening that there would be an extra allocation of around €18 million to deliver the measure.
Some relief appears to be on the cards for families who have more than one child in college through an extension of current discounts which apply to these families.
A plan had emerged to give a €100 voucher 16 year-olds in the Budget to be used for attending arts, music or culture events. A proposal to give such a voucher to 16 and 17 year-olds was part of the Programme for Government. It had appeared that this was going to be subject to further study, but the latest reports say the card will feature in some form in the budget speech.
The Government has made general promises on supporting businesses, but what could happen remains unclear. An extension of research and development relief could be one potential avenue, as well as measures aimed at encouraging investment in domestic industry.
Businesses are also looking for higher spending on training, funded by a surplus in the National Training Fund, but it is not clear is this will happen. It appears now that this is on the cards, with an allocation from the fund for training in AI related areas. A sum of €150 million over three years may be involved.
A fresh rebate scheme on beer kegs is aimed to help rural publicans.

title: Owen Doyle: Is there any other sport where referees are so fond of their own voices?
description: Rugby officials doing themselves no favours with ceaseless commentary and chummy approach to players
content:
“What we’ve got here is failure to communicate.”
The words are spoken by the prison boss to Paul Newman, aka Cool Hand Luke, in the movie of the same name. If you’ve never seen it, put it on your list.
The boss might well have been talking rugby. We’ve been hearing a lot of communication in recent weeks, both on and off the pitch, and some of it could indeed be placed in the “failure” category.
Let’s start with Italian referee Andrea Piardi, whose yellow cards in Australia’s win over South Africa caused quite a stir. Some – who should know better – have proposed that he should not be allowed to referee Australia again. It is a case of shooting the messenger and amounts to public criticism of Piardi, who is actually a very good referee. Yes, one card was an error, but that was compounded by an over-zealous assistant.
One of the cards actually resulted in the disciplinary panel handing a four-week suspension to Hunter Paisami for his dangerous tackle on Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu. That, no doubt, will give the pundits a few more messengers to gun down, but, gentlemen, you are totally out of order.
Piardi was applying World Rugby protocols and if players do not bend into the tackle, then they are at serious risk of heading to the bin. Suggestions that players should just be put on report for head contact are wide of the mark. They also ignore completely the reality that sub-concussive knocks to the head can cause long-term brain damage. This report system, we shouldn’t be surprised, is straight out of rugby league’s playbook. Unlike league, rugby union continues after a tackle, and needs the yellow card to maintain its deterrent relevance.
If players know they won’t be going off, we will have upright tackles that prevent the ball-carrier from passing by pinning his upper arms. Such tackles inevitably increase the number of head-on-head collisions. Having no immediate deterrent will not work. There was also the fiasco of a breakdown of the communication system, which has become the comfort blanket for too many officials, particularly below the top elite guys.
The coaches have also been having a public spat, with much toing and froing about the scrum. Dave Rennie, the New Zealand head coach, claims South Africa drive illegally across the scrum, which of course is stoutly denied. It can be very hard to detect and the jury of experts has been unable to deliver a unanimous verdict.
We have also been listening to how the referees communicate. While I would never wish to clone the match officials, some ‘dos and dont’s’ are surely necessary. The difference between Angus Gardner and Nika Amashukeli was chalk and cheese. Gardner was over-friendly, trying to cajole “Malcolm” (Marx) in an effort to get him to scrummage correctly. One scrum, constantly reset, took all of four minutes before Gardner awarded a free kick. John McEnroe’s stinging riposte to a Wimbledon umpire – “you cannot be serious” – comes to mind.
In contrast, Amashukeli simply said, and did not repeat it: “Remember what we agreed.” He was referring to the chat all referees have with the frontrows before the match when the requirements for good scrummaging are discussed. I’m clueless as to why referees feel they need to verbalise it all over again once play has started.
New Zealand referee Ben O’Keeffe was in charge of Argentina v Australia, and, boy, did we hear from him. Long, loud explanations were given as to the reasons for his sanctions, and also for his decisions not to whistle. It was way over the top, completely intrusive. Similar to Gardner, it all amounted to non-stop chatter, with the officials becoming the centre of attention. This is not confined to southern hemisphere referees, as England’s Karl Dickson demonstrated in the New Zealand v South Africa match in Baltimore.
There is much talk about preventative refereeing, it’s a tricky subject. I can understand it when a player may be unsure if he has the right to poach the ball at the tackle. But, if it has already slowed down the ball, or affected play in any way, then it’s too late.
A quite extraordinary incident saw O’Keefe telling the Argentina scrumhalf, Santiago Carreras, to go back. He shouted it three or four times. On the final occasion, the player did go back, only to be immediately told that he could now come forward as the lineout was over. That was just nonsense in terms of prevention. There’s also the problem of being consistent with prevention. It’s close to impossible to be equitable to both teams across 80 minutes, and indeed from match to match and from referee to referee.
There are protocols for just about everything under the sun, so a few for communication might not go astray. It would be an opportunity to get rid of the first-name, chummy-chummy stuff and the ceaseless commentary. Lord above, is there any other sport in the world where the arbiter behaves in such fashion?
Precise, concise reasons for sanctions, delivered firmly, is the only way to go. Referees should not enter into debates. Too often we see the match stopped while the referee listens to a player give his side of the story. And it shouldn’t be just any player appealing to the referee – everything should go through the captain.
Is it too much to ask that referees adopt a less-is-more communication policy in the forthcoming Nations Championship fixtures? Probably.

title: Uefa to investigate alleged spitting incident at half-time in Ireland v Israel
description: It was alleged that Ireland’s head of athletic performance, Damien Doyle, was spat at
content:
Uefa has launched an investigation into claims a member of the Republic of Ireland coaching staff was spat at during the heated Nations League encounter with Israel on Sunday.
The European governing body has confirmed that post-match reports submitted by match officials “contained an allegation of an incident in or around the tunnel at half-time” and that it will be the subject of a disciplinary investigation “regarding potential misconducts from player(s)”.
Witnesses at the match, held in the Serbian town of Backa Topola, reported hearing a member of the Irish staff – understood to be the fitness coach Damian Doyle – claim he had been spat on by an Israeli player as the teams went down the tunnel at half-time.
A spokesperson for the Israeli Football Association denied the reports, saying “no one had spat towards the coach”.
After the match Ireland’s coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson, said his team had been subject to a number of apparent provocations in the build-up and sought to defuse the incident.
“There have been a lot of those accidents and we were clever enough to avoid it before it went too far,” Hallgrimsson said. “I felt it was their intention to intimidate us and make us do something stupid. I give big credit to how the players handled their emotions.”
The investigation will probably extend the rancour that turned this double-header between Ireland and Israel into a geopolitical flashpoint. Ireland had been under intense pressure from supporters at home to boycott the matches and conducted a vote over whether to fulfil the opening fixture in Hungary.
The second match, nominally an Ireland home fixture, was held in Backa Topola after the Football Association of Ireland said “operational challenges” would prevent them from staging it safely in Dublin.
The build-up involved increasingly heated accusations made by both parties, and two Israeli journalists were banned from attending Ireland’s post-match press conference after Uefa found they had brought “football into disrepute by using a press conference for politically motivated purposes” and displayed “improper behaviour” during and after a pre-match press conference.
Hallgrímsson has asked that Uefa keep Ireland and Israel separate from each other in future draws. A Uefa spokesperson said: “Decisions to avoid certain teams being drawn against each other are made taking into consideration several factors, especially conditions between the two countries leading to structural risks for security. Uefa handles every situation very carefully on its own merits and monitors all facts and developments.” — Guardian

title: Four South American countries launch joint bid for 2035 Rugby World Cup
description: Plan is to stage games in 11 stadiums across 10 cities, with eight venues in Argentina
content:
Argentina, Uruguay, Chile and Brazil have submitted a ‌joint bid to host the Rugby World Cup in 2035, hoping to bring the quadrennial ‌tournament to South America for the first time.
The ​bid outlines plans to stage games in 11 stadiums across 10 cities, with eight venues in Argentina and one each in the other three countries, including the iconic ​Maracana in Rio de Janeiro.
Spain and Japan have also expressed interest in hosting the tournament. ⁠World Rugby will undertake site visits and feasibility assessments before identifying ‌a ‌preferred ​host by next May, with a final decision expected in November 2027.
“We have the opportunity to show the ⁠world our passion for this ​sport, our ability to host major ​events, and everything our countries have to offer,” Argentine Rugby Union president Felix Paez ‌Molina said in a statement.
“We ​take on this challenge firmly believing that our region deserves an opportunity ⁠of this size.
“It’s a project ⁠we’re excited ​about, and we’re building it together with the region’s unions and Sudamerica Rugby. Our hope is that, for the first time, a Rugby World Cup can be played in this part of the world.”
The next World Cup will be held in Australia in 2027, with the tournament making its first foray into the ‌Americas in 2031 when ⁠it will be hosted by the United States.
Argentina are the most successful rugby-playing nation in the Americas with the Pumas having ‌reached the semi-finals of the World Cup three times in 2007, 2015 and 2023.
Uruguay ​have competed at five editions, while Chile made ​their debut in 2023. Brazil have yet to qualify for the tournament.

title: Níl aon duine ag dul siar
description: Tá seandeighiltí sa talamh faoi cheantar Dhroim Crí ach tá ábhar misnigh le fáil ann chomh maith
content:
Tá eolaithe na meicnice candamaí agus fealsúna na meitifisice ag cur agus ag cúiteamh agus ag cíoradh bhun-nádúr an ama le fada ach, cé go bhfuil dul chun cinn áirithe déanta acu sa réimse rúndiamhair seo, sáraíodh iad ar na mallaibh a bhuí le turgnamh contúirteach, nach raibh aon choinne leis, a rinne baicle fear diongbháilte i dtuaisceart Ard Mhacha.
In ainneoin nach saineolaithe coibhneasachta ginearálta iad, go bhfios dúinn cá bith, d’éirigh le baill den Ord Oráisteach a chruthú gur féidir le buíon bheag daoine iarracht inbhraite a dhéanamh taisteal siar in am - ach fuair siad amach chomh maith céanna nach gcinntíonn gníomh aontaobhach dá leithéid go ngluaisfidh aon duine eile sa tsochaí siar in éineacht leo.
Cuireadh idir iontas agus alltacht, ní hamháin ar mhórphobal an Tuaiscirt ach ar dhaoine stuama i gceithre hairde na cruinne, nuair a athmhúsclaíodh taibhsí Dhroim Crí agus a tugadh ar mhuintir Gharbhachaidh Phort an Dúnáin dul siar ar bhóithrín na smaointe dorcha.
Droim Crí. Is dhá fhocal iad sin a chothaíonn réimse mothúchán, ó mhíchompord go múisc, i mbolg go leor againn a mhair trí 90idí na haoise seo caite agus a shíl gur sa mhílaois seo a d’imigh tharainn a d’fhanfadh an ghoimh agus an nimh a bhain leis an mhórshiúl chonspóideach agus leis an fhoréigean a d’eascair as.
Ní hamhlaidh an scéal áfach óir is léir go bhfuil an tOrd Flannbhuí, agus sciar den Aontachtas, a gceannairí ina measc, meáite ar an ghoin a athoscailt agus na seandeighiltí - a bhí á gcneasú de réir a chéile - a leathnú an athuair. Na déithe idir sinn agus an drochrud.
Mar a tharlaíonn sé, bhí baint ag ceantar Dhroim Crí le deighiltí agus le heasaontas i bhfad sular bunaíodh aon bhráithreachas caithréimeach coilíneach sa dúiche.
Tráth dá raibh ba cheantar teorann é Droim Crí idir dhá thuath ársa Ghaelacha, Clann Chana san iarthar agus Clann Bhreasail san oirthear. Is é ‘críoch’ is ciall leis an dara mír den logainm go fiú agus meastar gur d’Abhainn na Banna, nach bhfuil ach scread Fir Bhuí ón droim, atá an focal ag tagairt.
Is iomaí scoilt agus gág a bhí i mbólaí thuaisceart Ard Mhacha faoin am a thosaigh na mórshiúlta Oráisteacha sa 19ú céad mar sin.
Ina dhiaidh sin, cuireadh an dá thuath le chéile agus faoin 16ú céad is é Uí Nialláin an t-ainm a tugadh ar an bharúntacht ar fad ar an taobh ó dheas de Loch nEathach. Is í Clann Uí Néill Thír Eoghain a bhí i gceannas ar an áit agus is cosúil go raibh tarraingt ar leith acu ar thailte Uí Nialláin - ba mhinic a chaitheadh taoisigh na Niallach am i measc chnoic chiúine an cheantair de rogha ar a gceanncheathrú ghnóthach i nDún Geanainn.
Is eol dúinn go raibh lonnaíocht eaglasta i nDroim Crí féin ó ré na meánaoise ar aghaidh agus go deimhin is ar an tsuíomh chéanna atá an eaglais inniu a tháinig an Taoiseach Seán Ó Néill agus Ard-Seansailéir Shasana in Éirinn, Thomas Cusack, le chéile chun idirbheartaíocht a dhéanamh in 1563. Creid é nó ná creid ach Conradh, nó Síocháin, Dhroim Crí an teideal a bhaist staraithe ar an chomhaontú ba thoradh don chruinniú - tá sé deacair a shamhlú go bhféadfaí cáipéis den teideal chéanna a dhréachtú inniu.
Ní cóir dúinn barraíocht béime a leagan ar an tsíocháin áirithe sin áfach mar ní i bhfad a mhair an dea-mhéin. Bhí Eilís I den bharúil gur géilleadh an iomarca don Niallach sna cainteanna agus sa deireadh níor chomhlíon na Sasanaigh coinníollacha an chonartha mar a aontaíodh iad. La perfide Albion go paiteanta plapach, agus tá macallaí na feallaireachta sin go fóill le brath ar an láthair chéanna breis agus 460 bliain níos déanaí.
Tamall beag dá éis sin, ar ndóigh, tosaíodh ar an ghlanadh eitneach agus ar an díshealbhú agus ar an ollslad ba thrúig bháis do na mílte Gael i gCúige Uladh agus a leag síos an dúshraith don Phlandáil le linn an 17ú haois.
Is iomaí scoilt agus gág a bhí i mbólaí thuaisceart Ard Mhacha faoin am a thosaigh na mórshiúlta Oráisteacha sa 19ú céad mar sin. Cuireadh cosc orthu ag tréimhsí éagsúla de bharr an achrainn agus an uamhain a spreag siad ach lean an claonadh forchiníoch ar aghaidh thar na blianta, agus leanann fós.
Má bhí leid bheag i logainm Dhroim Crí go mbeadh ábhar deighilte sa chré áitiúil, bhí teachtaireacht sa talamh i nGarbhachaidh chomh maith: is é sin nach mbeadh pasáiste réidh ag siúlóirí áirithe fríd an bhaile fearainn Ghaelach. D’fhéadfaí a rá gur mín an t-achadh é acu siúd a léiríonn meas ar mhuintir na háite ach cosán corrach ag suaiteoirí seicteacha.
Ní duairc ar fad atá scéal an tírdhreacha máguaird áfach. Creidtear gur ó ‘bandia’ a shíolraíonn ainm na Banna chugainn, í ag lúbarnaíl anuas trí cheo na gcianta agus ag athbheathú na talún arís agus arís eile, tailte Dhoirm Crí san áireamh.
Ansin tá Macha ann, an bhean chumhachtach a bhronn ainm ar an chontae iomlán. Caitheadh léi go héagórach, is fíor, agus d’fhág easpa comhbhá a léiríodh léi lorg ar na glúnta a tháinig ina diaidh, ach ní íospartach amháin í: agus í ag fulaingt go géar, saolaíodh cúpla di. Beatha nua, teacht aniar, dóchas.
Bíodh sin mar atá, i ndeireadh an lae is iad muintir Gharbhachaidh féin a chinnfidh an bóthar atá rompu, gan bhagairt gan bhrú. Tá an meaisín ama Oráisteach feicthe acu agus níor mhian leo léim isteach ann. Tuigeann siad an stair agus níor mhaith leo dul ar ais. Aithníonn siad na deighiltí agus ba thoil leo iad a dhruidim.
Gluaiseacht chun cinn, breathnú ar aghaidh, siúl chun tosaigh - sin an bealach ionsar shochaí shíochánta. Níl aon duine ag dul siar.

title: New camera at Kerry railway crossing to target drivers breaking red lights, speed limits
description: Automatic camera will photograph licence plates of drivers who fail to stop when red lights flashing at crossing
content:
A new automatic enforcement camera will go live at a Co Kerry railway level crossing on Tuesday to catch drivers breaking the speed limit or red lights.
The GoSafe camera, intended to combat persistent speeding at the Farranfore level crossing, will start operation at 12pm.
The automatic enforcement cameras will take pictures of the licence plates of drivers who fail to stop when the flashing red lights are showing at the railway crossing.
Offenders will receive an €80 fine and two penalty points. Drivers who attempt to speed through the crossing will be fined €160 and given three penalty points.
The camera installation is the second of six planned cameras set to be placed at problematic level crossings in the coming months.
The first installation was at the Merrion Gates in south Dublin, which Iarnród Éireann said was chosen because of “persistent driver behaviour issues” where motorists attempt to beat the barrier by continuing past the stop line when the red lights are flashing.
In addition to Farranfore, Iarnród Éireann intends to deploy the cameras at the level crossing at Minish in Co Kerry, and in Co Roscommon at Knockcroghery where “speeding is the primary issue”.
In Dublin, a number of level crossings are set to get cameras including at Serpentine Avenue and Sandymount in south Dublin, and Sutton and Coolmine on the northside.
The installation of the cameras comes as a result of Transport Infrastructure Ireland being tasked in early 2024 with developing a national strategy for the introduction of camera-based enforcement.
Garda assistant commissioner for roads policing Denis Ferry said the force “welcome this next stage of co-operation with our partners in transport safety”.
He said the “effective use of this kind of technology will greatly help us to keep rail and road users safe through enforcement”.
Gardaí and GoSafe, the company responsible for speed vans in Ireland, will operate the cameras alongside Iarnród Éireann, with co-operation from Transport Infrastructure Ireland and Kerry County Council.
Motorists and cyclists drove into level crossing gates 23 times last year, a minor improvement on 28 incidents in 2024.
This year, a 12-year-old boy was killed in Mayo when a train struck a car at a user-operated crossing at Kiltybo near Ballyhaunis. Eoin Doyle was fatally injured while travelling in a car with his father, Declan, who suffered non-life-threatening injuries.

title: Mercedes GLC review: A brilliant electric SUV that tries far too hard to get noticed
description: This is one of the most refined electric SUVs, so why dress it up like a newcomer desperate to make an impression?
content:
There are 942 issues with the new all-electric Mercedes GLC. And then a few more inside. All of them add up to a nagging question: Is Mercedes a leader or a follower?
The new all- electric GLC’s arrival sets us up for a fantastic ding-dong battle in the premium SUV market . Landing within months of the BMW iX3 and at the same time as the new Volvo EX60 , one of the most competitive segments in the Irish market now has a trio of tempting electric offers, all boasting headline-grabbing range claims and impressive driving dynamics.
But the question is not whether the GLC is nice to drive, nor whether it’s got the range or capabilities to cater to most, if not all, Irish motoring needs. It’s about the “942 light points” beaming out from the nose of the car.
This light show is where the grille used to go before the EV era made it redundant and left car designers with a quandary: what do we do with the front of the car? For more than a century, the grille was great real estate for carrying a badge or creating a brand identity. Indeed, Mercedes-Benz references models like its 600 Pullman, W108 and W111 of the 1950s and 1960s for the front of this new GLC.
Now it’s a dilemma, and just at a time when SUVs are all the rage. Some simply continue the bonnet metal downwards. Others have toyed with a faux grille halfway house. Then there are those who fill the gap with lights. No one has quite nailed it.
Mercedes designers decided this would be an ideal location for what they’ve billed as “status-accentuating front design”. Which, in layman’s terms, translates to a big “in your face, plebs”.
Not that it’s ugly. On these dark early autumn mornings and darker nights, it looks quite smart. But do you really want to light up the neighbourhood every time you open or lock your car?
Buried in one of the car’s menus is the chance to switch it off, but then what’s the point? Switched off, the faux grille looks a little garish and too big for the car’s facade, like a beefy Roman pillar on the porch of a terraced council house. At least when it’s lit, it seems to serve some purpose.
Inside there are the usual comfort features, but this time let down by overworked chrome-coloured plastics. Combined with the big screens, it’s a bit like Mercedes is trying to mimic the over-dressed Chinese newcomer brands. Which is a bizarre move by a brand with 140 years of automotive heritage to build upon. Mercedes should be following no one.
That’s when the argument becomes considerably more complicated.
[ Mercedes CLA hybrid – a car so good, we almost like it in spite of ourselves Opens in new window ]
For all the visual theatre, underneath is an exceptionally accomplished electric SUV that builds upon the brilliance of the CLA.
Our test car was the 400 4MATIC, which means four-wheel drive and an output of 360kW (489hp). You can also opt for the four-wheel drive GLC 300 with 310kW, or the entry-level rear-wheel drive GLC 250 with 260kW.
The GLC 400 test car features the larger battery pack with 94.4kWh of usable storage, for which Mercedes claims a range of 653km. That aspiration is close to reality, for we started out with the range tipping in at 600km on a 95 per cent charge.
After 280km, we had averaged 17.5kWh/100km, which would equate to 537km. That’s short of the official figure, but still enough to make range anxiety largely academic for most Irish journeys.
Mercedes claims the potential to hit 330kW DC peak charging power. That trails the BMW iX3’s 400kW and the Volvo EX60 P10’s 370kW, although these are peak figures achieved only under optimum conditions and tell only part of the charging story.
Having preconditioned the battery, we had 31 per cent left, with a suggested range of 182km. The max charge the car could take was 262kW. At an ESB 360kW station, we started getting 255kW, but within five minutes it had dropped below 200kW. After exactly 10 minutes it was 142kW, but by then the battery was 68 per cent charged and the suggested range was up to 403km. With access to fast chargers, you can see how after a long journey you can quickly get the percentages up to 60 per cent or so in a few minutes, then top up the rest at home on a slower but more cost-effective charger.
For all its comfort, the GLC is certainly no slouch. Hitting 100km/h from a standing start in 4.3 seconds is no mean feat for a 2.6 tonne SUV.
The GLC’s greatest trait is that it does this with little drama. It’s graceful, yet controlled and communicative. You feel the road without suffering from the undulations. And stopping is as progressive as in a petrol car, with a beautifully judged brake pedal and little sense of the transition between regenerative and friction braking.
The real strength of this all-electric GLC is not just its substantial range. Nor is it the elongated screens stretching across the dash.
The beauty of this car comes in its refined drive. One colleague put it succinctly: it drives and rides exactly as you’d expect a Mercedes-Benz to. That sounds like an unequivocal compliment, although we were discussing it in the context of its rivals. And there is no doubt that the new BMW iX3 is sharper to drive.
But that sharpness comes at a price, paid by the passengers in terms of its ride. The BMW is a great car to be behind the wheel; less so from the passenger seat. The GLC, on the other hand, delivers a smooth and silky ride for all its occupants, while not forgoing too much of its sharpness in the corners and bends.
[ BMW reinvents the petrol 3 Series for the Neue Klasse era – but there’s a price Opens in new window ]
Cruising on the motorway or down a country lane, keep the stereo off and the cabin is whisper quiet. There is not even the rumble of tyres to disturb the peace.
All this makes this GLC a Mercedes mile muncher. Like the best of cars to come from the brand, you can criss-cross the country without any real strain.
And that’s before you drop another €4,000 for the Airmatic air suspension and rear axle steering, which lifts the car’s comfort to a new level. Worth the spend? You will not miss it if you don’t have it, but you’ll appreciate it more than handing over €2,000 on the hyperscreen and a host of other features that wow for the first three days and then lie unused for the rest of your ownership.
All this is to say that Mercedes has overworked what is at its heart a fantastic car to drive and travel in.
And it’s relatively well priced. Starting at €72,085 for the rear-wheel-drive GLC 250 version, it goes up to €76,580 for the GLC 300 with 4MATIC four-wheel drive.
We haven’t yet driven the 250, but on paper the GLC 300 version looks like the sweet spot, given there’s only a marginal difference in performance.
At €76,580, it’s €3,575 cheaper than the GLC 300e 4MATIC plug-in hybrid and a whopping €9,980 less than the diesel GLC 300d. For buyers with home charging, the argument for choosing combustion is becoming increasingly difficult to make.
And design is a very personal choice. My well-clued-in neighbours, whom I trust on taste matters, thought the new look quite smart. They patiently listened to my rant on the grille and interior, remained spectacularly unconvinced and started drilling down on details of specification and price. Two fellow motoring hacks I somewhat respect told me in no uncertain terms to park it when I brought it up for the third time with them.
Do that, and you can really appreciate how good this car is to drive. The curious achievement of the electric GLC is that almost nothing about driving it shouts electric car. There is no needlessly brutal throttle response, no artificial sportiness and little sense that Mercedes is desperate to show you what its software can do. Instead, it has concentrated on the old-fashioned virtues of refinement, isolation and engineering thoroughness.
My qualm with this car is that there is an underlying sense that its visual theatre feels more appropriate for a young Chinese brand still trying to establish its credentials rather than a company whose history dates to the origins of the modern automobile.
[ Publicity drive: Mercedes-Benz issues birth certs for vintage cars Opens in new window ]
These newcomers are parvenus, not peers. Mercedes does not need to shout, and it certainly should not look as though it is following anyone.
On the road, it’s clear the engineers understand this perfectly. Can someone please CC the designers?
Power: Dual motor four-wheel drive putting out 360kW (489hp) and a battery pack with 94.4kWh of usable storage,
Price: €81,226 as tested (range starts at €72,085 for the GLC 250).

title: Irish Rail services into Dublin from Newbridge disrupted by signalling issues
description: Train services between Hazelhatch and Heuston have been affected, with delays of more than an hour
content:
Irish Rail services from Newbridge to Dublin are experiencing significant disruption due to an early signalling issue in Co Kildare.
While the signalling issue has now been rectified, knock-on delays are running up to 75 minutes.
Services between Hazelhatch and Heuston stations were affected, leading to initial delays.
The line includes stops at Adamstown, Kishoge, Clondalkin and Fonthill, Park West and Cherry Orchard before finishing at Heuston Station.
Trains to Heuston from Portlaoise, Carlow, Waterford, Galway and Cork are all delayed.
Irish Rail reminded customers that Leap cards can be used on all Transport for Ireland public transport. However, no relief buses were provided for passengers impacted by the disruption.

title: ‘I’m swooning as I come in the door’: A trip to Milan to buy cottons, linens and silks
description: Milan is an ideal choice of location not just for the fashion set but also the hobby sewist
content:
A city synonymous with fashion, Milan is the birthplace of major labels such as Prada , Versace , and Armani and home to the headquarters of many more. It hosts four fashion weeks a year, and during my time in the city, I see more than one runway model gliding through the crowds.
Milanese style is formal, with a focus on designer handbags and sleek tailoring. I’m here for a few days, and it’s difficult to ignore the allure of the fashion set. Sadly my hopes of discovering the perfect 1990s Versace slip dress or a Miu Miu co-ord in one of the city’s many vintage shops are quickly blocked by a frame unsuited to Italian sizing. After a changing room try-on ends in my calves getting stuck in a pair of psychedelic Dolce & Gabbana jeans for €90, I get chatting to Chiara Sodini, the owner of Hello Vintage.
A former fashion archivist, Chiara understands my desire to get involved in what she calls Milan’s second favourite pastime, shopping. (The first being the pre-dinner aperitivo.)
As a hobby sewist, for me fabric shopping is the way forward. While Milan is a mecca for the finished product, it is also a hub for the raw materials. Chiara thinks hard before giving me her recommendations, writing them out on a yellow Post-it. First on the list is the family-run Fonte Della Moda, on Via Marcello Malpighi in the elegant Porta Venezia area.
It’s a few kilometres away, so I walk there directly. A step inside this small shop is a step into Italian fashion history. There are hundreds of bolts of fabric neatly stacked on floor-to-ceiling shelves, thousands of trimmings and drawers and drawers of buttons, and everything is catalogued by hand. Gabrielle, who helps her daughter Monica run the shop, hands me three big binders of fabric swatches to go through.
My Italian is limited, but the language of fabric is visual and easily decoded. Lino for linen, cotone for cotton and seta for silk. As I leaf through the pages of linen gingham, chintzy cottons and floral poplin, Gabrielle sorts bags of pearly buttons, and Monica tells me about her grandfather, who first opened the shop in 1945.
“There are many more fabric shops in the past. But fast fashion and people not making their own clothes as much have changed things,” she says. “I couldn’t keep it going without the rent from the pop-up store we run next door, but it is important that I do. It is history for me and my family.”
Monica moves on to find a length of elastic for another customer, and unsure of what I want, I go to the restaurant next door, Pesa Pubblica, for a glass of white wine and the best panini of my life, toast with tomato, stracciatella cream and olive tapenade.
Buying fabric requires a different set of skills from buying clothes and, as a beginner, I still get confused when surrounded by so much choice. In need of inspiration, I walk to Bivio, a well-known second-hand designer shop with four outlets around the city; the closest is just a few minutes away on Via Lambro.
Picking out loose cotton dresses with bold prints and drawn to the row of silk Gucci scarves for €100, I realise I want to bring home bright patterns to work with rather than the solid colours that make up much of my wardrobe.
Emporio Tessile is my next fabric stop on Via Pier Lombardo in the Porta Romana area. I get there just before closing. The front of the shop is taken up with upholstery and oilcloths, so I head to the back rooms that are dedicated to dressmaking material. Here, hundreds of rolls of fabric are stacked 20 feet high.
The question of how anyone can choose anything, when I can only see a fraction of what’s available, is answered by Martino, a young shop assistant, who directs me to a wall of swatches on keyrings. We look through pretty cottons and striped linens before my eyes are pulled to the bolts of fabulous silks. Italy is famous for its silks, particularly the areas around Lake Como, an hour north of Milan.
Enthusiastic about one of his country’s most famous products, Martino unfurls a roll printed with lions and zebras prowling around in beds of ferns. It’s €45 a metre, and I imagine it as a full skirt, with a narrow waistband swishing with every step. Silk is slippery, and my skills aren’t there yet, so I land on a bold red and white striped cotton that reminds me of a 1930s swimming costume, buying three metres for €57.
The next morning, I head out to the Porta Nuova area, passing the Vertical Forest. A defining feature of contemporary architecture in Milan, the twin skyscrapers are designed by Stefano Boeri and are now home to more than 800 trees and thousands of shrubs and plants. It’s a beautiful reprieve in a busy city. I’m one of the first people in the door at Tessuti e Scampolii, which translates to Fabric and Scraps in English.
[ Florence like a local: The ultimate guide to eating and drinking, from a €6 pasta dish to Tuscan haute cuisine Opens in new window ]
Spread over two floors, this is by far the largest fabric shop I’ve ever been in. There is every combination of colour and cloth here: natural fibres as well as rolls of vinyl, leatherette, organza, polyester, rayon and baskets of bargain-priced remnants sold by weight. It starts to get busy with locals, calling out Buongiorno as they arrive and greet their friends. There are deals to be found here, but my capacity for decision making is weakened, so I go for an iced coffee in nearby Café Gorille before my final shop.
This is one came recommended by Vittorio Giomo, the founder of Textile Design Group Milan, and an expert fabric buyer who has worked in the industry for decades. We chat on the phone, and he directs me to Tessuti Lagosta on Piazzale Lagosta, an upmarket place that opened in 1957.
In the window under a red awning is one of the most beautiful fabrics I’ve ever seen: an ochre-coloured linen with boldly embroidered flowers. It’s €85 a metre. I’m swooning as I come in the door. Paula, who has been working here for 10 years, shows me around. It’s mostly fashion students and tailors who come here, she tells me. The shop orders new material twice a year, often in small batches, so it’s possible to find fabrics here that are unique.
This is the best laid-out, most intuitive place to browse that I’ve been to in Milan. I buy a sliver of green silk with violet flowers as a souvenir and make a promise to return for the vintage Italian herringbone wools that catch my eye at €19 a metre.
In need of a refresh, I get the metro out to Terme De Montel, one of Europe’s largest thermal spas, near the San Siro football stadium. Built within the grounds of early 20th-century art nouveau stables, De Montel underwent years of renovation and opened last year.
If the Milanese can’t go north to the lakes at the weekend, they come here. Thermal waters are pumped from 396m underground and flow into blue pools variously designed for floating, relaxing and a “cold shock” at 22 degrees.
On entry, I am handed a pair of beige sliders, a white robe and a white towel. Soon, I am one of the many uniformly clad people moving between the sun loungers, pools and saunas.
[ Discovering northern Italy’s charm: exploring five beautiful cities in just five days Opens in new window ]
After days of kaleidoscopic colour, the sight of white cloth on bare skin feels like respite. It makes sense why some designers who have the finest fabrics at their disposal, like Jonathan Anderson, creative director of Dior, or Sarah Burton, who holds the same role at Givenchy, are rarely seen out of cotton shirts and denim jeans.
Rosanna Cooney was a guest of Terme De Montel

title: Budget 2027 has become worst-kept secret in Irish politics – and that’s saying something
description: Simon Harris’s first budget is expected to bring reductions in tax for middle-income earners
content:
It is the only week of the year when the Inside Politics digest on Tuesday is an identikit of the Inside Politics digest on Wednesday. What’s not been leaked by Monday night is not worth knowing. Until a few years ago the two Ministers with responsibility for the fiscal wellbeing of the nation kept one or two big items in reserve, but they have largely given up on that pretence too.
Now, they could surprise us. After all we have a new Minister for Finance in Simon Harris and we will not truly know his budget “form” until we have read his speech.
But you can take it that the era of Charlie McCreevy – where nobody had a clue of what he was going to announce until he stood up in the Dáil – is well and truly gone. The chances of a decentralisation style announcement today are as remote as Rockall.
Pat Leahy, Jack Horgan-Jones and Dominic Coyle have been on manoeuvres all day Monday trying to winkle out as much information from the budget document as possible.
Reductions in tax for middle-income earners worth up to €1,500 for a couple with a combined income of €100,000 are expected.
Harris and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers are expected to highlight the introduction of an annual cost-of-disability payment of €500, paid as a lump sum first and a monthly payment after next year, as well as cuts to the cost of childcare.
The broad fiscal envelope has already been established. The Summer Economic Statement 2026 set out an €8.5 billion package for 2027, comprising €7 billion in additional spending and €1.5 billion in taxation measures.
If Harris had not been having sleepless nights in the run-up to unveiling the details, that certainly changed after Friday when his wife Caoimhe gave birth to the couple’s third child, a baby girl. Harris will take paternity leave once budget week is done.
It’s an expansionary budget. Sure aren’t they all? Total 2027 expenditure is predicted to be €118 billion. There was a self-imposed rule of restricting spending growth to 5 per cent that the Government was supposed to stick to but that was never achieved. Not by a long shot.
Chambers has made a big show of keeping it to 6 per cent – amid much howls of protest from line Ministers. It will be interesting to see if that is achieved. It will be an achievement if it is. As Martin Wall reported several weeks ago, health spending so far in 2026 is close to 9 per cent above projections . A public sector pay deal is also going to be an additional costly item.
No wonder the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council and the ESRI are fretting publicly on an almost weekly basis.
It’s budget day in the Oireachtas so other business is sidelined. The formal proceedings will start at 1pm when Harris presents the budget, followed by Chambers presenting the public expenditure side of the equation. The Opposition spokespeople will then get a chance to reply at length and at volume.
In the afternoon, Ministers will hold a series of briefings outlining how the budget will impact their departments. The Dáil will then take a break and resume at 8pm to hear financial motions, and to vote on any financial, welfare or excise measures that need to be implemented immediately.
Harris has made a virtue of his tax package. The big Fine Gael ask last year was the reduction of VAT for hospitality – that had a mixed reception. This year it’s the módh díreach with reductions in income tax.
The entry point for the higher rate of income tax is expected to rise from €44,000 to €46,000, while adjustments to the universal social charge and tax credits are also expected to add a few hundred euro annually in benefits for middle-income earners.
The Government will argue that the average worker will be hundreds of euro better off.
Despite the fuel crisis biting with a vengeance over the past two months, the Government has not signalled the return of any once-off energy credits (although all the Opposition parties have been baying for them).
On Saturday, Taoiseach Micheál Martin signalled there would be no further increases in the carbon tax applied to home heating oil. He also indicated there would be a Christmas bonus payment to pensioners and welfare recipients (in addition to existing bonuses perhaps?). And expect to see some increases in fuel allowance.
On the housing front, it is understood the rent tax credit could be set for an increase, with a higher level of €1,200 per person or €2,400 for a married couple or civil partnership said to be under discussion.
Fianna Fáil TD Séamus McGrath led the charge for the abolition of the 1 per cent stamp duty on homes for first-time buyers. Harris never showed any enthusiasm for it. Instead, it looks like first-time buyers will be able to access up to €35,000 towards the deposit on their first home after agreement was reached by party leaders. This increases the limit by €5,000.
Core welfare payments will increase by €10. That means the State pension is expected to increase by €10, and it’s also expected there will be movement in terms of improving the carers’ allowance.
Childcare is another potential pitfall for the Government, given it promised to reduce the cost of full-time childcare to €200 per month per child by the end of its term. It now looks like the cost will be reduced by a minimum of €1,000 per child annually today, between €80 and €100 a month. It’s a fair bit but there’s still a long way to go.
Harris is expected to reveal details of his new savings and investment scheme, with tax incentives.
Another thing to look out for is the reduction of €150 in student fees, somewhat short of the €250 that was being floated several weeks ago.
Inheritance tax has been another hot topic. Expect the tax-free rate for children inheriting to rise.
Teenagers will also benefit from a culture voucher but its amount has not yet been revealed after tense negotiations between Chambers and Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan.
There is also a €10 million support package for rural pubs, a measure that will satisfy the rural Independent TDs supporting the Government and also backbenchers such as Peter ‘Chap’ Cleere.
There is another election this year. It’s the byelection for the vacancy in the Seanad caused by Seán Kyne’s victory in the Galway West byelection last May.
Nominations close today, and only members of the Oireachtas can vote so the total potential poll is 234 politicians. The seat will be won by a Government TD and you would assume there is a deal between Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael.
It therefore looks very likely that the winner will be Fine Gael Dublin city councillor Ray McAdam, who is his party’s nominee.
Marie O’Halloran has a great report on Sinn Féin TD Mark Ward’s attempt to regulate the horse and carriage trade in Dublin. He says that unregulated operators have made it look like the “wild west”.
Fintan O’Toole compares the Drumcree stand-off to Monty Python.
The former Conservative MP and author Jeffrey Archer has died at the age of 86.
The novelist was a Tory MP for six years and was chair of the party, but he was then imprisoned in 2001 for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice. An Old Bailey jury in the UK found that he had lied in a libel action he had brought against the Star newspaper 13 years earlier, in which he was awarded £500,000 damages.

title: Offender with 114 convictions who helped gang in fatal shooting keen to change ways, says lawyer
description: Most recent offence for robbery and reckless discharge of a firearm in Lidl on the Malahide Road
content:
A criminal with 114 previous convictions who helped a crime gang “snuff out” a 22-year-old man’s life outside his family home has recently been baptised and has a “genuine desire” to change his ways, his barrister has told the Central Criminal Court.
The court was told during Monday’s sentence hearing for Paul Clarke (43) that just two weeks before the victim was shot dead, the defendant had carried out an armed robbery at a Lidl on the Malahide Road.
Clarke, with an address at Coolock Drive, Coolock, Dublin, pleaded guilty last June to the participation in the activity of a criminal organisation.
The court heard that Clarke, between November 23rd and 24th 2019, did, with knowledge of the existence of a criminal organisation, participate in, or contribute to, the killing of Eoin Boylan at Clonshaugh Avenue, Dublin.
Clarke was originally charged before the District Court in March 2025 with the murder of Boylan.
Boylan (22) was shot several times at his family home on Clonshaugh Avenue on November 24th, 2019. He was pronounced dead later at nearby Beaumont Hospital.
At the outset of the hearing, Det Garda Jason Flynn from Coolock Garda station detailed the background of the incident. He told Fionnuala O’Sullivan, for the Director of Public Prosecutions, that in the year preceding Boylan’s death, he was subjected to several attacks.
Counsel said gardaí were aware of confidential information relating to a threat to Boylan’s life, which was assessed as being high. The detective garda agreed that Boylan was aware of this information and suffered from stress around the time of his killing.
Counsel said Boylan lived at a log cabin at the rear of his family home on Clonshaugh Avenue.
The court heard that his father, Liam, was driving towards his son’s home when he heard gunshots and saw someone running out of the side gate carrying a gun with a strap.
The shooting at the back of the main house was captured on CCTV and occurred at 4.49pm. Counsel said footage showed Boylan running out of the log cabin and the shooter firing at him before jumping over a side wall.
After the killing, she said the assailant had run out a side gate towards the front garden of the house before fleeing the scene on a bicycle.
O’Sullivan said a silver Citroen, which was captured driving past the deceased’s address the day before the killing, had pulled up outside the Belcamp/Darndale centre one hour and 20 minutes after the shooting. She said an individual getting out of the vehicle was identified by gardaí in CCTV footage as Paul Clarke.
Flynn confirmed that during a drugs search in December 2019, the defendant had made reference to Boylan’s killing, saying the deceased had thought his house was a fortress but that someone was cleverer than him. Clarke also told gardaí that a “fast gun” was used in the killing.
The Garda witness agreed that Clarke was interviewed on five occasions following his arrest in August 2023, but denied murdering Boylan.
The court heard that Clarke has 114 previous convictions, with the most recent for robbery and the reckless discharge of a firearm in Lidl on the Malahide Road on November 13th, 2019, two weeks before Boylan’s shooting.
Clarke was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment in October 2023 after pleading guilty to robbing the supermarket. However, in February 2025 the Court of Appeal imposed a new sentence of seven years and six months, with the last five months suspended, for the robbery. Clarke is serving this term.
In his submissions, Michael O’Higgins, defending, said the circumstances in which Clarke grew up were “grim in the extreme”, with instances of multigenerational drug addiction.
He said the defendant began abusing drugs at 14 years of age and there was a significant downward slope after he took a considerable amount of cocaine and heroin, resulting in a long-standing drug addiction.
The lawyer suggested that the court could see if this was an appropriate case to exercise its discretion against imposing a consecutive sentence. He said Clarke was a religious person and was recently baptised by a pastor.
Mr Justice Paul McDermott remanded Clarke in custody until Friday, when he will be sentenced.

title: Separatists win Quebec provincial election in blow to Mark Carney
description: Result may hamper Canadian prime minster’s efforts to maintain national unity against Trump
content:
A separatist party narrowly won Quebec’s ‌ provincial general election on Monday, a result that could make it tougher for Canadian prime minister Mark Carney to maintain national unity against US president Donald Trump .
Provisional results showed ​the predominantly French-speaking province of nine million had opted for the Parti Quebecois of Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who is promising to hold a referendum on breaking from Canada once Trump leaves office.
“A referendum is a chance to decide things for ourselves ... our national destiny will be achieved one day,” Plamondon (49), ​a former lawyer, told cheering supporters.
But he faces challenges. The Parti Quebecoiswon 59 of the 127 seats in the Quebec national assembly, ⁠five short of a majority. The legislature must approve any referendum vote.
Plamondon conceded he would need support from opposition parliamentarians ‌to ‌proceed.
The ​widely expected result reflected voter fatigue with the centre-right Coalition Avenir Quebec government, in office since 2018, analysts said. The Coalition Avenir Quebec lost all of its 79 seats.
Carney, who has stressed the ⁠need for a united front to tackle Trump’s tariffs, ​must now work with a Quebec premier who is determined ​to break up Canada.
In addition, the energy-rich province of Alberta will hold a non-binding vote this month on whether its residents ‌want independence.
Independence votes held by previous Parti Quebecois governments in ​1980 and 1995 failed, and polls indicate support for the idea of breaking with Canada is at 30 per cent, near record ⁠lows.
Plamondon, citing the political uncertainty and economic damage done ⁠by the tariffs, says he ​will not call another referendum until Trump is out of White House.
In remarks addressed to Carney, Plamondon said he would defend Quebec’s interests above all, but reiterated that he was happy to work with Ottawa whenever it suited Quebec.
Despite the unclear referendum prospects, some Parti Quebecois policies look set to boost tension with Ottawa, however.
The party plans to resist any federal bid to boost immigration, cut Quebec’s ties to the British monarchy and block a proposed high-profile high-speed rail link with Ontario.
Carney congratulated Plamondon on X, saying, “Building a stronger Quebec is core to our ‌mission of building a stronger Canada.”
Carney ⁠said looked forward to working with Plamondon to support Quebec’s businesses and workers hit by tariffs.
The Parti Quebecois – which benefited significantly from vote-splitting between the five major parties in the fray – took just 27.9 per cent of the ‌vote, the lowest share of ballots captured by a winning party in Quebec electoral history.
The Coalition Avenir Quebec’s collapse reflects the fact that politics in ​Quebec is traditionally more volatile than elsewhere in Canada. The Parti Quebecois jumped from seven seats ​to take power.
The previous lowest vote share of a winning party in Quebec was the 32 per cent garnered by the Parti Quebecois in 2012, when it also secured a minority. – Reuters
