title: Drochthuar faoi phríomhstraitéisí Gaeilge an stáit
description: Ní dócha go mbainfear amach mórspriocanna an rialtais i dtaobh na teanga idir seo agus 2030
content:
Beidh 2030 ina bhliain chinniúnach don Ghaeilge sa mhéid is go mbeidh dhá straitéis thábhachtacha ag teacht chun aibíochta.
An chéad cheann ná an Straitéis 20 Bliain a foilsíodh in 2010. Is í sprioc mhór na straitéise sin ná líon na ndaoine a labhraíonn Gaeilge ar bhonn laethúil a mhéadú go 250,000 duine. Agus go dtarlódh é sin faoi 2030.
An dara ceann ná an straitéis a bhaineann le hAcht na dTeangacha Oifigiúla 2021, go háirithe an dualgas atá ar an Stát neartú a dhéanamh ar na seirbhísí poiblí atá á gcur ar fáil trí Ghaeilge. Aidhm lárnach na reachtaíochta ná go mbeadh 20 faoin gcéad de na daoine a earcaítear ó 2030 ar aghaidh inniúil sa Ghaeilge.
Cén seans go mbainfear amach na haidhmeanna sin? Diabhal seans i mo thuairimse. Tá difríocht mhór idir plean a bhreacadh síos ar pháipéar agus gníomhaíocht cheart a dhéanamh chun an plean a chur i gcrích. Agus is léir nach bhfuil an Ghaeilge ag bláthú faoi pholasaithe an Stáit i leith na teanga.
Faraor, ní an Ghaeilge amháin atá thíos leis. Mar a fheictear domsa é, bíonn gach uile phlean a chuirtear amach faoi bhráid an Stáit nó an Rialtais easnamhach, sa mhéid is nach n-éiríonn leo na spriocanna a bhaint amach. Easpa cur chuige. Easpa fola sa chraiceann.
Nílim ag iarraidh a bheith ródhiúltach, ach ar an iomlán sílim go bhfuil toradh na straitéisí sin idir dhá cheann na meá.
Má chaitheann muid súil siar go 2010 - nó díreach roimhe – bhí an Rialtas fíormhisniúil go n-éireoidh leis an bplean 20 bliain, go raibh an fhéidearthacht sin ann i ndáiríre.
Bhí an straitéis uaillmhianach, níl dabht ar bith faoi sin. Bhí (agus tá go fóill) naoi réimse gníomhaíochta i gceist chun an teanga a dhaingniú roimh lár an chéid.
Maidir leis an gcóras oideachais, bhí níos mó béime le cur ar an nGaeilge i scoileanna Béarla agus níos mó tacaíochta le tabhairt don oideachas lán-Ghaeilge sna bunscoileanna agus meánscoileanna.
Bhí níos mó cúnaimh le tabhairt do cheantair Ghaeltachta mar phobail labhartha Ghaeilge.
An tríú ceann ná an teaghlach. Bhí sé d’aidhm ag an straitéis uchtach a thabhairt do theaghlaigh Gaeilge a labhairt lena bpáistí sa bhaile.
In éineacht leis sin, bhí níos mó maoinithe agus tacaíochta le tabhairt d’eagraíochtaí, féilte, agus pobail Ghaeilge ó cheann ceann na tíre.
Bheadh réimse níos leithne ann i dtaca le seirbhísí craolacháin agus teicneolaíochta a chur ar fáil trí Ghaeilge.
Tá difríocht mhór idir plean a bhreacadh síos ar pháipéar agus gníomhaíocht cheart a dhéanamh chun an plean a chur i gcrích.
An ceann deireanach ná go mbainfí níos mó úsáide as na Gaeilge i gcúrsaí gnó, fógraíochta agus eacnamaíochta.
Cén toradh atá feicthe againn agus gan ach cúpla bliain fágtha sula gcríochnófar an straitéis?
De réir Dhaonáireamh 2022, dúirt 71,968 duine in Éirinn go labhraíonn siad Gaeilge go laethúil lasmuigh den chóras oideachais. Tá an chéad daonáireamh eile in ainm is a bheith ann an bhliain seo chugainn. An bhfeicfear claochlú ar na huimhreacha sin? Níl aon amhras orm nach bhfeicfidh muid agus ní bheidh muid i bhfoisceacht an fhigiúir 250,000 atá leagtha amach sa phlean.
Agus céard faoin Acht ó 2021 a leag síos go mbeadh 20 faoin gcéad d’fhostaithe nua san earnáil phoiblí inniúil sa Ghaeilge faoin mbliain 2030?
Bhí an Dr. Aodhán Mac Cormaic, Rúnaí Cúnta na Gaeilge agus na Gaeltachta sa Roinn Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail agus Gaeltachta os comhair Choiste Oireachtais na Gaeilge agus Gaeltachta le déanaí.
Bhí sé in ann cur síos a dhéanamh ar dhul chun cinn na reachtaíochta agus an chuspóra maidir le seirbhísí poiblí a chur ar fáil trí Ghaeilge.
“Tá obair shuntasach déanta ag oifigigh na Roinne…chun an Ghaeilge a neadú i seirbhísí poiblí an Stáit agus seirbhís phoiblí dhátheangach a chothú,” a dúirt sé.
An sprioc is mó, dar ndóigh, ná go mbeidh 20 faoin gcéad ar a laghad de na daoine a cheapfar i gcomhlachtaí poiblí inniúil i nGaeilge faoi dheireadh na bliana 2030 – tríd an earcaíocht nó ardú céime.
“Tabharfaidh sé seo spreagadh sa bhreis do chomhlachtaí poiblí cúrsaí uasoiliúna Gaeilge a chur ar fáil ar bhonn réamhghníomhach dá gcuid fostaithe,” a dúirt Mac Cormaic.
Leag sé amach cuid den obair atá déanta - cúrsaí oiliúna Gaeilge; gréasán Gaeilge na hearnála poiblí (a bhfuil 3,000 fostaí cláraithe leis); aonad faoi leith ag comhordú an phlean gníomhaíochta, agus mar sin de.
Dar leis: “tá méadú as cuimse tagtha ar líon na ndaoine atá ag tabhairt faoi chúrsaí Gaeilge sa státseirbhís le roinnt blianta anuas”.
Ach táimid ag caint faoi líon mór daoine a earcú a bhfuil Gaeilge ar a dtoil acu. Faoi 2030. Faoi cheann ceithre bliana. Níl na hacmhainní ná na huirlisí taobh thiar den reachtaíocht chun an sprioc sin a bhaint amach.
Is maith an rud é go bhfuil níos mó daoine ag déanamh cúrsaí Gaeilge ach ní hionann sin agus líofacht ná a bheith ar a gcompord leis an teanga.
Ó bunaíodh an Stát níl beart á dhéanamh de réir a mbriathair maidir leis an nGaeilge. Agus tá sé deacair a shamhlú go bhfuil aon seans ar domhan ann go sroichfear sprioc lárnach an phlean seo.
Feicimid samplaí den mheon lagmhisniúil seo arís agus arís eile. Seo thíos dhá shampla a tharla le déanaí.
Dúirt an tAire Cumarsáide agus Meán Patrick O’Donovan nach mbeadh sé de dhualgas ar chúigear den 15 atá ar chomhairle féachana TG4 a bheith líofa sa nGaeilge. Tá sin beagnach dochreidte - ní fheicfeá a leithéid le haon seirbhís i mBéarla.
Chomh maith leis sin, d’eisigh an eagraíocht a bhíonn ag agóid ar son cearta tithíochta i nGaeltachtaí na tíre, Bánú, ráiteas an tseachtain seo caite. Maíodh go bhfágfadh an ráiteas pleanála náisiúnta nua do na ceantair Ghaeltachta muintir na gceantar sin níos measa as ná mar a bhí siad faoin seanráiteas i dtaobh tithíochta.
I gceantar Chois Fharraige i gConamara, faoi na rialacha pleanála atá i bhfeidhm faoi láthair tá dualgas ann 80 faoin gcéad de na haonaid a chur in áirithe do chainteoirí Gaeilge ar feadh 15 bliana.
Ach faoi na rialacha nua atá ar na bacáin, ní bheidh ach 58 faoin gcéad de na tithe curtha in áirithe ar feadh 10 mbliana amháin.
Ní dul chun cinn a bheas in 2030 ach a mhalairt.

title: Has your child settled in to school? The essential prep has nothing to do with reading or writing
description: In junior infants, the key skills to practise with a child at home include toileting, getting dressed and having a generally positive outlook
content:
S tarting school is a big milestone for everyone involved: children, parents and their teachers. And while the idea of gaining independence, making friends and learning new skills might be daunting for youngsters, helping them to achieve these goals can also be challenging for teachers, particularly if children are unprepared for the journey ahead.
Long before they donned their first uniform, parents will have been preparing them for the big event, both emotionally and practically, to help make the transition easier for the young students and their educators.
Now, more than a month into the school year, many of the junior infants are finding their feet and settling into school life. However, according to a recent study in the UK, many children are ill-prepared when they start school, with one in four who started last year not even toilet-trained.
The annual survey of primary school staff by the early-years charity Kindred Squared revealed that 26 per cent (36 per cent in the northeast of England) of children in reception class (junior infants) were having “frequent toilet mishaps”. The report also showed that 28 per cent of school starters were unable to eat and drink independently, while 25 per cent struggled with basic life skills such as being able to dress themselves, sit, play and listen and 28 per cent were unable to use books correctly, with many trying to swipe or tap them rather than turning over a page.
Irish psychologist Peadar Maxwell says that although parents might assume that helping their child to be school ready, and to settle in quickly, involves having them reading and writing before they start junior infants, this is not the case. It simply means arming them with the skills necessary to be a little bit independent for their first foray into the world.
“Teaching preparedness is a life skill,” he says. “I would advise parents to think about what their child needs to be able to feel confident, happy and relaxed in school. Feeling content while separated from their parents is the mindset that will allow a child to learn and, importantly, enjoy school. This is important as they will be there for many years, so set them up from the beginning to have a positive outlook for the next, at least, 13 years.”
Maxwell, who is based in Wexford, says children are more likely to be school ready when they are toilet trained and can also attend to basic needs. “This means that taking the time to be patient and teach your child the skill of opening their clothes, using the toilet, cleaning and dressing – with minimal prompting at first, and moving day by day to no prompting,” he says. “It means being able to dress themselves and fix their clothes and also the basics of washing their hands and keeping their nose clean.
“Never assume that a child should know these so-called basic skills. Every child needs to learn these tasks one at a time, and don’t expect perfection as you teach a skill.
“So help your child to express their feelings and opinions. Model positive observations and say please and thanks to people in your child’s company. Your child will be better able to deal with school problems if they have an optimistic view of the world and that includes a positive view of their school and teacher. But when your child needs to express negative feelings, allow that too.”
[ ‘I have 16 different feelings’: Test of emotions for pupils and parents as school starts Opens in new window ]
low” of the class, and the psychologist says parents can help their children cope with this by also having a routine at home – for mealtimes, bedtime and even activities or days out.
“A child who has been introduced to education and learning as a joy rather than a chore will be more ready for classroom work and more likely to see the point of school,” he says. “This can be encouraged by modelling curiosity about the world, nature and fun facts. Make learning fun by encouraging drawing, colouring, boardgames or puzzles.
“Also, encourage your child to be physically active to whatever degree they are comfortable with, as this will prepare them for PE, yard play and activities they may encounter. You might also try using even a few words of Irish such as ‘madra’, ‘rothar’ or ‘scoil’ just to introduce an Gaeilge as a new facet of your child’s world.”
Áine O’Rourke says she made sure to prepare her children for school as she was “a late starter” herself and knows how being behind can make children feel self-conscious. “I was probably a little bit spoilt when I was young, as I was an only child and my mother did everything for me,” she says. “I really wasn’t able to do much when I started school, aside from going to the bathroom and, even then, I didn’t like to go alone and often had accidents. I was used to being fed, having my coat zipped up and generally getting everything done for me.
“So when my own children (now aged seven and nine) started, I was determined that they would be better prepared as I remember feeling quite foolish when the other kids would be doing things themselves and I would have to wait for the teacher. Because of that, when my two started school, they were able to put their coats on or take them off, button them up, use the toilet, wash their hands and eat their lunch unaided.
“It is so important, not only for the children, but also for the teachers who are not childminders: their job is to give our kids an education, not spend their days wiping bottoms.”
According to the Kindred Squared report, school staff in the UK estimated they were spending almost 1½ hours a day changing nappies or helping children who are not toilet trained, and about 2½ hours of teaching time a day is lost due to pupils lacking basic skills.
The situation doesn’t seem to be mirrored in Ireland, with teachers finding a “very high level of school readiness” in junior infant intakes.
[ Starting school means parents must ensure children are prepared Opens in new window ]
Colm Byrne, principal at the Holy Family National School in Rathcoole, Co Dublin, says this could be attributed to the Early Childhood Care and Education ( ECCE ) scheme. “Prior to the introduction of the scheme, we could easily identify the children who had been to a private preschool service in comparison to those who had not received a formal preschool programme of learning and development such as now enjoyed through the ECCE scheme,” he says.
“Indeed, it’s a testament to the ECCE and the brilliant, underpaid teaching staff and struggling preschool managers who strive to continue to provide this service. We are all conscious of the financial struggles many of these services are experiencing. Our State, however, also deserves commendation for the provision of the scheme.”
The school principal says that “with the exception of children with additional needs”, most junior infants are expected to be fully toilet-trained and steps are taken to help them be independent in other ways.
“We also require children to wear Velcro shoes/runners until they are able to tie their own laces,” he says. “I ask mams and dads to imagine a junior infant child requesting teacher to tie their laces of both feet, even once per day, then to multiply that by the number of children in the class and you have the equivalent of 30 minutes of teaching time lost with just one lace tie per child. You can now extend this scenario to imagine a teacher taking a child to the toilet once per day.
“So it is imperative to ensure optimum learning and contact time that the teaching staff is allowed focus on progressing the child through the learning and developmental milestones which are outlined in our crowded curriculum. Teachers are not in a position to provide one-to-one care in a structural sense.
“Obviously, they will always provide care in an emergency situation, but it’s not appropriate to expect classroom teachers to be responsible for ensuring a child learns how to toilet themselves. I think there is space to discuss additional time in schools to develop skills regarding eating and hopefully the new curriculum time allocation will be more generous regarding school autonomy on allocating eating and break time to provide further opportunities around this, especially in the context of the provision of the much welcome and beneficial hot meals scheme.”
[ Here’s how to do hot school meals right Opens in new window ]
The experienced educator says there are a “range of observations regarding language literacy” but he does not believe that children will be impacted long term by an early introduction to digital devices. “While the junior infant intakes are increasingly digitally literate, there would be decreasing numbers of children who you would identify as having experienced language from reading time with parents,” he says. “These pupils will display some emergent reading skills such as reading orientation, but children are experiencing language and the written and spoken word in formats not available when I was a child.
“But I am not confident that language literacy is threatened by the fact that a junior infant child is not as familiar with how to orientate through a book as a junior infant child might have done 20 years ago. The manner and media through which infant children experience language has simply changed.
“So, typically, we find junior infant children primary school-ready. Of course, there is always the exception, and most junior infant intakes take until Christmas to fully assimilate to their new environment, but the ECCE scheme has delivered much success in this regard.”

title: Treating oesophageal cancer: ‘The service delivered here is on par with the best in the world’
description: Working as a surgeon for more than 30 years, Prof John Reynolds has been at the forefront of improving Ireland’s survival rates from the disease
content:
T here is no greater gift than years of survival for people with a life-threatening cancer – or being spared that diagnosis altogether.
This is what surgeon Prof John Reynolds has delivered for thousands of patients in Ireland, whether he operated directly on them for oesophageal/gastric cancer or they benefited from improvements he has driven within care systems and inspired among colleagues. He has been at the forefront of initiatives that have led to a doubling of overall survival for the 500-plus people diagnosed with oesophageal cancer in the Republic each year. That is the greatest increase in survival rate among seven high-income countries, according to a comparative study published in the Lancet in 2019.
Patients have been able “to return to their families, to walk daughters down the aisle, to tend to their gardens, or to embark on a pilgrimage on the Camino”, says Noelle Ryan, a founder and current board member of the Oesophageal Cancer Fund (OCF). Those under his care “would speak of John with a reverence that went far beyond medical gratitude”.
That is not to suggest for a moment that he radiates any sort of “god complex”.
In fact, nothing could be further from the truth.
There will undoubtedly be tributes to him at an academic symposium hosted by Trinity St James’s Cancer Institute, Trinity College and St James’s Hospital , Dublin, on October 16th to mark his retirement as professor of surgery, a role that combines teaching and research with clinical practice. But sitting down with The Irish Times, a day after his 69th birthday, to reflect on a career that spans a time of extraordinary medical advances since his graduation from University College Dublin medical school in 1981, the quietly spoken Reynolds is more comfortable focusing on patients, rather than the man behind the scrubs.
A surgeon’s relationship with a cancer patient is paramount, he explains, right from the first consultation. “You’re trying to have their confidence, and you usually have ... they trust you.”
The patient is struggling to cope with a very serious diagnosis that is “just pure bad luck”.
“They’re naturally in a terrified state and so is their family.”
He regards it as “an incredible responsibility” to guide them through the decision-making process and to prepare them for treatment. “But the real intensity of the relationship is from the time you take knife to skin, basically, and you operate on your patient. It could be a four-hour, eight-hour operation. The patient might be in for one week, two weeks or 10 weeks, depending on how they do.”
Surgery for oesophageal cancer is typically complex, as it involves removing part, or sometimes all, of the affected food pipe and pulling up the stomach to rejoin what is left. No matter what way the surgery is done, whether with a hand-held scalpel, through a minimally invasive, keyhole operation or using robotic surgery, the consequences of having your stomach up in your chest, or near your neck, or no stomach at all if that is a cancer site, are going to be significant. “It’s really looking after that patient in the immediate aftermath of the surgery as best you can, to make sure that they get safely through that treatment. That requires seeing the patient a lot.”
He admits he probably “freaked out” some patients by appearing at their bedside at 6am or midnight. “My natural bias was to overdo it,” he smiles. Other professors may like to travel the world attending conferences, “but I never did because I never wanted to leave the patients ... and the family, of course”. (No doubt his wife, Muriel, and their three now grown-up children are well used to him having vulnerable patients at the forefront of his mind.) “If I had done some major operation, I hated getting phone calls if I was away, ‘what do we do?’”
In addition to the dedication to his own patients, “the very special thing about what John did,” says one of his proteges, consultant upper gastrointestinal surgeon Dr Jessie Elliott, was how he went far beyond that to create a system, and a team around that, both in clinical care and broader research.
“He’s built a phenomenal multidisciplinary team at the national centre for oesophageal and gastric cancer here in James’s.”
Between dietitians, speech and language therapists and specialist nurses, not to mention ward catering staff and healthcare assistants, as well as doctors, it’s like a 360-degree model of care for the patients, she says. The effectiveness is underscored by the outcomes from surgery. “It’s really not an exaggeration to say that the service that’s delivered here is on par with the best centres in the world for oesophageal and gastric cancer.”
[ What to look out for: Symptoms of oesophageal cancer Opens in new window ]
The centralisation of expertise for these types of cancer, along with the establishment of the Barrett’s registry, have had the greatest impact on survival rates in this country, she says. Reynolds was instrumental in both.
The registry, funded by the OCF, is a system for monitoring people who have Barrett’s, a condition arising from severe or chronic acid reflux, which increases their risk of developing oesophageal cancer. A study published last year, analysing the outcomes of more than 9,400 patients on the registry, found only 1.6 per cent needed to have major surgery and nobody died from oesophageal cancer. That 100 per cent survival rate is “incredible”, she stresses, for a disease which, if it progresses, is very high risk. Elliott describes him as a “phenomenal mentor”, whose guiding principle is always, “what’s best for the patient?”
“Everything else flows from that. People get distracted by other things but John doesn’t. He is always focused on quality and quality doesn’t just mean doing an adequate job, it means doing an excellent job.”
That was never verbalised, she says, simply inherent in the way everything was done.
He also always had an eye to how there might be a better way of doing things, she adds, pointing to his support for having four senior scientists involved in the department. They work predominantly on tumour biology. In the lab it is now possible to grow small representative tumours from any given patient, to test how different drug treatments might work best for them. Research and clinical practice go hand in hand for Reynolds, who talks about the need for clinicians to immerse themselves in trying to learn from every small detail, both through experience and study. Also “to know your own data” about patient outcomes.
He spent two “fascinating” years in a tumour immunology lab while doing a master’s at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia from 1986-1988. It was a time when the potential of immunology to treat cancer was becoming front-page news. Another formative US experience was a clinical fellowship at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Centre in New York, where the chairman of surgery, Dr Murray Brennan, was “my greatest influence/role model”. Reynolds’ surgical specialisation dates from presenting himself as a clinical scientist at St James’s University Hospital in Leeds, England, in the early 1990s. “The whole area of cancer, but particularly, for me anyway, oesophageal and gastric, was rich in opportunity for improvement.” It was regarded as one of the “hopeless” cancers at the time. Seeds of this interest had been sown years previously, when he was a surgical senior registrar at St Vincent’s University Hospital, Dublin. He attended thoracic surgery weekly and was captivated by lung and oesophageal operations.
[ Can exercise give cancer survivors a better quality of life and avoid a recurrence? Opens in new window ]
Upper gastrointestinal surgeons are unique, he explains, in that they operate in three different compartments of the body – the neck, the chest cavity and the abdomen – and sometimes all three in the one operation.
“Anatomically, for a surgeon, it’s a beautiful aesthetic,” he purrs, describing the three compartments as “stunningly beautiful”, particularly the chest cavity. “Excuse me for my bias, but that would be one of the things you’d be drawn to.”
He returned to Dublin 30 years ago to take up a surgical post in St James’s. In 2001, he became professor of surgery, heading the department of clinical surgery at the hospital and Trinity College Dublin. On asking how that role breaks down between clinical and academic work, it becomes clear that it is best described as straddling two full-time jobs. But “it’s an absolute pleasure to teach medical students”, he says, and one of the privileges of being in a teaching hospital.
If he were Minister for Health, what would he prioritise? “Definitely more capacity,” he replies without hesitation, “particularly in the teaching hospitals that look after so much extra and are under pressure and stress on a daily basis. “I don’t know how people can do their jobs sometimes, when they come in and there’s no beds available and so many people waiting in A&E to get in. Limerick is the clarion call for that, but there’s elements of that throughout the system.”
There is no doubt about the excellence of oncology care in this country, he says, but he would like to see the infrastructure to support it. There should be some “meaningful, joined up connection” with “excellent private hospitals”.
When cancer patients get priority within a challenging system, it is difficult for non-cancer patients needing surgery. He acknowledges the surgical hubs , already open at Mount Carmel, Swords and Cork, will improve matters, “but we’re still chasing our tails”.
[ Oesophageal cancer: ‘I was fine, there was nothing wrong with me’ Opens in new window ]
He also mentions the plight of 100-plus people a year who experience gut failure and need to go on to total parenteral nutrition (TNP), administered through a central line into the chest. Unlike in the North, there is still no national centre of expertise in the Republic to care for “a group of patients who have no voice”. Without such a unit, it is estimated there are up to 12 avoidable deaths a year here . This is one systemic change he could not usher through, despite encouraging engagement, he says, by former health minister Simon Harris in 2019. Then Covid hit.
What does “semi-retirement” look like for Reynolds after such a full-on career sketched above, not to mention 500-plus published papers and various leadership roles within Irish and European professional associations?
“Like this,” he says, pointing to our immediate surroundings of an anonymous consulting room in the Beacon, where he spends a couple of days a week “seeing patients who want advice about their oesophagus and stomach”.
But it does mean more time for walks with his beloved Fox terrier Kobe, who appears with “scrubs” and stethoscope as his owner’s profile photo on a messaging app. There is also the chance to play “incredibly bad golf” more often.
Meanwhile, he and his wife have the wedding of “baby son” Jack to look forward to next month in the Cayman Islands, where he lives and works as an accountant. Their other two children are here: David is a vet in Ranelagh, Dublin, and Sophie is following in her father’s medical footsteps, not oesophageal surgery but is currently on hospital rotation in emergency medicine.
[ Oesophageal cancer: ‘People definitely rally around when they think you are going to pop your clogs’ Opens in new window ]
After an interview close on two hours, Reynolds is still worried he might have forgotten to mention someone or something important. But the resulting article was always going to be full of omissions, the author’s not his.
“My biggest reflection in reality is feeling beyond blessed in both my personal and professional life,” he adds in a follow-up text message. “Career wise, to have an ambition to be a surgeon investigator and to have ended up at St James’s and Trinity was a perfect match for me.”
A match that has paid huge dividends for patients and fellow professionals too.

title: Gerry Thornley: Munster’s problems cannot be laid at the door of one person
description: Province has the chance to address years of underperformance with a reboot
content:
When Ian Flanagan last week announced his decision to step down as chief executive of Munster at the end of the month, it represented big news. Yet after a season of upheavals and negative headlines, it also wasn’t the least bit surprising. It was time for Flanagan to do the honourable thing.
However, pending the outcome of an independent governance and organisational review by the Governance Company, commissioned by the Munster Branch, there’s an even bigger question than the identity of Flanagan’s replacement.
It’s a particularly significant question as Irish rugby tends not to turn over its CEOs. Munster have only had two since 1999. Flanagan’s predecessor, the late Garrett Fitzgerald, served in the role for almost 20 years from 1999 until his retirement in 2019.
So, after the tumult of last season and pending the outcome of this review, this is a huge opportunity to implement the kind of root-and-branch reboot, so to speak, that is evidently required. If this chance is passed up, you’d wonder how long it would take before the appetite do so again exists.
History will therefore judge this as a defining moment in the sometimes exhilarating, often troubled but rarely dull history of Munster Rugby.
In theory, Munster have the exact same structures as the other three provinces, but in practice, it has always somehow seemed much more divided, with key elements pulling in different directions. The IRFU have slightly remodelled their four provinces along the New Zealand lines, with a general manager (in effect, a chief operations officer) working alongside the CEO. The latter oversees the province as a business, such as bringing in funds, while the GM assumes control for much of the rugby matters, be it the men’s, women’s or underage teams, as well as overseeing their pathways and dealings with the clubs and schools. They are hired and employed directly by the provincial branches. In Munster’s case, this is Ian Costello.
Save for a five-year spell in England with Nottingham and Wasps, he has been with Munster since 2011 when becoming skills and kicking coach, as well as Munster A manager alongside Anthony Foley. He continued as defence, kicking and skills coach for two more seasons and returned in 2021 as Munster’s academy and pathway manager.
In 2023, Costello was appointed Munster’s head of rugby operations and then in 2025, became Munster’s general manager. In between those appointments, he had taken over as interim head coach – above the existing assistant coaches – following the sudden departure of Graham Rowntree in October 2024.
The head coach or director of rugby is equally influential and, like the CEO, is appointed and employed by the IRFU. In Munster’s case, of course, this is Clayton McMillan.
Augmenting, or complicating, all of this are the influential volunteers, primarily the board of directors, which in Munster’s case includes nine members and is chaired by Ger Malone, father of the former Garryowen backrower Peter, and comprised mostly of club nominees. They do have executive decision-making powers, as in commissioning the aforementioned reviews when, frankly, you’d prefer it to have been commissioned by the IRFU.
Each province also has a professional games board and a commercial board, both of which act in advisory capacities. Perhaps the sense of Munster being pulled in different directions is compounded by the oft-discussed Limerick-Cork divide, with the rugby operations based in the former and the Branch offices in the latter.
Yet the Cork-Limerick divide didn’t stop Munster reaching four Heineken Cup finals between 2000 and 2009, winning two of them, or winning the Magners League in 2011 or indeed the URC in 2023.
Munster have also had an influential and important group of private benefactors, who prefer to keep a low profile and maintain their anonymity. Alas for Munster, this column understands they became so disaffected that they have effectively disbanded and no longer supply the kind of funding which helped the province sign RG Snyman, Damian de Allende and others before them.
Compounding this loss of outside income, in the last five seasons Munster have not generated one Champions Cup home knockout tie and only two in the URC. Indeed, in the last five seasons in Europe, Munster have won seven matches out of 22.
The succession planning has been at best ineffective, when you think of them losing Peter O’Mahony, Conor Murray, Keith Earls, Simon Zebo and co. In this, the IRFU took their eye off their problem child, as for 10 years all their focus went into the national team.
But a golden generation needs replacing and ideally from all four provinces. David Humphreys has sought to rectify that by appointing six directors of rugby to schools in Munster, as well as Ulster and the clubs in Connacht. Yet like all such investments, that will take years to bear fruit and ultimately it is up to the provinces themselves to produce their own players.
Charlie O’Shea’s brilliant first start and the performance of other young players in last Saturday’s win over the Bulls was energising and timely. After years of instability among their coaching tickets, this McMillan-Jared Payne-Mossy Lawler-Denis Leamy ticket is high quality and more aligned than last season.
But young players will invariably struggle for consistency. Munster need to dip into their global brand name and generate monies off the pitch with a revised business model, perhaps making more use of the players, to attract the three or four world-class team-mates they will need after the World Cup to become the force of old.
The recent memoirs of Murray and O’Mahony have shone a light on Munster’s poor governance. One sincerely hopes David Duffy of the Governance Company, and the review’s independent chair Dr Martin Kelleher, speak to recently retired players. They will reveal more than anybody.
One of the latter could recount that no-one had spoken to him about a new contract from January onwards before he informed them in April of his decision to retire. Another younger player only learned he had become surplus to requirements when his name was announced at an end-of-season presentation thanking him for his services.
When you stack up everything, namely the decline in performances on the pitch, the declining attendances, the huge dissatisfaction among past and present players, the clubs and volunteers as well as supporters, and the apparent lack of leadership, all Munster’s ills cannot be laid at the door of one person. Flanagan tried his best, was particularly adept in organising fund-raisers and he ought not be made a scapegoat.

title: A crazy idea about pensioners and the cost of living
description: Something seems to be missing
content:
Sir, – In 2025, the minimum wage increased by 5.5 per cent to €13.50 per hour, whereas the State pension rose by 4.3 per cent, adding €12 per week.
This year, the minimum wage has increased by a further 4.8 to €14.15 per hour while the reported proposal for Budget 2027 is a 3.3 per cent increase in the State pension, just €10 extra per week.
I had the crazy idea that the cost of living rises the same for pensioners as for everyone else – am I missing something in my dotage? – Yours, etc,

title: Trial by everyone: Cornell case shows why Ireland’s strict court reporting rules matter
description: The ground will not stop shifting, but the principle that people are tried on the evidence in court, and nowhere else, remains worth fighting for
content:
The Michaelmas law term opened on Monday, with upcoming cases that will almost certainly dominate the news agenda. Louth man Robert O’Connor will stand trial in the Central Criminal Court accused of murdering three members of his family. Riad Bouchaker , convicted in July of the attempted murder of three children at Parnell Square, will be sentenced next week. Daniel Kinahan appeared via video-link before the Special Criminal Court on Monday.
Readers following these cases may notice how the coverage rarely strays from straight reportage. Before anyone is charged, an Irish journalist’s main legal constraint is defamation. Once a charge is laid, the far stricter law of contempt takes over. Reporting is then largely confined to what is said in open court. Previous convictions, background colour, speculation about motive and anything implying guilt or innocence must wait for a verdict. In rape and sexual assault cases, the complainant is entitled to lifelong anonymity, and the accused cannot be named unless convicted.
Media organisations do not always accept the manner in which these limits are applied and challenge them, sometimes successfully. But the penalties for getting it wrong can also be heavy. In 2019, the publisher of the Irish Independent was fined €111,000 after an article published mid-trial caused a rape case to collapse.
Much of the public has little idea these rules exist, and reporters covering big trials grow used to accusations of timidity or cover-ups. Further confusion can be caused by coverage of cases in different jurisdictions. In Northern Ireland , a man charged with rape can be named, which is why former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson was identified long before his conviction this summer. South of the Border, he could not have been.
Farther afield, when Dublin man Lorcan Murphy was convicted in July of murdering US nurse Mackenzie Michalski in Budapest , the Hungarian practice of shielding the identities of accused and convicted people meant he went unnamed for some time in Irish reports.
We are witnessing a vivid demonstration across the Atlantic of what can happen when few of these protections apply.
In October 2024, a Cornell University student went to a party at the Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York. Weeks later, she told campus police she had been sexually assaulted by several fraternity members after being given alcohol and ketamine. The local district attorney declined to prosecute, saying her sworn account described the encounters as consensual. The university disciplined a number of students. Last month the woman, identified only as Jane Doe, sued seven men, the university and others. Lawyers for the men have denied wrongdoing. The DA promptly reopened the case before New York governor Kathy Hochul removed him and appointed state attorney general Letitia James as special prosecutor.
[ Man’s triple-murder trial and Riad Bouchaker’s sentencing among cases coming in new legal term Opens in new window ]
What followed has been trial by everyone. Because the men are named in the lawsuit, their names and photographs are everywhere. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez , a potential candidate at the next presidential election, told an audience the woman had been gang-raped for hours, as though it were fact. Hollywood actors demanded arrests. Donald Trump said whoever James investigated would not be treated fairly. Websites sprang up to name and shame the seven, and the student newspaper opened an editorial by listing them, after which its own editors were doxed in turn. A commentator set out to unmask Jane Doe, prompting social media users to declare en masse that they were her. Leaked statements, texts and transcripts continue to surface daily, each seized on by one camp or the other.
All of this is made worse by the dysfunction of US politics. Legislators have abdicated responsibility, leaving the rules on contested issues to swing wildly with each administration. Into that vacuum have stepped an increasingly politicised judiciary and elected prosecutors for whom high-profile cases double as campaign messages. Hochul is seeking re-election next month. James is one of Trump’s most prominent adversaries. It would be hard to argue that either the accuser or the accused has been well served during this process.
Ireland is largely free of such pressures, although the system has sometimes struggled with the challenges posed by new media technologies. In the early years of digital publishing, judges were faced with the fact that old reports were suddenly a click away. During a 2009 criminal trial, the judge ordered newspapers to remove archived reports from their websites. When one accused asked the High Court to make the DPP scrub the internet of references to him, Judge Peter Charleton refused, holding that clear directions to juries were the proper safeguard. That view has largely prevailed, and jurors are now told, in blunt terms, not to search online. Whether all of them comply is another matter.
[ How Cornell University punished seven men accused of sexual assault Opens in new window ]
The focus has since shifted to individual users and the platforms they post on. Several people received suspended sentences for posting images of the boys convicted of murdering Ana Kriégel , and a woman in Co Down awaits sentence for a post likely to identify one of Donaldson’s victims.
Meanwhile, crime journalism has become one of the fastest-growing corners of digital media, from established players such as CrimeWorld, launched last year to replace the Sunday World’s website, to a crowded field of podcasters and content creators with no lawyer on call. Add in the new challenge of AI tools that can assemble a profile of any defendant in seconds. The ground will not stop shifting, but the principle that people are tried on the evidence in court, and nowhere else, remains worth fighting for.

title: Community Sport Facilities Fund: How it works, how much funding is available, and how to apply
description: The Community Sport Facilities Fund will open to applications from 9am on October 19th
content:
Last Friday, sandwiched in the middle of the most contentious international football window in memory, the Government launched the 2026 Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF).
Given the commotion and acrimony around Ireland ’s fixtures against Israel, the launch of the CSFF might understandably have slipped below your radar over the weekend. And yet, there may not be a more consequential announcement this year for sports clubs and organisations across the county.
Formerly known as the Sports Capital and Equipment Programme – more commonly referred to as the Sports Capital grants – the CSFF scheme provides an opportunity for clubs to apply for centralised funding.
Here’s everything you should know about the CSFF:
In its simplest form, it is the Government’s mechanism for providing grants to clubs and organisations to support the development of sports facilities and the purchase of non-personal sports equipment.
In the past, clubs have successfully applied for funding to help develop pitches, install energy efficient floodlights, build dressingrooms, refurbish sports halls, and erect security fencing and ball-stopping nets.
Your club, most likely. All voluntary, not-for-profit sports clubs, community groups, national governing bodies and local authorities are eligible.
Schools, third level colleges, diocesan trusts, and education and training boards can also apply in conjunction with associated sports clubs.
Traditionally, that might indeed appear to have been the case. Gaelic games grants of almost €97 million were awarded in the last round (2023) – a total of 787 applications coming in at €96,901,302. Soccer grants totalled €41.4 million (371 grants), while golf received €11.4 million (107 grants) and rugby got just under €10 million (76 grants).
Prior to the 2023 round, the previous tranche in 2020 saw Gaelic games receive €65.5 million, while soccer got €25.1 million, golf €8.8 million and rugby €8.7 million.
However, the Government has indicated this new round will specifically target multi-sport projects and sports that might have been overlooked in the past. In other words, there seems to be a real opportunity for some less high-profile sports to receive backing this time around.
There is a new registration management system this year, SPRAOI, through which clubs can apply for grants.
If your club has never previously applied, then the first step is to register on SPRAOI. The portal can be accessed through www.gov.ie/SportsCapital.
If your club was registered on the old system, the details should be automatically transferred to the new system.
If you are unsure of your club’s status, or require guidance on the registration process, further information is available by e-mailing: csff2026queries@ccs.gov.ie.
The system will be open for applications from 9am on October 19th, 2026, and closes at 5pm on February 26th, 2027.
Well, that depends on your club and the nature of the application. There is a tiered system with set parameters on the level of funding available.
No, stick with us. There are three tiers: Local grants, Regional Tier One, and Regional Tier Two.
Local Grants: Funding of up to €250,000 which is open to individual clubs for capital projects, such as renovations to a clubhouse or relaying a pitch. This is the scheme through which most local clubs and organisations will apply. The maximum amount of funding available for equipment is €70,000. For equipment-only applications, ownership of the property is not required. So, for example, boxing clubs or badminton clubs that rent premises can apply.
Regional Tier One: Funding of between €250,000-€550,000. This is intended for larger scale projects with a multi-club or multi-sport character. There is a push towards encouraging more all-weather facilities to provide teams with more certainty around pitch availability throughout the year.
Regional Tier Two: Largest possible grant allocation of between €550,000-€750,000. It is not open to individual clubs, but is instead aimed at encouraging local authorities to be proactive in considering facilities that would benefit their area.
Government ministers have been consistent with their messaging around these grants, stressing the focus is to promote multi-sport collaborations and on synergies between clubs and schools to deliver more shared sporting facilities.
If there was any doubt, Minister of State for Sport Charlie McConalogue outlined as much at the launch: “For the past year, I have travelled across Ireland to visit, listen and engage with sports clubs and organisations for their feedback on how best sports capital grants can work for them. No matter where I went, one message was clear: sports clubs and organisations are under pressure for facilities and resources.
“This new round of CSFF will specifically target sports and geographic areas that have been historically underinvested in. After a winter to forget, we will push to see increased collaboration in multi-sport and multi-club artificial surfaces for training and matches.”
Each application will be judged on its own merit, so if your club has plans or ambitions around improving facilities, or advancing infrastructure projects, then undoubtedly the best advice is simply to get registered and begin the process.

title: Depleted Connacht need to iron out wrinkles against Glasgow, says Woodman
description: Province aiming to build on victory over Benetton, but must do it without several key players
content:
Connacht will again be without a number of key players for their visit to Glasgow Warriors in the URC on Friday.
Dave Heffernan (calf), Will Connors (calf), Ben Murphy (ankle) and Harry West (hamstring) remain unavailable, while David O’Connor (quad) and Byron Ralston (knee) will also be out of action.
But in some good news for the province, Shamus Hurley-Langton has recovered from the rib injury that saw him miss last weekend’s away win over Benetton .
Despite the positive of last Friday’s win after an opening-round defeat to the Stormers in Galway, Connacht scrum coach Trevor Woodman feels there’s room to improve against the Warriors.
“I see players taking more responsibility and that’s impressed me,” he said. “But if I were Glasgow, looking at our last two games, I definitely would say, ‘well, let’s go after them’.
“We’ve looked at the issues against [Benetton] and there’s a couple of things we can put right easily, so it’s up to us to go out there and put it right on the field.”
Woodman expects Glasgow to be looking for a solid response after their draw against Ulster at Scotstoun last Saturday. Juarno Augustus denied the hosts victory in that match with his 73rd-minute try, which was followed by Nathan Doak’s conversion.
“It’s going to be tough,” said Woodman, “but we’ve got plenty of belief in our game and what we’re about to get a win, and there’s no reason why we should shy away from that.
“Obviously, they won’t be happy with their performance at the weekend, so they’re going to be strong up front. Their mauling game is one of the standouts in the URC, their defence, their line speed – but we’ve got to have belief.
“It’s about us staying in control of the ball when we’ve got it, making sure we’re playing in the right areas and not allowing them multiple entries.”
The fixture also comes with added spice, with Connacht head coach Stuart Lancaster’s son Dan playing for the Warriors.
“He keeps them on the front foot, doesn’t he?” Woodman said of the 25-year-old back. “He’s a smart player. But there’s been no talk yet of ‘let’s run over the 10′. We don’t want to be annoying his dad at the moment.”

title: Ireland under-21s face England with Euros playoff spot on the line
description: Jim Crawford’s side must match Slovakia’s result against Andorra in Cork
content:
Jim Crawford says Ireland are prepared for every eventuality as they head into Tuesday’s final-day showdown against England with a European Under-21 Championship playoff on the line.
The Boys in Green hold the all-important second spot in Group D, but only a victory over Lee Carsley’s England, who are already qualified as table-toppers, will guarantee their progression.
Failing that, Ireland would require Slovakia to slip up in Andorra. Both sides are tied on 17 points, but Ireland possess the head-to-head tiebreaker.
This down-to-the-wire scenario at a sold-out Turner’s Cross looked unlikely after Crawford’s side were humbled 4-0 by the Pyrenean microstate, but three consecutive wins have put them in control of their own destiny.
Andorra remain unbeaten at home in this group (two wins, two draws) and were only denied a famous victory over England by a 90th-minute Rico Lewis penalty. Still, Crawford isn’t expecting any favours.
“The unfortunate thing is that Andorra, when they played against us, they dropped down quite a few first-team players. I don’t think that’s going to happen against Slovakia,” he said.
“We’re well aware of that, but it’s in our hands. You can’t ask for any more than coming into the last game against England at home in Turner’s Cross, where the playoffs is in our hands.
“If you said to us after the game away to Andorra or at home to Moldova (1-1) that you could be in this position, we would have said, yeah, all day, give us that opportunity in the final game, a final showdown with England.
“We’re grateful to be in this position, but we’re in this position through hard work.”
Crawford will have a staff member monitoring the other scoreline in case it affects Ireland’s approach.
“It’s important to know what we have to do,” he said. “If we’re forced to change shape or to get more attacking players on the pitch because of what’s going on in the other game, you have to. We’re prepared for that.”
Captain Seán Grehan had a counterintuitive attitude to Slovakia’s scoreless draw with England on Friday, hoping their closest challengers would hold out.
“I said it to a few of the lads when we were watching the game,” recalled the Doncaster Rovers centre-back. “I was glad in a weird way when Slovakia drew because it takes everything out of the equation.
“If you go into a game and you’re thinking, what’s the result there, you lose sight of actually going and trying to win the game. It’s in our hands now.
“We have a total focus on winning the game. I think it’s a better approach.”
That result does create some ambiguity around Carsley’s selection. The game is now a dead rubber for the back-to-back European champions, who are on a 12-game unbeaten run.
Man City star Lewis was drafted into Thomas Tuchel’s senior squad on Sunday. They still feature Premier League experience in Arsenal midfielder Ethan Nwaneri, who is on loan with Borussia Dortmund, Chelsea’s Josh Acheampong and Tottenham’s Archie Gray.
“It might give Lee Carsley an opportunity to dip in a couple of other players,” said Crawford.
“To the untrained eye, people will be saying, that’s great, they’re weakened a little bit, but we wouldn’t think so.
“The size of the squad, the player pools ... Players who haven’t made their 21 squad would get into a lot of other international teams, so they’ve got a wealth of talent.
“You look at the quality that England have, I’ve no doubt they’ll be very close to making it three in the bounce.
“The players that they have on the bench will still represent a huge challenge for us, but we’re not really focused on them.
“A lot of it’s been about us, how we can get better, what we can do to hurt England, and that’s where our concentration levels have been on the build-up to this.
“It’s just on the day, how we’re focused, how we’re organised. It’s a fantastic game for the players to play in, a real barometer of where they’re at.”
Crawford describes his group as “an exceptionally young squad”, hailing their evolution and strong mentality for getting to this juncture.
Their primary focus will be tightening up a defence that leaked three goals in last week’s chaotic victory over Kazakhstan.
When asked where this game ranks among the biggest of his young career, Grehan responds: “It’s definitely the biggest for me anyway. It probably is for most lads.
“With everything that’s on it, with the qualification, and that opportunity to be the first 21s team to qualify, there’s loads at stake.
“That’s the motivator for the lads. Having that on your CV, being part of that first group to do it, is massive.”

title: Clock ticking on Aidan O’Brien’s pursuit of new Group One world record
description: Chelmsford set to resume hosting racing next month after ARC secures multiyear lease on track
content:
Aidan O’Brien has reached 20 Group One successes in 2026, but faces a battle against the clock if he is to threaten his own world record haul of 28 top-flights wins set in 2017.
True Love hit number 20 when supplying her trainer with a first success in Sunday’s Prix de la Forêt on Sunday’s Arc de Triomphe programme at Paris-Longchamp.
Now the Group One spotlight switches to Newmarket this week and the establishment of the two-year-old pecking order with O’Brien’s Ballydoyle team set to come up against a familiar foe.
Charlie Appleby’s Godolphin squad have the unbeaten Musical Times as hot favourite for Friday’s Fillies Mile.
However, the prospect of a mouthwatering clash between Godolphin’s unbeaten Desert Castle and O’Brien’s exciting Darkness Falls in Saturday’s Darley Dewhurst Stakes could dominate the spotlight.
The Irishman needs one more Dewhurst victory to claim an outright record nine wins in Britain’s most prestigious two-year-old race. O’Brien is on eight alongside the great 19th-century trainer John Porter and Frank Butters.
Darkness Falls tops an O’Brien trio in an entry of just seven horses left for the Dewhurst after Monday’s latest acceptance stage. Godolphin also have three with the Champagne winner Desert Castle favourite to give Appleby a fourth win in eight years.
The son of Frankel beat a Ballydoyle runner, Sergei Diaghilev, when landing the Champagne at Doncaster last month by three lengths under Billy Loughnane despite hanging notably to his left in the closing stages. He was quickly made an odds-on favourite for the Dewhurst.
The only interloper into the potential superpower clash is Gentle Hurricane – fourth in the Champagne – for Andrew Balding, a Dewhurst winner last year with the ill-fated Gewan.
O’Brien can also call on both the Coventry winner Great Barrier Reef and the recent Curragh maiden winner Raging Bull.
Darkness Falls, though, earned rave reviews when landing the new Group One Golden Fleece Stakes over nine furlongs at last month’s Irish Champions Festival in Leopardstown.
He is already an 8/1 favourite for next year’s Derby while Desert Castle is a general 4/1 market leader for the 2000 Guineas. City Of Troy in 2023 was the last of O’Brien’s Dewhurst winners.
O’Brien has half of the dozen entries in Friday’s big fillies race and it is the outcome of a series of upcoming Group One juvenile contests that are likely to determine his chances of threatening his own world record.
Doncaster’s Futurity at the end of the month is another opportunity while there are two more Group One contests for juveniles left at Saint-Cloud later in the month. There are also a series of two-year-old races on turf at the Breeders’ Cup .
The $34 million Breeders’ Cup at Keeneland is likely to see True Love try to add to her top-level haul in the Mile while O’Brien hasn’t ruled out going to Kentucky with Sunday’s Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe third Diamond Necklace.
“The funny thing about her is it’s only in the last month that she’s been able to take a normal horse’s work, so there’s every chance she’s been weak all year and is just starting to progress now,” O’Brien said.
“She could go to the Breeders’ Cup Turf and the lads [owners] could keep her in training next year. It depends on what they want to do.”
In other news, racing is set to resume at the Chelmsford track in Essex, southeast England, next month with live pictures at the all-weather circuit switching to Sky Sports Racing from Racing TV.
There has been no racing at Chelmsford since March when the track’s previous licensee went into administration.
Arena Racing Company (ARC) has secured a multiyear lease for the facility and, subject to the British Horseracing Authority (BHA) granting a licence, it plans to begin racing again on November 2nd. Five other fixtures are planned before the end of the year.
“We are delighted to confirm the signing of the lease with the freeholders and that racing will return to Chelmsford City Racecourse,” ARC operations director Kieran Gallagher said.
“We are grateful to the BHA for their ongoing support during the process currently under way of relicensing the racecourse and we look forward to getting everything prepared to welcome horses, owners, trainers and racegoers back in November and starting a new era under the ARC banner.”
Tuesday’s Galway action is over jumps and a handicap chase there looks a good opportunity for Mount Shenshan, who justified some hefty market support over hurdles at Clonmel on Thursday. That was a step up on previous form and she can maintain that momentum in a contest where she gets a lot of weight from the course and distance-winning topweight Hees Dynamite.
Gordon Elliott’s bumper newcomer Ellen Imlach, in the later 5.15pm race, has a Ballybrit pedigree given she is a half-sister to the 2023 Galway Plate hero Ash Tree Meadow.

title: Shane Lowry returns to action in Madrid ahead of busy end of season
description: Lauren Walsh is one of four Irish women at the Aramco Korea Championship in Seoul
content:
Shane Lowry skipped the Alfred Dunhill Links – usually one of his favourite weeks on tour – but returns to tournament action at this week’s Spanish Open in Madrid to kickstart a strong finish to the DP World Tour season.
Lowry, currently 18th in the Race to Dubai standings, which is led by American Patrick Reed ahead of Rory McIlroy, is playing the Spanish Open and next week’s DP World India Championship before finishing up at the two big-money events in Abu Dhabi and Dubai in the UAE next month.
Tom McKibbin , who is 85th in the Race to Dubai standings, is also playing in Spain and is in need of some big finishes if he is to move into the top 50 players who make it to the Tour Championship.
The globetrotting continues this week for Kildare woman Lauren Walsh who has moved on to the Aramco Korea Championship in Seoul on the Ladies European Tour, following a missed cut at Lotte Championship in Hawaii on the LPGA Tour.
Walsh is one of four Irish women competing in the Korean tournament which has a $2 million purse, with Anna Foster, Sara Byrne and Áine Donegan also competing.
Séamus Power, meanwhile, has a week off after failing to get into the field for this week’s Baycurrent Classic in Japan on the PGA Tour. Power’s tied-21st finish in the Bank of Utah Championship – won by Austin Smotherman – moved the Waterford player up three spots to 101st on the FedEx Cup Fall standings in his quest to break into the top 100 who retain full tour cards for next season.
Still soldiering away on the Champions Tour, Darren Clarke will revert back to playing captaincy for the Skechers Cup – which takes place at Feather Sound Country Club in Clearwater, Florida on December 3rd-6th – for what will be his third stint in that role.
Europe defends the title it won last year against the USA and International teams and Clarke has added another Major champion in Henrik Stenson to his line-up for the match.
In a statement announcing the first six players with two more to be added next month to complete the line-up, Clarke said: “Claiming the title last year was incredibly special, and I couldn’t be more excited to bring this European Team back together to defend in 2026. There’s a tremendous amount of pride that comes with representing Europe, and this group understands what it means to compete for one another. We know the US and International Teams will be coming in strong, and we wouldn’t want it any other way.”
Clarke has named himself, Jesper Parnevik, Colin Montgomerie, Bernhard Langer, Miguel Angel Jimenez and Stenson as the first six members of the team for the three-way team event that features players over 50.
“This feels absolutely mental!” – Liam Nolan , after his breakthrough win in the Abu Dhabi Championship on the Hotel Planner Tour. The 26-year-old Galway man’s win propelled him up 31 places to 12th on the order of merit.
The Hotel Planner tour has back-to-back weeks in China – starting with this week’s Hainan Open, where Nolan and Gary Hurley are the only two Irishmen in the field – and concluding with the Grand Final in Mallorca on October 19th-November 1st. The leading 15 players on the standings after the Grand Final will earn full DP World Tour cards for next season.
The centenary edition of the Amgen Irish Open – when Shane Lowry defends his title – will take place at The K Club from July 1st to July 4th next year, with the advance ticket sales portal now open with prices for general admission starting from €40 on tickets.europeantour.com .
Four years into his professional career, Tim Simpson finally made the breakthrough on the PGA Tour when he used some advice from the legendary Arnold Palmer to get over the line to win the Southern Open tournament.
“This is something I’ve waited for, for 22 years. It’s one of the happiest days of my life,” said an emotional Simpson after a closing round 67 for a total of 16-under-par 264 gave him a two strokes winning margin over runner-up Clarence Rose.
Noted as one of the game’s best ball strikers, Simpson had said he was his own worse enemy on the golf course in past attempts to secure a breakthrough win and had sought out the advice of Palmer.
“‘I said, ‘Arnold, what did you think about when you were playing and winning tournaments?’ He said, ‘Tim, I never felt like the lead was big enough. If I had a three-shot lead, I’d try to make it five’.”
Simpson took those words of wisdom on board in finally claiming the first of four PGA Tour wins, saying: “I would have to say it was a very, very solid 72 holes of golf. It seemed like all aspects of my game were at their peak. I putted well, hit my irons incredible and drove well.
10 years. That’s how long I waited for this moment. 🏆 2016: my debut at St Andrews, quietly dreaming of winning here. 2026: champion on my 10 th start. Thank you to my team, my family and everyone who believed. 🤲 Dreams take time. Sometimes exactly 10 years – Adrian Meronk showing how much his win in the Alfred Dunhill Links meant. The win for the Pole, a former Irish Open winner, secured his playing rights on the DP World Tour in returning from his time on LIV.

title: Punishing public servants will not cut class sizes or A&E waits or solve housing crisis
description: Anger over pay awards for those who provide vital services should be redirected towards Government
content:
Sir, – Kevin Doherty’s letter (“ Public sector has consistently failed to deliver but feels entitled to better pay ”, October 3rd) makes a basic but unsupported leap: because public-sector pay is a large part of Government expenditure, he implies that public-sector pay is responsible for failures in our public services.
That does not follow. First, our public services rank highly in comparison to other states while also remaining cognisant that significant improvements are still required.
Second, public sector pay is a cost of employing the people who deliver those services; it is not, in itself, an explanation for inadequate capacity.
No evidence is offered to establish that connection or to show that holding down public servants’ pay would reduce waiting lists, ease emergency department overcrowding, increase housing supply or expand classroom capacity.
Furthermore, it should be noted that public-sector pay deals have historically set pay levels below the rise of inflation with the last pay deal similar – contrary to Government declarations and espoused by Cabinet ministers.
The capacity issues raised by Doherty are fundamentally issues of capacity, planning, staffing, infrastructure and the allocation and use of resources. The public servants working in our hospitals, schools, Garda stations and public offices are the people dealing with these pressures every day. They did not create the demand they are being asked to meet.
If Government expenditure is failing to produce the required improvements, the appropriate question is whether sufficient capacity has been planned and whether resources are being allocated and utilised effectively.
Reducing the pay of the people providing those services would reduce the cost of employment, but it would not create hospital beds, housing units, classrooms or additional staff.
Nor would it address the underlying causes of inadequate capacity. Indeed, retention of staff within already-stretched public services is becoming a significant crisis, particularly in the health service.
The reference to child poverty is particularly striking. It is difficult to argue that child poverty is a national crisis while simultaneously suggesting that restraint should be imposed on the incomes of working public servants.
Many public servants are themselves ordinary working households facing the same pressures of housing, childcare, energy and living costs as everyone else. Reducing their real incomes cannot credibly be presented as a response to poverty; for lower-paid workers, it risks making financial hardship worse.
If tackling child poverty is the objective, the focus should be on policies that increase household incomes and reduce the costs families face, rather than treating public servants’ pay as a convenient source of savings.
There is certainly a legitimate debate to be had about productivity, accountability, grading structures and value for money.
But that debate should be evidence-based and should distinguish between the cost of staffing a service and the capacity of that service to meet demand. Ordinary public servants should not be presented as the cause of problems not of their own making.
If Government has failed to provide sufficient capacity to meet demand, the focus should be on identifying and correcting that failure, not on making public servants pay the price for it. – Yours, etc,

title: A teacher’s take on the ‘selfishness’ behind the teachers’ work-to-rule
description: If the label of ‘selfish’ is to be bandied about, perhaps it should also be directed at successive governments
content:
Sir, – Paul Gethings ( Letters, October 3rd ) points out that “most working people invest in their careers ... and contribute over and above what they are contracted to do”. He further suggests the teachers’ work-to-rule is “a very selfish action for teachers to take”.
My selfishness, it seems, extends far beyond the classroom and the school day.
I correct hundreds of exams every year on weeknights and weekends (my wife calls it selfish). I attend evening debates all over the country (my children call it selfish). I coach school teams and bring them all over the county – and, if we are good enough, my selfishness may extend to all over the province and country.
I go on school tours where my selfishness goes international. While there, it can extend to walking the corridors of a European hotel at 4am, ensuring students are safe.
I mentor students during my “free” classes. I write references for students during those same “free” classes. I attend open nights, award nights, graduation nights and the three nights of the school musical, where I selfishly ask parents for tickets.
I do all of these things, and more, willingly. I will continue to do most of them during the work-to-rule – and all of them when it inevitably ends.
So, if the label of “selfish” is to be bandied about, perhaps it should also be directed at successive governments who, since 2010, have seen fit to impose 33 unpaid Croke Park hours on teachers (and other public servants), while failing to properly recognise or take into account the considerable amount of additional work teachers already undertake.
Teachers are not suddenly becoming selfish. We are simply, for a period, choosing to do the job we are contracted and paid to do. – Yours, etc,

title: Air travel in Ireland is ‘growing faster than expected’
description: Carbon-dioxide emissions from departing flights rose to 1.7m tonnes in first half of year
content:
Air travel grew at a faster pace than expected in the State in the first six months of the year, new figures show.
The news comes as industry regulator the Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) confirms it will allow extra take-off and landing slots at Dublin Airport next summer, paving the way for further growth.
Flights in and out of the Republic increased almost 7 per cent to 157,515 in the first six months of the year, according to an IAA report on Irish air travel’s environmental performance.
European air navigation body Eurocontrol’s latest forecast had predicted an increase of 2.7 per cent for the year as a whole, the authority’s report said.
The latest figures indicated “stronger early-year growth” than the Eurocontrol forecast, it said.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
Overall last year, 316,784 flights carrying 43.5 million passengers arrived at or left the State’s airports, the IAA said.
Carbon dioxide emissions from departing flights grew 7 per cent to 1.7 million tonnes in the first half of this year, the highest since air traffic recovered from wholesale grounding during the Covid pandemic.
Eurocontrol ranked the State’s air traffic control agency, Airnav Ireland , as second best in Europe for efficient management of air space, which played an important part in cutting or limiting emissions, the IAA said.
The IAA report, Operational Environmental Performance of Irish Aviation Entities, showed the Republic’s air travel industry beat European averages across most emissions measurements.
Meanwhile, the IAA said on Monday it would add 28 new take-off and landing slots at Dublin Airport for summer 2027.
Its decision does not take into account the 32 million-a-year limit on passengers imposed by planners on the airport’s two terminals.
The IAA noted that the High Court has barred it from taking this into account pending a ruling from the European courts on a several questions raised by airlines in a legal challenge to the limit.
Those in the air travel industry expect Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien to have increased the so-called passenger cap to 40 million by the time the decision takes effect at the end of March.
A new law gives him the power to increase or axe the cap, subject to certain conditions.
In August the State company DAA asked the Minister to increase the cap to 40 million.
Planning appeals body An Coimisiún Pleanála is now assessing this.
Monday’s decision by the IAA confirms a draft proposal that the authority published last month.
Separately, the European Commission has previously told An Coimisiún Pleanála that a ruling imposing a yearly limit of 35,672 flights at Dublin Airport between 11pm and 7am breached EU law.
The European Commission asked the State to examine the ruling, meant to limit noise at the airport.

title: Better homes for communities, not taller apartment buildings, are the solution
description: Lower-quality flats are wrong way to meet urgent need for affordable properties
content:
Sir, – In response to your correspondent David McWilliams (“ What is really going on in the Irish housing market? The numbers don’t add up ”, Opinion, October 3rd), I agree that we need urgently to build more affordable homes.
However, in his concluding remarks he states that “obviously, the more floors in a building, the cheaper the apartment ultimately built will be” .
Taller buildings attract additional structural and fire safety requirements with significant associated costs as they go up.
Taller apartment building types typically require 20 per cent of their floor area given over to circulation corridors, stairs and lift lobbies.
In simple rounded terms, a €10 million apartment building construction cost (say, 28 apartments) must divide €2 million across the construction cost of each dwelling. They also require greater maintenance and servicing costs associated with shared circulation.
The State’s Land Development Agency is promoting such an assumed cost-driven model of taller apartment development in which 12 apartments per floor share a central corridor and residents’ front doors open directly into their livingrooms, all of which are accessed by a single lift and stair.
Build costs are intended to be further reduced by mandating smaller minimum size apartments and single aspect apartments. Apartments would be permitted that only face north and never receive sunlight or that face only south and overheat.
Balconies are to be the projecting variety that provide no sheltered outdoor private space. Blocks sit in isolating landscapes without enclosure or passive surveillance.
A cost assumption relating to this model that warrants economic appraisal from McWilliams is at what cost to society such a model of housing will impose in the long term?
Who do we envisage living well or thriving in such apartments? Do State officials or politicians envisage themselves and their families living thus?
Is the shorter-term return on capital more important than longer-term formation of neighbourhoods and communities?
There is strong converse professional evidence that low-rise high-density own-door housing of stacked duplex homes and town houses, together with taller terraced housing, enclosing shared neighbourhoods of pedestrian streets and squares, can deliver similar densities of homes without the capital cost or the annual management and maintenance costs of shared internal circulation areas of taller apartment blocks.
Instead of expensive and low-quality internal circulation, the landscape setting of convivial streets and squares offers more positive outdoor spaces of sociable public realm for future neighbours, and one that can integrate into existing street patterns.
The success of various street-based low-rise medium- to high-density design approaches is evident in the work of the UK’s Peter Barber Architects, or at London’s landmark Alexandra Road Housing, Cambridge’s Sterling Prize-winning Accordia Housing, with recent exemplars in Ireland including Sandford Lodge Residences, affordable homes at north Dublin’s Wilkinsons Brook and, indeed, similar recent work recognised by commendations in the RIAI’s silver medal for housing.
Low-rise high-density housing offers developers (be they private speculative or public bodies) a cheaper outlay on less-complex forms of construction and offers purchasers a corresponding more-affordable and preferable purchase opportunity for a place to become home.
It also has the added benefit of increasing housing supply with street-based front doors in more human-scaled neighbourhoods that may foster a greater long-term sense of community and belonging than taller blocks.
The longer-term vision offered by low-rise high-density street-based own-door homes, promoted as part of the solution to the housing crisis , offers an affordable and greater sense of future community for Irish society.
The current trend among State agencies, politicians and developers to favour taller apartment blocks and associated lower-quality homes must be re-evaluated. Assumptions that taller is obviously cheaper must be questioned. – Yours, etc,
Sir. – In his, as usual, instructive article, David McWilliams explains that the cure for high prices is high prices and ends with the hope that long may that last. It is a mild celebration of one of the self-correcting mechanisms inherent in market economics.
While supply and demand determine price, it is also true that, when it suits, there has always been room for intervention.
Our politicians need to be braver and legislate that until the crisis ends it should not be possible for someone who is not going to live in a house to be able to buy (or rent) one.
This would remove those who are buying as an investment and source of income from the demand side of the market and prices would fall. Drastic times call for drastic solutions. – Yours, etc,

title: Eamon Ryan: Should every motorway have a HGV lane? Ideas to tackle fuel crisis
description: On budget day we will see if the Government is capable of taking a long-term view
content:
W e are living in scary times, with many threats confronting us at once. How do you respond when you hear Bill Gates saying we are already at risk from biological or cyber attacks from artificial intelligence (AI)?
What can you do when extreme weather events could kill up to half a million people this winter because of a super charged El Niño? How will the wars in Iran and Ukraine end when Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin seem more desperate by the day?
The cost-of-living crisis caused by those wars is one thing we can quickly do something about. The crisis is real and could unfold dramatically as energy supplies continue to be attacked.
In Ireland, we are particularly exposed because we rely so heavily on imported fossil fuels in power generation, agriculture and transport especially.
Our ability to respond comes from the fact that we have the financial means to help protect us, but also a way forward to address the underlying cause of Ireland’s vulnerability. The question is how should those financial resources be best deployed and do we have the political will to make the switch happen? The budget on Tuesday should give us some answers.
To date, the political debate has been all about how tax cuts might lower fossil-fuel prices. The Government is already subsidising fossil fuels to the tune of €100 million a month and seems certain to do more in the same vein.
