What we need instead is to protect the most vulnerable householders and industries directly, while spending some of that money to lower the cost of the clean energy alternative, so we permanently reduce our expensive and insecure dependency.
Minister for Climate, Environment and Energy Darragh O’Brien was out the gate early last week when he announced a series of new grants to help people scrap their oil and gas boilers , which was very welcome.
The core of the transition has to be a move to the electrification of everything, so we rely on local power rather than some distant fossil fuel supplier. We need not only grants but also to lower the cost of electricity, so every electric appliance and vehicle becomes more attractive.
Ireland’s electricity prices are high because we still depend on burning gas for half the power supply. Nuclear is not the answer, as it would be more expensive and would take decades to deliver. Plug-in solar and batteries can provide a quick win and offshore wind will be a game changer.
We also need to incentivise householders to use power in a flexible way and invest in the electricity grid to better balance variable supply and demand.
We should start with the immediate building of the North-South interconnector, which is ready to go, but has been held up for years by local opposition. That connection would lower electricity bills by €100 million a year and improve Ireland’s energy security and enhance all-island collaboration. It could be followed by more interconnection with the UK, which would further drive prices down.
Tackling fossil-fuel dependency in agriculture is more difficult and has not been helped by the Government cutting the funding to help farmers move to a more productive and sustainable system.
That approach could change on Tuesday with the restoration of the multi-species sward measure , which supports new forms of grassland management. It cuts the use of fossil-fuel fertilisers by 75 per cent, which bolsters farm incomes, restores wildlife and provides greater resilience in both drought and flood conditions.
In transport, we also require a change of political direction. Each major city has plans in place for new bus corridors, but there is no funding to build them out. What we now need is an emergency response, where the Government directs each authority to introduce the bus corridors in the same way that experimental infrastructure was rolled out in the Covid era.
We could go further and introduce special HGV corridors on motorways and on the centre lanes of the M50. It would not be popular with motorists, but would be a much bigger boost for the haulage industry than any temporary cut in excise duties.
We would get an immediate leap in transport capacity, with less diesel being wasted from vehicles stuck in traffic. It would also be a lesson for the transport authorities on how we can build things quicker and cheaper, which has been one of our biggest failings.
It is never easy shaping a budget, but on Tuesday more than ever we need the Government to take a long-term view.
If it just opts for short-term interventions that cut the price of fossil fuels, then we do nothing about our dependency and miss the opportunity of addressing the root cause of the problem. We would only be setting ourselves up for the next oil crisis.

title: Time for US to rethink death penalty after failed execution of Christa Pike
description: Despite the macabre outcome, authorities are instead searching for more efficient ways to kill humans
content:
Sir, – Repeatedly beaten and raped as a child, Christa Pike became a troubled teenager who killed a classmate (“ The tragic life of Christa Pike: Death row inmate whose execution was botched ”, World News, October 2nd).
After a 30-year wait, the state of Tennessee decided the time had come for her to pay the ultimate price for her crime, so last week she was strapped to a gurney and injected with poison. In a macabre twist, two attempts to kill her failed and she was rushed to hospital for life-saving treatment.
Governor Bill Lee, who had declined to use his clemency power to spare Pike’s life, has paused further executions pending the outcome of an investigation into what went wrong.
It is a cause for dismay that rather than seizing the opportunity to (belatedly) abolish capital punishment, the authorities are instead searching for more efficient ways to kill other humans. If Pike regains her health the state of Tennessee may try to put her to death again.
Tennessee’s official slogan is “America at its Best”. It might be time for a rethink. – Yours, etc,

title: ‘He’s still young and learning’: Sam Prendergast’s development coming along nicely at Leinster
description: Leinster kicking coach Emmet Farrell says outhalf has ‘learned a lot over the last couple of years’
content:
The encouraging thing about Sam Prendergast , according to Leinster senior kicking coach Emmet Farrell, is not just his kicking ability, but also his understanding of the game around it.
Farrell, whose remit expanded last year to include the overseeing of regional kicking development across Leinster’s underage teams and clubs, has watched Prendergast develop from a precocious young player into an international outhalf. And he believes the 23-year-old is now putting all the parts of his game together.
In his season debut, Prendergast came off the bench in Leinster’s 26-20 defeat against the Sharks in Durban last weekend to deliver some standout kicks. They included a rocket into the opposition 22 and, at the death, the deft assist for Andrew Osborne’s late try that earned a losing bonus point.
He is poised to start against Cardiff on Saturday as the province return home to the RDS, playing at the redeveloped Laya Arena.
Farrell sees bigger development in Prendergast’s decision-making, knowing when to use the spiral, when to take distance or play shorter, and how to manipulate the two-man backfield.
“He’s a natural striker of the ball,” said Farrell. “Even from a couple of years ago, he’s kicking 50, 60-yard spirals in training and then he brings that to the pitch.”
He even looks to have bulked up a little over the summer. “It’s the hair, it’s fuzzier,” Farrell laughed. “No, he has bulked up a little bit. His first tackle of the season was on [Sharks centre, André] Esterhuizen, and then it was a turnover. He dropped it, so that goes down to Sam’s tackle, and he’ll be the first to point that out, I’m sure, when he gets back.”
Prendergast’s confidence has grown, too, despite the pressures of international rugby and the debate over the Ireland number 10 jersey.
“He’s still young and learning and growing, and we just all have to support him in that,” Farrell added. “He’s learned a lot over the last couple of years. As far as the pressure he’s under, and what he has to do, it hasn’t shook him.
“His attitude hasn’t changed, he hasn’t tried to become more compliant with everything he’s saying, he’s still trying to be himself, which is great, and we have to encourage that. I’m hoping this year he’s going to kick on. Definitely on Saturday [against the Sharks], it was a great start for him.”
Prendergast’s progress is part of a wider trend in Irish rugby, with young outhalves being asked to step up earlier than before. Charlie O’Shea made a superb debut for Munster against Benetton at the weekend, while Caspar Gabriel impressed in back-to-back starts for Leinster in South Africa.
“Casper is very relaxed, he’s got a great attitude,” said Farrell. “He doesn’t get flustered by mistakes. It wasn’t a surprise that he’d be comfortable.
“He was taking the ball to the line against South Africans and running at the line. He goes through for the third try – that’s pretty exciting for a 20-year-old to be doing that.”
“He can do lots of unbelievable things in training,” Farrell added of Gabriel. “There are other bits he’ll have to improve, and as a 10, there’s some discipline in how he runs the game. He’ll learn that the more minutes he plays.”
Farrell’s job is to bring Leinster’s kicking standards down the system, giving young players exposure to senior rugby, ensuring they arrive ready to play. Gabriel is clearly learning those lessons.
“Even just learning over the [South Africa] Tour to back up two professional games is insane,” Farrell said of the young kicker. “It’s a really good experience for him. No one has had that at his age.
“Hopefully now he’ll come back with lots of confidence and lots on how he can get better in his own mind. We’ll put an infrastructure around him and hopefully he kicks on.”

title: Fintan O'Toole: Drumcree is theatre of the absurd, straight from Monty Python’s Ministry of Silly Walks
description: Both sides are guilty of obscene exaggeration and competitive victimhood
content:
E conomists will tell us you can’t have inflation and deflation at the same time. But then they’ve never been to Portadown. The trick of tribal politics is to combine bigging-up with belittlement. Grievance is magnified; grief is diminished.
On one side of the Drumcree /Garvaghy Road standoff, there is a monstrous mismatch between the supposed grand purpose of the Orange parade and its mean little reality.
The march is claimed to be a commemoration not only of the Battle of the Boyne, but of the Battle of the Somme in 1916, in which there were over a million casualties, including about 300,000 deaths. This was a catastrophe shared by Ulster Protestants and Irish Catholics – around 3,500 men from the island of Ireland, serving in the 16th (Irish) and 36th (Ulster) Divisions, died.
How should a European cataclysm of such unimaginable dimensions be commemorated? What form of ritual solemnity could be expressive of a deep enough sorrow? How about walking down a road just to get a rise out of the neighbours?
There is only one thing that joins the Somme and the Drumcree parade – a profound sense of futility. In the theatre of the absurd, the Somme is the tragic epic, Drumcree the am-dram village-hall staging of Monty Python’s Ministry of Silly Walks sketch.
No one has ever tried to stop the Orangemen from marching to and from Drumcree. Their point is that they cannot bear to walk home the way they walked out – the route must, at all costs, be circular. A straight line represents intolerable oppression.
This hyping up is also a terrible dumbing down. It dishonours the memory of the dead. It does so in macrocosm by turning the immense tragedy of the Somme into desultory farce. And then it does so in microcosm by disregarding the 21 people, including the children Richard, Mark and Jason Quinn, who died in the violence surrounding the previous Drumcree conflict of 1996 to 1999.
But let’s not forget that there’s a similarly grotesque inflation on the other side. A banner reads: “From Gaza to Garvaghy Rd, Resist Occupation & Fascism”. Just as the Orangemen use the vast horror of the Somme to make themselves look epic, this comparison of the difficult situation faced by Garvaghy Road residents to the pulverising of three entire cities, the killing of at least 73,000 people and the wounding of 173,000, the killing or wounding of 64,000 children and the obliteration of schools, libraries, mosques and medical centres, is obscene overstatement.
Anyone with a knowledge either of history or of the contemporary world should know what occupation and fascism look like. Northern Ireland is not occupied – its sovereignty is entirely a matter to be decided by a majority of its population in a democratic vote. And 35 oul’ fellas in suits walking silently down a road at 8am is not fascism.
Nor does it need to be in order to be visibly wrong. The Parades Commission’s determination to allow the slimmed-down parade is foolish enough in its combination of recklessness and complacency not to require amplification into a world-historical catastrophe.
This egregious exaggeration is a return to what Liam Kennedy memorably called MOPE syndrome – Most Oppressed People Ever. During the Troubles, car bombs and the slaughter of civilians were justified by the pretence that the situation of Catholics in Northern Ireland was just like that of Black people under apartheid in South Africa or the Jim Crow regime in the southern states of the US .
This wasn’t true then. Anti-Catholic discrimination under the unionist monopoly of power was open, official and obvious. It was bad enough – it didn’t need overblown comparisons.
And it’s even less true now. There is no anti-Catholic discrimination in Northern Ireland now. The Orange state is long gone: the very fact that the First Minister Michelle O’Neill is out protesting on the side of the Garvaghy Road residents tells us so. But if you can’t credibly evoke apartheid or Jim Crow, reach for Gaza .
Why all this hype? Because the political soup of the day is competitive victimhood. Slights cannot be slight. Frustrations cannot be mere irritants. Disappointments cannot be just let-downs. Every insult must be existential, every provocation unendurable.
In this sense, the 2026 Drumcree/Garvaghy Road drama is not only a return to the nightmare of the 1990s. It’s also a very 21st century production. We live in a culture in which, for example, Liam Gallagher can compare the plight of his cheating club Manchester City to “Jesus prepared to die on the cross”. A sense of proportion doesn’t play well on X.
We used to pray that Northern Ireland would become more like the rest of the world – what’s happened, of course, is that the rest of the world has become more like Northern Ireland. Polarisation is the engine of politics across the democratic world – and it requires minor flashpoints to be stoked up into major conflagrations.
Everybody must be a victim. In reality, the Orange Order is a declining institution. Its membership halved between 1948 and 2009 and has continued to drop since. Its influence, once pervasive, is minimal. Its only hope is to be the vector, not of Protestant supremacy but of Protestant victimhood – not being allowed to walk in a circle is woeful oppression.
But to respond to toxic hyperbole with counter-hyperbole is not just unwise but profoundly disrespectful of real suffering. When you map Gaza on to Garvaghy, you inflate the latter but simultaneously deflate the former. In this false equivalence, the scale of the horror that is still being inflicted on Palestinians is brought down to the level of a nasty local row.
There is no need to summon the vast throngs of the dead from the Somme or Gaza. Portadown is haunted by far too many dead already. They died for the grotesque equation in which a human life is a point to be scored. Respect for their memories should be expressed in the only slogan that tells the truth: It is not worth it.

title: Opinion: The one thing Israel hasn’t managed to take from us in three years is hope
description: Thousands of women whose husbands have been killed, detained or have gone missing now carry the sole responsibility of protecting and providing for their families
content:
I t is three years since the start of the genocide in Gaza . Three years of sustained and brutal onslaught by the Israeli army , which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, injured more than 175,000, razed much of Gaza to the ground and left almost the entire population displaced.
The so-called ceasefire agreed a year ago is not a real ceasefire. The Israeli occupation force continues its attacks and has killed more than 1,400 people since it came into effect.
Meanwhile the humanitarian situation is catastrophic. Only 25 per cent of what is needed is getting into Gaza. Almost everyone is struggling to access enough food and water. The health system is dire. Living conditions are extremely crowded and dangerous.
Winter is approaching and will make conditions even harder. Much of the population is living in tents or makeshift shelters, which will do little to protect from heavy rains, strong winds and low temperatures. Communicable diseases are expected to rise, increasing pressure on the already hugely overstretched health system.
Women and girls have been hardest hit in this genocide. Access to essential services such as maternity healthcare and safe spaces has been severely disrupted. Thousands of women whose husbands have been killed, detained or have gone missing now carry the sole responsibility of protecting and providing for their families.
I was the director of Al-Awda hospital in Jabalia in northern Gaza during most of the genocide. Before then, I lived with family, including my wife, five children, sister and elderly mother in the northern Gaza Strip, and life was nice. At that time, I was MEAL (monitoring, evaluation, accountability and learning) manager with the Al-Awda Health and Community Association, one of the largest healthcare providers in Gaza. My wife worked in the Ministry of Health. We had a house. Our children went to school. We were eating good food every day.
That all changed after October 7th, 2023. Within 10 days, the occupation forces bombed my house. My family moved to live with my sister on the northern Gaza Strip. But her house and then all my relatives’ houses were destroyed. In the search for safety, my family moved south to Rafah, and I decided to stay with my colleagues in the hospital.
I did not see my family for 15 months. They and other family members were displaced 16 times during this period.
After the start of the war six of the Al-Awda Health and Community Association managers moved to Al-Awda hospital in the north, including me.
Those 15 months were horrendous as the staff of Al-Awda hospital found themselves under regular and sustained attack by the Israelis. Thirty-four people were killed in the immediate area of the hospital during that period, including three of my colleagues – who were killed inside Al-Awda on November 21st, 2023, by a shell – and one patient carer. Three more were killed in December by a sniper when the hospital was under siege: one nurse and two cleaners.
On December 18th, 2023, 12 people were arrested from the hospital including our director . Much of the hospital was destroyed. I took on the role of director at that point.
During severe shelling and bombing in May 2024 we were ordered to evacuate. But I, along with 13 other staff members, refused to move. There were no ambulances to evacuate the injured patients, so we stayed to care for them.
The worst period was the 106 days from October 5th, 2024, to the ceasefire on January 19th, 2025, when the Israelis did not allow supplies into the hospital including fuel, medication and medical supplies.
We had only one general surgeon in the hospital for those 106 days, and he was the only surgeon available to do all surgeries in the north. We lost many patients due to the lack of specialist doctors, medication and medical supplies. There was no vascular surgeon, no orthopaedic surgeon. Because of this we had to amputate limbs, some from children, as a last resort.
The lack of fuel meant we had to stop many of our life-saving interventions. We were working in a horrible situation but were putting all our efforts into helping our people.
A shortage of oxygen was a big issue. We had one patient to whom we gave manual oxygen for three days using an ambu bag to provide ventilation. As a team, we did this in half-hour shifts, but still we did not succeed in saving the patient.
Yet we showed that our humanity was stronger than all the armies.
On May 29th, 2025, we were finally forced to evacuate the hospital. The army attacked the upper floors and this went on from 1pm to 8pm.
Since August 2026, I am the director of PNGO, the Palestine Non-Government Organisations network, supporting humanitarian relief and advocating for international action. What is needed now is a real and permanent ceasefire, one that truly protects Palestinians.
Border crossings must be fully reopened and the continuous free flow of aid, including fuel, medical supplies and heavy machinery, into Gaza must be allowed without impediment. There must be full accountability and justice for all atrocities that have been committed, with alleged breaches of international humanitarian law, war crimes and crimes against humanity fully investigated and prosecuted.
Third states must uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law, including taking measures to prevent genocide as per the Genocide Convention. All forms of support that aids or assists Israel’s unlawful occupation, as per the advisory opinion issued by the International Court of Justice , must be prevented.
There must be accountability for what has happened. Robust sanctions, including travel bans and asset freezes, must be imposed on senior Israeli government officials linked to violations of international humanitarian law.
And all arms sales and transfers to the Israeli government where there is a clear risk they could be used to commit or facilitate violations of international humanitarian law must be ended.
I am one of the lucky ones. I have survived the last three years. And so has my family.
We have very little. But the one thing the Israelis can’t take away from us is hope. That is what keeps us going. We look forward to the day when we can all live in peace.
Dr Mohammed Salha is director of PNGO, the Palestinian NGOs network, which is a partner of ActionAid

title: Ireland on right side of global debt crisis
description: Advanced economies are flirting with full-blown crises because of excessive debt but not Ireland
content:
Irish Government debt as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP), the metric that creditors look at, fell to under 35 per cent last year, down from 38.4 per cent the previous year.
At the worst point of the financial crisis, it was over 120 per cent. It’s not that the State’s gross debt (€210 billion in 2025) has shrunk that much; it’s just that the economy here has grown dramatically in the interim, meaning the State’s debt-carrying capacity, again the metric that creditors focus on, has strengthened.
Even when you discard GDP because of the multinational factor, our debt-to-GNI (the bespoke measure of national income here) came in at 62 per cent at the end of 2025.
What makes these figures most interesting is just how out of kilter they are with peer group countries.
In the United Kingdom (at the end of 2025), the country’s debt-to-GDP stood at 101 per cent. In France, it was 115 per cent. In the US, 121 per cent.
The speed at which US debt has grown is mind-numbing. It first reached $1 trillion in 1941. It hit $20 trillion in 2017, then doubled to $40 trillion in the intervening nine years.
Advanced economies are flirting with full-blown crises because of excessive debt. A recent report by the Institute for International Finance indicated that “mature market governments now spend more on interest expense than the world invests in either AI [artificial intelligence], defence, or energy”.
[ Budget 2027: All you need to know Opens in new window ]
The Republic, however, sits outside the danger zone with debt metrics that the UK and France would bite their arms off for.
Even the European Union fiscal rules are redundant from the State’s perspective. Forcing member states to keep their debt ratio at 60 per cent of GDP is too loose for the Republic.
Judged against GDP, the State is a bit fitter than it actually is, hence the call by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council and others for the Government to adopt its own spending rule.
The new medium-term expenditure framework, adopted by the Government last year, seeks to put a 6 per cent cap on annual spending increases out to 2030.
Budget 2027 allows for a 5.9 per cent increase in spending, but as we’ve seen in the past, the Government has rarely kept to its budget spending plans.

title: Call for sporting sanctions is due to profound concerns over Israel’s actions in Gaza
description: Many who support engagement with Israelis also believe sports bodies should apply rules consistently
content:
Sir, – Chief Rabbi Yoni Wieder’s appeal for dialogue between Irish people and Israelis is both reasonable and welcome (“ All the good that might have come from Ireland v Israel has been lost ”, Opinion, October 3rd). Yet his article largely sidesteps the question at the heart of the controversy.
The calls for sporting sanctions did not arise because Irish people are unwilling to meet Israelis, listen to Israelis or recognise their humanity. They arose because of profound concerns about the actions of the Israeli state and the devastating human consequences of the war in Gaza .
By framing the debate primarily as a lost opportunity for conversation, the article focuses on the reaction while largely overlooking the cause.
Dialogue is important, but it cannot substitute for accountability nor can it be detached from the circumstances that prompt demands for action.
Many people who support engagement with Israelis also believe that international sporting bodies should apply their rules consistently. That is the issue under debate, not whether ordinary people should talk to one another.
Human contact builds understanding. It does not remove the obligation to confront difficult realities.
By reframing a question of state accountability as a question of interpersonal understanding, the article sidesteps the very issue that gave rise to the controversy. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Chief Rabbi Yoni Wieder wrote a considered and temperate article, which you published on Saturday.
It was a welcome and reasoned comment on the dilemma that faced Irish soccer followers and the correctness or otherwise of the Football Association of Ireland’s and the team’s handling of a very difficult situation.
It did not address the root cause of the unease, and often the condemnation, that an apparent majority of the Irish people feel about the retribution wreaked on Gaza after the slaughter wrought by Hamas on October 7th, 2023.
In that attack by Hamas, according to Wikipedia, at least 1,195 people were killed. These included at least 828 civilians of whom 36 were children, 71 foreign nationals and at least 367 members of the Israeli security forces.
The retribution that followed under Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu’s plans led in Gaza to 73,922 deaths, of which 21,638 were children.
As a teacher online of English, before Covid for the Hands Up Project, I got to know a woman in Gaza and her family of six.
Whenever I could, I was in contact with my friend as she was “hunted” by the Israeli government, from her bombed out apartment, through six tented accommodations across hundreds of kilometres.
I was in touch with her when her sister’s family was wiped out when they were bombed into the rubble and heard her tearful account of how the IDF soldiers “shooted” at the civilians frantically digging to try to reach any survivors.
Would that Chief Rabbi Wieder stand up and condemn the Israeli government’s handling of the Palestinian issue.
A really brave statesman-like rabbi is needed to lead Israelis out of the wilderness where their government has failed.
If I have missed any such expressions of opinion from Chief Rabbi Wieder, I apologise. – Yours, etc,

title: From minimum wage to affordable childcare: Tackling child poverty demands policies geared to ‘keep parents at work’
description: States must also provide adequate income support and accessible, high-quality services, says OECD report
content:
Governments intent on tackling child poverty must implement policies that support parents to work rather than simply relying on cash transfers, according to a significant international report published on Monday.
The document, published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), examined not just how much states spend on children but also how they spend it.
The largest gains from any additional investment in addressing child poverty will be from spending on “policies” that deliver for children, the report said.
[ The Irish Times view on child poverty: more needs to be done Opens in new window ]
Reducing child poverty is a key Government commitment. It will deliver its budget outlining spending and tax measures for next year on Tuesday.
A recent Economic and Social Research Institute report found the number of children in households below the poverty line – defined as having less than 60 per cent of median household income – rose to 200,000 (17.4 per cent) in 2024, up almost 30,000 children.
No single policy tackles child poverty, the report said. “The strongest results come from a coherent mix of three things: helping parents into work; adequate income support; and accessible, high-quality services.”
Poverty “affects multiple dimensions of wellbeing – health, cognitive, development, and socio-emotional – with long-lasting consequences”, it added.
It described child poverty as a drain on the economy through lower productivity, reduced tax revenues, and higher public spending over the life of anyone who has grown up in poverty.
“Reducing child poverty could generate sizeable economic gains through higher employment, earnings and tax revenues,” it added.
The report said social spending – on areas like health and wellbeing – in OECD countries has risen substantially, increasing from about 20 per cent to 25 per cent of gross domestic product and by nearly two-thirds in per capita terms since 2006.
This growth has been driven mainly by population ageing and rising healthcare costs, with expenditure on families with children remaining “comparatively modest”.
It said the areas with the greatest returns in tackling child poverty include supporting parents to reconcile work and care commitments.
These include paid parental leave, flexible working, and access to affordable early childhood education and care, as well as supporting parents to access work through training and job-search assistance.
Other key areas include income stability and good working conditions.
It said lower-income households need a good minimum wage and the option of income supports. It also called for quality, affordable, public services – including in health and housing – to address child poverty.

title: Mark Duffy’s last-minute tilt at PTSB muddies waters for budget ministers
description: Prospective buyer declined to say whether Axis Capital has investment banking advisers or financial backing
content:
Boom-era banker Mark Duffy, who oversaw Bank of Scotland (Ireland)’s introduction of tracker and interest-only mortgages as mainstream products in the Republic pre-2008 crash, knows how to stir things up.
A move by his fledgling corporate advisory firm, Axis Capital , on Friday evening to say it’s weighing making a tilt at PTSB comes weeks before the High Court is due to sanction the bank’s takeover by Austria’s Bawag . And 11 months after PTSB was formally put up for sale.
The promise by Axis, which Duffy cofounded three years ago with German corporate lawyer Lutz Hartmann, that any possible offer would be in cash at €3.20 per share – 7.7 per cent above Bawag’s €2.97-a-share offer – would result in Minister for Finance Simon Harris receiving just over €1 billion for the State’s 57.5 per cent PTSB stake.
It’s small change by the standards of the €125.5 billion expenditure ceiling on Budget 2027. But it is hardly nothing – particularly when Harris and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers face some difficult last-minute budget choices that will inevitably trigger criticism from Opposition, lobby groups and families believing they could have done more.
Duffy stepped down as Bank of Scotland (Ireland) chief executive in early 2009, months after its parent HBOS was taken over by Lloyds Banking Group in a shotgun merger in the UK. Lloyds recorded €14.8 billion in losses on the Irish loan book after the 2008 crash, including impairment charges and shortfalls on loan disposals.
Duffy helped initiate talks in 2025 between US equity firm Centerbridge, the Department of Finance and PTSB. Centerbridge later submitted a non-binding proposal for the State’s stake but was the underbidder when the formal sale process concluded in April.
Axis says its plan to turn PTSB into a “real third force” is based on “growth without gambling”, relying on “prudent capital, a transparent scorecard and no dependence on aggressive synergies”.
[ PTSB 'focused' on Bawag bid after ‘highly speculative’ Axis announcement Opens in new window ]
The problem is that the firm is only now engaging with potential financial backers. How could it even have put a price out there without financing in place?
More curious still is the absence of named financial advisers from Friday’s announcement. Duffy declined to say whether Axis has investment banking advisers or even indicative financial backing.
Even if Axis makes no further announcement in the coming weeks, observers say it’s likely some minority investors who are against the Bawag deal will ask the High Court to at least adjourn the sanctioning meeting on October 27 th to see whether Duffy can come up with the goods. There may be a few more twists yet.

title: Reader couldn’t believe it when she was charged €13 for ‘free’ Vanity Fair tote
description: EU fees and knock-on charges have quickly made online shopping much more expensive
content:
We have been writing a lot about new charges imposed on shoppers who have the temerity to buy on websites based outside the EU and one of our more recent stories has prompted a reader called Aideen to get in touch.
Revenue confirmed last week that online shoppers who buy from outside the EU will have to pay a fresh charge of €2 per item from November 1st .
The new Union Handling Fee is on top of a €3 charge per item that was imposed in the summer.
The charges and fees are being imposed by the EU, but delivery companies will have a legal responsibility to collect them if the levies have not been paid during checkout on the online store.
The charge is intended to cover the increased costs incurred by customs authorities as a result of the huge growth of ecommerce over the last number of years. It will apply to all goods, regardless of their value, once a seller ships them to Ireland from outside the EU.
And of course, the delivery companies will also charge fees of their own to collect the money. An Post , for example, has an administrative charge of €6.95.
The net effect of this can be pretty savage. A person who buys three distinct items on a website based outside the EU for a total cost of a tenner will end up having to pay €31.95 when all the charges are added to the mix.
It is in this context Aideen contacted us. She was less than pleased when faced with charges for a product she didn’t even buy.
“I’m sure you can imagine my chagrin upon receiving a customs duty notification from An Post just last week, in an envelope marked with bold, red and capital letters alerting to me the urgency of opening it,” she writes.
“What did I buy that originated outside of the EU? Might I have ordered Korean skincare direct from Korea? Hardly. I make a point of not shopping with Temu or Shein so it couldn’t be anything of that nature. Was I getting a present from an American relative for absolutely no reason?”
When Aideen logged into her An Post account “to try and shed some light on the situation (I would never scan a QR code as I always heed your warning about scammers), it was a thank you present from Vanity Fair in the US”. She adds: “Via Amsterdam, they were sending me a free tote for taking out a digital subscription.”
Aideen then remembered she had wanted to read one particular article in the US magazine. ”I had already cancelled my 30-day free trial by the time the customs notification was put through my door,” she confirms.
She looked closely at the notification and “was left bemused at the breakdown of charges”.
On top of the €3 charge imposed earlier this year, there was, she says: “No excise duty but a value added tax of €2.83 (again this was an unsolicited FREE tote bag), and a mysterious €6.95 handling charge from An Post.”
It brought the total to €12.78. Aideen acknowledges this would have been €14.78 if the parcel arrived after November 1st.
She marvels at the fact that she would have been faced with charges of close to €15 for a free tote, “and at a price the publishing company surely wouldn’t have paid its own wholesalers for”.
Aideen says: “Out of curiosity, I wondered where such a canvas receptacle might have been manufactured. Likely China or India ‘depending on the specific promotional batch or production run’, the internet tells me.”
She declined the charges and says the tote bag is on its way back to the sender.

title: Slánú na drámaíochta liteartha: an leochaileacht ag cothú an dóchais
description: Ó Pheann go Pár: Is ar na saothair ardáin atá Liam Mac Amhlaigh ag díriú ina alt is déanaí faoi litríocht na Gaeilge
content:
Le tamall de sheachtainí anuas, tá seasamh sheánraí liteartha na Gaeilge á chíoradh againn sa tsraith seo agus tá tagairt déanta don fhilíocht, don ghearrscéalaíocht agus don úrscéalaíocht.
Inniu tagaimid chomh fada le seánra leochaileach, ach spreagúil ar mhórán bealaí: drámaíocht na Gaeilge.
Tá stair shaibhir agus traidisiún amharclainne náisiúnta láidir in Éirinn go ginearálta agus i dtaobh na Gaeilge chomh maith. Tá cur chun cinn an tseánra suntasach freisin: in ainneoin lucht féachana atá beag, deiseanna gairmiúla atá teoranta, ionaid thiomnaithe atá caillte agus Béarla a bheith i gceannas i saol cultúrtha na hÉireann, lean drámadóirí agus comhlachtaí amharclainne orthu ag léiriú drámaí bunaidh, aistriúcháin, saothair nuachóirithe agus léirithe turgnamhacha.
Ag dul siar, bhí clocha míle ar nós An Triail (1964) le Máiréad Ní Ghráda, Lá Fhéile Míchíl (1963) agus Fornocht do Chonac (1979) le hEoghan Ó Tuairisc, agus saothar le Seán Ó Tuama agus le Críostóir Ó Floinn, léirithe ag amharclanna na Gaeilge.
Ní féidir le traidisiún amharclainne náisiúnta bláthú go héasca nuair a bhíonn an oiread sin ag brath ar aon ionad amháin.
Léirigh An Triail go háirithe go bhféadfadh an Ghaeilge teicnící amharclainne nua-aimseartha cumasacha a chur san áireamh agus ceisteanna sóisialta comhaimseartha deacra a phlé ag an am céanna. Tá buntáistí curaclaim scoile, aitheantas cultúrtha agus lucht féachana seanbhunaithe ag saothair ar nós An Triail, ach is féidir le spleáchas ar chanóin sách beag srian a chur le deiseanna do dhrámadóirí nua mar sin féin.
D’fhág dúnadh amharclann An Damer i mBaile Átha Cliath sa bhliain 1981, mar aon leis an laghdú a tháinig ar chomhlachtaí drámaíochta éagsúla, d’fhág sin amharclannaíocht na Gaeilge gan an líonra buan, nó leathbhuan, d’institiúidí léiriúcháin atá ar fáil don drámaíocht i mBéarla.
Mura mbeadh sé sin ar fáil, ba dheacair an bhunscríbhneoireacht liteartha féin a fheiscint ag dul in inmhe. Mar a mhaígh Brian Ó Conchubhair, tá saolré an-éiginnte tar éis a bheith ag earnáil amharclannaíocht na Gaeilge dá bharr, agus a todhchaí ag brath go mór ar chomhlachtaí beaga áitiúla. Go fiú ó aimsir na paindéime i leith tá tost ar chompántas clúiteach, Aisteoirí Bulfin, san ardchathair, go háirithe ó cailleadh Aodh Ó Domhnaill i mí na Feabhra 2018 - duine a bhí lárnach san aisteoireacht agus scríbhneoireacht scripte araon.
Bíodh go n-aithníonn an tionscadal ‘Playography na Gaeilge’ 796 dhráma Gaeilge ón mbliain 1901 chomh fada le 2010, bíonn laigí, nó go deimhin tanaíocht, le sonrú freisin. Is í an toirt an ceann is soiléire. Idir 1975 agus 2009, léiríodh 146 dhráma bunaidh Gaeilge i gcomparáid le 110 aistriúchán nó nuachóiriú; tá an méid sin le cur i gcomparáid le 1,282 dhráma bunaidh Béarla sa tréimhse chéanna.
Is í An Taibhdhearc - amharclann náisiúnta na Gaeilge i nGaillimh, a bunaíodh sa bhliain 1928 chun an amharclannaíocht Ghaeilge a fhorbairt agus saothar nua a choimisiúnú - an léiriú is soiléire ar a bhfuil á chur ar stáitse. Arís idir 1975 agus 2009, bhí 115 dhráma nua sa Taibhdhearc, beagnach 79% de na drámaí nua Gaeilge a taifeadadh sa tréimhse. Ach léiríonn lárnacht na Taibhdheirce ceann de laigí bunúsacha an tseánra.
Ní féidir le traidisiún amharclainne náisiúnta bláthú go héasca nuair a bhíonn an oiread sin ag brath ar aon ionad amháin.
Ach is í an ghné is bisiúla den seánra le tamall ná an éagsúlacht drámadóirí agus guthanna amharclainne. Ar an suíomh portraidi.ie, tá seacht ndrámadóir is tríocha luaite. Ina measc, tá Antoine Ó Flatharta tar éis léiriú neamhghnách ilchultúrtha ar shaol comhaimseartha na nGaeltachta a chur ar fáil; scrúdaigh Mícheál Ó Conghaile agus Joe Steve Ó Neachtain na contrárthachtaí a bhain le pobail tuaithe a bhíonn ag síorathrú; thug Éilís Ní Dhuibhne béaloideas, inscne agus castacht shíceolaíoch chun tosaigh; agus léirigh drámadóirí ar aon dul le Alan Titley, Biddy Jenkinson, Darach Ó Scolaí agus Celia de Fréine féidearthachtaí an ghrinn, na háiféise, na drámaíochta polaitiúla agus na scríbhneoireachta eachtrúla.
Níos cóngaraí do scríbhneoireacht an lae inniu, léiríonn saothar le HK Ní Shioradáin (Beards), Eoin McEvoy (ón chomharghrúpa AerachAiteachGaelach), agus Em Ó Ceallaigh go bhfuil sruth nua drámadóirí ag teacht chun cinn freisin: ealaíontóirí óga uirbeacha a aithníonn iad féin mar dhaoine aiteacha agus a úsáideann an léiriúchán lena bhféiniúlacht uile a chur in iúl trí mheán na Gaeilge mar uirlis amháin i measc go leor eile (an ceol, an fhilíocht labhartha, an greann).
Ní bhreathnaíonn siad ar ról an ‘drámadóra’ mar fhéiniúlacht ar leith a shainíonn gairm bheatha. Is athrú suntasach é sin ón bpróifíl a bhain le glúin reatha dhrámadóirí na bPortráidí, a bhí dírithe ar ghné amháin agus a raibh fréamhacha láidre Gaeltachta ag formhór a cuid ball.
Tá dea-chomharthaí glúine úire mar seo le sonrú in áiteanna eile chomh maith. Tá an amharclannaíocht á hathchruthú – léirithe le Aisling Ghéar agus Fíbín san áireamh, dhá chompántas a bunaíodh sa bhliain 1997 i mBéal Feirste agus sa bhliain 2003 i gConamara faoi seach. Tá forbairt ar fhoirmeacha amhairc agus fisiciúla in amharclannaíocht na Gaeilge, ina measc puipéadóireacht, maisc, ceol, gluaiseacht agus turgnamhachas.
Taispeánann léirithe Aisling Ghéar arís agus arís eile ar An Triail, mar shampla, conas is féidir téacs liteartha seanbhunaithe a athcheapadh go radacach do lucht féachana níos óige. Anuas air sin, tá infheistíocht ann le tacú leis an bpróiseas forbartha maidir le saothair nua ghairmiúla a chur ar stáitse. Tá an Roinn Gaeltachta tar éis ciste suntasach €4.085m a chur ar fáil d’Oireachtas na Gaeilge suas go 2027 le Plean Náisiúnta do na healaíona teangabhunaithe a chur i bhfeidhm. Figiúr ar leithligh is ea seo ón maoiniú €5.78m a tugadh do An Taibhdhearc féin sa tréimhse chéanna. Leis sin, sheol an amharclann ‘Taibhsín’, clár forbartha a thacaíonn le healaíontóirí atá ag obair go gairmiúil trí mheán na Gaeilge agus a thugann ardán do scríbhneoirí amhail Ciara Ní É, Louisa Ní Éideáin agus Seán Mac Dhonnagáin.
Samhlaím freisin, ó tharla gur uirlis an-chumhachtach is ea an drámaíocht i bhfoirm saothar foilsithe don aos léinn/teagascóirí ag gach leibhéal, go dtuilleann an seánra aitheantas faoi leith sa chóras oideachais. Bíodh agus go mbeadh argóint i gcónaí ann go mba cheart dráma nua a scríobh ar mhaithe le breathnú air ar stáitse, seachas a bheith á scríobh ar mhaithe le go léifí é, tugann an drámaíocht scríofa fhoilsithe deis an-láidir an teanga a shealbhú, treoracha breise a aithint i script agus agus stíl na cumarsáide ó bhéal a thuiscint ar shlí níos nádúrtha agus níos téagartha ná seánra ar bith eile dar liom.
Dá bhrí sin, ní leor breathnú ar an dúshlán atá roimh an gcéad ghlúin eile drámaíocht na Gaeilge a neartú; ina ionad sin, is gá í a normalú. Bíodh sé mar sprioc againn drámaíocht liteartha nua na Gaeilge a dhéanamh ina gnáthchuid de chultúr amharclainne na hÉireann seachas gníomhaíocht speisialaithe nó eisceachtúil. Más féidir infheistíocht institiúideach na mblianta beaga anuas a thiontú ina coimisiúnú leanúnach, camchuairt, foilsiú, léirmheastóireacht, aistriúchán agus forbairt lucht féachana, beidh na hacmhainní cuí ealaíon ag an seánra liteartha. Tugann an méid seo le fios nárbh ionann deacrachtaí agus easpa beatha i gcás dhrámaíocht na Gaeilge riamh; is é atá le déanamh ná struchtúir a aimsiú atá in ann ligean don bheatha sin bláthú.
ealaíontóirí óga uirbeacha = young urban artists

title: Irish taxi and food delivery drivers face headache as French insurer suspended
description: Paris-based firm Wakam directed to cease writing business amid concerns over capital reserves
content:
Competition to provide insurance cover here for taxi and delivery drivers has suffered a blow after French authorities ordered Paris-based insurer Wakam to suspend writing new business amid concerns over its capital reserves.
Broker NFP Ireland , a unit of Aon, had lined up Wakam as the underwriter of its scheme for taxi and food delivery drivers – known as RideSure – in February, after another player, UK-based insurer Zego, last year stopped taking on new business in the Irish market .
Wakam said in a statement posted on its website last week that the French Prudential Supervision and Resolution Authority had imposed a temporary ban on the company underwriting new contracts and renewing existing ones – as the regulator opened adversarial proceedings that could lead to the withdrawal of its authorisations.
Wakam said it was preparing a response and was continuing to implement a remediation plan, “which notably provides for strengthening its capital base”.
The temporary ban does not affect the management of contracts in force. Wakam continues to process and settle claims and to fulfil its commitments to policyholders and partners, the insurer said.
A spokesperson for NFP Ireland said: “We understand the uncertainty this creates for drivers whose renewal is coming up in the coming weeks. With new policies and renewals affected by the regulatory suspension involving Wakam, the underwriter, we are seeking clarity from Wakam on when normal service can resume. NFP’s priority is to keep its customers informed.”
A statement on NFP’s website added that policies that have already been offered renewal can be renewed, but the company cannot issue new quotations.
[ Budget 2027: All you need to know Opens in new window ]
While there are quite a few alternative insurance providers to the taxi sector – including Axa, FBD and RedClick – coverage is more difficult to find for food delivery drivers, according to market sources.
It is not clear what share of the taxi and food delivery markets Wakam has.
Promoting competition and market access is a key aim of the Government’s latest version of the Action Plan for Insurance Reform.
Wakam provides the insurance capacity to various distribution partners across Europe, including intermediaries known as managing general agents and brokers. It does business in more than 30 markets and generated €834 million of gross written premiums last year. It has dipped in and out of offering capacity to various segments of the Irish general insurance market over the years.
“Our priority is to protect the interests of our partners, policyholders and employees, and to provide a rapid, concrete and documented response to our supervisor’s expectations. We regret this decision for Wakam and its partners,” said Wakam’s chairwoman Catherine Charrier-Leflaive in the statement on the company’s website.
“Wakam has a robust operating model and the resources required to continue managing all its contracts currently in force.”

title: Budget 2027 tax cuts to benefit middle-income earners by up to €1,500
description: Tax-free threshold for inheritance tax from parents to children is expected to increase by €20,000 to €420,000
author_name: Pat Leahy, Jack Horgan-Jones, Dominic Coyle
content:
Reductions in tax for middle-income earners worth up to €1,500 for a couple with a combined income of €100,000 will be among measures unveiled by the Government in another giveaway budget on Tuesday.
In addition, it is expected there will be small reductions to the existing 33 per cent rate of capital gains tax.
The tax-free threshold for inheritance tax from parents to children is expected to increase by €20,000 to €420,000, though some of these details were still being hammered out late on Monday night.
The restoration of excise on petrol and diesel, due to begin on November 1st, is expected to be postponed until March 1st, while significant reductions in carbon tax on home heating oil will also be announced.
The higher gains than previously speculated from income tax changes will result in a bigger increase in the cut-off point at which people become liable for the higher 40 per cent rate, as well a significant hike in tax credits.
The final budget negotiating sessions at Government Buildings on Monday came after protracted and often difficult negotiations over the weekend at which Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers came under pressure to concede to spending requests from several departments.
Chambers has insisted on sticking to a ceiling of a 6 per cent spending increase across Government as a whole, which has meant many Ministers have seen increases for their departments set at considerably lower than this because of higher increases in some big spending departments. However, supplementary estimates – ie, budget top-ups – will still be necessary this year.
Minister for Finance Simon Harris and Chambers are expected to highlight the introduction of an annual cost-of-disability payment of €500, paid as a lump sum first and a monthly payment after next year, as well as cuts to the cost of childcare.
[ The budget I want: A home owner, house hunter, parent, pensioner and business owner Opens in new window ]
A €10 increase in core welfare payments was agreed over the weekend, while the income disregard for carer’s allowance will rise by €150 for a single person and €300 for a couple.
Fuel allowance will rise by a weekly rate of €5 with a higher income threshold for single people over 66 of €641, while the child support payment will rise by €6. The living alone allowance will rise by €3 per week.
After tense budget talks, a spokeswoman for Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan said money to “progress” a culture card for young people had been secured.
“All going well, we anticipate being able to roll it out by the end of the year,” she said. However, the introduction of the card, as repeatedly touted in recent weeks, seems some way off.
Families with more than one child attending third level will see fees come down through expanded grant access, while college fees will also fall by €150 a year.
A new fee cap of €550 per month for childcare will be introduced, with higher subsidies planned for under-sevens from next September.
An increase in the renters’ tax credit to €1,150 for a single person and €2,300 for a couple will also form part of Tuesday’s package. The amount available under Help to Buy will rise by €5,000 to €35,000.
There will be funding for up to 140 new public transport services, but fares will still rise as planned in 2027. The road transport support scheme is to be reopened for two months, with payments made before Christmas. A fund of at least €10 million to support rural pubs was agreed.
There will be money to hire 400 new Defence Forces personnel and 100 civilian staff, with a 10.5 per cent increase on defence spending, and an increase in international aid.
There will be funding for 1,000 new gardaí, additional prison officers and more for the International Protection Office – including more staff and funding for deportation flights.

title: Polish chocolatier in Clare: ‘There’s something very special about Irish people’
description: Burren-resident Kasha Maren says she didn’t really know how to do small talk until she moved to Ireland
content:
W hen Kasha Maren, who is now 44, moved to Ireland from Poland in 2007, she had no idea how to make small talk.
“Polish people they don’t really do small talk. They are maybe not as open,” she says.
According to Maren she had to learn to say, “How are you?” and talk about the weather when she walked into a shop.
“In Poland things are very transactional. You might say hello, you get your things, say bye. It definitely opened up some part of me that was ready to be opened up.”
Maren laughs as she says this, but the reason she moved to Ireland was because her sister had moved to the UK. They had both prioritised learning English in Poland and had trained as English teachers before moving.
“I think there was an element of: I’m not completely copying her by moving to Ireland. I am doing my own independent thing.”
Initially her plan was to move to Ireland for a few months and then join her sister in London. “I’ve always felt that Ireland was such a beautiful country and that there was a depth to it. It wasn’t just a big kind of industrial country.”
[ ‘Poland and Italy are wonderful, but our lives are in Cork now’ Opens in new window ]
She moved to Dublin and found a job in a Vodafone call centre. “What I discovered was how Irish people were really warm and open.”
A lot of the people she worked with had also moved to Ireland and were keen to see the country. This was how she met her now former husband.
The group had decided to go to Galway for New Year’s Eve, and while they were in the area, they did a hike in the Burren.
[ How a local Irish cafe can manage to sell 200 cups of hot chocolate every day Opens in new window ]
“He had a tour guide business, which he was operating out of his grandparents’ cottage.” The pair hit it off quickly and for a while had a long-distance relationship before she decided to move to the Burren to be with him.
She left her job to make the move to Co Clare , and, once she had settled in the Burren, she began baking in the cottage cafe. “My grandfather was a baker and my mum was a baker,” she says.
The move was quite an adjustment for her, and she felt lonely at the beginning.
She eventually found community through the cafe, as there was a continuous stream of customers from all over the world coming through. “I discovered that I had access to all these incredible people from all around the world that I probably wouldn’t have had if I still lived in Dublin.”
Over the next few years she began self-publishing cookbooks of the pastries she was making in the cafe. She and her partner began a chocolate making business to sell to tourists. Before long the chocolate became very popular. “It was such a heretical idea to have a little cafe in the middle of nowhere and then to add a chocolate factory to it.”
It was around this time that she decided that she was going to stay in Ireland for good. “After I published my first cookbook, my creative energy really got into motion and I felt very much alive. I felt: this is it.”
Since then Hazel Mountain Chocolate has featured on the perimeter of Aviva Stadium after it won Vodafone Ireland’s See Your Business Pitchside competition.
[ ‘We moved in with each other after seven days. We got engaged after eight months’ Opens in new window ]
During the pandemic Maren welcomed her daughter. “Not having family around was very, very difficult. Not just to help but also to share in the joy of having a baby.”
Her mother died suddenly and unexpectedly just as she opened the chocolate factory. She says this felt like losing both of her parents, because her mother had raised Maren and her sister alone.
After becoming a mother herself, she began to wonder if raising her daughter in Ireland was the right thing to do. But she found community through different play groups and by meeting mothers whose children were a similar age. “I met a lot of amazing mums.”
[ 'I feel much safer in Kerry than I would be in Poland' Opens in new window ]
“I think there is something so very special and unique about Irish people that you can very easily form a bond with someone you don’t know.”
Having lived in Ireland for 20 years, she feels the country has changed her somewhat. She that she has adopted an “It’ll be grand and things will work out” attitude, which is very different from how people act in Poland.
“In Poland you do worry and try to control it and feel like you are in charge of everything. What I’ve learnt from Irish people is that you can’t do it all and you do have to leave things to kind of sort themselves out.”
In the past year she and her partner have separated but they remain committed to raising their daughter as coparents.
Maren recently launched a YouTube show, Food for Stories where she interviews people about their relationship with food. Thinking about the future, she says that if the last year has taught her anything it is to be as open as possible and go with the flow as much as you can.
We would like to hear from people who have moved to Ireland in the past 10 years. To get involved, email newtotheparish@irishtimes.com or send us two lines about yourself using the form below.

title: Beer at €16 a litre? Oktoberfest drinkers cannot get enough
description: Even with super-premium prices and a cost-of-living crisis, visitors drank a record 6.7m litres
content:
E very four years you have the summer Olympics and the winter Olympics, but every year the German city of Munich hosts the “drink olympics”.
Also known as Oktoberfest, the 191st annual edition of the festival set new records this year after 16 well-lubricated days in the Bavarian capital. And, in the interests of accurate reporting, your tireless Irish Times correspondent was one of the record 7.4 million visitors at the fairground.
It was a high-risk mission that began with a civilised sausage-and-pretzel breakfast, was kept going by litres of Augustiner beer and concluded in a heaving tent with 5,000 lederhosen-clad revellers singing Take Me Home, Country Roads.
Dancing on a bench beside me, local man Basti said Oktoberfest was a sacrifice worth making.
“Every year I think, ‘Oh, not this again’, but you go along and the atmosphere just grabs you,” he shouts. As the band strikes up Sweet Caroline, he says: “There’s nothing quite like this.”
That much is clear as soon as you enter the sprawling Theresienwiese festival site. It’s four times the size of St Stephen’s Green and holds a garish mix of lights and smells, from old-fashioned carnival carousels to newer pneumatic rides that fling screaming visitors to infinity and beyond.
You can toss balls, shoot targets, pluck candyfloss or duck into the Schichtl variety tent which, since 1871, has offered goggle-eyed visitors theatrical executions by guillotine.
Not all attractions have lasted that long. Just once, in 1880, visitors were reportedly delighted by a family of Astrakhan Spitz dogs who could not just play cards and dance, but could also recognise Europe’s crowned heads from photographs.
Today’s longest-lasting attractions are its simplest. In the Teufelsrad (Devil’s Wheel), guests seated on a polished spinning disc do battle with centrifugal forces (and, for women this year, a rise in upskirting).
Another highlight is the Toboggan, where sober and semi-sober visitors try to remain standing on a long conveyor belt that rises at a steep incline at speed. Watching people lose their balance in public is therapeutic in our modern health-and-safety tyranny.
Oktoberfest has its roots in monarchy: a citywide booze-up in October 1810 to celebrate the marriage of Crown Prince Ludwig, later King Ludwig I.
He was later chased from the throne after a dalliance with a Sligo woman, but his wedding festivities concluded with a horse race on a Munich meadow. It was subsequently renamed Theresienwiese in honour of his bride, Princess Therese.
While locals call the festival “the Wiesn”, today’s horses are clad in elaborate leather-and-steel outfits with a medieval look and a Morris dancer jingle. Each brewery has its own fleet who pull carts laden with wooden beer kegs to the cathedral-like beer tents. There are 35 in total across the festival grounds, some with a capacity of up to 8,000 people.
All are miracles of engineering – both spacious and cosy – and logistical miracles that pop out food and beer with the efficiency of an airport luggage facility.
Without doubt the greatest miracle, however, is convincing people who complain about €2-a-litre petrol to pay nearly €16 for a litre of beer.
Even with these super-premium prices, beer sales were up nearly 3 per cent to a record this year of 6.7 million litres.
The trick is to win over visitors with a twinkling smile. That, at least was the approach of Munich’s new Green mayor Dominik Krause. As the first gay man in the role, Krause faced particular pressure with an opening day tradition, when he took up a wooden mallet to knock a beer tap into the first keg.
Relief was palpable on Krause’s face after he managed it with just two taps, securing himself a place in the premier league of Munich mayors rather than the hall of shame: a predecessor in 1950 succeeded only after 17 wallops.
In the beer buzz it is easy to forget how many Oktoberfest traditions are triumphs of cultural appropriation. In particular the traditional dress – women’s dirndls and men’s lederhosen – achieved popularity when Munich’s 19th-century upper-classes thought it would be a lark to dress like peasants.
While the popularity of such costumes rises and falls over the years, constants this year included 92 tonnes of rubbish and 4,000 lost property items.
This year’s treasure trove included 700 wallets, a pair of crutches, someone’s false teeth and an alcohol tester.
Oktoberfest organisers said the visitor record was boosted by good weather and a new security plan including crowd-management steered by artificial intelligence .
On Sunday evening, Mayor Krause raised his glass to a peaceful and profitable Oktoberfest – worth about €1.5 billion to the Bavarian capital. For anyone who missed out, the drink Olympics return next September 18th.

title: ‘They’re getting electricity for way lower prices’: Few regrets in Mayo over data centre refusal
description: ‘The price of energy is going up all the time and yet ... data centres are getting electricity for way lower prices than we ordinary people’
content:
D ata centres are not on the menu for the customers who still like to eat dinner in the middle of the day in The Village Inn, Killala, Co Mayo.
A huddle of them sitting at the bar when The Irish Times visited recently are more concerned about a couple of Irish-bred horses that had romped home at a race in Wolverhampton a few days earlier.
However, Marie Sweeney, who has run the pub for the last 32 years with her husband Aidan, is happy to talk about An Coimisiún Pleanála’s refusal of the development of a data centre near the village.
Mayo Data Hub Ltd, a subsidiary of US infrastructure and data centre firm Avaio Digital, had originally received planning permission from Mayo County Council last year for the proposed €1.5 billion project at the Killala Business Park, once the location of the Asahi factory.
However, this decision was appealed to An Coimisiún Pleanála, which ruled last month that “the applicant has failed to demonstrate that the proposed development would be in accordance with the overarching objectives of the Climate Action Plan 2025″.
[ Ireland can’t be a dumping ground for data centres other countries don’t want Opens in new window ]
The ruling also stated there was a lack of evidence that the project had any corporate power purchase agreement with a renewable energy supplier.
The increase in the number of data centres has drawn criticism in light of how much power they consume and the strain they are putting on the national energy grid. Data centres accounted for almost a quarter of the electricity consumed in Ireland last year.
Residents in Co Kildare are fighting plans to zone land for a data centre at Jigginstown near Naas, and protests were held last month outside Kildare County Council offices.
“It is not central to my thoughts and I don’t know a lot about it, just what we heard in the media,” says local Mayo woman Marie Sweeney of plans for the Killala data centre being refused.
“The data centre is just another plan that went in and has been refused. We’ve been there before with plans going in and being refused, or not coming to anything.”
Author and Mayo resident Sally Rooney was among those who had objected to planning permission. Rooney argued it would be a wasteful use of electricity that would require burning of fossil fuels to generate, and that it was not an acceptable development in a climate crisis.
[ Data centre opposed by author Sally Rooney has planning overturned on climate concerns Opens in new window ]
It is more than a decade since then taoiseach Enda Kenny announced that US-backed Mayo Renewable Power would develop a biomass plant to generate electricity on the site of the business park with an investment of €180 million and the creation of 350 jobs.
The proposed factory lies half-built to this day, with the development stalled due to funding shortages and regulatory problems.
“Sometimes we don’t miss what we don’t have,” says Sweeney. “So it is no surprise that I haven’t heard anyone mention the data centre refusal.”
The potential business it might have brought is also on her mind.
“It might have brought some employment to the area, but people are saying there wasn’t enough energy for it,” she says.
“I don’t know if AI is the way we should be going ... but I wonder if in time, it is going to be trouble.”
Indeed, she is not overly concerned about the possible loss of long-term employment due to the thumbs-down issued by the planning appeals board.
[ Podcast: Is it time to rein in the data centre boom? Opens in new window ]
“Killala is very quiet today, but we are very busy in the summertime and the weekends hold their own. We do have a lot of employment around, like Coca-Cola, Hollister and Baxter in Ballina [13km away],” she says.
“There is very little unemployment here, with a lot of locals commuting to Ballina, Sligo and Castlebar. My own son commutes to Sligo.”
Down the hill on Market Street, Uinsionn MacCraith has just completed a routine appointment with his GP. He is an Irish scholar and author who lives in the village of Glenamoy, some 30km farther northwest in remote Erris.
MacCraith says he was “absolutely delighted” the data centre was refused.
“Developers are just putting these data centres up here, there, and everywhere, without explaining anything to the local people or letting them know what they are doing,” he says.
“What it is costing the country as far as electricity is concerned is absolutely ridiculous. The price of energy is going up all the time, and yet the companies are making big money and the data centres are getting electricity for way lower prices than we ordinary people.”
Co Mayo Aontú TD Paul Lawless welcomed the refusal, noting that Ireland has become “Europe’s data centre”.
But local Fine Gael councillor Jarlath Munnelly is frustrated about the decision to refuse.
“This company has been working for in excess of seven years on this proposal, and they submitted a planning application to Mayo County Council, to which there were no local objections. They’ve met with all the regulatory bodies, and then for the project to be refused on appeal – it’s hard to understand,” he says.
Munnelly is concerned about how it has become “increasingly difficult” for businesses to invest in Co Mayo and is worried about “what type of enterprise we will ever be able to attract” to the locality
“As a country, if we actually got serious about offshore renewables, we can generate excess energy in a manner that I believe would be acceptable to communities,” he says.

title: ‘I feel broken’: Ukrainians in Ireland face an uncertain future
description: Contracts with hotels housing more than 4,000 Ukrainians end next month, while private host payments end in March
content:
H anna Skachydub (49), from northeast Ukraine , says she is “completely broken” by a choice she now faces: moving to Kilkenny with her children from the life they have built over four years in north Co Dublin, possible homelessness , or a return to their war-torn homeland.
The Department of Justice is ending its contract with the Howth hotel where they have lived and paid rent, offering the family just 30 days’ accommodation 150km away. They have not been told what will happen after that.
Like thousands of Ukrainians in State-supported accommodation, they face “really unpalatable choices”, says Brian Killoran, co-ordinator of the Ukraine Civil Society Forum.
Contracts with 158 private hotels housing more than 4,000 Ukrainians end between now and November 30th, while the accommodation recognition payment (ARP) for private hosts accommodating 40,000 Ukrainians ends at the end of March 2027.
Meanwhile, as the community’s temporary protection status comes to an end next year or in 2028, the vast majority will be ineligible to apply for the new temporary protection transition scheme (TPTS). It opened for applications on September 30th and closes at the end of March.
To qualify, Ukrainians must not live in State-supported housing, must earn a minimum of €29,432 a year and have lived in Ireland for at least a year.
Hanna Skachydub, her daughter Katya (24) and son Ivan (12) have lived in a single room in the Deerpark Hotel, Howth, since arriving. They pay €800 per month towards their accommodation. “It is not free,” says Skachydub.
She works in a local cookery school, her daughter works in a nursing home and Ivan has just started secondary school.
In July, they and the 200 or so other residents received Department of Justice letters informing them that “the accommodation you are currently receiving will come to an end on 18 October 2026. People currently living at this centre can: Apply for accommodation at a State-supported accommodation centre if they have specific needs. Or source independent accommodation.”
Since then, Skachydub has applied for scores of advertised rentals and has had two viewings. She and her daughter could afford a rent of up to €2,000 a month.
She believes some landlords will not let to Ukrainians. “People don’t give any chance for us. People understand we [are] Ukrainian, you know, don’t answer, don’t give any chance [to] rent.
“It’s very difficult for us, because we do everything right, everything legal. I learn English. I work, my daughter works, my son studies. We are good people.”
Returning home to the frontline city of Sumy, on the Russian border, would be “impossible”, she says. Elsewhere in the country is “too dangerous”, she adds. “If anything happens to my children if we go home, I would never forgive myself.
“I count every day, how many days to October 18th?”
She says her sleep and eating have been affected. Her son asks every day: “Have you found somewhere to live?” “I feel completely broken,” she says.
She applied for State-supported accommodation, asking to stay in the Dublin area.
On Friday, she received her answer – they will be provided with “accommodation in a short-term designated accommodation centre at Wallslough, Co Kilkenny, for 30 days”.
She and her daughter will lose their jobs, Ivan his school community, and they will be entitled to €107.40 plus a €175 food voucher per week.
She cannot apply for the TPTS, she says. “It’s really complicated.”
She says she would need to earn more than €29,000 and not live in social housing, “and it’s only [open] for half a year. It’s impossible for us. It’s terrible, really. I say to myself: ‘I’m strong, I’m strong’, but sometimes I am very soft. I cry,” she says, becoming upset.
“I need someone to give us a chance, give us a chance to rent, not break our life again.”
Thousands like Skachydub are making “huge strides” towards integration, says Killoran, co-ordinator of the Ukraine Civil Society Forum. “But the rug is being pulled from under them.”
[ Russian attacks continue during German chancellor’s solidarity visit to Kyiv Opens in new window ]
Ukrainians will not be eligible for homelessness accommodation, though “many will try to access it”, he explains. Others may apply for asylum, putting “more pressure on an already overloaded system”. Many will feel they have “no option” but to return to Ukraine.
“I heard Ukrainian parents have been asking how they can leave their children here in Ireland, how to contact Tusla, if they are forced to return to Ukraine. These are the desperate choices people feel they face,” he says.
“What we’re seeing in 2026 in particular is what I call an aggressive form of compassion fatigue among policymakers and Government.”
While thousands are now self-sufficient, many like Skachydub and her family are “well on their way to self-sufficiency, but it takes time”, he says.
A spokesman for the County and City Management Association, representing councils that provide homelessness accommodation, said it would “continue to work collaboratively with the Department of Housing and the Department of Justice, and partner organisations to support ... arrangements to assist individuals in accessing available supports”.
A Department of Justice spokesman said: “Ireland is progressing a phased withdrawal of State-supported accommodation. People who want to remain in State-supported accommodation were asked to apply.
“Following the termination of the ARP scheme, hosts can continue to have private arrangements with individuals.” Those seeking private rented accommodation may be eligible for a rent supplement.

title: Abu Dhabi mining firm makes bid approach for Kenmare Resources
description: Interest from International Resources Holding comes two years after group looked at pursuing a bid, say sources
content:
Kenmare Resources confirmed on Tuesday that an Abu Dhabi-based mining and trading group chaired by a brother of the president of the United Arab Emirates has made a bid approach for the Dublin-based titanium minerals miner.
It follows a report in The Irish Times that International Resources Holding (IRH), where Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan is head of the board, has been running a fresh rule over Kenmare two years after it previously looked at pursuing a bid.
“The board of Kenmare Resources plc notes recent press speculation and confirms that it has received a non-binding proposal from International Resources Holdings RSC Ltd regarding a possible cash offer for the entire issued and to be issued share capital of Kenmare,” Kenmare said in a statement.
Kenmare added that discussions are ongoing and that IRH has been given a deadline of 5pm on November 17th to at least declare a firm intention to make a formal offer or walk away.
Shares in Kenmare jumped 20.5 per cent to £2.185 in early deals in London, where they are more frequently traded than in Dublin.
Kenmare’s shares were trading more than 50 per cent below their 2024 highs before the news – their lowest level in more than seven years – amid ongoing falling prices for titanium minerals and uncertainty and protracted talks over a new royalties agreement regarding its key Moma mine in Mozambique.
[ Kenmare chief on shareholder frustration of being a ‘small cap, single country, single commodity’ company Opens in new window ]
The mine produces about 6 per cent of global titanium stocks. Its main products, ilmenite and rutile, are used in everything from paints, plastics and paper to aircraft, medical equipment and golf clubs.
Kenmare had a market value of about £163 million (€192 million) at the close of trading on Monday, having fallen 43 per cent in the past year.
News of the fresh interest of IRH comes 16 months after Kenmare Resources walked away from takeover talks with its former managing director, Michael Carvill, and another Abu Dhabi company, private equity firm Oryx Global Partners, after the consortium made it clear it would only be willing to proceed with a bid that was below an initial £473 million proposal previously made in March 2025.
Carvill told The Irish Times on Monday he is not involved in – nor aware of – any fresh bid interest in Kenmare. He added that he has no interest in pursuing another proposal in the future.
Industry observers said that mining companies are continuously assessed by potential bidders, especially businesses with a small portfolio of assets that make it easier to carry out due diligence and fold into larger entity groups. However, most bid approaches in the industry do not end up in a deal, they cautioned.
They added that it would be difficult to maximise value for shareholders in an offer situation without the price of titanium minerals showing signs of recovery and an agreement with the Mozambique government on a new royalties regime – or so-called implementation agreement – covering processing and exports of Moma products.
The price of ilmenite is in its fourth year of decline. Kenmare said in August that its mineral product revenues fell 16 per cent in the first half of this year to $134.5 million (€120.6 million), primarily due to a lower average price received as a result of weak product markets.
[ Kenmare secures further $30m loan facility amid covenants waiver after profit slump Opens in new window ]
However, the price of zircon, which accounts for about a quarter of revenues and is used to make ceramic tiles, has stabilised and is starting to increase again. Kenmare suspended its final dividend last year for the first time since it made a maiden payout in 2019.
Kenmare has been in talks for about four years with Mozambique on a new so-called implementation agreement. The previous 20-year accord expired just before the end of 2024, though the terms were to remain in place until a new one was reached.
The company said in August that it had made significant progress on a new accord. However, it added: “A failure to reach an agreement with the government of Mozambique on the IA [implementation agreement] and/or the imposition of a unilateral change of terms by the government on the company would be likely to lead Kenmare to resort to arbitration to enforce its contractual rights.”

title: Just 220 people opt to postpone drawing down State pension at age 66
description: Defering pension entitles people to higher weekly payment when compared to standard maximum of €299.30
content:
Just 220 people have so far taken advantage of the Republic’s deferred State pension scheme, opting to postpone drawing it down for a year or two.
New figures show that 194 people had chosen to take their pension at 67, instead of the normal age of 66. Another 26 had waited until they were aged 68, according to data from the Department of Social Protection .
Postponing the pension entitles people to a higher weekly payment when compared to the standard maximum rate of €299.30.
[ State pension: Is €300 a week enough to live on? Opens in new window ]
Opting to postpone for a single year until age 67 brings a €313.40 weekly payment, while waiting until 70 can mean it rises to €363.90.
Uptake of the scheme has been sluggish, and some financial advisers are telling clients not to defer even if they plan to stay in the workforce.
There are some cases, however, where a person does not yet qualify for a full State pension and deferral can be used to build up extra PRSI contributions.
Figures from the Department of Social Protection show 108 people deferred until 67 in 2025 while a single person drew down at 68. Up to September 14th of this year, 86 people opted to draw down at 67 while 25 waited until they were 68.
Nobody has yet started drawing down their pension at age 69 or 70 because the scheme has not been in operation for long enough.
[ Budget 2027: All you need to know Opens in new window ]
The department said there were a further 365 cases where people had indicated they wanted to postpone their pension. However, they had not provided information on when they planned to draw it down.
