The department also said that people were not obliged to notify them of their intention to hold off on claiming their pension.
“This means that people could decide to use the deferred drawdown option without contacting us.
[ Letters: Budget 2027 will cost pensioners Opens in new window ]
“Therefore, the figures ... are the numbers of people who have specifically indicated their wish to defer their pension drawdown date rather than the total number of people who may choose to defer their pension,” said the department.
Asked about the figures, a spokesperson for the department said international evidence showed that take-up of similar schemes tended to be “very small”.
They said people in their 60s who continued working were more likely to draw down their pension as soon as they became entitled to one.
“The objective of the measure was not that large numbers of people would necessarily defer claiming their pension, but rather to provide greater choice and flexibility for people approaching State pension age.
“The department is satisfied that the availability of flexible access to the State pension represents an important enhancement to the State pension system,” said the spokesperson.
The department said there were no current plans for a formal evaluation of the scheme or a review of the existing arrangements.

title: Modernised D3 redbrick on handsome street across from Fairview Park
description: Spacious Cadogan Road two-bed with converted attic room is a 20-minute walk from Clontarf prom
content:
Cadogan Road, a cul-de-sac off Annesley Bridge Road and directly across from Fairview Park in Dublin 3 , is sleepy on an early-autumn morning except for a couple of construction workers milling in and out of a renovation project midway down the row of redbrick terraced homes.
Renovation is not something prospective buyers of number 17 will have to worry about as the owners have taken care of upgrading works to a high standard. They made do with a basin as a kitchen sink for a few weeks so you don’t have to.
The couple bought the house in late 2019 and moved in just a few months before the Covid pandemic slowed the world down, causing the renovation to require about 50 per cent more effort, one of the owners estimates. They took the project room by room and wanted to make sure there was a cohesive flow through the home.
Number 17 Cadogan Road was previously owned by a man whose family had lived here since the early 1900s. They added a spacious kitchen/diningroom extension and a large bathroom on the return, so the current owners had a 139sq m (1,496sq ft) footprint to work with.
Now in search of more garden space, with two small children in tow, the couple are placing this C-rated home with two bedrooms and a converted attic on the market through Kelly Bradshaw, seeking €645,000.
Stepping from the street into the blue-and-white tiled front yard, selling agent Louise Kidney points out how the owners even thought to paint the electricity meter box in gunmetal grey to match the railings and the front door.
Inside, tiles with a grey and red Art Nouveau pattern on a white base command attention. The ceilings are high and framed by coving that continues into the sittingroom. The front of the room is a comfy space for watching TV, with a big wood-burning stove at its centre. Inside shutters on the front sash window allow you to block out the world. Beyond the sofas there is still lots of space, which could be used for a play area or even as a home office.
To the rear of the house is the spacious kitchen/diningroom which is flooded with light thanks to a southerly aspect and roof lights. The ceiling over the dining area is pitched with rooflights on both sides and spotlights to mimic the effect in the evening.
The kitchen provides extensive storage and counter space and the owners opted against an island to allow an easier flow in the room. The family spend most of their time here, the owner says, with the kids occupied at the table. They even tend to spend their weekend mornings here, she says, to make the most of the light.
Glazed doors off the dining space open to a small outdoor courtyard. To the rear of the kitchen is a secret door that looks like a cupboard but folds open to reveal a utility room.
Upstairs, the bathroom on the return is the size of a bedroom and is painted a luxurious moody navy shade and fitted out beautifully with terrazzo-style flooring, a free-standing bath and a separate spacious shower.
[ Georgian home and stud farm of up to 112 acres in Co Kildare Opens in new window ]
The main bedroom sits to the front of the first floor, with two sash windows framing leafy views of the trees beyond. Wardrobes are fitted on both sides of the room, along with a built-in dressing table, ensuring every inch of space is used. A second smaller double bedroom lies off the hallway.
Up another flight of stairs is a converted attic room with natural light from roof lights. It would make a fantastic home office or hobby room.
Cadogan Road is about a 25-minute walk or 10-minute cycle from Talbot Street on the north side of the city centre, with plenty of Dublin bus routes accessible nearby. As well as having Fairview Park across the road, Clontarf prom is a 20-minute walk away.

title: I’m about to buy a ground-floor apartment but am worried about noise from the duplex above
description: Property Clinic: What information should the developer provide to me on soundproofing before I sign contracts?
content:
I am considering buying a ground-floor apartment in a new-build development, with a separate duplex dwelling above. My main concern is impact noise and structure-borne vibration from footsteps. The planning documents say the upper duplex is timber-framed above a masonry ground floor, but they do not specify whether the separating floor is concrete/hollow core or timber, or whether it includes a resilient acoustic layer. What information should a buyer reasonably be able to obtain before signing contracts? Should the developer provide the detailed separating-floor specification, Part E acoustic details or test results if requested? And if not, can this information be obtained from the local authority or through a Freedom of Information (FOI) request?
With timber-framed construction, I am always concerned about sound insulation and how difficult it is to achieve good acoustic separation in a compartment wall or floor in an apartment development. A surveyor will be keen to understand how the floor/wall junctions and service penetrations are detailed to reduce sound (and fire) transmission. It is, therefore, a very reasonable first question – to ask the developer for these details.
The acoustic performance of the separating floor depends on the complete floor construction. Where a concrete slab is used, its mass provides much of the resistance to airborne sound. A resilient layer is generally used to reduce vibration and impact transmission.
The building regulations, through Technical Guidance Document E (Sound), sets out the requirements for both airborne sound and impact sound-insulation levels. For separating floors, these are 53 dB and 58 dB respectively. I appreciate these figures may not mean much on their own, but they provide a guide if you feel the sound insulation is substandard.
A duplex apartment arrangement can be more complicated than a simple apartment-to-apartment floor as sound may travel through structural walls and columns, staircases and landings, service penetrations and gaps around the floor perimeter. This is called flanking transmission and can significantly affect the performance of the separating floor.
[ ‘My apartment walls are paper thin. How can I reduce noise disruption to neighbours?’ Opens in new window ]
You should reasonably ask the developer for the following information ahead of your surveyor’s inspection:
The actual test results, if available, would be more informative in your case than simply being told that the development complies with Part E. A development can meet the requirements of the regulations while occupants may still hear some footsteps or low-frequency impact noise.
The FOI process may take too long if you are under pressure to sign a contract, and the planning file may not have that level of technical detail. So, I would start by asking the developer directly and, in parallel, contacting the local authority’s building control section to establish what relevant records it holds.
If noise remains a concern, consider arranging your own acoustic test to assess airborne sound, impact sound and flanking transmission.
Pat McGovern is a chartered building surveyor and a member of the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland

title: State subsidies, no VAT and lower costs: how Irish private schools are attracting UK students
description: The Irish State continues to subsidise 50 private secondary schools by a total of more than €140 million a year
content:
Second in line to the British throne, Prince George, has just started as a boarder at Eton College, where fees are about £65,000 a year (€75,688). But if his parents weren’t so flush, he might have considered an education across the water.
The cost of a private – or public as they call it – school education has been steadily rising in the UK, since the Labour government’s decision to add VAT – at an additional 20 per cent – as of January 1st, 2025. According to the Independent Schools Council, a UK lobby group, it means that average boarding school fees stand at about £54,000 a year. This has resulted in numbers attending UK private schools falling by about 30,000.
For example, at Roedean, a girls day and boarding school in Brighton, full boarding fees range from £17,778 a term to £21,330 a term (there are three terms in a year, so about £53k-£64K a year). But if VAT were excluded, fees would drop to £14,815-£17,775 a term.
Extra costs might apply for international students; at Eton, for example, an additional annual £3,000 charge applies to international students who need a visa.
Step forward Ireland and its network of boarding schools that, as in other EU countries, are not subject to VAT and still benefit from State subsidies. That means they can offer those who previously favoured a UK boarding school a significantly cheaper option.
Chris Lumb, headmaster of Clongowes Wood College , a Jesuit boarding school in Kildare, is starting to see an increase in interest from the UK.
“From our perspective, we are beginning to see an impact,” he says of rising costs in the UK, pointing to growing interest in Irish schools both from UK residents and farther afield.
Historically, it would have been children of Irish people living in the UK who might have been sent to Clongowes, Lumb says – but not necessarily those of UK families. Now this is changing.
“One of the challenges for us as we develop the UK market is for families in the UK to understand what an Irish education is,” says Lumb, noting that A Levels generally focus on three to four subjects, compared with seven typically for the Leaving Certificate.
“It’s about generating a greater understanding of the breadth and value of an Irish education,” he says.
Arthur Godsil is a former headmaster of St Andrews College in Booterstown who runs an education consultancy offering services to those looking to move to second level in Ireland, such as guardianship and registration requirements.
He has seen “a year-on-year increase in demand” across second-level boarding schools.
“I’ve no doubt the VAT imposed by Labour government will have had an effect,” he says.
Once on board with the Irish education system, UK-based families can find much cheaper options here.
Clongowes, for example, charges about €26,550 a year for boarders. On its website, it notes: “Our boarding fees are substantially lower than UK boarding fees, yet our grounds, facilities and results are on a par with some of the top UK boarding schools.”
Alexandra College in Milltown charges €28,667 for UK boarders, while Rockwell College in Tipperary about €17,928 – all significantly less than their UK equivalents.
One school actively targeting UK students is Kings Hospital, a mixed boarding school near Lucan, Co Dublin. Founded in 1669, it is one of Ireland’s oldest boarding schools and is promising “affordable fees for UK families”.
“Looking for an Irish boarding school with UK-level excellence and no VAT?” a message on its website asks. It charges €28,595 a year for UK residents.
Another reason, apart from VAT, for Irish schools being so competitive with their UK counterparts is that, in the UK, private schools operate outside the state system and don’t receive state funding. They are typically fully funded by school fees. In Ireland, however, private schools still receive significant public funding.
[ Inside Clongowes Wood: Who sends their child to boarding school in 21st-century Ireland? Opens in new window ]
While parties such as Sinn Féin and Labour want to end public funding of private schools, latest figures show the Irish State continues to subsidise 50 private secondary schools by a total of more than €140 million a year . The money largely goes toward salaries for teachers and special needs assistants.
This subsidy system is a key advantage when attracting students from abroad.
As the Kings Hospital website notes, “Ireland’s subsidised education system allows us to offer a world-class education and premium facilities at less than half the cost of UK independent boarding schools”.
Anthony Cheng, director and founder of the Irish International Education Center, an Irish education specialist based in Hong Kong that earlier this month held a webinar with the head of admissions at King’s Hospital, says Ireland remains “highly competitive” on total cost.
“Ireland offers excellent value for money on education quality, facilities, graduate employment prospects and the overall environment,” he says.
It’s not just UK students who are considering a move to Ireland. Students from other countries who may have typically boarded in the UK may be put off by the higher fees there.
“International families who may previously have chosen a UK school will now consider an Irish school,” says Godsil.
He has seen an uptick in applications from US students and has placed about a dozen or so students in Irish boarding schools in recent months. Elsewhere, he sees interest mainly from other European countries, the Middle East and China.
Brexit has also played a part in the declining attractiveness of UK independent schools.
“We now have an increased number of European families looking to us,” says Lumb.
Cheng says the imposition of VAT in the UK has “significantly increased” Hong Kong interest in Irish schools.
“Since tuition fees in Ireland remain VAT-free, it is becoming increasingly attractive to families looking for high-quality boarding education in an English-speaking country. Several of our recently enrolled students have explicitly stated that the UK’s VAT policy was one of the reasons they chose Ireland,” he says.
[ Private schools are not key to student success. I should know – I’ve taught in them Opens in new window ]
“Ireland is a safe, friendly and welcoming country with a high-quality education environment,” says Cheng, citing high academic standards, diverse pathways to higher education, an English-speaking environment, and visa-free entry to Ireland for holders of Hong Kong SAR [special administrative region] passports.
The “wealth” of extracurricular activities offered by Irish schools is also a plus, he says.
[ Life at Ireland’s biggest boarding school: ‘I have so much more independence’ Opens in new window ]
Most importantly, however, is the fact that the Leaving Cert offers a direct pathway to universities in Ireland and the UK, “which is traditionally the most popular higher-education destination for Hong Kong students”.
And, although the Irish Immigrant Investor Programme, which allowed nationals from outside the European Economic Area move to Ireland by way of making a long-term investment, ceased accepting new applications in 2023, “the demand for education for children from families who immigrate to Ireland through this programme remains”, Cheng says.
The UK opportunity comes at a time when schools here may have to start working harder to attract students willing to pay their ever rising prices.
Department of Finance figures show there were about 425,000 students enrolled across Ireland’s secondary-school sector in 2024/25. Of these, about 27,500 attended private schools.
However, numbers are on the slide. According to that same 2025 report, “enrolments in fee-charging schools, as percentages of total enrolments, are down since 2022/23 and represent a continuing pattern of falling attendance at fee-charging schools”.
[ ‘It makes them more resilient’: Life in Ireland’s only Irish-language primary boarding school Opens in new window ]
Back in 2008, private school enrolments peaked at just under 8 per cent, but have fallen back to less than 6.5 per cent since.
And demographics mean there is a declining pool of Irish-born candidates for such schools; CSO data shows that in the age cohort 1-8, there are fewer children now than there were in 2016. For example, there are an estimated 61,000 five-year old children in Ireland now: in 2016 there were 72,359.
“At the lower end of the primary sector, some schools may not be filling their classes,” says Godsil.
Continued interest from abroad is not assured either. Cheng says there may be a decline in Hong Kong students coming to Ireland.
“The Hong Kong SAR government is actively promoting the ‘Study in Hong Kong’ brand, extending its coverage from higher education to secondary education,” says Cheng. This added focus means more families may look to keep their children educated locally.
And State funding of Irish private schools may not continue at the same level.
“There is no doubt there’s a concern,” says Godsil, noting that private schools used to get the same level of funding as those in the non-private sector. The proportion has been reduced considerably and he expects it to continue to be eroded.

title: Is timing an issue when I am trying to offset losses against capital gains?
description: Reader queries benefit of delaying property sale to facilitate shares write-off
content:
I have recently agreed a sale on a property but have not yet agreed to a final closing date. I want time to organise old shares that I have made losses on to write off against the gains.
I pay my income tax at the end of October. Is there any value in delaying the sale until December or January and if I did, when would capital gains tax (CGT) need to be paid?
Dealing with capital gains can involve a certain degree of timing, especially when you are trying to offset losses against any gains arising to reduce your tax exposure.
You don’t clarify whether the losses you mention relate to the sale of shares in previous years or whether you are simply giving up the ghost on some shares you still own but which are trading below whatever price you paid for them.
The position with losses is that they are first set against any gains that arise in the same year. If, having done that, some losses remain outstanding, they can be carried forward for however many years are required until other gains arise to offset the losses outstanding.
So, if your losses relate to shares sold in previous years, there is no great advantage in messing around with the timing of closing the sale on your property – especially if there is any prospect that such a move could imperil the sale.
However, if you still hold these loss-making shares, then you might need a bit of time to sell them so those losses can be offset against any gain on the sale of the property. The key here is that losses cannot be offset against a gain or gains in previous years.
So if you sell the property this year at a gain and do not crystallise the losses until next year, they would be no good to you in reducing your CGT bill on the sale of the property.
When it comes to timing and tax, the rules are fairly straightforward but they have no relationship to the income-tax deadline.
[ My outstanding balance is about €59,000, do I really still need mortgage protection? Opens in new window ]
If a capital gain is crystallised – for instance by closing the sale of this property – between January 1st and November 30th in any year, the tax is due to be paid by December 15th the same year. For gains that arise in December of any year, the bill falls due one month later, at the end of January the following year.
So, if you close this property sale before the end of the year, any tax arising will fall due fairly quickly. If, however, you did not close the sale until January, the tax would not fall due until December 15th of next year.
But January is still three months away. You could well risk your buyer walking away if they felt they were being strung along in that fashion.
As long as you have your losses crystallised, I think, on balance, there is no real benefit in delaying the sale of this property unduly.
When it comes to filing details of any gain with Revenue , you actually have until October 31st the year following the one in which you sell the asset, though it may well make sense to act sooner given the payment deadlines.
Even if no tax was payable – either because of certain reliefs or offsetting losses – you are still obliged to file a return so that Revenue can keep track of things.

title: What will €295,000 buy in the heart of Dundalk and in the Meath countryside?
description: Two homes, one price: A three-bed townhouse in Co Louth town or a traditional cottage outside Kells
content:
This fine traditional cottage is on a quarter of an acre of mature grounds about a 20-minute drive from Kells in Co Meath. It is set back from the road and surrounded by trees and hedges for privacy. The grounds are neatly landscaped, and the facade features a charming duck-egg-blue panelled door and matching window shutters. Extending to 92sq m (990sq ft), the home features two bedrooms, a sittingroom with an exposed-brick hearth and a kitchen/diningroom with a range cooker and light-green cabinetry. There is also an attic room that works as a home office. Ber D2
This three-bedroom terraced townhouse has been extended to the rear and measures 126sq m (1,356sq ft). It’s about a 20-minute walk from the town centre and about a 10-minute drive or cycle from the train station, from where you can take a trip of between an hour and 90 minutes to Dublin city . It features two sittingrooms to the front of the house, the smaller of which could be used as an office or a fourth bedroom, and a bright, spacious kitchen/living/diningroom to the rear. Upstairs is an en suite main bedroom, two further bedrooms and the bathroom. It has off-street parking for two cars to the front and a paved garden to the rear.

title: US ban on diesel exports would hit Ireland harder and could lead to rationing, RSM warns
description: Ireland ‘uniquely vulnerable’ because of reliance on home heating oil
content:
A US ban on diesel exports would significantly exacerbate the current inflation surge, possibly resulting in fuel rationing, with Ireland being hit harder than other countries, Tom Pugh, chief economist with UK consulting firm RSM , has warned.
He also predicted inflation was likely to keep edging up as utility bills reset higher in October and indirect energy effects add to airfares, manufactured goods and food inflation.
This will result in inflation peaking at 4.5 per cent in the new year, Pugh said.
US president Donald Trump has indicated his support for a possible ban on diesel exports to reduce the price of the fuel in advance of midterm elections.
Under pressure from Trump, the G7 nations last week agreed they would release 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks, but experts say such a move will only act as a temporary buffer.
“Ireland is uniquely vulnerable because of its reliance on home heating oil,” he said. Home heating oil prices tend to rise alongside diesel prices as both are crude oil distillates.
About a third of households here (more than 700,000) use home heating oil as their primary source of heating, and the price of a standard household tank has already jumped by almost 60 per cent since the start of the Iran crisis in February.
Pugh said Ireland’s strong economy and labour market put it in a good position to weather the current period of high energy prices.
The main risk to the outlook would be if the current energy shock “turned much worse” because of an extremely cold winter or because of a ban on US diesel exports.
[ Oil refiners US and China have the leverage amid rising fuel prices Opens in new window ]
According to Reuters, Trump has warned France and Germany to release diesel stocks or face a potential US exports ban.
“It depends on how high diesel prices go, but I suspect if this did happen you would probably be quite quickly into rationing,” Pugh said.
Since the ban on Russian energy, Europe relies on the US for between a third and a half of its diesel imports.
The average price of diesel across Europe hit a record high of €2.24 per litre last week, compared with €1.59 before the Iran crisis, according to the European Commission.
Pugh did not discount the possibility that Trump might announce a ban but later backtrack.
He warned that the current spike in energy prices would eventually translate into higher food prices.
“It’s inevitable that we’re going to see another round of food price inflation early next year given all of your input costs have gone up by 50 per cent,” he said.
“I don’t want to be alarmist ... I don’t think we’re going back to the kind of 10-12 per cent inflation that we had in 2022 but considering in February we were talking about inflation around the 2 per cent mark and now we’re talking about 4.5 per cent,” he said.
He predicted inflation was on course to peak at 4.5 per cent in the new year, “with the risks skewed to an even bigger rise unless the Government announces further cost-of-living measures in Budget 2027 ”.
On the wider economy, Pugh said Ireland was insulated more than its peers because of the huge level of corporate tax flowing into the exchequer.
“When I speak to my friends in the UK treasury [about Ireland] the world’s tiniest violin comes out,” he joked.
While the concentration risk of having so much tax flowing from a handful of companies was real, Ireland was still “starting from a much better place than other economies”, Pugh said.
[ Tomorrow’s budget may be the worst since Charles Haughey’s wild spending Opens in new window ]
On the budget, he said: “When I look at the Irish economy I don’t see an economy that is crying out for a big injection of fiscal stimulus.
“You’ve already got domestically-generated inflation creeping up ... the labour market looks close to full employment, you’ve got an economy that is doing very well and is bumping up against those real constraints of infrastructure and labour supply,” he said.
“If you inject a dose of fiscal stimulus into that, all you get is inflation.”
The Government’s proposed €8.5 billion budgetary package for next year represents a near 6 per cent jump in spending, which economists warn is not sustainable.
A lot of Government spending is going into inflation-adjusted budgets, he said.
“It doesn’t feel to me that you’re solving the problem; it feels like you’re just papering over because you have the budget to do it,” he said.
“The risk is, you get into an escalation where, say, inflation is going to be 3.5-4 per cent next year ... so if you want to do above-inflation pay rises for the public sector then you need another 7-8 per cent, and you get into this circle rather than addressing the underlying issues of infrastructure,” he said.

title: The Weight of Angels by John Boyne: What if Oscar Wilde had lived long beyond his 46 years?
description: A poignant, moving, sometimes funny novel about regret and atonement
content:
Oscar Wilde was 46 years old when he died in 1900, his health broken after two years in prison for the crime of sodomy. His arrest came after he challenged the Marquess of Queensberry, who had called him a sodomite. Wilde sued for libel and lost.
But what if he hadn’t? What if he had, for once, practised restraint and ignored the taunt?
In The Weight of Angels, novelist John Boyne has imagined a different life for Wilde – one that lasted another 50 years and was rich with writing, success, young men and love. Also, heartbreak, failure and regret.
Boyne has done a remarkable job of writing a compelling tale that contains almost no action or introspection; he tells the story almost entirely through dialogue. The third-person objective narrator serves primarily as eavesdropper.
To break up the conversations, Boyne includes newspaper articles, letters and sections written as plays. He is a marvellous imitator and does an excellent job channelling Wilde, giving him witticisms that sound authentic. He has a subtle touch; as Wilde ages, the reader senses that he grows weary of always being “on”.
“The tragedy of the young is that they endlessly seek the spotlight,” Wilde says at one point, almost automatically. “The tragedy of the old is-” to which an American responds, “Knock it off. I’m not in the mood for any of your bon fuckin’ mots.”
The title refers to Wilde’s regrets, but there is another weight that courses through the book: society’s attitude toward homosexuality. Even Wilde’s friends use language that disparages his gayness; this disapproval pervades his life and helps explain his ostentation: it hides the pain of wanting what he thinks he can never have.
“A reciprocal love between men who both desired and treasured each other. Even the idea made him feel a wealth of sorrow, for such contentment, he was certain, would surely be impossible to find.”
Imagine, the book suggests, how fruitful a life could be if people were accepted, rather than punished, for who they are. Boyne imagines a wealth of new works for Wilde – plays, mostly – and gives Wilde’s young lover Bosie the death that the real Wilde suffered. In the novel, it is Bosie who challenges the Marquess and ends up in prison. And it is the narcissistic Bosie who writes the splendid The Ballad of Reading Gaol. Given Bosie’s nature, this is hard for the reader to swallow, but it is an elegant way of explaining the existence of the poem in Boyne’s reimagined world.
[ John Boyne: ‘Wilde was gay, he went to Trinity, he went to England. That’s me, me, me’ Opens in new window ]
As the book progresses, Wilde is everywhere, meeting everyone -attending coronations, parties and opening nights, and sparring with other, primarily Irish, writers, with whom he feels a prickly rivalry. He is cautiously friendly with William Butler Yeats, less so with George Bernard Shaw and Bram Stoker. He dismisses James Joyce, saying he’ll read Finnegans Wake once it’s been translated into English.
The Weight of Angels is reminiscent in ambition and scope of Boyne’s epic masterpiece, The Heart’s Invisible Furies (2017), in which he traces the history of modern Ireland through the life of one gay man. That novel was sprinkled with cameos of historic figures. But in this book the historic figures are everywhere and as the book progresses they show up more and more frequently.
The last third of the book is like the movie Forrest Gump, where Wilde either runs into, sits next to, drinks Champagne with, works with, argues with, charms or otherwise interacts with just about every notable figure from the first half of the 20th century: Winston Churchill, Katharine Hepburn, Mickey Rooney, Wallis Simpson, Emmeline Pankhurst, Rudyard Kipling, Agatha Christie, André Gide, TS Eliot, Charlie Chaplin. Also EM Forster, who Boyne imagines writing mysteries and walking around naked in the sunshine of Papua New Guinea.
Not all of these interactions are crucial to the plot and certainly their inclusion accounts for the book’s 600 pages, but they are highly entertaining. Boyne’s Virginia and Leonard Woolf are hilariously bizarre. Still, Wilde confides in them. “I am writing about a fool,” he tells them. “A man who makes a grave error and suffers the consequences. He hurts all those around him.” In other words, himself.
The Weight of Angels is a poignant, moving, sometimes funny novel about regret and atonement – regret for the people Wilde betrayed, or hurt, or made promises to that he did not keep, and an atonement that he hopes does not come too late.
Laurie Hertzel is the author of two memoirs. She has reviewed for the Washington Post, the Boston Globe, the Los Angeles Times and elsewhere

title: Best used electric estates: what should replace my diesel Mazda6?
description: Practical advice on your motoring queries, from buying, selling or issues you have with your current car
content:
I drive a 162-registration diesel Mazda6 Tourer estate. I’m looking to buy a used EV estate. I’m in my 70s and do a bit of sea kayaking, so I like an estate for its carrying capacity and low roof height (for loading a sea kayak on to the roof). I also find an estate a very practical car. I’m open to buying from Northern Ireland as well, as the car spec is usually higher. Would you have any recommendations? – Tom M, Co Louth
Let’s start with two cars: the MG 5 EV if price is the priority, and the Volkswagen ID.7 Tourer if you can stretch the budget to €40,000.
Estates, almost without question, make the best all-round cars because you get the aerodynamic sleekness of a saloon combined with the kind of load space that most people think – wrongly – only SUVs provide.
Until very recently, there were only a few estate options with all-electric power on the Irish market: the MG 5 EV and the Porsche Taycan Cross or Sport Turismo, for example. So that limits the choices for older, more affordable options on the used market right now.
The MG 5 EV is, unsurprisingly, rather more affordable, and you can easily pick one up for less than €20,000, but just be aware that the 5 EV, even in its updated form from 2023 onwards, isn’t all that big inside and feels really cheap in the cabin.
The touchscreen controls can be infuriating if you are coming from the wonderful world of button controls. Decent range for the money, though, at circa 400km.
There’s another possibility: a Kia EV6. A Kia dealer will probably try to convince some buyers that an EV6 is a crossover or SUV, because that’s apparently what people want, but it really isn’t. It’s too low-slung for that.
It’s also not really an estate, because the boot isn’t quite big enough, but it still manages to be roomy, good-looking, good to drive and comes with a long warranty. Perhaps it’s not on a par with your Mazda6 in terms of space, but it’s been a big seller in Ireland, so there are plenty from which to choose, and prices are down to the low €20,000 range.
There are estate versions of both the Opel Astra Electric and the Peugeot E-308, which are also worth a look. Both have been recently updated with improved batteries and longer ranges – now up to almost 450km on the official test. The older cars could manage about 420km, which doesn’t sound like a massive difference, but every little helps. If you can live with that range or a little less, both make a solid buy, with massive boots and, just as you are looking for, a low roof.
Remember, however, that strapping a kayak to the roof is going to impact the aerodynamics of the car and therefore the range. You already know that from the diesel fuel economy with or without the roof rack loaded. A rule of thumb would be a reduction of 10-20 per cent on what you would normally get on the same journey (not the official range but the real-world range) without it.
The Volkswagen ID. 7 Tourer is one of the unsung heroes of the VW ID line-up. True, its new price is a touch eye-watering, but the cheapest used examples are now under €40,000, so there are relative bargains to be had.
Massive inside (the rear legroom is properly limo-like) and smooth to drive, it also has a real-world 500km range in mixed driving. A really good choice, if it doesn’t bust the budget.
BMW’s i5 Touring could be another good choice. It’s very roomy inside, has a very decent boot, and feels every inch the “proper Beemer” to drive. We once drove one from Munich to Dublin in 24 hours, so although the usable 400-450km range doesn’t sound all that great, it’s better than you’d think. Still pricey even used, though – north of €50,000.
Stretch to €60,000, and you could pick up a demo or new Mercedes-Benz CLA Shooting Brake. It can carry a kayak on the roof and claims a range of more than 500km, with a spacious front boot for all your wet gear. There are CLA 200 versions of the award-winning EV for sale for circa €62,000.
Surprisingly, given Ireland’s general reluctance to embrace the estate, there are actually some used Taycan Turismos on sale. At €69,900 the cheapest one we could find isn’t exactly what you’d call affordable, but equally it’s maybe not quite as much money as you might think you’d have to spend on a massively powerful, four-wheel-drive Porsche .
You will get a little more in the way of choice by shopping in Northern Ireland. This is as long as the car has either been originally registered in Northern Ireland or brought into the North under the auspices of the Windsor Framework, then you won’t have to pay VAT or customs duty. VRT is assessed separately, using Revenue’s market valuation, but electric car relief may reduce or eliminate the amount payable.
For our money, we’d opt for the VW ID.7 as the best all-rounder for your needs. Like the best estates, it’s spacious both for passengers and loads, so it’s probably the closest to your current Mazda6. The roofline is at the right height.
It’s a comfortable distance traveller, but if you go for a test drive, be sure to pay particular attention to the touchscreens. Coming out of the Mazda6, you might find the controls a little annoying at first. Be sure to bring your kayak measurements and confirm the permitted roof load.
Also, check the battery size of the cars on offer. The 77kWh has an official range of 600km, and the rear-wheel-drive with 86kWh claims up to 690km. However, those are the test figures: winter weather, motorway driving and your kayak on the roof will shorten the distance between charges.

title: ‘The word meningitis came up and I was like absolutely stuck to the floor’
description: Siobhán and Noel Carroll following the death of their four-year-old daughter, Aoibhe, to meningitis
content:
A woman whose son contracted bacterial meningitis as a baby, which will result in lifelong impacts on the child’s health, has highlighted the importance of parents trusting their gut if they suspect their children have contracted the condition.
Helena Power (37), from Ballyroan in Co Laois, said “we will live with the impact of meningitis forever more”, in advance of World Meningitis Day on October 5th.
She gave birth to her first baby, a boy named Tom, in July 2021, but became ill a week later. Power attended the Midland Regional Hospital in Portlaoise and found out she had group B streptococcus (GBS) sepsis, a type of infection. After a few days of antibiotics, she was discharged.
One night, when Tom was around three weeks old, he did not sleep and had a high-pitched cry. He also had reflux and Power decided to bring him to the GP.
She had “a huge instinct” that Tom was unwell despite him not having any other symptoms such as a high temperature or a rash. She brought him to the hospital, under the GP’s recommendation. There, Tom’s blood was drawn and a lumbar puncture was performed.
By this stage, she said he was also vomiting and his hands were “freezing”.
“The word meningitis came up and I was like absolutely stuck to the floor.”
She said that in the space of one day she could see an increased sensitivity to light in her son and how his head went backwards as if there was a weight on his head.
He was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) at Children’s Health Ireland (CHI) Temple Street in Dublin, and she and her husband, Kelvin, were formally told that Tom had late-onset Group B streptococcus meningitis, which is the swelling of the membranes that cover and protect the brain and spinal cord.
After receiving this news, she said they didn’t know what the future held. It was a “devastating time” for the new parents.
“It’s not just us that’s impacted by this ... it’s my family, it’s Kelvin’s family,” said Power. “I remember saying to Kelvin, like ... let’s take this day by day.”
Tom spent two days in ICU and a week in Temple Street.
“It’s an out-of-body experience ... you’re just like you’re surviving.”
He then spent another three weeks in the Midland Regional Hospital and was on antibiotics for a further six weeks after getting home.
She said it’s “no coincidence we both were sick” but added that it cannot be proven that her GBS sepsis and Tom’s meningitis came from the same infection.
“It is definitely a mother’s instinct ... I just knew something was wrong.
“Trust your gut and ... act when you feel you need to,” she advised.
In January, Tom was diagnosed with hydrocephalus, which is a build-up of fluid in the brain putting pressure on the brain, and a shunt was fitted.
Power said hydrocephalus is a “lifelong illness” which can be caused as a result of meningitis. “We have to be extremely vigilant with Tom.”
“He’s impacted for life, like, that does not go away,” she said.
She and her husband were “worried” about him hitting milestones. “We were told, like, you know, we don’t know what damage this has done.”
However, last month, he started primary school and “is absolutely flying it”.
She said it was “a big relief” for him to start school.
“It’s just after everything Tom’s been through, he’s had, like, two major surgeries, one with getting the shunt in, one with [the] shunt revision, you know, he is as resilient as ever.”
She described him as a “wild” five-year-old, adding that he plays football and hurling.
Power praised the support of Siobhán Carroll of ACT for Meningitis, a national meningitis awareness and support charity. The charity was founded by Siobhán and Noel Carroll following the death of their four-year-old daughter, Aoibhe, to meningitis.
It was set up in 2011 to raise awareness, provide education and free support to families and individuals affected by meningitis.
[ How do I spot if my child has meningitis? Opens in new window ]
Meningitis can develop very quickly and anyone of any age can contract it but babies and young children, teenagers and young adults are among the groups at greater risk, as well as older adults.
Signs and symptoms can include a high temperature, severe headache, vomiting, stiff neck, sensitivity to light, aches and pains, rapid breathing, cold hands and feet, confusion, drowsiness, difficulty waking, seizures and a rash that does not fade under pressure.
For babies, symptoms can include refusing feeds, irritability, an unusual high-pitched cry, a bulging soft spot or being floppy or difficult to wake.

title: Northern Ireland rue missed penalty in Georgia draw
description: Wins for France and Italy in Group A1
content:
Isaac Price missed a late penalty as Northern Ireland were held to a goalless draw by Georgia but nevertheless maintained the top spot in Group B2 in the Nations League .
Liverpool goalkeeper Giorgi Mamardashvili guessed right to keep out Price’s 84th-minute spot-kick after a combination of Nodar Lominadze and Saba Sazonov fouled Ruairi McConville as he sent a header against the crossbar during a goalmouth scramble.
Jamie Donley and Josh Magennis also brought saves out of Mamardashvili and Tom Atcheson felt he had should have had a first-half penalty, but Northern Ireland were held to a stalemate for the second time in a week at Windsor Park.
Georgia, still yet to score in this season’s Nations League, responded to their 1-0 loss to Northern Ireland in Tbilisi 11 days ago by sacking Willy Sagnol, but Ramaz Svanadze is still awaiting his first win in charge despite Khvicha Kvaratskhelia showing flashes of his brilliance in the second half.
Northern Ireland started the night as the only side yet to concede in this season’s Nations League, and Pierce Charles made big saves from Zuriko Davitashvili and Giorgi Tsitaishvili to make it four competitive clean sheets in a row for the first time since 2017.
The 21-year-old goalkeeper’s seventh clean sheet in nine competitive appearances ensured Michael O’Neill’s side remain top of Group B2 by a single point from Hungary.
Meanwhile in Trnava, second-half goals from Milán Tóth and Márk Csinger saw Hungary take a 2-1 win over Ukraine to climb to second, a point behind Northern Ireland.
In Group A1, there were wins for France and Italy, Zinedine Zidane securing his first home win in charge after they came from a ‌goal down to beat Belgium 4-1 at the Stade de France.
Belgium’s Dodi Lukebakio put the visitors ‌ahead ‌in ​the 35th minute, but Desire Doue, Rayan Cherki and Michael Olise, all on ⁠the bench at ​kickoff, turned the match on ​its head in the final 15 minutes.
Doue levelled ‌with a left-footed shot ​from the edge of the box in the 77th ⁠minute. Four minutes ⁠later, Cherki ​put his side in front, finishing from an Olise cross. Olise then completed a brace from close range just before and during stoppage time.
Italy ​took a 3-1 win over Turkey in Bologna, Riccardo ⁠Calafiori and Pio Esposito scoring after Aral Simsir cancelled out Gianluca Scamacca’s opener.
France sit top with 10 points, three ahead of Italy ​and four clear of Belgium, while Turkey ​have four defeats from their opening four games.
In Group B4, an 84th-minute penalty for Ivan Basic earned Bosnia and Herzegovina a 1-0 home win over Poland, and Viktor Gyokeres fired home the winner for Sweden against Romania in Bucharest.
And in League C, Cyprus beat Latvia 2-1 while Montenegro and Armenia played out a goalless draw.

title: Former politician and novelist Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86
description: Former Conservative MP died suddenly at home on Monday
content:
Former politician Jeffrey Archer has died aged 86, his publisher said in a statement.
Archer, who was a Conservative MP for five years before serving as the party’s deputy chairman, died “suddenly and peacefully at his home between writing sessions” on Monday, Harper Collins said.
He had a successful career as a novelist alongside politics and was made a life peer in 1992.
His political career was paused in 2001 with the disgrace of his being imprisoned for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice.
An Old Bailey jury in the UK found that he had lied in a libel action he had brought against The Star newspaper 13 years earlier, in which he was awarded £500,000 damages.
He was released early in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.
Archer made millions out of his best-selling novels, most notably Kane and Abel.
[ ‘Tony O’Reilly should have been president of Ireland’: Jeffrey Archer on life, books and his God-given gift Opens in new window ]
Harper Collins said the author had met and signed books for hundreds of fans at a sold-out event with broadcaster Gyles Brandreth at the Leicester Square Theatre in central London on Sunday.
Writing on X, Brandreth said: “Just yesterday I did a show with Jeffrey Archer to celebrate his new novel – he said it was to be his last.
“He was in the most wonderful, ebullient form and had such a great reception from a packed house. He was funny, engaging and self-deprecating – a great storyteller to the last.”
Archer was due to be at the Cheltenham Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel, Adam and Eve.
He had his wife Mary had celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year. They had two sons and five grandchildren.
Former Tory minister Nadhim Zahawi paid tribute to Archer, writing on X: “Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey’s company.
“Jeffrey, it was a privilege to call you my friend. You were one of a kind. May you rest in eternal peace.”
Kate Elton, Harper Collins UK chief executive and Archer’s editor, said: “It has been one of the great privileges of my publishing life to have been Jeffrey Archer’s editor.
“He was the master storyteller and an editor’s dream – phenomenally hard-working, utterly committed to completing draft after draft to get every word as perfect as possible, and a true champion of the ‘team’ nature of great publishing.” - PA

title: All-Ireland winning Armagh captain Aidan Forker announces intercounty retirement
description: Maghery man led Armagh to first All-Ireland title in 22 years in 2024
content:
Armagh ’s 2024 All-Ireland winning captain Aidan Forker has announced his decision to retire from intercounty football.
The 34-year-old is one of just two Armagh men to captain the Orchard County to Sam Maguire glory, alongside current manager Kieran McGeeney, who led the county to their first title in 2002.
Forker struggled for game-time this season as he battled to overcome ankle and calf problems.
The Maghery clubman announced his retirement on social media on Monday night: “After 15 seasons, I’ve made the decision to step away from Armagh football.
“There will probably never be a right time to write these words for me. Armagh has been part of my life since I was 18 years old. Some very difficult days and, eventually, days that I could only ever have dreamed about. I’ve loved every bit of it.
“I leave with no regrets. Just enormous gratitude for the blessings I received in my football life. God is good. I hope, in some small way, I’ve left the jersey and Armagh football in a better place.
“I’m so excited for this group for 2027 and beyond. I arrived as an 18-year-old who just wanted to play for Armagh. I leave as a husband, a father, and always a proud Armagh man. Thank you for everything.”
Forker is the latest of the 2024 crew to step aside, his announcement coming just days after the retirements of Ethan Rafferty, Rory Grugan and James Morgan.

title: Air campaign against Houthis under way in Yemen, says Saudi-led coalition
description: Houthis have in recent weeks made lightning advances down the west coast of Yemen
content:
Leaders of a Saudi -led coalition in Yemen claimed a broad air campaign involving 100 jet aircraft was under way on Monday against the Iran -backed Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coastline and farther north in the capital, Sana’a.
The Saudi coalition spokesman, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the 100 fighter jets participating in Operation Dawn of Yemen were providing support to forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets. He claimed hundreds of Houthi fighters had been besieged in the Dhubab district, including the airport, close to the Bab al-Mandab strait, with some Houthi fighters fleeing across the Red Sea in boats.
Southern Yemeni forces known as the Giants Brigades, who are allied with the government, earlier on Monday launched a ground offensive against the rebels on the eastern flank of the coastal areas that the Houthis seized in their latest advances. The government forces also claim to have cut the road between Mocha and Dhubab, and that Houthi forces were deserting the recently captured city of Mocha as residents stayed behind closed doors.
Previous Saudi-led statements about territorial gains in recent weeks have often proved partial, but footage appeared to back up the Saudi claims of Houthis retreating by the seashore.
The president of the Saudi-backed government, Rashad al-Alimi, had promised a new offensive on Sunday, saying patience with the Houthis had run out. “Today we are embarking on a decisive phase in the history of our nation,” he said.
Air strikes were also reported on Monday in Sana’a and the Houthi stronghold of Saada in the north of Yemen. Command and control centres, camps and weapons depots were targeted.
The Houthis, who captured Sana’a in 2014, have in recent weeks made lightning advances down the west coast of Yemen, reaching the Bab al-Mandab and seizing strategic islands on the strait.
On Monday, Houthi sources denied reports of a retreat, and pointed to the explosions at a Saudi Aramco plant in Riyadh as a sign of the damage the group could still inflict on exposed Saudi oil installations, and by extension the world economy.
It appears a political agreement reached between the two main external Arab actors in Yemen – Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates ( UAE ) – permitted the UAE-backed Southern Giants to co-ordinate with the Saudi air force in the attack towards the coast.
It is being stressed by the Giants Brigades that no other ground forces supporting the Saudi-backed government are involved in the offensive. The brigades, who are linked with the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a political group outlawed in Yemen for trying to set up a secessionist state, are certain to have sought political commitments about the future status of Yemen in order to have thrown their military weight behind it.
It is not clear how the Saudis propose to address the age-old southern question. Concessions to the STC about the future governance of the south are certain to have been demanded, even if the UAE itself does not return to Yemen.
But the co-operation between the Saudi air force and the Giants Brigades is a remarkable turnaround, since as recently as January the Saudi air force was bombing UAE shipments of arms arriving in Southern Yemen for STC-backed forces.
The Saudi bombing triggered the UAE pullout from Yemen in January, the sudden dissolution of the STC, and the exile of its leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi. At the weekend, his supporters vowed to hold demonstrations later this month in support of the return to a separate southern state.
Houthi government officials claimed British fighter jets were supporting the Saudi air force with refuelling, something the UK ministry of defence has already announced.
The fighting was under way as senior ministers from Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia met in Riyadh to discuss the support Saudi Arabia might need to protect itself from the Houthis. They have formed a joint defence pact, but it is not known how it will operate. – Guardian

title: Would-be Galway mosque bombers made video warning they would carry out further attacks, court hears
description: Court hears ‘Irish Defence Army’ members shared information on making explosive devices in Signal chat group 'Shadows of Eire’
content:
A group styling itself the “Irish Defence Army” planned to smash the windows of a mosque using sledgehammers and throw pipe bombs inside to make a “public statement”, the Special Criminal Court heard on Monday.
The three-judge court also heard evidence that the defendants had a Signal group chat called “Shadows of Eire”, in which they shared information on making improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and discussed their plans to attack a mosque.
The plan was foiled when a Garda drug unit stopped two of the organisation’s members in a car and noted that one of them, Garrett Pollack, was evasive, seemed nervous and his leg was shaking. They searched the car and discovered written oaths, crests and a group manifesto along with materials related to the making of IEDs.
Further investigations showed that the group had prepared a statement written in the past tense taking responsibility for bombing a mosque in Galway. They had also filmed a video in which they warned that they would carry out further attacks and that “an eye for an eye is going to be our approach going forward”.
They said legitimate targets would include mosques, anyone who facilitated the development of accommodation for international protection applicants and estate agents who “house these thugs ahead of our own”. They said they would not target women or children “unless the woman is a threat to our country or loved ones”.
Det Insp Alan McDevitt told barrister Edward Doocey that the Irish Defence Army formed in October 2025 as a splinter from a larger group known as the Irish Citizens Army. He described the splinter organisation as a right-wing extremist, terrorist group with an anti-immigration ideology.
Karolis Peckauskas (39), with an address at Newfoundwell Road, Drogheda, Co Louth, previously pleaded guilty to a charge of attempting to engage in a terrorist activity or a terrorist-linked activity.
Darren Gorman (34), of O’Moore Place, Portlaoise, Co Laois, and Garrett Pollock (36), of Kilhorne Greene, Annalong, Co Down, both pleaded guilty to the same offence.
The details of the offence are that between November 4th and 5th, 2025, the defendants attempted to engage in terrorist activity or terrorist-linked activity by attempting to set fire to the Maryam Mosque at Old Cottages, Monivea Road, Galway, an offence which was aggravated by hatred.
[ Far-right group ‘laughed, joked’ about imminent attack on Galway Mosque, court hears Opens in new window ]
Pollack on Monday pleaded guilty to a further count of possessing an explosive substance on November 4th that year.
McDevitt said that when gardaí stopped Pollack and Peckauskas in a black BMW in Portlaoise on November 4th, 2025, they were each carrying knives. In the car’s boot, gardaí discovered a Tricolour, cable ties, tactical vests, hatchets, a lump hammer, knives, masks, pipe cap ends and five litres of peroxide, which can be used in manufacturing pipe bombs.
They also discovered the organisation’s emblem, gloves, further knives, changes of clothing and knuckle dusters. When gardaí asked Pollock to account for what was found, he said: “We’ve done nothing yet.”
Gardaí searched Pollack’s van, which was parked outside Peckauskas’s home in Drogheda, and found a hidden drawer containing four IEDs.
Peckauskas’s barrister Morgan Shelley told the court that his client offers his “sincere remorse and a sincere apology”. He said Peckauskas wants particularly to apologise to the mosque-going community of Ireland who must have found the offence “extremely traumatising”.
Shelley said Peckauskas became radicalised after joining various online groups and was affected by conspiracy theories, in particular those he learned from a group run by a former broadsheet journalist.
Lawyers for Gorman and Pollack will make their pleas in mitigation to the court next Friday.

title: Man accused of importing crystal meth worth €32m seeks access to witnesses’ phones
description: State’s case is the drugs were imported from Mexico and stored at the Ballyseedy Garden Centre before being transported to Cork
content:
The trial of a man charged with the country’s largest-ever crystal meth seizure, valued at more than €32 million, has been adjourned until Friday after he sought access to witnesses’ phones.
James Leen (43) of Pilgrim Hill, Kilmorna, Listowel, Co Kerry , faces five charges including one for directing the activities of a criminal organisation between February 7th, 2023, and February 16th, 2024.
Leen is also charged with the importation of methylamphetamine, better known as crystal meth, at Cork Port, Ringaskiddy, Co Cork , on October 16th, 2023.
He is further charged with possession of crystal meth at Ballyseedy Garden Centre in Tralee between October 27th, 2023, and February 12th, 2024.
The case relates to the seizure of 564kg of methamphetamine, or crystal meth, with an estimated value of €32.8 million from a container at Cork Port on February 16th, 2024.
The State’s case is that the drugs were imported from Mexico and stored at the Ballyseedy Garden Centre before being transported to Cork, where they were destined for export to Australia .
Leen’s trial at the Special Criminal Court was expected to get under way on Monday.
However, Colm Smyth, counsel for Leen, asked for an adjournment so an expert in Texas in the US can analyse data from phones belonging to various proposed witnesses in the trial.
John Berry, for the Director of Public Prosecutions , said gardaí have already disclosed to the defence all relevant material from those phones.
He said a difficulty arises because the defence wants access to all data on those phones, including that which is deeply personal to the witnesses and not relevant to the trial.
He said Irish courts have no jurisdiction to impose conditions on an expert working in the US that would safeguard that information.
Judge Caroline Biggs, presiding at the three-judge, non-jury court, said there are experts in Ireland who can carry out the work suggested.
She said it was not appropriate to come into court on the day of the trial and ask for an adjournment for the same reason an adjournment was given a year ago.
She asked that every effort be made to secure an Irish expert this week and adjourned the matter until Friday.
If there are no Irish companies who can do the work, she said the court would consider whether it is appropriate to allow the data to be analysed outside the jurisdiction.

title: Almost all schools to close for second day in coming weeks as unions turn the screw
description: Leaders of country’s four largest public service unions met on Monday to consider escalation of their dispute over a new pay deal
content:
A second one-day strike in the coming weeks is set to close almost all the country’s schools as well as cause substantial disruption across the health, local government and justice systems.
Teachers’ unions will formally serve notice to the Government on Tuesday of strikes on October 14th and 21st after leaders of the country’s four largest public service unions met on Monday to consider escalation of their dispute over a new national pay deal.
Irish National Teachers’ Organisation ( INTO ) general secretary John Boyle said the unions had previously agreed there would be a one-day strike on the 14th with the 21st to be decided upon.
However, he said the lack of progress since a work-to-rule started across many sectors of the public and civil service last Wednesday had persuaded officials to press ahead with notification of the second strike.
The INTO and Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland commenced work-to-rules on Monday, and Boyle said the experience of members with parents was generally supportive.
However, he noted children could not, in many cases, be dropped at schools before their official start time and had to, in many instances, be picked up immediately after classes finished.
“Some of the parents didn’t understand why we are doing this, but it makes sense to people when you tell them we want these pay talks to be first and foremost about pay.
“People do understand that, including private sector workers and the many parents who are public servants themselves.”
[ ‘They deserve to be on a good wage’: Dublin parents back teachers on industrial action Opens in new window ]
“We have three school weeks of work-to-rule, which is pretty much looking like it is going to be guaranteed. In that period, there’s going to be two school closures.
“So there’s no doubt that by the time the 21st comes, and all these workers across the public service, teachers, nurses, guards have been taking action, the general public is going to be feeling it.”
Members of the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation , Siptu and Fórsa are already engaged in the work-to-rule, with hospital doctor members of the Irish Medical Organisation , teachers in the Teachers Union of Ireland and members of Unite among those set to join in the action and strike next week.
Boyle said that, while the unions were being accused of setting preconditions about any talks, “all we are looking for is certain assurances that it’s not all about going forward into 2027, that there is some acknowledgment of the pressures that people are under in 2026″.
Speaking in advance of Tuesday’s budget , Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said he would make “a very significant allocation” for public pay for 2027.
“This disruption is completely unnecessary,” he said. “The Government wants to get a pay deal with all public workers.
“A pay negotiation is about engaging on a whole range of matters, and there is a well-structured process to do that with trade union representatives. I would encourage all the public sector unions to engage in substantive talks.”

title: Sinn Féin seeks to regulate ‘wild west’ horse-drawn carriage industry in Dublin
description: Arcane Victorian laws allowing ‘unregulated, irresponsible drivers’ to operate in the capital, says TD
content:
Legislation to regulate horse-drawn carriages in Dublin has been introduced to deal with the “wild west situation” of “irresponsible” carriage drivers operating in Dublin amid concerns about animal welfare.
Sinn Féin Dublin Mid-West TD Mark Ward said Dublin has a “long-standing cultural tradition of proper urban horsemanship” that goes back centuries in parts of the south inner city and Liberties.
But this tradition is “being undermined by gaps in regulations and arcane Victorian legislation”. He said previous licensed carriage drivers who meet Dublin City Council ’s standards and requirements under old bylaws are “working alongside unlicensed carriage drivers”.
“This has led to a wild west situation, where unregulated, irresponsible carriage drivers are operating in our city,” he added.
Traditional horse-drawn carriage drivers – or jarveys – have appealed for regulations to be brought in amid complaints from residents, tourists and animal welfare charities.
Sinn Féin TD Máire Devine said there has been a “legal lacuna” for more than seven years, and enforcement around Dublin’s horse carriage industry is “conflicting, outdated, inconsistent and inadequate”.
Informal regulation has been in place since a review of legislation in 2018, which found Dublin City Council did not have power to regulate horse-drawn carriage operators under legislation dating to back to 1853.
Devine said horse carriages in the capital are currently governed by three Victorian-era Acts that “effectively prevent Dublin City Council from making and enforcing modern bylaws to regulate carriage operators, licensing, safety and insurance”. She said this placed passengers, pedestrians and motorists “in peril”.
The Dublin South-Central TD said the party’s Local Government (Control of Horse Drawn Carriages) Bill repeals the 1853 Dublin Carriage Act and subsequent 1850s amending legislation with a 90-day period to allow the enactment of new bylaws to “ensure carriage operators are reputable and, most importantly, safe”.
The legislation would also introduce bylaws to deal with the disposal of dung. “The constituents in Dublin South-Central and the at least 1.5 million visitors to the Liberties area are dealing with streets full of dung , as the Dublin City Council stopped accepting it last year for disposal,” said Devine.
She said residents are “not just frustrated by the dung, but also by the antisocial behaviour and mistreatment of horses by unlicensed operators”.
The Government is not opposing the Sinn Féin legislation, which has to wait for the lottery system for Private Members’ legislation to be debated.
The Department of Transport has said it expects a draft general scheme for legislation on horse-drawn carriages to be ready by the end of 2026 or early 2027 following a consultation with stakeholders.
The National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals has also called for reform of the legislation to ensure animal welfare “remains the primary consideration in any future decisions affecting the industry”.
The charity called for stronger welfare protections and oversight but wants a phased removal of horse-drawn carriage operations because modern urban environments are “increasingly incompatible with the welfare needs of horses”.
Ward pointed to a social media post in April of a “terrifying video of a terrified horse going down O’Connell Street during rush hour”.
“We have also seen tourists being ripped off by unscrupulous carriage drivers by overcharging them.”
He said it was not uncommon in the Temple Bar area at 2am to see a horse-drawn carriage “bringing drunken tourists from one part to another”.

title: The Irish Times view on Spain’s  snap election: Sánchez plots another escape
description: Right bloc enjoys a comfortable poll lead, but victory is not guaranteed
content:
For some time, EU politics has been conducted in anticipation that France’s presidential election in 2027 will define the union’s next phase. Pedro Sánchez’s decision to call a Spanish general election for November 29th has added an unexpected twist.
Spain is not as central to the union as France, but it is the EU’s fourth-largest economy, and Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition is the most prominent left-wing government among the 27. On migration, defence spending and Palestine it has defied the prevailing centre-right consensus. If, as seems possible, it is replaced by a right-wing bloc including the far-right Vox, the balance in Brussels will tilt further, and the most visible model of social democratic resistance to the prevailing mood will have fallen.
The right enjoys a comfortable poll lead, but victory is not guaranteed. Sánchez is a wily operator who confounded similar predictions of defeat in 2023, returning at the head of a minority administration propped up by Catalan and Basque nationalists. That arithmetic was always fragile, as last week’s defeat of his emergency housing measures demonstrated.
He clearly calculates that housing, which has brought thousands onto the streets since the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid, can galvanise left-wing voters already alarmed by the prospect of Vox entering national government for the first time. He may be right. But he must contend with a steady drip of corruption cases involving former lieutenants and members of his own family. He also needs the fragmented parties to his left, now scrambling to agree a common platform, to avoid squandering seats under Spain’s electoral system.
There is a contradiction in fighting an election on housing. Sánchez can point to real achievements, including labour reforms, a big increase in the minimum wage and growth forecast at roughly three times the euro zone rate. On housing, however, his record is thin. Rents have soared, public building has lagged, and allies on his left accuse him of offering gestures rather than action.
If he loses, his successor will be Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the centre-right Partido Popular, with Vox either joining a coalition or supporting a minority government. That would mean a sudden change of course on defence, immigration and the Middle East, where Spain has stood alongside Ireland as one of the EU’s most outspoken critics of Israel’s conduct in Gaza.
With almost eight weeks of campaigning ahead, there is room for twists and turns. If Sánchez repeats his 2023 escape, he will cement his reputation as one of the great survivors of modern European politics. But escapology alone is not enough, and even an unlikely victory would leave him hostage to the fractious arithmetic of Spanish politics.

title: At Plaid Cymru’s annual party conference, it wasn’t always clear who the protesters were
description: After destroying Labour in May’s Senedd elections, Plaid Cymru is now in charge
content:
I t was a century in the making, but Welsh nationalist party Plaid Cymru ’s ascension this year to lead national government for the first time still seems to be in transition.
Governing party conferences always attract protests. Yet at Plaid’s conference last weekend in the north Wales seaside town of Llandudno – its first gathering since it swept Labour from power in May – it wasn’t always clear who the protesters were, and who they were protesting against.
Llandudno is a pleasant old Victorian resort town, more attractive than others of its ilk. The town’s genteel air was reflected in the halfhearted protests that showed up as Plaid members gathered at Venue Cymru on the promenade.
A seemingly ridiculously over-policed pro-Palestine protest ambled along the seafront in Saturday’s glorious sunshine, halting outside the venue for a rally. Plaid is already one of the most pro-Palestine parties on the island of Britain.
Instead of lambasting the government, as protesters tend to do, the first speaker spoke about how “refreshing” it was to have a party in power that shared their views – a few of the crowd actually wore Plaid conference passes.
The second rally speaker was one of the Welsh government’s most senior figures, deputy first minister Sioned Williams. Amid a sea of fluttering Palestine flags, Welsh dragons, Lebanese flags and even a few Iranian ones, the “protest” crowd clapped Williams as she criticised Israel.
Another apparent protester in a green Morris Minor pickup drove up and down the promenade outside the venue, beeping his horn. Attached to his vintage van were the national flags of Wales, Scotland, England and a British Union Jack.
Nobody, including bemused security, could figure out what he was saying, but it was widely assumed he must be pro-union. If he was, he was very friendly about it, waving at Plaid delegates each time he zoomed past.
The only real animus towards Plaid came from striking Unite union health workers. They accused party leader and new Welsh first minister Rhun ap Iorwerth of backtracking on a promise to support them. “Plaid lied” said their alliterative t-shirts.
[ Behind the mystery that first set off fears of Iranian threats at a UK military base Opens in new window ]
Beyond that, it was plain sailing for ap Iorwerth, a former BBC political journalist. His conference speech was well received, although with less of the visible giddiness that greeted his speech a year ago when it was becoming obvious Plaid might win.
Ap Iorwerth complained after May’s Senedd elections that he couldn’t even secure a meeting with then UK prime minister Keir Starmer . Will new UK leader Andy Burnham be any better for Wales?
“Yes, I think so,” ap Iorwerth told The Irish Times. He says Burnham assured him in a meeting he was open to the idea of devolving policing and justice powers to Wales, a key Plaid demand, and would look at other issues.
Ap Iorwerth thinks Burnham “instinctively believes” in more devolution for Wales: “But he is surrounded by people in the parliamentary Labour Party who have shown in recent years they are ideologically opposed.”
In Cardiff, the new Welsh government’s first big task is to pass a budget – it is five seats short of a majority.
Many of the rump of Welsh Labour that survived in May are said to be followers of old leader Vaughan Gething, rather than another former Welsh Labour leader, Mark Drakeford. “Drakefordites” are thought by Plaid delegates to be bigger believers in Welsh power, while “Gethingites,” it is claimed, look more towards UK Labour for leadership.
Plaid previously helped minority Welsh Labour governments pass budgets, but so far, it is unrequited. The Plaid government has already lost one supplementary budget vote after Labour refused support. Ap Iorwerth is seeking support for a draft budget vote in six weeks. If Plaid cannot pass a budget, it will struggle to govern.
One of Burnham’s big recent announcements was a plan for a national social care service for the elderly. Speaking on the margins of the Plaid conference, Delyth Jewell, the Welsh government minister with responsibility for social care, said she had already written to Burnham’s government about the plans.
“It was in our manifesto already, so England is just catching up with us in Wales. But I welcome the fact that the UK prime minister has brought this to the top of the agenda,” she said. “Burnham’s sincerity on this issue really does shine through.”
Liz Saville-Roberts, leader of Plaid’s four-strong group of MPs in Westminster, also said the ascension of Burnham made her more “optimistic” for co-operation with Wales.
“He is more prepared to have conversations. Starmer was just: ‘close it all down.’ But while I may like Burnham, he is not my friend,” she said.
A recent poll suggested that if Burnham called an early election, Plaid could win up to 15 Westminster seats in a hung parliament. That could give it the balance of power. She was “cautious” about the possibility, but that is a card Saville-Roberts said Plaid should be “pragmatic” about playing.
Her party leader agreed. Would Plaid prop up a Burnham government if it meant winning more powers for Wales?
“If we are in the position of more influence in Westminster, to push forward on empowering the people of Wales ... absolutely that is what we are there to do,” said ap Iorwerth. Maybe Plaid’s pivot to power isn’t such a big transition after all.
[ Andy Burnham raises prospect of UK rejoining European Union after next election Opens in new window ]

title: Man (43) to be sentenced for manslaughter of mother of two in Mallow stabbing incident
description: Joseph Butler inflicted an 11cm wound when he stabbed 31-year-old Paula Canty in Mallow, Co Cork, on January 3rd, 2025
content:
A 43-year-old man has been remanded in custody for sentence after he pleaded guilty to the manslaughter of a young mother of two.
Joseph Butler, of the Belfry, Bridewell Lane, Mallow, had been charged with the murder of 31-year-old Paula Canty at the Belfry, Bridewell Lane, Mallow on January 3rd, 2025.
However, his plea of manslaughter was accepted by the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), the Central Criminal Court in Cork was told.
Det Sgt Mícheál O’Regan of Mallow Garda station outlined the background to the killing after Paula Canty and her partner, Michael John Butler, and his brother, the accused, had been socialising at different houses in Mallow late on January 2nd.
All three had been drinking and returned at separate times to the apartment they shared at the Belfry. Joseph Butler returned home at 1.50am, his brother Michael John Butler at 2.21am, and Paula Canty at 2.31am.
A row subsequently broke out and Joseph Butler stabbed Paula Canty in the chest. When Michael John Butler rang the emergency services at 10.16am, paramedics attended the third floor flat and found Paula Canty lying unresponsive in a pool of blood. She was pronounced dead at the scene.
A postmortem by Assistant State Pathologist Dr Margot Bolster found Paula Canty died from haemorrhage and shock due to a single stab wound to the chest. The 11cm deep wound was such that she would have collapsed immediately.
Garda investigations led them to identify Joseph Butler as a suspect, and he was identified on CCTV carrying a knife as he left the apartment at 4.07am on January 3rd. He was later arrested and brought to Mallow Garda station for questioning.
O’Regan told how Joseph Butler told Det Garda Aidan Long as his details were being entered into the custody record at Mallow Garda station: “ If I did it, it was an accident – she was a friend, family,” before going on to tell Long where he had thrown away the knife.
[ Man (43) pleads guilty to manslaughter of mother-of-two Paula Canty Opens in new window ]
“Back to the house, Michael and myself were fighting, throwing boxes, missing more than we hit. I was calling Paula bad words, bringing up her past. Paula pulled a knife, struggle. I pushed Paula away and grabbed the knife. Accident over the struggle.
“I said ‘keep the house’ and I left with the knife. Paula was grand when I left. I went up Chinese Lane and threw the knife away on the grass. Had to happen in the struggle. I couldn’t see Michael John stabbing Paula to death.”
