Joseph Butler then asked the detective: “Would you feel guilty if you murdered someone?” When Long replied he would, Butler responded: “I don’t feel guilty. It was an accident, she’s family – I didn’t know she was dead until I got a phone call at 10.30am from my niece.”
O’Regan said Paula Canty was found lying in a pool of her blood, but there was no blood spatter pattern, which disproved Joseph Butler’s claim that she Canty was fine when he left, and confirmed the pathologist’s view that she collapsed immediately after being stabbed.
Det Garda Ann O’Flynn read victim impact statements on behalf of Paula Canty’s mother, Sinead, her brother, Darragh, and her sister, Rianna, in which they spoke about how their lives had been changed irrevocably by Paula’s death.
Prosecution counsel Donal O’Sullivan said it was the DPP’s view that the crime merited a sentence of between 10 and 15 years. He also said the court should give consideration to Joseph Butler’s criminal record, which comprised 50 previous convictions including ones for assault, assault causing harm, aggravated burglary, possession of a knife, threats to kill, harassment, criminal damage and public order offences.
Defence counsel Ray Boland pleaded for leniency, pointing out Joseph Butler was genuinely remorseful as evidenced by the fact that he had offered a guilty plea of manslaughter at an early stage, and he suggested that suspending a portion of his sentence would incentivise rehabilitation.
Judge Eileen Creedon thanked both for their submissions and said she would need time to consider those along with the victim impact statements and the evidence she had heard. She remanded Joseph Butler in continuing custody until October 16th, when she will sentence him.

title: Galway City Council ordered to pause tree felling by High Court
description: The local authority ordered the felling in response to damage caused by Storm Éowyn in January 2025
content:
Galway City Council has been ordered by the High Court to pause the felling of trees at a forest on the outskirts of the city following an injunction application by local residents.
Friends of Merlin Woods allege the city council is engaged in the unlawful removal of trees from lands at the forest.
Tom Flynn was granted a temporary injunction on Monday on behalf of the advocacy group, ordering the council to stop felling works at the forest. Judge Richard Humphreys said the case could return next week.
The injunction application follows the commencement of the felling works at the forest by a contractor working on behalf of Galway City Council.
The council ordered the felling in response to damage caused by Storm Éowyn in January 2025. The council said it plans to replant native trees at the impacted area.
In written evidence, Caroline Stanley, spokeswoman for Friends of Merlin Wood, said the group supported the council’s initial plans to remove storm-damaged trees.
“However, subsequently it has become clear that the project is now to fell 15.41 hectares of Merlin Woods, almost half of the entire woodland, and with a proposal at some stage to apply for funding to replant the trees,” Stanley said.
“For the avoidance of doubt, the [group] unreservedly opposes how this plan is now being implemented, and never consented to it,” she said.
The council has already cleared about 3.5 hectares of woodland, and intends to fell the balance of the 15-hectare area, the group said.
[ Galway’s Taaffes shop, empty for 30 years, has a new owner Opens in new window ]
The group has concerns about the impact of the felling on the biodiversity of the forest.
The group said it has engaged an expert who has expressed concerns about the council’s plans for the forest, and the need for the felling of trees in the manner proposed by the local authority.
Stanley said the group asked the council to pause the felling in order to discuss the impact of its plans on the biodiversity of the woodland.
“We feel that our voice has fell on deaf ears, and we have been left with no option but to seek recourse to legal action,” she said.

title: Judgment reserved in legal challenge to Orange Order parade on Garvaghy Road
description: Drumcree standoff: Three senior judges promised to deliver verdict on latest legal challenge to the march ‘swiftly’, but did not provide a date
content:
A Belfast court hopes to issue its decision on an appeal against the controversial Orange parade at Drumcree “within a swift enough time frame” following a highly anticipated hearing.
However, following proceedings on Monday, the Court of Appeal was unable to give a specific date for its ruling over the dispute at the centre of the ongoing standoff in Portadown .
Three senior judges at the Court of Appeal in Belfast heard submissions on Monday from barristers representing the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition and the Parades Commission .
The residents are challenging an earlier High Court decision to refuse leave to apply for a judicial review of the determination by the commission to permit the Orange Order to parade from Drumcree church along the Garvaghy Road on September 27th.
They were not able to proceed after the road was blocked by residents, and a standoff is continuing in the area with protesters maintaining a presence.
Denise Kiley, appearing for the residents, argued the Parades Commission had failed to “properly weigh” information from the Police Service of Northern Ireland ( PSNI ) around the potential for disorder.
She said it “didn’t properly understand the police assessment”, and therefore reached an “irrational conclusion” in permitting it to go ahead.
The barrister for the Parades Commission, Tony McGleenan, said the body was “fully briefed” by police, including “about the police resource and their ability to contain any disorder or reaction that occurred”.
He said the suggestion it had made a legal error “doesn’t bear scrutiny” and that just because people disagree with the outcome “doesn’t make it irrational”.
Richard McConkey, who represents a member of the Orange Order from Portadown, said: “Our position is obviously that the appeal should be dismissed.”
At the conclusion of several hours of proceedings on Monday, Chief Justice Siobhan Keegan told the court she and her fellow judges “will reserve our decision”. She said it would “hopefully” be delivered “within a swift enough time frame” but she was unable to give a date.
Inside the Court of Appeal, the public gallery was full, with DUP MP Carla Lockhart sitting beside loyalist activist Jamie Bryson in the front row, and Breandán Mac Cionnaith and other Garvaghy Road residents seated behind.
[ Breandán Mac Cionnaith profile: The ex-IRA man who Tony Blair said ‘took unreasonableness to an art form’ Opens in new window ]
Speaking to reporters after the conclusion of the hearing, Bryson – who is providing legal representation to the Portadown District Orange Lodge – said they would “abide by the law”.
He condemned the “mobs” who, he said, had resulted in Lockhart requiring security protection. “The contrast we have here is the law and the mob, and we stand on the side of the law,” he said.
Lockhart said it was “a sad reflection on society when you stand outside court, and you are abused, threatened” and the Orangemen “deserve the right to fulfil their legal determination to walk the Garvaghy Road”.
Also addressing reporters afterwards, Mac Cionnaith said their legal team was “very clear on what the situation was in relation to the parade, and I don’t think we have anything to regret so far. I am not going to prejudge the outcome”.
[ Drumcree consequences will be profound. That’s why it’s a line in the sand for nationalists Opens in new window ]
In court, Kiley described the Drumcree march as “one of the most polarising parades in the history of Northern Ireland ”.
She said it was not accepted that the Parades Commission’s determination remained live – “we say that it is spent because the date and time within has passed” – but this did not form part of Monday’s case.
Outlining a number of grounds for the appeal, she said there was a “public interest” in ensuring the Parades Commission “comes to correct and lawful determinations”.
The barrister said it had a “duty” to explain its decision but had failed to do so, arguing that “where a decision has consistently been made on one basis for 28 years, then a change cries out for explanation”.
She also argued the body had failed to take into account the potential for the parade to trigger “wider disorder”.
McGleenan told the court the commission’s determination was a “detailed 31-paragraph written analysis” which “has to be read in its totality”.

title: ‘Appalling attack’: Man forced into bin and pushed on to railway tracks at Dublin Dart station
description: Gardaí appeal for witnesses to incident at Harmonstown station on Sunday night
content:
Gardaí have appealed for witnesses after a young man was forced into a bin and pushed on to railway tracks in Dublin .
The male youth was hurt in the incident at Harmonstown Dart Station on Sunday night, but managed to climb back on to the platform despite his injuries.
However, the bin was still on the tracks when the next train arrived.
Barry Kenny of Irish Rail said the driver spotted it and was able to stop in time, but if an express train had been due, it would have taken longer to bring it to a halt.
He said if the injured person had been incapacitated on the tracks, the outcome could have been tragic.
“This was an appalling attack which had the potential to be much worse,” he said.
The attack happened at the station on Dublin’s northside at around 8pm, and it is understood a group of people were involved.
Gardaí at Raheny are investigating the incident and are asking anyone who was at the station between 7.45pm and 9pm and who may have witnessed it to contact them.
Anyone who may have camera footage is also asked to make that footage available.
Irish Rail, which has provided CCTV footage to gardaí, backed the call for the public’s help.
Trains were delayed for a time on Sunday evening while the track was cleared and the injured youth received medical treatment.

title: Ireland v Israel was no ordinary match assignment. Irish journalists were watched and filmed
description: Recurring presence of out-of-place people combined with blatant filming of reporters made for a deeply uncomfortable week
content:
War is peace, freedom is slavery, and football doesn’t mix with politics.
We began this international window about eight years ago in Kosovo, where Ireland manager Heimir Hallgr ímsson expressed gratitude to the Taoiseach for defending him and his use of the word “genocide” while talking to reporters at the United Nations General Assembly.
Each night in Pristina was scored to the sounds of protesters demanding the release of four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), recently sentenced to prison for war crimes committed during the war of independence from Serbia. Stalls lined the boulevard to Mother Teresa Square, selling KLA-branded hats and t-shirts along with Kosovo football scarves. The same KLA merch was sold duty free at Pristina airport.
The match against Kosovo was a party political broadcast: the stands were a patchwork of red KLA flags, the Kosovan fans continually chanted for the KLA and when Vedat Muriqi scored the only goal, he held up a t-shirt in support of the jailed leaders.
The following day we stopped in Munich on our way to Debrecen, where an Israeli TV journalist approached us in the airport. His greeting came with a slap on the back so firm it still stung as he began talking. He asked us about rumours the Irish team were going to cancel their press conference, then offered to trade some team news and told us where both teams were staying in Debrecen. It was at this moment The Irish Times learned we were going to be checking into the Israeli team hotel.
We arrived at the hotel as the Israeli FA were unloading their gear. This inelegant piece of scripting around a baggage-laden fixture had us stepping over Israeli kit bags to get inside the front door. The eight Irish journalists staying in the hotel were all given rooms beside one another in a corner of the third floor, while armed, plain-clothes security personnel kept a round-the-clock watch on the lobby and the hotel restaurant.
This sense of being watched extended to the Irish team hotel, where FAI security couldn’t help but notice the regular presence of a burly man in the lobby. They saw him check out shortly after the Irish team left. There were also some Irish fans staying in the Israeli team hotel and when their tickets were cancelled a couple of hours before the game, they wound up watching the game in that hotel.
Saturday in Debrecen was an extraordinary day, and not just because of the story we were covering. The principal drama was taking place at the Irish team hotel, but there was a feeling of covering it from a theatrical stage, onto which Irish journalists had been unwittingly cast as actors in the production.
It felt as if we were being constantly watched and filmed, and when we gathered outside the Irish team hotel after the squad missed their training session, we were persistently photographed by an Israeli press photographer. Another journalist took videos of us on her phone and whenever an Irish TV reporter did a piece to camera, she filmed the entirety of the report. This was a strangely dissociating experience: trying to report on what you are seeing and hearing while also feeling watched in some way.
Earlier, at the stadium, two Israeli journalists had approached me to talk about the horrors of the October 7th, 2023 attacks. They segued into telling me that the Irish people did not understand the truth because they are being presented with an “alternate reality”. Several Irish colleagues had the same experience.
These approaches were conducted behind a veneer of friendliness that quickly wore thin. While I was frantically filing news of Gavin Bazunu’s withdrawal from the squad on Saturday morning, an Israeli journalist stormed up to me, haranguing me over a comment on X I had supposedly posted minutes earlier describing the two national flags hanging in the stadium as surreal. The thrust of her argument was that the use of the word “surreal” was another attempt to delegitimise Israel’s presence.
An Israeli colleague filmed the confrontation on his phone, as I finally persuaded them that this was a case of mistaken identity. They left the room, returned a minute later to abashedly apologise, and then marched across the room to find the Irish journalist who had actually posted the comment. Again she harangued him, and again her colleague filmed it on his phone.
The atmosphere in the press room chilled and an Israeli TV journalist did a piece to camera, during which he said: “My gut feeling is the Irish journalists don’t really like us.”
Which is not to say there was no collegiality at all, for it was an Israeli journalist who told us outside the team hotel that the Irish squad had confirmed they would be going to train at the stadium. Another regular refrain from the Israeli media was, “Wow, your FA really doesn’t tell you anything”. If the ambition here was to drive a wedge between the Irish press and the FAI, both parties would bleakly laugh, knowing we have never needed any help in that regard.
Amid the head-spinning tumult of it all, I took a call from TalkSport outside the Irish team hotel to do a quick piece on air to explain what was happening. Once I hung up, a friend from home sent me a screengrab of the image they had used of me during the call. It was a screengrab from a spoof social media video I did with a former employer 10 years ago, in which I wore a novelty hat and a garish green blazer embossed with shamrocks.
Standing in front of Israeli photographers, this was a suboptimal time to be outed as some sort of Irish partisan. I had an attack of self-regard and complained to TalkSport about the use of the image. They told me they found it on Instagram, assumed I was simply a “wacky dresser” and assured me they didn’t think the begorrahness of it all undermined my authority on this diplomatic firestorm.
By the time Ireland’s former minister for justice Alan Shatter walked into the press box on Sunday, accredited to write a match report for the Jerusalem Post, the general reaction from the Irish press was the collective shrug of a group of people deeply weary of surprise.
Amid the hyperreality to which the game belonged, the Irish players created a resonant image of their own, bowing their heads for the Israeli national anthem. Some Kosovo players would re-enact the picture against Israel a few days later. As Ireland cruised to victory in Debrecen , there was another moment of choreography in the stands – a telegenic Israel fan recording himself leading supporters in chants for the IDF. He wore a t-shirt bearing a giant QR code beneath a slogan stating, “Hallgrímsson, this is a genocide”.
In Serbia, ahead of the second meeting between the teams, Israel’s head of communications did not condemn the chanting as he rejected the notion that the IDF is a political entity.
Before the trip to Serbia, though, we had returned to Dublin for our more traditional blend of politics and football at an Oireachtas Committee . In this setting, the FAI were subject to the usual staccato blend of forensic questioning and scattergun grandstanding. Meanwhile, the Irish football writers who had covered the game in Debrecen had become besieged by anonymous social media accounts attempting to further distort reality. The faceless accounts argued that the playing of the game in Hungary, and the subsequent muted protests against Austria in Dublin, proved the whole Israel controversy was the latest concoction by hysterical left-wing activists posing as sports journalists.
Backa Topola proved a fittingly alien stage for the fortnight’s final act, with Saturday’s pre-match press conference going viral across the world. The FAI assertively shut down the press conference after an Israeli TV journalist accused the Irish players of calling the Israel players “monkeys” a week earlier. He insisted he was asking a question, but the FAI had found no evidence for the accusation when they looked into it as it was not included in the referee’s report. The Israeli FA subsequently confirmed they had not yet made a complaint to Uefa about the allegation.
As the FAI press officer took the microphone from the journalist’s hand, an Israeli colleague was filming the incident on their phone. This footage was briskly posted online and quickly condemned in Israel as another episode of Irish censoriousness and hypocrisy. “They respect freedom of the press provided you only ask the questions they find comfortable to answer,” posted Israel’s ambassador to the EU. The FAI employee in the video was subsequently subjected to appalling online abuse.
This spectacle caused Uefa to intervene, and they excluded the Israeli journalist and a female colleague from the post-match press conferences on Sunday. The latter journalist tried to access the press room nonetheless, and spent several minutes in a standoff with security guards at the door, one of whom checked our passes to allow us to slip quietly inside.
A Uefa media relations official was scrambled to the match on Sunday, and he began both press conferences with a disclaimer warning not to ask any political questions. This felt, at the very final moment, a sort of vindication: this was not Uefa telling us that football and politics do not mix, but that they should not mix. Uefa’s unspoken subtext, of course, was that both had been mingling to the point of indistinction and they now had to do something about it.
Their intervention came two weeks too late.

title: The Irish Times view on the PTSB sale: stick with the plan
description: Another expression of interest has appeared, but the only offer on the table is from Bawag
content:
The proposed sale of PTSB to Austrian Bank Bawag has reached a crucial stage. Shareholders have voted in favour of the deal. The High Court has to give the go-ahead in a hearing due later this month and could face a demand from some minority shareholders for a separate vote.
Into this evolving picture came an unexpected development, when on Friday a corporate finance firm, Axis, said it was considering making a bid. This came late in the day – some 11 months after the bank was put up for sale.
Axis, co-founded by Mark Duffy – who previously headed Bank of Scotland (Ireland) – has promised to pay a higher price than Bawag. But, unusually, it as yet has no funders and no corporate finance advisers. Both would be expected from a potential bidder with serious intentions.
The Government and the bank’s board are thus correct to say they will stick to the plan to sell to Bawag. The High Court hearing on October 27th is the next step in this process. It remains to be seen if some minority shareholders will use the Axis expression of interest to try to bolster their case that the valuation of the Bawag bid is in question and that minority shareholders should be granted a separate vote on the sale.
A majority of these shareholders voted to accept the Bawag offer, but less than the 75 per cent normally required in such votes. The Government’s vote was thus vital. PTSB says it has strong legal advice that this was a correct procedure. Clearly it is now up to the High Court to decide.
The purchase of PTSB by a large, well-resourced EU bank would appear to be the best route to developing the bank and turning it into a genuine third force in the Irish banking market. This is important, as competition has been limited in some areas of the market in recent years , given the dominant position of AIB and Bank of Ireland. Smaller competitors have chipped away at parts of the market, but the huge deposit bases of the big players puts them in a strong position. A purchase of PTSB by Bawag is the best available route to addressing this.

title: Ethiopian government forces claim control of Tigray’s capital
description: Government-allied militia says it gained control of Mekelle after rebel offensive left country on brink of civil war
content:
Pro-government forces have claimed control of Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray region in northern Ethiopia , in what would be a major blow to the rebel alliance fighting to overthrow prime minister Abiy Ahmed.
The Tigray Peace Forces, a militia allied to the government, said on Facebook that they had gained control of Mekelle over the weekend, paving the way for the Ethiopian National Defence Force to follow.
That came after the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) withdrawal from the city in what it portrayed as a tactical retreat designed to preserve civilian lives.
Last month, the TPLF joined an alliance with six other regional rebel groups to launch a wide-scale offensive on several fronts, in a revival of the devastating 2020 to 2022 civil war that claimed up to 600,000 lives.
The latest fighting threatens to plunge Africa’s second-most populous country into full-scale crisis, potentially drawing in regional powers and endangering the country’s economic growth – among the fastest in Africa, despite near-constant insecurity.
According to the World Bank, Ethiopia’s economy has grown at between 5 and 10 per cent annually over the past decade, averaging about 8 per cent.
This time, fighting has spread into the Afar and Amhara regions, where ethnonationalist militias allied to the TPLF have claimed some gains. But a counteroffensive by the Ethiopian army has now made significant advances into Tigray.
Analysts say divisions among former commanders within the region, some of whom are now aligned with the government, may have weakened the TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 but was sidelined after Abiy took office.
[ Who is poisoning Kenya’s elephants? Opens in new window ]
Debretsion Gebremichael, the TPLF chair, said on Thursday that the movement would not seek to hold fixed positions. It would instead choose where it attacked the Ethiopian federal army, he said in his first televised statement since the outbreak of fighting.
“We know where and when to hit,” he said, suggesting that his forces would repeat the guerrilla tactics they deployed in the mountainous region during the last conflict.
The eruption of fighting in Ethiopia, a country of 130 million people, comes at a febrile moment in the Horn of Africa, with rising tensions between regional power blocs. Analysts have warned for months that a return to war inside the country risks provoking a regional conflagration.
The federal government in Addis Ababa claims that the rebels are backed by Egypt – at loggerheads with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and its potential impact on the flow of the Nile – Sudan and neighbouring Eritrea, with which it broke diplomatic ties last week.
Sudan in turn has accused Ethiopia of training and supporting the Rapid Support Forces militia with which it is fighting a bloody civil war.
Egypt’s foreign minister denied backing the TPLF and its allies. “I have to be very clear, we are not party to the domestic crisis facing Ethiopia now. It has nothing to do with us,” Badr Abdelatty told Reuters on Sunday. Eritrea and Sudan also deny helping the rebels. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026
