title: I saw Switzerland’s Alpine treasures melting away. It was a sobering experience
description: It remains a spectacular vista, but the snow caps and glaciers are now fading before our eyes
content:
In late October 2022, I travelled on Switzerland ’s Jungfrau Railway to Jungfraujoch, a saddle between the Jungfrau and Mönch mountains in the Bernese Alps. Stepping out into the freezing cold, I had arrived at Europe ’s highest railway station, 3,454 metres above sea level.
I boarded the cogwheel train at a mountain pass called Kleine Scheidegg (2,000 metres) where I had an uninterrupted view of the large 10km long wall comprising the north faces of the Eiger, Mönch and the Jungfrau.
From there, I could admire the majestic, snowy beauty of their presence against the pale winter sky, much as Clint Eastwood had while filming The Eiger Sanction.
To get there, I had taken another train from the valley floor in Lauterbrunnen. On the winding ascent, I could not but notice how threadbare the snow cover seemed to be on the lower reaches of these three icons of Swiss alpinism.
The winter wonderland that I was half-expecting was not quite materialising in front of my eyes and I was inclined to put it down to the fact Europe had just experienced its hottest summer on record.
A more nuanced picture would emerge two years later when the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation issued a report detailing a record-breaking 6 per cent reduction in Swiss glacier volume in 2022.
Apart from three summer heatwaves, other factors were the low snow cover from the 2021/2022 winter months followed by deposits of Saharan dust which reduced further the glaciers’ capacity to reflect radiation.
That year, snow disappeared at all elevations about four weeks earlier than usual, exposing the ice to the relentless heat of the sun. Swiss glaciers were becoming the squawking chicken in the coal mine of climate change.
It took tunnelling crews 16 years to blast their way through the Eiger and Mönch mountains to reach the Jungfrau so that the 9km railway line could finally open in 1912. Today it can whisk tourists up to the Jungfraujoch from Kleine Scheidegg in 35 minutes.
To my relief, there was snow on the ground when I made my way out of the concrete labyrinth that is Europe’s highest railway station and let my gaze swing back and forth between the summits of the Mönch and the Jungfrau.
As I stood outside the Glacier Cafe nursing a paper cup of tepid tea, I could see below me the Konkordiaplatz. This is the great gathering point of the Aletsch glacier system, the largest ice mass in the European Alps. The Great Aletsch Glacier is a corrugated 22km carpet of ice and snow swirling its way down to the Rhone Valley.
Unknown to me at the time, in 2022 the Aletsch was undergoing record-breaking mass loss with thinning rates beyond four metres. Things did not get much better in 2023. A tenth of the total glacier volume disappeared in those two years.
I was reminded of my visit to Jungfraujoch when I saw new data this month. It found that while the record melt rates of 2022 were not reached, Swiss glaciers lost more than 5 per cent of their volume in 2026 following a winter with exceptionally little snow and record-breaking summer heatwaves.
It’s a sad commentary on the state of the planet and fossil fuel consumption that over the last five years, Switzerland has lost nearly 20 per cent of its total glacier volume and several of its smaller glaciers have now completely disappeared and are not coming back.
Swiss glaciers are estimated to have lost around 2.2 trillion litres of water between July and September, which is more than four times the annual drinking-water consumption of Swiss households.
Further denting expectations of a pristine Alpine experience, scientists report that in September there was little or no fresh snow at Jungfraujoch, so exposing the glacier directly to further melting.
On busy days, the Jungfraujoch can be overcrowded. Post-Covid, it is back to attracting more than a million visitors per year. They struggle their way around the Ice Palace, the luxury watch stores, the viewing platforms, the photo ops with the Swiss flag, queues for the lifts and the restaurants.
My own memory is that the tourist plateau on the Jungfraujoch required maintenance in the form of a piste machine to push snow on to it from the foot of the Jungfrau. This was to support the claim of an all-year-round “snow and ice” experience.
That experience was at its maximum in August 1858 when a young man from Wicklow, Charles Barrington, crossed Konkordiaplatz on his way to the summit of the Jungfrau. Remarkably, he was walking across an ice surface roughly 200 metres above today’s level. He famously went on, a few days later, to become the first person to climb the Eiger.
Changed times. The Ice Palace attraction in the Jungfraujoch now requires cooling systems to avoid a meltdown caused by the warmth emanating from the large numbers of tourists passing through its ice-lined corridors.
Despite the Aletsch glacier’s reduced size, the panorama remains spectacular. It’s a vista fully appreciated even by those who complain about using such an environment to stoke mass tourism.

title: Corinna Hardgrave, restaurant critic of The Irish Times, dies
description: Corinna Hardgrave was widely respected for her skilled food writing, but always ensured her first duty as a critic was to the reader
content:
Corinna Hardgrave , restaurant critic at The Irish Times, has died after an illness. She was 64. Corinna Hardgrave had worked with The Irish Times for six years, having previously been a wine columnist for the Irish Independent, a food writer with The Sunday Times and restaurant critic and wine writer with Irish Tatler.
She was widely admired and respected for her authoritative and skilled food writing. She won numerous awards, most recently the Restaurant Critic Award at last year’s Irish Food Writing Awards. She also wrote lively and knowledgeable travel articles for The Irish Times, combining her critic’s eye for the best destinations at home and abroad with her expert knowledge of both food and wine.
[ Never flippant or headline grabbing, our restaurant critic Corinna Hardgrave always kept the reader in mind Opens in new window ]
Speaking on Monday, her husband Steve Hardgrave described his wife’s role as restaurant critic at The Irish Times as “her dream job” and “the culmination of all her writing and eating”.
Irish Times editor Ruadhán Mac Cormaic said: “Corinna Hardgrave joined The Irish Times in the midst of the Covid pandemic, that period of food boxes, social distancing and outdoor dining. Already a noted restaurant critic, she quickly became an expert on the byzantine rules and etiquette of dining in those strange days.
“Corinna had an easy and personable writing style, always wrapping her deep knowledge of the Irish food scene in entertaining prose.
“Fairness and credibility were hallmarks of her journalism during her six years as restaurant critic. She never set out to skewer a business; nor was she afraid to call out poor service, too-high prices or bad food. She bestowed praise, but only on places that deserved it, and she knew that her first duty as a critic was to the reader.
“Corinna’s untimely death is a deep loss to The Irish Times and its readers.”
Chef and co-owner of Michelin-starred restaurant Chapter One, Ross Lewis, said: “Corinna will be a great loss to us all, because she understood our industry and always told it as she saw it. She also had an amazing ability to champion new Irish restaurants and food producers.
“Her praise meant something, and her passion inspired those in hospitality. Her words changed how we saw and consumed food just as much as anyone on our side of the pass.”
Corinna Hardgrave’s extensive body of work also displayed her talent as an interviewer, with her renowned chef subjects over the years including Ferran and Albert Adriá, Michel Roux, Yotam Ottolenghi, Madhur Jaffrey and Clare Smyth.
She was born in Co Carlow and grew up in Dublin. Her first job was with Guinness, which she joined from school. She subsequently worked in the Middle East, initially as a flight attendant and subsequently in promotion and public relations. This brought her to England, while her food writing career began after they moved back to Ireland when their first daughter was born.
Corinna Hardgrave is survived by her husband Steve and their two daughters, Katherine and Isabelle.

title: Daniil Medvedev disqualified from China Open semi-final after ball hits fan in the eye
description: Russian player struck rebounding ball into the crowd
content:
Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final with Novak Djokovic on Monday after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd that struck a ​spectator in the eye.
The Russian world ‌No 5 was ‌trailing 7-5, 5-3 and had lost a point ‌when, in frustration, he struck a ball that had come off the back wall. The spectator, sitting in the first row, clutched his left eye and appeared in pain as he left the gallery, assisted by the stadium’s ‌staff.
Not the ending we expected 😮 @DjokerNole advances to the Beijing final after Medvedev is defaulted whilst down 5-7 3-5 #ChinaOpen pic.twitter.com/Pae5eNrJ6W
“Terribly sorry to the spectator, first of all,” Medvedev said, adding it was “100 per cent an accident” and that he wished to apologise in person. “The ball was bouncing back so I tried to just hit it anywhere so it doesn’t go out from the court. When I saw the result, I felt horrible.”
The incident added further to 2021 US Open champion’s fiery reputation, born of a series of incidents where his temper has flared. At the Monte Carlo Open in April, he smashed his racket several times and placed the remnants in a courtside dustbin during his 6-0, 6-0 defeat to Matteo Berrettini.
At the 2025 US Open, he received a $42,500 (€38,000) fine after losing his temper when a photographer interrupted Benjamin Bonzi’s serve for match point. Play was held up for more than six minutes as Medvedev riled up the crowd and insulted the umpire.
“What I say and what I do, in my head, I want to do worse, and I cannot because there are rules, because we’re on a tennis court,” he said.
At the 2025 Australian Open, he was fined after breaking a net camera by repeatedly smashing it with his racket. He also had to pay for the camera.
“I was shocked. I hope that person is not badly injured,” said ​Djokovic, who was disqualified from the 2020 US Open under similar circumstances.
“On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil, because I know exactly how it feels to be disqualified in a big match. I’m sure Daniil didn’t ​want to do this intentionally.”

title: ‘Cost-of-college crisis’ locking people out of higher education, says advocacy group
description: Students want Government to reduce contribution fees by €500 and address the price of transport
content:
Daniel Walsh (25), president of Aontas na Mac Léinn in Éirinn (AMLÉ), the student advocacy group, says students want to see “meaningful action on the cost-of-college crisis” in Tuesday’s budget .
Walsh, a graduate of law at Trinity College Dublin , noted that his union had organised a recent protest outside Leinster House in Dublin demanding the abolition of college tuition fees and the closing of gaps in funding.
Students want to see the Government honour its commitment to reduce student contribution fees by €500, as well as “action on the price of transport”.
They also want students to be protected from the scheduled 15 per cent fare increase across bus and rail services from January.
The union also wants to see State investment in purpose-built student accommodation, Walsh says, as well as closing the gap in core funding of the third level sector to bring down class sizes and hidden course fees.
“The average cost of going to college in Ireland is over €16,000 a year, and that is so plainly out of reach for thousands of students and families all across the country. We know that this crisis is locking people out of higher education,” Walsh says.
The hidden cost means students are “impoverishing themselves” to get through their studies.
“That can include students who are working 35 or 40 hours on top of their full-time studies, or it includes the students who are commuting five hours a day because they couldn’t get accommodation anywhere near college. And we’ve heard from students who said that they are skipping meals or making choices as to whether they can afford to make it in as far as their lecture,” he said.
“We ​​speak about college being the best years of your life, but that phrase really rings hollow in current circumstances where so many students are struggling to get by.”

title: Why reducing the €2,500 student registration charge would be a double-edged sword
description: Do we really want our universities to be much cheaper than others in the EU?
content:
Is Ireland on the way to becoming the most attractive country in the European Union for students seeking to study through English?
Dutch universities offer hundreds of degree programmes taught through English and about 3,500 Irish students are studying there. EU law requires Irish students’ applications for places on these programmes to be treated on an equal footing to those from Dutch and other EU students. The fees for undergraduate degree programmes in the Netherlands are €2,790 annually.
Until Brexit, Ireland attracted about 2,000 applicants from continental EU applicants, who, even then, had to pay less to study here than they did to study in the UK, where they would be charged £9,760 (€11,500). Since Brexit, continental EU applicants have been classed as international applicants in the UK and are levied fees of up to £35,000-£40,000.
Since Brexit, the number of continental EU applicants seeking to secure a place in an Irish third-level institution has grown from about 2,000 to 7,000. As with Irish students seeking places in European universities, these applicants have the same right as Irish students to be offered a place.
There is an agreed template for the school-leaving exams throughout every EU member state and its transposition into CAO points for the purpose of the round-one competition that occurs immediately after the publication of our Leaving Cert results.
These applicants should not be confused with international applicants, who are offered places at €30,000-plus in our universities. These places are separate to CAO places and our school leavers are not competing with these applicants. Although some years ago, one Irish student took a High Court challenge to seek entry to the international pool of places, stating he was perfectly happy to pay the higher international fees. He lost the case.
We have seen demand from students and Opposition parties for an ongoing reduction in the €2,500 student registration charge.
On the face of it, who could object to such a proposal if the funding were available to implement it?
If the registration charge were to be reduced further to €2,250 or €2,000, this would place Ireland more than €9,000 cheaper than the mainstream charge in the UK and €500-€700 cheaper than the Netherlands.
[ ‘Is a year studying abroad of sufficient value to justify the cost?’ Opens in new window ]
We have seen since the Russian invasion of Ukraine how the levels of benefits on offer to those seeking protection in Ireland had a significant effect on the numbers presenting. In recent months, the Minister for Justice Jim O Callaghan has begun the process of bringing the Irish regulations in line with European norms. This is having an effect on the numbers presenting, which seems to be in line with public opinion on this issue.
We are a welcoming nation but we can only cope with our fair share of applicants.
By reducing our registration charges significantly from their relatively low levels of €2,500, would we inadvertently be opening up our universities to a further growth in EU applicants, who will be competing for places on an equal footing with our own Leaving Cert students?
[ Study abroad in the Netherlands and Italy: ‘It all started with a leap of faith’ Opens in new window ]
We are very pleased EU law has allowed thousands of Irish students to travel to the Netherlands and secure their dream course there.
But would we be happy if and when the reverse happened?
Irish students have been somewhat protected from the competition from our fellow EU applicants since Brexit took effect, by virtue of the fact that, since 2021, all our Leaving Cert students have had their corrected Leaving Cert scripts enhanced, initially by 7 per cent, and on a reducing scale of a little over 1 per cent per year since 2025. Following a further reduction of 1 per cent in 2027, all enhancement will cease in 2028. The competition with our EU cousins will only intensify.
Maybe we should be looking at a further improvement in the Susi (Student Universal Support Ireland) grant structure to bring more students within its remit, which ensures a complete exemption from the registration charges, rather than a reduction in the charge itself.
The Government has also acknowledged that the university sector is underfunded. If money can be found down the couch it might be appropriately allocated to third-level funding, rather than reducing a registration change that is still one of the lowest around.
[ Irish colleges should focus on teaching abroad, not attracting foreign students – Minister Opens in new window ]
Yes, we want to be welcoming to our continental cousins to come and study in our third-level colleges. It increases cultural diversity and builds relationships across the EU.
But maybe not to the extent that our own students find it progressively more difficult to secure places at home.

title: ‘They deserve to be on a good wage’: Dublin parents back teachers on industrial action
description: Parents who spoke during school pickups on Monday were supportive of action, though acknowledged it may ‘upset’ jobs
content:
“I didn’t even know there was anything going on with the teachers. Now, his ma probably knows,” says Caroline Anglim as she holds her young grandson’s hand.
She has just collected him from playschool in The Liberties in Dublin city centre and takes out her phone and rings her daughter.
“Hang on,” she says, as she learns that primary schoolteachers from the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation began a work-to-rule on Monday amid a public sector pay dispute involving more than 100,000 public sector workers.
“Nikita, did you know there was anything going on with the teachers and nurses and all that? Oh you did? I’m standing here with a journalist, and I just said I’d ring you,” she says.
Anglim believes it will affect all parents, “especially working parents”, though it is unclear whether she is telling The Irish Times or her daughter.
“She says they’re not getting the recognition,” Anglim says, passing on her daughter’s thoughts.
No longer on the phone, Caroline says teachers “deserve what they’re getting and probably more”, adding they are “taking on an awful lot”.
Several parents collecting their children from primary schools in the area were unaware of the work-to-rule action taken by teachers from Monday. Even more were unaware of a planned 24-hour strike next Wednesday.
“I didn’t even know there was a strike on, to be honest,” says Laura, who is collecting her two children from St James’s Primary School. She works in a GP surgery in the area.
“They deserve to be on a good wage,” she says, though she accepts a potential 24-hour strike next week could “upset my job”.
“I have no clue about that yet,” says Charlyne, an IT worker originally from France, who was frantically rushing with her daughter to get back to work.
She was one of a wave of parents to collect their children from Canal Way Educate Together National School.
The vast majority of parents who spoke to The Irish Times on Monday were supportive of the action.
“The strike is obviously very different to the work-to-rule. It will affect parents a lot more, but I get where they’re coming from,” says one father in his 40s, who describes the current cost of living as “crazy”.
A short time later, Edel Kearney is leaning against the wall of Canal Way, waiting to pickup her two children, aged eight and 10.
Kearney, who is in her 40s, works as a career coach in the public sector and has been engaging in work-to-rule action since last week.
Her husband also works in the public sector, and both will be taking part in the 24-hour strike next Wednesday.
With schools also expected to close, she believes she will be “bringing the kids with me to the picket line”.
Describing the job of a teacher as “serious work”, Kearney says “everyone” is struggling financially.
“Myself and my husband even were sitting around yesterday trying to figure out how we were going to afford it until the end of the month. It’s literally at that stage,” she says.
During the same pickup, Kathy Foley says she will “of course” be affected should the 24-hour teacher strike go ahead.
“I won’t mind,” adds her 10-year-old daughter, Nancy.
[ Budget 2027: Improved childcare supports to include after-school care Opens in new window ]
Despite the potential disruption, Foley says she supports the teachers’ right to take industrial action.
“It’s really important that they get paid properly and in line with inflation for the work that they do,” she says.
“I am fortunate that with my child at this age, it’s not a huge challenge for us if there’s a day off school. I can work at home, and she can manage.
“But I know for parents of more than one child, younger children, children with additional needs, people with inflexible work situations, it’s really, really tricky,” she says.

title: Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash into Israel’s Ben Gurion airport, say Israeli officials
description: Co-pilot told interrogators in United Arab Emirates he planned the attack before being hired by the airline
content:
The Flydubai co-pilot who stabbed his captain in an ‌alleged attempt to crash the plane last week told interrogators in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) he planned the attack before being hired by the airline, according to two Israeli officials with ‌knowledge of the investigation.
A third source briefed on the UAE probe said the co-pilot, an Omani national, had planned to crash Wednesday’s flight into Ben Gurion airport ​near Tel Aviv. He had also operated a flight to Tel Aviv earlier this year and intended to hijack and crash the plane then, but opted not to, the source added.
It was not immediately clear why the co-pilot changed his mind on that previous flight, although the co-pilot is thought to have ​known someone onboard, the source said.
All of the sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation. UAE and Israeli authorities did not immediately respond to ⁠a request for comment, nor did Flydubai.
The co-pilot of Flydubai flight FZ1073, which was bound for Israel from Dubai ‌last ‌Wednesday, ​attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the UAE prosecutor general has said, calling the incident a “terrorist attack”.
Two sources have said the co-pilot is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami. ⁠Israeli officials have not named the co-pilot but have ​said he is from Oman. UAE authorities and Flydubai have not ​publicly disclosed the co-pilot’s identity.
[ Flydubai hijacking attempt could aid Netanyahu’s re-election bid Opens in new window ]
Reuters has not been able to independently reach al-Hammami, who is in UAE custody, for comment. The ‌UAE has not announced any formal charges against him ​and it is not known if he has appointed legal counsel. Oman has not commented on the incident.
The two Israeli ⁠officials said the co-pilot told interrogators he had ⁠applied for a job at ​Dubai state-owned Flydubai after searching for airlines that fly to Tel Aviv.
The third source said Israel was being continuously updated about the investigation from the UAE.
Disaster on board flight FZ1073 was averted after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot. The pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, survived the attack and has been described as a hero for managing to open the cockpit door. The plane was carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, most of them Israeli.
A reserve Flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in northwestern ‌Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot ⁠was detained by Saudi authorities and later transferred to the UAE on Thursday.
Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu has said pilots who are citizens of countries that Israel does not have diplomatic relations with, such as Oman, are not ‌permitted to operate flights to Israel. It is not clear how the co-pilot came to be assigned to the flight to Tel Aviv, and Netanyahu has since ​ordered a review of foreign airlines flying to Israel.
New Zealand assistant police ⁠commissioner Michael Johnson said on Monday the co-pilot had spent time in the country and New Zealand police were looking into the period. He did not say when the co-pilot allegedly visited the country or name him.
A multi-agency Australian counter-terrorism unit is investigating ​links to Australia of the co-pilot, who was once enrolled at RMIT University in Melbourne, Victoria. A fourth source said the co-pilot studied there around a decade ago. - Reuters
[ Flydubai co-pilot’s time in Australia under investigation after cockpit incident Opens in new window ]

title: Ireland v Kazakhstan World Cup playoff: Team news, kick-off time, where to watch
description: Everything you need to know ahead of Ireland’s trip to Kazakhstan
content:
Carla Ward’s Republic of Ireland side will play Kazakhstan in the first leg of their Women’s World Cup qualifying first-round playoff on Friday.
The game at the Astana Arena, in the Kazak capital Astana, will kick-off at the unusual time of 12pm on Friday.
The second leg will take place at Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Tuesday at 7.30pm.
Ireland are missing a few key players for the game in Astana. Katie McCabe and Marissa Sheva are suspended, while Denise O’Sullivan is nursing a knee injury she picked up with her club, but all three should be available for the second leg in Cork.
Meanwhile, Tara O’Hanlon (hamstring) and Saoirse Noonan (ankle) have been ruled out for both fixtures due to injury.
Crystal Palace midfielder Shanade Hopcroft is the surprise inclusion, qualifying through her Sligo grandmother. Heather Payne returns to the squad for the first time in a year after spell hampered by injury.
Goalkeepers: Courtney Brosnan (Everton), Grace Moloney (Southampton), Sophie Whitehouse (Charlton Athletic).
Defenders: Aoife Mannion (Newcastle United), Heather Payne (Leicester City), Anna Patten (Aston Villa), Caitlin Hayes (Brighton), Jessie Stapleton (Leicester City), Megan Connolly (Lazio), Hayley Nolan (Crystal Palace), Chloe Mustaki (Nottingham Forest), Katie McCabe (Chelsea).
Midfielders: Denise O’Sullivan (Gotham FC), Marissa Sheva (Sunderland), Aoibheann Clancy (Watford), Jamie Finn (Burnley), Lucy Quinn (Sheffield United), Tyler Toland (Burnley), Jess Ziu (Leicester City), Shanade Hopcroft (Crystal Palace).
Forwards: Kyra Carusa (HB Køge), Amber Barrett (Strasbourg), Abbie Larkin (Crystal Palace), Emily Murphy (Brighton), Leanne Kiernan (Newcastle United).
Yes. Tickets are still available for the game at Páirc Uí Chaoimh, selling for a very reasonable €30.
The winner of these first-round playoffs over the two legs proceeds to the second (and final) round, where a stiffer challenge awaits in the form of Belgium or Poland.
Of the eight second-round playoff winners, seven will qualify for the World Cup, while the eighth (based on league phase rankings) has another shot at qualification through the inter-confederation playoffs.
Ireland are 21st in the world rankings and currently play in Nations League A, while Kazakhstan are ranked 98th and compete in the third-tier League C.
Looking further down the line, Ireland beat Poland twice (at home and away) earlier this year, and in last year’s Nations League beat Belgium 4-2 in the first-leg relegation/promotion playoff in Dublin before losing 2-1 in the return leg four days later. So, in short, they’re both opponents Ireland are capable of beating.
But first, they must do the job in Kazakhstan on Friday if they’re to stay on track for a place at next year’s World Cup in Brazil.

title: Ireland records one of lowest rates of house price inflation in euro zone
description: Latest Eurostat figures provide more evidence of slowdown in Irish house prices
content:
Ireland recorded one of the lowest rates of house price inflation in the euro zone in the second quarter, Eurostat said.
The agency’s latest owner-occupied housing price index, which excludes homes bought as investments, indicated prices across the 27-member bloc rose by 4 per cent – in annual terms – between April and June this year.
The level of inflation recorded in Ireland was 3.5 per cent.
Only Luxembourg (-1.7 per cent), France (1.5 per cent), Belgium (1.8 per cent), Slovenia (2 per cent) and Finland (2.4 per cent) recorded lower rates.
The highest increases were recorded in Croatia (12 per cent), Bulgaria (11.7 per cent), Lithuania (10.8 per cent) and Portugal (10.6 per cent).
[ What is behind the slowdown in Ireland’s property prices? Opens in new window ]
The quarter-on-quarter increase in owner-occupied home prices in Ireland was 0.7 per cent, half the euro area average of 1.4 per cent.
The findings appear to back up claims that the housing market here is softening.
They come in the wake of a report from property website Daft.ie that indicated house prices, both new and second-hand, rose by 3 per cent in the year to September, about half the rate of inflation seen a year earlier.
That report found prices in Dublin rose by 0.8 per cent in the year to September, the slowest rate of increase since 2020.
The slowdown in price growth has been linked to expectations of higher borrowing costs with the European Central Bank (ECB) in the process of raising interest rates and comes amid the uncertain geopolitical outlook.
A global bond market sell-off is also pushing up borrowing costs in many countries.
In the euro area, loans with an initial fixed-rate period of 10 years-plus rose by 8 basis points to 3.43 per cent in August and the surge in euro zone government yields in recent weeks is expected to push rates even higher.
[ Irish house price growth slows as higher interest rates bite Opens in new window ]
Ireland’s housing has been adversely impacted by a shortage in supply.
The Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) recently forecasted that 39,200 new homes would be built in 2026 and just under 40,500 in 2027, while warning that planning permissions had not risen enough to support a sustained increase in construction.
The Government is targeting about 300,000 new homes to be built between 2025 and 2030, a pace of construction that the State has not witnessed since the Celtic Tiger era.
However, several industry leaders here claim the Government has the right policies in place to deliver 50,000 homes a year.
In the past 24 months, it has changed design standards, overhauled the rent rules and reduced VAT on new builds in a bid to entice investors back into the Irish market.

title: Budget 2027: Rent tax credit could increase to €1,200 per person at higher level
description: Universal reduction of €150 in college fees on the cards
content:
An increase in the rent tax credit is understood to be on the table as budget talks enter their final phase and the focus shifts to the final touches to the tax package.
The Coalition will reveal an €8.5 billion package of tax and spending measures on Tuesday after a budget process that has seen tensions flare even with significant extra spending and tax cuts predicted.
While the vast majority of the spending increases have been agreed, the tax package was still being worked on in Government Buildings and the Department of Finance on Monday afternoon.
It is understood the rent tax credit could be set for an increase, with a higher level of €1,200 per person or €2,400 for a married couple or civil partnership said to be under discussion.
The current maximum value is €1,000 for a single person or €2,000 for married couples or civil partners. However, the higher threshold may not kick in until later in 2027.
The tax-free rental income allowance will be extended to backyard cabins, which the Coalition has encouraged through planning reforms.
[ Budget 2027: Improved childcare supports to include after-school care Opens in new window ]
First time buyers will be able to access up to €35,000 towards the deposit on their first home after agreement was reached by party leaders. This increases the limit by €5,000.
The entry point for the higher rate of income tax is expected to rise from €44,000 to €46,000, while adjustments to the universal social charge and tax credits are also expected to add a few hundred euro annually in benefits for middle-income earners.
It is expected that there will be an across-the-board €150 cut to student fees. There had been suggestions over the weekend that a €250 cut could be on the cards, but hopes for this had expired by Monday morning. Across the course of the day, however, the idea re-emerged, with indications on Monday evening that there would be an extra allocation of around €18 million to deliver the measure.
It is expected there will be greater access to subsidies for parents with more than one child attending college.
There will be an increase in the income disregard for the carer’s allowance, which currently stands at €1,000 for single carers or €2,000 for a couple. However, it is expected to be more modest than last year’s.
[ Social welfare, tax changes and childcare costs: Everything we know about Budget 2027 so far Opens in new window ]
An increase is also expected on the living alone allowance, with €5 floated but not yet confirmed, and a separate increase on the child support payment.
Again, the increase to the child support payment is expected to be less than last year, when it went up by €16 weekly for kids aged 12 and up, and €8 for the under-eights.
On the pre-budget suggestion of a “culture card” for young people, originally mooted as being worth about €100, a spokeswoman for Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan said “money to progress” the idea had been secured “so the department will now be able to continue its work in this area”.
She added: “So far, we have been engaging with our EU counterparts on their approach. We now need to engage with the cultural sector and draw up the terms of the scheme, and develop a framework of approved venues.
“All going well, we anticipate being able to roll it out by the end of next year.”
Extra funding has been agreed for An Coimisiún Pleanála and local authority planning departments in an effort to speed up decision making.

title: O’Neill accused of choosing politics over ministerial responsibilities in Drumcree standoff
description: Emma Little-Pengelly said First Minister ‘chose to follow the law of the mob instead of the law of the land’
content:
Northern Ireland ’s Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly has accused First Minister Michelle O’Neill of choosing “ Sinn Féin politics” over her ministerial responsibilities.
In sharp exchanges between the Democratic Unionist Party ( DUP ) and Sinn Féin at Stormont , Little-Pengelly claimed O’Neill refused to issue a joint call for calm amid tensions over the Orange Order ’s attempt to parade down the Garvaghy Road.
The exchanges came as the Court of Appeal in Belfast reserved judgment in a case brought by Garvaghy Road residents challenging the Parades Commission ’s handling of the Orange Order’s original march application.
[ Judgment reserved in legal challenge to Orange Order parade on Garvaghy Road Opens in new window ]
The scene on Garvaghy Road on Monday was calm, though locals and supporters – who gathered in their thousands over the weekend – intend to maintain a presence while the court prepares its ruling.
A small group of Orangemen remain at Drumcree church and will continue to make their token attempts to parade, though they are quickly turned back by police officers.
In the Assembly, Little-Pengelly accused Sinn Féin of exploiting Drumcree for political gain in advance of next May’s Stormont election, saying the party had “flooded the Garvaghy Road for electioneering”.
“I reached out to the First Minister, and I asked her to put out a statement to call for calm. I reached out to the First Minister and asked her to stand with me to call people off the streets, and in terms of moving forward together,” she said.
“This is the reality – she chose to follow the law of the mob instead of the law of the land. She chose Sinn Féin politics over her responsibilities as minister, and that is shameful.”
[ Michelle O’Neill says the law is ‘wrong’ in Orange Order Drumcree march row Opens in new window ]
The Stormont clashes marked yet another day of bad-tempered exchanges between the Northern Ireland Executive’s two main governing parties, raising serious questions about its survival.
Replying to Sinn Féin’s Linda Dillon, Little-Pengelly said Sinn Féin needed “to get real if you genuinely think that you have not done significant damage” to the Executive.
The primary responsibility facing anyone holding the top positions in the Executive, or ministerial roles, is to uphold the law.
“That has to be at the very heart of it,” she told members of the Assembly.
“Key to this is the fact that you cannot demand equality and then claim an exemption for yourselves time and time again. I have proven by my track record that I show respect, but I also demand respect.”
O’Neill insisted in the face of challenges from Traditional Unionist Voice MLA Timothy Gaston that she was “the First Minister for what is right and that she would continue to stand up for Garvaghy Road residents”.
Gaston, an MLA for Antrim, asked her: “Will you now be supporting all those who dislike legal decisions and ultimately will take to the streets, or is it only when it’s ensuring there’s not a Prod with an orange sash allowed about the place?”
[ Drumcree consequences will be profound. That’s why it’s a line in the sand for nationalists Opens in new window ]
O’Neill, who was not present in the Stormont chamber for questions last week, replied: “Everything that I have been doing is about trying to calm tensions. Everything I have been doing is to support a community that’s under siege. I make no apology for it.”
Replying to the DUP’s Brian Kingston, she questioned why the Drumcree parade had re-emerged after being quiet for nearly 30 years.
“Why did you think this was a good idea to open this up? And the only answer I can take from that is because of the election,” O’Neill said.

title: Gardaí seized nearly 2,000 fireworks, worth €347,000, in past 10 years
description: Operation Tombola targets the importation, sale and distribution of illegal fireworks
content:
Gardaí have seized 1,883 fireworks, valued at €347,516, over the past 10 years.
Operation Tombola, which targets the importation, sale and distribution of illegal fireworks, is conducted through intelligence-led operations, visits to local car boot sales, searches and seizures of fireworks. It also aims to prevent firework-associated public disorder and antisocial behaviour.
An awareness campaign was launched in collaboration with An Garda Síochána, the National Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (NSPCA), the Irish Guide Dogs, Dublin Fire Brigade and the National Office for Community Safety at the Dublin Fire Brigade Training Centre in Marino on Monday.
The fireworks awareness campaign also emphasised the penalties associated with the sale and use of illegal fireworks.
Penalties associated with the sale and use of illegal fireworks include fines of up to €10,000 and five years’ imprisonment for those possessing fireworks with intent to sell or supply, or those convicted of throwing an ignited firework at a person or property.
Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan urged people “to think hard before they use fireworks this year, and am asking people to consider not just their own safety, but the safety of others who may be impacted by their actions over the Halloween period”.
[ Over 200 solicitors and barristers protest outside Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin Opens in new window ]
Halloween night last year saw a return of the declining trend of call-outs, 320 compared with 494 in 2024. Emergency ambulance services across Dublin received 516 calls during this period. Although this is the largest recorded in 21 years, there was only one fireworks-related injury that required a response by paramedics. In the run-up to Halloween 2025, local authorities removed bonfire stockpile materials, which aided the decrease of Halloween-related calls.
Chief fire officer of Dublin Fire Brigade Greg O’Dwyer warned of the devastating physical injuries illegal fireworks can cause.
He also urged people to only attend officially organised fireworks displays over Halloween.
“Firefighters and paramedics have had to deal with some horrific injuries caused by illegal fireworks over the years.
“These fireworks are completely unpredictable and these injuries can occur by fireworks igniting earlier than anticipated, exploding in some young person’s hand, causing disfigurement to their fingers, or going off in their pocket, severely burning their leg.”
NSPCA inspector Shane Lawlor has seen first-hand the consequences of firework use for domestic pets and working animals.
“I’ve seen how quickly a frightened animal can panic and try to escape,” he said. “Dogs and cats can bolt from homes and gardens, horses and livestock can injure themselves in fright, and wildlife can also be badly affected. It’s important to remember that animals have no understanding of where that sudden noise is coming from or when it is going to stop.”
[ Irish drug dealers use ‘impressionable’ teenagers to receive cannabis by post Opens in new window ]

title: Europe’s Stoxx 600 gains on banks boost but fiscal fears hit French stocks
description: Euro sinks to 17-month low amid renewed sovereign-debt worries
content:
European shares closed higher on Monday, while French equities slid to a six-month low on fiscal concerns ​and Schneider Electric’s fall after acquiring US software firm PTC.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 index ended 0.4 per cent higher, after hitting a four-month low last week as global bond yields surged on inflation, higher corporate bond issuances and worsening fiscal outlooks.
France’s CAC 40 fell 0.8 per cent, the biggest loser among regional peers, ​while the euro hit a 17-month low on fears of a return of sovereign debt crisis dynamics in the euro zone.
“What we’re seeing in bond ⁠markets is obviously impacting the euro, but it’s also having a knock-on effect on the stock market because ‌of ‌the ​impact that it could have on earnings,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.
France’s 2027 budget last week included politically contentious spending cuts and savings measures aimed at narrowing its deficit.
Dublin’s Iseq closed the session marginally up at 14,315. AIB was one of the main movers, increasing by 2.2 per cent to €11.29.
The positive move was linked to the group’s ongoing share buyback scheme. Rival Bank of Ireland rose by 0.8 per cent to €18.96. The recent oil price surge has squeezed airlines including Ryanair . The Irish airline’s stock fell by 0.5 per cent to €23.67.
The State’s largest institutional landlord, Ires Reit , continued in positive territory after last week’s takeover bid from Baring International Investment, closing up 1 per cent at €1.29.
A 10 per cent drop in Schneider Electric weighed on the CAC 40 after its $23 billion swoop for industrial software firm PTC.
While analysts could see the strategic rationale behind the deal, they questioned the increased exposure to the software sector at a time valuations are under pressure.
RBC Capital Markets analyst Mark Fielding said: “Valuation of industrial software assets has been under pressure due to AI concerns and while we think this is largely misplaced, it does not change the fact [the deal] will increase Schneider’s exposure to this concern.”
AkzoNobel rose ​1.8 per cent after agreeing to sell its Southeast Asian decorative paints business to Nippon Paint for $1.35 ​billion. Genmab rose 5.3 per cent after presenting updated data from a trial for its ovarian cancer drug Rina-S that showed a clinically meaningful response rate.
The United Kingdom’s FTSE 100 ‌rose on Monday, steadying after its steepest drop since April last week, as prospects of higher ‌crude supplies kept prices in check.
The blue-chip FTSE 100 index closed 0.34 per cent higher at 10,497 ​points.
A survey on Monday showed British services ‌firms ‌reported stronger ​cost pressures last month as fuel prices surged due to the Middle East conflict
Fuel prices have ⁠been under scrutiny owing to ​their impact on inflation expectations and ​the Bank of England’s interest rate trajectory
Ithaca Energy rose 2.2 per cent and was among top gainers on the ‌FTSE 100 after ⁠it agreed to acquire Suncor Energy’s offshore oil assets for $842 million in upfront cash
“This deal for Canadian assets provides a ‌level of diversification,” said AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould.
BT Group rose 1.4 per cent after ​it agreed to buy troubled broadband provider TalkTalk for £400 ​million (€470 million) in a government-backed rescue deal.
The benchmark S&P 500 rose and ‌the Nasdaq reached all-time highs on Monday as most megacap and growth stocks advanced, though risk sentiment remained in check as treasury yields held near multiyear highs.
Heavyweight tech stocks ​took the lead, with Nvidia rising 1.2 per cent, hovering close to its record high hit in the previous session. Meta Platforms, Microsoft and Tesla were up between 1.6 per cent and 2.4 per cent.
Ten of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were trading higher, with communication services and energy leading gains. Real estate was the sole laggard.
“The AI and tech story continues ​to drive the bus ... it is so strong that it can fight the headwind from higher interest rates,” said Dennis Dick, founder and market structure analyst at Triple D Trading.
PTC was the top gainer on the S&P 500, rising 34 per cent after France’s Schneider Electric agreed to acquire the software firm in a $22.6 billion all-cash deal.
Optimism about robust corporate earnings has helped US stocks outperform global rivals in the last ‌six months, despite the shaky geopolitical landscape and inflation worries.

title: Legal aid dispute a matter of concern, says Chief Justice
description: Revised payment structure provides a flat €520 solicitor fee irrespective of the number of clients or appearances
content:
An ongoing dispute between solicitors and the Department of Justice over a new payment model for District Court legal aid work is a “matter of concern” to the judiciary, the Chief Justice has said.
Donal O’Donnell, the most senior judge in the country, mentioned the dispute briefly during an address to mark the opening of the legal year in the Four Courts in Dublin on Monday.
“Some issues relating to [the dispute] are before the courts – including the Supreme Court – and that limits what I can say. But I think I can say that the continuation of the dispute is a matter of concern to me and, I believe, judges generally. I do hope the dispute can be brought to a conclusion soon,” he said.
The revised payment structure, introduced on July 1st, provides for a flat €520 solicitor’s fee irrespective of the number of clients or appearances. It led to a widespread withdrawal of services by criminal defence solicitors, leading to thousands of case adjournments.
The new-year event was attended by senior legal figures, including Judge Tomoko Akane, president of the International Criminal Court (ICC).
O’Donnell’s address focused on protecting the rule of law and judicial independence, both abroad and at home.
Addressing judges’ pay, O’Donnell said it was “frustrating” that the Government had failed to implement a 2014 Council of Europe recommendation to establish an advisory body whereby questions “in connection with [judges’] employment conditions could be examined in close dialogue with judicial representatives”.
While acknowledging constitutional guarantees against reductions in judicial pay, O’Donnell noted this protection “has less real effect in an era of growth and inflation”.
The judge said the establishment of such a body could benefit issues relating to judges’ pay and pensions.
“The proposed structure would not fix remuneration, but would simply provide the Government with independent expert advice,” he said.
In her address, Akane highlighted sanctions placed on the court’s members by the United States, as well as other measures “aimed at interfering with judicial proceedings and changing our course”.
The ICC is a global court based in The Hague, with powers to bring prosecutions for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.
The United States has sanctioned the court, which US president Donald Trump accused last year of engaging in “illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel”.
Twelve of the court’s 18 judges are subject to either US sanctions or a conviction in absentia handed down by Russia in response to the ICC’s reaction to the Ukraine war.
“Such attacks against independent servants of the law are couched in narratives that are specific to the ICC and its activities, but they are also part of a broader assault against the rule of law,” Akane said.
“It is of vital importance that courts, whether that is the ICC or any other court, remain independent and free from political pressure or any kind of coercion. But at times, it feels to me that this very foundational notion is corroding before our eyes,” she said.
Following on from Akane’s remarks, O’Donnell said the protection of courts, judges and the legal system at large should be the concern of “anyone who wants to live in a free society that respects the individual and protects their rights”.

title: Michelle O’Neill says the law is ‘wrong’ in Orange Order Drumcree march row
description: Court of Appeal in Belfast has reserved judgment on a fresh legal challenge to Portadown march
content:
Judgment has been reserved in the latest legal challenge to the Orange parade at the centre of the Drumcree standoff in Portadown , writes our Northern editor Freya McClements .
Three senior judges at the Court of Appeal in Belfast heard submissions on Monday from barristers representing the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition and the Parades Commission .
The residents are challenging an earlier High Court decision to refuse leave to apply for a judicial review of the determination by the commission to permit the Orange Order to parade from Drumcree church along the Garvaghy Road on September 27th.
They were not able to proceed after the road was blocked by residents, and the standoff is continuing in the area with protesters maintaining a presence.
Denise Kiley, appearing for the residents, argued the Parades Commission had failed to “properly weigh” information from the Police Service of Northern Ireland ( PSNI ) around the potential for disorder.
She said it “didn’t properly understand the police assessment”, and therefore reached an “irrational conclusion” in permitting it to go ahead.
The barrister for the Parades Commission, Tony McGleenan, said the body was “fully briefed” by police, including “about the police resource and their ability to contain any disorder or reaction that occurred”.
He said the suggestion it had made a legal error “doesn’t bear scrutiny” and that just because people disagree with the outcome “doesn’t make it irrational”.
Richard McConkey, who represents a member of the Orange Order from Portadown, said: “Our position is obviously that the appeal should be dismissed.”
You can read the full report from McClements here.
In a joint statement, the Catholic Archbishop of Armagh Eamon Martin and his Church of Ireland counterpart, Archbishop John McDowell, have appealed for peace and respect for the rule of law to build trust between communities.
The standoff at Drumcree Church sees no sign of ending. A ruling in the legal challenge against the decision to allow an Orange Order parade along the Garvaghy Road has been reserved by the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal.
Three judges heard the appeal by an applicant on behalf of residents who live on the route of the contentious parade.
In their joint statement, the archbishops posed the question: “How can we be good neighbours to each other?”
They also encouraged Christians to consider what would be generous and for the common good.
“We acknowledge the real hurt left by past violence, and the fragility of the present situation. We caution against language that inflames division and urge people to make space for a peaceful way forward,” they said.
“We call for an urgent, constructive, inclusive and reconciling initiative to help find a way through this crisis.
“We ask all Christians, and all people of good will, on the island and beyond, to pray for peace, healing and reconciliation at this time. This prayer offers a way to pray, and a challenge to live: to let the love of God and neighbour shape our words and actions.”
Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill has said she would continue “turning up” for residents of the Garvaghy Road and described the law as “wrong”.
Appearing for an urgent oral question in the Northern Ireland Assembly, O’Neill said that “when the law is wrong, I will stand firmly against it”.
“It is morally wrong what’s happening to the people on the Garvaghy Road,” she added.
The First Minister has been accused of “breaking the law” for supporting the Garvaghy Road residents who opposed a determination by the Parades Commission to allow an Orange Order parade along the road for the first time in almost 30 years.
The parade has not taken place because police said they could not facilitate it with the crowds gathered on the Garvaghy Road in opposition.
Sinn Féin Ministers and elected representatives from Sinn Féin, the SDLP and People Before Profit have also been criticised for being present on the Garvaghy Road.
Earlier at Parliament Buildings, DUP leader Gavin Robinson insisted it cannot be “business as normal” at Stormont following alleged “law breaking” by Sinn Féin Ministers, claiming 40 political representatives had “broken the law”.
There were sharp exchanges between MLAs over Drumcree during questions for the Executive Office in the Assembly, which were taken by Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly.
Sinn Féin MLA Deirdre Hargey challenged her on the Loyalist Communities Council giving evidence to the Parades Commission.
Little-Pengelly responded saying Sinn Féin’s “brass neck beggars belief” after the party stood “shoulder to shoulder with dissidents, with Provos, with those with appalling convictions”.
SDLP MLA Justin McNulty said he was “very proud to stand with the residents of the Garvaghy Road”, and Little-Pengelly responded that she was “disappointed” by him “justifying your actions” and “dancing to the beat of a dissident drum”.
“I do think it’s deeply disappointing, and I would suggest that you should apologise for that,” she added.
TUV leader Jim Allister challenged the DUP to ensure consequences for Northern Ireland’s “First Minister of lawlessness” by withdrawing its Deputy First Minister, Emma Little-Pengelly, from the Executive.
Breandán Mac Cionnaith from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition said it had been made very clear to Appeal Court judges what the situation is in relation to the Drumcree parade.
He said: “We believe all the arguments have been made, have been listened to.”
“Our legal team put forward all the arguments.
“They were very clear on what the situation was in relation to the parade and I don’t think we have anything to regret so far.”
He added: “I am not going to pre-judge the outcome.”
Jamie Bryson said there was a contrast between Orangemen in Drumcree and what he described as a “mob” on the Garvaghy Road.
He said: “What has happened today is that those who have disobeyed the law all week, defied the law, stood in defiance of it, have come back before the court and are now trying to use the law.”
Bryson added: “We will abide by the law, we have abided by the law from the start and whatever the decision is, we will abide by it.
“We approached this as a question of law.
“Last night, while more mobs were brought on to the Garvaghy Road, Orangemen were holding a prayer meeting, praying for the people who hate them.
“The contrast we have here is the law and the mob and we stand on the side of the law.”
DUP MP Carla Lockhart has had to receive security protection due to abuse received over the Drumcree parading dispute, Jamie Bryson has said.
Speaking outside the Appeal Court in Belfast, Bryson, who acts as legal adviser for the Portadown Orange Order, was loudly booed and heckled as he tried to speak to the media.
He said: “Those who stood on the steps of this court and called the mob down here have to take responsibility for what the mob has done.”
Turning to Lockhart, he added: “The abuse this woman has taken is absolutely vile. The behaviour at the weekend is absolutely vile.
“Those who called this mob to this court have to take responsibility.
“I don’t care about me, but what has happened to this female politician is absolutely scandalous.”
Lockhart said: “It is a sad reflection on society when you stand outside court and you are abused, threatened.
“It has been utterly disgraceful, some of the behaviour over the last week.
“I want to say to all of those abusing, they won’t deter me from doing what I do and for standing up for Portadown Orange District LOL Number 1 who deserve the right to fulfil their legal determination to walk the Garvaghy Road.
“It is a difficult day for Northern Ireland whenever you see lawbreakers trying to flout and use the courts,” she said.
Northern Ireland’s Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly has accused First Minister Michelle O’Neill of choosing not to issue a joint statement with her calling for calm at Drumcree.
Speaking during questions for the Executive Office, Little-Pengelly claimed Sinn Féin “flooded the Garvaghy Road for electioneering”.
“I reached out to the First Minister and I asked her to put out a statement to call for calm,” she said.
“I reached out to the First Minister and asked her to stand with me to call people off the streets and in terms of moving forward together – and this is the reality – she chose to follow the law of the mob instead of the law of the land.
“She chose Sinn Féin politics over her responsibilities as Minister, and that is shameful.”
Judgement has been reserved in the fresh legal challenge to the Orange march at the centre of the Drumcree standoff in Portadown, reports Northern Editor Freya McClements .
Lady Chief Justice Siobhan Keegan told the Court of Appeal in Belfast she hoped to give a decision “within a swift enough timeframe” but could not give a date at the conclusion of Monday’s hearing.
Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, which opposes the march, is seeking leave to apply for a judicial review of the decision by the Parades Commission to allow it to proceed.
Barrister Tony McGleenan, representing the Parades Commission, said the residents were attempting to “make some forensic play” in asserting a difference between what the police told the commission and what the commissioners then recorded as the police assessment.
He said “one accurately reflects the other”.
The barrister said legal jurisprudence placed a positive obligation on facilitating the right of assembly.
McGleenan said the residents’ contention that the commission had made a legal error “doesn’t bear scrutiny”.
He described the determination as an “expert judgment by the body set up by Parliament to make these evaluations”.
The barrister said that legal precedent made clear that considerable “deference” should be afforded to statutory decision making bodies.
On the residents’ case that the commission should have explained why it was changing its determination after almost 30 years of prohibiting the parade, McGleenan insisted the commissioners had explained why.
He said the reason lay in the fact that what was proposed by the Orange lodge was very different to what had been applied for before, including in respect of numbers, time of year and symbols and emblems displayed.
McGleenan added: “The folk memory of what happened in the 1990s relates to something that’s categorically different.”
The DUP said it would “not abdicate its responsibilities” in the political fallout over the Drumcree dispute.
However, DUP leader Gavin Robinson insisted it cannot be “business as normal” at Stormont following alleged “law breaking” by Sinn Féin Ministers, claiming 40 political representatives had “broken the law”.
He was speaking at Parliament Buildings as the parading standoff enters its second week and another legal challenge is being heard.
The DUP has been challenged to ensure consequences for Northern Ireland’s “First Minister of lawlessness”.
TUV leader Jim Allister said the DUP should withdraw its Deputy First Minister, Emma Little-Pengelly, to “ensure political consequences for law breaking”.
Allister said the “First Minister of lawlessness says: ‘We’re above the law, the law does not apply to us, we do not accept the law’.”
Michelle O’Neill has said she is standing by the residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown, and “it’s up to all of us to collectively and unequivocally stand with the Garvaghy Road residents and to say no to a sectarian, unwanted march”.
The First Minister is scheduled to face an urgent oral question from DUP MLA Phillip Brett on Monday afternoon. - PA
Barrister Tony McGleenan, representing the Parades Commission, told the Court of Appeal that the determination to permit a limited parade down the Garvaghy Road should be read in its entirety.
“It is a detailed 31-paragraph written analysis,” he said.
“And it has to be read in its totality. And there is a grave danger of cherry-picking sentences here and sentences there to suggest a wrong legal test or a misdirection, or that something hasn’t actually been considered.”
McGleenan said police had given an assurance to the commissioners that they had the capacity to deal with any disorder that may have been triggered if a parade was permitted.
He insisted that the commission was “fully briefed” by police on the uncertainty around what might happen.
“They met with the PSNI on the 23rd [September] at a lengthy meeting with them. They were read intelligence briefings. They were briefed about the police resource and their ability to contain any disorder or reaction that occurred. So they have all of that.” - PA
Barrister Denise Kiley, representing the Garvaghy Road residents, described the Drumcree parade as “one of the most polarising parades in the history of Northern Ireland”.
She said the Parades Commission had a duty to promote an understanding of parading and it had failed to explain why it had reached its determination to permit the parade, particularly as it was the first time in 28 years it had not been banned.
“There is a duty to explain decisions,” said the barrister.
“And where a decision has consistently been made on one basis for 28 years then a change cries out for explanation.”
The residents’ barrister Denise Kiley said the Parades Commission failed to “properly weigh” what the police had told it about the potential for disorder if the parade was given the go-ahead.
She said the commission’s assertion that there was no specific information from police about a risk of violence did not fully reflect what a senior commander had told it.
The barrister said PSNI Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson told the commission although police had no clear intelligence about any planned disorder, he had also stressed that officers were dealing with an “unclear picture” and that, as a result, police were planning for various scenarios – from a peaceful passing of the parade to an outbreak of violent disorder.
Kiley said the commission’s subsequent conclusion that there was no specific information about the prospect of disorder was “only part of the picture”.
“It doesn’t go on to record the uncertainty and the fact that the position remained unclear,” she said.
The barrister added: “It is clear that what the police were telling the commission was this is unclear, it’s uncertain, and we are preparing for all eventualities.”
She said the commissioners “didn’t properly understand the police assessment” and this impacted their decision to permit the parade.
Kiley said the commission had therefore reached an “irrational conclusion”.
The International Federation of Human Rights (FIDH) and the Committee on the Administration of Justice (CAJ) have issued a joint statement on the ongoing standoff at Drumcree, saying a “transparent and rights-based approach is essential to prevent further escalation”, reports Northern Editor Freya McClements.
“The protection of human rights must remain at the centre of any resolution to the Drumcree dispute,” the organisations said.
In their statement on Monday, the FIDH and CAJ stressed “the authorities have a duty to balance competing rights under the European Convention on Human Rights, including freedom of assembly and the rights of others.
“In this context there have long been recommendations for the ‘right to freedom from sectarian harassment’ affirmed within the Good Friday Agreement to be expressly incorporated in the parading decisions framework,” the bodies said.
“Freedom of assembly is a fundamental right for both those who parade and counter protestors. Where necessary in a democratic society it can be proportionately restricted to protect the rights of others,” said Daniel Holder, vice-president of FIDH and director of CAJ.
“The Parades Commission decision did not properly consider that the Drumcree parade was inevitably going to require balancing two competing rights of assembly, nor is there consideration of the risks of sectarian intimidation.
“Transparency and a human rights-based approach across all relevant issues are essential for future decisions,” he said.
FIDH and CAJ welcomed that to date all assemblies have been peaceful and that there has been no use of force by the police, but raised “concerns at the continued discourse of ‘illegality’ being applied to counter-protesters.
“We also draw attention to ECHR-case law which has held that in certain circumstances rights to hold spontaneous peaceful protests in immediate response to events where the protest would be pointless if delayed may override notification requirements,” they said.
A barrister for the Garvaghy Road residents, Denise Kiley KC, has told the Court of Appeal in Belfast that it was in the public interest to ensure the Parades Commission came to correct decisions on parading applications.
The residents are challenging a decision of a High Court judge – made in the early hours of Sunday, September 27th – to refuse leave to apply for a judicial review of the commission’s determination to permit an Orange Order march down the predominantly nationalist road in Portadown later that Sunday.
Opening the case, Kiley said the question of whether the determination remained live – given the time and date of the originally permitted parade have now passed – remained an unresolved issue. However, she said the residents were not currently seeking a court determination on that point.
Outlining the basis of the appeal court challenge, she added: “There is a public interest in ensuring that the Parades Commission – a body charged with making these significant decisions on contentious parading issues – comes to correct and lawful determinations.”
The fresh legal challenge to the Orange march at the centre of the Drumcree stand-off in Portadown is under way at the Court of Appeal in Belfast, reports Northern Editor Freya McClements .
Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, which opposes the march, is seeking leave to apply for a judicial review of the decision by the Parades Commission to allow it to proceed.
On Sunday, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald rejected Taoiseach Micheál Martin’s suggestion that her party has an “overly simplistic” view of how to resolve the Drumcree dispute.
Sinn Féin has repeatedly called on the British government to intervene and stop the Orange Order march.
Martin, on Saturday, said he did not agree with Sinn Féín’s assessment that “Drumcree could be sorted by me simply telling Andy Burnham what to do” and accused the party of lacking “sincerity”.
Asked on the BBC’s Sunday Politics programme if she accepted that “the reality is, it’s not that simple”, McDonald replied: “Well, it is, actually.”
She also accused the Dublin and London governments of creating a “vacuum” by not working towards Irish unity.
While they “sit on their hands and fail to create the democratic space and dynamic for all of us to engage, to discuss, to plan about Ireland’s future, while there is a vacuum there, we are sitting ducks for this kind of reactionary sideswipe from small elements in society who want to upend our progress.”
I’m pleased that events have passed this weekend in Portadown without major incident. I continue to speak with people of goodwill on all sides and believe a mutually agreeable solution is still possible if people can show leadership based on openness, compromise and magnanimity.
Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant said he is continuing to speak with “people of goodwill on all sides,” in a post on X
He believes “a mutually agreeable solution is still possible if people can show leadership based on openness, compromise and magnanimity.”
He was “pleased that events have passed this weekend in Portadown without major incident.”
On Monday, the ninth day of the sustained stand-of, Northern Ireland First Minister and Sinn Féin deputy leader Michelle O’Neill is expected to face an urgent question on her participation in the protest during plenary business at Stormont.
Under parading laws in Northern Ireland, protests must be notified to and approved by, the Parades Commission adjudication body.
Police have confirmed the protest was unnotified to the commission and therefore unlawful.
Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald has said she and her party will “of course” co-operate with the PSNI over any potential investigation into the Garvaghy Road protest. – PA
On Sunday, Irish rap trio Kneecap visited the Garvaghy Road to show their support for the protesters.
They went to a local school before meeting residents at the Drumcree Community Centre on Sunday evening.
In a statement after the visit, the trio said: “Kneecap support the residents of Garvaghy Road, they’re a determined and strong community.
“No community should have to live with sectarian intimidation, racism or hatred. Not here, not now, not anywhere.”
A fresh legal challenge will be heard at the Court of Appeal in Belfast on Monday regarding the Orange march at the centre of the Drumcree stand-off in Portadown.
Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, who oppose the march, is to seek leave to apply for a judicial review of the decision by the Parades Commission to allow it to proceed.
The hearing was originally listed for Friday but was postponed until Monday.
The two sides remain deadlocked despite days of talks facilitated by Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant last week.
