title: Waste firm Panda sent for trial over worker’s death at Dublin plant
description: Company failed to ensure the safety, health and welfare of its employees, according to the charges
content:
Waste company Panda has been sent forward for trial over a fatal workplace incident at a Dublin recycling plant.
The prosecution follows a Health and Safety Authority investigation into the death of 32-year-old Radu Alexandru Chertes of Five Lamps, Cappagh Road, Finglas.
The case of Tallaght-based Starrus Eco Holdings Limited, trading as Panda Waste Management Solutions, was before Judge Anthony Halpin at Dublin District Court on Monday.
He noted that the Director of Public Prosecutions has decided that the company, which has yet to enter a plea, will face “trial on indictment”.
The State served a book of evidence on a representative for the company before the judge granted a return for trial order, formally sending the firm to the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court, where the case will be listed for mention on November 19th next.
The company faces six charges under the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 relating to an incident on April 6th, 2022, at its premises on Cappagh Road, Finglas, Dublin 11.
According to the charges, the firm failed to ensure, so far as was reasonably practicable, the safety, health and welfare of its employees.
Specifically, the prosecution claims the company failed to maintain a safe system of work, adequate control measures and proper training, instruction and supervision for clearing blockages in an M&J Pre-Shred 4000S machine.
The charges state that, as a consequence of these alleged failings, an employee, Radu Alexandru Chertes, suffered injuries and died.
At the opening of the inquest in November 2022, the deceased man’s brother, Andre Chertes, who had also worked at the Panda plant in Finglas, gave evidence of formally identifying his brother’s body to gardaí. The inquest has been adjourned pending the outcome of the judicial process.

title: Ticketmaster trial over prices for 2025 Oasis Croke Park concerts delayed
description: Case now set to be heard in new year as company is obtaining an expert report
content:
Ticketmaster’s “misleading commercial practice” trial over prices for the Oasis 2025 reunion concerts at Croke Park has been delayed while the company obtains an expert report.
The case, which first came before Dublin District Court last month, stems from an inquiry by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC).
It was originally thought the four-day hearing would be held in December, but Judge Anthony Halpin said on Monday that it would have to be pushed back into the new year.
The company faces two charges under section 47 of the Consumer Protection Act surrounding information provided to concert-goers who bought platinum tickets.
Platinum tickets give fans access to some of the most popular tickets at a price set by the organiser.
The alleged offences relate to tickets for the Gallagher brothers’ concerts in August 2025. Last month, the defence counsel said: “I anticipate that this matter will be fully contested.”
When the case was listed again on Monday, Brian Gageby, for Ticketmaster , said an expert report had to be obtained.
Prosecutor Ronan Kennedy, for the CCPC, said there had already been correspondence between both parties.
The judge said it was a complex case, adding that he wanted both sides to marshal witnesses and have them ready when the hearing gets under way. A new hearing date will be scheduled when the case is listed for mention on November 9th.
Ticketline Unlimited Company, trading as Ticketmaster, faces two charges under the Consumer Protection Act 2007 over Oasis concert tickets sold on August 31st, 2024.
The first charge alleges that the firm engaged in a misleading commercial practice by offering “platinum” tickets in a manner likely to deceive consumers regarding the product’s main characteristics and specifications.
The second alleges that Ticketmaster provided material information concerning ticket prices in a manner that was unclear, unintelligible, ambiguous or untimely.
The court has heard that the defence expects to call around a dozen witnesses.

title: Heimir is the right man for the job, and four other things we learned from international window
description: FAI will continue discussions around future Israel fixtures
content:
The decency and calmness of the Republic of Ireland manager was a constant over the past fortnight despite relentless criticism from sections of the Irish and Israeli media.
The Icelandic coach navigated the aftermath of his “we are playing against genocide” comment, that he made last month, by repeatedly stating it was poor leadership to express a personal view about what is happening Gaza.
Acting as a lightning rod during nine separate press conferences, from the Ireland squad announcement to post-match in Serbia, the 59-year-old shielded his players from direct abuse. He deserves credit for publicly supporting Gavin Bazunu’s right not to play against Israel. He also took sole responsibility for not playing Finn Azaz in the Israel matches, noting that Azaz’s family ties to both countries “tested him more than all of us”.
The FAI is expected to petition Uefa to keep the Republic of Ireland and Israel apart in future qualification draws, starting at the annual gathering of 55-member associations in Berlin on Thursday. David Courell, the FAI chief executive, and president Paul Cooke are travelling to Germany.
Hallgrímsson stated over the weekend that European football’s governing body should consider keeping the countries apart “just for the players’ welfare”.
As things stand, Ireland and Israel cannot be paired in qualifying for Euro 2028 as they are both in Pot 3 ahead of the draw on December 6th. This would change, however, if Ireland beat Kosovo in Dublin on November 17th and finish runners-up in Group B3 behind Austria. This would promote them into Pot 2.
Teams finishing second in League B will earn a two-leg promotion playoff in March, potentially against Serbia, Italy, Turkey, Germany, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Wales or Norway.
Ireland still lack a midfielder who demands ball into feet before turning to initiate forward momentum. Azaz is the obvious solution.
Ceadach O’Neill’s competitive appearances for Northern Ireland, coming off the bench in the recent Nations League games against Georgia and Ukraine, mean that the 18-year-old cannot switch to the Republic of Ireland.
Conor Coventry and Jayson Molumby could be retained as the holding midfielders next month, against Austria away on November 14th and Kosovo three days later in Dublin, unless Jack Moylan’s emergence keeps Azaz as a number six. The Southampton playmaker showed grit and technical quality in a deep-lying role during the 2-2 draw against Austria.
Alternatively, Josh Cullen is due to return for Burnley after 10 months sidelined with a knee injury and there is time for Rory Finneran, who Hallgrímsson capped last summer, to progress from the under-21s to the senior ranks before Euro 2028. The 18-year-old Newcastle United midfielder is currently on loan to Notts Country in League One.
It felt like Groundhog Day as Ireland struggled to a 1-0 loss in Kosovo on September 24th. Starting five centre-halves behind two defensive midfielders stymied the creation of any goalscoring opportunities.
Hallgrímsson reacted against Israel by keeping a similar shape, albeit with Adam Idah, a natural striker, alongside Moylan and in behind Troy Parrott. Against Austria, Idah’s flick prompted Parrott to skin two Austrians and score a stunning goal. Evan Ferguson, when he returns from ankle surgery, will see an opportunity to challenge Idah as Ireland’s attack appears to work with two centre forwards rotating at the tip of the spear, Moylan as the 10 and Azaz initiating the play.
Nathan Collins, Dara O’Shea, Liam Scales or James Abankwah are likely to fill the back three against Austria in Linz, following some glaring defensive errors by Jake O’Brien and Liam Kitching against Kosovo and Austria.
Kosovo, during their victory in Pristina, looked comfortable whenever the Irish wing-backs, Abankwah and Scales, had possession. If Séamus Coleman can find a club and regain match sharpness at 38, he could come straight back into the team. Ryan Manning replaced Scales for the other three games, but nobody has claimed the left wing-back position since Robbie Brady’s injury.

title: Budget 2027: Ministers put finishing touches to package as final measures agreed
description: Inside Politics: Childcare costs, student fees and public service pay among issues still in focus ahead of Tuesday’s budget
content:
It’ll be like the night before Christmas in the Department of Finance this evening.
Nearly all the little presents have been tied up with civil service bows, the stockings stuffed with tax cuts and the milk and cookies laid out for Simon Harris and Jack Chambers ’ speeches on Tuesday.
Despite reports that the busy budget workshop, at times, may have resembled more of a nightmare before Christmas, as Ministers supposedly squabbled over the naughty and nice list - the big day is almost finally upon us.
Given the modern budgetary way, the politicians have been leaking like proverbial sieves and most concerned citizens will have a fair idea of what will be in the document come time for the official reveal.
Indeed, some of the measures we’ll be hearing about , such as the new savings scheme, have been trailed for months.
Discussions on the remaining minutiae are likely to continue throughout the day, with a reported boost to childcare subsidies one of the key elements.
For families with a young child attending a creche full-time, a €1,000 per annum reduction could be on the cards. It will be lauded by the Government, but most likely panned by the opposition as still being well-off its pledge to cap such costs at €200 a month.
As of last night, there were still senior ministers pushing for their preferred pressies - like James Lawless and his “last ditch” effort to secure a €250 cut to the student contribution . It sounds like the Minister for Higher Education’s forces were left spent on the battlefield - with sources cautioning against such an idea.
On Saturday, the Taoiseach signalled there would be no further increases in the carbon tax applied to home heating oil - and there would be a Christmas bonus payment to pensioners and welfare recipients.
Public servants will be tuning in tomorrow to get a sense of what may have been left in reserve for a potential pay deal .
Over 70,000 teachers belonging to the Irish National Teachers Organisation and the Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland have today embarked on a work-to-rule that brings the total numbers involved to over 250,000. The Teachers Union of Ireland will join the action next Monday.
With Ministers pleading for engagement, full-blown strike action is still planned for October 14th and 21st - and is likely to shut nearly every school in the State.
Speaking of being shut down, efforts to bring some sort of resolution to the dispute over the Orange Order’s intention to parade down the Garvaghy Road are continuing.
With the British Secretary of State Chris Bryant still clinging to the notion that a mutually acceptable compromise can be struck, residents have taken to the Court of Appeal in Belfast.
They are seeking leave to apply for a judicial review of the Parades Commission decision that reopened the whole saga.
The uneasy peace surrounding the stand-off managed to survive the weekend. The Belfast Irish rap trio Kneecap paid a visit to residents on Sunday, saying no community should be subjected to sectarian intimidation.
There will, meanwhile, likely be a bit of political noise this week, with First Minister Michelle O’Neill today expected to face an ‘urgent question’ during plenary business at Stormont.
Unionists want to know why she took part in an unlawful protest on the road in question, while her party leader Mary Lou McDonald has said Sinn Féin will “of course” cooperate with a PSNI investigation.
Getting back briefly to the Budget talk, one man who could only imagine the joy of being able to actually deliver one is Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez.
Under pressure due to an on-going housing crisis, Sánchez this morning called a snap election for the end of next month .
Street demonstrations have engulfed his administration following the eviction last month of an 87-year-old woman with disabilities.
Such are the controversies and difficulties surrounding his tenure, Sánchez hasn’t been able to present a single government budget since retaking office in 2023.

title: ‘They want to kill all of us’: Life on Israel’s anxious frontier
description: Three years after the October 7th attacks, real security feels elusive in the Israeli community nearest the Gaza border fence
content:
I n recent weeks, a number of kites from Gaza landed on the Israeli side of the border. In 2018, Gazans sent incendiary balloons and kites over the border, causing fires in fields and farmlands, in what they said was protest at the Israeli blockade of the Strip. The recent kites were not attached to explosives or inflammatory materials. However, the Israeli assumption is that Hamas is behind the actions.
Israel has warned the so-called Board of Peace – established by US president Donald Trump to chart a new future for the enclave – that there will be a military response if the kites keep coming.
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim ​wrote on X that ​children launch the kites “in search ⁠of their innocent childhood amid the rubble”.
But for residents of Israeli communities along the Gaza border, the kites were a trigger, bringing back memories of what became known as the policy of containment before the October 7th, 2023 Hamas-led invasion , when Israel had turned a blind eye to a series of Hamas border infringements.
Most residents who fled in the wake of the October 7th cross-border invasion have returned to their homes and many of the communities are flourishing, but the sense of insecurity is palpable.
[ Israel plans big settlement push across occupied West Bank Opens in new window ]
Some 1,200 people were killed in Israel the October 7th attack and 250 people, living and dead, were taken as hostages into Gaza. More than 74,000 people have been killed by Israeli attacks in Gaza since then, according to Gaza’s health ministry.
During the October 7th Hamas attack, 20 people were killed in the moshav, or semi-collective agricultural community, of Netiv HaAsara, which borders the northern tip of the Gaza Strip.
Between 1973 and 1982, Netiv HaAsara had been an Israeli settlement in the Egyptian Sinai, but it was disbanded after the two countries signed a peace agreement and the Sinai was returned to Egypt. The community relocated to the Gaza border, which at the time was not considered dangerous. The Gaza neighbourhoods of Beit Hanoun and Beit Lahiya to the south are clearly visible, along with Gaza city’s sprawling northern Jabaliya neighbourhood.
Hila Fenlon (48), remembers an idyllic childhood growing up in the community. She cycled to the Gaza beach and went with her parents to shop or eat hummus inside the Strip. There was no border fence or soldiers. She also remembers the day everything changed for her.
“I remember the day clearly. April 9th, 2001. I was nine months pregnant with my first son, and a rocket fired from Gaza landed inside our community. Our reality changed,“ she recalls. ‘’The next day we had another rocket, and then another and another.”
Fenlon was speaking to reporters on a tour facilitated by Jerusalem-based Media Central, which describes itself as a non-profit liaison service for journalists and which organised transport and access to interviewees.
Whereas residents of Jerusalem or Tel Aviv have about 90 seconds to reach a bomb shelter if a rocket is launched from Gaza, members of Netiv HaAsara have fewer than five seconds. Bomb shelters have been built in every home and along all of the streets for people caught outside during an attack.
At 6.30am on October 7 th , three Hamas militants succeeded in penetrating the community using motorised paragliders, before residents even realised that Israel was at war. A larger Hamas force failed to breach the concrete barrier, likely preventing a much bigger massacre.
“We lost 20 members in one and a half hours on October 7 th . We all knew each other, we all grew up together and now we will overcome this together,” Fenlon says.
The community’s 300 families were evacuated after October 7 th , but returned last July. Fifty families chose not to return: the trauma was too great. New members have joined the community and a new neighbourhood is being built.
“When you live in a kibbutz or a moshav you are part of a community, part of something, you are not alone,” Fenlon says. “And if you ask me why I stayed here, raising my kids and teaching them to run to the bomb shelter when they could barely walk, it’s because as a community we try to stay together and try to remain strong and have the best life we can.”
The sense of community is repeated across the communities on the periphery of Gaza.
Kibbutz Be’eri, some 25km south of Netiv HaAsara and home to 500 families, was one of the communities worst hit on October 7 th . One hundred and two people were killed as dozens of gunmen went from house to house, killing indiscriminately. The first Israeli soldiers reached the besieged community that evening.
Two neighbourhoods on the kibbutz that were badly damaged have been demolished and new homes will be built on the site of the ruins. A few charred skeletons of burned homes remain as a memory.
At the time of the attack, after hearing shouts in Arabic, Avida Bachar (52) locked himself in the family bomb shelter together with his wife and two of his four children who were at home that weekend. He spent hours trying to keep the door handle locked as the gunmen fired into the room, threw grenades and tried to suffocate them by lighting fires.
By the time the first soldiers reached the neighbourhood, his wife Dana and 15-year-old son Carmel had bled to death from bullet wounds.
[ Condemnation as Israel passes law imposing death penalty on convicted Palestinians Opens in new window ]
Carmel’s last request was to be buried with his surfboard.
The soldiers pulled Bachar and his 13-year-old daughter, Hadar, from the bomb shelter window and applied tourniquets to their wounds. Bachar’s right leg was amputated in hospital, but he and Hadar survived.
He believes nothing will change as long as Hamas remains in control in Gaza. “Before October 7th I thought they just wanted to live like us. But they want to kill all of us. I think they should leave Gaza and go to a real country. They can’t stay there. If they stay they will just try to kill us again,” he says.
Bachar rejected an offer from prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu for a reserved spot on the Likud’s party list in October’s election. “I am not entering politics and certainly not with the Likud that failed on October 7th and continues to tear us apart to this day,” he says.
Bachar has no expectations for the Gaza peace plan. “We have to stay here on the land, and if someone wants to take our land we have to take their land.”
Rafi Babian, security officer for the Sdot Negev regional council along the Gaza border, says the arrangements currently in place provide an adequate layer of protection. He says the yellow demarcation line inside Gaza and a series of IDF outposts further east, closer to the Israeli border, afford a sense of safety to the communities, but he is concerned that this is only a temporary solution.
“The kites are a trial balloon to see how we will react. They are testing us. I’m very, very, very worried that the IDF will be forced to redeploy in Gaza and withdraw to the border. I hope Trump can be persuaded that the IDF needs to stay there,” he says.
In a few days, Israel will mark the third anniversary of the October 7th attack, but for the residents of communities on the Gaza periphery, lasting security remains as elusive as ever.
Fenlon considers herself an optimist, but believes Hamas will never lay down its arms. “Three years ago we were told Hamas will be replaced, and it didn’t happen. Israel can no longer destroy Hamas because there is the Board of Peace and they are responsible for whatever happens in Gaza. It’s no longer in our hands.”

title: Key Limerick hurling management team members return for 2027
description: Paul Kinnerk and Caroline Currid have recommitted for another season alongside John Kiely
content:
Paul Kinnerk and Caroline Currid have recommitted to the Limerick senior hurling management team for 2027.
It was confirmed last month that John Kiely was remaining at the helm of the county’s senior hurlers for an 11th season and it appears all the key members of Limerick’s backroom set-up are also to remain in place.
There had been doubts on whether Kinnerk, the team coach, and sport psychologist Currid would return but they are to be on-board again, as are selectors Donal O’Grady, Liam Cronin, John Flavin and Alan Cunningham.
Kiely told The Limerick Leader: “We had to have a bit of reflection to see what was the best thing to do going forward.
“We’ve obviously committed to going forward again for 2027 and we’re very much looking forward to that.
“Since that decision was made then, it was a case of ‘let’s start getting to work’ then with the backroom team.
“I’ve been meeting lots of the members of the backroom team for conversations just to get a bit of feedback from them, just to pick up on things that we can maybe do a little better, areas of improvement.”
Limerick completed a clean sweep in 2026 – winning the Munster Senior Hurling League, the National Hurling League, the Munster SHC and the All-Ireland SHC.

title: Mountjoy prison officer killed in Madrid road incident
description: Liam Donoghue (52) died after being hit by a taxi early on Sunday morning
content:
An Irish prison officer has died after being hit by a car in the Spanish capital of Madrid in the early hours of Sunday morning.
The man was hit by a taxi at about 2.20am while crossing the Ronda de Toledo, a major road in Madrid’s city centre near the Toledo Gate.
He has been named locally as 52-year-old Liam Donoghue, who worked in Mountjoy Prison as a prison officer.
He was considered a popular and well-known officer in the Dublin prison. The man’s immediate family has been notified.
Paramedics and law enforcement attended the scene and treated the prison officer for cardiac arrest, local officials said.
He was transferred to the nearby Hospital Clínico Universitario San Carlos and was later pronounced dead.
The Department of Foreign Affairs said it was aware of the case and is providing consular support to the family.
“As with all consular cases, the department does not comment on the details of individual cases,” it said.
The Madrid municipal police said in a statement: “Preliminary indications suggest that he was crossing the road at an unauthorised location, but an investigation is currently underway.”

title: Chicken producer Moy Park paid £143m dividend to US parent as it cut 1,000 jobs
description: Meat firm reports 34% jump in operating profits
content:
Moy Park, the Co Armagh -based chicken producer, raised dividend payments to its US parent by almost 50 per cent last year to £143 million (€168.7 million) as it slashed its headcount in Northern Ireland and cut more than 1,000 jobs across Europe.
New accounts for the company, which is part of the US poultry group Pilgrim’s Pride, also reveal that operating profits at the Craigavon-headquartered entity climbed by 34.4 per cent to £134.5 million in 2025 from £102.7 million in 2024.
Moy Park substantially reduced headcount across its European operations last year as it restructured the business. In the UK and France , the company employed an average of 7,960 people in 2025, a reduction of 1,092 from the previous year, concentrated mostly in the UK.
Still, the chicken producer’s employee-related costs increased slightly to £321.6 million in 2025. In a report attached to the filings, the directors said that redundancy payments increased employee costs relative to headcount in the year.
However, they said the transition from a seven-day to a five-day production schedule would “reduce wages” in the future.
The directors said Moy Park, “the industry-leading manufacturer of organic, free-range and higher welfare chicken”, supplies branded and own-label poultry products to retailers and food service businesses throughout the UK, Ireland and Europe. It also produces beef products, vegetarian dishes and desserts.
Moy Park is also one of the North’s largest companies, working with 700 farms globally. It has 35 million chickens on the ground at any given time.
Turnover increased by 9 per cent to more than £2.1 billion in the year.
The company paid a £143 million dividend to its US parent in 2025, up from £98.3 million in 2024, an increase of more than 45 per cent year-on-year.
“Moy Park made significant progress in 2025 by focusing on driving operational improvements and securing contracts with key customers,” the directors said in their report. “Moy Park’s trading models and customer negotiations, together with commodity deflation towards the end of 2025, offset higher labour costs.”
Moy Park also invested in its factory infrastructure.
The directors said the group was “exposed” to commodity price fluctuations. Global poultry prices increased between 2 and 3 per cent in 2025.
Moy Park incurred raw materials costs of more than £1 billion in 2025, up by almost 10 per cent from 2024.
The company traces its roots back to the setting up of a small farming company in Co Tyrone and has had several owners over the past three decades.
It was acquired by US food giant OSI Group, best known as a meat supplier of McDonald’s, in 1996 before being sold to Brazilian meatpacker Marfrig 12 years later.
The then heavily indebted Marfrig sold the business to Brazil’s largest food processing company, JBS, in 2015. JBS sold the business in a $1.5 billion (€1.38 billion) deal in 2017. The buyer was US-based chicken producer Pilgrim’s Pride, which is more than 80 per cent owned by JBS.

title: Fitzwilliam tennis club seeks permission to enclose two padel courts with 10.5m-high cover
description: Dublin 6 organisation already in dispute with some residents over plans to put ‘air dome’ over tennis court
content:
The Dublin 6 tennis club already in dispute with some local residents over plans for a 10-metre tall white “air dome” over a tennis court is now planning to construct a separate 10.5m-high enclosure over two padel courts.
In new plans lodged with Dublin City Council , Fitzwilliam Lawn Tennis Club is seeking planning permission for the cover over two padel courts at the club’s premises on Winton Road, Ranelagh .
The structure is to consist of a metal frame covered by a white canvas.
A planning report lodged with the application by planning consultants Tom Phillips and Associates said the applicant was one of the oldest tennis clubs in the world.
It said that “2027 will be the 150th anniversary of the club and the proposed upgrades will facilitate celebrations associated with this anniversary.”
Julie Costello, associate director at Tom Phillips, said the enclosure over two padel courts “has been carefully considered and designed to ensure that the proposed cover would not result in any adverse impact on the residential amenity of the neighbouring residential dwellings along Leeson Street Upper ”.
Costello said the sole purpose of the proposed reorganisation of the padel courts “is to ensure that the cover would not result in any overshadowing or overbearing impact on the neighbouring properties”.
The report said the cover would be set back 25 metres from the rear wall of the original houses at Leeson Street, so the new structure would “not cause overshadowing to the open space associated with those houses, nor will it appear overbearing from within those houses”.
The proposed development would also provide for enhanced recreational facilities, allowing for the existing courts to be used during bad weather, Costello’s 20-page planning report said.
She said the development would achieve the realisation of many city development plan policy objectives and would make an important contribution to sport, active lifestyle and physical recreation within the area.
Plans by Fitzwilliam Lawn Tennis Club for its 10m “air dome” over a tennis court have been stalled. Two appeals have been lodged by local residents to An Coimisiún Pleanála against the Dublin City Council’s decision to grant planning permission.
Objectors have described the air tent or dome as a “colossal glowing orb”.

title: Royal Hospital Kilmainham conservation plan edges closer as OPW and Imma tensions ease
description: Office of Public Works and Irish Museum of Modern Art hold ‘constructive’ talks following previous disagreement
content:
A contentious plan for the future of the Royal Hospital Kilmainham site in Dublin 8 could soon be finalised following progress in talks between the Office of Public Works (OPW) and the Irish Museum of Modern Art (Imma).
Representatives from both organisations held a “constructive” meeting about the conservation management plan (CMP) last week.
The plan has been at the centre of heated discussions between the OPW and Imma in recent months amid disagreement over its content. Imma sought legal advice on the matter, saying an earlier version of the plan “entirely” overlooked the museum’s cultural significance .
Ali Curran, chair of Imma’s board, earlier this year said issues between the museum and the OPW had been “escalating for some time” and may require the intervention of Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan .
Curran made the remarks in a letter to Feargal Ó Coigligh, secretary general at the Department of Culture, in January.
The draft plan, the letter argued, “strays some distance from what may be expected ... into areas of constitutional revision and dilution of Imma as the operator of the site with an emphasis on the strategic repositioning of the OPW, undermining the museum’s mandate”.
In separate correspondence, John McLaughlin, an architect who sits on Imma’s board, said elements of the plan were “at odds” with best practice guidance published by the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS).
The OPW took exception to these remarks . An internal memo, dated April 16th, noted: “Imma state that CMP is not [in] line with best practice, ie ICOMOS principles. This opinion is wholly incorrect.”
Shaffrey Architects was commissioned by the OPW to draft the plan in 2023. The memo said the CMP was “built on best practice, drafted by an internationally recognised architect firm” and the comments were “disparaging and completely unacceptable”.
Representatives from the OPW, Imma and Shaffrey Architects were present at a meeting last Thursday.
A spokeswoman for Imma said “alternative wording” would be suggested for certain sections of the plan later this month, before another meeting will take place.
“We all feel rather confident that this will be finalised before the end of the year,” she said.
A spokeswoman for the OPW said the State body “is working closely with Imma to complete” the plan. She also referred to last week’s meeting as “collegiate and constructive”.

title: ‘We can all see you’: Gillian Anderson addresses ‘distracting’ fans in front row
description: Anderson was filmed outside Soho Place theatre where she’s performing in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?
content:
Gillian Anderson has come under fire after the actor was filmed telling a group of fans that they were “distracting” her by repeatedly sitting in the front row while she performs in London’s West End.
The Sex Education and X-Files star was filmed outside the Soho Place theatre where she’s performing in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, telling a group of fans: “You guys cannot sit in the front row. I do not care; you cannot sit in the front row. It’s so distracting.”
Anderson, who is playing frustrated wife Martha in Edward Albee’s play about an unhappy marriage, then said: “You can’t come 20 times and sit in the front row, it’ll drive me mad.”
The fans, who were not shown in the video, can be heard responding to Anderson’s comments with “I’m sorry” and “I know”.
After the video was uploaded to TikTok, the 58-year-old actor shared a statement on social media in an effort to clarify her position.
“The video doing the rounds is me talking with women I go back over 20 years with – so please don’t say anything negative to or about them,” she wrote on X.
“We’re thrilled to be doing this show but for people in the front row, please be aware that in such an intimate venue we can all see you and sometimes, it can be a tad distracting.”
Anderson signed off with: “That’s all. All good. On with the show and love to everyone and thank you to all of those coming.”
It’s not the first time this year an actor has made headlines with comments about theatre etiquette. Last month, Cate Blanchett asked the audience of her production Electra/Persona to put away their phones during curtain call.
[ Gillian Anderson: I want women to tell me what they think about when they think about sex Opens in new window ]
“I understand you like filming the curtain call – and it is kind of flattering in a way,” Blanchett said. “But for anyone who is filming the show, please don’t, because it spoils it for the next group of people who come in and are present with us.”
Rosamund Pike criticised an audience member for texting during her West End play Inter Alia in May. “I just wanted to say for anyone going to the theatre, it’s a huge thing that we’re trying to give you,” she told the audience .
“Somebody was texting in this part,” she said. “You know who you are … Maybe it was very important, and maybe you’re a doctor, and you’re saving someone’s life, and I hope you are, but we do see these, we do feel them.”
In April, Wicked star Cynthia Erivo halted her one-woman performance of Dracula – in which she played all 23 characters – after spotting an audience member recording the show.
In May, The Pitt star Isa Briones told fans to stop yelling references to the medical drama during her Broadway musical Just in Time. And Kristin Scott Thomas, who is due to perform in The Cherry Orchard this month, told the Financial Times she witnessed an audience member eating “a ready meal in the front row once” – but said she still prefers theatre to screen acting, adding: “For me it is telling a story to live, breathing, coughing, eating people and trying to drag them along with you. Which I find incredibly thrilling.”
Other actors, including Andrew Scott, Daniel Craig and Hugh Jackman, have spoken out about the decline in theatre etiquette. Lesley Manville told BBC Radio 4 earlier this year that she finds audience members who take photos during the curtain call “insulting”.
“Clap or don’t clap, but don’t just stick up your phone in our faces,” she said.
It’s not just the performers who have complaints either. Theatregoers at the Royal Shakespeare Company’s The Tempest starring Kenneth Branagh took issue with a baby cooing and gurgling through the first half of a performance in June. The mother and baby were asked to leave the Stratford-upon-Avon theatre for the second half after audience members asked for refunds. – Guardian

title: Major Denmark breach exposes personal data of 8.8 million people
description: Hackers gain access to names, addresses and personal identification numbers
content:
Denmark has suffered a major data breach that has given unauthorised individuals access to names, addresses and personal identification numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people registered in the country’s central population database.
The breach occurred after unidentified individuals misused a private Danish company’s legitimate access to search the Central Person Register (CPR), the government said in a statement Monday.
The company has since been blocked from the system while police investigate the matter, with authorities saying it is too early to determine who was behind the breach.
“This is a deeply serious incident,” digitalisation minister Christina Egelund said. She has ordered a comprehensive security review of the CPR system and urged Danes to be vigilant about suspicious calls and emails.
The CPR system is a cornerstone of Denmark’s highly digitised public sector. Every resident is assigned a unique 10-digit CPR number that is widely used to identify individuals when dealing with government agencies, banks and healthcare providers. While Denmark has a population of about six million, the register contains records on roughly 11 million people, including those who have died or moved abroad.
The administration first detected irregular activity on October 2nd and determined over the weekend that unauthorised searches had taken place during September. People registered in the system for name and address protection were not exposed, it said. – Bloomberg

title: Inside the school protests in France that have spiralled into arson and street violence
description: Sense of chaos feeds into election campaign, with Marine Le Pen promising to reestablish ‘order’
content:
T he boom of protest bangers starts soon after 9am. The crowd is visible from streets away, spilling across the road. The students of the local high school have once again emptied out of their building in central Paris to protest.
The blackened detritus of a burnt bin and a rental e-bike lie to one side. The teenagers are largely dressed like any 15- to 18-year-olds who went off to school that morning, carrying backpacks and wearing light autumn jackets. But moving among them are the daredevils and instigators, with their faces concealed by balaclavas.
Every now and again one of them tosses a banger and groups of girls in little tops and make-up surge shrieking away from the blast. Mostly, the young people stand around.
What’s the protest about? I ask one of the boys.
His friend steps in. “It’s for the teachers,” he begins. “Their salaries are too low.” He lists a series of complaints aired by student protesters across France: teacher absences, poor building conditions, long days that can stretch from 8am to 6pm.
The protests began at a school in a Paris suburb on September 17th and spread from there, developing into a nationwide movement from last Tuesday when they coincided with a strike of public sector workers that included many teachers.
The disruption is widespread. Up to 500 schools were partially or fully shut in France on Monday due to the protests, including a third of high schools in the greater Paris region.
Blocked roads can make journeys torturous: last week, the protests turned a 25-minute trip through Paris into an hour and a half.
[ France closes up to 500 schools on Monday as more protests planned Opens in new window ]
Protest is taken seriously in France as a civic act, and the involvement of young people can give it a sense of moral force.
However, the arson and violence that have accompanied some protests has soured the attitudes of some.
Across France, 24 schools have been “burned or ransacked” since the start of protests last month, according to the government.
Footage of some students attacking police has gone viral, and on Sunday a 16-year-old was arrested in southern France after a serious assault on a teacher.
For their part, riot police – never much known for their leniency in France – have stormed the protests with tear gas in a bid to get control and seriously wounded some students with rubber bullets and batons.
With France in election mode in advance of a presidential vote in the spring, response is polarised along political lines.
“Faced with chaos, re-establish order” read the call from the far-right National Rally party of Marine Le Pen this weekend, promising to increase teacher salaries, restore respect to the profession, and stand on the side of “authority” and “law and order”.
The party accuses the hard-left France Unbowed movement of orchestrating protests and of bearing “direct responsibility” for violence – a running theme.
The leader of France Unbowed, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is the nearest challenger to Le Pen in polls.
The veteran left-winger has supported the student protests from the outset. He has led condemnations of the “sickening” police response, calling for supporters to form protective lines around the young people and demanding that the interior minister “rein in this gang that’s beating up our children”.
“The student protesters are harmless. The ... government has ordered repression. This brutality is irresponsible and has a clear racist undertone,” Mélenchon wrote – a reference to accusations that the police response was tougher in diverse neighbourhoods.
There are signs that the protest movement may develop into something larger.
Over the weekend, the teachers’ unions issued a joint statement endorsing the student protests and declaring they would join them on Tuesday for a “day of mobilisation”.
The unions described students’ complaints as “legitimate” and said the problems were “the direct consequence of the education policy of the various governments of Emmanuel Macron”.
This is a negotiating move: the unions have their eye on the budget, which has a freeze on teacher salaries among its proposed belt-tightening measures and has just begun its torturous pathway through France’s hung parliament.
But there is a sense of momentum building around general discontent, with fuel prices soaring and France already on alert for a potential return of the Yellow Vests movement.
[ Yellow Vests protest in 2018: ‘They smashed the window with fists. There’s blood on the glass’ Opens in new window ]
The stakes are high: the government collapsed while trying to pass a budget this time last year, and financial markets are on alert. As trading opened this week, concerns about France were blamed for causing a slide in the euro.
Their differences aside, both left and right agree that the underlying complaints of the students have merit, and that Macron’s policies are to blame.
When Macron came to power in 2017, he promised reform and to restore France as an economic powerhouse.
But efforts to rein in spending, while received as punishing austerity by the public in France, have nevertheless failed to get a handle on the country’s towering debt pile and stubbornly high deficit, which ran wild during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Macron is at the end of his term limits, but the situation looks unfavourable to the various “Macronist” candidates who had been vying to be his successor.
[ Students in France take to the barricades over conditions Opens in new window ]
A teenager’s hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France yesterday, a local official said, on the eve of a national demonstration by the pupils’ union against underfunding, overcrowding and dilapidation.
The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police dispersal grenade that detonated in the town of Lens as the wave of school protests entered its third week.
François-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, declined to comment on the exact circumstances, saying some 200 to 250 protesters had been hurling objects at police.
It was uncertain if the incident had involved a police stun grenade or how the injury happened. Lauch said an investigation had been opened. - Agencies

title: US ‘monitoring’ suspected case of plague in Russia after lab worker dies
description: Mystery death at plague research institute in Irkutsk sparks quarantine measures across Siberia
author_name: Anastasia Stognei in Berlin and Katya Arenina in Vilnius
content:
The US has said it is monitoring developments relating to a suspected case of pneumonic plague in Russia , which has imposed sweeping quarantine measures in Siberia over the incident while insisting there has been no outbreak.
On Monday, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said Washington was watching the matter “closely” after an employee at Siberia’s Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute was admitted to hospital outside the city on September 29th.
“It seems there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there was concern that that could have spread,” Rubio said. “Like anything else, if something like that gets out, it could quickly spread so we are watching and monitoring it closely.”
Daria Shipilova (28), died two days later from what public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor described as “pneumonia of unknown” origin. Local media reported that pneumonic plague may have been the cause of death.
If confirmed, it would be Russia’s first case of plague in a decade. Europe has not seen a human plague outbreak since the immediate aftermath of the second World War.
However, Rubio cautioned that he did not think the incident was “cause for alarm”.
Russian authorities have not confirmed a recorded plague infection. The public health watchdog said tests on samples from Shipilova did not detect micro-organisms “connected with her work”.
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov urged them “not to listen to rumours about a plague outbreak” and to “rely on Rospotrebnadzor’s statement”.
But the scale of the Russian authorities’ response suggested they were treating the situation as exceptional. Irkutsk region governor Igor Kobzev said in a social media post on October 2nd that he held an “emergency meeting” with Rospotrebnadzor over “a suspected case of a highly dangerous infectious disease”.
Rospotrebnadzor was “carrying out the full range of anti-epidemic measures”, while everyone who had been in contact with Shipilova had been “placed under medical observation”, he added.
As many as 200 people were placed under observation, according to local media. The inpatient section of the Shelekhov district hospital was quarantined alongside several hospitals in Irkutsk, the independent People of Baikal outlet reported.
Only the quarantine at the Shelekhov hospital has been officially confirmed.
Staff at Shipilova’s institute were also isolated inside the building, “sleeping on chairs”, RFE/RL’s Siberia.Realities reported, citing sources.
On October 3rd, the head of the Irkutsk aluminium factory wrote on his Telegram channel that employees must wear face masks because of “contradictory information about plague”, but quickly edited the post to remove the mention of the disease.
According to the pro-Kremlin Telegram channel Mash, which has close ties to Russia’s law enforcement agencies, Shipilova had recently returned from a work trip to the country’s Buryatia region near the border with Mongolia.
Mongolia regularly records plague cases, with 17 confirmed instances reported to the World Health Organisation between 2019 and 2025. But Alexei Tsydenov, head of Russia’s Republic of Buryatia, said the woman who had “possibly died of plague” had not entered the region.
The US state department said “many details have not been confirmed” about the matter, adding that “we encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly”.
“Plague is a known disease and is treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early,” the official added.
Shipilova joined the Irkutsk institute in 2022 and had served as a researcher in its plague microbiology department since 2023. This spring, she was listed among the authors of a presentation on antibacterial drug susceptibility of the plague-causing bacterium Yersinia pestis.
The last confirmed plague case in Russia was in 2016, in a tiny Altai Republic settlement near the border with Mongolia, when a 10-year-old boy contracted the disease after contact with a marmot that his grandfather killed while hunting. The boy survived after receiving treatment.
The authorities did not dispute the diagnosis, isolated the boy’s contacts, disinfected affected areas and carried out an extensive campaign against marmot hunting.
