title: Drug barons ‘a cancer’ on State, says judge, as two boys sentenced for drug-debt intimidation
description: Teenagers were 16 at the time of incident in Mullingar in which home-made shotgun was fired, houses were attacked and four cars set ablaze
content:
The president of the Circuit Court has branded drug barons using children as foot soldiers as being “like a cancer”, saying “all State resources should be used to catch and lock them up”.
Judge Keenan Johnson’s comments came in the case of two boys involved in a drug-debt intimidation shooting at a house in Mullingar, Co Westmeath .
One of the pair also carried out attacks on houses, torched four cars and carried out a drug-debt intimidation campaign across three midlands counties. He was given a six-year suspended sentence.
That youth, now 17, and a second boy, the same age, pleaded guilty to recklessly discharging the home-made “slammer” shotgun at about 1.30pm on July 14th at Ardleigh Park in the Co Westmeath town.
The teenager who fired the gun admitted a further charge of criminal damage to the door of the house.
The pair cannot be named because they are minors with the right to anonymity.
They were 16 and had no prior convictions at the time of the incident, Mullingar Circuit Criminal Court heard.
One youth also admitted to criminal damage and arson offences in 2025 targeting seven properties mainly in Westmeath but also in Offaly and Longford.
The same teenager also pleaded guilty to possessing a blank-firing handgun, blank rounds of ammunition and €7,000 of cannabis.
Johnson described the incidents as “really shocking and very, very disturbing”.
The case reminded him, he said, of the Charles Dickens character Fagin and his team of child offenders, but the drug barons were “far more sinister and a lot more dangerous”.
Sentencing, he rebuked the “malignant forces” who “prey on children like the accused, plying them with drugs, building debts, to manipulate them to act as their foot soldiers in completion of their nefarious activities”.
He characterised them as “the lowest of low”.
Det Garda Kevin Lennon was part of a team assembled to investigate incidents of arson and criminal damage connected to drug debts in counties Westmeath, Offaly and Longford.
In evidence, he said one of the youths was charged after his home was searched and his phone was seized as part of another investigation into a drug and firearm find.
An examination of the device uncovered a series of videos and messages linking the boy to the drug-debt intimidation incidents in Mullingar, Tullamore, Rochfortbridge, Finea and Edgeworthstown from February to May 2025.
A video on the teenager’s phone showed him destroying evidence by setting a petrol can and gloves on fire.
The footage captured the sound of victims screaming. His phone messages contained discussions with another individual about whether he would produce a gun if occupants came out of the houses.
Victim impact statements were read to the court, including one from a woman who said she feared for her baby’s life. Another victim stated she was left living in fear, and the court heard that some families were left with boarded-up windows until they could afford replacements.
Two videos of the incident were found on the boy’s phone, including a message from a character known in his interactions with the teenager as either “D” or “Bob Marley”.
The teenager had explained that some of the videos were filmed on his phone and others were sent to him. He told gardaí he was afraid to speak out, believing he would end up dead, and stated that “it was them or me”, adding that individuals higher up the chain had drawn him into the activity and placed him under intense pressure.
Both defendants told the court they had drug debts at the time and were forced to take part in the gun attack.
The teen who fired the gun had already served a period in custody on remand in a detention centre, and the judge sent him into custody until a date in December, after which he will have a three-year sentence suspended over him for the next five years.
His co-accused, who faced the bulk of the charges, stopped coming to Garda attention after moving and getting work.
He received a series of concurrent sentences, the longest being six years on condition he does not reoffend in the next eight years.
He must also pay €14,500 to his victims in a series of instalments to be completed by June 1st, 2027.
The teen will also have to complete 240 hours of community service. The judge indicated the suspended sentences will also come into effect after he turns 18 and the order is to be finalised in December.
The judge noted their remorse and the severe pressure that led to them being “preyed upon by sinister forces”.

title: Behind the mystery that first set off fears of Iranian threats at a UK military base
description: A mysterious call near Fairford airbase set in motion a huge counterterrorism response and days of uncertainty
author_name: Michael D Shear, Eric Schmitt, Megan Specia and Adam Goldman
content:
T he three white vans navigated through a picturesque stretch of rural England in the middle of the night, winding toward a British airbase that the US is using to wage war on Iran .
It was 12.45am on Sunday, September 27th, when one of the men inside the vans – for reasons still not clear – dialled emergency services, giving authorities their first sign that a terrorism plot they had received intelligence on almost two weeks earlier might be in motion.
Police scrambled an urgent, armed response, speeding to the scene and arresting the man and four associates. A grainy photograph later leaked to the media showed the five men sitting shirtless on the side of a road, their hands bound behind their backs.
Why the man called police remains the subject of debate among investigators trying to unravel what happened that night, security officials from several countries told The New York Times. They asked for anonymity because the inquiry remains open.
It is one of many puzzles that authorities have yet to piece together.
The call did set off a cascade of events, including the arrest of the men on suspicion of terrorism, the frantic evacuation of 85 homes, a bomb disposal robot searching the vans for explosives, and a national security meeting convened by British prime minister Andy Burnham. He said later that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part.”
But a part in what, exactly? Burnham and other British authorities have offered few answers. The vans contained no explosives when police searched them. And within a day, all five men were released on bail, the kind of treatment typically given to common criminals, rather than terrorism suspects. Authorities could also have been hamstrung by the need to keep evidence classified and thus unable to be cited in criminal court.
Police have cast a wide net in trying to find those responsible for hiring the men, whom one official described as “unwitting chumps”. US and British officials believe the operation is connected to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard or a separate military headquarters in Tehran, Iran’s capital. Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, has rejected the accusations.
[ Trump says Iran may be linked to co-pilot who tried to crash Israel-bound plane Opens in new window ]
This account is drawn from interviews with investigators, local officials and residents as well as security officials in Britain, Germany, Israel and the United States who had knowledge of warnings about a plot to target US bases in Britain and elsewhere in Europe. Some officials declined to reveal details of the case. Others conceded that the full story remains hazy, even to them. Most spoke on the condition of anonymity, citing the sensitive nature of the investigation.
For Britain, the events of the past six days have been a vivid – if at times mystifying – reminder that the US- and Israeli-led war against Iran that began eight months ago has the potential to do more than raise the price of oil.
In July, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard issued a statement warning that allowing the United States to use the base “makes London responsible” for their actions. “Any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory,” the statement said, “is a legitimate target for our forces”.
In the end, officials found no concrete signs the men in the vans were in the final stages of an attack. But for a while last Sunday, it looked like Iran might be preparing to make good on its threat.
In mid-September, US military commanders received a chilling warning from US and other western intelligence agencies, according to US officials briefed on the information. Royal Air Force Fairford, the base in southern England primarily used by the US Air Force to deploy some of its largest bombers, was the target of a potential Iran-backed attack.
The murky outlines of a plot had been pieced together through a combination of intercepted communications, informants and other intelligence. Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu said his intelligence officials also warned their British counterparts of a probable Iranian-sponsored attack, though they did not provide a specific target. Follow-up attacks were likely to include drones, the confidential assessments warned.
The warnings were general. Analysts could not pin down a date or concrete details about the plotters, other than concluding they were guided and supported by Tehran. Base commanders in Britain raised security levels, already elevated since the start of the war with Iran.
[ After two decades, US forces leave Iraq to an uncertain future Opens in new window ]
Residents of the nearby town of Fairford, and the villages of Kempsford and Whelford, began noticing changes. There were “rumbles that things were being moved around the base in terms of protection and levels of warnings”, said Dom Morris, a local councillor.
On September 16th, 11 days before the episode at the base, a resident posted in a private neighbourhood Facebook group that he had seen something unusual: a man in a balaclava running through the village around 9pm. At least three other villagers said they had seen a masked man wearing black. It was unclear if they were speaking about the same person, or who it was.
Across Europe, concern among officials was growing rapidly. According to a senior US official, Israel warned Germany that US bases there were at heightened risk, noting Spangdahlem and Ramstein in particular.
On September 23rd, four days before the events at RAF Fairford, an Iranian-backed media site posted comments from Yahya Rahim Safavi, former chief commander of the Revolutionary Guard. According to Site Intelligence Group, which tracks the online activity of jihadi organisations, Safavi condemned Europe as a “logistics hub” for the US war on Iran, naming airbases that US forces have used to conduct the war, including Ramstein in Germany, Aviano in Italy and Fairford.
But without concrete intelligence about a specific target or timing, there was little authorities could do – except tighten security and wait.
That changed, dramatically, on Sunday, September 27th.
A local farmer returning home from a party found her driveway blocked by the three white vans.
“I looked at it and thought ‘that is not real’,” the farmer, who declined to be identified, later told BBC News. She told reporters she saw eight to 10 people in masks running.
At 1.36am, she said, she called 999 and later said she believed her call “foiled whatever plans they had”.
The police timeline suggests, however, that she made her call about 50 minutes after the man in the van. It isn’t clear whether the people she saw were the suspects, or security operatives responding to the initial alert.
[ ‘It’s off the charts’: Satellite images show how three years of war have devastated Gaza Opens in new window ]
“This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation,” Vicki Evans, the deputy assistant commissioner for Britain’s counter terrorism police, said later last Sunday, adding: “Our activity is in the interest of national security.”
By Monday, however, the case took a surprising turn.
The men were released on bail, a rare outcome for terrorism suspects. Police said later they had discovered some fuel, but no explosives, in the vans. Laurence Taylor, Evans’s supervisor, told reporters the men were “subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others. They absolutely remain under investigation”.
Behind closed doors, officials were trying to determine the suspects’ role, and whether Iran was using them to undermine Britain’s willingness to let the US use its bases. It is not yet clear how much investigators have learned from the men about their plans.
Were they a diversion from another attack that was in the works? Had they been intercepted before they could link up with other confederates? Or was the episode an elaborate hoax designed to sow fear and create propaganda?
Some intelligence officials believed the initial call by one of the five men was part of a plan to distract police while a broader plot unfolded. Others thought it was more likely that the five men were low-level criminals, one of whom called when they realised they had been hired to do something serious.
Taylor shared little about the investigation in his statement on Monday. But he hinted at the complexity of the case.
“Often this threat becomes visible to us as criminal activity,” he said, “often at a small scale and committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain”.
The head of MI5, Britain’s domestic security agency, has warned for years about Iran-backed plots, which have often involved targeting opponents using local criminals.
“Iranian state actors make extensive use of criminals as proxies – from international drug traffickers to low-level crooks,” Ken McCallum, the group’s director general, said in 2024. Iranian journalists and dissidents in Britain have received death threats and been physically attacked.
When he was prime minister of Britain, Keir Starmer initially refused to let the Trump administration use RAF Fairford for strikes on Iran, saying he would not join “regime change from the skies”. But he later gave permission for what he called “defensive” operations, and US B-52 and B-1 planes loaded with bombs began flying to Iran from Fairford. Burnham has continued the policy.
After Starmer announced the change on March 1st, Iranian proxies appeared ready to act against a wider range of targets in Britain. Four ambulances belonging to a Jewish volunteer group in London were set on fire. Molotov cocktails were thrown at several synagogues in the middle of the night.
The goal appeared to be to stoke fear in the Jewish community, while signalling that Britain’s changed posture had consequences. The attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, or Hayi, which, US prosecutors said, is a front for Kataib Hizbullah, a US-designated terrorist group and one of the most powerful Iranian proxies in Iraq. A commander from the group was charged in the US in May with leading the attacks and other incidents in Europe as part of a retaliation campaign by Tehran.
[ Justice or stability? Syria confronts the legacy of Assad Opens in new window ]
In April, Hayi posted a video claiming that the Israeli embassy in London would be attacked by drones carrying dangerous substances. Suspicious items, including two jars of a powdered substance, were found in the nearby Kensington Gardens. A huge police response was triggered, involving chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear teams. But the police later concluded that there had been no attack on the embassy and the powdered substance was not hazardous.
An actual assault on a US airbase in Britain would be a drastic escalation, officials said.
By the end of the week, the evacuated families had returned to their homes and a 400m cordon around where the vans had been was taken down. But concrete barriers were installed around the entrance of RAF Fairford. As the investigation continued, the police arrested a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian citizen in London, on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. He, too, was released on bail.
The US withdrew its bombers from the base over the weekend. – This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: Daniel Kinahan case adjourned for one week to allow solicitor to apply to represent him
description: Kinahan appears via video link for brief mention but will attend court next week
content:
Alleged crime gang leader Daniel Kinahan appeared by video link from prison when his case came briefly before the Special Criminal Court on Monday afternoon.
Kinahan was charged last August with directing an organised crime group between 2015 and 2017 and remanded in custody to Portlaoise Prison.
When the case was called just after 2.30pm on Monday, barrister David Perry said he was asked to appear by solicitor Darragh Mackin of Phoenix Law.
Counsel said Mackin was not in a position to attend court on Monday due to unexpected other matters elsewhere. Mackin wished the matter to be put back for a week to allow him to make a formal application to come on record for Kinahan, Perry said.
Counsel also asked the court to direct that Kinahan appear in person in court next Monday.
Judge Caroline Biggs, presiding at the three-judge court, adjourned the matter to then to facilitate the application to come on record and ordered that Kinahan be brought to court as requested.
When Kinahan appeared before the court in person on August 9th last, two hours after arriving in Ireland following his extradition from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), he was not legally represented.
It is understood he later approached a number of criminal lawyers in relation to taking on his case privately. If he applied for legal aid, he would have to provide a statement of means.
At the August 9th hearing, he said he did not have time to arrange representation and had assumed a family member would have contacted some legal representation. He was told he would have time to put in place a legal team before the case returned to court.
He was also told he had the option of appearing in person or via video link at the next hearing. He had indicated he wished to appear in person but then opted for video link for Monday’s brief mention of the case.
Kinahan faces a single charge of “directing the activities of a criminal organisation” between October 18th, 2015, and April 6th, 2017, contrary to section 71a of the Criminal Justice Act 2006, as amended.
He was the first Irish person extradited from the UAE under a new permanent extradition treaty, which came into force last year. He had lived in Dubai with his wife and five children for the last 10 years. He was arrested in Dubai in April on foot of an extradition request from Ireland and was in custody there until he was extradited.

title: Five Ireland players who impressed in a difficult international window
description: Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson appears to have a solid foundation to build on
content:
A former captain of the under-21s, Abankwah showed a different side to his game in this window, being used as a right wing-back rather than his usual position of centre-back on the right of Udinese’s back three. As a wing-back, he impressed going forward, being involved in two of Ireland’s best moves against Kosovo before showing composure to set up Troy Parrott for the opening goal in the first match against Israel.
Abankwah was lively against Austria , particularly in the first half, causing havoc with Jack Moylan on the right as Ireland went into half-time 2-0 up. In the absence of Séamus Coleman, he offered more at right wing-back in this formation than Jake O’Brien does, and at 22 and playing regularly in Serie A, he should continue to improve.
It was hard for Parrott to enhance his already glowing reputation with Ireland fans, but he did so with four goals in four games, one of them staking a claim as the greatest goal scored at the Aviva Stadium. Parrott’s virtuoso display against Austria – his best performance of the four games – showed once more that he is a big-game player. It comes after his famous goals against Portugal and Hungary last year, while for Real Betis he scored in his Champions League debut and also notched the winner against Real Madrid.
“As long as he was on the pitch, he was probably man of the match, not only because he scored a brilliant goal but also because he was involved in any of the offensive situations that Ireland created,” Austria manager Ralf Rangnick said after watching his team play against Parrott. His mazy dribble and finish for Ireland’s opening goal was a rare moment of an Irish player creating something out of nothing, an ability that is priceless. Parrott has shown a consistency in scoring that Ireland has been missing since Robbie Keane, with 10 goals in his last seven competitive matches.
The attacking midfielder was a find of the summer window games, impressing against Grenada and Qatar (albeit getting a red card in that friendly). However, given the end-of-season vibe to those matches, as Ireland had not qualified for the World Cup, it was up to Moylan in this window to establish himself. That he did with a brilliant goal and assist in the first game against Israel , which impressed Heimir Hallgrímsson enough to include him in the team to play Austria, even with Finn Azaz back in the side.
Moylan was a constant threat and showed an ability to beat a man in a way that few other members of the squad are capable of doing. He also has pace and an eye for a pass. With an average of 1.5 key passes per game, he was Ireland’s most creative player. For now, it seems like he has moved ahead of Chiedozie Ogbene in the pecking order.
The striker had a mixed time at Celtic, saying after leaving that he felt “hate” and “torture” at the club as he got the brunt of fan abuse when the team underperformed. As his confidence took a hit, it also affected his Ireland form and he did not start any of the six World Cup qualifying group matches or the playoff.
Since moving to Swansea City in the Championship, the Cork man has gradually got his mojo back. His goal in the first match against Israel was classic centre-forward play, beating the offside trap with a clever run and slotting the ball past the goalkeeper. He links up well with Parrott, who he first played alongside in youth football.
Holding the record for most Ireland under-21 appearances, the 26-year-old midfielder took longer to break into the senior international team, making his first competitive start in this window against Israel in a 3-0 win. The Charlton Athletic player looked assured against Austria, offering more on the ball than other options in midfield in the absence of Josh Cullen. Hallgrímsson also said Coventry has had a big impact in keeping the squad calm in difficult situations.
“One change that we’ve done in the last games is before we go on to the pitch, we do a little prayer and a huddle with the players and all the staff, just to cool our heads before we go on to the pitch,” the manager said. “Conor Coventry has taken that part, so he is now called Brother Coventry in the squad.”

title: Social media influencer Lisa McGowan pays herself €1.9m
description: Tullamore-based fashion entrepreneur Lisa McGowan’s company returns to profit
content:
Tullamore-based fashion entrepreneur and social media influencer Lisa McGowan paid herself a pay package of €1.9 million last year.
Accounts filed by McGowan’s Lisa’s Lust List Ltd show the company returned to profit last year to record a post-tax profit of €419,268 for 2025.
The firm returned to profit after McGowan cut her pay by more than €1.16 million in 2025 from a record package of €3.063 million in 2024. It was made up of €2.67 million in emoluments and €384,002 in pension contributions.
Last year, McGowan’s pay package was made up of €1.51 million in emoluments and €384,002 in pension contributions.
The pay of €1.51 million for the 54-year-old businesswoman equates to average pretax pay of €29,172 per week or €4,167 per day for 2025.
McGowan is the firm’s only director and McGowan’s pretax pay – excluding pension contributions – across the four years from 2025 and 2022 totals €6.1 million, which includes €969,275 in 2023 and €986,067 in 2022.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
The company returned to post-tax profit last year after incurring post-tax losses of €736,075 in 2024, which was due to the pay package that McGowan awarded herself.
The profits for last year resulted in the company’s accumulated profits rising from €459,677 to €878,945. Its cash funds rose from €727,254 to €999,427.
The abridged accounts don’t disclose revenues generated last year.
McGowan only started her online promotional work after she won the best-dressed lady competition at the Galway Races in 2016.
[ Social welfare, tax changes and childcare costs: Everything we know about Budget 2027 so far Opens in new window ]
An insurance broker by profession in the family firm, McGowan incorporated Lisa’s Lust List Ltd in November 2017.
The business has expanded with McGowan now selling clothes, accessories and beauty products on her lisaslustlist.ie website under her “Lisa & Co” brand.
She has also set up a joint venture company, LMLB Beauty Ltd with business partner, Linda Blanchfield in which McGowan has a majority 51 per cent share.
The new accounts show that in 2025, Lisa’s Lust List Ltd provided consultancy services to LMLB Beauty Ltd to the value of €737,521.
LMLB Beauty Ltd recorded a loss of €293,574 in 2025. At the end of December last, the company had accumulated profits of €243,109.
The firm’s cash funds reduced from €357,576 to €221,799.
McGowan’s Lisa’s Lust List site specialises in promoting products including fashion items, beauty, health, travel and homeware, mainly produced by Irish-based SMEs.
The fashion blogger’s Facebook page has 214,000 followers while on Instagram it has increased to 197,000.

title: World’s oil stockpiles are ‘scarily thin’, says Saudi Aramco boss
description: Amin Nasser says inventories depleted by Middle East conflict could take up to two years to rebuild
content:
The world’s oil stockpiles are “scarily thin”, the chief executive of Saudi Aramco said, adding it would take up to two years to rebuild inventories depleted during the Middle East conflict.
Amin Nasser said the seven-month war between the US, Israel and Iran had reduced oil supply from the region by “nearly three billion barrels”, equivalent to roughly half the crude oil and refined fuels that would have passed through the Strait of Hormuz over that period.
More than one billion barrels of oil have been drawn from reserves to try to cushion the shortfall, Nasser added.
Governments have released more than 300 million barrels from strategic reserves and agreed on Friday to release more, but Nasser said the majority that have been deployed have come from the reserves of companies, which held “the last major tool in the box”.
In his first public speech since the war began, the boss of the state-run Saudi Arabian company said he estimated that “less than six billion barrels of commercial inventories remain today, with the vast majority not practically available”.
“The system is already straining,” he told the Energy Intelligence Forum conference in London. “And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin.”
[ Catch up with all your Budget 2027 news and analysis here Opens in new window ]
He added that modern technology, including “open data such as satellite imagery and shipping logs”, was “increasingly being weaponised against infrastructure and tankers”.
In recent weeks, Iran has hit ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz while its proxies in Iraq and Yemen have attacked Aramco’s pipelines, refineries and ports. “Tools of transparency should not become ammunition for aggression,” Nasser said.
His warnings underline the damage to the global oil market from the conflict, even as a complicated system of shuttling oil through Hormuz is helping to restore flows.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
Shipments from Gulf countries rose to 15.5 million barrels a day last month, the highest level since the war began and more than 80 per cent of the pre-conflict volume, according to data provider Kpler.
However, these shipments have been hugely expensive, and oil markets remain extremely tight, with prices for physical North Sea crude cargoes to be delivered this month rising to their highest levels since April.
Nasser said that even at the end of the conflict, “replenishing inventories while meeting demand could take up to two years”, and called on governments to focus more on energy security and resilience.
Aramco was studying additional routes for exporting Saudi crude and exploring further overseas storage facilities to help protect customers against future disruptions, he said. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Norway becomes first major country to propose temporary ban on AI glasses in public places
description: Proposed law would prohibit use of the technology in parks, beaches, schools and kindergartens
content:
Norway has become the first major country to propose a temporary ban on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) glasses in selected public places amid growing privacy concerns over wearable technology.
The rich Scandinavian country’s centre-left government said on Monday that it would introduce a law to parliament soon on a temporary ban for places such as parks, beaches, schools and kindergartens. It will also set up an expert group to propose permanent national rules.
“I am concerned about the introduction of powerful new technology where people risk being photographed, filmed or recorded without their knowledge,” said Torgeir Micaelsen, Norway’s digitalisation minister. A temporary ban “will give us time to conduct a thorough assessment and hold an informed debate that can lay the foundation for permanent regulation”, he said.
Governments around the world are grappling with how to regulate AI glasses – including those from Facebook owner Meta and cheaper copycat devices – amid worries that they are being used to film people without their consent, including children and women in settings such as changing rooms.
Parts of Norwegian society have already reacted with their own bans, including schools in the capital Oslo and the country’s biggest company, oil and gas major Equinor, which has banned them from its offices and offshore facilities.
Australia is considering a ban on smart glasses in certain public spaces while courtrooms in several countries have issued bans as the use of wearable technology increases.
[ With Meta’s ‘pervert glasses’, we really are going through the digital looking glass Opens in new window ]
Norway’s government said it did not want to propose a total ban. It said appropriate use could be where there was no risk of filming people without their consent.
It added that the proposed ban was a “high priority” and that a draft law would soon be presented to parliament.
“We do not want a society where people are concerned about hidden audio recordings, photography and filming in places and situations where they are used to being without being monitored. Such a society can be experienced as unsafe and cause us to withdraw,” said Micaelsen.
US tech companies such as Meta , Google and OpenAI believe wearable technology, such as smart glasses, has the potential to replace mobile phones as our main gateway to AI. They believe that talking to AI – which will listen to people’s conversations and daily life – is easier than opening an app and typing in queries. Analysts at Counterpoint Research estimate consumers will spend more than $1tn between 2026 and 2032 on wearable devices.
But that has raised widespread privacy concerns about what such smart glasses could see or hear, and led to them being dubbed “pervert technology” by some campaigners. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Spain’s prime minister calls snap election after protests over housing crisis
description: Political crisis over housing started last month with the eviction of an 87-year-old woman with a disability
content:
Spain ’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , has called a snap election prompted by the housing crisis, which has seen a wave of protests and a resounding parliamentary defeat for his government in recent days.
Sánchez, a socialist who has been in power since 2018, has called the election for November 29th, the earliest date possible. The next general election had not been due until next summer.
“There remain many injustices to correct, many challenges in public services and housing,” Sánchez said in a live address as he announced his decision.
“What is true is that, in order to do more, we need the support of people; we need to ensure that parliament gives us a broader progressive majority.”
His coalition has been governing in minority, mainly with the support of an array of Basque and Catalan parties.
However, his lack of a parliamentary majority was underlined on Friday when Congress rejected a series of emergency measures his government presented aimed at tackling the housing crisis. The reforms sought to give tenants more rights, protecting them from eviction and ensuring their rental contracts were automatically renewed to prevent abuses by landlords.
The last-minute withdrawal of support for the legislation by Together for Catalonia (JxCat) was key in preventing its approval.
Sánchez had presented those measures in response to a sudden wave of social outrage on the housing issue, prompted by the eviction last month of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old wheelchair user, from her flat in central Madrid.
Hundreds of demonstrators turned out to oppose the eviction, which was followed by a nationwide series of protests, including people pitching tents in the squares of cities.
On Saturday, tens of thousands of protesters turned out in Madrid and other cities to protest the rental market, which has seen costs soar in recent years, and Congress’s refusal to approve the government’s reforms.
These elections come at a difficult time for the Sánchez government. His Socialist Party has been mired in scandals and his wife, Begona Goméz, is due to go on trial for influence peddling. Sánchez has defended her innocence against what he says is meddling by the political right in the judiciary.
His government has struggled to manage a crisis in the Spanish city of Ceuta, in North Africa, where more than 70,000 migrants arrived over two days in July. Most have returned to Morocco, but the city has become a logistical and political headache for Sánchez.
The opposition welcomed the prospect of elections, which they have been demanding for some time. The conservative People’s Party (PP) has been leading polls, which suggest it would need the support of the far-right Vox to govern.
“This is not about the PP beating the Socialist Party; these are not like previous elections,” said Alberto Núñez Feijóo. “This is about Spain defeating Sánchez.”
[ How an elderly Madrid woman’s eviction became a new flashpoint in Spain’s housing ​crisis Opens in new window ]

title: Over 200 solicitors and barristers protest outside  Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin
description: Minister urged to enter talks before High Court decision next week on challenge to new payment model
content:
More than 200 solicitors and barristers protested outside the Courts of Criminal Justice in Dublin on Monday as the criminal courts face more disruption with criminal defence solicitors extending their withdrawal of services.
Solicitors and barristers from around the country were also due to protest on Monday and Tuesday, including in Mayo, Wicklow, Monaghan, Galway, Meath and Donegal.
The dispute has been under way since mid-June over a new payment model, introduced on July 1st, for criminal defence work in the District Courts.
Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan said the new model, involving a €520 flat fee irrespective of the number of clients or court appearances, will achieve cost savings and efficiencies.
Solicitors have said it means they will not be paid for the work they do in more complex cases, including ones involving children and people with addiction and mental health issues.
The dispute has led to thousands of criminal cases, including rape and murder cases, being adjourned across all court divisions, with implications for all court users, including victims of crime and accused persons.
Members of the Irish Criminal Bar Association joined solicitors on Monday in urging the Minister to enter talks with the Law Society, which is the solicitors’ representative body, with a view to resolving the dispute.
O’Callaghan has previously said he is awaiting the outcome of a judicial review challenge by solicitor John Quinn to the new payment model. The High Court is due to rule on October 13 th on that challenge, aimed at quashing the statutory instrument introducing the new scheme.
Legal sources have suggested, if the High Court upholds the statutory instrument, that will lead to more solicitors resuming criminal legal aid work.
Since the widespread withdrawal of services from July 1 st , some solicitors have returned to work in locations including Laois, Naas, Limerick and Kilkenny.
Most solicitors, particularly in Dublin, continue to participate in the withdrawal but sources believe that could change depending on the outcome of the Quinn case.
[ Barristers urge Jim O’Callaghan to ‘engage further’ with defence solicitors to end pay dispute Opens in new window ]
Among the barristers who joined criminal defence solicitors on the steps of the Courts of Criminal Justice on Monday were Barry Ward, Fine Gael TD, and Mary Hanafin, a former Fianna Fáil TD and minister for education.
Ward said barristers agree with the position adopted by the criminal defence solicitors and were protesting as a gesture of solidarity.
He was “disappointed” the Minister had not to date accepted the Law Society’s offers to mediate the dispute. “If we’ve learned anything in Ireland, it is that talking does yield results.”
The reality is the new law term has started, important cases need to be disposed of, and that the action will impact victims, accused people and many others, he said.
“It’s not fair on everybody that it has not been resolved and any step that can resolve it should be taken.”
Whatever the outcome of next week’s High Court decision, he hoped “we can all move on and both sides will accept the judgment of the court”, added Ward.
Barrister Luke O’Higgins said the incomes of junior criminal barristers have been “devastated” by the dispute.
He strongly disagreed with the Minister’s insistence the courts continue to operate effectively. “I’m in these courts every day,” he said. “I was in Dublin District Court last Friday and about 85 per cent of cases were adjourned.”
“The only end to industrial action is engagement and I call on the Minister to engage. I don’t think what the solicitors are asking for is controversial. They are simply asking to be paid for the work they do.”
Solicitor Amanda Connolly, vice chair of the criminal law committee of the Law Society, said: “This crisis was created by the Minister and only the Minister can end it.”
O’Callaghan “changed the system without properly consulting the people who make it work, and three and a half months on he has still failed to engage meaningfully with us”, she said.

title: Seapoint links set for temporary closure in 2027 as Pádraig Harrington leads €7m redesign
description: Course will close in January for project work to take place, with estimated reopening in spring 2028
content:
Pádraig Harrington will add another string to his bow when the three-time Major champion adds course design to his portfolio in heading the redesign of Seapoint links in Co Louth in a €7 million project that will see the temporary closure of the course through 2027.
The 55-year-old Dubliner will link up with noted course architect Giulia Ferroni of Leeds Golf Design and Roddy Carr on the redesign of the course that will include four entirely new holes, seven new green complexes, significant changes across the existing course, new and repositioned bunkering, natural sand areas, an upgraded and extended irrigation system and upgraded amenities and practice areas.
“I’m hugely excited that Seapoint will be my first 18-hole golf course design project. I’ve known the course for many years, and it provides a tremendous natural setting, so having the opportunity to help shape its next chapter is very special to me,” said Harrington.
“There is enormous potential here. Our ambition is to create something distinctive and memorable that members will love playing regularly, while also offering the quality and challenge of a leading links course,” added Harrington.
The significant financial investment by Genesis Links Limited is aimed at transforming the 220-acre property in Termonfeckin into a stronger, more distinctive golfing experience while also addressing long-term infrastructural requirements.
The links has hosted events including the OFX Irish Legends on the Legends Tour and the Flogas Irish Men’s Amateur Open Championship since Genesis acquired the property in 2021.
Originally designed by Des Smyth and Declan Branigan, Seapoint – which neighbours the Co Louth Golf Club at Baltray – first opened for play in 1993.
Club members were informed of the investment on Monday afternoon, with the links due to close temporarily in January when project work will commence with a reopening timeline of spring 2028.
Harrington will collaborate with Ferroni and Roddy Carr on the redesign of the golf course. Ferroni is a protege of renowned golf course architect Martin Hawtree and has worked on some of the leading courses in Ireland and the UK, including Doonbeg, Sunningdale and Trump International Golf Links Aberdeen.
Carr, a former Walker Cup player and tour professional, also brings his extensive international golf industry experience – having worked for Jack Nicklaus Design and IMG – to the project.
“I’m really looking forward to working with Giulia and Roddy, getting into the detail of the design and seeing the new Seapoint take shape,” said Harrington of moving into a new area of a golfing career that saw him win three Majors – the 2007 and 2008 Open Championship and the 2008 US PGA – and successfully retained his US Seniors Open title this season.
Marty Carr of Genesis Links Limited heralded the investment as “a significant opportunity to realise more of its potential.”
He explained: “Seapoint has an exceptional piece of linksland ... this investment is about creating a golf course that is more distinctive, more consistent and better equipped for the future, while retaining the character that makes Seapoint such a special place to play.
“The scale of the programme reflects our long-term ambition for Seapoint. We want to create an outstanding links experience for members and visitors and further strengthen Co Louth’s reputation as one of Ireland’s great golf destinations.”

title: Deepfake Ireland on Virgin Media One: Gráinne Seoige’s distress in this grim film is palpable
description: Television: Seoige revisits her experience of AI-generated deepfake images while looking at the wider issue of misogyny on the internet
content:
Gráinne Seoige’s public persona is that of the understated and often sombre newsreader – giving us the facts and just the facts. So it is shocking to see her on the brink of tears as she recalls how she became the victim of deepfake pornography created using AI while canvassing for election in 2024 .
“It is so sickening that someone could do that to you,” she explains in Deepfake Ireland . (Virgin Media One, Monday, 9pm) This grim film sees Seoige revisiting her own experience of AI-generated deepfake images while looking at the wider issue of how misogyny is embedded in the source code of the internet. How it has become, in essence, a holy treatise of tech bro-dom that has brought immense pain to people around the world.
Seoige’s distress as she recalls the incident makes for uncomfortable viewing and – as is only proper given the subject matter – the entire documentary has a skin-crawling quality: what a horrible world it is out there.
Of course, “out there” in this context means the internet and the hellscape of social media, where more than 95 per cent of fake images are of women. “We’re there for their entertainment – there are no consequences,” says model and presenter Maria McGuigan, who, like Seoige, was targeted by deepfakers.
Victims are often extorted by their harassers – which can add to their trauma, says poet Darragh Fleming. Recalling his experience of being blackmailed over intimate images, he says that, to teenagers, “things like this are world-ending”. “I was blackmailed for nude images of myself – the stats around suicide linked to this, especially among teenagers, are really scary.”
Seoige believes that, in her case, the image was “politically motivated” because it surfaced at a time when she was standing for election for Fianna Fáil in Galway West , and the action was intended to diminish and humiliate her in the eyes of voters. There was, she says, a perception that she was “a celebrity candidate – lightweight, ill-qualified to stand... this was done for a very specific reason”.
Since then she has had nightmares in which faceless men attack her. Her experiences echo those of secondary school student Isabella, who, at age 15, was blackmailed with deepfake images and had dreams in which faceless men assaulted her. “It completely destabilises our sense of safety in the world,” says Seoige.
But her nightmare is not over. She meets Žilvinas Padolskas of Dublin-based technology company Ceartas, where she discovers that further images taken from her Instagram account have been manipulated by deepfake software. This is news to Seoige, who is understandably appalled.
The EU has announced a ban on AI “nudifier” apps that create non-consensual intimate imagery, to take effect from December 2026. But Seoige wonders if this will meaningfully improve the situation – changing the law is well and good, but how do you enforce the regulations?
She’s not sure that this will be possible. “It’s absolutely disgusting,” she says. “It could not be more personal – it’s all about control over women.”

title: ‘It turns out the magnets don’t work through double-glazed windows’: Fiachra Garvey on money
description: The concert pianist on his first car, buying a London flat and learning to haggle in Morocco
content:
Concert pianist Fiachra Garvey is a member of the international jury for the 2026 Irish Freemasons Young Musician of the Year Competition. The finals take place on Saturday, October 10 th .
I have fond memories of performing at a festival in Spoleto, Italy, in 2016 and spending the entire fee on a supermarket sweep-style shopping spree in an outlet mall outside Florence. Now, at the ripe old age of 39, I think I’m a bit more responsible with the saving versus spending ratio.
What was the first job you received money for, and how much were you paid?
On the piano side, it was probably the Late Late Toy Show in 2000, performing a waltz by Chopin. I was 13, and I was paid £100.
I actually do. I recently switched my broadband and electricity provider. With the latter’s very affordable night rate, I time all my household appliances to come on between midnight and 7:30am. Before people reading this think my neighbours must hate me, there is a silent setting on them.
What has been your most extravagant purchase, and how much did it cost?
Probably my little flat in London which I bought in 2023. I bought it for £189,000 and spent around £45,000-£50,000 renovating it. I’m not sure it counts as extravagant when it’s my only home, but it’s certainly the biggest financial noose around my neck. Every month I enjoy that I own a little bit more of it and that I’m no longer paying a landlord.
What purchase have you made that you consider the best value for money?
In 2007, at the age of 19, I bought my first and only car to date, a VW Polo. She was three years old at the time (a 2004 model) and is now 22 years old. She has been to every corner of Ireland, and from Cornwall to London to Edinburgh. As we say, she owes me nothing.
Is there anything you regret spending money on?
My flat is on the third and top floor of the building I live in. I jokingly call it ‘the penthouse’ as there’s no one above me, other than the pigeon population of Chiswick. Despite my relatively long arms, I can’t quite stretch around to wash the outside of the windows, so I bought what was advertised online as a magnetic window cleaning solution. It turns out the magnets don’t work through double-glazed windows.
[ ‘I’m looking to buy a home. It is a daunting task on an average single income’ Opens in new window ]
I did when I was in Morocco. I learned from the locals that, as a tourist, I should essentially halve the quoted price and start bargaining from there. I was fleeced for the first two or three days.
Do you invest in shares and/or cryptocurrency?
No. My parents had their small amount of savings go down the Swanee when they took the government’s advice at the time to invest in Eircom shares, so I steer clear of all of that.
Do you have a retirement or pension plan?
I finally started a pension two years ago. As a self-employed person, the fear of being completely destitute when I’m older finally got to me. For the amount I’m putting in each month, I’ll probably have to play piano until I physically collapse off the stool.
What was the last thing you bought, and was it good value for money?
The last amount of money to leave my account was to pay the M50 toll yesterday. It’s terrible value for money. The last personal item I bought was a new pair of hiking boots. Considering my last pair served me for about 10 years, I’m confident that these too will be considered value for money.
Have you ever successfully saved up for a relatively big purchase?
The deposit for my flat was the largest savings target I’ve had to date.
We’ve all lost a wallet here, or had a €20 fly out of our pocket there.
Are you a gambler and, if so, have you ever had a big win?
I’m not a gambler. I do the lotto now and then and am genuinely shocked and dismayed when I don’t win.
What is your best habit when it comes to money?
Most of my good habits regarding money are invested in raising funds for the West Wicklow Chamber Music Festival. The festival receives about 30-35 per cent of our running costs from the Arts Council and Wicklow Arts Office, and I have to raise the other 65-70 per cent myself.
If any wealthy people are reading this and want to support a wonderful charity, please do get in touch.
I’ve completely nipped my worst habit in the bud in that I used to spend a fair amount of money on takeaway coffee.
I’ve just come back from walking my lovely rough collie dogs, Luas and Bláithín, so I’ve no money in my pocket, but I have a few doggy treats to get them back on the lead!
