title: Kestrel Capital swoops on Dublin-based wealth and investment manager Kinsale
description: Deal reported to be worth around €10m
content:
Kestrel Capital , the private equity-backed Irish wealth manager, has agreed to acquire investment advisory firm Kinsale Capital for an undisclosed sum.
The transaction, which is subject to regulatory approval, extends Kestrel’s reach into the Irish wealth management market after taking on investment from European private equity firm IK Partners last year.
Financial details have not been disclosed, but citing sources familiar with the transaction, The Sunday Times reported recently that the deal was worth about €10 million.
Founded in 2015, Kestrel provides services to high-net-worth individuals, corporate clients and family offices. The deal for Kinsale will bring its assets under management to around €1.5 billion, it said.
Dublin-based Kinsale, meanwhile, was founded in 2005 by Gearóid Doyle, who has led the firm along with Seán Ó Flannagáin and George Dargan. Dargan will join Kestrel to “support the transition”, the firm said in a statement, and “ensure continuity for Kinsale’s clients”.
Kinsale has established itself as “one of Ireland’s most respected wealth management firms, with a strong reputation for client service and long-term investment stewardship,” said Kestrel chief executive John Crowe.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
“This acquisition represents an important step in Kestrel’s growth ambitions, strengthening our presence in Ireland and enhancing our ability to serve clients across the country,” he said.
Doyle said he is “immensely proud” of Kinsale’s achievements. “This transaction marks an important stage in Kinsale’s evolution. Since founding the business, our focus has been on building long-term relationships and helping clients achieve their financial goals through independent advice and trusted guidance.”
Ireland’s wealth management industry is forecast to expand in value to $9 trillion (€7.9 trillion) by the end of the decade from about $5.2 trillion now, amid strong and growing demand for EU market access among international fund managers.
Further consolidation is expected within the industry as firms look to capitalise on the Republic’s position as a global fund domicile and administration hub.

title: ‘It is traumatic for the parents’: How Irish drug gangs are using teenagers’ addresses in operations
description: Cannabis grow houses that once boomed in Ireland have become a smaller part of the trade
content:
I rish drugs gangs have begun aping tactics deployed by the Black Axe international fraud group.
The group’s members in Ireland recruit young people, often students, to allow their bank accounts be used to move the proceeds of the gang’s frauds.
The tactic is designed to frustrate gardaí in their efforts to find out who has control of the money and who it is ultimately on the way to.
Copying this tactic, members of small Irish drugs gangs are going to countries such as Canada and the US, where cannabis is legal, and buying relatively small quantities.
They are then sending it back to Ireland, usually in parcel post in quantities of 5kg or less. Rather than using their own addresses, or properties that could be linked to them, they are convincing or pressuring teenagers to allow their addresses to be used.
[ Cannabis now as profitable as cocaine as supply from legal markets surges Opens in new window ]
They often select minors; teenagers of an age that may not be prosecuted via the courts to the point of criminal conviction, or whose convictions as minors will not follow them into their adult lives.
Det Chief Supt Seamus Boland, the head of the Garda’s Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau , told The Irish Times that the Garda was seeing more and more cases of parcels of herbal cannabis being intercepted on their way to minors.
“It is very traumatic for the parents,” he said of people who find their child suddenly involved in drug smuggling, which only comes to light when gardaí turn up on their doorstep.
He added some of those who become involved were “impressionable” or were being “pressured” by small-time criminals in their communities.
“There is no risk on the purchase side, because the drug is legal there, full stop,” added Boland of the dealers travelling to the US and Canada to buy drugs in an environment where they did not need to come into contact with dangerous organised criminals.
The Irish dealers are sourcing cannabis through legal means in the US and Canada at knock-down prices. Once brought into Ireland the value of each kilo rockets on the illicit market.
Cannabis herb is so plentiful in Canada, for example, that some international research suggests a lower-grade kilo can be bought for little more than €500. And even a kilo of much more potent, higher-quality weed can be purchased for about €1,000.
Once smuggled into the Republic, if criminals opt to sell it on immediately, acting as wholesalers to street dealers, each kilo can fetch between €3,500 and €4,000. If they decide to break it down into street deals and sell it themselves, they can generate as much as €14,000 per kilo.
Though the parcel trade is only a small component of the overall smuggling landscape – most drugs still come into Ireland in freight by sea and air – it has surged as the drug has become easier to buy legally abroad.
[ Inside the Black Axe raid: What gardaí found in operation targeting global crime gang Opens in new window ]
Cannabis from the US and Canada – as well as from Thailand, where laws around the drug have been relaxed – accounted for 60 per cent of all of the cannabis seized at the point of entry into Ireland last year.
Garda sources said the supply from those three countries has become cheap and plentiful in recent years. As a result, cannabis grow houses that once boomed in the Republic have become a smaller part of the trade here.

title: Let Me In review: A brilliant premise, but this play ultimately feels underdeveloped
description: Dublin Theatre Festival 2026: Esosa Ighodaro is interested in the emotional reality of belonging to a country that doesn’t always seem to want you
content:
Let Me In has a brilliant premise. Written and directed by Esosa Ighodaro , it follows an Irish-Nigerian firefighter during the recent arson attacks on accommodation where immigrant families have been living. But rather than turn this into a high-stakes action story, Ighodaro brings us to her home, where the drama unfolds in intimate scenes with her white Irish boyfriend.
The play, which is being staged as part of Dublin Theatre Festival , goes straight at a contradiction in Ireland’s national myth: the land of a thousand welcomes can also be viciously hostile to migrants. Let Me In is interested in the complicated emotional reality of belonging to a country that doesn’t always seem to want you, and how that feeling plays out in your most intimate relationships.
Yet the way the story is told feels increasingly thin and implausible. The characters’ actions and emotions scan on a level of pure sense but lack the ring of lived truth. Lola (a gritty, worn-out Ebby O’Toole-Acheampong) comes home after an exhausting shift to her boyfriend, Seán ( Naoise Dunbar ). They canoodle on the sofa and make out – which can feel painful to watch, as they seem to have zero chemistry.
It’s Seán’s birthday, and his friends are coming over. Before they arrive he accidentally proposes. Lola is furious. Work is relentless; now this. She just wants a night off.
Then the friends arrive. Gaz (an excellent Darragh Feehely) is the kind of guy who calls women “birds”. Within minutes he’s warning Seán about African women being feisty and doing an impression of a woman carrying water on her head.
Another friend, played by the very funny Alexandra Conlon, is a white woman in cornrows who gives Lola’s name what she imagines is an African pronunciation and makes aggressively weird, possibly eugenics-coded remarks: “You’ve a lovely-shaped head.”
The problem isn’t that people like this don’t exist. I’m sure they do. It’s that the characters are so awful, and Seán himself has so little to recommend him beyond being caring and inoffensive, that another question starts to take over: why is Lola here?
This could be the beginning of a much more interesting play. Lola is in a relationship with a white man whose closest friends are casually and spectacularly racist. What does Seán’s apparent niceness mean if these are the people he chooses to keep around him?
And when she cites being overworked as a reason not to hang out with him on his birthday, or to engage with his marriage proposal, is that really all that’s going on? What buried contempt for him might lie underneath it? And, beneath that, what depths of self-hatred?
But Let Me In doesn’t dig very far into any of the psychological intrigue. The characters are so broadly drawn that the events onstage feel like dramatic contrivance. Sabine Dargent ’s set, a collection of crates, gradually builds throughout the play towards a faintly ridiculous climax.
Let Me In is at Smock Alley, as part of Dublin Theatre Festival , until Saturday, October 10th

title: Female-looking AI agents were paid less than male ones in virtual office, study finds
description: Workplace gender bias may be replicated in interactions with artificial intelligence, according to research from University of Limerick
content:
Gender bias in the workplace can be replicated in interactions with artificial intelligence , new research from the University of Limerick (UL) has found.
The study examined whether the way AI assistants are presented influences how people treat them in a workplace setting.
It was co-authored by Dr Mary Hausfeld of UL’s Kemmy Business School.
Researchers placed 189 workers in a virtual reality office and asked them to complete work-related tasks with different AI assistants, including human-like agents presented with either male or female appearance.
Participants were then given real money to divide between themselves and the AI assistant for completing the tasks, allowing the researchers to “recreate a real-world transaction and examine how much people were willing to pay AI for its work”.
AI agents with a female appearance were paid less than their male-presenting counterparts, despite using the same underlying technology, according to the research.
The AI agents had the same underlying capabilities, yet participants treated them differently depending on how they were presented.
The male-presenting AI agent, Johan, received higher monetary rewards than the female-presenting agent, Johanna. The male agent was also perceived as more human-like.
Johanna was paid 10.25 per cent less than Johan for completing the same work.
The researchers concluded that their findings suggest gender biases familiar from human workplaces could be reproduced in interactions with AI.
Hausfeld said the results raise important questions as AI agents increasingly become part of people’s working lives.
“What is striking about our findings is that the technology behind these AI agents was exactly the same, but people did not treat them in the same way.
“We often think of AI as being neutral, but the way we design and present these systems can activate those same assumptions and biases that exist in our interactions with other people.
“As AI agents become more common in the workplace, we need to think carefully about the characteristics we give them and the behaviours those choices may encourage. We don’t want to inadvertently reproduce existing inequalities in a new technological setting.”
The study was part of a larger investigation into how the human-like appearance of AI influences workplace interactions.
Although the systems were powered by the same underlying AI, participants trusted the human-like assistants more and gave them more credit for their contribution than the robot.
Participants also suggested they had no preference for an AI with female or male attributes, but “their behaviour told a different story”.
The study was conducted by Isabelle Cuber and Tarek Alakmeh of the University of Zurich, Mary Hausfeld of University of Limerick, Anand van Zelderen of SKEMA Business School, and Moritz Jenny, Jochen Menges and Thomas Fritz of the University of Zurich.
Human-Like and Male? How AI Assistant Design Relates to Trust and Monetary Reward at Work in VR will be presented at the 14th Nordic Conference on Human-Computer Interaction in Vaasa, Finland, from October 5th to 7th.
It will also be published in the conference proceedings by the Association for Computing Machinery.

title: ‘I didn’t even dream of it’: Ciarán Frawley enjoys a madcap Connacht debut
description: Outhalf loving life out west as he renews partnership with ‘mentor’ Stuart Lancaster
content:
When Ciarán Frawley’s head hit the pillow in Connacht’s Treviso hotel last Friday night, he couldn’t have dared to dream of a debut quite like this. A pulsating, helter-skelter of a game , both throwing punches and rolling with them, before springing off the ropes to snatch a bonus-point win with his second try of the night.
“I didn’t even dream of it to be honest, I didn’t think I’d be close to that, but it was great character shown by the lads because I kind of put us in a bit of a pickle when I kicked it out on the full here,” he said, speaking from the in-goal area where the mistake occurred in the 55th minute.
That, coupled with a madcap few moments which lead to a prolonged sequence of five-metre put-ins for a dominant Benetton scrum, had seemed like a seminal moment in a game which saw the lead change hands five times, with never more than five points between them.
“We ended up in our own half for the guts of 10-15 minutes and if it wasn’t for Billy Bohan and Sam Illo digging in, and then we turned the ball over and we exit, but that was a massive moment in the game.
“That was actually what made it possible for us to win, so I owe them a lot of pints and, yeah, I’ll give myself a kick up the arse for that,” said Frawley, still irked by his miscued kick more than pleased with his two tries.
He was also part of a critical moment in between two scrum penalties during that pivotal siege when he and Paul Boyle held Leonardo Marin up over the line. Otherwise, Connacht would have fallen 26-17 behind entering the last 10 minutes.
“That’s the thing I admired watching this team last year. I knew they always showed great character and the way they ended last season I was excited to join because they’re a group of winners and they put themselves in contention to play European rugby by having moments like that,” said Frawley.
“It’s brilliant to share a moment like that with Boyler because I came up through the youth system with him. We played Under-18s together and it’s a great story to be here with him now. He’s another big reason I actually came here, and they’re a great bunch of lads.
“They try hard, they have great character and with Stu [Lancaster] coming in and settling in for the year I think you’re starting to see players improve and Connacht essentially improving as well.
“So, it’s looking like we’re on the up but we have to back it up next week. We have Glasgow away, it’s going to be a tough game, essentially playing against, you could say, Scotland,” said Frawley, having just beaten the core of the Italian side.
[ AIL round-up: St Mary’s hold off Clontarf comeback on day of eye-catching results Opens in new window ]
Of course, renewing a coach-player relationship with Lancaster was another big factor in Frawley’s decision to join Connacht from Leinster.
“I worked, obviously, with Stu in Leinster. He was defence coach but he did a lot of what he’s doing now as a head coach. He’s brilliant for the development of young players but also for the development of me, on and off the pitch, with my leadership.
“It’s an area I need to improve in, so I think he’s brilliant to have as essentially a coach, but also like a mentor. So yeah it’s brilliant to get back with him and get to winning ways.”
The last time he scored two tries was for Leinster away to the Lions in April 2024.
“And we got hammered that game,” he recalled of a 44-12 defeat. “So, it’s nice to win and scoring two tries is one thing but winning is the main thing.”
He certainly has no second thoughts about his move now.
“Galway’s a lovely city as well so myself and my girlfriend [Charlotte Murphy] moved down. We’re living with Will Connors. We’re renting at the moment together so we’re like one big happy family. It’ll be great when Will gets back as well and he’ll be humming. He’s another great addition to the squad so I’m looking forward to lacing up with him as well.”
[ Malachy Clerkin: Pep Guardiola said Manchester City destroyed football – he didn’t know how right he was Opens in new window ]
Frawley moved in August and along with Connacht’s other six Irish summer tourists, missed the pre-season trip to Vannes.
“But then we had a great few weeks together and we were set up perfectly for tonight. Off the back of last week, a disappointing performance against a good Stormers team, it was nice to bounce back because we needed to win this week. We didn’t get any points last week so it was great to come away with five.”
And with the move west, of course, was the rebirth of his ambition to be an outhalf.
“Well, I played there when I was younger and I played a lot of football growing up and I think that’s why I can sort of play other positions, but I played 10 my whole life growing up, and yeah it’s great to basically get back to where you started, do you know what I mean?”
It’s swiftly become an even more interesting move now, not least for Andy Farrell’s widening cohort of outhalves. Frawley’s Connacht career has had some lift-off.

title: The terrifying, unbeaten Chiefs would like you to know your predictions were wrong
description: Kansas City beat the surprisingly feisty Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. They already look like a very real contender after a lost season in 2025
content:
The rivalry between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Las Vegas Raiders goes back to the formation of the American Football League in 1960, when the Chiefs were the Dallas Texans, and the Raiders resided in Oakland. At no time in that rivalry had both teams faced each other with a record of 3-0 or better until Sunday’s game at Las Vegas’s Allegiant Stadium. An unbeaten record wasn’t entirely surprising for the Chiefs with Patrick Mahomes, but the Raiders? The team won only three games in the whole of last season, but this new Raiders team under Klint Kubiak presents all kinds of challenges for opponents.
At first, it appeared that the Raiders might go on to their first 4-0 start to a season since 2002, when they made it all the way to the Super Bowl, where they were vivisected by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and their former head coach, Jon Gruden. Kubiak’s team held a 13-10 halftime lead on Sunday, and Kubiak told CBS’s Tracy Wolfson at half-time that his team was going to win the game.
Things looked promising for the Raiders until running back Kenneth Walker’s two fourth-quarter touchdowns put the score at 30-19 in Kansas City’s favour, and as game as the Raiders were to stage a comeback, it didn’t quite happen. Kirk Cousins’ amazing 20-yard touchdown pass to tight end Brock Bowers with 1:46 left in the game, and Cousins’ successful two-point conversion to receiver Cody White, put the score at 30-27, and the Chiefs went three-and-out on their subsequent drive after an unsuccessful onside kick by the Raiders. But Chiefs punter Matt Araiza placed the ball perfectly at the Las Vegas one-yard line, and Chiefs safety Xavier Nwankpa’s interception of a Cousins pass with 10 seconds left sealed the game.
The Raiders may not have won the game, but they continue to win respect they haven’t earned in years. Kubiak brought all the smarts he showed as the Seattle Seahawks’ offensive coordinator last season, and defensive coordinator Rob Leonard has a bunch of lesser-known players (as well as edge demon Maxx Crosby) playing above their projected stations. And it doesn’t hurt that Cousins, at the age of 38, is playing some of the best football of his career.
As for the 4-0 Chiefs, they are officially back to the top of the NFL after a disastrous 6-11 2025 season. Everybody who picked other teams to make the Super Bowl (and that includes just about everybody) may want to check those opinions at the door. Mahomes isn’t the force who blew away opponents at his peak, but he has been careful with the ball this season. He only has two interceptions to go alongside his seven touchdown passes, and is still unflappable on third downs. Two of his main targets were injured in Sunday’s game – Rashee Rice left with a hamstring issue and Tyquan Thornton was carted off after suffering a dislocated ankle – but the offense has been boosted by the arrival of Walker, who has rushed for 173 yards, 117 yards, 70 yards and 177 yards in his first four games since arriving in Kansas City from the Seattle Seahawks. And that’s before we get to the now routine brilliance of Steve Spagnuolo’s defensive schemes.
The Week 18 rematch between these two teams may be for a lot more than just AFC West bragging rights.
CeeDee Lamb, WR, Dallas Cowboys: Lamb’s work against the Houston Texans in Dallas’s 34-30 win may have been his single-game masterpiece. Lamb saw 21 targets, catching 17 passes for 189 yards and the game-winning touchdown with 40 seconds left. The 21 targets in a game is tied for fifth-most since records began, and the 17 catches is tied for fourth all-time.
Moreover, had Dak Prescott seen Lamb wide open on a play where he didn’t get the ball (much to Lamb’s extreme frustration), the receiver’s final numbers could have been even better. One week after the Cowboys’ coaching staff failed the players in all three phases, Lamb apparently decided to take care of business by himself – though he did have a little help from running back Javonte Williams and his three touchdowns.
As for the 0-4 Texans, we’re sure they already know that the only team ever to make the postseason with that kind of opening deficit are the 1992 San Diego Chargers.
Efton Chism III ARE YOU SERIOUS?! 🤯 One-handed grab to put the Patriots on top 🔥 (via @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/BZaRpD7Wxe
Through the first three weeks of the season, the regression of Drake Maye was one of the league’s most disconcerting stories. The 2025 MVP runner-up hadn’t resembled that player all season long, but Maye looked good in a crucial 29-26 win over the Buffalo Bills on Sunday. Maye completed 22 of 37 passes for 269 yards, three touchdowns, one interception, and a passer rating of 97.7, and his game-winning touchdown to Efton Chism with 1:50 left was certainly a highlight for the second-year undrafted free agent from Eastern Washington, who had caught two passes on three targets for minus one-yard this season before his 23-yarder here.
It had been one of the weirdest streaks in football history. The New York Jets failed to record an interception last season, and the drought continued through the first three games of the 2026 campaign.
It appeared that relief had finally come in the first quarter of the Jets’ Sunday game against the Chicago Bears when defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat came up with a Tyson Bagent pass, but the interception was called back due to an illegal use of hands penalty on cornerback Azareye’h Thomas.
The Jets’ long nightmare would end later in the half, though, when Minkah Fitzpatrick nabbed a deep Bagent pass to Colston Loveland. It was the Jets’ first interception in 637 days, 636 opponent pass attempts, and 20 games.
We’re guessing that no team will come anywhere close to that “record” for a very long time. Aaron Glenn’s team lost the game 23-12, and the Bears had more first downs (34) than the Jets had offensive plays (32), but you take the wins wherever you can.
♦ Philadelphia Eagles fans are not generally patient with their team, and they have reasons for angst after Sunday. With 7:31 left in the game, and the Eagles up 20-10, Philly had fourth-and-goal at the Los Angeles two-yard line. At this point, the Rams had a win probability of 3.2%. Jalen Hurts threw an incompletion to Darius Cooper (who had already caught two touchdown passes in the game), and the Rams – who were fighting to avoid a 1-3 start to their season – started their own drive 98 yards from the end zone.
Sean McVay’s team travelled that entire distance in a 10-play drive that included four Eagles penalties, and ended with Kyren Williams’s one-yard touchdown run. The Eagles went three-and-out on their next drive. Then the Rams went 79 yards on 10 plays and ended that drive with a Williams run that put the Rams up 24-20.
It was up to the Eagles to respond, and they didn’t. On their final drive of the game Hurts was sacked twice, and threw two incompletions. Overall, the Eagles went 0-12 on third down, their 172 yards of total offense was their lowest in a game in 12 years, and their 68 net passing yards was the lowest total for the team in 23 years.
Yes, the Eagles were missing key players, including right tackle Lane Johnson, receiver DeVonta Smith, and running back Saquon Barkley, but this is going to be a tough one to swallow for the entire city of Philadelphia.
♦ It used to be that the field goal of 60 or more yards was pro football’s ultimate rarity. Just four such field goals were made in the entire 20th century. That has certainly changed over the last few seasons, as better kicking balls and better kickers have invaded the NFL. Kickers made 12 of 22 attempts of 60-plus yards last season, and it’s become even more commonplace in 2026.
In Week 4’s early slate alone, three kickers attempted kicks of 60 or more yards near the end of the first half, and two successfully converted them.
Brandon Aubrey of the Dallas Cowboys, who has made at least one such field goal in each of his four NFL seasons, was the guy who missed. But Chad Ryland of the Arizona Cardinals nailed a 60-yarder with two seconds left in the first half – sadly, that wasn’t enough to beat the New York Giants, who triumphed 36-24. And in his team’s 24-18 win over the Tennessee Titans, Baltimore Ravens kicker Tyler Loop hit a 64-yarder.
♦ Drake Maye has returned to form (at least for the moment), which means that the travails of Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert remain the most baffling story of the season. Herbert was supposed to match his rare physical gifts to new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel’s schematic genius, but that has not happened in any way. Against the Seattle Seahawks, Herbert threw an interception on the first play of the game. On the very next play, Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold threw it right back to the Chargers, via edge-rusher Tuli Tuipulotu. This marked the first time in pro football history that quarterbacks traded interceptions on the first two plays of a game. From there, though, the Seahawks took care of business. And now the Chargers sport an 0-4 record, which very few people expected when the season began.
♦ Some well-deserved praise for Brian Flores, the Minnesota Vikings’ defensive coordinator. Flores’s crew has already been one of our pleasant surprises of the season, and in their 15-10 win over the Miami Dolphins, the Vikings didn’t score a touchdown. They also didn’t score a touchdown in their 9-3 Week 2 win over the Chicago Bears. Why is this relevant? Because it hasn’t happened since the earliest days of pro football. The last teams to start 4-0 while failing to score touchdowns in two of those games were (in order) the 1922 Chicago Cardinals, the 1923 Chicago Cardinals, and the 1934 Detroit Lions.
♦ Don’t worry Bryce Young, we see you turning into a competent NFL quarterback (with some help from Tetairoa McMillan).
[Schultz] An NFL ref appears to say “Fuc* you” to Cardinals TE Trey McBride 🤦🏻‍♂️ twitter.com/Schultz_Repo... [image or embed]
♦ Finally, if you’re going to swear please remember that the cameras are everywhere on an NFL field. — Guardian

title: Trio awarded Nobel Prize in medicine for research on mysteries of brain
description: Optogenetics makes it possible to switch on, ​or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain
content:
Scientists Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or ‌medicine for “discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics,” the award-giving body said on Monday.
Karl Deisseroth, a 54-year-old US citizen, Hegemann, a 71-year-old German, and ​Georg Nagel, a 73-year-old German, were selected by the Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute medical university and receive a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns (€1 million), which is shared if there are multiple winners.
Optogenetics “makes it possible to switch on, ​or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain,” the prize-givers said.
“This method is now being used in laboratories ⁠around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries.”
The physiology or medicine prize traditionally opens the annual ‌Nobel ‌announcements, ​with awards in physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics to follow over the coming days.
The five original Nobel Prizes were created under the terms of Swedish ⁠inventor and industrialist Alfred Nobel’s will ​and have been awarded since 1901, with only limited ​interruptions, chiefly during the first World War and second World War.
A sixth award, the economics prize, was ‌established in 1968 by Sweden’s central bank, ​the Riksbank.
The medicine prize has honoured some of the most influential scientific discoveries of the past ⁠century, including Alexander Fleming’s work on penicillin, recognised ⁠in 1945, and ​Karl Landsteiner, who won in 1930 for his discovery of human blood groups.
Last year, US scientists Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell and Japan’s Shimon Sakaguchi won the prize for work shedding light on how the immune system spares healthy cells, creating openings for possible new treatments of diseases such as cancer.
Nobel laureates are chosen by expert committees appointed by the prize-awarding institutions. The awards are presented in Stockholm, with the exception of the Peace Prize, which is handed out in ‌Oslo, a tradition often ⁠linked to the union that bound Sweden and Norway during Nobel’s lifetime.
More than 125 years after Nobel signed his will, the prizes retain many of their long-standing traditions.
The celebrations ‌culminate on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death, when laureates receive their awards in ceremonies attended by Sweden’s and Norway’s ​royal families and are feted at gala banquets held in their honour. – Reuters

title: ‘Hypocrisy of the Irish is unbelievable’: Israeli media reacts to draw with Ireland
description: ‘Just like the first game, the most important thing for the Irish team was to show disrespect’, says Israeli daily newspaper Yisrael Hayom
content:
While the Israeli media praised the national team’s performance in the 1-1 draw against Ireland in Serbia as a marked improvement over the 3-0 defeat a week ago, once again much of the coverage focused on the charged atmosphere surrounding the game.
The Irish players’ refusal again to shake hands and their decision to bow their heads when the Israeli national anthem, Hatikvah, was played was criticised as unsporting and hypocritical.
“Let the Irish stew in their hatred for us in their dressingroom and let’s hope we don’t get drawn against them in the future,” the Israeli commentator said just before the final whistle.
The panel members on Channel 12 television’s Morning News show on Monday were also critical.
“The hypocrisy of the Irish is unbelievable,” said one panellist. “Not long ago they shook hands with the Afghan national [cricket] side – that’s the same Taliban that oppresses and kills women. That’s okay but when it comes to the Jews it’s not okay. This is pure anti-Semitism.”
Another panellist suggested the Israel Football Association should lodge a complaint with Fifa and that Ireland should be banned from future competitions.
Another argued that the Irish behaviour was just the latest manifestation of a wider boycott against Israel that many Israelis were unaware of, that affected culture, academic and medical research and other areas, and she argued the actions of the Israeli government were not helping.
Coverage of the game in the Israeli media was somewhat subdued as the country on Monday marked, according to the Hebrew calendar, the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel in October 7th, 2023, when 1,200 people were killed and 250 taken hostage to Gaza.
“It happened again: Ireland’s players bowed their heads during Hatikvah,” was the headline in Ynet, the digital platform of the Yediot Aharonot newspaper.
“Once again the Irish disgraced the anthem and did not shake hands,” wrote N12, Channel 12’s digital platform.
Israel’s largest-circulation daily newspaper, Yisrael Hayom, wrote about Irish “cheap provocations”.
[ Ken Early: At the end, Ireland’s players just wanted to get out of the nightmare Opens in new window ]
“Just like the first game, the most important thing for the Irish team was to show disrespect. In a series of petty and stupid gestures, including showing disrespect to Hatikvah, they ruined the sporting element of the game and came away looking small-minded.”
The popular Wallah! news website quoted Israel’s captain Dor Peretz, who said foreigners could not really understand Israel’s reality and suggested they should visit Israel and learn more before forming opinions.
There was widespread coverage in all the media outlets over Dor Peretz’s gesture after scoring Israel’s goal, when he kissed his black armband, worn by all the Israeli players last night, commemorating the October 7th victims.
Sport5 described the Irish behaviour as a “disgraceful spectacle”. It described the match as “another tense and ugly game” but said Israel looked substantially better and should have won after creating several chances in the second half.
The Sport One website noted Israel hit the woodwork twice in the second half, and said the Irish media themselves acknowledged Ireland were fortunate to escape with a draw.

title: Survey seeking information on sexual abuse at Irish schools opens
description: People who were sexually abused at schools between 1927 and 2013 are being invited to take part in survey
content:
People who were sexually abused in Irish schools between 1927 and 2013 are being invited to take part in a survey opened by a new commission of investigation.
All day and boarding schools, both religious and non-religious, are within the scope of the commission’s work.
These include primary or national schools, secondary schools, community schools and comprehensive schools, both fee-paying and non-fee-paying schools, and special schools.
The Commission of Investigation into the Handling of Historical Child Sexual Abuse in Schools, set up in July of last year, was established to examine the handling of concerns of child sexual abuse related to schools in Ireland.
As the first stage of its work, it has published a survey, inviting survivors and others with relevant information or knowledge to take part.
This survey offers a confidential and voluntary way to participate, with access to an independent specialist support service.
People who were sexually abused as children and others with relevant information are invited to share initial information, which will help to inform the work of the commission.
These include survivors who were sexually abused as children in a school, or related to a school, between 1927 and 2013. A family member may complete the survey on behalf of a person who was sexually abused and is deceased or who cannot participate themselves.
Other participants could include people with relevant knowledge of concerns relating to sexual abuse in schools, including teachers, former pupils and others who may have witnessed abuse, or been aware of concerns, or been involved in reporting concerns.
Survivors and people with relevant information who no longer live in Ireland are also invited to take part.
The survey will inform the commission’s selection of sample cases for its formal investigation of the handling of concerns of child sexual abuse. Participants can indicate if they would be willing to provide further information to investigators if requested to do so at a later stage.
The commission will focus on identifying where concerns of child sexual abuse were not handled appropriately, why this occurred, and who was responsible. It will also conduct a survivor engagement programme to hear directly from survivors and will consider the impact of childhood sexual abuse in schools.
Judge Michael MacGrath has been appointed chair of the commission and is supported by four commissioners: Judge Mary Ellen Ring, Roddy Bourke, Michele Clarke and Kieran McGrath.
The survey is available online at commissionofinvestigation.ie
A detailed survey participation guide is available on the commission website. Printed copies are also available on request at info@commissionofinvestigation.ie or phone: (01) 920 8787.
An independent survey Participation Support Service is available from One in Four, which assists adult survivors of child sexual abuse. Email: coi@oneinfour.ie : phone (01) 611 4654

title: Jake Xerxes Fussell: Why I’m bringing my Napoleonic sea shanties to Ireland
description: The American singer has become a category of one: a singer with two feet in the past and his head in the present
content:
E very so often, when the mood takes him, Jake Xerxes Fussell will grab his guitar and travel backwards through time.
“You can go back to ancient folk songs that are hundreds of years old, and you can find themes in there that are still the stuff that we’re singing about now,” the singer says as sunshine streams into his office in his home in Durham, in North Carolina.
Fussell is a songwriter, but he is also a time traveller, a musical Indiana Jones recovering largely forgotten relics and introducing his discoveries to audiences who would otherwise never have encountered them.
He isn’t an academic, and he rejects terms such as “folklorist”, yet over the course of his career he has become a category of one: a singer with two feet in the past and his head in the present.
He presses onwards with that mission on his charming new album, The Old Beloved Path, a homespun collection of folk that revitalises music that has lain dormant for decades, if not centuries.
One striking example is Boney, which has its origins as a maritime work song, a “short drag” shanty associated with the age of sail, and which he revives as a fingerpicking blues track – think Dire Straits by way of a Ken Burns American civil war documentary.
It’s an extraordinary act of preservation, but it is also a song about missing home and about a war that consumed everything in its path – even Napoleon in the end (“Boney broke his heart and died / way in St Helena”).
That humanity is where Fussell finds the crucial connection. These songs, he says, are about all the big themes. “I find that I relate to a lot of songs that are quite old.”
Napoleonic sea shanties are nobody’s idea of mainstream entertainment but there turns out to be an enthusiastic audience for this kind of music, and critics have swooned over Fussell’s sonic reclamation. Pitchfork has heralded his talent for finding “ingenious ways to pull old obscurities into the anxious present”, while Spin has praised his “knack for unexpectedly astute arrangements”, saying, “The music of old, weird America has never sounded so spry”.
Fussell wears this praise lightly. He has the affable, ambling quality of someone who knows when to hurry and when to slow down. He’ll be doing a bit of both this month as he crosses the Atlantic for a short Irish tour.
It will be a homecoming, in a certain sense. The connection between Irish and American traditional music is long established, and Fussell has swapped notes with artists on this side of the ocean such as Lankum , to whom he was introduced after a show at Bello Bar in Dublin.
His interest in Irish folk extends to the Traveller singer Thomas McCarthy , through whom he discovered the ballad Michael Was Hearty, about a young man who marries for wealth rather than love and comes to rue his decision.
Fussell was introduced to the tune by Nathan Salsburg, curator of the archive of the 20th-century ethnomusicologist Alan Lomax , and instantly understood that he had to record his own take, which he did in 2019. He adds that he and McCarthy have yet to cross paths, but he would love for them to one day play together.
“I want to meet him. At some point we were in contact, we wanted to do a show together. It just didn’t pan out. I think we were going to do [it] and then Covid happened.
“Nathan Salsburg sent me a video of Thomas McCarthy singing that song. I thought it was the most beautiful thing I’d ever seen. I had the melody kicking around in my head for a long time.
“Irish music is such a thing. And I’m not Irish. It wouldn’t normally be something I’d try to fool with that much, to re-create an Irish song. That one I couldn’t get rid of. I’ve played it in Ireland a few times, and it’s been well received.”
Folk music has a long history of activism; the question of whether politics and the arts should mix has acquired a fresh relevancy since Macklemore was chucked off Ed Sheeran ’s tour after speaking out about Gaza.
This interview takes place before that incident galvanised opinions, but, speaking more generally, Fussell has a nuanced take on folk and its affiliations. He is certainly versed in the history.
“There’s a big tradition of that going back at least until the 1930s and 1940s, if not earlier. There was a first big wave of protest singing with people like Woody Guthrie , Pete Seeger and The Almanac Singers, and that sort of early folk revival of the 1930s,” he says.
“Then there was sort of a revival of that revival in the 1950s and 1960s, mostly in New York and Boston, which of course led to Bob Dylan , Joan Baez and those people. And singers like Phil Ochs , who were deeply political, and then people like Dylan, who could skim along the surface of those sort of topical songs but weren’t necessarily in their personal lives deeply political.
“There’s a long legacy of that. It’s always been around. You see it crop up here and there with different singers. Certainly, there’s an association there with the left wing for a long time.”
Does Fussell see himself in that tradition? “I definitely relate to it, and at different times I have sung songs that have been topical in that way. I have mixed feelings about it, because I don’t necessarily see music as having an immediate material application to geopolitical problems.
“There’s something to be said for people having a big benefit concert, when they raise a bunch of money for a cause. That’s a very material way of applying music or performance. Or at least giving attention to a cause.
“I also see a lot of strength in songs that can bring attention or have a transformative effect on someone on an individual level; certain protest songs can do that.”
He isn’t sure whether music itself can change things, however. “I don’t necessarily delve into that world too much, just because I feel like it isn’t the best use of my time in music.”
Fussell is looking forward to returning to Ireland; he sees an affinity between Irish people and those from the American South. Growing up in Georgia, close to the border with Alabama, he had an “acute awareness” of his southernness and the assumptions people would make about, for instance, racism.
“Especially when I travelled outside of the region, and people would comment on my accent a lot of the time. I never took that as an insult. It’s more sometimes ‘otherised’, in a way. ‘Oh, you have an accent.’ When, in fact, everybody has an accent.”
He’ll bring a little bit of the south with him when he comes to Ireland, singing songs steeped in the American past but brought to life with a passion that locates them firmly in the here and now.
“It’s a lot of the same basic stuff – about life and death and love and relationships and family, loss,” he says. As he pauses to smile you can hear a bird twitter outside. “It’s all sorts of things.”
The Old Beloved Path is released on Bandcamp and via Fat Possum Records . Jake Xerxes Fussell plays Cyprus Avenue , Cork, on Thursday, October 8th; Róisín Dubh , Galway, on Friday, October 9th; and Button Factory , Dublin, on Saturday, October 10th

title: Dear Éanna, have I spotted a penguin in Portmarnock?
description: Our readers bring their pictures and queries to wildlife consultant Éanna Ní Lamhna
content:
I spotted this bird on Portmarnock shores in mid-September. By any chance is this a South African penguin? Marie Purcell
Ah now. Penguins are flightless birds that only live in the southern hemisphere. They are indeed excellent swimmers, but there is no way that a penguin could swim more than 20,000km, cross the equator and turn up on a beach in Portmarnock.
This is a member of the northern hemisphere equivalents – the auk family. All our auks are able to fly. The only one that couldn’t – the great auk – was made extinct by humans by 1844. This particular one is a razorbill. Thousands of these breed around our cliffs and this is a juvenile one. They don’t usually stand at the water’s edge unless sick or exhausted.
What is this creature? It looks like a very small robotic lawnmower. I am in Lithuania on holiday. Carmel McGovern, Ennis, Co Clare
What a lovely way to describe it. This is a European firebug – Pyrrhocoris apterus . Like our own very familiar shield bugs, it is a true bug – a particular group of insects that possess a tube-like mouth which pierces plants and sucks their juices. This species is native to Europe and occurs widely on the continent and there are a few records for southeast England. It has only ever been recorded once in Ireland, in 1982, when Dr James O’Connor of the Natural History Museum identified one that was accidentally imported with bananas in the Dublin fruit market.
With reference to your account of the caterpillar of the lime hawk-moth on Saturday September 12th, I recorded one on the grounds of Cnoc Buí in Union Hall last July. It had just fallen out of a lime tree as I walked by. So, if they are in Co Cork they must be on the move. Cormac Leggett
This would be real scientific news, as so far, this species has only been recorded in Co Dublin, in Clonee in Co Meath and in Newcastle in Wicklow. I consulted with Michael O’Donnell of mothsireland.com who welcomes all such observations. He has identified it as an eyed hawk-moth caterpillar which, in fact, has a completely blue spike almost like the lime hawk-moth. It doesn’t, however, have the small reddish protrusions below the spike, which are another characteristic feature of the lime hawk-moth. The eyed hawk-moth has been widely recorded over the country and there are many Cork records.
I saw this interesting little creature walking in the dunes on Bull Island in mid-September. Part ant, part beetle, channelling its inner scorpion. Richard Butler, Raheny, Dublin
You must be reading too many comics – hybrid creatures, such as you describe, don’t actually exist. You have taken a most excellent picture of a rove beetle. This particular species goes by the name of the devil’s coach-horse. It is a common, nocturnal predator which feeds on slugs, and indeed any other invertebrates it can find. When alarmed – as in your picture – it opens its jaws and raises its tail over its back. It can release a foul-smelling liquid and bite too, so it is not to be messed with.
We found this creature on a towel in our back garden in Co Dublin. Could you tell us what it is? Vanessa (14) and Ruth Costello 11
It is a hoverfly – Volucella pellucens . This is an adult, which lays eggs in the nest of the common wasp. The larvae, when they hatch out, are scavengers, feeding on nest debris, dead wasp grubs, dropped food scraps, and dead adults. When fully grown, they leave and pupate in the soil below the nest, emerging as adults the following year.

title: Cannabis now as profitable as cocaine as supply from legal markets surges
description: Cannabis herb trade from US, Canada and Thailand is now so significant that economics of Irish drugs market have shifted
content:
Profits made by Irish drugs gangs from cannabis now rival those from the cocaine trade, as criminals source it at low prices from countries where it has been legalised or laws relaxed.
Changes in the international cannabis wholesale market are so significant that the economics of the Irish drugs trade have fundamentally shifted, Garda sources told The Irish Times.
It has become much easier to buy good-quality herbal cannabis – from the US , Canada and Thailand – at lower wholesale prices, greatly increasing the profits to be made in the Republic and reducing the risks for the Irish criminals involved.
Det Chief Supt Seamus Boland, who leads the Garda’s Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau (DocB), told The Irish Times the barriers to entry to the cannabis trade, by those buying at source abroad, have reduced, encouraging smaller operators.
He explained that even relatively minor figures in the Irish drugs trade were now travelling to places such as Canada and buying small quantities of cannabis herb, intended for the legal market in those countries, but then smuggling it into the illicit market in Ireland.
They did not need to deal with dangerous cartels abroad, and there was little risk from local law enforcement because the drug is legal in these locations. The only major significant risk was losing a consignment if it was seized when being smuggled into Ireland.
“Usually it’s in quantities of less than 5kg, and they are sending it back to Ireland in parcel post,” he said of smaller Irish drug dealers travelling abroad to countries where the drug has been legalised. “We have seen a number of times now that they’re using the addresses of minors, 16- or 17-year-olds.”
[ ‘They’ll use AI for new drugs’: Ireland’s arms race with organised crime Opens in new window ]
Boland added the dealers were often pressuring these young people into allowing their addresses to be used to take receipt of the drugs sent by courier. This shifted the risk of detection on to the younger people.
Garda research in recent months concluded cannabis herb is now being bought from Irish wholesalers, after being smuggled into the country, for between €3,500 and €4,000 per kilogram. It fetches €14,000 on the streets of the Republic, allowing a profit of up to €10,000 per kilo.
The Garda has now officially revalued a kilogram of cannabis herb at €14,000, down from €20,000 just months ago, reflecting the changing trade. Though the value of the drug has fallen in Ireland, profits have still increased.
The wholesale cost is so low because the supply lines are overstocked at a time when demand from drug users is at record levels.
[ US becomes main cannabis supplier to Irish market as drug smuggling booms Opens in new window ]
The Garda has recently gained specific intelligence proving the biggest domestic gangs are clearing a profit of circa €10,000 per kilo of cocaine, after the high cost base is taken into account. Cocaine needs to be bulked up with mixing agents and repackaged in a labour-intensive, thus costly, process.
No such processing is required with cannabis herb. That means, unlike with cocaine, that most of the differential between buying a kilo of cannabis herb wholesale in Ireland for about €4,000, and selling it in smaller street deals for about €14,000 per kilo, is profit.
Large quantities of the drug are being smuggled into the Republic in freight through ports and airports. Some 60 per cent of the cannabis seized at Irish ports, airports and at parcel-sorting centres last year was from the US, Canada and Thailand.
[ Large increase in cannabis being smuggled into Ireland through postal system Opens in new window ]
In 2019, the total value of cannabis seized at point of entry into the Republic that originated in the US, Canada and Thailand combined was €4 million. That grew to €64 million last year. This recent spike in drug smuggling, especially from the US, has resulted in a 10-fold increase in the value of cannabis seized by Revenue’s Customs officers since 2019, to almost €110 million last year.

title: Hallgrímsson relieved difficult international window is over
description: Two Dublin greats set up a county final shootout
content:
The highlight of that international window for the Republic of Ireland’s players was, you’d imagine, the final whistle in Backa Topola on Sunday evening. Come the end of their draw with Israel, they “just wanted to get off the pitch, on to their aeroplane and out of this nightmare at last,” writes Ken Early.
It was a pairing that “was drenched in rancour from the moment the draw was made,” says Gavin Cooney, “a fortnight of fierce sound and fury” culminating on a silent stage in Serbia. From start to finish, it was “bleak and acrimonious”.
Gavin Cummiskey reports on a game that came at the end of “a gruelling four-match, 15-day camp” , one that featured another flare-up at half-time when an Ireland backroom staff member alleged that he was spat at by an Israeli player .
“I’m absolutely delighted the window is finished,” said Heimir Hallgrímsson, the head coach understandably relieved it was all over . “I think we will look back on these two weeks as a defining moment. Every problem from now on will seem lesser.”
In rugby, Gerry Thornley reviews a URC weekend that saw two wins, a draw and a defeat for the Irish provinces , a bit of an improvement on round one’s whitewash. Charlie O’Shea had a night to remember in his first start for Munster, scoring two tries in their win over the Pretoria Bulls, while Ciarán Frawley achieved the same feat on his debut for Connacht, helping them to victory away to Benetton.
Ulster shared 10 tries in a thriller of a 33-all draw in Glasgow , but Leinster suffered their second defeat on the trot, this time to the Sharks in Durban. They did at least pick up a late bonus point in their 26-20 defeat, John O’Sullivan reporting on an invaluable experience for a young side.
And Ireland’s women helped themselves to seven tries in their second win over Japan in a week , Alana McInerney and Sophie Barrett both marking their debuts with tries in a 43-19 win in Cork.
Denis Walsh uses his column today to look at “Munster’s descent into tortured mediocrity” . He struggles to recall “the last time a Munster team didn’t feel dwarfed by the legacy of the jersey”, the organisation in need of a change of leadership at the top – “but there are no miracle cures”.
In Gaelic games, Gordon Manning rounds up the club weekend during which two Dublin greats set up a county final shootout after Con O’Callaghan’s Cuala and Ciarán Kilkenny’s Castleknock won their semi-finals. Gordon has all the results from around the country, Kerry’s Dingle and Meath’s Summerhill among the champions to fall.
And in racing, Brian O’Connor reports on Daryz becoming the first colt in close to half a century to win back-to-back Prix de l’Arc de Triomphes . title: Refuge review: A thrillingly weird opening becomes a true story from Ireland’s past
description: Dublin Theatre Festival 2026: In her new play, directed by Jim Culleton, Deirdre Kinahan focuses on the persecuted Palatines who arrived in Co Limerick
content:
An old carriage shed at Castle Matrix, in Co Limerick. A broken-down carriage, a dusty mirror, walls thick with ivy. A tree.
In expressionistic dance movements, a man in a grey tracksuit (Matthew Williamson) beats up a young Afghan man, Zabi (Sabah Qalo). Zabi runs, crawls under the carriage and falls asleep. When he wakes, a red-haired woman in 18th-century peasant dress, Hannah (Hannah von Peinen), is kneeling beside him.
This is the thrillingly weird opening of Deirdre Kinahan ’s new play.
Refuge tells the true and not well-known story of the Irish Palatines. Beginning in 1709, thousands of Protestants fled the German Palatinate after years of war, religious persecution and a devastatingly cold winter. Sir Thomas Southwell was among the Anglo-Irish landlords who settled Palatine families on his Co Limerick estate, around Rathkeale. His settlement there became one of the few Palatine communities in Ireland to endure.
The historical story centres on Hannah and her husband, Peter (Holger Kraft). Peter embraces their new life and the colonial project. Hannah is more ambivalent. “These low grey skies are not ours, Peter; these soft hills, they do not belong to us; and I cannot pretend, I will not pretend, it is ours like you do.”
Part of her ambivalence comes from her friendship, and growing romantic attachment, with an Irish poacher and Hougher (Aidan Kelly), one of the people being dispossessed from the land on which the Palatines are settling.
The play, which is staged at Dublin Theatre Festival by Fishamable and Staatstheater Mainz , a German company from Rhineland-Palatinate, at first feels like a strange pastiche of Brian Friel ’s Translations crossed with the enchanted atmosphere of A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Kinahan’s writing is full of simple, declarative, lyrical statements: “To take a man’s home is a terrible thing.” “I sinned against God.” “I like the bogland. I like the rivers. I like the delicate cotton flower that can be found in the grasses.”
There is a simplicity and limpidity to this high poetic register. Under another director it could easily fall apart, but Jim Culleton ’s excellent direction understands that the play should not be naturalistic. The lines are delivered starkly, with great sincerity. Steve Wickham sits to one side of the stage, providing a beautiful live score that moves between violin, piano and percussion.
[ Daughters of Destiny – Frank McNally on a forgotten immigrant community, the Irish Palatines Opens in new window ]
Matthias Werner’s set creates an uncanny, almost mythological vision of Ireland: deliberately tacky and elfish but dreamlike and unsettling too.
Quickly the twist is revealed, and the reason these stories are paired. Hannah is a ghost, wandering a land that isn’t hers, and now tends to lost souls in the same predicament. “I didn’t come to Ireland to conquer or steal another family’s future. I came here for refuge,” she says.
Kinahan is very good at holding both sides of this historical story at once. There is sympathy for the dispossessed Irish but also for the Palatines: people seeking refuge who have little choice about where they are sent, even as they become instruments of colonial oppression. Peter is essentially the bad guy, yet the play insists on his humanity.
Curiously, that generosity disappears in the present day. We understand Zabi, but the man in the grey tracksuit who attacks him remains a faceless racist. There is a certain squeamishness in this omission. Understanding what might drive a young man to such violence is not the same as excusing it.
I would have liked the play to extend its historical curiosity into the present: we are unlikely to get very far without some willingness to properly look at the people whose actions we find most repellent.
Refuge is at the Pavilion, Dún Laoghaire, as part of Dublin Theatre Festival , until Sunday, October 11th

title: Seasamh prionsabálta poiblí
description: Is féidir ceacht a fhoghlaim ó Kylian Mbappé
content:
Glacann sé misneach neamhchoitianta agus coráiste faoi leith dul in aghaidh an tsrutha. Bhí tráth nach bhfuil rófhada ó shin nuair a bhí formhór an phobail ina gCaitlicigh dhílse de réir gach tomhais phoiblí, ach ba dhána an mhaise do dhuine anois giob ciúin ar bith a rá ag cosaint na heaglaise céanna, is é sin, mura mbeadh sé ina cheap magaidh ar fad. Sa tslí chéanna, ba ghránna an bheart é an ginmhilleadh, ach tá an dealramh anois air gur cuid den saol laethúil é agus gur lag ar fad na cogair chiúine atá ina choinne, ní áirím an cheist a thógaint in aon chomhluadar measúil.
Cé go ndeir an rialtas go poiblí go bhfuil siad go láidir ar son na Palaistíne agus in aghaidh an tslada gan stad atá ar siúl in Gaza agus RTÉ gan dul i bpáirt le sorcas bliantúil seócheoil rinciúil pramsálach Chomórtas Amhránaíochta na hEurofíse, fós féin bhí glas ar a mbéal nuair a fágadh foireann sacair na Poblachta idir seacht gceann na meá agus gach adharc gabhair nuair gurbh éigean dóibh imirt in aghaidh Iosrael.
Chun a gceart a thabhairt do na himreoirí, bhí sciar maith acu in aghaidh an chluiche a imirt, ach ní raibh ach aon duine amháin a dhiúltaigh scun scan béal na gclár aon pháirt a ghlacadh sa ghruaimdhráma. Ba é sin Gavin Bazunu, cúl báire, a d’imir 22 uair cheana don Phoblacht. Ní hé go raibh aon sochar faoi leith le baint aige as an ngníomh seachas aithis agus maslaí ó dhaoine áirithe, ach b’fhéidir coinsias glan dála mar a choinnigh sé scláta glan ina chúl báire go minic. B’fhéidir gurbh uaisle fós a sheasamh má tá aon fhírinne sna líomhaintí go raibh liúnna ciníocha á séideadh le hAdam Idah le linn an chluiche toisc nár bhain sé le roghachine geal Dé.
B’fhéidir nach raibh beart Kylian Mbappé chomh dalba céanna nuair a d’fholaigh sé suaitheantas ag tabhairt tacaíochta do Ceuta ar gheansaí a chlub, Real Maidrid, an tseachtain cheana. Tar éis an tsaoil, agus is é an saol atá i gceist, tá sé ar cheann de na peileadóirí is fearr ar domhan ar fad thar amhras anonn, agus ní raibh aon ní i bhfoirm maoine nó cáile le cailliúint aige. Ina choinne sin thall, áfach, tá lucht leanta Real Maidrid chomh confach le lucht leanta ar bith agus ní mhaithfidís go furasta do dhuine ar bith a sheas i leataoibh na slí ón sluasmaoineamh.
Is é an scéal ná gur shocraigh Real Maidrid go gcaithfeadh imreoirí na foirne mana ‘Todos Somos Caballas’ a chaitheamh, nuair is leasainm nó ainm ceana é ‘caballas’ ar mhuintir Ceuta. B’fhéidir nach cúrsaí iontais é sin nuair is eol dúinn gurbh iad an club sin rogha Franco, agus gurbh ó Ceuta a sheol an Convoy de la Victoria, an sluamhuirí agus an armáid a ghabh port ar mhórthír na Spáinne d’fhonn tús a chur leis an gcogadh cathardha nócha bliain ó shin agus Franco ar thús an chabhlaigh.
Níorbh fhada gur éirigh an liú ina choinne ar na meáin lofa shóisialta, an sloc gránna sin ina maireann táirspíd na smaointe. Thug freagra uaidh chomh huasal, chomh dínitiúil is a gheobhaidh tú an taobh seo de chlaí na muice binbe.
Dúirt sé go tomhaiste gur sheas sé go daingean le muintir Ceuta gan cheist, ach, agus is é seo an ‘ach’ nach gceadaítear, go raibh bá aige chomh maith leis na híospartaigh, leis an mbreis is céad a báthadh, is nár chóir fulaingt amháin a chur chun tosaigh ar fhulaingt eile.
“Sula rabhas im imreoir peile, ba dhuine daonna mé.”
Nath é ar chóir é a ghreanadh i gcloch lasmuigh de cheanncheathrúna an FAI.

title: France closes up to 500 schools on Monday as more protests planned
description: Lessons will be ‘totally or partly suspended’ in some second level schools after clashes between riot police and student protesters, France’s education minister says.
content:
Up to 500 schools in France will be closed or partly closed on Monday as authorities brace for another week of student protests .
Lessons will be totally or partly suspended across hundreds of schools because security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, the education minister, Édouard Geffray, said on Sunday.
The minister said 24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and 78 education staff members injured. The number of school closures on Monday would be comparable to Friday’s but the government envisaged a “partial, progressive return to lessons”, said Geffray.
Thousands of teenagers staged widespread demonstrations and erected barricades last week to protest against what they said was underfunding and neglect of the education system.
Clashes with riot police left hundreds of people injured, led to more than 5,000 arrests, mostly of minors, and jolted president Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration.
There was a lull at the weekend, but protest organisers called for renewed demonstrations on Tuesday because the government had failed to produce “concrete measures”.
Authorities say political agitators have infiltrated the protest, which started at a Paris school on September 17th and spread across the capital and the rest of France.
“There are activists – particularly from the far left – who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence,” said Geffray. “Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students.”
The injured education staff members were deliberately targeted, “something we have never seen before”, said Geffray.
The protests caught the government by surprise and confronted Macron with his worst crisis in months. Images of burning barricades and police using teargas, batons and other methods to disperse protests have dominated TV news.
Student grievances include overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other factors are an opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the sweltering temperatures in classrooms during heatwaves.
Protesters have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education and cited difficult conditions such as leaks, cockroaches, collapsed ceilings and decayed buildings. Others have complained about excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff.
The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. On Sunday, police detained a 16-year-old in relation to an assault of a teacher in La Ciotat, a town on the southern coast between Marseille and Toulon. The teacher (59) was doused with gasoline and struck during a protest on Friday.
The government is also under pressure from trade unions that called a day of strikes last week to compel the new prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, to rethink budget cuts and consider a form of wealth tax on the super-rich. The CGT trade union exhorted workers to sustain the pressure with demonstrations this week. - Guardian

title: Mild, cloudy, occasionally wet weather to continue until midweek
description: Met Éireann expects temperatures to hit 20 degrees on Monday but dip expected on Wednesday
content:
The mild start to October is to continue for another few days before conditions take a cooler turn in the middle of the week, Met Éireann has forecast.
After a very mild night with temperatures of 13-15 degrees, Monday morning is to begin cloudy in most places with patches of rain, drizzle and mist.
It will stay humid for most of the day but whereas the north and west will continue to have some rain, the south and east will become drier, with temperatures reaching as high as 20 degrees.
Another warm night will follow and then Tuesday morning will see more dull and wet weather across the north and west which will move southwards across the country during the day.
Again, it will be mild for the time of year, with temperatures of up to 18 degrees forecast and the southeast likely to be the warmest.
Once the rain clears, temperatures will begin to fall and Tuesday night is expected to be cooler than of late, reaching just 5-9 degrees.
That drop in temperatures will continue into Wednesday, which will be cool and bright with just the occasional shower and some moderate to fresh breezes keeping it feeling more like autumn.
Temperatures are not expected to rise above 14 degrees anywhere.
Thursday will begin much the same, with most places dry and enjoying some early sunshine, but rain will move into the north and west later on.
No dramatic change is expected towards the weekend, with most areas having a mix of cloudy and clear spells but not a lot of rain, and highest daytime temperatures still hovering around 13-15 degrees.

title: Oíche mhór na n-amhrán is ansa linn
description: Beidh an cheolchoirm speisialta Cóisir Cheoil – An tAmhrán is Ansa Linn ar siúl i dTír Chonaill an tseachtain seo.
content:
“Beidh mé ionraic leat, tá mé ag déanamh go mbeidh oíche ann nach mbeidh a macasamhail sa cheantar go ceann fada go leor.”
Sin a dúirt an láithreoir raidió Dónall Mac Ruairí agus é ag trácht ar na ceoltóirí a bheidh ar an ardán i gceann de na ceolchoirmeacha is beoga dá bhfuil súil leis i saol na Gaeilge i mbliana.
De dheasca feachtas de chuid Mhic Ruairí, a chuireann an clár Cóisir Cheoil i láthair ar RTÉ Raidió na Gaeltachta, reáchtálfar an cheolchoirm Cóisir Cheoil – An tAmhrán is Ansa Linn an tseachtain seo.
“Bhí mé ag déanamh gur cineál smaoineamh beag simplí a bhí ann go ndéanfainn feachtas beag do mo chlár féin,” a dúirt Mac Ruairí le Tuarascáil.
“Is maith linn uilig liostaí ar nós cé na deich bpeileadóir is fearr in Éirinn, cé na deich leabhar is fearr agus cé na deich scannán is fearr.
“Agus is ón bhunsmaoineamh sin a mhéadaigh sé,” ar seisean.
D’iarr an láithreoir ar a chuid éisteoirí rogha amhrán a sheoladh isteach chuig an gclár, agus tiomsaíodh liosta de na hamhráin Ghaeilge is fearr leo as na freagraí.
…is annamh a bhíonn gach duine ar aon fhocal faoi liostaí mar seo, agus dá ndéanfaí lá eile é, seans gur liosta iomlán éagsúil a bheadh ann.
Cé go bhfuil dáimh ar leith ag Mac Ruairí leis an lucht éisteachta, chuir líon na bhfreagraí ionadh air.
“Bhí na céadta i dteagmháil liom, idir théacsanna agus ríomhphoist agus ghlaochanna ar an stáisiún agus is cinnte gur chuir an pobal suim ann,” a dúirt Mac Ruairí.
“Tá tú i gcónaí, mar láithreoir, ag iarraidh go mbeidh an t-eolas sin ag teacht go nádúrtha ó na héisteoirí agus is cinnte gur chuidigh an cleas beag seo iad a spreagadh.
“Ach níor shíl mé go n-iompódh sé insan behemoth seo a bhfuil muid ag déileáil leis anois,” a dúirt sé.
Ar na gnéithe ba shuimiúla a bhain leis an bhfeachtas bhí na scéalta a d’inis na héisteoirí faoi na hamhráin, agus na fáthanna ar roghnaigh siad iad.
“Tá tábhacht ag amhráin ar leith do dhaoine ar leith,” a mhínigh Mac Ruairí agus é ag trácht ar na freagraí a seoladh isteach chuige.
“Ní hamháin go raibh siad ag inseacht domh faoi na hamhráin a raibh meas acu orthu, ach bhí siad ag inseacht dúinn fosta cad chuige.
“Bhí nótaí beaga galánta ag teacht isteach leis na moltaí. Bhí siad ag rá, b’fhéidir, ‘Ba é seo an chéad amhrán a bhí á cheol sa chéilí nuair a casadh mo ghrá geal orm tríocha bliain ó shin’, nó ‘Seo an chéad amhrán ar éist mé leis nuair a bhí mé imithe as baile - nuair a chuirim an píosa ceoil seo ar siúl, cuireann sé an baile i gcuimhne domh’.
“Bhí sé galánta go raibh na scéalta beaga sin ag teacht isteach ó na héisteoirí,” arsa Mac Ruairí.
Bronnadh fadliosta amhrán ar na moltóirí agus roghnaigh siad sin gearrliosta de na cinn ba mhó a thaitin leo.
“Shuigh siadsan leis an chúpla céad moladh a tháinig isteach agus nuair a bhí muid san aon seomra amháin, roghnaigh achan duine na deich n-amhrán ab ansa leosan.
“Bhí sé le feiceáil láithreach bonn go raibh muid ar aon intinn, déarfainn, faoi sheacht gcinn acu sin.
“Cuirim i gcás Samhradh, Samhradh [Thugamar féin an Samhradh Linn],Bruach na Carraige Báine [amhrán ar an sean-nós as Corca Dhuibhne], An Cailín Álainn [amhrán a chan Tomás Mac Eoin], Pócaí Folamh is Cloigeann Tinn [clasaic le John Beag Ó Flatharta], Amhrán Mhuíse [amhrán ar an sean-nós as Conamara].
“Bhí siad sin ag beagnach gach moltóir,” a dúirt Mac Ruairí.
“Lean muid ar aghaidh ansin agus fuair achan duine deis cúpla amhrán eile a mholadh agus cás a dhéanamh fána gcoinne. Ach sin mar a d’oibrigh muid tríd.
“Shíl mé féin go mbeadh sé iontach deacair, go mbeadh míshástacht ann, ach ní raibh. D’oibrigh achan duine go tomhaiste agus go cúramach le chéile.
“Tá torthaí ár gcuid oibre curtha i gcrích ach déarfainn gur beag a d’aontódh leis an liosta, ach measaimse gur sin rud folláin – cuireann sé daoine ag caint faoi na hamhráin, cuireann sé daoine ag smaoineamh faoi na hamhráin a raibh meas acu féin orthu.”
Oíche Dé Céadaoin na seachtaine seo, cruinneoidh plúr na gceoltóirí Gaeilge in éineacht le Ceolfhoireann Coirme RTÉ i dTeach Pobail Chríost Rí i nGort an Choirce, Gaeltacht Dhún na nGall, chomh maith le hocht gcéad duine sa lucht éisteachta le ceiliúradh a dhéanamh ar rogha de na 40 amhrán is mó cáil agus is ansa le pobal na Gaeilge.
“Beidh John Beag inár gcuideachta, beidh Altan inár gcuideachta, beidh Iarla Ó Lionaird inár gcuideachta, beidh Séamus agus Caoimhe Uí Fhlatharta ann, agus níl ann sin ach cúpla duine.”
Tá Cóisir Cheoil – An tAmhrán is Ansa Linn á reáchtáil mar chuid de chomóradh céad bliain RTÉ agus tá sé ar cheann de na himeachtaí atá luaite le hUachtaránacht na hÉireann ar Chomhairle an Aontais Eorpaigh. Craolfar an cheolchoirm beo ar an raidió, agus déanfar taifeadadh air a chraolfar ar RTÉ One amach anseo.
“Beidh rud speisialta ag tarlú an oíche sin,” arsa Mac Ruairí. “Ní hamháin go mbeidh pobal na háite ag teacht ach beidh ceoltóirí mór le rá a bhfuil an oiread sin measa orthu fríd an tír inár gcuideachta fosta.”
Agus ar ndóigh, is iad na hamhráin a roghnaigh an lucht éisteachta a bheidh i gcroílár na hoíche.
“Oibreoidh muid fríd an liosta, ceann ar cheann agus iad á ceol i gcuideachta Cheolfhoireann Coirme RTÉ, agus tá mé ag déanamh go mbeidh cúpla aoi speisialta, cúpla ceoltóir óg atá ag teacht i méadaíocht le bheith inár gcuideachta fosta, agus sílim go mbeidh sé galánta.”
Ar ndóigh, is annamh a bhíonn gach duine ar aon fhocal faoi liostaí mar seo, agus dá ndéanfaí lá eile é, seans gur liosta iomlán éagsúil a bheadh ann. Ach mar sin féin, tá luach ar leith leis an bhfeachtas a reáchtáil Mac Ruairí.
“An rud atá deas faoi seo ná go dtarraingíonn sé aird an phobail ar amhráin an phobail,” a dúirt sé.
“Rud folláin atá ann sin, go bhfuil muid fós ag caint ar na hamhráin Ghaelacha seo”.
Cé go bhfuil móramhráin aitheanta na Gaeilge i measc na gceann a roghnaíodh, tá amhráin níos nua-aimseartha ar an liosta freisin.
“Rud eile ba dheas liom a rá, bhí sé galánta go raibh amhráin nuachumtha air, go raibh Séamus Barra Ó Súilleabháin air agus go raibh Huartan air, agus go raibh IMLÉ air agus go raibh Eoin Ó Ceannabháin air.
“Ní rud stálaithe atá ann seo. Bhí cuid mhór amhrán ón traidisiún ann, cinnte, agus tá sé galánta aird a tharraingt ar amhráin atá go mór i mbéal an phobail le díreach bliain nó dhó anuas, agus thóg sin mo chroí fosta.”
Tá ticéid do Cóisir Cheoil – An tAmhrán is Ansa Linn ar fáil ar eventbrite.ie .
