title: PTSB says takeover by Bawag still on track despite ‘highly speculative’ bid by Axis Capital
description: Axis, cofounded by former boom-era banker Mark Duffy, has yet to line up funding needed to make offer for bank
content:
PTSB said it remains focused on concluding its takeover by Austria’s Bawag as it characterised an announcement by a corporate advisory firm cofounded by a former boom-era banker as “highly speculative and conditional”.
Axis Capital, cofounded three years ago by former Bank of Scotland (Ireland) chief executive Mark Duffy, said on Friday evening it was considering a bid for PTSB , almost six months after the bank agreed to sell itself to Austria’s Bawag for €1.62 billion.
While it said any possible offer would be in cash at €3.20 per share – 7.7 per cent above the agreed price with Bawag – it also signalled it has yet to line up funding for such an offer.
Shares in PTSB rose 1 per cent to €3 in early trading on Monday.
PTSB, which is 57.5 per cent Government-owned, said in a statement on Monday morning that “no offer has been made by Axis for the company and that the announcement by Axis is highly speculative and conditional”.
It added that the bank’s board “is focused on delivering value and certainty to the company’s shareholders and, in accordance with its legal obligations, is continuing to work with Bawag to satisfy the remaining conditions” of the agreement.
The High Court, which is overseeing the sale, which is being carried out by a so-called scheme of arrangement, is due to hold a sanctioning hearing on October 27th.
“The announcement may increase the likelihood of a higher-value outcome for shareholders and reduces the perception that the Bawag scheme is a foregone conclusion,” said Denis McGoldrick, an analyst with Goodbody. “However, until Axis can demonstrate a credible funding solution and progress to a firm offer, we continue to view Bawag’s agreed transaction as the option offering the greatest certainty of value realisation.”
Axis, which Duffy set up with German corporate lawyer Lutz Hartmann, had €100 of assets as of May 14th, the end of its financial year, according to an abridged set of financial accounts for the period filed with the Companies Registration Office. It said on Friday it will now engage with “a number of potential funding and investment partners” with a view to raising the necessary financing that would support the announcement of a firm intention to make an offer.
[ Former banker Mark Duffy’s Axis Capital ‘considering PTSB bid’ Opens in new window ]
Axis Capital helped initiate talks in 2025 between New York private equity firm Centerbridge, the Department of Finance and PTSB. Centerbridge later submitted a non-binding proposal for the State’s 57.5 per cent stake but was the underbidder to Bawag when the formal sale process concluded in April.
The Business Post reported in July that Axis was urging minority shareholders to oppose the planned sale. In a circulated note, Axis said it was “increasingly uncomfortable” with the process, citing “inordinate involvement from one shareholder”.
Duffy said on LinkedIn that Axis had asked the panel to reopen the sale process so “all credible bidders” could make final bids to shareholders.
PTSB secured 91.3 per cent shareholder backing for the Bawag takeover at a late-July extraordinary general meeting (egm), led by the Government’s 57.5 per cent stake. However, about 36 per cent of minority investors voted against it.
Some small investors are expected to seek a second minority shareholder vote through the courts. PTSB says it has strong legal advice that only one vote count is required.
“Even if there is no further announcement from Axis Capital in the next couple of weeks, it is possible that minority shareholders who are resistant to transacting with Bawag at 297c per share might apply to adjourn the sanction hearing until Axis Capital’s position becomes clearer,” said John Cronin, founder of SeaPoint Insights, an independent research and analysis firm specialising in the banking and finance sectors.
“But would any such adjournment application succeed on the back of an announcement by Axis Capital of just a possible offer, with no certainty of funding in place?”

title: Brazil turns right: Bolsonaro in pole position as election goes to run-off
description: If Flávio Bolsonaro wins, Brazil will be the latest country to swing right in Latin America, a trend championed by Donald Trump
content:
S unday witnessed the far-right wave rolling across Latin American politics break over Brazil . Senator Flávio Bolsonaro defied polls, financial scandal and even claims of orgies with prostitutes to pip incumbent leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of the presidential election.
Flávio’s lead over Lula was narrow – 47.03 to 45.16 per cent – but he goes into the run-off in three weeks as favourite.
Nearly all those candidates now eliminated were on the right and he will be expected to grab a majority of their votes. History is also on his side. Since Brazil introduced two rounds for presidential elections in1989, the winner of the first has always gone on to triumph in the run-off.
It is a remarkable turnaround for the scandal-plagued Bolsonaro family whose leader Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence for a coup attempt after he lost the 2022 presidential election to Lula.
Now, after Sunday’s count, Bolsonaro senior sees his wife Michelle and son Carlos elected senators, another son Jair Renan elected a federal deputy and his eldest son Flávio now in pole position to become president.
Should Flávio win in three weeks’ time he has vowed to negotiate an amnesty for his father or pardon him.
Sunday’s result is a bitter blow for Lula. It is his first setback as a candidate since 1998 when he lost his third bid for the presidency. In the three victorious races he has contested since then he has always been in front.
Now he must pull off an unprecedented feat and come from behind. A wily old campaigner, he will back himself to overturn the small gap to his 45-year old rival. His best hope of doing so is tapping into the 21 per cent of the electorate who abstained. He still has the powerful weapon of the apparatus of Brazil’s federal government at his disposal.
[ Brazil’s poor once propelled Lula to power. Now many are wavering Opens in new window ]
But having taken advantage of an incumbent’s privilege to spend wildly in the campaign already, it is not clear if more financial inducements will work in the short time left.
Even more challenging, Lula is now operating in a political environment that has decisively turned to the far right.
Flávio’s allies won eye-catching victories in down-ticket races across Brazil, with the exception of the northeast region, now the last big redoubt of Lula’s Workers Party. They won more governorships and senate seats than any other grouping and will dominate the new congress.
While Brazil’s left was Sunday’s most notable victim, the country’straditional right emerged nationally a much reduced force. Another big loser was the supreme court, which last year convicted Jair Bolsonaro for his coup attempt.
The far right’s decision to put revenge for this historic verdict at the heart of its campaign has been vindicated, helped by the fact that Alexandre de Moraes, the justice who led the effort to jail Bolsonaro senior, is now mired in a corruption scandal.
[ The Bolsonaro comeback: can Brazil’s most divisive dynasty reclaim power? Opens in new window ]
A push to impeach the court’s most compromised members now beckons in the new congress.
As he looks to defy history, Lula appears set to double down on negative campaigning. In his speech after Sunday’s results he pointed the way referring to his opponent’s “dark connections ... regarding organised crime”.
But Flávio’s long-established links to Rio de Janeiro’s criminal underworld have so far not proved a political liability. Even a well-sourced report last week by an award-winning investigative reporter of his participation in orgies with call girls did little to damage his campaign.
Lula must be left wondering just what sort of scandal might derail the Bolsonaros’ march back to power.

title: Last-minute budget lobbying and the challenge of keeping money in the family
description: Business Digest: The best news, analysis and comment from The Irish Times business desk
content:
In advance of tomorrow’s Budget 2027 presentation by Ministers Simon Harris and Jack Chambers, film and television producers and studios across Ireland have launched a last-minute push, spearheaded by David Puttnam, to secure an enhanced tax break for regional productions in Budget 2027, three years after the Government phased out a previous scheme. Ian Curran has the details.
And while there is talk of some adjustment to inheritance tax thresholds , Eoin Burke-Kennedy reports on calls for more fundamental reform. Dave O’Brien, the head of tax at business advisory group Xeinadin Ireland, says making it easier for parents to transfer wealth to their children would be a more effective way of getting the €170 billion held on deposit back into circulation, potentially more effective than the Government’s proposed savings scheme.
John Loughran has stewarded the Sandymount Hotel business established by his parents through difficult times, including the post-2008 property crash and financial crisis, when it narrowly avoided the appointment of receivers. Having handed over the reins now to his son Gerard, he talks to Ian Curran about his determination to retain the business’s family-owned status and the challenges of doing so in Ireland.
Too many bosses leave it to managers to do the communicating with staff, writes Pilita Clark. Or they burden staff with long, repetitive and widely unread emails that reek of little thought or care. Against that background, the mildly chaotic half-hour weekly online sessions of cheeky, rapid-fire presentations from Octopus Energy founder and chief executive Greg Jackson and his team are certainly engaging.
Economic consultant and former senior Teagasc executive Brendan Kearney argues that replacing beef farming with forestry would boost incomes in the sector and help the State meet its climate goals.
Ireland may not be managing its current exchequer abundance, writes John FitzGerald, but it does not have to worry about the scale and growth of public debt which looms large for several of the world’s largest economies, presenting a big challenge for governments.
Closer to home, activity in the State’s services sector expanded again in September with “new business growth” hitting a 10-month high. But AIB’s latest purchasing managers index also highlights rising inflationary pressures from higher wages and energy costs. Eoin Burke-Kennedy reports.

title: Oil refiners US and China have the leverage amid rising fuel prices
description: Donald Trump’s recent threat to halt diesel exports would have had calamitous consequences for Europe
content:
Rising fuel prices have highlighted a shift in the geopolitics of energy, with leverage moving from countries that produce oil to those that refine it. The United States and China are among the winners; Europe is not.
When the leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) major industrialised states agreed last Friday to release 100 million barrels from their strategic oil reserves, they described the action as a “decisive, co-ordinated” measure to protect households and businesses from price shocks.
But the will of just one of the seven, the United States, was the decisive factor that forced the other six into a co-ordinated response to the recent surge in the price of refined oil products, especially diesel.
Days earlier, Donald Trump had threatened to halt the export of diesel from the US, a step that would have had calamitous consequences for his European allies. The US supplied almost half of the diesel imported into the European Union in August so when Trump demanded that they open up their strategic reserves to help lower the price of the fuel, the Europeans had to comply.
Despite the standoff between the US and Iran in the Strait of Hormuz , crude oil is moving again, if not quite at pre-war levels. The greater shortage is in refined oil products like petrol, diesel and jet fuel, and it is one that is likely to persist well into next year despite the G7’s action last week.
While petrol fuels cars, diesel is the workhorse of the economy, powering the trucks, tractors and diggers that are indispensable to production. When the price of diesel goes up, it makes everything from farming and mining to transport and construction more expensive and drives up the cost of essential goods for households, particularly food.
Iran has attacked refineries in Gulf states that host US military bases, and Ukraine and Russia have struck one another’s energy infrastructure, reducing a global refining capacity that was already under pressure. The EU had already all but halted the import of diesel from Russia and earlier this year, it extended sanctions to imports from countries such as India of refined products made from Russian oil.
About 30 refineries have closed in Europe since the start of this century and last year alone saw two refineries in Germany and two in Britain halt the processing of crude oil. The closures could affect Ireland, where the Whitegate refinery in Cork produces about a third of the country’s retail fuel, with most of the rest coming from Britain.
China has the world’s biggest refining capacity, followed by the US, with a handful of other net exporters of refined oil products including India and South Korea. In the winter of 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Chinese exports helped to ease the price of diesel and they played a similar role at times this year during the Iran war.
But just before its National Day last week kicked off a weeklong holiday in China, Beijing told its refineries to pause exports, according to a report from Reuters. The move was probably in the name of energy security and a legal requirement Beijing introduced last year to maintain reserves at a certain level but it highlights the leverage enjoyed by states with major refining capacity such as China and the US.
China displayed the diplomatic utility of its refining capacity during one of its export pauses earlier this year when it continued to supply diesel to the Philippines, a country with which it is engaged in an intense maritime dispute. And Trump showed last week that he is willing to use diesel exports to persuade his allies to take action that could reduce prices ahead of next month’s midterm elections.
The medium-term prospects for the EU are unpromising and the structural factors exacerbating the fuel shortage could even get in the way of the common European project of rearming the Continent. A report last month by the Lithuania-based Nato Energy Security Centre of Excellence found that even if Europe continues to spend hundreds of billions of euros on weapons, without more refining capacity it might be unable to fuel them.

title: Gerard Howlin: Tomorrow’s budget may be the worst since the days of Charles Haughey’s wild spending
description: Despite all the promises, the day after tomorrow will be one of disappointment
content:
T he thing to know about tomorrow’s budget is that, like it or loathe it, you don’t have a choice. The Opposition cannot credibly outspend this Government and can’t afford to underbid it. In the absence of any broader vision, what we are getting is a great frittering of money for ever-less return. We are heading into a winter of loadsa money and a lot of discontent.
This budget will rival Gene Fitzgerald’s in January 1981 in its purposelessness – and that budget was until now a nadir of Irish budgets. Fitzgerald was finance minister in the throes of rising public debt, unemployment and inflation. Under then taoiseach Charles Haughey ’s direction he ignored reality and kept spending in advance of an imminent general election, but it didn’t work. The circumstances now are very different but eerily similar. Modest but firm control of public spending, under a government with clear priorities and a willingness to articulate them, could be transformative. But it is not to be.
What we have in its place are bitty promises, a chaotic budgetary process that feels made up as it goes along, and fragmented politics. Much of the Cabinet and civil service are left to follow developments through the media. Inside the Government – insofar as there is any inside – there is a lot of feral scrapping for a share of a diminishing political centre. It is all short term and tactical. But even on the purely tactical front, it doesn’t work.
Because despite all the promises, the day after tomorrow will be one of disappointment. Expectations have been raised across multiple fronts for months – not least by Minister for Finance Simon Harris . No one has been prepared to face down any of the demands.
The chutzpah of the hospitality industry in hitting the Government for an expected €681 million in 2027 in the form of a reduced VAT rate was an omen of what was to come. We are now spending €100 million a month on cutting excise duty on fossil fuels as farmers face a severe shortage of winter fodder after a summer drought linked to global warming . Presumably the fodder shortage will require another subsidy.
Like the water charge protests of more than a decade ago, the fuel protests were about far more than the ostensible issue. Both resulted in not just a U-turn on the issue, but a real political setback more generally. The momentum for structural reform in the State stalled with the abandonment of water charges. Likewise, the pretence of fiscal discipline ended with the hauliers’ blockade after Easter – and this budget is part of that. It is now a political truism across much of Government that appeasement is the only possible policy.
An exception, for now, are the trade unions which have set down preconditions for pay talks to replace the public pay agreement that has expired. A standoff with Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers has escalated into work-to-rule across parts of the public service and planned one-day strikes on October 14th and 21st. There would be a strategic prize for the Government if it could negotiate an agreement that would take them to the other side of a general election at the end of 2029. But it is unclear if this Government can do strategy.
Meanwhile, Government backbenchers are being assailed by fuel protesters and by public servants seeking better pay and conditions. As belated attempts are made to contain the rate of growth in public expenditure, public services will be affected by industrial action.
All of this feeds into a general mood of dissatisfaction. Ireland is awash with money, yet there is not enough to get younger people who are paying high rents on to the housing ladder, or for modestly paid people to do a weekly shop and pay their fuel bills without feeling the pinch. Critically, there is no persuasive political narrative to convince voters that the Government has a plan for how to tackle any of this.
[ Budget talks enter ‘banging fists on the table’ phase – metaphorically at least Opens in new window ]
Budget 2012 was the first after Fine Gael and Labour took power in 2011 and split the Department of Finance in two, creating a new Department of Public Expenditure. That was a political decision about sharing economic power within the Government. It worked well for a time.
Until last year, when Paschal Donohoe and Chambers presented Budget 2026, there was largely a unity of purpose between the two ministers concerned.
But for the first time since 2011, there is now a split team in the Government trying to manage the economy.
Feeding into that dynamic is increasing dysfunction in what, 15 years later, are separate but siloed economic departments, neither of which has or feels responsibility for the big picture. The senior cadre in each department lacks experience in the other – institutionally, this is a step backwards and means the collective powerhouse that took charge in the post-crash period has been diminished.
Compounding all this is the rotation of the office of Taoiseach, which started in 2020, and by the next election will be a decade-old phenomenon. This has profoundly altered the dynamic of government to its detriment. It means that a new taoiseach has hardly arrived, but people are looking over their shoulder towards their successor.
If there is any consolation to be gleaned from all of this, it is that we have few problems that don’t have solutions – and many can be solved far more easily than in 1981. All that is lacking is the political will and courage to get on with it.

title: Una Mullally: A very touching thing happened on Capel Street last Thursday evening
description: When we talk about those on the ‘margins’, we are talking about real people
content:
L ast Thursday, I met a friend for a drink on Capel Street on the north side of Dublin city centre. Walking down the street at 7.30pm was a chance to experience the kind of genuinely thrumming street life that only exists where pedestrians have space and safety from traffic (the street is pedestrianised). The street has a diversity of businesses, architecture that is human scale and public seating. There were even children kicking a ball, a great sign of a healthy urban habitat.
But as we sat outside a pub on the street we also saw a steady stream of people experiencing the kind of destitution and addiction that are now familiar sights in the city centre. One after the other, people young and old approached, asking for money. There were maybe half a dozen people in total, including a man holding a child’s hand, a little girl who had all the chirpiness of a kid being brought to the amusements, as opposed to a trip around the streets looking for change from strangers.
Most of the interactions were friendly. One was edgy, a young woman fizzing with the kind of energy anyone who spends a lot of time in the city centre will now recognise. Writing in this newspaper in August, the chief executive of Merchants Quay Ireland and former governor of Mountjoy Prison Eddie Mullins detailed the rapid rise of crack cocaine, writing that it “reveals a deeper and more uncomfortable reality exposing the consequences of homelessness , trauma, poverty and social exclusion. It demands a response that goes beyond treatment alone.”
Recently, the head of the Dublin City Taskforce, Robert Watt – who is being paid a salary of €280,000 to do that job – made remarks about people on, as he called it, “the margins of society” in Dublin city centre, specifically Dublin 1 . Watt was speaking at the Irish Planning Institute ’s autumn conference, and said Dublin’s north inner city had a “massive overconcentration” of services. This is true. For example, Gardiner Street , parallel to O’Connell Street , should be a grand street of public and affordable housing, with all the shops and amenities any populated city neighbourhood requires. Instead, a tenth of Ireland’s homeless population lives there, amounting to about 1,700 emergency accommodation beds on one street. Raising this in the Dáil last April, local TD Gary Gannon said the North City Centre Residents’ Alliance concluded that 7,000 people were living in homeless accommodation in the north inner city.
The taskforce has a subgroup concerned with “vulnerable groups”. Their first job was to map and list all locations and services for vulnerable groups in Dublin 1, Dublin 2 and around Heuston Station, with the goal of managing the overconcentration of such groups in “small geographical areas, and relocate existing provision, where possible and appropriate”. Watt also suggested other local authorities step up and share the burden of services, because it isn’t fair on the residents and workers of Dublin 1. This is logical, especially when it comes to densely populated working-class areas with less political power to address spatial inequality, and left to soak up Government failures. But what also must be addressed is the housing crisis that is driving this reality.
It is neither the job nor the remit of the Dublin City Taskforce to solve all of society’s ills. The Government states the taskforce will take a “holistic view” of what is required to “rejuvenate” the city centre. But unless there is major action on addiction and homelessness, such improvements risk being superficial rather than socially transformative. The taskforce has ambitious goals. But for genuine change to be achieved, the Government needs to match those with equally ambitious actions and funding for addiction services and public housing. There are 15,000 people on the council’s housing list.
When the streets are gussied up and the landmark projects – the GPO, the Parnell Cultural Quarter, the Fruit and Vegetable Market – progress, none of it will matter if fundamental failures are not addressed. We need taskforces, leadership and political heft to tackle destitution, homelessness and addiction in our society.
[ ‘What’s happening is not working’: Dublin needs homelessness ‘tsar’, says charity Opens in new window ]
A very touching thing happened on Capel Street that evening. With no change in my pockets, I walked up to a shop with one man who had approached me for money and bought him what he wanted. He said he was living in a tent, and insisted we do a scratch card together. There were a few other people begging outside the shop. My new pal with his scratch card didn’t have a coin to scratch it. One person sitting outside the shop handed him one. When he went to hand it back, he was told to keep it. A kind gesture in an often cruel context.
When we talk about those on the “margins”, we are talking about real people. People who smile when they’ve won a fiver on a scratch card, a smile that broadens when they’re told to keep a coin. A child on an evening stroll with an adult begging. A woman down to skin and bone who can seemingly no longer make sense of the world. These are Dubliners too, not just on the margins, but in the heart of the city, scrambling around to survive. Unless we address that – in such a “rich” country – then I’m not quite sure what rejuvenation really means.

title: Munster have been digging this hole for years as they slide into tortured mediocrity
description: Change of leadership at the top of the organisation is desperately needed but there are no miracle cures
content:
F or everybody with feelings for Munster , there is an image of the club they refuse to give up. It is romantic and rooted in the past and, somehow, it has survived Munster’s descent into tortured mediocrity. It is not blind adoration, but it is heartfelt.
In his new autobiography and in interviews promoting the book, Peter O’Mahony has not spared the Munster leadership for what he perceives to be years of mismanagement. He was wounded by Munster’s disrespectful vacillating over his final contract extension, and it troubled him that in 10 years as captain he lifted just one trophy. But he never renounced his original feelings for the jersey.
“There’s always something different, though [about Munster],” he said in conversation a couple of weeks ago. “Whatever happens it will be a special club. We travel anywhere in Europe, and you’ll get bigger crowds because we’re there. It’s a really critical time now that Munster hold on to that and realise how important it is.”
But is that not living in the past, I asked him?
“Yeah, well,” he said, “you have to build yourself on something.”
[ Peter O’Mahony: ‘There was stuff that I shouldn’t have done – the pressure I was putting on people’ Opens in new window ]
Munster’s history, though, is never entirely in the past. There always seems to be an upcoming anniversary of some event from the glory days. Munster rarely play a European game that doesn’t have an historical resonance of some kind. Creamy pints of nostalgia are filled from a pouring tap.
“We know the history,” said Ian Flanagan, the outgoing chief executive, in an interview with Simon Lewis in May. “We know what we want to live up to.”
That fixed standard, though, has magnified every shortcoming over the last 15 years. When was the last time Munster had a team that could remotely live up to the overbearing achievements of the teams that set the standard? When was the last time a Munster team didn’t feel dwarfed by the legacy of the jersey?
“Things have deteriorated and the notion that Munster ‘aren’t far away’ comes off as a little fanciful now. Frankly, I don’t remember Munster as low,” wrote Ronan O’Gara in his Irish Examiner column towards the end of last season. “Just because Munster are a big brand does not mean that the brand can’t fail.”
The resignation of Flanagan as chief executive last week, before the publication of an independent review into the governance of Munster Rugby, has promoted the possibility of another “line in the sand”. It is a familiar chorus. The problem for Munster is that Ground Zero has kept shifting.
It is 10 years since Alan Quinlan’s famous outburst on Sky Sports after Munster lost to Stade Français by 20 points in Paris, even though the French team had played for 40 minutes with just 14 men. Only a try by Conor Murray with five minutes left prevented Munster from suffering their first shutout in 21 years of European rugby up to that point.
“Embarrassing, humiliating, disgraceful – these are the words that spring to mind,” said Quinlan in the live broadcast. That season Munster failed to qualify from the pool stages of the Champions Cup for the second year in a row and didn’t reach the play-off stages of the Pro12, as it was then.
The bracing thing, though, is to compare that team to the current squad: the starting 15 against Stade Français contained nine players capped by Ireland and four players who had toured with the British and Irish Lions.
Nothing like such depth exists now. When Munster lost by 31 points to the Bulls in the quarter-final of the URC last season, only four of the starting 15 had ever been capped by Ireland and they had made just 63 appearances between them – 31 of which belonged to Craig Casey. None of the Munster players had toured with the British and Irish Lions.
[ United Rugby Championship: Munster 26 Bulls 22 Opens in new window ]
In these things despair is always relative to expectation. Our memories are short too. It is only five years since, in the space of a week, Munster lost the final of the Pro14 to Leinster and ran Toulouse to seven points in the Champions Cup in Thomond Park. Both defeats were held up as harrowing examples of how far Munster had fallen off the pace at the elite level of the club game.
How would a week like that be received now?
The context for such despair at the time was hope. At the beginning of that season Damien De Allende and RG Snyman, World Cup winners with South Africa, had arrived on massive contracts. It was seen as a demonstration of Munster’s renewed ambition.
Trophy signings are off the menu now. Last season ended with a round of redundancies and further cuts to the playing budget. At the end of June, Munster announced a €1 million cash flow deficit in their 2024-25 accounts, which they expected would be repeated in last season’s accounts.
In his autobiography, Conor Murray wrote bluntly about the cost-cutting that had impacted on the first team and dragged the club into a swamp.
“Travelling on the cheap has become an issue in the last few seasons,” he wrote about an away trip to Zebre in September 2024. “It’s another manifestation of the ongoing financial spiral. They don’t buy big-time players because they’ll cost too much so you end up with fewer box office talents who’ll get supporters coming through the turnstiles.
“Your squad becomes progressively weaker season upon season and inevitably, then, the results start to suffer. That in turn affects the gate receipts which in turn means the quality of the recruitment goes down and the vicious circle continues. An air of stagnation starts to hang over everything. And eventually you end up sending your squad cattle class to Italy and the Munster brand name takes another embarrassing hit to its prestige.”
Zebre won that game, their first victory over Munster in 21 attempts.
[ Owen Doyle: World Rugby must tackle laissez-faire policy spreading like a virus in southern hemisphere Opens in new window ]
The feelings that surround the club now are estranged from hope. The crowds at home games have boiled down to the hard core. Tickets for the glamorous Champions Cup game against Racing 92 in Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Saturday, October 17th, are not selling fast. Filling Thomond Park for any European game now is a relic of another era.
A change of leadership at the top of the organisation is desperately needed but there are no miracle cures. Munster have been digging this hole for years.
“The past is a foreign country,” wrote LP Hartley. “They do things differently there.”

title: ‘My son has just started secondary school and seems a little overwhelmed’
description: ‘Should I be worried?’
content:
My son has just started secondary school and seems a little overwhelmed by the step up in level. Gone is the bubbly little boy who could not wait to recount the day’s events in the car on the way home.
I have spoken to his year head, who was very reassuring. She stated that it takes a few months for children to adapt to the new challenges of second level.
Should I be worried at his seeming reticence to talk about how he is getting on?
I would concur with your son’s year head. The transition from primary to second level is a huge one in any child’s life.
Overnight they have gone from being the senior students to the most junior. This can be quite intimidating and the potential for bullying – both within his new peer group, as certain students begin to mark out their territory, or older students taking advantage of the vulnerability of the new arrivals – is something that all the teachers but particularly the year head will be keenly observing.
He has to learn the names of up to a dozen, if not more, teachers. Previously he had a single teacher for an entire year, whose every action quickly became familiar.
Now he has to adapt to each one’s teaching styles.
Most schools also accommodate a number of both first- and second-year postgraduate master’s student teachers, who often share a subject with an experienced teacher. After all, how do aspiring teachers learn their trade? PME students tend to be allocated first- and second-year classes so the number of new faces can often exceed fifteen or sixteen. This is an awful lot of change to take on board when you are 11 or 12 years old.
Apart from the multiple teachers, there is also the constant movement from the moment he enters his school building each morning. Instead of heading for a familiar classroom, he instead heads for a set of lockers where all his school based texts are stored. He has to remember which subjects he has for the early morning classes and what homework, if any, he must bring to class.
He will return to his locker at least three to four times a day to extract the latest classroom requirements, and deposit those he has just used. You can imagine the state of his locker at the end of a day’s activity.
Getting it in shape before leaving the building when tired, so that he can manage the following day’s requirements, is a big learning experience.
Given the nature of the second-level school timetable, when he arrives home he will have to organise his homework to ensure that he prioritises what is due the following day, remembering when he has physical education so that he brings in his sports gear on the right day.
It has always amazed me over a lifetime of teaching how incoming first-year students adapt to the radically changed environment. By Halloween, the vast majority have fully integrated themselves into the day-to-day routine of the big school.
Having said that, I would not in any way dismiss your concerns. If his mood remains subdued I would definitely contact his year head again to see if the teachers have any observations on his adaptation to the new challenges he is grappling with.

title: Most neurodivergent children have a neurodivergent parent – diagnosed or not
description: Part two: Neurodiversity and your parenting style
content:
Knowing yourself is the beginning of all wisdom – Aristotle
A s well as being immensely rewarding and satisfying, parenting can be one of the most challenging and stressful roles we take on in our lives.
In studies, a parent dealing with a child’s meltdown experiences a higher level of real-time stress than an air traffic controller dealing with a near miss. Because we so love and are invested in our children our deepest emotions, positive and negative, are evoked as we parent.
Our childhood experiences and how we were parented ourselves, as well as our values and beliefs, come strongly to bear on our parenting and we are easily triggered by our children’s words, actions and feelings. A critical comment from our own children can wound us in a profound way, just as a loving comment can bring us immense joy and satisfaction.
As we embark on the parenting journey we are called to empathically understand our children but we are equally challenged to empathically understand ourselves. In the first article we discussed how important it was to develop a compassionate understanding of your children’s needs and strengths. It is equally important to become self-aware of your own needs and the strengths of your parenting.
When faced by a challenge such as a struggling or anxious child, as well as empathically understanding what is going on for your child, it is important to reflect about what is going on for you as a parent:
What is triggered in you as you respond?
This self-awareness is the key to becoming an effective parent. Indeed, one of the great benefits of becoming a parent is the journey of self-discovery it brings.
Neurodistinct (ND) conditions such as autism , ADHD and dyslexia are genetic and hereditary. This means that most ND children have a parent who is ND also – whether they have a diagnosis or not. Indeed, it is often during the process of their child’s assessment that many parents wonder about their own neurodiovergence and are motivated to explore this possibility either formally or informally. In anonymous surveys of parents attending my “parenting exceptional children” courses, 79 per cent say they are or think they might be neurodivergent in some way and 85 per cent think the other parent might be.
Without necessarily seeking a formal diagnosis, I encourage parents to explore and embrace their neurodiversity as this increases their self-understanding and can improve their relationship with their ND child. Many of the ND children I have spoken to over the years tell me they don’t like their diagnosis, not because they disagree with how it describes them but because it makes them feel different in the family – ND children can feel sidelined in the family as “the autistic or ADHD one”.
[ What happens when your therapist or GP asks: ‘Have you ever wondered if you might be neurodivergent?’ Opens in new window ]
Sharing with your children how you might also be ND or have a similar way of thinking and processing the world can help them feel more connected to you and included in the family. A sense that “Dad is ADHD too” or that “Mum has particular sensory preferences too” can help a child feel more bonded in the family. Even when parents have different ND traits from their children an open discussion about family neurodiversity can help children feel better – “you know the way you like to chill by dancing to loud music, I’m the opposite and need a few moments quiet to calm myself”.
Being self-aware of family ND differences can help you understand conflicts and challenges as they arise. For example, you may be an autistic mum who often prefers a quiet evening routine to regulate after a busy day, struggling with an active ADHD son who needs high-energy physical activity and chatting time as part of his routine. Or you may be a highly social ADHD dad who loves family social events and finds it frustrating when his autistic daughter is stressed and overwhelmed.
Appreciating a parent’s neurodiversity can have a profound impact on everyone in the family. I was working with a father whose son was struggling in school and was being assessed for ADHD. The father was initially critical of his son, feeling he just needed to “knuckle down” and apply himself – however, putting pressure on his son drove a wedge between them.
When I gave the father space to talk about what was going on for him, it turned out he had a similar experience in school and had “dropped out” and had a lifelong feeling he had “failed”– he didn’t want his son to “repeat [his] mistakes”. As he told his own story the father realised he might also have ADHD and this helped him develop a more compassionate view of both himself and his son. Rather than their education challenges being failings on their part, it was simply that the structures in school didn’t support their way of learning. He became focused on ensuring his son’s wellbeing and advocating for him to get better supports in school. The two of them developed a special bond over both being ADHD and as they explored their passions for biking and outdoor pursuits.
This changed perspective also transformed the father’s relationship with his wife, who now understood her husband better and really appreciated his increased positive involvement with their son, which considerably reduced her own stress.
Whether you are neurotypical or neurodivergent, it is really important to identify your individual preferences and needs as a parent. A good way to start this is to consider your sensory preferences and needs. What sensory experiences do you love and which ones do you hate? Which sensory experiences regulate or relax you and which ones distress or agitate you? People have very different sensory profiles and something that deeply relaxes you may agitate another parent. For example, you may:
Your sensory preferences will vary depending on context and what you can manage in the moment. The important thing is to not judge or deny what works best for you and instead to compassionately understand your needs.
When your needs come into conflict with your children’s needs, it is important not to immediately override your own. Instead, it is worth taking a pause to consider whether there is a way to respond to your child’s needs while making sure you meet your own.
Although you sometimes have to sacrifice your own needs to support your children, you have to be careful to not overdo this and end up overstressing yourself to the extent you can no longer meet anyone’s needs. It takes a lot of time and often trial and error to think through how you might creatively adapt to your child’s needs while meeting your own.
One mother I worked with who used to meet her needs in a highly social job where she was out and about all day was very challenged by parenting three young kids and felt lonely and depressed during the day at home with them. We worked on a series of “physical resets” she could punctuate the day with to boost energy and wellbeing – these included doing a music and dance session with the kids, scheduling a time to take everyone out for a playground trip, phoning a friend, doing weight exercises, putting on a face mask, engaging in her own interests when the children were napping or had screentime (rather than striving to “be productive” or engaging in housework). She also increased creative activities at home that she too enjoyed, sorting family photos and making collages with the kids.
When co-parenting, sharing the parenting tasks according to respective needs and strengths can make life more manageable. One mother found the executive function demands of organising and providing daily meals for children really overwhelming. To manage, the father took over grocery shopping and brought the children out for the afternoon every Saturday and she batch cooked for the week in a quiet kitchen. This played to both parents’ strengths: she liked having quiet time and being alone at home and the creativity of putting together a set of meals; her husband liked getting out of the house, doing messages and being on the move. This helped both feel regulated and recharged.
This article is the second in a four-part series on neurodiversity and families. The next article looks at neurodivergent relationships.

title: Erling Haaland turns to the law to protect his signature hairdo
description: Thierry Henry singing Zinedine Zidane’s praises, Ronaldo’s posse wade in
content:
Manchester City fans will be glued to this particular legal battle. No, not that one, rather the case Erling Haaland is taking against airline Norwegian Air for alleged trademark infringement during last summer’s World Cup .
The case is due to be heard in Oslo this Friday, the claim being that the airline “unlawfully exploited Haaland’s commercial characteristics and registered trademarks”.
What did they do? They edited his ponytail on to one of their planes during the World Cup, captioned it “we’ve never looked more Norwegian” and posted it on social media.
Their defence is that it was just lighthearted banter, although they could just point to his current hair-do and ask: “What ponytail?”
“We’ve been hit with an infection or a bug. In terms of how many withdrawals, we’ve had a similar number to Man City’s charges.” – Sweden’s head coach Graham Potter on losing a bunch of players to illness ahead of the game against Bosnia and Herzegovina, although not quite 114.
“Zizou’s arrival is extraordinary. It’s having someone who is on a par with God. I say this without intending to offend believers.” – Thierry Henry on the divine Zinedine Zidane becoming manager of France.
“Bored beyond belief. I have got three kids so I am a full-time Uber driver, basically. It is a strange transition. It wasn’t one I was ready for.” – How much is Kasper Schmeichel enjoying retirement? Not a great deal.
“Can I just say to all those United fans who’ve been gloating all week, you’re still crap and you know you are.” – UK education secretary (and Manchester City fan) Lucy Powell . A bit unparliamentary, but she had a point.
That’s how many days (over 18 years) it was since Cristiano Ronaldo was last an unused sub for Portugal in a competitive game, until Norway last week. He took it well.
When Portugal’s manager Jorge Jesus left Cristiano Ronaldo on the bench for their game against Norway last week, and then (allegedly) let him know he wouldn’t start against Denmark either, it was an act of extreme bravery on his part.
Not just because there was a chance it would result in Ronaldo departing the camp in a huff (which he did), but also because it would inevitably attract the ire of the mega-protective and exceptionally bolshie women in his life.
Did they keep their counsel after his walkout? Did they heck.
“CR7 deserved more respect,” said his sister, Elma. “As for the Portuguese people, well... they don’t deserve to have the best [of] anything. We are envious, disdainful, ignorant, and we deserve to return to the mediocrity we always had in football before CR7.”
And his wife, Georgina Rodriguez? Of Jorge Jesus she said: “I don’t know how this man can carry the name of Christ.” Oh Lord.
“Kimmich runs somewhere. Everyone immediately gives him the ball. I don’t know why. Nothing comes from him.” – Former German international Mario Basler struggling to see the point of Joshua Kimmich.
“Very good. Very, very good. Very good in the duels. He was, once again, very good. I said it four times!” – Zinedine Zidane ’s verdict on Jeremy Jacquet’s display against Italy? Well, very good.
“I always felt that in England, people never actually respected the quality and IQ that I play with. In Spain, they really do.” – He’s a confident lad, is Anthony Gordon .

title: Parents scramble for childcare as Dublin creche announces it is closing
description: Oakview Tallaght, located on grounds of locality’s TU campus, issues three months’ notice
content:
Parents of almost 50 children have been left scrambling for childcare after a west Dublin creche announced its intention to close with just three months’ notice.
Oakview Tallaght, located on the grounds of TU Dublin’s Tallaght campus, wrote to parents last week informing them that the creche would close in January 2027.
Ciara Kirby, who has two children in the creche, says she rang another provider after receiving the letter, but they had almost 400 people on the waiting list already.
She was due to return to work after the birth of her third child, but now has to consider taking a sabbatical due to the impossibility of getting alternative childcare at such short notice.
“I would love to get back to earning, but I suppose the main thing is I’ve worked really hard for my career. The idea of putting that on pause for a year or two, and maybe not having my job at the end of it, that’s kind of killing me now,” said Kirby, who is a speech and language therapist.
“If there was clarity as to why that was closing, if we knew what the reason was, we would probably be able to accept it better.”
In the letter from Oakview to parents, seen by The Irish Times, the creche said the decision to close “follows consideration of the works required within the service, exclusively, the installation of appropriate care Room Temperature Controls and works needed to address safety issues within the outdoor area”.
[ Minister defends record on childcare spending as protest is held outside Dáil Opens in new window ]
However, when asked why the creche was forced to close, TU Dublin said Oakview had chosen to leave the facility at the end of its licence period in December 2026.
“This is not a new date recently imposed on Oakview,” said the university. It also said the creche had contacted TU Dublin in May 2026, saying it would end its services early, in September 2026, before withdrawing that request and deciding to continue operating until December 2026.
Regarding the temperature issues cited by the creche, TU Dublin said the elevated room temperatures identified by Tusla in a 2025 inspection had been addressed by Oakview through portable cooling measures, and this had been deemed adequate by Tusla.
“Oakview subsequently sought a permanent capital air-conditioning solution funded by TU Dublin. The contract did not require TU Dublin to provide or fund such an installation, nor had Tusla required it based on their report,” the university said.
TU Dublin also confirmed it would not be seeking a new licensee for the service.
Aisling Barry is another parent with a two-year-old child, Kerri Marie, in the creche who said the news was devastating.
“It’s just so difficult to find a creche these days anyway. We were looking around for one since I was about six months pregnant and it was just no, after no,” said Barry.
She has also contacted other facilities since receiving the letter, with some telling her they are fully booked until 2028 and others with waiting lists extending to 400 people.
“With the late notice of the closure, I don’t know what we’re going to do. The cost of living has just skyrocketed and this is the last thing we need now,” said Barry.
“We’re not really getting any sort of information on what happened, it’s coming in dribs and drabs, and it’s very unclear. We don’t know if TU Dublin or Oakview were aware that they were planning on closing the creche in January 2027. It’s just very difficult to get any solid verified information. So, I mean, frustration-wise, it’s just more of a panic,” said Barry.
Oakview Creche has been contacted for comment.

title: Service sector activity strengthens despite price pressures
description: Latest PMI for State’s services sector indicates growth with inflationary pressure
content:
Activity in the State’s services sector expanded again in September with “new business growth” hitting a 10-month high.
AIB ’s latest purchasing managers’ index (PMI), however, highlighted rising inflationary pressures from higher wages and energy costs .
The prices or fees charged by service businesses – which covers everything from hotels and hairdressers to IT firms and telecoms – rose at their sharpest rate in five months, it said.
Economists expect the price squeeze on businesses from higher energy prices to worsen in the short term, even if a deal in the Middle East is reached.
AIB’s latest PMI for services fell from 55.4 in August to 54.1 last month, signalling slightly slower growth. Any figure above 50 indicates expansion.
“Activity levels were boosted by existing and new business, alongside renewed gains in employment,” AIB chief executive David McNamara said.
He also noted that rate of growth was ahead of the flash euro zone and UK PMIs at 53.0 and 51.7 respectively, but below the US PMI at 58.7.
“New business continued to grow strongly following a dip in activity earlier in the year, although new export business growth eased on the month,” he said.
“Higher activity was driven by new clients and marketing efforts. In that context, the volume of outstanding work rose at the fastest pace in over two years,” McNamara said.
[ Brown Thomas considers launching Planet Beauty concept as separate brand online Opens in new window ]
AIB’s report indicated that input price inflation rose further in September, reaching its highest since May.
The bank said increased input prices reflected elevated wage pressures, alongside higher fuel and energy costs.
There were signs of rising capacity pressures in the Irish services sector with growth in the level of outstanding business, it said. Nonetheless, all four sub-sectors of AIB’s barometer registered higher activity in September.
The technology, media and telecoms sector posted the fastest expansion (58.3), followed by transport, tourism and leisure (56.3). Business services (51.5) and financial services (51.2) both registered more moderate growth.
[ Will AI really kill most desk jobs ‘within the next 12 to 18 months’? Opens in new window ]
The report said new business at Irish service providers rose for the fifth consecutive month running in September, and at the strongest rate since November 2025.
“Increased demand reflected new clients and greater marketing efforts,” it said.
Firms in the sector were also confident about the 12-month outlook for business activity.
“Overall confidence improved for the sixth month running to the highest since February 2025, linked to planned business investments, new contracts and marketing efforts,” it said.

title: Ken Early Ireland Israel troy parrott Heimir Hallgrímsson
description: Finn Azaz’s creativity was missed against Israel but leaving him on the bench spared him from the criticism that would inevitably have come his way
content:
It doesn’t happen that often in football that you have to play a match against an opponent you beat 3-0 only last week. The exception is two-legged cup ties, when the aggregate score is a factor conditioning the way the second game is played.
The aggregate score was not a factor in Ireland v Israel II, which was not a second leg or even really a return fixture but a pure rematch . Above all it was a chance for the Israeli team that had been demolished in Debrecen to redeem themselves after a week in which they had been battered by the Israeli media and public. You got the impression they would gladly accept relegation from League B in exchange for revenge against Ireland.
Actually, only five of the Israeli XI that lost the first game 3-0 started in Backa Topola. They had clearly resolved to be much more solid defensively this time, and the first quarter of the game was mainly Ireland passing the ball around the perimeter of the Israeli block, too slowly to open up any space.
Last time out Ireland had repeatedly skewered Israel with quick passes through the centre, but here they struggled to make that happen. They also struggled to harness the direct running of Jack Moylan, a live wire in Debrecen but peripheral here.
The assured passing of Dara O’Shea was missed at the back, likewise the craft in midfield of Finn Azaz, who was there on the bench but did not play. Jayson Molumby took Azaz’s place in central midfield, and it soon became apparent that Israel had targeted him for special treatment.
When Dor Peretz fouled Molumby 30 yards from Israel’s goal it was the fifth foul the Irish midfielder had suffered in 39 minutes. It looked as though the Israelis were trying to get a reaction out of him and Molumby has been known to respond to provocation. He kept getting up and grinning but as the fouls kept coming the grin was developing a slightly wild-eyed, Private Pyle-like edge.
But this foul was worth taking. As Ryan Manning stood over the ball, Israel were preparing for either a shot or cross to the far post. Somehow they left Troy Parrott standing completely unmarked in the D. Manning simply rolled a pass to the Irish centre forward, whose quick but weak shot was parried by Israel goalkeeper Assaf Tzur. Jimmy Dunne was first to the loose ball and was brought down by the scrambling Israeli defenders.
Ireland screamed for the penalty – they have got better at these kinds of appeals – and after a VAR review the Spanish referee gave it. Parrott nailed it into the bottom corner for his 10th goal in his last seven competitive internationals.
A scuffle at the entrance to the tunnel at half-time – sparked by the allegation that an Israeli player had spat at an Irish coach – was defused by the Spanish referee, calling out in a soothing tone: “Be clever guys. Be clever.”
But there was nothing clever about the way Ireland conceded the equaliser. Conor Coventry slipped as he tried to pass upfield and Israel counterattacked. Oscar Gloukh’s shot struck Liam Scales and the deflection just killed the ball perfectly for the lurking Dor Peretz, who beat Caoimhín Kelleher from close range.
Israel twice struck the outside of Kelleher’s post and looked the slightly more dangerous side in a dire second half. Ireland looked tired and out of ideas, as though the exertions of the last two weeks were catching up with them. The obvious move from the tactical point of view was to introduce Azaz to bring some creativity and direction to Ireland’s play in the centre, but the Irish staff evidently felt that was impossible.
By not picking Azaz to start they had evaded the question of whether he would bow his head for the Israeli anthem along with his team-mates, but would he wear the black armband for the dead of the Gaza conflict, while the Israelis wore their own black armband to mark the third anniversary of October 7th?
Azaz would be targeted for criticism no matter what he did, and the Irish staff decided the game was not worth forcing him into that situation. Instead Chiedozie Ogbene, Rocco Vata, Joel Bagan and Bosun Lawal came on and only Ogbene had any impact on the game, forcing a save from Tzur late on. Jason Knight missed Ireland’s best chance in the 89th minute, mistiming a header at the far post. He had battled gamely in the right wing-back role but James Abankwah has looked more comfortable, and much more imposing, in that position.
There was further aggressive posturing after the final whistle. The Israelis were clearly happier with the 1-1 than Ireland, who just wanted to get off the pitch, on to their aeroplane and out of this nightmare at last. The atmosphere of paranoia and enmity in which these games have played out is unprecedented in their international careers.
On Saturday afternoon two Israeli journalists had asked Heimir Hallgrímsson about the Flydubai attempted hijacking and the Israeli claim – immediately and forcefully denied by the FAI – that Irish players had called Israeli opponents “monkeys”. On Sunday the two were told that they had been banned from the postmatch press conferences, a decision apparently taken at the highest level in Uefa.
They had done more than their fair share to stoke up the bad feeling that surrounded these games. In Israel’s press conference on Saturday, Irish journalists had asked whether it would not just be better to make sure these two countries didn’t have to play each other again.
[ Austria pull off another late show to stay top of Group B3 Opens in new window ]
“Coach, what do you think of that idea that maybe it’s better for everybody if there’s, like, an amicable divorce,” the last question went. “If we say to each other, we had a nice two games but ... let’s not do this again.”
The question provoked laughter that eased the tension in the room, but in the end the answer from the Israelis was no, there can be no question of divorce, we must stay together for the sake of the children.
On Thursday the presidents and general secretaries of Uefa’s member FAs head to Berlin for their annual meet-up. The rules for the next set of qualifiers have not yet been finalised. The FAI’s delegation would have a chance to raise the matter again and see whether Uefa’s thinking has evolved.
But it sounds as though any such suggestion will be firmly opposed on the Israeli side. For Uefa to agree to keep Ireland and Israel apart because Ireland no longer wants to play them looks to Israel like a slippery slope towards exclusion.

title: Pilita Clark: Dear all ... how bosses should talk to the troops
description: What matters most is understanding priorities and conveying them as thoughtfully as possible
content:
Some chief executives send a weekly email to tell their staff how things are going. Others hold an online Q&A every few months, or post their thoughts on LinkedIn.
I am not sure any do exactly what Greg Jackson does at Octopus Energy, the British household energy supply group he founded in 2015.
Every Friday at 4.15pm, he encourages Octopus’s 13,000-odd staff in eight countries to join “family dinner”: a mildly chaotic half-hour online session of cheeky, rapid-fire presentations from Jackson and his top managers on the latest company news.
Here’s what happened at one I watched the other week at the group’s London headquarters on Oxford Street. As 4.15pm neared, staff began to log off, grab drinks from company fridges and settle in front of a large screen in an office auditorium.
Jackson soon materialised online to talk about people he had met at Octopus Live customer sessions being held around the country.
A couple in Manchester had brought their bills down to £12 (€14) a month with a home battery, heat pump and solar panels. A breast cancer survivor had cried as she told him how Octopus had helped her manage bills.
Then the group’s country heads came on to deliver their news, amid video clips, jokey animations, a stream of online staff comments – and a lot of Jackson interjections.
“Jesus!” he exclaimed as his chief executive for Germany reported the company had just swept all 36 categories in industry awards for customer service and innovation. “That is unbelievable,” he said, joking that his Italian equivalent would be furious.
“Absolutely f**king great!” he hooted, as his man in Tokyo revealed 600,000 Japanese customers. He liked the news from Japan and China so much he announced that a prize of a free trip to both countries would go to the two employees who could say how many solar panels were installed in China in 2025.
Entries will be “off the charts” by competition cut-off time on Tuesday, he told me later. It’s all part of the effort to entertain staff while reinforcing company priorities such as industry leadership, prices, clean energy and customer service. The format alternates each week.
A global session like that one is followed by a country one, then another global one and then one for individual teams. Jackson hosts all except the team events, meaning he is doing a session three out of every four weeks.
It’s time-consuming, he agrees, but crucial “if you want to keep a global company focused on the same objectives and know what we really want”. A lot of organisations would do well to adopt this type of approach.
Too many bosses leave it to managers to do the communicating. Or lumber staff with long, repetitive and widely unread emails that reek of little thought or care. Or livestream rare, stilted and largely uninformative presentations.
Saying that, Jackson is hard to imitate. He has a good sense of comic timing that he can deploy with relative ease since Octopus is privately held, plus a background in tech where playful online town halls are more common.
It is more complicated when you run a listed company with more than 200,000 employees in 56 countries and you are axing some of the most expensive ones, as Georges Elhedery is at HSBC.
He has made internal communication a priority for his senior managers since becoming chief executive in 2024 and does plenty of it himself. Along with emails at quarterly results time, he appears at regional town hall meetings and at panel discussions with top executives, and has online chats with outside guests, such as DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis.
Matt Brittin, the BBC’s new director general, has taken a similar approach, appearing at online Q&A sessions for the broadcaster’s 20,000-plus staff, hosted by presenters such as Adam Fleming.
At McKinsey, global managing partner Bob Sternfels writes a regular blog about anything from the forces affecting clients to what he has seen on his travels. He also pens less frequent but more substantial letters about news affecting the firm, or ideas he wants everyone to know about.
I know of other bosses who send out videos, or write chatty emails about family holidays, or hold ask-me-anything staff Slack chats.
Ultimately, what matters most is understanding one’s priorities and conveying them as thoughtfully, regularly and non-tediously as possible. Anyone who can do that while making people laugh is well ahead. The rest can gain a lot by trying. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Over-regulation is choking the property market
description: The law now tilts almost entirely towards tenant protection
content:
Sir, – Jenny Curran’s claim that the Government has done “nothing in reality” to address housing ignores the raft of tenant-focused legislation enacted in recent years (Letters, September 29th).
From Rent Pressure Zones to tenancies of unlimited duration, the law now tilts almost entirely towards tenant protection.
But this framework has completely backfired. By piling on compliance burdens while leaving landlords with a Residential Tenancies Board that takes months to resolve unpaid rent or property damage issues, the State has made private letting an unviable risk for small property owners.
It is little wonder they are leaving the market in droves.
Alongside this, our housing policy suffers from a kind of regulatory perfectionism. Under the Building Regulations 2019, every new home must achieve Nearly Zero Energy Building and top-tier Ber standards.
While the environmental goal is admirable, mandating these specifications drastically inflates build costs and slows down delivery. It is the policy equivalent of telling someone in emergency accommodation they must stay on a waiting list because we refuse to build anything less than a pristine, high-spec dwelling.
By regulating lower-cost or entry-level options out of existence, the State is forcing lower-income tenants into direct competition with middle-income earners for standard units. This drives open-market rents higher across the board and pushes the most vulnerable into an unregulated black market.
State funding alone cannot fix the housing deficit without a functioning private market. Until we balance tenant security with basic landlord rights and swift dispute resolution, and replace rigid building perfectionism with pragmatic delivery, over-regulation will continue to choke off the exact supply renters so desperately need. – Yours, etc,

title: How hubris is shaping the latest Greek-Turkish confrontation
description: An ancient Greek concept helps explain modern tensions in the Aegean, where disputes over maritime rights risk deepening a long-running rivalry
content:
H ubris was the word used by the ancient Greeks to describe extreme pride or arrogance, leading to a disastrous fall. In Euripides’s play Medea, hubris might be one of the characters, so deeply is it embedded in the drama: Jason portrays hubris in his arrogant betrayal of his wife, Medea, and she, in her own hubris, kills her children in revenge. Result? Utter tragedy. Today, for modern Greeks, it means much the same: the overconfident display of blind pride, coupled with indifference to the fate of others. It is, basically, an insult to the values and intelligence of the rest of us.
“Hubris” leapt out at me recently, from a press release by an environmental group in Corfu , where I live. Commenting on our neglect of living tradition, and the consequent loss for future generations, the group’s statement read: “Culture is part of the identity of Corfu. It is what we choose to pass on to our descendants. Indifference towards this culture is not simply negligence. It is hubris.”
These words struck me as a succinct summary of the way “progress” is greeted as inevitable and as somehow superior to more old-fashioned ways of doing and thinking. It certainly sums up the way Greece has almost blindly welcomed the phenomenon of tourism , with the consequent sweeping aside – or even sweeping away – of traditional modes of travel and hospitality. I recently astonished a young person by saying that in 1969 I had visited Mykonos “before they had built the airport”, to which she replied: “But how did you get there, then?” – so ubiquitous has air travel become.
Modernisation is difficult for those who enjoy stability and the assurance it affords. It comes very easily to those anxious for change and with new ambitions. In my experience, working on similar topics with the Council of Europe, the necessary balance between old reliables and new opportunities is a public-private matter which very few societies can accommodate. The Greek islands, in their response to tourism, are a sad example of missing that balance.
Hubris of a different, but comparable, order exists in Greek-Turkish relations, but it, too, involves one of the most central of Greek concepts, the islands – and some of the most popular for holidaymakers, such as Rhodes, which has been part of Greece only since 1947.
We are still in a situation where increasingly blatant hostility could become lethal: a tragedy where hubris supersedes diplomacy. Turkey , having declared a “blue homeland” to extend its claims over the eastern Mediterranean, is now majoring in the creation of two marine parks, one of which will effectively sever contact between two Greek islands near the Turkish coast, Limnos and Samothrace (originally home to the legendary sculpture The Winged Victory, today in Paris’s Louvre museum).
In the Greek experience, it is what ‘slips through the cracks’ in diplomatic talks with Turkey which so easily reveals Turkish hubris: the lack of dialogue, the absence of meaningful understanding and a sublime indifference to the nuances of history
The other marine park would surround the tiny island of Kastellorizo, also part of Greece since 1947, and only a mile off the Turkish coast, with a population of fewer than 600. It is feared that the creation of these marine parks might lead to further aggressive action on Turkey’s part to interrupt Greek island life: ferries, fishing and the vital area of tourism.
As of last week, Greece has diplomatically rejected the legality of Turkey’s marine parks. But should Turkey attempt to escalate the tension by implementing its unilateral claim to Greek waters, the answer from Athens could have military consequences.
Despite its tiny size, Kastellorizo is the home of a documentary film festival, ironically entitled Beyond Borders, which held its 11th annual event last month. The festival viewed 42 films on the theme of “the human experiences that slip through the cracks of dominant narratives, overlooking the subtle nuances of history”. Its aim is to facilitate dialogue, critical thinking and meaningful understanding.
In Greek-Turkish relations, each side has its “dominant narrative” which is diametrically opposed to the other. Greece has emphasised that it will “take any action necessary to protect the national interest”, which of course includes its territorial waters. Turkey appears to lay unilateral claim to these waters, despite the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (to which Turkey is not a party).
As Manos Karagiannis (a Greek professor specialising in international security at King’s College London) observes: “For the Turkish government, the Aegean Sea is not neutral or friendly: it is a space for confrontation.”
In both classical and modern Greek, “sevas” means respect for that which commands loyalty and adherence. Greece, in demanding respect for the rule of law and the facts of history, meets its opposite in Turkish hubris.
In the Greek experience, it is what “slips through the cracks” in diplomatic talks with Turkey which so easily reveals Turkish hubris: the lack of dialogue, the absence of meaningful understanding and a sublime indifference to the nuances of history. Turkish provocation in the matter of the Aegean (and, in effect, the entire eastern Mediterranean) certainly has the air of arrogance – a “blind” pushing aside of political history to assert a point of view without apparent concern for the consequences.

title: Inheritance tax reform could unlock €170bn sitting on deposit, expert says
description: Current system incentivises families to hold assets until death because of tax implications
content:
Reforming the inheritance tax system could be a more effective way of getting the €170 billion held on deposit in Ireland back into circulation, a leading inheritance specialist has said.
Dave O’Brien, the head of tax at business advisory group Xeinadin Ireland, said a significant part of this wealth is owned by older people who have no incentive to pass it on to the next generation because of the tax implications.
The tax-free threshold for children inheriting from their parents is €400,000, after which a capital acquisitions tax (CAT) of 33 per cent applies. The threshold was €542,000 and the tax 20 per cent before the financial crisis.
O’Brien said the Government should consider the seven-year gifting rule adopted by the UK which encourages earlier transfers of wealth by allowing the transfer to be tax free if the donor survives for seven years.
“If there was an incentive to give those monies away during a lifetime without a tax liability then there would be nothing to stop parents giving the money to their children,” he said.
“And then you’re giving the money to people who are younger, who are in their 30s and 40s, and they’re either spending the money [incurring VAT] or investing the money,” he said.
The current system can incentivise families to hold assets until death, “when policy could instead encourage money and assets to move earlier through the economy”, O’Brien said.
While the Government is planning to introduce a new State-sponsored savings and investment scheme as part of Tuesday’s budget with the aim of channelling some of the €170 billion sitting idle on deposit back into the real economy, O’Brien said offering more tax-efficient ways of transferring wealth between generations could work better.
[ Coalition leaders discuss last ditch bid to cut student fees by €250 in budget Opens in new window ]
Another mechanism might be to lower the CAT rate from 33 to 20 per cent, where it was before the financial crisis.
“If I was the Government I’d be more leaning to that as you’re getting an intake of 20 per cent in tax, you’re not losing the full 33 per cent, and you’re still getting the money to go around,” O’Brien said.
The Government is expected to lift the tax-free thresholds for each category of inheritance or gift in the budget, amid criticism they have not kept pace with rising property values.
The Category A threshold (€400,000) governs inheritances received by children, while the Category B threshold (€40,000) covers inheritances received by siblings, nieces, nephews and grandchildren.
“We have discussed, and are considering, broader adjustments to inheritance tax across different categories but it will be within what’s available,” Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers told the recent Dublin Economics Workshop event in Wexford.

title: Visible speed limit signs often nowhere to be seen
description: In my experience this is common all over the country and especially in cities
content:
Sir, – On a recent visit to Carlow, I unfortunately received a fixed penalty notice for being in excess of a speed limit.
There was a sign advising speed cameras in operation but what was missing completely were visible speed limit signs to advise drivers of the speed limits in the area even, if not especially, before approaching after the speed camera sign.
In my experience this is common all over the country and especially in cities where road users are ‘supposed to know what the speed limit is’ in the absence of speed limit signs.
On a recent visit to London, while driving there, the roads are littered with speed limit signs leaving the driver in no doubt as to the speed limit and further, the local authorities paint the speed limit on the road, leaving no room for error.
This signage is supported by monitoring cameras and the result is an obedient procession of cars moving through the city, all at the same speed and getting to their destinations in a similar time scale.
These cameras also serve to penalise drivers who ignore yellow junction boxes. In Ireland, it seems to be a sport as to how many drivers can squeeze into the yellow box, which at busier times causes gridlock.
Information and communication through visible and plentiful road signs backed up by cameras is perhaps a very simple solution to assist drivers and to stop the “gotcha” culture perpetuated by Gatso vans hiding around corners. Prevention is surely better than cure. - Yours, etc,
Sir, – We are told that the GoSafe speed-camera operation is not about making money. This is reassuring, particularly as the company is expected to receive more than ¤30 million from the Garda this year.
Indeed, the figures suggest that GoSafe is becoming one of the more successful enterprises in the country with €138 million in speeding fines generated between 2021 and 2025, of which €85.7 million went to the company.
Despite these huge profits, it is comforting to know that the principal purpose of the cameras is road safety rather than revenue generation. The fact that the operator receives €99.20 from every €160 fine is, presumably, merely a happy byproduct of keeping us safe.
I wonder if there is a business opportunity here – perhaps the Government could extend the same principle to other areas of public policy. A company could be contracted to monitor littering, illegal dumping, dog fouling with the State receiving the benefit of improved behaviour and the contractor receiving, say, 62 per cent of the fines – the possibilities are endless. This could help to keep us all safe and well, and at least we would know that it wasn’t about the money. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – The Government is to be commended for the lightning speed with which they have acted on e-scooter legislation, although it is unclear if their actions are appropriate or will be effective.
