In July, serious concerns were highlighted by the medical profession about serious injuries involving this mode of transport, and new laws are in place in just a few months.
Contrast this with the appalling failure to tackle the deaths and serious injuries on our roads involving motor vehicles. We know that lower urban speed limits, average- and fixed-camera enforcement for speeding and phone use, and better road design will result in fewer collisions and save lives, yet this Government has delayed or reversed progress in this area.
The same level of urgency given to e-scooters is needed to make our roads safer for all users. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – In her letter on right sizing, Sandra Ní Dhubhda (October 1st) raises issues that, I’m sure, are familiar to many in the same situation.
Cohousing could offer a solution. Members of cohousing communities design their own homes and shared spaces and set their own rules and management fees.
In addition to her suggestion that policymakers address the obstacles she outlined, they might also consider the Dutch government’s approach to housing for older people, given both countries are experiencing similar demographic changes and housing crises.
In addition to providing financial support for cohousing initiatives, the Dutch government also has a team of technical experts to advise new groups on the practical steps to setting up a new housing community.
This fits with their policy of encouraging older people to stay longer in appropriate, right-sized, future-proofed homes, thus delaying or avoiding the need for institutional care.
Presumably they believe the short-term investment will lead to greater savings in the long term. I wonder if the fledgling cohousing community movement in Ireland can look forward to a similar level of support in the near future? – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I recently read with interest “BusConnects Dublin Construction Newsletter” with the following logos and slogans: “Bus Connects, Your City, Better Connected, Core Bus Corridors, Project 2040 Government of Ireland and NTA”.
The truth be told I never felt as disconnected in the 10 years that I have been commuting from Galway to Dublin to my place of work, Leinster House.
Back in 2016 when I started this weekly journey the very reliable Dublin Bus no 145 from Heuston Station was always on time and traversed the city with various stops along the way passing my place of employment on Kildare Street, then onwards to UCD. The 145 has now been replaced by the unreliable No 4 Bus that goes all the way out to Monkstown. It is often overly crowded, rarely arrives on time, frequently disappears off the live TFI digital display, is regularly seen to go down a cul-de-sac of no return at the back of Heuston Station, only to reappear again about 20 minutes later – if at all – to the Stop 4320 at the front of Heuston Station, if one is lucky.
Dublin Bus is the face of public transport in Dublin and receives hundreds of complaints due to ghost buses which, in my opinion, is not of its making but is as a direct result of the NTA, TFI and Government and poorly thought-out bus connections.
It’s hard to believe that in 2026, one must take two buses from Heuston Station to our national parliament on Kildare Street. Many UCD students I have met along the way also have to get two buses to go from Heuston Station to college.
The most difficult part of my three-hour commute from Galway to Dublin is the final leg of the journey from Heuston Station to Nassau Street; it used to take 20 minutes but can now take close to an hour and that is if the No 4 turns up.
Assuming that Project 2040 is achieved, does this mean 14 more years of BusDisconnections? – Yours, etc,
Sir, – The elephant in the room in the dispute about the banning of plastic refuse bags by Dublin City Council is the fact that the council itself relies on private waste collectors. Residents have no choice but to use these firms, regardless of how efficient or reliable they may be.
In an effort to get in advance of the upcoming plastic bag ban, in my house we moved waste provider to avail of caddie bins. The bins themselves were poorly constructed, and could not be sealed against rain; in addition, they were very frequently left uncollected by the company, with no satisfactory explanation. When we cancelled our contract with that provider, the only option was to return to plastic bags.
Dublin City Council is leaving its residents at the mercy of a wasteful and unreliable system. If the council is going to dictate to residents the means of waste collection, they should take responsibility for it and establish a proper system of municipal waste collection. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – The Garvaghy Road stand-off serves as a reminder that, despite the huge progress made since the Belfast Agreement, Northern Ireland remains a society divided.
Children do not enter the world believing that there is an “Us” and a “Them”. That concept is learned. It can be instilled and reinforced by family, community, religion, and politics, but also, crucially, by an education system in which children are still overwhelmingly segregated along religious lines.
Integrated education will not, by itself, resolve Northern Ireland’s constitutional or political issues, but bringing children of different traditions together from a young age and providing them with an opportunity to get to know each other as individuals rather than “others” is surely a sine qua non for long term integration and peace in Northern Ireland.
Segregation breeds tribalism and a sense of the “other”, of the unknown. This in turn can breed fear, prejudice, even hatred.
A child who grows up learning, playing, and forming friendships with children from another tradition is less likely to be prejudiced against them.
The scenes on the Garvaghy Road should prompt an obvious and fundamental question. If we genuinely want a peaceful and shared future in Northern Ireland, why should religiously divided education remain the norm?
Around 93 per cent of schools in the North are religiously segregated. In a 2021 survey, 71 per cent of respondents said that integrated education should be the “main model” for Northern Ireland’s education system. Yet integrated education in the North remains largely an aspiration.
Segregating children on religious grounds is neither natural, nor healthy, for a society.
The children of Northern Ireland have far more in common with each other than what separates them. They deserve an education system that reflects that reality and gives them the hope they all deserve. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – As a mother of three young children, I read with the letter by Ursula Hough-Gormley (September 30th) with familiarity.
The woman on the bus could have been me. Ignoring her child, looking at her phone or more specifically answering an email, supporting my staff following a difficult meeting, paying the creche fees that were due yesterday, booking the camp that sells out in five minutes, buying a present for the birthday party at the weekend, ordering groceries so I don’t miss the delivery slot, or writing a to-do list so I don’t forget these tasks and more.
Admittedly, sitting on a bus is not the ideal time to do any of this, but is usually the only time between 6am, when my children awake, and 11pm when I put my laptop away for the second time in the day, having caught up on the work I couldn’t complete between 9 and 5.
I wonder was the woman on the bus doing any of the aforementioned tasks. Or maybe she just wanted to look at her phone.
I dream of the day when I can sit on a bus in peace, observing my fellow passengers and writing a narrative about their lives. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Walking from my parked car to work this morning a schoolbus paused beside me in the traffic. Every occupant looked to be wearing headphones, absorbed in private worlds.
No one seemed to be speaking. For all our lamenting the effects of smartphones on attention spans in the classroom, this seems a much greater loss to me.
It’s likely during secondary school such pupils may spend a thousand or so hours in each other’s company but not interacting. The close links not being formed must be a huge missed opportunity. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Occasionally when prompted by an ad for the Lotto I’m transported into a temporary reverie where I bask in that feeling of having won the thing. And knowing that I’ve only a slightly better chance of actually winning it if I buy a ticket, I’m doubly delighted that I had the feeling without experiencing the cost. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I’m 90 and disabled, but my wife, who is younger than me, in her 80s, recently decided to eschew the car and give public transport a try. She took the train to Galway and was left standing for the entire journey.
Hardly an encouragement to use public transport. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I would like to add some more examples of the misuse of grammar: an urban/rural “divide”, a “disconnect” between ... the search has been “stood down”, should have” went”. – Yours, etc,
Sir , – I agree with recent correspondents about the misuse of grammar. However phrases such as “I was sat there ” seem to be peculiar to the English rather than the Irish.
One example of misuse is “He invited Mary and I ” instead of ” Mary and me”. It is incredible how many acclaimed authors are guilty of this error. – Yours, etc,

title: Budget 2027 Ireland: Improved childcare supports to include after-school care
description: Families with a young child in creche could save €1,000 a year, while an income-tax package is expected for workers
content:
Measures to cut the cost of childcare in Budget 2027 are to be targeted at families with younger children, including those in aftercare during their first two years in primary school .
Families with a young child attending a creche full-time could save as much as €1,000 a year per child under the plans.
Coalition leaders met for several hours on Sunday as part of efforts to finalise details of Tuesday’s budget.
While talks on the childcare package are expected to continue today, The Irish Times understands that subsidies available under the National Childcare Scheme are to go up for younger children up to and including those attending senior infants.
The changes would take effect from September 2027.
Meanwhile, under the plans from Minister for Children Norma Foley , there are due to be separate cuts to the maximum fees that all creches and aftercare services can charge. It means parents of older children could also be in line for at least some reduction in fees for after school-care.
Funding will also be made available to increase pay for early-years educators.
Senior Government figures have promised help with childcare costs in Budget 2027, including progress towards fulfilling the pledge of reducing costs to €200 per month per child by the end of the Coalition’s time in office.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin , Tánaiste Simon Harris and Minister of State Seán Canney, along with Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers, were all involved in the talks on Sunday.
Chambers told RTÉ that the Government “wants to make an impact when it comes to the affordability of childcare for Budget 2027″. He added that “a central focus as well is wider issues around cost of living”.
A €10-per-week increase in the State pension and other welfare payments are expected to be announced as part of the budget.
Another social protection measure understood to be agreed is a €500 cost-of-disability payment. A €5-per-week increase in fuel allowance is also expected.
[ Prospect of a €250 cut to student contribution fees unlikely ahead of Budget 2027 Opens in new window ]
Over the weekend, the Taoiseach confirmed that welfare recipients and pensioners can expect a Christmas bonus payment this year.
As the energy crisis caused by the Iran war continues, Martin also signalled carbon tax increases on home-heating oil will be halted for the remainder of the Coalition’s time in office.
It is expected that the budget will include an income-tax package for workers. On inheritance tax, there is set to be an increase in the tax-free thresholds on the value of bequests across the three bands. However, sources said these increases will be “modest”.
On transport measures, there is to be a focus on funding more than 140 new public transport services next year. This will be facilitated through an increase in Public Service Obligation funding, with routes that are not commercially viable being subsidised. The expansion of routes will also be part-funded by fare increases from January.
Meanwhile, it is understood that Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport Patrick O’Donovan is to use part of his budget allocation to provide extra funding for the Arts Council.
It is also anticipated that Budget 2027 will include finding for the recruitment of 1,000 gardaí in 2027 as well as additional prison officers, with resources going to the International Protection Office for more staff and deportation flights.
Funding is also understood to be allocated for 400 new Defence Forces recruits and almost 100 new civilian staff.
On housing, one area of focus for Minister for Housing James Browne is trying to ensure necessary funding for the forthcoming Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan.
Last-minute negotiations are expected to continue today in advance of the budget being unveiled by Harris and Chambers on Tuesday afternoon.

title: ‘We’re not going back, are we?’: Courts may be the only way to end Drumcree standoff
description: Garvaghy Road residents return to the Court of Appeal on Monday
content:
Claire Hanna, the SDLP leader, was in Dunnes Stores in the Annadale shopping centre off the Ormeau Road in Belfast on Friday afternoon when she was approached by an anxious couple.
“He was, like, ‘God, we’re not going back. We’re not going back, are we?’,” she says, referring to the danger of the Ormeau Bridge parade riots of the 1990s and 2000s happening again.
Drumcree 2026, however, is not the same as the 1990s. Thankfully, it has not witnessed violence, and Portadown has mostly gone about its business quietly over the last week, free of disturbance.
However, Hanna’s quick conversation in the aisle reflects conversations across Northern Ireland over the last week in the wake of Drumcree erupting again after nearly 30 years dormant.
Garvaghy Road’s residents return on Monday to the Court of Appeal to challenge last week’s block on their bid to have the Parades Commission ’s original Drumcree march permission reviewed.
For now, there are lots of “ifs”. If the courts rule that a judicial review is now warranted, and if the Orange ’s permit is judged to have lapsed, then the matter must go back to the commission for a new ruling.
Despite confusion about what the Police Service of Northern Ireland ( PSNI ) told the commission the first time, it is hard to believe it would say now a parade can peacefully take march.
However, it could rule that the permission is still valid, heightening the pressure on the PSNI to clear the way – even though Chief Constable Jon Boutcher has already made his disapproval clear.
Drumcree is both unique and not. Its history, the violence and bitterness that surrounded it during the 1990s, and before, gives it the primary place in Northern Ireland’s list of flashpoints.
However, it is but one of 3,813 parades notified to the Parades Commission in the year to March 31st– 2,507 of them are Protestant/unionist/loyalist; 96 are Catholic/nationalist/republican; 171 are sensitive; 141 have conditions imposed.
[ Taoiseach questions Sinn Féin ‘sincerity’ over Garvaghy Road situation Opens in new window ]
The concern now, not just for those living near the Ormeau Bridge but elsewhere too, is that hard-won local compromises will fray if Drumcree intensifies – or even that the damage is already done.
But it is not just about parades. For many, the crisis has awoken sectarian hatred that had drifted into the background, but not disappeared.
Standing outside Garvaghy’s local Catholic Church on Thursday night, resident Paul Larkin talked of how Portadown has changed in the last 10 years or so, with Catholics now broadly comfortable in town.
Broadly comfortable, but not entirely so: “You’d still have that little bit of fear. They’re not happy with us mingling in around the town in GAA tops. But before, if you went into the town in one, you’d have got the shit kicked out of you.”
Larkin is comfortable leaving the past in the past: “Children today don’t know anything about this, shouldn’t know anything about this.”
The danger is that the poison released by Drumcree’s latest chapter will seep into broader society’s bloodstream. “I have a niece, a curious 10-year-old, never knew anything about the Troubles,” said one local.
“She’s actually turned bitter. She wouldn’t have known anything about Orangemen, or anything like that. For the first time today, I heard her actually saying ‘Orange bastards’.”
Frankly, a solution is now likely only from the courts, since the binary “march, or no march” choice facing politicians is one from which most of them will not vary their oft-repeated stand.
Watching Sinn Féin on Garvaghy Road in the last week has been instructive: locals elect Sinn Féin representatives, yet they follow local residents’ leader, Breandán Mac Cionnaith’s lead.
The former jailed IRA bomber is not a Sinn Féin member, having quit the party 20 years ago over its decision to support the police. Since then, he has been a leading member of the politically dissident Éirígí.
[ Breandán Mac Cionnaith profile: The ex-IRA man who Tony Blair said ‘took unreasonableness to an art form’ Opens in new window ]
His local influence leaves Sinn Féin walking on eggshells, but that is a price worth paying because Drumcree is a political gift for the party in advance of next May’s Stormont elections.
Sinn Féin has been in difficulties – its Stormont accomplishments few, its polling figures rocky. However, Drumcree has galvanised broader nationalist opinion – not just people who once supported the IRA, even if they do not want violence on the streets.
The danger, perhaps, is over-confidence. Having thousands on Garvaghy Road over the weekend’s rally, or a widely circulated social media video of “My Old Man’s A Provo” from Thursday night, contrasts with Taoiseach Micheál Martin’s urging to “dial it down”.
Relations between Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) are poisonous. Neither is truly invested in making the Stormont Executive work, yet would prefer if the other was blamed for collapsing the institutions.
On Friday, DUP leader, Gavin Robinson, clearly displayed his concern that matters could go over the edge, saying “too many people have acted in a deeply reckless way”.
For the DUP, a successful march a week ago could have done much to defend its right flank from the predations of Jim Allister and the Traditional Unionist Voice in the coming elections.
[ The south sees Drumcree and thinks: we don’t want that sectarian mindset down here Opens in new window ]
Today, however, the still-blocked march poses higher hurdles for Robinson, especially since so many of his own people, such as local Portadown MP, Carla Lockhart, are less invested in Stormont’s survival than he is.
In the meantime, the hope of a Hillsborough talks genie is unlikely, especially since there are grumbles that Secretary of State Chris Bryant, newly in office, has yet to understand local politics’ grim realities. “Pollyanna-ish, at times,” said one observer.

title: Jack Rowan: It’s ridiculous how many people say I look like a Hollywood star who was huge in the 80s
description: The English actor on his Irish roots, filming in Connemara, and striving for happiness
content:
I am very agreeable. I want to please people. The worst thing for me is to upset somebody. When it comes to agreeing to something, I am always up for it if someone else is too. I mean, if someone says, “Let’s just jump off this bridge together,” I’ll say: “Yeah, lets do it.” If it’s daredevil stuff I will always do it. If somebody says, “Will we do this?” I always say yes.
My middle name is Jordon. Now that I am older and I get bills to my house it’s funny when I get a letter and Jordon is spelt like Jordan, with an A. I want to say “Who’s that guy?” But I love my middle name. If there was another actor called Jack Rowan, I would have been happy to have gone by Jordon Rowan.
My grandparents’ house in Co Tyrone . There is no other place that I feel so safe or loved. My dad is from there, and I loved visiting his family. When you look at a map of the world and you’re looking at certain places I zoom into Co Tyrone and the house and I feel like that’s where I belong.
My second favourite place is Coral Strand in Connemara , Co Galway. My last job was filmed there by the coast. Me and my girlfriend drove up and down the Wild Atlantic Way and parked up and watched the sunset. It was just beautiful.
Compassionate. I’ve been an actor now for 10 years and you get the luxury of meeting people from everywhere. You’re playing different types of characters and meeting new people and I think that makes you compassionate. I owe acting a lot that way – and I think I’m kind and caring.
Playing with my WWE wrestlers. I grew up in the time before kids had phones. I spent a lot of time playing with the only toys I had, which was my WWE wrestlers. It was a world in and of itself. I did storylines, accents, just getting lost in the imagination of it all. I didn’t know it was my introduction to storytelling. Subconsciously it was showing me where my future was going to go.
I suppose as an adult you lose your innocence. You kind of miss the bliss of waking up in the morning and not having adult worries.
I have an older sister. She is eight years older. When I was 10, she was 18. What was great about that dynamic is we never had that period when we fought. I looked up to her as someone who had the answers. Almost like a second mum. When she got older all her friends would come over and she would let me come into the room and we’d all watch movies. It opened up my mind being around older people. I felt like they always had my back.
[ From the archive: Boys from County Hell a decent slice of Irish bog horror Opens in new window ]
I strive for happiness all the time. I am an optimistic person. But sometimes things happen that are out of your control. That is always ebbing and flowing. But on my last job filming in Connemara, swimming in the sea, and travelling around. I had a few days off and we just had so much exploring. I was just so happy to be in Ireland.
I think it’s a luxury in life to love people and miss them when they’re gone. When it’s my time to go I would love a moment to tie up any loose ends, to meet those people I have lost and hug them and see them again. To finish my life with no lose ends and tie it all up.
It’s ridiculous how many people say I look like Matt Dillon. He’s older than me but I’m going to cheat with my answer. I’m going to flip it and say Matt Dillon, if he was younger than me.
When I was a kid I did karate. I was really good at it and it was getting really serious. I don’t know why but one day I burst into tears and begged my mum not to bring me and I never went back. It was just a loose end, and I would love nothing more than to say right now that I had a black belt. I loved The Karate Kid growing up. If I did a karate movie that would be a great excuse to start again. There’s still time.

title: Irish film and TV industry mounts late push for enhanced regional tax break in budget
description: Film producer David Puttnam calls for Government to ‘spread Ireland’s screen industry across the country’
content:
Film and television producers and studios across Ireland have launched a last-minute push to secure an enhanced tax break for regional productions in Budget 2027 , three years after the Government phased out a previous scheme.
In an open letter seen by The Irish Times, high-profile film producer David Puttnam has urged Minister for Finance Simon Harris to “spread Ireland’s screen industry across the whole country” by adding an 8 per cent regional uplift to the section 481 tax credit.
Aimed at bringing more productions to areas outside Dublin and Wicklow and boosting capacity, the enhanced rate for regional productions was in place from 2019 to 2023.
Production companies can claim section 481 relief against their corporation tax liabilities to a value of 32 per cent of eligible expenditure or a maximum of €125 million.
However, just 14 per cent of the €502 million spent on film and TV productions in the Republic in 2025 related to projects outside Leinster.
Puttnam, a British life peer who lives in west Cork, said because of the concentration of television and film productions in the east of the State, people living elsewhere had to uproot to follow a career in the industry.
“Skibbereen has been my home for more than 30 years,” Puttnam wrote. “In 1993, we made War of the Buttons in west Cork, with scores of local young people on the crew and cast. At least four went on to very successful careers in film. Every one of them had to move to Dublin or Belfast to do it.”
Puttnam cited the example of Everybody Digs Bill Evans , which was filmed at West Cork Film Studios in Skibbereen. The film, which stars Anders Danielsen Lie as the influential titular jazz pianist, was awarded the prestigious Silver Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival this year.
“The studio has brought a sense of vibrancy to the town, and people are finding jobs there who never would have considered our sector before,” Puttnam said. However, west Cork remains an “exception”.
“Films and series take three years or more to make,” Puttnam wrote. “The uplift should run for as long as section 481 itself. Nobody builds a regional company on a tax credit that might end before the work is finished.”
Screen producers across the State have echoed Puttnam’s call in advance of tomorrow’s budget. West Cork Studios cofounder Steve Park said his business had lost out on €20 million of productions this year “because we can’t be as competitive”.
“The last regional uplift was designed to [be] phase[d] out,” said Darach Ó Tuairisg, cofounder and chief executive of Fíbín Media in Galway. “A permanent 8 per cent regional uplift would give producers the certainty to commit to the region and the confidence to take ambitious projects to market, turning Galway’s promise into a lasting production hub.”
Susan Kirby, chief executive of Screen Producers Ireland, which has spearheaded the regional uplift push, said her members wanted to “work where they live” and develop businesses in their own communities but needed “the right conditions”.
[ David Puttnam: ‘The Irish invented immigration and went through every single form of the immigrant experience’ Opens in new window ]
She said the regional uplift would “generate wider economic activity” in the regions.
During budget week last October, Minister for Culture and Media Patrick O’Donovan said he would like to revisit the regional uplift despite its exclusion from the tax package. However, the Coalition did unveil a separate enhancement to the section 481 specifically aimed at the State’s growing visual effects industry.

title: Dua Lipa to Dior: How books became fashion’s hottest new accessory
description: Dior has chosen Trinity’s Old Library for it’s first runway show in Ireland in December – it’s no coincidence
content:
D ior generated quite a buzz recently by announcing the fashion house would stage its first runway show in Ireland this December, in Trinity College Dublin ’s Old Library. Derry-born designer Jonathan Anderson , the brand’s creative director, will present Dior’s Fall 2027 collection in the Long Room on December 4th.
Anderson often references Irish symbolism in his designs. Showing at Trinity is “a dream come true” for him, he says – “I began my career in fashion in Dublin, so returning here feels deeply personal” – but for the rest of us, it is simply rather fabulous to think of a Dior runway among those majestic shelves of old books.
The library setting is far more than just a pretty backdrop for the Dior show. Right now, fashion seems to be obsessed with books, libraries and the whole idea of being literary. Dior already has its book cover collection, which has turned the covers of classic works including Ulysses, Dracula, Pride and Prejudice and Moby Dick into book totes and items of clothing. The current collection even includes a €420 book-cover card holder.
Coach has taken this fascination with books a step further. In its Spring 2026 collection, the brand teamed up with Penguin Random House to create a collection of mini book charms containing the actual text of literary works. You can now hang a tiny copy of Sense and Sensibility from your shoulder bag and, technically, carry the whole book with you.
Meanwhile, Miu Miu’s fourth Literary Club, held in Milan in April, brought readers, writers and thinkers together around the work of Nobel Prize winner Annie Ernaux, and Ama Ata Aidoo, Ghana’s former minister of education and a Commonwealth Prize winner.
[ Irish tweed is having a moment in fashion from Jonathan Anderson to Anne Hathaway Opens in new window ]
Our social media feeds are cluttered these days with filtered images of a trendy book on a cafe table with some fancy latte art on the side, curated “shelfies”, books casually featuring in “What’s in my bag?” reels, and women on Substack raving on about the same viral book. “Literary It Girl” is the internet’s new favourite label.
The Guardian recently published an article with the headline “ The rise of the hot literati ” about how reading became sexy, while GQ is telling us why “Guys are wearing slutty little reading glasses now”. All of a sudden, being seen as a bookish person is in vogue.
Celebrity book clubs are also pushing the trend forward, with other famous people following in the footsteps of the likes of Oprah and Reese Witherspoon by launching their own. Dua Lipa’s Service 95 is a new and very successful example, as well as Dakota Johnson’s TeaTime Book Club.
Helen Shenton, librarian and college archivist at Trinity College Dublin, thinks there’s a reason why books still have such a strong pull beyond their practical purpose. The Old Library is still a functional library housing 700,000 of Trinity’s most valuable and vulnerable items, and “collectively, those books represent knowledge, wisdom, curiosity, and evolution,” Shenton says. “This resonates with people.”
This “resonance” is of huge importance when we wonder why a luxury fashion house would want to stage a show in the Long Room. Dior is not borrowing the Old Library just for its beautiful interior; it’s stepping into a space that carries enormous cultural meaning in itself.
Much of digital culture is designed around interruption, novelty and rapid switching ... novels and poems demand the habit of dwelling
“[The Long Room is] often used to represent and illustrate the country internationally,” Stenton says. “It has enormous cultural significance, housing the Brian Boru harp which is the very symbol of the nation.”
Katriona Flynn, lecturer in Fashion and Luxury Goods at TU Dublin, says her experience working on catwalk collections taught her that “very little is left to chance” at these shows.
“There is a thread running through each touchpoint presented to the audience, from the collection and casting to the music, set design and venue. The space itself becomes part of the language of the collection.”
A library can therefore do something that a conventional runway venue cannot. It is capable of communicating the intellectual and cultural world behind the clothes before the audience has even seen them. It “becomes another layer of storytelling”.
“A literary reference can ... also offer an insight into the mind of the creative director: what they are reading, researching, looking at and responding to beyond fashion,” she says.
[ Jonathan Anderson is a reminder why we shouldn’t push our kids into ‘bullshit jobs’ Opens in new window ]
While the image of the reader is having its cultural revival moment, the actual practice of reading is in decline. Children’s Books Ireland’s 2025 report found that 24 per cent of Irish teenagers aged 13 to 18 do not read for pleasure. The report also describes a noticeable decline in reading for enjoyment and book ownership among children and young people. Across the OECD, average reading performance fell by about 10 points between 2018 and 2022. That is a startling cultural contradiction.
But Prof Ronan McDonald, Gerry Higgins chair in Irish Studies at the University of Melbourne, says we need to separate the book itself from the act of reading when it comes to this latest fashion trend.
“The cultural prestige of the book may remain remarkably strong even where the practice of sustained reading is weakening,” he says. “A society can, in that sense, become more ‘bookish’ in its imagery while becoming less readerly in its habits.”
We can surround ourselves with books without making time to read them, post images online of our bookshelves full of unopened books, join a fancy book club, wear our “slutty little reading glasses”, carry a literary tote bag, know which books are fashionable and mention them in small talk at gatherings. But that doesn’t necessarily make the whole trend shallow, he says.
“Much of digital culture is designed around interruption, novelty and rapid switching, and there are powerful commercial incentives to keep pulling our attention elsewhere,” he says.
[ Ireland’s falling reading rates: ‘There’s a crisis of literacy. There’s a crisis of reading’ Opens in new window ]
But novels and poems demand something else from readers: “The habit of dwelling.”
“Books suggest duration in a culture of immediacy, an inward life that cannot be entirely externalised, and the possibility of giving something our attention,” he says. We are suddenly so nostalgically attached to the idea of books because they represent something that is now very difficult to find in the modern world.
Dior understands that too. And perhaps that’s why the Long Room will look so right behind a Dior collection. Because fashion does not only sell us clothes and accessories. It sells us an ideal.

title: Joe Humphreys: Please don’t tell me you hope I am well - because I might just answer
description: Suppose I’m in the depths of existential dejection; are you really ready for me to offload my feelings on you?
content:
D ear reader, I hope you are well. Let me get that out of the way, because I won’t be saying it again.
I’m fed up with the “I hope you are well” trend in emails, WhatsApps and other communications.
The use of the phrase really took off during the Covid-19 pandemic, according to business observers – an understandable urge given the deadly virus then circulating. But today we just have the usual hazards that come with being human. So what’s wrong with a simple “hello”?
I’m not against inquiring into another person’s welfare, but “I hope you are well” has become too reflexive, too automatic for my tastes. Literally, it’s on auto-prompt. Starting typing “I hope ... ” and then swipe right to complete the rest.
Responding meaningfully to “hope you’re well” has become another task to tick off. And when the phrase is in corporate communications, it seems cloying or indecently chummy.
A more honest greeting might read: “The world’s gone to shit, and no one really knows why we’re here, but have you got that report I was looking for yesterday ...”
Obviously, I do hope you are well, but can’t we take that for granted? I mean, I’m not a psychopath. Also, call me naive, but I generally assume people don’t wish me to be unwell. So, like, thanks for the concern, but suppose I’m in the depths of existential dejection; are you really ready for me to offload my feelings on you?
What does an expert think? Dr Emma Farrell is an assistant professor in mental health in the department of psychology at Maynooth University . She offers another view as today’s Unthinkable guest.
“No. I can hope someone is doing well without necessarily having a close relationship with them. Indeed, the Buddhist loving-kindness meditation invites us to wish others well as a practice that connects us to our shared humanity. So while your email reflex may not have the wellbeing of humanity at its heart, it’s not likely to do any harm.”
“It’s very hard to establish how somebody is without direct information from the person themselves. If we see someone in person, particularly someone we know, we can often tell how they are by reading their body language, facial expressions and general energy and demeanour. I’m struck by the philosopher and sociologist Hartmut Rosa’s account of resonance: the experience of being reached by something in another person – a shadow of pain, despair or joy on their face – and responding in a way that changes the encounter. I’m not sure that kind of resonance is possible without presence.
“Without presence, we are relying much more on what people say in response to ‘I hope you’re well’. As with many social courtesies, the answer may be as reflexive as the greeting – ‘I’m great thanks, I hope you’re well too’. There’s nothing wrong with that, but we all need some people in our lives with whom we can answer that question honestly.”
“A resonant relationship is one in which we feel that the other person reaches us, that we are safe and welcome to respond as ourselves, and that something in us shifts or is moved through the encounter. This can happen online. For someone who finds it difficult to meet people or connect in person, an online encounter may even offer a much-needed opportunity to meet someone who understands their experience.
“But I don’t think resonance comes from using the right greeting or platform or playing the ‘communication’ game well. It relies on an openness and willingness to be present to how someone actually is, what they say, what they express, or what they struggle to convey ...
“Resonance calls for space, time, attention and an openness to being affected by the other person. This openness can be hard to summon when we’re distracted, exhausted or caught up in our own worries and concerns.”
“There’s no special toolkit for building a connection through a screen. The same things matter in remote working contexts as physical working contexts – doing good work, being kind and showing, over time, that you’re a decent person to work with.”
“The words we use to greet one another reflect the conventions of our culture and the moment we’re living in. In Ireland in 2026, ‘I hope you’re well’ is an acceptable way of saying ‘I recognise there is another human being on the other end of this exchange who has a life and needs and feelings that are worth acknowledging’ before getting down to business. Perhaps what we feel compelled to do is greet one another, rather than assess the wellbeing of everyone on our organisation’s mailing list. And that’s no bad thing.”

title: Three firefighters killed in 1936 Pearse Street tragedy to be honoured
description: It remains the greatest loss of life suffered by Dublin Fire Brigade in a single incident
content:
Monday marks the 90th anniversary of a tragedy in Dublin city, as three firefighters lost their lives in the line of duty.
On October 5th, 1936, Dublin Fire Brigade responded to a serious fire at the Exide Batteries premises on Pearse Street.
Fire safety laws were not what they are now, and the premises was located in the basement with housing above.
Believing that a family might still be trapped inside, firefighters entered the burning building. A series of explosions followed, and much of the building collapsed. Peter McArdle, Robert Malone and Thomas Nugent were buried beneath the ruins; their remains were recovered the following morning, after many hours of searching and the removal of some 30 tons of rubble.
It remains the greatest loss of life suffered by Dublin Fire Brigade in a single incident.
Las Fallon, a retired firefighter and fire service historian, has advocated for a tribute for the men, and this will come to fruition with a commemorative plaque to be unveiled by Lord Mayor of Dublin Cllr Daryl Barron.
“The fire brigade got very little in the line of money, very little in the line of resources,” Fallon told The Irish Times. “In 1936, we paid the price for it when a fire started in 163 and 164 Pearse Street. There were tenement houses, but the basements were being used by the Exide battery factory. That was quite within the law at the time
“Exide batteries were producing batteries there, so there was highly flammable gas stored on the premises.”
[ Firemen killed in 1936 fire honoured Opens in new window ]
McArdle left a wife and seven children – his youngest daughter was born three months after his death. Malone, also married, was a veteran of the 1916 Rising, having served at Boland’s Mills. Nugent was engaged to be married.
The three men lay in state at City Hall before a civic funeral to Glasnevin Cemetery, and more than 80,000 people lined the streets of the city to pay their respects.
However, the fire brigade did not treat them with the same respect as their widows were forced to move out of accommodation designated for the service.
“I remember when I started looking into this back in the 80s, there were people who lived through the 1930s,” Fallon said. “And if you talk to Dubliners who remembered the time, they remembered two things. They remember the Eucharistic Congress and they remembered the Pearse Street funerals.”
A fourth firefighter, Tommie Potts, escaped. A renowned fiddle player, Fallon thinks his survivor’s guilt was evident in some of his melancholic tunes.
His nephew Seán Potts was a member of the famous Irish trad band The Chieftains.
There will be a commemorative service in Glasnevin Cemetery on Sunday before the plaque unveiling on Monday, with family members of the men set to attend.
They will include McArdle’s daughter, now 90, and a niece of Nugent, Cáit Kendall.
Kendall said her mother was very close to Nugent, who they called Gerard rather than his official name of Thomas.
His death left a heavy mark on the family, and she recalled how her grandfather learned of his son’s passing through the newspaper.
His fiance Maye, who subsequently married another man, remained close to the family, which she said “helped keep my uncle’s memory alive”.
While she never met him, she always felt close to him and is delighted that he will be honoured on Monday.

title: A message for Ireland from one of the lesser-known Irish-American Kennedys
description: Letter to Ireland: One Patrick Kennedy left for Boston, but mine went to New Orleans, never to return home
content:
I grew up on the Kennedy compound. My summers were full of days jumping off piers, casting nets, boating, and climbing trees. I’ve been thinking a lot about that time. I’ve been thinking a lot about the man who brought my family here.
In the mid-1800s my great-great-great-grandfather Patrick Kennedy embarked on his journey to the US. Leaving all he knew behind in southeast Ireland for the promise of the American dream. When he came to the US, he worked as a barrel-maker. Patrick’s wife was also an Irish immigrant and they had multiple daughters and two sons.
Their sons would become established businessmen and one of them would also become a well-known politician. Their daughters would become wives and mothers playing vital roles in their husband’s successes.
Now, before I go any further, you may be thinking I’m talking about the famous Kennedys. However, I’m not. My family’s hometown, Gaulstown, Co Kilkenny, just 13km from Dunganstown, Co Wexford. While their Patrick went to Boston. Ours went to New Orleans.
Although we may not be at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner or make international news, I think it’s important for Ireland to also know what happened to its unsung emigrants and their descendants.
Writing to family back home was a lifeline for Irish immigrants during this time and left a trove of documents known as The American Letters. They shared news of success and survival, longing and love. These would often be accompanied by money to help family or boat tickets as part of chain migration.
And so as a descendant of the lesser-documented Irish-American Kennedys, this is my American Letter to Ireland.
You may have seen the 2019 movie Dumbo. It stars Danny DeVito and your own Colin Farrell. Well, Danny’s character bought Dumbo’s mama, Jumbo, from my hometown Biloxi, Mississippi. It’s where Patrick relocated our family to after 30 years in New Orleans. His brother, Michael, who came through the east coast during the famine was a Union Soldier. He was stationed in New Orleans after the American civil war. We think Patrick came on a cotton trading ship from Liverpool during the 1860s.
I’m saddened to tell you, that William, their younger brother who accompanied Patrick, died from yellow fever only a year after arriving. He was among thousands of Irish who died from the mosquito-borne disease. Many worked long days in harsh conditions, digging ditches and canals in stagnant water where such deadly diseases spread quickly.
When Patrick finally got to Biloxi, many years after arriving, he used his savings to start investing. He opened The Kennedy Hotel with his sons, the first hotel within Biloxi city limits. This was a big deal. At the time, Biloxi was considered “the seafood capital of the world”. Patrick, a multi-entrepreneur, also took part in that booming enterprise.
His son John would later become the first full-time mayor of Biloxi and his other son William worked in a pharmacy business and also in seafood.
Another Kennedy business came with the next generation. William’s son later opened Kennedy Engine, an essential service to the marine and industrial sector. The business was taken over by William’s grandson. Later, my own father was one of its top salesmen, providing engines to big companies all over the US’s south region.
Now, we are at my generation. We’ve done our own thing. Three of us have worked in yet another family business, a restaurant back in New Orleans managed by my brother. Parkway Bakery and Tavern is a po’boy shop, where visitors from all over the world try its celebrated sandwiches. Much like your pubs, it’s a place that brings joy and people together.
So, Ireland, why is it so important that you know this? Every time I go visit you, the Irish want to know where I come from. I can’t describe my history without going back to where it started.
I was 23 when I first visited you; I had just graduated college and was the same age Patrick was when he left for the US. Like Patrick, I bartend for a living. Unlike him, much of my income goes toward travelling instead of a family. Visiting you over the years, I’ve learned more about myself, my heritage, and about humanity. In many ways you feel like home, a place to recuperate, gain perspective and commit to reverence.
I recently saw you again this past February when I took a trip to honour St Brigid. Once again you provided solace. I had escaped a violent situation over three years before. And the dream that kept me going through that dangerous time was to one day see you again. And gladly for me, I did.
But Patrick, like so many Irish, never got to go back home. Maybe, in some way, I keep visiting you for him.
Catherine Kennedy is a writer and bartender living in New Orleans. Her substack is at https://catkennedy.substack.com/

title: Daniel Geary: This year won’t see the end of Trumpism. But it might see the beginning of the end
description: Worldview: Unless the polling is very wrong, Democrats are on course to retake the House of Representatives. But they also have a strong chance of capturing the Senate
content:
I f you’re a Democrat and have been following the polls, you might have a sore arm from repeatedly pinching yourself to ensure you’re not dreaming. Donald Trump ’s approval ratings are so far under water that they are sinking Republicans ’ chances. If Democrats’ dreams come true come this November, it will have long-term consequences for politics in the United States .
Unless the polling is very wrong, Democrats are on course to retake the House of Representatives. But they also appear to have a decent chance of capturing the Senate, which would have been nearly unthinkable this time last year. After some disastrous 2024 Senate results, Democrats need to flip at least four seats, requiring multiple wins in Republican states.
In a country with such a close partisan divide, it is very difficult to overcome a double-digit deficit. And yet polls favour Democrats to win not just one, but three states that Trump carried by more than 10 points in 2024: Alaska, Ohio and Texas. The race in another – Iowa – appears to be a toss-up. Other deeply red states are improbably in play. Republicans have had to pour money into defending a seat in Kansas, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1932. And in neighbouring Nebraska, independent Dan Osborn (who would vote with Democrats more often than not) is threatening to unseat a Republican incumbent.
In North Carolina, which Trump carried three times and which like Texas has a history of breaking Democrats’ hearts, popular former governor Roy Cooper is running away with the race. Democrats are poised to hold a seat in the battleground state of Michigan despite a divisive primary that chose progressive Abdul El-Sayed as the Democratic candidate. The lone bright spot for Republicans is Maine, where crafty Republican incumbent Susan Collins is running neck-and-neck with Democratic candidate Troy Jackson. The only other worrying sign for Democrats is that one of their sitting senators, John Fetterman, has been flirting with Republicans; he addressed their midterm convention via video earlier this month.
It is normal for opposition parties to pick up Congressional seats in midterm elections, but the scale of swing predicted – and the usual health warnings about polls apply of course – would be extraordinary. We haven’t seen anything like it since the 2010 Tea Party wave by Republicans. In some cases Democrats benefit from having selected strong candidates, while in others Republicans suffer from having chosen – partly at Trump’s behest – weak ones.
Yet every election is also a referendum on Trump’s presidency and Democratic gains on this scale are only made possible by his dismal popularity. The Trump team trumpeted 2024 as giving him a mandate to enact his radical agenda, but this is one lie they seem to have believed themselves. Trump would probably not have been elected without the inflation that voters blamed on Joe Biden and which Trump promised to control. He also won votes with his promise to keep the US out of foreign wars. He managed to break both promises in a single stroke.
More Americans than not now disapprove of Trump’s handling of immigration , which had typically been his strongest issue. Here Trump clearly overplayed his hand by sending Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Ice) agents to invade American cities and by the open and wanton cruelty of their treatment of suspected undocumented migrants. Many Republicans are now asking Trump not to campaign with them.
Even losing the Senate and winning the House of Representatives narrowly – which currently seems like the Democrats’ realistic worst-case scenario – would give them the ability to block Trump’s budget proposals and to amplify their opposition to him by holding public hearings.
But a large victory would have significant longer-term consequences. Senators serve six-year terms, meaning that flipping seats that Democrats typically have no business winning would give them an advantage in the chamber until 2032. A big win is especially important because the Senate structurally favours Republicans. Every state, no matter its size, gets two senators, meaning that the whiter, more rural and more conservative populations of smaller states are over-represented and the less white, more urbanised and more liberal populations of larger states are massively underrepresented. Imagine if Leitrim had the same representation as Dublin how that might distort Irish politics.
[ A Trump electoral project to make Steve Hilton the next governor of California Opens in new window ]
In order to reverse the damage that Trump has done and advance the ambitious reforms the US badly needs, any Democratic president elected in 2028 would need a majority in the Senate. Really, they need a decent majority. Biden had a tie in the Senate in 2020, meaning that just two troublesome Democratic senators stymied much of his agenda.
The size of the win would also have an impact on who Democrats next nominate for president. Democratic voters have been inclined to choose moderate candidates for their ostensible electability. But if they are more optimistic about a win in 2028, they may choose the candidate who best represents their values and is most likely to enact significant reforms.
In the long run, the only way Trumpism will be defeated is if Democrats win consistently large victories at the polls and implement an ambitious agenda that addresses the country’s obscene wealth inequality.
So, 2026 won’t be the end of Trump or of Trumpism. But it might just be the beginning of the end.
Daniel Geary is Mark Pigott Professor in American History at Trinity College Dublin

title: The budget I want: A home owner, house hunter, parent, pensioner and business owner
description: Parents, homeowners, professionals, farmers, healthcare workers and people with disabilities discuss their priorities
author_name: Dara Bradley, Jack White, Emmet Malone, Barry Roche, Kitty Holland, Stephen Conneely
content:
A s Minister for Finance Simon Harris and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers prepare to deliver Budget 2027 , The Irish Times has spoken to parents, homeowners, professionals, farmers, healthcare workers and people with disabilities to hear about their priorities and concerns.
Ailish Scully has delayed ordering heating oil this winter for her home in Moycullen, Co Galway, until after the budget – in the hope the Government cuts fuel taxes.
The native of Swords in Dublin bought 500 litres last February for €475 and her tank is running low.
“It was dear then, but now it’s just gone mad altogether. Last time I looked, it was nearly €900 for 500 litres,” she says.
The 62-year-old mother of five adult children volunteers with Cancer Care West. Her husband Declan, from Santry in Dublin, is an accountant with PennEngineering in Mervue, Galway city.
Their Moycullen home of almost 25 years has an open fire and wood-pellet stove, but oil heats their radiators and water.
Retrofitting an air-to-water heating system would be “very expensive” but Ailish would like more State grants to help install solar panels, windows and insulation to improve their home’s energy rating and “save money” on bills.
Ailish acknowledges that international events caused oil prices to spike – by more than 60 per cent in the past year, according to Fuels for Ireland – but she feels the Government could ease the burden.
Until then, Ailish says: “I’ll be sitting here in my big fleece blanket keeping myself warm.”
Damien Owens seems less concerned about what the budget can do for him than for young professionals like his daughter.
Aged in her late 20s, she moved home in recent years to save for a house.
“No adult child wants to be living with their parents. They should be living their own life, getting out there and doing it,” he says.
The 64-year-old, who lives in Clontarf, Co Dublin, has been an engineer for more than 40 years, the last four of which he has spent as director general of the representative body Engineers Ireland.
When Owens was starting out as an electronic engineer, having graduated in the 1980s, he says the “social contract” was “largely facilitated” at the time.
“Housing is one thing that young people are finding demoralising because they’ve fulfilled their part of the social contract in getting the education, getting a job to keep the economy going and pay tax.
“The other part of the social contract then, is that they should be able to get affordable housing.”
[ Budget 2027: Measures on pensions, welfare, income tax and more take shape Opens in new window ]
Believing that most new builds are for rent, he says measures should be introduced in this year’s budget to encourage a “purchasable supply” of houses.
Lamenting increasingly costly groceries, energy and fuel, alongside the housing crisis, Owens believes there could be a “bigger exodus” of young professionals if Budget 2027 does little to alleviate pressure.
“If you’re a professional, you’ve invested in your future, you’ve invested in your career, and now really what people want to see is the State investing in them,” he says.
Owens believes workers are entering the higher rate of tax “very early”, which is a “key issue” that should be addressed.
“We all know that Ireland isn’t a cheap place to live, but I think you’re happy to pay the taxes when you get the services that you need and that’s the key to it.”
When The Matcha Bar opened for business in July 2024, so many people queued for a taste of the Japanese green drink that the line wrapped around the internal courtyard of the Powerscourt Townhouse Centre in Dublin 2.
[ Ian O’Riordan: Does the Government truly understand the value of sport? Opens in new window ]
“We started as a six week pop-up,” says owner Elaine Fitzsimons, “then I spoke to the landlords and asked could I extend the lease.”
A little over two years later, “it’s going really well”, she says. “I think there was definitely an appetite for matcha in Ireland. When I started it, it was my own problem I was solving – I selfishly wanted a good matcha place.”
But running a busy cafe with six staff total is no mean feat. “I think hospitality is extremely difficult in that it’s really hard to get staff,” Fitzsimons says.
And new staff means more tax obligations: auto-enrolment in a pension scheme, employer PRSI rates, and an increasing minimum wage.
While auto-enrolment is “a fantastic initiative”, Fitzsimons says, “I do think small businesses need supports with that because it adds a whole chunk on top of your bills”. Lower PRSI rates would be beneficial too, she says.
“And then energy bills,” she says, followed by a sigh. “My last few months of bills – oh my God.”
“We had to get air-con because it was so hot this summer, I think that tripled our bill over the course of the month,” Fitzsimons says. “That makes it super challenging – and, probably, had I known all of this before, I don’t know if I would have opened.”
Cork farmer Noel Hurley has a long list of measures which he would like to see addressed in the budget to assist farmers – from rebates on diesel to increased support grants.
A native of Kilbrittain in west Cork, Hurley (58) moved to Kildorrery in north Cork almost 40 years ago as a farm manager and today he farms 300 acres and milks 200 cows there, along with his son Sean. Hurley and his wife Elizabeth, daughter Lisa and Sean all live in their modern farmhouse.
When they built the house in 2007, the Hurleys put in geothermal heating so they don’t have a home heating fuel bill, and solar panels on the farm buildings have cut his electricity bill for milking and cooling machines from €17,000 to €8,000, but there is no escaping the issue of diesel prices.
Hurley says that “everything that goes into this yard and goes out of this yard runs on diesel” and while he would like to go green, he doesn’t believe he will ever see an electric tractor capable of doing the work required.
Hurley burns 5,000 litres of green diesel annually and while green diesel was 90 cent a litre last year, this year he is paying at least on average 150 cents, so his own fuel bill has gone from €4,500 to over €7,000 and he is paying €9,000 more to contractors to cut silage this year.
“The Government gave €85 million for the Fuel Income Support Scheme in April as a 20 cent a litre rebate – €45 million of this is still to be used, we need to see this paid out and ring-fenced for farmers and contractors. Carbon tax also needs to be scrapped. My milk production costs are up by €90,000 on last year and milk prices are down an average of 10 cent a litre so we need all the help we can get on costs.”
September can be a slow month for selling bicycles: the summertime spike in sales has begun to fall off, and it’s a while away until children’s bikes are bought en masse as Christmas gifts.
But within 15 minutes on a Wednesday morning, Donnybrook Bikes sees three customers, two deliveries and two phone calls in its small premises off the Dublin 4 village’s main street.
[ Budget builders: the money Ministers who are two sides of the same coin Opens in new window ]
“Sometimes, you make great margins on the sale of bikes, but you can’t rely on that alone,” says Ruairi Parsons, the general manager of the shop that opened in 2014. “You also need to concentrate on repairs,” he says, which make up about half of the business’s revenue.
“Especially over the winter months … if the weather is brutal, there’s not many people thinking of buying bikes”. Budget 2027’s release date in early October may then provide well-timed assistance.
Parsons’ immediate response to what the Government could do to enhance his business’ results is not to reduce tax or alleviate energy costs. “I suppose, the obvious one would be to put more money into bike lanes on the roads,” he says.
“A lot of people are put off by” sharing the road with buses, he says, “and just won’t hop on a bike”.
The Cycle to Work Scheme “definitely has” attracted more customers, but it caps the price for eligible electric bikes at €1,500. Parsons says this could be increased to €2,000 to allow for more customers to avail of the scheme and better quality bikes to be sold.
The margin on bike sales “aren’t great”, he says, before pointing to a red road bike with a €1,000 price tag below its handlebars. “That probably cost me €600 and the tax man gets €230 … so I’m making €170 on that,” and that 23 per cent VAT takes its toll: “We’re forever paying the tax man,” he says.
With Budget 2027 looming, childcare is once again a key area of interest with parents hoping for additional supports.
A €200 cap per month per child is a stated goal, but it remains to be seen whether this will be delivered on.
[ Alternative budget ideas: A €500 ‘everyday costs’ card, cheap e-bikes, a State building firm Opens in new window ]
Caroline De Bank is a mother-of-three who lives in Tubbercurry, Co Sligo. Her daughter Millie (4) attends creche at the local Family Resource Centre. She says the care her daughter receives is “exemplary” and she feels recruitment and retention should be an area where additional funding is allocated in the childcare sector.
“It’s a bit of a postcode lottery at the moment,” she tells The Irish Times.
While grants of €750,000 have been available to purchase or construct new premises for community early learning or childcare services since 2025, De Bank feels staffing issues in these centres will persist without additional supports as staff can find better pay and conditions elsewhere.
She adds that these issues also exist in private childcare facilities. DeBank, who is a community nurse, says she has friends who own creches and “constantly find themselves in the red”.
She feels “headway has certainly been made in the last four years” regarding childcare costs in Ireland. However, she wants to see plans to support childcare staff and families.
She hopes for more strategic thinking from Government and the relevant stakeholders, saying “a 10-year plan would make more sense than stopgap measures”.
Robert Walker (75), who lives alone in north Co Dublin, wants to see a “fair” increase in the old-age pension and greater investment in the health service.
A retired steel fabricator, he bought his one-bedroom apartment after the break-up of his marriage
“I don’t have a mortgage or rent, but I have management fees of €1,800 a year [€34.60 a week],” he says.
“I live on the pension [€299.30 weekly] and the living alone allowance [€22 a week]. I’ll get the fuel allowance [€38 a week, for 28 weeks from late September], which is a great help.
“I still struggle to pay the bills. The ESB bill can be high – €200 every two months. The storage heaters are electric, which are very expensive so I don’t have them on much.”
He also has bin charges and broadband, mobile phone and insurance bills.
A pressing worry is that his water-pump is failing, meaning water pressure is often too low to take a shower. “That will be €600 or €700 to replace and I just don’t have that.”
He buys ready-meals for dinner. “They’re about €6. Sometimes I do scrambled eggs or a sandwich for dinner. I wouldn’t do a full dinner every day. Everything is so expensive. A pound of butter – that’s €5. That used to be about €2.50.
“I heard the increase in the pension is to be €7.50. It doesn’t sound fair to me. And they need to spend more on the health service. I was in A&E for 40 hours a while ago. It never used to be like that.”
Catherine Rossiter (52) is a single mother of 13-year-old twins, one of whom is profoundly disabled and one who was recently diagnosed with autism. She works full-time in third-level education.
She wants to see greater targeted supports, through refundable tax-credits possibly, for single parent families and for families with disabled children.
“My [disabled] daughter needs to be warm as she is immobile. I keep the sittingroom at 22 degrees. I feel very lucky I have a wood-burning stove, which keeps costs down,” she says.
“I had to convert the garage to provide a downstairs bedroom and bathroom for my daughter. That cost €60,000, which I had to borrow. I couldn’t get any grant help. The income threshold for the adaptation grant needs to move.
“I have a significant mortgage which I’ll be paying until I am 70. The groceries are about €200 a week – and that is about €40 more than a year ago. I am counting pennies at the end of every month.”
She thinks the Government “is very disconnected from the ordinary person”.
“I would like to see more tailored supports, especially for single-parent families. Married couples get advantageous tax credits. I think single parents should get something similar.
“And I’ll be watching out for the new cost-of-disability payment, to see who gets it and how much it is.”
Martin Hoey (54), who sustained a brain injury in 2006, has a hidden disability. He has had huge anxiety for years after he was the victim of an assault and still has difficulties.
He would like to see a “good start” to the new disability support payment and funding for disabled people’s organisations (DPOs).
Hoey had to retire from his job as a paramedic, initially receiving invalidity benefit. Gradually he re-entered the workforce and now works part-time.
[ Middle earners could be €750 better off post-budget, but they may not be impressed Opens in new window ]
He receives a half-rate partial capacity benefit of €127 a week, plus €185.40 in respect of his adult dependent wife, and €78 in respect of their 14 year-old daughter – €390.40 per week for the three of them.
His wage from his work fluctuates, depending on the hours he is needed.
His partially blind wife lost her means-tested blind-pension when he got part-time work.
“We have a council house in Dublin and the rent is €230 a week. We have two adult children at home and their wages are counted for the rent, but it all comes out of my payment,” he says.
“I wouldn’t say we have a life of luxury. We are doing okay, but we are looking at the cost of ESB, which is going up all the time.”
Because he cannot work full-time he is home more than he would be otherwise. He is dreading a cold winter. “The gas heating is on very sparingly. It is too expensive.”
Lifford-based healthcare assistant Dermott Foy spends a good part of his time on the road between visits to service users in rural Donegal.
Working to support a mix of older people, those just out of hospital and those with disabilities, he has been hit by the cost of running the car he relies on to get around while they, he says, are highly dependent on domestic heating to stay warm heading into the winter.
Fuel, then, is top of his priority list in advance of Tuesday’s budget.
In addition to the already increased maintenance costs on a car he cannot afford to let him down, he says: “My fuel spend has maybe doubled this year because you’re completely reliant on your vehicle in this job,” he says.
“I’d say I’m looking at €60 to €70 a week extra now on top of what I had been spending.”
Foy receives mileage from the HSE, but he says: “It might have been close to break-even on what I was spending before, but it doesn’t even come close now.”
For Foy, action on fuel prices, car costs and home heating, is the absolute priority in this budget. “It’s hitting a lot of people really hard,” he says.

title: ‘It’s off the charts’: Satellite images show how three years of war have devastated Gaza
description: UN says number of destroyed structures in Gaza up by 9% since ceasefire of October 2025, amid mass displacement and acute humanitarian need
content:
O n Thursday last, Palestinians gathered to bury the remains of 105 people killed in an Israeli attack on Gaza City three years ago. The victims were killed in a series of Israeli air strikes involving dozens of bombs that levelled a seven-storey building and destroyed several other residential buildings in the Yarmouk Square neighbourhood on the afternoon of October 25th, 2023, local authorities say.
Three years after the Gaza war began, and almost a year since a ceasefire came into effect, the extent of devastation and the severity of the continuing humanitarian crisis faced by the territory’s 2.1 million people continues to be revealed.
The presence of human remains still buried under the rubble remains one of the most urgent humanitarian issues in Gaza. According to estimates cited by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), between 8,000 and 10,000 bodies may still be buried in this way.
Newly released satellite images on Google Maps, taken in June this year, show the extent of devastation. Thousands of homes, businesses, places of worship have been wiped away. Any available open space in Gaza City is packed with shacks, tents and huts.
The images also show fresh damage to towns such as Beit Lahiya and Beit Hanoun, as well as the destruction of places of worship such as the Istiqlal mosque in Khan Younis. Large neighbourhoods in Gaza City such as Jabaliya and Shuja’iya, which were targeted in repeated Israeli offensives, are clearly now uninhabitable.
[ Irish citizens are already ashamed of Israel and inaction, Taoiseach Opens in new window ]
Swathes of rubble are visible in the south of Gaza, where a wide strip appears to have been cleared by Israeli forces along the border with Egypt. The town of Rafah appears to have been almost entirely reduced to rubble and Tel al-Sultan razed.
More than two million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters in Gaza, where an estimated 80 per cent of structures – roughly 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with about two-thirds of those destroyed, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa.
A recent UN assessment estimated that the number of destroyed structures across Gaza had increased by 9 per cent since the declaration of a ceasefire in October 2025.
“The estimate of the total amount of rubble in Gaza is 61 million tonnes. It is approximately 20 times the amount of rubble generated in all wars across the world over the last 18 years,” Jaco Cilliers, the UNDP’s special representative in Palestine, told the Guardian last month.
The destruction is staggering; the human toll even more so. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the start of the war, mostly civilians. The conflict was triggered by a surprise attack by Hamas into Israel in October 2023, in which militants killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage.
Gaza’s health ministry attributes the deaths in the territory directly to Israeli military action, but does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.
[ ‘World’s richest nations’ facilitating ‘undisguised genocide’ in Gaza, says Sally Rooney Opens in new window ]
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) disputes the ministry’s figures, saying there is “no basis to assume” that all those listed were killed as a result of IDF activity. It says it operates in “a precise manner to remove threats and protect its troops and Israeli civilians, in accordance with the agreement”, and that it works to mitigate any civilian harm “to the greatest extent possible”.
Meanwhile, the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains perilous, according to United Nations agencies and humanitarian organisations.
Addressing the UN General Assembly last month, secretary general António Guterres said of Gaza that while the resumption of assistance since the ceasefire was announced last October has brought some relief, conditions remain intolerable.
“International law, including international humanitarian law, is brazenly violated. Humanitarian access remains severely restricted, and the level of human suffering is still off the charts,” he said.
Conditions in Gaza remain catastrophic, with widespread destruction and severe shortages nearly a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, according to the British Red Cross and Médecins Sans Frontières.
Human rights groups say the Israeli military maintains direct control of or imposes buffer zones over roughly 60 per cent of the territory; during military operations this expands to 70 per cent of Gaza’s 365sq km. This confines 2.1 million Palestinians to devastated neighbourhoods and tent camps in the 30-40 per cent of the coastal enclave where homes and infrastructure have been reduced to rubble.
The UN secretary general’s spokesman, Stéphane Dujarric, has warned of yet another catastrophe. “Our humanitarian colleagues warn that funding shortfalls, as well as continued Israeli restrictions, are severely limiting preparations for the rainy season,” he said.
While heating points and reinforced tents have been established at displacement sites, they can only host 10 per cent of the population. “Many more tents are needed, along with shelter kits, heaters and sustained fuel imports. Thousands of heating points will be required to meet the needs of people when the temperature drops,” he said.
Israel reports that approximately 600 to 800 trucks enter the Gaza Strip daily, although humanitarian organisations say only 20 per cent carry vital humanitarian aid. In addition to the trucks that get through, UN deputy special coordinator for the Middle East peace process Ramiz Alakbarov has accused Hamas of disrupting aid distribution, increasing the hardship of civilians ​already facing a humanitarian crisis in the devastated enclave.
He said humanitarian workers halted work after armed men entered a food distribution hub in northern ​Gaza and assaulted two truck drivers in a World Food Programme warehouse.
“These ​incidents are not isolated. They are completely unacceptable and reflect an ⁠increasingly dangerous pattern of intimidation, violence and obstruction, including smuggling attempts, targeting and ​abusing humanitarian operations,” he said.
[ Bono compares Israeli minister’s comments on Gaza to Nazi leader Heinrich Himmler Opens in new window ]
Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu and the Israeli foreign ministry stated that Israel does not have a policy of starvation and facilitates the entry of humanitarian supplies.
Against this backdrop, the charge of genocide in Gaza has been levelled at Israel. During his recent address to the UN General Assembly, Netanyahu claimed that these allegations were “the biggest lie of the century”.
The US refused entry to Palestinian Authority president Mahmoud Abbas, who delivered his UN address by video-link. He called Israel’s Gaza offensive a “genocidal war that has created an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe” and accused the media of failing to tell the truth about Gaza.
For nearly three years Israel has banned foreign journalists from entering Gaza. Satellite images, meanwhile, provide a stark reminder of the conflict’s lasting impact. Gaza remains a landscape of rubble and displacement, where the dead are still being recovered and the living are still waiting for recovery to begin. – Additional reporting: Guardian
74, 000 – The estimated number of Gazans killed during the war, according to Gaza’s health ministry. The war was triggered by a Hamas attack in which militants killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage.
175,000 – The estimated number of injured in Gaza during the war, according to Gaza’s health ministry.
21,000 – The estimated number of children among the fatalities, local health authorities, and international monitoring groups report.
2.1 million : The estimated population in Gaza, with one million under the age of 18, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics.
8-10,000 : The estimated number of bodies still buried under rubble in Gaza, according to the UN Development Programme.

title: ‘It’s a fashion thing, to show your Irish identity’: Belfast’s GAA jersey surge
description: Students move around the campus in a variety of county shirts, including Armagh, Donegal and Kerry – in contrast to the Troubles era
content:
Tuesday night is jersey night at The Hatfield bar on Belfast’s lower Ormeau Road.
GAA county flags hang from the ceiling over its magnificent hand-carved mahogany counter in the downstairs lounge.
It’s freshers’ week nearby Queen’s University, and wearing your club or county jersey “breaks the ice” and becomes a talking point, says Hatfield co-owner Stephen Cassidy ahead of festivities.
During the late 1990s, the nationalist lower Ormeau was the scene of a sectarian flashpoint during the Orange Order marching season.
In a week that saw the Drumcree parades dispute erupt after being dormant for almost three decades, a friend got in touch from the States – we shared a house in the Holylands student area beside Queen’s in 1998 – despairing at the newly inflamed tensions.
Back then, violent clashes against the backdrop of the Garvaghy Road standoff between Protestant Orangemen (and their supporters) and Catholic residents of the Portadown road led to tensions across Northern Ireland, forcing shops and pubs to close early in this part of Belfast.
Police sirens roared down our street as armoured vehicles raced to block rioters and seal off the Ormeau Bridge.
Today, students stroll down Rugby Avenue in the Holylands – our tiny matchbox house was on the corner – towards Queen’s University in autumn sunshine.
Two young men carrying large coffees are wearing the county jerseys of Down and Tyrone.
Bulky security guards stand at the side entrance of the students’ union where a queue is four deep by noon.
Across the road, hundreds of students spill out of Elmwood Hall. Flashes of the Donegal jersey’s bright green and gold are among the crowd.
A young man wearing a Kerry jersey is heading towards the glass-fronted union building. Despite his county allegiances, he is from the North.
“I’m not wearing this to make a point. I’m wearing this because it’s what I know,” says the 20-year-old student, who doesn’t want to be named.
At traffic lights, another is wearing a pair of Down shorts.
