Inside the students’ union, Éanna Nig Riabhaigh is signing up members to An Cumann Gaelach, the university’s Irish language society. She is wearing an Antrim jersey she bought on eBay.
“It was £30 (€35.20) and I got it from Canada actually – and me from Belfast,” she says, laughing.
“I think it’s from 2000. I like the looser fit.”
Nig Riabhaigh comes from a musical background and thinks the increased presence of GAA jerseys is also linked to pop culture.
Many people wearing jerseys neither play nor watch Gaelic games, she says.
“It’s definitely a fashion thing, trying to look and present in a way that shows your Irish identity. I think that’s a very big thing culturally within young people,” she says.
Earlier this year, loyalist activist Jamie Bryson urged unionist students to wear Orange Orders sashes and T-shirts in response to the presence of GAA shirts.
“You will see more GAA tops at Queen’s University than you will at Croke Park,” he told the university’s Orange societies.
They must join the “culture war against nationalism” on campus, he said.
Law student Caolan Turley shakes his head in disagreement.
The Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann festival took place in Belfast for a week in August and included loyalist marching bands. “It wasn’t sectarian at all,” Turley argues.
“What’s the big deal? If someone’s wearing a Rangers top, I wouldn’t be offended,” adds the Belfast student.
“If you’re offended by someone wearing a GAA top, it shows you’re insecure.”
In March, a referendum aimed at reintroducing Irish language dual signage in the students’ union following its removal almost 30 years ago won the overwhelming support of voters.
Hip-hop group Kneecap were among those to back the campaign.
Members of the Young Unionists society at Queen’s opposed the move, saying it would create a “chill factor”.
Standing outside the gates of the university, Eoghan Ó Conghaile says he’s looking forward to the signage being erected “soon”.
He points to a student in an Armagh jersey in front of us.
“I’ve definitely noticed a lot more people wearing them. I think it’s indicative of the changing demographic, not just in Queen’s but across the North,” says Ó Conghaile, the face of the referendum’s ‘Yes’ vote.
“It shows also that the GAA is normalised now, it isn’t this different counterculture in society.”
Back at the Hatfield, Cassidy is enjoying the calm before the night ahead when they’ll open upstairs for “club and county” colours.
Bananarama’s Cruel Summer is blasting out from the speakers of the family-run bar.
Cassidy’s late father bought the Hatfield at the height of the Troubles in 1976.
It’s a place that welcomes everybody, he insists, where there’s no dress code.
He mentions their ties with East Belfast GAA, a club established during Covid in a historically unionist stronghold of the city.
“A few of our staff played for them, they have people from all different backgrounds and different nationalities,” he says.

title: ‘I decided to take a leap of faith’: Largest ever number of GPs graduate
description: Largest ever graduation of GPs, as State moves to increase numbers to meet demand
content:
W hen Dr Hannah McCauley was a child, she was used to her father Denis working all hours as a general practitioner (GP) in rural Donegal .
“People would come to the house and every third night he would be on call. I grew up knowing the hard work that was involved in medicine but I saw how much enjoyment Dad got out of it,” she says.
Despite getting the Leaving Cert points to study medicine in Trinity College Dublin, she decided to “take a leap of faith” and study abroad in Dundee, Scotland .
After graduating in 2016, she worked in Edinburgh for two years, before working in Northern Ireland for another two. But after working in hospitals and seeing “patients come and go”, she realised she wanted a different speciality.
“In general practice, it’s very much patient focused. You know his whole history. He is a person and the illness happened to him,” she says.
“There is that classic GP cradle to grave situation, where we see them for their newborn check and you can see them through adolescence into adulthood into old age.”
McCauley is one of 274 new GPs graduating from the Irish College of GPs at Dublin’s Convention Centre on Saturday.
She started her GP training in 2020 during the early days of the Covid pandemic, but had two children during the process.
[ GP numbers rise by just 185 in five years despite healthcare needs of growing population Opens in new window ]
“I had my first baby in 2022. At that point, I was out in rural general practice and came back from maternity leave pregnant,” she says.
“I had two [babies] in 18 months. I was learning the art of being a GP while learning to be a mother and everything else that comes with that.”
The 35-year-old is so excited to be able to work as GP in her beloved Donegal, following in the footsteps of her father.
She was even more surprised to discover she, and another graduate, are both being given the Ellard Eppel award – a recognition of the GP trainee with the highest exam score in the country.
“The GP training programme is normally four years, but I took six because I took a year off for each of my babies. I had thought the babies had fried my brain. I did the last exam last year. My son didn’t sleep for two years, so I don’t really remember it,” she says, laughing.
She added that the Donegal GP training programme was such a “supportive learning environment”.
[ GP shortages: Where are the most acute problems across the country? Opens in new window ]
The Government has increased the number of GP training places in recent years in a bid to meet the growing supply and demand gap, particularly in rural areas.
Speaking about the newly qualified GPs, Fintan Foy, chief executive of the Irish College of GPs, said it was the “largest graduation in the college’s history”.
“Behind that are 274 new specialist GPs who will care for patients and families in communities right across Ireland,” he says.
“These GPs will help to address the GP workforce crisis and to ensure that we have sufficient specialist GPs to care for our population. I congratulate every one of them, and the families and friends who supported them along the way.”
Of the new graduates conferred at the weekend, 32 had completed the international medical graduate rural programme, which is a two-year supported work and learning initiative run by the Irish College of GPs, alongside the HSE to help experienced non-EU general practitioners integrate into rural Irish healthcare.
Dr Velma Harkins, president of the college, paid particular tribute to these individuals, adding that they have “kept its doctors’ surgeries open”.
Dr Arsalan Naqvi is originally from Pakistan but moved to Ireland in 2021 because he wanted to focus on more community-focused care.
“For me, Ireland is a country that is very welcoming and has beautiful scenery. It has a healthcare system where primary care plays an important role,” he says.
The 31-year -old worked as a senior house officer (SHO) in Portiuncula hospital in Galway for the year after he moved.
[ At least 1,000 new GPs required to maintain patient ratios, says representative group Opens in new window ]
“During that year, I really enjoyed the relationship between the hospital and the primary care and how general practice co-ordinates care in the community,” he says.
“I applied to the GP scheme and got the Sligo GP scheme. The day I moved from the hospital to community and I felt like this is where I wanted to be.
Why does he love general practice so much? There are lots of reasons, he said.
“You’re seeing a variety, you’re doing chronic medical conditions, minor surgery. I find in terms of illness you’re dealing more with the social and psychosocial effect,” he adds.
“The relationship a GP has with a patient is different. You see them at different stages of their life.”
Now he has graduated, he will continue to work across two practices – one rural and one urban – though he thinks rural medicine might the home for him in the future.
“I would be more inclined to work in a rural practice that’s why I want to do both to see whether I enjoy them both. I haven’t decided yet,” he said.
“I wanted to see where I stand. I’m looking forward to learning more skills in general practice.”

title: Delay of children’s hospital would ‘impose considerable additional costs’, Minister warns
description: Jennifer Carroll MacNeill issued warning to contractor earlier this year over continued delays
content:
The continued delay to the completion of the national children’s hospital would “impose considerable additional costs on the State”, the Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill warned the contractor earlier this year.
The construction of the facility on the St James’s Hospital site in Dublin began in 2016 and was scheduled to be completed by the end of 2022, but has faced numerous delays.
The project has been marked by ballooning costs – from €987 million to €2.24 billion – with an increasingly fractious relationship between the builders, Bam, and the board overseeing the project, the National Paediatric Hospital Development Board (NPHDB).
In March, MacNeill wrote to Henk Rottinghuis, chairman of the Royal Bam group, the parent company of Bam Ireland, criticising the resources and progress on the project.
At that point the hospital was due for substantial completion by April 30th. It has still not reached this stage more than five months later.
“Any delay by BAM Ireland in handing over the NCHI beyond the 30 April target is untenable and would significantly disrupt downstream mobilisation and commissioning activities by Children’s Health Ireland (CHI),” her letter, obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, said.
“This is not a matter of mere inconvenience: such delays would impose considerable additional costs on the State, defer the commencement of critical clinical services in the new hospital, and prolong the elevated clinical risks to patients that the new facility is expressly designed to mitigate.”
A spokesman for the Department of Health said the main cause of delay has been “Bam’s failure to adequately manage and resource the project and maintain effective quality assurance processes in the delivery of the works”.
“There is no additional capital budget requirement and the revised budget of 2024 includes appropriate contingency to address legitimate claims on a project of this scale and complexity,” he said.
[ Complaints about doctors to the Medical Council were up 12% in 2025 Opens in new window ]
“However, the National Paediatric Hospital Development Board continues to robustly defend all claims considered to be without merit to protect the interests of the State.”
The spokesman said the additional costs arising from the delays are “primarily opportunity costs”.
“Delays to the completion of the NCHI has an opportunity cost to the healthcare service beyond financial concerns,” the spokesman said.
“The delays defer the clinical, operational and patient-centred benefits associated with the transition to a modern healthcare facility and prolong reliance on legacy infrastructure that is increasingly incapable of supporting the current requirements of our paediatric services.”
The spokesman said the delay to substantial completion has also delayed the operational commissioning phase.
“In order to reduce costs as much as possible, CHI has taken steps to streamline its commissioning team until such a time as the building is ready to be handed over,” he said.
“This reduction in the commissioning team includes releasing staff temporarily to other work within CHI and the Health Service Executive, holding vacancies, and building up the knowledge pool within the organisation so high-cost external specialists can be reduced.”
[ What is really going on in the Irish housing market? The numbers don’t add up Opens in new window ]
A spokesman for Bam said the project is in the “final stages of commissioning and certification”.
“The programme continues to be, and has always been, sufficiently resourced,” the spokesman said, adding that given the “late stage” of work, it is “entirely normal that there are fewer personnel on site”.
“BAM continues to work closely with the National Paediatric Hospital Development Board and Children’s Health Ireland to deliver the hospital as quickly and safely as possible for the children of Ireland,” he said.

title: Can the AA justify a 300% jump in travel insurance prices in under five years?
description: It really pays to keep an eye on your auto-renewal documentation. For years I  didn’t - and just look at how much it cost me
content:
I t’s not often that Pricewatch starts a reader query with our own experience, but we feel like we have no choice this week.
That is because what has just happened to us closely mirrors what has happened to several of our readers. We also have to highlight our story first, because the experiences that correspondents shared with us have just saved this page hundreds of euro.
Regular readers will know that we are big fans of travel insurance.
Well, truth be told, “fans” might be a stretch, but we have certainly highlighted the importance of travel insurance on many, many occasions and have always said it represents great value for money.
This is not, it has emerged, always the case, however.
In 2022, Pricewatch took out a multi-trip family travel insurance policy with AA Travel and paid what we considered to be a very reasonable €141.97 for cover for five people.
Luckily, we did not have to make any claims on the policy over the following 12 months, and when the auto-renewal time came round in October 2023 we stuck with the same company.
We did not notice that the cost of the same premium had climbed to €175.10, a jump of 23 per cent, but to be honest even if we had we are not sure we would have paid all that much attention to it. Decent cover for five people for a year for under 200 quid would have seemed like okay value for money.
Another 12 months passed, and again none of those on the policy had to make any claims – and again we let the auto-renewal do its thing.
[ Man paid about €400 on Booking.com for hotel that turned out to be closed Opens in new window ]
We are not proud to admit that we did not read the documentation when it was sent weeks in advance of the renewal kicking in, and as a result we did not know that the price of the same cover jumped this time to €265.54, an increase of 52 per cent on 12 months earlier.
In 2025, auto-renewal time rolled around again, and again we failed to go through the documentation that was sent to us. Yes, we are aware this displays a striking lack of Pricewatchiness (it is a word, look it up).
What we did notice was the money leaving our account. And how much was it this time? It was €374.83.
Now, bear in mind that in October 2022 the cost of the annual family policy with the AA was €141.97, so that was a hike of 164 per cent between October 2022 and October 2025. We are familiar with the impact of the cost-of-living crisis on us all, but even in such a context that increase seemed excessive.
Believe it or not, AA Travel were only getting started – but when renewal came around this year, we were ready.
[ Visitors arrive ‘almost daily’ at my house expecting to stay in tourist accommodation Opens in new window ]
We were ready, not just because of the €374 that left our account unexpectedly last year, but because of the experiences of readers – and we will get to them shortly.
Last week, the renewal notification came in again. And this time we did not ignore it.
The mail arrived on Monday with the “Travel renewal invite” in the subject field. We immediately opened it.
“As your annual AA Travel Insurance renewal date approaches, we’re here to remind you the peace of mind that comes with being protected wherever you go,” it began. “Whether it’s a spontaneous trip or a well-planned holiday, AA Travel Insurance has you covered with benefits designed to help you feel safe and secure at every step of your journey. Below is a summary of the comprehensive coverage your policy offers, giving you the confidence to travel with ease.”
‘I never intended to renew. The only notification went to a spam filter, so I only realised more than two weeks later when the money left my account’
In case you are wondering, the cover we were paying for included “as an extra treat ... access to an English-speaking GP abroad with the AA Virtual Doctor”. We also had cancellation or curtailment cover up to €6,000 and medical expenses up to an impressive-sounding €10 million.
All of this information and more was in the mail. But there was something missing.
We read through it carefully and could find no mention of the cost. We opened the attachment that was sent along with the invite, and there it was.
The cost of the policy for the next 12 months had jumped to €581.20.
Now, to save you doing the maths, that is a year-on-year increase of 55 per cent, and a jump of 309 per cent in just four years.
When we made it through to a human being, we said we wanted to talk about our travel insurance and he immediately assumed we were looking to cancel.
We think it is interesting that he was the first of us to mention the “c” word – and it suggests to us that such calls are not uncommon.
We talked about the mental – our word – jump in price, and explained that there was absolutely no way we could accept a rate of inflation of in excess of 300 per cent. There was no pushback, and the entirely pleasant call centre operative agreed to cancel the policy from the renewal date at the end of this month. He suggested that we might want to consider some single-trip policies in the short term.
[ ‘I assumed Complete Savings emails were junk but €18 a month was going out of my account’ Opens in new window ]
Then, for devilment, we went on to the AA website again and gave all the same details for the five people who are currently insured with the company, but supplied a different email address and intimated that we were a new rather than existing customer.
And how much do you think Pricewatch was quoted for a new multi-trip policy that includes cancellation and curtailment cover?
It was €148.29, or more than €400 less than they wanted to charge us as an existing customer who had made no claims at all over the past four years.
The reason why we were so on top of this business when the renewal mail landed is because of dear readers who got in touch with us to share strikingly similar stories.
“I am writing to flag an issue with AA Ireland travel insurance that I think may be of wider public interest,” begins the mail from Tom.
“My annual travel insurance policy was auto-renewed at €170, up from €117 last year – a 45 per cent increase for the same one-person cover,” he says.
“I never intended to renew. The only notification went to a spam filter, so I only realised more than two weeks later when the money left my account.”
He contacted the company to query the charge and was “told the 14-day cooling-off period had passed and there would be no refund. In other words: unless you proactively cancel, they can quietly hike your premium by almost 50 per cent and keep the money.”
He suggests that “€170 for a single-person annual policy is absurdly off-market – it’s not even close to what competitors charge. I suspect this practice could be affecting thousands of policyholders, many of whom will never spot it.”
[ ‘At my wits’ end’: Currys customer’s new fridge-freezer stopped working within days Opens in new window ]
And then there is Karl, who has a story that started a full decade ago when he took out a AA multi-trip annual travel insurance policy for his stepson for his 21st birthday.
Way back then, he paid the €40 or so that the policy cost on his credit card.
“I have the full details of the amounts deducted for the last nine years from my credit card with no policy changes to the original policy,” he says.
‘The increases arising from this control issue were not consistent with AA Ireland’s intended pricing approach and the company has put in place additional controls to ensure that this error will not be repeated’
Now, bearing in mind how much the policy cost a decade ago, how much do you think this year’s policy ended up costing Karl?
He says the AA came looking for €516. That amounts to a hike of more than 1,100 per cent in 10 years.
Like Pricewatch, Karl decided to price the policy as a new customer looking for the same benefits. “It has come in at €80.76,” he says.
“In my opinion, this raises a number of consumer issues. How does a 10-year loyal AA customer get charged circa 500 per cent more than a new customer for the same cover?
“How does AA justify a 1,000 per cent increase over 10 years for a policy that has no requested cover changes?”
Now, Karl acknowledges that his stepson “did not read the renewal emails sent out by the AA every year. He puts this down to the email subject ‘renewal invite’ and thought it was just an invitation and not automatic renewal”.
He also says that he “did not spot the charges on my credit card for a number of reasons. I was a member of the AA and did have car insurance policies over the years. I only identified the charges and investigated after I retired and had the time. When I spotted this earlier this year I did make contact with the AA customer service, but due to the policy being in my stepson’s name with the charge going to my credit card, they were not interested in our queries, relying on the fact that they send out renewal emails every year. They would not respond to any of our queries.”
He says he has not been able to prove or disprove “whether we ticked a box saying automatic renewal, due to the length of time since the original policy was taken out and information available online. AA would not provide confirmation.”
We contacted the AA in connection with this episode, and received a statement that is so remarkable that we shall carry it in full.
“AA Ireland is aware of an internal pricing control issue affecting the renewal of travel insurance for some customers and is working to rectify it.
“During the renewal process, 213 customers were inadvertently overcharged.
“This resulted in those customers receiving renewal premiums that were higher, or in some cases significantly higher, than they should have been.
“AA Ireland has completed a comprehensive review and has identified the impacted customers. We are in the process of contacting those customers, who renewed at an incorrect premium, and we have started the process to refund them automatically.
“Impacted customers will be notified directly, and no action will be required on the customer’s part.
“The increases arising from this control issue were not consistent with AA Ireland’s intended pricing approach and the company has put in place additional controls to ensure that this error will not be repeated.
“AA Ireland would like to again apologise and will always fully investigate any cases brought to its attention.”

title: How much protein should I eat in a day?
description: Q&A: Protein bars. Protein ice cream. Protein yoghurts. High-protein cheese ... but does the Irish public really need all of this protein-enriched food?
content:
A visit to an Irish supermarket in recent years shows a clear trend. Protein wraps. Protein ice cream. Protein yoghurts. High-protein cheese. The list goes on. But does the Irish public really need all of this protein-enriched food?
Protein is one of the main nutrients in food, alongside carbohydrates and fats.
The nutrient builds and supports damaged muscles, organs, skin, hair and nails using smaller units called amino acids.
It’s driven by a number of trends, according to nutritionists and dietitians, but social media is a big factor.
Online fitness and wellness influencers consistently tout protein as being an excellent tool in fat loss.
They maintain that higher-protein foods keep people feeling fuller for longer, reducing snacking and enabling people to more easily stay within their calorie deficit.
That largely depends on your activity level, age and weight.
The recommended daily intake for the population in general is 0.8g of protein per kilogramme of body weight, so somebody weighing 60kg would need 48g.
[ Protein: Are we eating enough of it? And is ‘high protein’ branding just a fad? Opens in new window ]
Those who do a lot of exercise or strength training would have higher protein requirements.
In a set of updated scientific recommendations for food-based dietary guidelines for older adults published in 2021, the Food Safety Authority of Ireland said healthy older adults should consume a more protein-dense diet than the general adult population.
It recommended that older adults at risk of frailty, sarcopenia and undernutrition eat a minimum of 1–1.2g of protein per kilogramme of body weight each day to preserve muscle mass.
Research would suggest yes. The National Adult Nutrition Survey II, published in 2024, found Irish adults got 18 per cent of their total energy from protein.
And this is a worldwide phenomenon. The US is also witnessing this explosion in protein products, but a government report found nearly 90 percent of Americans have enough protein in their diets.
Safefood research from 2019 found that the way these products were being marketed would lead people to believe they were healthy alternatives.
However, 77 per cent of the high-protein bars surveyed were high in saturated fat and a source of added salt and sugar, while high-protein yoghurts and quark, dairy drinks and smoothies surveyed were a source of added salt and sugar.
If company accounts are anything to go by, protein’s marketing success is undeniable.
Kilkenny-based nutrition group Glanbia reported a 7 per cent jump in revenue for the first six months of the year, which included a 25 per cent spike in demand for its premium protein powder product, Optimum Nutrition.

title: Changing the world of organ transplants while fearing he could die waiting for one
description: Dr Robert Montgomery pioneered the use of pig organ transplants – after his time on waiting list led to heart surgery in clinical trial
content:
The first time he went into cardiac arrest and died, briefly, Dr Robert Montgomery was hiking in Patagonia, near the southernmost tip of South America. He felt his heart racing as he lagged behind his son John and their guide.
Then he collapsed, face down into the snow.
Seconds passed before a medical device implanted in his chest delivered a shock that restored his heartbeat and saved his life.
It was 2010, and Montgomery, then 50, recovered quickly. But it was becoming painfully clear he needed a new heart. The one he was born with was failing.
The odds of him getting a heart transplant were grim and Montgomery knew this because he was a transplant surgeon himself.
In Ireland, there are approximately 660 people currently waiting for an organ transplant. Earlier this year The Irish Times reported that most were on the waiting list for a kidney transplant, with approximately 100 on the list for other organs. Of these, six patients were waiting for a heart transplant.
At the time of his Argentina trip, Montgomery was leading one of America’s premier organ transplant centres, at Johns Hopkins Medicine.
As a child, Montgomery wanted to be a veterinarian. It was only when, at age 14, his father developed symptoms of dilated cardiomyopathy that he reconsidered. The rare disease causes the heart’s chambers to stretch and enlarge and can lead to heart failure, irregular heart beats or arrhythmias, cardiac arrest and sudden death. His father became increasingly debilitated and eventually needed a feeding tube after suffering brain damage from a cardiac arrest.
[ People ‘My youngest child will probably be bearded before the national children’s hospital opens’ Opens in new window ]
By the time his father died in 1976, Montgomery, then 16, had decided to become a doctor. Eleven years later, he had just started a surgical residency at Johns Hopkins Medicine when he got the worst phone call of his life. His brother Rich, a 35-year-old father of two, had died that morning.
Pathologists discovered that Rich also had dilated cardiomyopathy, likely caused by a genetic mutation. Robert was evaluated and learned he had the condition too.
Suddenly, his career was in doubt. Surgical training was gruelling, and a cardiac arrest or fainting episode could endanger patients.
When medication failed to keep his arrhythmia in check, Montgomery opted for a new medical device called an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, or ICD, that could shock the heart back into a normal rhythm.
Unsure if he could complete his residency, Montgomery and his wife at the time moved to England so he could study immunology. He decided to pursue a doctorate, just in case surgery didn’t work out.
Montgomery returned to Johns Hopkins in 1992. He wanted to specialise in transplant surgery. His own illness was a motivator. “I didn’t think I would live a normal lifespan – I knew I would need a heart transplant or I would die – so I was in a hurry, and I was hyperfocused.”
[ Irish Guide Dogs at 50: ‘He made the difference of being able to leave the house or not’ Opens in new window ]
So few heart transplants were done in the early 1990s that becoming a full-time heart transplant surgeon wasn’t an option. Montgomery focused on kidneys, the most commonly transplanted organ. At Hopkins, he helped develop a minimally invasive surgical technique for retrieving kidneys from healthy living donors, which doctors hoped would lead more people to donate a kidney. It did. Over the next few years, “we transplanted all the kids on our paediatric list”, Montgomery said.
In 2001, realising he could increase the number of patients who got an organ if kidneys were swapped between incompatible, donor-recipient pairs, Montgomery started a programme to do just that. Soon, he and his team were doing domino donations. An altruistic donor gave a kidney to a stranger, whose nonmatching donor gave a kidney to a second recipient and so on. “He was seen as a bit of a cowboy,” said Brigitte Sullivan, the transplant administrator who Montgomery described as his “fellow visionary”.
In 2016, NYU Langone Health recruited Montgomery to build an organ transplant programme, and he moved to Manhattan with his wife, opera singer Denyce Graves, and their daughter (Montgomery also has three children from previous relationships; his first marriage ended in divorce). He had met Graves on a flight to Paris. By the time the plane landed, she had invited him to hear her sing and he had invited her to watch him operate.
Despite his earlier near-death experience in Patagonia, Montgomery returned to the same spot in 2017. He wanted to spend time with his sons John and Max, but he went into cardiac arrest again. The closest hospital was nearly an hour away and John did chest compressions on him in a Jeep as they raced to it.
When he emerged from a medically induced coma more than a month later in New York, where he had been flown, Montgomery had to learn to walk, talk and eat again. “As I was having more of these near-death experiences, it became really clear to me that the likelihood of me getting a heart transplant was less than of me dying before I got on the list,” he said.
A few months later, his heart stopped in the middle of the Broadway show, School of Rock. He received CPR in the aisle. At a medical conference in Italy, in September 2018, he experienced four cardiac arrests, one after another.
The upside, he realised, was that he was now so sick he could finally join the waiting list for a heart.
[ A mother stalking her 19-year-old online is demented – but not in the way you think Opens in new window ]
Just before dawn on September 20th, 2018, he got a call that a heart was available – if he wanted it. The donor, who had died of a heroin overdose, was infected with hepatitis C.
There was reason for pause. The hospital’s heart transplant programme was brand-new; Montgomery had started it less than a year earlier. And transplants with hepatitis C-positive hearts were so novel that he would be part of a clinical trial if he received one.
“A lot of my colleagues thought I was crazy,” Montgomery said. But he believed in the programme and had encouraged his own patients to consider organs with hepatitis C, which could be cured with medication. “So why not me?” he said.
After a six-hour surgery, Montgomery had a new heart. Two days after the operation, he was sitting up in bed, reviewing cases.
After his experience, Montgomery began to see all the work he had done to find more viable organs as insufficient. “It’s never going to be able to provide enough organs for people with organ failure,” he said.
It was time for a radical move. Experiments had proved that organs from genetically modified pigs could be transplanted into monkeys. The next step was to build a case for transplants to humans. Montgomery decided to try it first in a patient who was brain-dead, something that had never been attempted.
In 2021, Montgomery announced he had for the first time transplanted a kidney from a genetically modified pig into a human. Scientists at United Therapeutics, which produced the pig, had knocked out a gene involved in an aggressive organ rejection response. Not only was the kidney not rejected, but it functioned, making urine and excreting waste for 54 hours, the limit set by a hospital ethics panel.
Over the next few years, Montgomery’s team and others in Maryland and Boston transplanted pig kidneys and hearts into a small number of living patients who were terminally ill and had exhausted other treatment options.
The patients died of underlying conditions within months, but none of them mounted the kind of devastating immune rejection that destroys an organ – a major accomplishment that showed that pig organs could be transplanted safely and function properly in humans.
Last year, the Food and Drug Administration in the United States gave a green light to clinical trials of pig organ transplants in very ill patients who aren’t likely to get a kidney any other way. Montgomery is leading two of them.
Since his surgery, he has gone salmon fishing in Alaska with his son John, travelled to Africa with Graves to celebrate her retirement and assisted kidney surgeons in Ukraine.
Every morning, to protect his new heart, he walks 3km to work. He sets out before 6am, to make it in time for patient rounds. – This article originally appeared in the New York Times

title: I want to add a dormer attic to my home. What do I need to know?
description: I’ve looked at the new planning exemptions, but am not sure if I fully understand them
content:
I have a question on the Government’s new planning exemption regulations. I am interested in building a dormer attic. On review of the new legislation, it looks like I can build a gable-to-gable dormer attic once I have the 20cm eaves setback and the attic is less than 30 cubic metres. Am I correct in this? I ideally want to turn all of my attic into a dormer (gable-to-gable).
This aspect of the legislation is becoming a very hot topic, and you have picked up on the main requirements. The new Class 1B exemption, introduced by statutory instrument (SI No 344 of 2026) and effective from July 27th, 2026, covers dormer roof extensions and dormer windows to the side or rear of a house. It sets out two conditions: the internal volume must not exceed 30 cubic metres, including other dormer roof extensions, and the dormer must be no higher than the existing roof ridge, with at least a 20cm eaves setback.
However, it is important that your proposal is reviewed in the round. It would be advisable to carry out an examination of the proposed drawings and the property’s planning history before confirming that your particular design is exempt.
A review of the drawings would help identify whether the roof has already been altered – whether the roof was raised or the pitch changed when first built, or subsequently, for instance. A planning search would discover whether the conditions of the grant of permission for the house specifically restricts additional windows or alterations to the roof.
There is also the cumulative rule. The 30-cubic-metre allowance applies to the proposed dormer in combination with other dormer roof extensions. Previous permissions and drawings can help establish what already exists and how much of the allowance remains.
One clarification is that the 30-cubic-metre limit relates to the dormer development, rather than the volume of your entire existing attic.
If you encounter any of these planning or construction issues, or if you have any qualms at all before starting construction, the way forward is to engage with your local planning office by way of a Section 5 Declaration. This submission will allow the local authority to determine whether your planned development is exempt or otherwise. The application form may be downloaded from the local authority’s website.
[ There is damp in our attic following an insulation upgrade. Am I right to be concerned? Opens in new window ]
If you are converting your attic, it is always advisable to get an experienced, qualified, insured designer. A good set of drawings will clearly show the dormer’s width, depth, height, relationship to the ridge and eaves, an internal volume calculation, and location of the stairs. Most importantly, the designer will generate construction drawings that will inform the builder of all requirements in your case, but also allow all interested builders you may be talking to to price for the exact same thing.
[ Bigger extensions, dormers, subdivided homes, bike sheds: What planning changes are coming? Opens in new window ]
Finally, planning exemption does not remove the need to comply with building regulations. Your construction drawings should address structural support, fire safety and escape, stair access, insulation, and ventilation regulations, particularly if the attic will become a bedroom or another habitable room. It is also important to note that exemptions do not apply to protected structures.
Brigid Browne is a chartered building surveyor and a member of the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland
