title: Replacing beef farming with forestry would boost incomes and help meet climate goals
description: Afforestation is the most significant climate change mitigation option available to Ireland’s land use sector
content:
In the early years after Independence, virtually no afforestation was undertaken in Ireland. Public funds were in scarce supply and subsistence farming was still prevalent in much of the country, and that pattern more or less continued for the next two decades because, as one government minister stated some time later, putting trees in the ground would not put more food on the table.
Years after the second World War , it dawned on the Government how dwindled timber stocks and forests had become, and despite considerable pressure being exerted within government not to support afforestation, a defined forest policy was established and actively promoted. However, as before, only poorer quality land could be afforded for planting. Until the mid-’80s, afforestation progressed, occasionally reaching an additional 9,000 hectares annually, and it was undertaken almost exclusively by the State.
Even as public afforestation was gaining a foothold, private planting was minimal, having a negative image and receiving little or no State support.
Then in the mid-’80s forestry was identified as having the potential to make a major contribution to national economic and regional development and rural incomes, and generous grants and annual premiums were provided by the State and EU.
Subsequently, afforestation trebled between 1987 and 1995, with private planting exceeding public planting for the first time in 1989.
Planting held up reasonably well in the decade after 1995, at an average of 13,000 hectares each year, but levels of planting have largely gone downhill ever since. In the past decade, new planting has averaged 3,800 hectares annually.
Afforestation in 2023 and 2024 was at its lowest level since the 1920s. Over the past 40 years a succession of ambitious planting targets were established, but all were missed by a wide margin.
The surge in private planting from the late ’80s would initially have occurred on the least intensively farmed land. Thereafter, it would have moved on to progressively better land. That would partially explain the very high planting early on.
While there are possibly many reasons for the general downward trend in planting since the mid-’90s, it began with the changed character of the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy (Cap) .
Cap shifted from price and market supports to restrictive measures on output, strengthening rural development and environmental policies and direct payments.
[ Does Ireland have the will to undo the disaster of plantation forestry? Opens in new window ]
The pattern of land use is now facing substantial pushback due to environmental pressures, and in consequence we have reached if not surpassed peak intensity in grassland utilisation. From here, there will be increased pressure on land use due to enterprises such as anaerobic digestion, while sectors such as solar panels and onshore wind turbines are also likely to show significant development.
The Cap Strategic Plan 2023-2027 also includes two heavily funded environmental measures heralding a new era addressing biodiversity, environmental issues, water quality and climate objectives, and increasingly offering rewards for alternative land uses that were not hitherto available. These schemes have attracted a high rate of participation from farmers and pose a real challenge for forestry.
Afforestation is the most significant climate change mitigation option that is available to Ireland’s land use sector, and is an essential and recognised factor to reaching net zero carbon dioxide emissions by 2050.
The rate of afforestation depends not only on the incentives available but also on such factors as awareness levels, promotion activities and technical support systems
So, from a future perspective, any increase in forestry planting is most likely to come from the cohort of 80,000 or so beef cattle enterprises. The great majority of those involved have the lowest incomes, are older than average, at least half of them have off-farm jobs and they have lesser levels of contact with support services.
The replacement of beef farming with forestry is a win-win action. It increases farm income, reduces GHG emissions, and significantly increases carbon sequestration. There also tends to be a prevalent negative attitude to forestry from this group, ranging from perceptions that forestry is inimical to agricultural development, to it being responsible for rural depopulation, social isolation and the limiting of land-use options.
Consideration must now focus on the shape of and ambition for the next Irish afforestation programme. It is now Government policy to expand forest cover from the current 11 per cent or so of the land area of the country to 18 per cent, but based on achievements over recent decades we will be waiting a long time to reach this target.
[ ‘Our purpose is to manage the State’s forests on behalf of the people of Ireland’ Opens in new window ]
The rate of afforestation depends not only on the incentives available but also on such factors as awareness levels, promotion activities and technical support systems. At a policy level, it is necessary to adopt an integrated approach in designing land-use schemes including forestry so as to achieve compatibility and complementability between the respective measures in the next national Rural Development Programme.
The role of forestry needs to be more strongly promoted across Government, and the sector’s role in adjusting to climate change and in terms of rural development given greater emphasis. The development of knowledge transfer groups representative of the relevant stakeholders or perhaps some form of European Innovation Partnerships could play a useful role in changing attitudes towards forestry. Meanwhile, every effort must be made to reach out to those particular landholders who are the most likely target category for forestry but who are the least likely to have contact with farm support services.
Finally, it could be an opportune time to establish a national forum of the respective interests such as existed in the mid-’90s, to identify the factors impeding more rapid adoption of farm forestry and how these might be addressed.
Brendan Kearney, an economic consultant, was formerly assistant director of An Foras Talú ntais, now Teagasc

title: Rising debt burden poses threat to economic growth
description: Ireland and the other ‘PIIGS’ find themselves in a better position than the US, UK and France
content:
Ireland has had a lot of experience of public debt crises. But right now, our main problem is poor management of the exchequer’s abundant, though vulnerable, resources. This compares with other major economies, where the scale and growth of public debt looms large and is a major challenge for governments.
In the UK, France and the US, government debt exceeds 100 per cent of national income. The sustainability of their public finances is posing major political challenges.
We will see this month how the UK government proposes to square the circle of political ambition and fiscal prudence. In France, the absence of a government majority in parliament may prevent any resolution, at least until after next year’s presidential election. As for the US, thus far it is ignoring the problem, as its fiscal situation deteriorates.
We know from Ireland’s debt crises in the 1980s, and again from 2008 to 2013, that once the debt burden exceeds 100 per cent of national income, there can be no resolution without serious pain.
By 1987, our debt interest payments were absorbing 10 per cent of national income, and 20 per cent of all government expenditure. The rapid growth in these outlays over the 1980s squeezed resources for government services, and also necessitated extremely high taxes. Together that made a recipe for national misery.
Reversing the rise in indebtedness proved very painful, and took most of that decade.
Although Ireland’s national debt in the wake of the 2008 financial crash peaked at more than 160 per cent of national income, higher than in the 1980s, the burden of debt proved much more manageable.
This was due to the assistance of the bailout, and a much lower external interest rate environment in its aftermath. While the necessary austerity was very painful, it only lasted four years, not a decade. Debt interest payments peaked in 2012 at less than 6 per cent of national income, and nearly 10 per cent of government expenditure.
With a rapid economic recovery, and low interest rates internationally, our indebtedness fell dramatically. Today, government interest payments account for only 2 per cent of Ireland’s national income, and almost half of that cost is covered by interest income from the Government’s investments.
Ripping the plaster off slowly in the 1980s was more painful. A lesson from the Irish experience over both debt crises is that the faster action is taken, the less damage there will be to the economy and society. The EU and IMF, which lent us large sums, also pressed for faster action in the more recent debt crisis.
Right now, the external environment has turned nasty for governments needing to borrow. Interest rates have been driven up by the huge scale of financing needed by governments, especially the US, alongside giant borrowings to fund the AI investment splurge, and by rising inflation linked to oil and gas.
[ Grafton chief bets on ‘PIIGS’ boom as northern European markets stall Opens in new window ]
Interest rates could well climb further if major economies cannot bring their public finances under control and if the energy crisis is not resolved.
However, interest rates in Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Greece have risen more modestly over the last three years than in countries with major fiscal problems such as France and the UK. We the “PIIGS” [Portugal, Italy , Ireland , Greece and Spain] dealt with our debt problems a decade ago. Today, Ireland can borrow at rates very close to those of Germany, reflecting a very similar levels of indebtedness.
The US is particularly exposed, because much more of their debt is short-term, unlike most European countries, which will only need to refinance 20-30 per cent of their national debt in the coming five years
Between now and 2030, we will have to refinance 30 per cent of our national debt at today’s higher interest rates. While this will mean some rise in interest payments, the change won’t be very significant. Moreover, some of the extra cost should be offset by a higher return on government financial investments.
For the UK (whose interest bill is already 3.4 per cent of national income) and for the US (paying interest amounting to 4.8 per cent of national income), the cost of refinancing at today’s higher interest rates will add to their budgetary problems.
[ Greece is Ireland. Ireland is Greece Opens in new window ]
The US is particularly exposed, because much more of their debt is short-term, unlike most European countries, which will only need to refinance 20-30 per cent of their national debt in the coming five years. The high interest rates needed to dampen US inflation will hit their public finances hard.
The US president has floated a $5,000 cash inducement for all if the Republicans win the midterms. Meanwhile, in the real world, higher debt payments will squeeze resources in the UK and France for social services, health and defence, unless taxes are raised.
If public debt continues to climb, interest rates will again ratchet up. That will slow down growth in the private sector, limiting any growth dividend to spend on public services, and stifle the housing market.
Ireland’s Minister for Finance has it far luckier than his international peers.

title: Sandymount Hotel’s John Loughran: ‘I don’t see this as an asset that you flip’
description: John Loughran on passing the baton at the Sandymount Hotel to a new generation
content:
A third generation of the Loughran family has taken over the running of the Sandymount Hotel in Dublin 4 , 71 years after its doors were first opened to guests.
Recently filed accounts for Mount Herbert Ltd and its parent company, Loughran Investments, reveal that hotel director Gerard Loughran has taken ownership of the ordinary shares in the business from his father, John Loughran, who retired last year.
In a 2025 restructuring of the company behind the 190-bedroom hotel, two of Gerard Loughran’s three siblings – Oisín and Sinéad – were also issued a new class of preference shares in the business.
[ Budget 2027: All you need to know Opens in new window ]
Speaking to The Irish Times, John Loughran said there are no voting rights attached to the preference shares and Gerard, who has worked in the hotel for 20 years, is “free to run the business as he sees fit”. John is also retaining some preference shares in the company “in the event I need a few bob in the future”, he said.
Mount Herbert Ltd has also acquired one of the hotel’s eight buildings from John Loughran’s wife, Audrey Loughran, for about €5.7 million, according to the filings.
John Loughran said the proceeds were used to pay taxes associated with the transfer of the business – including capital gains tax, capital acquisitions tax (CAT) and stamp duty – in the order of about €4.5 million. He said the company, which had accumulated profits of more than €13 million by the end of last year, was in a “fortunate” position.
Formerly called the Mount Herbert Hotel before being renamed in 2011, the property sits about 200m from the Aviva Stadium. It comprises eight Victorian buildings, which were first converted into a four-bedroom hotel by John Loughran’s Tyrone-born parents, Gerard and Rosaleen, in 1955.
John and his brother Paul inherited the business before John bought out his sibling’s shareholding in 1999. He has stewarded the business through difficult times, including the post-2008 property crash and financial crisis, narrowly avoiding the appointment of receivers to the hotel.
However, Loughran said that when it came time to pass the torch to his children, the process was anything but smooth.
“I was coming up to my 66th birthday in 2021,” he said. “There were Government incentives to transition a family business where you got business relief [for CAT], and you got retirement relief [for CGT] if you transition the business before you are 66.”
At the time, there was a €3 million cap on the value of business assets that could be transferred within families tax-free for those aged 66 or older.
[ ‘You might have five stars but it will be soulless if there is no connection with the staff’ Opens in new window ]
“Then Covid hit, and it was off the table, so the window of opportunity had passed,” he said.
Loughran said he contacted the Department of Finance in 2024 to lobby for an extension of the retirement age, which led to a meeting with officials. “I said my business is going to go to foreign ownership, when it could remain an Irish family-owned and run business because there won’t be an Irish buyer for this hotel,” he recalled.
Due to its reputation and prime location, the hotel has had countless suitors over the years, Loughran said, including some “big offers”. However, he said that he felt he had a duty to his “legacy staff” – the longest-serving of whom has been with the business for 46 years – to maintain family control.
“I don’t see this – and Gerard would be of the same view – as an asset that you flip,” he said. “It is the livelihoods of 130 people.”
In Budget 2025, the Government moved to raise the age at which the €3 million cap applies from 66 to 70. The reforms came into effect in January 2025, giving the Loughrans five months to complete the transfer before John’s 70th birthday that May.
“The fact that I had a motorbike accident in February and was off the page for a month didn’t help things,” he said. “But anyway, we just about got it done.”
Loughran said that due to inheritance tax rules, Gerard is “handcuffed” to the business for 12 years, meaning it will “remain an Irish family-owned and run business” for years to come.
Even with the changes to the CGT regime, the experience of dividing a family business was challenging, Loughran said, and costly. “Whereas other countries recognise the value of family-owned businesses and have policies and tax incentives to support them, that’s not really the case in Ireland,” he said.
Still, Loughran said the hotel is lucky to have traded well in 2025 and into 2026. Mount Herbert Ltd reported turnover of €9.8 million in 2025, up by about 5 per cent year-on-year. The company also swung to an almost €1.4 million profit last year from a loss of close to €688,000 in 2024.
He put the turnaround down to a sizeable drop in administrative costs related to pension transfers that were conducted in 2024, which dragged on the hotel’s bottom line in that year.
“The other big cost, which won’t be there in 2026, is probably close to €200,000 of professional fees,” which were paid to three different advisory firms in the run-up to the transition. “I was paying handsomely for three conflicting opinions,” Loughran said.
“So the business as it sits now and moves forward into the next generation is in a strong place,” he added. “It’s debt-free. I suppose I learned my lessons from the financial crash.”

title: Alice Cooper’s new book lacks bite, but the definitive story of The Shadows is masterful
description: Plus an enlightening overview of Ultravox and the fickleness of fame, and an eloquent broadside against the US country music industry
content:
Never say die and all of that, but does a third autobiography from the man dubbed the Godfather of Shock Rock stretch a tall tale to breaking point? Devil on My Shoulder: A Memoir by Alice Cooper (Ebury Spotlight, 464pp, £25) does its best to shove a narrative salad around a large plate, but ends up being too familiar and too sparse.
Written by Cooper (real name Vincent Furnier) to, he says, trace his “evilution” and to unravel the “embellishments, elaborations and outright fabrications” he has admitted to throughout his 60-plus-year career, there is a sense here of a last-gasp appeasement towards a dwindling fan base. “For much of my time on Earth I’ve rarely allowed facts to get in the way of a good story,” he writes, setting the tone.
There is a wealth of name-dropping – all the way from Frank Zappa, John Lennon, Bette Davis, Groucho Marx, Vincent Price and Frank Sinatra to his golfing buddy Tiger Woods – and his career highlights are well covered. Overall, though, Cooper covers old ground with falling autumn leaves. More than two-thirds of the book details events from his birth in the late 1940s to his 1970s heyday; the remainder, as with most celebrity memoirs, hastily rakes subsequent decades into a tidy heap of information.
Rather more substantive is the first authoritative biography of an instrumental group that from 1958 to 1968 racked up 49 Top 20 hits in the British pop charts. The Shadows: The Definitive Story by Bob Stanley (New Modern, 352pp, £25) is a masterful telling of the story of one of the most successful and influential pop groups of all time.
Too obscure, perhaps, for contemporary music fans to want to investigate but dedicated pop historians will lap up Stanley’s thoroughly detailed rags-to-riches account of the group that would become the original blueprint for a post-second World War teenage upheaval. “They would revolutionise and rebuild British popular music,” writes Stanley. The Shadows, with and without their singer, Cliff Richard , “were a national soundtrack, cajoling a country to emerge from the rubble”.
From the group’s origins in Newcastle-upon-Tyne and their Sliding Doors-style lives with The Beatles (the members of each group were the same age) to their later career dip playing their hit songs whether they liked to or not (“they would never shake the dust of The Shadows from their clothes”), Stanley documents the halcyon days and fallow periods, full of relevant information as well as previously unknown nuggets, with his customary poise.
[ ‘It was tribal and sexual’: Alice Cooper on the debauchery of Detroit rock Opens in new window ]
There was poise aplenty, too, in the early music of Ultravox, who formed in London in 1974, but if there is ever a group unjustifiably defined by one song, then it is the batch of misfits who pioneered the use of drum machines in pop music. The defining song is, of course, Vienna, which arrived in all its monochrome splendour in 1980.
As the highly informative Looking Backwards Towards the Future: The Story of Ultravox by Richard Evans (Omnibus Press, 400pp, £25) recounts, however, there was much more to the band than their most successful song. What has been forgotten by all but their most committed fan base are the group’s before-and-after editions, the first of which (1974-79) was driven by a sleek hybrid of art-school ideas and glam rock.
Pre- and post-fame is smartly detailed, from an art-school project devised by coalminer’s son Dennis Leigh (who would change his name to John Foxx) to a more streamlined hit-making machine spearheaded by Midge Ure (who would go on to co-write, with Bob Geldof, Band Aid’s all-conquering song Do They Know It’s Christmas?).
[ Bob Geldof: ‘I never read about myself. I can’t stand the stupid f**king things I say’ Opens in new window ]
The hits didn’t last, of course, but for an enlightening overview of one of Britain’s less celebrated pop acts of the 1980s, and how fame can be fickle and fleeting, this book is invaluable.
Pursuing a music career in the male-dominated area of country music has, perhaps, been viewed through a sharper lens since the recent death of Dolly Parton. Reissued in paperback, Her Country: How Women Reclaimed Country Music by Marissa R. Moss (Omnibus Press, 320pp, £14.99) is an eloquent and righteous broadside against a US country music industry where, writes Moss, “you can be penalised for speaking your truth in a genre that is supposed to be built on it”.
Primarily, Moss uses the background stories of three Texas songwriters/performers (Mickey Guyton, Maren Morris and Kacey Musgraves) as a sometimes shocking primer for too many other females who “never made it to Nashville, never felt welcomed because of the colour of their skin or who they loved or the language they were born speaking, or who left the industry because of sexual harassment or abuse”.
[ https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/music/rock-memoirs-worth-their-salt-1.2178412 Opens in new window ]
In full activist-journalist mode, Moss, who also weaves in second-tier stories with artists such as Margo Price, Patty Griffin and Mindy Smith, pulls zero punches. She is justifiably critical about genre-formatted radio and how, despite breaching the borders of the genre, female singers and songwriters receive backhanded compliments and little support. Essential reading.
Compiled and curated by Olivia Harrison, with essays by Irish author Colm Tóibín (a former chancellor of the University of Liverpool) and Booker Prize-winning US writer George Saunders, The Third Eye by George Harrison (Ebury Spotlight, 352pp, £45) is equal parts coffee-table design, enthusiastic amateur snaps and a chronicle of a paradigm shift in pop culture.
Of more than 200 images taken from 1963 to 1969, on Harrison’s Pentax SV and 8mm film cameras, while professional techniques are absent, many are superb. On-the-road and off-duty shots of his bandmates dominate, with their relaxed nature presenting the level of close-up intimacy you get when the photographer is a trusted part of the inner circle. Inevitably, some images don’t have the same impact (“His camera etiquette was non-existent,” notes his widow) but as the years progress, Harrison’s skills assuredly improve. The real visual treats arrive when monochrome turns into colour, with the tranche of images taken in India in 1966 being particularly good.

title: In a Word... Curse
description: Mayo’s infamous All-Ireland ‘curse’ that never was is not forgotten, you know
content:
No doubt you’ve heard the story about the old Irish woman who, when asked whether she believed in fairies, said: “Ah, the Little People. I don’t believe in them – but it doesn’t mean they’re not there.”
That, clearly, is the view of Mayo ’s All-Ireland senior footballers, who ended a 75-year famine for their county in glorious fashion last July to win the Sam Maguire. It followed 13 heartbreaking near misses [including two All-Ireland replays] since 1989. Lucky 14th, therefore.
The celebrations continue since, with those generous young men bringing Sam to every school and club in the county, Electric Picnic, the Ploughing, and – bravely – Corduff in west Dublin.
Yet, the infamous “curse” is not forgotten. You will recall how it was alleged that the last All-Ireland winning Mayo team, of 1951, was cursed by the parish priest in Foxford after it failed to pay due respects to a passing funeral. The priest – allegedly – pronounced that Mayo would never win another All-Ireland as long as any member of that 1951 team lived.
In 2013, current Foxford parish priest Fr Padraig Costello, a fine footballer in his day who has always dismissed the “curse”, gave that year’s Mayo team an official blessing at the exact spot on the bridge over the river Moy in the town where it was – allegedly – imposed.
However, Mayo continued to lose All Irelands afterwards – six times, including a replay, up to now.
That included the All-Ireland final of September 11th, 2021. The last member of the 1951 Mayo All-Ireland team died two weeks later, on September 25th, 2021. This year’s All Ireland final was the first Mayo played in since 2021.
Meanwhile, the current, successful, Mayo All-Ireland team are taking no chances. On Monday, July 27th, the day after their victory in Croke Park, they returned home to Castlebar by train, bypassing Foxford. Yes, they visited that town eventually, symbolically carrying Sam across the bridge there.
But when the team, on its county tour, met a funeral in the village of Balla, between Claremorris and Castlebar, the coach driver stopped suddenly, followed by a spontaneous silence on board, until the funeral passed.
[ UK prime minister to Taoiseach: Any chance of All-Ireland final tickets? Opens in new window ]
Of course there was no curse – but that doesn’t mean it didn’t happen.
Curse, from Old English curs for “prayer that evil should befall one”.

title: Heimir Hallgrímsson: ‘When you are lying on the ground you can see who is kicking you’
description: Ireland manager hopes Finn Azaz and Gavin Bazunu will remain key players in Ireland squad
content:
“Political or non-related questions about the football match will not be entertained,” stated Uefa ’s head of communications Brian Orsini before Heimir Hallgrímsson ’s press conference after Ireland ’s 1-1 draw in Backa Topola against Israel. The Uefa official flew into Serbia following heated scenes at the Irish press conference on Saturday.
His presence seemed to have the desired effect, as all was calm in the briefing.
“It felt like a friendly,” said Hallgrímsson. “There were no people watching. There was no spark, especially for players playing their fourth game [in 10 days].
“Six international flights, playing in four countries, and all the things that have been going on ... We needed the same spark that we got in the Aviva for the Austria game.”
Clearly, the high of last Thursday’s 2-2 draw against Austria in front 45,000 fans in Dublin could not be replicated inside an empty stadium.
Hallgrímsson repeated his praise of two Ireland players in particular, Gavin Bazunu and Finn Azaz, although neither played in Serbia. Bazunu opted not to line out against Israel, while Hallgrímsson decided not to play Azaz in either game.
“With Finn, we spoke a lot together. It was just tough on him. I could feel it when I spoke to him. It was tough for him that we were wearing black armbands. It was tough on him that we looked down when the national anthem was sung. It tested him more than all of us. I just felt it was better to leave him out today than play him.”
Hallgrímsson intends to select both players in the Ireland squad next month against Austria and at Euro 2028.
“I surely hope so,” Hallgrímsson said when asked if concerns about Azaz’s international future have been allayed. “I have not asked. He wants to be with us in Euro 2028.”
Hallgrímsson’s nature is to find the positive from every situation. Sure enough, he highlighted the appointment of Gerard Perry, a clinical psychologist and former referee, since last week’s 3-0 defeat of Israel in Debrecen.
“One hundred per cent, this team is stronger for what we’ve come through,” he added. “The bond between players has grown so much.
“Leaders are born in tough times, when the true characters step up. In these times, you find your true friends who you want to work with in the future.
“Even though it was tough on us, I think we will look back on these two weeks as a defining moment. Every problem from now on will seem lesser. That is the gain from all this, we need to look at it positively, this negative two weeks.
“This is also the time to find your enemies. When you are lying on the ground you can see who is kicking you.”
Hallgrímsson noted that the leaking of information to the media from within the Ireland camp, mainly in Hungary last week, is something that must be identified and stopped in the future.
“We can definitely fix our systems. There was a lot of leakage of information. A closed vote was in the papers in real time. We don’t want to go to the Euros with my team in the papers before we pick it.
“It’s about finding your friends, and your enemies, and to get them away. There is a lot of opportunities from this.”
He added: “I’ve been fresher. It’s been tough. I’ve learned a lot myself, personally, in these two weeks. I learned not to mix my feelings, my emotions as a person into me as a leader, as a spokesman for the association. It was difficult sometimes.
“At the beginning, I shouldn’t have told you where I stand about what is happening in Gaza, that was a mistake. My opinion and feelings should be set aside as a leader of a group.
“I normally journal, so there is a lot to read when I’ve some time off.
“I’m absolutely delighted the window is finished. Credit to the players, they were amazing. I wish that no international team goes through the tough times we have experienced.”

title: US withdraws bombers from RAF Fairford after suspected terror plot
description: A sixth man arrested in connection with the incident has since been released on bail
content:
The US Air Force has withdrawn all its bombers from RAF Fairford after a suspected terror plot at the base in Gloucestershire.
The bombers have been sent back to their home bases in the US , with aircraft monitoring sites showing B-1 bombers flying out of the base on Sunday.
On Saturday, UK Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said a sixth man arrested in connection with events at RAF Fairford had been released on bail.
The 25-year-old, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under section 5 of the UK’s Terrorism Act 2006.
Five British nationals, all in their mid-20s, were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism and then bailed .
Three suspicious vans were spotted near the military site on September 27th.
A Pentagon official said on Sunday: “US Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.
“The airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime.”
Senior CTP national co-ordinator Vicki Evans previously said the investigation was “hugely complex”, adding that specialist teams were “interrogating multiple lines of inquiry”.
She added: “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles, including possible foreign state involvement.”
UK prime minister Andy Burnham said there were “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident.
RAF Fairford has been used in recent months by US bombers after former prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran during the Middle East war.
Counter-terror police have said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found in the vans that sparked the security alert.
Last Thursday, Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu claimed Israel had handed Britain intelligence about the suspected terror plot.
Netanyahu said his country warned UK authorities about the “Iranian-sponsored attack” shortly before Britain’s announcement of a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
Earlier in the week, US president Donald Trump said he was “disappointed” after the five men were released on bail.
He told reporters: “We were involved in [the investigation], but as you know, your fellow countrymen let them go.
“Well, they didn’t let them go. They put them out on bail. I assume they haven’t watched closely… they should not have done that.” – PA

title: Ireland staff member allegedly spat at by Israel player during half-time tunnel scuffle
description: Israel FA offers no comment to allegation made by head of athletic performance, Damien Doyle
content:
The Israel Football Association say they have no comment to make on an allegation of spitting made by a Republic of Ireland backroom staff member.
The Ireland squad’s head of athletic performance, Damien Doyle, alleged that he was spat at by an Israeli player as the teams left the pitch for the half-time break during Sunday’s 1-1 Nations League draw in Backa Topola, Serbia.
Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrímsson declined to comment on the allegation after the match, saying it may be subject to a disciplinary committee. Speaking separately to Off the Ball, Hallgrímsson confirmed the accusation was made but added he did not see the incident which led to the allegation.
“I felt like they were trying to intimidate us from kick-off, so I give a lot of credit to the players to keep calm, it could have been a game of yellow and red cards,” he said.
Asked about the allegation during his post-match press conference, Israel head coach Ran Ben-Shimon said he did not see the incident as he was already in the dressingroom. When the Israel FA’s press officer was asked about the allegation, he replied: “No comment. I didn’t see anything, so I can’t comment on that.”
Ireland led at half-time through Troy Parrott ’s penalty, but Israel captain Dor Peretz equalised two minutes after the break. Israel twice hit the post during the second-half, and their coach believed they would have been worthy winners.
“We showed we are a good team, we deserved to win tonight,” said Ben-Shimon. “We were very dangerous in the counter attack. Of course it was very difficult for us to deal with the set pieces against Ireland, but otherwise we were better on the pitch. This is my opinion.”
He praised his players for better handling the emotional pressure of playing Ireland, which he said they failed to do in last week’s 3-0 loss in Debrecen.
“The situation in sport is that sometimes you lose games, and sometimes in these games, we lose ourselves,” he said. “In the first game, it wasn’t us, we didn’t react well. But for us, it is a long history. We came to the game today with a balanced approach between emotion and tactical thinking. We showed specifically in the second half that we are a very good national team.”
Asked whether Israel lacked that emotional balance last week, the coach replied: “I am sure about that. We tried our best to isolate our national team from the noise. We made a good job of coming to this game much more ready and much more balanced with the right approach. I am very proud of my players.”
He also denied that his players specifically targeted Jayson Molumby across the game after he reported alleged racist chanting by Israeli fans to the referee in Debrecen last week. The Irish midfielder suffered several fouls in Backa Topola, including one which led to the penalty which Parrott scored.
“From the last game, one of our conclusions was that we became very soft and were not aggressive enough,” said Ben-Shimon. “There is nothing personal against Molumby, we tried to win all the battles and the 50-50 balls, and I think we did good in this game. Come on, we just don’t do it [target players]. We are not men like this.”
The press conference began with a disclaimer read by a Uefa official, stressing that only questions focusing on the game could be asked, and not on separate political issues. This was a response to the chaotic scenes at Ireland’s press conference on Saturday, which was cut short when an Israeli journalist made an allegation of racism against the Irish players, which the FAI press officer rejected as “a lie”.
The journalist in question was one of two Israeli media members excluded by Uefa from the post-match press conference on account of the political questions they asked Hallgrímsson.

title: Biljana Plavsic, the only woman charged with war crimes in the Balkan wars, dies aged 96
description: Known as the Iron Lady of the Balkans, she expressed remorse after pleading guilty but later recanted
content:
Biljana Plavsic, a Bosnian Serb biologist and ultra-nationalist political leader during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in Serbia ’s capital, Belgrade, aged 96. She pleaded guilty to one count of crimes against humanity and expressed remorse, but later recanted, saying she “would do the same again”.
Her death was announced on Thursday by Serbian state media. No other details were provided.
Plavsic, a former professor at Sarajevo University who studied in Zagreb, Croatia , New York, London and Prague, and wrote more than 100 scientific papers, became notorious in the 1990s for applying biology to politics when the multi-ethnic state of Yugoslavia disintegrated. She declared Bosnia’s Muslim population “deformed genetic material” and railed against mixed marriages, common before the war, as leading to “the degeneration of Serb nationality”.
Often coldly indifferent to the suffering of non-Serbs, she was known as the Iron Lady of the Balkans, a nickname inspired by Soviet descriptions of Britain’s Margaret Thatcher . But the name Plavsic relished most was a tribute that Serb fighters daubed on the side of their tanks: Empress.
“She was educated, a professor but a real hard-line nationalist,” recalled Laura Silber, co-author of The Death of Yugoslavia, who interviewed Plavsic several times during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia. “She was prim and proper – school marmish in demeanour – so it was especially shocking to hear the ugly nationalist rhetoric coming out of her mouth.”
Olivera Simic, an Australian scholar from Bosnia who interviewed Plavsic for hundreds of hours in her later years, remembered her as highly intelligent but often blind to the suffering of non-Serbs. “She was not a monster and would express from time to time that she felt sorry for everyone – and then quickly start talking about Serb victims and cry over them,” Simic said in a telephone interview.
For nearly four years, Plavsic served as vice president of Republika Srpska, a Serb enclave in Bosnia that declared itself a separate state in 1992 and began a programme aimed at driving out Muslims, Croats and other non-Serb residents. In that role, she worked closely with Radovan Karadzic, the self-declared state’s president, who in 2016 was convicted of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity by a United Nations tribunal.
She rejected the term “ethnic cleansing” in her interviews with Simic, a law professor at Griffith University in Australia, describing the separation of different peoples as a “natural process.” According to Simic, Plavsic believed that “everyone should live with their own tribe” and, as a result, “willingly turned a blind eye” to the suffering this caused when ethnic groups were separated at gunpoint “because she was only interested in protecting her own tribe.”
Testifying as a witness at The Hague trial of Serbia’s wartime leader Slobodan Milosevic, Vojislav Seselj, the founder of a far-right Serb political party who was also charged with war crimes, said that Plavsic “held very extremist positions during the war, insufferably extremist, even for me, and they bothered even me as a declared Serb nationalist.”
After the war ended, Plavsic muted her anti-Muslim fervour, broke with Karadzic, accusing him of corruption, and in 1996 took over as president of Republika Srpska with support from the West, which viewed her as a partner for peace.
She was for a time hailed as a symbol of reconciliation after she expressed remorse during a 2002 sentencing hearing in The Hague. “I have now come to the belief and accept the fact that many thousands of innocent people were the victims of an organised, systematic effort to remove Muslims and Croats from the territory claimed by Serbs,” she said.
Serbs, driven by “an obsession to never become victims,” had “allowed ourselves to become victimisers,” she told the court.
Plavsic was the only woman among more than 150 people indicted by the international court for war crimes in former Yugoslavia. In 2003, she received an 11-year sentence for persecution, a crime against humanity, as part of a plea bargain that allowed her to avoid a trial on charges of complicity in genocide.
In contrast with Karadzic, who went into hiding for more than a decade and, after his arrest, boycotted parts of his trial in The Hague, Plavsic surrendered voluntarily and cooperated with the tribunal.
After initially pleading not guilty, she later pleaded guilty on one count, acknowledging that Serb forces had committed crimes and her own responsibility for these. “The knowledge that I am responsible for such human suffering and for soiling the character of my people will always be with me,” she told the court.
The judge said that Plavsic had not conceived or planned the violent Serbian campaign of ethnic separation that killed tens of thousands of Muslims and Croats and expelled many more from their lands with “great brutality,” but that she had embraced, supported and contributed to it. “This is a crime of utmost gravity,” he said.
Victims of the war and some human rights groups criticised her sentence as too lenient. But others said the major issue in Plavsic’s confession and guilty plea was that they would make denials by other Serbian leaders more difficult.
“In a region where denial and revisionism are central and where the tribunal is seen with scepticism, Ms. Plavsic’s gesture is striking,” Alex Boraine, a member of South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, told the court.
Fellow Serb nationalists, appalled by the confession in The Hague, denounced her as a traitor for deviating from the narrative that Serbs were innocent victims. They embraced her as a hero when she later recanted and declared herself and Serbs blameless.
The grip that the narrative of innocence still holds on many Serbs was on ghoulish display in September when thousands, including Serbian government ministers and the son of President Aleksandar Vucic, turned out in Belgrade for the funeral of Ratko Mladic, a Bosnian Serb general convicted of genocide and known as the Butcher of Bosnia.
Plavsic’s contrition, if ever more than a ploy to avoid a lengthy trial and escape genocide charges, did not last long. Released early from prison in 2009 for good behaviour, she settled in Belgrade and quickly retreated from what Simic, author of the 2025 book “Madam War Criminal,” concluded was “fake remorse” in The Hague.
Divorced with no children, she lived alone in a modest Belgrade apartment decorated with Orthodox Christian icons and a wooden cross made for her by a fellow inmate convicted of genocide for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre.
“She believes she sacrificed herself for ‘her people’ and did not show any ability to critically reflect on her actions but persistently justified and rationalised her behaviour, which she always perceived as highly ethical, moral and legitimate,” Simic wrote in her book. “She told me on many occasions during our conversations that if the circumstances would arise again she would most likely respond the same way.”
The debate rages in former Yugoslavia, where the 1995 massacre of Bosniaks at Srebrenica has been legally recognised as genocide but atrocities committed by Serb forces against Croats in Vukovar in 1991 and by Croats against Bosniaks in Mostar during a 1993-94 siege have been classified as war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Biljana Plavsic was born on July 7th, 1930, in Tuzla, then part of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. She grew up in Sarajevo, to which her affluent family moved when she was four. Her father was a prominent scientist who had been educated in Vienna, and she was raised on books and stories celebrating an infamous relative — Gavrilo Princip, a Serb nationalist who precipitated the first World War in 1914 by assassinating Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo.
Eleven years old when Nazi Germany invaded Bosnia in 1941, she witnessed Serbs being executed in the street and lost dozens of relatives to brutal ethnic purges carried out by the Ustashe, a Croatian fascist group that led the Independent State of Croatia, a puppet state of Germany formed during the second World War.
After the defeat of the Nazis, Bosnia became one of six republics in the newly declared Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Despite her family’s hostility to communism, Plavsic, who never joined the party, embarked on a highly successful academic career focused on plant virology. This included two years of botany research in the 1970s at Cornell University.
A popular biology professor in Sarajevo, she had a reputation as an exacting but fair-minded scholar who held all students, no matter their ethnicity, to the same high standards. Elected dean of Sarajevo University’s faculty of natural sciences and mathematics in 1987, she turned to politics in 1990 when she became the Serb member of a collective, multiethnic presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then still part of Yugoslavia.
When Slovenia and Croatia, two other Yugoslav republics, broke away to declare independence in 1991, Bosniaks began demanding their own state, too — a prospect that terrified Plavsic and many other Serbs.
In interviews with Simic, the Australia-based scholar, before her death, Plavsic often referred to 1991 as “the continuation of 1941,” a replay of the World War II conflict between Nazi-aligned Croats and anti-fascist Serbs that, she believed, “never finished.”
She told Simic years later in Belgrade that everything she did was motivated by a desire to avoid “the extinction of the Serb people.” Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats all suffered and, Simic said, Plavsic’s obsession with crimes against her own people was part of a bigger problem across former Yugoslavia.
“Everyone talks about their own victims, never their own perpetrators — no one,” Simic said. “This is the problem. Everyone wants to talk about their victimhood, never their perpetrators. They think nobody acknowledges crimes done against them, no matter how big or small.” - This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: Ireland 1 Israel 1: Draw in Serbia as Troy Parrott penalty not enough – as it happened
description: Ireland in Serbia for ‘home’ leg against Israel following 3-0 win in Hungary last week
content:
“An unforgettable Nations League window ended in disappointment for the Republic of Ireland at the TSC Arena in Backa Topola, as Troy Parrott’s first-half penalty was cancelled out by Israel’s Dor Peretz,” Gavin Cummiskey writes, summing up the last two weeks.
“There is an almighty debrief ahead for the FAI and the players, with one lingering regret likely to be that the move to a behind-closed-doors match in a small Serbian town denied them the chance to play a home game inside a sold out Aviva.
“Arguably, the near constant travel and inevitable fatigue cost them two important points.”
[ Troy Parrott penalty cancelled out by Israel equaliser as tempers flare in Serbia Opens in new window ]
That’s all from us for now. Keep an eye on The Irish Times website for reaction from both the Ireland and Israel post-match press conferences, and we’ll have analysis from Ken Early online tomorrow morning and in Monday’s paper.
“Ireland v Israel was drenched in rancour from the moment the draw was made, and across months it filtered down from fan groups to football associations to coaches and press officers and, finally, to the players,” Gavin Cooney writes from Serbia.
“And so the final act in this bleak and acrimonious series was to keep both sides separated as they left the field in Backa Topola. In the end, all these teams could share was a draw.”
Read his take on the game in full below:
[ Ireland and Israel’s fortnight of fury ends on a bizarre stage in rural Serbia Opens in new window ]
And so ends Ireland’s 2026 duties with Israel. Both sides will be delighted not to have to see each other again for a while. Ireland finish the international window on five points, level on points with Kosovo but behind them on head-to-head thanks to the defeat in Pristina. The group will conclude in November with Austria away and Kosovo at home.
FULL-TIME: Ireland 1 Israel 1 It ends with a whimper, as Israel clear Vata’s low ball in the game ends with honours even. The draw was a fair enough result - neither side had enough quality to deserve all three points.
Another yellow card for ISrael, this time for a stamp by Levi on Parrott. It’s getting testy again as the game winds down. One last chance for Ireland to get the ball into the box here - Vata’s ball is disappointing and that’s that.
Ireland under pressure now with two minutes to play, Jimmy Dunne concedes a corner - he was looking for a free kick but didn’t get it. Kelleher comes to claim, calm as you like. You feel there will be a chance for someone here - to whom will it fall?
Chance for Scales! It fell to the Celtic defender after a Vata long throw but he jabbed it over the bar. More changes for Ireland - Joel Bagan and Bosun Lawal on for Manning and Coventry. Six minutes to play.
Israel hit the post again! Oscar Gloukh has been excellent in this second half and he almost put Israel ahead there, whipping a right-foot volley against Kelleher’s post. Think Ireland would probably take a draw here.
SAVE! Ogbene chests down a Parrott flick-on and spears one towards the top corner but Assaf Tzur is equal to it. Fine save. The corner is cleared but Ogbene is fouled out on the right for yet another free kick. Fifteen minutes to go and we’re still at 1-1.
Huge let-off for Ireland. Oscar Gloukh finds Gandalman on the penalty spot and his shot catches the bottom of Kelleher’s left-hand post and deflects wide. Ireland were aspeel at the back there. Feels like Jimmy Dunne isn’t really at the races here - time for John Egan to shore it up maybe?
Manning spears one into the box that causes huge confusion but Israel survive. Hallgrimsson takes that as his cue to make changes. Chiedozie Ogbene and Rocco Vata on for Moylan and Idah. Not sure about that one, Heimir - Moylan was really coming into his own and seems fairly miffed to be taken off.
Brilliant work from Moylan down the right to force a corner, turning this way and that and riding two Israeli tackles. The corner is half-cleared and Moylan does brilliant again to win Ireland a free kick on the edge of the box...
An hour gone and this game is anyone’s now. Peretz gets in behind Dunne but Kelleher is out to tidy up. Idah has a swing at one from a Moylan lay-off but he skies it into the empty stand. Hard to imagine there won’t be more goals.
Ireland are labouring a touch in possession. They’re trying to get Moylan into the game but he’s getting crowded out a bit too easily. Parrott and Idah almost combined for a chance there but it came to nothing.
Chance for Israel, as Abada find himself in the clear in behind Scales. He’s forced wide and has to shoot early, so Kelleher is comfortable in getting down to it. But the Israel tails are up.
Very disappointing from Ireland, who had looked quite comfortable as the Israelis lost their discipline. The shot kind of skittled through Scales’s legs, hitting him on both ankles before falling to Peretz. They’ve had more of the ball since the goal but this is a dangerous fixture now.

SAVE! And a penalty shout! Manning fed a lovely ball into Parrott whose snapshot was saved. On the follow-up, Jimmy Dunne was brought down and now there’s a VAR check by the Spanish referee, who initially gave a corner...
The Israelis seem to be taking turns fouling Molumby. That’s seven fouls for them already, at least four of which have been on the Waterford man. This one brings a free kick in a good position for Ireland, Ryan Manning standing over it...
Approaching the half-hour mark and that’s the first booking of the night, with Israel centre-half Idan Nachmias carded for taking out Idah after the Ireland striker had rolled him. Free kick to Ireland in the centre of the pitch, 40 yards out. Comes to nothing. Ireland were 3-0 this time last week but it’s a much more even game tonight. Ireland probably have marginally more quality but haven’t really threatened in the box.
Inches wide by Molumby, whose shot from the edge of the box almost brings his first ever Ireland goal. It was a lovely lay-off from Moylan, who is starting to look lively. Better from Ireland.
First corner of the game goes Israel’s way. For all of Ireland’s possession, they had only that quick couple of shots from Idah and Parrot to show for it. Israel don’t make them pay this time but they soon force another one, with Kelleher diving to tip a shot from Abada round the post. It comes to nothing but Israel are having a decent spell here.
First shot of the night belongs to Adam Idah, turning onto a Manning pass on the edge of the box. It’s pushed away by Israeli goalie Assaf Tzur, who only made his debut on Thursday against Kosovo. Parrott soon has him scrambling again but he drags his shot wide. Ireland completely dominating possession in the early stages.
Off we go. Ireland start as expected, with Knight at right wing-back and Moylan looking to scurry ahead of him.
No handshake from Kelleher, as with O’Shea last week. Kick-off imminent.
The teams come out of the tunnel to the silence of the empty stadium. Covid vibes. Now the anthems.
Irish heads bowed once again for Israel anthem pic.twitter.com/rPUDTZvmST
Finn Azaz played well on Thursday but has been left out here, although Hallgrímsson doesn’t rule out using him at some stage in the match. “It’s mostly fitness,” the manager told RTE. “Obviously, emotional fitness is also an important factor in players. He played 90 minutes against Austria. It took a toll, got a little knock, but he is available to play and we might see him in the end of the game or middle of the game.”
Heimir Hallgrimsson confirms Jimmy Dunne replaces the absent Dara O'Shea for Israel game in Serbia, while Finn Azaz starts the game on the bench due to fitness - 'obviously emotional fitness is an important factor in players' #rtesoccer pic.twitter.com/E9uNkWFa2j
Gavin Cooney has this update from the stadium...
“The Israel squad have been affected by a virus in the lead-up to this game, with members of their backroom staff wearing face masks. Israeli media report all of Omri Glazer , Manor Solomon, Guy Mizrahi, Thai Bribo and Raz Shlomo are ill. Israel have been unable to name a full squad, and so have only 22 players available tonight.”
So four changes for Ireland from the team that drew with Austria on Thursday night. Jake O’Brien comes in for John Egan, Jimmy Dunne for captain Dara O’Shea, Jayson Molumby for Finn Azz and Jason Knight for James Abankwah, who is suspended. You’d imagine it will be a fairly straightforward formation - O’Brien, Dunne and Scales as the three at the back, Knight and Manning as wing-backs, Coventry and Molumby anchoring the midfield, with Moylan, Idah and Parrot making up the attack.
And as Gavin Cummiskey reminds as four Irish players are a booking away from missing the Austria game in November: Molumby, Idah, Coventry and Manning.
The other match in the group tonight has ended in a draw, with Austria grabbing a late equaliser against Kosovo. Fisnik Asllani scored for the home side in Pristina, putting Kosov ahead on 70 minutes. But a Christoph Lang header after a flick on from a long throw snatched Austria a share of the points five minutes from time.
That’s probably a good result for Ireland, all in all. It leave Austria on eight points after four games, with Kosovo on five. An Ireland win over the next few hours would leave them on seven points after the opening international window. To say we’d have taken that after Pristina is world-class understatement.
Of course, there’s no RTE coverage again tonight. The game will be carried live on RTE Two but it will be the world feed, with no studio and no analysis.
Our starting XI to face @IrelandFootball ! 🇮🇱 pic.twitter.com/XKeYWiHCdC
ISRAEL: Assaf Tzur; Ilay Feingold, Idan Nachmias, Nikita Stoinow, Roy Revivo; Eliel Peretz, Dor Peretz (capt), Ethane Azoulay; Liel Abada, Oscar Gloukh; Dor Turgeman. Subs: Eliasi, Glazer, Dasa, Gandelman, Shua, Baribo, Solomna, Levi, Mizrahi, Kanichowsky, Abu Farchi.
How we line-up in Bačka Topola pic.twitter.com/sCysPB2pDv
REP OF IRELAND: Caoimhín Kelleher (capt); Jake O’Brien, Jimmy Dunne, Liam Scales; Jack Moylan, Jason Knight, Jayson Molumby, Conor Coventry, Ryan Manning; Adam Idah, Troy Parrott. Subs: Max O’Leary, Josh Keeley, Laim Kitching, John Egan, Joel Bagan, Bosun Lawal, Finn Azaz, Killian Phillips, Rocco Vata, Chiedozie Ogbene, Thomas Cannon, Owen Elding.
Still no sign of the starting line-ups just yet, so while we wait, here’s some Troy Parrott magic from Thursday’s game against Austria:
Troy, that is beautiful 🤩 A fantastic run and finish from Parrott has us in the lead 💪 pic.twitter.com/gPJRFPc1nY
Mary Hannigan has named the striker ‘Paradona’ for his “twisty, turny, dribbly, nutmeggy piece of art” to put Ireland ahead at the Aviva.
[ Troy Parrott goal lights up the Aviva in a twisty, turny, dribbly, nutmeggy piece of art Opens in new window ]
Ken Early has made the trip to Serbia for the game.
“Backa Topola, a little town separated from Belgrade to the south by more than 100km of dead-flat cornfields, has been selected to host Ireland v Israel mainly due to its remoteness even from the rest of Serbia,” he writes.
“The Ireland team have played away games against Georgia in Mainz, Ukraine in Lodz and, last week, Israel in Debrecen, but this is the first time a game has been taken away from Dublin due to war. Ireland is involved only in the informational dimension of the current, diffuse, many-sided war, but even that is intense enough to overturn normality.”
[ Ken Early: Israel’s war in Gaza brings Ireland to remote cornfields in Serbia Opens in new window ]
Gavin Cooney has news for us from Serbia:
“Uefa has confirmed to The Irish Times that the two Israel journalists who asked questions of Heimir Hallgrímsson yesterday have been excluded from both of today’s post match press conferences. The decision was made by Uefa, and it is understood they are being excluded because of ‘their political-based questions’ to Hallgrimsson.”
In case you missed it, here’s Gavin Cummiskey ’s report from yesterday’s press conference:
[ Heimir Hallgrímsson’s press conference ended after ‘verbal attack’ from Israeli reporters Opens in new window ]
The venue for this evening’s game: TSC Arena in Backa Topola, Serbia.
Gavin Cummiskey’s report on the press conferences from yesterday is well worth reading, just for how it all went down.
[ Heimir Hallgrímsson: ‘They can’t have this happening again, just for the players’ welfare’ Opens in new window ]
Should have some team news in the next while. Until then, there’s plenty of reading about the game and everything surrounding it in the weekend Irish Times. Gavin Cooney’s account of another mad day in the Ireland-Israel circus is here.
[ Israeli media call Ireland press conference incident ‘disgraceful’ as fury swirls Opens in new window ]
Tony O’Donoghue had some interesting news to relay from the ground to RTÉ Radio just now. In the wake of yesterday’s pre-match press conference, two Israeli journalists have been banned by Uefa from attending the post-match press conference.
The scenes at Heimir Hallgrímsson’s press conference yesterday included one of them invoking the attempted hijacking of a FlyDubai flight during the week and the other accusing an unnamed Irish player of using racist language during the first game. Uefa have clearly taken a dim view of their behaviour and they won’t be allowed into the post-game media rooms.
The longest international window (in every sense) limps towards its end. Ireland are in the back of beyonds in Serbia, an out-of-the-way town called Backa Topola, ready for their second game against Israel. The temperature around this one has been raised relentlessly but, as we saw last weekend, at a certain point the whistle goes and the football takes over. We’ll be here to bring you whatever developments there are to report.
Already today there have been a couple of extraneous curve balls thrown at this game. Around two o’clock this afternoon, Uefa confirmed that they would been allowing Israel’s request to wear black armbands in memory of the October 7th attacks in 2023. Ireland will be wearing their black armbands again and there won’t be any handshakes or exchanges of pennants.

title: Troy Parrott penalty cancelled out by Israel equaliser as tempers flare in Serbia
description: Dor Peretz’s equaliser at the start of the second half secures his side a point as Nations League window closes with a draw
content:
An unforgettable Nations League window ended in disappointment for the Republic of Ireland at the TSC Arena in Backa Topola, as Troy Parrott’s first-half penalty was cancelled out by Israel’s Dor Peretz.
The result leaves Heimir Hallgrímsson’s side third in Nations League Group B3, level on five points with Kosovo after they drew at home to Austria.
The Irish players return to their clubs following a gruelling four-match, 15-day camp before the next outing against Ralf Rangnick’s Austrians in Linz on November 14th. The campaign ends three days later against Kosovo in Dublin. Austria sit on top of the pile, undefeated with eight points and on course for automatic promotion to League A.
There is an almighty debrief ahead for the FAI and the players with one lingering regret likely to be that the move to a behind-closed-doors match in a small Serbian town denied them the chance to play a home game inside a sold out Aviva.
Arguably, the near constant travel and inevitable fatigue cost them two important points.
“This is you, Ryan,” bellowed Hallgrímsson as Ryan Manning stood over a free-kick, about five yards outside the Israel box.
Manning scored twice last season for Southampton from a similar distance, but he went short to Parrott, who drew a save from Assaf Tzur before Jimmy Dunne was felled by Dor Peretz in the scramble for breaking ball.
The referee seemed happy to move on before he was called to review the incident by VAR. Peretz was yellow carded before Parrott slotted his 39 th -minute spot kick into the bottom left corner.
It was the Real Betis striker’s 15 th international goal, leaving him two behind Shane Long and one clear of Noel Cantwell, Jonathan Walters and Kevin Doyle.
With 10 goals in his last seven competitive caps, dating back to the brace against Portugal 11 months ago, he could climb over Don Givens, Frank Stapleton and Tony Cascarino, all equal on 19 goals, before the year is out.
The free-kick that led to the goal had been awarded for the fourth of five fouls on Jayson Molumby in the first half. Molumby felt the impact of three further late challenges that the Spanish referee Juan Martínez Munuera did not see as Dor Turgeman, Dor Peretz and Eliel Peretz all charged into the West Brom midfielder. He continually dusted himself down and smiled at his Israeli opponents.
Parrott’s goal sent Ireland in ahead at the break, but as the teams left the field the FAI’s athletic performance coach Damien Doyle could be heard claiming he was spat on as he approached the tunnel.
But Ireland’s dominance of an Israel team without their injured Crystal Palace winger Anan Khalaili and West Ham’s Manor Solomon, who was benched until the last 20 minutes, came unstuck less than two minutes after the break when Dor Peretz equalised.
The Israel goal was created by an Irish error as Conor Coventry slipped, allowing Roy Revivo and Liel Abada to combine down the right before Liam Scales deflected Oscar Gloukh’s shot, which fell kindly for Peretz to finish.
Peretz removed his black armband and jogged to the Israeli bench where the entire squad huddled in celebration.
Adam Idah, Parrott and Jack Moylan have gelled in the Ireland attack since defeat to Kosovo in Pristina 10 days ago, but Hallgrímsson felt the need to change, reverting to Parrott as the lone forward. Moylan and Idah made way for two wingers in Rocco Vata and Chiedozie Ogbene.
But the swing in momentum was confirmed as Oscar Gloukh grew into the game; the Ajax attacker found Omri Gandelman, whose shot beat Caoimhín Kelleher only to hit the post.
As the temperature rose on the pitch, and sideline, Ogbene wiggled free to draw a fine save from Tzur.
Confusion among Ireland’s new defensive combination of Scales, Jake O’Brien and Dunne invited Gloukh to strike the post again – both teams beginning to live on their nerves as four games in a relentless window began to take a toll.
The niggle between the teams was evident in every duel. Yarden Shua appeared to aim an elbow at Kelleher before the Brentford goalkeeper denied the same player in a one-on-one situation. The linesman’s flag was only seen after the new Irish skipper saved with his legs.
Ireland had better chances towards the end but the final ball continually let them down.
At full-time, Gloukh was blocked by Israeli staff from rushing towards the Irish players who wasted no time disappearing down the tunnel.
Republic of Ireland: Kelleher; Dunne, O’Brien, Scales; Knight, Molumby, Coventry (Lawal, 84), Manning (Bagan, 84); Moylan (Ogbene, 69), Idah (Vata, 69); Parrott.
Israel: Tzur; Feingold (Dasa, 78), Nachmias, Stoinov, Revivo; E Peretz, D Peretz (Shua, 78), Azoulay (Levi, 58); Gloukh, Abada (Solomon, 72); Turgeman (Gandelman, 58).

title: Austria pull off another late show to stay top of Group B3
description: Ronaldo-less Portugal won against Norway while Jurgen Klopp’s frustrating start with Germany continued
content:
Austria pulled off a second comeback in the space of four days to earn a draw against Kosovo in their Nations League meeting in Group B3.
Having salvaged a share of the points with two second-half goals in Dublin on Thursday, Austria conjured a late reply to Kosovo’s opener in Pristina.
Fisnik Asllani put the hosts ahead on 70 minutes, but Christoph Lang denied Kosovo a second win of the group stages – the first coming in their opening game against Ireland last month – with his equaliser five minutes from full-time.
The result leaves Austria unbeaten at the top of the group, with eight points from their opening four fixtures, while Kosovo sit second on five points, ahead of Ireland on account of their head-to-head result.
In League A, Joshua Zirkzee scored the winner as the Netherlands snatched a 2-1 win over Serbia in Group 2.
Teun Koopmeiners put the Dutch ahead with a free-kick from out on the right which flew straight in, before Mihajlo Cvetkovic equalised with a header.
But half-time substitute Zirkzee secured the three points with a tap-in from Ruben van Bommel’s cross.
Elsewhere in the same group, Germany’s frustrating start under new boss Jürgen Klopp continued with a goalless draw in Greece .
In Group 4 of the top tier league, Portugal – without Cristiano Ronaldo following his walk-out last week – beat Norway 2-1 thanks to a Goncalo Ramos winner.
Brentford defender Kristoffer Ajer fired Norway ahead with a spectacular goal, chesting down Martin Odegaard’s long ball before volleying home from the edge of the box.
But seven minutes later Joao Cancelo came up with anther scorcher from 20 yards to equalise.
Norway striker Erling Haaland appeared to be struggling with an injury when he went off after 67 minutes.
Ramos tapped in the deciding goal at the far post 12 minutes from time before Portugal lost Francisco Conceicao to a second yellow card.
A calamitous piece of goalkeeping by Wales ’ Danny Ward gifted Denmark a 1-0 win.
Ward sliced a clearance straight at Gustav Isaksen and then brought down the Danish winger to concede a penalty.
Ward survived a VAR check for a red card but was then sent the wrong way from the spot by Rasmus Hojlund.
Dor Peretz cancelled out Troy Parrott’s penalty as Israel drew 1-1 with the Republic of Ireland.
Elsewhere, Kosovo drew 1-1 with Austria, Malta were 1-0 winners over Andorra and Azerbaijan beat Lithuania 1-0.
On Saturday, a 70 th -minute penalty strike from John McGinn earned Scotland full points away to North Macedonia in Group B1, while England served up a 7-0 demolition away to Croatia .
Kane and Bukayo Saka both scored twice, Jude Bellingham scored one and made three more, while Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers were also on the mark.
Kane, who is now on 89 international goals from 124 games, says the performance has to be the blueprint for how England play.
“Even when we were 1-0 up, we went for two, went for three, went for four, and that’s got to be our mentality,” he said. “When you have a certain style of playing, you can’t just pick and choose when you want to do it. It’s just relentless. It’s non-stop.
“We’re playing against a really good side. We can’t take this type of win for granted because it could have been a really tricky game for us.
“And it’s always just sending messages – not just to yourself, but to the other teams around Europe. I think we’ve done that again.

title: Ireland and Israel’s fortnight of fury ends on a bizarre stage in rural Serbia
description: Heated scenes in Backa Topola as Ireland let slip another half-time lead
content:
Ireland v Israel was drenched in rancour from the moment the draw was made, and across months it filtered down from fan groups to football associations to coaches and press officers and, finally, to the players. And so the final act in this bleak and acrimonious series was to keep both sides separated as they left the field in Backa Topola. In the end, all these teams could share was a draw.
The Irish players responded much better to the intense pressure in Debrecen last week, but the Israeli media were in no mood to lessen their players’ load for this rematch. The Israeli coach was asked on Saturday why his team had “choked” with the nation’s honour on the line, and the same journalist wrote on Sunday of the need to avenge last week’s “humiliating” defeat. And, of course, everything was cast in a wider context.
“The Israeli team wants to achieve sporting revenge on the team and the country that has no idea what is happening here and allows itself to intervene, tell lies, and take the wrong and inhumane side,” wrote Lian Bitan of ONE, an Israeli football outlet.
The same journalist spent much of the preamble to the game in animated discussion with security and Uefa officials, as she was one of two Israeli journalists told ahead of the game by Uefa that they would not be welcome at the post-match press conferences. The other journalist excluded was the TV reporter who made an allegation of racism against the Irish players that led to the abandonment of the press conference. Uefa made the decision, saying it was due to their political line of questioning. Uefa also scrambled in additional help from their media relations team for the press conferences, with a brief to oversee the questions and ensure that they would be solely about the game.
It was a strangely dissociative experience, then, to experience this noxious enterprise in a boxfresh, empty stadium adjoining a hotel in a rural Serbian town. That a fortnight of fierce sound and fury would culminate on a silent stage was bizarre. Perhaps this is what it would be like to scream underwater for 90 minutes.
The pregame playlist over the PA was smooth jazz at a low volume, sounding like we were all sitting in a hotel bar clinking glasses. However, true to custom, Gala’s Freed from Desire kicked in a few minutes before kick-off. The music died for the final few minutes before the players entered the pitch, meaning the only sounds in the stadium were the waspish distortions of the walkie-talkies of security guards. The PA announcer ran through the team line-ups, perhaps out of sheer force of habit, and twice read Uefa’s standard pregame message of respect.
“This game should be played in the spirit of respect and fair play, and remember, there is no room for racism.”
The game was prefaced by the now-familiar formalities – Irish heads bowed for the Israeli anthem; no handshakes exchanged – and then slowly the temperature was cranked higher. Without the white noise of the crowd, every single yell and claim and recrimination made by players and benches were audible, accentuating the contention of every contested moment. Jayson Molumby came in for particularly close attention, and Israeli captain Dor Peretz left a foot in on the Irish midfielder in the second minute. Molumby took the challenge in his stride, reacting only with a slight smirk.
Molumby was officially fouled five times – there were many more kicks that went unpunished – but it was from one of those five that Ireland wound up scoring. Hallgrímsson yelled at Ryan Manning, “This is you, Ryan!,” which was the signal to unveil some training ground choreography. Manning slipped the free-kick into a gap in the Israel defence for Troy Parrott – think the Wout Weghorst routine for the Netherlands against Argentina in the 2022 World Cup – at the end of which Jimmy Dunne was fouled by Peretz. Parrott scored from the spot, obviously, moments after Manning tried to draw the officials’ attention to an alleged kick by an Israeli player. Meanwhile, Molumby appeared to exchange some words with the Israeli bench.
The mood further soured as the sides made their way off at half-time, with Ireland’s head of athletic performance, Damien Doyle, audibly alleging that an Israeli player spat at him . The FAI confirmed at half-time that Doyle made the allegation. The players had to be separated as they made their way down the tunnel, Hallgrímsson with his arms stretched wide as an ersatz steward. “Guys, be clever, be clever,” pleaded the referee.
Hallgrímsson spoke on Saturday of the need to cool down his players before playing Israel last week, asking Conor Coventry to lead the squad in prayer before kick-off. Perhaps the half-time flashpoint disturbed Ireland from their focus, for they lost their lead within two minutes of the game’s resumption and lived on their wits’ end from there. The game became stretched and the Irish players harried; and twice the clank of Caoimhín Kelleher’s left-hand post echoed around the empty stadium. An Israeli journalist thumped a glass panel behind the press box at frustration at the second of these near-misses.
The game ended in one more flash of rancour, with an Israeli player restrained from approaching Molumby. “Calm, calm,” yelled the referee. The Irish players disappeared down the tunnel, with the Israeli squad held back on the pitch.
“Thank you for attending the match,” concluded the PA announcer, now either thoughtlessly reading a script or else possessed with mischievous humour. The few who did attend did so out of obligation, and none will want to do this ever again.

title: Prospect of a €250 student fee reduction unlikely ahead of Budget 2027
description: The programme for government commits to continuing to reduce the student contribution fee over the lifetime of the Government
content:
There have been moves to pour cold water on the prospect of a €250 cut to the student contribution being considered for Budget 2027 .
On Sunday there were reports that the measure was set to be discussed in Budget talks with a last ditch bid by Minister for Higher Education James Lawless to secure the cut.
There was a suggestion that the cost of the €250 cut to the student fee was put at under €30 million, and an expectation among some sources that it could be considered by senior Coalition figures.
A spokesman for Lawless declined to comment on the matter.
Later in the day, some Government sources cast doubt on whether such a proposal was being proposed or considered for the Budget.
One source suggested the matter should be “treated with caution”.
The programme for government commits to continuing to reduce the student contribution fee over the lifetime of the Government.
A €500 cut in the student contribution was announced in last year’s budget.
One Department of Higher Education measure that has been agreed is a €16 million support package for students aimed at helping squeezed middle families through extending grant eligibility for households with more than one child in third level education.
There is also a plan to use €150 million from the National Training Fund to be invested in AI skilling and reskilling.
The Departments of Children and of Social Protection are among those yet to see their budget packages finalised.
[ Budget 2027: Measures on pensions, welfare, income tax and more take shape Opens in new window ]
At a Fianna Fáil event on Saturday night, Taoiseach Micheál Martin was asked if promised childcare cost cuts would be targeted at any particular age group.
He said: “There’s no question that the significant costs arise in the early years, in the zero to five years, and I think that’s something that the minister and public expenditure, people are looking at. But that all remains to be discussed.”
In terms of social protection measures, a €10-per-week increase in the State pension and core welfare payments are expected to be announced as part of the budget on Tuesday.
* This article was updated and amended on October 4th.

title: Con O’Callaghan sets up shoot-out with Ciarán Kilkenny as Cuala beat Ballyboden
description: Dublin football greats to square off after Castleknock beat Thomas Davis
content:
Two of the most decorated forwards in the history of Dublin football have set up a county final shoot-out after Cuala and Castleknock progressed to the capital’s 2026 showpiece event.
It will be Con O’Callaghan against Ciarán Kilkenny after 2025 champions Ballyboden St Enda’s relinquished their grip on the Dublin title at Parnell Park on Sunday.
O’Callaghan scored 0-3 as Cuala dethroned Ballyboden with a 0-21 to 0-17 victory in the second of the weekend’s Dublin SFC semi-finals.
