Kilkenny, who announced his intercounty retirement in July, helped Castleknock beat Thomas Davis 0-26 to 3-12 on Saturday night at the Donnycarney venue to progress to only their second ever senior football county decider after losing to St Vincent’s in 2016.
O’Callaghan has been the Dublin captain for the last two years. Kilkenny was his vice-captain in 2025. In any debate on the greatest Dublin players of all time, both are certain to feature. They were pillars in a Dublin team during a history-making era of unprecedented dominance.
A Dublin SFC is the one standout medal missing from Kilkenny’s collection, whereas O’Callaghan has garnered county titles in both football and hurling.
Still, the final in a fortnight will only be Cuala’s third appearance in the senior football decider – even though the Dalkey outfit not only won the title in 2024 but also progressed to be crowned All-Ireland club champions in January 2025.
Their first final appearance came in 1988 when Parnells proved too strong. Peter Dunne was the Cuala manager that year and fittingly the man taking the club to this year’s county final is his son, Derek.
“My father was involved in 1988, it’s a long time ago but it’s a nice connection to it,” said the Cuala manager after watching his side beat Ballyboden.
It is a Cuala team stuffed with intercounty experience – including O’Callaghan, Peadar Ó Cofaigh Byrne, Eoin Kennedy and Charlie McMorrow. And nine-time Sam Maguire winner Michael Fitzsimons continues to shore up the defence at full back.
[ ‘I wrestled with it a lot’: Galway manager Éamonn Fitzmaurice on potentially facing Kerry Opens in new window ]
Fitzsimons was as tigerish as ever at the heart of the Cuala defence on Sunday as they largely frustrated a talented Ballyboden attack.
“In the Dublin championship anyway, the referees are just great for allowing the ball into contact, it’s your responsibility to get it out so long as there are no jersey pulls,” said Fitzsimons.
“So it allows for more turnovers and end-to-end contests. That was even great in the All-Ireland final this year, Mayo have been pressing up on teams for years and are very good at it.
“It is important in the new rules for there to be a possibility for defenders to get turnovers because that’s what makes it exciting. If you get turnovers you get quick transitions, you get better offensive play and you avoid the basketball style a bit more, which is great.”
For Ballyboden, Sunday’s defeat marks the end of a long campaign. After winning the Dublin championship last October, the Firhouse outfit went on to win the Leinster club title in December before ultimately losing the All-Ireland decider to Dingle in January.
They were guilty of trying to force matters too much in the first half on Sunday, kicking seven first-half wides – with half a dozen of those coming from ambitious two-point efforts. Cuala led 0-9 to 0-6 at the interval but Ballyboden turned the screw on the resumption – destroying the Dalkey side’s kickout in the second half.
Ballyboden won Cuala’s first eight kickouts after the break to hit the front in the 50th minute. But Cuala had spent 12 months stewing over last year’s semi-final loss, when Ballyboden staged a late surge to end their reign as Dublin champions. Some payback was due.
With the sides tied on 0-17 apiece as the game entered the final minute of normal time, Cillian Dunne – Derek’s son – nudged Cuala ahead.
The push was on. Cuala added three further points in injury-time from David O’Dowd, Conor O’Brien and McMorrow to win by four.
“There was an awful lot of hurt there building up over the year,” said Derek Dunne. “Maybe it did help us get over the line in the end in the last three or four minutes.”
[ Gaelic Games All you read is love: The books about Mayo’s All-Ireland win that just had to be written Opens in new window ]
Ballyboden weren’t the only champions dethroned over the weekend. Indeed, All-Ireland club kingpins Dingle exited the Kerry SFC on Saturday, losing 1-17 to 1-11 against Spa.
And in Meath, 2025 winners Summerhill exited at the semi-final stages following a 1-17 to 0-14 defeat to Wolfe Tones in Dunganny on Sunday.
Loughmacrory’s defence in Tyrone also ended at the semi-final stages with Errigal Ciarán running out 0-19 to 1-13 winners in Omagh.
The fall of the champions continued in Wexford too where St Martin’s beat 2025 winners Castletown 4-12 to 1-16 at Wexford Park.

title: Egypt condemned by more than 80 rights groups after detaining newsroom of journalists
description: Arrests follow US waiving of Egypt’s human rights responsibilities linked to receiving military aid
content:
An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.
Last week, Egyptian security forces arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.
On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, an NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.
Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.
Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.
“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”
Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.
The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.
More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.
The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320 million (€284 million) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.
The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human rights record, but has largely kept funds flowing.
This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total, as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, according to a state department memo revealed by Reuters.
While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”
Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.
Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.
Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on the Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsadaash are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS. - Guardian

title: Fresh legal challenge to Orange march at Drumcree scheduled for Monday
description: Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition to seek leave to apply for judicial review of Parades Commission decision
content:
A fresh legal challenge to the Orange march at the centre of the Drumcree stand-off in Portadown will be heard at the Court of Appeal in Belfast on Monday.
Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition , who oppose the march, is to seek leave to apply for a judicial review of the decision by the Parades Commission to allow it to proceed.
The march, which was due to take place on September 27 th , was unable to proceed after residents from the nationalist Garvaghy Road blocked it.
The two sides remain deadlocked despite days of talks facilitated by Northern Secretary Chris Bryant last week.
On Sunday, Irish rap trio Kneecap visited the Garvaghy Road along with their solicitor, Darragh Mackin – who also represents the residents – and folk singer Radie Peat to show their support for the protesters.
They went to a local school before meeting residents at the Drumcree Community Centre on Sunday evening.
In a statement after the visit, the trio said: “Kneecap support the residents of Garvaghy Road, they’re a determined and strong community.
“No community should have to live with sectarian intimidation, racism or hatred. Not here, not now, not anywhere.”
The stand-off at Drumcree has been continuing since September 27th, when a limited march by 35 members of the Orange Order – which had been given the go-ahead by the Parades Commission and subsequently by the High Court – was prevented from proceeding due to the presence of protesters on the Garvaghy Road.
The Orangemen have made several attempts to parade down the road since then, but their way has been blocked by police Land Rovers, and protesters continue to maintain a watch along the sides of the road.
On Sunday, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald rejected Taoiseach Micheál Martin’s suggestion that her party has an “overly simplistic” view of how to resolve the Drumcree dispute.
Sinn Féin has repeatedly called on the British government to intervene and stop the Orange Order march.
Martin on Saturday said he did not agree with Sinn Féín’s assessment that “Drumcree could be sorted by me simply telling Andy Burnham what to do” and accused the party of lacking “sincerity”.
Asked on the BBC’s Sunday Politics programme if she accepted that “the reality is, it’s not that simple”, McDonald replied: “Well, it is, actually.”
She said Martin had “described the Parades Commission determination as incomprehensible and wrong and he and I agree on that matter.
“We have impressed upon him and on all the others, on the British government, that there is a resolution to this, which is that the Secretary of State call this, make it clear that he puts a stop to this march, and thereby creates a space for a mediation and a dialogue.”
She also accused the Dublin and London governments of creating a “vacuum” by not working towards Irish unity, saying that while they “sit on their hands and fail to create the democratic space and dynamic for all of us to engage, to discuss, to plan about Ireland’s future, while there is a vacuum there, we are sitting ducks for this kind of reactionary sideswipe from small elements in society who want to upend our progress.
“So the government in London [and] particularly Micheál Martin and the Government in Dublin, need to pay attention to that.”
On Saturday, rallies took place on the Garvaghy Road and in the loyalist Edgarstown estate in support of the two sides in the dispute.
Addressing the several thousand who gathered in support of the residents, Sinn Féin vice-president and Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill said that “if the British government is not prepared to end this crisis, then it’s up to every single one of us ... to collectively and unequivocally stand with the Garvaghy Road residents and say no to a sectarian, unwanted march”.
DUP MLA and Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly described it as “electioneering” and accused O’Neill and Sinn Féin of “a complete abdication of leadership”.
The district master of the Orange Order in Portadown, Nigel Dawson, said: “We’re still waiting for the Chief Constable to do his job and put the parade down the road, as per our legal determination and backed up by a High Court judge.”
Lawyers for the residents argue the Parades Commission “materially misdirected itself” on the police assessment of the potential for disorder, and had not given an “accurate representation of the evidence received from the PSNI” in its decision.
McDonald defended Sinn Féin’s participation in the protest against the march and said there was “no question of us co-operating” with any potential police investigation.
A big police operation remains under way at Drumcree and evidence gathering is “ongoing”.
Assistant Chief Constable Anthony McNally said, “anyone blocking the Garvaghy Road will still be treated as participating in an unnotified and therefore illegal protest” and “anyone found to have broken the law will face criminal justice consequences”. Additional reporting – PA.

title: Macarons and Mounjaro as Daryz turns beauty into destruction in Paris
description: Harry Kane shows his goalscoring pedigree as England show the kids how it’s done
content:
O nce in a blue moon, some of us decide to take a break from sport-watching, the very brief hiatus usually prompted by a dismal set of events, like the ones we witnessed in Serbia on Saturday afternoon. That’s when you opt for some light entertainment of the non-sporting kind, just to cleanse your skull, so it was a choice between Shrek 2, Formula One and horse racing come Sunday afternoon.
The Qatar Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe in France, the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, not to mention Ireland at home to Israel in Serbia. It’s a complicated world. But in the end the horses won out.
Virgin Media brought us Racing TV’s coverage of the occasion, and safe to say they were rather up for it. “Paris begins in light, a soft gold rising over the Seine, the first shimmer on the iron lace of the Eiffel Tower,” our host Tom Stanley began, before Frankie Foster joined in on the ode.
“The Qatar Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe is more than just a horse race, it’s a test of balance and bravery, of poise and power, where everything is asked for and nothing is hidden.” The contenders? “When the moment comes they must turn beauty into destruction.”
And there was us thinking it was just a horse race.
But a very special one in the horsey world, of course, staged at the highly lovely setting of Longchamp. And Frankie had quite the view over the course when he joined Francesca Cumani in a big airborne glass box that appeared to be dangling from a single wire in the sky.
“You can have a glass of champagne, a macaron and watch the racing from on high,” he said of the “Sommet de l’Arc”; the fellah looking a little green around the gills as he noted just how far he was from earth. Francesca was perfectly chilled, but you feared the macaron Frankie had just eaten was about to make a reappearance.
Those of us who wouldn’t know an important horse race from an onion ring do, of course, need to become invested in some manner so as to pique our interest, so the only way, really, to do this is to pick a winner.
[ Daryz emulates Alleged by winning the Prix de l’Arc Triomphe back-to-back Opens in new window ]
Arrow Eagle was tempting, simply because its owner is a person called Waltraut Spanner, and there was a soft spot too for Kalpana because when Frankie spoke to her trainer Andrew Balding he was quite rude about her. “Until last year, she was always carrying excess condition,” he said, which was as good as calling her a fat bird. “But this year she’s sleeker, leaner ... I have no idea why.” Mounjaro? He didn’t say.
Then there was Bay City Roller, and you kind of had a vision of him hollering “Bye bye baby” as he overtook a rival in the final inches, but in the end it was Daryz who subjected that very fate to the Roller.
[ ‘Getting medals does not equal cash’: The Irish Olympians struggling to make ends meet Opens in new window ]
Kalpana, perhaps still carrying a bit too much weight, finished fifth, while Arrow Eagle was a distant 12th. You could but hope his backers didn’t label him a spanner.
Daryz, then, as commentator Simon Holt told us, became the first colt to win the Arc two years running since 1978, although Tom pointed out that this stat isn’t all that it’s cracked up to be because most Arc winners are retired and sent off to make babies, studs that they are.
There’s a chance England will send Harry Kane to stud soon, such is their hope that he can sire more goalscorers of his quality. He was at it again against Croatia in Rijeka, scoring twice in a slightly comprehensive 7-0 triumph.
An odd occasion it was too. The game was technically played behind closed doors, because of unruly behaviour by the Croatians before, but the stadium was in fact populated by 6,000 local schoolchildren.
Some rude people suggested that their high-pitch screaming was a welcome smothering of Lee Dixon’s co-commentary, Virgin Media’s Tommy Martin suggesting at half-time that “the only hope for the home side is that England get done by the prevention of cruelty to children people”.
“Croatia look ancient,” said Richard Dunne. “Their midfield pairing have a combined age of 74,” said Tommy. “They look 74 each,” said Richard.
Come full-time, the 6,000 kids in attendance probably wished they’d taken a break from watching sport too.

title: Drumcree consequences will be profound. That’s why it’s a line in the sand for nationalists
description: The resurrection of this march of all marches, with its bitter, bloody history, has tapped into something visceral in the northern nationalist psyche
content:
T he Garvaghy Road is northern nationalism’s line in the sand, its watershed moment, its crocodile.
The reptiles were the defining image of the Assembly election in March 2017, which played out in a not dissimilar atmosphere of rancour and division between nationalists and unionists. Referring to the demand by Sinn Féin for an Irish Language Act, the then first minister and Democratic Unionist Party ( DUP ) leader Arlene Foster , remarked that “if you feed a crocodile it will keep coming back and looking for more”.
The widespread sense of nationalist outrage was embraced by Sinn Féin; turnout increased by almost 10 per cent and unionists lost their overall majority at Stormont for the first time.
Now, nearly 10 years on, another Assembly election beckons, by next May at the latest. It does so against the backdrop of a crisis that has revealed the extent of the sectarian divide still permeating politics and society in Northern Ireland. It has further weakened, perhaps fatally, the Northern powersharing institutions.
But the standoff at Drumcree, still ongoing in advance of yet another legal challenge on Monday, is more than just another crocodile.
The resurrection of this march of all marches, with its bitter, bloody history, has tapped into something visceral in the nationalist psyche, into that collective memory of discrimination, of marching for civil rights, and of being batoned off the street by B Specials in Derry exactly 58 years ago on Monday.
Sinn Féin has taken the lead at the protests – and is certainly making political hay – but also present were the SDLP, People Before Profit , Aontú and dissident republicans. In conversation after conversation over the last week with people from nationalist backgrounds of all shades of green, it is clear they are united in their resolve that the Orange Order cannot be allowed to march down the Garvaghy Road.
There would be no going back to the days of being “second-class citizens”, many said. As one lifelong SDLP voter put it, “no more Croppies lie down”, in a reference to the British folk song that celebrates the defeat of Irish rebels in 1798.
[ ‘There’s so much change’: Young Spencer on finding common ground with Kneecap in Belfast Opens in new window ]
Yet, even in Northern Ireland, time has moved on. The civil rights movement is 60, the Belfast Agreement almost 30, and this is not the Drumcree of those days.
A whole generation has grown up proud of its Irishness and its culture – from the Irish language to the GAA to Kneecap – and has the freedom to express it.
Witness the musicians who have performed for the Garvaghy Road protesters; not just the likes of Christy Moore , but mainstream Irish acts such as members of Beoga and The Mary Wallopers .
Several thousand people attended the protest on Saturday, with its near-festival atmosphere. This was young, confident nationalism, ready to stand up and be counted, and with others ready to stand beside them.
It is highly significant that more than 1,000 “concerned individuals from a Protestant background” have thus far signed an open letter calling on the Orange Order to end the parades impasse “in the interests of our entire community”.
[ ‘Everybody wants this to end’: Protestant group pushes UK government to end Drumcree standoff Opens in new window ]
Speaking on the BBC’s The View on Thursday, SDLP leader Claire Hanna explained why, in 15 years as an elected politician, it was the first time she had objected to a parade.
“I wish to see the traditions of this region flourish together, and I am very, very clear that’s not what I think was happening,” she said. “People – Catholic, Protestant and dissenter – are not buying this.”
As the standoff continues, it is already clear its consequences will be profound; for the people of the Garvaghy Road, for the politics of Northern Ireland, and for the debate about its very future.

title: The Irish Times view on Budget 2027: time to slow the runaway spending train
description: Credibility needs to be restored to the budgetary process
content:
Tomorrow’s budget is important for a number of reasons. There will be much focus on its political implications for the Coalition and its likely impact on the economy.
However, another key issue is also worthy of attention. It is the need to produce a package which is credible, in the sense that the forecasts, for spending in particular, are firmly based. This has not been the case in recent years as spending has repeatedly come in well ahead of target.
There are times when this is understandable – perhaps even inevitable. Following Russia’s full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, for example, the resulting surge in inflation required a response to protect households and businesses . In a turbulent world, things happen, some requiring a budgetary response.
Looking at Ireland’s recent budgets, however, it is clear that other factors are also at work. The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council has pointed to two trends. One is unrealistic budgeting which fails to properly provide for the year ahead, particularly in the light of a rising population There appears an understanding in the background that this can be dealt with via supplementary estimates as required.
The other related issue is poor budget control. Departments often work with poor information systems. In some cases there seems little commitment to stick to the budgeted figures. In terms of major capital projects like the National Children’s Hospital big overruns are the norm. But the key issue relates not to investment but to current spending on public services.
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers is seeking to bring this under better control and the Government has signed up to a 6 per cent target for spending growth in 2027. This may be adhered to in the budget sums. But whether it can hold in practice is the real question. Already it appears that spending this year is forecast to run €1.5 billion ahead of target and this may well be exceeded by the end of the year. If a realistic starting point for 2027 is not written into the budget, then failure becomes inevitable.
Over recent years soaring corporate tax has given successive governments budgetary room for manoeuvre and paid for significant overruns. The key goal for next year must be to remove unplanned overspending which emerges without any Govenrment sign-off. In turn this leaves more scope to make decisions to adjust if conditions really do demand it. A proper contingency provision could provide scope to pay for this.
As the Economic and Social Research Institute has pointed out, the mood in borrowing markets is changing. Any wobble in Ireland’s tax take could quickly lead international investors to examine the vulnerability of Ireland to potentially volatile corporate taxes. Building credibility is vital in uncertain times.

title: Support for Gaza and Garvaghy Road residents in ‘anti-fascism’ march through east London
description: Thousands attended demonstration to mark the 90th anniversary of the Battle of Cable Street
content:
Thousands of protesters have made a call to “stop the far right” as they marched through the East End of London to mark the 90th anniversary of the Battle of Cable Street.
Demonstrators marched from Tower Hamlets Town Hall in Whitechapel to St George’s Gardens in Cable Street on Sunday to mark the anniversary of the clashes.
The Battle of Cable Street on October 4th, 1936 saw demonstrators block Oswald Mosley’s British Union of Fascists (BUF) from marching through the East End of London.
The anti-Semitic BUF’s decision to march through the area, then home to a large Jewish population, was regarded as a deliberate provocation and anti-fascist organisations rallied large crowds to prevent the march.
Protesters at Sunday’s march carried placards which said “Stop Islamophobia, Stop the far right” with pictures of activist Tommy Robinson , as well as others saying “Stop Trump, Stop Farage”.
Those at the front of the march carried a banner reading: “No to: Antisemitism, Islamophobia, all racism. 1936 they did not pass. 2026 they will not pass.”
Other protesters carried “From Cable Street to Garvaghy Road, smash fascism” banners in reference to the Drumcree parade dispute in Northern Ireland .
Groups participating in the march included trade unions such as Unite and organisations including Jewish Bloc for Palestine.
Protesters joined in chants of “Zionists are not welcome here” and “Zionism is fascism”.
There was a brief confrontation between marchers and two counter-protesters carrying flags with “Campaign Against Antisemitism” written on them.
The Metropolitan Police said one man was arrested for breach of the peace and public order offences.
Speaking at a demonstration after the march, former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn criticised “racist language used today by Farage and Reform and all the others who are now blaming refugees and migrants”.
Corbyn, an MP for Islington North, said: “Anti-racism means we oppose every form of racism, whatever it is, wherever it raises its head, because it destroys the unity that we need in order to improve the living standards of the poorest people within our society.
“The biggest proponents of, now, Islamophobia are the far right across Europe.
“They are funded by Elon Musk . And the big money that flows into those parties, you need to know where it comes from and who is providing it.”
Tower Hamlets mayor Lutfur Rahman said “migration, immigrants, the indigenous communities together have made Tower Hamlets what it is – a great borough”.
He added: “The 1930s and the early 1940s was a taint of dreadful, dreadful world history. Mosley ran riot across the country and tried to run riot in Tower Hamlets.
“Our forefathers said, ‘No, you’re not coming here. You shall not pass’. And they couldn’t pass.
“And we say that again now: the fascists, the far right, will never run riot in Tower Hamlets.” – PA

title: The Irish Times view on Irish prisons: inhumane conditions
description: As overcrowding grows, early release programmes may come onto the agenda
content:
The harrowing picture of condition in Irish prisons painted by the Irish Penal Reform Trust (IPRT) is of a piece with the findings of the Government’s own watchdog, the Inspector of Prisons. One figure stands out from the recent report of the IPRT, which campaigns for prisoner rights. More than two thirds of the current prisoner population of around 5,400 cannot go to the toilet in private. Prison is meant to be a deterrent and a punishment, but that does not require daily humiliation.
The IPRT and Inspector of Prisons reports confirm that the increased jailing of criminals has clearly outpaced the ability to house them in humane conditions. The average number of people in custody on any given day rose by 10 per cent last year, while the number of places added to an already overcrowded system rose by 4 percent.
The current plan to deliver another 1,500 places by 2031 will not even meet the existing shortfall, never mind any increase in the numbers being committed to prison as a consequence of demographic or policy changes.
The Minster for Justice Jim O’Callaghan and his colleagues should look across the Irish Sea to see where the current trend of sending more and more people to already overcrowded prisons is inevitably headed; wholesale and politically damaging early release programmes.
The British government freed around seven hundred prisoners under early release provisions last week in order to address overcrowding in prisons in England and Wales. Some 2,000 prisoners are expected to be released over the next month, some of them with convictions for domestic abuse and violent offences. Another 3,000 will be released over the next year from a system considered less overcrowded than the Irish one.
The Irish equivalent would be releasing 270 prisoners on top of the more than 500 already on temporary release under various schemes. It would doubtless provoke a similar reaction from sections of the media, victims groups, Garda representatives and Opposition politicians as seen across the water.

title: ‘They never made it out’: The biggest loss of life in the history of Dublin Fire Brigade
description: The Pearse Street fire of 1936 broke out at the premises of Exide Batteries 90 years ago this Monday, October 5th
content:
“See this man here?” says George O’Connor. “He was about 7ft tall. They called him ‘the Horse’ McDonald.” We’re poring over photos spread out on the kitchen table of George’s home near Dunshaughlin, Co Meath.
“The Horse” is one of numerous firemen whose names George – now aged 103 – can still recall from his childhood. They were comrades of his father, John O’Connor, who was station officer in the Central Fire Station on Dublin’s Tara Street.
John O’Connor witnessed a lot over the course of his fire brigade service, which included the revolutionary period. George shows me a photo of him pumping water in the aftermath of the Custom House fire in 1921 .
George and his siblings grew up in the station’s family quarters. “It just became normal,” he says of his unusual childhood home, but he concedes that “there was always a lot of activity”. There was an ambulance based out of the station, and George recalls blood having to be washed off the stretcher when the crew would return from an incident.
A snapshot in George’s collection shows two firemen posing at Tara Street with a terrier named Minnie. “She used to go to all the fires,” explains George. “When the alarm would go off she’d hop up on the vehicle.” Until, that is, the occasion of a big fire on Bachelors Walk when someone stole Minnie, abruptly ending her career with the Dublin Fire Brigade.
Of all the fires in Dublin which occurred in George’s childhood, perhaps the one which stands out the most is the Pearse Street fire of 1936 , which took place 90 years ago this Monday, October 5th. George was 13 at the time.
The fire broke out on a Monday night at the premises of Exide Batteries at 163 and 164 Pearse Street. The Central Fire Station was just up the street, and a tender of 11 firemen under Lieutenant Howard was on the scene within two minutes of receiving the call, followed shortly afterwards by reinforcements. The first turnout included John O’Connor, Thomas Potts – better remembered now as musician Tommie Potts – and Leslie Crowe, subject of the RTÉ television documentary “Camera Tripod Bicycle” a few years ago.
Some time prior to the fire, in an attempt to remedy water shortages, Dublin Corporation had reduced night-time water pressure. This made the firemen’s task considerably more difficult from the outset, forcing them so close to the flames that their uniforms were scorched.
Minutes after the first turnout arrived on the scene, there came a deafening explosion followed closely by another. John O’Connor was thrown from the second landing of the building to the hallway by the force of the first blast.
The explosions – which were apparently caused by cylinders containing coal-gas and oxygen – accelerated the fire, which engulfed the upper floors of the burning premises, trapping three of the firemen. George lists their names: “McArdle, Malone and Nugent.” Those three never made it out of the building alive.
The fire raged for hours and destroyed all of No 164 and most of No 163. It was not until about 2.30am that the firemen could begin digging for their comrades. Their progress was impeded by falling masonry and the still-smouldering debris but they moved determinedly, and by about 7am the remains of Robert Malone and Thomas Nugent had been recovered.
The men were given a public funeral and their remains lay in state in City Hall for two days before a Requiem Mass in St Andrew’s Church on Westland Row
The men were assisted by comrades on holiday who, hearing what had happened, arrived in uniform and joined in the search. The final body, that of Peter McArdle, was not recovered until the following night. It was estimated that the men had to dig through 30 tons or more of debris to recover the remains of their comrades.
The men were given a public funeral and their remains lay in state in City Hall for two days before a Requiem Mass in St Andrew’s Church on Westland Row. It was estimated that at least 50,000 people lined the streets as the cortege made its way to Glasnevin Cemetery, where the three comrades were laid to rest alongside each other. So numerous were the floral tributes that they had to be transported on a 10-wheeled Guinness lorry.
George’s father was particularly friendly with Thomas Nugent, known as Gerard to his family. “They were great pals.” Nugent had been engaged to be married to a young woman named May Craddock and they had already bought furniture to set up a home. Peter McArdle and Robert Malone were both married with families.
“It was a terrible tragedy,” recalls George, “really shocking.” Ninety years on, the Pearse Street fire remains the biggest loss of life in the history of the Dublin Fire Brigade.
Thanks to the efforts of historian and retired fireman Las Fallon, a new plaque is to be unveiled at the site of the fire on Pearse Street (beside the Trinity College gym) this Monday at 11am, 90 years on, inscribed with the names of the three firemen.

title: ‘Today Brazil is a divided country’: Brazilians in Ireland turn out in force for presidential vote
description: Voting followed campaign marked by deep political divisions
content:
Thousands of Brazilians travelled from across Ireland to Dublin on Sunday to cast their ballots in Brazil’s presidential election first round, with voting at the Royal Dublin Society (RDS) beginning at 8am.
“[It] doesn’t matter how long I spend away from Brazil, my roots are there. I want everyone to be well and I still feel I belong,” said Renato da Cunha Melo, who has lived in Ireland for 11 years with his wife, Andrea Carla Soares.
“It was living abroad that made me see Brazil more clearly and it was living here in Ireland that made me learn more about politics, social programmes and support for vulnerable people and immigrants,” Soares said.
For many Brazilians, election day is called “celebration of democracy” and this year, the political polarisation that has divided Brazil crossed the Atlantic.
Families could be seen chanting the names of their candidates, carrying flags and wearing the colours of their preferred candidates. Some even brought their pets dressed for the occasion.
“My Brazilian identity abroad is also expressed through my vote. Despite living in Ireland, the people I love most are there, and today Brazil is a divided country,” said Saruana Martins, who has lived in Dublin for seven years and came to vote with her young daughter Ella.
Nearby, Cenira Fernandes (65) was praying outside the RDS for her candidate to win.
“Brazil needs change. My life is good here in Europe and I want that for Brazil too,” she said.
Brazil’s ambassador to Ireland, Flávio Macieira, said the engagement of the community had grown significantly. The embassy estimates that about 80,000 Brazilians live in Ireland, and 16,794 are registered to vote here. According to Brazil’s superior electoral court, the number of registered Brazilian voters in Ireland has risen by 41 per cent since the last presidential election. In 2018, there were just 2,111 registered voters, meaning the electorate has grown almost sevenfold in eight years.
The election pits president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro , who is serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted over a plot to overturn the 2022 election.
The latest Datafolha poll, published on Saturday, put Lula on 45 per cent of valid votes and Flávio Bolsonaro on 42 per cent. If no candidate wins more than half of the valid votes, a second round will be held on October 25th.
The campaign has been marked by deep political divisions, concerns over the economy and crime, and tensions with the United States.
Seeking a fourth term at 80 years old, Lula warned Washington against interfering, while the White House denied any intention to do so.
Meanwhile, 80 international observers arrived this week to follow the election.
Presenting Brazil as an independent country, Lula supports multilateralism and stronger connections with Europe, China and South America. His political story includes spending a year and seven months in prison on corruption charges before his convictions were cancelled by Brazil’s supreme federal court, opening the way for him to return to politics and win the presidency in 2022. Trying to secure his re-election in the final days, Lula announced several new measures: increasing the income tax exemption, adjusting social welfare payments for low-income families, creating programmes to help people negotiate their debts, banning sports-betting apps nationwide and offering free weight-loss injections through the public health system.
Flávio Bolsonaro (45) defends his father’s conservative and tough-on-crime ideas. However, his father’s legacy is still marked by how his government handled the Covid-19 pandemic, a period when the elder Bolsonaro repeatedly called the disease a “minor flu”.
While Flávio relies heavily on his father’s loyal voters, he tries to distance himself from the negative image of the previous government, even though he promises to pardon his father and others convicted for the coup plot.
Flávio also tried to get closer to Washington during president Donald Trump’s administration, meeting him at the White House in May and receiving public praise from him.
For voters in Ireland, however, the election was also about maintaining a connection with a country many had left years ago.
Soares summed up the feeling among voters on both sides of the political divide.
“This election will determine the future of Latin America,” she said.

title: Green Empress enhances Sun Goddess’s reputation with Group One win in France
description: Aidan O’Brien lands first Forêt success as Guineas heroine True Love emerges on top in thrilling finish
content:
Out of luck with Thundering On in the Qatar Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe, Joseph O’Brien still secured Group One glory with a filly at Paris-Longchamp on Sunday as Green Empress delivered in the Prix Marcel Boussac.
Ridden by top local jockey Christophe Soumillon, the 13/8 favourite got the better of Data by a head to earn 12/1 quotes from some bookies for next year’s 1,000 Guineas.
It was a success that advertised the talents of a filly not even at Longchamp, as the outstanding Sun Goddess has beaten Green Empress three times this season, the only defeats the new Boussac heroine has endured.
“It’s really special for us to have a Group One winner on this day and she has been progressive – she’s only ever been beaten by Sun Goddess all year,” said O’Brien, who isn’t ruling out a tilt at the Breeders’ Cup in Keeneland later this month for the winner.
“She has a super pedigree, being by Saxon Warrior out of a Sea The Stars mare. We see her as a miler that might go 10 furlongs at some stage. We’ll see how she comes out of today and discuss with the owners whether she’ll go to America or whether we wait for next year,” he added.
The sense that this year’s juvenile fillies are superior to the colts was underlined again in the following Prix Jean-Luc-Lagardere as Amusingly put her male opponents to the sword in some style.
Supplemented into the shorter Lagardere rather than tackling the Boussac, Amusingly showed a withering turn of foot under Colin Keane to beat O’Brien’s National Stakes winner Folsom Blues.
The Juddmonte-owned star was the first filly since Happily in 2017 to win the race.
Arc-winning trainer Francis Graffard said: “She beat the filly that finished second in the Marcel Boussac (Data) very easily, so I was hoping I didn’t make a mistake!”
Keane added: “She relaxed a lot better today, she wasn’t as fresh and gassy and did everything right in the first half of the race. When she did that part we thought she’d run a good race and she showed how well she can quicken.”
O’Brien was quick to describe Folsom Blues’ conqueror as “very special”. Having regularly bumped into Sun Goddess with his own Group One filly, it looks a verdict with some authority. All of it makes for a potential 1,000 Guineas to relish next spring.
This year’s 1,000 Guineas winner True Love got the better of an exciting finish to give Aidan O’Brien a first success in the seven-furlong Prix de la Forêt. It was the champion trainer’s 20th top-flight victory of the year.
“She’s a serious filly,” said O’Brien. “She’s been on the go since early on. She’s a Guineas winner, a Cheveley Park winner, a Queen Mary winner and now to come back at the end to win this race, she’s a very good filly. She could go to the Breeders’ Cup Mile.”
It retrieved an otherwise largely frustrating Arc weekend for the Ballydoyle team, with Precise earlier finding Miss Scott too good in the Prix de l’Opera after a less than clear passage. It was another success in the Thoroughbred Corporation colours for Soumillon aboard the Gosden-trained winner who’d previously scored at the Curragh.
“It was her first time in at the real deep end here after winning a Group Three at the Curragh last time out with Christophe on board,” said Thady Gosden. “The plan was to come here and give it a good go. Obviously Aventure (unplaced) is a top-class filly and we were a little bit scared of her coming into the race. We were thinking we might step her up to a mile and a half next year.”
Saturday’s Prix du Cadran proved a race too far this season for Aidan O’Brien’s outstanding stayer Scandinavia. He was outpointed by Caballo de Mar in a close finish that resulted in a stewards’ inquiry where the positions were left unchanged.
Killarney’s Monday programme has been boosted by the Listed Navigation Stakes, transferred from Cork’s cancellation due to conditions last week.
The contest includes Magnum Cor, a winner at Bellewstown on Thursday and who sports first-time cheekpieces. Action has been freed from pacemaker duties to try to add some winning black type to a CV that includes a Group One second in last year’s Futurity.
The solution, however, could be Donnacha O’Brien’s Shaihaan. Jockey Chris Hayes can have a happier time than when third on Dermot Weld’s Purview in Saturday night’s Canadian International behind Arabian Crown after being badly checked before the turn-in.
There is jumps action at Fairyhouse on Monday, where Drumadeise can build on a 40/1 second at the Listowel festival in the concluding hurdle.

title: Judge compares wind farm objectors to ‘dogged Japanese soldier’ still fighting second World War
description: Kilkenny manager Henry Shefflin among locals who objected to planning permission
content:
A High Court judge has compared court objectors against a €175 million wind farm in Co Kilkenny to “the dogged Japanese soldier still fighting World War II in the Philippine jungle, decades after everyone else has admitted defeat”.
Judge Richard Humphreys made his comment when dismissing the High Court bid by Save the South Leinster Way and writer Tara Heavey to quash An Coimisiún Pleanala’s decision to grant planning permission for the 21-turbine wind farm at Castlebanny four years ago.
The planning commission granted leave in September 2022 despite opposition from local residents, which included 10-time All-Ireland-winning hurler Henry Shefflin.
The recently appointed Kilkenny senior hurling manager was one of 70 parties to make submissions when the case was before the planning commission in 2021-22.
The applicants’ challenge has been before the courts for almost four years after the launch of a High Court judicial review application in November 2022.
In the new ruling, Humphreys has refused to quash the grant of permission for the wind farm despite finding in favour of the objectors’ grounds of challenge concerning objectives relating to the freshwater pearl mussel and the kingfisher.
However, he has found that the opposing parties in the case, the planning commission and Minister for the Environment, have established that the errors concerning objectives for the kingfisher and the freshwater pearl mussel were “harmless”.
Humphreys said that discretion weighs decisively against the quashing of the grant of permission here, particularly due to the harmlessness or lack of effect of the error.
On the issue of harmless error, Humphreys said that “generally speaking it would trivialise judicial review and be an exercise in self-indulgence to quash decisions because of things that make no difference”.
The wind farm scheme by Springfield Renewables Ltd is a joint venture between FuturEnergy Ireland – comprising Coillte and the ESB – and ART Generation.
In a new 41-page written judgment on the legal challenge, Humphreys said “the applicants began this case scrambling for the last seat on the last helicopter off the embassy roof in Saigon, by lodging their papers on the last possible day”.
In a previous judgment in October 2023, Humphreys made his initial “Saigon” comment when ruling the judicial review challenge was one day out of time.
However, the applicants were subsequently successful in a Supreme Court challenge where the court ruled that the judicial review application was made within time and the case was remitted back to the High Court.
In October, 2025, Humphreys dismissed the challenge apart from several core grounds, including the mussel and kingfisher, pending the outcome of a separate case.
Now, in refusing the applicants’ challenge, Humphreys said that the applicants “end like the dogged Japanese soldier still fighting World War II in the Philippine jungle, decades after everyone else has admitted defeat”.

title: Irish mining-waste facilities ‘a curse on future generations’, conference hears
description: Toxic waste-storage plants do not meet industry standards, says geophysicist Steven Emerman
content:
Facilities in Ireland that store toxic mining waste use technology dating from the ”first World War" that does “not meet industry standards”, a conference hosted by An Taisce has heard.
Geophysicist Steven Emerman, a specialist in mine waste and hydrology, said the use of outdated mining waste-storage facilities, which had been banned in several countries, was “quite common in Ireland”.
The State of Mining in Ireland conference, held in Dublin on Sunday, was attended by communities opposed to mining or mining waste-storage facilities associated with the Aughinish Alumina refinery in Limerick, Tara lead-zinc mines in Meath and the proposed Curraghinalt Gold mine, also known as the Sperrin Mountains mine, in Tyrone.
The plants use, or propose the use of, “upstream” dams for storing mining waste, Emerman said. He added that these dams have been denounced by the mining industry and have been implicated in some of the worst toxic-waste disasters associated with mining, resulting in deaths and destruction of habitat.
The dams are used to store “tailings”, which are “the wet, crushed rock particles that remain after the commodity of value has been removed”. He said they are “almost always toxic”.
Ore deposits of commodities such as gold, copper or lithium are “heavily depleted”, he said.
Emerman added: “Those ancient, high-grade deposits are long, long gone. Nothing like that exists anywhere anymore.
“What is being produced by the modern mine is very little commodity. A modern mine’s principal product is toxic waste. That is what is being produced, with the commodity as a very minor subproduct. It is quite rare for any modern industrial process, except mining, to produce so much waste.”
Upstream dams are used because they require a minimum amount of construction material, making them inexpensive. But they are particularly susceptible to failure, Emerman said.
“What can go wrong is the catastrophic failure of the tailings storage facility.”
These facilities must be maintained “in perpetuity”, he said. As humans have no experience in designing something to last forever, “catastrophic failure is guaranteed”. Because of this, he says the facilities are “a curse on future generations”.
Knowing these risks, Emerman underlined the importance of asking pertinent questions.
“Who is getting the benefit from this commodity? And who is suffering the damages and bearing the risks from the production of this commodity? Is it the same people who benefit and who suffer the damages and bear the risks?
“If you have one group of people who get the benefits and another who bears their risks and the damages, that is simply profoundly unjust, and there’s no basis for even asking this question: ‘is the commodity worth the price?’.”

title: British Green Party votes to equate Zionism with racism
description: Move expected to be challenged by some party members under equality legislation
content:
The Greens in England and Wales have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.
The move is expected to be challenged by some party members under equality laws.
Members voted at the party’s annual conference in Brighton to back a motion that calls for Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, to be “treated as any other form of racism”. It passed by 1,022 votes to 813.
It has been publicly opposed by four of the party’s five MPs, although Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales , has said he believes Zionism is a racist idea.
The motion, which is now formal policy, calls for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel, “with equal rights for all”.
Adrian Ramsay, one of the MPs and a former party co-leader, said after the vote that he was “deeply saddened” by the decision, and that the idea of endorsing a single Palestinian state did not match Green commitments to self-determination.
The motion argues that Zionism is necessarily racist as it “privileges one ethnic group on the basis of the subjugation of others”. It adds: “This motion is aimed at the political ideology and practice of Zionism, as defined, and not at the religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists. Not all Jews are Zionists and not all Zionists are Jews …”
While the proposers of the motion argue it will not be used to discipline Jewish members who support Zionism, it is understood that some members are consulting lawyers over whether the policy could be challenged.
Adam Wagner, the barrister who led a case which concluded that the Labour Party under then leader Jeremy Corbyn broke equality laws over anti-Semitism, said that such a case would have a good chance of success. “I think there is a strong risk that the motion as passed contravenes the Equality Act 2010, which applies to political parties, as it will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally,” he said.
There is considerable disquiet among some senior Greens who feel that Polanski, who is Jewish, could have taken a stronger stance on the issue. The party leader, who missed the vote to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a parliamentary byelection next week, has justified the motion’s argument by pointing to the death toll in Gaza during Israel’s assault on the territory.
[ ‘Terminally online’: Frustrated Greens want leader to hand over his social media Opens in new window ]
Asked on Saturday if he believed Zionism was racist, Polanski told the BBC : “Well, in the motion, it is defined as the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people. I think that is clearly racism.”
The Movement for Progressive Judaism, one of the main Jewish denominations in the United Kingdom, condemned the vote.

title: Man dies in overnight apartment fire in Mount Merrion, Dublin
description: Fire quickly brought under control but man pronounced dead at the scene
content:
A man in his 50s died over night in an apartment fire on the southside of Dublin .
Dublin Fire Brigade said it was alerted to a fire at 1.20am in the Stillorgan/Mount Merrion area of the city and firefighters and paramedics from Donnybrook, Rathfarnham and Dolphin’s Barn were sent to the scene.
The blaze was quickly brought under control but the body of a man was recovered. He was pronounced dead at the scene and his body was removed to the mortuary at St Colmcille’s Hospital in Loughlinstown.
The coroner was notified and a postmortem examination will be carried out.
An Garda Síochána took control of the scene at about 3am and a technical examination was being carried out on Sunday morning.
It is understood, however, that foul play is not suspected.

title: Charlie O’Shea shines for Munster on encouraging weekend for Irish provinces
description: Ciarán Frawley enjoys dream debut as Connacht beat Benetton in Treviso
content:
After the four provinces lost on an opening weekend for the first time since 2009, when Ireland ’s summer tourists were still on the sidelines, the tourists’ gradual return sparked a more encouraging second round of the United Rugby Championship , with just one province suffering a loss. The quartet remain in the bottom half of the table, but each could take positives from their latest outings.
Connacht welcomed back six of their seven-strong summer tour contingent, with Billy Bohan and Sam Illo locking a key scrum as Benetton pushed for a two-score lead entering the last 10 minutes. But then a second try for Ciarán Frawley, on his debut for the province, secured a 22-19 bonus-point win, the westerners’ first victory at Stadio Monigo since April 2022.
“It’s a huge result, to get five points away from home in Treviso,” said Connacht head coach Stuart Lancaster . “I’ve never come here at any point in my career and had an easy game. We had so many players playing the first game for a long time, and we had a lot of combinations not having played together, Ciarán [Frawley] obviously being one at 10. There’s always going to be that element of clunkiness and rustiness. But we dug in there, we got the win and I’m delighted for the lads.”
Lancaster said of Frawley: “It’s a dream start for him. He managed the game really well. He saw space in the backfield early on. As a 10 he put in a really accomplished performance. But it wasn’t just that, it’s his involvement and his enthusiasm off the field, how he’s conducted himself and integrated with the lads, how he’s trained. So, it’s been a huge bonus for us.
“It allows me to mix and match with Josh Ioane. He made a big impact at 15, which is obviously a great change up for us, and Sam Gilbert went to 13. We’ve got Harry West and Byron Ralston injured, but Bundee [Aki] will be around next week.”
“Italy last week, Scotland next week,” added Lancaster before a long trek home to Galway and in advance of next Friday’s game away to another international bulk supplier in Glasgow.
Munster beat the Bulls 26-22 at Thomond Park on Saturday thanks to a stunning, two-try, man-of-the-match full debut by 20-year-old academy outhalf Charlie O’Shea. In front of an attendance of 10,318, such a shot in the arm was timely on the back of the positivity generated by a rebooted coaching ticket.
“It was just unbelievable,” said O’Shea. “I probably got lucky there with one of the tries but the fans were great. It’s the loudest crowd I have played in front of and they really gave us energy there to kick on and get the win.”
Munster face Ulster in Belfast next Saturday (5.30pm) after the latter shared 10 tries in a 33-all draw in Glasgow. Leinster picked up a third bonus point from their early-season trek to South Africa, two more than last season, after a 26-20 loss to the Sharks in Durban.
They will welcome back a tranche of Ireland frontliners for next Saturday’s first competitive outing at the redeveloped Laya Arena in more than two years when hosting Cardiff (kick-off 7.45pm).

title: Daryz emulates Alleged by winning the Prix de l’Arc Triomphe back-to-back
description: Francis Graffard-trained star beats Bay City Roller and Diamond Necklace in €5m Longchamp highlight
content:
French favourite Daryz became the first colt in close to half a century to win the €5 million Qatar Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe back-to-back at Paris-Longchamp on Sunday.
Bred by the late Aga Khan, and carrying his famed green and red silks, Daryz pounced from the pack to beat the English outsider Bay City Roller, with Aidan O’Brien’s Diamond Necklace best of the Irish in third.
A surprise winner in 2025 when running down Minnie Hauk, Daryz emulated the Vincent O’Brien-trained Alleged, who won Europe’s richest race in 1977-78.
Since then, the fillies Treve (2013-14) and Enable (2017-18) have doubled up in the Arc, and Daryz is the just the ninth horse in all in the 105-year history of France’s greatest race to win twice.
The commercial breeding imperative of cashing in on an Arc winner at stud has meant most winning colts don’t get a shot at repeating but the Aga Khan organisation’s pluck was rewarded.
The confidence of French racing’s new dominant trainer, Francis Graffard, also got vindicated in style as jockey Mickael Barzalona delivered Daryz with another withering run up the Longchamp straight.
Irish jockey Oisín Murphy’s hopes he might hold on aboard Bay City Roller flickered only briefly as the winner won with more authority than the length and a quarter margin might suggest.
“He’s a champion. I said that before. It’s rare I’m confident before a race as it is so hard in a race like this, but I knew things were going right and he’d be very hard to beat,” said Graffard.
“I was confident, but I was putting so much pressure on myself before the race, and you can make yourself look a fool, so it is easier not to speak and not say anything. But I think for the sport we have to be transparent, and I was confident and his rider was confident, so we had to say it.
“Mickael rode a beautiful race again. It’s so beautiful for the sport, I’m lucky to have horses like that,” added Graffard.
Having announced his arrival at elite level as a 19-year-old when celebrating his narrow 2011 Epsom Derby success on Pour Moi well before the line, Barzalona’s big-race nerve has never been in doubt, although it got tested here.
“To win this kind of race twice proves that Daryz is an exceptional horse,” he said.
“It didn’t go as we expected but he showed his talent and that made the difference in the end. The pace was not strong, it was a rough race and nothing went to plan, but the horse deserved to win again, and he’s proved all season he is the best one,” the rider added.
Diamond Necklace did best of the Irish quartet with her Ballydoyle stable companions Benvenuto Cellini and Minnie Hauk finishing ninth and 10th respectively.
Christophe Soumillon made light of Diamond Necklace’s wide draw and briefly looked a threat before finishing a neck behind Bay City Roller for second. Joseph O’Brien’s Oaks winner Thundering One was eighth.
Both Treve and Enable failed in their attempts at a historic third Arc and it doesn’t look like Daryz will get a shot at it. The Aga Khan’s daughter, Princess Zahra, who now oversees the famed bloodstock empire, suggested a new stud career beckons for the son of 2009 Arc hero Sea The Stars.
It was another landmark for Graffard however. He set a new French record of 14 Group One victories in 2025 and is currently on nine for the year. Earlier on the Arc undercard, his supplemented filly Amusingly beat the colts in the Prix Jean Luc Lagadere.
“It is different when you are favourite and you are the one to beat. There was pressure, you can’t deny it, but it’s good and it’s why I show emotion. It’s great for the owners, it’s such a wonderful breeding operation.
“We kept losing position early, we were too far back, but we were lucky Daryz has good acceleration. Without any trouble I knew he’d run a big race” he commented.
There was Group One success for both Aidan and Joseph O’Brien on the Arc undercard. O’Brien Jnr landed the Prix Marcel Boussac with Green Empress. His father won the Prix de la Forêt for the first time through True Love.
