title: Russian attacks continue during German chancellor’s solidarity visit to Kyiv
description: Friedrich Merz pledged €1bn in military aid and said his ⁠visit ‘demonstrates ​that we will not be intimidated’
content:
German chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv in a show of support as Russia stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian cities.
The aerial war has intensified, with Moscow attacking cities across Ukraine with hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, while Kyiv has been striking Russia’s oil industry and businesses.
Merz said he travelled to the Ukrainian capital on his second trip as chancellor to demonstrate his country’s solidarity with Ukraine. He announced ‌military aid for Ukraine worth ​about €1 billion and an energy support package, ⁠as the Ukrainian ‌capital ‌came ​under renewed attack on Sunday from ⁠Russian ​drones.
Merz said ⁠his ⁠visit “demonstrates ​that we will not be intimidated. Nor will we be intimidated by a drone ‌attack occurring at ⁠the very time of our visit.”
Germany is Ukraine’s largest donor, sending Kyiv more than €43.3 billion since the war began, along with equipment and weapons.
“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said in a statement on Sunday, adding that he told Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy : “You can continue to count on our help.”
The chancellor said the partnership between the two countries was “not a one-way street”, pointing to German and Ukrainian companies jointly developing technologies that benefit both sides.
“This makes us safer and stronger,” he said.
In a post on X, Zelenskiy thanked Germany and said the two countries would make “important agreements” during the visit to strengthen Ukraine’s defences and those of the rest of Europe.
“Russia must be stopped together,” he wrote.
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said Merz would hold talks with Zelenskiy.
Writing on X, Sybiha said the agenda would focus on “strengthening Ukraine, our defence and resilience, and our shared European security”.
Russia’s foreign ministry said on Saturday it would continue to carry out “mass retaliatory strikes” on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, urging foreign nationals and diplomats to leave the country.
It previously issued a similar warning in May.
The German and Russian foreign ministers met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly’s annual gathering of world leaders last month. It was believed to be the first such face-to-face meeting since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russia’s Sergey Lavrov rejected German calls to ease off its “dangerous path of escalation” towards Ukraine, and instead accused Germany of being Ukraine’s main sponsor and seeking to be a leading military power in Europe.
Ties between Russia and Germany have soured even more in recent weeks, following an attempted drone attack in early September at Leipzig airport .
Germany has blamed Russia for the incident and announced the closure of the German consulate in St Petersburg, the latest in a cycle of tit-for-tat moves.
Meanwhile, Merz’s power inside Germany has taken a blow after a string of state election defeats last month, including losses to the anti-migration and Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany party.
However, he said he intends to remain chancellor.
On Sunday morning, Russian attacks continued with a drone hitting Kyiv’s Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River again, Zelenskiy said.
Video circulating on social media showed the drone flying into the bridge and the explosion as vehicles crossed.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were wounded in the attack.
The latest strike came after Russian assaults forced the full or partial closure of three of Kyiv’s six road bridges over the Dnipro river earlier this week, suspending traffic and causing tailbacks in Moscow’s latest effort to disrupt life in the Ukrainian capital.
Previously, Russia has hit apartment blocks, supermarket warehouses, petrol stations and data centres, among other targets.
One person was killed and 16 wounded on Sunday in a Russian aerial bomb attack on the Ukrainian city of Sumy, local officials said.
Russia’s ministry of defence said on Sunday it would intensify its strikes “against military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure, in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine”. It delivered the warning in response to Zelenskiy’s comments, in an interview with Reuters published on Saturday, that Ukraine would escalate its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Russia invaded its neighbour more than 4½ years ago and there are no concrete signs that a peace settlement might be possible.
Fighting along the roughly 1,250km frontline, snaking through northern, eastern and southern Ukraine, has been virtually deadlocked in recent months. – AP and Reuters

title: Max Verstappen wins chaotic F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia after rain causes farcical scenes
description: First win of season for Dutchman after long rain delay sees Kimi Antonelli close in on the championship
content:
Victory in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia for Max Verstappen was surely as sweet as any he may have tasted, the Dutchman on top after what was an extraordinarily dramatic and, indeed, chaotic afternoon at the Sepang circuit. But in a race which had opened in an embarrassing farce for Formula One, it held in contrast only bitter disappointment for George Russell, whose retirement has left his title hopes shattered and his Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli within touching distance of the championship.
It is nine years since Malaysia hosted a grand prix and, standing in this weekend for the cancelled meeting in Bahrain, the much-loved circuit proved to be the grand stage to showcase a dominant drive for Verstappen and Red Bull, his and the team’s first win of the season, beating Antonelli into second.
Moreover, as the champion in waiting demonstrated his credentials, there was a timely reminder that the driver whose success he hopes to emulate, Lewis Hamilton, has lost none of his touch. He took third for Ferrari, a remarkable comeback after a torrid afternoon, starting on the slick rubber in the wet which dropped him as far back as 17th and 80 seconds off the lead. He delivered a superb drive, determined and decisive, including a late pass for the podium place on Isack Hadjar, who finished fifth behind Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc.
For Antonelli, even given Mercedes were no match for Verstappen and Red Bull in Sepang, he did what was required in leading his team-mate for most of the race until Russell, who was in third place behind the Italian, had a power unit problem and had to retire. Heartbreak for Russell who has endured more than his fair share of bad luck this season.
For Mercedes it was a disappointment allied to a doubtless sense of deja vu, suffering an engine problem at the same track where Hamilton had a similar failure in 2016, which all but cost him the title. Russell acknowledged this had been a similar body blow, as Antonelli takes an 84-point lead with seven meetings remaining.
“You’ve almost got to laugh, I’m beyond disappointment,” Russell said. “I don’t need to say I think it’s [the title] gone or whatever but of course it’s exceptionally unlikely, and that’s just the reality. I knew if I wanted to come back, I needed luck on my side. Unfortunately, I had luck not on my side.”
Verstappen is out of the title fight but clearly took huge pleasure in a win as dominant as some of his best drives. Having passed Antonelli for the lead in the early stages he was untouchable out front, taking the flag nine years after he won in Malaysia.
Yet his win was preceded by farcical scenes as this season’s engine formula was found sorely wanting the first time it was tested in wet conditions. F1, which prides itself as the pinnacle of motorsport, was brought low by a spot of rain and, of all things, some dicky software. Hardly the stuff of the gladiatorial arena it wishes to present.
After a downpour swamped the circuit before the off, this was the first time these cars had run in the wet this season and the engines, with an almost 50-50 split between electrical and combustion power and already facing fierce criticism, proved to have problems that had not been anticipated.
The start was delayed by 45 minutes but as the rain eased the cars took to the track for two formation laps, Hamilton was swiftly among a swathe of drivers who had a software problem. He slowed and had to effectively reboot his car but he was not alone and there were similar issues affecting other competitors, including Verstappen, noting he could not accelerate, and two of the Ferrari-engined Haas and Cadillac also stopping, with many drivers reporting the same problems to varying degrees. It left the field out of order and in some cases not even on the same lap and the start was suspended.
That, in turn, prompted a further delay of 53 minutes as the cars were re-sorted into grid order and the governing body, the FIA – now it appears functioning as the sport’s IT department – uploaded new software parameters to the cars to deal with the problem. The issue was caused by the engines’ software, now so intrinsic to delivering the power, and incapable of coping with the low revs used in wet, low-grip conditions because of, it is believed, the complex algorithm that is designed to prevent teams using traction control.
None of which takes the sheen off Verstappen’s victory, which represents an extraordinary turnaround delivered with no little fortitude. For the opening half of the season the car was a handful to drive and even Verstappen, for all his skill, was struggling to master it. Since which, Red Bull have delivered upgrades perhaps beyond expectations and securing a win was a mighty achievement.
Once he retook the lead from Antonelli, who had swept past at the start, the Dutchman was in control throughout, while Russell made up places to be in third, only to have to climb despondently from his car with five laps to go. The victory belonged to Verstappen but Antonelli emerged from Sepang very much on top while F1 is left to consider why “computer says no” was another foible that had not apparently been foreseen in possibly the least popular regulations the sport has ever delivered. – Guardian

title: How Cornell University punished seven men accused of sexual assault
description: After a woman accused fraternity members of assaulting her in 2024, the university conducted a closed disciplinary process
author_name: Sharon Otterman, Hurubie Meko, Debra Kamin
content:
The lightest punishment called for writing a paper and completing training. The most severe was expulsion from the college.
After a woman attending Cornell University accused seven fraternity members of sexually assaulting her in 2024, the university convened a closed proceeding to determine what had occurred and whether those men should face discipline.
Since then, the sanctions imposed on each of the men, and the reasoning behind those decisions, have remained secret. The college has said little.
But detailed summaries of the punishments obtained by The New York Times provide the first look at how Cornell administrators apportioned blame for the alcohol- and drug-fuelled gathering that the woman has said left her shattered and degraded.
Two of the fraternity members were expelled. Another, who had already graduated, was barred from campus. Two more were suspended. The remaining men were handed lighter punishments, the summaries show.
All of them have denied any wrongdoing, and the district attorney for Tompkins County, New York , where Cornell’s Ithaca campus is located, declined to prosecute in 2024. None of the men has been charged with a crime. Their fraternity, Chi Phi, has been banned from campus.
Still, since allegations from the woman who has become known as Jane Doe surfaced in a lawsuit on September 16th, they have touched off intense anger over sexual abuse on campus and why more is not done to punish those responsible. Others have criticised what they see as a rush to judge the seven men involved.
[ Keith Duggan: Cornell rape allegation scandal brings an early bleakness to upstate New York Opens in new window ]
In her lawsuit, Jane Doe claimed that, from the start of her encounter involving the seven fraternity members, she was incapable of consent because she was severely intoxicated. The lawsuit inflamed particular ire by stating the defendants were all “afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell”, an assertion Cornell has said did not accurately reflect what occurred.
Combined with more than 1,000 pages of interview transcripts, police reports and other records gathered by Cornell investigators, the discipline summaries show the university based its decisions on a broad and complicated body of evidence.
[ How Cornell University alleged rape victim went from shame to seeking justice Opens in new window ]
In the end, the punishments handed out by the three-member panel, which met on Zoom over 12 days in May 2025, varied widely. The panel, which enforces federal civil rights at the university prohibiting gender-based discrimination, did not conclude Jane Doe was sexually assaulted by all the men she had accused, according to the discipline summaries.
The university investigative files outline in excruciating detail what the fraternity members were accused of doing on the night of October 19th, 2024.
It was Matthew Ingalls whom Jane Doe originally went to visit at the Chi Phi fraternity house at about 11pm. She walked there alone from a bar to see him, with her intoxication level from drinking through the evening at a level of about a five out of 10, she told investigators.
After she arrived, Ingalls asked her if she wanted to have a threesome with Jonathan Newell, Jane Doe said. During that encounter, she said, the men gave her ketamine and alcohol. Eventually, other men engaged in sex acts with her without her consent and while she was incapacitated, she said.
At the end of the night at the fraternity house, when Jane Doe was near hallucinating, there was more sex, she told investigators.
Expulsions were handed to Ingalls and Newell – the man who sent a Snapchat message to other fraternity members encouraging them to enter the bedroom where Jane Doe was undressed, the discipline summaries show.
The discipline summaries show that the panel found Ingalls responsible for sexual assault, judging that he was willing to manipulate, exploit and endanger Jane Doe for his own self-interest and the entertainment of others.
A lawyer for Ingalls declined to comment.
Newell was also accused of sexual assault, the university files show. Jane Doe told police on November 14th, 2024, that he had struck her buttocks with enough force during intercourse to leave bruises, and that he had manipulated her to ingest ketamine. He also sent a Snapchat message apparently inviting other fraternity brothers to join in, the files show.
It was not clear whether Newell had hired a lawyer, and he did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Suspensions and disciplinary probation were given to Winston Lee and Gillio Lopes. Jane Doe had accused Lee of inhaling ketamine off her body and forcing oral sex on her. She alleged that Lopes had sex with her without her consent.
Lee was suspended for two years, with several semesters of disciplinary probation upon his return; Lopes received a three-semester suspension and two years of probation, the discipline summaries show. Both men also were ordered not to contact Jane Doe, and were required to study sexual harassment and to write reflection papers.
Lawyers for Lee and Lopes did not respond to requests for comment.
A persona non grata order was issued to Diego Sarabia, who had graduated by the time of the discipline panel’s ruling. Sarabia, whom Jane Doe accused of forcibly kissing her, was barred from campus for three years.
The remaining two men, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar, were ordered not to contact Jane Doe, to study sexual harassment social media use and bystander intervention, and to write “reflection papers”. They were accused of being part of a group of men who entered the room after reading Newell’s Snapchat message.
A recently unsealed lawsuit filed by Kretzschmar against Cornell shows he was not found responsible for sexual assault. Instead, Cornell ruled he had committed a lesser offence of attempted sexual exploitation.
Jeremy Saland, a lawyer for Kretzschmar, said in a statement on Friday that the discipline his client received showed he was “never accused of, nor found responsible for, rape”.
“He was not even present during any sexual activity,” Saland said.
It was not clear whether Norris was represented by a lawyer, and phone calls and text messages to numbers listed for him and his family members went unanswered.
Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said in a statement on Friday that the punishments “did not reflect the severity of the charges”.
“With the exception of two of these men, all of them will be able to graduate with a Cornell diploma and live their lives reaping the benefits of this coveted degree,” Giuffra said. “In contrast, as of today, it is doubtful whether Ms Doe will even graduate college or ever live a normal life due to what these men did to her.”
A spokesperson for Cornell declined to comment, citing federal laws protecting student privacy.
[ New York governor attacks law enforcement’s handling of 2024 Cornell rape investigation Opens in new window ]
In the wake of Jane Doe’s lawsuit, New York governor Kathy Hochul last week ordered an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the case. On Thursday, she appointed the state attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor with the power to bring criminal charges.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: Motorcyclist (50s) killed in Co Meath crash named as award-winning photographer
description: Colin Keegan remembered by colleagues as an outstanding photographer and devoted father
content:
A motorcyclist who died following a crash in Co Meath on Saturday has been named as award-winning press photographer Colin Keegan.
The incident, which involved a motorcycle and a car, occurred on the R156 at Harlockstown, Co Meath, at 12.15pm on Saturday.
Colin Keegan, who was in his 50s, was pronounced dead at the scene. His body was subsequently removed to Navan Mortuary. The driver of the car, a woman in her 70s, was uninjured.
Colin Keegan worked for Collins photo agency for three decades, and won a number of awards through the Press Photographers’ Association of Ireland for his work capturing news, politics and entertainment across Ireland.
His photographs were published widely across Irish media, including by The Irish Times.
Charlie Collins, proprietor of the agency, paid tribute to his colleague, describing his death as an enormous loss.
“He worked with us for 30 years. He was one of the best news photographers in the country. He was an enthusiastic motorcyclist. He was just out on a leisurely ride,” he said.
“He was such a total gentleman, that’s all there is to say.”
Niall Carson, press photographer with PA Ireland, described Colin Keegan as a “complete professional” with whom he had a “friendly rivalry”.
“Colin was my main competitor but he was very friendly about it. He would often text you if you got a better picture to congratulate you on it,” he said.
“He was a tough guy. I would trust him to have my back in very dangerous or tough situations.”
Carson singled out Colin Keegan’s 2005 photograph of then-minister for defence Willie O’Dea holding a gun – an image that sparked significant controversy at the time.
“I knew his photographs before I knew him. He was one of the best photographers for the country and he won many awards in the difficult categories. He was a devoted father as well,” he added.
Photojournalist and friend Gary Ashe said the photography community is “heartbroken to hear of his passing”.
“Colin was, in my opinion, the best news photographer in the country . . . few would argue. He was a great colleague and an absolute professional at his trade. His many press photo awards are testament to his skills in photojournalism,” he said.
“On a personal level, I consider Colin a great friend and someone I shared a great, cheeky sense of humour [with]. I have known Colin for over 26 years and he will be sorely missed, not only by myself, but his loving family and the greater press photographer community.”
Laura Hutton, deputy head of visual media at The Irish Times, said colleagues rang each other in disbelief at the news of his death.
“A motorcycle accident in Meath, coming just over a year after the death of Colin’s good friend, photographer Mick O’Neill , in a similar motorcycle accident,” she said.
“His loss is devastating, my thoughts are with his family, his two children especially. He was one of the best hard-news photographers in the country, and his hunger and talent never waned.”
She added: “He was quick, he was sharp and he always got the shot. He will be sorely missed in photography circles, as well as the wider news industry, which will be poorer for his loss.”
The scene of the crash was examined by Garda forensic collision investigators and an incident room has been established at Ashbourne Garda station, Co Meath.
A senior investigating officer has been appointed.
Gardaí are appealing to anyone who witnessed the crash, particularly anyone in the area between 12pm and 12.30pm on Saturday, or anyone with dashcam footage, to come forward.

title: Newry’s Conor Wallace comes up short in world title eliminator against Ben Whittaker
description: Wallace had the former Olympic medallist badly hurt in the final round
content:
Newry light-heavyweight Conor Wallace came up short on the scorecards against Ben Whittaker after having the home fighter badly hurt late on in their fight in Birmingham, England, on Saturday night.
Whittaker (now 13-0-1) won both the unanimous decision and the right to challenge unified champion Dmitry Bivol, but after the fight he expressed interest in a rematch with Wallace (17-2), having had to hold on to survive the final minutes of his first 12-round fight.
Whittaker’s boxing pedigree and sharp reflexes saw him coast through the majority of the fight, while Wallace took a cautious approach that left him way behind on the judges’ scorecards. Whittaker displayed his customary Prince Naseem-like showboating throughout the early rounds.
After nine one-sided and subdued rounds, the 10th proved to be the first where Wallace found success, landing with hard left straights, and Whittaker’s coach, Ireland’s Andy Lee, instructed his man to stick to outboxing his opponent after that session.
However, the Newry man continued his success in the 11th, and the 12th was perhaps the toughest round of Whittaker’s career so far.
Whittaker was caught early with a straight left and tried to hold on, eventually slumping to the canvas, which referee Kieran McCann ruled a slip. Immediately after, Whittaker dodged low to avoid a punch and grabbed on to Wallace’s leg, forcing both men down.
Wallace finally threw caution to the wind, attempting to finish the fight, while Whittaker held on where he could throughout the last round, making one more visit to the canvas; again ruled a slip.
At the final bell, the deficit built in the early rounds proved to be too great for Wallace to overcome and he lost via unanimous decision.
Despite earning a shot at a world title, Whittaker said in his postfight interview: “I want to thank Wallace, great fight. I think we should do it again and I’ll beat him down even better.”
Lee also expressed interest in a rematch, claiming illness leading up to the fight had affected Whittaker’s performance.

title: Celtic condemn tennis ball protest aimed at Dermot Desmond at St Andrews
description: Tennis balls throw at club’s principal shareholder during Alfred Dunhill Links Championship
content:
Celtic have condemned a protest which saw tennis balls thrown towards principal shareholder Dermot Desmond during his visit to the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship at St Andrews.
Desmond – who has been criticised by supporters for a lack of progress on the pitch – was taking part in the pro-am event on Saturday when the protest took place on the green of the 15th hole.
Tennis balls with pictures of Desmond’s face crossed out were thrown on to the green. The 76-year-old was escorted off the course by security.
The Celtic Fans Collective later posted a statement on social media, which included video and pictures of the protest, calling for change at the top of the club and more “accountability”.
On Saturday evening, Celtic issued a lengthy and strongly-worded statement against the “premeditated action” which “brought shame upon” the name of the club.
“Celtic Football Club has never sought to prevent supporters from expressing criticism of the club, its board or its shareholders,” the statement read. “Supporters are entitled to disagree with decisions, to make their views known and to protest peacefully. What occurred at St Andrews represents a significant and unacceptable escalation.
“Those responsible have brought shame upon the name of Celtic Football Club and upon a reputation which generations of Celtic supporters have spent more than a century building.
“The club no longer accepts that the Celtic Fans Collective can credibly claim to represent the wider Celtic support. Those responsible for today’s events certainly do not speak for the many thousands of Celtic supporters who express their views passionately, peacefully and responsibly.”
Celtic said the club would not be “intimidated or coerced by organised acts of disruption”, adding “there is a line between protest and deliberate disruption. Today, that line was crossed.”
The statement concluded: “No supporter requires the permission of Celtic Football Club to disagree with its board. But equally, no supporter group has an entitlement to repeatedly disrupt events, intimidate individuals, or seek to coerce the club and then claim to do so on behalf of the Celtic support.
“Celtic will continue to listen to and engage with supporters who wish to make their voices heard constructively and responsibly. There are many established channels through which supporters can do so, and today’s decision does not diminish the club’s commitment to meaningful supporter engagement.
“But engagement requires responsibility. The club will protect its employees, directors, shareholders and supporters. The reputation of Celtic Football Club is non negotiable.”
A spokesperson from the Scottish Police confirmed no injuries were reported from the incident, adding “enquiries are ongoing”.
Martin O’Neill ’s side, who won the domestic double last season, currently sit top of the table, two points clear of Rangers.
However, Celtic lost their last three fixtures before the international break – two defeats to Rangers, and a 3-1 home defeat to Ferencvaros in their opening Europa League clash.

title: Brazilians head to polls in high-stakes, polarised election
description: Election campaign has offered meager policy debate, as both leading candidates skipped major TV debates
content:
Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday in the first round of a narrowly split election after a campaign dominated ‌by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling.
Leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , 80, is seeking a fourth term, while senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the 45-year-old son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, hopes to return his father’s right-wing movement to power.
A victory for the senator ​would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US president Donald Trump , while Lula’s re-election could create a headache for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
Despite growing worries over Brazil’s public finances and sluggish economic growth, the campaign has offered meager policy debate, as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates.
If no candidate wins more than 50 per cent of valid votes, the top two will face off on October 25th. Surveys show Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro polling roughly even in a likely runoff.
Other ​candidates, including former state governors Ronaldo Caiado and Romeu Zema, have struggled to break through with the polarised electorate, even as Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro are each rejected by roughly half of voters, polls show.
Flavio Bolsonaro has promised to seek amnesty for his father, who is serving a sentence ⁠of more than 27 years for plotting a coup after his narrow election defeat in 2022. Lula has cast the election as a choice between “democracy and denialism” and repeatedly warned of foreign interference.
The ‌fallout ​from Jair Bolsonaro’s conviction last year has coloured much of the campaign.
Trump, who called that case a “witch hunt” imposed a 50 per cent tariff on Brazil in 2025, explicitly linking the tariffs to the trial of Bolsonaro after lobbying from the Bolsonaro family to pressure Brazil’s Supreme Court to drop the charges.
This year, Trump levied new tariffs over alleged unfair trade ⁠practices. Lula has cast the move as an attempt to sway the election and portrayed the ​Bolsonaros as too eager to please Washington at Brazil’s expense.
[ Brazil’s poor once propelled Lula to power. Now many are wavering Opens in new window ]
Lula’s allies have warned that the Trump administration might ​refuse to recognise election results if he wins. They point to a failed effort to send US officials to Brazil in order to “discuss electoral integrity,” according to the US state department.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that Brazilian intelligence officials briefed a French and ‌German delegation on alleged US and Russian interference before the election. The US ​has rejected claims of interference in Brazil’s affairs.
Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, though he hosted senator Flavio Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly.
The senator, who has pledged closer ties with the ⁠US and Israel, welcomed the Trump administration’s designation of Brazil’s major gangs as terrorist groups, which Lula ⁠rejected.
Also in play is US access to Brazil’s vast ​critical mineral reserves, key to Washington’s push to reduce dependence on China for those materials.
Despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over voters grappling with high living costs, heavy household debt and the threat of street crime and more pervasive gang activity.
Flavio Bolsonaro has sought to capitalise on cost of living concerns, while Lula has moved to ban online gambling and, as the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief for families.
Rising spending and public debt above 82 per cent of GDP have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil’s president may need to address. The government lowered its economic growth forecasts for this year and next to just 2 per cent and 2.3 per cent respectively.
“Lula would likely preserve a state-led model with only modest spending restraint; Bolsonaro would likely pursue a more market-friendly agenda centered on spending cuts, privatizations, concessions, and a stronger fiscal anchor,” said Alberto Ramos, chief Latin America economist at Goldman Sachs.
Overshadowing the policy debate, a scandal surrounding the now-defunct Banco Master has engulfed much of Brazil’s political class and renewed public anger over corruption.
Daniel Vorcaro, ‌who ran the bank, was arrested earlier this year ⁠and accused of a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme. The investigation has probed the banker’s ties to figures from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes to Flavio Bolsonaro, who is being investigated for money laundering tied to the case by the federal police.
The senator has denied any wrongdoing, although he confirmed raising millions of dollars from Vorcaro to make a movie about his father.
The banker’s connections to Moraes, seen ‌by many as a Lula ally, plunged the court into crisis a month before the vote, creating fresh problems for the president. Moraes has said the case is politically and electorally motivated for his conviction of the elder Bolsonaro.
Lula has also tried to distance himself from a ​federal police investigation into his son over alleged influence peddling, which his son denies.
On Sunday, voters will also elect all 513 lower house members and two-thirds ​of the Senate, where some lawmakers have pushed to impeach Moraes.
Congress has gained greater influence in Brazilian politics since the impeachment of former president Dilma Rousseff, a Lula ally, in 2016, raising the stakes of those legislative races. - Reuters

title: AIL round-up: St Mary’s hold off Clontarf comeback on day of eye-catching results
description: Young Munster stun a stacked Terenure side for a fifth successive victory over Dublin side
content:
Where to start? On a glorious October day, the Energia All-Ireland League rained tries and thrillers, with hexes extended and surprises plentiful among some truly eye-catching results.
St Mary’s withstood a thunderous second-half comeback by Clontarf in front of a large and rapt Templeville Road crowd to repeat their win in last May’s final. Dan Goggin’s try, to augment earlier efforts by Richie Bergin and Conor Pierce, earned Mary’s a 33-14 interval lead and Mick O’Gara’s fifth penalty in a 21-point haul had them 36-19 ahead. But the prolific Dylan Donnellan scored three of Tarf’s five tries before Mary’s repelled one final attack.
“We played some great rugby in the first half,” said Mary’s head coach Mark McHugh. “But they’re an excellent side and have a great scrum, lineout, maul and pick-and-goes. If there had been another five minutes there was only one winner, so we’re delighted. But I’m glad we don’t have to play them for another eight months.”
Where to continue? All the other four wins were standout results. After a summer turnover and opening thumping at home to Old Belvedere, Young Munster travelled to Lakelands Park and stunned a stacked Terenure side for a fifth successive time.
Terenure laid siege early on, but Oisín Minogue won a turnover, Munsters went wide on their own line, Ihechi Oji broke clear and Tom Waters scored. Seán French levelled matters, Waters scored again before Aran Egan converted his own try and made it 17-14 past the hour. But a monster Munster maul earned a 78th-minute penalty try and they were pushing for a bonus point at the end.
Munsters coach Ger Slattery said: “We didn’t make many changes but Luke Murphy had a great game and credit to the guys who’ve stuck with us, like Alan Kennedy, Fintan Coleman and Kelvin Langan. We can take huge confidence from this.”
Similarly, after last season’s double, UCD again stunned Lansdowne 43-26 at the UCD Bowl. With some good launches from scrum and lineout, and a big performance from Arthur Ashmore, Maxim Aschenbrenner and Charlie Molony both scored twice, while Paddy Clancy contributed 23 points in a kicking masterclass.
Old Belvedere joined them as the early pacesetters after an emphatic 56-10 win over Ballynahinch at Ollie Campbell Park, with Robbie Russell scoring four of their eight tries and Sam Wisniewski crossing twice and landing five conversions in their respective 20-point hauls.
Last but not least, Old Wesley registered a first win in 1A for three decades by beating Cork Constitution 36-33 at Energia Park. Páidí Farrell crossed twice for Wesley, with Tom Larke’s 79th-minute penalty decisive.
In 1B, Nenagh Ormond and Blackrock College maintained unbeaten starts, while Trinity scored six tries to defeat Garryowen 46-22. Cashel and Corinthians lead 2A after 36-29 and 26-19 wins away to Queen’s and Greystones, Dominic Williams’s injury-time try securing all five points for the Galway side.
Remarkably, Clogher Valley, Malone, Ballyclare, Skerries and newcomers Enniskillen lead a five-way tie on maximum points in 2B North, suggesting the IRFU’s 2B and 2C carve-up has not worked.

title: Young woman knocked down in fatal Henry St incident urged to come forward
description: Congolese man in his mid 30s died on Dublin’s Henry Street in May
content:
Gardaí investigating the death of Yves Sakila on Dublin’s Henry Street in May have issued a renewed appeal for witnesses, including asking for a woman in her late teens or early 20s to come forward.
During the incident, “a male and a female” were knocked to the ground, gardaí said in a press release, but while they have spoken to the man, they have yet to reach the woman.
Sakila, who was Congolese and was in his mid-30s, was suspected of shoplifting from Arnotts and was pursued by security personnel on May 15th at around 5pm.
When gardaí arrived on the scene, Sakila had been held on the ground by a group of security guards for a period.
The responding gardaí handcuffed Sakila in an apparent bid to get control of the situation and attend to the injured pensioner.
However, almost immediately after the handcuffs were applied, gardaí realised Sakila was unwell, removed the handcuffs and began performing CPR. He was then taken to the Mater hospital where he was later pronounced dead.
Video footage of the first part of the incident, involving a group of men restraining the deceased, circulated on messaging apps. It showed the group, at least some of whom are security personnel, holding Sakila to the ground as he is face down on the pedestrianised street.
The woman gardaí wish to speak to was described as “a white female, dark hair, in her late teens to early twenties, wearing a khaki-coloured waist length coat, black crop T-shirt, blue jeans cut at the knees and black Adidas runners”.
“After being knocked to the ground she got up herself and stayed around for a few minutes before making her way to O’Connell Street,” gardaí said.
The force asked that she contact the investigation team at Store Street Garda Station, the Garda confidential line or any Garda station.
It also said that investigating gardaí “believe that there are also still other persons who were in the area at the time who have not come forward”. They encouraged them to do so.
Gardaí received the results of a postmortem investigation but have not released them for operational reasons.
The high-profile death of Sakila led to protests on the streets of Dublin in its wake attended by members of the Congolese and other African communities as well as members of the wider public.
The Congolese minister for foreign affairs, Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner, met Sakila’s family and Irish ministers over the matter on a visit to Ireland.
Ebun Joseph, the special rapporteur on racism, called for an “urgent” independent investigation into the incident, expressing “profound shock and grave concern”.

title: Flydubai co-pilot’s time in Australia under investigation after cockpit incident
description: Australian federal police says multiple agencies are investigating man’s connections to the country
content:
Australian security agencies have launched an investigation after it emerged that the Flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel -bound flight spent about two years in the country as a student.
Disaster was narrowly averted on Wednesday when passengers and crew intervened to stop the co-pilot’s attempt to take control of the Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv, which had 182 people onboard and plunged 5,067m in just over 30 seconds.
The United ⁠Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general has said the co-pilot had used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air. Numerous media outlets have named the co-pilot as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national.
A source familiar with the case, but not authorised to speak publicly, said the man was granted an Australian student visa in 2014, before arriving in the country to commence a university course the following year.
He left Australia in 2017, and his visa was cancelled in 2019 after authorities confirmed he was no longer enrolled in the course, the source said.
The Australian federal police (AFP) on Sunday said multiple agencies – including the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (Asio) – were probing the man’s connections to the country.
“The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team (VIC JCTT), comprising the AFP, Victoria Police and ASIO, can confirm it is investigating the man’s links to Australia,” an AFP spokesperson said.
“An update will be provided at an appropriate time.”
[ Flydubai flight: Co-pilot had ‘Islamic radical indoctrination’, says Netanyahu Opens in new window ]
US media outlets, including CNN, reported that a now-deleted LinkedIn profile said al-Hammami had studied engineering at an Australian university.
It came after a British university, Buckinghamshire New University, said a student named Hamam al-Hammami had “previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management” at the institution. It added: “He did not undertake any pilot training at the university.”
A Flydubai spokesperson on Saturday said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still ‌under investigation and the airline was not in a position to comment further.
The airline’s flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv have been suspended until further notice after the attack. The Omani co-pilot and the flight’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, were taken to the UAE, as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.
The Wall Street Journal has reported that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. He was then moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, according to the official, before being hired by the UAE-based budget airline Flydubai.

title: Fund manager charges are taking a chunk out of my retirement fund
description: Average charges for an Approved Retirement Fund are around 1% but better deals are available if you shop around
content:
I’m approaching retirement and, as my pension fund has grown quite well over the years, I’m interested in taking out an approved retirement fund (ARF).
I have a query about the charges involved. A fund value of €1 million would give a pension of €40,000 a year, but you can expect to pay 1 per cent of the fund value or an additional €10,000 a year in charges.
As these charges will continue to be taken as you’re drawing your pension, they could realistically amount to hundreds of thousands of euro in total.
My pension fund has done well partly because I’ve kept costs to a minimum. So, I want an ARF with:
ARF providers, however, all seem to charge a percentage of the fund value. It doesn’t make sense that drawing a pension from a €1 million fund should cost you 10 times more in charges than a pension from a €100,000 fund.
Do you know of an ARF provider with flat-rate charges, and can you recommend anything else I should be doing to minimise these charges?
Approved retirement funds (ARFs) are one way a person can take their pension on retirement.
Your pension funds will have built up over your working life either in a pensions scheme attached to your workplace where you can be one of many members or small personal schemes. When it comes to retirement you have some choices about what happens those funds.
First, you can take a certain amount of your fund tax-free. That is generally a quarter of your fund up to a maximum of €200,000. If a quarter of your fund amounts to more than this, you will pay just the standard 20 per cent rate of income tax on anything between €200,000 and €500,000.
Some people, including those employed in the public service before a certain date, are entitled to take one and a half times their salary instead.
Thereafter, there are generally two ways of drawing down your income in retirement – an annuity or an ARF.
With an annuity, you hand your fund over to an insurance company in return for an agreed annual income for life. Generally an annuity will die with the owner unless they have made provision for a survivor’s payment to a spouse from the fund.
You can choose certain features – payment of a reduced pension to a surviving spouse, minimum term of payment so the fund pays out for a set minimum number of years even if you die earlier and a provision to allow for inflation, for instance. Each of these comes at a cost, reducing the amount you receive initially.
How much you receive will also be gauged by how much you have in your fund and your general health. Smokers and the less healthy, ironically, can get a higher payment as they are not likely to be needing the fund as long as someone who can reasonably expect to live close to 20 years in retirement.
ARFs were introduced widely in 1999 and have proved popular for several reasons, not least that the rates offered under annuities became less attractive.
They allow your pension to stay invested so that it can (hopefully) grow further and, among other things, they do not die with the holder. They can be left to a spouse, a child or children, or to some other beneficiary.
Each of those scenarios has different tax treatments that we will not go into here.
You clearly know all this but it is worth explaining in some bare detail as pensions have an awful habit of confusing most people out there.
Importantly in the context of your question, there are rules in place on the minimum you must draw down from your ARF each year – a percentage figure that changes with age and can also change with the sum in the fund.
Under the age of 70, you must draw down 4 per cent of the value of your fund each year (you will be taxed by Revenue as though you have even if you draw down less) – hence your €40,000 income from a €1 million fund.
Over 70, that drawdown rises to 5 per cent. And if your fund is over €2 million in value, you need to take 6 per cent each year.
The tax you pay is determined by your income from the fund – as it is for other citizens – but, with an ARF, the responsibility for deducting that tax falls to your qualified fund manager. This is the person you have an issue with.
Under the legislation, your ARF must be managed by this qualified fund manager and they are also responsible for the paperwork involved in setting up your ARF. Under section 784A of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997, this qualified fund manager can be a stockbroker, a life company, credit union or bank.
Critically, you are also looking for ongoing growth in your fund and they are responsible for managing that. You are not just paying a fund manager to cover the costs of paying your pension monthly; you’re paying them to grow or maintain the value of the fund.
There is no provision for bypassing this fund manager so you are stuck with them. You cannot manage the fund personally.
And you are right. Income in retirement is limited and your capacity for future earnings is diminished, so it stands to reason that you would query or challenge significant costs.
As you say, a 1 per cent fund management charge translates as €10,000 lost from your fund if the fund is around €1 million in size. For most people, with more modest funds, the charge will amount to something in the single figure thousands – €1,000 a year on a fund valued at €100,000 for instance.
To put it in context, if you are in your sixties and your fund is less than €2 million in size, this charge is equal to a quarter of the income you are expected to live on for the year from the fund.
It increases the return you need to make on your remaining investments if the fund is not to be at risk of running out of cash before you die.
You are correct that 1 per cent seems to be the “average” fund management fee – although I have also come across significantly larger figures – but that is not to say that you cannot do better.
In general, the larger the fund, the more leverage you will have to negotiate down the percentage fund management charge. Certainly, with a fund of €1 million, you should be able to find a fund manager who will oversee the fund for a percentage charge closer to 0.5 per cent or 0.4 per cent.
Royal London, for instance, says it offers funds with charges ranging from 0.4 per cent to 0.9 per cent whereas someone like Zurich opts for a flat 1 per cent rate. What you get for each of these you would need to check for yourself.
I am not permitted under Central Bank rules to recommend any specific product as I am not a registered qualified financial adviser, just a journalist.
Of course, apart from the size of your fund, the charge will be determined by the type of investment you are considering. Those looking for very active management of their fund can expect to pay a higher charge all other things being equal. Clearly, investing in ETFs, which have low costs, should be at the lower end of the range.
The other thing worth saying is that choosing who should be your fund manager is not simply a hunt for the lowest fund management fee; you also want to be comfortable that the fund manager is going to deliver the best growth for your fund over time.
This can mean a trade-off. It may well be worth paying a slightly higher for someone with a better record of returns over the long term – bearing in mind the old investment manager get out that there is never any guarantee that past performance will be replicated in the future.
When looking at performance be very careful of managers that focus on particularly successful returns in recent years. You want a fund manager that can deliver returns across volatile market cycles – not just in an equity bull market.
You also want to check whether there are other charges connected with the ARF over and above the fund management charge. If you buy your ARF through a broker, for instance, they could be getting commission which will also eat into your fund. And there can be other charges associated with actual trading of investments within your fund.
The bottom line is that there is no way of self-managing your ARF, for instance tapping the industry on an execution-only basis when you want to make a change to your investments or actually draw down funds. You are obliged to use a qualified fund manager and their annual costs will reduce the size of your fund. You need to be happy that you have the lowest possible charges for the best possible investment returns.
That’s a tricky balancing act, one that can never be certain. What is true is that those prepared to do the work in comparing ARF fund managers are more likely to get a better deal.
Please send your queries to Dominic Coyle, Q&A, The Irish Times, 24-28 Tara Street, Dublin 2, or by email to dominic.coyle@irishtimes.com with a contact phone number. This column is a reader service and is not intended to replace professional advice.

title: Tenant who lived in car for months with partner and child due to rent hike awarded damages
description: Kildare landlord David Massey also ordered to repay ‘goodwill payment’ he had allegedly sought from family to secure rental home
content:
A Kildare tenant who said he had to live in a car with his partner and young child for months as he could not afford an invalid rental increase has been awarded almost €16,000 in damages and overpaid rent.
A Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) tribunal heard landlord David Massey also allegedly sought a “goodwill payment” from the “desperate” family to secure the house in Kilbelin Close, Newbridge.
Dylan Keating, who had been approved for the Homeless Housing Assistance Payment (HAP), began renting the property from Massey in December 2022.
Rent had previously been set at €1,650, meaning the highest Massey could charge Keating was €1,683 under Rent Pressure Zone (RPZ) rules, which restricted increases to 2 per cent per year.
However, Keating claimed Massey told him another party was willing to pay more and it was suggested he pay an additional €200 per month, bringing the rent to €1,883.
Massey, however, claimed the €1,883 was agreed “at the outset”, though he accepted he “overlooked” the 2 per cent rule.
Keating agreed to pay the €200, saying he was previously homeless and “desperate” to secure a home for his family. He also claimed Massey had asked “what else he could offer”, and suggested a “goodwill payment” of €1,000, which Keating said he paid in cash.
Massey claimed Keating had offered the payment, but that he “definitely” did not receive it.
About three months after they moved in, the monthly €200 top-up was increased to €466, with Massey telling the tribunal it had emerged HAP was only covering €1,417 of the rent.
On December 23 rd , 2024, Keating received a notice of termination from Massey, who said he intended to sell the house.
Massey, who said he changed his mind once he realised he would be “hit” with a capital gains tax bill of €50,000 upon sale, then offered Keating a new lease.
The new lease set the rent at €2,150, meaning the top-up payment would be increased to €766.
Keating claimed Massey also sought a further deposit of €1,750, which Massey said he did not recall.
Unable to afford the new rent, Keating and his family left the house, telling the tribunal he and his partner lived in their car for six months with their child, who was less than 12 months old at the time.
He argued Massey “forced” them “into homelessness”.
The couple’s two other children lived with both sets of grandparents at the time, Keating said, adding they were “overwhelmed by the family being split up”. The family ultimately moved into a property provided by the council last December.
Noting Massey had increased the rent by 14 per cent from €1,650 to €1,883, despite the RPZ rules, the tribunal found Keating had overpaid more than €7,000 in rent from 2023 to 2025.
It said the landlord had “ignored the legal provisions around rent” and “attempted to impose a higher-than-permitted rent”, and ordered him to repay the sum.
The tribunal found Massey’s conduct amounted to an “abuse” of the termination procedure, saying a termination on the grounds of sale cannot be used to “place pressure” on a tenant to accept an invalid rent review.
It was satisfied Keating left the house as a consequence of the notice and Massey’s “reliance on that notice as leverage for the invalid rent review”.
The tribunal ordered Massey to pay €7,500 in damages, which it said was proportionate to the “seriousness of the breach” and the six-month period Keating and his family spent homeless.
It also accepted Keating’s evidence that he paid €1,200 in cash, being the “goodwill payment” and the initial €200 top-up, which it ordered Massey to repay.

title: Gardaí investigate after man shot and injured in Limerick
description: Thomas O’Neill (37) previously convicted of rape and drug offences
content:
Gardaí are investigating after a man was shot and injured in Limerick city on Saturday night.
Thomas O’Neill (37), of Lenihan Avenue, Ballinacurra Weston, sustained a gunshot wound to an upper leg.
The gun attack happened outside a house at Hyde Avenue, close to where O’Neill is living.
O’Neill, who was identified by reliable sources, was taken from the scene in a private car to University Hospital Limerick .
His injuries were not immediately life-threatening.
The shooting occurred around 8.20pm, gardaí said.
Gardaí did not identify O’Neill. A Garda spokesman said “one male was injured” in a “shooting incident”.
The force has appealed for witnesses or those who may have relevant CCTV or dashcam footage to come forward.
O’Neill has a substantial criminal record. He was one of four youths and an adult man who raped a woman at Cratloe Woods, Co Clare, on January 23rd, 2004.
They were armed with a golf club, a screw driver, a shovel and a wheel brace, and threatened a woman and a male who had travelled to the wood.
O’Neill and the others pleaded guilty to rape, false imprisonment and assault causing harm, and were jailed for a total of 31 years.
At his sentencing hearing, O’Neill was described by judge Paul Carney, now deceased, as the “ringleader” and the “director of operations”, and jailed him for 10 years with the final 12 months suspended.
O’Neill was released from prison in December 2025, after he served part of a two-year sentence for drugs offences, which was imposed in November 2024.
O’Neill had admitted six counts under the Misuse of Drugs Act, including possession of heroin and cocaine for sale or supply, and simple possession of cocaine and heroin, at Hyde Avenue, Limerick, on dates in June 2023.

title: Message from the Editor: How The Irish Times is covering Budget 2027
description: Follow our live news updates, analysis, videos, newsletters and podcasts and ask your budget questions in a live Q&A
content:
One of the big set-piece events of the Irish political calendar will take place on Tuesday, when the Government publishes its budget for 2027. The news for weeks has been filled with leaks and speculation on how Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers will decide to spend the public money at his disposal (it will emphatically be a spending budget) and what Minister for Finance Simon Harris might do on tax.
The tightly choreographed event is easily dismissed as theatre. Yes, the format can feel jaded. We know, based on the evidence of recent years, that the budget itself is more of an opening position; as Cliff Taylor points out in his column , the Government will in all likelihood make decisions next year which change the spending and tax plans outlined next Tuesday. We know the budget Ministers will solemnly over-claim and that the opposition will fall back on its own pre-baked cliches about missed opportunities. We know, too, that if journalists such as ourselves are doing our job, you will have a good sense of the key measures in the budget before it is announced (our latest insights can be read here ).
For all that, however, the budget remains one of those rare moments when politics attracts a mass audience. From political anoraks to those who ordinarily feel disengaged, everyone’s attention will be on Leinster House on Tuesday. That’s partly because the budget will give us the clearest sense of the Government’s priorities and its vision for the period ahead – one that will be profoundly shaped by economic, technological, military and ecological crises. It is also because, at a time when many people are feeling real uncertainty and stress in their lives, the effects of the decisions set out by Chamber and Harris on Tuesday will be felt in every household in the country.
For everything you need to know in advance of Tuesday, visit our Budget 2027 site , where you will find the latest news, analysis and commentary from our own reporters and guest contributors.
We will have comprehensive coverage over the coming days, as set out below by my colleague Siún Lennon.
We will tell the stories of a range of people across Ireland, each hoping for different things in Budget 2027. Once the budget is published we will return to these people to see how it has affected them.
Join The Irish Times for our live Budget 2027 coverage from 8am on our website and app. Our Business and Politics teams will bring you news and analysis as it happens in our live blog, while our live main points synopsis will give you the highlights.
You can also stay up to date by following us on our social media platforms.
We will provide live coverage of the budget as it is announced along with snap analysis and explanations of notable measures.
You can track the main points and watch a live stream of the speeches.
Once the budget speeches are finished, we will provide analysis from our Politics, Business and News teams; including columnist Cliff Taylor and Political Editor Pat Leahy.
We will also explain what the changes mean for you.
Our budget calculator, in association with PwC, will let you work out how it affects you.
Look out for a special Budget 2027 newsletter on Tuesday evening. You can sign up to our daily newsletters here . Subscribers to our daily Business newsletter will also receive a special Budget Day edition on Tuesday afternoon.
Along with our live stream from the Dáil chamber, we’ll have video analysis from Consumer Affairs Correspondent Conor Pope with his take on the budget.
Business Editor Ciarán Hancock will host a special edition of the Inside Business podcast , available for download on Tuesday afternoon.
Deputy Business Editor Dominic Coyle and experts from PwC will answer your Budget 2027 questions from 7am on Wednesday. You can submit questions via a form on irishtimes.com from Tuesday afternoon.
Hugh Linehan and our politics team will assess how Chambers and Harris performed, in a special Inside Politics podcast that will be available on Wednesday morning.
Published on Wednesday – and available via the ePaper – The Irish Times’s Budget 2027 print supplement will spell out exactly what the budget means for you with the latest news, analysis and comment as well as reaction from individuals and businesses around the country.
We like to hear from you. Feel free to send comments, feedback or suggestions for topics you would like to see covered to feedback@irishtimes.com .
To subscribe to The Irish Times for more budget coverage, visit here .

title: Latvian PM on track to lead pro-Ukraine coalition after election win
description: Kulbergs pledged continuing support to Ukraine and to keep a hard line towards Moscow
content:
Latvian prime minister Andris Kulbergs was set to retain power and form a pro- Ukrainian coalition ‌after his centrist United List secured the biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence in 1991.
With 97 per cent of ballots counted after Saturday’s election in the Nato ​and EU country bordering Russia , United List was on 35.3 per cent, enough for 42 seats in the 100-seat parliament.
A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs (47), came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray Ukrainian military drones flew undetected into ​Latvia.
Latvia’s economy has underperformed its Baltic neighbours for more than a decade and Kulbergs has vowed to improve governance, cut red tape and reduce public spending, ⁠political scientist Roberts Kits said.
“Kulbergs played on being a get-things-done type of guy and has persuaded the voters that ‌he ‌can ​do things differently, bring some fresh energy,” he said.
“This means the responsibility is huge. People expect him to deliver, but the question remains whether he has the team to do it.”
United List ⁠appeared able to secure a parliamentary majority with ​either the nationalist National Alliance or the liberal Progressives, Kits said.
Kulbergs pledged continuing support to Ukraine and to keep a hard line towards Moscow.
[ Latvians vote in election in shadow of drone incursions and war in Ukraine Opens in new window ]
“Any ‌economic ties with Russia makes us weak. Yes, ​it can bring some extra money, but it’s a weakness Russia might exploit,” he told reporters at his party’s headquarters ⁠on election night as supporters celebrated the scale of ⁠the win.
“It’s remarkably good. ​I was not expecting such a result,” Kulbergs said.
Voter turnout was 51.8 per cent, down from 59.4 per cent in 2022.
United List was followed by the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First, which was on 13.1 per cent. Latvia First had courted the country’s substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote.
Third in the ranking was the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party, on 11.7 per cent, followed by the National Alliance, which promotes a hardline approach to the Kremlin, at 8.9 per cent.
Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs promised more anti-drone capability for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5 per cent of gross domestic product, one of ‌the highest levels in Nato.
His pro-Kremlin ⁠rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and instead focus on tackling cost of living issues, particularly among the country’s Russian-speaking minority.
Although pro-Russian parties increased their representation, Kits said they remained sidelined and were unlikely to ‌influence government policy.
Latvia’s ethnic Russian minority is split between those who oppose Moscow’s war in Ukraine and others who voice frustration with policies at home aimed ​at limiting their influence on public life, which many of them see as discriminatory.
Latvia, with ​a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea and Russia and Belarus to the east, with EU and Nato allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south. - Reuters

title: Japan protests after US marine arrested on suspicion of murder in Okinawa
description: Prime minister Takaichi described alleged murder as ⁠'extremely brutal and vicious incident’
content:
Japanese prime ‌minister Sanae Takaichi registered a protest with the United States on Sunday after a US marine was arrested on ​suspicion of robbing and murdering a Japanese woman in Okinawa.
Devin Jacob Ballard (20) is suspected of killing Anna Yagi (39) in a hotel in Naha, the capital of the southernmost prefecture, on Saturday and ​taking her wallet and backpack, police said. Ballard denied the allegations, police said.
“The occurrence of such an ⁠extremely brutal and vicious incident is extremely regrettable,” Takaichi said in a statement.
“The government ‌of ‌Japan ​strongly protests to the US side and strongly seeks maximum cooperation with the investigation,” as well as the tightening of discipline ⁠and thorough measures to prevent a ​recurrence, she said.
The US embassy and ​the marine corps expressed condolences over the incident and said they were cooperating with ‌the Japanese authorities.
The marines said in a ​statement that the suspect, who is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force and ⁠based at Marine Corps Air Station ⁠Futenma, was in ​Japanese custody.
“The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior [sic],” it said.
Most of the 18,000 Japan-based marines are stationed in Okinawa, which the US held from the end of second World War until 1972. Their presence has repeatedly stirred resentment among residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct ‌of personnel.
The 1995 rape ⁠of a 12-year-old Okinawan girl by three US servicemen sparked mass protests.
Saturday’s killing could complicate Takaichi’s efforts to relocate some Marines from the busy ‌Futenma air base to a more remote facility at Henoko. Opponents want the troops moved out of the ​prefecture.
Okinawa, which is 100km (60 miles) from Taiwan at ​the closest point, is viewed by Tokyo and Washington as key in deterring potential military aggression from China. - Reuters

title: Cornell rape allegation scandal brings an early bleakness to upstate New York
description: Case suggests college years are more challenging and, in some cases, troubling than ever
content:
W inters in Ithaca, in upstate New York , are infamously grey-skied and excruciatingly bitter, so students at Cornell learn to make the best of the late autumn colour. But this term, the bleakness has arrived early.
On Thursday night, more than 100 people, most of them students, attended a public hearing arranged by Cornell University’s student government. The attendance, out of a student body exceeding 25,000, was small but the subject matter, and the emotional charge, carried weight.
There were, according to reporting, raw testimonies and tears and repeated calls for a better response from the college leadership in guiding the institution through the fallout from a sexual assault case that has convulsed a certain stratosphere of United States society.
By then, governor of New York Kathy Hochel had tasked New York attorney general Letitia James, nemesis of Donald Trump, to lead a new investigation into the case that has been reopened following the filing of a lawsuit by a former Cornell student referred to as Jane Doe .
The woman is taking a legal action against seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity house, and Cornell University, claiming that she was drugged and gang-raped at a fraternity party on the campus two years ago.
She initially reported the alleged assault on November 14th, 2024, explaining that what began as a consensual sexual encounter with a man, who suggested another male join them, gradually led to a situation where she was unclothed, intoxicated, having taken ketamine, and surrounded by a “ring of men”. “I don’t remember the very end of the event where I was raped,” she said over the course of a detailed conversation with a campus police officer. “I can say with 100 per cent confidence I was raped.”
While the details of the events were included in the condensed voluntary statement forwarded to the district attorney, the woman’s assertion that she had been raped was not included, something that Hochel identified when she spoke on Friday morning.
“We don’t know enough. But what is coming out is very contradictory and I want the truth.”
Cornell’s response at the time of original complaint was to mete out punishments, which included two suspensions and two expulsions. The seven defendants deny the charges they are facing.
In the curiously loose way of the American legal system, the details of the night in question, and its repercussions, are already under a furious firestorm of argument, point and counterpoint, in both the social media sphere and dominating media and political discourse. The disturbing details, including degrading, misogynistic messages traded between members of the fraternity house, have been pored over. So too has the plaintiff’s testimony. Although the identities of those involved have been officially withheld, their names have been published online and elsewhere.
[ Texts about alleged Cornell University fraternity house gang rape released after investigation reopened Opens in new window ]
The scandal has raised broader questions about consent; about prevailing sexual mores among young men raised in a culture where the pornification of women is rampant; about the safety of women on campuses; and about the subculture of the US collegiate fraternity house tradition, which is as old as the country itself. Just last week, a Wisconsin university launched an investigation into an “unregistered” frat house in which 30 male students were found shirtless and sitting in squalor in the hot basement, undergoing a prolonged hazing test.
The plaintiff’s lawyer gave a television interview on Friday in which he asserted his client had arrived at the frat house that night too intoxicated to give consent to anything.
“Testimony was she was slurring her words before she even got to the Chi Phi House, that she was stumbling around. I think most people, particularly a bunch of college, a bunch of frat boys, know when somebody is intoxicated.”
In late summer, The Princeton Review published a list of those US colleges whose academic year fees will now exceed $100,000 (€88,000). Harvey Mudd College came in at number one, with everywhere from Duke to the University of Southern California to appearing. Cornell is notionally in the same full-fees bracket although it offers significant public-tuition programmes, unlike other elite colleges – although students with excellent academic achievements are often accepted by those elite colleges irrespective of financial status.
[ How Cornell University alleged rape victim went from shame to seeking justice Opens in new window ]
For centuries, attending US elite universities was a badge of distinction, a signifier of the class system, and a perceived golden ticket into the slipstream of elite professional and public opportunity and society. Almost four million Americans will graduate high school next spring. There are just 165,000 Ivy League places on offer each year. Today’s generation are arriving in campuses at a time when the fees are more exorbitant than ever while the traditional pathway careers in finance or law are no longer as easily navigated or as certain.
And the disturbing accounts and testimonies of campus life emanating from the Cornell revelations suggest that merely navigating a path through their college years is more challenging, and in some cases, troubling than ever before.

title: Britain scraps heavily criticised plans to curb jury trials after backlash
description: Case backlog awaiting trial by jury in Crown Courts in England and Wales was nearly 81,000 in June
content:
Britain will scrap ‌plans to remove the historic right to trial by jury for defendants in less serious criminal cases, the UK government announced on Sunday, in response ​to sustained criticism of the proposals by many lawyers and politicians.
The decision by Andy Burnham , who became prime minister in July, to drop his predecessor Keir Starmer’s policy comes as hundreds of prisoners were released early to stop prisons becoming full, in just one ​element of a criminal justice crisis.
Plans to curb jury trials for cases where a jail sentence was likely to be less than ⁠three years would be abandoned, the ministry of justice (MoJ) said, which was broadly welcomed by the Criminal ‌Bar ‌Association (CBA) ​and other groups.
But lawyers raised concerns over the MoJ’s decision to increase sentencing powers for magistrates – who hear trials for more minor offences without a jury – and ⁠the removal of defendants’ right to elect trial ​by jury.
“I have heard the strength of feeling ​on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the Crown Court and have made the decision ‌to change course,” secretary for justice Alex Norris said.
CBA ​chair Andrew Thomas thanked the government for “listening to the evidence and reaching the right verdict”, though he ⁠said “a severe threat to our trial by ⁠jury remains”.
The Bar Council’s ​chair Kirsty Brimelow agreed, saying that giving magistrates greater powers when the backlog in magistrates’ courts is increasing could be counterproductive.
The current backlog of cases awaiting trial by jury in Crown Courts in England and Wales was nearly 81,000 at the end of June, almost double the figure in 2020, and victims, defendants and witnesses often wait years for cases to come to trial.
[ Lawyers lose out on €6.6m in payments amid criminal legal aid dispute Opens in new window ]
Starmer’s minister for justice David Lammy last year said reducing jury trials would speed up ‌justice, but met a ⁠furious backlash from lawyers who said it curtailed the fundamental right of defendants to be tried by a jury of their peers.
Critics also argued that years of neglect and underinvestment by successive ‌governments, rather than jury trials, were the root cause of delays, while the head of England’s judiciary raised “grave security concerns” for judges.
The ​MoJ said it would maintain plans that complex fraud trials could be heard ​by a judge alone, which has long been mooted to avoid jurors sitting on months-long cases, though a government-commissioned review this year rejected the idea. – Reuters

title: Mark O'Connell: A handful of companies profiting from a sick planet is obscene
description: If it’s bad for humanity, it’s invariably good for the oil industry
content:
The calculus could not be more simple: if it’s bad for humanity, it’s good for the oil industry. This year, after the US and Israel started a war with Iran and caused one of the most serious supply disruptions in the history of the oil market, many of the world’s largest fossil fuel companies recorded massive increases in profits.
In August, the Guardian published a report detailing the huge windfalls enjoyed by major oil companies as a result of the conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In the spring quarter of this year, the first full financial quarter after the war began, eight of the largest companies in the sector – among them BP , Shell , ExxonMobil , Chevron and the state-owned Saudi energy giant Aramco – almost doubled their combined profits compared to the same period last year. Throughout that quarter, these companies made some $93 billion in profit, or almost $700,000 (€620,000) every single minute.
Aramco recorded the largest increase in profits, a 34 per cent leap above the same period last year, despite the damage caused to its infrastructure by Iranian and Houthi missile strikes. According to the group Carbon Majors , which traces emissions to the organisations and states that produced the fuels, Aramco is allegedly responsible for more carbon emissions than any company in history.
It’s worth recalling what else was happening in the world while such gigantic war profits were being raked in by these companies and their shareholders. There were successive extreme heatwaves across Europe, with temperature records broken in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain and the United Kingdom, and some 36,000 excess deaths during the heatwaves .
Here in Ireland, it was the hottest summer in history ; according to Met Éireann, July was the driest month ever recorded in the country. Meanwhile, continental Europe experienced a season of catastrophic wildfires . Across France and Spain, hundreds of thousands of people were evacuated from their homes – the largest such mass evacuations in peacetime since the second World War. And last month’s catastrophic flash flood in Nepal , which killed at least 1,400 people, was triggered by the collapse of a glacier – precisely the kind of extreme event we know to be increasingly common as a result of human-caused climate change.
That these oil companies and their shareholders are recording such healthy profits at a time when their product is so visibly sickening the planet is a moral obscenity. And as with many moral obscenities, it is the result of a business model proceeding precisely as intended by those who designed it. All of these companies have invested massive amounts of money over many decades in preventing the application of the kind of policies – at the level of individual governments and at the level of collective international action – that might have stopped or mitigated the consequences we are now forced to live with.
The Saudi government in particular, as one of the world’s top exporters of oil, has been relentless in undermining international efforts to transition to renewable energy. Here’s how Al Gore put it after last year’s UN Cop30 Climate Summit in Brazil: “Saudi Arabia appears to be determined to veto the effort to solve the climate crisis, only to protect their lavish income from selling the fossil fuels that are the principal cause of the climate crisis.”
According to a recent report by climate-focused investigative organisation DeSmog , the UK’s Reform Party has received £24 million (€28.15 million), about two thirds of its total funding, from donors with financial interests in the fossil fuel industry. The party, which essentially acts as the political wing of the oil industry in the UK, has committed to scrapping the government’s net zero policies. Its manifesto talks about this in terms of cutting the cost of living for consumers (“British households and business are being crushed by among the highest energy costs in the world – driven by bad ideological policy”), but the real aim seems to be to keep profits flowing into the coffers of the fossil fuel industry.
There is, surely, a gap in the electoral market here in Ireland. If I were an oil industry representative thinking about making a long-term play in Irish politics, I would be taking a good look at the meeting held in Westmeath last weekend by some of the organisers of the fuel protests that brought the country to a standstill earlier this year.
