The meeting was led by Christopher Duffy – a prominent figure in April’s fuel protests – who announced that the group would block roads again if their demands to abolish carbon tax and reduce excise and VAT on fuel were not granted. The abolition of carbon tax would certainly reduce the cost of doing business for hauliers and agricultural contractors like Duffy; it would also be of huge benefit to oil companies.
‘Those who polluted the most, and profited the most must do far more to repair the damage they caused. Polluters must pay’
These business owners’ aims are entirely in sympathy with those of the fossil fuel industry. (Despite the populist framing of their outrage at the Government and the costs it is forcing ordinary Irish people to bear for transport, the protesters seem to have nothing to say about the recent announcement that public transport fares will be increased by an average of 15 per cent from next January.) It is ultimately depressing that the protest movement currently threatening to bring the capital city to a standstill once more is not one demanding that the Government does more to reduce emissions, or to mitigate the effects of climate change – but one demanding that it does less.
The companies now raking in huge profits, after decades of preventing any attempt to move away from a fossil fuel-driven global economy, are directly responsible for incalculably vast environmental and economic devastation. Just as consumers – and, yes, business owners such as the fuel protesters – are being forced to absorb the cost of fuel hikes resulting from the war with Iran, humanity as a whole is being forced to pay for those profits with its future.
In his final address to the recent UN General Assembly, the outgoing secretary general António Guterres reiterated a call he has been consistently making since the start of his tenure in 2017: that the oil companies must be made to pay – in the form of compensatory payments and windfall taxes – for the damage they have inflicted on this planet, its ecosystems and its inhabitants. “Those who polluted the most, and profited the most,” he said, “must do far more to repair the damage they caused. Polluters must pay.”
The US president , though he famously believes climate change to be “the greatest con-job ever perpetrated on the world”, takes, in his own way, no less dim a view of the massive profits the oil companies have been making as a result of the global chaos he himself unleashed this year . “They’re making too much money based on a shortage,” as he put it. “I don’t like it.”

title: Clare Moriarty: As a religious teen, I was against abortion. But even I could see the flaws in the logic
description: There is a middle ground between effective altruism and what is really a very niche fixation on the welfare of blastocysts, embryos and foetuses
content:
T here are men who stand on the street corner opposite the National Maternity Hospital performatively praying for what their metaphysics tells them are babies’ souls. For them, personhood begins at conception and a fertilised embryo is as morally significant a life as a fully fledged human. If it weren’t so prevalent in populations that overlap with ours, this would be more obvious for what it is – a strange opinion.
If your interest is the welfare of the vulnerable – as I’m sure these men say theirs is – there are many clearer cases of need. I’m not one of these utilitarians who think we need to direct our philanthropic attention only to the most urgent cases, but there is a middle ground between effective altruism and what is really a very niche fixation on the welfare of blastocysts, embryos and foetuses.
As I‘ve swerved around these men on my way to appointments in Holles Street, I’ve wondered whether they also pray at Tuam or Bessborough, or the many sites across Ireland where spiritual and physical harms to very real children were committed.
I think of Matthew 6:6 and wonder why they’re there are all: “[W]hen you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.” This discretion is contrasted with “hypocrites” who love praying on, you guessed it, “street corners”. Why, one wonders, do these men focus their biblically contraindicated prayer where they do? Is it because of a welfare concern, or because they dislike women exercising agency over their sexual and reproductive lives?
[ Three-day abortion wait adds ‘unnecessary barriers’ to care, campaigners say Opens in new window ]
Protests last weekend challenged the mandatory three-day waiting period imposed on families trying to access abortion services. To be clear, the waiting period isn’t a response to some pre-existing rule that dictated that, as soon as one mentioned the possibility of a termination at an appointment, they were tied to a gurney and forced down the corridor for surgery. People are already free to have a think about their options, and I suspect that it’s only in very exceptional circumstances that plenty of consideration hasn’t taken place before that initial appointment.
As someone who has had basically the same procedure as a surgical abortion, albeit to remove an already-deceased foetus, I also waited three days, but because of public waiting lists rather than policy. I hated the wait; I felt like a wandering coffin as circumstances forced me to continue to carry a pregnancy I’d already lost. It’s a physical upset I remember viscerally. With abortion, forcing people to continue to grow within them something that they’ve decided to terminate is a complex kind of cruelty that will be hard for many to imagine. If only the seriousness reflected in waiting period policies could be summoned for miscarriages, like by perhaps finally legislating for decent paid leave.
We recently heard from Dr Cliona Murphy, clinical director of the HSE’s National Women and Infants Health Programme that “there is no clinical requirement for a mandatory three-day waiting period”. Withdrawing the mandatory wait does nothing to stop people from having an initial appointment and taking a few days to think about things before deciding.
[ Removing three-day wait would lead to rise in ‘already massive’ number of abortions, GP says Opens in new window ]
Beyond practical concerns about forced delays causing women to time out of eligibility, and the practical challenges (childcare, missing work and so on) of splitting up appointments, is the offensive supposition that women are somehow incapable of uncompelled reflection – that they wheel into medical appointments without thinking about the treatments they pursue. In most medicine, we trust patients to think about things.
I was once against abortion. I was a religious teenager. I enjoyed the devotion inherent in Christianity and enjoyed the comfort and structure it offered. Throughout my teens I went to Mass, I confessed my sins (especially around exam-time, as my dad would note) and, when I got to university, I wrote meandering essays about the logical validity of the ontological argument in Anselm’s Proslogion. I knew the church forbade abortion, so I was against it.
I understood that ours was a pretty peculiar metaphysical position. As soon as certain necessary conditions are met, pop, God imparts a soul and we have a being as fully precious as any other. I thought there was beauty in that strangeness.
[ Fine Gael TD Peter Roche compares three-day abortion wait to duration of hangover during committee debate Opens in new window ]
But even in my religious days, I appreciated that the modern Catholic account of personhood was a bit untethered from the more obvious priorities issued in the Bible. In Exodus 21, my Bible said “Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death” and then “When men strive together and hurt a woman with child, so that there is a miscarriage, and yet no harm follows, the one who hurt her shall be fined, according as the woman’s husband shall lay upon him. If any harm follows, then you shall give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth (...)”. I’m no biblical scholar, but it seemed there was plenty of scope to think that the “ordinances set before [us]” suggest that causing the end of a pregnancy is morally and forensically very different from killing a fully developed person.
When my thinking changed and I realised that I no longer believed, my respect for sensible religious autonomy didn’t change. If someone believes their blastocyst or foetus is a complete moral being, they should be allowed to make decisions about their body on that basis. Beyond that, men should get off that corner, and the Government should trust us to manage mature reflection without being legally compelled.
Clare Moriarty is a Research Ireland enterprise fellow, working at University College Dublin and the National Library of Ireland

title: Daughter claims father threatened to kill her if she did not ‘follow family ideals’
description: Woman got protection orders against parents over alleged isolation and emotional abuse in family home
content:
A young woman who alleged her father threatened to kill her if she did not “follow family ideals” and that both parents had isolated her in the family home got protection orders against them.
Her parents did not want her to be educated or to work outside the home “as it was against family morals” and withdrew her from school to be home-educated for a number of years, the woman told the emergency domestic violence court at Dolphin House in Dublin .
Her father removed her bedroom door at one point and slept outside her room, she said.
On an occasion earlier this year he attempted to strangle her and threw her down the stairs, she said.
He subjected her to emotional and financial abuse, threatened to kill himself if she did not follow his rules, followed her if she went anywhere and both parents blamed her for him having a serious illness, she said. He would remind her of his illness “in scary ways”, she said.
Her mother also subjected her to financial, psychological and emotional abuse, she said.
She was prevented socialising or having contact with friends and was “very isolated”.
On occasions she was denied food, allowed only limited showers and not permitted to use a hairdryer.
“I fear for my safety,” she said. “I always felt safer when I’m not at home.”
Judge Gerard Furlong granted her application for a protection order against both parents.
[ ‘He was incredibly entitled and manipulative’: The grim pattern of femicide in Ireland Opens in new window ]
It was among several made ex parte (one side only represented) before the judge on Friday.
Due to industrial action by public sector workers, the emergency domestic violence court was one of just two courts sitting in the Dolphin House complex on Friday. Three other family courts did not sit due to the action.
During Friday’s hearing Furlong was given a cake by solicitor Sandra McAleer to mark his 26 th year sitting as a District Court judge.
In another application a woman who alleged her long-term partner “dropped a door” on her after pulling it off its hinges sought protection from him.
They lived together for many years from when she was 17 but in recent years she realised she had “endured what I thought was love”, she said.
[ Pregnant mother-of-two’s murder ‘one of the worst cases of domestic violence’, Belfast court hears Opens in new window ]
While they were in a homeless hostel with their teenage children, the man came into a room and hit her, causing her to fall to the floor after which he threw a mobile phone at her head. She had promised her children, if he hit her again, she would call the gardaí and screamed for her daughter to call gardaí, she said.
She was sitting with her back to the door of the room, blocking it because she was “so scared he would get out” to her daughter and he pulled the door off the hinges and dropped it on her, she said. Gardaí removed the man from the hostel and charged him with assault, she said.
The man had not always been like this during their relationship but he was consistently “a narcissist and a gaslighter”, she said. In more recent years she had “learned so much” and realised he had been emotionally abusing her.
He was a drug user “with a very short fuse”, she said. He never hit their children but they witnessed his behaviour towards her, she said.
He had pushed her and held her throat a few times and thrown things at her. He once punched her so hard she fell and hit her head off a corner that “nearly split me open”, she said. He started kicking her “until the kids begged him to stop”.
“He scares me, we’re only homeless because of him.”
She and the children are doing well away from him, she said. “I don’t want him to take any of that away from us.”
The judge told the woman he would “absolutely” grant her protection order application.
Another woman, whose children include a child with severe disabilities, got a protection order against her former partner.
He was “extremely controlling” and verbally abusive to her during their relationship, calling her names including “fat c***”, she said. He sent constant messages asking where she was, had “taken chunks out of parts of the kitchen” and smashed a hob.
The woman sobbed as the judge read her sworn information including that her young daughter had asked her: “Why are you putting up with this?”
Since she recently ended the relationship, he has “bombarded” her with abusive messages as well as flowers and messages saying he loved her, she said. She received 70 messages in one day, the court was told.
He had told her he would kill himself and demonstrated erratic behaviour in front of their children and a member of his family, the woman said.
“I feel I cannot continue like this, it’s having a huge impact on me and the kids,” the weeping woman said. She cannot sleep or eat and finds doing her job difficult, she said.
“I want this to stop and us to get on with co-parenting the kids in a positive way.”
Granting a protection order, the judge said: “I hope this works and gives you and the kids some peace.”

title: Krispy Kreme rage, Teresa Mannion, HomeToVote: The moments that made the Irish Internet truly great
description: The viral moments we’d like to preserve if the vast online archive disappeared tomorrow
content:
I f you’ve ever spent time poring over the details of the 1911 or 1926 census , or holed up in a library researching newspapers from a long-ago decade, you’ll appreciate the value of a physical archive. The past comes alive to us because of artefacts, writings and records maintained for future generations. The National Library of Ireland holds around 12 million items that document the life and culture of Irish society – books, manuscripts, newspapers, photographs, maps. But what about the artefacts that exist in relatively new spaces: online, in the cloud, in digital format?
When journalist and writer Carl Kinsella discovered recently that a digital record of his own had been deleted, it was a bit of a wake-up call. Kinsella had worked for the website Joe.ie in the 2010s, writing social and political commentary and humour pieces and covering events like the dramatic arrival of the Irish public to the country’s first Krispy Kreme doughnut drive-through: “We have so much pent-up rage and frustration and hunger that it behoves us to converge upon our first 24-hour doughnut drive-through and slam the shit out of our horns until they feed us tasty, soft, sugary, doughy doughnuts into our grateful mouths.” Kinsella’s Krispy Kreme quotes live on only in a Guardian article about the doughnut hysterics, with the original Joe.ie piece cast to the digital wind. He’s practical about the deletion, saying, “I always had a feeling something like this would happen, and I think there’s a degree to which we’ve all trusted platforms – whether it’s a small online media organisation or a social media platform – to serve as archives for our work or our photographs or our personal memories”.
And Kinsella’s right. There’s a precariousness and impermanence to what exists online. Even though resources like the Wayback Machine – which trawls the web taking snapshots of pages – can resurrect material from defunct websites, there is no guarantee that any or all content will be saved. Already so much digital history has been lost. “Any platform could go bust tomorrow and rob us of online artefacts whose security we’ve taken for granted. It underscores the need for all of us to find ways to be our own archivists for the things that matter to us,” Kinsella says.
The National Library of Ireland does have a “Born Digital” archive among its collection. In 2023 it published its first digital preservation policy to recognise the importance of materials that represent the online life of Ireland, although the library acknowledges that the exponential growth of the volume of content continues to provide a challenge. Among the Born Digital artefacts are websites relating to the Repeal movement, the archive of the Yes Equality campaign and digital materials donated by author Marian Keyes .
Journalist and entrepreneur Mark Little recently published a book called The Last Good Day on the Internet – the title derived from the viral photograph in 2015 that got people all over the world debating the colour of a dress. It was a time before toxic algorithms and AI slop, when the world wide web felt like a community.
[ Mark Little on his new book ‘The Last Good Day on the Internet’ Opens in new window ]
All this got us thinking: if we were to build an ideal Museum of the Irish Internet – the viral moments we’d like to preserve if the vast online archive were to vanish tomorrow – what else should be on its intangible shelves?
When Ireland briefly legalised class A drugs thanks to a legal loophole, the #YokeGate hashtag made the US late-night talkshows. DJ, cook and content creator Marcus O’Laoire posted: “Bought some of those legal yolks in Tesco earlier. Can’t wait to get scrambled.” Blindboy Boatclub called in to Tom Dunne’s Newstalk radio show claiming to have taken ecstasy.
YokeGate was a banner day on what was, at the time, Twitter.com. Back then, unique slang, turns of phrase and cultural, political and historical in-jokes by Irish Twitter users and accounts like Not The RTÉ Guide and Motherfocloir provided rich and humorous commentary on life in Ireland. The site hasn’t been the same since Elon Musk took over and renamed it X . The golden days of Irish Twitter are firmly in the past.
“Props to anyone who tries to be fashionable in Ireland. I wore a red beret once in Waterford and someone called me Super Mario,” tweeted @janky_jane in 2021, highlighting how difficult it is for anyone to get away with anything in this country. The tweet encouraged others to share sartorial traumas of their own, including one person who had returned home to her rural village and, while queuing in the chipper, was told: “You think you’re so great, coming back here, in your HAT” (@awedandflawed). Another tweet in 2019 by @Ciara87C told a similar story: “One day I was wearing a dress and knee boots, in Armagh, and someone shouted across the street to me “Someone thinks they’re in Hollyoaks”.”
Author and Irish Times columnist Séamas O’Reilly went viral in 2018 when he used Twitter to tell a story about the time he was 18 and accidentally ended up in a room with his boss and then president of Ireland Mary McAleese , while high and “sweating like microwaved bread”. The story has since been turned into an animated short film featuring Chris O’Dowd and Aisling Bea .
Do you remember where you were when Pat Kenny referred to Ireland’s celebrity mattress tycoon Mattress Mick as simply “Mattress” on live television? It was 2019, and Kenny was hosting a debate on Pat Kenny Live on Virgin Media One. Pat introduced the bed magnate as “Mattress Mick” but then moved to the more familiar “Mattress”, before stuttering and adding “ ... eh Mick”. The online reaction to the show is vital to our nation’s digital history.
And we couldn’t mention viral TV without acknowledging how we as a people embraced the liveblogging and livetweeting of #RoseOfTralee and #LateLateToyShow, triggering global confusion when both hashtags trended worldwide year after year.
Normal People first aired on RTÉ in the midst of the pandemic, causing a stir across the internet and on the airwaves. Liveline played host to a debate about the sex scenes in Element Pictures’ adaptation of the Sally Rooney novel, and poor old Joe Duffy was driven to tweet “I’m calling in sick. Who do I ring?”. Normal People star Paul Mescal also used Twitter to simply declare “I’m Irish” after the British press was suddenly desperate to claim him. In fact, any Irish digital archive should include a comprehensive record of the many times Britain has tried to claim an Irish high achiever as their own.
[ Daisy Edgar-Jones: ‘It was great practice for Sense and Sensibility, all that time in Fermanagh fields with cows’ Opens in new window ]
In 2015, RTÉ broadcaster Teresa Mannion became a global viral sensation when her outdoor reporting during Storm Desmond turned “don’t make unnecessary journeys” into a mantra for anyone taking on inclement weather. Mannion became an internet meme; her enthusiastic warnings were remixed into a dance tune, and her image was edited with clips from disaster films like The Day After Tomorrow. More recently, her famous quote went viral on TikTok.
We wouldn’t be Irish if we weren’t obsessing over the weather and its effect on road conditions, school closures and supplies. More than once, the availability of bread and accusations of hoarding Brennans have taken over our online spaces. And who can forget when empty supermarket shelves turned into all-out looting in 2018, when a JCB was used to break into a Lidl in Tallaght?
Irish mourning has moved with the times, from death notices broadcast on local radio to livestreaming funerals during Covid and beyond. The deaths of public figures like Manchán Magan in 2025 and Sinéad O’Connor in 2023 precipitated outpourings of respect and grief on social media platforms, with people sharing clips and tributes and personal reflections on what their work meant to them. Our greatest innovation, though, has to be RIP.ie , a website that not only serves the Irish need for community (and nosiness), but also allows for the collection of memories and tributes through online books of condolence.
The internet has always been a great mobiliser for both public and private causes. #HomeToVote was a rallying call during the 2015 marriage equality campaign and ballot, and again in 2018 for the referendum to repeal the Eighth Amendment. Arguably as important was #HomeToRide, a hashtag started in 2015 by Twitter user Linda Kavanagh, which collected stories about prodigal Brendans and Siobháns coming back from Vancouver or Perth or Rathmines for Christmas to congregate in the local pub on St Stephen’s night.
When Irish Times journalist Patrick Freyne wrote about Oprah’s infamous interview with Harry and Meghan, his opening paragraph, which regularly goes viral, read:
“Having a monarchy next door is a little like having a neighbour who’s really into clowns and has daubed their house with clown murals, displays clown dolls in each window and has an insatiable desire to hear about and discuss clown-related news stories. More specifically, for the Irish, it’s like having a neighbour who’s really into clowns and, also, your grandfather was murdered by a clown.”
In 2017, Amy O’Connor published the findings of a canvass of every TD in Ireland and their views on Beyoncé on DailyEdge.ie, the now-defunct pop culture wing of The Journal. Her vital work, which must be preserved for millennia, inspired articles in Vanity Fair, Teen Vogue and the Washington Post.
We must make space in the Museum of Irish Internet for a wide and varied collection of other Irish viral moments online, including but not limited to: Comic Shane Dan Byrne’s Easter Sunday sketch , the 2025 Cherry Tomato Bridge fever dream , The Rubberbandits’ Horse Outside , the man who slipped on the ice ( who has his own Wikipedia page ), Clisare’s Shite Irish Girls Say , Senan Byrne’s helium balloons Vine , Catch Him Derry , my limes!, Carl Kinsella’s free Luas and many, many more.
While our museum is largely a digital archive, it’s imperative to make room for some of the physical representations of how the internet came into Irish homes in the first place. Prepare a display case for the ESAT Telecom and Eircom promotional CD-ROMs which delivered dial up software to the huge grey family computers in the corners of sittingrooms around the country in the mid to late 1990s. We might as well include some of those computers too, to round out the collection.

title: ‘I constantly have to see my ex and the woman he cheated on me with in work’
description: Ask Roe: ‘I cannot stomach the sight of them, and it pains me that they seem so happy while I continue to relive the moment I found out about the cheating’
content:
A few years ago, I dated a former coworker for about four months. Despite it being a brief relationship, I left feeling entirely damaged, confused and worthless. While we were together, he slept with and began a relationship with another one of our coworkers. Said coworker knew I was dating him and did not tell me she had also begun dating him. She even gossiped with me about how “terrible” he was (as he had seemingly slept with an additional third woman), and when I found out she had been with him too, my trust in everyone was shattered. They are still together and happy, three years later. Last year I even skipped a mutual friend’s wedding as I knew they were attending. I cannot stomach the sight of them, and it pains me that they seem so happy while I continue to relive the moment I found out about the cheating every day. I am ashamed I haven’t had a successful relationship in the meantime, and they seem blissfully happy. We live in a similar part of town, and every time I walk outside I am nervous I’ll bump into them . How do I move on ?
I’m really sorry you went through this. Having a partner cheat on you is horrendous, and you also had layers of extra pain on top of it: a confidante also betraying your trust, having to see the people who hurt you at work and so never getting space to heal, and then having to see them in your town and shared social world. That’s really hard.
Cheating hurts so much because it feels like we don’t have any control over our most intimate life, and because the people who are meant to care for us become sources of pain. It breaks a social contract, and can erode our belief that we can trust people. The hypervigilance you’re feeling – not being able to relax around them, thinking about the painful moment constantly, scanning your world for them – is the symptom of a body that still feels like it’s in danger and is trying desperately to keep itself safe. You keep looking out for this couple so you can avoid them, in order to avoid reliving the pain they’ve caused.
The problem is you’re stuck in that mode and are shrinking your life down and hurting yourself in other ways. The obsessive ruminating, constantly comparing your lives with this couple’s, organising your movements to avoid them, and missing out on events that would allow you to connect with your actual friends – you didn’t do anything wrong, yet you’re paying a very high cost. Ironically, your world has become organised around the very event you want to leave behind, and I don’t think that’s what you want. You need to decide you no longer want your life to be tied to and defined by these people, and take back control.
I want you to take a moment and think of all the millions – MILLIONS – of people throughout history who have been cheated on. I want you to imagine your best friend came to you and told you they’d been cheated on. Are you sitting there thinking that all those people are pathetic, or that there’s something wrong with them, or that they’re less worthy of love or a beautiful life than anyone else? Or are you thinking “That’s awful, and so hurtful, and so unlucky, they deserve better”?
That’s what you need to start thinking about yourself. You deserve better. And until you start truly believing this, the more your world is going to continue folding in on itself – and it will be become a self-perpetuating cycle. Because the smaller your life becomes, the more disconnected from your friends you feel, the more you let your inner monologue judge and criticise and blame yourself, the more you will believe that the world doesn’t have anything to offer you – because you won’t be letting yourself receive evidence it does.
And trust me, it does. There is so much love and joy and happiness out there waiting for you. It’s been three years. It’s time to get back out there and find it.
I know if it were that easy, you would have done it already. The fact you’ve felt stuck for so long is a sign you need and deserve some help. A good therapist will give you tools to help you reframe your thoughts, interrupt your ruminating, change your inner voice from one of self-judgment to one of compassion, and will teach you how to calm your body down so that you’re not stuck in such a state of panic and hypervigilance. Think of therapy as the first step back to your life, with a guide who will support you as you start walking forward.
You can also start taking some steps yourself. One thing you can do is interrupt yourself when you start comparing your life with theirs. You’ve created an internal scorecard that says these people hurt you and found love, and you got hurt and feel lonely. With that framing, of course it feels intolerably unfair. But your relative relationship statuses are not the outcomes of a moral trial. Their happiness does not retroactively make the deception acceptable; and equally, their unhappiness would not automatically erase what they did.
A reality of betrayal that feels unfair but is also necessary to accept is that the people who hurt us do not have to become unhappy for us to heal. Sometimes they thrive. Sometimes they never understand what they did. Sometimes they tell themselves a completely different story – and sometimes, infuriatingly, they don’t think much about us at all. It’s unfair. But healing sometimes requires us to tolerate that injustice. Sometimes after a betrayal, a trauma, an injustice, we can resist healing because it can somehow feel like conceding. We can think “If I’m happy again, does that mean they’ve got away with it?” – but you don’t need to keep suffering to prove that what happened to you was wrong. It was wrong. That will always be true, no matter what they do or what you do. So you might as well move towards happiness.
[ I worry my sister’s lack of selfishness is damaging her health Opens in new window ]
You don’t need to forgive them, you don’t need to wish them well, you don’t even need to stop disliking them. You just need to stop letting them define the way you live your life.
Start reclaiming some of the parts of your life you’ve abandoned, in manageable ways. Find a cafe or walk-in that you like, reach out to some friends and organise a fun night out, go on a date in a great outfit with no expectations. When you start thinking about them, say to yourself: “My life belongs to me. My attention belongs to me. My future belongs to me.” This will remind you that you have power and agency, and your happiness is no longer tied to them – it’s entirely in your hands.
And if you ever see them in the street or at a party and feel yourself shrinking, unbow your head. Stand up tall. This is your life, and these people are merely background extras in it. Your life, all its great plot developments, twists, turns and your great love story all lie ahead of you. Look beyond them to the road ahead of you, and walk towards it.

title: ‘Getting medals does not equal cash’: The Irish Olympians struggling to make ends meet
description: A proposal to Government in advance of Tuesday’s budget is aimed at enabling elite Irish athletes to keep competing amid the cost-of-living squeeze
content:
Several Irish Olympic athletes have laid bare the increasing financial burdens associated with high-performance sport, with sailor Eve McMahon saying there is “barely an income to survive the day-to-day costs of a normal person”.
McMahon receives the maximum annual Sport Ireland podium-tier funding of €40,000 – the international carding scheme amount has not changed since 2006, becoming progressively stretched as the cost of living has increased.
“I would pay for absolutely all of my entry fees to every competition that I do,” McMahon says. “Every boat charter, sails for new competitions, all my equipment, all my flights, all my accommodation, all my day-to-day expenses, fuel, ferries, drivers to drive all the kit around.
“The list is honestly endless, and that is what the carding money goes towards. I’m very fortunate to have additional sponsors, and if I didn’t have them, then I wouldn’t be able to cover that.”
Paris Olympics swimmer Tom Fannon, who at age 28 receives €18,000 in annual funding from Sport Ireland, says his sporting career is “not sustainable” without additional funding from his parents: “If it was just down to Sport Ireland funding, I wouldn’t be able to do it,” he says. “And if you don’t have [the funding], you can’t continue. Especially after a certain age.”
Aifric Keogh, who won a bronze rowing medal at the Tokyo Olympics , is chair of the Olympic Federation of Ireland (OFI) athletes’ commission. She says athletes are being lost to the system because they can’t afford the cost of placing their lives on hold, either in simple financial terms or because of career opportunities lost.
“It can be an anxious time in an athlete’s life when you’re out there trying to perform,” Keogh says. “But there’s a kind of a financial cost or a financial burden associated with your performance too.
“There’s this perception that if you’re out there winning medals, and I was one of those athletes winning medals back in the day, then you’re doing okay. But getting medals does not equal cash. Essentially you’re still relying on Sport Ireland funding.”
One of the few sport-related proposals to the Government in advance of Tuesday’s budget directly concerns the financial health and future wellbeing of elite Irish athletes. Despite significant increases in sports funding in recent years, there is a sense it’s not trickling down to the athletes at anywhere near the same pace.
A proposal, essentially a decade in the works, put forward by the athletes’ commission aims to modernise tax measures to better reflect the realities of high-performance sport in Ireland. It would not amount to a lot of money but it would afford athletes the chance to keep a little more of whatever they did earn in their pockets.
For most of them, particularly in Olympic sports, it is seen simply as a long overdue tax break like ones that exist elsewhere in professional sport. Given that it is getting harder for many athletes to earn any sort of income beyond funding, and we are in a cost-of-living crisis, this would be a welcome time to introduce such a measure for these athletes.
In some sports – such as rowing, swimming and boxing – prize money and additional personal sponsorship rarely if ever come into the equation. Which means athletes aiming to reach the top of their game are entirely dependent on Government funding, distributed by Sport Ireland.
Central to this funding model is the international carding scheme, which has three tiers of direct athlete funding, distributed annually: podium-level funding of €40,000; world-class level of €25,000; and international class of €18,000. The podium-level amount has not changed since 2006 even though inflation over the 20 years to August 2026 was 38.4 per cent. Furthermore, although all the funding coming from taxpayers, it is also still further taxable for the athletes.
In more recent years, investment in the various sporting organisations has soared, with Sport Ireland allocating €33.36 million in core funding support for 2026. This represents an 87.4 per cent increase on the €17.8 million investment in 2018, when the National Sports Policy was published, and covers the general sporting operations of 57 national governing bodies (NGBs) of sport, including participation and competition programmes.
At the high-performance end, the investment for 2026 was €28.5 million, up by €1.8 million on the previous year, while the increase in direct athlete funding for 2025 (€4,424,352) to 2026 (€4,750,000) was just €325,648.
[ Let them eat crumbs: Growing wage inequality is bad for both workers and businesses Opens in new window ]
In athletics, as a further example, direct athlete funding went from €645,000 in 2025 to €689,000 in 2026, an increase of just €44,000. Over the same period, Athletics Ireland’s overall income grew by €1.2 million, while wages and salaries went from €2.54 million to €2.86m.
Sport Ireland is supporting the OFI proposal, saying: “We are mindful that it is the request of the athletes’ commission and that would be meaningful to all Olympic and Paralympic athletes. It is not simply a financial measure but a recognition to the athletes who make such a contribution to Irish sport.”
[ Elite athletes’ harsh financial reality: ‘Vast majority are struggling to make ends meet’ Opens in new window ]
Paul McDermott, director of high performance and NGBs at Sport Ireland, says the top-tier podium funding amount of €40,000, which 29 Irish athletes currently receive, is “always under review”, but that other support pathways, around the Sport Ireland Institute, such as strength and conditioning, physiotherapy and nutrition, have significantly increased in recent years.
“All recipient athletes have access to the full array of services provided by the institute, so the performance programme covers nearly everything else, including the coaching. What the athlete has to do with that €40,000 has changed very substantially since that time,“ McDermott says.
[ Ciarán Murphy: Mark Zuckerberg’s few coins thrown to the GAA should not fool us Opens in new window ]
“The carding scheme is still absolutely vital, to allow athletes to train, but the real difference will be training in the right environment, with the right services, the right coach, the right facilities, all of that.”
As Ireland’s fastest swimmer, breaking his own 50m freestyle record this summer, Tom Fannon knows exactly what is required to get the best out of himself. At 28, he’s also heavily reliant on his Sport Ireland international-class funding of €18,000, while his parents continue to make up the shortfall necessary to exist in his sport.
“If you think about junior swimming, a lot of the funding comes from your parents,” says Fannon. “And that happens for a number of years. Then maybe if you’re going through university, you get universities to fund you as well.
“But the moment you’re no longer in that, and you’re still in the chance of fighting for medals at games, if you don’t have a basic level of Sport Ireland funding to see you through, you end up retiring. Which is a shame.
“That’s where the funding from Sport Ireland is crucial, it helps you keep going. But I’m also having to get funded by my parents, because if it was just down to Sport Ireland funding, I wouldn’t be able to do it. It’s not sustainable.”
Fannon remains intent on swimming at the LA Olympics in 2028. In Paris 2024, he missed out on the 50m final by just 0.1 of second, finishing 10th overall. Based at the National Aquatic Centre in Dublin, Fannon’s accommodation is part-subsidised by Swim Ireland, but he’s not able to earn any additional income himself.
“It’s not quite Dublin prices, because we can’t afford Dublin prices, that’s the reason why it’s subsidised. And I’m in the pool twice a day, in the gym in between, so there’s no time in the day to work outside of that.
“There’s rarely any prize money, and even sponsorship is not great. Unless you’re winning the Olympic Games, it’s not the easiest. Even Mona McSharry, she’s like the rest of us. It’s a tough gig, but you don’t do it for the money. You do it for the love of it.
“Obviously, it would help to have slightly more subsidies. It allows you to actually reach the pinnacle of what your performance could be. But if you have people finishing their career early, you never know what they could have done. Maybe win more medals for Ireland.”
Which is where the proposal to create a €50,000 annual tax credit that athletes could use during or after their sporting careers would also help.
“Even a small gesture is better than no gesture. It’s not like we’re trying to cheat the system, living these lavish lifestyles. I’d say 95 per cent of every carded athlete are not living lavish lifestyles.
“And you can’t keep earning 18 grand, at the age of 28, 30, 32. At some point, something has to give. Because of the level of funding, you have no backing behind you, in terms of investments, or savings. When I eventually finish swimming, the likelihood is I go into the working world at the age of 30, 32, with no financial backing behind me at all.
“That’s another sacrifice that we’ve all made, and again, 95 per cent of us are in that same boat.”
The Paris Olympics was among the high points of Eve McMahon’s sailing career to date. Finishing 13th in the ILCA 6, the then 20-year-old realised her Olympic dream with aplomb, and her performance also put her in the shop window for sponsors. She needs financial backing if she’s to excel again in Los Angeles and Brisbane.
Without her personal sponsors, it’s hard to see how she could make ends meet.
“I am fortunate enough to be on that top level of carding,” McMahon says, referring to her €40,000 “podium” designation under the current system. “It is really important to me, and it is allowing me to compete as a full-time athlete, but it never will cover an Olympic campaign.”
While support from Irish Sailing covers costs such as coaching, strength and conditioning, and physiotherapy, the Sport Ireland funding is quickly gobbled up by the demands of her sport.
“I would pay for absolutely all of my entry fees to every competition that I do, every boat charter, sails for new competitions, all my equipment, all my flights, all my accommodation, all my day-to-day expenses, fuel, ferries, drivers to drive all the kit around. The list is honestly endless, and that is what the carding money goes towards,” McMahon says.
“I’m very fortunate to have additional sponsors, and if I didn’t have them, then I wouldn’t be able to cover that.”
With athletes “coming out with barely an income to survive the day-to-day costs of a normal person”, she says, “the reward financially at the end of the day is very little to none.”
It amounts to a far less glamorous life than many presume elite sport to be and entails a huge opportunity cost.
“I still live at home,” says the 22-year-old. “My brother [Ewan] is competing as well for the Olympic Games, and he’s still living at home, and the two of us are saying we would absolutely love to move out of home.
“It is amazing to come home to a family environment and have those people in your corner, but at the end of the day, we are starting to be in those stages in our lives where we have to spread our wings.
“But when you’re competing at such a high level with other countries who are so heavily funded and who do have better tax systems, you have to make the sacrifice of going, ‘I can either spend the money on buying an apartment, or I can invest it fully into my campaign’.”
Her commitment is yielding results, with McMahon ranked second in the world behind American Charlotte Rose, but sometimes the what-ifs are hard to take.
“It’s like a confidence [shaker] to know that another athlete who’s on the start line beside you has got a completely different system and completely different funding.
“No matter how much hard work you put in, you [wonder] will the financial element make a difference, which is pretty killer for us as athletes, because we can only do the best we can do.”
After retiring shortly after the Paris 2024 Olympics, Aifric Keogh felt a need to put her rowing experience to further use. Particularly her journey towards winning Olympic bronze with the women’s four at the delayed Tokyo 2020 Games.
In April of last year, she was elected chair of the nine-person Olympic Federation of Ireland athletes’ commission, which is behind the proposal to introduce a new tax break for all Irish athletes as one small way of easing the increasing financial burdens associated with high-performance sport.
“This conversation first started probably about two commissions ago,” says Keogh, “when the likes of Derval O’Rourke were serving on the commission [in 2017]. The next cohort took over, then we kind of inherited it, and were finally able to put that last piece of the puzzle together in terms of bringing that submission forward.
“Without a doubt, all the federations, and all the high-performance programmes, are much better funded now. And we’re obviously seeing that coming through with all the results. Which is fantastic.
“But every athlete has a different story. Or a different struggle maybe. If you look at the likes of a rower, for example, if you want to row for Ireland, you have to relocate to Cork. You look at sailing, there’s a huge personal cost there with all the travel and equipment.
“In athletics, how many are training abroad, for coaching? That’s all funded by the athlete. There’s this perception that if you’re out there winning medals, and I was one of those athletes who were winning medals back in the day, it’s all okay. But getting medals does not equal cash. Essentially, you’re still relying on that on Sport Ireland funding.”
After her Tokyo medal success, Keogh received the annual top-tier funding of €40,000, but for most athletes the struggle is to find any source of funding.
“I would definitely say it’s a barrier to entry. I came to that point when I was graduating from university, and was kind of making the decision, do I go down to Cork, try to give this a go? And what if it doesn’t work out?
“It is a tough decision, and obviously your family is going to be involved too. Because you’re going to have to rely on them for all the support, financial and just general support. If those opportunities aren’t there for those athletes, where they can rely on others to support them, it’s definitely going to stop them from pursuing that.
“I can’t obviously speak for every sport, but I know myself, when I went down to Cork first for rowing, I had to have my own boat. You need a car. You need to be able to eat a lot of food. There is a huge cost to that lifestyle. And there’s also a cost of going abroad, competing, it all adds up. That’s if you’re lucky enough as well to be on one of those carded athletes.
“And I never won a cent for rowing. You know that when you get involved, and every sport is quite different in terms of opportunities and funding. But something like this tax relief would be of benefit to all.”
Days after winning her three medals at the European Para Swimming Championships in Turkey last month, Róisín Ní Ríain was back in the lecture and study halls at the University of Limerick, starting into her final year of pharmaceutical chemistry. And back in the swimming pool too.
At 21, even with 20 international medals already won across various competitions, including silver and bronze at the 2024 Paralympics in Paris, Ní Ríain can afford to feel like her swimming career is only getting going.
“I’m really lucky down in UL, where I’m also a sports scholarship athlete,” she says. “It’s a dual scholarship, so the way they look at it, they support both your academics and your sport as well as they can.
“And it really helps us to get the best out of both. I’m part of a big training group of swimmers down in Limerick, most of us are in college as well, and also balancing the academics and training to the best of our abilities.”
Among the three medals she won last month , Ní Ríain defended her 100m backstroke title in the S13 class for visual impairment, along with silver in the 200m IM and the 100m freestyle. Since her Paralympics success in Paris, she’s also been on the Sport Ireland podium-level funding of €40,000, although she’s not yet sure that will be enough to sustain her in swimming beyond her college years.
“Fortunately there is the funding by Sport Ireland , and for me at the moment, I’m also a college student, but I haven’t decided yet what I’m going to do after college.
“If I’m going to go looking for a job, or something like that, it’s going to be a little bit different, and I’m sure things will change over the coming years. But I’m definitely blessed to also have all the facilities that I do down in Limerick, and with that funding, and support staff, and I have absolutely wonderful people behind me, all that’s helped me get to where I have been.”
Of the 139 Irish athletes in receipt of direct Sport Ireland funding for 2026 under the international carding scheme, 29 are in Paralympic sports (21 per cent of overall athletes), including seven pilot/guide athletes from para athletics, para cycling and para triathlon. Derry swimmer Dearbhaile Brady, who won four medals at the European Para Championships last month – three silver and one bronze – also receives the top podium grant €40,000.
Ní Ríain recognises that this medal success on the international stage is largely reliant on the increased recognition of Sport Ireland for athlete funding.
“I think it’s definitely improved over the last couple of years, absolutely,” she says. “Even from when I first got into para sports, six or seven years ago now, I didn’t have that many to look up to when I was younger.
“So I do think we’ve definitely come quite a long way since then. But I also think, as always, there’s probably still plenty more that we would hope to grow, to create more awareness around people with disability in sports.”
The proposal submitted by the Olympic Federation of Ireland (OFI) to Government in advance of Tuesday’s budget outlines two key recommendations designed to reduce the significant financial and career-related opportunity costs faced by Olympic and Sport Ireland carded athletes.
Despite Ireland’s growing success on the world sporting stage, many high-performance athletes earn little or no income from their sport.
As a result, they cannot access existing tax supports such as the Sportspersons Relief, which was introduced in 2002 to much applause, by then minister for finance Charlie McCreevy. It gives professional and semi-professional athletes in 13 specific sports relief from income tax at up to 40 per cent on their direct sports earnings for up to 10 years (chosen after the year of their retirement) as long as they are living in Ireland, another EU state, Switzerland, Iceland, Norway or Liechtenstein at the time of their retirement.
Currently, this only applies to athletics, badminton, boxing, cycling, football, golf, jockeys, motor racing, rugby, squash, swimming, tennis and cricket.
The tax relief also only applies to earnings directly from participation in the sport, such as wages or prize money. Any income earned from items such as personal appearances or sponsorship does not qualify.
The OFI Athletes’ Commission proposal seeks to update and expand the Sportspersons Relief so that all Olympic sports governed by recognised National Governing Bodies qualify, and allowing sponsorship and philanthropy income – now the primary income source for many athletes – to be included where it is wholly and exclusively derived from the athlete’s professional trade.
Parallel to this, they are looking to align Olympic and Sport Ireland carded athletes with the artists’ exemption scheme, which was introduced in 1969 by Charles Haughey to encourage creative work in the State.
This would allow athletes to earn €50,000 a year before paying income tax during their sporting careers, directly reducing the opportunity cost of remaining in high-performance sport. It could also encourage athletes to stay resident in Ireland post-retirement.
Currently, any direct athlete funding under the Sport Ireland international carding is regarded as taxable income.
The focus on these two reliefs is that they build on existing legislation and established legislative definitions (under Section 847AA of the Taxes Consolidation Act) to ensure clarity, ring fencing and ease of implementation.
Recent European heptathlon champion Kate O’Connor is among the athletes backing the proposal, saying: “I think that it’s definitely something that the Government needs to look at. It’s such a huge positive for people sitting at home watching athletes do well. So I think it [the tax break] would be a huge benefit, to enjoy all the hard work that we put in, then maybe having some savings to be able to buy a house at the end of it.”

title: Department’s €130k ‘turf agent’ a masterclass in loose oversight
description: Plus: Jeffrey Donaldson’s Down home on the market, Alan Shatter’s mixed debut as a football hack, and Ireland-Israel game nets a big viewership
content:
The Comptroller and Auditor General , who runs a fine-tooth comb through public spending, this week set out a masterclass in loose oversight.
In his 2025 public services report, spending watchdog Séamus McCarthy examined the “management of compensation for cessation of turf cutting”, a matter the Department of Heritage has been in charge of since 2020.
The European Commission announced in March 2024 that it was referring Ireland to the European Court of Justice for failing to halt turf cutting on designated/protected bogs. The expectation was that financial penalties were looming, so the department took “urgent action”.
It had appointed “a bog plot owner” within a month to “leverage their expertise and networks” with a view to increasing the numbers signing up to be compensated to stop cutting turf on designated bogs.
There was no competitive procurement process and the selected agent paid was almost €130,000 (€105 per hour for 1,234 hours) for services provided between April 2024 and August 2025.
“The evidence available to support and verify the agent’s work is limited,” the comptroller said, adding that “records of engagement between the agent and turfcutters were not available” as the department requested they be disposed of for data security reasons.
The department told the comptroller there were 392 new applicants for the scheme arising from the agent’s work, but it was unable to say how many succeeded. The agent benefited from the scheme’s lump sum payment while doing the job, which the department did not consider a conflict.
The comptroller reviewed a sample of 30 compensation files, with seven not containing “any evidence of checks to ensure turf cutting had ceased”.
The department said when indications of illegal cutting on plots linked to the scheme arise, it seeks a declaration saying the beneficiary did not cut turf or that the cutting was done without their consent. It then “considers that the matter is closed, and does not conduct any further checks or investigations to verify this statement”.
The comptroller suggested that the department should conduct more robust checks. The department agreed. No turf war there.
Some have argued, including Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín, that the Democratic Unionist Party’s determination around the ongoing Garvaghy Road standoff seeks to distract from an upcoming event involving a former party figurehead.
Jeffrey Donaldson , who was party leader when he was arrested and charged with child sex offences in March 2024, is due to be sentenced this month for rape, gross indecency and indecent assault. His wife, Eleanor Donaldson, who faced a trial of the facts on mental health grounds, was found to have aided and abetted her husband.
The couple are estimated to have run up legal costs of some £500,000 (€585,000) and this is likely to rise, with each seeking to appeal their outcome. Their four-bed home on Dublinhill Road, Dromore, Co Down, has gone on the market, with £649,950 (€760,142) being sought for the four-bed property.
The “substantial detached country home enjoys beautiful, uninterrupted views of the Mourne Mountains”, according to an ad on PropertyPal.com. Features include a traditional maple kitchen with granite worktops and an oil-fired Aga, reclaimed pitch pine flooring, an impressive twin flight staircase, electric gates, landscaped gardens and a secluded barbecue area.
The Bel­fast Tele­graph reports, citing Land Registry documents, that the couple bought the house for £380,000 in 2003 and that a charge was put on Jeffrey Don­ald­son’s interest in it earlier this year by a company connected to his solicitor.
Many people insisted they would not tune into Ireland’s politically charged Nations League game against Israel, which took place in a near-empty neutral stadium in Debrecen, Hungary, last Sunday. But many people say a lot of things.
RTÉ viewership figures show its stripped-back coverage did little to deter hundreds of thousands of football fans from tuning in for Ireland’s 3-0 win. No crowd, no pundits, no local commentary – no bother.
The broadcast had an average audience of 478,000 people, peaking at 573,000 viewers, with a further 230,000-plus following via the RTÉ Player. The figures were better than those for the previous Thursday’s loss to Kosovo, which had an average audience of 383,000 viewers, peaking at 486,000.
Context is important, however, and audiences for both games were significantly down on those for March’s heartbreaking World Cup play-off defeat to Czechia, and the preceding victories over Hungary and Portugal. All three high-stakes games had in and around one million viewers.
RTÉ had a contractual obligation to broadcast the Israel game, as it does again for Sunday’s return “home” fixture in Serbia, but it opted to take commentary from an international feed and to leave the punditry team in Dublin.
The broadcaster also chose not to take any advertising or sponsorship around the game, meaning a reasonable pay-day was abandoned for a fixture overshadowed by significant public revulsion over the huge death toll in Palestine.
Plenty will tune in again this weekend, with Troy Parrott’s wonder goal against Austria (a game that drew 449,000 viewers on average) having whetted appetites. What happens behind closed doors, stays behind them.
There were surprises aplenty surrounding the Israel match. But a byline on a Jerusalem Post piece from Debrecen provided another, as did the arrival of the writer, former minister for justice Alan Shatter, to the Nagyerdei Stadium press box.
“After a berserk, topsy-turvy couple of days, of course the press box would include a former minister of justice,” said one of the travelling reporters.
Shatter has been a critic of much of the Irish response to events involving Israel and Palestine since October 7th, 2023, with the campaign to stop last Sunday’s game (and the return fixture) a particular bugbear.
His article focused on the drama in the build-up, including goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrawing, citing his “belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong”.
Pointedly, Shatter reported: “Bazunu was one of Ireland’s reserve goalkeepers and was unlikely to have played.”
He noted that Bazunu was Southampton’s goalkeeper in the Premier League last season when they were relegated (Southampton were not in the Premier League last season). He also mentioned that Irish players Finn Azaz and “Brian Manning” (aka Ryan Manning) and Israeli goalkeeper Daniel Peretz were now team-mates at Southampton while Bazunu “interestingly” now plays for Bolton Wanderers in League One.
His report dedicated three paragraphs to the match itself, another to how Israeli supporters chanted “IDF, IDF” in the dying minutes, and one to how “this writer” saw his X feed “hit by a deluge of anti-Semitic hate originating from Ireland” when posting updates.
Shatter also took issue with a line in The Irish Independent’s reporting from Debrecen, which he felt singled him out by mentioning his age (75) when referencing his press box appearance. “Is this ageist or a tribute to my vim & vigour? Total mystery,” he posted on X.

title: Swapping an office job for the Great Blasket Island: ‘It drove me to a remote island’
description: Working as caretakers on the island off the Co Kerry coast was a transformative experience for Conor Jones and Aisling Costello
content:
W orking as caretakers on the Great Blasket Island from April to September has been “a magical experience” for Aisling Costello and Conor Jones, who lived on the island for the 2026 season.
Reflecting on the couple’s six-month stint on the island off the coast of Co Kerry , Costello, from Cork, says: “I think people who might be applying for the job or reading about the job, think, ‘Oh fab! I’m going to go and chill on the island now for six months.’
“People don’t realise it’s a job. You are employed. It is really full on. I was definitely very idealistic about it, and I still am – it is beautiful, but I think a lot of people probably think that they’re going to just get to frolic through the fields and dance with the sheep all day, but like there’s a lot of working in June, July, and August – you don’t get a second to do any of that.”
“Until September,” says Jones. “In September you can frolic away.”
Once a job with 80,000 applicants when the role was first posted in 2019, and 23,000 in 2020 , the Blasket Island caretaker listing has had a 300 application cap since 2025, making it one of the more competitive job processes in the country.
Local couple Alice Hayes and Billy O’Connor are the owners of three cottages and a coffee shop on the Great Blasket, and organise the role of caretaker.
Jones says: “We had one interview with Billy and Alice. I was expecting more because I’ve worked in recruitment.
“Because we gave a very detailed application, mainly it was them just trying to tell us that there is loads of work. I think they were trying to scare us off.” He laughs.
The Blasket Islands are a group of uninhabited islands located about two kilometres from the Dingle peninsula ; the Great Blasket Island was evacuated in 1954 . There is running water, but no running hot water, and limited electricity. A small wind-powered generator allows the couple enough electricity to charge mobile devices.
“There’s a 5g mast on Dunquin. Actually, reception is the least of your worries. The reception here is much better than the reception in Cork city. My internet’s never been faster,” says Costello.
[ Life as a Great Blasket caretaker: I knew I would go back, but I would not live it the same way Opens in new window ]
“You need that because if something went wrong, we need to be able to call someone. But electricity-wise, you know, we are limited. Everything is limited.”
In exchange for bed, board and a stipend, the couple run the cottages as well as the cafe on the island, along with any other odd jobs that need doing, such as building a sheep pen or installing a pump for the island’s back-up water tank.
Costello was working in an administration role when she decided last year that she wanted a career break.
“That job nearly drove me around the bend. I mean, yeah, it drove me to a remote island,” she says, laughing.
Although the location is remote, between guests and wildlife, they have had plenty of company, she says.
“Rabbits and hare, sheep and lambs, loads of seals. We’ve got the largest grey seal colony in Europe, and at the moment it’s their pupping season. So down on the beach and in all the little coves, you can see the tiny little white ones.
“When we first came out, it was the lambing season, so we had all the little dotey pets running around. And now, as we are coming to the end, it’s the pupping season, so we’ve got more little cutie white dotey pets to be looking out for.”
Other creatures are the burrowing Manx shearwater, whose exit coincides with the couple’s – “they actually only left the island a week or so ago” – while the swallows took flight further south long ago.
The 2026 solar eclipse was billed to be a blockbuster natural phenomenon, and best seen in western Europe, but proved to be somewhat of a let down on the Great Blasket, Costello says.
“The eclipse was really cloudy here and it was supposed to be the best spot to see it. People came to stay especially for it. We were all standing outside, hoping to see something. But it was just loads of the midges biting us, and then it got kind of dark for a while, and then it got bright again. So we didn’t really get to see anything,” she says.
When it is not cloudy, Costello says, “the sky here is just so gorgeous. We’ve had like some really amazing moon rises recently with the full moon, and we saw shooting stars.
“You really feel like you’re on the edge of the world.”
There are mainland comforts that they have missed, however.
“I have dreams about going to the supermarket and browsing the aisles,” says Costello, while Jones adds: “I miss the middle aisle.”
Another convenience they miss is the option of eating out in a restaurant, or having a meal that has not been cooked by themselves.
“I’m very excited about getting a Chinese takeaway. I’m mad to have a spice bag,” says Costello.
Spice bags and supermarket middle aisles will soon be within reach for Costello and Jones, as they are set to leave the island, possibly as early as Sunday.
“There’s no date on it yet – the sea is our master out here,” says Costello.
[ ‘It’s how life should be’: Inside a summer on the Great Blasket Opens in new window ]
Despite all of their hard work – Jones says the pair worked for 40 days without a break over the summer – the couple say their big takeaway is the slower pace of life.
“I know we’ve been really busy, but also at the same time it’s this nice slow pace of life. So I’m definitely going to try and bring that into city living. Just kind of take it easy and not rush everything because I guess you can get burnt out quite easily,” Jones says.
“I just think we’re really appreciative of having had this opportunity,” says Costello.
“It is the most amazing thing I have ever done, ever in my life. I know I’m always going to look back on this.
“To be honest, I’d love to never leave, but obviously all good things must come to an end.”

title: ‘It can be magical’: Galway’s swimming, kayaking underwater volunteers
description: One volunteer in Connemara says monitoring these underwater meadows has increased her sense of connection with her part of the world
content:
A group of Connemara volunteers spent days this summer swimming and kayaking through elusive underwater meadows, helping to map a coastal plant that could be a useful weapon in Ireland’s fight against climate change .
Initially formed to oppose the Sceirde Rocks offshore wind farm, the Connemara Coastal Protection group plotted a number of large seagrass meadows off the Galway coast.
Seagrass removes carbon from the environment much more quickly than land-based plants and can store up to twice as much carbon per metre as a mature forest. The plant removes carbon directly from the air through photosynthesis and can trap it in seabed sediment for thousands of years.
The proper mapping, protection and management of Ireland’s seagrass meadows could also significantly reduce penalties of up to €26 billion that Ireland will face in 2030 if it does not meet its climate targets.
Seagrass grows in shallow salt water, often around small islands, and is a distinct species from seaweed, which is a form of algae. Once common all over Irish coastal waters, seagrass meadows have been devastated over the past 100 years by a combination of pollution, high nutrient run-off from land, invasive species and destructive fishing techniques.
While records from the early 20th century are sparse, it is thought that a large portion of Ireland’s seagrass may have also been damaged by a wasting seagrass disease in the 1920s and 1930s.
[ New era of climate obstruction requires pretending things are okay when clearly they are not Opens in new window ]
As well as mapping the seagrass meadows, the Connemara Coastal Protection volunteers have also committed to ongoing monitoring and protection of these ecologically valuable underwater meadows.
The four Connemara sites are part of a network of 100 meadows mapped by citizen science volunteers across Ireland over the past year, all working in conjunction with the environmental NGO Coastwatch.
According to Coastwatch, if the Irish State was to formalise the mapping and monitoring work currently being undertaken by these volunteers, the seagrass meadows could count as a large blue carbon store, a term which refers to carbon captured and stored by ocean and coastal ecosystems.
This would significantly boost Ireland’s chances of reaching its 2030 carbon targets and decrease the €3 billion to €26 billion of compliance penalties that the State is expected to face.
Connemara local Siobhán Kennedy has played a significant role in mapping the seagrass meadows around Inishlacken near Roundstone; Mweenish close to Carna, Moyrus and Eyrephort in recent months.
Kennedy and other volunteers, trained by Coastwatch, used boats and kayaks while others swam carefully through the seagrass meadows to map their exact size, shape and condition.
“It is really beautiful. If you do manage to get out there into the water, it’s just like a large meadow. It is beautiful to see it, a meadow but underwater,” she says.
[ Seagrasses are a precious resource and need protection Opens in new window ]
“When we were off Inishlacken, for example, we saw quite a few shoals of young fish moving through the seagrass. Seagrass is so important for a lot of these species.
“When we were off Eyrephort, close to Inishturk and Inishturbot, we saw a lot of young eels. When you are there and you see it, you feel like you are part of protecting this marine environment in a teeny-tiny way. It can be quite magical.”
Marine ecologist Karin Dubsky believes that the protection and development of Ireland’s seagrass meadows could have a positive effect on climate.
Under the current EU Nature Restoration Law, Ireland is required to put 30% of its degraded seagrass into effective restoration by 2030, based on the 2020 levels of seagrass cover.
Coastal local authorities became responsible for planning and development management near coastal areas following the enactment of the Maritime Area Planning Act in 2021.
Dubsky believes that a collaboration between these county councils and local volunteers could open the door for this seagrass to act as blue carbon credit for Ireland.
“Ireland can get carbon credits for this seagrass, but Ireland can’t just say that it has this seagrass there, it has to be able to show that these beds are managed and monitored,” says Dubsky, aprofessor at Trinity College Dublin and cofounder of Coastwatch Europe.
“The community volunteers are are doing the day-to-day work of watching, monitoring and managing the seagrass.
“All the Government needs to do is to give just one officer to each local authority, who is specifically there to work with local communities on the management of seagrass and blue carbon, then you have monitoring, management and reporting.
As well as mapping the seagrass meadows, volunteers are trained to examine local pressure points that could be affecting the health of the seagrass meadows and examine ways in which these pressures could be mitigated.
Kennedy says mapping and monitoring her local seagrass meadows has increased her sense of connection with her part of the world.
“Even if you don’t want to get into a kayak and get out on to the water, seagrass will often wash up on shore. If you know what to look for, then that can be valuable information. It means that somewhere out there are seagrass beds.
“It makes you feel connected with how it all works, all of these ecosystems.
“But there are two parts to this: one part is discovering areas that have not been mapped and the other side is looking after the areas that have already been mapped.
“These seagrass meadows are susceptible to the elements. They can be destroyed altogether. They have stressors such as nitrates from agriculture, dredging, storms, there are lots of things that can damage them. So this is an ongoing process for us.”

title: ‘There’s so much change’: Young Spencer on finding common ground with Kneecap in Belfast
description: Rapper says music is bringing young people together in Northern Ireland and talks about how his association with nationalist rap trio ‘divides opinion’
content:
Passing cars slow to beep their horns at Gareth Spence when he walks through the rain-soaked streets of Belfast ’s Shankill estate. This is the loyalist stronghold where the rapper, known as Young Spencer, grew up.
Neighbours wave from doorsteps under a sea of red, white and blue bunting as two enormous dogs attempt to jump their owner’s gate.
It was “UDA country”, says the 32-year-old, nodding his head in the direction of paramilitary murals on gable ends.
“Welcome to Loyalist Lower Shankill, 2nd Batt C Com” is daubed on a blue wall, a reference to the notorious C Company unit of the Ulster Defence Association . The unit – linked to dozens of sectarian murders – was embroiled in a bloody loyalist feud more than 25 years ago.
“There’s a big distinction between coming from here and further up the Shankill Road … some people see you as coming from down in the gutter when you’re from this part,” says Spence.
“Growing up as a teenager, you’re thinking, ‘maybe change that?’ There’s been people making change here for years. Youth workers, football coaches, community workers – these people were integral to my upbringing and how I’ve been raised.”
In August, Young Spencer performed at a sell-out concert headlined by rap group Kneecap, during the Féile an Phobail community arts festival in west Belfast.
Fans draped in Tricolours chanted his lyrics at the Uppa Falls charity gig in Falls Park. Climate activist Greta Thunberg was among many in the crowd wearing Kneecap’s signature balaclavas.
“As a proud British born and raised Protestant from the Shankill estate, I thought I’d died and gone to Fenian heaven for about two hours,” Spence says, with a smile, about the performance.
“But do you know what, you live here with a curiosity because often when you’re young, you’re told, ‘don’t mix with themuns’. They’re not you and you’ll never mix’. So then you grow this curiosity and you confront it. I was the type that always liked asking ‘why’.”
Our interview took place before the resurrection of the Drumcree parades dispute in Portadown.
Asked about its fallout on Tuesday, Spence admits he is worried.
“It’s really starting to separate people again in my community. Tensions are rising,” he says.
He is speaking on his phone while walking up the nationalist Cliftonville Road in north Belfast.
A motorist beeps the horn and gets out of his car.
It is day three of the standoff between Garvaghy Road residents and the Orange Order.
“That’s it right there in a nutshell. I’m coming up the Cliftonville and there’s someone called Kevin - who I don’t know - pulling in to shake my hand.
“So I still feel confident in the future generation and its abilities - regardless of what happens politically.”
Back in early September, when we meet on the Shankill Road, he has rushed from his day job at a school in north Belfast. Dressed in a green leather jacket, white top and jeans, headphones hang round his neck. Four teenagers shout his name from their car outside a KFC.
Despite the visible support, Spence is aware that his association with Kneecap “divides opinion on this road”.
It is the second time in two years he has shared a stage with the Irish language rappers. Online critics have accused him of selling out.
“Of course, there’s the hatred. There’s people who just don’t understand what you’re doing,” he says. “But mainly I’ve have been blown away by the love and appreciation. It always outweighs any negativity.”
Others have claimed he is “chasing headlines”.
“I’ve had people complain that we’re not really conscious of kids watching us. We are. That’s the whole point,” Spence says.
“We’ve had to deal with the ramifications of not growing up directly in the Troubles but being raised by families who were. That’s created a sense of worry within us. We’re just young people who have our ways and methods of how we feel we can bring people together, through music and art.
“Kneecap and Young Spencer could not have supported each other 30 years ago because somebody was dying; someone was getting killed.”
In an interview with The Irish Times earlier this year, Kneecap’s Mo Chara expressed his respect for the Shankill rapper. Their relationship highlights how young people are “moving on”, he said.
“I’m a republican and I suppose he’s a unionist. But he is being authentically himself, and I respect that. I respect him. He has this tune, P.R.O.D., and I love that. I think that’s unreal,” Mo Chara said.
[ Stevie Wonder releases four unheard tracks from Songs in the Key of Life sessions Opens in new window ]
‘I don’t agree with everything the lads say and they don’t agree with everything I say, but I respect the artistry,” he says.
“I see more than the headlines that people want to create. I see genuine lads that’s telling their story of how they grew up in west Belfast – that’s what I’ve always related to.”
Passing a playpark close to his home in the estate – it was waste ground known as the “Muckhills” when he was a child – Spence points to a street where children from a nearby Catholic school cut through on their way home.
“These are still very much impoverished areas, it’s the same on both sides. But it’s different to when I was growing up,” he says.
“I saw two guys the other week at a car wash on the Shankill wearing Celtic tops. It was all right to me. I’m a Rangers fan but I thought, ‘go do your thing, go get your car washed’.”
Not every fan of Kneecap is from the “Catholic/nationalist side,” he says.
“Kids come up in the school where I work and tell me quietly, ‘I listen to Kneecap too’. What’s amazing for me is to see that barrier start to become broken down.”
Walking up to Beatties fish bar (a “staple” of Shankill life, he says smiling, “my granny used to come here”), Spence speaks a few words of Irish. He has started taking classes.
“A lot of people say that’s not my language. But should that deter me from learning Irish? How many proud Irish Protestants have spoken it?
“I think it’s a very poetic language because there’s a multitude of things you can say for one thing.”
[ New Irish albums reviewed and rated: Driven Snow, David Geraghty, Andy Irvine, Last Apollo, Sorcha Richardson Opens in new window ]
Windows are misted up in Beatties, where a pensioner is tucking into a chip butty and mug of strong tea before the evening rush. Union flag bunting criss-crosses the entire ceiling of the small premises.
Spence orders a pastie before returning to the Irish language.
“If you go on holiday, you always think about learning the language. To me, any genuine person would respect you for trying.
“What makes that any different from me being over in west Belfast saying to someone, Sláinte a chara, míle buíochas [cheers my friend, thanks a million]. It’s just a term of endearment.”
A so-called Peace Wall divides the Shankill Road from the Falls Road.
Built at the beginning of the Troubles, it reaches 14 metres (45ft) in height at certain points and stretches for 650 metres, making it the highest and longest of the remaining interface structures in the city.
