Outside the shop, Spence acknowledges that if he “grew up 10 minutes the other side of that wall” he’d be “campaigning for the same things”.
“I’d be wanting the Irish language to be as pivotal as the English language is.”
The P.R.O.D acronym he uses on his social media platforms is a “set of principles to live by” as opposed to a label, he says, adding: “Passion, persistence, respect, resilience, opportunity to overcome, dedication, determination.”
Music has been “therapy” since his early teens. Educated in an integrated primary school – “my mum was big on us mixing with other kids” – he spent childhood summers playing cross-community football tournaments.
“I was bullied in school and things got bad. Thankfully I got help and the writing took over.”
He beams in torrential rain recalling the moment “some random person” posted a tweet suggesting a Young Spencer-Kneecap collaboration during Covid. “Kneecap reposted it. I thought it was crazy but it showed there was mutual respect.”
When the band’s film was released in 2024, Spence says he remembers watching it and “wanting to reach out to them even if nothing ever comes back”.
[ Westside Cowboy at Whelan’s review: Like watching tomorrow’s superstars grow up before your eyes Opens in new window ]
“The conflict in my own mind was that right away I knew someone from where I’m from is going to have a problem. I then wrote a song called Shankill Son. I said in the song, ‘Salute the Kneecap from P.R.O.D.’ and I knew it would start the spark and start the conversation.
“I thought then we could build some sort of connection. We don’t have to be best mates but I thought we could do something for the city that we both come from, that we’re both proud of and not be deterred from the fact that you’re from the Falls and I’m from the Shankill.”
A month before Kneecap’s pre-Christmas SSE Arena performance in 2024, he received a message from them.
“It was Móglaí Bap. He asked if I wanted to do a few songs in the SSE.
“Right away, I’m pacing up and down the livingroom, thinking ‘oh my God’. I’ve been dreaming of this ... but I was worried about telling my family.
“It wasn’t normal for where I was from. And fair play to the lads, I’ll always have respect for them. Not too many people on my side have been offered an opportunity like that.”
Last month he was invited to perform at the Fleadh in Belfast. The event has been hailed a watershed moment for the city; loyalist marching bands were among those who took part.
“There was something like two billion eyes and ears on Belfast because of the Fleadh,” says Spence.
“A lot of people are going to say, ‘well that’s not us’. But I think now, the conversations we’re having, the news we’re making, the unity we’re bringing among this city and this country regardless of what it’s called – Northern Ireland or the North – is breathtaking.”
At traffic lights on our walk back down the Shankill, Spence laughs when he spots a blue sticker on a lamp-post.
“Belfast Groove Collective” is written on it.
“That’s my cousin, he’s part of it. He’s in a band,” he says. “Right now, everyone wants to be a rapper. Everyone wants to be an artist.
“The thought that you could be a rapper and perform to a sell-out crowd in Belfast was unthinkable 20 years ago. You were a laughing stock to even talk about it.

title: Benjamin Alire Sáenz: ‘As an ex-priest, I understood what it meant to have a calling to poetry’
description: Benjamin Alire Sáenz, the Texas-based poet and author, was the man to speak to if you wanted to learn about the ‘world of in-between’ of the US-Mexico border
content:
“Y ou’ll hallucinate out there, on the road.” I was standing in Benjamin Alire Sáenz’s kitchen in his home in El Paso, Texas . It was after midnight, and we had just finished a meal of Mexican stew, a recipe Sáenz learned from his grandmother. I had arrived after a 15-hour flight from Dublin . The desert skies over El Paso were dark and filled with stars. I knocked on Ben’s door, and when he answered, I was greeted with his lined face, open eyes, and wide smile.
The moment I crossed the threshold into his sittingroom I was hit by the smell of stew simmering on the stove. We sat and ate for several hours with a group of people I didn’t know. Ben had hundreds of friends, and any were likely to turn up for dinner, any night of the week. The conversation was lively, a mix of Spanish and English.
I did my best to keep up. I told him my plans. I was going to travel the length of the Texas-Mexico border, from El Paso and Juárez in the west to Brownsville and Matamoros in the southeast. Driving along the scarred, rigid spine of one of the most contentious borderlands in the world. And I was going on my own.
Ben raised a glass of wine and toasted my journey. “You’ll hallucinate out there,” he repeated. And then added, “tonight, you sleep in my bed. I’ll take the couch.”
I slept fitfully and rose before dawn, loading the few things I brought from Ireland into a tiny white rental car. Ben stepped out on to his front porch and handed me a bag full of leftover food from the night before. He lit a cigarette, took a drag, and coughed into the wind. We were both dead tired, and I was suddenly daunted by the journey ahead of me. Ben smiled and offered one last piece of wisdom. “At the other end of the border, in the southern valley, they can’t cook for shit.”
We both laughed. I settled into my compact car and reversed out of the driveway. In the rear-view mirror, I saw Ben standing still on the porch, his lit cigarette glowing in the dark. I pulled away and set off into the desert.
That was the last time I saw Benjamin Alire Sáenz before his death in July. In the intervening years, we shared dozens of hours of phone conversations, many of which I recorded. Only weeks before he died, we completed a manuscript of a collaborative book, an account of our shared experiences on the border. My enduring image of Ben is of the poet standing alone in the dark, puffing a cigarette against the high desert winds, sending me off into the borderlands. Smiling.
When I first started visiting the US-Mexico border, more than a decade ago, I was asked one question over and over again: “Have you met Benjamin Alire Sáenz?” The name itself sounded like a mystery. Friends and fellow writers across Texas assured me this was the man I needed to speak to, if I wanted to learn about the “world of in-between”.
In 2015, as writer-in-residence with the Lannan Foundation, I met the border journalists Angela Kocherga and Alfredo Corchado. We spent evenings under the cosmic Marfa sky, chatting over tequila in the Hotel Saint George. When I asked them about Sáenz, Angela answered quickly. “You want to meet Ben? Sure, I’ll take you to him.”
A year later, I flew from Ireland back to El Paso and met Angela at the airport. She drove straight to Sáenz’s house downtown, passing long stretches of border fencing along the Rio Grande. The river was barely a stream. Concrete slopes on either side were painted with colourful murals and slogans, words and images defying the barriers erected between people who see themselves as one. From the hill above Sáenz’s house, I could see the border crossing into Juárez. One city split into two. Many border dwellers refuse to acknowledge such crude divisions.
[ From Donegal to Texas: ‘I felt part of an Irish community for the first time in years’ Opens in new window ]
Angela and I interviewed Ben for a documentary film. He invited us into his kitchen, where he was kneading dough to make polvorones. We talked as he baked. When our interview ended, Ben pulled me aside and said, “you’re a poet. That’s why we understand each other. As poets.” For Sáenz, poems expressed the contradictions of life on the border. He lived many lives on the page.
After that first meeting, Sáenz and I shared a correspondence and friendship over 10 years, grounded in poetry and its possibilities. When he died in July, at the age of 71, we were working on a collaborative poem. I showed Ben how to use a shared Google doc, where we wrote back and forth, across continents. That doc is bookmarked in my search browser, above the words I’m writing now. Our collaborative piece, We Live Most Days in Light, was planned to be much longer than it turned out to be. But it might well contain the last lines of poetry Ben Sáenz ever wrote.
Benjamin Alire Sáenz was born in 1954 in Old Picacho, New Mexico, near Las Cruces, in a borderland floodplain along the Rio Grande. His family ran a small farm, and he grew up speaking both Spanish and English. From an early age, he was drawn to Catholic ritual and discipline, which led him into seminary and the priesthood in his early 20s. He was influenced by Latin American liberation theology and liberal Catholic figures like Dorothy Day, the Berrigan Brothers, and the poet-monk Thomas Merton.
After a few years serving as a parish priest, Sáenz left the church – not because of his as-yet unacknowledged homosexuality, but because of the painful sense that he had not been given a religious vocation. Travels and study in Europe opened his eyes to histories of oppression and colonialism, and back on the US-Mexico border, Sáenz engaged in the anti-war and anti-poverty actions of the Chicano Movement. Though he left the priesthood, a sense of vocation, justice, and discipline never escaped him.
Ben once told me, “I didn’t leave the Catholic Church. The Catholic Church left me.”
[ ‘I arrived in Arizona to 48-degree heat; being Irish, I decided to go for a cycle’ Opens in new window ]
With characteristic conviction, Sáenz set a new path, as a writer. First, he won a scholarship to the University of Iowa, home of the famous Iowa Writers Workshop. “I hated Iowa,” Ben told me. “There were no Mexicans, no Latinos there at all. When Los Lobos came to play the auditorium, every Mexican in the city came out of the woodwork!” Ben beamed at the recollection.
One day in the sub-zero Iowa winter, he received a phone call from sunny California. He’d been awarded the Wallace Stegner Fellowship at Stanford, perhaps the most prestigious and competitive writing award in the country. When the woman calling from Stanford broke the news, Ben blurted out, “I want to marry you!” “I get that a lot,” she said. “I love my job.”
At Stanford, Sáenz realised, “I understood what it meant to have a calling. As a former Catholic priest, I know that word is serious business. You have to respond to it. I wasn’t afraid to write, to experiment, to discover what was inside me.”
The most influential figure Sáenz encountered at Stanford was the poet Denise Levertov, who became Sáenz’s champion and mentor. She told him, “You have a passion for history. Don’t lose it, it will be part of your work.” Ben reflected to me, “She believed poets have to look outward, listen for the people who talk about necessary things in whatever form they come in.”
[ The ‘other Americans’: 20 books that celebrate US literature’s rich diversity Opens in new window ]
At Stanford, Sáenz produced his first book of poems, Calendar of Dust (1991), which won an American Book Award. Literary success meant that Ben could pursue artistic and academic opportunities in the major cities on the east coast, or in Europe. Instead, he decided to return to the border, where he helped found the first bilingual creative writing programme in the US, in the University of Texas at El Paso.
Sáenz would go on to publish six poetry books and 11 novels. He was a prolific painter and a revered figure on the border for his politics and public addresses. After decades as a “kept secret” in the borderlands, at the age of 57, he published Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe in 2012, a novel for Young Adult readers. It sold (as he was always delighted to tell me) 11 copies in its first week. Ari and Dante, a coming-of-age story about two gay boys on the Texas-Mexico border in the 1980s, went on to sell more than 30 million copies and be translated into 70 languages. It’s a modern classic.
In 2013, his collection of border stories, Everything Begins and Ends at the Kentucky Club, won the Pen/Faulkner Award, making Sáenz the first Latino writer to receive the honour.
Ben always told me that it was a blessing to have commercial success late in life because it allowed him to develop his art without overwhelming scrutiny, and to enjoy success without ego. He continued to live modestly in El Paso, in view of the border, and he gave most of the money away.
Perhaps Sáenz’s bravest publication is the poetry book, The Last Cigarette on Earth (2017). It’s a deeply personal reflection (in part) on his coming out, in middle age, as a gay man; and his descent into drug use and addiction. Ben recovered, always telling me that his brush with the El Paso drugs underworld was “anthropological”. But the suffering of that period, and his clarity in writing it, is not to be diminished. In a poetic prologue to the book, Sáenz writes about himself in the third person: “He wants to remember/ and understand the crooked roads/ he has walked. He will step into the landscapes/ where he lost and broke himself.”
Ben traversed many borderlines – those in the land, in the body, in the spirit. For a man filled with warmth, he had a raging politics on the side of the disenfranchised. He would laugh as quickly as he would cry. He was my guide. And he was my friend.
Sure enough, I did hallucinate driving along the border. Mountains rise out of the desert, with a kind of unreality surrounding them. Hot, unrelenting sun. Endless miles of highway that blur your vision. I drove late into the night and early into the morning. I was alone, but Ben travelled with me. A stack of his books on the passenger seat.
I kept returning to a sequence of meditations on the border that appear in Sáenz’s The Book of What Remains: “Jesus spent his entire life living in the desert./ This is why he is not bothered by the impure language/ and the impure thoughts and the impure people/ that inhabit the border./ He knows what it has cost us to survive.”
Along the border, I visited poets, painters, conservationists, and historians. Many of them were introduced to me by Ben, and they contributed to the vast picture Sáenz had been painting for decades. When I arrived back home in Ireland, Ben and I began work on our collaboration.
I said before that my enduring image of Sáenz is the poet smoking in a dark doorway, bidding me off on a journey. But I think now mostly of the lonely cursor flickering on my computer screen, marking the final, unfinished poem Ben and I were meant to make. His last contribution was this:
In our final phone conversation, Ben couldn’t contain his excitement at the idea of visiting Ireland when we were on book tour together. He had been hospitalised for months, but was home and planning for the future. On the call, we ranted over politics, talked about art and poetry and publishing, and we laughed.
We always laughed. He ended the call, as ever, with a simple, “I love you.” And the phone went dark.
Jonathan C Creasy is a writer, film-maker, musician and broadcaster based in Dublin.

title: Can you drink whiskey with dinner?
description: How to Drink Better: The author of a new Irish whiskey cookbook would argue that you most definitely can, and should
content:
Can you drink whiskey with dinner? Oisín Davis thinks you can, so much so that he has written a book about it. Davis has always been an avid promoter of Irish drinks through tastings, podcasts, events, and, in his first book, Irish Kitchen Cocktails. Next week, he will release his second, The Irish Whiskey Cookbook.
“My first book was all about encouraging people to make cocktails at home – it was very focused on the domestic enjoyment of Irish-made cocktails,” he says. “This one I see as a guide for people who want to enjoy Irish whiskey in a more elevated manner both at home and when they are out.
“With the book, I am trying to do is celebrate something that is very unique to Ireland, which is our Irish whiskey – it’s GI-protected. From a culinary perspective, it’s something we have been masters of for centuries. If we want to have a culinary culture that is unique to Ireland, then we really need to start showcasing the items that are truly unique to the island of Ireland.”
In the new book, Davis aims to highlight a different approach to whiskey, firstly by bringing it into food: “Literally cooking it in a sauce, mixing it into a cheese fondue, bringing the whiskey into a Irish coffee brownie”.
His other “core message” is that if you buy a bottle of whiskey and cook with it, you can keep it open and drink it alongside the food.
But does he believe that whiskey does go well with food as part of a meal?
“Absolutely it does. It may not be something that you would have throughout the entire meal but it an Irish whiskey cocktail or even a nice straight serve is lovely as an aperitif. But if you want to have an Irish whiskey paired with your main course, where we would normally veer towards the wine, I suggest you look at cocktails. That’s what we’ve done in the book; for every dish, there is an Irish whiskey recommendation, whether it’s a straight serve or a cocktail. I love a straight whiskey at the end of the meal at the cheese board. Irish cheeses go absolutely wonderfully well with Irish whiskeys. I think restaurants that have cheese boards and don’t bring out the Irish whiskey, or at least suggest it, are missing out.”
Davis looks at how other producer countries such as the US and Scotland view their whisky and reckons we have “a lot of catching up to do”.
“In both those countries their whiskys are far more integrated into their culinary cultures and into their menus, whether it’s bourbon and a nice barbecue sauce, or how well they pair seafood and their cheeses over in Scotland. It may not be to everyone’s taste to enjoy an Irish whiskey with every course of food at a meal but if you haven’t had an Irish whiskey alongside a nice dessert or an Irish cheese board, I would highly recommend starting there.”
Davis’s book has 50 recipes, all containing Irish whiskey and each with a suggested pairing. “I have recipes that go back as far as the 19th century and I have recipes that are my own and then others that are just kind of twists on other whiskey classics,” he says.
Dishes include duck breast with spiced redcurrant whiskey sauce, chicken and whiskey hot wings, baby back ribs with whiskey, ginger ale and lime, scallops with a whiskey soy glaze, and chocolate whiskey mousse.
Does he have a favourite whiskey recipe?
“There’s definitely a couple of very approachable, very easy recipes that everyone can give a go. From the sweet side I would say that the Irish coffee brownie is very easy to pull off and complements an Irish coffee beautifully. And then the Irish whiskey cream sauce for steaks. I think that any gastropub or restaurant that is celebrating Irish food but is not serving something like an Irish cream sauce with their steaks should be fined.”
The Irish Whiskey Cookbook: 50 Recipes to Cook, Sip and Savour is published by Nine Bean Rows

title: Malachy Clerkin: Pep Guardiola said Manchester City destroyed football – he didn’t know how right he was
description: There is no sanction that will feel satisfactory for their cheating, no way of undoing what the serial Premier League champions have done
content:
There’s a Pep Guardiola speech that bubbles up every once in a while on the internet, like the gristly foam on the surface of a boiling ham. Taken from one of the Amazon glaze job documentaries, it’s always a good reminder that you’re spending more time than you should in the For You wastelands of X. Sort of like Robin Williams’ gag about cocaine being God’s way of telling you you make too much money, just with added Bernardo Silva.
It’s from the end of the 2017/18 season, Guardiola’s second at Manchester City, their first league title won under him. Except they didn’t just win it; they swallowed it in one gulp. They put up 100 points; they set or equalled records for consecutive wins (18), consecutive away wins (11), and consecutive wins in all competitions (20). They scored 106 goals, 22 more than the next-highest. They finished with a goal difference of +79, a full 33 better than the next best.
It was a Pantera season, a vulgar display of power. And in keeping with the general tone of muscular, macho bravado, Guardiola’s speech to his players, captured by the Amazon cameras, leans into the language of obliteration. The supposed intent of it is to deflect praise from himself on to them, but there’s a serious bang of the humblebrag off it too.
"I destroyed football like you destroyed the Premier League" Pep Guardiola's speech to his @ManCity players after their first Premier League triumph 🏆 pic.twitter.com/3rFW4wXWd5
“Can you imagine a ball boy?” Pep begins. “In his own country, a small country. Going to the academy when he’s 13 years old. And after playing in the first team, his own team, in his heart, who stayed there a lot of years and after became the manager – 37 years old and in four years he destroyed football.
“It’s me. I had the privilege to live that. I destroyed football like you destroyed the Premier League. Like you destroyed the Premier League this season.”
Sheesh! Talk about saying the quiet part out loud. Just to put a bit of context around the season Guardiola is eulogising here, City went into it off the back of a summer window in which they bought Ederson, Kyle Walker, Bernard Mendy and Bernardo Silva. They added Aymeric Laporte in January. This was on top of the previous season where they bought John Stones, Leroy Sané, Ilkay Gündoğan and Gabriel Jesus. Of those nine players, six went on to feature in at least one PFA Team of the Year over the next decade.
They didn’t come cheap either. Ederson cost a world record fee for a goalkeeper. Stones was the world’s most expensive defender until they bought Walker, who held the tag for four months until being passed by Laporte. Silva played 460 games for City, Ederson played 372, Walker 317. Stones, Gündoğan and Jesus all played at least 200 matches; Laporte played 180. The money did what it was supposed to. It built Guardiola’s best-ever team.
[ Manchester City or Scam FC – the €1bn scandal Opens in new window ]
We know now that it was all a con job. The Premier League confirmed on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of inflating their sponsorship totals for a decade leading up to that season, that they filed inaccurate accounts to hide the true state of their finances and that they arranged sham contracts with commercial partners. This was worth almost £900 million to them over the period that was investigated. City have stated their innocence and are appealing.
In the forest of numbers, it’s useful to try and find a clearing where we can give ourselves room for a better look. Helpfully, the report breaks down City’s connivance on a season-by-season basis. And so we are able to see that in 2017/18, the club recorded £145.73m (€166.34 million) in commercial revenue, with only £11 million (€12.56 million) paid by actual sponsors. That means City’s owners put up £134.73 million (€158.38 million) in disguised funding for that season, against the rules.
[ Manchester City guilty of Premier League charges after £900m of ‘sham’ contracts Opens in new window ]
Cut to Guardiola standing in front of a white screen in a Holiday Inn meeting room in 2018, all grave tones and manly gesticulation, giving his players their due for destroying the Premier League. “This belongs to you,” he says. “The football, guys, belongs to you. It doesn’t belong to me. It belongs to you.”
It belongs to them all now. Guardiola presumably didn’t mean to be quite so on the nose with all his talk about destroying football and so on, but look where it has all led to. Nobody has been able to give a proper sense of where this is going to end up for City, but regardless of what form their punishment ultimately takes, football has been destroyed here.
Not just Premier League football, either. English football as a whole is going to have to wrestle with what to do with them over the rest of the decade. The past 15 years of European football is a tainted, asterisked thing too. There’s no satisfying way to sanction them, no undoing what they’ve done. You can’t take the eggs back out of the cake once it’s baked.
The comet’s tail is going to be longer than we can even imagine here. City’s rapacious, lawless tentacles have been attached to every corner of the elite game throughout the Abu Dhabi adventure and so their name is blackened permanently for future generations. They were one of the greatest club teams the game has ever known, playing football that reinvented an entire sport.

title: Budget day looms amid first hints of uncertainty over corporation tax
description: Department admits that while business tax take will rise this year, it will not meet even recent forecasts
content:
Easily lost in the bumper corporation tax numbers published with Friday’s exchequer returns was the admission by the Government that the State will not collect as much corporation tax this year as it had expected.
The number will be up for sure – hardly surprising given that the headline rate for some of our largest multinationals has risen to 15 per cent from 12.5 per cent – but it will fail to match Government projections.
Back in April, the Department of Finance anticipated corporation tax receipts would come in at €35.3 billion. As recently as last month, it was reported that figures prepared for Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Tánaiste Simon Harris suggested that number would be exceeded by a wide margin .
Now, just weeks later, it has been revised down to €34 billion, fractionally below the fairly conservative estimate in last year’s budget white paper.
Addressing the issue, even as the department unveiled an unexpected €3 billion take from the business tax in September, a spokesman said some payments expected this year would not now arrive until early next year.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
That is very likely but as Harris and his ministerial colleague Jack Chambers put the finishing touches to the budget package for 2027, the first hint of uncertainty about the outlook on corporation tax suggests the time for playing fast and loose with “windfall” corporation tax revenue is coming to an end.
No one should need the Economic and Social Research Institute think tank or the budgetary watchdogs at the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council to realise that using exceptional tax income to fund recurring day-to-day spending is simply irresponsible, especially in a State just one generation on from a catastrophic international bailout.
This time last year, in the budget white paper, the then finance minister Paschal Donohoe saw strong growth in corporate tax underpinning his budgetary arithmetic, alongside income taxes.
Donohoe did add that he expected the tax to top out at some stage. That may be sooner than we think, especially as we are so reliant on a small cohort of companies.
Just three companies, Eli Lilly, Apple and Microsoft, account for close to half of all business tax income. A few years ago during the Covid pandemic, Pfizer would have featured in that sentence. Its subsequent travails illustrate just how fast fortunes can change – and how exposed we might be.
As for income tax, that is certainly delivering on Donohoe’s expectation for now, but even there, the employment outlook is clouded by concerns over geopolitical factors and the impact of artificial intelligence.
[ The issue that keeps Simon Harris awake at night Opens in new window ]
Regardless of political party, the focus of every deputy in the Dáil in advance of budget day is on spending, not sound fiscal practice. Politically, expectations have been raised; economically, we are mortgaging the future of our younger generations.

title: ‘What’s the best way to clear brambles from my overgrown garden?’
description: ‘It contains some lovely trees and shrubs that we want to keep’
content:
We recently bought an old 1960s-style bungalow with a large, established garden. It contains some lovely trees and shrubs that we want to keep, but is very badly overgrown with brambles. What’s the best way to clear these without resorting to weedkillers? Áine F, Cork
The first step is to cut their long, thorny, arching stems right back to the ground, so arm yourself with a strong pair of thorn-resistant, protective gloves, eye-protective goggles, and an old thick overcoat that you don’t mind getting torn and then use a long-armed, extendable loppers to slice them to the ground. Then use the loppers to chop these thorny stems up into smaller pieces before piling them into a heap in a quiet corner of the garden to rot down.
The next step is to excavate as much of the bramble plants’ deep, suckering root systems as you can. A hardy, vigorous, woody perennial that can quickly colonise new ground, the root systems of this very widespread native plant can go very deeply into the soil and can regenerate quite easily from just small fragments left behind. You’ll need to use a mattock, pickaxe or strong garden fork or spade to prise them out as thoroughly as you can, concentrating particularly on removing the main central root system of each plant while taking care not to damage the root systems of any nearby trees, shrubs and perennials that you want to keep.
Bear in mind that you’ll almost certainly need to repeat this process several times over the course of a year or two to properly eradicate them, so it will be a slow and laborious business, but worth it in the end. Although wild brambles don’t regularly produce viable seeds, it’s also important to watch out for any baby seedlings that may appear in the interim and remove these quickly to prevent them establishing.
Once you have the ground reliably clear of brambles, mulch it generously with an organic mulch to suppress further weed growth as well as to boost the health of any remaining ornamental plants, which have presumably been neglected for some time. In large open areas of the garden, you could also consider sowing a lawn, with regular mowing being another very effective way to eradicate brambles and other stubborn perennial weeds without resorting to herbicides.

title: TV guide: the best new shows to watch, starting tonight
description: October 4th-9th highlights: including How to Shop Well Now, Deepfake Ireland with Gráinne Seoige, and RTÉ Investigates: Fertility Uncovered
content:
We’re all seeing our grocery bills rise on the regular, and with the changes in climate come fears about the impact on food prices and farmers. So what’s a shopper to do? This two-part documentary looks at these and related issues, and features the popular content creator Sophie Morris, who’s known for her videos about supermarket products. She’s joined by journalist Claire Brock as the pair ask how we can all spend smarter during a time when the average annual family grocery bill is up by about €3,000 since 2020. Not to mention the fact we are an island nation depending on imports and exports to keep us afloat. Morris will meet food producers and find out more about what’s behind the rising cost of products, while Brock will look at supermarket psychology and how to shop smarter.
It’s a new series of DIY SOS, where Baz Ashmawy and team help to improve the lives of people across the country by transforming their homes and gardens. It’s always a tearjerker to watch people row in to help folks like the Connolly family in episode one, who live in Kildare. Ramona Connolly and her five-year-old son Oran have been dealing with the aftermath of their husband and dad Daragh dying suddenly in December 2025. Ramona and Daragh had been in the process of building their forever home at the time, and Ramona was left without a mortgage, life insurance or the means to complete the house. Enter Baz and the DIY SOS team, who step in to complete their home. There won’t be a dry eye in their house – or ours. There are three more builds to come in this series, in Limerick, Bray and Offaly.
Back in 2019, author Lisa Taddeo’s non-fiction book Three Women made waves for telling the stories of three different women’s sexual and emotional lives. A six-part drama based on the book aired in the US in 2024 and is now making its way to this side of the Atlantic. We’ll meet grieving writer Gia (Shailene Woodley) who plays a Taddeo-like character who wants to write a book about female desire in America, and her three subjects: a suburban homemaker named Lina (Betty Gilpin), an entrepreneur named Sloane (DeWanda Wise), and a waitress named Maggie (Gabrielle Creevy). We follow as the women try to break free from the relationships and thought patterns that are holding them back in life.
This hugely popular British TV show has been presented by Richard Osman since 2017, but this latest series marks a new era. Osman has stepped back (well, he’s very busy with his bestselling cosy crime books) and into his shoes is stepping the Welsh actor Michael Sheen. On this first week back on our screens, the celebrity contestants are actor Stephen Mangan, broadcaster Andi Peters and former EastEnders Shona McGarty and Nina Wadia. They will compete in a series of trivia games, and an overall champion will be named on Friday.
Journalist and broadcaster Gráinne Seoige discovered in 2024 during her general election campaign that a nonconsensual explicit deepfake image of her was being widely circulated. The person behind the image has never been identified, and in this new one-hour documentary, Seoige speaks about the impact of the incident on her life. She also meets other people who have been impacted by this sort of AI-generated image abuse, as well as experts, campaigners and policymakers. One of the victims she interviews is just 15 years old, while she also speaks to Cara Hunter MLA, who was targeted by a deepfake pornographic video. This is a timely look at how technology is being used to target women in particular – and how difficult it can be to bring anyone to justice for these 21st-century crimes.
Even if you don’t harbour much artistic ability, it’s extremely entertaining to witness the incredible skills of the contestants in this long-running series. In series 13, host Stephen Mangan is joined by three new judges: art historian and broadcaster Katy Hessel, director of Frieze London Eva Langret, and one of Britain’s best-known contemporary portrait painters, Jonathan Yeo. In this first episode, the contestants will be trying to capture the likeness of Lennie James, Sheridan Smith and Vanessa Williams.
It’s 40 years since the first baby was born in Ireland via IVF, and now RTÉ Investigates is turning its lens to Ireland’s fertility industry. The industry is booming, and publicly funded IVF is now available in Ireland, helping people on the journey to fulfil their wish of having children. RTÉ Investigates looks at what it’s like to undergo fertility treatment, including how well the system serves individuals and couples during what can be an emotionally vulnerable time.
In this one-off documentary, former Ireland rugby international and theology graduate Andrew Trimble looks at the Belfast upbringing and background of the author CS Lewis, who wrote The Chronicles of Narnia. Trimble sets out to examine why Lewis is not always seen as an Irish writer , as well as exploring the impact that Belfast had on his work. He visits the author’s family home, discovers more about the childhood trauma that led to him leaving the city, and how his upbringing impacted his work. Then he heads to Oxford, where Lewis spent most of his life, and speaks to historians and writers about Lewis’s legacy.
If you’re looking for a comedy fix, try the new series of No Worries, which returns this week. We can expect regulars such as Emma Doran, Justine Stafford, Killian Sundermann, Seán Burke and Michael Fry, as well as new faces including some of comedy’s bright new talents. Pat Shortt and his daughter Faye are on board, as are Siobhán McSweeney, Rachel Galvo and Aoife Dunne. You’ll recognise all of these names as people who are making the Irish comedy scene a very vibrant place indeed. In this series, Ali Fox plays a terrible antenatal coach, Michael Fry murders half a pub, Emma Doran is inappropriate with her niece and Justine Stafford goes on a series of unsettling romcom meet-cutes.
On the sofa this Friday night is actor Bill Murray . He’s certainly not someone we see doing a lot of media these days, but he’ll be chatting about his BBC golf show, A Course Called Ireland. This involved Murray and celebrity pals such as Chris O’Dowd, Joanne McNally and Jason Kelce taking a wacky trip around the golf courses of the island of Ireland. Also on the show will be Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård to chat about their bonkers comedy fantasy Wicker, and Penélope Cruz to chat about her upcoming film La Bola Negra. The musical guest is queer alt-country star Orville Peck.
Stephen King’s shocking story of school bullying and paranormal powers spawned a hit horror film starring Sissy Spacek, and in recent years the Duffer brothers paid homage to Carrie via the character of Eleven, in Stranger Things. Now King’s debut novel has been turned into a full-length series that promises to bring the story up to date, exploring cyberbullying and toxic social media while sticking firmly to the old-fashioned gore of the original book. Summer H Howell stars as Carrie, who has to navigate family tragedy and the cruelty of her classmates while discovering her own scary powers of telekinesis. It’s a lethal combination that’s bound to end in tears – and probably bucketloads of blood. Kevin Courtney
Mackenzie Crook’s comedy for the BBC has been renewed for a second season, to air in 2027, so it’s handy that Apple TV has bagged the first season of this acclaimed series, to give us a chance to recap on this gentle and surreal suburban drama. Pearce Quigley stars as Michael Sleep, an eccentric type who has never got over the disappearance of his beloved partner, Clea, seven years ago. When his dad, Brian (Michael Palin), gives him an ancient recipe, he discovers he can conjure up strange water-dwelling creatures in his shed – not sea monkeys but homunculi, magical spirits with the power to predict the future. Crook costars as Gordon, the unlikeable manager of the DIY store where Michael works, with Lauren Patel as Michael’s colleague Kacey, with whom he strikes up a friendship. KC

title: Jason Moran: ‘I have a lot of gratitude for Cork Jazz Festival. And I still have that wonderful crystal vase’
description: The American composer won the festival’s rising star award in 2002. He returns this year as one of the defining jazz pianists of his generation
content:
When Jason Moran played Guinness Cork Jazz Festival early in his career, he received a very welcome surprise. The American pianist and composer, who was 27 at the time, had already been given considerable critical acclaim – he had signed to the celebrated Blue Note label in 1998 and released four diverse and widely praised albums – but he was still largely regarded as an exceptionally promising New York newcomer rather than being recognised internationally as one of the more important emerging figures in jazz.
Moran maintains that being presented with the 2002 festival’s rising star award helped change that. “To receive that kind of push and acknowledgment as a young artist just felt like I was being seen,” he says from the music room in his apartment in Harlem, New York City. “That small gesture really helped me stand up. So I have a lot of gratitude for the Cork festival. And I still have that wonderful crystal vase.”
In the intervening years Moran (pronounced muh- ran rather than Mor -un) has continued to stand tall and be counted, so much so that he’s now firmly established as one of the defining and most creative jazz pianists of his generation.
He made five more albums for Blue Note, and has released 12 further records on the independent label Yes Records, which he set up in 2016 with his wife, the mezzo-soprano Alicia Hall Moran – all united by a commitment to innovation, experimentation and a certain multiplicity of approach. “I’ve tried to build my career on the premise that no one in the public would ever know what I’m going to do next,” Moran once said.
He has succeeded. While his agile and highly interactive trio The Bandwagon, with Tarus Mateen on bass and Nasheet Waits on drums, has remained together since 1999, Moran has also embarked on a series of historical projects that have celebrated and reimagined the music of such wildly original pianists as Thelonious Monk and Fats Waller .
He has also shone a light on the pioneering early jazz bandleader and composer James Reese Europe, who led the all-black “Harlem Hellfighters” regimental band during the first World War, both surviving brutal combat and helping to bring jazz to Europe. Moran is interested in who gets remembered and how.
This month, in a solo concert that sees him return to Guinness Cork Jazz Festival for his first Irish performance in nearly nine years, he turns his “deconstructionist” gaze – a perspective that advances both personal interpretation and contemporary relevance – to one of the greatest (if sometimes criminally overlooked) composers in 20th-century music, Duke Ellington .
“I’m always looking for that single thread from the past that is still evident and continues to resonate today,” Moran says. “It could be, ‘This is how you lift people’s spirits up.’ Fats Waller is able to do that. Or it could be, ‘This is how you create a kind of bravery that has never been witnessed before.’ That’s what James Reese Europe and his band do.” Moran’s method is about looking backwards as a way of moving forwards.
He was awarded a $500,000 MacArthur fellowship, the so-called genius grant, in 2010, the same year Moran joined the faculty of the illustrious New England Conservatory in Boston.
In 2014 he became artistic director for jazz at the Kennedy Center in Washington, DC. During his 11-year tenure Moran played a crucial role in radically expanding the programme of jazz-related concerts and events, taking what he calls a cross-discipline approach to the role by exploring jazz’s relationship to, among others, opera, dance, theatre, visual art, poetry, hip-hop, comedy and skateboarding.
He also helped redefine what the organisation meant as a national cultural hub – in 2017, for example, Moran was instrumental in bringing Q-Tip to the Kennedy Center as its first director for hip-hop culture. “People didn’t have to like it all, but I wanted to see if I could change the blood flow of the centre and bring in as many people as possible,” he says. “Our mandate was: support the artists, let the art show the people, and let it be provocative and make people ask questions.”
[ ‘It was like Moses coming down from the mountain’: John Coltrane and the creation of A Love Supreme Opens in new window ]
Moran resigned on Juneteenth last year, following the organisation’s extreme political upheaval under US president Donald Trump. “There was no way to work in an environment like that,” he says. “But nothing has stopped because the building is closed and vacant. I continue to do work that was spawned during my time at the Kennedy Center. As artists we keep it moving; we and our ideas are mobile.”
A number of jazz musicians have made visual art. A shortlist would include Ornette Coleman , Miles Davis , Cécile McLorin Salvant , Milford Graves and Sun Ra . Yet Moran is highly unusual in that he has made music and visual art symbiotic and inseparable parts of the same practice.
As well as collaborating with some of the United States’ most prominent contemporary artists, including Adrian Piper, Glenn Ligon, Kara Walker, Theaster Gates and, in particular, Joan Jonas, Moran has made drawings, paintings, sculptures and installations, often linked to, or generated by, live performance. He has exhibited at the Venice Biennale and in 2019 had his first solo museum show at the Whitney in New York.
Some of this artistic and intellectual fire comes from his upbringing. Moran grew up as the middle child of three boys in a culture-loving, middle-class family in Houston, Texas. His father, Andy, was an investment banker with a strong interest in art, photography and music (he played the flute, and his record collection was 10,000-strong); his mother, Mary, was an educator, mentor and entrepreneur who started a bakery. “They were both really loving, caring and supportive,” Moran says.
He also once explained that “a lot of my confidence comes from my parents; they really instilled a sense of self-worth in my brothers and me”. It is part of the reason, you suspect, why Moran left Blue Note and went out on his own. Yes Records’ releases are not on streaming services and are available only on Bandcamp; valuing, controlling and “owning your own canon” are critical to Moran.
He began classical piano lessons, through the Suzuki method, at the age of six, but he only really discovered a love for the instrument at 13, after hearing his parents play Monk’s haunting and enigmatic ballad ’Round Midnight.
Moran was drawn to the tune’s deceptively simple melody and sense of space. Later he would also find a connection between Monk’s offbeat rhythms and rebellious nature and the late-1980s hip-hop he was avidly listening to.
“The big thing, though, was: he’s playing the same instrument as me, but why does my piano not sound like that?” he says. “I was jealous; I wanted to try to find Monk’s notes, to search for his sound.”
At 18 Moran made a conscious choice to move to New York to study at Manhattan School of Music for four years with a respected elder, the hugely versatile pianist Jaki Byard, whose playing ranged across the broad sweep of jazz history. Through the pianist’s deep knowledge and experience, Moran came to think of the piano’s potential as limitless. “Jaki Byard says to always keep your hands in history because it’ll free you in the future,” Moran recently told JazzTimes.
That combination and aesthetic have been defining characteristics of his music ever since – none more so than on Jason Moran Plays Duke Ellington, an album he released earlier this year. It’s a wonderfully engaging and surprising solo piano recording that honours both Ellington the incomparable composer and, more unusually, spotlights Ellington the too-often-undervalued pianist. It also manages to be faithful and highly original at the same time.
Moran has a long history with Ellington, right back to playing his tunes with the saxophonist Greg Osby, whose band he joined in 1997. He also has a deep connection to the long and expansive solo-piano tradition in jazz; his landmark 2002 solo album, Modernistic, brilliantly synthesised such divergent elements as stride, Schumann and Afrika Bambaataa’s Planet Rock into a cohesive and compelling whole.
[ Cécile McLorin Salvant: ‘My sister was, like, you don’t have to fit in – you’re weird, and it’s okay that you’re weird’ Opens in new window ]
But he waited to combine the two, regarding Ellington’s music as “too important” and his contribution “so monumental ... so vast, so complex”. Is he ready now?
“Yes, because, at 51, I feel like it’s my turn to be in the garden and tend to the big trees,” he says. “Do they need a little pruning? Do they need some water and nutrients? Do they need some sun? Or do they simply need someone to sit under them for a while?”
Jason Moran plays Triskel Christchurch on Friday, October 23rd, as part of Guinness Cork Jazz Festival . The festival runs from Thursday, October 22nd, until Monday, October 26th. Jason Moran Plays Duke Ellington, and other Yes Records albums, are available digitally on Bandcamp and physically via yesrecords.bigcartel.com
Lyrical and cinematic English pianist and keyboardist best known as an original member of the popular modern fusion band Snarky Puppy.
Leading American pianist and keyboardist – playing here solo and in duo with the trumpeter Peter Evans – whose adventurous music ranges from free improvisation and contemporary classical to rock, hip-hop and electronics.
Lauded American pianist and composer (and tenured professor at Harvard) who vividly reconceives jazz as something that can encompass chamber, contemporary classical, Asian, hip-hop, film music and more.

title: Two thumbs up for Tom Cruise in Digger. Also, two thumbs down
description: The promotion for Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film shouts that its mixed critical reception is a feature, not a bug
content:
W arner Bros has just paid critics and influencers the greatest compliment imaginable. You might reasonably expect the media giant to be a tad peeved at the mixed word on Alejandro G Iñárritu ’s film Digger.
The sprawling satire, starring a heavily made-up Tom Cruise as a deranged oil magnate, once looked like one of the company’s big Oscar players. Anything could still happen. Cruise may well get a best-actor nomination in honour of his status as the Last Movie Star.
But the advance eye-rolling will not have helped. Mike Ryan called the film “unpleasant” and “baffling” on X. His fellow critic Hoai-Tran Bui referred to it as insufferable.
Why single out these comments? Because they appear in a new advertisement for the film. The canny little video begins with a quote from one @thejonathansim: “Digger is an ambitious film sure to polarize audiences.”
We then cut to Cruise’s title character spitting, “You know what? F**k those people!” There follows a series of juxtapositions between apparently negative and positive one-word reviews: “Masterpiece” vs “Unpleasant”. “Baffling” vs “Brilliant”. And so on.
We see footage from the film’s centrepiece, in which furious politicians, beneath the legend “Same film different truth”, yell dissent while Digger holds the parliamentary floor. “They’re afraid to tell the truth – whatever that is,” he remarks closing a door on the viewer.
Fair enough. The film’s distributor is noting there is much disagreement about the movie and inviting potential attendees to decide for themselves (as they always should).
[ Digger review: Tom Cruise can’t be faulted for effort. But it’s still wasted Opens in new window ]
In truth, the brief negative notices flit by so quickly one can barely take them in. Those with healthy cinematic knowledge will think back to all those masterpieces that emerged to early disdain: The Thing, The Shining, Withnail and I.
Will Digger also end up acclaimed a masterpiece? This critic is saying it won’t, but, yes, you really should decide for yourself.
Decide for yourself. DIGGER – in theaters and IMAX FRIDAY. Tickets on sale now. https://t.co/Z1IpSpFnXd pic.twitter.com/e5ID4WUxbL
Anyway, Digger joins a shortish list of titles that have dared to use negative notices in their publicity. Among the most notable examples is David Lynch ’s Lost Highway , from 1997. The characteristically surreal noir emerged to largely positive reviews, but Roger Ebert and Gene Siskel, then the most powerful critics in the United States, were less than impressed.
“It’s a shaggy ghost story, an exercise in style, a film made with a certain breezy contempt for audiences,” Ebert wrote. “There is no sense to be made of it. To try is to miss the point.” He and Siskel offered their notorious “two thumbs down” to the picture on their television show.
Lynch (or his people) leaned into the negativity. A poster later appeared with the words “Two Thumbs Down – Siskel and Ebert” sitting above the legend “Two more great reasons to see ... Lost Highway”.
The advertisement could, to continue with the digital analogies, be read as two fingers up to the school of mainstream white-bread criticism that Siskel and Ebert seemed to exemplify.
This is not entirely fair. Both men were more open to challenging material than is now remembered. Though Ebert was unconvinced by Lynch’s work until the arrival of The Straight Story and Mulholland Drive, in the millennial years, Siskel pushed back with enthusiastic reviews of earlier films such as Blue Velvet and Wild at Heart.
For all that, this felt like a win for Lynch.
The marketing team behind Darren Aronofsky’s Mother! , from 2017, created a poster that placed an array of positive notices down one side and negative reviews down the other. “A circus of grotesque debauchery,” Rex Reed didn’t exactly rave in The Observer. “Some people are going to f@#ing hate this movie,” Scott Maslow equivocated in GQ.
There is a linking theme. All of these films are, in their different ways, deliberately provocative. Core audiences for this version of Aronofsky, this version of Lynch and this version of Iñárritu fully expect their idols’ films to enrage the unconvinced. (See also the Lars von Trier tendency.) That is part of the appeal.
If you see a distributor displaying negative reviews of its romantic comedy or high-end literary adaptation then the word “brave” really can be used with confidence.
To my knowledge, no advertisements for the much-derided 2022 take on Jane Austen’s Persuasion, the one with Dakota Johnson, dragged out any of the critical brickbats.
“It appears to have lifted sentences from the novel and fed them through some kind of Instagram-filtering, catchphrase-generating, text-summarizing idiot bot,” Justin Chang wrote in the Los Angeles Times – but not on any poster.
The real winners in the current case are, however, the most underappreciated and misused class in world media. I speak, naturally, of film critics.
For all the dry snark in that Digger promo, its focus on reviewers confirms that we brave folk do still matter. A bit. In certain contexts. For now.

title: Christopher Eccleston on Chasing Millions: A tale from Ireland’s biggest bank heist
description: Christopher Eccleston’s new film is set after the Northern Bank robbery of 2004, when £26m was stolen in Belfast. Amazingly, what happened isn’t very well known, writes Donald Clarke.
content:
We have something to clear up first. Taking the cheap and easy route, I begin by jokily venturing that, as a son of Manchester, Christopher Eccleston must have a bit of Irish in him.
“I have to stop you there,” he says with a dry smile.
I immediately twig where he’s coming from.
The good burghers of that city, inspiration for the fictional Coronation Street, are proud of their distinctive identity within Greater Manchester.
“There is a worrrrrld of difference,” Eccleston says, cackling. “This is our centenary. It’s 100 years a city. So yeah. We know little about my mum’s side. But my paternal great-grandmother was Katy Connor from Dublin . That much we do know. My mum’s side are a bit more mysterious. We think Mum’s side were canal people.”
At any rate, Eccleston has done both Lancashire and the Irish diaspora proud over the past three or four decades. Breaking through with fine early TV work on Jimmy McGovern’s Cracker and the campaigning movie Let Him Have It, he went on to become a defining actor of Britain’s millennial years: part of a stellar rising cast in Our Friends in the North; reviving an icon in Russell T Davies’s disinterment of Dr Who. He admits to slowing down a little in recent years, but gaps in the CV are rare.
We meet as he takes on the role of a harried Northern Irish police officer in Stephen Burke’s diverting Irish comedy Chasing Millions. Positioned as a mismatched-buddy flick – Madeleine Madden plays a younger, visiting Australian officer – the film is about the aftermath of the Northern Bank robbery of 2004. More than £26 million was stolen in the largest such heist in British or Irish history. It is surprising the extraordinary story is not better known.
“So much more was going on in terms of the peace process, which of course we know it impacted on massively,” Eccleston says. “I was aware of the broad headlines at the time and then forgot about it. It was only when they came to me with the script that I listened to a brilliant podcast on BBC Sounds, which was forensic in its detail for background.”
Chasing Millions, written by Burke and Katherine Thomson, finds the humour in some grim circumstances.
“That was the tone we tried to go for,” Eccleston says. “I think it’s fair to say it’s true of Salford and Manchester – and it’s true of Belfast – that when these things happen that humour is there. Think of the joy that Manchester United supporters are getting from Manchester City. Humour always foregrounds in those great working-class cities,” he says with a laugh.
We speak just hours after Manchester City were found guilty of more than 100 charges related to breaches of the Premier League’s financial regulations. As a lifelong United supporter, Eccleston would not be human if he didn’t take some relish in the decision.
He is proud of his working-class roots. Dad was a fork-lift driver. Mum worked as a cleaner at a launderette. I had read that the acting bug didn’t set in until he was at sixth-form college.
“I failed all my GCSEs and my O-levels, so I went to a sixth-form college,” he says. “It was a very middle-class environment, and I was the lunatic. A drama teacher spotted me f**king around in the communal area and said: ‘Well, if you’re going to do that, you might as well do this play.’
“I did this play, and they allowed me to put mascara on, which I left on when I went to the pub. We were around postpunk. So that whole thing was happening.”
His initial motivations were uncomplicated.
“There was a very beautiful woman playing opposite me. I was 17. I fell in love with her. Yeah, wine, women and song. I’m afraid that there was no depth to my ambitions. Avoid the factory. Avoid the nine to five. Of course, when you get old you realise you really wanted a creative life. But then I just wanted to get out of a very specific environment and lifestyle.”
Eccleston has spoken of how, 40 years ago, financial assistance was still available for working-class folk seeking a career in the theatre. It is much tougher now for people from his background.
“I had no academic qualifications – which, fortunately for me, were not needed at the Central School of Speech and Drama, which was grant-assisted,” he says. “Also, I was given a discretionary grant by Salford council.
“Again, I had no academic qualifications, but because I’d got myself a place in one of these drama schools, Salford gave me a discretionary grant. I am the luckiest man on the planet compared to the equivalent of me nowadays. Somebody like me is not getting there.”
[ Film Four new films to see this week: Sense and Sensibility, The Lost Children of Tuam, Her Private Hell, Stupid August Opens in new window ]
This is a peculiar story. In the 1950s and 1960s, British theatre, hitherto the preserve of the middle classes, woke up to working-class and northern voices. The Royal Court Theatre in London staged plays such as John Osborne’s Look Back in Anger and Edward Bond’s Saved. Actors such as Tom Courtenay and Salford’s own Albert Finney became stars. It feels as if the business is heading back to the days before that social revolution.
“It’s not shifting back. It’s there,” Eccleston says. “They’ve just done a play at the Royal Court in London, and they had a f**king red carpet outside. A red carpet outside the Royal Court Theatre? What the f**king hell’s that about?”
This appears to be a reference to the opening of Manfred Karge’s Man to Man at the famously radical theatre on Sloane Square last month. “Unusually, there was a first night red carpet outside the Royal Court,” Mark Lawson wrote in The Guardian, “leading a writer long associated with the venue to express ‘shock’ to ushers at such Hollywood vulgarity.”
[ Daisy Edgar-Jones: ‘It was great practice for Sense and Sensibility, all that time in Fermanagh fields with cows’ Opens in new window ]
Speaking of red carpets, that is not where Eccleston ever expected to find himself. He remembers the Irish actor John Lynch, who was at Central with him, heading off to make Pat O’Connor’s Cal before graduation.
“One Sunday morning we were playing football – Central versus Rada. We all turned up, getting changed by the goalpost, and out of the mist, he came. Here’s Johnny Lynch with his boots. He was back, and he’d made a feature film. It was mind-blowing.”
Who knew the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art had a soccer team?
“At drama school from 1983 to 1986, you never saw a camera,” he says. “Everything we did was theatre based. I can’t believe how naive I was, because it never occurred to me that I might be on television. I had no ambition to be on screen. The great passion was to be on stage – to play the lead, big classical roles and the contemporary roles.”
Eccleston sees himself as a theatre actor who became a screen actor by accident. After drama school he didn’t work for three years. He moved back to Salford. He eventually wangled an Equity card and landed the role of Derek Bentley, a young man controversially hanged for murder in 1953, in Peter Medak’s acclaimed Let Him Have It.
“So I went from being the least successful in my year to the most successful,” Eccleston says. “Complete lottery. Sir Alex Ferguson said it about himself. He said: ‘Apart from everything else, I’ve always been lucky.’”
Talent and charisma also mattered. Eccleston was suddenly everywhere. He appeared in Danny Boyle’s debut feature, Shallow Grave, in 1994. He was DCI David Bilborough in the first two series of Cracker. And then there was Our Friends in the North.
Screened on the BBC in 1996 in nine feature-length episodes, Peter Flannery’s series followed four Geordies from the early 1960s to what was then the present day: from Harold Wilson’s first general election victory to the birth of New Labour.
The casting could hardly have been cannier: Eccleston, Daniel Craig, Mark Strong and Gina McKee. A James Bond. A Doctor Who. And two more of the most versatile actors of their generation.
“I remember feeling in awe of all three of them in terms of their ability,” he says. “Daniel, as well as being a brilliant actor, had a kind of sexual, physical, leading-man rock-star charisma. Whenever he was on set, you thought, wow, that’s charisma.
“Mark’s a brilliant actor. And Gina, of course, was the best of the bunch in terms of the performance. Very good. Talk about performance on television for camera.”
A degree of controversy still surrounds Eccleston’s time as Doctor Who. The 2005 rejuvenation – the first formal series since 1989 – was a critical and ratings success. Eccleston’s hard-edged northern Doctor went down well. Billy Piper excelled as a smart assistant. But the lead left after just one season.
“My relationship with my three immediate superiors – the showrunner, the producer and co-producer – broke down irreparably during the first block of filming and it never recovered,” he told Radio Times in 2018. “They lost trust in me, and I lost faith and trust and belief in them.”
Is there anything he wants to say about it now?
“No. Just that I’m very proud of the 13 episodes that I was part of, because they were made, from a professional point of view, under the most difficult circumstances,” he says, politely. “The establishing of a series like that – the first series – when you’re shooting it, that’s a tough one to do. I’m very proud of what I did. And I adored the character.”
Eccleston survived. He had good roles in the US series Heroes, True Detective and the cult favourite The Leftovers, among others. He brushed against the MCU in Thor: The Dark World. He was an acclaimed Scrooge on stage at the Old Vic in London.
Yet I have read him saying that, if he had another go round, he might not become an actor again. He would prefer to get his hands on the levers of power.
“You’re not going to level up the playing field as an actor,” he says. “If I’d have gone to try and run the National Theatre then I might have levelled the playing field. Then I can effect change. Then I can affect taste. But all those jobs, we know, go to the Oxbridge, public-school lot. They’re only going to lean towards the culture they know. They’re going to lean to the people they know. It’s just got more and more unfair.”
Eccleston admits he is not as busy as he once was. Time to stretch out.
“It’s been quiet for me for a good few years,” he says. “Changes in the industry. Changes in my age. It’s been a tough time, but the biggest part of being an actor is being unemployed. I’m very good at being unemployed.”
“I need a little bit of luck to get going again.”
Chasing Millions is in cinemas from Friday, October 9th

title: A Galway kitchen ‘refresh’ ended up gutting half the house, but the owners couldn’t be happier
description: It can make sense to embark on a bigger renovation project to get the right outcome, as this Galway household discovered
content:
A decision to refresh one room in your home can sometimes trigger a much larger renovation project. This was the case for one couple from Tuam, Co Galway .
Their original plan was to replace the kitchen they had bought when they moved into their home in 1999. By the time they had finished, almost half their house had been gutted but they couldn’t be happier with the result.
After 26 years of service, they say their kitchen didn’t owe them anything and it was time for something new.
“Lack of worktop space, storage and the impracticality of having the fridge in the utility room, meant that the kitchen didn’t flow or function correctly.”
But when they started looking at kitchens, they realised that a new one wouldn’t solve all their problems.
“The cost was going to be quite high for something we weren’t going to be 100 per cent happy with, because we would end up with a lot of the same problems we had in terms of storage, space and light,” they say.
Nor would it address their wish to have a direct connection between the kitchen and their garden.
“Our garden is quite mature, but it never felt part of the house. The garden and trees weren’t visible from the kitchen because the kitchen window was quite small.”
They also had a conservatory that was freezing cold in winter and too hot in summer.
It became clear that a bigger renovation project was needed, so plans were drawn up for a 40sq m (431sq ft) extension and the demolition of the conservatory. After realising they would need professional help to make the best use of the space, they commissioned Galway interior design company Dubh House Studio on the recommendation of friends.
“That made all the difference to the project,” they say.
“They turned it into a contemporary space that was also sympathetic to the rest of the house. Dubh House worked with the kitchen supplier, the electrician and the contractor and it took many headaches away from us.
“Instead of us traipsing around to retail outlets, they gave us the links for everything in terms of furniture and fittings, the type of lamps or lighting to select and where to source them. This saved us so much time.”
The studio’s interior architect Claire Finegan and interior designer Orla Tighe say they came in at the right time for the project. “There were a lot of little tweaks that we were able to make as regards the layout, and it was great to be involved at that early stage,” Tighe says.
The original plan had placed the living area at the back of the house beside the kitchen and overlooking the garden, but the designers saw that it would pose problems. There was no wall space for the television and there was a risk of glare on the television screen from all the glass.
“They wanted to have a cosy space for their living area, but they probably wouldn’t have gotten that, and it wouldn’t have been as functional with all of the glass on that side, so we suggested they flip it with the dining area on the opposite end of the room,” Finnegan says.
The original plan also had a bi-folding glass door across the back of the house and they suggested breaking it with a piece of wall.
“At the time the clients were like, oh my goodness, we’re trying to get light in, and you’re suggesting putting another piece of wall in there? But we were confident that there was enough glass and breaking it up slightly with a bit of wall defined the space.”
A roof light over the kitchen island was moved to make space for pendant lights. They also suggested wall lights to illuminate the sink area. “When you put the sink against the wall, I think a lot of people forget that even though you’ve got your line of spotlights, they are shining down on your back and not giving you light when you’re washing the dishes,” Tighe says.
Strip lighting at kickboard level brings an added warmth to the area at night.
Underfloor heating was included in the extension, but the designers suggested carrying it through the living area, utility room and adjoining bathroom.
And when the floor of the utility room was being dug up, the designers got the chance to improve the layout there. Anyone who is fed up with clothes horses permanently on display will envy their new hot press.
“Our old utility room always had a couple of drying racks out on display,” the homeowners say. “Now, the hot press in the utility has room for drying racks. And the washing machine and dryer have been raised for easy access which is great too.”
They also appreciated the fact that they could do a 3D walk-through of the plans before anything was agreed, giving them a feel for what it would be like to live in the space.
Their storage issues have now been comprehensively addressed. Getting rid of their old kitchen led to a major decluttering exercise, but they are still surprised at the amount of storage space they have.
A kitchen cupboard door disguises a walk-in pantry which holds all their food supplies and appliances while another kitchen cupboard door conceals their breakfast station. “That leaves all the kitchen surfaces free of clutter,” Tighe says.
Their media wall in the living area also has ample storage, making it very easy to keep the clutter at bay. One of the homeowners’ favourite features is the large picture window in the kitchen. A remote-controlled blind box conceals the blinds on this window and on the glass doors.
“We wouldn’t even have thought of that but if you had a blind in front of that window frame it would totally take from this feature,” they say.
While some people baulk at the cost of hiring interior architects or designers, they believe it saved them money because they didn’t make costly mistakes and weren’t asking tradespeople to change something at a later stage.
“We didn’t paint the wall with an incorrect colour and have to change it. Imagine if you select a worktop that doesn’t tie in with the rest of the kitchen and have to replace it? We probably could have visited up to 20 different tile shops and still not selected the floor tile we have, but Dubh House saw the overall picture.”
The designers say many of the mistakes people make with home renovations often stem from the panic that sets in when tradespeople start looking for decisions.
“They might forget to have the room wired for a wall light or they might decide they want to look at underfloor heating when the floors had already been screeded over,” Finegan says.
This couple moved into their new space in November and were happy to find that nothing had been overlooked in their renovation project. They say that they constantly gravitate towards the kitchen and living area now.
“Everything we need is here. We are delighted with the result. When the mood lighting is on around the island in the evening, it’s such a lovely area to relax in.”

title: New crime fiction books, including Jasper Fforde’s funny triumph of human creativity
description: A 19th novel in the Jack Taylor series from the late, great Ken Bruen, plus compelling works from Carrie Lee South, Mick Herron and Jonathan Ames
content:
Every reader understands there is an “entirely separate reality that exists within books”, but few writers have leaned into that idea as strongly as Jasper Fforde with his series of Thursday Next novels.
Thursday, a literary detective who debuted in The Eyre Affair (2001) and is currently head of the Swindon Library Service, has the capacity to move between the real and literary worlds, defending literature against bad actors who try to manipulate fiction.
The eighth novel in the series, Dark Reading Matter (Hodder & Stoughton, £25), delivers Thursday’s toughest case yet. Plagued by villainous literary characters trying to assassinate her (a not uncommon occurrence), Thursday discovers that the Martians from HG Wells’s The War of the Worlds are wreaking havoc in rare editions of Hamlet. But who is behind this latest invasion of Martians? And what is this mysterious Word Engine that seeks to absorb every literary text ever written, including the chaos of dark reading matter – ie the impossibly vast amount of the world’s unpublished fiction?
With its “interfictional travel”, “reality field distortions” and “unintentional self-fictionalisation”, Dark Reading Matter is a deliciously mischievous blend of crime, sci-fi and literary fiction, with Fforde’s deadpan style perfectly pitched to undercut the increasingly bizarre events (“You’ve been playing fast and loose with almost every literary convention there is,” the Muse Calliope sternly informs Thursday).
But as charming, funny and whimsical as it appears on the surface, Dark Reading Matter is fundamentally a serious novel: not only does Thursday’s adventure allow us to reimagine the way we read fiction, Fforde also raises the spectre of the Word Engine – the existential threat, to literature, of AI -generated fiction – in a story so surreal, so brilliantly imaginative and superbly cohesive, that it makes a mockery of the possibility that a non-human intelligence might duplicate it.
The final instalment in the Thursday Next series, Dark Reading Matter is an absolute triumph.
Set in the Devil’s Den State Park in the Ozarks, Carrie Lee South’s In the Woods They Wait (Little, Brown, £16.99) centres on Audrey Figg, a park ranger and trail guide. When a young girl, Ivy Summers, goes missing during a hike, Audrey is unusually invested in finding her: the reason Audrey became a park ranger is because her younger brother Benny disappeared in the Devil’s Den 15 years previously - while in Audrey’s care: “Some part of her felt that if she could find some evidence of Benny’s final whereabouts, if she could prove something, she could rewind the spool of years and start over from the point that she’d ruined everything.”
Moving back and forth between 2004 – the year Benny vanished – and the present day, the novel initially derives its tension from the ticking clock: when a young child goes missing in the 1.2 million acres of the Ozark National Forest, every minute counts. Gradually, however, South introduces a strange and sinister element, one that – without giving away any spoilers – means that In the Woods They Wait unexpectedly mutates into a cross-genre thriller. The storytelling is lean and driven, but where South really scores is in her lyrical but unsentimental descriptions of the Ozark wilderness.
The late, great Ken Bruen ’s private eye Jack Taylor first made his way down Galway’s mean streets in The Guards (2001). Galway’s Edge (Head of Zeus, £25) is the 19th novel in the series, and Jack is still taking on all comers, and particularly those who abuse their power (he’ll use a gun if he has to, will Jack, although his preferred weapon is his trusty hurl).
Galway is in thrall to a vigilante group calling itself The Edge as the novel opens, a group with a renegade priest pulling its strings; even so, no one is more surprised than the resolutely anticlerical Jack when he is commissioned by the Vatican to put a stop to The Edge and its violence.
Nineteen books in, though, the plot is almost superfluous to a Jack Taylor novel. All the interesting stuff happens on the fringes of the story as Jack wanders from pub to pub on his quixotic adventures, encountering the colourful characters who live on the fringes of society and keeping us updated on his latest reading while decrying the state of the world, all the while putting away heroic quantities of Jameson. One of the true (and few) mavericks of Irish crime fiction, Bruen’s loss is keenly felt.
Mick Herron ’s series of Slough House novels, featuring the spectacularly slovenly Jackson Lamb, has reinvigorated the modern spy novel since he published Slow Horses in 2010. There have been nine novels in the series to date, most recently last year’s Clown Town, but Herron has also published an intermittent series of novellas featuring some of the minor characters from Lamb’s world.
Watch the Quiet Snow (Baskerville, £22) brings together those novellas in a single book, opening with The List (2015) and John Bachelor, a former spook now grinding out a living as a “milkman” checking in on former spies and defectors. Glamour is at a premium, as we might expect, and especially when John has the misfortune to make a mistake that causes First Desk, aka Diana Taverner, to turn her icy glare upon him: “It’s hardly Tinker, Tailor, John. You wipe their noses, feed their cats, make sure they’re not blowing their pensions on internet poker.”
With Lamb absent for the most part, the writing is a little more restrained, the mood more elegiac, than in the Slough House novels, and especially in the pick of the bunch, The Last Dead Letter, which is a bona fide spy love story set in cold war Berlin.
The smallest of minor characters in the first of Jonathan Ames’s series of private eye novels, A Man Named Doll (2021), LAPD detective Maria Cole takes centre-stage in A Past Without Pictures (Pushkin Vertigo, £9.99). Suspended from duty after killing a Mexican teenage boy on her first night working as a detective, Maria travels to Fair Port on Alabama’s Gulf Coast to bury her estranged father Billy, an ex-convict she hadn’t seen since she was a child and who was murdered during a robbery at his home.
Expecting to observe the formalities and depart again, Maria quickly discovers that the murder suspect is a young black man who knew her father through their AA meetings, and that Fair Port’s chief of police, Rawlins, is an old-fashioned bigot: “Hard thing to get over,” Rawlins tells Maria. “Killing somebody. But I guess you know that now. Even if it was a Mex.”
[ Crime fiction: Hitchcockian flair in modern Ireland, and a note-perfect Mexican noir Opens in new window ]
Ames has published eight novels, including the stand-alone You Were Never Really Here (2013). There are echoes of that novel in Maria’s past traumas and her unusual coping mechanisms, and fans of Daniel Woodrell’s country noir will find parallels in this elegantly crafted southern noir of corruption, racism, violence and redemption.
[ The true-crime dilemma: ‘Family of people who have been harmed could hear these stories’ Opens in new window ]
Declan Burke is an author and journalist. His latest novel is The Lammisters (No Alibis Press).

title: Author Niall Williams: ‘I will always be an outsider, even here after 41 years’
description: Author describes how he arrived ‘fictionally home’ in the imaginary village of Faha and how he celebrates the generosity, dignity and humour of his community
content:
The elegant first paragraph of Niall Williams ’s latest book, O Now!, reminds me why my first child is called Isobel, named (with a vowel shift) after a character in his tender debut novel, Four Letters of Love, from 1997, which he adapted for the 2024 film starring Pierce Brosnan , Helena Bonham Carter and Gabriel Byrne .
