O Now! begins with elderly neighbours Bat and Ganga, sitting in companionable silence in the latter’s thatched cottage, which “had not taken the electricity when it was passing”, waiting to see who will die first, “the ashes of evening fallen through the grate”.
It’s the end of October, “a month so needled with rain it seemed the heavens wanted to stitch themselves onto the earth and make life and afterlife all the one”.
Originally commissioned for BBC Radio, it is a warm, wise and witty short story, set in Faha, the imaginary west Co Clare village that has inspired his writing since the 2014 Booker Prize -longlisted History of the Rain, followed by This Is Happiness, from 2019, shortlisted for An Post Novel of the Year, and Time of the Child, from 2024, winner of the Kerry Group Irish Novel of the Year Award .
In an enlightening afterword, the author explains how Faha was invented on Easter Sunday in 2011 after dinner with his old friend and neighbour Martin Keane, to whom the book is dedicated, when a large Ordnance Survey map of southwest Clare and the Shannon Estuary was produced.
His previous book, John, about the Evangelist’s resurrection of the fading story of Christ, had spiritually exhausted him. He withdrew from writing into reading.
Then his father died. In his handwritten will, his father had written: “To Niall, my books.” “It remains one of the most moving sentences I have ever read,” Williams writes – four words of love, to play on the title of his debut novel.
Connecting with his late father through his books, “the idea of books as reliquaries of spirit, not just of those of their writers but those of their readers too, I began to imagine a girl whose father had died and left her his books”. This would become History of the Rain, whose protagonist, Ruth, is confined by illness to bed so learns of Faha through stories. She is entranced, as is her creator.
Williams had moved to west Clare in 1985; it and its people had got under his skin and filled his imagination. He wanted to celebrate their generosity, largeness of spirit, community, endurance, dignity and humour. To write, in short, out of love and about love.
[ A Bigger Life by Louise O’Neill: A willingness and openness to surprise at its best Opens in new window ]
“I knew the risks of this, the pitfalls of sentimentality, nostalgia and all the rest, as well as the courage that would be needed during these fraught times to write this way.”
As a method, he had two examples to follow, the winding local roads that followed the contours of the land and traditional Irish music with its sinuous digressions and ornamentations.
“Music has been really important to me, when I was younger especially, in feeling less alone in the world and less peculiar. Writing the Faha novels, I listen to the music of Martin Hayes and The Gloaming. I feel fortunate to be living in a time when Martin Hayes exists.”
And he had the wisdom of an early inspiration to follow. “It is a great blessing,” Flannery O’Connor wrote, “perhaps the greatest a writer can have, to find at home what others have to go elsewhere seeking.”
When I am planning my trip to visit him, Williams recommends a slight detour along the broad, majestic Shannon Estuary to Labasheeda, which means Bed of Silk in Irish, before turning inland to Kilmihil, the nearest village to the home in Kiltumper that he has shared with his wife, Chris Breen, since they moved from New York, in 1985.
Theirs is a beautiful home, the original four-roomed cottage that once belonged to Breen’s grandfather tastefully extended and modernised but with a reverence for tradition. There is the conservatory where Williams writes for a couple of hours each morning, and the old sittingroom with its huge hearth and wood-burning stove, where he used to run his creative-writing workshops. They are now held in the Old Ground Hotel in Ennis, with alumni such as author Helen Cullen.
By the stairs is a framed poster of his play The Murphy Initiative, from 1991, a comedy about Americans looking up their roots. Talent-spotted by Garry Hynes, he was the first Irish playwright since O’Casey whose debut premiered on the Abbey’s main stage.
It was a calamitous production, however, the details of which must remain off the record, he says, but I am left cringing with second-hand embarrassment. The Irish Times review was headlined : “Total waste of a bad idea.”
“I now look on it as thank God, because otherwise I’d still be trying to make it as a playwright, and I know how hard it is. It’s a miracle if you see a good play. Everything has to align.”
More happily, the downstairs bathroom is decorated with two framed short stories from The Irish Press: Apples in October, by Williams, and Queens’ Irish, by Breen. He was 19 or 20 when his first story, Love, was published by David Marcus in The Irish Press, resulting in a cheque for £25 before he had a bank account but, more importantly, gifting him self-belief.
“You saw your name in the paper. It almost didn’t seem like it was you, but you recognised something of your spirit had gotten outside you and is there.”
His style was not yet formed, but he identifies his preoccupations, “older people, and ruralness or nature, and somehow not of the place and time that I was living in”.
Breen shows me a framed news story from the National Enquirer, headlined “Couple Give up $70,000 a Year to Become Dirt-Poor Farmers”, with a photograph of their younger selves walking the land in their wellies as a cow looks on sceptically.
Over a lunch of butternut squash Thai curry, followed by home-made wheaten bread and blue cheese, it becomes clear that Williams and Breen are not just husband and wife but a close creative partnership.
“The ideas that we both had from the start is that we are creating a life, and that that is a joint creation, which includes everything from the garden to the family, the books, Chris’s paintings.”
The flowers on the table are from the beautiful garden that wraps around their home. He points out Breen’s drawings on the wall behind me, which illustrated In Kiltumper, from 2021, their book marking a fifth decade in this place.
The couple met in the cafeteria in University College Dublin, where Williams was writing a master’s on William Faulkner and Breen, a New Yorker of Irish heritage, was doing one on John Banville.
[ Mary and Padraic Colum - Lives and the Dream: Bringing a singular literary duo back to life Opens in new window ]
“Those were our chat-up lines, basically,” Williams says. “I had never heard of John Banville,” he adds.
“There’s my headline,” I joke, but of course he was 21, and Breen says that Declan Kiberd, her mentor, hadn’t heard of Banville then either.
University meant the luxury of four years’ reading. He went to very few lectures. He loved Faulkner’s passionate intensity, his raw emotional power married to extraordinarily powerful, at times biblical language.
Williams found UCD ugly where he wanted beauty, and wished he had gone to Trinity College Dublin, but he recalls the fierce intelligence of his lecturer Denis Donoghue and the brilliance of Frank McGuinness acting in Richard II.
He felt he was “a person of no parish, just a floating intelligence and sensitivity”, not just because he was from suburban Kilmacud rather than idyllic Kiltumper, but also because of “my sensibility, shy, socially awkward and a bit removed”.
He had found a home in literature but was looking for the source.
“So here’s the thing. This will sound grandiose, but when I’m in college and I’m reading Yeats, I’m getting an imagined idea of the west of Ireland, with no lived experience whatsoever. And as I read more, I eventually came to think about Synge as a model.”
James Joyce said the shortest way to Tara was via Holyhead. Williams and his future wife spent five years commuting to Manhattan from upstate New York before they resigned from the rat race to try out the good life in her grandfather’s old cottage in Clare.
The early years were a struggle, but they wrote a successful series of nonfiction books – sample title O Come Ye Back to Ireland, which appeared in 1987 – about their new life, which sold well in the US. “I view them now as a kind of apprenticeship,” he says.
It would take almost 30 years for Williams to know the place well enough to fictionalise it. A stellar review in The New York Times led to a 20-minute segment on Good Morning America and St Patrick’s Day appearances alongside Pierce Brosnan and The Chieftains. Then readers started tracking them down. They stopped taking names after the 300th visitor.
Fiction was always the goal. Unlike his debut play, his debut novel was a triumph. To what extent was Four Letters of Love his own love story?
“Nothing in my fiction is autobiographical, in the sense of taking incidents from my life, returning them into fiction. It’s against the idea that fiction is the art of other people. However, obviously all of it comes through you. Looking back at it all these years later, I can say, okay, William’s [note the name] decision to quit the Civil Service and follow a vocation which may not be real to become an artist is certainly our decision to leave paid jobs in New York, move to the west of Ireland, in the hope that you have some talent.”
His father had risen to be head of the ESB but was from a modest background in Ringsend, Dublin. Class, though, is not a preoccupation of the writer. Or any agenda.
“When I’m writing fiction, he says, “I’m trying to be inside the person, and inside the other person, and inside the place. I’m not writing from the point of view of an idea or ideology. I have no plot. I’m making it up, one sentence at a time, each time trying to be the person. Iris Murdoch said fiction is the art of other persons, and I believe that to be true.
“For me, all writing begins in reading. The reason I became a writer was that I wanted to repeat the intensity of the pleasure of my experiences as a reader. Living in another world. When Mr Mason, our English teacher in Oakland CBS, read Great Expectations aloud, and Pip fell in love with Estella, I fell in love with Estella. I try to achieve that closeness in my writing. And for the reader to feel it, you have to feel it first.”
[ Exposed – The Scandals that Shook the Irish State: Drawing a line from the past to today’s hot issues Opens in new window ]
This also informs Williams’s teaching. “I read fiction, largely, to meet people. The goal of fiction writers is to put a person on the page, to do the highest possible justice to a human being in all their complexity and richness.
“I get students to notice where a physical detail becomes dynamic and takes you below the surface of a person and suggests a depth. Like when Pip sees Mr Jaggers with the black dots where his beard keeps trying to come through.”
The goal is also to find one’s own voice. Just as Williams learned to speak by imitating his mother, he learned to write by imitating Faulkner until he developed his own voice.
Ann Patchett, a famous fan of Williams, interviewed him and Breen for her bookstore’s podcast. He recounted how Chris, his first reader, read the first draft of Time of the Child before pronouncing it “pure Niall Williams”. He responded: “You mean, Niall Williams with all his redundancies, excesses and sentimentality?”
It is part of Breen’s job as editor to prune. But he now recognises that her verdict is his mission.
“The goal is actually ‘Kilroy was here’, to be true to yourself, your own signature.
“Where I go ‘wrong’ is where I fall in love too much with the same rhythm. And that’s where Chris has a really clear eye and a great ear. She’s always right.”
[ AK Blakemore: ‘The best historical fiction is comfortable living with the sheer weirdness of the past’ Opens in new window ]
I ask Breen to define the essence of Williams.
“Besides the relationships, which are so important, this compassion, empathy that he has for all sorts of people. His humour, and his language. Sometimes I say cut that back a little bit, change the pace here. Sometimes when I read it I’m just amazed how great the sentences are, so lyrical, beautiful,” she says.
“Maybe people think it’s too purply or flourishing. I don’t. I think Niall has a kind of direct line from Irish writers starting even before Oscar Wilde, like Jonathan Swift. I love that he wants to stay now in this little village of Faha. I can’t wait to see what’s next.”
History of the Rain, although set in Faha, takes place in the attic room of the Williams home, transported to somewhere like Labasheeda on the Shannon Estuary, and close to the present day.
“I felt something released in me writing it,” the author says. “By the time I finished it, I thought, do I dare walk out into Faha itself?”
And so This Is Happiness, set in 1958 as electricity comes to Faha, begins with a stranger, Christy [again, note the name], walking into town. “In the writing of it, something happened to me that had never happened before, and that is that I didn’t want to finish it. I really loved being there. The 40 years that I’ve spent living in west Clare was coming through.
“My main experience of living here is of people’s goodness. People are extraordinarily decent. If I broke down anywhere in the parish, I would be certain that people would help me. People have been helpful to us when Chris had cancer, when we were adopting our children.
“I fell in love with the characters, their world, and before finishing it I realised that I would not again leave that parish, that I was home. I was fictionally home. For better or for worse, fearing how it might be received in Ireland, you’re thinking nostalgia and sentimentality and you’re aware of all of that. But yet this is what I have to offer.”
Williams quotes the Latin construction “non solum sed etiam” – not only but also. “That’s my experience of life: there’s this, but there’s also that.” His gift is to focus on the good stuff. “The force of darkness is understood to be there, but I write with a sense of ‘despite’ – despite all the terrible things, there yet endures goodness.”
He has spoken of feeling bereft as a lover of language after the Catholic Church replaced Latin with the vernacular, a translation devoid of exaltation. It makes me think of the heightened language of his fiction as a kind of Latin, a transcendent tongue for talking of things spiritual and metaphysical.
“That’s centrally important to me, absolutely,” he says.
Time of the Child takes place in 1962, a Christmas story where the local doctor and his daughter Ronnie take in an abandoned baby. The author and his wife have two adopted children, Deirdre and Joseph. One works in fashion in New York, the other for a homeless charity in Dublin. “The adoption in Time of the Child is definitely inspired by that.”
And the relationship between Ronnie and the baby is inspired by Williams first holding his grandchild in his arms and feeling his heart expand. “It is also one of the planks of Christianity to love a stranger.”
“I’m trying to do justice to these people,” Williams says. “We know people like Ganga and Bat and how they are. You’re trying to make it as physical as possible, the body, the smoke and the fire. At the same time you’re trying to reach for something spiritual out of that physical groundedness.”
He plans to stay in Faha, moving forward four or five years with each novel, for as long as he is able. He turns 70 in 2028, and his next novel is set in 1968. It follows Jude, who finds the baby in Time of the Child and is now 18.
I’m not trying to write realistic fiction about what it’s like to live in west Clare
Williams agrees that he has a mythic imagination, like his heroes Faulkner, Melville and Márquez, focusing on a place and connecting it to something universal and timeless, the larger picture, as in Patrick Kavanagh’s poem Epic: “I made the Iliad from such / A local row.”
He also has a strong affinity to Synge. “The people that he writes are imagined, a marriage between the imagined and the actuality of being with the people. And I feel the same thing.
“I’m not trying to do exact verisimilitude; that’s not at all interesting to me. In the same way nobody ever spoke like Synge’s characters spoke. It’s imagined, poeticised. I’m not trying to write realistic fiction about what it’s like to live in west Clare.”
Williams’s novels began with a strong shade of magic realism that over time has become a granular realism.
“When I first started writing fiction,” he says, “literature was my biggest experience, so I was writing fiction that’s born of fiction. The influence of Gabriel García Márquez, Faulkner, all the South and Latin American writers was more important to me than where I was.
“I will always be an outsider no matter where I am, even here after 41 years, And that’s okay. I understand that is my nature and my role and who I am. I feel a novelist should be on the margins and not in the centre.
“As I’ve lived longer, and put more roots into a place, met more people, become a little less shy, experienced more humanity, I’m therefore writing from a different place. I’ve lived here a long time, and I’ve had the courage to try to do justice to the rich, extraordinary time we’ve had living here.”
The day we meet is the anniversary of 9/11, and the back roads of Clare are unusually busy with gardaí providing security for Donald Trump’s imminent visit to Doonbeg. How does he keep the outside world at bay? These things too shall pass, he says.
Earlier he had quoted Wendell Berry: “A person who is growing a garden, if he is growing it organically, is improving a piece of the world.” He aligns that with his friend Martin Keane, who talked about inhabiting the place you live in.
“We realised that we couldn’t fix the world but we could improve this space here. We’ve been trying to do that for 40 years, combining to make it beautiful but also more productive.”
O Now! is published by Bloomsbury on Thursday, October 8th

title: Today’s Bible accurately represents what was originally written, despite differences in style
description: Rite & Reason: William Tyndale’s translation of the Greek New Testament into English appeared 500 years ago
content:
T his year marks the 500th anniversary of the appearance in England of William Tyndale’s translation of the Greek New Testament into English. It was one of the first such translations into the vernacular making the New Testament accessible to the general population.
Originally from Gloucester in southwest England, Tyndale studied at Oxford as well as Cambridge and subsequently decided to set out on his translation of the scriptures.
His story is one of religious devotion, intellect and independence of mind, determination and, as recounted below, ultimate brutal tragedy.
In the Introduction to the History of Christianity, edited by Tim Dowley (London, Lion, 2014) , it is explained that Tyndale’s self-appointed task arose because, while working as a tutor after his university years, he was struck by the lack of education of the parochial clergy, and is reputed to have told one cleric: “If God spare my life, ere many years pass, I will cause a boy that driveth the plough shall [ sic ] know more of the Scriptures than thou dost.”
An immediate obstacle he met in his great project was the refusal of the then Bishop of London, Cuthbert Tunstall, later Prince-Bishop of Durham, to give his approval.
This was a decisive blow because Tunstall was immensely influential with the Tudor monarchs.
Indeed, in a popular account of the man, entitled The Calculating Bishop, Durham University has phrased it appealingly to the modern reader by observing that Tunstall’s name was to be found “in the address book of kings and queens, scholars and diplomats, heroes and traitors”.
Everyone apparently wanted, and many had, Tunstall’s ear.
This was of course before the English Church broke with Rome and the bishops did not favour the idea of the Bible in the vernacular, as the opening up of the Bible to ordinary people risked strengthening the Reformation process that was already under way.
[ ‘He was only 88’: There is a cosy familiarity to Irish funerals Opens in new window ]
One might expect that Tyndale would have known of this immense difficulty as far as his plans were concerned, but he seems to have been the type of person who believes so much in a course of action that all such obstacles are deemed surmountable.
Alas, life is not quite as simple as that. There is always politics, in both state and church.
A late 14th century English text, the Wycliffe Bible, was a translation from the Latin Vulgate but, as a translation of a translation is a risky affair, it was not as dependable as a translation from the Greek.
The bishops had already effectively banned the Wycliffe Bible in 1407-08, not because of any unreliability but because of the danger of its fomenting ecclesiastical unrest encouraged by the Lollards, followers of Wycliffe.
The Lollards formed what is sometimes known as a “pre-Protestant” faction, were fiercely critical of Roman doctrine and practices and, perhaps needless to say, were much persecuted. Their nomenclature is not controversial today but at the time it was derogatory, being suggestive of mumbling.
Faced with the continued aversion to the Bible in the vernacular among the hierarchy, Tyndale fled to Germany in 1524. He completed his New Testament translation in 1525 but faced legal jeopardy over its printing. Nonetheless, it proceeded and Tyndale’s translation began circulation in England in the following year. Tragically he was martyred in 1536 by strangulation and burning at the stake, his final words having been recorded as, “Lord, open the King of England’s eyes.”
[ Is Ireland still a place ‘open to everything except for God’? Opens in new window ]
When it comes to the history of the text of the New Testament, there are many twists and turns.
The first unpalatable fact is that we do not have any of the original manuscripts, and nor did Tyndale or Erasmus (1466?-1536), on whose Greek text Tyndale relied. Erasmus had used a relatively small number of Greek manuscripts to compile his Greek text, but none of these is understood to have dated to before the 11th century.
The original texts of the New Testament were written in Greek because it was a common language used by officialdom and merchants across the region. Indeed, this assisted the spread of the Gospel beyond the Holy Land.
What happened was that the original texts were copied by scribes, often in a group setting in a scriptorium, with one person dictating. As a result of this, sometimes errors crept in or indeed changes were made because of doctrinal preferences.
The discipline of textual criticism, involving the assessing and comparing of many ancient manuscripts, has advanced remarkably since Tyndale’s time. As a result, we can be confident that our Bible today represents much more accurately what was originally written, although versions differ in style, and the number of books in the Protestant, Orthodox and Roman Catholic versions of the Old Testament differ.
The development of the canons of the Old and New Testaments is another story.
One of the earliest extant New Testament manuscripts, known as P45, dates from the mid-3rd century and is held at the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin.
Canon Ian Ellis was rector of Newcastle, Co Down, until retirement in 2020, and edited The Church of Ireland Gazette from 2001-2017.

title: Heimir Hallgrímsson: ‘They can’t have this happening again, just for the players’ welfare’
description: FAI will have opportunity to raise question of avoiding Israel at Uefa gathering in Berlin next week
content:
Heimir Hallgrímsson believes Uefa should consider keeping the Republic of Ireland and Israel apart in future qualification fixtures.
The Ireland manager was speaking in advance of the second Nations League game against Israel in Serbia on Sunday night.
“I think Uefa must take that into consideration,” he said. “They can’t have this happening again, just for the players’ welfare. It raises awareness of the things that are going on. If it changes anything, I think that’s worth it. But I think it’s not me to answer this one. It’s a good question to Uefa.”
FAI chief executive David Courell recently revealed that Uefa declined to keep Israel and Ireland apart following February’s Nations League draw as the countries are “not in direct conflict”.
Uefa subsequently stated that: “Decisions to avoid certain teams being drawn against each other are made taking into consideration several factors, especially conditions between the two countries leading to structural risks for security. Uefa handles every situation very carefully on its own merits and monitors all facts and developments.”
[ ‘We are not doing questions like this’: Sound and fury continues to swirl around Ireland and Israel Opens in new window ]
When approached on Saturday, a Uefa spokesperson had no comment.
However, Courell and the FAI president Paul Cooke will attend the annual gathering of all 55 Uefa associations in Berlin next Thursday when the issue is expected to be raised again.
Currently, Armenia and Azerbaijan; Bosnia & Herzegovina and Kosovo; Serbia and Kosovo; Spain and Gibraltar; and Ukraine and Belarus cannot been drawn together in qualification groups.
Russia was previously blocked from being drawn against Ukraine and Kosovo before they were suspended by Fifa and Uefa in February 2022.
On Saturday, when Hallgrímsson was asked by an Israeli reporter to comment on an “ideology that is based on murder” the question was interrupted by an FAI press officer who said: “We are only concentrated on football questions today. Heimir respected that question last [Saturday in Hungary].”
When a second Israeli reporter then asked about allegations that the Ireland players had abused their Israeli counterparts during the match last Sunday in Hungary, the Ireland press officer interjected again, saying: “That is completely untrue. You just broadcast a lie.”
The press conference was cut short and Hallgrímsson subsequently spoke to the travelling Irish journalists in a changing room before training at the TSC Arena in Bačka Topola.
“The FAI has provided good protection for us,” he said. “We’ve always felt safe in our environment.
“Obviously it’s never nice to be verbally attacked. But it’s just the world today, it is so easy to access through social media or through media, players, families, et cetera.
“Now you realise how much pressure is on a national team player. I think it’s a good time to look at what these players have gone through and respect that they still are here and they still want to represent Ireland.
[ ‘We are not doing questions like this’: Sound and fury continues to swirl around Ireland and Israel Opens in new window ]
“They’ve done it with grace and dignity and they’ve done it the way that footballers can do on the pitch as well, showing good performances in difficult environments. So I think that’s the way footballers like to express themselves. Given everything, I think they’ve done that magnificently.”
Hallgrímsson distanced himself for the suggestion that he is considering his position as the senior men’s head coach. The 59-year-old’s contract is until after Euro 2028.
“It is not on my mind now. My focus is just to finish this and survive in this camp. Coming out the best way we can.
“We obviously know and respect that some people might not be happy with us playing this game. In the end, not allowing politics or anything else to control football – we like our game to be disconnected from politics.
“Hopefully, in hindsight, we will look back and say this was the right decision.”
[ Ken Early: Israel’s war in Gaza brings Ireland to remote cornfields in Serbia Opens in new window ]
The Ireland players intend to repeat last Sunday’s break in protocols, before and after the 3-0 defeat of Israel in Debrecen, by wearing black armbands, refusing to exchange pennants or shake hands with the opposition, and they will bow their heads during the Israel anthem in memory of “all lives lost in the conflict”.
No Ireland player is obliged to do any of the above.
“It is what the players decided,” said Hallgrímsson. “We support their decision. There’s no demands to it.”
An FAI spokesperson added: “No one is ever going to be forced to do something they’re not comfortable with.”

title: Charlie O’Shea produces dream display and guides Munster to important win over Bulls
description: Outhalf making his first start for the province scores two tries in URC victory at Thomond Park
content:
Finally, some real respite for Munster after another week of turmoil. Not just a win to get their season up and running, but the unearthing of a gem of an outhalf who produced a dream first start with 20-year-old Charlie O’Shea steering them home with the authority of a veteran.
It’s not that O’Shea has come from nowhere. The opposite; he has followed a well trodden path through Dolphin, Christians, UCC and the Irish Under-20s. Throw in some Gaelic football skills from the Erin’s Own club and it was easy to see why he is held in such regard.
Yet throw a 20-year-old academy player into a senior team under pressure and who knew what might happen?
“Ah, it was just unbelievable,” said man of the match O’Shea. “I probably got lucky there with one of the tries but the fans were great. It’s the loudest crowd I have played in front of and they really gave us energy there to kick on and get the win.
“It’s class, just to get the opportunity to play. Craig [Casey] mentioned we are the smallest halfback partnership in the world! I was so happy to get the nod and I was so happy it went well then,” he added.
Munster were forced into a late change when lock Fineen Wycherley cried off to be replaced by Evan O’Connell, meaning that Diarmuid Kilgallen, Seán O’Brien and Michael Milne were the only survivors from the side which lost the opening game to Glasgow Warriors at Thomond Park.
But Milne lasted just seven minutes, not recovering from a leg injury picked up in the opening foray and he had to be replaced by Jeremy Loughman.
But it was clear young outhalf O’Shea was quickly settling into his first competitive start with authority, a superb penalty touchfinder in the second minute providing the Cork native with an early boost.
The Irish Under-20 outhalf also showed good hands in that early Munster onslaught but they could not find a way through and it was the Bulls who hit the front after 15 minutes in their first attack.
A couple of penalties to the left corner yielded an almost inevitable score, lock Ruan Vermaak getting over and Curwin Bosch adding a good conversion from the left.
That subdued the relatively small attendance and a moment of magic was needed to lift Munster. O’Shea duly delivered in the next attack, spotting former Munster player Thaakir Abrahams had come in from his left wing, and his pinpoint crosskick was collected over the line by Kilgallen to score. O’Shea then curled the conversion from the right touchline to tie the game at 7-7 and get the crowd on their feet.
Munster’s injury woes continued when Kilgallen had to go off but his replacement Gordon Wood, a late addition to the squad when Wycherley was ruled out, came on and made a couple of big impacts.
O’Shea’s night got better and better nine minutes from the break when he blocked down a clearance from his opposite number Bosch and beat scrumhalf Zak Burger to the touchdown. A penny for his thoughts as he tried to compose himself before tapping over the conversion to make it 14-7.
The lead only lasted five minutes, with the Bulls scoring from a scrum on the 10m line on the right, running it through several pairs of hands, all of whom made ground, not least Abrahams, before tighthead Francois Klopper got over from close range. Bosch converted to make it 14-14 at the break.
Bosch edged the Bulls back in front with a 35m penalty before a dink from O’Shea bounced kindly for fullback Shane Daly, but he was nabbed by Sebastian de Klerk a few metres shy of the line.
But O’Shea and Munster were not denied seven minutes later, O’Shea sneaking in at the right corner with a sublime finish from close range. He narrowly missed the touchline conversion but his second try left Munster 19-17 in front going into the final quarter.
A Bulls handling error presented Munster with an attacking scrum 11 minutes from time with Wood, Dan Kelly and skipper Craig Casey involved as Alex Kendellen powered over. O’Shea converted to make it 26-17 before making way for JJ Hanrahan to a standing ovation from the Thomond Park crowd.
The Bulls were given a lifeline when Jeandre Rudolph in the right corner cut the gap to four points with seven minutes remaining.
Munster hit back with JJ Hanrahan executing a superb 50:22. With new prop signing Kieran Brookes in as replacement hooker, they lost the lineout but won back possession through Wood and Gavin Coombes and deservedly held on to the end to get their season up and running.
SCORING SEQUENCE — 15 mins: Vermaak try, Bosch con, 0-7; 19: Kilgallen try, O’Shea con, 7-7; 31: O’Shea try and con, 14-7; 36: F Klopper try, Bosch con, 14-14; Half-time: 14-14; 44: Bosch pen, 14-17; 55: O’Shea try, 19-17; 69: A Kendellen try, O’Shea con, 26-17; 73: J Rudolph try, 26-22. Full-time: 26-17
Munster: S Daly; D Kilgallen, S O’Brien, D Kelly, S McCarthy; C O’Shea, C Casey (c); M Milne, M van der Merwe, J Aungier; T Ahern, E O’Connell; S Edogbo, J Hodnett, B Gleeson. Replacements: J Loughman for Milne (7 mins), G Wood for Kilgallen (22), G Coombes for Edogbo (52), A Kendellen for Hodnett (57), K Brookes for van der Merwe (61), R Foxe for Aungier (61), Edogbo for Gleeson (65), JJ Hanrahan for O’Shea (69).
Scorers - Tries: C O’Shea (2), D Kilgallen, A Kendellen. Cons: C O’Shea (3).
Bulls: H Kunene; S de Klerk, S Gans, S Jacobs, T Abrahams; C Bosch, Z Burger; A Tshakweni, J Else, F Klopper; R Vermaak, R Ludwig; M Coetzee (c); H Liebenberg, J Rudolph. Replacements: C Jooste for Jacobs (45 mins), W le Roux for Abrahams (61), J Uys for Else, S Sithole for Tshakweni, K Mchunu for Klopper, JF van Heerden for Ludwig and P de Wet for Burger (all 65), N Carr for Coetzee (72).
Scorers - Tries: R Vermaak, F Klopper, J Rudolp. Cons: C Bosch (2). Pen: Bosch.

title: Taoiseach questions Sinn Féin ‘sincerity’ over Garvaghy Road situation
description: Micheál Martin says one football match is not going to get Israeli government to ‘change direction’
content:
Taoiseach Micheál Martin has accused Sinn Féin of a “lack of sincerity” and an “overly simplistic” view on resolving the Drumcree dispute.
Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald previously called on Micheál Martin to tell British prime minister Andy Burnham and Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant that they have a responsibility to stop the march on Garvaghy Road.
McDonald and Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill , the party’s deputy leader, met Martin to discuss the impasse during the week.
On Saturday, the Taoiseach said he does not agree that the dispute could be solved by telling Burnham to stop the march.
Martin had been criticised at a rally on the Garvaghy Road on Saturday which was held in support of the residents against the Orange Order march.
The rally was organised by residents and featured speeches by McDonald and O’Neill.
There were also boos and chants of “shame” at the mention of the Taoiseach by Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín, who accused the Fianna Fáil leader of “standing idly by”.
Tóibín concluded his speech by saying: “They [the Irish Government] have a moral responsibility to be here with you to defend your rights and to make sure that this march never comes on this road again.”
O’Neill and McDonald applauded the remarks.
[ Thousands attend rallies as Drumcree stand-off enters seventh day Opens in new window ]
Asked about being booed at the rally and the calls for action from Sinn Féin, Martin said: “I met with the leader of Sinn Féin and I met with the First Minister last week, and I worry about their sincerity at times in respect of these issues.
“Because I met them in good faith but the meetings seem to be more about press choreography than substance.
“I just feel that the meeting last week lacked a degree of – at the end of the day – sincerity, because there were comments made before the meeting, there was comments made after the meeting. Every meeting can’t be about a press release.
“They think Drumcree could be sorted by me simply telling Andy Burnham what to do, and that’s it. Now I think that’s overly simplistic, and I don’t agree with them on that.”
Martin said the approach and language used by Sinn Féin would not help “bring about a united Ireland”.
The Taoiseach said it was the Government view the dispute would be resolved through continuing dialogue.
[ Two US Air Force fighter jets land at Shannon after issue over the Atlantic Opens in new window ]
“We’ve been in close contact all week with the British Government. There have been talks between the community and between the Orange Order. They do not yield a result, there are further legal actions.”
“Everyone needs to be calm, and everybody needs to be very sensitive in terms of what they say right now, because we simply do not want to go back to the visions of the past.”
He said both Governments were “very keen” for mediation and building a foundation for reconciliation.
Meanwhile, the Taoiseach said one football match is not going to get the Israeli government to “change direction” on policies towards Palestinians.
He said a boycott of the Republic of Ireland men’s international team’s next fixture against Israel on Sunday could do harm to Ireland with “no consequential gain” for Palestinians.
Pro-Palestinian groups have called on the FAI and players to scrap the Uefa Nations League fixture over Israel’s war in Gaza and illegal settlements in the West Bank.
Asked if the next game should go ahead, Martin said: “There’s two things I think that we need to bear in mind. One is that if this was to have an impact – I don’t believe it would – it’s actually possible it would do harm to Ireland with no consequential gain in terms of the Palestinians.
[ ‘We are not doing questions like this’: Sound and fury continues to swirl around Ireland and Israel Opens in new window ]
“And Ireland will continue to press very hard at every international forum we have to press for the rights of Palestinians.”
Addressing the calls for a boycott, Martin said “there’s been too much pressure put on the players”.
“The FAI and the footballing community took a decision to play the match.
“The FAI did everything to promote the expulsion of Israel from Uefa and didn’t succeed and people are putting undue pressure on the players to unilaterally take a decision in respect of the match.
“I’ve no doubt every footballer playing with Ireland abhors what has happened in Gaza, abhors what’s happening in the West Bank.
“But I believe that Ireland, overall diplomatically, politically, has done everything it possibly can, and continues to do everything we possibly can to put pressure on Israel and indeed others within the European Union and internationally to get Israel to change direction in respect of its policies towards Palestinians – and that’s a very challenging endeavour.
“One football match isn’t going to sort that. We need to be clear-eyed about that. I don’t believe the Israeli government or Prime Minister [Binyamin] Netanyahu cares whether Ireland plays that game or not.” – PA

title: Israeli media call Ireland press conference incident ‘disgraceful’ as fury swirls
description: Press conferences for both teams were tense, with the two head coaches saying they wanted to stick to talking about the game
content:
Heimir Hallgrimsson says the Irish have found the calm and quiet they need in the remote, rural surrounds of Backa Topola, the incongruously muted setting for the sound and fury that has swirled around Ireland versus Israel .
The Irish squad are also practising a traditional sort of mindfulness, with Hallgrimsson asking Conor Coventry to lead the Irish squad in becalming prayer before last week’s game against Israel. He’s become known as Brother Coventry as a result.
Alas, the serenity did not last for the entirety of Hallgrimsson’s pre-match press conference. Ten minutes in, an Israeli journalist who last week spoke emotively of “Hamas terrorists” and the horrors of the October 7th attacks while asking Hallgrimsson about his time working in Qatar, read from a pre-prepared question. She referenced the attempted hijack of the FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv earlier this week, asking Hallgrimsson about the “people you support, their ideology is based on murder.”
The FAI press officer sitting beside Hallgrimsson stepped in, saying “we are not doing any questions like this, we are doing football questions, we are concentrating on the football today.”
The journalist continued her question, with only some words audible between the press officer’s responses. “Innocent children, thousands of others ...”
“We respected your question in the last press conference, Heimir respected the question the last time,” replied the FAI press officer.
She eventually committed to a football question, asking Hallgrimsson if Finn Azaz would play tomorrow. Hallgrimsson said she would see tomorrow, and that he would not be revealing his team selection to the media.
The microphone was passed to another Israeli journalist, who last week asked Hallgrimsson about Ireland’s game against Nazi Germany in 1936. This time he made an allegation of racism against the Irish players, a claim that emerged in the Israeli media in the aftermath of last week’s game in Hungary. The FAI press officer jumped in, telling the journalist the claim was “completely untrue.”
“We are going to finish the press conference there,” said the press officer, to which the journalist protested, “I am doing my job, I am doing my job!” Amid the din and scraping of chairs, the FAI press officer directed Hallgrimsson and the Irish journalists outside the door to conclude the interview.
“You have just broadcast a lie,” said the FAI press officer while another FAI staff member took the microphone from the Israeli journalist.
He protested that this was a press conference at which he has a right to ask questions, to which the FAI staff member responded that there is a difference between asking a question and making an accusation.
The Uefa official on the ground, the venue broadcast operations manager, was not in the room for the press conference, much to the frustration of some FAI staff.
Hallgrimsson and the Irish media then stood in an open area outside the press conference room, trying to resume the questions and some semblance of normality. The Irish manager was asked about player availability, having earlier said Dara O’Shea was doubtful as he attends the birth of his child.
“Contractions were starting,” said Hallgrimsson when he was brought to a halt by a shout nearby. “Don’t touch me!” The Israeli journalist who made the racism allegation had followed us out to the hall, and appeared to be seeking access to the Irish huddle with Hallgrimsson, citing his employers’ status as rights holders. He was engaged in a stand off with several FAI staff, and threatened to call the police. The FAI staff spoke without raising their voices, one of whom called for the Uefa official.
Hallgrimsson and the Irish media were then whisked down the corridor, and ushered into a dressing room that had been commandeered for FAI use. The press conference was concluded without interruption there. The journalists stood in a tight huddle around Hallgrimsson, as the FAI’s head of security stood over a laptop in the background, a stadium map and various official-looking documents spread out on the table before him.
Hallgrimsson left to oversee the Irish training session.
Meanwhile, the press conference flashpoint was spreading quickly online. An Israeli journalist recorded footage of the FAI official taking the microphone from the Israeli journalist, and the journalist’s employer posted it online, calling it a “disgraceful incident.”
While their video included the allegation made in the question, the caption on the video said their journalist asked Irish players about “allegedly swearing at the Israeli players.”
Among the people to react to this video was Israel’s ambassador to the EU, who posted “they respect freedom of the press provided you only ask the questions they find comfortable to answer.” The FAI chose to publish the entire 13-minute press conference, unedited, to their YouTube channel.
The media returned to the stadium at 5.30pm for the Israeli press conference, braced for further rancour. It began on a very pointed note, as the press officer first invited questions from the Israeli journalists “as they didn’t get many chances to ask questions in the Irish press conference.”
One Israeli questioner laid bare the residual anger at losing to Ireland last week by telling the coach that the players “choked” despite the fact they were playing for “our honour.”
“I know we disappointed the nation,” the Israel manager Ran Ben Shimon said, vowing that Sunday’s game would be different.
The first Irish question quoted the communications director’s comments of last week which called for the separation of sport and politics, and in that context asked if he condemned fans’ chanting “IDF” during the Irish game. He replied that Israel is very proud of their armed forces and angrily rejected the premise that the IDF is a political entity.
The press officer intervened, saying: “I won’t take your microphone away, but we will not answer your question.”
The Israeli FA also confirmed they had not yet contacted Uefa about the racism allegation made in the Irish press conference earlier, while the coach cited a blinkered focus on football to dodge the many contentious topics asked of him.
The questions eventually wended their way to whether it might be best in the future for this simply to never happen again; that it might be time for both associations to go to Uefa and request an “amicable divorce.”
The Israel coach disagreed, citing personal experience to say that “divorce is not pleasant.”
Nor has been this enforced, fortnight-long union.

title: Taoiseach signals halt to home heating oil carbon tax increases for lifetime of Government
description: Micheál Martin also confirms welfare recipients and pensioners can expect Christmas bonus
content:
Taoiseach Micheál Martin signalled that carbon tax increases on home heating oil will be halted for the remainder of the Coalition’s time in office, while also confirming that welfare recipients and pensioners can expect a Christmas bonus payment this year.
He was speaking in advance of the Cáirde Fáil dinner in Dublin which is being held this year as Fianna Fáil celebrates its centenary.
Negotiations are continuing this weekend as senior Coalition figures finalise Budget 2027 which is due to be announced on Tuesday.
There will be much focus on measures aimed at helping households amid the continuing energy crisis caused by the Iran war.
Asked if carbon tax increases on home heating oil – already postponed this year – could be stopped for the lifetime of the Government, Martin said: “In respect of the home heating dimension of the carbon tax, yes, that’s the direction of travel.”
“We are conscious of home heating this winter and given the nature of the crisis now, the view is that there is no real sign of an easing of the pressure on energy.”
He said there is a hope that the G7 decision to release oil reserves will help reduce prices, but added: “What really is required is the end of the conflict and a sustainable agreement between Iran and the United States and also the end to the Russian-Ukrainian war. Because, as you know, a lot of oil stocks are being destroyed in respect of that war also.”
The last Government used household electricity credits to respond to rising fuel prices caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
[ Budget 2027: Measures on pensions, welfare, income tax and more take shape Opens in new window ]
Martin said that energy credits have not been discussed in budget talks as yet. “I can’t anticipate what new measures people might put forward at the 11th hour but they haven’t been discussed to date,” he said.
Meanwhile, social welfare recipients and pensioners can expect a Christmas bonus payment this year.
“Yeah, I think they will [receive the payment]. I mean, I don’t think that’s a big surprise, and we do that every year. And certainly, we’re in a position to do it this year,” he said.
A €10-per-week increase in the State pension and other welfare payments are expected to be announced as part of the budget on Tuesday.
Martin was also asked if childcare cuts would be targeted at any particular age group. He said there has been an “enormous expansion” in investment in childcare in recent years. “There’s no question that the significant costs arise in the early years, in the zero to five years, and I think that’s something that the minister and public expenditure, people are looking at. But that all remains to be discussed.”
[ Budget builders: the money Ministers who are two sides of the same coin Opens in new window ]
He said that budget spending measures will be within a fiscal framework of a 6 per cent growth in public expenditure.
Earlier, Martin said the budget will be “about trying to ease the pressures on families and households, in respect of the cost of living, which is bearing down on people because of the war in Ukraine, and the war in the Middle East”.
He said “cost of living is a key issue” and there will be a variety of measures including in the areas of income tax, support for people with disabilities and social protection “to alleviate pressures on families”.

title: Young Leinster side outmuscled by physical Sharks in Durban
description: Exposing young players to high-level rugby will be arguably more valuable as the season unfurls despite defeat
content:
Regrets, they’ll have a pocketful, but Leinster won’t fixate unduly on the negatives because despite two defeats a large tranche of the younger contingent were exposed to the brutally physical rigours of rugby in South Africa.
Several thrived in that adversity, none more so than Conor O’Tighearnaigh, Josh Ericson and Todd Lawlor, while Caspar Gabriel and Fintan Gunne have a better understanding of running a game from the get-go. It wasn’t always perfect but that would have been an unrealistic burden or expectation.
There were collective game management issues, basic mistakes from handling to the more technical, but Leinster didn’t lose because of system issues. Individual lapses when well set territorially were more prohibitive in cost terms.
And then there was the scrum. Sharks wing Edwill van der Merwe was named player-of-the-match, but it should have gone to Springboks loosehead Thomas du Toit, who alone squeezed six penalties from the Leinster scrum and had Thomas Clarkson sinbinned for good measure. It was singularly corrosive to the visitors’ aspirations.
Leinster captain and hooker Rónan Kelleher admitted: “There were times when we put ourselves in good parts of the pitch to capitalise, but we just didn’t through ill-discipline. And then there were times when the scrum started to creak, so that’s obviously a big work-on going forward.”
The Irish province fell afoul of referee Craig Evans whistle. There were occasions when they were unlucky and got the rough edge of the officiating but throughout the running ticker tape of penalty offences the lion’s share were eminently avoidable.
Yet for all their tribulations, Leo Cullen’s side trailed 21-16 with four minutes remaining only to hand van der Merwe an intercept try. It appeared a cruel ending to a brave effort but to their credit Leinster dredged a response; replacement Sam Prendergast’s cross-kick to Andrew Osborne for a try allowed the visitors to earn a tangible reward in defeat.
It wasn’t all about the tyros. Prendergast had several standout moments, Ryan Baird, Josh van der Flier and Andrew Porter were tireless and effective in equal measure while Robbie Henshaw had a fine game at centre and latterly flanker. Alan Spicer stepped up, while Hugh Cooney and Tommy O’Brien scrambled brilliantly in defence.
The first 15 minutes of the match were borderline unwatchable, an endless succession of “contestable kicks” that, given the number of knocks-on, sucked the atmosphere out of the stadium. It led to scrums. Scrums led to penalties. Penalties led to lectures. Lectures led to warnings. Eventually Evans produced a yellow card for Clarkson who he had pinged for the fourth time.
Clarkson’s replacement Niall Smyth, on for wing Andrew Osborne, was then going to be penalised but Sharks wing Lili Bester, on penalty advantage, scored in the corner vacated by the Leinster wing. It was the second time in the half that the scrum was a conduit for a try for the home side, one that gave them a 14-7 lead at the break.
The first moment of rugby cogency in the game came when Josh Ericson won a breakdown penalty. Caspar Gabriel kicked into the Sharks 22, Robbie Henshaw broke the gainline with his first carry and the try-line 60 seconds later after Leinster’s “heavies” launched a prolonged and direct frontal assault. Gabriel kicked the conversion to put Leinster 7-0 up.
Sharks’ flanker Manu Tshituka waltzed over for a try soon after as Leinster abandoned both discipline and scrum efficacy over a three-minute period.
Outhalf Vusi Moyo kicked the conversion as he did again from the touchline in first half injury-time. Leinster had at that point conceded 12 penalties and two free-kicks, the sort of figures that make coaches go grey.
And yet they never gave up, never stopping playing, the only criticism was that they overplayed the box-kicking. Clarkson, who battled manfully for 73 minutes against du Toit and then Ox Nche for good measure, burrowed over for a try. Gabriel hit a post with the conversion, his last act.
Prendergast’s first half a dozen actions were impressive and there were flickering moments in which the visitors demonstrated their attacking prowess, but little mistakes, handling, decision-making, late to clear out at the breakdown, cost them a scoring chance here and there.
Leinster conceded in deflating fashion, losing possession in contact in the Sharks 22, and from there van der Merwe was involved several times as was Eben Etzebeth, as the home side raced downfield for captain and centre Andre Esterhuizen to dot down. Moyo kicked the conversion.
The visitors though showed great resilience, Porter won a scrum penalty and once again they found their way into the Sharks 22, but this opportunity perished from a knock-on in the lineout maul. Van der Merwe’s try looked to have sealed a night of frustration, but the combination of Prendergast and Osborne delivered a cutting edge to complement excellent continuity in building the opportunity.
It was what they deserved. What Leo Cullen’s squad will take home from South Africa is a great deal more than the three points from the two games. Exposing young players to high-level rugby will be arguably more valuable as the season unfurls.

title: Ulster draw with Glasgow in high-scoring URC thriller
description: Terrific game saw both sides reduced to 13 men at different points in Scotstoun Stadium
content:
A remarkable game ended with both sides locked together in a clash which saw them both reduced to 13 men at different points in the game.
For Ulster , coming away with three points from Scotstoun is some result though they will be frustrated at not sealing the deal as the Warriors were the ones missing two players as the game entered its final phase.
Ulster withdrew Jacob Stockdale prior to kick-off with an injury which meant that the returning Ethan McIlroy shifted from centre to fullback with Ben Carson coming in to fill the gap in midfield.
The province made light of that though and, in sharp contrast to the Edinburgh clash, they started with real venom. After sweeping into Glasgow’s red zone, they tapped a penalty under the posts and Bryn Ward smashed through on three minutes. Jack Murphy’s conversion put them seven up.
Stung into action, the Warriors tied things up on nine minutes though this was through a fortunate penalty.
From the lineout they found Sione Tuipulotu and with Dan Lancaster on the wrap, Josh McKay was put through a gap in Ulster’s defence to run in under the posts unopposed, allowing George Horne to convert.
The Warriors couldn’t then capitalise as Lancaster was yellow carded on 18 minutes for a deliberate knock-on off Murphy as Ulster’s attack put them under pressure.
From the lineout near the line, David McCann broke through the maul and with penalty advantages for Ulster, Murphy’s long pass put McIlroy over. The provider though missed the extra two points which looked potentially costly.
Ulster then handed the advantage straight back to 14-man Glasgow, gifting their hosts presence in the province’s 22 which led to Stafford McDowall throwing a long pass to Kyle Rowe who ran in unopposed, Horne kicking a superb conversion from the touchline to give them the lead for the first time.
Then with the clock in red, a moment of petulance from Horne saw a penalty reversal after he threw the ball at Tom Stewart, and how it cost them.
Ulster kicked to the corner, mauled and recycled on the line before spreading the ball and McIlroy’s reverse pass returned the favour to Murphy who crashed over, the outhalf then converting his own score to give Ulster the lead 19-14 at the halfway point.
They increased it too, McIlroy feeding Mullins who stormed his way to the line. Murphy converted too and the visitors now led 26-14.
However, two quick yellow cards then undid their cause, Ben Carson getting the first and McIlroy being binned as well shortly afterwards.
Glasgow had to score against 13, Jamie Dobie crossing and Horne converting, cutting Ulster’s lead to four. Sam Talakai was next, Horne converting to put Glasgow in front just as Carson returned.
Glasgow kept coming, and Kyle Rowe got his second though Horne missed the extras.
The Warriors couldn’t seal it though. Rory Darge and Talakai were shown yellows and they ended the game with 13. Ulster had to score and Juarno Augustus did with Nathan Doak’s conversion tying it all up.
Both sides had chances to win the game, but neither could manage it.

title: England score seven as they turn on style to crush shambolic Croatia
description: Dominant performance for England with Kane and Saka both scoring twice in behind-closed-doors game
content:
Nations League: Croatia 0 England 7 (Kane 8, 53, Bellingham 21, Gordon 39, Saka 45, 68, Rogers 87)
England produced one of their most dominant performances in recent years as they dismantled Croatia in a stunning 7-0 victory.
Their attacking quality came to the fore in the Nations League clash in Rijeka as Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka all made hay.
Kane and Saka both scored twice and got an assist, Bellingham notched one and made two others, while Gordon scored one and created another.
Substitute Morgan Rogers added a late seventh as Thomas Tuchel’s side posted a memorable victory.
This was a free-flowing performance that will fuel huge excitement at what this side is capable of achieving with a set of attacking players at the top of their game.
England have had plenty of high-stakes battles with Croatia over the last eight years, but Slaven Bilic’s outfit are now a far cry from the team that made it to the 2018 World Cup final and the semi-finals four years later.
Victory saw England consolidate their position in the top two of Group A3 and another three points against Czech Republic on Wednesday will put them on the brink of qualifying for March’s quarter-finals.
This was officially a behind-closed-doors game as Croatia were punished for their fans’ racist behaviour in a 2025 match against France.
But there were over 6,000 schoolchildren in attendance and they had to watch as their country was taught a lesson.
England were in control from the off and went about dismantling their hosts in the opening half.
They opened the scoring in the eighth minute as two of their star players combined brilliantly.
Bellingham superbly threaded the ball through to Kane and the marksman made no mistake, firing home his 88th international goal after a fine first touch.
Tuchel’s side almost doubled their lead straight after as Lewis Hall’s through-ball sent Gordon clear, but the in-form Barcelona winger shot straight at Dominik Livakovic.
It was all England and they did make it 2-0 in the 21st minute.
They worked the ball out to the right, where Saka’s cross found Gordon at the back post. He brought the ball under control and squared it to Bellingham, who converted from close range.
This was irresistible stuff from England and it should have been three soon after, but Gordon missed from close range after Bellingham had tried to repay the favour.
The third goal came in the 39th minute as Gordon finally got on the scoresheet, heading home Jarell Quansah’s cross for a third goal in three games.
A dreadful Croatia should have reduced the deficit after Manchester City’s Mateo Kovacic danced past three challenges after Elliot Anderson’s slip, but he embarrassingly shot wide from six yards with the goal gaping.
And England rounded off a stunning opening 45 minutes as Saka joined the fun.
Gordon and Bellingham combined down the left and the Real Madrid man teed up Saka for another close-range finish to send England into the break 4-0 up.
They needed just seven minutes of the second half to make it five with another picture-book goal.
A patient passing move saw Anderson eventually break the lines after a one-two with Saka and his low cross was converted by a sliding Kane.
Bellingham could have then brought up the half-dozen when Gordon sent him clear but he stabbed wide.
The sixth did come in the 68th minute as Saka got his second after he intercepted Josip Stanisic’s wayward pass then got it back off Kane to fire home.
He should have been celebrating a hat-trick soon after but somehow skied a far-post effort from a yard out.
Rogers completed the rout in the 87th minute as he rounded the goalkeeper and tucked home.

title: Israeli and Irish press conferences: Hallgrímsson’s ends after allegation was made
description: Israel manager says ‘we know what we are playing for’ against Ireland
content:
The press conference concludes with a statement from the Israel press officer.
“After the match I met Irish fans in our hotel. They said the most enjoyable match they attended in the last 25 years was in 2005 in Tel Aviv: the hospitality, the parks, the celebration with Israeli fans,” claiming the Irish fans said they want to return soon. He also says the Israel FA received an email on the eve of the Debrecen game from an Irish fan who said he had not missed a game for 30 years aside from during Covid, and so the Israel FA gave him a VIP ticket. “We believe in that, football should be for everyone.”
From Gavin Cooney : Ran Ben-Shimon, Israel’s manager, says the Israel squad did not deal with the pressure going into the previous game against Ireland - “We felt the pressure - we did not react well, I believe something like this can happen on the pitch when you are overthinking, I am trying to prepare our national team the best way, probably I didn’t do a good job. I hope tomorrow will be much better.”
The Israel head coach is asked about Manor Soloman’s comments that “we have a country that is 10 times better than theirs,” and he swerves the question. “I am just not going there, I am staying focused on the professional matters,” he says, before adding that “Manor is a great human being.”
From Gavin Cooney : The Israel coach and FA are quizzed on the details of the allegation made by the Israeli journalist earlier, which led to the cutting short of Hallgrímsson’s press conference.
They do not divulge any details, saying they are focusing on the football and, once that’s out of the way, they may then raise it with Uefa. The Israel FA confirmed they have not yet raised the issue with Uefa.
From Gavin Cooney : An Irish journalist cites a comment last week by the communications manager of the Israel FA that “sport and politics must not mix” and, in this context, whether the Israel FA condemns the pro-IDF (Israel Defence Forces) chanting among their supporters during last week’s game in Hungary. Israel’s head of communications says “We are proud of our military forces,” and that “I am sure each nation is very proud of the army that defends its nation.”
When the Irish journalist repeats the question, the communications manager rejects the premise that the IDF is a political entity. The Israel press office then steps in, saying “we will not take the microphone from you,” but that “we will not answer the question.”
Israel head coach Ran Ben-Shimon admits their team “disappointed the nation” with a 3-0 defeat against Ireland last week, but tomorrow’s game he promises, will be different. “We know what we are playing for”.
From Gavin Cooney : The Israel press officer says the first questions will come from the Israeli journalists as “they didn’t get many chances to ask questions in the Irish press conference”.
The Israeli press conference will start in five minutes, Gavin Cooney and Gavin Cummiskey are in Serbia at that one.
Here is Gavin Cooney on the update on the footballing side of things:
[ Ireland captain Dara O’Shea is doubt for Israel match as partner is giving birth Opens in new window ]
The FAI press officer ended Heimir Hallgrímsson’s prematch press conference early ahead of the Uefa Nations League meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on Saturday morning, after what the Ireland manager later described as a “verbal attack” from Israeli reporters.
[ Heimir Hallgrímsson’s press conference ended after ‘verbal attack’ from Israeli reporters Opens in new window ]
Reports from the press conference and training will follow from Gavin Cummiskey and Gavin Cooney, while we will back with updates from the Israeli press conference at 4.30pm.
From Gavin Cooney: After that accusation from the Israeli media, it led to the premature ending of the press conference in Serbia, with the Irish media taken elsewhere in the stadium to speak with Hallgrímsson.
Chaotic scenes at Ireland press conference. An Israeli journalist makes an allegation against Irish players which FAI press officer rejects, cutting short the press conference. Led to angry verbal confrontations within the room and again outside...1/2
A question from the Israeli journalist about the plane incident earlier this week, the FAI communications officer says only football questions. Another journalist asks will Finn Azaz play this game.
“I will not give the starting lineup to journalists before the game,” says Hallgrímsson.
Then a chaotic moment in the press conference as the Israeli journalist makes an allegation about the Irish, which the press officer says “that is not true” and the live part of the presser ends.
Heimir Hallgrimsson speaking in Backa Topola: 'Surviving this camp and coming out of this together would be a massive win for me. That is coming from my heart.'
Hallgrímsson says whatever the players have done, they have done it with respect, all obstacles they face will be lesser than they are in the future after this week. He says this will be the moment we grew.
On the alleged racist abuse of Adam Idah: “I just hope we can focus on football, and football will be the winner after this. I have not gone into details.” FAI press officer says: “That investigation is ongoing”.
Hallgrímsson says Dara O’Shea has stayed in London as his wife is due to have a baby. “Hopefully it will be a good centre back for Ireland in 16 years.”
Hallgrímsson says it is his job to keep players focused on football. He says there has been a lot of emotion from the people of Ireland, the challenge is focusing on the football side. He says they have done a lot of work in that area, he says they do a little prayer and huddle before they go onto the pitch, he says Conor Coventry has taken a lead and he has a nickname “Brother Coventry”. He says they try to cool players down.
“It’s a quiet location. The hotel is at the stadium so it is absolutely a perfect location for us.
“It is more travelling for us than most other teams, because we are playing three games away from home.
“It is new for national coaches to rotate players in this window.”
We (him and Gavin Cummiskey) are at the TSC Arena in Backa Topola, awaiting Heimir Hallgrimsson. He won’t have far to travel to get here: the Irish team hotel is part of the stadium, so he will just have to pop downstairs
Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson will speak to the media ahead of their match against Israel in Bačka Topola in Serbia at about 11.15pm Irish time. This is designated as a “home” game for Ireland, but has been moved here for security reasons. Last Saturday, it was a wild day for Irish football after goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the squad, not feeling comfortable to play. He won’t take part for this match either, the rest of the team is here apart from James Abankwah, who is suspended after a yellow card against Austria.
“No,” replied Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson earlier this week when asked if his players are planning another vote to boycott the upcoming Israel fixture. “But we thought that as well before the first game,” he said.
