Sterling chose to rebuild under Robin van Persie at Feyenoord. It was disastrous: ruthlessly mocked on social media by the club’s fans, laughed at in the stadium.
One source who worked with Sterling compared his career trajectory with Michael Owen’s – two teen prodigies whose speed was their greatest asset, and whose careers faded as that diminished. Owen played his final season at Stoke, making eight Premier League appearances from the bench, and retired at 33. Sterling will be 32 in December. Another source questioned whether winning so much and earning vast sums had dulled the desire required to stay at the top.
Sterling returned home from the Netherlands and, 11 days later, drove his Lamborghini for more than an hour on motorways during rush hour while inhaling nitrous oxide from balloons. It seemed like a cry for help. He admitted to officers, when arrested in May, that he had a “problem” with nitrous oxide – a stark admission from an athlete with hopes of playing again.
Standing in the dock in court dressed in black last month, while Liverpool were preparing for a League Cup game against Tottenham, Sterling learned he faces the real prospect of prison when the court reconvenes in November.
“Before he was Raheem Sterling the international footballer, the Premier League player and the name everybody knew, he was simply a young boy with a football who somebody had to believe in,” Anderson says.
Will anyone still believe in him now? – Guardian

title: Breda O'Brien: If we’re going to listen to women, we need to listen to all women
description: The three-day wait protects the essential time needed in a way that voluntary waiting periods do not
content:
L isten to women. Trust women. Women must be heard. These slogans were the cornerstone of the 2018 Repeal campaign.
Yet powerful people seem unwilling to listen to one group of women – those who had an initial consultation for an abortion but decided to keep their babies during the mandatory three-day wait.
Marie O’Shea, who conducted the abortion legislation three-year review, carried out qualitative interviews with three women who chose abortion; six abortion-providing GPs, 16 hospital providers, and nine senior HSE / Department of Health officials. She also attended the Southern Taskforce for Abortion and Reproductive Topics annual conference, then representing 300 abortion providers.
But she did not conduct even one interview with a woman who did not proceed to abortion. Nor did she include an examination of HSE Primary Care Reimbursement Service figures obtained by Carol Nolan TD, which indicate that between 17 and 19 per cent of women do not return after a first consultation every year.
O’Shea still recommended abolishing the three-day wait.
She relied on IFPA data and the HSE-commissioned Unplanned Pregnancy and Abortion Care qualitative study that interviewed 58 women, none of whom chose to keep her baby.
The Irish Family Planning Association (IFPA) asserts that only 2 per cent of its clients do not proceed to abortion, a conclusion not borne out by its own non-peer-reviewed data. Its figures surprisingly exclude the 104 people it recorded (4.3 per cent of 2,390 first consultations) who did not return after their first appointment. This group would seem to me the most likely to have had their babies.
Adjusting for approximately 98 women who miscarried, had ectopic pregnancies or had negative pregnancy tests, the true figure is that roughly six per cent are not recorded as having accessed abortion care (2,146 of about 2,290). IFPA estimates are at least 11 per cent lower than the HSE statistics mentioned above, an unexplained discrepancy.
Several women who kept their babies formally requested to speak to the Joint Health Committee conducting pre-legislative scrutiny of the Sinn Féin Bill to abolish the three-day wait. The committee decided to hear only from clinicians.
It had emerged at a previous committee hearing that the Irish College of General Practitioners representatives had not consulted with their membership, of whom 90 per cent do not provide abortion services, before recommending removal of the reflection period.
As a result, Fine Gael TD and health committee member, Colm Burke – who voted for Repeal – and other members, believed the committee should hear from GPs providing abortion who support the three-day wait. A doctor was identified and was willing to testify, but because that happened outside an arbitrarily imposed and restrictive window from 4.30pm one day until 9.30am the next, was not allowed to be heard.
Instead, an extra committee session was organised to hear from two pro-life doctors . The way some legislators treated Dr Kirsten Fuller and Dr Andrew O’Regan , compared to other witnesses, was jarring and, in my view, disrespectful.
The Pro-Life Campaign organised a briefing for politicians to give a voice to the women whom the committee had refused to hear.
One little blonde-haired two-year-old nearly stole the show. He held up his arms to his mammy as she spoke. She expertly juggled her toddler, a microphone and a script as she explained what she faced when she discovered she was pregnant with him. She was having problems with her partner. They were living in a mobile home. They already had two children, and she was also studying for a master’s. She had voted for Repeal. She just wanted the problem taken away, but was also conflicted.
She was crying when she rang the My Options helpline, but she says all she received were contact details for abortion providers. No one suggested she consider other choices. “Lauryn” (a pseudonym) said that if there had not been a three-day wait, she would have taken the pills there and then. Today, she and her partner cannot imagine life without their third child. She completed her master’s three weeks before giving birth.
“Meg” (another pseudonym) also voted for Repeal. She was very young when she discovered she was pregnant. Meg felt My Options was only steering her to abortion providers, which was presented as “a simple and routine solution”. She was shocked to discover she would have to wait three days. Those three days changed her life so much for the better. She thought pregnancy would mean her life was over, but instead, it motivated her to succeed both for herself and her daughter.
All the women’s testimonies confirmed that mandatory waiting periods protect the essential time needed in a way that voluntary waiting periods do not.
Removing the three-day wait will almost certainly increase the already shocking figures of nearly 60,000 abortions to date. Bizarrely, Michéal Martin and Simon Harris supported the Sinn Féin Bill, while the majority of their party TDs voted against it.
I suspect this Bill is seriously out of kilter with public opinion, but voters need to let their TDs know that, firmly but respectfully. Whatever way you voted on abortion, my guess is that you did not vote for some women’s voices to be ignored.

title: A striking similarity between health insurers on recent changes
description: In particular there is a new 40% shortfall in orthopaedic and ophthalmic operations between multiple companies
content:
Sir, – I have been following correspondence in your letter pages about increased premiums and cuts to cover by private health insurers.
I have received my renewal pack from my health insurer.
This states that apart from increased premiums, they intend to reduce our cover for certain procedures.
In particular there is a new 40 per cent shortfall in orthopaedic and ophthalmic operations.
I immediately looked up the Health Information Authority comparison website and called other insurers, and surprise, surprise they all have the same shortfalls.
This made me wonder if there is a cartel operated by private health insurers in spite of the HIA and other authorities banning collusion. – Yours, etc,

title: Tax-rich Ireland at one remove from debt zeitgeist
description: Bank of Ireland delivers upbeat assessment of economy despite international headwinds
content:
Ireland, 15 years ago, was Europe’s austerity poster boy. The export-driven Celtic Tiger economy had come undone. The banking system was bust and the then government, controlled by a troika of creditors, was forced into implementing a swingeing series of cutbacks.
Ireland was the zeitgeist of the financial crash period. Everything bad about it played out here.
Fast forward 15 years and we now find ourselves at one remove from the debt and fiscal troubles infecting most of our peer group, largely because of windfall corporation taxes and an economy that is still growing strongly despite the international headwinds.
[ Budget 2027: All you need to know Opens in new window ]
Contrast that with the UK or the US or France, where mounting public debt and elevated inflation are pushing bond yields, which determine everything from car loans to mortgages, higher and higher.
Bank of Ireland yesterday upgraded its growth forecast for the economy on the back of what it said was “resilient consumer spending and the AI-related investment cycle”.
The bank revised up its forecast for modified domestic demand, a bespoke measure for growth here, to 3.8 per cent for 2026, reflecting what it said was the strength of AI-related investment in ICT and other machinery equipment, which rose by 37 per cent to €8 billion in the first half of 2026.
“FDI [foreign direct investment] into Ireland is also benefiting, evident in recent announcements from Intel, Anthropic and OpenAI amongst others,” it said.
While warning that elevated inflation, which is now expected to rise to 4 per cent in the final months of 2026, would keep the price squeeze on households, Bank of Ireland’s assessment is more upbeat than downbeat.
It forecasts consumer spending growth would moderate to 1.8 per cent this year because of inflation, while noting this was “still positive and a sharper expansion than expected in the UK and European countries”.
Job creation (1.5 per cent), pay growth (3.5 per cent) and the €1.5 billion of tax cuts planned in Budget 2027 will help real household incomes to grow despite inflation, it said.
This time around, we seem to be residing outside the financial zeitgeist of debt and fiscal constraint.

title: Judging the scrolling parent
description: Modern life, and thus modern parenting, is conducted to an ever-increasing extent online
content:
Sir, – I write to you in response to two recent letters “ The sadness of not being present for your child, ” (October 1st) and “ A sad sight ”, September 28th) written by well-meaning observers who felt that children were being neglected because their parent(s) was using a mobile phone in their presence.
Modern life, and thus modern parenting , is conducted to an ever-increasing extent online. As a parent of four young children, I use an app for grocery ordering and delivery in order to feed my children.
I use a SmartHome app to adjust the heating, open the blinds, answer the doorbell and turn on the sound system in our family home.
My children’s national school uses an app to send information to, and make requests of, parents. I make and confirm GP and dental appointments for my children online. I browse, select and purchase clothes, sports gear, Halloween costumes and books for my children online.
I browse, book and confirm sports, clubs and after-school activities for my children online. I read and reply to countless messages from the WhatsApp groups to which my fellow parents and I belong.
The children observed by the writers of the aforementioned letters were, in the first instance, enjoying an al fresco breakfast in a cafe. The observed parent may have been on their mobile device researching the location of a local playground, or even e-mailing some family photos to a beloved grandparent.
In the second instance, the child observed was taking public transport with their parent; perhaps they were en route to a child-friendly activity which had been booked online and the parent was now searching for directions to that destination using an app on their phone. From the reading of both letters, neither child was observed to be unsafe or unloved.
Perhaps, all members of society need to look more kindly on parents who are doing their best to raise their children in an increasingly judgmental and isolating world. However, I don’t know any parent who wouldn’t look up from their digital To Do List when told by a smiling stranger that their child is beautiful and they must be doing a great job as a parent. – Yours, etc,

title: Man’s triple-murder trial and Riad Bouchaker’s sentencing among cases coming in new legal term
description: Daniel Kinahan expected in court on opening day of new legal year
content:
A Co Louth man’s trial on triple murder charges and the sentencing of Riad Bouchaker for the attempted murder of three children in Dublin are among the cases due before the courts in the new law term starting next week.
The new legal year opens on Monday amid mounting concern about the adverse impact on the entire criminal justice system of the continuing withdrawal of services by criminal defence solicitors over a new criminal legal aid payment model for the District Courts introduced by Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan .
A big security presence is expected on Monday outside the Courts of Criminal Justice, where alleged crime gang leader Daniel Kinahan is due to appear before the non-jury Special Criminal Court (SCC).
Kinahan (49), charged with directing an organised crime group between 2015 and 2017, will be updated on the preparation of the book of evidence.
Last August, the Dubliner became the first Irish person extradited from the United Arab Emirates under a new permanent extradition treaty, which came into force last year.
Separately, at the SCC on Monday, James Leen faces trial on charges connected with the largest ever seizure of crystal meth in the State.
Leen (43), of Pilgrim Hill, Kilmorna, Listowel, Co Kerry, is accused of importing methylamphetamine, more commonly known as crystal meth, into Cork Port on October 16th, 2023, with the value of the drug being greater than €13,000.
He is further charged with possession of the drug at the former Ballyseedy Garden Centre between October 27th, 2023 and February 12th, 2024, possession of crystal meth worth more than €13,000; possession for sale or supply and directing the activities of a criminal organisation within the State between February 7th, 2023, and February 16th, 2024.
In the Central Criminal Court on Monday, Robert O’Connor, of Drumgowna, Co Louth, is due to go on trial charged with the murders of his mother Louise, father Mark and brother Evan at Drumgowna on September 29th, 2025.
That same day, the Court of Appeal will hear an appeal by the Director of Public Prosecution over alleged undue leniency of an eight-year sentence imposed on Richard Brennan, a former priest, for sexually abusing his three sisters in their south Dublin home.
[ Brothers’ abuse of sisters was hidden in Dublin family for years Opens in new window ]
Brennan’s sisters – Paula Fay, Catherine Wrightstone and Yvonne Crist – had expressed “deep disappointment” over the sentence imposed at the Central Criminal Court in July 2025.
The global eight-year sentence was imposed after Brennan admitted 24 offences, including raping Fay and Wrightstone when they were minors, in the family home in Rathfarnham when he was aged between 16 and 24.
The Court of Appeal is to rule on October 6th on the appeal by former Irish soldier Lisa Smith against her conviction by the SCC of membership of a terrorist organisation, Islamic State.
Smith (43), from Dundalk, Co Louth, became the first person to be convicted in an Irish court of an Islamist terrorist offence committed abroad when the SCC found she joined Isis when she travelled to Syria in 2015.
Smith had denied membership of an unlawful terrorist group, Islamic State, between October 28th, 2015, and December 1st, 2019. After being refused an appeal against her 15-month sentence, she appealed her conviction.
On October 8th, directions are due to be made by the High Court to manage the hearing of an appeal by teacher Enoch Burke over his dismissal from his position as a teacher at Wilson’s Hospital School in Co Westmeath. The appeal is another step in the long-running litigation between Burke and the school dating back to his August 2022 suspension as a teacher arising from his behaviour at a school religious service in June 2022.
On October 12th, Riad Bouchaker, a native of Algeria of no fixed abode, faces a sentencing hearing after being found guilty by unanimous jury verdict last July at the Central Criminal Court of the attempted murder of three young children at Parnell Square, Dublin, on November 23rd, 2023.
One child, then a five-year-old girl, suffered what doctors described as “lifelong” and “life-limiting” severe brain and other injuries, requiring 24-hour care, when she was stabbed in the heart. Another five-year-old girl underwent surgery to repair a non-penetrating laceration to her scalp and dislodging of a skull fragment and was discharged the following day. A six-year-old boy had a nick on his neck treated with paper stitches.
Bouchaker will also be sentenced on other charges, including intentionally inflicting serious harm on childcare worker Leanne Flynn, who suffered serious injuries requiring life-saving surgery after being stabbed in the back when she tried to protect the children.
In all, Bouchaker was found guilty of eight charges connected with the attack at Parnell Square which sparked violent riots in Dublin that night.
[ The inside story of the Riad Bouchaker trial: Horror and heroism at Parnell Square Opens in new window ]
In the High Court, there will be intense interest within the legal world in an October 13th judgment from Judge Mary Rose Gearty on a judicial review challenge by criminal defence solicitor John Quinn to the legal-aid payment model introduced by O’Callaghan on July 1st.
It sparked the withdrawal of legal-aid services by many solicitors, resulting in the adjournment of thousands of cases, with adverse impacts for accused people, crime victims and all involved in the criminal justice system. Quinn’s case is aimed at quashing the statutory instrument underpinning the new payment model.
The legal-aid dispute has separately led since July to a flood of applications to the High Court over the legality of the detention of accused people, including on behalf of people unable to secure legal representation when seeking bail. The High Court applications, which must be prioritised because they concern a person’s liberty, are expected to continue into October.
Later in October, the Supreme Court will hear appeals by Kerry Sinn Féin TD Pa Daly and Dublin South-West People Before Profit-Solidarity TD Paul Murphy against the High Court’s rejection of their challenge over “super junior” ministers attending Cabinet meetings.
In separate cases, both deputies contended only Government Ministers could attend Cabinet meetings and the attendance of super junior ministers, who are appointed by the Taoiseach, breached Cabinet confidentiality.
In November, Samantha O’Reilly (38), and Steven Cummins (39), both of Cherry Orchard Green, Ballyfermot, are due back before Dublin District Court on charges alleging they committed perjury during Conor McGregor ’s appeal against a civil High Court jury finding that he raped Nikita Hand.
Both are charged with giving a statement they knew to be false at Lincoln Lane, Dublin 7, on January 14th, 2025. O’Reilly faces an additional charge of giving a statement she knew to be false on May 6th, 2025. When they appeared before Dublin District Court on September 29th last, they were remanded on bail to appear again on November 9th.
The DPP has opted for trial by indictment, meaning the case will ultimately proceed before Dublin Circuit Criminal Court.
Later in November, an appeal by jailed solicitor Michael Lynn against his conviction for stealing more than €18 million from six financial institutions during the Celtic Tiger era is listed for hearing before the Court of Appeal. Lynn previously lost an appeal over the severity of the 5½-year sentence imposed for those offences.
[ Disgraced former solicitor Michael Lynn carries out community service in lieu of detention Opens in new window ]

title: James MacGuill obituary: Criminal law expert who won landmark cases against the State
description: MacGuill successfully defended an IRA escapee and the State’s first female genital mutilation prosecution, among other landmark cases
content:
“In September 2022, when most of the world was watching Ukraine on the news, James MacGuill got on a plane and came to see us,” wrote Valentin Gvozdiy, a Ukrainian advocate, on learning of the death of the Irish solicitor and senior counsel.
As president of the Council of Bars and Law Societies of Europe, MacGuill travelled to Mukachevo to sit with the Bar Council of Ukraine “in person, in wartime, to discuss how lawyers keep defending people when the country itself is under attack”, said Gvozdiy.
“He simply believed that if Ukrainian advocates were doing their job under fire, European colleagues should stand next to them, not send messages from a safe distance.”
The Ukrainian advocate’s heartfelt tribute to his friend was among many paid to MacGuill following his death earlier this month after a short illness. He was 63.
MacGuill was one of five children born in Dundalk, Co Louth to Comhghall MacGuill, a solicitor, and his wife, Maeve, an educational psychologist.
He was educated at St Mary’s College, Dundalk, and later University College Cork, graduating with a law degree in 1983. He was admitted to the roll of solicitors in 1986.
He joined his father in the family practice, later succeeding him. The mixed practice involved considerable criminal defence work, including cases affected by the Troubles.
MacGuill’s lifelong commitment to human rights law and scepticism of State authority was influenced by his abhorrence of behaviour of certain gardaí and prosecutors. He labelled a senior garda whom he regularly battled with as the “prince of darkness”.
As managing partner of MacGuill and Company, he specialised in litigation, with an emphasis on public law, especially criminal law.
“He strongly believed everyone, without exception, is entitled to a defence, and the best possible one,” said Ken Murphy, a friend and former director general of the Law Society .
MacGuill undertook several landmark cases, including for a former senior IRA member, Brendan “Bik” McFarlane , who won a significant battle with the Irish State in the European Court of Human Rights.
McFarlane was charged in the Republic in 1998 with kidnapping supermarket executive Don Tidey in 1983. As commander of IRA prisoners in the Maze prison during their 1981 hunger strike, McFarlane had led the mass escape from that prison in 1983.
In 2010 he won a declaration from the ECHR the State proceedings against him had taken too long and he was entitled to compensation. The State paid €15,000 damages and legal costs and his victory was all the sweeter for MacGuill because he had taken on a State legal team headed by the attorney general and representing the cream of the Irish Bar.
Another client, Yusuf Ali Abdi, who spent 16 years in prison before his murder conviction was overturned , never forgot the solicitor who stood with him. In a message of condolence on MacGuill’s death, Abdi said: “I am glad to have you in my corner.”
An asylum seeker whose father was murdered during the civil war in Somalia, Abdi was convicted in 2003 of the murder of his infant son in April 2001 after a prosecution psychiatrist disagreed with defence experts he was suffering from paranoid schizophrenia.
At a retrial, ordered following an appeal, the prosecution psychiatrist accepted that, in 2003, Abdi may have shown signs of mental illness and had a history of paranoid schizophrenia.
Abdi was found not guilty by reason of insanity and the Court of Appeal later upheld a miscarriage of justice finding, entitling Abdi to seek compensation from the State.
More recently, MacGuill won a significant victory when representing an African couple at the centre of the first ever criminal prosecution here for female genital mutilation.
Those proceedings concluded last June as a declared miscarriage of justice , based on new medical evidence the couple’s young daughter was never subjected to the procedure.
MacGuill notched up another big win when he took a test case on behalf of a man who suffered injuries after a violent assault but was offered just €645 compensation under the State’s criminal injuries compensation scheme.
After the Court of Justice of the EU last year upheld the Irish High Court decision that the scheme unlawfully excluded compensation for pain and suffering, the State paid the man damages estimated about €60,000 and announced reforms aimed at bringing the Irish scheme into line with European law.
Although he was a tough opponent in court, MacGuill had the same approach to law as to rugby, a sport he loved and had played enthusiastically. Once a case concluded, he would, as Circuit Court judge and former solicitor Simon McAleese put it, “leave everything on the pitch”.
MacGuill was actively involved in the Law Society, the solicitors’ representative body. He chaired its criminal law and human rights committees and served as its president in 2007-2008. In 2022 he served as president of the Council of Bars and Law Societies of Europe, the only Irish solicitor to be president of both bodies.
MacGuill particularly despised lawyers whom he considered had embarked on a legal career with the primary aim of enriching themselves.
Some colleagues affectionately referred to him as “Comrade MacGuill” because of his strong belief in solidarity. He was seen as politically to the left, an Irish nationalist, an internationalist, and not typical of the Law Society establishment.
He was the only Law Society president who invited Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams as a guest to the presidential suite at Blackhall Place, a colleague recalled. “That caused some to reach for their smelling salts.”
When appointed president, MacGuill summed up for the Law Society Gazette his own motivation for entering the profession: “The greatest satisfaction for me in being a solicitor is where your client is the person against whom all the odds are stacked – but has justice on their side.”
Many clients involved in complex cases appreciated his dedication. Mary Kavanagh, in a condolence notice, recalled MacGuill’s work over years on behalf of her and three other Co Louth residents when they took legal action against British Nuclear Fuels over the nuclear reprocessing plant at Sellafield, whose discharge pipeline was directly across the Irish Sea from the Cooley peninsula.
“He was always totally prepared and well informed on the complexities of our case, and assured and confident when we were facing into yet another court appearance ... Exactly the guy you wanted in your corner. He was a charming man and remained passionate and committed to our case throughout the many years it ran and for that we owe him a big thank you.”
A retired Garda detective, Maurice Downey, posted a condolence recalling dealing several times with the “capable and caring” MacGuill over cold cases in Ireland and abroad.
In 2020 MacGuill’s skill as an advocate led to him being one of the first Irish solicitors to be granted the title senior counsel by government.
Friends and colleagues particularly highlighted his assistance and kindness towards aspiring lawyers starting out on their careers.
Outside the law, MacGuill was an adoring father and best friend of his son, Conor. He was a bon viveur, opera lover and great wit. As Ken Murphy put it, he was a man who “licked the lid of life” and was “always happiest when he was not part of the establishment”.
MacGuill is survived by his son, Conor Kirby MacGuill; his brothers, Colm, Ciarán, Daire and Conor; and his sister, Eithne.

title: Increasing number of foreign-born recruits joining Defence Forces
description: Trend mostly seen as a positive by military management, but can pose operational difficulties in relation to overseas service
content:
The Defence Forces are increasingly recruiting foreign-born troops as the military aims towards a strength of 11,500 by 2028.
Between 13 and 18 per cent of new recruits since 2022 were born outside the State, according to data obtained by The Irish Times.
Prospective soldiers do not have to be Irish citizens, but candidates seeking to join the Defence Forces must have the right to live and work in Ireland on a long-term basis. In practice, this means the organisation is open to EU citizens, people with refugee status and those who have held Stamp 4 Visas for the previous five years.
Between 2022 and the first half of this year, 2,762 recruits joined the military. Of these, 362 (13 per cent) are confirmed as non-Irish-born. However, this figure may be higher.
According to the data, provided following a Freedom of Information request, country of birth is not recorded for a significant minority of new personnel.
If these recruits are included, just over 18 per cent of new soldiers, sailors and aircrew since 2024 were born outside Ireland, a figure broadly in line with the general population. Most are from the EU , but in recent years there has been an increase in recruits from outside the bloc.
The Commission on the Defence Forces in 2022 recommended increasing diversity within the organisation. A Defence Forces Inclusion Office has since been established, and officers have met representatives of minority groups to discuss removing barriers to enlistment.
However, contrary to online rumours, recruitment does not occur in direct provision centres as asylum seekers are not eligible for military service, the Defence Forces said.
The growing number of foreign-born troops is mostly seen as a positive by military management. A spokesman pointed out that demographics in Ireland are changing generally and the organisation is reflecting this.
[ Defence Forces purchase of armoured vehicles wasted ‘millions in taxpayer funds’ Opens in new window ]
“Inclusion is essential in any organisation in adapting to changing environments; it enhances innovation and serves as a force multiplier, driving greater effectiveness.”
However, the increase in foreign-born troops has presented some operational difficulties, sources say.
Some members do not have an Irish passport, meaning they sometimes cannot obtain travel documents required for overseas service. This means they are unable to serve on certain peacekeeping missions. The issue has been repeatedly raised by the bodies representing Defence Forces personnel.
There have also been calls for citizenship fees to be reduced or waived for Defence Forces personnel. The Government is currently considering a recommendation from the Commission on Defence to fast-track citizenship for serving personnel. Currently, immigrants must wait nine years before applying.
The proposals under consideration are similar to the system in operation in the US, which allows military members with one year’s service to apply for citizenship.
One recent recruit is Private Al Cheikh, who wore his Army uniform to his citizenship ceremony last month in Co Kerry.
“I came to Ireland from Syria in 2019, and today, as a member of the Defence Forces and an Irish citizen, I feel very proud of how far I have come. It is a moment I will always remember”.

title: Ireland is the last stand for rare coastal machair habitats in the EU – but it’s failing
description: Funding nature restoration looks like an easy line to leave blank in the budget. That would be an expensive mistake
content:
E arlier this week I stood on Murvey Beach in southwest Connemara , between Roundstone and Ballyconneely. The scene was fresh: blue skies, wispy white clouds, green grasslands, and, on a section of the beach, 42 piles of seaweed sourced nearby and carted on to the beach, being spread by local farmers across the sand. Within about 10 minutes, the brown piles became a carpet of seaweed covering the sand.
Murvey has something rare: Ireland is the only country in the European Union with machair habitat. This coastal grassland formed over thousands of years from a unique combination of geology, weather and people. The sands are rich in shell fragments and calcareous seaweeds, which makes the machair soil lime-rich. Strong westerly winds pushed this sand inland, behind the shore, flattening it out across a mix of wet and dry ground.
All of this creates conditions ideal for herb-rich grasslands and flowers. In the late spring and summer, the few remaining machair sites in Ireland dazzle with colour from plants such as harebell, ox-eye daisy and marsh orchids, and attract insects such as the rare great yellow bumblebee, as well as the northern colletes bee, and breeding waders such as lapwing, redshank and dunlin – all under immense pressure elsewhere.
Why should we care about restoring the machair? If it disappears here, it disappears from the EU. We’re legally obliged to do it. An EPA -funded study published in September found that natural habitats such as machair and salt marsh could potentially reduce exposure to storms along 38 per cent of Ireland’s coast, but only if those habitats are in good condition. Most are not.
Murvey, about 43 hectares, is a severely degraded machair site. Overgrazing by sheep and rabbits has reduced the habitat’s resilience and left it more vulnerable to extreme storms. In 2013 a storm hit Murvey Beach, and significant parts of the machair disappeared, leaving depressions of exposed sand. To restore the machair, seaweed is being spread on sand slumps, in the hope it will add organic matter and nutrients, hold the surface against the wind, and give new vegetation a chance to establish.
It’s part of a €7.4 million EU-funded nature restoration project that’s trying to protect the remaining machair along Ireland’s northwest coast, on nine sites from Connemara to Donegal. The project ends in 2028. Murvey’s recovery, like the rest of Ireland’s legal obligation to restore nature, cannot run on a six-year EU grant, which brings us to next week’s budget .
On October 6th, Simon Harris and Jack Chambers will stand up in the Dáil and share out €8.5 billion. We know the shape of it – cost of living, energy bills, childcare. Funding nature restoration looks like an easy line to leave blank. That would be an expensive mistake.
Where are we with nature? Nine in 10 protected habitats are failing. More than half are getting worse. These are our rivers, bogs and meadows, our woodlands and seas – the landscapes we see on Fáilte Ireland posters selling the country as natural and healthy. The Instagram post and the data tell completely different stories.
[ Public to be asked for input as first Nature Restoration Plan takes shape Opens in new window ]
We have a deadline. Under the EU Nature Restoration Law, we have agreed to have restoration measures in place on 30 per cent of degraded habitats by 2030 – just four years away – rising to 60 per cent by 2040 and 90 per cent by 2050. That leaves four budget cycles before the first target in 2030 is due. A bog, river or machair site cannot recover in a single budget cycle – stop-start funding is a waste of public money.
This isn’t a luxury only for those who like rare plants or golden eagles in the sky. Degraded peatlands leak carbon that counts against our climate targets. Polluted and drained rivers worsen flooding and make water treatment more expensive. Nature restoration is often the lowest-cost way to tackle problems the State is paying to fix. Healthy wetlands, rivers and coastal habitats can help buffer flooding, drought and storms.
[ Grief, anger and lack of trust expressed in community meetings on Nature Restoration Plan Opens in new window ]
Our first draft National Restoration Plan went to Brussels on September 1st. What is lacking is money, so as it stands, it’s little more than a long press release. The Independent Advisory Committee on nature restoration estimates the cost at €450 million-€700 million a year and economic modelling shows that restoration benefits are at least 10 times the cost. The State owns about a 10th of the country, including Bord na Móna bogs, Coillte forests and national parks. If we’re to lead on public land, only money will deliver it.
If we’re serious about restoration, Budget 2027 needs a named, multiannual budget line for restoration so farmers, fishers and local authorities know the money will be there year on year.
Farmers could be forgiven for not trusting the Government’s restoration promises. In 2007 the State designated six upland areas for the hen harrier, leaving 4,000 farmers with new restrictions on what they could do with their land. Farmers say they were promised compensation. A scheme opened but closed in 2010 after just 377 farmers joined. The areas were signed into law in 2012, with no financial package, and the plan to save the bird took more than a decade to publish. A results-based programme paid 1,600 farmers to improve the habitat, but the hen harrier’s long-running decline continues.
So when farmers hear “You’ll be paid for nature”, many will roll their eyes. The scepticism reflects a reality farmers feel: the State cannot be trusted with long-term, successful, well-funded restoration. Most farm lobby groups aren’t opposed to restoration outright; they just want the money, guaranteed.
The farmers who spread seaweed on Murvey are paid through a scheme that ends in 2028. The machair will still need them in 2029.

title: In pictures: All-Ireland Hedge Laying Championships
description: ‘There’s something really ancestral about staying in touch with the land, staying in touch with the old ways’
content:
U nder the heat of a late September sun, traditional hand saws, axes, beadles and billhooks are put to skilled use at the All-Ireland Hedge Laying Championships 2026 in Monasterevin, Co Kildare . Hedge laying is an ancient craft that increases growth and cover on agricultural land through specialist cutting and laying of hedgerow stems and appeals to many who hanker for the old ways.
“There’s something really ancestral about staying in touch with the land, staying in touch with the old ways, and remembering that knowledge and bringing it back to modern, modern times, where it’s as applicable today as it was 200, 300, 400 years ago. It’s a great day out – when it’s not raining,” says hedge layer Lucy Cowles.
Clean cuts close to the ground with strong hinges are a big consideration for judges, as that ensures a healthy flow of sap, which encourages growth, leading to cover that takes away the need for fencing, and creating a complete barrier to livestock that can be as effective as expensive fencing. Competitors work their hedge section in the novice, contractor, ladies and pairs classes with grit and dedication.
“The bogs died out for a while, and they came back again,” says novice hedge layer Pat Boylan, who is 78. “We cut turf until we were banned. But then we went back to this, the hedge laying, and started this Hedgerow Association in 2004. The thing is, now the tractors and machinery create a disconnect.”
Dedicated participants argue that hedge laying keeps a tradition alive while also performing an important ecology service.

title: BlackBee founder claims liquidators failed to exhaust all assets before compensation call
description: Blackrock Office Bond II was first BlackBee investment to be classified a ‘compensatable event’
content:
The founder of BlackBee , the Cork investment group whose key arms have succumbed to liquidation over the past three years, claims liquidators failed to exhaust all assets available to investors in a property-backed bond before declaring that investors could access a special compensation fund.
David O’Shea, the founder, warned in a letter to the Investor Compensation Company DAC (ICCL) last week that if it proceeds with compensating investors in the bond without exhausting all available assets, he will apply to the High Court for leave to seek a judicial review.
The liquidators said they “reject outright” the contents of O’Shea’s letter.
Luke Charleton and Alan Large of EY , the liquidators of the various BlackBee entities, wrote last month to investors in Blackrock Office Bond II – which raised over €11 million in 2019 to buy Block 2 at Blackrock Business Park in south Co Dublin – saying they were entitled to compensation from ICCL.
It was the first BlackBee investment to be classified as a so-called compensatable event. The maximum payout for ICCL-eligible claims is 90 per cent of the compensatable loss, up to a cap of €20,000.
O’Shea noted in his letter to ICCL that the property had been sold by a receiver for €8.75 million in August 2024, resulting in a net €5.88 million being transferred to the liquidators. That was after a loan from a property company associated with wealth manager Warren Private, called Futuredale, was repaid.
Meanwhile, the liquidators said in letters to investors that a total compensatable loss of €4.25 million had occurred. This comprised loan repayments and interest received by City Quarter Capital II, a bond issuance vehicle within the BlackBee group, that was not made available for distribution to the Blackrock Office Bond II investors.
However, O’Shea claimed in his letter to ICCL that Blackrock Office Bond II had recourse to between €3 million and €4.5 million of additional “super senior” collateral held by City Quarter Capital II, to protect investors in the product against property shortfalls. This was secured against a portfolio of unencumbered healthcare properties, which a receiver has been actively selling down, he said.
“The combination of physical sale proceeds (€5.878 million) and additional assets (the €3 million–€4.5 million) yields a recovery in the range of 80-95 per cent of notional noteholder capital,” he said.
O’Shea said the ICCL should not be paying compensation “while millions of euro in registered collateral sit uncollected in the hands of an active receiver”.
He also alleged that BlackBee’s core IT system, Hive, which held investment records, had been decommissioned after BlackBee Investments, the group’s Central Bank-regulated entity, went into liquidation in May 2023. He said this led to “data corruption” until Hive was recommissioned last September.
“We reject outright the contents of Mr O’Shea’s letter,” EY Ireland said in a statement on behalf of the joint liquidators.
O’Shea and Carl Dillon, an accountant and adviser to O’Shea, will be examined in early November in the High Court on the affairs of the BlackBee entities in liquidation.
BlackBee Investments had about €180 million of client assets when it was put into liquidation.
“The joint liquidators have returned over €30 million to investors to date. Investors are informed directly of the status of their investment. The joint liquidators will continue to work with asset owners, other receivers and liquidators to realise assets and to return funds to investors,” EY said.

title: Doing business with Olive: The sports star, the fitness guru and the minister
description: Kavanagh boasted of his connections with Tánaiste Simon Harris and proposed hosting a podcast with him
content:
E ducational technology entrepreneur Brendan Kavanagh has a knack for persuading current and former sports stars to get involved with his businesses.
Kavanagh leads the Olive Group of companies, which has substantial contracts with public education and training boards (ETBs) , statutory bodies that manage both primary and post-primary school provision, and also supplies dozens of schools with laptops and tablets.
The businessman is in the news this week after it emerged that he resigned as chairman and director of Grinds 360, the country’s biggest online grinds company that he cofounded, following a boardroom dispute.
The Wicklow man has succeeded in attracting an array of former sportsmen, from former GAA star player and manager Babs Keating to rugby player Brian O’Driscoll , to become involved as investors, business partners and staff in his companies, including Olive for Education, Olive Media and Grinds 360.
One of the sports figures he wooed was former Irish international footballer Richie Sadlier , who is speaking publicly for the first time about his experience out of concern that others have also been drawn into Kavanagh’s businesses and projects.
In January 2020, Sadlier received a text from Kavanagh.
The message said Kavanagh was launching a mental health project and was also “working with the minister for health [then Simon Harris ] in a personal way”.
Sadlier, one of RTÉ ’s leading soccer pundits, was also presenting a series with Second Captains at the time featuring in-depth interviews with sports stars.
Given Sadlier’s high profile, Kavanagh pitched him an idea for a new podcast. It would involve Sadlier, Kavanagh and Harris discussing mental health issues. Sadlier said Kavanagh claimed to be “a mentor” and friend of the Fine Gael minister and Wicklow TD.
With the 2020 general election scheduled for February 8th, Sadlier declined, feeling he would be “unavoidably politicising myself”.
The conversation turned to a sex-education course that Sadlier, a qualified psychotherapist, had developed with Elaine Byrnes, a researcher at the University of Galway , which they had run in a south Dublin secondary school. Kavanagh proposed scaling it up through his company Olive Media.
“He said: ‘Listen, I’m CEO of the leading e-learning company in the country, this is the stuff we do,’” said Sadlier of Kavanagh’s pitch.
Telling them that “the sky is the limit” for the project, Kavanagh said all he needed was the content, he told the pair.
Sadlier and his partner Byrnes supplied it through their company Cherry Blossom Productions. They agreed that Olive would sort out the technology and production and there would be a 50/50 revenue split.
“I was quite impressed by him,” said Sadlier. “He had links with the minister for health, so I assumed that carried some weight. I trusted him.”
Sadlier worked with Byrnes to create an online course that could be accessed by schools across the country. Share – Sexual Health Awareness Relationship Education – was launched by Simon Harris, then minister for further and higher education, in July 2021.
Harris said at the launch, in a video of the event posted on YouTube , that he was “hugely impressed” with the accessibility of the Share platform for parents, teachers and students. He described the course as “a hugely helpful tool” in the fight against sexual violence.
Share was ready to launch in July 2021, before the new school year. The fee for schools was €20 per student, up to a maximum charge of €2,000. Sadlier said Share generated some €60,000 of revenue in the months after its launch.
Sadlier first had concerns about the joint-project when Olive was late providing figures or late paying fees. Olive kept a dashboard of financial information showing how many Share licences were bought.
However, it was not until November 2021 that he became seriously worried.
At that stage, Sadlier had been out of action for three months. Spending 22 hours a day in bed after spinal fusion surgery to treat back pain, the former professional footballer had time on his hands.
As he recovered from surgery, he began to hear from schools that had signed up to the platform, but he could not see those sign-ups reflected in Olive’s figures.
“There was a little bit of a mismatch between what I knew was happening and what I was being told was happening, so I started to ask very politely, very clearly, just questions, looking for explanations, and every answer I got was more of a red flag,” said Sadlier.
As he questioned the data, his access was cut off. He was told he would get monthly figures only. Another red flag for Sadlier was when Olive refused to tell him which schools were clients, with the strict data protection law, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) , cited as the reason.
When he managed to talk to schools involved, many were unhappy.
“I started to understand just why there was so much resistance within Olive for me talking directly to teachers,” he said.
‘I do remember how I felt that day when I just read an article which said he had a new venture, and I think [rugby players] Brian O’Driscoll and Caelan Doris [Kilkenny hurler] Walter Walsh, three people who I’d have a lot of time for, were investors’
“Some schools would say: ‘Listen, we paid them months ago and we still haven’t had access to the course.’ Others would say: ‘We paid for them and then had tech difficulties. They keep telling us they’ll send someone to service and we just haven’t heard from them.’”
“I was mortified by this, because I was very much the person that was sent out to speak to the media about how good this was, how reputable and brilliant the company was,” said Sadlier.
From Kavanagh being an enthusiastic partner, Sadlier said he soon found the Olive boss would not speak directly with him.
There were attempts to arrange a meeting, but it never happened. In one email responding to Sadlier’s questions, Kavanagh accused Sadlier of trying to “bully” his staff by asking questions.
“I knew at this point that not only had the working relationship completely broken down, but they weren’t doing what they claimed they would do to a high standard,” said Sadlier.
The final straw came when the mother of a teenage client receiving therapy from Sadlier asked him to contact her sister – a teacher who was frustrated that Share was not providing what her school had paid for.
[ Charity received more than 170 warnings from regulator about overdue accounts Opens in new window ]
“At this point, I knew I needed to get out and the lawyer said: ‘You have grounds to terminate’, and I immediately sent a letter: ‘Agreement terminated’,” said Sadlier.
The letter sent by Cherry Blossom Productions, the company owned by Sadlier and Byrnes, sent in April 2022, claimed Kavanagh’s company had breached their contract nine times.
Thomas Cullen, then Olive’s chief financial officer, in a responding letter to Cherry Blossom, said he did not accept their complaints, but confirmed termination of the contract “by mutual agreement”.
Sadlier said the final payment from Olive arrived without any breakdown of what it was for. The whole experience left a bad taste in his mouth.
“For a long time, I was really angry that I had invested so much of my time and work in something that I really wanted to work and I was kicking myself that I partnered up with him and that after all the time and work that was put into it, we were back to square one,” he said.
One ETB recently confirmed to Sadlier that it had paid Olive €565.80 in February 2022 for Share, but it could not get the programme to work – and no one from Olive responded to repeated requests for assistance.
A refund was requested and despite Sadlier being told by Kavanagh that he would handle it, no refund was ever paid.
Sadlier earlier this year launched a new online course aimed at secondary schools called “Let’s Talk SPHE” – referring to social, personal and health education, a mainstay of the curriculum.
This project has no link with Olive and Kavanagh.
Sadlier is prepared to talk about his bad experience because sports stars he admires have invested in Kavanagh’s businesses.
“I do remember how I felt that day when I just read an article which said he had a new venture, and I think [rugby players] Brian O’Driscoll and Caelan Doris and [Kilkenny hurler] Walter Walsh, three people who I’d have a lot of time for, were investors,” he said.
Sadlier was not the only content provider to have such a negative experience with Olive.
Mr Motivator, the leotard-clad fitness instructor whose live workout sessions and fitness tips on British breakfast TV shows made him a household name from the 1990s, had a similar ordeal.
Mr Motivator, or Derrick Evans, partnered with Olive in 2021 to launch an online fitness and wellbeing website after Kavanagh pitched the idea to him.
“I should have listened to my inner spirit, really, which always told me if something sounds too good to be true, it normally is, right?” he said.
“Because they promised everything; they over-promised and underdelivered.”
Rather than build a bespoke site, Evans was unhappy to learn Olive built his Mr Motivator Club on an existing template and he had to operate within those constraints.
Soon after the launch, Evans heard complaints from customers who were not having their inquiries answered. People who joined but then cancelled their membership complained that they continued to be charged and had difficulty getting refunds.
Even though the JLR deal was terminated in 2023, Olive still has a page on its website claiming to be providing the technology that will ‘revolutionise’ JLR’s employee learning scheme for 30,000 staff
When Evans promoted a live chat with Kavanagh on his Facebook page, a woman complained in the comments: “Please when you chat to Brendan please ask why his website overcharges for access following IT failures their end, and I’m being charged twice for services I don’t use.”
Evans said: “Quite a number of people were having all those kind of problems.”
He said Kavanagh told him Olive had a deal to run the staff rewards and training system for Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), the giant UK automobile manufacturer, and promised thousands of customers could be recruited for him through that. As part of the rewards and training, staff could claim credits to use for self-improvement classes, ranging from golf to fitness classes to music lessons.
In reality, the Olive deal with JLR that was signed in early 2022 with much publicity was terminated in 2023 after golf pros and guitar teachers complained Olive had failed to pay them for months after they gave lessons booked through its system.
Even though the JLR deal was terminated in 2023, Olive still has a page on its website claiming to be providing the technology that will “revolutionise” JLR’s employee learning scheme for 30,000 staff.
Evans said his deal with Olive involved him receiving a set monthly fee, while Olive kept the rest of the revenue until it covered development costs.
In 2022 Olive stopped paying him, he said, and he could not get transparency on how the site was performing. Coupled with rising customer complaints in 2023, he became disillusioned and cut dealings with this Irish company.
“There were all these things that they promised with different people like JLR, and none of it was ever materialising,” Evans said.
“And then I realised that it was all the Blarney Stone.”
Evans estimates he lost between £10,000 (€11,650) and £12,000 (€14,000) through his dealings with Olive, but decided not to pursue any legal action. He has since set up a new Mr Motivator website without Olive.
“We just cut our losses because it just got really bad,” he said. “You just could not get anything back from them.”
While Kavanagh had pitched his idea directly to Evans, at home he has used his network of connections to attract other investors and partners.
One of those key connections is a senior political figure.
A number of Olive sources have said Kavanagh, who is lives in Wicklow, often boasted about having a close relationship with Simon Harris, a TD for that constituency, and claimed his companies helped Harris with some of his social media. The relationship had helped Kavanagh with his approach to Sadlier.
Kavanagh arranged for Harris’s constituency manager John Kelly and other campaign workers to meet one of his video production partners to get advice on targeting and retaining younger voters. A request was made by Kelly at one point to add an Olive worker as an administrator on the Simon Harris Facebook page.
One Olive source said Kavanagh privately admitted he does not support Fine Gael but said Harris was “good for business”.
The ETBs have been valuable clients for Olive in recent years, with four of them having paid more than a combined €1.5 million to Olive since 2020.
By far the most important ETB client for Olive has been Louth & Meath ETB, which paid €1.28 million to the company from 2020 to 2025. There is no suggestion that Harris played any role in helping Olive win those contracts.
Harris, now Tánaiste and Minister for Finance, was minister for health from 2016 to 2020 and minister for further and higher education from 2020 to 2024. He was chosen as Fine Gael leader in March 2024 and became taoiseach in April of that year.
Kavanagh was among Harris’s Wicklow supporters in Leinster House on the day he was elected taoiseach.
Kavanagh shared a letter with colleagues that Harris sent him as taoiseach, dated January 5th, 2025.
“I wanted to take a moment to thank you for all the friendship and support over the years,” Harris wrote.
“Not only did this make the general election in Wicklow possible, but it allowed our party to enter the Dáil term with a renewed vigour and energy, and for this I am immensely grateful.
“Please do keep in touch and do not hesitate to let me know if I can ever be of assistance,” the Fine Gael leader wrote.
More recently, Kavanagh posted a photograph on LinkedIn of himself meeting Harris in Leinster House in late May 2026. Kavanagh thanked Harris for his “authentic interest in what’s happening in technology and how Government can support”.
At the time, Harris’s spokesman said the meeting was “a visit by some constituents of the Tánaiste’s to Leinster House which was organised by his constituency office”.
“The Tánaiste dropped in to greet them and had an informal conversation with them about a number of constituency matters.”
The Irish Times sent 10 questions to the Tánaiste’s press advisers on September 11th asking about what assistance Kavanagh had provided him.
A spokesman for Harris phoned The Irish Times on Tuesday, September 15th to say that the Tánaiste’s office would not respond on the record to the questions. He asked whether he could speak off the record, meaning his responses could not be quoted. The Irish Times declined and said it only wanted the questions answered on the record so they could be quoted in this story.
The Irish Times asked Olive and Brendan Kavanagh a series of detailed questions on September 2nd.
On September 29th, a spokesman for the Olive Group complained that they had not had adequate time to consider and respond fully to the questions.
“Olive Group and Brendan Kavanagh do not accept a number of the assumptions, characterisations and conclusions reflected in the questions submitted,” the spokesman said.

title: Back on the Garvaghy Road, people are wary and rather worried
description: More than 20 deaths have been linked to Drumcree, a problem most people thought was settled. On Portadown’s Garvaghy Road, its resurrection is causing deep apprehension
content:
We are back on the Garvaghy Road again. People who live there and in the vicinity are wary and rather worried. What the ultimate fallout will be is unpredictable.
Things have been said at political level that may be hard to retreat from and that could threaten the stability of the Northern Ireland Executive and Assembly, and undermine some of what was achieved by the 1998 Belfast Agreement.
Here at local level, it is not like the 1990s but there is fear of the unexpected, that some crazy or maverick action could make a bad situation infinitely worse.
The formal opposition to the Orange Order parade is being led by the likes of Breandán Mac Cionnaith and the residents’ coalition and Sinn Féin, with some well-known dissidents such as Colin Duffy regularly in attendance. The Orangemen ’s legal representative Jamie Bryson and local DUP MP Carla Lockhart respectively characterised nationalists protesting against the parade as a mob and a rabble.
Most local people not directly linked to the protests are reluctant to talk but some are prepared to venture their opinions anonymously. Paul, a 62-year-old local man, says the community is “pulling well together”.
“To let the town go back 30 years is ridiculous, but that’s the way it is here,” he says.
He thought Alliance leader Naomi Long had a good idea when she suggested the Orangemen should exhibit their Christian credentials by adopting the high moral ground in having won permission to parade but then agreeing not to do so.
“They could take the big win in the interests of community relations,” he adds, but, shaking his head, doesn’t think it will happen. “That’s just the way they are.”
He remembers the bad times and says he can’t understand how the Parades Commission arrived at its decision to permit the parade . “We don’t want any violence but if the parade is forced down, that would change things. It would bring the youngsters out, and they are easily led. I think there would be a few petrol bombs and the like of that.
“We don’t want to go back to that. We all thought that those days were long gone.” Over recent days there has been talk of a possible “one and done” solution whereby a small group of Orangemen would get their parade along the Garvaghy Road but that there would be no more such parades. Paul has his doubts over whether that would work. “I can’t see what the resolution can be. They want to walk, we don’t want them to walk. There is no middle ground. It’s the old Mexican stand-off, it’s about who blinks first but nobody is planning to blink here.”
He agrees there is no comparison with the 1990s but adds: “That could change.”
Paul is not enamoured of Jamie Bryson. “Jamie can start an argument and then get out of the way,” he says. “He has no connections to Portadown. It is strange he is the Orangemen’s legal adviser.”
There is a similar comment from a middle-aged local woman walking near the community centre. “Jamie Bryson and Carla Lockhart have a lot to answer for,” she says. Asked about the mood of the place, she responds: “What is the word you are looking for when you don’t know what it is?” Then she quickly fires out a few: “It’s uneasy, it’s anxious, it’s worried; it’s like Groundhog Day. We don’t know what’s going to happen.”
[ Who is Jamie Bryson, the unelected loyalist standing ‘front, back and centre’ at Drumcree? Opens in new window ]
Her friend, a young woman, adds: “My 12-year-old daughter, every Saturday she goes into the town centre, but I can’t let her any more. Before she could go into town wearing her Donegal or Kerry GAA jersey without any bother, but not now. Whenever she goes out now she is afraid.” Remembering Robert Hamill, a 25-year-old Catholic beaten to death in Portadown at the height of the Drumcree violence almost 30 years ago, the woman adds: “I worry what might happen to her.”
She says reactivating Drumcree has caused real trauma: “Every time my dad starts thinking about it, he cries.”
The middle-aged woman says her son is married to a local Presbyterian and the couple have three children: “They don’t want this; this has put back community relations.”
Observing parents going to collect their young children from school, she adds: “The youngsters, they don’t know what is happening, but they know something is wrong; they can feel it.”
The two women are at one that the parade must not go through. “We were second-class citizens, but we’re not any more,” says the middle-aged woman.
Other elements of life have changed since the 1990s. Two African women approach along the road, one of them wheeling a child in a buggy. One of the women cheerfully agrees to talk, but her comment is short. “I have really no idea what this is all about so I am afraid I can’t help you.”
[ Why is the Orange Order so set on Garvaghy Road? Opens in new window ]
The mood among ordinary people here generally is calm. There is a stoicism; there is no great bitterness. The feeling is more despairing than angry with the Orange Order. But there is real concern and apprehension.
“I still feel terrified,” says one woman. “I don’t want my children and my grandchildren to have to go through this again.”
“The road the Orangemen took to Drumcree is a perfectly good road for them to walk back on; they should take that road back and leave us alone,” says her companion, the two women out for a regular afternoon walk.
Just 100 metres from them about 50 men and women are gathered on the road at a makeshift encampment close to a banner declaring “Garvaghy Road Says No”. They operate in shifts, ready at a moment’s notice to mobilise more protesters to block the road should the Orangemen back about a mile away up on Drumcree hill get the go-ahead to march. Tricolours and starry plough flags flutter from lamp-posts along the road.
Firmly behind the protest, the first woman says admiringly: “The people, the community here, are absolutely brilliant. We have great support this time.”
She fears, however, that if the Orangemen ultimately get their parade that the “whole thing will blow up again”.
What “blowing up again” might mean is difficult to predict. The road feels much different from the mid- to late-1990s but the apprehension among ordinary people is palpable.
The women are of an age where they have strong memories of the early Drumcrees. They do not want a rerun.
But that determination to march is going nowhere. Alistair Power, the deputy district master of the Portadown district of the Orange Order, insists: “It is the Orange Order’s legal right to march down the Garvaghy Road. We will continue our campaign. The permission granted by the Parades Commission remains live. We have told police we are ready to walk down the Garvaghy Road when the PSNI is ready to facilitate it.”
Rank-and-file Orangemen will not engage with the press outside the Orange hall next to the Church of Ireland, though there is much mention of “British subjects being blocked from the King’s highway”, and sometimes a few mentions of the “Queen’s highway”.
“We will be here until we are allowed to go down,” one told a small group of journalists, before walking off.
Jamie Bryson, meanwhile, is adamant that there will be no compromise: “The Portadown District will not be doing any deal which doesn’t deliver on the fundamental legal principle, and the fundamental legal principle is this: that the Portadown District will walk the Garvaghy Road and nothing else will do.”
The first eruption was on Sunday July 9th, 1995 when locals, with former IRA prisoner Breandán Mac Cionnaith first coming to public prominence as leader of the residents’ group, decided there should be no march.
[ Reluctant Garvaghy Road resistance point man Breandán Mac Cionnaith rises to Drumcree challenge Opens in new window ]
The Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) blocked the return parade at the bridge close to the church, and the first of numerous stand-offs began. Rallies on the hill were thunderously addressed by the likes of DUP leader Ian Paisley, the then local Ulster Unionist MP David Trimble, and future DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson.
Orange and loyalist blood was up and on the second night, they broke through the police lines, with Ian Paisley, for a time, at their vanguard. Pitched battles were fought in the fields close to the church between, on one side, the police, and on the other, loyalists and Orangemen. Several plastic bullets were fired – I still have a casing from one of the bullets that sits as a pen holder in my office.
For a period it seemed the mob would rampage through the Garvaghy area. I remember terrified women in the houses at the Ballyoran estate off the Garvaghy Road saying, incongruously, “thank God for the RUC”. Eventually the protesters were pushed back.
Amid the tumult, several groups, from professional mediators and politicians to clergy and representatives of the Orangemen and residents, engaged in various forms of talks. Eventually a compromise was reached where the Orangemen silently marched down the road, with placard-carrying nationalists standing equally quietly on the footpaths. It was strange and eerie, many nationalists turning their backs as the Orangemen passed by.
It seemed like an honourable resolution but then, as most nationalists saw it, Paisley and Trimble did their giddy hand-in-hand jig of triumphalism when they reached the Portadown town centre. That ended the brief feelgood factor.
Trimble added insult to injury by insisting there was no compromise with the residents when the police, the mediators, the residents and even some members of his own party agreed that a formal accommodation had been reached.
[ Drumcree: ‘I want to stop all this in its tracks. I have five grandchildren; it’s breaking my heart’ Opens in new window ]
There would be no more accommodations. Such was the loyalist and Orange threat that the parades were forced through the Garvaghy Road in 1996 and 1997. The leader of the Loyalist Volunteer Force (LVF) known as King Rat, Billy Wright, later murdered in prison by the INLA, was on the scene, menacing, marshalling and managing his troops. In 2000 Ulster Defence Association figure Johnny “Mad Dog” Adair arrived with about 100 UDA members plus his dog Rebel, they and the dog wearing a T-shirt bearing the slogan “Simply the Best”.
Drumcree-related violence and disruption spread throughout the North. At times such was the toxicity it seemed Northern Ireland was on the verge of civil insurrection.
The killings began. During the 1996 dispute the LVF murdered Michael McGoldrick, a 31-year-old married Catholic taxi driver from Lurgan, Co Armagh who had just graduated from Queen’s University Belfast with plans to become a teacher. In April the following year amid deep sectarian tensions a loyalist group beat Robert Hamill to death in Portadown town centre. In all, 21 deaths have been linked directly or indirectly to the Drumcree stand-offs.
Over the years several other parading disputes arose in places such as Derry, the lower Ormeau area of south Belfast, at the Ardoyne shops in north Belfast, in Dunloy and Rasharkin in Co Antrim, in Bellaghy, Co Derry and in other areas. It is only in recent years, to the relief of most people, that parading disputes have dissipated and mostly died down.
[ Drumcree standoff puts a significant achievement of the peace process at risk Opens in new window ]
Unionists accused Sinn Féin of conspiracy to cause trouble, citing how Gerry Adams in 1996 told a private Sinn Féin conference that opposition to Drumcree and other contentious parades did not “happen by accident” and was the sort of issue that needed to be developed and exploited.
Then in July 1998, again during the Drumcree stalemate, the three Quinn children, Richard (10), Mark (nine) and Jason (eight) were killed when loyalists petrol-bombed their home in Ballymoney, Co Antrim.
It caused such outrage that there would be no more Drumcree parades after that, even though Portadown District continued to press for a march. The protests and troubles continued into the 2000s but gradually these became weekly token gestures, with marching permission always refused until this procedural foul-up by the Parades Commission resurrected a problem most people thought was settled.
[ Drumcree, 2026: ‘It’s mad they want to go down the road and start all this again’ Opens in new window ]
In the Assembly this week, the new leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, Jon Burrows, who was sure the police would never act to force through an Orange parade, remembered a happier time pertaining to Drumcree.
He recalled how as a former senior PSNI officer in the Portadown area members of the Orange Order walked up to the police line every Sunday at Drumcree knowing that under the Parades Commission rulings they would be denied permission to march along the Garvaghy Road.
“They would stop at that line not because there was a line of police or there were barricades – the sergeant was often late to turn up – but because the law said, ‘Stop’. In fact, they often rang the police and said, ‘You need to hurry up and get here because we’re at our point and want to hand over a letter’.”
Everyone along the Garvaghy Road and most people in Northern Ireland including many unionists, would love that relaxed peaceful situation to return.

title: Why has rugby largely avoided gambling sponsorship?
description: Other sports are awash with money from betting companies, but rugby is a different story – for reasons that could change
content:
The opening rounds of the United Rugby Championship campaign see Leinster visit two of South African rugby’s most celebrated grounds with less than glorious new names.
Ellis Park, the venue for last weekend’s defeat to the Lions , was the site of the 1995 World Cup final, Nelson Mandela famously sporting a Springboks jersey when presenting the Webb Ellis Cup to his compatriot Francois Pienaar. Round two brings the province to Kings Park, a ground forever etched into Irish rugby lore by Ciarán Frawley’s match-winning drop-goal back in 2024.
Technically speaking, these names are no longer the correct nomenclature. Since 2023, the Durban venue has been known as Hollywoodbets Kings Park thanks to an agreement with a betting company that extends to naming the team the Hollywoodbets Sharks. Similarly, as of a deal announced in July, the team that beat Leinster last weekend is called the 10Bet Lions. They play their home games at 10Bet Ellis Park.
Although team-naming rights partnerships are not new (Leinster beat the Fidelity SecureDrive Lions in last season’s URC knockouts), such gambling-themed franchise titles are “unprecedented in the world of sport”, according to Darragh McGee, an academic researcher in the field of gambling sponsorship.
Betting partnerships themselves are also no novel phenomenon. Even if Premier League football clubs have agreed to ditch betting companies from the front of their shirts, the league is awash with jersey sleeves and pitchside hoarding featuring gambling partners. Staying in the UK, multiple county cricket teams have partnerships with Dafabet, an Asian bookmaker. Across the pond, all four major sports leagues – the NFL, NBA, NHL and MLB – have official betting partners. Add to that list a host of individual North American franchises.
By contrast, gambling sponsorship within rugby has been conspicuous by its absence. These South African examples stand out simply by having any sort of relationship with betting operators. In Europe, professional rugby union has largely avoided such partnerships – with a handful of exceptions.
The Ospreys sport Quinnbet on their playing shorts. In 2018, Leicester Tigers announced a similar arrangement with LeoVegas lasting two years. In France, Toulouse have a partnership with OlyBet, while both Ligue Nationale de Rugby (Top 14 and ProD2 organisers) and the Federation of French Rugby have signed deals with Betclic.
Compared with other sports, these examples are limited. At domestic level, rugby has well-known money problems. In the UK, multiple clubs have disappeared under financial pressure, in theory creating a scenario where cash-strapped organisations are prime candidates to hold their noses and take whatever deals they can get. When sports with a larger share of the viewing market are taking on gambling companies as sponsors, the obvious question is why not rugby?
The answer depends on the appetite of both sides, the sponsor and the team accepting the cash. In Irish rugby, there is next to no desire to be seen partnering with the betting industry.
Provinces and the IRFU alike get approaches from companies but they are quickly rebuffed.
Ulster , for instance, recently changed their shirt and stadium sponsor. The club is understood to be comfortable partnering with healthcare company Affidea for multiple reasons, among them avoiding negative attention after receiving criticism for their relationship with Kingspan (in 2024, a report on the Grenfell fire found that the Irish building materials company “ knowingly created a false market ” for its insulation that was used in the tower. Kingspan expressed their sympathy to families of the victims, acknowledged “wholly unacceptable historical failings” and said their product was not the principle reason for the fire spreading).
“It’s been a set trend over the years from generation to generation that gambling is just not right for Irish sport,” says Colm Roche, a strategic sponsorship consultant. “It comes down to the market and the fans themselves, if gambling is accepted.
“If you look at Ireland as a sporting nation, sport is built from the community up, steeped in culture, history, from kids to clubs to schools to international level. From a betting brand perspective, it would have a negative effect on that pathway and be seen as a step backwards. Irish rugby in particular has always stayed away for that reason.”
[ Generation gamble: the invisible addiction crisis gripping Ireland’s teenagers Opens in new window ]
Rugby is not alone within Ireland. In 2018, the GAA introduced a blanket ban on sponsorship from gambling companies. The FAI opted not to pursue gambling partners, albeit this does not apply to League of Ireland clubs. Shamrock Rovers sport NetBet on their jersey sleeves as the club’s responsible gaming partner.
On the flip side, how keen are the gambling companies?
Many operators question the viability of rugby itself. The sport lacks cultural relevance in the two biggest markets targeted by bookmakers, Asia and the US. The white-label companies – lacking a local presence and mostly targeting Asian bettors – that sponsor Premier League clubs are unlikely to be keen on rugby considering the sports their target audience consumes. Rugby doesn’t have the numbers.
According to McGee, assistant professor at the University of Bath and author of Imitation Games: How Gambling Hijacked Sport, rugby punters are less likely to be profitable customers than fans of other sports. Although rugby has worked hard to break out of its private-school stereotype, education and class are nonetheless factors in all this.
[ Imitation Games by Darragh McGee: Football in the grip of a gambling addiction Opens in new window ]
“With education comes a degree of critical consciousness about the traps that lay in wait for all of us,” McGee says. “Economic literacy allows people to see through gambling and its extractive mechanisms.
“Gambling firms will have analysed and profiled this very carefully and decided that the rugby market is small. If they thought it was profitable, they’d be there.”
One gambling industry figure pointed to the lack of time spent on their rugby product compared with other sports. “The reason some sports are big gambling sports is they’re on all the time,” they sayyid. “Look at darts, table tennis, esports. There isn’t as much televised or organised rugby.”
[ Gambling and soccer: ‘I want the likes of Roy Keane to say we can no longer endorse this’ Opens in new window ]
As a result, most websites don’t offer significant in-play markets on rugby matches. You’d struggle to place a bet on the number of rucks hit by James Ryan in a single match, whereas you can wager on the number of corners in a Premier League contest. “In-play is much more immersive, impulsive and profitable,” says McGee. “In-play is designed to eventually move fans into the online casinos which are the most profitable, addictive and harmful.”
Another wrinkle is the impending laws regarding gambling sponsorship within Ireland. In 2024, the Gambling Regulation Act was signed into law. Section 159 of the act makes it clear that any company licensed by the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI) cannot sponsor a team where children are members or a public activity that appeals to children.
