title: David McWilliams: Is the Irish housing market beginning to turn?
description: The current easing is not driven by new supply - buyers have reached the limit of what they can afford and the homes available don’t match what people want
content:
Over the last few months, house prices have not been rising as quickly . Although national asking prices are up 3.0 per cent on a year ago, this is about half the 5.8 per cent pace of last year, meaning that sellers are adjusting down what they think they can get when they put their homes on the market.
Meanwhile, agreed sale prices are up just 0.8 per cent, the slowest in six years. This is a big shift. Another signal is that the premium that buyers were prepared to pay over the asking price has narrowed from 6.8 per cent to 2.6 per cent. Buyers are no longer being bullied into paying way over the odds because they fear being outbid by someone else. Given the role psychology plays in markets, such a change in dynamics is significant.
We forget the role of emotions in markets at our peril, because the “mood” plays a huge part in the way people see prices and bargains. Sometimes, my profession, the economists, don’t get this. When economists see a price, we see a number; when ordinary people see a price, they get a feeling. It is this feeling that makes them confident, or anxious, as the case may be. Confidence pushes people to pay the extra bit over the asking price; anxiety has the opposite effect.
We are seeing a sharp reversal of behaviour. For example, in Dublin, according to the latest Daft report ( Daft Q3 2026 ), sale prices fell 5.2 per cent year-on-year, the largest annual fall since 2014, and this fall has accelerated over the summer, with prices dropping 2 per cent in the three months to September. Asking prices are still up 2.7 per cent, so the gap between what sellers want and what buyers will pay is wider in Dublin than in any other region in the State.
Before you go thinking the housing crisis has been solved, hold on. What we are seeing is not evidence of that. Prices nationally remain 44 per cent above pre-Covid levels. The easing we’re seeing is not driven by new supply. It reflects two developments: first, buyers are reaching the limit of what income, lending rules and support schemes allow them to pay, and second, the homes that are being built don’t match what people want.
We are still building three-bed semidetached homes in commuter towns, in a country that wants urban apartments, because the size and nature of the Irish household has changed. We are having fewer children, and more people are single and want to live alone or in a couple without necessarily wanting two extra bedrooms.
Let’s look at the first development. Prices are simply too high, and potential buyers have hit the price ceiling. The expression “the cure for high prices is high prices” is one of the oldest in economics. Eventually, very high prices fix themselves by depressing demand, because people run out of money and can’t afford to pay the higher prices. In addition, the high prices usually imply higher profits for builders and the higher prices prompt higher supply, which brings down prices in time. However, in Ireland right now, it is a simple fact that buyers are “maxed out” and can’t afford relentless rises in house prices – so they cannot play the game any longer.
Since Covid, although wages have been more or less rising in line with inflation or a small bit more, house prices across the country are up massively. In Munster, outside the cities, prices are up 72 per cent since the pandemic. They are up 62 per cent in Leinster outside Dublin; the four regional cities have seen prices rise by 57 per cent, while in Connaught/Ulster, traditionally the most moribund of housing markets, prices are up a whopping 72 per cent since Covid.
[ If Irish property is overvalued, will house prices fall? Opens in new window ]
Dublin lags behind, with prices up by 32 per cent in the same period. The current asking price for a three-bed semi is €635,000 in Dublin, €431,000 in Cork city, €424,000 in Galway city; €376,000 in Limerick City and €313,000 in Waterford city.
The font of all borrowing is income, so let’s look at these prices relative to wages and the ability to borrow, and then let’s see where prices should be. Real wages are roughly flat: earnings were up 3.9 per cent against inflation of 3.7 per cent last year. First-time buyers – half of all buyers – can borrow, at most, four times their income, with a 10 per cent deposit.
This is a numbers game – and the numbers don’t add up. We need far more apartments in our cities, and the asking prices for these apartments must fall
So take a couple in their 30s, both on average earnings of €1,046.88 a week, or €54,400 a year. This gives them €108,900 combined. Four times income in borrowings means a maximum mortgage of €435,500. When adding their 10 per cent deposit, the maximum purchase price they can afford is about €484,000.
Based on these figures, the Dublin family home is out of reach on their income alone. The couple would need a dual income of about €145,000 to afford the three-bed semi, or a cool €200,000 in cash.
In terms of getting an apartment in Dublin, the average two-bed costs €406,000, so it is within lending limits, and repayments are below 20 per cent of gross income. The challenge for this couple is saving up the €41,000 in cash for a deposit, roughly 4.5 months of combined gross pay.
This is not insurmountable if they have been saving, or can rely on family, and parents giving a house deposit to young couples is very common. But let’s say they would like to have a family in an urban setting, in, say, a three-bed apartment. At a cost of €502,000 it is about €18,000 over the couple’s maximum threshold, and it would require €66,500 in cash.
[ The Irish Times view on the ESRI housing report: house prices alarmingly overvalued Opens in new window ]
Even if taking the completely stretched first-time buying couple who’ve looked down the back of the couch to put together every cent they have, they are still well short of the needed funds in Dublin. Is it any surprise prices are adjusting in the capital?
Apologies for all the numbers in the last few paragraphs, but this is a numbers game – and the numbers don’t add up. We need far more apartments in our cities, and the asking prices for these apartments must fall. The State must fast-track building in the cities. We need to build up, because obviously the more floors in a building, the cheaper the apartments ultimately built will be – and we also need to reduce the ability of serial objectors to put spurious spanners in the works.
For now, the market has spoken – prices are adjusting downwards, because the cure for high prices is high prices.

title: Housing the Nation by Lorcan Sirr and Brittle by Ronan Lyons: indictments of an untenable system
description: Insightful, illuminating works by leading housing commentators both ultimately ask: remembering our past, while looking to the future, what kind of Ireland do we need to build?
content:
At what point does the term “crisis” become inaccurate? It implies the need for an urgent solution but, after 12 years of an acute crisis in our housing system, we are still waiting.
Governments come and go. New plans and schemes are launched. A group of experts is appointed to a Housing Commission , their report almost immediately forgotten. Election cycles see political parties promising to build a fantastical number of new homes, but the numbers climbing stubbornly higher are rents, house prices and the people (many of them children) experiencing homelessness .
Into this morass come new books from two of Ireland’s leading commentators on housing. Lorcan Sirr is a housing policy analyst, senior lecturer at Technological University Dublin and a regular contributor to The Irish Times. Ronan Lyons is associate professor in economics at Trinity College Dublin, and widely known for his quarterly Daft.ie reports on the Irish housing market.
Sirr’s Housing a Nation: Seven Generations of Land, Politics and Power reflects on the history of land and housing in Ireland, starting before the Famine and exploring the context and consequence of past approaches to housing policy up to the present day.
In Brittle, Lyons focuses on analysing our present housing situation, before he shifts his attention to future solutions. Each book looks at housing through a different lens but it is the many points of consensus that stand out upon reading.
Both texts offer insight and illumination, not only into the technical challenges of housing but the political, cultural and social context in which housing choices are made. This effort to relate how housing shapes broader society leads both Lyons and Sirr to narrativise the lives of invented characters and use their stories to demonstrate and highlight the human cost of policy shortcomings.
This choice is wise, and it works. It ensures that the human consequences of mistakes and delays are not lost in debates over data.
Sirr examines what happened over the centuries to bring us to our current impasse. Behind housing policy, he writes, are “decisions … shaped by dogma, influenced by power … often ideological in nature, divorced and removed from the reality of everyday life”. He returns to this theme throughout the book, revealing how the same pressures and processes of the past recur in the present and lead us to reproduce the same failings and inequalities.
Sirr begins in 1821 with a vivid description of the small cottage inhabited by “Will and Eliza”. The pernicious threat of eviction hangs over these powerless tenants at the mercy of their landowners, standing in contrast to the living conditions of the Anglo-Irish landlord in the Big House.
From this starting point, Sirr spans seven generations of a fictional family to take the reader through the first census, the mapping of Ireland, Griffith’s valuation and the construction of the workhouses.
He describes how the conditions that produced the Great Famine rested, in large part, on a dysfunctional land system. The decades of emigration that followed held back any prospect of economic growth and decimated the population. Land reforms, brought in to undermine popular support for the Home Rule movement, were not sufficient to arrest momentum towards self-governance.
Post-independence, Sirr focuses on the interplay of land, housing and power with a perceptive review of the political and social influences on Irish housing in the 20th century.
The role of the architect Herbert Simms and the building of new suburbs in Dublin to meet the needs of a growing population highlight the successes of earlier eras. The influence of Archbishop John Charles McQuaid on suburban planning in the mid-20th century seems remarkable at this juncture, and shows the enormous change Ireland has undergone in recent decades.
Sirr also points to an anti-urban bias that dominated for decades, and the idealised vision of a rural, agrarian lifestyle that left the planning and development system with a cultural distrust of dense housing, where illicit activities and subversive ideas might spread.
A detailed account of the Ballymun flats project gives greater context to the pressure to provide alternatives to slum conditions in Dublin’s tenements, and the fatal tragedies that befell families when these tenements collapsed.
While visions of urban neglect and decay remain all too familiar to Dubliners, efforts to tackle the appalling squalor of the tenements have improved life for many. The continued, if slow, expansion of the social and affordable housing sector should offer hope.
[ ‘Two of the kids can’t stay overnight’: Mother of seven on her overcrowded Dublin council flat Opens in new window ]
In Brittle, Lyons foregrounds the invisible nature of many forms of housing precarity, including the absent households that are never formed or counted in homelessness data by virtue of emigration, couch-surfing or the lost opportunity for new family formation. He highlights the many young people who have had their lives delayed or truncated by the lack of housing options, observing the invisibility of many people’s experience of this crisis.
He defines a category of people – the “blocked” – who earn too much for State subsidies but too little to access accommodation provided by the private market. This group includes young people, the newly arrived and those experiencing relationship breakdown. Their experience, Lyons says, is evidence that “Ireland increasingly produces households who are expected to fend for themselves in a system structurally incapable of serving them”.
It is this structural failing that Lyons attacks. With his extensive technical command of economic and tax policies on housing, he pinpoints a series of decisions that have contributed to our current situation. These include the abolition of domestic rates, the expansion of section 23 tax relief, and the transfer of social rental properties into private ownership. Though popular with those in a position to buy, this left the State’s public housing stock heavily diminished by the time of the global financial crash.
Lyons’s analysis is lucid and persuasive, arguing that the overarching political push for home ownership since the 1930s has undermined the health of the rental sector and left many tenants unprotected and living in poorly maintained accommodation.
He speaks of “assumptions that policymakers carry into the room with them” that may explain why our housing patterns reflect an Ireland that no longer exists. Given our familiar history of emigration, decline and stagnation, we never planned for economic success or sustained population growth.
It is this pessimism that creates structural underprovision. When future projections are proved wrong, the panicked rush to plug gaps exacerbates the problems by avoiding the harder work of restructuring the system as a whole. As Lyons puts it, “[m]any of the interventions addressed symptoms of the housing crisis rather than the mechanics producing it”.
Lyons argues that, while individual policy choices may have seemed reasonable in isolation, when combined with other political decisions, they created a wholly untenable housing system even before the Celtic Tiger bubble. When the economic crash occurred, despite thousands waiting on local authority housing lists, construction fell to historic lows that did not match the scale of outstanding demand. Almost immediately, the knock-on effect was a spike in homelessness – particularly, family homelessness – as far back as 2014.
Lyons does not only diagnose our housing maladies but offers detailed suggestions for solutions. This includes expanding supply in urban centres through a model that plans housing and infrastructure together at the city level.
One of the challenges posed by Lyons’s suggested solutions is that they confront embedded cultural beliefs around participation in planning and ownership of the family home. Sirr captures the history behind this preference for home ownership, while Lyons shows why our demographics – smaller households living longer – would suggest that we may be too focused on larger family homes for owner-occupiers.
While each book differs in scope and emphasis, both Sirr and Lyons ultimately pose the same question: remembering our past, while looking towards the future, what kind of Ireland do we need to build?
Regardless of whether the current tax windfalls continue, we will emerge from this period with a much larger population, crammed into sprawling cities and traffic-clogged suburban towns. As we grow and change as a country, so too must our housing system. The system inherited from previous decades has failed to produce the housing we need for today’s Ireland, let alone Ireland of the future.
Real policy solutions may require a change in our politics and mindsets. Certainly, as we attempt to tackle and correct past mistakes, honest and frank conversations about available trade-offs and choices are not just advisable, but essential.
[ Ireland’s housing policy needs greater coherence Opens in new window ]
Housing a Nation and Brittle differ in emphasis and details, but Sirr and Lyons would appear to agree on this: if we do not adapt at a policy level, we will continue to limp on indefinitely, hoping for the best.
Housing is a complex policy problem. A “house” means different things to different people. It is, simultaneously, the bricks and mortar that represent a financialised asset, and a person’s home and place of safety. In industry parlance, the house is a “unit”. The number of units that will be delivered in a given year is determined by either the purchase price or the rental yield that can be achieved.
For the lone mother raising her small children in a single cramped hotel room, this “unit” is a dream she longs for every day of her life: a secure home where she can raise her children. At the heart of our problem in Ireland is this contradiction.
As a country, we’ve come a long way since the abject misery of subsistence labourers surviving in smoky mud cabins, so vividly evoked in Housing a Nation. But we didn’t intend to throw off one form of subjugation only to find ourselves trapped in a “brittle” housing system that cannot meet the needs of the population.
When housing is secure and affordable, it fades into the background. When it is absent or precarious, there is nothing more urgent or pressing. Lyons writes that we’ll know we’ve succeeded when we’re no longer talking about housing.
Rather than continuing to tinker at the edges of a broken system, a much more fundamental shift is needed. Future generations will thank us.
Rosemary Hennigan is a novelist who previously worked in housing and homelessness policy in the NGO sector.

title: Not the Perfect Victim by Nikita Hand: An immense and ongoing act of courage
description: The voice is clear, natural and readable, staying within the realm of personal testimony
content:
The fact that “rape memoir” has become a literary genre in its own right is a depressing reflection of our society; more sobering still is the knowledge of how many stories remain unwritten and untold. Within the genre, different structures and styles emerge. Some memoirs, such as Know My Name by Chanel Miller, use a personal narrative to give broader systemic and cultural critiques about the societal construction of justice and victimhood. Gisèle Pelicot’s memoir, A Hymn to Life , explores the nature of memory and reconstruction of the self after trauma, while Lucia Osbourne-Crowley’s I Choose Elena asks what medicine, trauma theory and literature reveal about the impact of trauma on the body and self. Writers such as Roxane Gay and Dorothy Allison have written more thematic and literary memoirs, where sexual violence is the originating wound but the writers then use essayistic and poetic writing to explore subjects such as embodiment, fatness, queerness, class and occupying space.
[ ‘I still get panic attacks’: Nikita Hand on impact of Conor McGregor trial Opens in new window ]
Nikita Hand ’s memoir Not The Perfect Victim, cowritten with Kathryn Rogers, acts primarily as testimony, recounting Hand’s experience of being sexually assaulted by Conor McGregor , the PTSD she suffered in the aftermath and her fight to bring McGregor to justice via a civil case when the DPP decided not to press criminal charges. As the media coverage of the case was so relentless, many details will already be known to many readers, but the description of all the ways the trauma and relentless reminders of McGregor impacted Hand’s daily life is affecting. What also emerges is the trauma inflicted by the trial itself, and the shame she internalised from the endless attacks on her character. “I was made out to be a liar, a loose woman, a bad mother, a habitual drinker, a drug taker and a homewrecker in the courtroom. The inference was always there below the surface: I was ‘asking for it.’”
The voice is clear, natural and readable, staying within the realm of personal testimony without explicitly veering into the realm of social critique or advocacy. This choice makes sense. Hand was silenced and intimidated, branded a liar and forced to contend with a man whose fame, immense resources and depressingly large international fan base gave him extraordinary power over the narrative. In that context, telling her story in her own words is a reclamation of voice, credibility and narrative power - and an immense act of courage.
Roe McDermott is an Irish Times columnist

title: Female Life on Planet Earth by Laleh Khadivi: Too many perspectives, not enough of an emotional thread
description: Despite qualms, the ending comes together beautifully
content:
In the run-up to the anniversary of her mother’s death, Heti, an Iranian-American woman, receives a photograph from an unknown source of her mother, veiled in black, holding an assault rifle to the head of another woman. A building burns in the background.
It’s enough to throw anyone into disarray. Tasked with organising the anniversary ceremony, she now searches to reconcile the woman in the photograph with the mother she thought she knew. In the process, she will have a series of conversations with friends, family and strangers, that will answer as many questions that they raise.
And so Female Life on Planet Earth develops its structure of loosely connected episodes in which Heti encounters a memorable cast of characters ready to speak at length about life in a sometimes funny, and often thought-provoking mannner, telling personal stories that highlight and explore the complexities and contradictions of womanhood, of what is expected of them and by whom, cycles of repression perpetrated by culture, lineage and society.
The voices are distinct, the settings richly rendered in a distant, dreamlike prose, and the characters Heti encounters are well drawn and memorable.
The novel is a chorus of perspectives, but Heti’s is kept at arm’s length. We don’t see what moves her from moment to moment, and the episodic structure reveals the artifice as each chapter starts and end in much the same way. Heti will meet a character, who will flood the pages with monologue that by the chapter’s end gives way to some form of enlightenment.
It is insightful to see where and to whom Heti offers her own perspective, but for much of the novel her role is that of receptacle. Her feelings about the photographs are presented in dialogue, but we are not privy to her inner reflections. It might leave readers wanting an emotional thread that would better serve the impact of the ending, which despite those qualms comes together beautifully.
When the anniversary ceremony is in full swing, Heti presents her family with the photographs of her mother. It gives way to a moving sequence of events, with each added voice lending a new perspective to a complicated historical and social tapestry where multiple truths exist side by side.
Djamel White is a novelist from Dublin. His debut novel, All Them Dogs, was longlisted for the Booker Prize 2026

title: Glorious Monsters by Martina Devlin: An engrossing novel about Frankenstein author Mary Shelley
description: There’s a breathless energy to this novel that celebrates real-life figures in all their genius and flaws
content:
It’s remarkable that Mary Shelley was only 20 years old when Frankenstein was published. The daughter of 18th-century feminist Mary Wollstonecraft, and the wife of the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, she was surrounded by books all her life but also by disappointment. Her husband was a philanderer, she suffered from depression and her future work was overshadowed by the incredible success of her debut.
Martina Devlin’s engrossing novel explores a period in 1819 when the Shelleys were living in Rome with Mary’s stepsister Claire, who had a child with Lord Byron and was now Shelley’s mistress. If this sounds like the summer from hell, add Amelia Curran, an Irish painter, into the mix, who finds their commune simultaneously repugnant and fascinating.
Devlin does a terrific job at describing the claustrophobic tensions that surround the quartet. Shelley believes in “free love”, Claire is persuaded to the idea, Mary is forced to put up with it, while Amelia observes in disapproval.
Each becomes interested in the historical story of Beatrice Cenci, who was executed for revealing her father’s incestuous and sexually abusive relationship with her. The two writers are drawn to telling her story while Amelia wants to paint her image. A clash of three art forms – poetry, prose and painting – then ensues, along with a competitive feeling over who might represent Beatrice’s story best. And when Lord Byron himself swans into Rome in his gilded carriage, it’s fair to say that matters grow even more complicated.
Glorious Monsters represents the third volume of Martina Devlin’s informal trilogy about female writers. The first centred on Edith Sommerville during the early 1920s while the second explored the romantic life of Charlotte Brontë. This is a worthy addition to that sequence, presenting Mary Shelley in such a rounded fashion – creative, frustrated, in love, in despair – that one reaches the end feeling the urge to read all the non-Frankenstein books simply to understand her better. (I happened to read The Last Man a few years ago and it’s an extraordinary book that should have a wider audience.)
Well researched, with vivid characterisation, there’s a breathless energy to this novel that celebrates the real-life figures in all their genius and all their flaws.
John Boyne’s latest novel is The Weight of Angels

title: Shauna Lawless: ‘This is always what I’ve loved about Irish mythology: the drama and the magic’
description: The author of historical fantasy on the latest book in her Gael Song: Era II series, the importance of research, and reasserting women’s perspectives
content:
In the fifth volume of the Gael Song series, the Anglo-Norman army is preparing to invade Ireland. While the Irish kings argue over how best to deal with this threat, Ireland’s immortals discover new magical powers.
The challenges always revolve around accuracy. If you’re telling a story set in the past, it must be authentic and feel like a real place, otherwise, what’s the point? I didn’t want my retelling of Clontarf or the Anglo-Norman invasion to be invented within my imagination. I wanted it to be as accurate as possible, but when you’re going as far back as the 10th century, this can be difficult. An author truly must become a detective. What style of houses did people live in? How has the language evolved between now and then? How was religion perceived and structured? Was there a legal system? What did people eat?
These questions are sometimes difficult to answer, and I’ve had to delve into archaeological digs, source documents, translations of source documents, monastic annals, historical textbooks, as well as my own site visits.
The opportunities, however, are immense. It’s an opportunity to explore humanity and how we’ve changed (and how we have not). I’ve had so many people read my novels and say it’s inspired them to read the historical sources themselves or to pick up historical nonfiction books – and I’m quite often told by readers that it has reignited an interest in Irish history and mythology that they’d had in childhood but let slip away. This is the greatest compliment of all.
I have five novels out in the Gael Song series. The sixth novel will be out next year, and these six books are split into two eras. The first era (made up of the first three books) is set around the Battle of Clontarf. The second era is set around the Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland.
The Children of Gods and Fighting Men is the first novel and begins in AD 981. Not only do I follow the historical timeline, but there are characters with magical gifts derived from Irish mythology. If you want to read my work, begin here.
It was honestly just the way the story came out. I suppose I was very influenced by the Irish mythology I had read. The Táin, for example, is a story about a battle between Ulster and Connacht, but within the story there are magical elements and characters. This is always what I’ve loved about Irish mythology: the drama and the magic. And so it felt natural for this story, a story which revolves around a historical battle, to contain elements of mythology and magic.
I was helped by the source documents too. Though they don’t often make it into textbooks; they are full of magical happenings. Gerald of Wales writes about werewolves and ghost armies roaming the forests. Njal’s Saga (an Icelandic saga that documents Clontarf) records incidents of scalding blood rain and of attacking flocks of ravens that seem to have claws and talons made of steel.
[ ‘Merging Irish myths and Irish history gave my story its soul’ Opens in new window ]
They are two magical tribes of people who lived in Ireland and they are documented in Lebor Gabála Érenn (also known as The Book of Invasions). The Tuatha Dé Danann have a range of magical gifts, and they include the Morrígan, Manannán mac Lir, the Dagda and Brigid.
The Fomorians are described as cruel and greedy, and they fight against the Tuatha Dé Danann. Their king, Balor, has one eye with seven eyelids that can destroy everything around him.
In Irish mythology, the Tuatha Dé Danann defeated the Fomorians at the Second Battle of Moytura. However, in my story there are some surviving descendants of each tribe who are still secretly at war with each other.
Very deliberate. Historical retellings are traditionally told via the perspectives of kings and warriors. I understand why – they are often the more active characters. However, that is only one way to view history, and the perspective of women needs to be brought to the forefront more often.
Brian Boru and the Battle of Clontarf by Seán Duffy; Viking Pirates and Christian Princes by Benjamin Hudson; Strongbow: The Norman Invasion of Ireland by Conor Kostick.
I have written three novellas. They are all prequel stories connected to the main Gael Song series. I’d recommend reading Dreams of Fire if you want to read a story about characters with mythological powers. Dreams of Chaos is about the early life of Brian Boru and his son Murchad, and Brian’s bid to become king of Munster. Dreams of Sorrow is a novella I would read after reading the second book in the main series, as it gives the backstory of a crow called Senna.
Book: May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry; film: The Odyssey ; podcast: The Ancients (for history buffs) and Plot Twist (by Victoria Aveyard and Soman Chainani for publishing and writing gossip).
Son of the Serpent is published by Head of Zeus

title: A most enjoyable memoir from a great sportswriter
description: The Lost Sportswriter: A Life Up Close with Irish Sporting Greatness by Vincent Hogan
content:
The great Irish-American journalist Pete Hamill said that at a certain point down the road of a long career, filing copy for newspapers felt like “writing while you are double parked”, and he eventually moved to writing novels.
After 43 years working as one of Ireland’s finest sportswriters, Vincent Hogan felt something similar, deciding to park his talent once and for all, and admitting in this absorbing, self-effacing and candid memoir: “For my entire adult life, deadlines had me in a headlock ... [when] I turned 60 I reached a point of realisation that this was something I did not want to do any more.”
A pity on one level; if Hogan was double-parked during his impressive career he, like Hamill, was passing his words through the window of an Aston Martin. A big sporting occasion meant seeking Hogan’s byline in the Irish Independent for the insights and instincts that made sports pitches sparkle from his craft.
Hogan was a deadline artist, and even if the existential dread of eternal deadlines may have forced his hand at times, he never let it show in his writing on big occasions; and there were plenty of those: Gaelic games’ grandest days, World Cups, prize fights, Olympics – too many to list fully here.
Some of the most intriguing parts of the memoir are when Hogan has justifiable pops at the shameful corporatisation and commodification of sports now, and when he recalls the good, the bad and the ugly that he met over decades of reporting.
It’s depressing to hear how the other side of the sports media coin (active athletes and officials) have all but ended their relationships with journalists nowadays; coverage is desired, but criticism is disavowed. No one wants to say anything of note any more, and Hogan says: “That the GAA has become the worst offender only deepens the frustration ... the sense of connection ... has withered into a kind of soulless, tiptoeing, faintly corporate exercise”. Strange days for an association based on its community connections.
Finishing this most enjoyable book, you sense that Hogan deserves his full-time whistle now – no more deadlines – and he should feel content in the realisation that this Lost Sportswriter (who helped write one of the great sports autobiographies with Paul McGrath) found greatness in his trade. His writing will be missed.
NJ McGarrigle is a journalist from Co Tyrone

title: How much is anyone to blame for anything? Kathryn Paige Harden seeks an answer
description: Plus a wonderful and unflinching book from Trish Bourke and an enlightening read from Christopher Insole on questions about God
content:
Aristotle tells us choice is the beginning of moral responsibility: we are answerable only for what we freely choose to do. It’s a simple piece of logic that has underwritten most jurisprudence and moral philosophy since. And yet, Kathryn Paige Harden argues, the more we understand behavioural genetics, the more problematic this thinking becomes. With stark statistics and fascinating cases, Harden suggests that an act of “sin” is driven less by choice than by genetic inheritance, upbringing and environment. This raises the question: how should we attribute blame when the conditions for wrongdoing begin before the perpetrator is even born? Beyond her rigorous research, Harden has a real talent for memoir, detailing with candour and vulnerability a personal reckoning with fate, fairness and blame. Ferdia Roche
[ Poetics by Aristotle: An essential read Opens in new window ]
The similarities between religions or cults is astonishing: complicated origin stories and regulations; fear or hatred of women; sexual abuse of minors by elders. Trish Bourke’s father, hungry for truth, opened the door to Jehovah Witnesses. Cue a life of surveillance, shame, guilt and threat of Armageddon. As her teens, pop music and hormones loomed, the religion’s embrace began to stifle. A man 20 years older groomed her, resulting in her banishment from home and the loss of her dream: university. A few years later, he raped her. She met other boys but relationships foundered, she “flitting from sharp wit to floundering despair”. A wonderful, unflinching book ending with this brave author thriving, and reconciling with her parents. Rosita Sweetman
Philosophy, as Socrates and Russell knew, is at its best not when providing answers but when discovering which questions are worth asking at all. Christopher Insole evidently agrees. His new book is an erudite exploration of “what is really going on, for and between you and me” when we speak about God. The motivation is simple: believers and atheists could argue forever over the existence of God and never reach a satisfying conclusion. So, what sort of questions can we ask about God that might help us better understand ourselves and others? Insole weaves through heavy hitters such as Spinoza and Kant with grace, delivering complex arguments in a tangible form and relatable context. An enlightening read for those of all faiths, or none. Ferdia Roche
[ Joe Humphreys: Why you should quit the coding job and retrain as a philosopher for hire Opens in new window ]

title: All About My Mother: An engaging account of family life from Diana Rigg’s daughter
description: Intimate family interactions explored in portrayal of an evolving mother/daughter relationship
content:
On the first page of this biography of her mother and fellow actor, Diana Rigg, Rachael Sterling recounts how at the kindergarten gates: “There was always something fishy about how other people’s dads looked at my mother: it was as if they were hungry or could smell something delicious. This, I later understood, was hot, unbridled lust.”
Here I must hold up my hand and plead guilty – except that I was not a 1980s dad, but a four-year-old boy in the 1960s, and her character Emma Peel in The Avengers was my first small-screen crush.
Early on, Stirling acknowledges that hers is not a detached narrative, and inevitably she is an unreliable narrator. Yet, while there is a jolly-hockey-sticks tone to some of the more intimate family interactions recounted here, this is a well-written and engaging read, which functions best as a portrayal of an evolving mother/daughter relationship.
Rigg emerges as a practical, ambitious woman with a strong work ethic tempered by a good sense of humour, who at the same time did not suffer fools, especially lecherous men who overidentified her with what remains her most famous role.
Indeed, one gets the impression that embodying Emma Peel was just another job, albeit one which represented huge opportunities as a career stepping stone. Equally, after her big-screen experience as a Bond girl making On Her Majesty’s Secret Service (1969), it would seem she never quite took film and television work seriously again, at least not in comparison with her first love, the theatre – outside of it being a lucrative way of paying the bills. Treading the boards, she went on to win acclaim in many productions, highlight hits being her starring turns in Medea and Mother Courage.
[ Octomum by Patrick Eades: third in The Moth Short Story Prize 2026 Opens in new window ]
A grande dame (and she really was a Dame, receiving the royal honour in 1994), she liberally dropped F-bombs, particularly on whippersnapper directors who had the temerity to try giving her notes.
It’s all acting, of course. Can you see the real Diana Rigg, as distinct from Emma Peel, or any of the other parts she played? Her daughter does, at least of the role Rigg played as her much-missed “Ma”.

title: Gathering at John McGahern’s grave became a ritual for my friends
description: Writing a biography of an author with quiet, unshowy charisma has been a humbling and exciting experience
content:
M y mother rang me to say that John McGahern had died. It came as a tremendous shock and I sat looking out at a flock of lapwings turning black and white in the air over the fields behind the house for a long time, trying to absorb what it meant. I did not quite know it until that day, but no public figure had ever made a greater impression on me, or ever would again. It was lunchtime on March 30th, 2006.
I thought briefly about going to the funeral but felt it wasn’t my place, despite having met McGahern on several occasions. I had been taught by him in my final term as an undergraduate at University College Galway in the spring of 1993 and had been struck by his quiet, unshowy charisma. We had shared a couple of pints of bitter in a pub by Preston railway station on a cold February night in 2003 after a reading at the nearby university. Me and a few of my students had driven up from Liverpool to hear what he had to say. When I insisted that he not buy another round for them he stopped me firmly me with his half smile, declaring: “I have more money than life.” It was an unforgettable phrase, made all the more so when I discovered later that he knew he was dying.
In the months that followed that reading I heard rumours that he was unwell with cancer but was then cheered by the news in the summer of 2005 that he would appear at Galway ’s Town Hall that September to read from Memoir. For anyone who was fortunate enough to get a ticket that night to a packed venue, it was a reading of extraordinary emotional depth, a mixture of levity and seriousness, looking back at a childhood punctuated by the death of his mother, when McGahern was just nine, followed by his move to the garda barracks in Cootehall to live with his eccentric and sometimes fearsome father. “It was a night,” wrote Keith Duggan (who had been part of those 1993 McGahern seminars in UCG) in this newspaper, “that most people in the attendance will carry with them through the remainder of their lives.”
I queued up to get my copy of Memoir signed along with what felt like the rest of Galway, but McGahern still made time to chat with me and share some wry memories of that winter night in Lancashire. This proved to be the last time we would speak.
In the months that followed his death I found myself preoccupied by the fact of his absence, by the painful idea that there would be no new work to read. That Faber have now reissued four of his books with newly commissioned introductions in addition to releasing a series of new audiobooks is a joy. Through that autumn of 2006, the feeling that I needed to visit McGahern’s grave to pay my respects nagged away at me. I contacted a few close friends to see if we might do something as a group and so, just before Christmas, some of us met up in Galway and drove to Leitrim. It was near sunset when I asked a man sitting at the bar of a Ballinamore pub if he could point me towards Aughawillan. “You’re lookin’ for McGahern?” he asked and pointed me on my way. It was as though he had been waiting for us.
Gathered at the grave in the gloaming, we chatted, caught up with each other’s lives. To meet up had become a rarity, as happens with all friends. Things were moving on. Some of us had recently become parents, others were thinking about it. We were silent for a bit, some blessed themselves, a cigarette was lit. Then we hit on for Carrick-on-Shannon. This visit to the grave on the hill in Aughawillan became a Christmas ritual.
Within two years of that initial graveside visit, I published my first essay on McGahern as part of one of four stylish Yearbooks edited by John Kenny at what was then called NUIG, having taught for a few days in Ballinamore library the previous June at a lively summer school dedicated to honouring the author’s work. Another essay appeared the following year as I became more interested in the oblique presence of WB Yeats across McGahern’s fiction. These essays soon grew into an idea for a book on influence and literary allusion and I passed a year among McGahern’s papers in Galway, spending most of my waking hours in 2013 reading McGahern drafts. The resultant book, Touchstones: John McGahern’s Classical Style, was published in 2016.
[ A Bigger Life by Louise O’Neill: A willingness and openness to surprise at its best Opens in new window ]
In July 2014 I was contacted by Madeline McGahern, the person who would become by far my most important source in assembling a biography. New York-born and two weeks her husband’s senior, she had already lived a fascinating life before ever meeting John in a Manhattan restaurant in 1966. I was happy to agree to lunch in Mohill to discuss a few ideas around her late husband’s work. By the end of that day, I had visited the McGahern home in Foxfield, been shown an impressive range of archive boxes and read a couple of McGahern’s letters. For someone like me, a devotee of the work who had begun to commit my professional life to its elucidation, these hours were a humbling and exciting experience.
On leaving that day, Madeline asked me to consider editing John’s letters. While I felt instinctively that it was a job I wanted to undertake, she was happy for me to think about it for a couple of weeks before getting back with an answer. My hesitancy was about the scale of the job – I knew this would be my life for many years to come and had to be sure. A fortnight later, I said yes.
Editing the letters took seven enjoyable years. There were frustrations: letters that could not be found, letters whose recipients did not wish to share them, glancing references that I never managed to trace. But for the most part the work was extraordinarily enriching. As the project grew, I became closer to Madeline and we began to work well together, with me sometimes visiting Foxfield over several days armed with hundreds of questions. This growing closeness and trust led, by 2017, to us tentatively talking about a possible biography, and in February 2018, over a London lunch with Madeline and McGahern’s agent, Bill Hamilton, I signed up to write the book.
For a few years, work on the Letters ran alongside thinking about the biography, occasionally drafting parts of a possible chapter and thinking hard about structure. I was fortunate to win a British Academy/Leverhulme Senior Research Fellowship for the academic year 2018-19 that allowed me to all but finish editing the Letters, which were published by Faber in 2021.
[ Exposed – The Scandals that Shook the Irish State: Drawing a line from the past to today’s hot issues Opens in new window ]
I was now ready to work full-time on the biography and had a lot of the hard lifting done. I had gone through the entirety of the McGahern papers (about 50,000 pages) in Galway courtesy of funding from the Leverhulme Trust and from the University of Galway’s Moore Institute. I had transcribed and annotated some 1,200 letters, interviewing dozens of figures known to McGahern over the course of his life, leading to an 850-page book. A subsequent visiting fellowship at the National Humanities Center in North Carolina gave me enough peace and solitude to bring the biography to completion over the 2024-25 academic year. It would be hard to overstate the importance of these various funding bodies who still believe in the humanities and in the need for long, silent contemplation.
I was acutely conscious that time was running out: most of those I wished to interview had been born in the 1930s and 1940s and that generation was rapidly disappearing. I never got to speak to Seamus Heaney, Edna O’Brien, Brian Friel. I cold called Richard Murphy in Sri Lanka on a Friday from my Liverpool office. He died the following Monday.
I did not expect many surprises about my quiet, private subject over the course of my research, and that supposition proved correct. I had learned about the existence of John McGahern’s son, Joseph, while editing the Letters, discovering that after McGahern’s decision to have no part in this boy’s life, the pair subsequently met on several occasions beginning in 1979 and running through to the 1990s. I was able to isolate the precise moment when McGahern and his son’s mother, Joan Kelly, first met, when she interviewed him for the Irish Press on the publication of his debut novel, The Barracks, in 1963. I did not find Joseph, despite being given several leads – all of them dead ends. And, frankly, I was torn about this whole aspect of the research, not wishing to impose on the privacy of people who had never asked to be discovered, whether that be McGahern’s son or his first wife, Annikki Laaksi, who I also failed to find despite a number of Finnish searches.
[ New poetry: ‘The most horrifying, exquisite and staggering poems I have ever read’ Opens in new window ]
I had better luck with unveiling other aspects of the life: one especially moving moment came when McGahern’s cousin, Liam Kelly, put me in touch with Fr Peter Dolan, a Leitrim priest in his 90s, who had spent much of his life ministering in Florida. Amazingly, he had been taught by McGahern’s mother, Sue, in Lisacarn national school and shared with me his vivid memories of her kindly teaching style.
A former student of McGahern’s, Shep Ranbom, who had been taught by the writer in Colgate University, New York, in the late 1970s and is now living in Washington, was another terrifically useful find, with a photographic recall of the writer’s preoccupations and classroom habits. Similarly, my correspondence over several years with Bob White, a former teaching colleague of McGahern’s at Newcastle University, and now a retired professor in Western Australia, allowed me to form a much clearer picture of the otherwise largely undocumented mid-1970s.
So what is it about McGahern that makes him such a worthwhile subject for biography? He lived an undramatic life after all: he never fought in a war, he didn’t win the Nobel Prize, nor score the winning goal in an All-Ireland final. He never broke the bank at Monte Carlo. But he worked hard, he thought carefully about who we are and why we’re here. He told the truth about things others would have preferred to stay hidden.
But it is, of course, for the unparalleled quality of his prose that he will be remembered. Hilary Mantel recognised him as “one of the greatest writers of our era”. Deirdre Madden has written about the fact that “there is almost something eerie about the way that McGahern’s language works. The words seem to disappear and you see the thing itself, as if unmediated.” Andrew O’Hagan comments of him: “McGahern is, in some way, in some priceless way, out on his own: his prose is richly odd, and has none of the mannered simplicity much-loved by the world’s Creative Writers. He is a writer with nerve.”
Over the course of my work on McGahern over this past 20 years I had cause to visit Paris on a number of occasions. John and Madeline spent many happy times there and it was where he wrote large sections of Nightlines and The Leavetaking in particular. When the beautiful old Irish College on rue des Irlandais was converted into the Centre Culturel Irlandais in 2002 it was to McGahern that the authorities turned for the opening. Around the corner is the magnificent Panthéon, celebrating the great figures of French civilisation, above its pillars as it peers down over rue Soufflot the words: “Aux Grands Hommes La Patrie Reconnaissante”.
McGahern thought the categorisation of writers under national tags an idle endeavour, but nonetheless he was Irish and his work can make us feel rightly proud. We have no Panthéon to honour him – he lies with his mother in the still beauty of an Aughawillan churchyard. But we have his books to which we can return alone and in silence. “For all art,” McGahern reminds us, “approaches prayer”.
John McGahern: A Writing Life by Frank Shovlin is published by Faber. Shovlin is Professor of Irish Literature in English at the University of Liverpool

title: Ten-man Bohemians survive late scare to win at Dundalk and go joint top
description: Colm Whelan and Ross Tierney put Gypsies in front, but late penalty for home side set up nervous finish
content:
Bohemians survived a late scare before holding out for victory against Dundalk at Oriel Park to move joint top of the SSE Airtricity Men’s Premier Division table.
A first-half penalty from Colm Whelan and a 68th minute strike from Ross Tierney looked to have Alan Reynolds’s men cruising to victory, but a Daryl Horgan penalty two minutes from the end, followed by the dismissal of Cian Byrne for a last-man challenge a minute later, set up a nervous finish, in which the home side hit the crossbar.
In the end the Gypsies held out for a huge win that sees them go second in the table, ahead of Shamrock Rovers but just behind St Patrick’s Athletic on goal difference.
The destiny of the title is now very much in the Phibsborough outfit’s hands as they face both of their Dublin rivals in their four remaining league matches. Before that, they have a chance of making the FAI Cup final, with a semi-final at home to Waterford FC to come next Friday.
Both sides had chances which never looked likely to beat either Enda Minogue or Paul Walters before Bohemians hit the front from the penalty spot on 26 minutes.
Referee Damien MacGraith initially saw no problem with Aodh Dervin’s challenge on Connor Parsons that saw the 25-year-old go down in the box, but he did point to the spot just seconds later after Dawson Devoy went down softly following a challenge from Mayowa Animasahun.
The Mayo official – taking charge of his first Premier Division game in almost two years – then angered the home support even more on 28 minutes when he opted to only book Parsons following a lunging challenge on Harvey Warren.
Bohs had the best chance to add to the scoreline before the break, but Senan Mullen couldn’t direct his header on target after being picked out at the back post by Tierney’s cross on the break.
The Louth men would register the first chance of note in the second half in the 58th minute as Gaxha found space on the right to pick out the inrushing Bobby Burns, but his effort was blocked by Patrick Hickey.
Bohs had been on the back foot at that point, but doubled their lead from their first corner of the night on 67 minutes. Jordan Flores’ delivery to the back post was headed back across goal by Hickey with Tierney flicking it to the net with his outstretched right foot despite the efforts of Horgan on the line to keep it out.
With the visitors passing up a couple of chances after that, the game looked to be petering out until Dundalk were awarded a spot kick which Horgan blasted home two minutes from the end after Norman Garbett had been fouled by Niall Morahan.
The visitors were then reduced to 10 with a minute remaining after Byrne took down Harry Groome, who was quickest to react to a panicked clearance from Walters.
From the follow-up free kick Burns then clipped the top of the crossbar as Bohs held out for what could be a huge three points.

Bohemians : Walter; Power (Morahan 81), Hickey, Byrne, Mullen (Diallo 62); Devoy, Flores; Tierney, Vaughan (Myers 62), Parsons (Rooney 77); Whelan (James-Taylor 62).

title: Ciarán Frawley’s stunning debut try helps Connacht pull off away win over Benetton
description: Irish province had the kitchen sink thrown at them against a stacked Benetton team
content:
Connacht rode their luck against Benetton, but dug deep and opportunistically struck at the death through a second, stunning try of the match by Ciarán Frawley on his debut. They could hardly have scripted it better. Some debut.
Against a stacked side who threw the kitchen sink at them in a helter-skelter game, this was a huge win for Stuart Lancaster’s gritty team
Despite the 8.45pm kick-off local time, the temperature was 19 degrees at the start of the game. Furthermore, the Azzurri football team were also reacquainting themselves with Zinedine Zidane in Paris for the first time since Italy won the 2006 World Cup final in Berlin.
Yet with a new stand being built at one end of the ground, both stands in the picturesque Stadio Communale di Monigo were fairly full with the well-heeled locals and a good smattering of Connacht fans. Rugby in Treviso operates in a bubble within the bubble of Italian rugby.
On a pristine pitch, neither side were inclined to pause for breath, with quick lineouts, off-the-top ball and an array of launch plays choreographed in preseason the norm in a blistering start.
Frawley’s first touch from one such launch play was nearly a 50:22 but Jacob Umaga did well to keep the ball infield when tackled by the chasing Finn Treacy.
Even so, Connacht soon struck off another lineout strike play, Cathal Forde trucking up after a good take by Sean O’Brien, before Cathal Forde went back against the grain. Sean Jansen was the link for Cian Prendergast to bump and swivel out of tackles by Umaga and Onisi Ratave to score. Surprisingly, Sam Gilbert missed the conversion.
Connacht’s biggest cause for concern was their scrum, which was under increasing pressure and conceded the first of a couple of penalties to the corner from which their defensive maul was splintered for Bautista Bernasconi to score.
Connacht’s response was swift, Gilbert and Mack Hansen each counter-attacking effectively before Hansen came off his wing to make further inroads. From the recycle, Frawley’s deft, no-look offload led to Francois van Wyk before O’Brien picked up sharply to score.
Again though, unusually for him, Gilbert missed another kickable conversion, and the scrum issues remained, albeit Prendergast disrupted another close-range Benetton lineout.
Instead, it was Benetton who struck off first phase from a lineout inside their own half, the impressive Alessandro Garbisi working a wrap in midfield and taking the ball to the line to dummy and line with Matt Gallagher, who splintered Forde and Frawley to put the talented Leonardo Marin away for a 40-metre finish. Umaga converted for the lead.
But a 50:22 by Treacy led to yet another try off a lineout strike move as Blade wrapped around Forde to link with Frawley, who sped through a gap before dummying one tackle and taking Umaga’s hit to score.
Gilbert converted, although Connacht finished the half with 14 men after Bernasconi theatrically clutched his face after a glancing clash of heads with Finlay Bealham. He also signalled for a yellow card, which Hollie Davidson duly brandished.
An even worse decision followed early in the second half when John Devine was harshly penalised for side entry, and the ensuing penalty to the corner led to another maul try for Bernasconi, Umaga’s conversion putting Benetton 19-17 up.
After Frawley misjudged a kick over the end-line from 40 metres out, a superb Sam Illo turnover was undone when Jansen’s offload eluded Devine and Hansen could not regather, forcing Gilbert to concede a five-metre scrum.
Somehow Connacht survived two scrum penalties and a host of resets, Frawley and Paul Boyle holding up Marin over the line, before a big scrum by Billy Bohan, Illo et al, and a brilliant tackle by Devine on Michele Lamaro forced a turnover to complete a fine night’s work.
Connacht’s replacements made a significant impact, none more so than hooker Eoin de Buitlear. Although it looked like their last chance was gone when he was tackled wide out and Mirco Spagnolo won a turnover penalty.
Indeed, nothing seemed on when Gilbert cleared from inside his 22 but the ball found grass and bounced high for Shane Jennings to jump, gather and offload inside for Gilbert. Connacht went wide off the recycle for de Buitlear to glide past one defender and line with Frawley, who showed real strength in fending the last tackler and score.
Gilbert missed another kickable conversion but atoned with a thumping hit on Odogwu which forced a spillage, which led to Connacht running down the clock and Colm O’Reilly to kick the ball dead. Some win.
Scoring sequence: 4 mins: Prendergast try 0-5; 12: Bernasconi try 5-5; 16: O’Brien try 5-10; 35: Marin try, Umaga con 12-10; 38: Frawley try, Gilbert con 12-17; HT: 12-17; 5 mins Bernasconi try, Umaga con 19-17;

Replacements: Jean Smith for Odogwu (34 mins), Mirco Spagnolo for Medrano (53 mins), Tiziano Pasquali for Ferrari (56 mins), Siua Maile for Bernasconi (60 mins), Ignacio Mendy for Otave (65 mins), Sootala Fa’aso’o for Marini, Andy Uren for Garbisi (both 71 mins).
