Liev Schreiber and Stephen Graham are the heavyweight names on opposite sides of the law in this dark crime series based on the bestselling Scandi-noir novels. For this series the action has been moved to the United States, where Schreiber is the former soldier Jonah Lynn, a homicide detective in Philadelphia who has decided to get away from the pressure cooker of big-city policing and move with his family to a small town in Pennsylvania. But if he thinks he’s in for a relaxing time, he’s in for a shock when the town is terrorised by a serial killer, Jurek Walter (Graham), who likes to bury his victims alive so he can taunt their loved ones. No prizes for guessing that Lynn’s own family is targeted by Walter, and he’s forced to make some agonising choices to save those he loves the most.

title: Extra Geography review: Nerve-rackingly brilliant boarding-school cringe comedy
description: Debut feature by Molly Manners culminates in an unforgettably spiky denouement
content:
Molly Manners’s auspicious debut feature follows Flic (Marni Duggan) and Minna (Galaxie Clear), two best friends at an English girls’ boarding school who decide that academic success is not enough: if they really want to impress the Oxbridge authorities, they need to become “worldly”.
Their solution is to fall in love. Their somewhat deranged plan, inspired by Shakespearean magic, guides them towards their bespectacled geography teacher, Miss Delavigne (Alice Englert). Let the games begin!
This curated romantic obsession is complicated by rehearsals for A Midsummer Night’s Dream, an interschool venture that brings – ew – boys into their previously closed world.
Brilliantly adapted by Miriam Battye from Rose Tremain’s 2007 short story, the film treats adolescence as a nerve-racking rollercoaster of exaggerated stakes and cringe comedy, allowing both girls to be selfish, mean, insecure and, simultaneously, endearing.
School, exams, romance and companionship become emotional landmines and existential crises. Flic and Minna are touchingly close but fiercely competitive, constantly measuring themselves against each other.
Minna’s self-pity when she is cast as a mound, while her best pal is named Titania, queen of the fairies, is matched only by Flic’s quiet smugness. Their friendship is simultaneously their bedrock and a gladiatorial arena for their insecurities.
Duggan and Clear blaze up the screen. Duggan’s Flic is anxious, intense and frequently uncertain; Clear’s Minna is more assured but equally preoccupied with status and approval. Their note-perfect performances capture the shifting balance between quasi-Sapphic intimacy and alpha-girl rivalry. The young Irish star Aoife Riddell, as a goofball chum, adds to the queasily unstable hierarchy of adolescent attachment.
Manners pitches the film just askew of realism. The historical period is deliberately fudged; this boarding-school setting has the same stylised quality as the institute in Enid Blyton’s Mallory Towers or Kazuo Ishiguro’s Never Let Me Go.
Andrew Commis’s cinematography zooms in on the physical details of teenage life, from bruised knees to shared dorms. The screenplay makes merry with the girls’ eccentric dialogue and games.
There are more prickles here than in the similarly themed comedies Booksmart and Mean Girls, and they finally coalesce into an unforgettably spiky denouement.

title: Targeted finance helps Kildare community expand its facilities
description: Leixlip Amenities Centre €3.3m extension an example of a committed local organisation, specialist sector expertise and long-term finance coming together
content:
A €3.3 million extension to Leixlip Amenities Centre has demonstrated how targeted finance, specialist banking expertise and a strong community organisation can combine to deliver new local capacity with lasting social value. AIB supported the project with €2.1 million in Strategic Banking Corporation of Ireland (SBCI) backed green finance over a 10-year term.
“We are delighted to support Leixlip Amenities Centre as it invests in modern, sustainable facilities for a growing community,” says Niall Morrissey, AIB head of business banking capital markets, Dublin South, West, Wicklow and Kildare. “This expansion shows what can be achieved when a committed local organisation, specialist sector expertise and long-term finance come together.
“AIB Business Banking works closely with customers to understand their ambitions and provide the funding and practical support they need to invest and grow,” he continues. “In this case, that investment will benefit not only the organisation and its members, but also the many clubs, families and community groups that rely on the centre. It is a strong example of how backing a local enterprise can help build healthier, more connected and more sustainable communities.”
Founded in 1981, Leixlip Amenities Centre is located at Collinstown, Leixlip, on a 15 hectare (38-acre) campus. Its catchment extends beyond Leixlip to Celbridge, Maynooth, Lucan and surrounding communities that continue to experience population growth and rising demand for sport, recreation and wellbeing services. Individuals, couples, families, sports clubs and community organisations use the centre throughout the year.
The centre offers a fully equipped gym, a high-performance training area and dedicated studios for exercise and wellness classes. Its indoor sports hall accommodates basketball, badminton, indoor soccer, gymnastics, martial arts and a variety of community activities. All-weather floodlit pitches support organised and recreational sport throughout the year, while meeting and activity rooms provide space for classes, events and local groups.
Long-standing links with local stakeholders, including Kildare County Council and major employers, strengthen the centre’s role as a venue for community engagement and active living. Beyond physical activity, the organisation has supported employment, training and skills-development initiatives, extending its social contribution to local people.
The organisation is overseen by a voluntary board, whose members contribute professional expertise and time. Its not-for-profit model means surpluses can be reinvested in facilities, services and community initiatives.
Membership now exceeds 2,600 people and is open to anyone aged 16 or over.
Designed to modernise the centre and accommodate growing demand from members, clubs and community groups, the extension has increased the premises by 82 per cent (1,772sq m) bringing the overall building to 3,933sq m, or approximately 42,300sq ft.
The centre sought term debt to help fund the extension, Morrissey explains. “We brought together our relationship management and sector teams, visiting the customer on site to understand the organisation, the proposed development and assist with guiding the application process.”
Following a series of meetings, site visits and the collection of the required information, AIB provided €2.1 million in SBCI-backed green finance over a 10-year term. “The funding was drawn in four stages as the development progressed, with support from a bank-appointed monitor,” he adds.
The completed extension has achieved a B building energy rating, reinforcing the project’s environmental credentials and helping create a more modern and efficient community facility.
“The phased structure matched finance to construction milestones, bringing oversight and certainty to a significant capital project while supporting the organisation’s long-term financial sustainability,” says Morrissey.
AIB Business Banking combines local relationship management with specialist sector expertise, helping customers assess opportunities, structure investment and navigate the lending process, he continues.
“Support can range from everyday banking and working-capital needs to larger investment projects, including facilities, equipment, expansion and sustainability improvements,” he explains. “For projects such as Leixlip Amenities Centre, on-site engagement allows our banking teams to understand the customer’s operating model, community purpose, sector dynamics and long-term ambitions, not simply the financial request.
AIB can also connect eligible customers with SBCI and government-backed finance, supporting investment in growth, resilience and the transition to more sustainable operations, Morrissey points out.
“Our relationship-led approach brings together financial analysis, sector knowledge and practical oversight. This can include phased drawdowns and project monitoring where appropriate. By backing viable organisations that create facilities, employment and services, business finance can have an impact far beyond the individual borrower, supporting stronger local economies, healthier communities and more sustainable regional development.
“Leixlip Amenities is an example of this multiplier effect,” he concludes. “Finance for one organisation has supported a larger, more energy-efficient facility that can be used by thousands of members as well as clubs, groups and partner organisations.”

title: Cornering the market for machines that make Nvidia’s AI chips
description: Christophe Fouquet has built Europe’s biggest business through a total monopoly over the most advanced chipmaking equipment
content:
Anyone worried about the short-termism of the technology sector, the bravado of so many tech bros and the easy prickability of the AI bubble should take a reality-check trip to Veldhoven, the unremarkable Dutch municipality that is home to Europe’s biggest company.
ASML, arguably the most consequential yet low-profile company in the AI ecosystem, employs nearly half the town (population: 47,902) and another 25,000 besides, doing the no-nonsense work of making and marketing the ever-larger machines that churn out ever-smaller computer chips.
As for the company’s chief executive, Christophe Fouquet, a tech bro he most certainly is not. This grounded French physicist is both a refreshing antidote to the salesmen of Silicon Valley and a more convincing advocate for the durability of technological advance.
The secret of this 42-year-old company’s success, Fouquet tells me in a nondescript meeting room at ASML’s headquarters, has been teamwork.
“If I had to summarise it, this has been a lot about extreme co-operation with the ecosystem, which is, first, our customers, but also our supply chain,” he explains, portraying ASML as the epitome of the collaborative European company, in stark contrast to a thrusting American one.
ASML, though still unknown by many people outside the tech sector, is an increasingly crucial linchpin in the global manufacture of chips. It has an extraordinary share of the market for chipmaking lithography machines, including a total monopoly on the most advanced extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, machines that are essential in the manufacture of chips for complex AI applications.
“I think there’s been a bit of a catch-up moment for a large part of the world, how a few companies have become critical for the future of the entire economy,” Fouquet says, pointing to the 88 per cent jump in the company’s share price over the past year and its market value of €591 billion.
He explains how investors enthused by Nvidia ’s AI vision for chip design first realised how vital Taiwan’s TSMC was to the manufacture of those chips. “And then they started to wonder, ‘Oh, by the way, how does TSMC make those chips?’ And then they realised that they used this EUV machine [and] suddenly everyone realises there is only one company, ASML, making those machines.”
In a competitive global economy, how on earth did the world allow only one company in a small Dutch town to become another AI choke point to add to the squeezes on data centre construction and energy supply?
“It’s complexity really,” Fouquet says, and I remember the jaw-dropping physics behind the $400 million (€352 million) EUV machine I had seen earlier in the day. The size of a double-decker bus, the machine prints circuits on to silicon wafers by firing 60,000 droplets of molten tin per second at them, using mirrors, lasers and short-wave light in a kind of vacuum-sealed nano-photocopier.
“Our customers were asking themselves ... ‘If I only have one supplier, am I okay?’ ... You could always say, ‘I’m going to get a second one’, but the amount of learning, the amount of investment and the amount of time you need to create that is huge.”
So trust is essential. “Our profit will grow with the [profits] of the industry but we are not going to abuse the situation.”
He admits “this is sometimes a difficult discussion” with shareholders: they might prefer the company to boost profit margins and put more debt on the balance sheet to accelerate investment and juice returns.
“We have that question every day ... But it’s not about the money, that’s the beauty of it. If I could put a few billion down and get another 20 per cent capacity, I would do that. But because of the supply chain, it’s far more complex than that.”
ASML’s supply chain is something else. Where a typical industrial product might have a few dozen suppliers, an ASML EUV has more than 100,000 parts provided by 200 principal suppliers and 2,000 companies overall. That, Fouquet says, might limit the ability to increase production rapidly, but it has been key to the company’s performance, as the science has become ever more elaborate.
“The more complex our products became ... the more advantage we got in terms of competitiveness. We could [develop] a lot faster than anyone else.”
Rather than trying to make everything itself, ASML outsources to the best manufacturer of each component – Zeiss for optics, Trumpf for lasers, VDL for mechatronics. This has helped it crack problems that its competitors, notably Japanese groups Nikon and Canon, have failed to, leaving them focused only on previous-generation deep ultraviolet (DUV) technology.
“We really needed the best brands across the world to get it done. I can tell you, if we had taken it upon ourselves ... to do everything on EUV, there is no way we could have done it.”
On occasion, when suppliers have looked vulnerable, ASML has bought them to safeguard production. Laser maker Cymer, acquired in 2013, was one example. More recently ASML has taken an 11 per cent stake in French AI challenger Mistral. But collaboration normally trumps acquisition.
There is one big fly in the ointment: the US government. Its ban on exporting EUV technology to China blocks ASML from selling its most advanced, most profitable products to an AI market that is second only to the US.
Although president Donald Trump has no direct jurisdiction over ASML (and is far less strict on Nvidia, which is allowed to sell its own EUV-made chips to China), the US has put pressure on the EU and on the Dutch government to impose an embargo on ASML – a source of clear frustration for the company.
“We understand that some technology may be restricted for obvious and legitimate concerns but if we go too far, we are going to create the opposite results of what we’re trying to achieve in the first place,” says Fouquet. Namely, he says, China will be spurred to innovate itself.
[ Rules of AI etiquette: be upfront, check accuracy, and don’t burden people with ‘workslop’ Opens in new window ]
Huawei recently emerged as a pivotal force in China’s development of DUV machines, for example. “If you over-restrict, you bring desperation,” he goes on, no longer mild-mannered but exercised now. “And desperation creates a huge appetite for people to accelerate their own technology and, potentially, at some point, become strong competitors.”
“It’s not a message to Trump. It’s a message to all people who make those decisions,” he says bluntly. “I think the Dutch government decides for itself what it wants to export, or not, to China. So that’s first a message to the Dutch government [and] a message for the EU.”
We have yet to discuss the most cliched question of all: whether AI – and thus the demand for the EUV machines and the other tech that underpins it – is a bubble ripe for bursting.
[ Google fights EU attempt to open Android to rival AI Opens in new window ]
Fouquet admits the markets are jittery. But he insists this is no short-term sugar rush: the AI “revolution” will endure. “I think the AI effect on society and industry is going to take 10 to 15 years. We’re only seeing the tip of the iceberg.”
ASML is confident its EUV technology will evolve over a similar period. Transistor circuits will be stacked on top of each other. Mirror apertures will be increased to focus light more precisely.
Fouquet presents himself as an accidental chief executive, a career semiconductor engineer who just grew with the industry. After studies in Grenoble and London, he worked in Israel and the US before landing at ASML 18 years ago and becoming the boss two years ago. (Having a physicist in charge again, after a financial manager, was a relief, confides one colleague.)
What tech is he most excited about now? “Humanoids will be among us ... a few years from now,” he says. “We are just at the beginning of that cycle. [They] will be doing some of the tasks we all hate doing – the gardening, or emptying the dishwasher.” (He skates over my protest that many people love gardening.)
But what about truly transformative inventions?
He is enthusiastic about the scope for “space tech” to revolutionise telecoms and energy production. But does he believe, for example, that nuclear fusion is finally within commercial reach? Are there lessons to learn from ASML’s success in developing a pioneering technology such as EUV after 20 years of trying?
[ Mark O'Connell: For 10 years, I’ve listened to people say AI will kill us all. Here’s what I think Opens in new window ]
“For EUV.” Fouquet explains, “ASML thought the need would be absolutely there, therefore we put all our energy in it, almost at some point putting even the company at risk to get it done. I don’t think that you have that in some of those technologies [such as fusion]. You need at some point people to believe that this is absolutely critical to get it done.”
And rather than “200 people or 200 companies” pursuing the idea with splintered inefficiency, you need a monomania, “[you need] concentration when it comes to technology.”
After all this highbrow talk, I’m curious to know quite how the ASML boss reconciles running a company in the vanguard of the AI revolution with being a father to six children.
Fouquet’s answer is refreshingly unscientific. “You could see the children as a burden,” he says. “But for me, it’s always made me stronger because the time I spend with my family, the time that I spend outside this office, is my rebalancing art ... It gives me joy, and I think coming to work with joy is a lot better than not.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Dublin Theatre Festival: Theatre for a great night out
description: Book your tickets now for Dublin Theatre Festival before it’s too late
content:
Looking for a great night out? Dublin Theatre Festival opened last week with a programme of home-grown and international productions that will make you laugh, surprise you and send you out into the night on a high. From the holy bangers and emotional belters of Lourdes! The Musical and the playful old Hollywood glamour of Radio Bette, to the wit and provocation of Heroes of Tomorrow and the warmth and humour of Let Me In, there are plenty of reasons to make a night of it at Dublin Theatre Festival.
The Gaiety Theatre from October 8th to 10th
Irish National Opera stages Testament at The Gaiety Theatre from October 8th to 10th, a haunting new opera by Tarik O’Regan with a libretto by Colm Tóibín, adapted from his novella The Testament of Mary. This new opera will delight fans of Tóibín and anyone curious about the secret thoughts of the mother of all mothers. The story unfolds in the final years of Mary, mother of Jesus; Mary is old and watched by three men, Paul, Marcus and John, who are determined to shape the story of her son. They want what is written to define the future. Mary wants only to recount what she witnessed and knows to be true.
The opera unfolds inside her memory. Past and present coexist, often without clear boundaries, as performers move in and out of roles. What emerges is a struggle between lived experience and the versions others seek to fix in words. The Gospels were written years after Jesus’s death, shaped by memory rather than direct eyewitness record. Testament imagines a figure who was there, who saw and remembered.
Civic Theatre Tallaght, September 25th to October 10th
A fun night out that will rip your heart out and leave you thinking for days. You’ll laugh, you’ll cry and you’ll emerge changed from this pilgrimage.
A musical about miracles and the people who stage them. On the day Matthew’s life is finally about to begin, he receives news that changes him forever. Forever and ever, Amen. Instead of facing reality, he runs to Lourdes, where faith is spectacle and a ragtag troupe of pilgrims are staging an amateur musical about St Bernadette. From the company behind the award-winning musical Oliver Cromwell is Really Very Sorry comes a new musical packed with holy bangers, emotional belters and a nun with a habit for DJing. Behind the irreverence and spectacle is a story with real heart. As Matthew tries to escape a reality he isn’t ready to face, Lourdes! The Musical explores faith, friendship, hope and the things we turn to when life changes in an instant. Funny, moving and unexpected, this is a pilgrimage with much more on its mind than miracles.
The cast brings together some brilliant musical theatre and performance talent, including Riain Cash, seen in the Tony Award-winning Fun Home at the Gate Theatre; Danielle James, award-winning actor, writer and performance artist and a finalist for the 2025 Women’s Prize for Playwriting; and Molly Lynch, whose musical theatre credits include Eliza Doolittle in My Fair Lady and Cathy Hiatt in The Last Five Years.
Project Arts Centre, September 25th to October 4th
When we can’t even agree on what’s true, how do we know what’s right? Who is a hero, who is a villain – can we even tell the difference?
Created by internationally renowned and award-winning Dublin-based company Brokentalkers in collaboration with acclaimed theatre-maker Andy Smith, Heroes of Tomorrow is a new work for theatre that considers some of the complexities and contradictions of living in the world today, and asks questions around the purpose of art and what part it can play.
Heroes of Tomorrow tells the story of celebrated artist Jan Hansen. Born in 1974 in Tromso, Norway, along with his partner Caoimhe Keenan, Jan has been resident in Ireland since 2020. His 30-year career has seen him win awards, exhibiting work worldwide at prestigious venues including Astrup Fearnley in Oslo, Tate Modern in London, The Guggenheim Bilbao and Imma in Dublin. Hansen is an artist who likes to explore what art is; ask questions of what it can do and where it can happen. Critics have written how his work recognises the humanity in a world of changing power and perception.
Hansen has recently been announced as the latest recipient of the Beyond the Future commission. Sponsored by a consortium of three global tech companies, they set it up “to support art that reflects their principles, values and intentions”. Hansen has announced that his work will be called The End of it All.
Considering art, power and protest, Heroes of Tomorrow is a story of possibility, connection and corruption. An epic tale of oil, trade, weaponry, technology, colony and creativity. Of Vikings, empire, exploitation and extraction. It’s a story of how we got here: a world where things feel a bit fragile and fragmented. Where it feels like there is a gentle rumble underneath everything.
And it’s hard to know what to do, right?
O’Reilly Theatre, Belvedere College, October 1st to 4th
Presented by Dead Centre & Théâtre de Liege and adapted by from the book by David Van Reybrouck, this production takes place from October 1st-4th at O’Reilly Theatre, Belvedere College. Dead Centre, one of Ireland’s greatest theatre companies explores the roots of power in Europe within a story that couldn’t be more relevant to the geopolitical mess we are in.
This is the story of something that came into existence by accident, was exploited, extracted from its place of origin, and sent to far off places. That something was a man called Joseph Rixen. This is also the story of zinc.
Over the course of his life, without ever moving, Rixen was a neutral, subject of the German Empire, resident of the Kingdom of Belgium and citizen of the Third Reich. He did not cross any borders, borders crossed him.
Blending the testimonies of five cast members from across Europe, with the extraordinary true tale of Joseph Rixen, ZINC will explore how the human body becomes a map – a site where the struggles of politics and history determine who we are.

title: Mixed messages unhelpful on hitting climate targets
description: Doubt over sustainability of microgeneration credits from solar panels may give consumers cause to pause
content:
The Green Party may no longer be in government, but taking steps to address climate change and meet targets set for the State by the European Union still ranks high among the stated priorities of the ruling Coalition.
Climate is mentioned 48 times in the 162-page programme for government, shy of education, housing and health but in advance of tourism, for instance, a sector long seen as key for the indigenous economy.
The Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland is targeting people aggressively with an advertising campaign promoting grants on offer to undertake energy upgrades for their homes.
And just this week, the Minister for Climate Darragh O’Brien announced enhanced retrofit and renewable energy supports, including a new €2,000 grant for people replacing an existing fossil fuel boiler.
For all that, the State is well behind its 2030 targets on climate emissions in areas including the number of electric vehicles in circulation and retrofitting. As of now, there appears to be little or no chance of meeting our commitments, a position that opens the State to financial penalty.
Part of the issue is that, for all environmental merits of home upgrades, the financial benefits for households are longer term. Crunching the numbers, many households struggle to see how they can afford such upgrades.
That is why the Government has been forced to increase the incentives available.
When it comes to solar panels, part of the attraction has been the ability to sell surplus power back to the grid. People can make up to €400 from this without any tax liability – and if the utility account is in joint names, that rises to €800.
However, when UCC academic Paul Deane flagged earlier this month that payments for selling power back to the grid would eventually be phased out, the Government very consciously refused to rule it out.
[ Benefits of Ireland’s solar boom should not go only to the big energy firms Opens in new window ]
Deane’s comments came as electricity suppliers failed to raise the amount they pay households under the microgeneration credit even as they announced chunky rises in the unit rate they charge those same households for energy supply.
A lecturer in clean energy futures, Deane knows the area but if the Government is serious about incentivising retrofitting, raising a doubt on a benefit of up to €800 a year can only be counterproductive.
The department may say, as was reported, that the main bene­fit of installing solar panels “is based on the bene­fits of self-consumption, rather than any addi­tional revenue from selling sur­plus elec­tri­city to the grid”, but as the Government prepares to announce this year’s budget, it should bear in mind that any doubt on the financial return from retrofitting just undermines the policy it wants to promote.

title: Blackthorn restaurant review: Much skill on show at this stylish Galway bolthole
description: Chef Nathan Hindmarsh has an adventurous style that pays off, helped by his Mibrasa charcoal grill
content:
I’m standing at the reception of a Galway hotel that can’t find my weekend reservation – cue panic because we’re travelling with our dog and not every establishment is pet-friendly. There are dramatic mentions of driving back to Dublin , but eventually we think of The Twelve Hotel in Barna and, happily, it can come to our rescue. And in even better news, it can slot us in for dinner at its Michelin-listed Blackthorn restaurant without a reservation.
Located a stone’s throw from the sea, the family-owned Twelve will shortly celebrate its 20th birthday. Over the years, it has received many restaurant awards but the last time I dined upstairs at The West restaurant, the room felt dated and out of sync with the adventurous cooking of chef Nathan Hindmarsh.
Now renamed Blackthorn in homage to the family’s tradition of making walking sticks, the restaurant has received a glow-up. Elegant mid-century style chairs and tables are arranged around the room with two large live edge (cut from a solid tree slab) tables in the middle. The room is bright, with a moody focus wall drawing attention to the wine display. Suspended wicker lampshades and potted plants round out the relaxed natural feel. I can feel my shoulders relaxing.
The menu is printed on rough-textured paper, which long-time restaurant manager Fergal Guiney tells us is studded with wildflower seeds. The dog drama has meant we’re eating late, so we decide against the six-course chef’s menu (€100) and opt for a la carte instead. This involves choosing from three raw dishes, three starters, and seven “embered” mains including a 30-day dry-aged Hereford sharing côte de boeuf.
To begin, sous chef Gabriela Torres delivers a trio of bites – croustade of Killeen cheese, duck liver parfait sandwiched between dainty sablés, and an intense tartlet of cod’s roe and Bullaun Ark herbs. They’re a solid start to the meal even if the croustade could have been crispier.
A glossy Parker House roll is torn apart and laden with cultured butter, which is made in house over two days using Cuinneog milk. Dainty wholemeal scones release warm nutty notes of Kylemore cheese, pairing well with fresh bright green herb butter. Somebody in the kitchen clearly likes butter and who am I to argue?
No self-respecting restaurant is without oysters these days and two plump Connemara specimens are topped with tangy buttermilk dressing popping with Ibérico ham and trout roe (€10). A ribbon of kohlrabi conceals a generous mound of Inis Mór crab (€19), surrounded by a fragrant tom yum sauce whose subtle spiciness marries well with the sweet fresh meat. Hidden underneath, I find a single smoky prawn.
If that prawn hinted at open-fire cooking, then my main course trumpets its presence beyond doubt. Wild seabass (€44) has a crunchily delicious salted skin giving way to soft white flakes. Along with a silky lemon verbena beurre blanc, it is delicate and precise, a contrast to the rustic large South Atlantic wild prawn, the likes of which I see more often in Portugal than in Ireland.
Given the presence of the Mibrasa charcoal grill in the Blackthorn kitchen, I had expected Connemara lamb to arrive perhaps as a grilled rump. Instead, it took a sharp swerve into classic cooking, served as two impeccable slices of ballotine with a refreshing cucumber raita and a shiny, sticky demi-glace sauce that has me ‘swiping my fingers on the plate’.
Mains are accompanied by a little pot of boulangère potatoes and grilled potatoes but for me, the stand-out is an intriguing bowl of charred Padrón peppers, courgette flowers and green beans. Hindmarsh certainly has a penchant for mixing things up, fusing open fire with French techniques honed at the Chesterfield Mayfair Hotel and Restaurant L’Audacieux in Paris.
A wine pairing is available for €75 (€90 with the chef’s menu) but I’m lured in by the wine list, which is as strong as ever. It’s organised by grape rather than region and, as a result, guides the diner down paths they might not have considered. A Chardonnay fan, I choose a bottle of Slovenian Gasper (€42), whose fresh minerality delivers pleasant smoky notes against the food. A glass of herby Magnolia Montepulciano (€11) goes well with the lamb.
[ The best places to eat and drink on a weekend break in Galway Opens in new window ]
For desserts, Guiney ignites a shot of Diplomático rum over my lemon verbena baked Alaska, flames dancing blue before quieting. It’s good but I feel a bit of residual alcohol heat and I prefer my companion’s fresh summery Wexford strawberries with sheep’s yoghurt and basil (both €13) before finishing with petit fours.
After dinner, we roll upstairs to our snoring dog, the earlier panic forgotten thanks to the smooth service and good food. Guiney and Hindmarsh are very much at home in their new setting, working as a formidable team. And even though the main course prices initially caused me to raise an eyebrow, the fact that all bites, breads and sides are included means that I really feel as if I got value for money by the end.
The verdict: Skilfully executed modern cooking with an elegant kiss of fire
Food provenance: Dexter beef from McGeough’s Butchers Oughterard, lamb from Gilligan’s Farm, pigeon and game from Gourmet Game, vegetables from Burke’s Fruit & Veg and Ballymakenny Potatoes, seafood from Glenmar Shellfish and Moycullen Seafoods, wild sea bass from the English Channel
Vegetarian options: None listed, but can be easily accommodated. Options include wood-roasted girolles and hen of the woods, or St Tola goat’s curd agnolotti with Hare Tree Irish truffles and aged Killeen cheese
Wheelchair access : Fully accessible, with an accessible toilet

title: Event guide: Tim Wheeler, Kate Nash and the other best things to see in Ireland in the week ahead
description: October 3rd-9th, 2026: Our pick of music, art, theatre and more coming your way
content:
When he isn’t throwing shapes on stage with a Gibson Flying V guitar as a member of the punk-pop band Ash, Tim Wheeler is a deft, sensitive songwriter blessed with the ability to create lasting and memorable tunes out of thin air. On his debut solo tour of Ireland, Wheeler will be delivering acoustic versions of some of Ash’s sterling guitar-pop songs as well as digging into the band and solo archives for a few long-lost nuggets. Also Saturday, October 10th, John Lee’s, Tullamore, Co Offaly, 8pm, €26.50, leesbar.ie ; Sunday, October 11th, Grand Social, Dublin, 7pm, €27.80, thegrandsocial.ie .
The Icelandic musician and composer Ólafur Arnalds returns to Ireland for three shows, subtitled Falling Apart Together, that, through almost 20 pieces of music, attempt, he says, to loosen “the distance between us”. With an ensemble of musicians plus an immersive visual production, Arnalds presents a hybrid concert featuring fusions of electronic and neoclassical music.
The London-Irish singer-songwriter Kate Nash has been popping over to Ireland more often than usual this past year, and now we know the reason: she has been recording her forthcoming album, Cailín, at Stiúideo Cuan, in Spiddal, Co Galway. In February she’ll follow the album release with a more extensive Irish tour. Before that, this is a golden opportunity to see the acerbic performer play in small venues. Alongside a batch of her pop gems, expect a tin whistle to make an appearance, as well as her fine cover version of Sinéad O’Connor’s song Famine.
One of Ireland’s most admired storyteller songwriters embarks on a rare nationwide tour in support of Oceanic, his eighth studio album, which is released on Friday, October 16th. Expect a bundle of new material alongside fan favourites such as Galileo, Big Bad Beautiful World and Caterpillar DNA. Also, Saturday, October 10th, Town Hall, Westport, Co Mayo, 8pm, €38, westporttheatre.com ; Saturday, October 17th, Vicar Street, Dublin, 8pm, €45, ticketmaster.ie ; Thursday, October 22nd, Spiegeltent, Wexford, 8pm, €35, lantern.ie . Touring throughout November.
Referencing a popular 19th-century New York vaudeville act featuring songs and sketches, Muldoon’s Picnic sees the US-based Pulitzer Prize-winning Irish poet Paul Muldoon preside over an array of prose, poetry, song and banter with the Horslips members Jim Lockhart and Barry Devlin, the writer Anne Enright, the author and film-maker Neil Jordan, the sean-nós singer Iarla Ó Lionáird and the songwriter and performer Paul Brady.
Celebrating its 30th birthday, the festival this year features dance, circus, theatre, music, literature, visual art and pop-up shows. Highlights include Shapeshifters (from Saturday, October 10th, until Sunday, October 18th, Outset Gallery, various times, free), Shades of Shadows (from Wednesday, October 14th, until Sunday, October 18th, An Taibhdhearc, various times, €15) and Bake, an outreach show touring to Galway school halls.
When Ryan Hennessy isn’t bouncing across stages, taking off his top and launching into any one of the band’s impressive list of hit songs as the lead singer of Picture This, he sits in quiet spaces and writes poetry. His first collection, Syncopated Blue, was published by Gill in 2021; his latest collection, In Another Lifetime, is published by Faber. Hennessy will read from his new collection and, we will safely bet, have an acoustic guitar close at hand.
Representing a more experimental facet of her work, Elizabeth Magill’s new exhibition features smaller-scale works that investigate, she says, “the tension between abstraction and observation”. Most of the paintings are named after lyrics from Northern Sky, the song by the late English musician Nick Drake. To coincide with the exhibition, a new monograph, featuring text by the writer Colm Tóibín (“There is much ambiguity and strange, coiled beauty”), will be available.
Building on the legacy of the Indie Cork film festival, which was shuttered last year, Gearr will feature the work of Irish and international short-filmmakers. Categories include thriller, comedy, horror, noir and sci-fi. The festival will close with the presentation of four awards: best international short, Blacknight award for best Irish short, best made in Cork, and spirit of Gearr.
