title: Munster’s Jack Crowley focused on rest and reflection amid uncertain injury lay-off
description: Outhalf has been dealing with a lower limb vascular injury since the end of last season
content:
There was no moment of pain to signify the damage. Jack Crowley went to run. He couldn’t. He went to do some kicking. He couldn’t. It took a while before the prognosis was replaced with a diagnosis of a lower limb vascular injury. That hiatus between not knowing and knowing was the excruciating part.
“It could be two things,” he said. “It could be an accumulation of time and wear and tear, or it could have just been a once-off incident. But, I suppose, we weren’t aware of either, and it just came about.”
“I tried to go out to run and kick and I couldn’t. It was very evident straight away, but (not) evident walking around.”
Wearing his Munster clobber in the Ascil building in Lyons – the French city will host the 2027 Champions and Challenge Cup finals – he looked in good nick, ready to play. Except he can’t. A recent statement issued by the province clarified he wouldn’t feature again until the new year. Crowley confirmed that timeline hasn’t changed.
His last match was against Benetton in April. He had been due to feature in their home game against Ulster the following week but withdrew during the warm-up, and three weeks later was pencilled in to play against the Lions, but again was a late withdrawal. The jig was up. He’s tried to remain stoic. Meditation helped him cope.
Rest is the prescribed cure. Upper body weights are permitted, but no running. He spoke about the advice to “take things slow,” week to week, but “in terms of healing, it’s going pretty quick.” The most salient marker will be when he sets foot on a pitch again in earnest. That’s still some way off.
“It’s frustrating, but it’s also part of the game. I’ve been very fortunate up until now that I haven’t had any serious injuries. Everyone gets [one] at a certain point. Now, it’s my turn. It’s just dealing with that.
“I suppose when there’s a period of uncertainty and nothing’s known, everything can be thrown into the mix. It is the natural tendency to question everything when something goes wrong. There was uncertainty, 100 per cent; I’ve had no problem in saying that.
“If it was a known [issue], it would be a lot easier to diagnose quicker and stuff like that. Who knows what way my body will respond. That’s just the nature of it. So right now, I don’t know, being perfectly honest with you. I don’t know what complications could come, but like anything, you cross that bridge when you come to it.
“I’m currently in a period of just rest. It’s just allowing everything to heal, to get strong. I can do upper body work, but in terms of running and stuff, that’s not happening right now. The thing is, if it was a 12-month injury, it’d be a different story. It’s just that we didn’t know the timeline.”
His absence from the match environment has reminded him of how much he loves the sport, and it has also fostered a little introspection.
“I’d be a deep thinker in terms of utilising time and space as best I can to just be a better person day in, day out. A period like this has given me time to reflect on that. Ultimately, that’ll hopefully make me a better team-mate and a better person.”
He still prowls training sessions, watching, chipping in with ideas and advice. He speaks out when the need arises. He views it as an important role to fulfil as a senior player, and he’s taken a pastoral role with Tom Wood and Charlie O’Shea.
“They’re two unbelievably talented young players,” he said of the two young outhalves. “Whether I was playing or not in training, in terms of environment, it’s massive for lads that have experience to help lads out. But equally, it’s also up to young lads to go about asking people how they can improve. It’s a two-way street.
“And the two lads have been brilliant. Likewise, you learn something from them as well. We’re not always right, it’s just our opinion. It’s been really cool seeing their evolution. Obviously, Tom’s unfortunately injured but, again, I’m sure he’ll come back very quickly.”
But he’s careful not to be a hurler on the ditch.
“You don’t want to say, ‘oh, you should have done this; it’s clear as day, you should have picked this opportunity or moment’. Hindsight’s brilliant, and it’s about just delivering in the way that it’s compassionate, not that I would do it better,” he said.
“It’s from a place of going, ‘oh, maybe, look, this is where I’ve struggled in the past’. Or ‘I found seeing this space difficult’. And it’s just sharing your perspective. The most important thing is if the person wants to hear it or not, it’s only if it’s invited.
“We have a brilliant group that is receptive. But, at the same time, when you’re a leader in a group and something needs to be said, you say it. That’s what standards are about.”
Crowley was asked about criticism from former players regarding governance issues at Munster.
“There’s a review going on. There’s been trust in that and the processes that will come of it. As a playing group, it’s solely around how we can deliver performances consistently.
“And you can’t do that if you’re putting your focus elsewhere and expending your energy in areas that you can’t control. It’s important – and we have it – the sense of connection and moving forward together. We’ll see what will come of that.”
Hopefully he’ll be back sooner rather than later to add his weight to that forward push for both Munster and Ireland.

title: Ireland goalkeepers were not spoken to about Israel matches, FAI tells committee – as it happened
description: Safeguarding issues also on the agenda, with politicians pressing the association on the level of Garda vetting among soccer referees
content:
And with that, the meeting ends. Some interesting lines out of it, not least the claim that the Ireland manager had a one-hour sit-down with Gavin Bazunu in August. And also John Martin’s admission that nobody spoke to the goalkeepers before the Israel game. This was not the impression given on Saturday in the various media dealings with the Irish management.
Alan Kelly asks why there was two votes by the players. Cooke says it was to get greater clarity around the decision. “It was felt by everyone in the room that greater clarity was needed.” Kelly says a vote was taken, ye knew the position of the players, why do a second vote?
“The view in the room was that greater clarity was needed. The manager, the captain, the players, ourselves, it was felt by the people in the room that a second vote was required.”
“The players took the vote. And it was felt that now with those numbers, in light of knowing the amount of people who were against playing the game, would it affect anyone’s decision? We wanted them to be armed with full information so that we could have a confident read on the room before we made our decision. And again, we will own that. We took the decision to play the game.”
Kelly: “Was the much of a change in the second vote?”
Courell: “We’re not going to get into that.”
Peter Cleere asks what they would change about how they handled everything. Courell speaks for a while about how difficult the situation and says that when they reflect on it in a few weeks, they might find things they would have done differently. But he says he suspects not much could have changed where things ended up.
Daniel Ennis criticises John Martin for not making the Irish players aware of the record of racism from Israel fans. He gets Courell to agree that Israel fans have a history of racism, as adjudicated by FIFA. But Courell does not agree that the reaction of the FAI should be to not engage with the opposition country.
Courell asks to respond to Byrne’s accusations about a lack of leadership from the FAI and the claim they’ve brought shame on the country. “We are all here to do our best for Irish football. I strongly reject any claim that we have brought shame on the game.”
"You're a football woman. You know the game." FAI CEO David Courell responds to Sinn Fein TD Joanna Byrne after expressing a belief that the organisation has done lasting damage to Irish football by playing Israel. pic.twitter.com/IVlnkzD6lV
Joanna Byrne asks Martin about the issue of whether any players were threatened by their agents about playing the game. Martin replies that no, as far as he knows, that didn’t happen.
Byrne asks Courell about the Adam Idah incident and Courell says he understands the players are reviewing the video.
“Considering the racism incident, would you not go to ask government to underwite any financial fall-out from not going ahead with the fixture?” Courell replies no, the decision has been left to them and they have taken it.
Malcom Byrne asks about the friendly against Qatar in the context of human rights abuses there. Courell says obviously the FAI considered it but there were certain requirements for that window. in the hope of Ireland being at the World Cup, he says they had to play a team that was going to the World Cup, which narrowed the field.
Evanne Ní Chuillin asks if there have been any investigations into underage coaches this year. Aoife Rafferty says there has been one but can’t comment any further.
The questions go back around. Barry Brennan asks what the decision would have been had the players’ vote gone against playing. Courell says it wouldn’t have been possible to play without 11 men. Also says there is no plan for a vote this week.
Richard Boyd Barrett’s turn. He starts of talking about genocide and it being the opposite of what sport represents. He quotes the Israeli captain as being proud of their state and their soldiers. “Is that not a reason, as well as the abuse that was thrown at our players and the chants for the IDF, is that not a reason to reconsider playing the second game?”
Courell: “I think we’ve been clear throughout that there are many elements of this situation that we are uncomfortable with. I know people want us to be a vehicle for change but we are charged with the future of Irish football. As things stand, I don’t see us changing our position on playing the second game.”
"I know people want us to be a vehicle for broader statement and change but the reality is we are tasked to do a particular role to protect the interest of Irish football." FAI CEO David Courell explains why the Republic of Ireland will play the second match with Israel. pic.twitter.com/vzncAJf8xq
Murphy asks why Hallgrimsson retracted his use of the word genocide in his press conference. “There are multiple viewpoints on this particular topic, including with our own dressing room.”
Paul Murphy’s turn now. He pays tribute to Gavin Bazunu. Then he asks Courell if he will say that Israel are committing genocide in Gaza. Courell says he’s not qualified to adjudicate that.
Garry Gannon is up now. He asks if anyone from the FAI threatened defamation proceedings against Virgin Media. Paul Cooke answers that he contacted Virgin looking for clarification but never threatened defamation proceedings.
Ruth Coppinger is up now. She accuses the FAI of deceiving people, now that is has emerged that nobody spoke to the goalkeepers. Why was Gavin Bazunu excluded?
Martin: “He wasn’t excluded. The players went back to their rooms and spoke to loved ones. They came back and took a vote. Gavin didn’t take part in the vote. We assumed his vote was a no vote when we tallied the votes.”
Kelly: “At any point did you go to the government and ask them would they underwrite any shortfall as a result of not playing the matches?”
Kelly: “You said David that there was a consensus the day before and then this one player changed his mind. You said the manager had an hour-long chat with that player in August. But in a press conference on Saturday, the manager said he didn’t speak to the goalkeepers.”
Courell: “That was in terms of the call-ups. The meeting in August was a general catch-up.”
Kelly: “In the week leading up to this, was there an individual check-in with each of the players.”
John Martin: “Heimir is on record as saying he spoke to the outfield players.”
Kelly: “So who spoke to the goalkeepers?”
Martin: “Truthfully, it appears nobody talked to the goalkeepers.”
"Who spoke to the goalkeepers?" "Truthfully it doesn't appear like anyone spoke to the goalkeepers." Deputy Alan Kelly TD asks FAI Director of Football John Martin about individual consultation with Republic of Ireland players prior to the Israel game. pic.twitter.com/YvO04dpk6A
Alan Kelly is up now. Says the manner in which Uefa dealt with the Israel game is a stain and unacceptable.
Kelly asks Courell about the idea of pivoting from child to adult safeguarding. Courell seems surprised by the word pivot.
Kelly reiterates that he can’t understand why Courell won’t answer certain questions, given that other FAI officials are happy to do so.
Senator Mark Duffy is up now. He asks about the mental health of the Ireland players after the weekend. Aoife Rafferty says the FAI is acutely aware of the need to support them. She cites the medical team and the addition of a clinical psychologist to the staff for this window.
John Martin says the group dynamic is exceptionally strong. Says that if anyone saw the departure lounge in Hungary on Sunday night, they would see a group that is together.
Out of the clear blue sky, Carrigy asks if there will ever be an all-Ireland league. John Martin says it’s not on the agenda in the short-term.
He asks Courell a general question about safeguarding and Sport Ireland about FAI governance and any concerns they might have. Courell welcomes the opportunity to filibuster for a while.
Michael Carrigy (FG) is up now. He’s taking an interminable amount of time to get to a question. We’ll let you know if he does.
This is interesting claim. Courell says that the player - Bazunu - had a one-hour sitdown with Heimir Hallgrimsson in his club in August to talk about the Israel game. Up to now, we were under the impression that he hadn’t been asked before the camp at all.
Peter Cleere is up now. He asks Courell about players being asked before the camp whether they wanted to play. Courell says 13 or 14 were asked immediately after the draw and they said they’d go by the wishes of the FAI. Around 25 players were asked over the summer as well. They had meetings with the players and there was consensus that the games would be played.
Cleere then has a bit of a kerfuffle with FAI lawyer Deirdre Ardagh over garda vetting.
Deputy Peter Cleere, chairman Alan Kelly and FAI general counsel Deirdre Ardagh clash over coach garda vetting and use of the word 'soundbite' #rtesport pic.twitter.com/sc7CThBnTk
Ennis asks Cooke about is comment that the FAI handled the situation quite well. Cooke goes back to the 68 per cent and stands by his claim.
Ennis asks if the numbers from the straw poll had been flipped, would the FAI have called the game off? It’s an interesting question but Courell swerves it.
Daniel Ennis subs in for Sinead Gibney. He asks about the vote between the players on Saturday morning. Who called it?
“It was the players themselves. Maybe including the staff. Certainly not the executive.”
Ennis: “Nine players did not want to play...”
Courell goes into the timeline again, rehashing what people mostly already know.
“One player said: ‘I’ve changed my mind, Gaffer.’ The players had a straw poll. That was not what decided whether to play the game. The FAI decided to play the game.”
Byrne asks Courell where the concerns for player welfare were over the weekend.
Courell: “I note that you were watching from home. The reality was that in the environment where we were, player welfare was paramount. No player travel alone... We are very satisfied that we wrapped around the player in question [Gavin Bazunu hasn’t been named here but it’s accepted that’s who he’s talking about]”
Heated exchange between Sinn Féin deputy Joanna Byrne and FAI president Paul Cooke regarding the handling of the first fixture against Israel #rtesport pic.twitter.com/ONtbdOHBQm
Cooke takes the opportunity to talk about the 68 per cent who voted for the game to go ahead. It’s an easy out for him. She asks him where his leadership was over the weekend. He falls back on the vote.
Cooke replies that he was there, he did an interview after the game, as he did after the EGM. Byrne starts talking about bubbles and ivory towers, letting Cooke slightly off the hook here. She’d be as well to make him answer a question.
Byrne asks Paul Cooke of he was “for real” in saying he thought the FAI handled the events of last week quite well.
Joanna Byrne: “I do believe there have been catastrophic failures from the FAI in terms of leadership over the past few months.”
The issue of sanctions for missing the game comes up.
Courell: “The challenge we have with regards to Uefa’s decision making on a rule breach is that it’s subject to a disciplinary hearing. So if I talk to someone in Uefa and ask what the probably sanctions are, they can’t say because they don’t know. It’s an independent committee who decides.”
Back to Israel. Courell says the FAI have had upwards of 20 meetings with Uefa in the past year about the game.
“It’s fair to say Uefa are sympathetic to the situation we found ourselves in. But they have to make their decisions int he context of the 55 members of their organisation.”
FAI chief executive David Courell describes the level of communication with UEFA over the Israel issue #RTEsport pic.twitter.com/GruVgZSazz
Byrne returns to a question posed by Ní Chuillin regarding his refusal to answer questions about historical abuse cases. Other FAI officials have answered questions on it at past hearings but Courell continues to say he doesn’t want to prejudice Garda investigations. Chairman Kelly takes a dim view of his stance.
Malcolm Byrne is up now. He asks Sport Ireland and the Department of Sport if they have governance concerns about the FAI and both replay that the FAI have made improvements.
Ní Chuillin: “There are three concerns so far in this meeting.”
Courell: “I’m not sure what the concern is.”
Ní Chuilinn: “The concern is that a man in a towel and nothing else came into the team room. The concern is that the Ireland women’s team, with quite a few young players, were stalked and harassed and the police were called. The concern is that Aoife Rafferty has no memory of what must have been a quite striking conversation.”
Ní Chuilinn brings up an incident in Budapest in 2023 when the Ireland women’s team were stalked and harassed and police were called.
Aoife Rafferty says she’s aware of the incident.
Ní Chuilinn: “Do the women’s team have security with them on international trips?”
Courell: “They do. It was doubled in 2025.”
Evanne Ní Chuilinn asks if any coaches who find themselves officiating at matches might not be Garda-vetted. John Martin says he doesn’t know but will find out.
Senator Alyson Comyn is back to safeguarding and asking about referees. She presses John Martin about a guarantee that all referees from the past four years have been fully vetted. Martin says he can’t say it for certain.
Courell: “This is a very specific area. We came in here expecting to answer questions on one area...”
Alan Kelly: “This is about safeguarding. This is part of it.”
Courell: “We can give a guarantee that all 1,400 referees in the system are fully vetted.”
Courell: “I would have to revert on that.”
Brennan: “The players have been thrown under the bus by the FAI. And the FAI have been thrown under a juggernaut by UEFA. Why is that?”
Courell: “It’s simply because Uefa is a 52-member organisation. Sentiment is high in Ireland with regard to this issue but there are 51 other members.”
“A lot of questions there Deputy,” says Courell, “is there any one area you’d like me to address?” He goes on to say it’s not for the FAI to dictate government policy.
Brian Brennan (FG) is asking about the Israel game now. He asks what supports Gavin Bazunu got, who decided that the call to play would be left to the players and what happened during the game. He also asks about the timeline over the past year around the game. He’s grandstanding a bit now, talking about his own trip to Gaza and the kids playing football over there, very much getting into comment-not-a-question territory...
O’Sullivan asks if all referees in Irish soccer are Garda-vetted. John Martin assert that is the case. O’Sullivan asks if this was the case three years ago, Martin replies he’ll have to look into it.
O’Sullivan asks why the FAI’s safeguarding officer isn’t here. CEO David Courell points out that the association’s four most senior executives are here.
Chairman Alan Kelly (Labour) opens the meeting and we’re underway. Pádraig O’Sullivan is the first TD up. “Welcome everyone, here we go again...”
Welcome to the Irish Times liveblog of the FAI’s appearance in front of the Oireachtas Committee on Arts, Communications, Culture and Sport. Proceedings will get underway in the next few minutes - all the main protagonists are in the lobby outside Committee Room 1 for now. As soon as they’re called in, we’ll let you know.

title: ‘Leomania’: How secular France fell for the Pope
description: Macron makes sudden decision to attend Mass as pope draws large crowds
content:
I n college I read the arch-conservative Joseph de Maistre. He wrote at a time when French revolutionaries were renaming the months “Brumaire” and “Thermidor” according to “rational principles”, and banning religious festivals in favour of civic ones such as the “Cult of Reason”.
De Maistre argued that this would fail. The crowds would not come. No secular festival would ever have the pull of the sacred.
I couldn’t help but chuckle to see staff at the Élysée Palace – usually hardened to the appearance of dignitaries in the court of honour, which happens every week – crowded around a small window to catch a glimpse of the arrival of Pope Leo XIV .
It was quite an image for a state founded in opposition to Catholicism. De Maistre was having the last laugh.
The pope has been an unexpected hit in secular France.
Regional daily La Dépêche described “a surge of popular jubilation” accompanying the pontiff’s itinerary through Paris and Lourdes.
“Some talk of a ‘Leomania’ that has gripped the capital, not to say the whole country ...” reported the broadcaster RTL.
The insidery political newsletter Playbook Paris titled its Sunday edition “Pope star”, and reported that Leo’s open-air Mass for hundreds of thousands in the Place de la Concorde was “the place to be for much of the political class”.
Attendees were advised to start queuing at 11am for the 3pm Mass. I took a “boat bus” down the Seine, evading security cordons that blocked off a large chunk of central Paris.
The crowds lined the bridges and the quays for miles. Priests took confessions along the Champs-Elysées.
France’s famous laïcité, or state secularism, was set down in a 1905 law that ended state subsidies for any religious group and transferred Church property to the state.
Nowadays, debates about the display of religious symbols and clothing in public settings are all about Islam, but they have their origins in fierce anticlericalism directed against the Catholic Church .
Both Macron and Leo reflected on this history when they met at the Élysée.
A true secularism “consists not in excluding religion from the public sphere or from education, but in striving to ensure that the state and religious institutions maintain dialogue and join forces in the service of the common good”, the pontiff said, mentioning the state-subsidised restoration of Notre Dame.
France’s laïcité is “in no way the negation of religion”, Macron said, adding that all were free to worship.
[ Pope Leo’s family secret: a birth in a mother and baby home Opens in new window ]
Yet the protocol over which events the French president can attend during a papal visit is delicate.
In 2023, president Emmanuel Macron caused a minor furore and was accused of disrespecting his office by attending a Mass by Pope Francis in Marseilles, the first time a president had done so since 1980.
This time, however, it was Macron’s absence from the huge Mass in Paris that was noticed, especially when a good number of next year’s presidential election hopefuls were there.
Close to midnight before Leo’s final day in France, Le Monde and Le Figaro reported a sudden change to the president’s agenda.
“In a surprise move, contrary to the original schedule,” Le Monde wrote, “Emmanuel Macron will in the end be attending the mass celebrated by Pope XIV in Metz cathedral.”
The local mayor slated to be the official host was bumped. Macron was getting in on the popular feeling.
There was an official explanation. Courtesy demanded it, and Macron hoped to continue his “fruitful” discussions with Leo about peace and artificial intelligence, Élysée sources briefed.
There were legal technicalities to draw on too.
When the separation of church and state was introduced in 1905, Metz was part of Germany. It means an older “Concordat” signed under Napoleon in 1801 is still in force there.
Schools include religious education. The clergy of the officially recognised religions – Protestant ministers, Jewish rabbis, but mostly Catholic priests – receive salaries from the state. This is a less secular part of France.
Now that Leo has departed, France is taking stock of its moment of fervour.
For some, it is part of a broader conservative turn, as polls show the far-right Marine Le Pen as the clear front-runner for president in advance of an election due next year.
However, Leo doesn’t fit neatly into a right-left divide. He spoke forcefully against abortion and euthanasia, while also making a point of visiting an assistance centre for migrants.
Europe’s Christian heritage provides the template for managing “the arrival on the Continent of so many men and women fleeing war and persecution or seeking a better life far from poverty and hardship”, he said in Metz.
“Human dignity demands legal and safe pathways,” he said – but this is not enough. “To welcome a person means to integrate them as if they were part of one’s own family.”
Some point to an appetite for a figure who shows moral leadership, and the appeal of authenticity in an age when democratic representation has become professionalised.
The pontiff, who was visibly moved at a spectacular celebration of faith attended by 80,000 young people at the Stade de France, had his own explanation, reflecting after his visit that: “especially young people ... are obviously searching for something”.

title: Substantial sums paid to asylum seeker accommodation providers represented ‘no value’
description: Settlements were reached with three providers who sued after precontract deals cancelled, State spending watchdog says
content:
The State paid out “substantial” sums in legal settlements to the providers of accommodation for asylum seekers after it cancelled precontract agreements, the State spending watchdog has said.
A report from the Comptroller and Auditor General published on Wednesday said “no value” had been secured from the money paid out, which represented “a substantial loss to taxpayers”.
The report says precontract agreements entered into by the Department of Children in 2024 and early 2025 – with a combined value of more than €100 million – represented commitments to significant future expenditure.
It said such deals “therefore represented significant contingent liabilities for the Exchequer”, which should have required the approval of the Minister for Public Expenditure.
The watchdog said the Department of Public Expenditure was not consulted before entering the precontract agreements and no contingent liability in respect of these arrangements had been disclosed by the Department of Integration in its accounts for 2024.
Details of the settlements were not included in the watchdog’s report, but were described as “substantial”.
The report said in March 2024, the Government approved an accommodation strategy aiming at reducing the State’s reliance on commercial providers for accommodation for those seeking international protection by 2028.
It said the Department of Children launched an “expression of interest” process to source suitable properties. More than 134 submissions were received but no contracts were entered into.
It said precontract agreements were entered into with potential accommodation providers in respect of 15 properties, and these “did not emerge from the expression of interest process”.
[ More than 1,100 asylum seekers have voluntarily left the State this year Opens in new window ]
The Department of Justice, which now has responsibility in this area, told the watchdog that precontract agreements were first used by the International Protection Procurement Service in May 2024.
“The purpose of introducing such agreements was to provide security for potential providers of temporary emergency accommodation for their investments in larger-scale accommodation centres.”
The report said potential accommodation providers had maintained they were finding it increasingly difficult to access the credit necessary to refurbish large properties.
After taking over responsibility from the Department of Children in mid-2025, the Department of Justice proceeded with one of the precontract agreements, while three others were considered to have lapsed.
The department then decided to terminate the remaining agreements. Five accommodation providers who had signed precontract agreements subsequently sued the Minister for Justice.
“The department has stated that the potential combined value of the related agreements was more than €100 million. Following mediation, the Department of Justice made settlement payments in three of the legal cases.
“Plaintiff costs in those cases remain outstanding for agreement and payment. The settlement amounts are significantly less than the estimated contract values. Settlement was not reached through mediation in the other two cases.
“The Department of Justice expects that those cases will proceed to hearing by the Commercial Court in due course.”
The watchdog said the Department of Justice “expressed concern” that publication of details relating to the settlement payments or to the department’s response to claims could “hamper the State in the legal proceedings”.
“The Department of Justice’s view is that costs incurred could only have been avoided if the department had proceeded with greater expenditure for services that the department did not want or need,” the report said.
The Department of Justice told the watchdog the use of such precontract agreements “is now entirely discontinued” in favour of long-term plans for State accommodation and an “overhaul of commercial contracts”.
[ Sharp fall in number of asylum seekers since EU migration pact, says Jim O’Callaghan Opens in new window ]

title: Pilot who stabbed co-pilot may have tried to crash Israel-bound aircraft, says Netanyahu
description: Officials investigating if incident was attempted terror attack on Israelis
content:
One of the pilots of an aircraft flying from the United Arab Emirates to Israel stabbed his co-pilot and appeared to try to crash the aircraft, the Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu said, as Israeli officials said they were investigating if the incident was an attempted terror attack on Israelis.
The aircraft was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after the apparent attack, with the two pilots wounded but other passengers safe, according to a statement by Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz international airport, more commonly known as Tabuk airport.
The pilot accused of carrying out the attack was being questioned by Saudi authorities, Netanyahu said. Israel’s transport ministry said it would carry out a joint investigation with the defence establishment.
It was not immediately clear what motivated the attack, which threatened the lives of the about 170 passengers on board.
The Israeli defence minister, Israel Katz, described the incident as an “attempted jihadist attack”.
“The terrorist had a single objective: to crash the plane, killing everyone on board,” Katz said, adding that the attack was stopped due to the “heroism of several passengers”.
The passengers of the diverted flight landed in Israel on Wednesday evening on a replacement aircraft, eight hours after their emergency landing. Netanyahu praised the bravery of the crew members and passengers who subdued the attacker and landed the aircraft safely.
“They saved many lives. They prevented a heavy disaster,” he said.
Israeli officials, speaking on condition of anonymity to reporters, said the attacker was an Omani national and that Israel’s current assessment of the incident was that it was a terror attack. There was no comment on the attack from either Oman or the United Arab Emirates.
Two and a half hours after taking off from Dubai, the aircraft sent out an emergency signal – squawk code 7700, indicating a general emergency – before sending out another – code 7500, indicating a potential hijacking attempt.
Passengers heard screams from the front of the aircraft, and the wounded pilot managed to open the latch on the cockpit door, leaving it ajar.
The aircraft also abruptly descended, falling about 5,200m in a two-minute span. As the aircraft began to dive, passengers and a crew member pushed their way into the cockpit, subduing the attacker. Other crew members then stabilised the descent of the aircraft and began to land it safely in northwestern Saudi Arabia.
Videos of the incident showed passengers screaming as the aircraft descended, as well as a blood-covered man who appeared to be the pilot injured and on the floor.
“The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon told reporters via her mother’s phone at Tel Aviv airport.
“It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him,” she said, adding that a doctor on board treated the wounded pilot.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu: "This morning, there was a serious security incident on a flight from Dubai to Israel. Almost all the passengers on the flight were Israelis. During the flight, as they approached the country, one of the pilots stabbed the second pilot, and… pic.twitter.com/PrK7f7gS1P
Israeli officials initially scrambled fighter jets after the emergency signals were sent out, fearing an attack on Israel or that the aircraft would be diverted to a third country. A spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister’s office then said the incident was not a hijacking, as media reports circulated of a fight between the two pilots.
As more information emerged about the violent nature of the attack, Israeli and international media began to report officials anonymously saying an investigation had been opened into whether this was an attack on Israelis.
The head of the Israeli military, Lieut Gen Eyal Zamir, postponed his planned visit to the United States next week over the incident, where he was meant to have a meeting with US joint chiefs of staff and the head of US central command, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East.
The incident came just days after Netanyahu, warned there were indications an attack would be carried out during Israel’s October elections. The Israeli military, quoted by Israeli media, said it had no intelligence that an attack was being planned on Israel.
Yair Lapid, an opposition figure and former prime minister, cast doubt on the connection between the alleged attack and Netanyahu’s warning, saying that a security briefing on Tuesday night gave no information about a possible incident similar to what happened on Wednesday.
Israel experienced a series of hijackings and attacks on aircraft by Palestinian militants in the 1960s and 1970s, but has not had anything similar in decades. The country maintains some of the strictest airport security procedures in the world, including security checks before passengers board Israel-bound flights.
Flights between Dubai and Israel started after the countries normalised ties in 2020. Israel does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, but in 2025 landed an aircraft in Riyadh because of a medical emergency.
Flydubai confirmed that flight FZ 1073 en route to Ben Gurion experienced an incident and landed safely in Tabuk on Wednesday. “Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities,” the carrier said. “Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available.”
Israeli media reported that a later Flydubai flight heading to Tel Aviv turned around in mid-air back towards Dubai after the incident. – Guardian

title: Public sector workers refusing to enter talks on pay deal, Chambers says
description: More than 100,000 civil and public servants commenced a work-to rule on Wednesday
content:
Public sector workers are “unwilling to sit down and engage” with the Government on a new national pay deal, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers has said.
Chambers said public sector unions have pre-emptively pushed ahead with industrial action when they could be in negotiations, as more than 100,000 civil and public servants commenced a work-to-rule on Wednesday.
Chambers told RTÉ Radio’s News at One that officials from his department were willing to meet union representatives for substantive talks on a new deal immediately, and are also willing to involve the Workplace Relations Commission .
Chambers said the last pay deal, which concluded at the end of June, protected public services workers, and cited the pay of one of the lower-paid grades in the Civil Service – clerical officers – which, he said, had increased by 33 per cent since 2019 while inflation had amounted to 23 per cent.
“The public pay bill overall has gone from about €21 billion in 2018 to €36 billion in 2026,“ he said.”
Responding to remarks by Fórsa general secretary Kevin Callinan that any talks needed to start with an undertaking that a new deal would address cost-of-living issues, Chambers said unions must first engage.
“We cannot predetermine the outcome before discussion commences,” he said. “This is just a parallel argument that is going on while unions are unwilling to sit down and engage.
“I am clear for weeks and months that the Government wants a pay deal. We want to sit down with trade unions, but the deal has to be safe, sustainable and affordable within our wider fiscal parameters and I think everybody understands that.”
[ Civil Service work-to-rule expected to disrupt EU presidency Opens in new window ]
Earlier, Callinan said the unions’ position is that the vast majority of their members have seen their pay outstripped by inflation by “at least 5 per cent over the past five years”.
“The last agreement made some inroads into that during 2024 and 2025, but we have fallen behind again in 2026, and that just isn’t sustainable,” he said.
Callinan acknowledged the impact of the industrial action could be serious for service users in health, education and elsewhere, but said the responsibility for the work-to-rule going ahead lay with the Government.
The industrial action taken by members of unions including Fórsa, Siptu and the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation is set to continue over the coming weeks if talks do not restart.
Two of the three teachers’ unions have said they will take action from next Monday, and Callinan confirmed a second one-day strike has been scheduled for October 21st.
