title: Dublin 4 office investment for €2.95m offers buyer scope for 7% yield
description: Six of seven own-door office units at Argyle Square off Morehampton Road are let at present
content:
Private investors and family offices looking for a well-located, income-producing property with asset-management potential may be interested in the sale of Argyle Square, a multi-let scheme comprising seven own-door office units located just off Morehampton Road in Donnybrook , Dublin 4 .
The development, which extends to 805sq m (8,671sq ft) of office space in total, along with 76sq m (819sq ft) of stores, is being offered to the market by agent Lisney at a guide price of €2.95 million. The price equates to a net initial yield of 5.93 per cent with a reversionary yield of about 7 per cent.
Argyle Square comprises seven self-contained two-storey office units, with six of the seven units let to tenants operating across the legal, professional services, telecommunications, security and interior design sectors. The weighted average unexpired lease term (WAULT) is approximately 2.8 years, and all the leases are on full repairing and insuring (FRI) terms. The tenancy profile includes open-market rent reviews throughout, providing an opportunity to capture rental reversion.
There is one vacant unit of 101sq m (1,088sq ft) which will provide the incoming owner with the opportunity for leasing and income growth. The investment also comes with 14 surface car-parking spaces.
Argyle Square occupies a high-profile position on Morehampton Road in Donnybrook and is situated approximately 2km south of Dublin city centre. The subject property is convenient to the shops in Donnybrook itself and to the nearby villages of Ballsbridge and Ranelagh.
The scheme sits just off the N11 and is served by numerous Dublin Bus routes. The Luas Green Line stop is a 20-minute (1.4km) walk from the property.
James Nugent of Lisney says: “This is an opportunity for investors to acquire a well-located Dublin 4 office investment with diversified income, embedded asset-management opportunities and exposure to one of the capital’s most sought-after commercial districts. The vacant unit provides potential to enhance income, while the freehold title and established tenant base offer a secure platform for future growth.”

title: Stripe’s former Dublin headquarters office seeks new occupier
description: The One Building on Grand Canal Street Lower expected to command rent in the region of €62.50 per sq ft
content:
Following the relocation last October of Irish-founded fintech Stripe to new and larger offices at nearby Wilton Park, the firm’s former Dublin headquarters is being offered to let through joint agents BNP Paribas Real Estate and Savills . Designed by a renowned architect, the late Sam Stephenson, and built in 1972, the One Building on Grand Canal Street had been occupied by Stripe for nearly 10 years following a full refurbishment in 2015.
The subject property comprises a seven-storey over basement office building with a net internal area of 4,287sq m (46,144sq ft). The ground floor features a reception area and offices to the rear. The building’s floor plates typically extend to 663sq m (7,136sq ft) and offer prospective occupiers the benefit of being fully fitted.
The specification includes raised access floors, exposed ceilings, a four-pipe fan coil air-conditioning system, two 13-person passenger lifts, male, female and disabled toilets located on all floor levels, and shower facilities at basement level. The floor-to-slab height is 2.75m (9ft) on the office floors.
There are 44 car-parking spaces with 37 of these located at basement level and seven at podium level. Additional shower and bicycle facilities in the basement are undergoing a full refurbishment, and these works are due for completion in December this year.
In terms of leasing, the top two floors of the building are currently under offer to an international occupier, leaving the remaining floor area of 3,210sq m (34,552sq ft) available to lease over five floors in its entirety or on a floor-by-floor basis. While a quoting rent has not been set, the One Building is expected to command in the region of €62.50 per sq ft. Further information on the property is available from Keith O’Neill at BNP Paribas Real Estate and Shane Duffy at Savills.

title: Site next to Square in Tallaght with planning permission for 199 apartments seeks €5.9m
description: Former Woodies site sold for €20m to developer Bernard McNamara at height of Celtic Tiger era
content:
A range of parties including developers, institutional investors and the Land Development Agency may be interested in the opportunity presented by the sale of a 1.19-hectare (2.94-acre) site at Tallaght Town Centre in Tallaght , Dublin 24 .
Located immediately adjacent to The Square shopping centre and within a short walk of both Tallaght University Hospital and TUD’s Tallaght campus, the former Woodies site has full planning permission for a residential-led mixed-use scheme and is being offered to the market by agent Hooke & MacDonald at a guide price of €5.9 million.
The disposal of the property is being conducted on the instructions of John Healy and Myles Kirby of Kroll joint receivers over certain assets of Ravensbrook Ltd, a company headed by Siobhán Quinlan, a property investor and the wife of financier Derek Quinlan , John Gordon, with an address in Monaco, and Michael Quinlan, with an address in Castleknock.
While Ravensbrook’s directors had been seeking originally to develop as many as 326 apartments on the site, that plan never came to fruition. The receivers commissioned a planning application earlier this year, and in May secured permission on appeal from An Coimisiún Pleanála for the development of 199 apartments along with 17 commercial units and a 58-space basement car park.
The residential accommodation is to be distributed across two blocks of up to seven storeys in height. Block A includes 49 senior-living apartments and communal amenity facilities, while Block B comprises 150 apartments. The approved units comprise a mix of studio, one-bedroom, two-bedroom and three-bedroom apartments.
The approved commercial accommodation consists of 17 units with a combined area of 2,123sq m (22,851sq ft) which would be suitable for healthcare, retail, cafe, pharmacy, childcare and neighbourhood service uses.
The site’s €5.9 million guide price represents just a fraction of the €20 million that developer Bernard McNamara paid for it at the height of the Celtic Tiger era. McNamara’s company, Laytar, acquired the property from a group of investors assembled at the time by Derek Quinlan. A plan to develop 350 apartments on the site never materialised and the property was put back on the market in 2016 for €4.5 million.
Commenting on the site’s arrival to the market now, Donald McDonald of Hooke & MacDonald said: “Belgard Square East represents a rare opportunity to acquire a fully permitted mixed-use development site of scale in one of Dublin’s most important town centre locations.
“With planning permission in place for 199 apartments, commercial accommodation and a highly accessible location beside The Square shopping centre and the Luas, we expect strong interest from developers, investors and housing providers.”

title: Four-storey home beyond humble cottage exterior in Bray
description: Architect Lindsay Johnston designed a unique property on a sloping site on Killarney Road
content:
There was nothing straightforward about this sloping site in Bray , Co Wicklow , when the owners bought it in the 1970s to build a home. Fortunately for them, renowned architect Lindsay Johnston was a good friend and agreed to take on the challenge.
In 1977, after a complicated build across different levels, Patchwork, named after the cottage that originally stood on the land, was reborn in a daring, innovative design that was ahead of its time. Or, as one of the family put it, “in a world of bungalow bliss, this was certainly a serious antidote”.
Located on Killarney Road, the house, which went on to be featured in the Architects’ Journal, feels totally secluded, yet it is just a four-minute walk from Bray town hall. Approached from the front, it has all the features of a cottage. The pink windows give a little wink as you walk up to the door, giving the house instant personality matching the owners’ sense of fun. It is difficult to tell from here that the back of the house drops down into the site, creating a house laid out over four levels.
The floor area is 178sq m (1,916sq ft), with the front door opening directly into the main living areas. Dividing the space is a central chimney stack, with a wrought iron spiral staircase running through the centre of the house.
A gallery-style mezzanine, set out as a study, overlooks the rooms below, including the bright livingroom with a cantilevered bay window and double-height ceilings. The clean white walls provide space for displaying art. On the other side of the chimney is the dining area, with doors leading out to the rooftop terrace. The kitchen, fully refitted a few years ago, is beside this, with a utility room for laundry and extra storage.
The owners’ son says the flow between these rooms meant the home provided the perfect setting for numerous parties over the years.
“It was a magical place to grow up. It was such a happy house. It adapts to all stages of life, like having dens in the garden as kids, and then as teenagers it was a great party house with the main living space connecting out to the garden and the kitchen. There would be different generations on different levels.”
The four bedrooms are spread across different floors. The main bedroom is on the lowest level, and leads out to a private terrace and gardens. Each bedroom looks out on the tiered gardens, and it’s the view from these windows that allows you to appreciate the thought behind the architecture, something the owners never tire of.
“The orientation is super, with the design responding to the site. In every room of this house, you’re in a different garden or a different link to the garden because the house is below the road almost, on this quarter of an acre site that just spreads itself down the land. It’s so private, and you feel like you are among the landscape and trees in all of those bedrooms. It’s super.”
There is also a loft room accessed by an outdoor staircase, creating an independent space for a home office or studio.
Fifty years of love, labour and local knowledge have gone into the gardens. There are mature trees, planted beds, secret spaces and the river Swan running behind it. The 42sq m (452sq ft) roof garden, which is effectively two storeys up, feels particularly private, surrounded by treetops and the sound of birds and the river below.
Although the design of the house has stood the test of time, it was due an upgrade in energy terms. The owners had it retrofitted 10 years ago, including high levels of insulation, as well as the installation of an A-rated boiler and a zoned heating system. This took it up to a C energy rating and banished the draughty 1970s vibe. The house also had a full decorative refit at that stage, with a new bespoke kitchen fitted and all the bathrooms completely redone.
Now that Patchwork is on the market for the first time with agent Garrett O’Bric guiding the sale at €1.295 million, leaving such a unique home will be difficult for the family, but they have nothing but fond memories.

title: Victorian villa providing peace and privacy a short walk from Dún Laoghaire main street
description: Mulgrave Terrace home is split level beyond a single-storey front
content:
Number 20 Mulgrave Terrace sits on a row of charming Victorian villa-style houses on a quiet street off Dún Laoghaire ’s main thoroughfare; you wouldn’t think that just 500m down the street lies a busy town centre. Mulgrave Terrace has the benefit of being close to amenities, including shopping, restaurants, cafes and public transport, but is also far enough away from the bustle to feel tranquil.
The house is set well back from the street, behind high gates and tall, evergreen screening, and at the end of private front garden with a gravelled driveway, manicured lawns, flowers and trees. Number 20 Mulgrave Terrace is single storey to the front and split level to the back, with three bedrooms. The Ber-exempt home measures 152sq m (1,636sq ft) and is for sale through Sherry FitzGerald, seeking €1.595 million.
The front door has glass surround and leads in to a wide, high-ceilinged entrance hall where there is a dado rail, ceiling coving and centre rose on display, along with wide-plank timber flooring stained in a rich mahogany hue.
The four large reception rooms at this level offer both space and versatility; to the right is an impressive drawingroom with a feature fireplace with an open fire, and a large sash window with shutters looking out to the front garden. Double doors lead to the diningroom, also with feature fireplace, with glazed double doors leading out to the back garden and a lovely stained glass window above the doors. Both these rooms have stained hardwood floors, a picture rail, ceiling coving and centre roses, and antique-style radiators.
To the left of the hall are two big double bedrooms. The principal bedroom looks out to the front garden and exudes comfort and luxury with a fireplace and large built-in wardrobes on each side. The second bedroom looks out on to the rear patio garden.
A half arch in the entrance hall leads into the inner hallway and on to a split-level stairway. Upstairs is the third bedroom, which has been designed as a child’s sanctuary, featuring a raised sleeping platform with storage and study/reading space underneath, and a built-in wardrobe.
The main bathroom has a tiled floor and tiled tongue-and-groove panelled walls along with an antique roll-top bath. To the back of the bathroom is a generous hot press and storage cupboard.
Downstairs there is a lobby with tiled floor, built-in shelving and recessed lighting, with a sash window looking out to the courtyard garden at the side. Off this lobby is a shower room.
The kitchen/breakfastroom to the back has large, bright tiles on the floor and white Shaker-style kitchen cabinets and fittings, with hardwood countertops and a Belfast sink. The dining area is spacious, with built-in display cabinetry and large double doors out to the garden. There’s a Velux window above the kitchen and recessed lighting all around.
[ Former church that’s now a modern home in Kilmainham Opens in new window ]
The back garden wraps cleverly around the house, providing multiple spaces for outdoor play, dining and relaxation, all enclosed by tall granite walls and panelled wood fencing for total privacy, and configured to catch the southerly and westerly sun. The double doors in the kitchen/breakfastroom open to a large patio garden with evergreen hedging and raised beds bursting with colour. Steps lead up to a lawned area at the back, and there is pedestrian access from here via a gate. Around the corner is a further lawned area, with a lovely patio just outside the diningroom.
Dún Laoghaire is distinctive for its seafront walks along the East Pier towards Sandycove. Among the attractions along the seafront are the Pavilion Theatre, Casper & Giumbini’s restaurant, the DLR Lexicon library, Haddington House Hotel and Oliveto restaurant, Teddy’s ice-cream shop and the People’s Park.

title: Fully let south Dublin residential investment for sale at reduced price of €2.25m
description: Roebuck House comprises five apartments and generates annual rental income of €150,720
content:
Having failed to find a buyer after it was offered to the market at a guide price of €2.8 million in April of last year, Roebuck House, a substantial period redbrick house comprising five fully let apartments in the south Dublin suburb of Clonskeagh , is seeking a buyer at a new and reduced price of €2.25 million.
The investment, which is now for sale through agent TWM, is generating gross rental income of €150,720 a year with the rents set at approximately 15 per cent below the prevailing market rate.
The accommodation at Roebuck House extends to an overall area of 557sq m (6,000sq ft) and is distributed across one three-bedroom and four two-bedroom apartments within a well-appointed, detached period redbrick house. The property retains numerous original features, and these are complemented by the house’s contemporary fit-out. Each apartment has its own individual Eircode, electricity meter and gas boiler.
Roebuck House is the centrepiece of a wider development known as Roebuck Court, with apartment buildings located either side of the subject property. The scheme occupies a prime location next to Clonskeagh village and close to UCD’s Belfield campus.
The area is well served by public transport, with several Dublin Bus routes to the city centre and Luas Green Line stops nearby at Milltown and Windy Arbour. There is a wide range of amenities in the immediate area, including schools, shops, restaurants, leisure facilities and sports clubs.
Stephen Aherne of TWM says: “We expect to see good interest in this property as it provides an opportunity to acquire a fully let residential asset in a prime south Dublin location. It will provide a secure investment which is easy to manage and is likely to provide excellent rental and capital growth.”

title: Musician Foy Vance: ‘I’m enjoying my sobriety. Everything gets better – including your bank account’
description: Musician Foy Vance is as self-aware as they come, which makes him impossible to dislike. His outlook has bled into his songwriting too
content:
Whenever someone tells Foy Vance that he ought to be a bigger name than he already is, he has a well-prepared answer ready for them. He has collaborated with, supported and earned the admiration of everyone from Elton John to Kacey Musgraves and Bonnie Raitt .
“I’m, like, ‘I’m getting away with it. The bills are paid, everyone’s happy, I get to do exactly what I want, release music whenever I want; I don’t have to speak to anyone.’ You know what I mean?”
The musician, who was born in Bangor in Co Down but spent years in the United States, sighs softly, smiling.
“So I guess, in a nutshell, if you want to play a stadium and you’re good enough and you’ve got enough contacts and all that bullshit, it’s just about working twice as hard as the next guy. Whoever’s the hardest-working f**ker out there, work twice as hard as them and then you stand a chance, if all the other stars are in place.”
He grins, a twinkle in his eye as he shrugs.
Vance is as self-aware as musicians come, and so impossible to dislike. His outlook has bled into his songwriting, too, with seven fine studio albums under his belt, including The Wake, produced by Ethan Johns, which was released earlier this year.
[ Foy Vance: Signs of Life – Acute and denouncing self-awareness Opens in new window ]
A soulful, tender album, it’s the culmination of a cycle that has defined Vance’s creative life, beginning with the death of his father, Hugh Bailie Vance, a pastor with the evangelical Church of Christ, in 1999. It was a soul-rattling experience that ultimately set Vance on the path to becoming a recording artist.
An accompanying tour, which will take him around the world after it kicks off, in mid-October, includes a string of Irish dates at the end of the month. Vance will also launch a new album cycle, releasing his eighth studio album, If, in three parts, each appearing as an EP between October and April.
“At one point we were looking at maybe getting me checked in somewhere, because I was starting to appear crazy,” he says of his creative purple patch, chuckling.
“I was writing scripts, books, new songs, painting, making films. I just couldn’t stop. I was barely sleeping. I just had an almighty surge. So I’ve already got more music to go, but I’m glad The Wake’s in the world. It’s one of the only things I’ve ever seen through.
“I used to say music and marriage are the only things I’ve ever committed to, but now that I’m three times married I can barely say that one.” He laughs hard. “I said I was going to do something, I set out to do it and I did it.”
A number of changes preceded the release of The Wake and If, most notably Vance signing with a new label. His association with Ed Sheeran , who signed him to his Gingerbread Man Records and championed him over the years, has been both a blessing and a curse, although Vance has nothing but good things to say about his friend.
On the one hand, it brought his music to a wider audience; on the other, being perennially linked to one of the most famous musicians in the world can come with its own pitfalls. The Wake was Vance’s first album since Joy of Nothing, from 2013, not to be released on Sheeran’s label, which was backed by Warner Music and distributed by Atlantic Records until recently.
“It was just, like, ‘Let’s call it what it is,’” he says, shrugging. “And this is not about me being in any way self-effacing, but I was a minor artist on a major label. The only reason I was on Atlantic was because of Ed. He was spearheading the whole thing. So I think they did their best by me. They’re all beautiful people, we’re all still great friends, there’s no bad blood. It was just sort of mutual.”
“I can imagine when my name came up in the meetings, they were, like, ‘Okay, right, that’s Rihanna done ... so this Foy ... who the f**k is this Foy? Is that Ed’s mate? Why do we keep talking about this old bald guy that writes about his dad?’”
“So I kind of went around looking for a viable partner, and I met the team at Rounder Records and just loved their vision, their support. They were very excited, and that charged me.”
Vance’s new clarity of purpose coincided with his decision to stop drinking alcohol. It hasn’t been a particularly difficult shift, he says. “I wanted to prove to myself that I wasn’t addicted to it. I said, ‘I’m going to do Dry January,’ and then a friend was, like, ‘Well, if you want to prove that you can break an addiction, it takes up to three months.’
[ Róisín Ingle on Dry January: Since giving up alcohol, I’ve developed some strong opinions about it Opens in new window ]
“But quite honestly, three weeks into it, it kind of dawned on me: there’s nothing missing. I thought I was going to be white-knuckling, trying not to drink every day. But I think as soon as you consciously do it because you want to, and if you take stock of what’s going on, you sleep better, you think better, you work better, you communicate better.
“I mean, just everything gets better – including your bank account. And the first time you go out with your mates and they’re drinking and you’re not, you realise three pints deep that everyone talks absolute shit,” he says, laughing. “So it’s not a constant fight at all. I’m enjoying my sobriety.”
Some of the songs on The Wake are testament to his newfound mindfulness. He wrote Call Me Anytime for his three kids, Ella, Sonny and Sol; it’s a track that admits to past failings but reaffirms his devotion to his children. The songs on If come from a collection of more than 100 hundred tracks, both old and new, that he reimagined with the help of the producer Anderson East.
Vance pauses, blinking back tears, when I ask whether his father factors into the songs that he writes in a more purposeful way these days.
“I’ve been so embarrassed over the years, talking about my dad: ‘Oh, my dad this, my dad that, my dad’ – I feel like I whinge on about him. But the truth of the matter is, his death was the greatest gift I ever got. It was the strangest and most heartbreaking gift I ever got, but that’s exactly what it was.
“I could hear after that. I mean, I could sort of always hear music, but just not that clearly or that intensely. Something happens in the body after trauma; something changes.
“So, yeah, it’s kind of hard to write about anything and not feel close to my dad. It’s hard to pick up a guitar and not feel close to my dad and not be aware of him.
“Especially being a dad now, when I’m going, ‘Lads, lads, lads!’ I’m thinking, ‘I’m so like my dad. I just turned into him, lads. Brutal.’”
There was another unexpected twist in Vance’s career in early 2024, when he found himself not only attending the Emmy Awards but also making his way onstage to accept one. A Beautiful Game, a song Vance had written for the TV series Ted Lasso with Sheeran and the pop Svengali Max Martin, won the award for outstanding original music and lyrics.
“It’s on top of my piano. I shouldn’t say this, but sometimes I hang keys from it. I did have it as a toilet-roll holder at first, and then I thought, ‘If someone takes a picture of that, they will take it off me.’”
“That was a mad experience. Ed wasn’t there, Max wasn’t there, so I took that as a sign of ‘We haven’t won this,’ or they would have called them and said, ‘Get here, we need you here.’
“The guy beside me, who was up for the same Emmy, was writing his speech the entire time. So I sat there the whole night with Bonnie [Bishop, his partner, who is also a musician], going, ‘This is a great night. We got a free hotel, we got flown out here, what more do you want?’
“I was genuinely surprised when my name was read out – I really, really didn’t expect it, but it’s a lovely thing. What’s that saying, ‘Awards only matter if you win them’? They don’t change anything. They don’t change the arc you make. But I guess, in certain worlds, it puts more eyes on you.”
There are perhaps more eyes on Vance than at any other point in his career, and he is making the most of it.
“I’ve never been less than content for the vast majority of my life,” he says. “My dad always said, ‘Foy, son, you could fall in shit and come out smelling of roses,’ and he’s not wrong. I feel like I’ve really lucked out here, by sort of coasting at my own pace. I’ve carved out something for myself that works for me. I feel excited about what’s coming next.”
If: We is released on Friday, October 30th. Foy Vance plays Wexford Spiegeltent Festival on Tuesday, October 27th; 3Olympia Theatre , Dublin, on Thursday, October 29th; Town Hall Theatre , Galway, on Friday, October 30th; and Lime Tree Theatre , Limerick, on Saturday, October 31st

title: Try! review: In this charming Irish documentary, everyone’s a winner
description: Oisín Mistéil’s debut feature follows four Irish players on their journey to the 2025 Mixed Ability Rugby World Cup
content:
Even the biggest wiseacre will happily forgive the on-the-nose pun in the title of this charming Irish documentary from Oisín Mistéil. Try! is, you see, about mixed-ability rugby . The title references how teams gain advantage and also the effort players expend. How could you call it anything else?
Mistéil’s debut as feature director goes among four Irish players as they prepare for the 2025 International Mixed Ability Rugby Tournament, in Pamplona.
Richie Philpott, of the Sundays Well Rebels, is an intense young man with a strong line in sporting banter. “When I step out on that pitch, only one thing crosses my mind: ruthless aggression!” he says.
Maeve Owens, of the Ballincollig Trailblazers, is delighted to be appointed captain in the run-up to the tournament.
Paul Deacon, from DLSP Vikings, is impressively blase about the 220km round trip he must take from his rural home to training in Dublin.
Tommy Crawford, of Malone Tornadoes (go, south Belfast), talks us through his extensive collection of whiskies.
[ The Lost Children of Tuam review: Historical evils lurk beneath a muted surface Opens in new window ]
The film is careful to introduce its characters as personalities rather than define them by their disabilities, but testimony from parents, particularly Maeve’s, on challenges met and overcome proves deeply moving. Try! gets across the sense that this sport is, for some, one of the few places they experience something like equality.
Try! is not much interested in explaining the tweaked conventions that allow able-bodied and disabled players to compete on the same pitch. We learn that scrums are uncontested, but we are otherwise just invited to enjoy the glorious inclusivity of it all.
Beginning 250 days before the tournament, the film takes us through the pressures and excitements as our four players train, plan and speculate.
One charming sequence sees Maeve and her pal clattering through a department store in search of holiday gear. Elsewhere, we meet Richie with his colleagues re-enacting second World War battles. “You committed treason,” he says casually of a colleague who looks to have accidentally shot one of their own allies.
The contest matters a great deal, but, unlike Murderball, the 2005 documentary on wheelchair rugby, Try! does not dwell in a cauldron of ruthless rivalry. Here is an enormously generous film that believes everyone on the pitch is a winner.
[ Pressure: Andrew Scott is brilliant in this intense D-Day drama Opens in new window ]

title: The Weight review: Ethan Hawke does the heavy lifting in this 1970s-style genre movie
description: Russell Crowe makes an impression in a gritty 1930s survival film that draws on classic Hollywood
content:
They don’t make movies like The Weight any more. This hoary genre picture, which might have featured on a double bill with Paper Moon or The Sting during Hollywood’s postclassical zenith, features Ethan Hawke spending much of his screen time bruised, exhausted or flexing under an impossible weight, in keeping with the characterful features of early-1970s cinema.
He heads an appropriately grizzled cast for an outdoorsy adventure. The plot shares DNA with William Friedkin’s underappreciated Sorcerer: four prisoners in 1933 Oregon are offered freedom in return for transporting stolen gold through the wilderness.
Hawke plays Samuel Murphy, a widowed mechanic and first World War survivor, separated from his young daughter during the Great Depression. At a labour camp, Warden Clancy ( Russell Crowe ) gives him a choice: take three other prisoners on the five-day journey and complete the illegal delivery, or serve out his brutal sentence. If any gold is lost, they will be killed.
This feature directorial debut from the veteran editor Padraic McKinley has a high-concept hook, a gritty period setting and bruising physicality. The men, who are improbably joined by Anna, a Native American fleeing servitude, cross rivers, forests and unstable bridges (with Bavaria standing in for the Pacific Northwest). Two goons hover nearby. Other interested parties follow close behind.
The weight of the gold is a constant logistical nightmare. An excellent rope-bridge scene requires a nervy game of pass the parcel as bars are transported individually.
[ Ethan Hawke: ‘My first screen partner overdosed. That was a big lesson to me’ Opens in new window ]
The group dynamics are less convincing than the brawn of the action sequences. Various disagreements are too fleeting and shallow to make an impression on the narrative or the viewer. Rather, this engaging and effective survival film depends on its older cast members.
Crowe inevitably makes an impression as the camp’s casually menacing warden. (Sadly, the New Zealander disappears far too soon.) Hawke maintains a hot streak dating back to the 2017 film First Reformed . His performance deftly balances urgency and pragmatism. In common with his character, he does most of the heavy lifting here.
[ Blue Moon review: Ethan Hawke and Andrew Scott make performances to remember Opens in new window ]

title: Celebrate 75 extraordinary years at Wexford Festival Opera this October
description: Over 17 days from October 15th to 31st, this year’s festival features a world premiere by Colm Tóibín alongside some of the world’s leading opera stars
content:
Every October, Wexford Festival Opera transforms the historic harbour town of Wexford into one of the world’s great opera destinations. This cherished autumn tradition returns from October 15th to 31st to celebrate its 75th anniversary.
Since 1951 the festival has welcomed artists and audiences from across the world to share something truly extraordinary, earning an international reputation for presenting rare and unexpected operatic works while launching the careers of many of the opera world’s leading stars.
What makes Wexford unique is that the entire town becomes part of the festival. Venues, cafes, restaurants and public spaces come alive with music as visitors and local residents celebrate together, forging lasting friendships and creating a sense of community that extends far beyond the stage. At the heart of it all is Ireland’s National Opera House, where the flagship festival events take place. Acoustically superb and visually magnificent, this venue is rightfully considered one of the country’s finest and is a destination in its own right.
This year’s landmark festival promises to be filled with memorable performances and the unique spirit that has defined the festival for 75 years. Speaking about the festival, artistic director Rosetta Cucchi says: “Wexford has always been about rediscovery and revelation. It has been about opening forgotten scores and finding within them beating hearts. It has been about young artists challenging themselves and seasoned performers finding new depths. It has been about that electric silence before the first note, when we hold our breath together in the dark.”
This year’s main stage operas are Iris by Pietro Mascagni, L’equivoco stravagante by Gioachino Rossini and Sergei Prokofiev’s The Gambler. The 17-day experience also includes concerts, lunchtime recitals, shorter pocket operas, talks, free pop-up performances around the town and the magnificent 75th anniversary concert, Croí na Féile.
Mascagni’s Iris is a rare opportunity to experience Italian opera at its most atmospheric and emotionally raw. Directed by the festival’s artistic director, Rosetta Cucchi and conducted by Mascagni specialist, Francesco Cilluffo, this production also sees the return to Wexford of one of the world’s most acclaimed tenors, Joseph Calleja, who will perform the role of Osaka in this striking, symbolic masterpiece. The production is sponsored by British Airways.
A joyous early work by Rossini, L’equivoco stravagante is a fast-paced, playful exploration of social climbing and the lengths we go to for love. Musically brilliant, it’s the ultimate fun night at the opera. A sparkling farce of absurd misunderstandings, youthful wit, rapid-fire ensembles and comic excess. The production is sponsored by Elavon.
The final main stage opera, Prokofiev’s The Gambler, looks at the price of desire. Based on Fyodor Dostoevsky’s 1866 novella, the libretto draws directly from Prokofiev’s own gambling addiction. The opera follows the protagonist, Alexei, a young tutor, as he spirals into gambling debt while being obsessed with his employer’s stepdaughter, Polina. The production is sponsored by Danone.
The 75th anniversary concert, Croí na Féile, is on Saturday, October 17th. Expected to be one of the defining events of the birthday celebrations, the glittering concert will bring together four of the world’s leading opera superstars on one stage: Ermonela Jaho, Joseph Calleja, Daniela Barcellona and Giorgi Manoshvili. They will perform iconic arias from Tosca, Carmen, Don Carlo, Rigoletto, La Traviata and so much more.
In this anniversary year the festival has commissioned two brand-new works. These world premieres celebrate the beginnings of the festival and the community at its heart. Performed by The Wexford Factory participants, The First Festival reunites celebrated novelist Colm Tóibín with his regular collaborator, composer Alberto Caruso. A heartwarming and joyous celebration of love, music and a town changed forever, this operatic tribute honours the festival Tóibín has loved and championed for decades. The Wexford Factory is sponsored by PwC Ireland with additional support from The Community Foundation Ireland and the Fundación Arnhold de la Cámara.
The Community Opera has become a hugely popular part of the festival where members of the local community perform alongside a professional cast. This year’s opera is Still, life…, a brand-new commission by Ailís Ní Ríain, composer-in-residence at the festival. The production is sponsored by Energia Group.
As well as the main stage operas, the shorter Pocket Operas are a beloved part of the festival, cherished by regular attendees and a brilliant introduction to opera for first-time visitors. This year’s Pocket Operas are: The Rose of Castille (Michael William Balfe) and Much Ado About Nothing (Charles Villiers Stanford). The performances are sponsored by Applegreen.
For those looking to enjoy a more intimate musical experience, the Lunchtime Recitals offer a wonderful opportunity to hear principal singers up close in a relaxed and intimate setting. Held at St Iberius Church and in the O’Reilly Theatre within the Opera House, these recitals are perfect for those seeking a daytime cultural treat.
The festival also offers an engaging talks series including the much-loved Dr Tom Walsh Lecture, which this year brings together five artistic directors representing the illustrious past and vibrant present of the festival.
The Impossible Interview is another festival favourite with host Michael Dervan, who this year interviews Rossini, performed by Peter McCamley, who was not only the most famous composer anywhere in the world in the 1820s, but also one of the wittiest people of his time.
Now one of the most popular treats of the festival, the free pop-up events feature festival artists who surprise and delight audiences in unexpected locations around Wexford town. The pop-up events are sponsored by Castleacre Insurance.
This year’s late-night event imagines Wexford Festival Opera 75 years from now. Step into the future with a world-premiere song cycle from the brilliant minds of novelist Colm Tóibín and composer Conor Linehan.
The always popular Gala Concert, hosted by artistic director Rosetta Cucchi and broadcaster Marty Whelan, will be an extraordinary evening, where artists step beyond their roles to share the music they truly love including the arias and songs that have shaped their journeys and captured their hearts. The concert is sponsored by Range Rover.
Whether you’re an opera lover or simply curious, this is your year to experience Wexford Festival Opera.
The 75th Wexford Festival Opera runs from October 15th to 31st. Book your tickets at 053 912 2144 or visit wexfordopera.com .
Wexford Festival Opera would like to acknowledge and thank The Arts Council, Wexford County Council, Fáilte Ireland/Ireland’s Ancient East and the festival’s friends, sponsors and donors for their invaluable and continued support

title: Portlaoise special school benefits from AIB Community €1 Million Fund
description: How AIB is helping Laois communities thrive through funding, advice and local support
content:
With 170 branches in communities across Ireland and the largest branch network in the country, AIB supports its customers to bank how they want, when they want and where they want. Through its Portlaoise and Rathdowney branches in Co Laois, AIB is a key enabler of economic activity in the area. AIB’s chief customer officer Orlaith Ryan recently visited the AIB Portlaoise branch and branch manager Adrian Cummins to engage with customers and members of the wider community.
“AIB is proud to be embedded in communities across the country,” says Ryan. “We’re committed to Laois through our branch network and people, and branch manager Adrian Cummins and his team are here to support their customers in achieving the life they’re after.”
The AIB Community €1 Million Fund enables customers, members of the public and AIB employees to support charities that matter most to them in their region. In Laois, one of the beneficiaries is Kolbe Special School, which caters for children with severe to profound learning disabilities and/or autism.
“It was wonderful to meet some of the thriving businesses and customers we’re supporting who will continue to help develop and benefit communities within the region,” says Ryan. “And it was especially heartening to see the amazing work that the Kolbe Special School does first hand.”
The Kolbe Special School received €20,000 after it was nominated by AIB customers and the public, as well as receiving an additional €6,000 through the AIB employee fund.
“On behalf of the pupils and staff thank you to the AIB Community €1 Million Fund for the very generous donation to Kolbe Special School,” says Orlagh Mahon, principal of Kolbe Special School. “All money will be invested in resources and equipment to enhance our pupils’ learning. This kindness and support is helping to create better learning opportunities and life experiences for our pupils. We greatly appreciate AIB’s generosity and everyone who took the time to nominate us and to AIB for creating a fund that recognises charitable organisations and the 49 children we support every day.”
Community support is one part of AIB’s wider role in Laois, where it has a long history of supporting local enterprise. Adrian Cummins pointed to the county’s thriving agriculture sector and growing interest among businesses in making their operations more sustainable.
That local presence helps branch teams build long-term relationships with households, farms and businesses, while gaining a close understanding of the opportunities and pressures facing customers across the county. Whether customers are planning a big life event, seeking finance to grow a business or investing in more sustainable practices, they can draw on experienced staff in the community alongside AIB’s wider digital services.
AIB’s community involvement extends beyond banking. As a sponsor of the GAA for more than 35 years, it works with the organisation to promote men’s Gaelic football, ladies football, hurling and camogie across the country.
That same local focus is reflected in the support available at AIB’s Portlaoise and Rathdowney branches, where advisers help customers plan for the life, they’re after through guidance on investing, retirement planning, protection and more.
Customers can also manage everyday banking through the new AIB mobile app, allowing them to bank when they want, how they want and where they want. That’s made easier by the ability to send instant payments using just a mobile number through the Zippay function. The new app also features new insights and budgeting tools and card management so you can freeze and unfreeze cards.
This combination of digital convenience and local expertise gives customers flexibility. Routine tasks can be managed through the app, while branch teams remain available for more detailed conversations about financial plans and decisions.
Whichever channel customers use, security remains central. AIB regularly shares advice to help people protect themselves from scams and provides 24/7 support to customers who believe they may have been defrauded. Its guidance is simple: wait a second and double-check any unexpected request for personal or banking details.
Pausing before responding, checking an unexpected message through a trusted channel and never sharing security details with an unsolicited caller can make a meaningful difference. Anyone concerned about suspicious activity should contact AIB through an official number or trusted channel as soon as possible.

title: How Tesco is helping build friendship, purpose and community under one Men’s Shed roof
description: ‘It’s about being shoulder to shoulder ... and the banter over a cup of tea’
content:
Mayo man Damian McHugh joined Claremorris Men’s Shed soon after it opened in 2012.
It was a time of recession when many, in sectors such as construction, were feeling the consequences of the financial crash. Damian was working part-time in hospitality, which was feeling the pinch too.
“It started out as a men’s support group, because at the beginning there were a lot of retired men that just wanted to meet up and do something, and it grew into a Men’s Shed,” says Damian, who went on to become its chairman.
The Irish Men’s Sheds Association was set up in 2011, based on a movement that had begun in Australia some years earlier, which aimed to improve the health and wellbeing of retired and socially isolated men.
The idea took off across Ireland, with today more than 400 Sheds registered with the association, and at least 12,000 men visiting one each week. It also led to the creation of Women’s Sheds.
Part of the rationale behind the Men’s Sheds is that working side by side, on joint projects, is conducive to conversation among men. “It’s about being shoulder to shoulder,” says Damian. “But it’s also about the chat and the banter over a cup of tea.”
Initially a group of about eight to 10 men would meet regularly at a local family resource centre. “It was somewhere comfortable we could sit down and have a cup of tea,” he says.
As the group grew, it secured the use of an actual shed nearby, a bigger space they could equip with tools and turn into a proper workshop, sharing and teaching a range of practical DIY-type skills.
“Lots of men had lost work at the time and they had all these skills but nowhere to go with them, because everyone was unemployed,” he says.
“Everyone in here has their own skills, whether they were chippies, or lads doing construction, or metal work, and everyone teaches everyone how to do things. That’s a huge part of the Men’s Sheds; they are teaching sheds. I work in hospitality, for example, so I didn’t know how to use an electric chop saw. Now I do. Over the years I’ve picked up all sorts of skills.”
When not working on specific projects they cut down wood for kindling which they sell to raise funds.
“Sheds are non-profit, so everything raised and all donations go back into paying the bills, whether it’s for electricity, tools – or tea,” he laughs.
Having projects to work on, and the purpose that comes with that, helps to support good mental health too, he points out.
Today there are 23 men in Claremorris Men’s Shed, which recently moved into its biggest premises yet, in the town’s old bacon factory.
“This one was a ready-to-go unit, which is great. We’re still in the process of moving in. At the moment we’re trying to set up a canteen area,” he says.
Drop in on any weekday between 10am and 2.30pm and you’ll find about a dozen members gathered there. Some might be making kindling, others enjoying a game of cards, a singsong or simply a cup of tea and a chat.
“You leave feeling great, not just because of something you might have worked on but just because of the lads. Everyone gets on,” he says. That’s not to say there aren’t disagreements, he says, but that’s all part of the fun.
“We always have the chats and a bit of craic. It’s a great way to get all the local news.”
The Shed provides a range of services for the local community, such as fencing for the town’s Christmas tree, running initiatives for Men’s Health Awareness Week, and regularly volunteering as marshals at local events such as the Claremorris Agricultural Show and the town’s parkrun.
“We’ll always try and help anyone we can,” he says.
The Shed has become a lifeline for men who are retired, living alone or rebuilding their confidence after illness and the group is always open to new members, something Damian is very solicitous of.
He knows it can be daunting to join a club of any sort, which is why he makes sure to introduce joiners to a few members at a time, reducing any feelings of stress and putting them at ease.
That includes his own father, who recently retired after a long career in a poultry factory.
“He’d been in the chicken factory for 30 years but had nothing to do after that, in retirement,” says Damian, who, of course, encouraged him to join the shed.
He did and hasn’t looked back since. “Now it’s something for him to do for an hour or two every morning,” he says.
The group’s profile in the town has been helped enormously over the years by being a beneficiary of Tesco Ireland’s Community Fund.
On three separate occasions, it has featured as one of the three local voluntary and charity groups to which shoppers in the town can donate the blue tokens they receive at the checkout.
This has raised valuable funds for the group, about €400 on each occasion, which has helped pay for new equipment, such as a table saw, and contributed towards general overheads.
Tesco’s Community Fund is a core part of the retailer’s That’s Every Little Helps campaign, alongside strong support for Irish suppliers, recognition of the hidden disabilities sunflower and reduced packaging, to name a few. Blue Tokens have helped more than 27,000 community projects secure €10 million since it launched in 2014.
The group depends on public donations for everything.
“The most recent Tesco Community Fund money we got will go towards rent and, the way I look at it, every little helps. The support from Tesco customers really does make a difference and helps us continue providing a place where local men can come together, learn new skills and enjoy each other’s company,” says McHugh.
For more information on the Tesco Community Fund, or to nominate a cause close to your heart to receive funding, visit tescoireland.ie

title: Letters to Our Sons by Stephen Graham and Orly Klein: On men living out a crisis
description: No overview or editorial explanation of the crux of masculinity is offered. This is just a book of testimony
content:
In the West, men, especially young men, are in trouble. The privilege they enjoy is undeniable, but so is their rate of suicide. As the correspondent described as “George • 35–44 • Tech Worker” puts it: “Suicide is the biggest killer of men under fifty, and for every awful end there are so many trips to the emergency room, so many men talked down from moments of crisis – myself included.”
George’s letter describes how, “with one silver suitcase only half full … some clothes, a battered laptop, an old gaming console" he walked out of his first marriage. “The suitcase,” he ruefully observes “had been a wedding present.” The detail of the half-full suitcase (at least for this reader) brought vividly to life an image of George storming out, proud, manly and determined, as he embarked on the journey that would end in ER. This collection is filled with such images, and like a splinter, they go on hurting long after one has finished the text.
Stephen Graham explains in his foreword how Letters to Our Sons came about. When his co-curator Orly Klein’s son “turned thirteen, she’d asked some men to write to him with some guidance on what it means to be a man”. Out of this acorn arose the idea of a book of such letters, by fathers to their sons.
Jude Marwa, the agent, sensed this might resonate with Graham as it would, as he puts it, “continue what we set out to achieve with Adolescence ” , the TV series in which Graham starred and that told so many discomforting truths about fathers, sons and masculinity . Marwa was right. He and Klein agreed to collaborate and together make such a book. The call for letters went out.
The ambition from the start was “to hear from dads who might not usually take part in something like this, who might not necessarily even have access to the portal”. In order to cast the net as wide as possible “application packs [went] to places like libraries, prisons, community centres and charities”. Sixteen hundred letters came back “from fathers from all corners of the world and with hugely different backgrounds, upbringings, religions and cultures” (“from bin men to barristers”, Graham proudly asserts,) and from this tranche he and Klein made their selection.
Their ambition was undeniably to produce a work that is democratic, but of course (and this is not a criticism, just an observation) the nature of the project was bound to appeal to a certain cohort. This would be the sort of men who watched Adolescence (as did the already-mentioned George, who watched immediately before his son was born) and felt threads of anxiety roiling in their guts as they did, because what they saw on the screen connected with insights, perhaps repressed, which they had already had.
These fathers, already troubled or perplexed, were the men moved to send their letters in. The untroubled, the unenlightened, the complacent, did not (or perhaps they did and were cut out). The result is a collection almost completely free of mansplaining bombast and swagger, but heavy with shame and misery, doubt and grief.
[ Netflix hit Adolescence gets a lot wrong about the reality of boys’ struggles Opens in new window ]
The letters in Letters to Our Sons have been grouped into three sections – Early Years, Adolescence and Adulthood – to reflect the different phases in a son’s life. At the foot of each letter, the same basic information about the letter’s writer is given: name, unless they remain anonymous as a few writers do, age bracket, and occupation.
I read Letters to Our Sons in a day, but the editors don’t expect this. The editors see this as “a communal book, the kind of book that can be in the bathroom, or on the coffee table, maybe at the doctor’s or in the dentist’s waiting room … a book that people dip into".
I think the editors might be wrong about that. These letters, so many of which are produced in defiance of what “Terry • 55–64 • Surrey, UK • Retired" memorably calls “hereditary masculine muteness”, make for compulsive if troubling reading. These are all writers trying to eschew the hierarchal and hoping to enable the next generation to live their lives better than they have.
[ Resilience and adolescence: ‘Pushing things away is not learning to ride the wave of emotion’ Opens in new window ]
There is a crisis within masculinity, and Letters to Our Sons captures the iterations, couched as letters, of a selection of men who have lived and are still living this crisis out in their lives. No overview or editorial explanation of this crisis is offered. This is just a book of testimony, and the only reasonable generalisation that can be made about these personal revelations (and this is the editors’ line) is that “We are all the same and all unique”.
It’s refreshing to read a book that doesn’t have designs on one. Will this book make the world a better, kinder place? Who knows? But it won’t make it a worse one.
Carlo Gébler’s memoir No One Tells You: the Last Years of Edna O’Brien, is published by New Island

title: Volkswagen ID.Polo first drive: The Germans remember how to make a VW
description: After missteps with the first generation of ID cars, Volkswagen goes back to basics with an electric Polo that majors on space, comfort and the fundamentals of driving
content:
Volkswagen is having a torrid time. Massive job cuts and ongoing financial challenges have been well aired in the media over the last 12 months. From the midst of this battle emerged the plucky little ID.Polo , carrying rather more weight on its shoulders than any supermini reasonably should.
Okay that’s a lot of pressure to put on the chassis of a little electric car , but it’s fair to say the timing of its arrival could not be more opportune. For in this car – and its siblings carrying sister brand logos – we have a reminder of the foundations of the German brand’s success in the past.
The new VW ID.Polo is not just another electric car tagged with a legacy model name. This is no cynical repeat of the Ford Capri marketing folly. Here we have a car that looks, feels and functions like a Polo but just happens to be electrically powered.
The ID.Polo is arguably Volkswagen’s attempt to draw a line under the first-generation ID era. The headline here is not just another EV but rather a new Polo. VW would have been wiser to drop the ID tag entirely from the name.
Competition in the car market tends to come in waves. Right now, the two most active areas are small affordable electric cars and premium mid-sized crossovers. Buyers in both markets are being spoilt for choice.
The EV supermini battle is defined by fun – often retro – design, smart functionality and the promise, at least, of entry-level prices within shooting range of €20,000. Some of the big names to arrive include the Renault 5, Fiat Grande Panda and Nissan Micra.
Now comes the Polo, a car that over the decades has grown ever larger, just as the Golf has bulked out above it.
We picked up the ID.Polo at the airport in northern Denmark, accompanied by two cases and two colleagues, both of whom tower well over 6ft 2’, for a 72km trip.
No problem with the luggage, but the big surprise was the legroom in this little car. Both passengers sat in line, neither chewing on their kneecaps or forced into the foetal position. Unlike the Renault 5, this car can cater for rear seat passengers with feet larger than size four.
While it retains the conservative exterior styling of past Polos, there’s something remarkable apparent on the inside. Volkswagen has rediscovered the button, that ingenious little device mastered by mankind some time after discovering fire. You can now turn up the temperature or turn down the volume without taking your eyes off the road. That’s cutting-edge ergonomic engineering.
VW spent years defending its touch-heavy interiors. So, a return of buttons is not just some trivial ergonomic detail. This seems like a corporate mea culpa.
There’s even an option to adopt a retro instrument cluster that mimics the old VW analogue dials and even the old calculator-style digital numerals.
About 45km of our trip was on the motorway, where you might expect an EV supermini to be approaching its limits. Yet, the ID.Polo settles in with the characteristics we’ve come to associate with the Golf. It was the same on the narrower rural roads and later, during extensive testing on tight, challenging country lanes.
The real strength of this new ID.Polo is in how mature it feels, delivering its power without any of the sudden surges you get with many EVs. Here, power is delivered in a linear way, not far removed from the best days of the nippy little three-cylinder versions of the past.
[ Forget bigger batteries: VW shows another way to boost EV range Opens in new window ]
Equally impressive is its ride and handling. The steering is beautifully judged. There’s enough weight around the straight-ahead to know what the front wheels are doing, but it doesn’t pile on artificial heft when you wind on lock. The weighting builds naturally through a corner.
The chassis set-up is firm enough to keep the body properly tied down through a sequence of bends, yet the damping takes the sting out of broken surfaces without allowing the Polo to become floaty.
This is a car you could take from Dublin to Cork and not find yourself passing Carlow wishing you’d opted for a bigger model.
One of the most welcome improvements is the braking feel. Earlier ID models haven’t always managed the handover between regeneration and friction braking gracefully, leaving an initially soft, slightly artificial pedal feel before the mechanical brakes bite. This Polo has a far more natural and progressive pedal feel. It sounds like a small thing; in everyday driving it’s anything but.
Across four different ID.Polos we tested, we managed to maintain economy rates of 18.4kWh/100km. On paper that equates to a range just shy of 300km from the 52kWh of usable battery power on offer from our test car. But our driving was hardly representative of everyday use. We were pushing to uncover any flaws in the chassis set-up, while about 40 per cent of our driving was on motorways where the limit was 130km/h.
A trusted colleague who previously spent his time testing the car in a mix of city and suburban driving showed me proof of achieving under 12kWh/100km, which should mean a range of close to VW’s claimed 450km. The firm also claims it can take a fast charge up to 105kW, but we’ll wait for the chance to test that fully before standing over the figure.
Our testing was in versions with the 52kWh battery pack, which carries a price of €33,788 on the road in Ireland after the various grants are applied. However, for those who can live with a range closer to 300km on a full charge, a 37kWh battery pack is also offered, carrying a price tag of €21,410 with a 116hp electric motor or €28,455 for the 135hp motor version. We didn’t get the chance to drive those, so we’ll have to wait for the Irish arrival to run the rule over them. But based on the larger battery and its 211hp motor, Volkswagen certainly has the basis of a supermini that may well outshine its rivals.
[ Renault 5 delivers retro fun and a nippy drive Opens in new window ]
Consider that entry-level version, for example. The equivalent entry-level Renault 5 currently starts at over €26,000. A cheaper Renault variant is due at the end of the year, but for now the ID.Polo has an edge not only on price but also on range, rear seat room and overall grown-up practicality.
Is it great fun to drive? Not quite on a par with the Renault 5 perhaps, but our test versions with the 211hp would qualify as warm hatches. But if it’s more enthusiastic driving you’re after, VW Group isn’t just going to hand you over to Renault.
The ID.Polo provides the grown-up baseline, while Cupra has been allowed to give the Raval more driving fun.
The same platform also underpins the Skoda Epiq, pitched as the more practical, family-friendly crossover, and more style-orientated ID.Cross. There’s even an ID.Polo GTI ready to take to the road. We got the chance to test drive all these different models and can attest to the noticeable difference in their offerings, both in terms of practicality and driving performance.
[ Cupra’s Raval steps forward with VW Group’s first front-drive, affordable EV Opens in new window ]
Like its predecessors, this ID.Polo isn’t showy, it’s not flamboyant, and it’s unlikely to turn heads. But the steering does what you want, the brakes stop where you intended, and the suspension keeps the worst excesses of the road surface outside the cabin. That might seem mundane, but in a car market where these motoring fundamentals seem to play second fiddle to touchscreens that can make farting noises, this ID.Polo perhaps shows that amid the turmoil VW has realised a world of EVs doesn’t require it to reinvent everything that made its cars good in the first place.

title: Joanne McNally on Celebrity Traitors: ‘We’re more than willing to throw each other under the bus’
description: Comedian Joanne McNally is among 21 stars taking part in the second season of the BBC show
content:
Joanne McNally has declared comedians will be “more than willing to throw each other under the bus” on The Celebrity Traitors .
The 43-year-old Irish comedian is among the 21 stars taking part in the second season of the BBC show, which returns this week.
Born in Co Roscommon and raised in Dublin, McNally’s breakthrough came with the one-woman show Bite Me.
While she is busy touring Ireland and the UK until December with her new show Pinotphile , McNally has found the time to appear on the celebrity spin-off of The Traitors, which is hosted by Claudia Winkleman .
This season there are six comedians in the line-up – many of whom have worked together before.
However, McNally said they had not planned strategies together before filming.
“We haven’t been in cahoots at all. There’s been no chatting because we know that we’re more than willing to throw each other under the bus,” McNally said.
“So, it’s not like we’re making fake allegiances. They are professional entertainers, and they will absolutely kill each other off for the craic.”
The other comedians featuring in this season of The Celebrity Traitors are James Acaster, Joe Lycett, Miranda Hart, Rob Beckett and Romesh Ranganathan.
Asked about signing up for the series, McNally said her main drive was for the “social circle”.
[ Traitors winner to use €22,925 prize to fund IVF treatment Opens in new window ]
“It’s all about the celebrity WhatsApp group. And what an eclectic cast we have. Like, you couldn’t predict it. It’s like lining up all my ex-boyfriends. There’s no consistency to it at all. I love it. It’s so frantic. It kind of has a bit of everything,” she said.
Aiming to be chosen as a Traitor, McNally said she was “quietly competitive”.
“I’m great at spotting lies. I can read body language, and I’ve dealt with a lot of snakes,” she said.
The comedian added that her friend and My Therapist Ghosted Me podcast co-host Vogue Williams encouraged her to do whatever it takes to go far in the game.
“She’s delighted. She’s like, get it, girl. She said it would be really funny if I went in fully two-faced. It’s not a bad game plan,” McNally said.
Beckett said he would probably find being on the show “hilarious”.
[ The Traitors Ireland: What makes this intoxicating show so utterly gripping? Opens in new window ]
“It’s just so surreal to be around that group of people, and to be with a few people I know,” he said.
“Romesh, obviously everyone knows we’re such good friends, but Joe Lycett and James Acaster, I did gigs with them nearly 20 years ago, in pubs in Soho in front of eight people, and now all of a sudden we’re in this situation.
“So it’s quite a reflective moment to consider this journey we’ve all gone on to now be on the biggest show on TV.
“Everyone wants to be on it, and we’re very lucky to be here and to be here with friends and people that I’ve come through the ranks with and been able to confide in over the years. It’s quite nice to see all of us here as grown-ups.”
But Beckett added he would be able to betray any of them if the game required it.
[ Joanne McNally: ‘In my early 30s I quit my job, moved into my mam’s attic and cocooned at the top of the house’ Opens in new window ]
“Oh yes, if it’s part of the game. And I’d expect vice versa. If I get done, I get done.
“I’ll be competitive, but if I get murdered or banished or whatever the situation is, of course I’ll be disappointed for a minute, and then I’ll think, do you know what? I’m going home and I’ve got a couple of weeks off!”
He added: “I’ve got no qualms about killing people off.”
Other stars set to join them in the castle include The Last of Us star Bella Ramsey, singer James Blunt, Little Mix’s Leigh-Anne Pinnock, Love Island host Maya Jama and actors Richard E Grant and Michael Sheen.
The first season of The Celebrity Traitors aired on the BBC last autumn, with the finale hitting a peak of 15.4 million viewers, according to the broadcaster.
The spin-off series brought in an average audience of 14.9 million people during its run, the biggest TV audience of 2025.
The Celebrity Traitors starts on October 1st at 8pm on BBC One and BBC iPlayer.

title: No breakthrough in Drumcree crisis as Taoiseach tells Sinn Féin he won’t intervene
description: Bitter dispute over Orange Order parade continues after second round of talks fail to deliver resolution
author_name: Freya McClements, Seanín Graham, Mark Hennessy
content:
The political crisis in Northern Ireland , sparked by last Sunday’s Orange Order parade dispute at Drumcree, is no closer to being resolved. The standoff was continuing on Tuesday night after a second round of talks failed to bring a breakthrough.
Northern Secretary Chris Bryant met separately with the order and the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition at Hillsborough Castle on Tuesday, but concerns are growing that the standoff could continue for some time.
Talks are expected to resume on Wednesday, but with neither side giving any indication on Tuesday night that their position had changed, the prospect of an agreement appeared slim.
Portadown district master Nigel Dawson reiterated that the Orange Order had the legal right to march. “We look forward to the law being applied to the parade,” he said.
However, Garvaghy Road residents’ spokesman Breandán Mac Cionnaith said their message was: “Reroute the sectarian parade.”
Speaking to The Irish Times afterwards, he asked to meet with Chief Constable Jon Boutcher, asserting he was “the only person still left for us to meet, if he has the courage to meet us”.
In the Northern Assembly, there was a second day of angry clashes between Sinn Féin and unionist politicians, while in the Dáil, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald told Taoiseach Micheál Martin the Northern Secretary could no longer “sit on his hands”.
McDonald asked the Government to encourage Bryant to use his powers by intervening and banning the march.
Martin said he did not think it is “as simple as that”, adding “one intervention is not going to resolve it”. He stressed the need for people to “stand back” and called for “some collective pathway . . . with some degree of mediation”.
[ Drumcree: ‘I want to stop all this in its tracks. I have five grandchildren; it’s breaking my heart’ Opens in new window ]
Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee said she believed it was “likely” an international mediator would be appointed to intervene.
There remained a police presence in the Garvaghy Road area of Portadown on Tuesday night. Members of the Orange Order were still inside Drumcree church, while protesters continued to keep watch alongside the Garvaghy Road.
Earlier on Tuesday, lawyers for the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition lodged a legal challenge to the court decision which overturned an earlier injunction banning the parade.
The original determination by the Parades Commission granted a limited parade of 35 Orange Order members permission to march from Drumcree Church last Sunday.
The fresh application argues the Parades Commission “materially misdirected itself” on the police assessment of the potential for disorder and had not given an “accurate representation of the evidence received from the PSNI” in its decision.
The hearing is listed for the Court of Appeal in Belfast on Friday.
McDonald and First Minister Michelle O’Neill , who is also Sinn Féin vice president, met the Taoiseach as well as Tánaiste Simon Harris in Government Buildings on Tuesday to discuss the crisis.
There have been calls from unionists for O’Neill and McDonald to be prosecuted for their participation in the “unnotified” protest which prevented the march from proceeding on Sunday.
Arriving at Government Buildings, O’Neill was asked by the media if she had been contacted by police and if she expected to be arrested.
“No, I have not, and no,” she replied, adding that she would “continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents”.
The PSNI has said it is reviewing the evidence gathered, and anyone who has broken the law will be prosecuted.

title: Gordon and Kane fire England to Nations League victory against 10-man Czech Republic
description: Trent Alexander-Arnold brought in from the cold to set up Antony Gordon opener
content:
Anybody can lose to Spain. But when England did so at Wembley on Saturday, it served to turn the temperature up on this trip to the Czech Republic, where England have form for finding it difficult. Remember the Euros qualifier in 2019 when they lost 2-1?
It was not easy at first. Thomas Tuchel shuffled his pack, making the surprise decision to start Jude Bellingham among the substitutes. It was all a little angsty and the Czechs, for whom this is the start of a new era under the Spaniard Santi Denia after their World Cup washout, dared to dream about another upset.
Then everything changed. It was a rash challenge in the 23rd minute by Pavel Sulc on Elliot Anderson, late and high, albeit nothing overtly nasty. The referee, Umut Meler, showed the Czech midfielder a yellow card and on we went. Yet the video assistant referee was not happy and when Meler was called to the monitor, everybody knew what was coming next.
It was a red card to disfigure the contest, but Tuchel was not complaining. His players made the most of the decision to get their Nations League campaign up and running, the standout moment being provided by Tuchel’s headline selection.
Trent Alexander-Arnold was in from the cold at the outset for only his second appearance under Tuchel; the first was as a substitute against Andorra in the summer of last year. And it was the Real Madrid player who helped to unlock the stalemate at the beginning of the second half, his whipped cross made to measure for Anthony Gordon.
Harry Kane added the second with his 87th England goal and, after all the focus on England’s defensive vulnerability, there was the bonus for Tuchel of a first clean sheet in seven matches. The team had conceded 13 times in the previous six. It did not start particularly well. By the end, it was a stroll.
The rare inclusion of Alexander-Arnold at right-back was the wild card. Any team with him in it feels more nuanced and it meant Tuchel retained only Marc Guéhi from the back four against Spain. Ezri Konsa and Nico O’Reilly had minor injuries. With Trevoh Chalobah in central defence and Lewis Hall at left-back, it was a completely untested unit.
England lacked cohesion at the outset. There were errors from them and it was easy to fret about their lack of care on the ball; the looseness of some of the passing. They looked to build through Elliot Anderson but the midfielder got away with one in the early running when he misjudged a high ball up the channel and Sulc had the sniff of an opening. Chalobah chased back to put him off.
The red card changed the feel of the occasion. The Czechs had been the better team until then. England could highlight the moment on 16 minutes when Gordon took a fizzed pass from Myles Lewis-Skelly and crossed low for Morgan Rogers. Lukas Cerv hit a sweet volley past the post. Sulc choose the wrong option when well-placed and was crowded out by Guéhi and Chalobah.
Sulc’s challenge on Anderson was late and a little high. In the moment, it felt as though the referee, Umut Meler, got it right with the yellow. Sulc had over-stretched in an effort to play the ball. It was not malicious and it did not feel crazily excessive in terms of the force. There was no outrage from the England players around Anderson. Meler was sent to the pitchside monitor and he concluded that it ticked the boxes for an upgrade to red. As always it looked worse on the slow-motion replays.
The hosts felt their attacking ambition evaporate. England came to dominate the ball. What could they do with it? Not much before the interval. Kane took another incisive ball from Lewis-Skelly and extended Matej Kovar in the 45th minute. England had to do more.
Tuchel finished the first half in an almighty funk at the fourth official after a decision had gone against Bukayo Saka.
The manager reset at the interval, sending on Eberechi Eze for Lewis-Skelly – who was booked on 35 minutes – and going to 4-1-4-1. Lewis-Skelly had lunged in on Cerv, whose screams could be heard up in the press box. The Czechs wanted a red card to even things up. It was not that bad but Tuchel could not take any chances with Lewis-Skelly.
England got the breakthrough almost immediately and it was one for the Alexander-Arnold lovers. When the Czechs coughed up the ball cheaply, he chased it down on the right, turned and did what he does. The pinged cross had a low trajectory and it bounced once before sitting up for Gordon, whose headed conversion was marked by precision. It was deserved reward for Gordon, who was quick and urgent; he was the player most likely to spark England.
Hall began to surge up the line. He shot inches wide after getting a pass back from Gordon while he watched Ladislav Krejci turn a low cross from him against his own post. The Gordon goal had relaxed England and the Kane goal was inevitable. It came when he drilled a loose ball into the far corner after a break into the box by Rogers.
Tuchel got Alex Scott on for his debut and he did well. Ditto Rio Ngumoha, who also came off the bench. England might have scored more with Kovar making a particularly fine save to deny Eze.
Next up for them is Croatia away on Saturday. – Guardian

title: Switzerland’s Rodríguez and Elvedi punish Scotland after early red card
description: Hosts reduced to 10 for almost 80 minutes after Jack Hendry sent off at Hampden Park
content:
Switzerland have responded exceptionally well from allegations of capers involving vaccination certificates that threatened to overshadow this international window. Make that six points out of six for Murat Yakin’s stylish team. Switzerland look comfortably capable of breezing out of Group B1 in the Nations League . They have not even played at home yet. Granit who?
Sébastien Pocognoli, conversely, has been left to ponder one step forward and umpteen back. Scotland’s second half in Slovenia at the weekend provided hope to the new manager and a supporter base who want to enter a brave new world. Age old, troublesome flaws remain.
Jack Hendry’s red card meant Scotland played almost 80 minutes of this encounter with 10 men. They were, however, outclassed in every department. Scottish patterns of play were not immediately obvious. The upcoming trip to North Macedonia carries importance as Pocognoli seeks to win hearts and minds. This was all pretty grim for anyone of a Scotland persuasion.
Scottish expectancy heading into a World Cup where they subsequently took tedium to new levels feels such a long time ago. They have scored only once in five games. Impotence can only concern Scotland’s Belgian manager, whose bow at Hampden Park was over as a contest long before full-time. A penny for the thoughts of Steve Clarke, Pocognoli’s immediate predecessor and a coach much-maligned in certain quarters. Were Clarke in charge of this ragged display, the public response would have been ferocious.
Judgment of Pocognoli on this occasion requires appropriate context. Switzerland had control of the early exchanges without creating anything until a slick move saw Dan Ndoye sent through on goal from the halfway line. It was quickly apparent ­Hendry did not have the pace to halt his ­opponent. Initially, the referee Nenad Minakovic booked Hendry and awarded a penalty for the clear pull on Ndoye which ­toppled the Swiss forward. Following a video assistant referee check that was unnecessarily lengthy, the official corrected his decision to a free-kick and sending off. Up stepped Ricardo Rodríguez to crack the ball beyond Angus Gunn from 19 yards.
Pocognoli’s immediate response was to withdraw Kieron Bowie, one of two strikers. The introduction of ­Stephen Welsh retained Scotland’s three-man backline. A noticeably subdued Hampden crowd feared a long evening. This is, after all, a Switzerland team that followed up a strong World Cup performance with a comfortable win in North Macedonia on Saturday.
John McGinn appealed in vain for a penalty after claiming he was held at a Scotland corner. The blunt truth is Scotland have needed more from McGinn than the seeking or winning of fouls for some time.
McGinn’s Aston Villa team-mate Johan ­Manzambi was unsurprisingly lively; he fired just wide of Gunn’s right-hand post moments after a delicious cross that found no Swiss takers. With half an hour played, the Scots were gasping for air against opponents who looked physically and technically superior. When in possession, far too much of the hosts’ play was sideways or backwards. Gunn denied Ndoye nine minutes before the break.
The half ended with a yellow card for Pocognoli, who protested a little too vociferously after McGinn was fouled. All the episode did was sum up Scottish frustration. There had been needle in the game but the coherent football had been played by those in red.
Manzambi had irritated the home support by embellishing fouls and entering into a verbal spat with Oli McBurnie. His play, though, was a compelling watch. Manzambi’s movement unnerved Scotland.
