His willingness to drop deep or wide to get involved in the game emphasised his versatility. Manzambi’s touch and dribbling ability set him apart; all at the age of just 20. Scotland’s lack of anything approaching such emerging talent is glaring.
Switzerland’s second came from a more unlikely source. Scotland only partially cleared a corner, with the ball funnelled wide right to Ndoye. The cross was pacy and low, with the central defender Nico Elvedi striding forward to flick home. Two nil was a more appropriate reflection of events to that point.
Pocognoli now made a triple change. McBurnie’s 18th cap had passed without the ending of his international scoring wait. As on Saturday, the alterations were like-for-like in positional nature. ­Pocognoli’s level of tactical flexibility remains open to question. Yakin withdrew ­Manzambi, in what could be classed as a humanitarian act towards Scotland.
Not that Switzerland had stopped dishing out punishment. The ­closing stages resembled an attack ­versus defence training exercise. A third from the Swiss was inevitable as they toyed with the Scots.
Gunn was pitifully weak in attempting to deal with Zeki ­Amdouni’s strike, which flew into the roof of the Scotland net via the goalkeeper. Cue a mass exodus from the stands. Pocognoli has been served a strong, painful reminder of the scale of task he chose to inherit. – Guardian

title: Éamonn Fitzmaurice front-runner to become Galway football manager
description: Pádraic Joyce stood down as manager earlier this month after seven seasons in charge
content:
Éamonn Fitzmaurice is understood to be the front-runner to replace Pádraic Joyce as Galway senior football manager, according to reports.
An All-Ireland winner with Kerry as a player and manager, Fitzmaurice is believed to be in advance talks with Galway GAA over his potential appointment.
Joyce stepped down as Galway manager at the start the month after seven seasons in charge of his native county.
Fitzmaurice won three All-Ireland titles with Kerry as a player, coming in 2000, 2004 and 2006, before retiring from intercounty action the following season.
The Finuge clubman took over as Kerry senior manager in August 2012, succeeding Jack O’Connor after his second stint in charge.
He spent six seasons at the helm, leading Kerry to an All-Ireland title in 2014, before stepping down after the 2018 championship.
Galway reached this year’s Connacht final, losing out to Roscommon, and came through the new All-Ireland series format, getting to the quarter-finals where their season was ended by Dublin.
The Tribesmen have contested two All-Ireland football finals in the last five seasons, losing out to Kerry in 2022 and Armagh in 2024. The county last claimed the Sam Maguire Cup with a win over Meath in the 2001 decider.

title: Garvaghy Rd residents say chief constable must meet them to explain parade advice
description: Garvaghy Road residents lodge legal challenge to parade ruling and seek ‘urgent hearing’
author_name: Jack White, Katie Mellett, Colin Gleeson
content:
The meeting of the Garvaghy Road residents has concluded, reports Mark Hennessy from the scene.
Shortly after 8pm, Breandán Mac Cionnaith and other residents’ leaders briefed hundreds of locals in the pastoral centre next to St John The Baptist’s Church on Garvaghy Road about the meeting held in Hillsborough with the Northern Ireland Secretary of State, Chris Bryant, following the latter’s return from the Labour Party conference in Manchester.
Mac Cionnaith said Chief Constable of Northern Ireland Jon Boutcher must meet with Garvaghy Road residents to explain how the force could have told the Parades Commission that an Orange Order march could take place from Drumcree Church without the risk of serious public disorder.
“Almost 93 per cent of people here signed a petition opposing this proposed march,” he told journalists after the briefing.
“Their voices need to be heard by the British government – and not only heard, but listened to. So that was made very clear to the Secretary of State. We also said that a march along Garvaghy Road in any shape, any form, would not be acceptable to this community.”
Demanding a meeting with Boutcher, he said: “The only person still left for us to meet, if he has the courage to meet us, is the PSNI chief constable.
“So, I’ll be waiting tonight and tomorrow morning for the chief constable to let me know when he is going to meet with us, or is he going to hide behind a wall of uniforms of police in riot gear? It’s up to him.”
He said Boutcher needs to be able to explain how the PSNI’s security briefing to the Parades Commission could have led to the commission clearing the way for the Orange parade.
“I’m sure the chief constable knows the questions that’s going to be posed to him,” he said. “Have the courage and come and meet with us.”
Earlier in the week, Mac Coinnaith demanded the appointment of an international mediator, though he sounded significantly less enthusiastic about this point when he spoke to journalists on Tuesday evening.
“Our past experience has been that mediation has always ended up in a march, so why should we get involved in a flawed process that leads to a flawed decision?”
Rejecting suggestions that he was back-tracking, he said: “No, I says why should we [get involved in mediation]? It’s up to others to prove why we should.
“We’re very clear, and don’t try to misinterpret anything I’m saying, and don’t try and publish wrongful information about what’s going on. We’re asking the questions. Nobody’s giving us the answers.”
Questioned about the residents’ group decision to launch a court challenge to seek sight of the PSNI’s security advice to the Commission, he said: “I think it’s quite obvious what we want to achieve through that legal action.
“So that’s another process has been put into play here. The Orange Order and Jamie Bryson aren’t the only ones that can take legal action. We’ll leave that to the courts to decide.
“But, as I said, our main priority now is to see if the chief constable will meet us and let us know what his views are, because he also has some questions to address, especially about his so-called security assessment that led us to be put in this position.”
He finished by insisting residents will stay on watch “until we get a decision”.
A meeting of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition has started, Mark Hennessy reports from the scene. The press have been left outside.
He tells us there were cheers for their representatives upon entering, but adds: “That tells little.”
Garvaghy Road residents have finished a meeting with Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Chris Bryant at Hillsborough Castle.
A representative of the community, Breandán Mac Cionnaith left without making comment, stating “it’s only fair” to brief residents first.
O’Neill earlier said police have not contacted her about her attendance at an unlawful protest against the Drumcree parade, adding that she does not expect to be arrested.
She and other senior colleagues were among a large crowd that blockaded the road in the predominantly nationalist Garvaghy Road area on Sunday to prevent the contentious Orange Order Drumcree parade from passing the route.
Under parading laws in Northern Ireland, protests must be notified to, and approved by, the Parades Commission adjudication body.
Police have confirmed the protest was unnotified to the commission and therefore unlawful.
Asked if she believed she was above the law, O’Neill told reporters: “Right is always right, and this community needs our support right now – and I will continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents.”
The Orange Order has said it had “a very positive and constructive meeting” with Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Chris Bryant.
Speaking as his group left the meeting at Hillsborough Castle, Orange Order Portadown district master Nigel Dawson said: “We have once again had a very positive and constructive meeting with the Secretary of State.”
“Obviously, the contents of the meeting is confidential but we look forward to the law being applied to the parade.
“We will not be taking any questions because this is a confidential meeting we had with the Secretary of State.”
Asked when the process will continue, he said: “That’s a question for the Secretary of State.”
Since early Sunday morning, 35 members of the Orange Order have been waiting at Drumcree Church to parade down the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown.
It is a march that, in the 1990s, sparked tension and violence in Drumcree, and with the result that the Protestant loyalist organisation has been refused permission to march through the Catholic area for nearly 30 years.
As of Tuesday, the Orangemen remain determined to march, saying they now have the legal right to do so. The local nationalist community is equally intent on preventing them.
And the repercussions are being felt at Stormont. The DUP and the Orange Order have made complaints to the PSNI about the presence of Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald and Northern Ireland’s First Minister, Michelle O’Neill, at the protest.
With tensions running high on the streets of Drumcree, and the DUP-Sinn Féin political partnership fraying, could this standoff bring down Stormont?
You can hear from Mark Hennessy, The Irish Times Ireland and Britain Editor, in our In the News podcast as he reports from the Garvaghy Road.
On the fresh legal bid to prevent the Drumcree march, lawyers for the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition have argued the Parades Commission “materially misdirected itself” on the police assessment of the potential for disorder.
The group has also claimed the Parades Commission had not given an “accurate representation of the evidence received from PSNI” in its decision.
The Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition has lodged a legal challenge to a ruling which found the Orange Order Drumcree parade could proceed at the weekend, reports Northern Correspondent Seanín Graham .
The residents’ solicitor, Darragh Mackin of Phoenix Law, confirmed on Wednesday that he had submitted an appeal seeking an “urgent hearing”.
Papers were lodged to the Court of Appeal in Belfast shortly before 3pm, ahead of their meeting with Northern Ireland Secretary for State Chris Bryant, at Hillsborough Castle.
“It is clear there’s a wider public interest in having these issues determined,” Mackin told The Irish Times.
The residents will challenge an appeal granted to the Orange Order following an overnight court hearing on Sunday, which resulted in an earlier injunction banning the parade being overturned.
Central to the residents’ appeal will be a PSNI submission to the Parades Commission.
The commission determined that a limited parade of 35 Orange Order members could proceed down the nationalist Garvaghy Road.
“The late disclosure at 1.30am on Sunday morning regarding the content of the police assessment given to the Parades Commission called into question the rationality of the Parades Commission’s decision in the first instance,” Mackin said.
“For that reason, it is important these issues are ventilated before the court at the earliest opportunity.”
It is not yet clear when the appeal hearing will take place.
Mackin also rejected claims made on Tuesday by an Orange Order member who said that the Parades determination remained “live”.
“There’s no rationale for saying it’s a live determination. It’s not. That’s wrong,” he said.
If the Portadown Orange Order members leave Drumcree Church, they know they will have “have to reapply” to the commission for another parade, he added.
“They police cannot extend a Parades Commission determination,” he added.
Sinn Féin Assembly member (MLA) Pat Sheehan asked unionist MLAs seated opposite why they had given over the leadership of unionism “to this buck idiot, Jamie Bryson,” reports Northern Editor Freya McClements .
The high-profile loyalist activist and “legal eagle”, Sheehan said, was “swinging you all around by the tail. Why do you not just stand up?”, he asked.
“The leader of unionism at the minute, who is calling the shots, is standing down at Drumcree,” he said.
In response, DUP MLA Diane Forsythe described Sheehan as an “IRA bomber,” in reference to a past conviction and emphasised she was “proud” to say DUP leader Gavin Robinson was the leader of unionism.
“He does a much better job than the part-timer [Sinn Féin vice president] Michelle O’Neill, First Minister on the run from the chamber.”
Ulster Unionist leader Jon Burrows criticised the Sinn Féin politicians who took part in the unnotified protest against the Drumcree parade on Sunday, saying “you have damaged the legitimacy of this place and that is shameful.
“A big challenge is coming down the road for Sinn Féin, because its members broke the law.”
SDLP MLA and Leader of the Opposition, Matthew O’Toole, highlighted the continued “dysfunction” of the Stormont Executive, not least over its continued failure to agree a budget and said Northern Ireland was “at a moment of acute political – possibly even societal – crisis, given what has become a stand-off.
“While I want a resolution to the issue at Garvaghy Road that upholds the rights of the residents, I also have to be clear about the unacceptability of walking away from the responsibility to govern this place,” he said.
The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) MLA Timothy Gaston repeated his call for the DUP to walk out of the Executive and collapse the power-sharing institutions, asking “how can she [O’Neill] remain a fit partner in government for [deputy first minister] Emma Little-Pengelly?
“The rule of law must be upheld,” he said. “No parade, no Stormont – and no surrender.”
The Assembly also heard O’Neill will attend the chamber to answer an urgent oral question regarding her presence at Sunday’s protest next week, after she failed to do so on Monday.
DUP MLA Philip Brett had tabled the urgent oral question asking O’Neill to explain how her attendance at the protest was in keeping with her pledge of office as an MLA.
O’Neill defended her presence at Sunday’s protest, which was not notified to the Parades Commission and was therefore deemed illegal, in the Assembly earlier on Monday, saying she had attended in her capacity as the vice president of Sinn Féin, not as First Minister.
On Tuesday, speaker Edwin Poots gave an update to the Assembly, saying O’Neill had initially indicated she would attend to answer the question that day, but later informed him she was unable to do so because of “another urgent engagement.”
O’Neill and McDonald were in Dublin on Tuesday afternoon for a meeting with Taoiseach Micheál Martin to discuss the ongoing stand-off at Drumcree.
Poots said he had been given an assurance O’Neill would attend next week and he was content the matter was resolved.
“The situation now on the Garvaghy Road is very urgent, there has to be an intervention,” said Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald, reports Political Correspondent Harry McGee .
McDonald, along with First Minister Michelle O’Neill, went to meet the Taoiseach and the Tánaiste at Government Buildings.
“The march has to be stopped and the person with the discretion to do that is the British Secretary of State.”
“They expect the Government here in Dublin — their government, because they are Irish citizens.
“They expect that their government intervenes and demands that the British Secretary of State stop sitting on his hands and delaying matters and intervenes now, as is his right and his power, to stop this march.”
She said she will be asking Simon Harris and Micheál Martin to “intervene directly now and ask the British Government to do the right thing.
“Every day that passes, the pressure on the community grows, and I think it’s fair to say that you couldn’t overstate the kind of trauma that has now been revisited on the community.
She said that community life and family lives are “completely disrupted”.
“The level of damage that has been done to relationships across all communities is immense, and the longer this goes on, the more that will deteriorate.”
She said that “28 years of peace” in the Garvaghy Road area is now “in jeopardy”.
“This proposal for a sectarian march, an Orange march, down the Garvaghy Road, travelling through a Catholic neighbourhood, is part of a broader charter, a rejectionist charter. People want to drag us all back to the past,” she said.
Northern Ireland’s First Minister Michelle O’Neill said she has not been contacted by the police over her attendance at an unlawful protest against the Drumcree parade in Co Armagh.
Arriving for a meeting with Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Tánaiste Simon Harris, O’Neill was asked if she had been contacted by the PSNI and whether she expects to be arrested following her attendance, she replied: “No, I have not. And no.”
O’Neill has faced criticism from unionists after she attended the unlawful protest in Portadown when she stood alongside residents on the Garvaghy Road.
O’Neill and other senior colleagues were among a large crowd that blocked the road in the predominantly nationalist area to prevent the Orange Order Drumcree parade from taking the route. - PA
Garvaghy Road residents will tell the Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant that they will not accept a parade, at a meeting on Tuesday evening.
Asked as he arrived at Hillsborough Castle for the meeting, what his message to Bryant is, representative of the community, Breandán Mac Cionnaith said “reroute the sectarian parade, that’s it”.
“That’s what our community wants. That’s what almost 4,000 people living in our community want and we gave that evidence to the Parades Commission last week.
“A signed petition, signed by 4,000 residents. That’s our mandate.” - PA
“No talking, no walking” was the position of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition from the outset of the dispute in 1995, writes Newton Emerson .
If Portadown District Orange Lodge would not talk to residents, they would not agree to a parade.
The Orangemen would not talk because they believed they needed no consent from residents to walk “the Queen’s highway”.
They did engage in shuttle diplomacy in 1995, with mediators moving between both sides until a parade was agreed. But the lack of direct contact led to mutual misunderstanding: residents thought they had a respectful compromise; Orangemen thought they had won.
Notorious scenes of jubilation outside Portadown’s Orange Hall destroyed the deal and have left residents wary ever since.
This deadlock has defined Drumcree and the British government’s strategic response: the creation of the Parades Commission in 1998.
Government Chief Whip Mary Butler rejected calls in the Dáil for a debate this week on the Garvaghy Road crisis, reports Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
“I think it’s important that efforts involved in the Minister of Foreign Affairs, the UK Secretary of State and importantly the communities, are allowed to continue,” she said.
She was responding to calls from People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd Barrett for an “urgent debate” about the Garvaghy Road crisis. He said his call last week was ignored, and the crisis had developed.
The Irish Government and British governments have a responsibility to make sure “communities are free from sectarian intimidation,” he said.
“That was ignored, and we saw the escalation last week and that is still not resolved.
“Can we have an urgent discussion to make sure this Government and this Oireachtas discharge its responsibility in that regard,” he asked.
Independent Laois TD Brian Stanley backed the call for a debate. He said the only reason the parade was given the go ahead for the Orange Order was to “demonstrate supremacy and dominance over the national community there”.
A delegation from Portadown Orange Order has arrived at Hillsborough Castle for talks with Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant.
The group was accompanied by their legal adviser, loyalist activist Jamie Bryson.
The delegation, which includes District Grand Master Nigel Dawson, did not speak to the media on arrival. - PA
In response to Labour leader Ivana Bacik’s question, the Taoiseach said “we need to be careful of” placing responsibility on the PSNI, reports Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
Micheál Martin said “I think the PSNI would say there were caveats to that”. He paid tribute Chief Constable Jon Boutcher who had one “clear objective” that he “didn’t want one ear and one head hurt or injured”.
“We should be clear about supporting the PSNI in that objective and avoiding any action that would precipitate injury or harm to people,” he said.
He said the manner in which the decision was allowed seemed to suggest there were “clear issues” if they were “only allowing 35”.
“We need to focus on how we can bring all different dimensions to this together and how we can have a conversation and develop a conversation between the communities involved to try and resolve this once and for all or to get a pathway to resolution of this.”
“I think we now need to concentrate on how we get a resolution to this, which will not be easy,” he said.
Labour leader Ivana Bacik said it was a “failure of Northern Ireland’s political system that the situation remains so tense and volatile today,” in the Dáil, reports Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
Residents “may well feel that the institutions set up to protect peace have abandoned them. So we must not abandon them.”
She said as co-guarantors of the Good Friday Agreement, the Taoiseach has a “role in restoring trust”.
She warned “there are sinister actors who want to see mediation fail, who want to explore the dysfunction in power sharing and in devolution to bring down the institutions of the Good Friday Agreement and we cannot allow them to win”.
Bacik asked if the Taoiseach had questioned the PSNI as to “why it told the parades commission that the Drumcree parade could safely take place, as it clearly could not”.
The DUP and the Orange Order have made complaints to police about the presence of a number of Sinn Féin representatives at the protest on Sunday - including Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald, vice president and Northern Ireland’s First Minister, Michelle O’Neill - which prevented it from proceeding along the Garvaghy Road, reports Northern Editor Freya McClements .
In the Stormont chamber on Monday, O’Neill defended her participation, saying she was “proud” to be involved and she would assert the rights of the residents of the Garvaghy Road “to live their life free from fear and intimidation … all day long and every day.”
The Police Service of Northern Ireland’s (PSNI) “significant public safety operation” remains in place on the Garvaghy Road.
In an update on the Drumcree policing operation, Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said: “Overnight, we have continued to engage and assess how best to balance the rights of all parties.
“We will continue to explore and keep under review a range of tactical options to safely bring this matter to a conclusion and keep the peace.
“Our dedicated enquiry team are continuing to review evidence gathered to ensure an effective criminal justice strategy,” he said.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin said he did not think “one intervention” was going to resolve the situation on Garvaghy road, reports Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
Responding to Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald’s call for him to call on the British government and Secretary of State for Northern Ireland to stop the parade, he said he had been in touch with British prime minister Andy Burnham and they had discussed the situation over the weekend.
Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee “has been in constant contact with the secretary of state”.
He said “if we’re honest, I don’t think it’s as simple as that” to have “one intervention” to stop the parade.
People “have to stand back and there has to be some collective pathway determined with some degree of mediation”.
Describing the situation as “deeply depressing” the Taoiseach said there are “a number of complications to this that transpired over the weekend”.
He said it “calls for creative thinking” to “create a pathway of reconciliation and trust, building on the platform of work that has been underway in this community for quite some time, building on that platform to create a long-lasting peaceful resolution of this”.
He added: “I understand fully that feelings are very high, but this is a time for all of us to be calm and to be careful in what we say and what we do.
“I am relieved that those directly involved are open to mediation” and he supported the idea of an “independent international figure, to play a role in supporting and encouraging mediation and negotiation”.
In the Dáil, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said the Irish and British governments have a responsibility to ensure “there is no Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road,” reports Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
She said the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland “can stop this sectarian march being forced down that road and that is what he must do, because the way to restore peace and calm is this”.
“That is the way to resolve this crisis,” she insisted and called on Taoiseach Micheál Martin to inform “the British prime minister and the Secretary of State of their responsibility to end this nightmare and to stop this march and to allow the people of the Garvaghy Road and beyond to return to their peaceful lives”.
She asked the Taoiseach to “impress upon the British government and the Secretary of State, that he can no longer sit on his hands. He has to intervene and stop this march.”
McDonald asked “why when a generation has grown up without this intimidation, without this fear, why is there such determination to reopen this dispute and override the clearly expressed wishes of the community”.
But she asked “how was such an incomprehensible and wrong decision arrived at? What changed?”
The “days of second-class citizenship are over” and there would be no return to the past.
For mediation to succeed “the community need to have the threat of this sectarian march lifted”.
Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant has arrived at Hillsborough Castle ahead of further talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parading dispute.
Bryant travelled to Co Down after delivering his speech at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool.
He is due to host delegations from the Orange Order and Garvaghy Road residents. - PA
Earlier, Portadown Deputy District Master Alistair Power told reporters that the determination by the Parades Commission to grant the parade remained “live,” reports Northern Correspondent Seanín Graham .
It had previously been suggested that the controversial determination – which was challenged in the High Court during a marathon series of 14-hour hearings at the weekend – lapsed by midnight on Sunday.
Portadown district also told police on Tuesday that they are ready to walk down the Garvaghy Road when the PSNI is ready to facilitate it.
The lodge has accepted a second invitation from Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant at Hillsborough Castle this afternoon.
Its statement added: “We must all be governed by the same law and expect our rights under it to be vindicated.
“Ours have been denied and despite having used the law and obtaining a clear determination in our favour, the message being sent now is that this counts for nothing and instead, it is those who break the law who are rewarded and prevail.
”If this persists then in general, the rule of law collapses but in particular parading regulation collapses as any group, on any side, will know all they must do to override the Parades Commission is to put a mob on the street and the Chief Constable will wilt.”
The Orange Order has made a criminal complaint against First Minister Michelle O’Neill and Sinn Fein leader Mary Lou McDonald over their participation in the Garvaghy Road protests, reports Northern Correspondent Seanín Graham .
Portadown District Lodge confirmed on Tuesday it made a formal complaint to the Chief Constable in relation to four alleged offences “including under the Serious Crime Act 2007”.
In a statement, it said the rule of law has been “hugely damaged”.
“Faith in the law continues to erode as the PSNI continue to facilitate an unlawful mob thumbing their nose at the legal determination and our courts,” it added.
“The impact of this cannot be underestimated. As a society, we must all be governed by the same law, and expect our rights under it to be vindicated.”
O’Neill and McDonald stood with thousands of protestors on the Garvaghy Road on Sunday morning ahead of the planned parade by 35 members of Portadown district, which was due to begin at 8am.
Sinn Féin has been contacted for comment.
It is “essential” that peace and order are maintained as the stand-off over the planned Orange Order march on the Garvaghy Road continues, said Tánaiste Simon Harris, reports Political Correspondent Cormac McQuinn .
The Fine Gael leader said what has happened and the decision of the Parades Commission to allow the march “has really been extraordinarily triggering, traumatic and devastating for a community that has suffered far too much.”
He expressed his hope that a solution can be found that understands this.
Harris also said: “We can never again see a nationalist community left behind in the North and this is simply an appalling situation”.
Speaking to reporters in advance of Tuesday’s Cabinet meeting Harris responded to a suggestion that Garvaghy Road residents believe the Irish Government was slow to respond to events.
Harris said he is “disappointed and saddened” to hear that and mentioned that he met Garvaghy Road residents last week and said there has been “very intensive engagement” and “very strong” comments from Taoiseach Micheál Martin over the weekend.
He said he himself has been in touch with political leaders in the North and “the Irish Government is very clear in relation to this.
“My very strong view is that the Parades Commission got this extraordinarily wrong.
“But that part perhaps is for another day.”
He added: “What is most essential now is that the very unique and traumatic circumstances and the history of that trauma are understood in finding a solution and finding a way forward and I really do also hope that at this very tense moment that the ongoing efforts to ensure that while this stand-off is in place that peace is maintained, that good order is maintained”.
He acknowledged that this has been the case “in relation to both sides of the dispute so far and it is absolutely essential that that continues in the hours an days ahead.”
An international mediator over the Drumcree parade dispute is “likely the direction that we’re going in” and “would be welcome on all sides,” said Minister for Foreign Affairs, Helen McEntee.
“I think it’s important that we have someone that would understand the situation first and foremost,” she told RTÉ.
“This is a very complex situation and as we know there has been significant trauma and there has been significant challenges over the years.
“That’s why we haven’t had a march in 28 years, that’s why it’s really important that we do not go back to the challenges of the past and to the trauma that was inflicted on communities there.
“So I think this is an option to move forward…with the agreement of the communities and with the wider political support today so I hope that we will be able to see progress in that regard."
To have been a fly on the wall when Breandán Mac Cionnaith met Northern Ireland’s Secretary of State Chris Bryant on Monday afternoon would have been interesting. Former Labour prime minister Tony Blair could have briefed Bryant on what to expect, writes former Northern editor of The Irish Times Gerry Moriarty .
In his memoir, Blair remembered the Drumcree “nightmare” that began in the mid-1990s. He didn’t specify whether he was referring to the Orange Order or the Garvaghy residents, or both,, but his view was that “the Drumcree people were the unreasonable of the unreasonable of the unreasonable”.
“In the Premier League of unreasonableness, they left every other faction and every other dispute gasping in their wake,” he wrote.
And then he lighted on “this one guy, Breandán Mac Cionnaith”.
He painted a picture: “He took unreasonableness to an art form. He conceded nothing, and I mean nothing. I’m not just talking about the substance of meetings, I mean where a meeting should be held. Who should be there. Who shouldn’t be there. When it began. When it ended. What its purpose was. Who spoke first. Who spoke last. Who spoke in between first and last.”
Bryant is to fly back immediately to Belfast from the Labour Party conference in Liverpool , though it is likely to be mid-afternoon before he will have the opportunity for direct talks with the Orange Order, the Garvaghy Road residents and political parties.
Bryant insisted he will go ahead of reforms of Northern Ireland’s legacy commission, though he pointedly insisted that such a body will be able to offer truth to the families of British soldiers and Northern Irish security forces, just as much as it will for any sector of Northern Ireland’s population.
The Drumcree parades crisis is setting Northern Ireland back years, Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant said, urging all sides to “double down” on compromise, reports Ireland and Britain Editor Mark Hennessy .
Addressing a half-full hall at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, Bryant said he had wanted to be speaking about all the things that are going well in Northern Ireland, “not about Drumcree”.
“I had wanted to stand up here and boast about the news that Northern Ireland has the fastest economic growth of anywhere in the United Kingdom, and the lowest unemployment ... But the situation in Drumcree is tense.”
The British government “like every Labour government, will always go the extra mile for peace,” he went on, adding that he will return to Hillsborough talks to end the crisis this afternoon.
“That’s precisely what I will be doing this afternoon. Bringing both sides together, talking over one bridging sectarian divide and giving compromise a chance.
“Because nobody, nobody, nobody wants Northern Ireland to return to the 1990s.
“That’s not going to be easy. As the last few days have shown, it’s really easy to stir up a grievance. Much harder to calm it down. Which is why I appeal to everyone. Believe in Northern Ireland and double down on compromise.”
Alistair Power, the deputy district master of the Portadown District of the Orange Order, said members will walk down the Garvaghy Road when police tell them it is safe to do so.
“Portadown district has accepted a second invitation to go and meet the Secretary of State today and we will be doing that this afternoon,” he said.
“The position of the district remains that we still have a live document, the 11/1, which is the parade from the 27th September to bring this district down along its traditional route, via the Garvaghy Road, to complete its parade in Carleton Street.
“That is the position. We have asked the police when they can take that road and bring us down the road safely; we will be here to do that.”
A senior Orangeman said further talks will take place with Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant to attempt to find a resolution to the Drumcree parading dispute.
The deputy district master of the Portadown District of the Orange Order, Alistair Power, is among a small group of lodge members who have remained at Drumcree Church waiting to take part in a march that would pass along the mainly Catholic Garvaghy Road in Portadown.
He said: “We are still at the stalemate from eight o’clock on Sunday morning.
“The police are still giving us an assessment that they cannot police us safely down the Garvaghy Road.
“We have left it with them that we are here and waiting until they can give us safe passage to complete our 1998 parade which was given to us by the Parades Commission with 35 Orangemen, under really restrictive conditions from the Parades Commission but we accepted that and we wish to bring our banner back home.”
Power said Bryant had not indicated what the further talks would be about.
He said: “Let’s see what’s on the table and hopefully everybody can come and get this done and resolved for everyone.” - PA
Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee has called for continued calm among communities in Northern Ireland as she acknowledged the “difficult few days” for residents on the Garvaghy Road.
Speaking on her way into Cabinet, Helen McEntee said: “It’s very clear that this has been very difficult for all communities in Northern Ireland. It’s been a very difficult few days for the residents on the Garvaghy Road and it has been difficult for all political parties.
“I want to acknowledge and commend the restraint that has been shown and to call for continued calm. It’s really important that people engage, that is the only way we will find a solution through this.
“I expect today that there will be further engagement with the community. I expect there will be further engagement with the Orange Order.
“I hope to see a process put in place that will allow people the time and space.
“People have been up late at night. It has been a very challenging time, particularly for the community, and it is really important that this is resolved through dialogue, but also it’s really important that people in the community do not have a march forced on them, where very clearly this is not something that people want.” - PA
Breandán Mac Cionnaith from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition has said he believed the British government has a “game plan” to make the residents appear “unreasonable” and the Orange Order “look good”.
Speaking to those gathered on the Garvaghy Road on Monday night, Mac Cionnaith said he accepted an offer of mediation provided they were an “independent mediator with no connection to here”.
He said an offer was made to host a meeting of the British government, the residents’ association and the Orange Order to agree on a mediator.
“That’s not how mediation works,” he said, adding: “Those involved in a dispute don’t appoint the mediator.”
There would be more engagement with the British government over the coming days, he said.
“But I believe the British government already have their game plan in place and it’s to make us to be the unreasonable ones and to make the Orange Order look good,” he said.
Mac Cionnaith said the issue went beyond Garvaghy Road, “because the British know that the political process here is already in crisis and that they need to be seen to give something to unionism”.
“And we make for the sacrificial lamb,” he said.
He reiterated that “Orange feet” on the Garvaghy Road was “not acceptable to this community” or nationalist communities “right across the North”.
Should the British government go down that path, “let it be on their head”, he told those gathered.
“Because they already know what the result of a march on Garvaghy Road will be,” he said.
While residents remain on the Garvaghy Road, so too do several Orangemen at Drumcree Church.
The Orange Order members made a number of attempts to proceed with their parade on Monday but were prevented from doing so by PSNI officers.
Further talks are due to be held today with Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant.
However, he is scheduled to speak at a Labour Party conference in Manchester at 10am, so any talks involving him to find a way through the Drumcree crisis are unlikely before the midafternoon, Mark Hennessy reports.
Bryant hailed “positive conversations” on Monday.
I am grateful to all for the positive conversations about Drumcree today. Constructive dialogue is the route to a solution. I continue to hope and work for progress in further talks tomorrow.
Former taoiseach Bertie Ahern has urged political parties in Northern Ireland not to return to the “tribal past” for the “short-term gain of winning of a few votes”, saying they would regret it by the end of next year.
Speaking on Tuesday morning as the Drumcree stand-off entered its third day, Ahern noted that the dispute over the Orange Order parade on Garvaghy Road “never finished” after the Good Friday agreement and the focus should be to “bring it to an end finally” by means of a resolution.
“I think really what we need to try and do is everybody calm down a bit. I think the First Minister and Deputy First Minister should have coffee or tea this morning and try and mend this because otherwise it’s a disaster because it will affect the institutions,” he said.
Ahern said Northern Ireland was now the fasted and strongest growth area for employment and investment across the UK, which the Executive “should be proud of”.
“So I really think if the parties believe for an election in six or eight months’ time, there’s some short-term gain of winning a few votes based on going back to the tribal past, I would really caution against that.
“They will regret that by the end of next year,” he said.
The next Stormont election is expected in May 2027.
Speaking on RTÉ Radio’s Morning Ireland, Ahern added he remembered “painfully” how several parades were mediated after 1998 and “sorted out based on the fact that we made progress”.
“So it could open all that up and there’s an awful risk of that and we should not let that happen,” he said.
Once the Parades Commission made its determination, “everything was too quick”, Ahern added, noting the High Court came to a decision at 2.30am on Sunday, hours before the parade was due to take place.
“So I think the whole thing was choreographed far too tight, far too dangerous, and I think with the inevitability of what happened,” he said, referencing the resulting fallout.
Garvaghy Road is quiet this morning, following another night when hundreds of people stayed to deter any possibility the Orange Order’s march along the road could go ahead, Mark Hennessy reports.
Throughout the evening and night, the atmosphere was calm, with no sign of a presence by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI). The nearest solitary squad car – not an armoured Land Rover – was hundreds of yards away.
Maintaining spirits, tea and sandwiches were given out free to residents and supporters, some of whom have come from south of the Border, while musicians played near tents erected near the junction where the road turns off for Drumcree.
Reporting back to residents on Monday afternoon following his meeting with the Northern Ireland Secretary of State, Chris Bryant, local residents’ leader, Breandán Mac Cionnaith urged people to stand firm.
Significantly, the residents’ group met separately with Bryant from Sinn Féin, and relations between the two sides have been prickly – with Sinn Féin doing much to stay on side with them.
Talks in Hillsborough are expected to resume later today after the Northern Ireland Secretary returns from the Labour Party annual conference in Manchester, though signs of likely compromise are few.
Last night, Bryant said he could “see a way through the mist”, but few others do, for now.
The residents are insisting on the appointment of an international mediators, while the Orange wants a written guarantee that its permission to march continues.

title: Ireland under-21s ride their luck to down Kazakhstan in Cork
description: Tommy Lonergan penalty seals the win at Turners Cross
content:
Tommy Lonergan’s late winner kept alive Ireland’s hopes of reaching the Under-21 European Championship finals after a thrilling encounter with Kazakhstan at Turners Cross.
Jim Crawford’s side rode their luck to make it back-to-back victories in four days after Friday’s win in Slovakia. Ireland moved a point ahead of Slovakia with Tuesday’s win, although with one game extra played.
Runaway group leaders England play Slovakia on Friday before Ireland host England on October 6th while Slovakia travel to Andorra, leaving the qualification play-off spot behind Lee Carsley’s side up for grabs.
Ireland lived on their nerves as Kazakhstan opened the scoring after just 12 seconds before having a second goal harshly ruled out for offside. Yan Trufanov flicked on a long punt to Artyom Litosh, who turned between two defenders before firing into the roof of the net.
Ireland responded calmly to that early shock, with Cathal McCarthy seeing a powerful shot saved before Lonergan was denied on the rebound.
But Kazakhstan thought they had doubled their lead in the 20th minute when Litosh found Trufanov, whose shot beat Noah Jaunty, only for the flag to go up. It was a let-off for the hosts and Ireland took full advantage, levelling a minute later when Alex Murphy volleyed home at the near post from Jamie Mullins’ corner.
Mullins, celebrating his 22nd birthday, then put Ireland ahead in the 29th minute, following up after Lonergan was denied by goalkeeper Sherhan Kalmurza.
But the Kazakhs levelled again in the 38th minute when Litosh picked out Ramazan Karimov, who fired into the bottom corner, while Miras Otamay also struck the far post before half-time.
Yet Ireland restored their lead three minutes after the restart when Sam Curtis met another Mullins corner, his header deflecting in off Ali Turganov. The advantage lasted only briefly, as the visitors punished poor defending from a long throw, with captain Sultan Askarov finishing well.
Mullins hit the crossbar with a header from Adam Brennan’s cross before Romeo Akachukwu was introduced with 20 minutes remaining and supercharged the Irish attack.
The home side pressed for the winner, with Kalmurza denying Kone-Doherty and Lonergan frustrated from close range before Crawford also threw on Michael Noonan and Leon Ayide as a last roll of the dice.
The decisive moment came in the 86th minute when Kalmurza fouled Lonergan just inside the box. The 22-year-old then showed real composure, chipping the ball down the middle as Kalmurza dived.
Litosh was sent off in the final minute, completing a dramatic night that kept Crawford’s side firmly in the qualification hunt.
REP OF IRELAND: N Jauny; S Curtis (D Lipsiuc, 70), C McCarthy, S Grehan (L Ayinde, 81), A Murphy; R Finneran (M Noonan, 81), J Devaney; T Kone-Doherty, J Mullins, A Brennan (R Akachukwu, 70); T Lonergan (D Okagbue, 87).
KAZAKHSTAN: S Kalmurza; S Malikaidar, S Askarov, A Turganov, R Karimov; Z Mukhametkhanov (S Zhumabekov, 77), A Nurymbet; Y Trufanov (M Birkurmanov, 77), M Omatay (M Abish, 66), S Popov (M Toktybay, 66); A Litosh.

title: A Krakatoa that nobody saw coming: Dáil united on grave business of Garvaghy Road
description: Sinn Féin leader agrees with Taoiseach that Parades Commission decision to permit Orange Order march was ‘incomprehensible’
content:
It was a Krakatoa that nobody saw coming, a political volcano long dormant that erupted with next to no warning.
It’s been a quarter of a century since the sectarian siege of Garvaghy Road in Portadown was lifted and finally ended.
But over the weekend it became apparent the supply of magma was never fully exhausted and it was threatening to erupt again.
At Leaders’ Questions, unsurprisingly, it dominated proceedings. The mood was glum but for once the political leaders were united, mostly agreeing in their downbeat assessments of what occurred over the weekend.
During the mid-1990s the protracted stand-off in mid-July in Portadown spawned sectarian violence, riots and murder. The Orange Order ’s insistence on walking what it claimed was the traditional route along Garvaghy Road to Drumcree church brought it into conflict with the residents there, the vast majority of whom were nationalist.
The march was finally banned in 1998 and there had been no incident of note since 2011. The decision by the Parades Commission to allow a small parade involving members of the Orange Order early on a Sunday morning re-stoked the fires, and brought a weekend of tension and the prospect of incipient violence.
Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald , her voice quivering with anger, raised the issue, asking how could it have happened after 28 years of peace.
She recalled the darkest moments of the mid-1990s stand-offs: the murders of solicitor Rosemary Nelson, Robert Hamill – who was “kicked to death” – and the three Quinn boys, aged between 9 and 11, whose home was firebombed by loyalist paramilitaries.
“I have spoken to those mothers and grandmothers who lived through the dark years and to parents, children and teenagers also who lived their entire lives free from that intimidation and fear,” she said.
“Why in God’s name would anyone seek to drag this community backwards?”
[ In pictures: How the Garvaghy Road standoff unfolded on day of high tension Opens in new window ]
In a very rare nod of assent to Taoiseach Micheál Martin, sitting across from her, she said he had “correctly” described the decision by the Parades Commission to allow the march as “incomprehensible”.
The solution, she said, was for the new Northern Ireland Secretary of State, Chris Bryant, to “stop this sectarian march being forced down the road”.
Given the gravity of the situation, it was a hard job for Martin to segue to a quite different, but monumental, seismic event that has affected Leinster House this week. And that is the retirement of a generational talent, Irish Times columnist and colour writer Miriam Lord, who was sitting in the press gallery, high above the Dáil chamber, for the last time.
“If you would indulge me for a moment,” Martin asked Leas-Cheann Comhairle John McGuinness, before launching into a paean of praise for the blushing Lord, who, for all her mercurial writing, is a low-key operator away from the keyboard.
“We would all agree that Miriam’s journalism, and in particular her oversight and accounts of our work in this house, has been a critical part our national conversation, and our nation’s democracy.
“I have to say, in her unsparing but sharp analysis I sometimes felt that she was rather unfair about me but was always spot on about everyone else.”
Cian O’Callaghan of the Social Democrats, Ivana Bacik of Labour and Ruth Coppinger of Solidarity all gamely added their tributes to Lord, who was “only scarleh” at this stage.
And then Martin and the others segued back to the grave business of Garvaghy Road.
There was general agreement that an international mediator was required. Given the intractable stuff that blew up over the weekend, they might be better off calling for a volcanologist.

title: Reluctant Garvaghy Road resistance point man Breandán Mac Cionnaith rises to Drumcree challenge
description: ‘Nobody saw this coming. I never thought we’d see this again. It’s like we’ve woken from a bad dream’
content:
On a wet afternoon in the Drumcree Community Trust centre off Garvaghy Road, Breandán Mac Cionnaith wends his way through tables filled with local residents having a late lunch in search of a quiet room.
Thirty years ago, Mac Cionnaith was the face of Garvaghy Road when the Orange Order’s attempt to march from Drumcree made global headlines for four difficult years in a row.
Now 69, he is not glad to be back in the spotlight, as some have charged.
“Nobody saw this coming. I never thought we’d see this again. It’s like we’ve woken from a bad dream,” he says.
In a long conversation, the former IRA man, jailed for bombing a local Orange Order hall, tries to explain to those far away from the town of Armagh the tempers and tensions that govern 2026 attitudes, even drawing upon a 200-year-old example.
Twenty-one people were killed in, or around Portadown, or because of the Drumcree crisis in the 1990s.
“The Orange Order cannot dissociate themselves from that, no matter how much they want to do so,” he says.
“They didn’t tell the loyalist Volunteer Force leader Billy Wright and his comrades, or Johnny Adair and his people, to get away from them. They welcomed them with open arms,” Mac Coinnaith says, referring to the loyalist hardmen.
The families of some of those killed still live on the route that would be passed by the Orange Order if it manages to make its way from the church at Drumcree into the centre of Portadown through Garvaghy.
Marie-Therese Matchett, the mother of 12-year-old Darren Murray, is one of these. He was chased down by a gang of loyalists in 1996 when playing near the Orange hall. He died two days after being struck by a car in the Garvaghy Road area.
“They gave him a few slaps around the head. He got away and they came running after him. He was in a panic – you can imagine a 12-year-old boy with a dozen after him. He ran smack bang across the road and into the path of a car,” says Mac Coinnaith.
“His mother was here the other night. She doesn’t do interviews. But she got a poster made with her son’s picture on it and marched with us. I don’t know how she had the courage to do that.”
The family of 29-year-old Catholic council worker Adrian Lampf, who was shot and killed by a loyalist gunman in Portadown on April 21st, 1998, is among others who live on the route.
He was singled out because he was a Catholic at the Duke Street council recycling site. A lone gunman wearing a scarf and baseball cap rode up to him on a mountain bike and shot him in the head and neck. No one has ever been convicted for his murder.
Mac Coinnaith, a member of the republican political dissident group, Éirígí, lists others.
“This is a march in place like no other and it will reopen questions about Orange marches elsewhere where there were no problems,” he says.
“No matter where you walk around, you’ll see the scars in this place. Some of the first sectarian murders were carried out here,” he adds, remembering local publican Jack McCabe, killed in 1972.
[ Breandán Mac Cionnaith profile: The ex-IRA man who Tony Blair said ‘took unreasonableness to an art form’ Opens in new window ]
In Mac Coinnaith’s telling, the 48-year-old McCabe was killed by an off-duty Royal Ulster Constabulary officer who chose him because he was a “successful Catholic businessman”.
“I met his son and daughter-in-law this week. They joined us, saying they had moved away to get away from all of it, but they couldn’t let this happen again. The memory of their da’s killing is still as strong as ever,” he says.
In a place like Garvaghy Road, where memory is searing but often seen through a single lens, a records check shows that McCabe died alongside a Protestant customer, William Cochrane, who was sitting at the bar when hooded killer Ralph Henry, a member of the RUC and UDA, entered and killed both.
During the early days of the Troubles, Portadown was known as the centre of “The Murder Triangle”.
Some 52 people were killed in the town or in the surrounding town lands over 30 years. The killings were almost evenly spread: 28 Protestants and 24 Catholics, shot at work, in their homes, on their farms, in RUC or British army uniform.
Speaking before heading to Hillsborough for a meeting with Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant, Mac Coinnaith says he realised early that this year’s Orange Order application was different from those refused since 1998.
“Why this year? I don’t know. There’s no logic behind it. Nothing’s changed,” he says.
“The Orange could have challenged in the courts every year up to now; you don’t need to be a top lawyer to know that. Somebody wanted to use it this year.”

title: The Irish Times view on Ireland’s education system: a detailed comparison with some surprises
description: Despite spending  less than the OECD average, its educational outcomes are impressive
content:
Few Government departments have faced pre-Budget skirmishes as fierce as those surrounding the Department of Education this year. An overspend of €640 million led Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers to recoup €446 million through a levy on other departments. The row has intensified pressure on Minister for Education Hildegarde Naughton, who argues the real problem is persistent, systemic underfunding of schools. Meanwhile, teachers’ unions and parents’ groups say more resources are needed to reduce class sizes and meet growing demand for special education.
Tuesday’s publication of the OECD’s Education at a Glance report, which compares spending and outcomes at every level across its 38 member countries, brings welcome clarity to the argument, though not all of its findings will be welcomed. Measuring government expenditure per student, adjusted for purchasing power, it places Ireland slightly below the OECD average. Beneath that headline lie some intriguing results. Spending per primary pupil is marginally above average, while at secondary it falls well short. Ireland is one of few countries to spend less per student at secondary than at primary. Third-level funding also lags, with the State meeting 58 per cent of the cost of degree-level education, against an OECD average of 68 per cent.
Nonetheless, Ireland’s educational outcomes are impressive. Almost six in 10 adults hold a third-level qualification, against an OECD average of 43 per cent. Just 4 per cent of 25 to 34-year-olds lack an upper secondary qualification, down from 9 per cent a decade ago. The proportion of 18 to 24-year-olds neither working nor in education or training has halved since 2015 to 9 per cent, well below the OECD figure of 13 per cent.
Despite recent talk of teacher shortages, Ireland outperforms most countries in recruiting and retaining qualified staff. Only 0.3 per cent of teachers are not fully qualified, compared with 9.1 per cent across the OECD, and just 2.1 per cent left the profession in 2024/25, a third of the international rate. Irish teachers earn less than other graduates, but the gap is narrower than in much of Europe. Less creditable is the imbalance in leadership, with women making up 84 per cent of primary teachers but only 62 per cent of school management.
Interest groups will doubtless cherry-pick these findings. The Department has already done so, celebrating progression and employment outcomes while ignoring the spending comparisons. But the report also flags a looming challenge. The population aged five to 14 is projected to shrink by 17 per cent by 2033, reducing the number of teachers required. Whether the State responds by cutting posts or by further reducing class sizes will be a telling test of its priorities.

title: Manchester City guilty of Premier League charges after £900m of ‘sham’ contracts
description: Manchester City CEO Ferran Soriano says guilty verdict the result of a ‘Premier League conspiracy theory’
author_name: Will Unwin, Matt Hughes, Paul MacInnes
content:
The Premier League has confirmed Manchester City have been found guilty of all charges of breaching its financial rules over a nine-year period, with the club found to have boosted their income by a staggering amount of more than £900 million.
In a bombshell announcement, the Premier League revealed an independent commission had found City guilty of arranging “sham contracts” with commercial partners to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs, and of filing inaccurate accounts to hide the true state of their finances, which if accurately reported would have led to significant breaches of Premier League and Uefa spending limits.
The club were also found to have entered into “sham” image rights deals with players and the then manager Roberto Mancini to artificially inflate their earnings.
City have said they will appeal by Friday’s deadline “on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. The club’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano, said in a video to employees that the decision was based on a “Premier League conspiracy theory”.
The appeal is expected to run aside a sanctions hearing presided over by the independent commission, with the Premier League eager to conclude matters as quickly as possible.
The extraordinary scale of what Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, has described as City’s “financial doping” has sent shock waves throughout the world of football, leaving executives at other Premier League clubs stunned.
The Premier League’s chief executive, Richard Masters, described the case “as the most significant in Premier League history”. It seems inevitable it will lead to an unprecedented punishment, likely including a points deduction that will condemn City to relegation.
Although there is no direct precedent given the scale of City’s offences, Everton’s 10-point penalty for breaching profitability and sustainability rules by £19.5 million over a period ending with the 2021-22 season was based on a Premier League tariff of six points for the initial breach, plus an additional point for every £5 million the club overspent.
The commission made damning comments regarding the behaviour of City witnesses during the hearings. “Evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses called to give evidence on behalf of the club was false in a number of key respects,” it wrote, arguing that some witnesses had given evidence “they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest”.
City were found to have operated a “disguised funding scheme” worth £830.6 million over nine seasons, from 2009-10 to 2017-18, and to have hidden costs by a further £70 million. In addition the club have been found guilty of multiple breaches of failing to co-operate with the Premier League and act in good faith. The commission concluded the club had made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the investigation.
The Premier League published a redacted 40-page “core decision” from the independent commission, which has taken almost two years to produce after a 42-day hearing that concluded in December 2024.
The league said: “The independent commission found City arranged ‘sham’ commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.
“As part of the scheme, further ‘sham’ arrangements, funded by ADUG, were entered into to enable the club to record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred, as well as a ‘sham’ circular arrangement with Fordham, an entity that purchased the club’s players’ image rights, that was funded by ADUG.
“The purpose of these schemes was found to have been to artificially inflate the club’s revenues, and reduce its costs, by more than £900 million during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules.
“The consequence of this, as the commission found, was that the club filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators.”
ADUG bought City on behalf of Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan for £200 million in 2008, with the new owners making an immediate impact by paying £32.5 million to sign the Brazilian superstar Robinho from Real Madrid. That was the start of a spending spree City struggled to afford with their existing revenues, and the independent commission concluded the only way to match the owners’ ambitions for the club was for ADUG to “provide very significant funds by way of equity contribution”.
The commission report states that in 2010 City devised a scheme whereby sponsors would pay a “base sum” and ADUG would pay a “tagged sum”, despite the base sum being the only true revenue. The recorded sponsorship fee would be the total of them both.
City’s lawyers claimed that the “tagged sum” was a loan by the Abu Dhabi government on liabilities on sponsorship fees. The commission rejected that argument.
The judgment is a huge victory for the Premier League and Masters. Despite the commission demonstrating that City breached Uefa’s spending limits there appears little prospect of Uefa’s case being revisited because there is a five-year statute of limitations on its disciplinary proceedings. Uefa’s punishment of City in relation to alleged financial fair play breaches was largely overturned in 2020 by the court of arbitration for sport, which found “most of the alleged breaches were either not established or time-barred”.
Masters said: “The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade. It also vindicates the Premier League’s decision to pursue this case against Manchester City.”
He said in relation to sanctions: “Now we have the commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the league, our clubs and fans.”
Other Premier League clubs are surprised City have not reached an agreed sanction with the Premier League, given the judgment, but City continue to deny wrongdoing. “Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League commission, that has been published today,” the club said.
“The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.” – Guardian

title: Irish citizen pleads not guilty in Hungarian court to murder of his ex-wife
description: California native David Anderson, who holds Irish passport, denies setting fire to woman’s apartment to stage her death as an accident
content:
An Irish citizen has pleaded not guilty in a Hungarian court to murdering his ex-wife and setting her apartment on fire to stage her death as an accident.
David Anderson (45), who is originally from California but who holds Irish citizenship, appeared at Buda Central District Court of Budapest on Tuesday for the first time since he was charged with the premeditated murder of his ex-wife, Megumi Anderson, a Japanese national, who died in January 2025 aged 43.
Anderson was escorted to the courtroom on Tuesday by three Hungarian police officers in balaclavas, with his hands and feet cuffed and wearing a hoodie with a slogan reading, “Just do nothing.”
During the pretrial hearing on Tuesday, the Irish citizen denied that he murdered his ex-wife 20 months earlier.
He also denied setting her apartment on fire or that he staged the scene as if his ex-wife had fallen asleep with a cigarette in her hand and that the subsequent fire was responsible for her death.
Anderson refused a plea deal that would have seen him spend 17 years behind bars and being expelled from Hungary for a further 10 years after the conclusion of his prison sentence.
“I believe I have a very strong case,” Anderson told the court at the end of the hearing.
He said he wanted to represent himself during the trial, even though, under Hungarian law, every defendant must have a defence lawyer present to be able to provide legal advice.
The court heard on Tuesday that Anderson was born in Santa Monica, California. He later became an Irish citizen, qualifying through his mother, who had married an American in Dublin in 1979 before moving to the US.
In 2002, Anderson and Megumi were married in Honolulu. The pair moved to Hungary and settled in Budapest in 2013 where they raised their two children, who were aged seven and 11 at the time of Megumi’s death.
The court heard that by 2020, the couple’s marriage had deteriorated and they filed for divorce in 2023. Anderson later remarried and moved to the Netherlands, while the children stayed with their mother in Budapest.
Prosecutors in Hungary claim that he was motivated to murder his ex-wife because of her desire to move with their children to Japan. Megumi Anderson filed a request to Hungarian authorities in March 2024 to be able to move with the children to Japan, where her parents lived.
Anderson opposed this, even though the divorced couple made arrangements to ensure he would be able to stay in touch with his children if his ex-wife’s move to Japan went ahead.
The process was still continuing when Anderson arrived in Budapest 10 months later. On the morning of January 29th, 2025, he brought his younger child to her swimming lesson, while the older one went to school by himself.
A few hours later, upon his return, Anderson alerted firefighters, who found Megumi Anderson’s lifeless body in the apartment engulfed in flames.
In the following days, Hungarian police said their initial investigation found no signs of foul play and that it was likely Megumi Anderson died after falling asleep while smoking.
A Hungarian women’s rights organisation claimed that Megumi Anderson had been in touch with them for years and had repeatedly accused the Irish-American of physical and psychological abuse, while others highlighted the fact that she never smoked.
The police arrested Anderson five days after the incident, following the discovery of CCTV footage allegedly showing him changing clothes and returning to the flat much earlier than he had originally told the authorities.
A man wearing a balaclava and a bicycle helmet is seen on the videos entering the building at around 10am and leaving an hour later, with Anderson in his original clothes returning after 1pm.
The prosecution argued in court on Tuesday that Anderson decided to kill his ex-wife and stage it as a household accident months before, fearing an unfavourable decision in his bid for the custody of their children.
They allege that during the hour he spent at the flat, after returning in disguise, he covered Megumi’s nose and mouth, who suffocated to death.
Afterwards, he is accused of laying his ex-wife’s body on the sofa and placing a cigarette in her hand as well as candles and wine bottles around the livingroom before setting the sofa on fire.
Anderson’s trial will start in November.

title: Budget 2027: Staggered introduction of childcare fee reductions under review
description: Negotiations on size and structure of package to intensify in coming days, say sources
content:
The Government is considering a staggered introduction of childcare fee reductions in 2027 as part of budget negotiations.
The programme for government notes a reduced cost to households of €200 per child monthly, with senior Coalition figures repeatedly flagging significant progress in this budget recently.
Negotiations on the size and structure of the package will intensify in the coming days, sources said.
[ Budget 2027: All you need to know Opens in new window ]
Some Government figures said that a level of fee reduction could be seen in January, followed by more in September, with the precise timing of introduction to be thrashed out in the days ahead.
Others noted that previous cuts have taken effect from September onwards, suggesting that would make an introduction in September more likely. Another source said depending on how the package is structured, they could also come entirely in January or September
Timing of subsidy changes kicking in has moved around in recent years. Budget 2023 introduced them from January, whereas changes announced in Budget 2024 came in from September.
At the weekend, Fine Gael Minister for Finance Simon Harris flagged that childcare bills could be reduced from January.
There is also the possibility of targeting the fee reductions towards younger children, with one source saying families are under most pressure when children are younger. The National Childcare Scheme (NCS), which pays a universal subsidy, is available for children up to 15 years old.
It is unclear if any split by age would be done on a lasting basis, or if there would be a phased extension of the reductions to older age groups, with sources saying discussions had not honed in on that yet and that final decisions had not been made.
However, limiting or delaying cuts for parents of children attending after-school care could potentially lead to a political backlash from parents of children left out or waiting longer for an increased subsidy – and it is understood that such an approach is not viewed favourably on the Fine Gael side of Government.
It is understood that the precise timing and structuring of the package hasn’t yet been discussed in detail.
But calibrating when cuts would take effect, how broadly they might apply, and the timescale for that will be key to talks. One Government source said the Coalition was “looking at different ways to maximise the impact”, with options to narrow down later this week.
The programme for government says the Coalition will progressively reduce the cost of childcare to €200 per month through the NCS and explore options to cap costs for larger families.
Last year, new ceilings were introduced which capped fees for those parents with children attending a service participating in the Government’s core funding scheme for between 40 and 50 hours per week.
Meanwhile, it changed the subsidy scheme, increasing income limits for eligibility for the higher income-assessed subsidy. The lower income threshold increased from €26,000 to €34,000, and the higher threshold increased from €60,000 to €68,000. The Coalition said this would provide increased subsidies for up to 47,000 children.
However, these changes are generally seen as benefiting those on the margins – either at the higher or lower ends of the income distribution, while many tens of thousands of children are covered by the NCS. Earlier this year, Minister for Children Norma Foley said that new data showed about 245,000 children benefited from the scheme last year, an increase of 12 per cent on 2024.

title: No explosive devices found in vans searched near UK airbase
description: Counter-terrorism police defend decision to bail five British nationals in connection with incident at Fairford
content:
No explosive devices were found in three vans searched near RAF Fairford in England as part of a terrorism investigation but a quantity of petrol was recovered, police have said.
Five British nationals were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after a resident living near the Gloucestershire airbase reported suspicious activity involving three vans.
Defending the decision to bail the men , Laurence Taylor, the head of Britain’s Counter Terrorism Policing, said: “Yesterday we released the five men on police bail. They remain under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions while we continue our work. The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision making, and this was certainly the case yesterday.
“I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers.”
Taylor said of the van: “Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered.”
The vans were marked by the logo of a legitimate fuel transit company that later denied ownership of the vehicles, which prompted speculation online and in the local community that the men could have been fuel thieves.
Residents were returning home on Tuesday after spending days evacuated from their village.
Marco Rubio , the US secretary of state, claimed the events were the work of a “foreign actor” but did not provide further details. He said “a lot of people are disturbed” after the release of the suspects from custody. US president Donald Trump had earlier said he was “surprised” the group had been freed.
Speculation has been growing about a connection between the weekend’s incident and Iran . The potential link was a key reason behind Andy Burnham’s decision to call a meeting of Cobra, the UK government’s crisis committee, on Monday, attended by senior police and security officials among others.
The same day Taylor said he knew there was “significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident”.
He added: “But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”
In March the British government gave the US permission to use the base for “specific defensive operations into Iran”.
Iran’s London embassy has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement.
Eighty-five households were forced to decamp to a leisure centre on Sunday as the bomb squad and counter-terror police descended on the village of Whelford, where five British nationals were arrested for terror and explosives-related offences.
Mark Richings, a butcher in Fairford, told the Press Association: “There’s no change in here and we just got on with it as normal. We are a bit quieter today, but everybody seems to be okay, and we are having a bit of a chat about it.
“We just carried on as normal. We have enough to do to occupy our minds. If anything did happen, there isn’t a lot we could have done about it.”
[ UK prime minister Andy Burnham rises to his big moment with emotional conference speech Opens in new window ]
Some of the evacuated residents were able to stay with families, about 60 people received support from a Cotswold district council rest centre in Cirencester and 28 people were accommodated overnight in hotels.
Fr Michael Robertson, the priest at the nearby St Thomas Catholic church, told PA: “A lot of parishioners didn’t think they could get to church. Those that came were worried but perfectly happy with the situation.
“In fact, quite a lot of Americans who have deployed here actually come to Mass and some of the permanently deployed Americans are full members of the parish. We’re quite contented with the situation generally. Obviously, the disruption upsets people.” – Guardian

title: ‘Devastating tragedy’: Father and daughter killed in workplace incident are named
description: Mihai and Denisa Chinez died at Banagher Precast Concrete, Co Offaly, on Monday
content:
The tragic deaths of a father and daughter in a workplace in Banagher, Co Offaly , have affected the “whole town”, locals say.
Mihai Chinez (49) and Denisa Chinez (24) were killed in an incident at Banagher Precast Concrete on Monday morning.
An Garda Síochána and emergency services were called just before midday, but the pair were pronounced dead at the scene.
It is understood the two workers were preparing a concrete mould at the time of the incident.
The father and daughter were from Romania , but lived and worked in the locality for many years. The woman’s mother and boyfriend also work in Banagher Precast Concrete, locals say.
The town has “gone quiet” following the tragedy, residents have said.
In Flynn’s Bar and Restaurant, on Main Street, the customers and staff were coming to terms with the news.
“It’s nearly like an eerie feeling [in the town],” said Amy Connaughton (20), from nearby Meelick Eyrecourt, Co Galway.
Connaughton, who works in Flynn’s, said she only knew the father and daughter to see and that they had been working “for years” with Banagher Precast Concrete.
“You can tell that there’s sadness in the town. It’s so sad. When it happens in your own community, it’s hard to process it,” she said.
Retired Army commandant, John Murphy (76), originally from Cabra, Dublin, but now living in Roscrea, Co Tipperary, was in Flynn’s with a friend and said he was “shocked” when he heard of the tragedy.
Murphy, who spends “quite a lot of time” in Banagher, did not know the father and daughter, but has come to know many people in the town, who were “very close knit, welcoming and friendly”.
