The pair purchased Strancally Castle in August in an off-market deal. The castle is located in west Waterford, a 30-minute drive from Youghal on a 440-acre estate on the banks of the River Blackwater.
It is close to a number of other residences owned by overseas billionaires, including James Dyson’s Ballynatray House.
Discussing how the donation came about, Shamrocks GAA chairman Tómas Roche said the club secretary had received a call from a Dublin solicitor which led to a call with a representative of Zuckerberg in Los Angeles in which the club made its case for how money would benefit the community.
“We sent on detailed account of our club and what our aspirations were and he explained there was a donation due that would help the club, so it’s very welcome because we are a small rural club with 200 members in a parish of 750... it will help us redevelop our dressing rooms,” he said.
Lismore GAA Secretary Emer Barry said she met the couple’s personal agent from America in Lismore some weeks back to make her case.
“I brought him up to the pitch and explained that we were in the process of developing a second pitch and then two weeks ago we were told that we would be getting funding which is great news for Lismore,” she said.
Tallow GAA chairman Terence McSweeney said that Zuckerberg’s representative told the club that the billionaire “likes to give back to an area”.
“[The] €50,000 will come in very handy because we have finished gym but that will be open to everyone, not just club members, and we have a community walkway and we will be looking to tarmac that but we will also use it for games development and coaching so it’s very welcome," he said.

title: O’Brien defends bus and train fares hike, says public transport affordable by EU standards
description: Public transport fares are to increase by 15 per cent on average from January
content:
Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien defended planned increases in public transport fares as he highlighted the need to fund new public transport services.
O’Brien, who is also Minister for Climate and Energy, was speaking as European energy ministers gathered at Dublin Castle for an informal meeting where energy affordability and security are on the agenda for talks.
The meeting is being held as part of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union .
It was confirmed by the National Transport Authority earlier this month that bus and rail fares are to increase by 15 per cent on average from January.
On Tuesday the Irish Independent reported that the Just Transition Commission, an independent advisory body, contacted the Government urging it to halt the planned increases in fares citing concerns over climate action and the cost of living.
O’Brien gave no indication the fare increases would be halted when asked if this would happen in the budget.
The Fianna Fáil Minister said the fuel measures brought in by the Government are to support society and the economy and are not a subsidy for fossil fuels.
He also highlighted the start of the Fuel Allowance season this week for households at risk of fuel poverty.
O’Brien said there has not been a fare increase for eight years and that the increases planned by the NTA “will go directly into new services” with an intention to roll-out 140 new services next year.
He added: “Ireland’s transport system and public transport is affordable by any comparison across the EU” and people “want more services for a growing population”.
Meanwhile, on the question of whether expected carbon tax increases on petrol and diesel will kick in the day after the budget – as has happened in recent years – O’Brien said: “we’re still in budgetary discussions at the moment.”
He said the carbon tax “provides us [with] the funding for us to retrofit homes and retrofit businesses”, that some 287,000 homes had been retrofitted so far and “we’ve seen a doubling of applications this year alone.”
He added: “They’re things that actually protect people from future price shocks and also reduce energy bills, reduce emissions.”
Asked if he was concerned a postponement of carbon tax increases for motor fuels or home heating oil would lead to less funding for retrofitting initiatives, O’Brien said measures like the planned €2,000 scrappage payment for oil boilers are “fully funded” through climate funds and the carbon tax “so I don’t envisage any reduction whatsoever in relation to the acceleration of the grants”.
Separately there has been discussions among EU ministers on US president Donald Trump’s suggestion last week that he would back a proposal to ban US diesel exports as part of efforts to ease prices for American motorists. US energy secretary Chris Wright subsequently said a ⁠diesel export ban would not work.
European energy commissioner Dan Jørgensen told reporters on Tuesday: “I’ve sent a very clear signal to my American counterpart and also the public, which is that it is not in the interests of anybody, not the US not us, to not have as free a flow of energy as possible in these difficult times.”
He also said he was “happy to see that Chris Wright has said publicly that he is also not supporting such a ban”.
O’Brien cast doubt on whether a diesel export ban will be implemented by the US. He said he was in Washington, DC, last week and “from the information that I was able to glean in DC last week there doesn’t seem to be a push to do that” but also “we’re not going to be complacent about it”.

title: Shanade Hopcroft earns surprise call-up to Ireland squad for World Cup playoff
description: Carla Ward’s side will travel to Astana to face Kazakhstan in the first leg on Friday week
content:
Crystal Palace midfielder Shanade Hopcroft is the surprise inclusion in Carla Ward’s Republic of Ireland squad for the upcoming World Cup qualifying play-off against Kazakhstan. The 28-year-old qualifies for Ireland through her grandmother Nora Hopcroft, a native of Tubbercurry, Co Sligo.
Born in Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire, Hopcroft helped Birmingham City win promotion to the WSL last season before rejoining Palace where she had enjoyed a successful first spell, also helping them earn promotion to the WSL and being named their player of the year.
She began her career in Chelsea’s academy, had spells with London Bees and Reading before taking up a scholarship at Daytona State College in the United States. She went on to play with Colorado Buffaloes before returning to England.
Leicester City’s Heather Payne returns to the squad for the first time in a year after an injury-interrupted spell, but Wolves’ Tara O’Hanlon and Watford’s Saoirse Noonan have both been ruled out with hamstring and ankle injuries, respectively.
While Denise O’Sullivan is named in the squad, she will not travel to Astana for the first leg on Friday week, the Cork woman nursing a knee injury since joining Gotham FC from Liverpool during the summer. Ward is hopeful, though, that she will be fit for the second leg in Páirc Uí Chaoimh on October 13th.
Captain Katie McCabe and midfielder Marissa Sheva are both suspended for the first leg but will be available for the second. Midfielder Aoibheann Clancy, who joined Watford in the English WSL2 from Shelbourne in August, is included again, but there is no place for any player from the domestic league.
If Ireland get past Kazakhstan they will face either Belgium or Poland in the final play-off round, the prize a place in next summer’s World Cup in Brazil.
Goalkeepers : Courtney Brosnan (Everton), Grace Moloney (Southampton), Sophie Whitehouse (Charlton Athletic).
Defenders : Aoife Mannion (Newcastle United), Heather Payne (Leicester City), Anna Patten (Aston Villa), Caitlin Hayes (Brighton), Jessie Stapleton (Leicester City), Megan Connolly (Lazio), Hayley Nolan (Crystal Palace), Chloe Mustaki (Nottingham Forest), Katie McCabe (Chelsea).
Midfielders : Denise O’Sullivan (Gotham FC), Marissa Sheva (Sunderland), Aoibheann Clancy (Watford), Jamie Finn (Burnley), Lucy Quinn (Sheffield United), Tyler Toland (Burnley), Jess Ziu (Leicester City), Shanade Hopcroft (Crystal Palace).
Forwards : Kyra Carusa (HB Køge), Amber Barrett (Strasbourg), Abbie Larkin (Crystal Palace), Emily Murphy (Brighton), Leanne Kiernan (Newcastle United).

title: Owen Doyle: World Rugby must tackle laissez-faire policy spreading like a virus in southern hemisphere
description: The centre cannot hold if teams continue to flout the laws of the game
content:
“Turning and turning in the widening gyre, The falcon cannot hear the falconer;
Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold; Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world.”
WB Yeats ’s powerful imagery, written in 1919 following the Great War, resonates strongly today. In society, and in politics, we are seeing and hearing things which would have been utterly unimaginable, unconscionable, not so long ago. The verse is also apt for what is happening in rugby union. South Africa v New Zealand , the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series, confirmed issues which many have feared for quite some time.
Firstly, the physicality. It was pure attritional brutality, which is rugby’s norm nowadays. Serious brain and skeletal injuries are greeted with little more than a shrug, the accepted price of playing a game of huge non-stop collisions.
Failed HIAs in the opening match led to three players being unavailable for the second Test. In the third match Ardie Savea was savagely cleared out by Malcolm Marx, which strangely was not reviewed. The New Zealand captain sustained a serious shoulder dislocation and surgery was required. Cheslin Kolbe left very early with a broken jaw – more surgery. Quinn Tupaea also departed – knee ligament damage – but has so far fortuitously escaped the scalpel.
South Africa bring ferocious non-stop intensity to the table. Huge starting 15s are aided and abetted by a big bench, and probably the two best frontrows in the game. While others might not like it, South Africa are quite entitled to play to their strength, but that doesn’t mean they are unbeatable. Les Kiss’s Australia – down to 11 men at one stage – demonstrated that on Sunday.
Four yellows to one team is rarer than me enjoying a long-distance flight, but did referee Andrea Piardi get these right? Two were for head-on-head tackles, and those can’t really be argued. Another was following a penalty try; that’s in accordance with established protocol, like it or lump it. But the card for Joseph-Aukuso Sua’ali’i was plainly wrong in my reading of it. Called in by assistant Ben O’Keefe, it was exceptionally severe and not obvious at all that the player was actually offside. So, three cards were obvious, and the one that wasn’t clear shouldn’t have been given.
The South Africa v New Zealand series also demonstrated an unwelcome, unacceptable split in how the game is refereed. Contests for possession are the unique identity of rugby union, its essential heartbeat. However, Super Rugby Pacific refereeing favours the team in possession to such an extent that it is becoming increasingly difficult to get the ball back.
Teams must be allowed opportunities to contest for the ball, to regain possession. These are crucial contests, which do not exist in rugby league, where a team must hand it over to their opponents after six tackles, so that the others can “have a go”, so to speak. Is that really what World Rugby wants? Because that’s where it’s heading.
[ ‘How to beat the bullies’: What will rugby look like heading into the World Cup next year? Opens in new window ]
A core principle of union is being left behind, forgotten: that continuity of play is not, repeat not, continuity of possession. And, unsurprisingly, lineout illegalities continue unabated. Teams flout the law, unhindered by fear of a sanction.
The first South African try in the second Test was a case in point. Angus Gardner is not alone in meticulously setting up the lineout, and then ignoring the law completely – it’s an absurd farce. Siya Kolisi took up position as receiver, so we knew what was coming. As the ball was thrown, several team-mates immediately left the lineout, which is expressly forbidden. They joined Kolisi to set up a powerful maul, which travelled about 20 metres before the outstanding Jasper Wiese broke off.
When Wiese was tackled a team-mate straddled on all fours over him, protecting possession. This straddling is not as blatant as a player throwing himself on top of the ball carrier, but is just as effective in preventing a fair contest. There was much the same at the next tackle as South Africa recycled the ball, before Jesse Kriel scored. And, to add insult to injury, there was a South African block on a New Zealand defender.
South Africa’s second try came from a similar maul driven, once again, around 20 metres. This “double-banking” maul formation raises a simple, fundamental question: Who gave permission for teams to action it and for referees to ignore it?
New Zealand, to avoid a contest in the lineout, occasionally tossed the ball in quickly, directly to their front man. It’s hardly a throw-in, more of a pass, really. In a fully formed lineout it is beyond belief to see how it can be construed as a legitimate, contestable throw. But, heck, who gives a damn?
More differences at scrum time. Gardner, not anxious to penalise, reset frequently. One scrum was reset four times, before a free kick on the fifth engagement. In contrast, Nika Amashukeli and Karl Dickson adopted a sanction based approach in the third and fourth tests. The Georgian was into the second half before he called a reset; until then the scrums had either been good, or had been sanctioned.
Amashukeli is very hot on sealing the ball-off and side-entry, and his reputation obviously preceded him. South Africa’s breakdown behaviour was markedly different under his watch, much more compliant in staying upright. As part two of the Nations Championship looms ever closer, Andy Farrell doesn’t need me to tell him that absolute clarity is needed as to exactly what is what.
The laissez-faire policy is widespread down under, a virus which cannot be allowed to spread, despite what Australia and New Zealand might wish. These two unions hold immensely powerful World Rugby positions in chairman Brett Robinson and Mark Robinson (no relation) in a newly created chief-of-rugby role.
Is there any chance that they will work to deliver a game which is played in accordance with its laws and charter?
Despite the chairman’s reassuring words earlier this year, I remain concerned at what will be proposed after the fast-approaching World Cup. There is every possibility of a boardroom battle royal on the way. The northern hemisphere unions, and South Africa, will not roll over in placid acceptance.
If necessary, they have the means to turn Yeats’s imagery around. They can ensure the centre holds.

title: An bhfuil na seanfhocail a mhaisigh ár gcaint uair amháin anois ag trá?
description: Tá cumha ar ár gcolúnaí i ndiaidh na nathanna saibhre a chloiseadh sí ní ba rialta tráth
content:
Tá an tsraith spraíúil theilifíse, The Traitors Ireland, a taifeadadh i gCaisleán Bhaile Shláine, thart anois ach tá sí fós i mbéal an phobail. Tá daoine á moladh, ag rá go raibh an Ghaeilge le cloisteáil in úsáid go nádúrtha babhtaí ag an láithreoir drámatúil Siobhán McSweeney, gan trácht ar na fealltóirí iad féin - bhí “ bíonn cluasa ar na ballaí” agus “ is minic a bhris béal duine a shrón” le haireachtáil in eipeasóid amháin, mar shampla.
An rud eisceachtúil é seo áfach? Arbh í úsáid na seanfhocal Gaeilge ar ardán poiblí ba chúis le cumha agus tnúthán ionam féin, a chuir ag smaoineamh mé ar na seanfhocail a chloisfeá go rialta sa chaint tráth? An gcloistear iad sa chaint a thuilleadh? An léiríonn an easpa úsáide seo gné chinniúnach de mheath agus de bhánú na Gaeilge?
Cá bhfuil frásaí agus nathanna rithimiúla ár sinsear? Cá bhfuil na seanfhocail seo a thug slí isteach dúinn ar ghaois agus ar sheantuiscint shaol na Gaeilge, agus atá mar acmhainn luachmhar againn i dteanga na Gael?
“Tugann seanfhocal cuntas dúinn ar an gciall a bhaineann pobal as an saol, ar na creidimh agus na luachanna atá mar bhunchlocha ina mbeatha agus ina slí mhaireachtála,” a scríobh Donla Uí Bhraonáin in 2010 i réamhrá an bhailiúcháin a chóirigh sí as an nua do Cois Life de Seanfhocla Chonnacht le Tomás Ó Máille, leabhar a foilsíodh den chéad uair in 1948.
“Tá comhairle iontu maidir leis an iompar atá oiriúnach i gcúinsí áirithe, rialacha faoi conas déileáil le gnáthchúrsaí an tsaoil. Cé gur teachtaireacht an-dáiríre a bhíonn ina bhformhór, cuirtear sin i láthair go minic le greann agus le híoróin.
“Léiríonn an úsáid a bhain scríbhneoirí as seanfhocla a dtábhacht mar chuid den chumarsáid agus mar threoir don saol agus an tslí ina bhfeidhmíonn siad sa ghnáthchaint,” a leanann sí. Admhaíonn sí go bhfuil athruithe móra le feiceáil idir dearcadh an lae inniu agus dearcadh na seanfhocal go ginearálta ar roinnt ábhar ar leith - mná, an lucht siúil agus creideamh spioradálta go pointe áirithe - ach, arsa sí, “ceann de na gnéithe is suntasaí de na seanfhocail is ea an ghontacht agus an deisbhéalaí a bhaineann leo”.
Seans go mbaineann siad le glúin atá imithe ach cloisim iad ag caint i gcónaí, macallaí ag aisfhuaimniú thar na céadta.
Nuair a bhí mo mháthair ag foghlaim Gaeilge sa Rinn sna seachtóidí, scríobhadh sí na seanfhocail ar fad ina leabhar nótaí. Is cuimhin liom í ag déanamh athrá ar “ Ní troimide an loch an lacha ” agus í faoi dhraíocht ag loighic an ráitis sin agus an rúndiamhracht a bhain leis. Is iad na seanfhocail seo a fháiscim chugam féin anois. Filleann siad orm, go háirithe na cinn a léiríonn sólás an chreidimh. “ Is gaire cabhair Dé ná an doras” - bhaineadh na seandaoine úsáid as an seanfhocal sin dá mbeifeá ag fulaingt nó in argóint leis an saol nó chun a mheabhrú duit a bheith dóchasach mar go “ bhfaigheann seanbhróg seanstoca ”.
Bhí seanfhocail agus frásaí cliste gonta fite fuaite i saol gach páiste tráth dá raibh, in úsáid ag múinteoirí dá mbeidís ag iarraidh rang a dhéanamh ciúin: “ is binn béal ina thost ” a chloisfeá á rá go cráifeach acu; nó duine éigin eile amuigh sa halla agus “ ní thagann ciall riamh roimh aois” in úsáid go feasach aige nó aici. Bhí na nathanna ar fad ar bharr a dteanga acu i gcónaí, iad réidh le húsáid mar chosaint ar chóras beatha nó mar cheacht nó mar rabhadh. Bhí ceann ann do gach aon ócáid. Nuair a shiúil cailín isteach agus an lá scoile faoi lánseol, “ is fearr déanach ná choíche ”, a d’fhógair an múinteoir foighneach.
Tá mé uaigneach in éagmais na seanfhocal a chloisfeá go rialta tráth. Fanaim leo. Mothaím teochroí clainne sna focail amhail is go bhfuil mo mhuintir, atá imithe ar shlí na fírinne, níos gaire dom. Cothaíonn na nathanna seo rúnmhaireacht agus foisceacht. Oibríonn siad babhtaí mar fhuinneog ar phobal, ar stair, ar shlí maireachtála nó ar nósmhaireacht a mhair tráth.
Chaithfí dul siar ar bhóithrín na smaointe chun spreagadh a fháil uathu na laethanta seo mar ní chloistear rómhinic nathanna amhail “an rud is annamh is iontach”, “ tús maith leath na hoibre” nó “ ní hé lá na gaoithe lá na scolb”, gan trácht ar an gceann a fhógraíonn “ nach bhfuil in aon rud ach seal” . Ó chianaibh i gcónaí bhí sé éasca teacht orthu, bhí siad so-aitheanta agus aithnidiúil agus bhí siad ag gach aoinne.
“Briseann an dúchas trí shúile an chait.”
“ An té nach bhfuil láidir, ní foláir dó a bheith glic.”
“ Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine.”
Seans go mbaineann siad le glúin atá imithe ach cloisim iad ag caint i gcónaí, macallaí ag aisfhuaimniú thar na céadta. Is bealach isteach iad ar thuiscint níos fearr a fháil ar chúrsaí éagsúla: creideamh, greann, spórt, bochtaineacht, slite beatha agus an grá.
Agus ná déanaimis dearmad ar an spraoi agus an spórt a ghabhann leo - nuair a deirtear “ go n-aithníonn ciaróg ciaróg eile”, is cinnte go bhfuil magadh i gceist. Sna nathanna a thug Micheál Turraoin do na béaloideasóirí a labhair leis agus a d’fhoilsigh An Sagart sa bhliain 2007 in aon bhailiúchán amháin, Leabhar Mhaidhc Dháith, saothar go raibh Máirtín Verling ina eagarthóir air, tá greann fite fuaite sna seanfhocail, mar shampla: “‘ Cúnamh gach aon rud,’ a dúirt an dreoilín nuair a dhein sé a mhúin sa bhfarraige”. Gan amhras tá gaois agus tuiscint chun tosaigh i roinnt eile a thug sé uaidh mar atá san abairt: “fuil a gheibheann an uaisleacht, airgead a gheibheann an uaibhreacht” agus sa bhfrása saoithiúil: “ Ní thagann an óige fé dhó choíche, is tagann an bhrón fé dhó san oíche”.

title: Heroes of Tomorrow review: What does ‘tarnished’ money do to art? Brokentalkers try to find some answers
description: Dublin Theatre Festival 2026: What lingers is not grand declarations of artistic purpose but the quieter channels through which conviction travels
content:
We never meet Jan Hansen onstage. The fictional Norwegian artist is the central figure of Brokentalkers’ focused and funny production, but he remains forever absent from the stage.
His existence is merely recited, parcelled out in portions by the actors Malua Ní Chléirigh, Alice Roots and Michael Tient, who fold his biography into fragments of history, tracing a restless network of connections between politics, art and protest.
We learn that Hansen was born in 1974 in Tromsø, Norway. His early college work had a certain rigorous clarity, and was conceptually honed and seemingly uncompromised. But there are signs that he has perhaps sold out these principles.
Not long after he received oil money, in the form of a Statoil art award in 2007, his interest in direct action was reignited through his brother-in-law and old college friend Cathal Keenan and his wife Caoimhe’s research into female protesters. Statoil, his former sponsor, is one of the targets for the Corrib gasfield protesters.
In the present day he has been chosen for a Beyond the Future commission, sponsored by three global tech companies “to support art that reflects their principles, values and intentions”. Equally tarnished money. Hansen has announced that this forthcoming work bears the apocalyptic name The End of It All. Surrounded with mystery, there are rumours that it could be his last.
Created by Feidlim Cannon, Gary Keegan and the British theatremaker Andy Smith, Heroes of Tomorrow is rich with connections showing that history is not so much a sequential timeline but isolated events that repeat and resonate in different eras.
Throughout the performance, these historical facts accumulate and soon begin to speak to one another. The words that tell these stories are primary, but they are bolstered by an economy of visual language.
At one point a red rope that has kept viewers a respectful distance from hanging artworks becomes three neckties, draped around the collars of the performers as they tell us about Hansen’s Statoil prize. A literal depiction of the corporate uniform is also the physical binding of Hansen’s artistic practice to the interests of fossil-fuel capital.
Should art be serving the needs of corporations and politics? And what responsibility does the artist, and each of us, have to society? Towards the end of the production, the connections have been made, the histories assembled and the contradictions laid out. Now it’s time to tackle the less manageable question of what, exactly, we are supposed to do with them.
As Alice Roots says to the audience: “It’s hard to know what to do, right?”
We never learn what exactly Hansen’s The End of It All entailed. Not that it matters. Leaving the performance, what lingers is not grand declarations of artistic purpose but the quieter channels through which conviction travels, from spouse to spouse, friend to friend or even stranger to stranger.
Heroes of Tomorrow is at Project Arts Centre, as part of Dublin Theatre Festival , until Sunday, October 4th

title: Ireland spends less on education than OECD average, new data shows
description: The report also found the number of primary teachers in Ireland increased by 27 per cent over the last seven years, which is much higher than the OECD average
content:
Ireland spends less on education per student than the average across all OECD countries, new data shows.
The data was contained in the Education at a Glance report, released by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Tuesday.
It uses internationally comparable data on the structure, financing and performance of education systems across the 38 OECD member countries and other key partner countries.
When looking at Government expenditure on education, the report found the average expenditure per student across the OECD countries was US$13,601 in 2023, while in Ireland it was US$13,113.
In primary education , expenditure per student was US$12,943 in 2023 in Ireland and US$12,893 on average across the OECD.
In secondary education , it was US$12,699 in Ireland and US$14,291 on average across the OECD.
The data comes as Ministers negotiate what share of Budget 2027 their departments will get in the annual announcement, which takes place next Tuesday.
The Department of Education came under scrutiny this year for a €600 million “overrun” in its budget , a spend that the department argued was required to cover teachers’ wages and ordinary running costs.
The department said in June this extra funding would be secured on an annual basis in a resetting of the base.
[ School closures loom on separate days next month as teacher pay dispute escalates Opens in new window ]
This year’s Education at a Glance report has a special focus on teacher shortages, examining their impact across countries and how education systems can respond.
The report says teacher shortages often manifest in a higher share of non-fully qualified staff, or unfilled teaching posts.
However, Ireland has one of the lowest rates of unqualified teachers across the entire OECD – behind Korea, Japan and Hungary.
In Ireland, 0.3 per cent of all primary and secondary teachers were not fully qualified in 2024/25, well below the OECD average of 9.1 per cent.
The report also found the number of primary teachers in Ireland increased by 27 per cent over the last seven years, while the number of students decreased by 1 per cent.
This is much higher than the OECD average, where the number of teachers in primary schools rose by 13 per cent while the number of primary students rose by 2 per cent.
[ As controversy grows over Leaving Cert reform, Northern Ireland is going the other way Opens in new window ]
This represents a significant change in policy here toward smaller class sizes as the State caters for an increase in the diagnoses of children with additional needs.
There are now almost 4,000 special classes across primary and post-primary schools in the Republic, almost double what there was six years ago.
These are designed for children with special educational needs, including autism , and have a lower student-to-teacher ratio than mainstream classes.
The report shows Ireland has also made headway in keeping young people either in education or employment.
Some 9 per cent of all 18- to 24-year-olds were neither employed nor in education or training (what the OECD calls NEET) in 2025, down from 18 per cent in 2015.
For comparison, the average share of NEETs across OECD countries with available data for both years was 13 per cent in 2025 and 16 per cent in 2015.

title: Australian firm to take 35% stake in Daft.ie owner
description: REA to pay about €248m for stake in Distilled
content:
Australian property group REA is to buy a 35 per cent stake in Daft.ie owner Distilled in a deal worth an estimated €248 million.
The company said the purchase of the minority stake would be funded from debt and existing cash reserves.
Distilled Media, which was founded by brothers Eamonn and Brian Fallon, includes property portals Daft.ie and PropertyPal, classified ads site Adverts.ie, and car marketplaces Used Cars NI and DoneDeal.ie.
Irish-based investment manager Blacksheep Fund Management led an acquisition of the listings group in 2024.
[ Who are the Fallon brothers behind Daft and DoneDeal? Opens in new window ]
“This is an exciting opportunity to extend our core property strategy into an attractive, profitable, high-growth market, with increasing adoption of vendor-paid advertising and where our intellectual property and technology is directly relevant,” said REA chief executive, Cameron McIntyre.
“The investment provides immediate exposure to an exceptional business with a strong growth trajectory and a portfolio of high-growth assets.”
The deal, which must clear regulatory hurdles, is expected to close before the end of the year.
Chief executive Eamonn Fallon will continue to lead the business and will retain, along with Brian Fallon, a “meaningful” holding following the deal. Asked for details, the company said it does not comment on individual shareholdings.
“REA is a natural partner for Distilled, combining leadership in digital marketplaces with capabilities that can support our growth,” he said. “There are clear opportunities for collaboration, and we look forward to tapping into REA’s experience to create new value for customers, consumers and partners.”
Recent Companies Registration Office filings revealed that Blacksheep’s deal for Distilled was valued at €627.4 million.
The transaction consisted of almost €450 million in cash, with €312 million of that sum paid to European online classifieds group Adevinta, which had owned 50 per cent of Distilled. Adevinta was a spin-off of Norwegian classified group, Schibsted, which acquired a 50 per cent stake in Distilled in 2015, merging it with its DoneDeal.ie platform.
The Fallons shared almost €240 million from the Blacksheep deal, which was “settled in part by cash consideration and part in exchange for shares”, according to the filings.
The deal also reduced the brothers’ combined stake in the group from around 38 per cent to 16.66 per cent.
In response to questions from The Irish Times last week, the Fallons said: “We love building this business, and we’re focused on continuing to grow it over the long term. With the support of our strategic partners, we see plenty of runway ahead, and we’ll keep investing in the platforms and the people behind them.”
Distilled also owns around 13 per cent of the shares in Journal Media, the online news platform the brothers established in 2010, according to its most recent annual return.
The Fallons continue to hold a controlling stake in that business through their company, DML Capital.
The Irish Times reported in 2024 that the Fallons were in talks to sell The Journal and the42.ie to Irish Independent publisher, Mediahuis. It was understood at the time that the Business Post, then controlled by Galway businessman Enda O’Coineen’s Kilcullen Kapital Partners, was an underbidder for the business in a sales process being run in-house by Journal Media, the parent of the news brands.
However, the deal, said to be valued in the low single-digit millions, was later called off.

title: Groundhog Day for Ireland as uncertainty remains over second Israel clash
description: It wasn’t a great weekend either for Irish rugby, as Gerry Thornley writes
content:
If last week felt like a never-ending one for Irish football, this week could prove to be the longest yet. Gavin Cooney reports on the latest state of affairs in the Irish camp , the squad set to decide on whether to play their game against Israel in Serbia next Sunday after Thursday evening’s meeting with Austria in Dublin. Much could depend on the reaction of the crowd in the Aviva Stadium, Heimir Hallgrímsson admitting that he is worried about what kind of atmosphere his players will face.
“We are all uncomfortable,” Gavin Cummiskey heard the head coach say. ” We have different opinions and we should allow people to have different opinions. But it is tough. It is just like politics where some parties just can’t work together.”
The fallout from last Sunday’s game has hardly eased matters, the FAI reviewing footage of alleged racist chants from Israel fans towards Adam Idah. And Israel captain Manor Solomon lashed out at the Irish players. “ Obviously, they hate us. We don’t like them . We have a country 10 times better than theirs.”
It wasn’t a great weekend either for Irish rugby, but purely in terms of URC results. As Gerry Thornley reminds us, it was the first time since 2009 that all four sides lost on the opening round of the season . The absence of “pretty much all of Ireland’s summer tourists” was, need it be said, a mitigating factor.
Leinster did at least take bonus points from their narrow defeat by the Lions, Michael Scully hearing from Tyler Bleyendaal about the plan to place a greater emphasis on their attack this season . And Connacht, who lost 29-15 to the Stormers, should be boosted by the return of some of their seven-strong Irish contingent for Friday’s game away to Benetton.
In Gaelic games, Gordon Manning talks to Derek ‘Fresh’ O’Connell after he helped his club win the Laois intermediate football title last Saturday - at the age of fifty-four. His secret? “ Eat cornflakes after your dinner and don’t train too hard!” Noted.
Gordon also has word on the list of nominees for the 2026 Camogie All-Stars , champions Cork with 14 of the 36 contenders, as well as two of three players on the shortlist for the player of the year award.
In his Different Strokes column, Philip Reid has the latest golf news from around the globe, including the women’s game being hit by its PIF Global Series reducing from five tournaments to just one next year.
An in racing, Aidan O’Brien is keeping a close eye on the weather forecast for Paris on Sunday, his plans for the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe “up in the air” . “Original expectations for an unusually quick ground are now being tempered with conflicting forecasts for the days ahead,” Brian O’Connor reports.
TV Watch : Football’s Nations League continues apace, among your viewing options this evening Scotland v Switzerland (BBC 2) and the Czech Republic v England (Virgin Media Two and UTV), both at 7.45pm.

title: Buenos Aires na gcluichí Gaelacha
description: Tá foireann CLG darb ainm Limerick Gaels i bpríomhchathair na hAirgintíne agus fear as Luimneach i lár an aicsin ann
content:
Fear óg as cathair Luimnigh is ea Ruaidhrí Ó Conaill atá ag obair in Buenos Aires na hAirgintíne ag cur na gcluichí Gaelacha chun cinn. D’imir sé peil agus iomáint lena chlub áitiúil, Na Piarsaigh, agus é ag fás aníos. D’fhreastal sé ar Ghaelcholásite Luimnigh agus, tar éis na hArdteiste, bhain sé céim amach i gCorp Oideachais agus Gaeilge in Ollscoil Luimnigh. Bhí spéis mhór aige sa spórt i gcónaí, idir lúthchleasíocht, dhornálaíocht agus rámhaíocht, ach deir sé go raibh nasc ní ba láidre aige le Cumann Lúthchleas Gael.
Bhog Ruaidhrí thar lear den chéad uair in 2021 nuair a chuaigh sé go Bilbao i dTír na mBascach. Thosaigh sé ag imirt peil Ghaelach ansin agus ba í sin an chéad taithí CLG a bhí aige taobh amuigh d’Éirinn. Bhain sé an-taitneamh as agus as a shaol ansin. Ach mar mhúinteoir, bhí sé deacair fostaíocht a fháil agus dodhéanta post buan a aimsiú mar nach raibh an Bhascais aige, cé go raibh Spáinnis aige ceart go leor. Mar sin, bhog sé ar ais go hÉirinn le bheith ag obair, agus ag imirt peile agus iománaíochta.
…bhog an-chuid Éireannach go ceantar darb ainm Hurlingham. Bunaíodh club CLG Hurling ann in 1922, agus imríonn siad sa tsraith chéanna le Gaeil Luimnigh…
Bhí fonn air dul ar imirce áfach. Bhí roinnt cairde leis ag bogadh chun na hAstráile agus bhí beirt deartháireacha leis ina gcónaí i gCeanada ag an am. Ba rogha easca é, dar leis, dul chun na hAstráile nó go Ceanada, áiteanna a mbeadh aithne aige ar go leor daoine cheana féin. Mar sin, shocraigh sé ar a bhealach féin a dhéanamh.
Bhí cara le Ruaidhrí ina chónaí san Airgintín roinnt blianta ó shin agus chuir sé Ruaidhrí i dteagmháil le Colegio Limerick, scoil atá i gcroílár Buenos Aires. Go stairiúil, bhí an-bhaint ag na hÉireannaigh leis an oideachas sa chathair. Tá cúpla scoil de chuid na mBráithre Críostaí ann, agus tionchar mór Éireannach orthu i gcónaí. Chuaigh bunaitheoirí na scoile ar thuras timpeall na hÉireann agus timpeall na hEorpa sna hochtóidí. Thug siad cuairt ar Luimneach agus chuaigh an áit go mór i bhfeidhm orthu. Nuair a d’fhill siad ar an Airgintín bunaíodh an scoil - Colegio Limerick. Sheol Ruaidhrí a CV chuig an bpríomhoide agus tá sé ag obair ansin le bliain anuas. Is é Ruaidhrí an t-aon Éireannach sa scoil ach deir sé go gcuirtear béim ar stair, ar litríocht agus ar chultúr na hÉireann ann, agus go gcuirtear an-bhéim ar an spórt. Imríonn na daltaí peil Ghaelach sa bhunscoil agus sa mheánscoil. Bhí sí mar chuid den churaclam corpoideachais sular tháinig Ruaidhrí chun na scoile, ach ní raibh sí ró-iomaíoch. Bhí na scileanna bunúsacha ag na daltaí ach bhí easpa liathróidí peile agus easpa acmhainní orthu, rud a bhí ag cur bac orthu dul chun cinn a dhéanamh. Dúirt Ruaidhrí go raibh sé an-éasca socrú isteach sa scoil agus sa cheantar nuair a bhog sé ann. Daoine cineálta cneasta atá i bpobal na scoile agus chuir siad fáilte mhór roimhe.
Shocraigh Ruaidhrí agus roinnt daoine áitiúla club CLG a bhunú ann. Club pobail is ea Gaeil Luimnigh Buenos Aires, nó Limerick Gaels, agus imríonn scoláirí, iarscoláirí, múinteoirí agus tuismitheoirí leis. Tá timpeall 120 duine ag imirt leis an gclub. Tá foireann shinsearach peile, foireann ban, foireann faoi 15 agus foireann faoi 13 acu, agus imríonn siad sa tsraith áitiúil in Buenos Aires. Breis is céad bliain ó shin, bhog an-chuid Éireannach go ceantar darb ainm Hurlingham. Bunaíodh club CLG Hurling ann in 1922, agus imríonn siad sa tsraith chéanna le Gaeil Luimnigh chomh maith le club eile, CLG Bulfin. Imríonn na hÉireannaigh atá ina gcónaí sa chathair leis na foirne sin. Deir Ruaidhrí nach bhfuil mórán Éireannach ag fanacht ann go fadtéarmach; Éireannaigh atá ag caitheamh tréimhse in Buenos Aires is mó ata ann. Bíonn an spórt ar siúl ag an deireadh seachtaine, agus bíonn asado - nó beárbaiciú tipiciúil de chuid na hAirgintíne - ann freisin. Fanann chuile dhuine siar don teacht le chéile sóisialta seo tar éis na gcluichí.
Ag deireadh mhí Mheán Fómhair, beidh 40 dalta ag taisteal ó Colegio Limerick in Buenos Aires chomh fada le hOllscoil Luimnigh chun cúrsa seachtaine a dhéanamh. Ina dhiaidh sin tá siad chun camchuairt a thabhairt timpeall na hÉireann - ó Luimneach go Baile Átha Cliath agus go Béal Feirste. Ní bheidh Ruaidhrí féin ag taisteal leo ach fuair sé deis taistil i rith an tsamhraidh nuair a d’fhreastal Gaeil Luimnigh Buenos Aires ar Chluichí Domhanda CLG i bPort Láirge. Turas an-spreagúil a bhí ann agus bhí cluichí an-iomaíoch ag foirne na hAirgintíne. Ba thaithí nua é sin nach raibh acu roimhe sin mar go bhfuil na foirne chomh scaipthe sin ar fud Mheiriceá Theas. Dá mbeidís ag iarraidh cluiche iomaíoch a bheith acu lasmuigh den Airgintín agus taisteal go Paragua mar shampla, bheadh sé ar nós turas idir Luimneach agus Maidrid!
Tá sraith eile ann freisin i Meiriceá Theas a eagraíonn CLG Cuenca del Plata. Beidh an comórtas mór ar siúl ar an 14 Samhain, is é sin La Copa Almirante Guillermo Brown. Laoch náisiúnta de chuid na hAirgintíne ab ea William Brown, a rugadh i mBéal Easa i gCo. Mhaigh Eo sa bhliain 1777. Chuaigh sé ar imirce agus bhunaigh sé cabhlach na hAirgintíne. Beidh Ruaidhrí agus Gaeil Luimnigh, chomh maith le foirne ó áiteanna eile san Airgintín, ó Pharagua, ón tSile agus ó Pheiriú ag glacadh páirt sa chomórtas.
Tá fonn ar na Gaeil na cluichí Gaelacha a fhorbairt sa chlub agus cúrsaí iománaíochta agus camógaíochta a chur chun cinn. Níl ach dhá chamán déag ag an gclub áfach agus níl aon chamán do leanaí acu. Tá sliotar amháin acu agus níl clogad ar bith acu. Tá cuntas Instagram @limerickgaels ag an gclub agus deir Ruaidhrí go gcuirfeadh sé fáilte mhór roimh chamán, clogad nó sliotar, dá mbeadh ceann nó dhó sa bhreis ag éinne!
Nuair a chroch foireann iomána Luimnigh Corn Liam Mhic Cárthaigh ar an 19 Iúil, bhí Ruaidhrí sa seastán i bPáirc an Chrócaigh. Ach tá fear Luimnigh an-sásta lena shaol in Buenos Aires. Tá ceart cónaithe san Airgintín aige anois agus saol an-mhaith mar mhúinteoir. Tá an lá scoile níos faide ann ná mar atá sé in Éirinn, ach deir Ruaidhrí go bhfuil rithim an tsaoil beagáinín níos moille ann agus go bhfuil sé i gceist aige fanacht. Go n-éirí leis.

title: One in four Irish shoppers has bought a product on AI’s advice, new research shows
description: Consumers are happy to ask AI for advice, but most are not yet ready to hand over control of their wallets
content:
One in four Irish adults has now bought something on the advice of an artificial intelligence (AI) tool.
That figure comes from new research by Dublin marketing agency Wolfgang Digital and Amárach Research, which surveyed a nationally representative sample of 1,000 Irish adults about how they use AI assistants when shopping.
Sixty-nine per cent of Irish adults now use at least one AI tool. ChatGPT is the tool of choice, reaching 55 per cent of the population. Alphabet’s Gemini reaches 28 per cent of Irish adults, followed by Microsoft’s Copilot and Anthropic’s Claude at 15 per cent and 10 per cent respectively.
“Most of the conversation about AI in business has been about productivity, headcount and cost,” says Brendan Almack, managing director of Wolfgang Digital. “Those are fair questions, but they’re distracting people from something more immediate. Customers are already using AI to decide what to buy, and who to buy it from.”
The study breaks the behaviour into stages: 46 per cent of Irish adults – or roughly 1.9 million people – have used AI to research, compare or choose a product or service. Of those, 56 per cent went on to buy. That works out at 26 per cent of all Irish adults – about 1.1 million people – who have bought something after researching with AI.
Beyond that, 26 per cent of Irish adults say an AI tool has recommended a brand, product or retailer they had never heard of. Among 18- to 24-year-olds, that rises to 43 per cent.
“People used to use AI to confirm a decision they’d already half made,” Almack says. “Now it’s introducing them to businesses they’d never have found otherwise. Brand discovery has gone from ads, to algorithms and now to AI assistants.”
Almack believes businesses now need to consider if and how they are showing up to potential customers. “Around 1.1 million Irish adults have been introduced to a brand by a machine. The key question to answer is: when an AI assistant makes a recommendation, does it recommend you or your competitor?”
The categories where people ask AI for help are broad, covering topics such as education and learning (38 per cent) and travel (38 per cent), followed by electronics and gadgets (35 per cent), health and beauty (30 per cent), recipes (28 per cent) and DIY (27 per cent).
Consumers are happy to ask AI for advice, but most are not yet ready to hand over control of their wallets. Asked how comfortable they would be allowing an AI assistant to make a purchase for them, based on criteria they’d set themselves, 63 per cent said they’d be uncomfortable, including 46 per cent who said very uncomfortable. Only 19 per cent said they’d be comfortable.
Almack doesn’t believe that this will slow down the industry’s move towards agentic commerce. “We saw similar scepticism in the early days of ecommerce; now we don’t give a second thought to making an online purchase. In a few years, the same will be true of agentic commerce”.
His read for business owners is that the audience they are targeting is changing. “You have two audiences: your customers and the AI systems they ask for advice. Most companies are only optimising for the first one.”
Wolfgang Digital’s full analysis of this research is available on its website , with further detail on how AI is changing the way Irish consumers discover, research and ultimately buy products and services, as well as what the shift means for businesses adapting to an increasingly AI-led marketplace

title: Almost 30,000 people opt out of State’s auto-enrolment pension scheme
description: Figure represents less than 4% of those enrolled and significantly below global levels, says Minister
content:
Almost 30,000 contributors have opted out of the State’s new auto-enrolment pension scheme , but Minister for Social Protection Dara Calleary said the figure represented less than 4 per cent of those enrolled, well below international figures.
The scheme aims to address the existing private pension coverage gap in the Republic and to “provide workers with greater comfort and security regarding their retirement income”.
Known as MyFutureFund , it began on January 1st this year and currently has more than 835,000 participants, working for approximately 115,000 employers.
Membership for workers is compulsory for the first six months, after which employees can opt out.
On July 1st, those enrolled in the scheme were given a two-month opt-out opportunity, and by the end of August, 29,352 had left the scheme.
[ The most tax-efficient savings product Opens in new window ]
In reply to a parliamentary question from Fianna Fáil TD John McGuinness, the Minister said the rate of opt-out was substantially below international comparators such as the United Kingdom, where the rate was approximately 10 per cent and New Zealand at about 12 per cent.
McGuinness welcomed the low opt-out rate as a good outcome and said people seem to accept the need for the fund. He called for those who withdrew to be interviewed to establish their reasons in an attempt to see what action could be taken to drive the positive momentum further.
Under the new system, employees not already in an occupational pension scheme, aged 23-60 and earning more than €20,000 a year, are automatically enrolled.
The starting contribution rate is 1.5 per cent per employee, 1.5 per cent per employer and 0.5 per cent from the State.
Refunds of €10 million have been made, with an average of €331 to employees, while an average of €400 was left in their fund.
Meanwhile, the Minister is expected to update Cabinet on the new pension regime on Tuesday.
The National Automatic Enrolment Retirement Saving Authority, which has responsibility for the operation of the fund, collected €553 million through the scheme for investment as of the end of August.
[ Time to stop demonising successful people for having large pension pots Opens in new window ]
Some €237 million were employee contributions, with the same sum coming from employers, and another €79 million in contributions came from the State.
There is another €33 million in investment returns, meaning the total value of funds under investment stands at €586 million.
Calleary said: “The high numbers of participants and low opt-out rate demonstrate the great level of success that MyFutureFund has achieved since its commencement.”
In a separate parliamentary question, 100% Redress Party TD Charles Ward expressed concern about reports from employers involved in the pension fund about “significant delays in the processing and reimbursement of payments due to businesses” that was affecting cash flow for small and microenterprises.
[ Budget 2027: All you need to know Opens in new window ]
Calleary told him the authority, the fund’s operator, had “processed more than 30,000 refunds with a value of over €10 million to date, including refunds to participants who have opted out of MyFutureFund”. The vast majority of refunds were processed within 15 days.
He added that a small number of employers requested a review where they believed they might have overpaid contributions through payroll error. “Each request must be assessed by an authorised officer” to establish any overpayment before funds can be disinvested from the employee’s pension pot. “There are approximately 500 such refunds on hand at present.”

title: ‘When I met my Irish partner in Brazil, I thought he looked very exotic’
description: When Juliana Germinio moved to Belfast she struggled with the accent and ‘couldn’t understand a thing’
content:
Since moving to Belfas t after leaving her native Brazil in 2014, Juliana Germinio (34), has packed her bag four times with the intention of moving back home.
Adjusting to life in Belfast was hard for Germinio, as she found both the weather and the culture colder than in her homeland.
She had moved to Ireland to be with her then-partner Killian, whom she met when they were both volunteering for housing charity Habitat for Humanity in her home city of Recife. Her manager had asked her to go and speak to the Irish man there, as she had the best English of their group.
“I thought he was very exotic. I remember the first thing I said to him was, ‘Did you apply suncream?’” Germinio says of Killian, now her husband. “I had never met anybody that had blue eyes, very pale skin covered in freckles, and bald. That combination of factors was so foreign and so unusual.”
It turns out that Killian had not applied any suncream, and so was grateful to be offered some as they worked out in the open in a city that sits on the equator.
Before long, the two became a pair, and by the end of that summer, Germinio, who was in college at the time, had decided she was going to move to Dublin with Killian and do an Erasmus year.
She says her father knew then that she would not be moving back home. “I had no idea, I am just go-with-the-flow, and it was one of those very immature things that we do when we are young.”
The couple did not stay in Dublin. Killian, a structural engineer, was soon offered a job in Belfast, to which the couple relocated. She admits she knew nothing of the city’s history when they moved there. Her only indication of its complicated past was when her father expressed concern about her moving there. “It was a massive learning curve.”
From the start, the Belfast accent was a struggle for Germinio. “I came to Belfast and I couldn’t understand a thing.” She was used to an American sort of English – not a Northern Irish sort of English.
It was only after they moved to Belfast that the full weight of moving away from everything and everyone she knew hit her. As neither Germinio nor Killian are from Belfast, they were both starting from scratch with no support network. “I could not wait to have my independence, but I did not know it was going to be this costly,” she says.
[ ‘I tell all my Irish friends that Ireland is the Brazil of Europe’ Opens in new window ]
Germinio, who then dropped out of her university course, succeeded in getting a job in an art gallery and framers’ in Belfast. She got the position by printing out her CV and going from door to door.
In a bid to make friends, Germinio decided to go to a Portuguese language meet-up in Belfast she had seen online. It was run by a Brazilian man and his girlfriend, who wanted to practise her Portuguese. “They are our best friends to this day. They opened up a whole plethora of Brazilian people living in Northern Ireland.”
While today she has a wide circle of friends, there were a number of social norms to which Germinio had to adapt when she first moved. “At the beginning I would give people two kisses, one on each side of the cheek, and people would find that off-putting.”
Eventually, someone told her that people in Ireland often shake hands when meeting, and only hug if they know them in their personal life. A moment that still haunts her is when she bumped into an old boss and his wife. “I pulled him in and gave him two kisses. Then I looked at his wife, and she was not pleased!”
After moving to Belfast, her father-in-law approached her and offered to pay to continue her education. “He said, ‘My son took you out of education and I don’t think that’s right – so I am going to put you back in.”
Germinio is quite emotional talking about this. She emphasises the belief that her father-in-law always had in her and the great financial commitment this represented. Being from Brazil, he had to pay international fees on her behalf.
“It was the craziest thing I had done, as I was working full-time, and then doing this programme for managers in UCD.” Once a month for four years, she would commute to Dublin for classes conducted over three-day weekends.
[ A Brazilian man in Ireland: ‘I was working nights just collecting drunk people’ Opens in new window ]
In 2023, the couple welcomed the arrival of their daughter Pippa. Since then, Germinio has founded creative agency Yellow Zest, which runs the East Belfast Business Meet Up connecting local entrepreneurs, and hosts a monthly podcast.
“I am very passionate about Belfast. I think we have so much to offer. I am very involved in the community,” she says.
Germinio has even considered getting into politics in Belfast, but her husband has so far talked her out of it. “I want to leave Belfast a better place than I found it. I can see the change – and that’s the exciting bit.”
In particular, Germinio points to the regeneration of Newtownards Road in Belfast’s city centre. “As time passes we can see more diversity in the food and activities, and the murals are now about hope and friendship.”
We would like to hear from people who have moved to Ireland in the past 10 years. To get involved, email newtotheparish@irishtimes.com or send us two lines about yourself using the form below.

title: Does going electric still save me money if my fuel is VAT-refundable?
description: Practical advice on your motoring queries, from buying, selling or issues you have with your current car
content:
I read the story on the estimation of the fuel savings of an electric car . Can you apply similar logic to my case? I drive a new Hyundai Tucson PHEV . It is very suitable for carrying equipment to deal with my wife’s mobility issue. I do only about 4,500km per annum. Because of the mobility issue, we get a refund of VAT on all petrol used. No such refund is available for electricity used in charging a car.
Because of our circumstances, we spend a lot of time at home each day, using quite a bit of daytime electricity. When one avails of a discounted night rate for electricity, the daytime rate is increased to compensate. In such circumstances, availing of night rates for electricity would have the effect of increasing our overall cost of electricity. So in estimating any saving in our case, I think we must use a rate which is similar to the daytime rate.
I understand that the cost of installing a charging point at my house is typically €1,500. It seems to me that it would take quite a few years to recover that cost through savings. I also understand that the cost of installing an outdoor 13-amp plug is about €250. I could use it to charge the battery on my present Tucson to give me about 50km on each charging, but even that is difficult to justify. From TC, Co Dublin
Yes, this could well be one of the cases where going electric actually wouldn’t save you money. In fact, it could end up costing you, but it depends very much on the way in which you use your Hyundai Tucson.
The Tucson plug-in hybrid (PHEV), as you note, has an electric range of up to 50km – actually that’s 60km on the official figures, and in our experience it’ll manage about 40km in day-to-day use, depending, of course, upon weather, driving conditions, and your driving style.
The average of 4,500km per year breaks down to just 12.3km per day, so on average you should only need to charge the Tucson up every three days, even in a worst-case scenario when it comes to electric consumption.
In terms of fuel use, this is hugely dependent on the way you drive and, crucially, charge your Tucson. According to the official WLTP fuel economy test, the Tucson uses only 1.2 litres of petrol per 100km. But of course that’s a bit of a fiction, and based on the way plug-in hybrids come off as far more efficient in the WLTP laboratory testing conditions than they do in real-world use.
You’d have to be charging up the hybrid battery every day and doing all but a tiny handful of your driving on electric power alone to match that figure.
If you could do that, then at current fuel prices (correct on the day of writing) you’d have to spend around €102 per year on fuel, assuming a pump price of €1.90 for unleaded.
[ https://www.irishtimes.com/motors/2026/09/03/range-rover-electric-can-you-save-the-planet-and-still-drive-the-archetypal-luxury-suv/ Opens in new window ]
Of course, as you point out, you can get the VAT back on your petrol which should reduce the price to around €1.55 per litre, which would give you an annual bill of €83.70.
So, could you save any money by switching to electric? Probably not, no, but let’s at least break down the figures.
To cover the same distance in an equivalent electric car, which we could take as being a Hyundai Ioniq 5, you’ll most likely see an average energy consumption of around 17kWh/100km. You might actually manage slightly better than that if you’re not doing much in the way of motorway miles, but let’s take 17kWh/100km as a reasonable assumption for average energy use.
The Ioniq 5 offers a claimed range of 570km on the WLTP test, and should be able to manage 500km in real-world use, there or thereabouts. Which means that you’d only need to fully charge the battery nine times each year, in theory.
As a benchmark, Electric Ireland’s current cheapest day rate for electricity is 32c per kWh, so nine full charges of an 84 kWh battery at 32c per kWh comes out at €242. So no, you wouldn’t save any money. In fact, you’d be spending three times as much compared to your Tucson at its most possibly economical.
But the Tucson can’t really manage to do that kind of fuel economy in real-world driving. Going by our experience, a PHEV of that sort, with minimal charging of its big hybrid battery, will burn fuel at around 8.0 litres per 100km. So that means your 4,500km each year are potentially costing you €558 a year, so there’s a potentially large saving to be made by going electric.
[ What can I do if I suspect the VRT applied to my camper van is wrong? Opens in new window ]
Of course, that saving is based purely on usage, which means we’re ignoring the cost of – as you pointed out – the installation of a charging point at home (€1,500) and the cost of trading in to buy an electric car of similar size to the Tucson, all of which are going to tip the balance back towards petrol power.
Possibly the best idea here is to actually get that €250 outdoor socket from which you can charge up your Tucson’s hybrid battery. As you say, a night rate is no good to you as that pushes up the pricing for your daytime rate, which is the one you use more, so let’s stick with the standard 32c per kWh rate.
The 13.8kWh battery will cost you €4 each time you need to fully charge it, and at an average of 50km per charge, you’ll need to charge it 90 times throughout the year, which adds up to €360. Which is potentially a significant saving over our (in fairness, assumed) 8.0 litres per 100km fuel consumption rate of driving the Tucson around without charging it. You’d just about make back the cost of the outdoor socket within a year in that case.

title: A Bigger Life by Louise O’Neill: A willingness and openness to surprise at its best
description: Commitment to being out in the world with other people may  reveal one of the book’s most vital messages
content:
There are a lot of rules about how women are supposed to love, and author Louise O’Neill has heard them all. From her mother, from TikTok , from endless discourse about attachment styles, boundaries and emotional unavailability; and from increasingly bleak declarations that heterosexual dating is essentially a humiliation ritual.
In A Bigger Life, O’Neill wonders what all these rules are doing to us.
The memoir begins in the aftermath of the breakdown of O’Neill’s formative relationship with “Jonathan”, with whom she had bought a house and imagined a future. At 38, the loss brings not only heartbreak but the particular fears reserved for women over 35: the fear that she has missed her chance, that men will choose younger women, that motherhood may no longer be possible, that she is falling behind.
O’Neill is particularly astute on the ways time is weaponised against women. She writes about time lost to an eating disorder, trauma, Covid , and relationships, before suddenly finding herself confronted with a culture insisting she is ageing away from desirability, options and the chance at a fulfilling life. She notes how fearmongering about women’s ageing and “the biological clock” becomes another mechanism encouraging women to panic, settle, and accept less than they want.
But A Bigger Life refuses to accept less. Again and again, O’Neill asks herself – and the reader – what do I actually want? Women, she argues, are trained to subsume their own needs and pleasure in favour of other people’s; taught to distrust and disconnect from their own desires. At one point, she wonders whether the partner, house and mortgage she had accumulated represented the life she actually wanted, or merely an attempt to prove that she had successfully achieved respectable womanhood.
After the break-up, she decides to find out. Her journey undeniably holds similarities to Elizabeth Gilbert ’s self-discovery memoir Eat, Pray, Love , and fans of the 2006 phenomenon will adore O’Neill’s journey through alternative therapies, spiritual retreats, beautiful cities and beautiful men. O’Neill travels to Paris , London and New York , challenging herself to date a new man every day; no repeats, no commitment, no pressure to shrink or compromise herself in a relationship – just a woman rediscovering herself, and embracing what makes her feel alive.
[ Books Louise O’Neill: ‘The rhetoric around dating was that for women over 35, you may as well be dead’ Opens in new window ]
Nowhere is this aliveness more present than the chapters about O’Neill’s adventures in Paris, where she is willingly seduced by the city’s atmosphere of pleasure. The writing pulses with sensuality and possibility as O’Neill notices clothes against her skin, the pleasure of food, the brush of another person’s hand, the intoxicating rush of realising a person wants to kiss you, the feeling of her own beauty.
[ Louise O’Neill: ‘Fairytale of New York makes me grit my teeth’ Opens in new window ]
The writing becomes more meaningful when layered with O’Neill’s own history. After years spent battling an eating disorder, surviving sexual assault, and living in a culture that teaches women to experience their bodies primarily as objects to be judged, her insistence on female embodiment, desire and self-love feels like a reclamation.
Though not explicit, O’Neill’s focus on embodiment and committing to being out in the world with other people may actually reveal one of the book’s most vital messages. In brief paragraphs of cultural analysis, O’Neill notes the increasingly cynical, one-dimensional and dismissive narratives about heterosexual love and dating that permeate online discourse. Algorithms feed us stories about narcissists, gold-diggers, body counts, and impossible standards until entire genders become abstractions.
There are places where A Bigger Life might have pushed its own questions further. O’Neill is sharp about the industries selling women thinness, youth and beauty, but less curious about the enormous wellness economy she embraces
But through her experiment, O’Neill discovers something considerably less fashionable: most people are interesting, curious, hopelessly flawed and much harder to discount when you actually spend time with them. Contrary to popular rhetoric, O’Neill writes that “the more dates I went on, the more good men I encountered, the more optimistic I became about the state of the world.”
Perhaps this is A Bigger Life’s most persuasive argument: to get off your phone and to prioritise embodied connection,; real-life encounters and experiences that become lessons or just good stories. These are the point of life. We are all we’ve got.
This idea is beautifully shown through O’Neill’s description of friendships and family. Imbued with unconditional acceptance, love and support, they illustrate that while romantic love is beautiful, it does not have a monopoly on meaning.
There are places where A Bigger Life might have pushed its own questions further. O’Neill is sharp about the industries selling women thinness, youth and beauty, but less curious about the enormous wellness economy she embraces through acupuncture, somatic therapies, ayahuasca, chakra clearing, breathwork and spiritual retreats.
The question of who can afford this expensive pursuit of wellbeing is worth more exploration, as is how the market for women’s self-regulation sells women coping mechanisms for patriarchy that are delicate, feminine, strategically individual and apolitical.
[ Louise O’Neill: ‘The hardest place to maintain my feminism is in a relationship with a straight man’ Opens in new window ]
There is another productive tension around vulnerability, and where rhetoric around boundaries and standards can simply become more ways to armour up against the vulnerability that intimacy requires. O’Neill is perceptive enough to recognise this herself, but in a dating culture fluent in the language of boundaries and self-protection, I was greedy for more of this exploration.
The real joy of A Bigger Life lies in O’Neill doing the opposite. In New York, she writes, “I said yes, and I said yes again. I was willing to be surprised”, and that willingness and openness is the book at its best. We cannot recover lost time, guarantee love, prevent ageing or construct lives in which nobody disappoints us. A bigger life necessarily contains risk. O’Neill’s warm, funny and vulnerable memoir makes a compelling case for embracing that reality, and taking the leap.
Roe McDermott is an Irish Times columnist

title: Ireland’s EU presidency may be about to hit a snag
description: Inside Politics: Civil servants’ work-to-rule could cause ‘serious disruption’; meanwhile, this is a dangerous moment in the North
content:
Ireland’s EU presidency has gone without a hitch, but could that be about to change?
European energy ministers are assembling in Dublin Castle for informal talks on energy affordability and security.
Speaking in advance of the meeting, Ireland’s Minister for Climate and Energy, Darragh O’Brien , said: “The ongoing conflict in the Middle East underlines why Europe must accelerate the deployment of renewables across all sectors.”
He said that during Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union he was “emphasising the need for the accelerated deployment of clean energy” to “deliver affordable and sustainable power”.
The meeting comes – the August break notwithstanding – halfway through Ireland’s EU presidency, which, so far at least, has progressed smoothly.
However, as Europe Correspondent Jack Power reports in our lead today , there may be trouble ahead.
Senior Government officials have warned Ministers that a planned work-to-rule across the Civil Service starting this week has the potential to cause serious disruption to Ireland’s EU presidency.
Against the backdrop of the battle over public-sector pay there are fears a prolonged industrial dispute will cause a slowdown in the Government’s attempts to conclude political deals on a wide range of European legislation and reforms during its six-month presidency.
The work-to-rule, whereby staff are restricted to working within the letter of their contracts, will be in place from Wednesday onward.
The industrial action follows ballots passed by Fórsa, Siptu and other unions representing public-sector workers.
A one-day strike by public-sector workers is planned for October 14th, to raise pressure on the Government in advance of expected pay talks.
There are concerns the work-to-rule restrictions will disrupt Irish efforts to guide EU policy negotiations in Brussels, work that can regularly run late into the evenings and take place over weekends.
Guidance about how civil servants should approach the work-to-rule action differs between unions.
The Association of Higher Civil and Public Servants, which represents higher-ranked staff, has instructed its members not to carry out additional duties.
Any travel – including to EU meetings in Brussels, or ministerial “informals” organised in the Republic – should be undertaken only during working hours, according to the guidance.
It is understood Ministers have been privately briefed by senior officials that this could create challenges for civil servants based in Dublin, who had been expected to accompany Ministers to meetings and discussions in Brussels and Luxembourg.
Today’s meeting in Dublin Castle will be unaffected by any industrial action but waters could turn more choppy soon.
The events in Northern Ireland over recent days offer a deeply worrying and unwelcome reminder that tensions from the past can quickly resurface and escalate into political crisis.
As Freya McClements and Mark Hennessy report , the Irish and British governments have stressed the need to safeguard the North’s powersharing institutions amid the row over a controversial Orange Order parade at Drumcree.
The stand-off in Portadown, Co Armagh, continued on Monday night, with hundreds of residents and supporters remaining on watch in case members of the Orange Order tried to force the march through.
During Monday, the order made a number of attempts to parade from the Church of Ireland church at the centre of the dispute. However, they did not try to breach the barrier of Police Service of Northern Ireland Land Rovers blocking their route.
At Stormont, there were heated exchanges in the Northern Assembly, with the Democratic Unionist Party accusing the First Minister, Sinn Féin ’s Michelle O’Neill, of breaking the law and a “total abdication of leadership”. Sinn Féin told the DUP the Drumcree parade was “steeped in a history of murder, violence, intimidation and supremacy”.
“It’s very important the institutions are protected,” Taoiseach Micheál Martin told reporters in Cork. In Hillsborough, Northern Secretary Chris Bryant said the “most important thing is we have to have powersharing”.
Bryant on Monday met members of the Orange Order, the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition and political parties in an attempt to find a solution to the stalemate. He admitted to reporters afterwards that “it’s not quite clear what that will look like yet”.
Ireland and Britain Editor Mark Hennessy spoke to residents on the Garvaghy Road .
In her analysis, our Northern Editor Freya McClements writes that although Stormont staggers on, this is a dangerous moment for Northern Ireland .
On the Opinion pages, Fintan O’Toole writes that Ireland stood up to Israel – then left it to 26 footballers to follow through .
It is not fully clear whether the Central Bank will no longer have the role of approving Israeli bonds for sale in the European Union , according to the chair of the Oireachtas finance committee Sinn Féin TD Mairéad Farrell. Harry McGee has the story .
Health Correspondent Shauna Bowers reports on how the contractor behind the new national children’s hospital has submitted claims for an additional €983 million over disputed costs incurred during the project.
Work Correspondent Emmet Malone has a feature on the cybersecurity implications of artificial intelligence agents hacking government agencies.
The Cabinet meets this morning. Our tee-up story – which includes details of how a rule that limits workers from outside the European Economic Area to 50 per cent of an organisation’s workforce is being relaxed to address critical healthcare staff shortages – can be found here .
Dáil proceedings begin with Leaders’ Questions at 2pm.
Legislation proposed by Fianna Fáil TD Malcolm Byrne aimed at protecting children from AI companion chat bots is to be introduced at 3:04pm.
Government Business later in the afternoon – from 3:55pm – is a second stage debate on the Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation Bill 2026.
Next up is a debate on a Sinn Féin motion on the recently announced public transport fare increases.
Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris is due to take Parliamentary Questions at 9:29pm.
There will be an opportunity for TDs to raise Topical Issues at 11:05pm.
A Government motion on the Defective Concrete Blocks Social Homes Scheme 2026 will be before the Seanad at 3:30pm.
Artificial intelligence and the environment will be the topic for discussion at the Committee on Artificial Intelligence from 11am. Representatives from ESB Networks, EirGrid and the Commission for Regulation of Utilities will be in attendance to take questions.
European Union climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra will be before the Committee on Climate from 11am.
The Committee on Foreign Affairs will be looking at diaspora engagement from 3pm.
There will be pre-legislative scrutiny of the heads of the Legacy of the Troubles Bill at the Committee on Justice from 3pm. Organisations due to attend include Amnesty International Ireland, Relatives for Justice, The Pat Finucane Centre and the Irish Council for Civil Liberties.

title: Cabhair an cheoil
description: Tá a céad albam eisithe ag Lucy Rice, nó Last Apollo mar is fearr aithne uirthi. Labhair sí le Emma Ferrari faoin saothar agus faoin bpróiseas.
content:
Ar ardán, d’fhágfadh glór cumhachtach Lucy Rice i do staic thú. I bpearsa tá sí cáiréiseach, séimh, cairdiúil.
Tá sí fillte ar Bhaile Átha Cliath i ndiaidh seal trí bliana a chaitheamh i Londain. Tréimhse foghlama: “chaith muid an t-am ag staidéir próisis taifeadta, seónna beo, albaim dhifriúla. Sin a deirim faoin am sin, go raibh mé ag staidéar.”
Bhí cáil ar Last Apollo - a hainm stáitse - roimhe sin, ach le haird tháinig súilíochtaí, ar féidir iad a bheith ina n-ualach agus ealaíontóir ag aimsiú áite sa saol.
“Bhí muid ag déanamh gigeanna, ach ní raibh mé compordach leis an aird. Bhíodh slua ann, gach focal acu, ach bhí mé ar ardáin ag smaoineamh ‘ní maith liom an ceol seo’. Bhí ‘ reputation’ agam. I Londain bhí spás ann le haghaidh rudaí a thástáil. Daoine nua gan réamhchlaontaí. Sin agus Serigio…”
Léiritheoir is ea Sergio Maschetzko a raibh meas mór ag Lucy air agus a d’oibrigh le leithéidí Black Country agus New Road. Ba gheall le tairngreacht ar deireadh é: “Ó mo dhia! Bhí muid go léir inár luí ar leaba Naoise. Chuir Naoise Snow Globes ar siúl le Ants From Up There… Agus muid ag stánadh ar an tsíleáil dúirt mé ‘b’fhéidir go n-aimseoimid léiritheoir cosúil le Sergio, agus taispeánfaimid an t-amhrán seo dóibh lena thuiscint céard atá uainn’. Anois, i ndiaidh a bheith ag obair leis, ag ithe dinnéir ina theach, smaoiním faoin oíche sin, muid ar fad caite ag ár bpostanna deacra, sa teach garbh sin… a leithéid de rud?!”
Cé go raibh siad tógtha le fuaim Black Country, níl amhras ach go bhfuil a bhfuaim shainiúil féin mar thoradh ar a gcuid oibre, an t-albam I’ll Walk Towards You, ar a mbriseann téaduirlisí téagartha ina dtonnta i gcoinne carraigeacha rac-cheoil.
Is é an cúlra clasaiceach atá aici a saintréith agus a bua, ach bhí Lucy drogallach tagairt dó ar dtús. “Bhuail mo bhanna le chéile ar an ollscoil - ag staidéar cumadóireachta . Bím neirbhíseach go mbíonn cuma mhóiréiseach air sin, nó go gcothódh sé coimhthíos.”
Tá a machnamh déanta aici ar an ábhar, agus aistí scríofa aici ag impí ar shaol an cheoil chlasaicigh oscailt do sheánraí eile.
“Níl a lán daoine nua ag teacht chuig an seánra. Baineann sé le hairgead agus fachtóirí eile ach ceapaim go bhfuil sé tábhachtach gan smaoineamh faoi sheánraí mar spásanna nach bhfuil cead dul isteach iontu. Is fuath liom nuair a chuirtear ceoltóirí i gcúinne amháin, cosúil leis na 1950idí agus buachaillí agus cailíní ar thaobhanna difriúla an halla - sin an íomhá atá i mo cheann! Táim sásta go bhfuil daoine ábalta mo cheol a úsáid mar thúsphointe.”
Más láidir ceol an albaim is láidre an scríbhneoireacht leochaileach chruthaitheach chroíúil.
Is léir scil na gceoltóirí a bhíonn ag seinm le Last Apollo, ach míníonn Lucy nach í sin a bpríomhbhua: “Níl mé ábalta a rá cé chomh tábhachtach is atá siad. Is iad mo chairde ar dtús iad, ansin mo bhanna. Fuair siad glaochanna gach lá: mise ar an tolg ag rá ‘nílim ábalta, tá sé ródheacair, tá daoine i bhfad níos fearr ann.’. Níor chaill siad foighne, dúirt siad ‘is féidir, tá tú á dhéanamh ar na fáthanna cearta’.”
Tá gá le misneach in earnáil nach bhfuil an t-infreastruchtúr ag freastal ar chruthaitheoirí, bac atá tugtha faoi deara ag Lucy: “Níl mo bhanna buartha faoi thóir a bheith orainn nó faoi cheirníní a dhíol - tá an taobh gnó tábhachtach domsa mar táim ag iarraidh ár slí bheatha a dhéanamh - ach tá siadsan ar nós cuma liom faoi. Is brea leo ceol, tá siad ag iarraidh seinnt. Tá sin tábhachtach mar ní bheadh mé in ann rátaí seisiúin a íoc - níl a fhios agam conas is feidir le daoine é a dhéanamh.”
Caitheann muid seal ag iarraidh an córas a réiteach, earnáil a shamhlú a d’íocfadh táille chothrom nuair is deacair cíos ionaid a íoc fiú. Ní thagann muid ar réiteach.
“Ach tá sé go breá,” arsa Lucy, “tá mo chairde agam!”
Léiriú eile ar an gcairdeas ná freagra an bhanna ar chéadéisteacht chéad amhrán an albaim: “is albam é seo, ní amhrán é”, agus “ar dtús, an bhfuil tú ceart go leor?”
Más láidir ceol an albaim is láidre an scríbhneoireacht leochaileach chruthaitheach chroíúil. Filltear ar mhóitífeanna mar a bheadh i suite rómánsach, a fhiosraíonn grá, cneasú croí, agus na fírinní éagsúla a chuimsíonn eispéireas saoil.
Labhraíonn Lucy lena lámha. Síntear amach iad, ag iarraidh téada éagsúla an albaim a shnoí le chéile.
“Bhí mé ag iarraidh smaoineamh an-chumhachtach a leagan síos. Ní thagann sé nádúrtha dom smaoineamh faoi aon fhírinne amháin, mar bím ag smaoineamh faoi gach duine eile. Bhí mé níos óige, agus gafa le gach rud a thuiscint. Tuigim anois gur feidir rudaí a thuiscint cé nach bhfuil tú in ann glacadh leo agus vice versa.”
In ainneoin leochaileacht an togra, fágann an sprioc mhisniúil nach dúshlán é a roinnt: “b’fhéidir go bhfuilim ait, ach mothaím ceart go leor faoi! Cruthaím ceol chun comhluadar a ofráil. Agus tú i spás deacair, ceapann tú nach dtuigeann éinne, agus tá sé sin aonaránach. Ach cloiseann tú amhrán agus tuigeann tú go raibh an taithí chéanna ag duine éigin eile, gur mhair daoine i gcónaí tríd, agus go tobann tá tú timpeallaithe ag daoine. Mar sin de mothaím ceart go leor faoi. Ta súil agam go bhfuil mé ag cabhrú le daoine.”

title: Stevie Wonder releases four unheard tracks from Songs in the Key of Life sessions
description: Songs are released as a new EP of the same name to mark 50th anniversary of classic album
content:
Stevie Wonder has expanded the scope of what was already the most epic studio album in his catalogue, 1976’s Songs in the Key of Life.
Four unheard songs from the recording sessions have been released today as a new EP of the same name, marking the 50th anniversary of an album which won album of the year at the Grammys and contains a number of Wonder’s landmark tracks including Sir Duke, As and Isn’t She Lovely.
“We’ve lived with Songs in the Key of Life for 50 years, but there’s still more to hear,” Wonder said in a statement. “We didn’t add these songs to the album, but they were part of what I was feeling and discovering as we made it. They bring me back to that time in my life, and now they get to become part of yours.”
The songs are suffused with the style Wonder had crafted during the 1970s, and which arguably reached its apotheosis on that 21-track double album: a sunlit, spiritually attuned type of soul and R&B, celebrating love and the richness of existence while acknowledging emotional strife and social struggle.
