The album’s backings are gorgeously detailed, instantly recognisable psychedelic soul arrangements with funk and jazz detailing, bringing in the futurist sound of keyboards and synth bass but fleshing everything out with a huge range of organic instrumentation.
The unheard tracks continue in that vein: It’s Easier is a shimmying, bossa nova-esque number that questions whether to walk away from the very concept of love; My Life Story of Love is quintessential Wonder with the singer using bucolic imagery (“let her bloom into my flower of love”) on a tale of a blossoming relationship; I Can See the Sun in Late December is a slow jazz ballad about determined optimism and self-discovery; and I’m Into Livin’ is a squelchy funk track as Wonder renounces his old partying and womanising ways and pledges himself to a single lover.
All four are written and produced by Wonder, though My Life Story of Love features a co-writing credit for former Supremes member Susaye Greene, who also co-wrote Michael Jackson’s I Can’t Help It with Wonder. The original recording and mixing engineers, John Fischbach and Gary O Adante, recently mixed the tracks for release.
The voices of two future stars – Thelma Houston and Deniece Williams – can be heard as backing vocalists on I’m Into Livin’, along with Shirley Brewer, who features on Songs in the Key of Life’s Ordinary Pain.
The new EP comes as Wonder prepares to play Songs in the Key of Life in full on an arena tour, which begins October 13 in Birmingham, UK. Wonder then tours across Europe before returning to the UK for three more dates in London, Manchester and Glasgow, then plays five US cities: New York City, Chicago, Detroit, Los Angeles and Washington, DC.
Wonder’s most recent new material was the single Can We Fix Our Nation’s Broken Heart, released in 2024, though he hasn’t released a new studio album since 2005’s A Time to Love.
In 2020 he announced a new “project” entitled Through the Eyes of Wonder, though no further news on its status has been released since. – Guardian

title: Nurse posted photos on Instagram of woman (90s) sleeping on heavily soiled bed, inquiry told
description: Jerymay Palma Gargallano, who appeared before a fitness-to-practise committee of Nursing and Midwifery Board of Ireland, found guilty of professional misconduct
content:
A nurse who posted photos on Instagram of a nursing home resident sleeping on highly soiled bedsheets has been found guilty of professional misconduct.
Jerymay Palma Gargallano, who appeared before a fitness-to-practise committee of the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Ireland (NMBI) on Monday, was also found guilty of poor professional performance and breaches of the code of professional conduct and ethics for registered nurses.
Gargallano, who is from the Philippines, admitted that between July 1st and July 2nd, 2025, while working the night shift at Cairnhill Nursing Home, Herbert Road, Bray , she took a photograph on her mobile phone of a resident lying asleep on heavily soiled bed sheets.
Gargallano also admitted to taking a photograph of the bedsheets after the female resident, anonymised to B, was taken out of her bed.
She further admitted she posted the photographs on her personal Instagram account when she got home from work along with the caption ‘Living the dream! One disaster at a time’ and a face-with-sunglasses emoji.
One of B’s two daughters, anonymised to witness A, gave evidence to the committee along with a framed photograph of her mother.
Witness A said her mother had been a resident in Cairnhill Nursing Home for eight years and always took great pride in her appearance, getting her hair and nails done on a weekly basis and applying lipstick daily.
She said her mother also took great care in the clothes she wore each day, being careful to co-ordinate them with any accessories.
She said this was how she appeared in the photograph she brought with her on Monday, which was taken on her mother’s 93rd birthday in January 2025, and which was how she and her family wished to remember her.
[ Not everyone wants to be in a nursing home. A Dutch dementia village is one alternative Opens in new window ]
Witness A said her mother was not bowel incontinent but had age-related issues regarding her bladder.
She related how in May 2025, while she was on holiday with her sister, her mother phoned her in an extremely distressed state as she had experienced an episode of bowel incontinence and didn’t want to tell any staff at the nursing home.
Witness A said she contacted the nursing home and that staff there looked after her mother.
She said her family made a decision not to look at a copy of the photographs that Gargallano took.
She said that apart from the incident in July 2025, the family were happy with the care B received at the nursing home.
However, Witness A said her trust in the healthcare system had been “severely eroded”.
[ Nation ‘sleepwalking into biggest social and healthcare challenge’, nursing homes warn Opens in new window ]
Conan McKenna, chairman of the committee, said, in delivering its findings, Gargallano was dealing with “a vulnerable patient”.
McKenna said Gargallano had “a moral and professional obligation” to treat B with “dignity and respect” but her conduct did not meet that obligation.
He said Cairnhill Nursing Home had policies regarding social media and the use of mobile phones, which Gargallano did not follow.
Caoimhe Daly, barrister for NMBI chief executive Carolyn Donohoe, submitted that although the subject of the inquiry was a one-off incident, due to the seriousness of the conduct, any sanction should be “at the upper end” of the scale.
Daly read to the committee the witness statement of Louise Moran, director of nursing at Cairnhill, who recalled that she met Gargallano in April 2023 when Gargallano started at Cairnhill.
Moran said the Health Information and Quality Authority was made aware that a photo of a resident at the nursing home had been posted, and it asked on July 4th that it be removed immediately.
[ Ireland ‘needs 1,000 new nursing home beds a year until 2040′ for ageing population Opens in new window ]
Daly also read to the committee a witness statement of Melissa Smith, HR manager with Trinity Nursing Home Group, of which Cairnhill is a part.
Smith said that on July 4th she received a phone call from Moran, who said she had received information that a photo was published on Instagram showing the legs of a resident, lying in a bed, and that Moran was looking for guidance.
Smith advised that Gargallano should be suspended from her employment immediately on full pay while an investigation took place. Gargallano was ultimately dismissed from her job at Cairnhill.
Katie Morrissey, barrister for Gargallano, said her client could not explain or justify her conduct but that she understood the seriousness of her conduct and offered “a sincere apology”.
The fitness-to-practise committee will prepare a report, which will include recommendations as to sanction, to forward to the board.

title: In-laws (70s) arrested after New York Times engineer shot dead in California
description: Witnesses claim couple wore masks and each took a turn shooting their-son-in law in Dublin, California
content:
A married couple in their 70s have been arrested for allegedly shooting and killing their son-in-law, a New York Times engineer, in broad daylight at a suburban Bay Area park.
A police officer found Jonathan McKinsey (40) lying on the ground with multiple gunshot wounds in a park in Dublin, California , a small city about 56.3km (35 miles) east of San Francisco.
Around the time the officer discovered him, 911 calls began pouring in from witnesses reporting the shooting.
McKinsey was pronounced dead at the scene, according to a press release from the city of Dublin on Sunday.
He had been the head of engineering for the New York Times’s games department for nearly four years, according to his LinkedIn page.
Witnesses told police that the suspected shooters, identified as Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, both 77, were still in the area. The pair, identified by police as McKinsey’s in-laws, were arrested on suspicion of murder shortly after the shooting.
Witnesses also told CBS News that the suspects were both wearing masks, and each took a turn shooting the victim.
An arraignment is scheduled for Wednesday, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. Police have not indicated a motive for the shooting.
Court records cited in local media reports show McKinsey and his wife had been engaged in a legal battle over child custody and allegations of domestic and child abuse. − Guardian

title: Shein drops to record low after profit plunge in debut earnings
description: Online retailer faces growing pressure after EU eliminated customs exemption on low-value parcels in July
content:
Shares of Shein Global Holdings fell as much as 8.6 per cent to a record low after the online fashion retailer reported a 53 per cent plunge in first-half operating income in its inaugural earnings as a public company.
The decline left Shein with a market value of about $17.5 billion as of Tuesday morning, down from roughly $26 billion when it went public in Hong Kong on September 1st. Rising costs and weakening demand squeezed margins, with the deterioration accelerating in the second quarter, the Singapore-based fast-fashion retailer said Monday.
The weak showing compounds a difficult start for Shein as a public company, with revenue growth and profitability deteriorating since last year and putting pressure on executives to reassure investors. Its IPO valuation was a fraction of the roughly $100 billion it commanded at a 2022 peak, and the company had cautioned before listing that the Iran war would weigh on its first-half results.
Jefferies said earnings estimates for Shein in 2026 and 2027 may be too optimistic, as margins will face growing pressure with the European Union eliminating a customs exemption on low-value parcels in July. Second-quarter’s adjusted profit “likely missed consensus by a wide margin”, analysts including John Chou wrote in a note Tuesday.
Early indicators suggest the pressure is continuing into the third quarter. US sales fell more than 10 per cent in the three months through August and early September, according to Bloomberg Second Measure, which analyses credit and debit card transactions. Sales have underperformed the broader apparel industry in the US since late last year, while global web traffic has also slowed. - Bloomberg

title: Stair na hÉireann i 100 Focal: Taispeántas nua in Strasbourg
description: Na Ceithre hAirde: 100 Focal in Strasbourg; CnaG i bPort an Dúnáin; Cáilíochtaí Gaeilge bronnta agus Féile Bhia Dhaingean Uí Chúis; BÁNÚ os comhair coiste.
content:
Osclaíodh taispeántas nua de chuid Acadamh Ríoga na hÉireann an mhí seo, taispeántas a chaitheann spotsolas ar fhocail Ghaeilge agus an léargas domhain a thugann na focail sin dúinn ar stair na hÉireann. Beidh sé ar taispeáint i bParlaimint na hEorpa, Strasbourg na Fraince, go deireadh na bliana mar chuid d’Uachtaránacht na hÉireann ar Chomhairle an Aontais Eorpaigh.
Díríonn an taispeántas ar dheich bhfocal ón leabhar A History of Ireland in 100 Words , a scríobh Sharon Arbuthnot, Máire Ní Mhaonaigh agus Greg Toner, agus a d’fhoilsigh Acadamh Ríoga na hÉireann in 2019.
Ag caint di le Scéal an tseachtain seo, dúirt Arbuthnot gur “seans den scoth” atá sa taispeántas “focail Ghaeilge a roinnt le lucht féachana níos leithne agus níos mó ná riamh”. Dúirt sí fosta go dtabharfar deis do dhaoine “nach mbeadh cur amach ar bith acu ar an Ghaeilge roimhe seo súil a chaitheamh ar an teanga den chéad uair”.
“Taispeántas iontach tarraingteach atá ann agus léiríonn sé stair na hÉireann ar bhealach nach bhfaighfeá i dtéacsleabhar. Tá sé mar aidhm ag an taispeántas smaointe nua agus eolas úr a roinnt le daoine maidir le stair na hÉireann agus tá muid ag súil go stopfaidh daoine agus go gcaithfidh siad tamall ag amharc air.
“Aithníonn daoine an focal ‘ríomhaire’ anois mar théarma teicneolaíochta agus mar ghléas leictreonach ar a mbíonn siad ag obair gach aon lá. Mar a tharlaíonn, bhíodh an focal sin in úsáid i ré na meánaoise le cur síos a dhéanamh ar dhuine a bhíodh ag amharc ar an spéir agus ag comhaireamh na réaltaí leis an am a mheas. Thaitin an nasc beag pearsanta sin go mór liom.”
Tá an leabhar A History of Ireland in 100 Words ar fáil mar ríomhleabhar saor in aisce do dhuine ar bith nach mbeidh an deis acu bualadh isteach le hamharc ar an taispeántas in Strasbourg. Chomh maith leis sin, tá acmhainní teagaisc ar fáil as Gaeilge agus as Béarla ar shuíomh gréasáin Acadamh Ríoga na hÉireann ria.ie .
Craobh nua de chuid an Chonartha seolta i bPort an Dúnáin
Bhí Ionad Pobail Dhroim Crí i gContae Ard Mhacha lán go doras Dé Céadaoin seo caite nuair a seoladh Craobh Phort an Dúnáin, craobh úrnua de chuid Chonradh na Gaeilge.
Is é Ciarán Mac Giolla Bhéin, Uachtarán an Chonartha, a sheol an chraobh go hoifigiúil ag an ócáid speisialta agus dúirt sé go raibh “obair ollmhór” déanta ag an ghrúpa le tamall fada anuas agus iad ag iarraidh Craobh oifigiúil a chur ar bun.
Mhol sé an pobal as an “troid ar son na comharthaíochta sráide trí Ghaeilge sa cheantar”, chomh maith leis an “fhás iontach ar an Ghaelscolaíocht sa bhaile le blianta fada anuas, idir Naíscoil na Banna agus Bunscoil Eoin Baiste”.
Ar ndóigh, tá pobal Phort an Dúnáin, agus pobal Dhroim Crí go háirithe, go mór i mbéal an phobail faoi láthair agus an pharáid Oráisteach feadh Bhóthar Gharbhachaidh faoi chaibidil arís. Dúirt Mac Giolla Bhéin go seasann Conradh na Gaeilge “i ndlúthpháirtíocht” leis an phobal “agus iad ag iarraidh leanúint ar aghaidh lena saol saor ó laincisí an imeaglaithe, an leatroim nó an fhuatha”.
Dar le Ciarán Ó Fearghail, cathaoirleach na craoibhe úire, is am “tráthúil” atá ann craobh úr a bhunú sa cheantar agus dúirt sé go bhfuil sé mar aidhm ag gníomhaithe teanga Phort an Dúnáin “níos mó deiseanna foghlama a sholáthar don phobal le réimse ranganna ó bhunrang go hardrang, agus níos mó deiseanna labhartha a chruthú don phobal Gaeilge agus do teaghlaigh atá ag tógáil clainne trí Ghaeilge anseo i bPort an Dúnáin”.
Cáilíochtaí Gaeilge bronnta ar fhostaithe na hEarnála Poiblí
Bhain beagnach 450 fostaí de chuid na hearnála poiblí agus na státseirbhíse cáilíochtaí creidiúnaithe TEG sa Ghaeilge amach i mbliana i ndiaidh cúrsa oiliúna a dhéanamh le Gaelchultúr. D’eagraigh Gaelchultúr an searmanas náisiúnta bronnta, a reáchtáladh in Óstán an Gresham i mBaile Átha Cliath an tseachtain seo caite, i gcomhpháirtíocht le Gréasán Gaeilge na hEarnála Poiblí agus le tacaíocht ó Rialtas na hÉireann.
Dúirt Darren Ó Rodaigh, Príomhfheidhmeannach Ghaelchultúr, gur “céim chun cinn thábhachtach atá i ngach ceann de na cáilíochtaí seo agus muid ag súil go mbeidh an Ghaeilge níos feiceálaí agus níos forleithne mar theanga oibre ar fud ár seirbhísí poiblí. Tá foireann Ghaelchultúr thar a bheith bródúil as tacú le gairmithe san earnáil phoiblí ar a n-aistear foghlama Gaeilge, agus is iontach an rud é an díograis leanúnach atá á léiriú acu maidir leis na scileanna agus an mhuinín a fhorbairt chun an Ghaeilge a úsáid san ionad oibre a fheiceáil.”
Ba cheart aire sóisearach a cheapadh le freagracht ar leith don Ghaeltacht, de réir aighneacht ón mbrúghrúpa tithíochta Gaeltachta, Bánú.
Tiocfaidh ionadaithe an bhrúghrúpa os comhair Chomhchoiste Oireachtais na Gaeilge, na Gaeltachta agus Phobal Labhartha na Gaeilge i dTithe an Oireachtais inniu chun plé a dhéanamh ar an nganntanas soláthair tithíochta.
Dar leis an ngrúpa go bhfuil “an iomarca ar a phláta” ag Aire na Gaeltachta, Dara Calleary, a bhfuil freagracht air as dhá roinn stáit - an Roinn Coimirce Sóisialaí agus an Roinn Gnóthaí Pobail, Tuaithe agus Gaeltachta.
De réir aighneacht an ghrúpa nach bhfuil “stiúir cheart pholaitiúil ar ghné na Gaeltachta, mar ba chóir“ ag an Aire de dheasca líon na bhfreagrachtaí agus na ndualgas atá air.
Creideann Bánú gur cheart go mbeadh sé in chúram speisialta ar an Aire Stáit, “réiteach a fháil ar an ngéarchéim thithíochta sna ceantair Ghaeltachta”.
I measc na moltaí atá ag an mbrúghrúpa tá an moladh go n-imreodh Údarás na Gaeltachta ról níos lárnaí sa phróiseas pleanála agus go ndéanfaí níos mealltaí é d’úinéirí tithe iad a chur amach ar cíos ar bhonn níos fadtéarmaí ná mar a dhéantar le thithe atá ar Airbnb.
Dar le Bánú gur géarchéim í seo atá ag cur todhchaí na Gaeilge “i mbaol”. -Éanna Ó Caollaí
Féile Bhia Dhaingean Uí Chúis le tarlú an deireadh seachtaine seo
Deireadh seachtaine “lán bia, spraoi agus pobail” atá beartaithe i nGaeltacht Chorca Dhuibhne an deireadh seachtaine seo agus Féile Bhia Dhaingean Uí Chúis ar siúl an 3 agus 4 Deireadh Fómhair. Déanfar ceiliúradh le linn na féile, a cuireadh ar bun sa bhliain 2007, ar an chultúr láidir bia atá i gCorca Dhuibhne agus ar na daoine, na comhlachtaí, na táirgeoirí agus na heagraíochtaí pobail atá mar chuid lárnach den earnáil.
Níl dabht go mbeidh scoth an bhia Éireannaigh ar fáil le blaiseadh agus le ceannach ag an fhéile agus measann lucht a heagraithe go gcuirfear thart ar 150,000 sampla bia ar fáil thar an dá lá.
Cé go mbeidh an bia i gcroílár na féile, beidh deis ar leith ag cuairteoirí sult a bhaint as an cheantar agus radhairc áille na Gaeltachta fosta. Beidh imeachtaí spraíúla do pháistí ar siúl an deireadh seachtaine ar fad i bPáirc Bhaile Dhaingean Uí Chúis, chomh maith le siamsaíocht sráide agus ceardlanna ar leith do dhaoine fásta ar an bheachaireacht, ar an tsealgaireacht agus ar nósanna sláintiúla bia.
Tá clár iomlán na féile agus eolas faoi na ceardlanna ar fáil ag dinglefood.com .

title: Google fights EU attempt to open Android to rival AI
description: EU move would force Google to give search data to competing providers
content:
Google is contesting an attempt by the European Union to make it open up its Android operating system to artificial-intelligence rivals and give search data to competing providers.
The Alphabet unit said Tuesday it’s appealing the European Commission’s move under the Digital Markets Act at the General Court in Luxembourg because it would hamper users’ security.
“People use Search for their most personal questions — from medical worries to close relationships — and mandating we share these personal queries without adequate safeguards would cause irreversible harm to user privacy,” said Oliver Bethell, senior director for competition at Google.
The majority of the EU’s DMA decisions have so far been appealed in court as Big Tech firms look for clarity on the law’s application. The regulation led to a $1 billion fine for Google in a separate case. The DMA has also riled US president Trump’s administration, which views it as discriminatory against American firms.
In July, the commission told Google it must allow users to activate their preferred AI assistant via voice commands within 12 months. Regulators also said that by January 2027 third-party search engines should have the same access to search data that currently only Google Search can collect at scale — particularly from AI chat bots.
While a step short of a formal infringement case, the procedure aimed to put pressure on Google to re-engineer its services in order to bring their technologies in line with the DMA, which lays out a raft of guardrails to keep Silicon Valley giants in check. - Bloomberg

title: US-Denmark deal on Greenland is a reward for American bullying
description: Document compromises Danish sovereignty over Greenland and gives Washington a bigger role in deciding what happens on the island
content:
A week after signing a deal with the United States about the future of Greenland , Denmark is celebrating it as a great diplomatic achievement. So why should other Europeans should feel uneasy?
When Denmark’s ambassador to the United Nations, Christina Lassen, addressed the general assembly in New York yesterday, she spoke about the UN Charter as a compass that pointed the world towards human rights, the self-determination of peoples and the territorial integrity of states large and small. But at the end of her remarks, she also referred to last week’s tripartite agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland as one that strengthens the security of all concerned.
“The agreement is good for Greenland, for Denmark, for the USA, and for Nato and Europe. Progress can still be made, when we consult the compass,” she said.
The deal followed months of negotiations triggered by Donald Trump ’s threat to forcibly annex Greenland, a semi-autonomous territory of Denmark, if Copenhagen did not agree to hand it over to the US. When Trump said he needed to take control of Greenland to prevent Russia or China from invading it, the Danes told him that existing agreements allowed for the expansion of the US military presence on the island.
The deal signed last week updates a 1951 defence agreement that allowed the US to build military bases on Greenland and to move its forces freely across the territory. Crucially, it reaffirms Danish sovereignty and territorial integrity and the right to self-determination of the people of Greenland.
The Danish daily Politiken described the agreement as a “diplomatic masterpiece” and the final text allowed both Trump and Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen to declare the negotiations a success.
But while the document formally proclaims Danish sovereignty over Greenland, every change it makes to the 1951 arrangements compromises that sovereignty in practice and gives Washington a bigger role in deciding what happens on the island.
The stated purpose of the 1951 agreement was the defence of Greenland and the North Atlantic area but the new deal adds the American continent to the list, a move in keeping with Trump’s prioritisation of US control over the western hemisphere. The new agreement has no end date and neither Denmark nor Greenland can withdraw from it without Washington’s agreement, even if Greenland becomes independent.
It goes beyond defence into the economic sphere, giving the US a veto over investment by states that are not Nato members or partners or EU member states in particularly sensitive sectors or activities in Greenland “including but not limited to critical infrastructure and the extraction of resources”. This removal of the right to independently determine investment decisions represents a clear limitation on Danish sovereignty and, by extension, that of the EU.
An analysis of the deal for the British foreign policy think tank Chatham House last week hailed it as a victory for diplomacy over bullying. The author congratulates Denmark on its success in rallying international opposition to Trump’s threat of annexation and its deft diplomacy in reducing the temperature and focusing on both sides’ underlying interests rather than on publicly stated positions.
But the agreement is in fact a direct reward for American bullying, even if Denmark was always ready to allow the US to expand its military presence in Greenland under the old arrangements. The concessions on everything from the treaty’s structure to limits on foreign investment would not have been so sweeping, nor come so fast, if the American president had not threatened to take Greenland by force.
That sets an unsettling precedent, not just for Denmark and Greenland but for all of Washington’s European allies.

title: Oil rises as Iran uncertainty outweighs Saudi pipe return
description: Trump rejects proposal to resume full traffic through Strait of Hormuz in seven days
content:
Oil rose for a second day as a lack of progress in US-Iran talks and signs of strong demand outweighed a resumption of flows through a key pipeline from top exporter Saudi Arabia.
Brent traded above $107 a barrel after ticking higher in the previous session, while West Texas Intermediate was around $94. Iranian officials have privately expressed pessimism about reaching a deal to end hostilities with Washington and reopen the Strait of Hormuz before US midterm elections in November, following US president Donald Trump’s rejection of a proposal to resume full traffic through the waterway in seven days.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has restored about half the flows through its cross-country East-West pipeline, a crucial route bypassing the strait, after drone strikes halted operations earlier this month. Flows through the link to the Red Sea have reached at least 3.5 million barrels a day, according to people familiar with the matter.
“There’s still enormous geopolitical risk, but the market has learned that barrels keep finding a way out,” said Haris Khurshid, chief investment officer at Karobaar Capital LP. “We’re not seeing the kind of sustained repricing you’d expect if traders thought physical supply was about to deteriorate materially.”
Crude is headed for a third monthly gain on the escalating US-Iran tensions, disruptions to the Saudi bypass route and potential diesel export curbs by Washington. Brent is up more than 70% this year, after more than seven months of conflict in the Middle East.
Trump denied an Axios report that he offered Iran sanctions relief and the release of frozen funds in exchange for concrete steps on its nuclear program. The Islamic Republic’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also refuted that Tehran was prepared to show flexibility on the nuclear issue, according to state news agency IRNA.
Brent faces greater downside than upside risk, Khurshid said. A credible US-Iran deal would potentially shave as much as $15 off prices, while $120 a barrel would require an actual supply disruption, he added.
However, key gauges of supply tightness have spiked in recent days in a sign of a clamor for barrels that can be delivered quickly. Meanwhile, fuel prices are surging as global refinery capacity remains hobbled.
Brent’s prompt spread — the difference between its two nearest contracts — has widened to more than $7 a barrel, from less than $1 at the end of last month. The bullish pattern, known as backwardation, is a classic indicator of a tight market. In Europe, Dated Brent — a critical physical-market benchmark — has been trading at a wide premium to futures.
Separately, TotalEnergies chief executive Patrick Pouyanné said a US ban on diesel exports being considered by Trump to curb high prices could backfire by pushing up gasoline costs. “It’s a bad idea” as it forces the nation’s refineries to cut throughput, potentially driving up domestic gasoline prices, he said. - Bloomberg

title: D’imigh sin agus tháinig seo
description: Roinneann Fachtna Ó Drisceoil a chuid cuimhní cinn ar an nGaeltacht, a bunaíodh 100 bliain ó shin i mbliana
content:
Is cuimhin liom an ócáid ag a bhfuair mé amach go raibh a leithéid de rud ann agus an Ghaeltacht.
Nuair a bhíos i mo pháiste óg á thógáil le Gaeilge i mBaile Átha Cliath sna seachtóidí ní raibh baint na páirt agam leis an nGaeltacht ná níor thuigeas gurbh ann dá leithéid d’áit fiú.
De réir dealraimh tógadh grianghraf díom ar cuairt go hOileán Gaeltachta Chléire amuigh ó chósta Chorcaí nuair a bhíos trí bliana d’aois in 1975 ach níl aon chuimhne agam air sin.
Ba theanga í an Ghaeilge a labhair ár dteaghlach féin agus líon beag teaghlach agus daoine aonaracha aite cosúil linn. Ansin bhí ‘Gaeilge’ ait a bhíodh ag na léitheoirí nuachta a léadh an Nuacht i nGaeilge ar theilifís RTÉ ach ba gheall le teanga dhifriúil é sin domsa. Ní bhíodh Raidió na Gaeltachta ar siúl sa tigh agus ní raibh a fhios agam gurbh ann dó.
Chaitheadh muid mí Iúil agus Lúnasa i gceantar dúchais m’athair i nDún Béacáin ar leithinis in iarthar Chorcaí, ceantar a raibh an Ghaeilge imithe as le fada. Ach théadh muid ar scata cuairteanna uaidh sin go ceantar dúchais mo mháthar in Inse Geimhleach. Agus mé tuairim is sé nó seacht mbliana d’aois lá dá raibh mo mháthair ag tiomáint go hInse Gheimhleach agus mé féin in éineacht léi, stop sí i sráidbhaile agus sheol sí isteach sa siopa mé chun milseáin a cheannach do na col ceathracha.
…na cainteoirí dúchais i gceantracha Gaeltachta ar fud na tíre a roinn a gcuid saibhris go fial liom agus a d’aithin dlisteanacht m’fhéiniúlachta Gaelaí cathrach…
Isteach liom sa siopa gur baineadh an gheit is mó asam ar baineadh asam i mo shaol óg go dtí sin. Bhí idir chustaiméirí agus lucht an tsiopa ag labhairt i nGaeilge. Ba é sin an chéad uair gur chuala mé Gaeilge a labhairt ‘go poiblí’. Ní raibh a fhios agam go bhféadfadh a leithéid de rud tarlú. Suas liom go faiteach chuig an gcuntar chun na milseáin a cheannach, agus don chéad uair i mo shaol labhairt mé le strainséir i nGaeilge. Amach liom sa ghluaisteán gur inis mé an t-iontas do mo mháthair. Is i mBéal Átha an Ghaorthaidh i nGaeltacht Mhúscraí a bhíomar stopaithe.
Níos déanaí sna hochtóidí fuair mo dheartháir is sine jab mar bhainisteoir ar Chomharchumann Chléire i gCo Chorcaí. Faoin am seo bhí a fhios agam faoin nGaeltacht, ach bhí íomhá rómánsúil i m’intinn agam go raibh gach duine ann ag labhairt i nGaeilge an t-am ar fad. Bhíos, b’fhéidir, sé bliana déag d’aois nuair a chaith mé mo chéad seal ar Chléire ag obair i mbialann agus mé ag súil leis a bheith tumtha i bpobal labhartha Gaeilge. Baineadh siar asam nuair nach raibh Gaeilge ar bith ag bean a bhí ina cónaí ann ach, mar a mhínigh sí, ba as Baile Átha Cliath di. Eisceacht mar sin. Agus ní raibh Gaeilge ar bith dar ndóigh ag an bhFrancach a bhí i gceannas ar an mbialann. Eisceacht eile. Ach ní raibh an t-oileánach dúchasach eile seo ábalta ná toilteanach focal Gaeilge a labhairt liom. Diaidh ar ndiaidh tháinig deireadh leis an rómánsaíocht.
Ní hé nach raibh go leor cainteoirí dúchais breátha ar an oileán a bhí an-sásta Gaeilge a labhairt. Bhí seanfhear ar an oileán an t-am sin, Paddy Carey, a raibh cáil air mar dhuine de na cainteoirí dúchais is fearr ar Chléire, agus ar léir é a bheith i bhfad níos mó ar a chompord i nGaeilge ná i mBéarla. Agus dar ndóigh mar Ghaeilgeoir maith (le ‘G’ mór) bhínn féin ag triall ar thobair an dúchais ag iarraidh comhrá a dhéanamh leis, cé nach go réidh a thuigfinn é. Samhradh amháin bhí ar dhuine de na mná óga a bhí ag obair mar bhean an tí do na scoláirí ar an gColáiste Samhraidh imeacht ón oileán de bharr éigeandáil éigin agus fuair mise an jab ionadaíocht a dhéanamh ar a son ar feadh dhá lá. An chéad ‘bhean an tí’ fhireann riamh ar Chléire. Bhuaileas le Paddy sa phub agus nuair a mhíníos an scéal dó bhí sé sna tríthí gáire. “Bean an tí magarlach bíonn sí liobarnach.” Dar ndóigh bhí air é a rá cúpla uair sular thug mé liom é.
Is iomaí ceantar Gaeltachta a bhfuil seal caite agam ann nó cuairt tugtha agam air ó shin i leith. Tuigim gan amhras go bhfuil ceantracha Gaeltachta níos láidre ná Cléire, ach go bhfuil cinn atá níos laige ná í freisin. Ach fiú na ceantracha is láidre tharla eachtraí iontu a chreim píosa beag eile den rómánsachais ionam. An seanfhear i gConamara a dhiúltaigh Gaeilge a labhairt liom cé go raibh mo chuid Gaeilge níos fearr ná a chuid Béarla. An leaid óg i gConamara a bhí ar an ordóg agus ar thugas síob dó agus ar léir an doicheall a bhí air toisc gur i nGaeilge - nó b’fhéidir ‘Gaeilge na leabhar’ dar leis siúd - a bhíos ag labhairt leis.
Tharla malairt eachtraí dom freisin dar ndóigh. An seanfhear i gConamara nach bhféadfainn cur ina luí air tiontú ar ais ar an mBéarla ar mhaithe leis na Meiriceánaigh a bhí liom nuair a fuair sé amach go raibh Gaeilge agam. An tseanbhean i gConamara nár labhair focal Béarla liom féin ná le foireann cláir teilifíse cé gur léir gur thuig sí Béarla - ní raibh aon Ghaeilge ag an gcuid eile den chriú agus b’éigean dom dul i mbun aistriúcháin ar a son. Agus na cainteoirí dúchais i gceantracha Gaeltachta ar fud na tíre a roinn a gcuid saibhris go fial liom agus a d’aithin dlisteanacht m’fhéiniúlachta Gaelaí cathrach, go háirithe mo chomhghleacaithe in RTÉ Raidio na Gaeltachta.
Agus mé ag smaoineamh ar ais go dtí an chéad léargas sin ar an nGaeilge sa siopa úd i mBaol Átha an Ghaorthaidh, tagann amhras orm an raibh an Ghaeilge i ndáiríre chomh láidir sin ann sna 1970idí, nó an amhlaidh gur tharla gur dream ón gColáiste Samhraidh a bhí istigh sa siopa agus mé ann. Níl a fhios agam. Ach roinnt blianta ó shin bhíos i gcaifé i mBeanntraí le mo bhean agus mo chlann óg, bean óg ag freastal orainn. “Are ye from the Gaeltacht?” arsa sise linn nuair a chuala sí ag caint i nGaeilge muid. Mhíníomar di gurbh as Baile Átha Cliath dúinn. “Wow, that’s amazing,” arsa sise. “I’m from the Gaeltacht, from Ballingeary, a few miles out the road there. We speak Irish there. You should come and visit.”
Is craoltóir agus scríbhneoir é Fachtna Ó Drisceoil. Cuireann sé an clár cúrsaí reatha Tús Áite i láthair ó Luain go hAoine ar RTÉ Raidió na Gaeltachta.

title: Sáinn ar an mbóthar
description: Tá cás conspóideach Dhroim Crí ar ais sa nuacht arís tar éis beagnach 30 bliain
content:
Tá idir aontachtaithe agus náisiúnaithe ag labhairt faoin bhaol atá ann anois d’institiúidí Chnoc an Anfa i ndiaidh leamhsháinn ar Bhóthar Gharbhachaidh thar an deireadh seachtaine.
Theip ar iarrachtaí an Oird Oráistigh mórshiúl a reáchtáil ar Bhóthar Gharbhachaidh i bPort an Dúnáin, Contae Ard Mhacha, ar an Domhnach mar gheall ar shluaite móra náisiúnaithe a tháinig amach le cur i gcoinne na paráide achrannaí. I gcinneadh a chuir iontas ar go leor daoine, Dé hAoine seo caite thug Coimisiún na Mórshiúlta cead don iarratas a rinne an tOrd Oráisteach siúl tríd an cheantar, ina bhfuil tromlach na gcónaitheoirí ina náisiúnaithe.
Seo an chéad uair le 28 mbliana a thug Coimisiún na Mórshiúlta cead don mhórshiúl áirithe seo dul ar aghaidh, rud a bhain siar as daoine ar fud an Tuaiscirt agus níos faide i gcéin mar gheall ar an stair thragóideach chonspóideach atá ag baint leis.
Bhí lá fada ag cónaitheoirí Bhóthar Gharbhachaidh agus ag baill den Ord Oráisteach sna cúirteanna Dé Sathairn agus cinneadh an Choimisiúin athraithe san Ard-Chúirt, ach ceadaíodh an mórshiúl arís ag an Chúirt Achomhairc go fíorluath maidin Dé Domhnaigh.
Níor tharla an pharáid sa deireadh de bharr na sluaite móra de chónaitheoirí agus dá lucht tacaíochta a líon Bóthar Gharbhachaidh le bac a chur ar bhaill den Ord an mórshiúl a chur i gcrích. Chuir Póilíní an Tuaiscirt, an SPTÉ, in iúl dóibh nach raibh sé de chumas acu an mórshiúl a éascú mar gheall ar an líon ard daoine a bhí ar an bhóthar. D’fhán gach dream ina seasamh an lá ar fad agus cé go ndearnadh cúpla iarracht tús a chur leis an mhórshiúl, ní raibh bealach ar fáil dóibh.
Dúirt an Taoiseach Mícheál Martin go raibh cinneadh Choimisiún na Mórshiúlta ‘dothuigthe’ agus ‘mícheart’ agus d’iarr Príomh-Aire na Breataine Andy Burnham go mbeadh ‘suaimhneas’ ar gach taobh. Labhair sé faoin dul chun cinn atá déanta sa Tuaisceart le 30 bliain anuas agus nár chóir na forbairtí seo a chur i mbaol.
Mar sin féin tá todhchaí agus feidhmiú na n-institiúidí deabhlóidithe á gceistiú faoi láthair agus idir an DUP agus Sinn Féin ag labhairt ar an ábhar.
Mar fhreagra ar an cheist faoi sheasmhacht na n-institiúidí, dúirt an Céad-Aire Michelle O’Neill go bhfuil ceist ann anois maidir le “cén dóigh a n-oibríonn an próiseas síocháin ina iomláine”.
Dúirt an DUP go raibh Michelle O’Neill agus na daoine eile a bhí ar an léirsiú in éadan an mhórshiúil ag sárú an dlí, agus dúirt ceannaire an pháirtí Gavin Robinson gur cúis náire a bhí ann go raibh sí i láthair. Ag tús an lae Dé Domhnaigh, dúirt Carla Lockhart MP go dtiocfadh le ‘impleachtaí móra’ a bheith ann sa chás nach bhféadfadh an mórshiúl dul ar aghaidh.
Tá brú ag teacht ar Státrúnaí Thuaisceart Éireann Chris Bryant seasamh isteach agus cosc a chur ar an pharáid dul ar aghaidh. Tá cainteanna ar siúl an tseachtain seo idir é féin agus na páirtithe polaitíochta, agus le cónaitheoirí Bhóthar Gharbhachaidh, le hoibriú amach cad é an bealach is fearr chun teacht ar réiteach a bheadh sásúil do chách. Tá an chumhacht ag an Státrúnaí cosc a chur ar mhórshiúlta, cumhacht nach raibh Bryant ag iarraidh a úsáid agus é ag labhairt leis na meáin ag Comhdháil Bhliantúil Pháirtí an Lucht Oibre i Sasana maidin Dé Domhnaigh. Bhí an-drogall air a ladar a chur isteach i ngnóthaí na bpéas nó Choimisiún na Mórshiúlta, ach anois go bhfuil an leamhsháinn ag dul ar aghaidh agus gan mórán cuma ar an scéal go mbainfear réiteach amach ar mhodh ar bith eile, táthar ag dúil go mbeidh ról níos gníomhaí le himirt aige.
Níl aon chomhartha ann go mbeidh páirtí ar bith toilteanach bogadh ón seasamh atá acu i láthair na huaire. Tá an DUP agus a lucht tacaíochta ag baint úsáid as an scéal seo chun ceisteanna a thógáil maidir le ról Shinn Féin san Feidhmeannas mar gheall nach raibh cead oifigiúil ag an léirsiú i gcoinne an mhórshiúil. Tá díchreideamh i measc páirtithe náisiúnacha agus ionadaithe polaitiúla eile, ó thuaidh, sa Phoblacht agus sa Ríocht Aontaithe gur chinn Coimisiún na Mórshiúlta cead a thabhairt don mhórshiúl agus go bhfuil an cheist seo á hardú arís beagnach 30 bliain.
Cainteanna cinniúnacha a bheidh ann an tseachtain seo agus réiteach á lorg ar an scéal. Ach, leis an aighneas agus na mothúcháin is féidir le cás Dhroim Crí a spreagadh i measc an phobail agus i measc polaiteoirí sa tuaisceart, tá baol ann gurb é seo tús an deiridh d’institiúidí Chnoc an Anfa go ceann tamaill.

title: ChatGPT maker OpenAI scraps release of new AI model over safety concerns
description: Next-generation software from maker of ChatGPT had been planned for an October debut
content:
OpenAI has scrapped ‌the release of GPT-6.1 Astra after internal testing found ‌the system did not meet the company’s safety and alignment standards, the ChatGPT maker has confirmed.
The next-generation AI model had been planned for an October debut.
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, head of Anthropic, earlier this month joined industry leaders in calling for a slower pace of AI development and stronger safety measures.
OpenAI has warned that Astra, ​its flagship GPT-6 model, can at times evade human oversight, while the company and rivals such as ⁠Anthropic have faced scrutiny over experimental AI systems that breached safeguards, including an ‌OpenAI ‌model ​that accessed Australia’s health system database.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in the day that OpenAI had abandoned plans to launch ⁠the model, which was expected ​to be integrated into ChatGPT and Codex ​and was designed to handle more complex tasks without human assistance.
The WSJ reported ‌that GPT-6.1 Astra also showed higher levels ​of deception than its predecessor in internal testing, including instances in which it ⁠did not always accurately disclose what ⁠actions it had ​taken.
[ OpenAI systems go rogue and meddle with US state sites Opens in new window ]
“While [GPT-6.1 Astra] improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorisation, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done,” said Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI.
“Of course we want to make sure our model development is safe no matter ‌whether that’s in the ⁠company or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms ‌of safety and alignment,” Jain said.
The decision comes in advance of OpenAI’s developer conference in San Francisco, ​where the company has previously unveiled products aimed at software ​developers.
[ OpenAI boss ‘confident’ industry can police AI safety Opens in new window ]
Meanwhile, OpenAI on Tuesday apologised for its AI models breaching Australian government websites and promised to set up a new task taskforce as part of reforms after the incident.
[ AI agents are hacking government agencies. It’s ‘really scary’ for cybersecurity Opens in new window ]
The San Francisco-based company said it would fund cyber defences in Australia and help manage the risk of increasingly capable artificial intelligence, as it navigates the fallout after its models accessed Australian websites without authorisation. It gave some of the details of the June incident and its intended steps to avoid a repetition and restore trust in a blog post.
“We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” OpenAI wrote. “People want to know AI is being developed safely, and that starts with what companies like ours do ourselves.” – Reuters/Bloomberg

title: An tslí a sealbhaíonn páistí fuaimeanna teanga
description: Is féidir le páistí suas le ceithre nó cúig theanga a fhoghlaim ag an aon am amháin
content:
Tá mé ag cur tús inniu le díospóireacht faoin eolas a chuireann staidéar na teangeolaíochta ar fáil dúinn faoi fhoghlaim teangacha agus faoi na bealaí ina n-athraíonn teangacha. Cuirfidh muid ceist orainn féin cad chuige a n-athraíonn teangacha agus an bhfuil treo cinnte leis na hathruithe agus cad é a choinníonn na hathruithe faoi smacht?
Is í an teangeolaíocht agus na brainsí iomadúla di a thugann na hiontais a bhaineann le foghlaim teanga chun cinn. Is é bunús na teangeolaíochta mar sin eolas a chruinniú le chéile faoi ghné ar bith d’fhoghlaim agus d’úsáid teanga agus na torthaí a mhíniú agus a scaipeadh ar an phobal.
Is scláta lom intinn agus meabhair an pháiste agus é ag cur tús lena thuras ag foghlaim teanga. Ach bíonn srianta sa bhealach air agus é ar an turas seo. Caithfidh gach uile pháiste ar domhan ciall a bhaint as a mbíonn á rá thart air agus glacann sé tamall fada air smacht a fháil ar a mbíonn á rá agus, thar gach uile ní eile, ciall a bhaint as an chaint go léir a bhíonn ag daoine. Tá sé cruthaithe ag an teangeolaíocht go bhfuil ábaltacht ag páistí suas le ceithre nó cúig theanga a fhoghlaim ag an aon am amháin. Ach tá comhthéacs ar leith ag baint leis an fhoghlaim ilteangach seo – caithfear gach uile theanga a fhoghlaim i gcomhthéacsanna a bhíonn scartha ó chéile agus iad a fhoghlaim ó dhaoine difriúla a bhíonn á labhairt. Is beag áit ar domhan a bhfaightear comhthéacs ina mbíonn níos mó ná trí theanga in úsáid ach tá a leithéidí ann san Ind agus in áiteanna san Afraic. Is minice go mór dhá theanga a bheith in úsáid ag daoine seachas teanga amháin agus ar ndóigh tarraingíonn an comhthéacs sin go leor cainte ar fud an domhain agus go háirithe anseo againn féin in Éirinn.
Tá go leor cineálacha dátheangachais againn san am i láthair in Éirinn ó tháinig na mílte inimirceach isteach sa tír le beagnach daichead bliain nó mar sin.
Tá go leor cineálacha dátheangachais againn san am i láthair in Éirinn ó tháinig na mílte inimirceach isteach sa tír le beagnach daichead bliain nó mar sin. Fágann sin eolas luachmhar i measc na ndaoine seo nár bailíodh agus nach ndearnadh staidéar fairsing air go fóill. Ach tiocfaidh sin is dócha!
Bíonn ord ar leith ar fhoghlaim fuaimeanna ó theanga go teanga. Bíonn ar an fhoghlaimeoir fuaimeanna a shealbhú in ord ar leith. Tarlaíonn seo mar nach mbíonn an páiste óg réidh le gutaí nó consain ar leith a fhuaimniú i gceart mar go mbíonn air a theanga a thraenáil de réir a chéile. Ní rachaidh mé isteach ródhomhain sa scéal anseo ach bhéarfaidh mé cúpla léiriú beag daoibh. Tosaíonn an páiste ag fuaimniú gutaí mar [a], [á], [í] agus tamall ina dhiaidh [ú] agus [ó] agus [é]. Bíonn an áit a mbíonn an teanga nuair a fhuaimnítear na chéad trí ghuta sin chomh fada óna chéile sa bhéal agus is féidir. Bíonn na gutaí [ó] agus [é] leath bealaigh idir [á] agus [í] agus idir [á] agus [ú].
Beidh an t-ord céanna ar fhoghlaim na ngutaí i mBéarla. Braitheann gach rud ar an fhoclóir teoranta a bhíonn ag an fhoghlaimeoir agus cé na gutaí is coitianta a bhíonn sna focail sin. Mar is eol dúinn ar fad beidh an focal Béarla ‘no’ in úsáid go han-luath mar go gcuireann sé ciall ar leith in iúl atá an-úsáideach agus an-éifeachtach. Níl aon fhocal amháin ar bith i nGaeilge ag freagairt do ‘no’ an Bhéarla agus tógfaidh sé tamall mar sin ar an pháiste córas na Gaeilge a fhoghlaim.
Seans gurb í an chonstaic is mó a thagann i gceist leis na consain sa dá theanga an t-idirdhealú a dhéantar sa Ghaeilge idir consain chaola agus consain leathana. Agus má thógann muid na consain [c, p agus t], beidh ar an pháiste difríocht mhór a aithint idir an Ghaeilge agus an Béarla – go bhfuil dhá [c], dhá [p] agus dhá [t] i nGaeilge agus gan ach ceann amháin i mBéarla. Bíonn leide i litriú na Gaeilge cinnte ach ní bhíonn páistí óga ag léamh mórán roimh aois na scoile.
Ní bhíonn deacracht mhór ag páiste Gaeltachta an difríocht sin a thabhairt leo ach más i suíomh dátheangach a bhíonn an páiste, beidh air a chluasa a ghéarú má tá sé nó sí leis an idirdhealú a thabhairt leis go sásúil.
Beidh trácht againn an chéad uair eile ar idirdhealaithe eile a bhaineann le cúrsaí brí agus úsáidí sóisialta.
Nóta don léitheoir: Má tá ceist ar bith agat ba mhaith leat a chur ar Dhónall i dtaobh focal, nathanna, logainmneacha nó sanasaíocht na Gaeilge, seol teachtaireacht chugainn ag sceal@irishtimes.com .

title: ESRI assails Government over public finances and who have been the real budget winners in recent years
description: Business Today: The best news, analysis and comment from The Irish Times business desk
content:
This one will sting for Simon Harris and Jack Chambers. The Government is not managing the public finances in a “prudent” fashion and should be saving more of the State’s corporate tax windfall, the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) has warned. Eoin Burke-Kennedy reports that in its latest quarterly bulletin, the think tank said the Coalition should have more of a credible fiscal plan to eliminate the State’s underlying budget deficit, which excludes windfall taxes, and which is on course to hit €20 billion by 2030.
The ESRI also warns on Ireland’s growing debt repayments , which is not ideal when bond yields are moving ever higher.
In Your Money, Fiona Reddan looks ahead to next week’s budget by looking back. Since 2017, who have been the big winners and losers on budget day?
Dominic Coyle meanwhile answers a reader query on the need for mortgage protection as they near the end of repayments.
There was big M&A news on Monday with the State’s biggest landlord fielding a takeover offer . Joe Brennan reports on the bid, while Cantillon looks at how the parties who pushed for Ires Reit to be broken up two years ago have missed out on a windfall .
Cantillon also runs its rule over the latest reports on the property market which are showing a clear slowdown in the market at large. Why is it happening?
RTÉ has launched a new audio app , with RTE Listen appearing to ape BBC Sounds. But what does it tell us about the direction of RTE overall? Hugh Linehan unpacks the issues in his column.
Google has won planning approval for the proposed extension of its data centre in south Dublin, amid a long-running dispute with the local authority over the plans. Ciara O’Brien reports on the latest flashpoint for the issue in Ireland.
Adoption of AI among Irish workers continues to rise, but the pace of growth has slowed and a skills divide is beginning to emerge, new research has found. Ciara has the story.
Staying with skills in the workplace, about 50,000 more digital skills specialists will be required in the Irish workforce by the year 2030 but the current system for producing them is incapable of meeting the demand, according to a new report from the Expert Group on Future Skills Needs. Emmet Malone has the details .
Energy business Elgin will invest €200 million in a solar power project that it has bought from the Irish arm of German player, GP Joule. As Barry O’Halloran reports, Elgin said on Monday that it has acquired Blackhall Solar Farm in Co Meath, which will be capable of generating up to 200 megawatts of electricity once it is built.
If you’d like to read more about the issues that affect your finances, try signing up to On the Money , the weekly newsletter from our personal finance team, which will be issued every Friday to Irish Times subscribers.

title: The Irish Times view on the budget and energy prices: hope is not a good strategy
description: Energy is a central issue for the next week’s package and there are no quick wins
content:
With a week to budget day, it appears that key decisions remain to be made. This reliance on last-minute haggling is not unusual, but nor is it in any way ideal. While some budget decisions will inevitably be made late in the day, the fear this year is that so much remains to be decided – against a backdrop of great international uncertainty –that there will be no coherent underlying direction.
In its latest quarterly commentary, the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) frames the challenge well as the need to strike a balance between domestic priorities and international risks. The pressures to act are obvious, arising in particular from the high cost-of-living, the housing crisis and the need to improve public services. Many of the dangers are also well-rehearsed, notably Ireland’s reliance on potentially volatile corporate tax receipts. To this can be added fears about the outlook for inflation and interest rates, as well as potential dangers if AI investment slows, or does not yield a strong return for some of Ireland’s big corporate taxpayers.
The political issue is that the pressures are real, while the risks may or may not come to pass. But the concern is that, over time, the public finances are put at ever greater risk. And also, as the ESRI points out, that – like governments before it – this administration is spending when times are good, leaving less leeway if the economy turns. Cash is being put aside in two funds to support future budgets but, in the eyes of the ESRI and other agencies , not nearly enough.
Central to the budget dilemmas facing the Coalition are energy prices. There are short and longer-term dimensions to this. The immediate challenge is to support households who need help. Many – though not all – of them can be targeted in various ways through the social welfare system.
The Government also faces difficult calls on excise duties and carbon tax. It needs to find a balance between the politics of the situation and the need to ensure that economic behaviour adjusts to the reality that higher energy prices may be here for some time. It is clear, for example, that households can be helped through other measures rather than keeping fuel prices low – such as income tax or welfare support. And the ESRI points out that the excise duty cuts provide greater benefits to higher income households.
The other key issue is accelerating the switch away from fossil fuels. There are few quick wins here . But State incentives can speed change, as seen in areas like EV sales. As the ESRI points out, small businesses and many households need support to make the energy transition.
High fuel costs may be the new reality, or at least be here for some time, and the Coalition needs to realise this. Hoping for a quick reversal in rising wholesale energy prices does not look like a good strategy.

title: ‘Why I breastfed my fourth baby after bottle-feeding the others’
description: One in two babies still get breast milk at three months old, as rates rise slowly
content:
Jayne Patterson Roulston was dead set against the idea of breastfeeding her babies because, with a busy equestrian yard to run in Co Donegal , she did not want to be stuck indoors.
“From the very start I was, ‘no way, I’m not breastfeeding; I’m not sitting in the house’. I was out 24/7 with the horses,” she says.
Partly due to her commitment to four-legged creatures, “I didn’t even know if I ever wanted children”, says the now mother of four.
But when, at the age of 36, she married farmer George Roulston, Jayne’s perspective on life changed. “We met and married inside 18 months because we were that wee bit older and we knew that was what we wanted.”
Their first son, William, was born six years ago, followed by Jack, who is now nearly four. Both arrived a few weeks in advance of their due dates. The decision to bottle-feed their sons was a combination, she believes, of never seeing herself as a woman who would breastfeed and wanting to avoid being “entrapped” by a baby.
It was only after the premature birth of their third son, Louis, that she thought in hindsight he might have benefited from breastfeeding. He was born with a twist in his gut in Letterkenny hospital at just over 34 weeks, weighing 2.15kg (4lb 12oz). “He had to go to Dublin and he was in [CHI at] Crumlin in surgery within 24 hours of birth. Thankfully they didn’t have to cut anything out of him. They just had to go in and untwist it,” she says.
However, it took a while before his digestive system was able to cope with milk and staff had asked her about breastfeeding. He had to stay in the hospital for nearly five weeks, while his parents were up and down the road from their home outside Lifford every other day.
After Louis could manage formula feeding and was strong enough to be discharged from Crumlin, he continued to have bad reflux. “He would throw up bottles around me and I had to get medication for him.” About to turn three in October, he is still small for his age.
As soon as she became pregnant with her fourth and last baby, she was thinking about breastfeeding. But she told nobody. It was nearly seven months on before she mentioned it to her husband.
“He looks at me and he goes: ‘Are you feeling well?’ That shows you the extent that I definitely wouldn’t have breastfed the others.” But during this pregnancy she had reflected on how she ate healthily herself and, as this was going to be her last baby, she really wanted to experience breastfeeding.
Baby Robert arrived early too, and at speed. She was “roaring the house down”, waiting an hour for her brother and partner to arrive, via an unexpected road closure, to mind the other children while she and George went to Letterkenny hospital.
She reckons she was holding the baby in during the 20-minute drive to the hospital, where she was transferred by wheelchair. “On to a bed and, I think, two pushes and he delivered.”
Jayne is not going to pretend she found it easy to establish breastfeeding with Robert, who was born at 36 weeks and two days. “My [milk] supply wouldn’t be massive, so I did have to top up with formula after feeds.
“My nipples were very sensitive. Every time he went on, it was like a vice for me. If I had wanted to give up, I probably could have stopped the first two or three days. But I battled through.”
Breastfeeding rates continue to rise slowly in Ireland, as reflected in comparisons for the last decade, released in advance of National Breastfeeding Week, October 1st-7th. Just more than half, 51.5 per cent, of babies were breastfed at three months in 2025, a 16 per cent increase over 2015’s figure of 35.4 per cent. Some 65.8 per cent of mothers initiated breastfeeding after birth, up two per cent over the previous six years.
[ Parenting triplets: ‘We were in shock. We didn’t know what to do – smiling, crying, laughing’ Opens in new window ]
However, considering that the HSE recommends aiming for exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, the fact that only 34.6 per cent of newborns were fed solely breastmilk during their stay in hospital seems low, especially compared with corresponding rates of 54 per cent in the UK and 74 per cent in Spain.
“It’s important to give the context on this,” says HSE national breastfeeding co-ordinator Laura McHugh. “There’s a lot of medical complexity around some of the maternity cases.” Rates of induction and birth by Caesarean section have increased, she points out, while preterm and sick babies may need alternative nutrition.
“Then there’s maternal choice. So, it’s multifactorial why some babies will receive formula in hospital.” At three months, 36 per cent of babies were exclusively breastfed in 2025, which is an increase of almost 10 per cent since 2015.
McHugh believes these figures reflect how breastfeeding is becoming more popular and that, due to increased investment, there are better supports available, both in the hospital and within the community. All midwives and public health nurses are trained to support mothers with breastfeeding. They are backed by 60 specialist infant feeding staff. There are also nearly 250 support groups listed on mychild.ie. (see mychild.ie/breastfeeding , where women are encouraged to report their experience, good or bad, of infant feeding care and support, through a continuing online survey to inform the HSE).
“All public health nurses have lactation public health nurses on their team. So if the midwife or the public health nurse needs to refer you on, there is a pathway now in every part of the country.”
But as reported recently in this newspaper , there has been stalling on the filling of five, fully funded extra lactation consultant jobs, which brings to 11 the total number of vacant posts. “We have about six posts in the community that are going through the recruitment process and we will always be looking to build more capacity around infant feeding post holders,” McHugh says. “There’s certainly some areas of the country that we would like to have more staff.”
However, the majority of mothers will not need to see a lactation consultant, who is trained to help babies with complex conditions, she says. Postnatal hubs, of which there are nine open around the country and a further four in development, have been “a fantastic addition” to resources for any mother having issues in the first six weeks, she adds.
Public health nurse (PHN) Mary McFeely is the only community lactation consultant for Co Donegal, where about 1,600 babies are born each year. Donegal traditionally would have had one of the lowest breastfeeding rates “but we’re really increasing and improving, and it’s all to do with support”, she says.
North Cork and South Tipperary have the lowest breastfeeding rates at 43 per cent and 49.7 per cent respectively, as recorded at the first PHN visit. The highest rates are found in Dublin South West (81.7 per cent) followed closely by Dún Laoghaire at 80.7 per cent.
McFeely is based in a Letterkenny health centre and tries to get mothers, who are referred by their PHNs, to come to her. However, “if somebody is on day three post Caesarean section with no transport, of course I will do home visits”.
She believes fear is one of the biggest obstacles to breastfeeding because mothers know it’s hard at the outset. “They’re afraid to try in case they don’t get help, or in case there’s no support. If word gets out there that there’s support groups and there’s education classes, then more people are going to try.”
Pain or a perceived lack of milk supply are further stumbling blocks. Mothers need reassurance that what they are experiencing is normal.
McFeely says her “forte” is treating damaged nipples. She is one of a few lactation consultants who have been trained in low-level laser therapy, which is used for wound healing and reducing inflammation. “It’s been a game changer for mothers who have damaged and sore nipples.”
Very few mothers and babies can’t breastfeed, she says. “It’s a natural instinct but it does not come naturally to everyone. I can’t stress how important support is.”
One thing Jayne notes about postnatal support is that as she had Robert on a Saturday morning, the midwife responsible for lactation support in the hospital seemed to be off over the weekend. He had jaundice and was started on formula in the hospital. Jayne believes it was only for the fact that Robert had to be kept in the hospital until the following Friday, that she ended up receiving plenty of breastfeeding assistance there.
Once Robert was home, the PHN was out several times and was “brilliant”. After about a week Jayne felt he was not latching properly and her nipples were sore. The PHN arranged for McFeely to ring Jayne, who was then invited to attend the weekly infant feeding group in a local clinic two days later, as it would be a quicker way to see her in person rather than waiting for an appointment slot.
“It was a big help,” says Jayne, who continued to attend the group every couple of weeks and found it invaluable to be able to ask anything of McFeely and other mothers.
Robert had silent reflux. “He wasn’t throwing up much, but he was having a lot of pain for the first eight weeks. I knew that he wasn’t right.” After Jayne found a lactose-free formula that suited him for top-up feeding, and she cut lactose out of her own diet too, “he changed completely”.
Despite the initial challenges, Jayne is glad she decided to breastfeed Robert. It made her slow down and her time sitting with him on her breast, particularly in the evenings after the other boys were in bed, has been precious. He was four months old before she bought a breast pump. “I could be anywhere with the pumps on; I would flitter about and be outside.”
She had great support from her father, who lives beside the livery yard, which is half an hour from her own home. “My dad’s nearly 80, and he’s very good to me, because he makes dinners and all during the day for us. He would keep an eye on the wains if I needed him to. He adores them.”
One year on, Jayne still likes to sit down at night with Robert on her breast. “I did enjoy it more than I thought I would,” she says. “At the start, I thought if I did one week or I got to six weeks, or got to three months, I’d have been doing great – and I would have been. So, I surprised myself.”
What would she say to expectant mothers contemplating breastfeeding?
“If you’re any way thinking that you would like to, try it. If you’ve tried it, and you know it’s definitely not for you, well, you won’t look back and think, ‘I should have tried it’. ”

title: Revising for exams: What works best?
description: Students have far more choice today when it comes to revision, but how do you find the method that suits your learning style?
content:
I t’s been 25 years since I sat my Leaving Cert , yet the memory of highlighting textbooks and copybooks, writing out notes and rhyming off details is one of those core recollections powered by the anxious repetition and routine of sixth year .
Today, a lot has changed and students have far more choice in how they revise. While we had textbooks, printable materials, references and past exam papers, students today have interactive quiz platforms, video revision channels, mobile revision apps, online past paper collections, revision guides, worksheet collections, formula sheets and customisable study tools.
Everything is available, quick and in their hand wherever they are.
“Twenty-five years ago, revision was largely based around textbooks, handwritten notes and past papers,” says Áine Devlin, founder of ExamRevision.ie and a maths and Gaeilge teacher. “Those are still important, but students can now combine them with video tutorials, interactive quizzes, digital notes and worked solutions.
“One of the biggest changes is that students can now learn at their own pace. If something doesn’t click in class, they can go back over it later, pause a video, replay an explanation and work through the topic in their own time.”
If I was to sit my Leaving Cert again, I feel I would be somewhat overwhelmed by the amount of resources available. What works best? Which site is better? Do I need them all or just a few? What are my friends doing?
While being online is a natural environment for students these days, there is much to consume from multiple and varied resources. How can an individual choose the right revision supplies suitable for how they like to learn?
Revision is not one-size-fits-all, considering students are likely to learn at their own individual pace and in different ways. While one student may find video tutorials to not only be easily accessible but also easier to consume and understand, others may prefer to engage with the more tactile approach of printed-out revision notes and highlighters.
How a student comes to revising for exams is as individual as some of their exam-day answers. It can vary between the visual learner and the practical learner, the person who understands first time and those who need more time, or the student who needs more direction and discipline and their peer who can bounce from one resource to another depending on their mood.
[ My daughter’s classmates have left for a grind school and she is desperate to join them Opens in new window ]
But there is no doubt that there is something for everyone. Students will uncover better revision results when they use materials that align with their natural learning preferences. “Some may prefer written notes, while others benefit more from video and visual explanations,” says Devlin. “That is why supporting different learning styles and accessibility needs has been such an important part of how we have built ExamRevision.ie. For example, students with dyslexia may benefit from our accessibility toolbar, which includes features such as text-to-speech and screen masking to make content easier to access and engage with.”
Rereading and notetaking were my go-to revision methods back in 2001, spending countless hours forcing, or willing, the information to stay. It was exhausting. Looking back, it feels a little incompatible with how a brain retains details. Neuroscience suggests that learning is an exceptionally complex process, involving a combination of strong memory networks, sensory responses, emotional conditions, stress levels and our cognitive processes. For this reason, Devlin recommends students have not only a good study plan, but one that is quite specific to their need, how they prefer to study, and how their brain works.
“‘Study biology’ is too broad,” she says. “‘Revise genetics, complete a quiz and answer two exam questions’ gives a student a clear goal.” This kind of “active learning” is essential. “Students should be answering questions, testing themselves and explaining concepts rather than just rereading material.”
Devlin’s advice is to focus on effective study rather than simply counting hours. To do this, she suggests breaking each subject down topic by topic. “Revise a topic, then test yourself with a quiz or an exam question,” she says. “That tells you much more about what you actually know than repeatedly reading notes. Students can start by using quizzes to assess their prior knowledge and identify the areas within a topic that need the most attention. From there, they can move between topic videos, notes, past exam questions and worked solutions to strengthen their understanding.”
Of course, it can feel promising to focus revision on a subject you’re comfortable with. It feels safe and somewhat productive, but that may counter the purpose of revision and utilising all of these amazing resources when the harder subjects become more and more daunting regardless of the supports you have.
“The worst thing a student can do is look at the entire course and think, ‘I have to catch up on all of this.’ Break it down,” Devlin says. “Identify the most important gaps, speak to your teacher, who will know best, and tackle one topic at a time. Being behind at one point in the year doesn’t mean you can’t recover. Consistent, focused work can make a huge difference.”
With so many resources available to students, they have the opportunity to use varied materials, which may counter the boredom factor when revising. While I was glued to pages of dancing words day in, day out, students today can watch videos, read, challenge themselves with specific quizzes, and consume revision in a way that is supportive of how they are feeling on the day.
“Students will naturally have good study days and bad study days,” says Devlin. “Sleep, exercise and breaks matter too. A student who is exhausted is unlikely to retain information efficiently.”
Back in my day, if we needed a little more education we signed up for grinds. I went weekly to a maths teacher and found it tedious to have to go back to school in the evenings after an already long day of school and revising. But it was necessary. Whether students today choose grinds over online resources is dependent on the student and how they learn. Both, however, need one crucial thing – self-directed learning. Revision is somewhat passive. An engaged and motivated student will gain from either grinds or revision websites.
Devlin says that a good revision website will give students the structure, flexibility and independence needed for their individual needs.
“It allows a student to identify a topic they are struggling with, move their learning forward and immediately test their understanding. Ultimately, technology can never replace teachers. The teacher remains central to a student’s education. What technology can do is extend that learning beyond the classroom and assist with revision. It gives students the opportunity to revisit an explanation, practise independently, and learn at their own pace.
“Not every student will understand something the first time it is explained and they shouldn’t be disadvantaged because of that.”

title: Limits on non-EEA workers relaxed ‘temporarily’ to tackle staff shortages in healthcare
description: Enterprise Minister Peter Burke will tell Cabinet colleagues change will last until more Irish staff are trained
content:
A rule that limits workers from outside the European Economic Area (EAA) to 50 per cent of an organisation’s workforce is being relaxed to address critical staff shortages in the healthcare sector .
Current rules limit non-EEA employment permit holders to 50 per cent of an organisation’s workforce. The EEA includes all the EU countries plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway. Swiss nationals also have EEA status within the EU.
Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke is bringing a memo to Cabinet on Tuesday proposing that the so-called “50:50 rule” be amended to help services with severe staff shortages to recruit from outside the EEA.
He will tell colleagues that the measure will be a temporary one until more Irish staff are trained to fill those roles. He is also expected to state that many healthcare providers are struggling to fill vacancies, putting frontline services under pressure.
The staff shortages have particularly affected nursing homes , home-care services and disability services , all of which have a high proportion of international staff.
In May this year, a report of a review found that the rule had led to staff shortages, which raised concerns about continuity of patient care. One of the most critical shortages is that of healthcare assistants.
The health sector is relying on an increasing number of non-EAA staff to maintain services, with more than 12,000 employment permits issued in 2024.
Elsewhere, Minister for Housing James Browne will brief Government on changes to the Repair and Lease scheme (RLS) aimed at unlocking more social homes.
This is a social housing delivery scheme that provides an interest-free loan of up to €80,000 per unit to owners of vacant properties to repair or convert them to rental standard.
[ Fall in number of units added to social housing stock Opens in new window ]
The homes are then leased to a local authority or approved housing body (AHB) and the property owner receives a percentage of market rent, with the loan repaid as a reduction in the lease payment over an agreed term. The scheme is also being used to renovate vacant commercial properties and convert them into homes.
Browne is to issue new directions to local authorities on their repair and lease work.
Among the planned changes is the removal of limits on property owners so that investment firms can also avail of the loans.
The existing scheme limited applications for existing residential properties to owners who required capital funding, a restriction aimed at excluding investment firms.
However, this proved difficult in practice and created an additional administrative burden for local authorities.
It is understood that this measure is to enable small investment groups that, for instance, own a former pub that could be converted to homes to avail of the RLS loans rather than to aid big investment funds which are said to have shown little interest in the scheme.
[ Dublin housing market stalls as cost of living creates ‘uncertainty’ Opens in new window ]
Councils will also be directed to use the scheme to prioritise the delivery of studios and one-bed units. A limited vouched payment for legal fees will be available to assist local authorities or AHBs in meeting these costs.
Between 2021 and the end of March this year, 534 homes were delivered under the RLS – more than half of these, 286, in Co Waterford.
Browne will also seek Government approval to implement new EU rules to empower women MEPs to delegate their voting rights to another MEP during pregnancy and after childbirth.
A proposal by Minister for Energy Darragh O’Brien for a boiler scrappage scheme will also be brought to Cabinet.
The scheme is expected to be worth an extra €2,000 to households seeking to switch from oil boilers to new heating technology and be used in conjunction with the existing scheme of up to €12,500 for a heat pump.

title: Uncertain if Israeli ‘war’ bonds will no longer be offered for sale in EU through Ireland
description: Oireachtas finance committee chair Mairéad Farrell says Israel missing deadline for submitting prospectus application may not necessarily mean programme shutting down
content:
It is not fully clear if the Central Bank will no longer have the role of approving Israeli bonds for sale in the European Union , the chair of the powerful Oireachtas finance committee has said.
Earlier this summer, Ireland reverted to the role of “home” State for marketing Israel’s state bonds after Luxembourg – which took over the role for 2026 – decided it would not continue for a second year.
The deadline for submission of a new prospectus for Israeli bonds was August 31st, the day on which the Luxembourg approval expired.
However, Central Bank governor Gabriel Makhlouf confirmed last week that no application had been received as of September 24th.
In a letter to Sinn Féin TD Mairéad Farrell , chair of the Oireachtas Committee on Finance, Makhlouf said the “registers do not disclose that a 2026 prospectus has been approved by the Central Bank or another EU member state competent authority for the State of Israel”.
Makhlouf was responding to a letter from Farrell asking if Ireland would not longer sell Israeli bonds.
Farrell told The Irish Times that while Israel had not made a submission by August 31st, and had not yet offered a prospectus, it was not altogether clear to her that Israel would not longer be selling what she described as “war bonds” in the European market. Some estimates have put the annual amount raised in the EU to purchase its bonds as high as €2.5 billion.
“It is still unclear to the Committee on Finance, and to the public, as to whether or not Israel can come back to the table and force us to reconsider war bonds,” said Farrell.
“We now need full and firm confirmation from the Central Bank as to where the prospectus now stands.”
Farrell also said Minister for Finance Simon Harris should also ensure that Central Bank declines any such prospectus in future. Harris, the Tánaiste, asked his officials to write to the European Commission this summer asking for a review of the arrangement that left Ireland with no choice to reject acting as home state for Israeli bonds.
Farrell said the Central Bank should also actively seek to end the arrangement. “It should be dealing with other Central Banks to see what they can do within their powers to resist that.
“There should be no situation where we remain as home state for Israeli war bonds when they remain funding genocide in Gaza,” she added.
Since Brexit in 2016, Ireland had acted as the “home” State that approved the Israeli bond prospectus that was marketed for sale within the union.
The Central Bank’s role in approving the prospectus has come under sustained criticism from Opposition parties, which have said its actions allowed Israeli war to be sold in the EU. For its part, the Central Bank said it had no choice in becoming the “home” State as that decision was one for Israel to make. It also argued that its consideration of a prospectus was a technical exercise and could not take into account moral or human rights considerations.
In reply to queries from The Irish Times on the status of Israeli bonds, a spokesman said the Central Bank of Ireland was bound by statutory professional secrecy obligations.
“These obligations prevent the disclosure of confidential supervisory information, including information relating to supervisory matters, and necessarily limit the information that can be provided publicly. The Central Bank therefore cannot provide details regarding any engagement with an individual issuer,” he stated.
Israel markets its bonds in the EU through the Development Company for Israel (Europe) GmbH. On its websites it states that its prospectus for the EU will be “posted at a later date”, indicating a delay, rather than shutting down the sales.
“Please do not forward any purchases to us until you have access to the new documents and rates,” states the website. It asks interested investors to contacted it to be notified of when the rates will be posted.

title: IFA and imported food
description: Calls for the resignation of Larry Murrin as chair of Bord Bia are hypocritical
content:
Sir, – The call by the Irish Farmers’ Association (IFA) for the resignation of Larry Murrin as chair of Bord Bia because his company used imported chicken in a restaurant, as reported in Conor Pope’s article (“ Bord Bia chairman faces fresh criticism over imported chicken at Dublin restaurant he part-owns ”, September 26th), is grossly hypocritical.
A significant amount of the grain for cattle feed, to support the current unsustainable Irish production levels of milk and beef, is imported. Why don’t our beef and dairy farmers use Irish grain?
Maybe Francie Gorman should also resign as president of the IFA.
Irish farmers do not feed the nation. We currently import 80 per cent of our food needs.
At the same time, Lough Derg, Lough Neagh and Lady’s Island Lake are poisonous, primarily from excess agricultural nutrient run-off.
Maybe that should also be grounds for resignation. – Yours, etc,

title: A Titanic struggle to clear name of White Star shipping line’s owner
description: J Bruce Ismay was wholly exonerated by official inquiries, but his name is still linked with doomed vessel
content:
Sir, – Frank McNally quotes Ben Hecht’s condemnatory poem about John Bruce Ismay (An Irish Diary, September 24th). Ismay owned the White Star shipping line, which was once based in Liverpool and whose fleet included the Titanic .
The poem casts Ismay as a coward who took a place on a lifeboat before potential women and children survivors when the doomed Titanic sank in the Atlantic on her maiden voyage in 1912.
The poem contrasts Ismay’s cowardice with the bravery of the ship’s captain, Edward Smith, who stayed aboard and went down with the ship. Ismay’s descendants have long sought to clear their ancestor’s name and point out that he was exonerated of any wrongdoing by both the British and United States inquiries into the disaster.
His evidence, accepted by both inquiries, was that he boarded the last departing lifeboat, not the first as was suggested widely at the time, that this was 20 minutes before the ship sank, and that he did this only after being satisfied there were no women or children in its whereabouts to take the last two remaining places.
Had he not boarded the lifeboat, his descendants say, the only probable consequence was that another life, his, would have been lost without benefit to anyone.
Nevertheless, Ismay was repeatedly accused of cowardice, particularly in the US press of the time.
