Most of the flooring is manufactured hard wood, but some of the rooms have been carpeted.
This a well-insulated B-rated house with an east-facing back garden that has been landscaped. It could also be described as modern in its simplicity. An artificial lawn is flanked by decking and has cultivated trees and shrubs on either side.
There’s a shed at the back, which has been wired for electricity.
[ Why it pays to go green for lower costs when buying a new home Opens in new window ]
Durham Road is a mature residential street with many of the houses built in the 1950s. It’s just 500 metres from picturesque Sandymount village, with its mix of Georgian, Victorian and Edwardian buildings. It has a triangular green in the centre and a number of shops, restaurants and coffee shops.
It’s within walking distance of Sydney Parade Dart station and is well-served by buses to Ballsbridge and Dublin city centre. It’s also just 14 minutes by car to the city centre.
Sandymount has long been a desirable residential location due in part to its proximity to the sea and its long Victorian promenade on Strand Road, which has views of the Poolbeg Chimneys, Irishtown and Dún Laoghaire in the distance.

title: “Braithim go maireann meon na nGael go láidir lasmuigh den domhan gránna caipitlíoch ina bhfuilimid.”
description: Is aisteoir agus drámadóir é Timmy Creed atá le feiceáil sna sraitheanna teilifíse House of Guinness agus Vikings. Scríobh sé an dráma SPLICED, agus tá páirt aige faoi láthair in ZINC, dráma de chuid Dead Centre.
content:
Cad é an chéad phíosa ealaíne a d’imir tionchar ort mar dhéagóir?
Dr Dre, 2001. Ba é seo an chéad cheirnín a cheannaigh mé mar dhéagóir. Go dtí sin, do bhíos ag éisteacht le ceol mo dheartháireacha, ar nós Blur, Pulp, Oasis, Radiohead srl. Chomh maith leis na beats dochreidte, chuaigh an meon a bhí ag na hamhráin i bhfeidhm orm: spiorad an reibiliúnaigh.
Cén t-ealaíontóir atá beo is mó a bhfuil meas agat air?
An file, ceoltóir, saoi, Rónán Ó Snodaigh. Tugann a chuid ceoil, go háirithe na halbaim le Myles O’Reilly, an méid sin fuinnimh dom. Is aoibhinn liom an tslí a meascann sé doimhneacht, spiorad agus ceol le simplíocht na teanga. Osclaíonn sé bealaí dom isteach sa teanga.
Cén sórt talún cruthaithí ba bhreá leat a fhiosrú?
Feirmeoir de shaghas éigin. Do bhí an fhiosracht agam ó bhíos óg, agus tá sí fós ionam. Ba bhreá liom an deis a bheith agam domhan a chruthú le talamh, trealamh, plandaí, glasraí, ainmhithe, gan dabht, agus pé rud eile a bhaileoinn ar mo bhealach.
Cén t-éacht gairmiúil is mó a bhfuil tú bródúil as?
Is dócha gurb é an chéad dráma a scríobh mé, SPLICED, faoi shaol Chumann Lúthchleas Gael. Thug sé fíormhuinín dom mar scríbhneoir, agus léirigh sé dom go bhfuil guth agus scéal againn go léir.
Cad í an chomhairle is measa a fuair tú riamh?
An rud a ritheann liom anseo ná gan aon aird a thabhairt ar an gcuid is mó den chomhairle atá le fáil. Bíonn daoine ag caint ráiméise an chuid is mó den am. Éist leat féin agus cruthaigh bealach a n-oireann duitse, is cuma cé chomh hait nó trína chéile is atá sé.
Ní thuigeann daoine freisin cé chomh deacair is atá sé leanúint le bealach na n-ealaíon ó thaobh airgid, féinmhuiníne, fuinnimh, clainne agus frustrachais.
Caithfidh tú cónaí i mbuncar faoi thalamh, agus is féidir leat scannán amháin, sraith theilifíse amháin, agus leabhar amháin a thabhairt leat: cad iad?
Dead Mans Shoes le Shane Meadows; The Wire; agus Nostos le John Moriarty.
An raibh aon mhúinteoirí inspioráideacha agat?
Bhí beirt mhúinteoirí Gaeilge agam sa mheánscoil a spreag mé leis an teanga i gcónaí: Brian Tyers agus Finian Ó Drisceoil. Ach bhí múinteoir Béarla agam ar feadh sé bliana, Ger O’Kelly, agus ní raibh a fhios agam ag an am an tionchar a bhí aige orm. Chuir sé béim ar an bhfoghlaim de ghlanmheabhair; Shakespeare, T. S. Eliot, Yeats. Do bhíomar go léir ábalta na féinuiríll in Macbeth nó Hamlet nó The Love Song of J Alfred Prufrock a rá gan smaoineamh. Ní rabhas go maith ag an mBéarla go nádúrtha, ach chreid sé ionam agus bhaineamar rud éigin amach le chéile, measaim.
Conas a bhí do shaol cultúrtha mar pháiste?
Tá mo mháthair ana-mhaith ag péinteáil agus spreag sé sin rud ionainn go léir, measaim. Ba mhúinteoir Fraincise í freisin agus tá caighdeán maith Fraincise againn sa chlann dá bharr. Tá radharc agam i bhFraincis sa dráma, ZINC, atá ar siúl an tseachtain seo, ach is féidir leis an lucht féachana a chinneadh féin a dhéanamh ar mo chaighdeán.
An bhfuil saothar cruthaitheach amháin ar mhaith leat tabhairt faoi ach nach bhfuil tosaithe agat fós?
Ba mhaith liom píosa talún a fháil agus tígín beag a thógaint mé féin in áit éigin dhraíochtúil.
Cad iad na rudaí is fearr ar éist tú leo, a léigh tú, nó atá feicthe agat le déanaí?
Chonaic mé an scannán Paris, Texas le déanaí. Bhíos chomh tógtha leis an scéalaíocht, agus le cé chomh bog agus mothúchánach a bhí sé, agus ní fhacas aisteoireacht chomh caolchúiseach le haisteoireacht Harry Dean Stanton le fada an lá. Bhaineas an-taitneamh as ceolchoirm na Gorillaz i rith an tsamhraidh. Chonaic mé Fugit, dráma le comhlacht ón gCatalóin darb ainm Kamchàtka sa Cork Midsummer i mbliana. Spreagadar mé leis an méid is féidir a dhéanamh le lucht féachana agus le hamharclannaíocht.
Cad a cheapann tú faoi chaighdeán na n-ealaíon in Éirinn faoi láthair?
Tá rud éigin ag tarlú faoi láthair - tá na Gaeil ar na stáitsí móra agus tá an domhan ag breathnú orainn, mar go bhfuil spiorad éigin againn don am atá ann anois. Níl aon dabht ná go bhfuil ealaíontóirí ar ardchaighdeán againn in Éirinn. Tá cruthaitheacht agus ealaín le feiscint i ngach baile beag sa tír. Tá sé ionainn go léir ar shlí amháin nó ar shlí eile. Sin ráite, ní cheapaim go bhfuil go leor ama tugtha do dhaoine óga leis na healaíona, agus tá an iomarca béime ar an saol acadúil seachas ar an tsamhlaíocht agus ar an gcruthaitheacht. Teastaíonn níos mó tacaíochta, struchtúr, maoinithe agus spásanna uainn go práinneach sna laethanta seo.
Cad é an mhíthuiscint is mó atá ag daoine faoi do shaol mar ealaíontóir?
Ceapaim go bhfuil sé deacair ar dhaoine tuiscint a fháil ar an méid ama a chaitheann tú mar ealaíontóir ag dul timpeall agus timpeall ar an rud céanna - ag lorg bealach nua, difriúil, spreagúil isteach i rud chun é a choimeád beo duit féin. Ní thuigeann daoine freisin cé chomh deacair is atá sé leanúint le bealach na n-ealaíon ó thaobh airgid, féinmhuiníne, fuinnimh, clainne agus frustrachais.
Cad é do thuairim faoi fhorbairt na Gaeilge sna healaíona in Éirinn?
Tá níos mó daoine ag dúiseacht don tuiscint go bhfuil gach rud againn anseo in Éirinn: cultúr, teanga, agus pobal. Tuigeann daoine go bhfuil an domhan á rith ag cladhairí nach bhfuil dírithe ach ar an airgead, ar an tsaint agus ar a ndul chun cinn féin. Braithim go maireann meon na nGael go láidir lasmuigh den domhan gránna caipitlíoch ina bhfuilimid. Feiceann daoine go bhfuil saol eile ann, agus tugann ealaíona na Gaeilge an spreagadh agus an deis dúinn go léir aghaidh a thabhairt ar na rudaí tábhachtacha.
Beidh Timmy Creed le feiceáil sa dráma ZINC le Dead Centre sa Dublin Theatre Festival, an 2-4 Deireadh Fómhair, san O’Reilly Theatre i mBaile Átha Cliath.

title: Budget: Are we richer or poorer than in 2017? And who is saving €8,000 a year on taxes?
description: Our six family groups have all made savings in their tax bills over the past decade
content:
After months of kite flying and leaks, we now have a fair idea of what’s going to be announced in the budget on October 6th.
Income tax cuts, welfare increases, changes to energy prices and more housing supports all look to be on the agenda this year as part of an €8.5 billion package. But the challenge is making households feel richer.
“Families don’t measure budgets in tax bands and credits. They measure them by what’s left in the bank account at the end of the month,” says Katie O’Neill, a director with PwC .
But before we get caught up in Budget 2027, it’s an opportune time to consider how the Government’s tax strategy over the past 10 years has impacted on Irish households.
So, in advance of next week’s pronouncements from Minister for Finance Simon Harris, we take a look at the winners and losers in the income tax stakes over the past 10 years, from 2017 to 2026.
As this article clearly shows, Irish families are definitely getting to keep more of their incomes in their pockets, thanks to successive tax cuts since about 2015.
Our high-earning couple, for example, are saving more than €8,000 a year in tax, while a worker on €29,000 is saving almost €2,000 a year.
However, as O’Neill points out, while Budget 2027 might deliver a further easement on this front, “the broader challenge is ensuring that families experience a genuine improvement in disposable income”. Higher housing costs, childcare and other cost-of-living challenges have hit families hard.
[ Budget 2027 update: From income tax to energy excises and childcare – here’s what we know so far Opens in new window ]
“The key question is not whether incomes have increased, but whether disposable income has increased,” O’Neill says. “Many households are earning more than they were 10 years ago, but they are also facing very different cost pressures. Ten years on, most workers are better off from a tax perspective, but many are not convinced they are better off from a cost-of-living perspective.”
Here are how the families have fared in more detail:
Customer service representative Rebecca earns around the minimum wage, at €29,000 a year.
Thanks to successive changes in recent budgets, she now gets to keep an extra €164 a month, due to a lower tax burden. In particular, she has seen her annual income tax bill fall from €2,500 in 2017 to €800 today, while her USC charge also fell substantially, down from €740 in 2017 to €403 today.
It means that her effective tax rate has dropped from 15 per cent to 8.4 per cent, and she gets to keep almost an extra €2,000 each year, thanks to these tax savings.
Part of the reason for the cut in her tax bill was the introduction of the rent tax credit in 2022. Rebecca rents a one-bedroom apartment, and so benefits from this. She currently saves €1,000 a year on her rent because of this, and is hoping for a further increase in next week’s budget.
Single parent Tom has seen the second-largest percentage increase in tax savings over the period, with an 11 per cent jump, which means he is now retaining an additional €4,152 each year.
He has benefited from successive increases in the standard rate band over this period; for example, in 2017, the single band cut-off point was €33,800, or €37,800 if claiming child carer credit.
Now it is €44,000, or €48,000 with child carer credit, and further increases are expected come budget day.
As a result, the income tax he pays per year has more than halved, from €5,583 in 2017 to €2,281 this year.
He also benefits from the rent credit, as he is paying €2,000 a month for a two-bed apartment in north Co Dublin for him and his son.
They might earn significantly less than our dual-income family on €175,000 a year, but our pensioners have enjoyed, relatively speaking, greater savings over the 10 years since 2017, and are one of our families who have benefited the most since 2017.
While tax changes – such as broadening USC bands – have played a part, the biggest reason for the couple’s elevated income is regular increases to the State pension. In 2026, the State pension went up by €10 a week to €299.30 for those under age 80, and €309.30 a week for those aged 80 and above.
While the weekly State pension remains below the Fianna Fáil/Fine Gael pledge of €350 a week, it is expected that at least another €7.50 will be added to the weekly payment in the budget, bringing it up to close to €310 a week.
In 2017, our dual-income family, Ekene and Alison, with a taxable income of €175,000, gave up nearly €4 out of every €10 they earned to Revenue, at an effective tax rate of 39.6 per cent. This meant they got to keep just €8,809 of their €14,583 gross monthly income.
Thanks to successive tax reductions since, however, this year their net monthly income has risen to €9,235, which means that they are saving €5,112 a year. Part of the couple’s savings are down to the introduction of the earned credit income in 2016, which Ekene can claim as a self-employed hotelier.
Jian and Sean live on one income, of €47,500. In addition, they earn an extra €10,000 by letting out a room in their house – but they don’t have to pay tax on this, thanks to the rent-a-room relief.
Their tax burden has slid substantially over the past 10 years, to the point that they now get to keep an additional €3,444 a year.
In 2017, for example, they paid an effective tax rate of 16.8 per cent, which meant that they got to keep €3,295 of their income each month, once tax was deducted. This year, however, their tax rate has slid to just 9.5 per cent, and their net income has increased to €3,582.
The couple, who live in a four-bed house in Kilkenny, have also seen savings on the property tax front. In 2017, with a valuation band of €400,000-€450,000, their annual bill was €765. This year, despite an increased valuation of €550,000, their tax bill has shrunk to €601.
Our high-earning family Mark and Linda, on combined taxable income of €325,000, have seen their tax burden shrink since 2017. However, despite earning such a significant sum every year, their savings are not as great as one might have expected.
In 2017, they faced an overall effective tax rate of 44.1 per cent on their income, which meant they got to keep €15,145 each month. This was an improvement on 2011, when they gave up 45 per cent of their income to the tax man.
And last year they actually saw their net income drop by €1 a month, due to the PRSI hike. Their overall tax burden is still down from 2017, however, at 41.6 per cent, an improvement of about 6 per cent. It means that they now get to keep €15,825 of their €27,083 monthly income.
Overall, this is an improvement of €669 a month, or €8,028 a year. Indicating how tax changes in recent years have been aimed at the “squeezed middle”, this couple have the lowest percentage increase in tax savings, at just 4.4 per cent.
The couple, who also own a rental property that brings in an income of €25,000 a year, will have seen a slight easing of the tax burden on this property, due to the introduction of residential premises rental income relief in 2024. This gives relief at a rate of 20 per cent on a proportion of rental income profit, between 2024 and 2027.
The couple will have also seen an increase in property tax on their €1.5 million detached four-bed house in Dún Laoghaire – but not by much.
In 2017, their property was in a lower valuation band, of €900,000-€1 million, with an annual charge of €1,491. While the property’s value has jumped, the bill hasn’t, rising by just €36 a year to €1,527.

title: How many movie or TV characters with a physical disability can you name?
description: If more TV shows and movies included disabled characters whose disability was not a ‘thing’, I might be asked ‘what happened to you?’ by random strangers less often
content:
I f I asked you to come up with 10 movie or TV characters with a physical disability, would you be able to?
Depending on your age and taste, I’m thinking House might be on the list, or Tyrion Lannister from Game of Thrones . Maybe Walter “Flynn” White jnr, from Breaking Bad, or Isaac from Sex Education. If you go back further, you might think of Tom Cruise in Born on the Fourth of July or Lieutenant Dan in Forrest Gump.
This being Ireland, I assume you’d think of Christy Brown in My Left Foot.
Maybe you can’t think of anyone, but in any case, chances are it would take you a while to think of 10, if you’d get that many.
That’s not because you have a poor memory or can’t be bothered to notice. There simply are very few physically disabled characters on our TVs and screens, despite 13 per cent of the world population living with a disability.
And if I asked you to think of an on-screen happy physically disabled character, living a great life, chances are you couldn’t think of anyone.
For as long as they’ve been cast, physically disabled characters on screen have mostly been allowed two jobs – be cured or be a cautionary tale.
Shortly after becoming hemiplegic myself, I remember watching Artie in Glee spending an entire episode having a dream sequence in which he stands up and dances, clearly, the show’s not especially subtle way of saying that the “real” him is the walking one. Go back further and you’ve got Ron Kovic in Born on the Fourth of July and Lieutenant Dan in Forrest Gump, both wrestling with disability as the defining tragedy of their lives, all bitterness and broken masculinity, until the story either redeems them or doesn’t bother.
I used to think Hugh Laurie’s House was another exception. House is a successful doctor, after all. I was wrong, and it took a fair bit of arguing with myself (well, with a very patient AI, but let’s not get into that) to admit it. House’s leg is not incidental. It’s the catalyst of the entire show: his Vicodin addiction, his bitterness and his self-destruction all trace back to the infarction that caused his disability.
The problem is not that the show portrays House’s inner demons, many of them quite realistic, it’s that, once again, misery is shown as being part and parcel of a physical disability.
[ ‘When you have a physical disability, the world is a very unaccommodating place’ Opens in new window ]
Hardly ever does a character on screen have a physical disability without it being a “thing”: someone living a great life, with a fabulous career and a great group of friends, who just happens to use a mobility aid, is blind or hearing impaired. Someone like Patton Plame in NCIS – New Orleans. Or Marlee Matlin’s character in The West Wing. Their disability is a neutral fact. A thing that is true about a character in the same way their hometown or their taste in coffee is true. Present, occasionally relevant, but never the point.
Now you might sigh, question whether this is really what we should be worrying about with all that’s happening in the world, and wonder if it’s really necessary for everyone to see themselves represented. The answer is yes, and here’s why.
According to several studies, the more we are exposed to something, the more easily our brain processes it. This is called perceptual fluency, and it makes us perceive things as “safe”. With the lack of exposure to physically disabled people in the media, we don’t have any perceptual fluency when it comes to someone in a wheelchair, someone walking differently or someone with a prosthesis. We see these as “different”.
Media images also shape beliefs. When you repeatedly see a topic paired with a positive image, you will be conditioned to think positively about the topic itself. On the other hand, if all we see is physically disabled people dreaming of being able-bodied again, feeling miserable or being addicted to painkillers, then we will naturally assume that’s what the physically disabled are like. People to be pitied, avoided, and definitely not to be hired into any role of significance.
There is no doubt that lack of exposure to positive images of physically disabled people is contributing to the higher unemployment rate in this group.
Now imagine you’re a child with a physical disability, or an adult trying to piece your life together again after becoming paralysed following an injury. While you’re learning to navigate a world that wasn’t built with you in mind, you also struggle to find any role models. I’m hemiplegic, and a number of years ago I found myself crying in Penneys for no other reason than because they had an ad display for jumpers that featured a woman in a wheelchair. We all want to recognise ourselves, and when you’re a white, able-bodied man or woman, you don’t even think about these things because you see yourself reflected in some way, shape or form everywhere.
Fortunately, there are positive examples, too. Logan Calloway, a minor but memorable character in Locke and Key, is a double amputee whose disability is never once explained on screen. Isaac in Sex Education and The Pitt’s wheelchair-using psychiatrist make up a small but growing list. All three are played by actors with the same disability as their character. Because, yes, that matters. Marvel, of course, is a winner here, with Daredevil, who is blind, Hawkeye, who has a hearing impairment, and maybe the most famous of all, Professor Xavier, a wheelchair user. Stan Lee, Marvel’s creator, was once quoted saying he wanted his comics to reflect “the world right outside our window”.
If more shows and movies did that, our perceptual fluency would increase, and I reckon I’d be asked “what happened to you?” by random strangers less often. Young people with physical disabilities would feel more optimistic about their future in the workforce, and accessibility would be a given, rather than an afterthought. Representation matters, and casting directors and writers need to step up.
With that in mind, why wouldn’t Keeley Jones or Rebecca Welton, in Apple’s hit show Ted Lasso, have a physical disability? And if, like a friend of mine, your first thought is that they couldn’t be because they have to be pretty and powerful, then that’s exactly why they should be.

title: Scáth na nimhe sa tsochaí
description: Diaidh ar ndiaidh tá foréigean agus bagairtí ag méadú, i saol na polaitíochta agus lasmuigh de
content:
Thart ar choicís ó shin bhí an Teachta Dála neamhspleách Michael Healy-Rae sáite i mbrú tráchta i gceartlár Bhaile Átha Cliath.
Tá an Ciarraíoch ar dhuine de na polaiteoirí is so-aitheanta in Éirinn mar gheall ar an gcaipín a chaitheann sé agus ar a cholainn chaol.
In éineacht leis sin, tá comhartha mór ar an gcarr a deireann: Michael Healy-Rae TD.
Mar sin, is neach poiblí é, níl dabht faoi sin. Tá sé deacair air a bheith ag saothrú a choda i ngan fhios don saol mór.
Ar aon chuma, bhí fear ar an gcosán ag an am a bhí ag siúl lena ghadhar. Chonaic sé an carr agus an fear a bhí ag tiomáint agus ní raibh sé deacair air Healy-Rae a aithint.
Ach is léir nach eisceacht í an tír seo. Feicfimid na hathruithe san Eoraip agus sa Bhreatain ag tarlú in Éirinn amach anseo.
Tuairiscíodh gur caitheadh maslaí le Healy-Rae agus ansin, de phreab agus gan fainic, gur tugadh sonc sa bhéal don Teachta Dála trí fhuinneog an ghluaisteáin a bhí oscailte mar gheall ar theas an lae. Gortaíodh Healy-Rae, níl amhras ar bith faoi sin. Gearradh go dona san aghaidh é agus bhí air greamanna a fháil.
Is é seo an eachtra is deireanaí i liosta fada d’ionsaithe agus de bhagairtí atá dírithe ar pholaiteoirí na hÉireann le roinnt blianta anuas. Tá fear anois faoi ghabháil i dtaca leis an eachtra.
Agus ní hé seo an chéad uair a tugadh íde béil do Healy-Rae. Bhí agóid ar siúl lasmuigh de Theach Laighean in 2023 agus, nuair a tháinig Healy-Rae amach, thosaigh cuid den slua ag caitheamh maslaí leis.
Agus é ag siúl síos Sráid Chill Dara, lean roinnt den drong mhallaithe é agus b’éigean do na Gardaí cabhair a thabhairt dó éalú uathu. Sciobadh fón Healy-Rae an lá céanna.
Agus tar éis an mhéid a tharla le linn na míosa seo, chonaic mé físeán eile de Healy-Rae ag iarraidh sráid a thrasnú sa phríomhchathair agus slua ag plódú timpeall air ag béiceadh agus ag cur ina leith gur fealltóir a bhí ann.
Seo cuid den teanga a úsáideann an dream a dtugann tírghráthóirí orthu féin chun a naimhde a dhíspeagadh agus a chur faoi chois. É sin agus manaí frith-inimirce ciníocha a spalpadh ar líne agus go poiblí.
Go dtí Covid is beag den stuif sin a bhí le feiceáil i saol na hÉireann agus, faraor, ó 2020 ar aghaidh tá an claonadh seo i saol poiblí na tíre ag éirí níos nimhní bliain i ndiaidh bliana.
Ar ndóigh, tá sé ina scáthán ar na hathruithe suntasacha atá tarlaithe i ndreach na polaitíochta san Eoraip le glúin anois. Go dtí, b’fhéidir, deich mbliana ó shin bhí páirtithe ón eite dheas (iad siúd ag iarraidh inimircigh a dhíbirt) imeallach sa pholaitíocht. Bhíodar i gcónaí sách láidir i dtíortha cosúil leis an bhFrainc ach ní raibh aon seans acu cumhacht a bhaint amach.
Ach nuair a thosaigh an t-éirí amach go léir sa Mheánoirthear agus nuair a thosaigh na milliúin teifeach ag taisteal chun na hEorpa ag lorg cosanta, is ansin a chonaic muid athrú ag teacht ar mheon daoine áirithe ina leith.
De ghnáth leis hinimirce is go dtí na háiteanna is boichte a théann an pobal nua chun cónaí. Agus ní nach ionadh go mbreathnaíonn an pobal seasta sna ceantair sin go doicheallach ar an lucht atá tar éis teacht isteach. Úsáideann páirtithe agus grúpaí frith-inimirice an teannas sin ar mhaithe leo féin.
Níl na páirtithe de chuid na heite deise imeallach a thuilleadh san Eoraip. Tá roinnt acu i gcumhacht anois agus roinnt eile cóngarach do bheith sa rialtas - go háirithe sa Ghearmáin agus sa Fhrainc. Dealraíonn sin go bhfuil na teachtaireachtaí crua (agus ciníocha i gcásanna áirithe) ag dul i bhfeidhm ní hamháin ar dhream beag, ach ar sciar maith den daonra.
Agus tá sé ag tarlú in Éirinn chomh maith, diaidh ar ndiaidh, cé gur ar an imeall atá na páirtithe agus polaiteoirí den chlaonadh sin fós.Ach is léir nach eisceacht í an tír seo. Feicfimid na hathruithe san Eoraip agus sa Bhreatain ag tarlú in Éirinn amach anseo. Níl mé ag rá go bhfeicfimid páirtí den chineál sin sa rialtas. Ach feicfimid iad ag cur go mór lena lucht tacaíochta agus lena dtionchar.
Bhí mé ag breathnú siar ar eachtraí agus ionsaithe cosúil leis an méid a tharla do Healy-Rae. Ní tharlaíonn siad go rialta ach ní tharlaíonn siad go hannamh ach oiread.
Bhí cásanna coiriúla a d’eascraigh ó bhagairtí a rinneadh ar an Tánaiste Simon Harris agus a chlann; ionsaí a rinneadh ar Roderic O’Gorman, ceannaire an Chomhaontais Ghlais; agus bagairtí a rinneadh ar Helen McEntee nuair a bhí sí ina hAire Dlí agus Cirt.
Bhí sé deacair breathnú ar an bhfeannadóireacht nimhneach ó dhaoine gan ainm a cuireadh suas mar ráitis ar shuíomh meán sóisialta Helen Ogbu, iarMhéara na Gaillimhe, le linn na bliana. Bhí cuid de déisteanach ar fad.
Go dtí cúpla bliain ó shin, ní raibh drogall ar pholaiteoir ar bith sa tír seo - Taoiseach an lae san áireamh - dul i measc an phobail in aon áit. Ach tá sin athraithe, faraor, agus sa lá atá inniu ann ní dóigh liom go bhfuil an dara rogha ag polaiteoirí ach a bheith ar a n-airdeall maidir le hionsaithe. Sin é an saol ina maireann muid.
Agus dá dheasca sin, tá athrú tagtha ar an mbealach a smaoinímid ar ár sochaí. Caithfimid athbhreithniú a dhéanamh ar an tuairim go bhfuil Éire ina tír shábháilte do chách.
Mar is léir dúinn uilig nach amhlaidh atá an scéal níos mó. Níl aon amhras ach go bhfuil an saol poiblí in Éirinn i bhfad níos duairce na laethanta seo.

title: Modernised two-bed with attic room in Ringsend for €550,000
description: Hastings Street home is within easy distance of local amenities and Dublin city centre
content:
“We never had to worry about traffic, even at Christmas,” says one of the owners of 26 Hastings Street in Ringsend , Dublin 4 , referring to how convenient it is to get to the city centre – on foot or by bike, Dart or bus – from their midterrace redbrick home.
The owners bought number 26 as their first home together four years ago and have hit several milestones while living there, including an engagement, a wedding and the arrival of their child. Now moving just 10 minutes away to better accommodate their growing family, they are placing this turnkey two-bed on the market with Owen Reilly Estate Agents, seeking €550,000.
Residents of the street have provided a lovely community, they say, and there is always someone on hand to take in your delivery for you if you’re not home. They also have Ringsend Park nearby, where there are sports pitches and courts, and a playground. They say the opening of Boland’s Mills, which is home to cultural events, a bar, a coffee shop, a hair salon and a Pilates studio, has been a welcome addition to the vibrant area.
Extending to 63sq m (678sq ft) with a D2 Ber, 26 Hastings Street has two bedrooms and a converted attic. Its façade has been beautifully restored to its original redbrick and repointed, with a welcoming light-blue front door and matching sash window frames.
You enter the home via the open-plan living/diningroom, which opens into a galley kitchen at the rear. A floating shelf has been put up inside the door as a place to drop your keys, and a comprehensive bank of storage – including hanging space, deep drawers and a wine rack – was added under the stairs. French doors lead out to a small patio terrace off the dining space.
The owners updated the kitchen by painting the units baby blue – complementing the facade – as well as installing new handles, and adding a large, navy pantry storage unit.
The fluidity of the layout meant it was a great house for parties, one of the owners says with a tone of nostalgia, as parenthood has put a stop to those for a while.
A modern shower room flooded with light from a square inset roof light sits to the rear of the ground floor. It features floor-to-ceiling white metro-style tiling with a Crittall-style shower screen.
Upstairs, the main bedroom spans the width of the front of the house. It features a pop of colour from statement wallpaper behind the bed and an alcove in the wall for hanging clothes. A small bedroom sits to the rear, set up as an adorable nursery, and there is a loo off the hallway.
A staircase leads up to the versatile attic room, which has a pitched roof, under-eaves storage and natural light from a pair of roof lights.

title: ‘These works are still quite raw for me. I haven’t really talked about this before’
description: The art in Margaret Corcoran’s new exhibition weaves together Etruscan bronzes, Dante’s Divine Comedy and horrific images from Gaza
content:
I n 2022, remarkable images began to emerge from the small Tuscan commune of San Casciano dei Bagni, human figures in bronze rising from the mud, scarcely tarnished after 2,300 years underground.
Margaret Corcoran remembers seeing some of the photographs and immediately feeling that the figures would somehow enter her work.
The artist went to her studio and began to sketch them. It’s a familiar process for Corcoran, whose practice often begins with reading the news in the morning and carrying the images that affect her into the studio.
The following day, by coincidence, Corcoran was giving a talk about Aphrodite at Trinity College Dublin; as it happened, the archeological director of the Italian excavation, Jacopo Tabolli, had been a researcher in the Irish university’s department of classics, and he invited her to come and see the figures.
One thing that struck Corcoran was the apparent complexity of the sanctuary itself. The bronzes were votive offerings, many associated with healing, but there were also numerous small anatomical plaques – objects that could be held in the hand. To her, these suggested a place concerned not only with worship but also with healing and medical knowledge.
“Something about them stayed very firmly and strongly with me,” Corcoran says. “I still can’t fully articulate the draw other than that I really wanted to be near them and make art from them.
“I felt I had this real connection with them. I wasn’t sure at all how it would manifest in the artwork, but I was certain that a series would come out of these really powerful finds. And it all seemed so much about luck and serendipity, being able to have such close access to them. I wanted it, and then it happened.”
The artist allowed them to simmer in her imagination.
Then came 2023. Each day brought horrific images from Gaza : children killed, bodies in rubble, scenes of devastating violence and human suffering.
“All these horrendous images were coming through the media, particularly images of children,” Corcoran says. “The way I tried to bear witness was through my practice.”
In the studio, she found that the figures she was making as she tried to process what she had seen in the news bore an unsettling resemblance to the ancient bronze bodies emerging from the Tuscan mud.
The parallel troubled her. She worried that bringing the two sets of images together might be insensitive, that it might be wrong to liken the ancient beauty of the figures with the hideous images of genocide that were arriving each day.
“I kept questioning myself: am I allowed to express my opinion in this way? But I had this image of the baby coming up from the ground. It looked terribly like some of the scenes we were seeing.
“In my drawing I made the baby float above a crowd of people leaving Gaza, moving towards safety. At that point there was still hope for a ceasefire. So the baby is floating like a guide, almost like a soul, helping to lead them towards safety. I eventually made that image into a collage.”
As Corcoran researched the sanctuary further, she began to discover other ways in which the ancient material could speak to the present. The bronzes belong to a period of transition between the Etruscan and Roman worlds, yet the sanctuary appears to have remained a place in which those cultures coexisted even during periods of conflict.
As Tabolli has put it, “Even in historical epochs in which the most awful conflicts were raging outside, inside these pools and on these altars the two worlds, the Etruscan and Roman ones, appear to have coexisted without problems.”
Corcoran began to think of the bronzes as objects resurfacing from the earth in the way a buried memory can resurface: returning to the collective consciousness with something to say. It changed the way she understood her drawings and the political charge latent within them. She describes the resulting works as visual prayers.
“The Etruscan bronzes became characters in a narrative,” she says, “a plea for cessation, and for an arrival at safety and peace for those suffering.”
As the war continued, that narrative became more explicit in her work.
“Things were getting worse and worse, and I wanted to make that painting much bigger and include a scene from Gaza, with people coming into what I imagined as a place of safety.
“I used the figure of a baby extensively throughout the series. In Etruscan times a votive figure of a baby might have been placed in the spa in the hope of restoring that child’s health.
“These works are still quite raw for me – they’ve only just gone up on the walls – and I haven’t really talked about this before.”
She’s referring to the walls of the Kevin Kavanagh Gallery, in Dublin, where her exhibition, The New Life: La Vita Nuova, brings together the three strands that have occupied Corcoran over the past three years: the Etruscan bronzes of San Casciano dei Bagni, Dante’s Divine Comedy and the violence and upheaval of the contemporary world.
Across large canvases, charcoal and pastel drawings, watercolours and small oils, ancient figures and mythological characters reappear within contemporary landscapes, from Powerscourt to Palestinian olive groves.
One of the exhibition’s recurring figures is Apollo, who appears in a painting before an ancient Palestinian olive tree. Corcoran had encountered a photograph of the tree, one of the oldest in the world, and was drawn to the image of a man tending the earth around it. Into this scene she placed Apollo, weeping before the tree.
The association acquired another meaning at the exhibition opening, when the Palestinian ambassador to Ireland, Jilan Wahba Abdalmajid, saw the painting and pointed to traditions connecting the ancient peoples of Palestine with the Greek world.
For Corcoran, who had worried about how the work might be received, the encounter was reassuring. “I was so relieved, because I thought, ‘How is she going to see what I’m doing here?’ She thought it was absolutely appropriate.”
That process – making an image intuitively and researching its associations afterwards – is characteristic of Corcoran’s practice. “I generally do the work and then I’ll research after,” she says. “Because I don’t want to block it coming out.”
Alongside Apollo and the other male figures, Corcoran began introducing female deities into the work. Their presence became a way of responding to the images of mothers and children that had entered the series while shifting its balance of power.
“I put in a lot of goddesses,” she says. “I wanted to balance what was happening with motherhood with female deities, and try to redress the power.”
Another visual reference Corcoran returned to while making the series was the French symbolist Odilon Redon, an artist she had loved as a student, in her early 20s. The affinity is easy to see: both artists create dreamlike images populated by archetypal creatures that seem to come out of deep collective memory or myth.
Only recently, however, did Corcoran learn more about the trajectory of Redon’s work. His early career was dominated by the dark, often unsettling charcoal drawings and lithographs he called his noirs, while his later work opened into luminous colour, flowers and spiritual imagery.
Redon had lived through the Franco-Prussian War, an experience Corcoran found newly significant in light of her own work’s response to images of conflict.
“He starts with very, very dark imagery, lithographs, and he’d been through a war,” she says. “He was very traumatised after what he’d been through.” Later, she says, “he got into Buddhism, and all this colour flooded back into his work.”
For Corcoran, who had begun the series largely in black and white, it eventually felt necessary to infuse these “visual prayers” with colour. “There’s a great trueness in his works,” she says; “in the pigment, the bright colours.”
Redon’s movement from darkness into colour offered a kind of precedent. Corcoran had the sense that, through this transformation in his work, he had been reaching towards another state.
The New Life: La Vita Nuova, by Margaret Corcoran, is at the Kevin Kavanagh Gallery , Dublin, until Saturday, October 10th

title: A new home in older age: What are the benefits of downsizing to a new development?
description: New-build properties are becoming increasingly attractive to people who want to reduce running costs and make life simpler
content:
A fter decades of putting down roots, accumulating possessions and raising children, leaving the family home can be a difficult decision. Knowing that downsizing may be a practical move does not make it any less emotional. For a growing number of homeowners, however, the move is becoming less about giving something up and more about choosing a home that better fits the way they live now.
An older, larger house can come with significant heating bills, as well as the ongoing burden of maintenance. This is one reason new-build properties are becoming increasingly attractive to downsizers who want to reduce day-to-day running costs while making life simpler and more secure.
Gemma Moore, divisional director at Sherry FitzGerald New Homes, has found that older buyers no longer necessarily want to remain in the family home for the rest of their days.
“We see that there is a growing trend of homeowners downsizing to a more manageable and energy-efficient home that is better suiting their future needs,” says Moore.
“We’re seeing more apartments come on, with very strong interest coming from people in their late 50s and 60s who want to remain in their existing communities, but without the maintenance responsibilities that come with owning a larger home.”
Moore is quick to point out that although the release of more high-quality apartments is drawing homeowners towards the idea of downsizing, the location has to be right.
“Location and lifestyle are the biggest drivers,” she says.
“The importance of remaining in the community they are familiar with is always top of the list. It would be very rare for us to see a downsizer buying somewhere completely random, unlike a first-time buyer who is looking at a certain price point or transport network. This doesn’t happen with older buyers, unless, of course, they are moving somewhere new to be closer to kids and grandkids.”
Energy efficiency is not usually the main reason behind the move, Moore says, but once buyers start comparing the running costs of different properties, it can become a significant advantage.
Latest figures from climatejargonbuster.ie show that the average electricity bill is roughly between €1,750 and €1,850 a year in Ireland for a typical home.
When broken down, however, the savings between A-rated and G-rated homes cannot be ignored.
In an A-rated home, owners are paying €600-€900 annually. This jumps up to €1,500-€2,000 a year for a C rating, while an F- or G-rated home can cost more than €4,000 a year to run.
For downsizers coming from a home with a low rating and looking to live off a pension , the savings are hard to overlook.
Developers are moving with the times too. Where once new schemes were primarily marketed at first-time buyers, developers have taken note of the increasing number of downsizers in the market and are accommodating their needs when it comes to planning schemes.
“There is far more suitable stock on the market now,” says Moore. “With two- and three-bed apartments being built along with the likes of two-bed houses and bungalows, older buyers have more choice. With bungalows, I feel like the market is getting used to them more and planners are starting to offer semidetached options geared towards downsizers.”
Unlike younger buyers, downsizers can be reluctant to buy off plans, but Moore says developers are aware of this and work towards having a showhouse available as soon as they can, with this buyer type in mind.
The modern layout and high specifications of new-builds can also provide a novelty factor for those moving from older homes. In apartments, the absence of stairs is an obvious attraction, particularly for buyers thinking about how their needs might change over time.
“They are looking for simplicity and certainty at this stage of life, with not many looking for a doer-upper,” Moore says.
Most new-builds are turnkey, with only small decisions to be made around details such as floors and tiles, which downsizers like because they want some scope to make the property their own and choose finishes that make their home feel less standard.
It is not just apartments and bungalows that this cohort are considering. Moore has buyers who have moved into three-bed houses because they don’t want to lose out on a garden . On the other side of that, there are those who are happy to leave the garden and weeding behind and enjoy the communal grounds of a development without getting their hands dirty.
[ RTÉ’s Jacqui Hurley sets up business matching downsizers with those trading up: ‘There’s probably trepidation’ Opens in new window ]
Safety is another consideration for people who may be moving from living alone in a large house. Having neighbours nearby and effective alarm systems can provide reassurance. For anyone who travels frequently, owning a home in a secure development can make it easier to lock up and leave, rather than relying on family or friends to regularly check on the property.
Unsurprisingly, the biggest barrier for this buyer type is the lack of suitable stock. Options remain limited for those who are unwilling to move outside their existing community. Moore has also found that the practical hassle of moving can put potential buyers off before they have even begun the process, so urges people to plan ahead.
“Often they are selling and buying at the same time, which can be tricky to queue things up. We do it a lot so it can be done, but it may put people off,” says Moore.
“In an ideal world, anyone looking to make this move would speak to an agent as early as they can so they can have everything lined up. It is good to have an understanding of timelines like when developments are coming up and different phases coming on so you can time the sale of your home and not be left with a six-month gap between homes.”

title: My outstanding balance is about €59,000, do I really still need mortgage protection?
description: Mortgage protection is designed to pay off any outstanding balance on your home loan should you die
content:
I have a query about mortgage protection policy. I have just over six years left on my mortgage. The outstanding balance is about €59,000. A rough valuation of my house is about €325,000.
I’m paying €30 for mortgage protection. Can I have no mortgage protection policy in place at all given the value of the house outweighs the outstanding balance?
If I were to default on my mortgage payments, the bank would surely get its money if they had to repossess the house. Paying my mortgage repayments is not an issue, I just feel I don’t need the insurance policy.
Keeping tabs on household bills and cutting out unnecessary spending is always a good idea as we try to balance our household budgets. And, as you say, it is not always just a question of making the numbers fit: even where we can comfortably afford our current spending, there is no good reason to waste money on pointless spending when it can be put to better use elsewhere – invested for instance.
Having said that, our hands are tied when it comes to some things – and that includes your mortgage protection policy.
Although there are clearly very good reasons for such policies in the early years of a home loan when things are tight all round and the bank’s exposure to us is significant, the pressure can seem less imposing when we are closer to the end of the term.
In your position, you have a long history of meeting your mortgage commitments in full and on time. Just six years shy of mortgage freedom, you might think it is superfluous as there is plenty of equity in the property to ensure the bank could easily get paid if all came to all.
The purpose of mortgage protection insurance is to protect both the lender and your family or successors in the unfortunate event that you die before the mortgage is fully paid off. That is it. It doesn’t cover loan arrears arising from illness or unemployment, just repaying of the loan on your death.
Where a couple buys a home, normally such policies are worded to pay out on the death of the first partner in recognition that finances generally could become fairly tight for a surviving spouse or partner. It suits both them and the bank to ensure the home loan is not one of those things.
The way these products are structured, they match the amount outstanding on your loan – not the value of your property which, hopefully, rises over time.
So, when you took out the mortgage, it would have covered about 90 per cent of the value of the property. As you paid off the mortgage, the amount covered reduces year by year. If your outstanding balance is €59,000, that is what the mortgage protection policy would pay out if you were to die this week.
The bank would get its money and any surviving family – or your estate if you are single – would get your home unencumbered by debt.
If you accelerate payments either by making additional payments or making payments higher than the monthly sum due, you could find the policy providing greater cover than the outstanding balance.
[ Why it pays to go green for lower costs when buying a new home Opens in new window ]
But more importantly than common sense, it is a contractual commitment to which you agreed when you drew down the mortgage in the first place. And, under consumer legislation that came into force in the late 1990s, it is now a legal requirement for most people.
Section 126 of the Consumer Credit Act puts the onus on the mortgage provider to arrange a mortgage protection policy before releasing funds to a homebuyer purchasing their principal private residence, or family home.
Anyone over the age of 50 at the time they draw down the loan is exempt from the requirement, as are those borrowing for property other than a family home or, in Revenue parlance, a principal private residence.
Anyone who would struggle to secure insurance – for health or other reasons – or who would be hit with a premium “significantly higher than that payable by borrowers generally” can also get a mortgage without mortgage protection being in place – though you would imagine lenders might be careful of lending to anyone considered uninsurable.
The other exception is where the home purchaser has independently secured an acceptable mortgage protection policy elsewhere, which they are perfectly entitled to do.
So, no, it is not something you can simply dispense with on the grounds of financial management or household budgeting.
[ Irish mortgage holders warned to brace for ‘tough winter’ with two rate hikes expected Opens in new window ]
At €30 a month, and just over six years left on your loan, it might be academic for you but mortgage holders in general should certainly shop around for a better deal on their mortgage protection premiums – especially if they originally took the policy out through their lender.
Policies secured through lenders will, as a general rule, be noticeably more expensive than the same cover sourced directly in the market.
Your lender does have to be assured that the policy is fit for purpose but, given that these are fairly straightforward policies provided by a number of long-standing players in the markets, that should never be an issue.

title: It’s functionality over flamboyance in celebrity chef Rachel Allen’s kitchen
description: With a love for natural products, a thoughtful layout and her favourite Miele appliances, Rachel Allen explains what she deems necessary in a great kitchen
content:
Since selling her coastal home in Shanagarry, east Cork, five years ago, Rachel Allen has been planning her next house build, and for the chef, author and broadcaster, this naturally involves considering carefully what makes a truly great kitchen.
The celebrity chef explains that a well-designed kitchen comes down to one good-sized, well-organised workspace, where everything you need is close at hand and easy to reach. The classic design rule connecting the three main work areas – sink, fridge and oven – into a convenient triangular layout still holds true. “It’s all about convenience and proximity,” she explains. “And for me personally, I love being able to either wash up or cook while looking out of a window.”
Materiality is her next priority. “I love natural products and materials, so I’d choose either wooden countertops or marble. I love old French marble in a kitchen, and there are so many composites available now that look like marble but are much more user-friendly. They’re not porous, so it doesn’t matter if you spill turmeric or red wine or lemon juice.” Allen admits her Pinterest saves lean heavily towards old French kitchens with chicken wire and fabric-fronted cupboards.
This same love of texture reveals itself in her love of plastered shelves, beautiful serving plates on open shelving and copper saucepans, and she believes the wood you choose for your kitchen cupboards should be one you genuinely love the look of. “My mom always says, ‘Once you paint wood, you have to keep repainting it,’ so you need to be really happy with the look and shade of the finish.
The mother of three has, over the years, cooked in more kitchens than most of us have had hot dinners. From professional restaurant kitchens and country house hotel kitchens to international catering set-ups, television studio kitchens and the famous Ballymaloe Cookery School, Allen has spent a career quietly cataloguing what works in a kitchen and what doesn’t.
For the 54-year-old, a great kitchen is largely a matter of having the right kit, in the right place. “The kitchens in the Cookery School are really great; properly user-friendly,” she says. “It sounds ridiculous, but having a jar or pot in front of you with whisks, spatulas and wooden spoons – rather than having to rifle through a drawer – makes things so much easier. Having knives in a rack that’s within easy reach so you barely have to think just makes everything simpler,” she says.
Allen’s favourite kitchen appliance is her Miele oven. “It sounds like the most obvious thing, but an oven that actually cooks at the temperature it says it’s cooking at is the most important thing. So many people blame themselves for their cooking and say, ‘Oh, I can’t bake’ or ‘I always burn everything’, but quite often food is being cooked at the wrong temperature.” Allen has been using Miele ovens for years and trusts them. For anyone whose oven doesn’t run true to its dial, she suggests getting an oven thermometer. “If you have an oven that’s a bit older, get an oven thermometer; they cost just a few quid.”
Allen cooks on an induction hob during her Miele cookery demonstrations. “I find them really good; induction is just cleaner,” she explains.
One of Allen’s favourite new pieces of kitchen kit is Miele’s downdraft hob. By removing the need for an overhead extractor fan, it immediately opens up new design possibilities for a kitchen. “They’re really great because you don’t have to think about having a hood or extractor fan overhead, you can just position the downdraft hob on an island in the centre of your kitchen.”
Another favourite is a Gourmet drawer, an appliance designed to hold cooked food at a steady serving temperature without drying it out or overcooking it. “I think it’s a lovely thing,” says Allen. “The drawer is about 60cm x 30cm and it can be set to a variety of temperatures. It’s great for warming food, but also for warming crockery – I’m a big, big fan of warm plates. One drawer can hold about ten main-course plates and possibly ten side plates or bowls at the same time,” she explains. “And you can slow cook in it too.”
Her love of slow, low-effort cooking extends to dedicated countertop slow cookers too. “I love how so many people are slow cooking now, putting the ingredients on, then going to work and coming home to a delicious casserole.” Clutter creeps on to kitchen counters easily, however, so she advises thinking hard about which appliances actually earn their place. “You also don’t want to have too many kitchen appliances in cupboards because they just won’t come out – out of sight can be out of mind.”
Currently on her wishlist is a Miele gourmet griddle plate. “It’s a brilliant length – it spans the width of two hob cooking zones – and it has lovely ridges on it. You can cook six or eight steaks on it or lots and lots of slices of vegetables like aubergines and courgettes.” For someone who admits: “I don’t buy kitchen gadgets unless I know they’ll deliver”, this is high praise.
For all her enthusiasm about equipment, Allen circles back to the same principle – a great kitchen might not look the most impressive, but it will make preparation and cooking stress-free. The details she values emphasise functionality over flamboyance – from an oven you can trust to a Gourmet drawer that holds ten plates at once. It’s this practical approach to a kitchen, honed over decades of professional cooking, that she’ll be bringing to her next family kitchen.

title: ‘Are the house rules in my apartment building legally binding and enforceable?’
description: Property Clinic: ‘I have been told that these rules are obligatory and supported by the law’
content:
I live in a small apartment block of nine units. We have house rules, which are obligatory as a result of the Multi Unit Development (MUD) Act 2011. What I really want to know is – are these house rules legal?
The provision regarding house rules in a multi-unit development are set out in section 23 of the Multi-Unit Development Act and are binding on all occupiers and owners within the multi-unit development. The act specifies the following:
23.—(1) An owners’ management company may, as respects the multi-unit development for which that company has responsibility, make house rules as respects the development or part of the development relating to the effective operation and maintenance of the development and with the objective of enhancing the quiet and peaceable occupation of units generally in the development, and such house rules shall be binding on –
(c) servants, agents and licensees of persons referred to in paragraphs (a) and (b).[1]
A typical set of house rules in an apartment block may contain provisions around noise levels, construction works, animals, parties, obstructions etc.
[ How can you vet how an apartment building is managed before buying? Opens in new window ]
The house rules must be adopted at the annual general meeting or extraordinary general meeting of the company where members have the opportunity to add or amend the rules by a simple majority vote.
The rules are then binding on the parties providing that all proper procedures were followed and also that they are in the best interests of the owners’ management company (OMC). For example, the imposition of a house rule stating that construction works are not permitted whatsoever would be unlawful as it would contravene the covenants of the lease agreement which states that the property owners have the right to effect repairs or refurbishment of their own apartment.
Most of the listed house rules are also contained in the terms of the lease agreement and so there is a considerable overlap in this regard. However, unlike the lease agreements, the house rules can be relatively easily changed and added to at no cost while also remaining binding on the parties.
Aisling Keenan is a property managing agent, consultant and an associate member of the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland

title: How to furnish a smaller home with what you already own
description: How to identify the pieces that matter and make them work in your new home
content:
M oving from a large house to a smaller house or an apartment comes with lots of decisions, but one of the biggest is what to bring with you. Furniture, artwork and possessions collected over many years can be hard to part with, especially when you know you won’t have room for everything. But deciding what to keep isn’t just about taking the things that will fit.
Here are some ways to identify the pieces that matter and make them work in your new home.
Look around your home and identify the things you love and would genuinely miss. Don’t worry about style or whether an antique or traditional piece will work in a contemporary home. If you love it, put it on the list. Some pieces will have sentimental value, while others may be beautifully made, valuable or difficult to replace.
Once you separate what you care about from what has simply accumulated around you, deciding what comes with you becomes much easier.
With your shortlist in mind, measure the furniture carefully and plot it on an accurate floor plan. Better yet, if you have access to the new apartment, mark out the footprint of larger pieces on the floor using masking tape, newspaper or cardboard. Seeing how much space a sofa or dining table will occupy makes it much easier to judge whether it will work in the room. And don’t just focus on whether something fits.
Think about the space it needs around it. A dining table might appear to fit on plan, but can you pull the chairs out and still walk behind them?
Check the practicalities, too. Measure doors and lifts and find out about any restrictions around deliveries.
But don’t assume that moving to a smaller home means everything needs to become smaller. One generous sofa can work better than several smaller pieces. If family dinners are important, keeping a substantial dining table may make far more sense than replacing it simply because you have downsized.
One of the easiest traps to fall into is trying to reproduce the rooms you are leaving behind on a smaller scale. Your new home is different and the way you live in it is likely to be different too. Lamps from a livingroom could make perfect bedside lights or a chest that lived in a bedroom might work beautifully in the hallway. You are not trying to find a new location for every item. You are choosing the best pieces and allowing them to work differently.
People are often nervous about bringing older furniture into a contemporary apartment, worrying that it won’t work with clean lines and modern finishes. In reality, the opposite can be true. An old dining table can work beautifully with modern chairs and lighting, while a traditional armchair can take on an entirely new character when reupholstered.
The contrast between old and new can give a home far more personality than furnishing everything from scratch. Bringing furniture and objects with history also helps a brand-new home feel like home.
It’s also a more sustainable approach. Good furniture shouldn’t be discarded simply because the surroundings have changed.
Think twice before parting with artwork. Even traditional paintings can look wonderful in a contemporary apartment, while familiar artwork and photographs are one of the easiest ways to make a new space feel like home.
Don’t assume things need to be hung in the same way either. Pictures previously spread across several rooms might work together as a gallery wall. Look at the frames too. Reframing a painting or print can give it a new lease of life and help it sit more comfortably in a contemporary setting.
There will be inherited pieces you genuinely love and want in your new home, but holding on to something purely out of guilt can leave you accommodating furniture you neither use nor particularly like.
Consider whether a piece could be adapted instead. A chair can be reupholstered or a table refinished. If there are things you genuinely can’t decide about and you’re under pressure to make a decision, temporary storage can give you a little breathing space. Just don’t let temporary become permanent. Give yourself a time frame to revisit what you’ve stored once the move is behind you.
Don’t fill every available space before you have even moved in. Bring the pieces that matter and give yourself time to live with them. You may find you need much less new furniture than you thought, while living in the space will quickly reveal what is actually missing. A new home doesn’t need to look finished on move-in day. There is something very natural about allowing it to evolve.
Downsizing is often talked about in terms of everything you have to give up. Instead, think of it as an editing process. You decide which possessions deserve a place in the next home and give yourself permission to leave the rest behind. The goal isn’t to see how much of your old house you can squeeze into your new apartment. It is to bring the things that will make the new place feel like home.

title: Pope Leo says concerns about AI’s threat to humanity are not ‘fake news’
description: Pontiff’s remarks are in stark contrast to US president Donald Trump, who says fears about AI’s dangers are a ‘hoax’
content:
Pope ‌Leo XIV on Monday said concerns that artificial intelligence could destroy the world ‌are not “fake news” and should be taken seriously, in an apparent rebuke ​of US president Donald Trump.
The first US pope, who has warned of the dangers of AI throughout his 16-month papacy, ​also directly criticised technology CEOs who argued there should be no ⁠guardrails on the technology.
“I do think that the ‌concerns ‌raised ​by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously,” the ⁠pontiff said in a ​press conference on his flight ​back to Rome after a four-day trip to ‌France. “I don’t think that that ​is fake news, as some have said.”
Trump told the ⁠UN General Assembly ⁠last week ​that he believed fears about the dangers to humanity from AI were a “hoax”.
The pope said he had read on Monday that the head of chipmaker Nvidia had announced there could be a way to insert guardrails into certain ‌AI models. But ⁠he expressed scepticism, adding: “He’s the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed ‌and no government regulation.”
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang told CBS ​News this month that he agreed with ​Trump that safety concerns about AI were overblown. - Reuters

title: An tAire Cirt faoi bhrú de bharr eachtra Anderson
description: D’éalaigh an dúnmharfóir tar éis dó a bheith ligthe amach go sealadach as Príosún Mhaigh gCabraí
content:
Rinneadh athghabháil ar an dúnmharfóir ciontaithe Gary Anderson i dTír Chonaill an tseachtain seo caite i ndiaidh dó breis is seachtain a chaitheamh ar a theitheadh. D’éalaigh Anderson i ndiaidh dó cead a fháil imeacht ó Phríosún Mhaigh gCabraí le freastal ar shochraid a athar i gCathair Dhoire. Níor fhill sé ar an phríosún agus chuir an PSNI agus an Garda Síochána tús le tóraíocht trasteorann láithreach.
Ciontaíodh Anderson agus a dheartháir Sean as dúnmharú Karol Kelly i nDoire in 2018. Diúltaíodh d’iarratas Sean Anderson freastal ar an tsochraid chéanna agus dhiúltaigh an tSeirbhís Phríosúin cead do Gary Anderson sa chéad dul síos. Ach rinneadh aisiompú sna cúirteanna ar an chinneadh maidir le hiarratas Gary Anderson. I ndiaidh don scéal briseadh go raibh Anderson éalaithe ó na húdaráis, ardaíodh ceisteanna faoin phróiseas cinnteoireachta agus faoi cé acu an raibh deis ag an tSeirbhís Phríosúin cur i gcoinne rogha na Cúirte nó nach raibh.
Labhair an tAire Cirt Naomi Long leis an Tionól ar an ábhar seo agus an scéal fós i mbéal forbartha. Dúirt sí leo gur léir nach raibh an deis ag an tSeirbhís Phríosúin cur in aghaidh chinneadh na Cúirte. Níos déanaí sa tseachtain, nuair a foilsíodh tuilleadh eolais ar an ábhar, tháinig sé chun solais go raibh an deis sin acu, ach nár chuir siad i gcoinne aisiompú an chinnidh.
Dúirt an tAire Long gur léir go raibh polaiteoirí áirithe ag déanamh iarrachtaí cnámh spairne pholaitiúil a dhéanamh den chás…
Mar gheall ar an eolas nua seo, rinneadh líomhaintí go raibh an tAire Long i ndiaidh an Tionól a chur amú agus gur roinn sí eolas leis na Comhaltaí nach raibh cruinn. Shéan sí go láidir na líomhaintí seo, ag maíomh gur roinn sí cibé eolas a bhí ar fáil di ag an am agus, nuair a fuair sí amach nach raibh iomlán an eolais aici ag an phointe sin, rinne sí socruithe chun labhairt leo arís leis an eolas sin a cheartú láithreach.
Dúirt Jon Burrows, ceannaire an UUP, go raibh tráma as an nua déanta ar mhuintir Karol Kelly, go raibh eagla ar an phobal, agus, cé nach gceistíonn sé macántacht an Aire, ceistíonn sé an cumas atá aici. Bhí CTR de chuid an DUP Jonathan Buckley ar aon intinn le Burrows, ag rá gur “teip thubaisteach” ar an chóras cirt a bhí sa chás seo.
Dúirt an tAire Long gur léir go raibh polaiteoirí áirithe ag déanamh iarrachtaí cnámh spairne pholaitiúil a dhéanamh den chás seo ar bhealach nach raibh ag teacht leis na fíricí ar fad. Cheartaigh sí an taifead a luaithe agus ab fhéidir léi agus d’ordaigh sí athbhreithniú ar an dóigh ar saoradh Anderson go sealadach sa chéad dul síos. Ghabh sí a leithscéal le teaghlach Karol Kelly go poiblí, agus dúirt sí gur mhaith léi é sin a dhéanamh arís i bpearsa chomh maith.
Tá an cás seo i ndiaidh ceisteanna móra a ardú maidir leis an phróiseas taobh thiar de shaoradh sealadach a bhronnadh ar phríosúnaithe, agus tá ceist ar leith ann anois faoin dóigh ar ligeadh do shibhialtach aire a thabhairt do phríosúnaí agus é saor ón phríosún. Ar a bharr sin, beidh ceisteanna ag an Aire Long ar a Roinn agus ar an tSeirbhís Phríosúin maidir le cén fáth nár tugadh iomlán an eolais di sula ndeachaigh sí chun labhairt leis an Tionól ag tús an scéil.
Tá Naomi Long, atá ina ceannaire ar Pháirtí na Comhghuaillíochta chomh maith, ag teacht faoi bhrú faoi láthair ó roinnt foinsí éagsúla. Cuireadh an-chuid ceisteanna uirthi agus ar a Roinn i ndiaidh na gcíréibeacha ciníocha i mBéal Feirste ag tús an tsamhraidh, agus tá go leor dúshláin eile roimh an Roinn Cirt mar atá.
Lena chois sin, tá imní ag fás go mbeidh sé deacair ar Pháirtí na Comhghuaillíochta cosaint a dhéanamh ar na suíocháin úra a bhain siad amach sa Tionól in 2022 i ndiaidh dóibh titim a fheiceáil i bpobalbhreitheanna. Tá an páirtí anois ag suí ag thart fá 10% le tamall, agus tá ráta sásaimh Naomi Long mar cheannaire tite chomh maith.
Beidh próiseas anois i gceist chun Anderson a bhogadh ar ais chuig an Tuaisceart agus go Príosún Mhaigh gCabraí, agus is cinnte go leanfar leis na ceisteanna maidir le saoradh sealadach a bhronnadh. Scéal tubaisteach do theaghlach Karol Kelly a bhí san eachtra seo, agus rinneadh níos measa é mar gheall ar dheacrachtaí cumarsáide laistigh den chóras dlí agus cirt. Beidh brú anois ar Naomi Long a léiriú go mbeidh na ceachtanna foghlamtha. Beidh le feiceáil an leor sin lena lucht cáinte a chur ina dtost.

title: Base jumper killed following wingsuit failure in 213m descent
description: Gabe Reilly, a US firefighter, was with a group of eight to 10 people in a mountainous part of Utah
content:
A 27-year-old US firefighter died on Sunday after his wingsuit failed during a Base jump from a 213m perch in northern Utah, authorities said.
The man, Gabe Reilly, was with a group of eight to 10 people before he jumped in a mountainous area east of Millville Canyon in Cache County, according to chief deputy Doyle Peck of the Cache County Sheriff’s Office.
Emergency crews responded just after 9am to a report of an accident that involved a Base jumper, the Sheriff’s Office said. Reilly was “experienced in this type of activity,” Peck said, but on this jump “something went wrong and he did not have enough lift with his wingsuit”.
Reilly hit the ground “at a high rate of speed resulting in his death,” Peck said.
A flight medical crew removed his body from the area.
The Salt Lake City Fire Department said in a social media post on Monday that Reilly had worked for the department for four years. He had followed “in the footsteps of his father,” who retired from the department in 2024.
Peck said that the area where the accident took place, which is more than 70km north of Ogden, Utah, along the Idaho border, is popular for Base jumping, a high-risk sport that involves parachuting off buildings, bridges, cliffs and other surfaces. (BASE stands for “buildings, antennas, spans and earth”.)
The tragedy came months after two people were killed in Base jumps in southeastern Utah. Danny Joe Kregle and Andrew Lewis died during a jump at a canyon in Grand County, Utah, on June 14, the authorities said at the time. – This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: Safety warning issued over Tesla battery system ‘which presents a risk of fire’
description: US carmaker has launched a replacement programme for affected units of its Powerwall 2 batteries, which are used mainly in homes
content:
A regulator in the UK has issued a safety warning over a Tesla battery system which “presents a risk of fire”.
The US carmaker, founded by Elon Musk , has launched a replacement programme for affected units of its Powerwall 2 batteries, which are used mainly in homes.
Customers are asked to ensure their system remains online and check the Tesla app for a notification confirming whether their unit is affected, according to the Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS).
“The product presents a risk of fire as certain battery cells within affected units may develop internal defects over time,” the UK regulator said.
“An investigation identified that battery cells manufactured by a third party may contain excessive lithium plating, which can lead to cracking of the cell casing.
“This may result in an internal short circuit and subsequent thermal runaway, increasing the risk of the battery overheating and catching fire.”
Thermal runaway occurs when a battery generates more heat than it can safely release, causing its temperature to rise rapidly and uncontrollably.
“The product does not meet the requirements of the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016,” the OPSS added.
Tesla has remotely discharged most affected units and any remaining ones are in the process of being discharged.
Customers should contact their original installer to schedule replacements or contact the support team at Tesla.
Affected units will be replaced free of charge.
Powerwall batteries store energy generated by solar or from the grid, which can be used to power devices and appliances, even during outages, according to the Tesla website. - PA

title: O’Neill rejects ‘gross discourtesy’ accusations as large numbers remain on Garvaghy Road
description: Drumcree parade, which had previously sparked serious disorder, was due to go ahead for the first time in nearly 30 years
author_name: Jack White, Ronan McGreevy, Cian O'Connell
content:
That’s a wrap on today’s live blog. We’ll be back tomorrow morning with more coverage on the Drumcree standoff. You can read a summary of today’s events here .
In a post on X, Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald said the British Secretary of State, Chris Bryant, has been told he “must act to stop any unwanted sectarian march being forced through the Garvaghy Road”.
McDonald told media earlier on Monday that the “sense of uncertainty now needs to be removed” and that the community “needs to know that they can breathe easy again”.
We have told the British Secretary of State plainly that he must act to stop any unwanted sectarian march being forced through the Garvaghy Road. This community has lived in peace for 28 years. That peace is not up for negotiation. We stand with the people of Garvaghy Road. We… pic.twitter.com/NmzsjrZIcU
Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant has posted the following statement after a day of talks.
I am grateful to all for the positive conversations about Drumcree today. Constructive dialogue is the route to a solution. I continue to hope and work for progress in further talks tomorrow.
Mark Hennessy reports that there is still a large presence of supporters in Portadown this evening.
Hundreds of residents and supporters from elsewhere remained on Garvaghy Road late tonight, though the atmosphere was calm, with most people taking advantage of the free tea and sandwiches on offer at a number of tents erected during the day.
Earlier, a crowded meeting of residents in the pastoral centre of St John The Baptist’s church heard an update from representatives of the residents’ association, led by Breandán Mac Cionnaith.
Members of the media were excluded from the meeting, though it is understood that the residents were given a report on the meeting with Northern Ireland Secretary of State, Chris Bryant, at Hillsborough earlier in the day.
However, bar one rash of rumour at 7pm there is little expectation of anything happening.
A crowd of 200 or fewer Loyalists have gathered at Water Street, which lies between Garvaghy Road and Portadown’s main street. Though they were on the road, traffic could get through.
Throughout the day, policing was noticeably more low-key, with officers using far more ordinary patrol cars than Land Rovers as had been the case on Sunday, or earlier in the controversy.
First Minister of Northern Ireland Michelle O’Neill has rejected accusations of “gross discourtesy” by Stormont Speaker Edwin Poots.
“Well, I don’t agree with the speaker,” O’Neill said. “I’m very confident in my role in supporting a community that’s under siege. I’m very confident and proud to stand with the community in Garvaghy, and I will continue to do so.”
Poots described O’Neill’s failure to attend the Assembly at Stormont on Monday as “unprecedented” and said she “needs to come and answer to the community of Northern Ireland”.
“You may not like the call that the speaker’s office made, but it is gross discourtesy to everyone in the House that you choose not to do it,” he added. O’Neill had been at Drumcree alongside protesters over the weekend.
She said that she can see “political mixing in the assembly chamber” and “political opponents trying to use this as an opportunity”. O’Neill said that she did not attend the Garvaghy Road in her capacity as First Minister, but as a representative of those demonstrating and as vice president of Sinn Féin.
The Northern Ireland Secretary has said he is “very keen to get to some kind of solution” to the Drumcree dispute.
Chris Bryant said he has been speaking to as many people “as possible” and is “exploring every option to see whether there’s a solution”.
Asked for an update on his talks, which he said he was prepared to continue on Tuesday on return from the Labour conference in Liverpool, Bryant told reporters at Hillsborough: “It’s been positive so far today and sometimes people showing a bit of ankle, and I think an awful lot of people of good faith wanting to get to a good outcome.
“It’s not quite clear what that will look like yet, but kind of – a bit through the mist – I can see maybe what that might look like if I can persuade everybody to sign up.”
Asked if the determination around the parade was still live, he said he could not answer the question as he was not a lawyer.
There had been no requests from the PSNI to call off the parade under section nine of the Public Processions (Northern Ireland) Act 1998.
“I believe in the rule of law and I believe that the rule of law should be upheld.
“I’m trying to find a solution that really works for everybody so that everybody can hold their head up high – and it’s tantalisingly just a bit far away at the moment, but we’re working on it.”
“An awful lot of people of good faith wanting to get to a good outcome.” Secretary of State @rhonddaBryant reflects on discussions with politicians and community leaders to find a peaceful resolution to the situation at Drumcree. pic.twitter.com/3yqdBjhvSl
Taoiseach Micheál Martin says the Government remains “very, very concerned” about tensions in Drumcree, reports Barry Roche.
Martin said there is an “obligation on everybody now to stand back and to mediate an outcome” in the best interests of the people of Northern Ireland.
The Taoiseach said that events over the last few days have threatened to undermine community relationships.
Loyal order members remained at Drumcree in Portadown on Monday after a weekend of tension in the Co Armagh town. Their planned parade was stopped by police as officers were concerned about the scale of a mass protest on part of the proposed route – the predominantly nationalist Garvaghy Road.
Orangemen attempted to start their parade on several occasions, including in the early hours of Monday morning, but police halted them on each occasion.
The parading dispute has erupted again after the Parades Commission adjudication panel granted permission for a limited parade down the Garvaghy Road for the first time in almost 30 years.
Speaking to reporters in Cork, Martin said: “I pay tribute to the PSNI, who have been left in a very, very difficult – if not somewhat impossible – position, and I appreciate the leadership of Chief Constable Jon Boutcher, who said his over-riding concern was that no one would be harmed in the context of what was transpiring over the last 48 hours.”
He said no one wants to go back to the divisions of the past and the “trauma” experienced at the Garvaghy Road.
Asked about Sinn Féin calls for Secretary of State Chris Bryant to overturn the Parades Commission decision to allow an Orange Order march in the area, Martin said: “I would say to Sinn Féin and to everybody else: Time to dial back now and time to engage in dialogue, and to work this out in a sensible, community-based way.
“Over the last number of decades, community relations in this area has improved immensely and very significant work has been put in by residents’ groups, by community groups, to develop community relationships, put them on a much more sustainable level.
