Still, it’s not just about what future housing issues might look like. Life, parenthood and all that entails looks a bit different from what we might have imagined in our own youth, my friend and I agreed.
Which brings us back to back to my friend’s question at the beginning. And whether we as women feel we are always under a different kind of scrutiny.
“Don’t be visible as a mother at work,” a colleague once advised me. I think it’s safe to say, as a parenting columnist, she may have called that one wrong. But I could see where she was coming from. And I thought of the advice I might give to my younger self, if I could, and would give now to my own daughter.
[ Jen Hogan: You may be questioning the sort of company I keep Opens in new window ]
Such as bearing in mind that your career may never recover from motherhood. That’s not to say don’t do it – my children are the best thing that ever happened to me – but know that the motherhood penalty is real. A recent study published in the British Journal of Sociology found “motherhood significantly increases downward mobility and limits access to professional occupations”.
Meanwhile, a recent workplace report showed women make up two-thirds of low-paid jobs.
Women are disproportionately represented in part-time work. Mothers are more likely to avail of unpaid parental leave, or take time away from the work altogether to rear their family, than fathers. And there is a consequence to the choices we make as we try to juggle our family’s needs.
We, of course, as women are not allowed to think this, or say this out loud, because doing so clearly shows we must hate our children. Luckily for men, there is no expectation they clarify this. And thankfully there’s a fatherhood bonus. Phew.
Just like the toddler parent who really can’t appreciate what raising teens is like, it’s hard to imagine how working life will be when the kids are a little older and years of career sacrifices have been made, and life and its asks look a little different.
But whatever choices you make to suit your family, beware of the wolf in tradwife’s clothing, who ultimately cares little about women’s rights.

title: Worldview: If the EU continues to drift, disintegration is seen as a more plausible future
description: Worldview: Rightward-shifts in major EU states like Germany, France, Poland and Italy present a real threat
content:
G aps between the European Union ’s advocacy of ambitious policy goals and its ability to implement them matter greatly in a world changed from market integration through globalisation to one dominated by power politics and growing security threats. Such incoherence risks losing the public support vital to EU success, according to influential EU policy experts.
Ireland’s six-month EU presidency sits squarely astride these contradictory imperatives. Securing an EU budget deal for 2028-2034 is a priority made more difficult by the political contest between states supporting more resources for the EU and those who prefer a relatively smaller financial commitment. Ireland’s commitment to more market-driven integration along the lines of the 2024 Draghi and Letta reports now has to confront the reality of a more troubled and fragmented world.
Ireland’s existing economic and political model – based on an open transatlantic economy, multilateralism and global human rights – is sorely tested in this new world environment. It needs renewal based on far more critical public debate about its durability, realism and appropriateness. Can the model be renewed through alternative pathways involving Canada, a UK newly convergent with the EU and a pragmatically enlarged and re-empowered internal EU market? Is that pathway made more difficult by the emerging power-dominated and rightward-shifting trends in major EU states like Germany, France, Poland and Italy?
Canadian prime minister Mark Carney ’s eloquent advocacy of the first course comes up against his own and the EU’s reluctance to pool economic sovereignty outside formal membership. The Carney approach is seen as unrealistic because of this by a variety of critics like the columnists Wolfgang Münchau and Martin Sandbu .
The second scenario is foreseen by the Carnegie think tank group writer on EU affairs Stefan Lehne , who fears that elections in France, Italy, Poland and Spain next year could shift the EU in a right-wing sovereigntist direction, making it much less inclined to re-empower itself in economic competitiveness, security and defence or adapting to a multipolar world.
Lehne notes that there has been no fundamental EU treaty reform in 20 years. Instead, there has been secondary legislation and inter-governmental financial and political innovation in response to events like the 2008-2012 financial crisis and recent geopolitical changes. Such “failing forward” methods by political elites can undermine popular support and legitimacy for deeper structural changes. That opens the way to the right-wing populist movements so visible this week in Germany, while simultaneously exposing the pathetic mediocrity of Friedrich Merz ’s leadership and the vulnerability of other leaders.
A recent survey of public opinion on the EU in France, Germany, Britain, Poland, the Netherlands and Italy by the European Centre on Foreign Relations bears this out. Across the six countries there is a sense of general deterioration in everyday life and a loss of normality; fears about war, conflict and insecurity; feelings of political fragmentation and division; and of economic hardship and geopolitical turbulence. Political leadership is seen as lacking, poor or slow, hypocritical on Ukraine and Gaza and lacking alternative visions to the liberals’ preparation for war with Russia . The only leader commended is Pedro Sánchez in Spain.
The spring Eurobarometer survey across the 27 EU member states charted similar findings about current problems, but reported more positive feelings about the EU as a zone of stability and potential hope if uncertainties recede and leadership improves. In Ireland, 74 per cent see membership as a benefit – but 23 per cent do not; economic benefits of membership substantially outweigh security and international relations in Irish opinion.
[ Nostalgia and lost pride: the fuel that feeds Europe’s far right Opens in new window ]
The annual review of EU affairs by the Journal of Common Market Studies concluded in 2025 that what emerges across the agenda on climate, defence, enlargement and social policy “is a broader pattern of strategic drift, a context in which the EU articulates far-reaching policy goals and institutional reforms, often in response to ad hoc crises, but struggles to ensure the political cohesion necessary for effective implementation”. Integration without supranationalism lacks a unitary political demos; the term “demoicracy” – a growing politicised interaction of national democracies – may be more apt.
Academic debates on whether the EU is a federal, confederal, liberal intergovernmental, compound or differentiated polity continue. They are echoed in the surveys of public opinion. Emmanuel Macron ’s ideas about a strategically autonomous EU with its own sovereignty have not gathered support as he departs. Disintegration is now recognised as a plausible future.
Strategic drift no longer suffices as the EU awaits a firmer direction. It remains to be seen whether the next group of leaders can respond more creatively to the many crises facing it.

title: Kara Owen: By working together, Ireland and the UK can build prosperity in a challenging world
description: Both countries have complementary strengths in digital infrastructure, semiconductors, cyber and advanced technologies
content:
In recent weeks, the pace of engagement between the UK and Ireland has been striking.
On September 18th, UK prime minister Andy Burnham welcomed a foreign leader to No 10 North for the first time: Taoiseach Micheál Martin .
Later that day, John Healey, the UK’s chancellor of the exchequer, was in Dublin as a guest at Ecofin, seeing the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris .
The same week, Dublin hosted UK economic secretary Lucy Rigby for Eurofi. As well as this, UK defence secretary Wes Streeting and Ireland’s Minister for Defence Helen McEntee held their first detailed bilateral discussions.
That level of engagement is entirely intentional. For the UK , no international relationship is more closely woven into our prosperity, security and future growth than our relationship with Ireland. As the prime minister said, it “matters at every single level”.
Speaking recently at the Dublin Economic Workshop in Wexford, I argued that the countries best placed for long-term success will be those that remain open, invest in innovation and capability, and deepen co-operation with partners that share their values and outlook. For me, the UK-Ireland relationship demonstrates how, in this challenging global environment, trusted partnerships can be a strategic advantage.
During my five years in Singapore, I watched countries across Asia invest relentlessly in infrastructure, capability and innovation. I came away motivated that Europe had to be “match fit”, both economically and strategically, for what lies ahead.
It is a false choice to present openness and security as being in competition. We need to be neither protectionist nor complacent if we are to remain both competitive and secure. Fragmentation and reducing co-operation would only weaken our prosperity.
Businesses and governments have become more clear-eyed about supply-chain disruption, energy volatility, rapid technological change and unfair competition. In that clarity, Ireland and the UK remain absolutely integral to one another’s growth story.
The economic case for working together on infrastructure, energy systems and technologies is compelling. Bilateral trade surpassed €2 billion a week in 2025, making Ireland the UK’s sixth-largest trading partner.
Irish investment in the UK stood at £77.4 billion (€90 billion) in 2024. The Common Travel Area allows people, skills and ideas to move freely between our countries, underpinning deeply integrated labour markets and economies. Northern Ireland occupies a unique position in both the EU Single Market and the UK’s internal market.
These connections extend far beyond Dublin and London. Twenty per cent of Irish investment in the UK last year went to the north of England. According to Enterprise Ireland, 60 per cent of Irish companies operating in the UK plan to expand, creating jobs and supporting innovation partnerships. British firms are also helping to deliver Ireland’s €275 billion development and infrastructure ambitions.
Nowhere is the connection between growth and long-term security clearer than in our shared search for secure, affordable and sustainable energy to drive economic growth. Ireland possesses one of Europe’s richest untapped offshore wind resources, while existing interconnectors already demonstrate the benefits of practical co-operation. We are learning from Ireland’s success in deploying onshore wind and solar, while the UK is a global leader in offshore wind, second only to China in installed capacity.
Together we can reduce costs, strengthen energy security, attract investment and create skilled jobs on both sides of the Irish Sea.
The same is true in technology. Ireland is one of Europe’s leading technology hubs, hosting major operations for many of the world’s largest technology companies. The UK is home to a technology ecosystem worth more than $1 trillion (€890 billion), combining world-class research, deep pools of capital and an exceptionally international outlook. We rank among the world’s top three AI ecosystems alongside the United States and China. That is why European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen identified the UK as a priority AI partner for the EU.
Ireland and the UK also have complementary strengths in digital infrastructure, semiconductors, cyber and advanced technologies, and a similar approach to keeping these resilient.
The UK prime minister’s recent address to the United Nations General Assembly underscored a simple reality: the challenges that will shape the coming decade, from disinformation to AI, cannot be solved alone. The UK is strengthening resilience through a new National Centre for Information Defence while working with partners to shape the standards and safeguards needed for emerging technologies such as AI.
The consequences of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have reinforced the reality that European and UK security is indivisible. Strong economies are essential not only for citizens’ pockets, but because prosperity is required for real security.
As the EU pursues greater economic strength and resilience, the UK’s capabilities and partnership should form part of that picture. The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic co-operation. That is why we will continue to engage closely with the EU as it develops its plans, including on “Made in Europe”.
I am a deeply practical diplomat and am pleased that the UK-Ireland work programme to 2030 – developed for the summit in Liverpool and extended at the summit in Cork – provides a framework for making a real-world difference on growth, infrastructure, innovation and security.
Our governments already work closely on energy, customs, supply chains, critical infrastructure and emerging technologies. And as co-guarantors of the Belfast Agreement, we also share a profound commitment to peace, stability and prosperity in Northern Ireland.
In a more uncertain world, trusted partnerships are becoming one of the defining advantages of successful countries. The UK and Ireland have spent decades building the institutions, connections and relationships that allow us to tackle shared challenges and seize opportunities. We should be confident in that partnership and ambitious about what it can achieve.
Kara Owen is the British Ambassador to Ireland

title: ‘I want to dig the foundations for my house extension to cut costs. Is this wise?’
description: Property Clinic: ‘Should I ask my building surveyor to review my work before the builder pours the concrete?’
content:
I’d appreciate your advice about digging the foundations for a planned house extension myself, with a view to reducing overall project costs. I am planning a single-storey extension to my existing house. To keep the budget under control, I am considering doing the excavation for the strip foundations myself, then using direct labour for the concrete pour and the rest of the build. Should I ask my building surveyor or engineer to review this before the pour?
There is an old saying in the construction industry that when building houses, you should build the first one for your enemy, the second for your friend and the third for yourself. You learn a considerable amount as you go and good building contractors have accumulated knowledge that is hard to match.
It is understandable, given the cost of construction nowadays and the increases we have seen over the last number of years, that homeowners are looking at carrying out elements of building works themselves in order to make much-needed extensions or home improvements financially achievable. I would say, however, that if you are considering this, you need to pick your battles. Construction is good, honest, hard work, and it certainly helps to have a reasonably good idea of what you are doing. Ideally, you should have some background in construction or previous experience of carrying out this type of work as we are not talking about finishes here such as decoration.
That is not to say that a homeowner cannot successfully undertake certain elements of the work themselves. Sometimes, from a budgetary perspective, it is necessary. However, foundations are one area where particular care is required.
Despite ultimately being hidden below ground, the foundations and substructure are arguably the most important elements of the construction. Everything else rests upon them. Getting the foundations, levels and below-ground construction wrong can result in problems further up the building and, once everything has been built over, shortcomings at this level can be particularly difficult and expensive to rectify.
If you intend to undertake this element yourself, I would therefore do so with the agreement and involvement of your building surveyor/engineer overseeing the project. You should have a proper set of construction drawings and details covering the extension from foundation level through to the roof, rather than trying to work solely from planning drawings. You need to understand the required foundation depths and widths, finished floor levels, floor build-up, insulation, damp-proofing and radon protection, together with how the new construction will physically tie into the existing house.
Even relatively simple matters such as setting the blockwork out at the correct level and coursing can become important when you subsequently come to install insulation, membranes, the sub-floor and screed and need everything to marry correctly with the existing building. Consider services such as water supplies, drainage, ducts and cables – are there any in the ground you are about to excavate (or overhead) and where do you need these positioned to achieve the required outcome of the new building – both internally and externally.
None of this means that you cannot excavate the foundations yourself if you are comfortable doing so and understand the drawings and setting-out requirements. However, I would regard professional inspection before pouring the concrete as essential. The concrete should not be poured until the engineer or building surveyor overseeing the works has had an opportunity to inspect the excavations. They will want to satisfy themselves as to matters such as the ground conditions, depth and dimensions of the excavation and its general suitability before the foundations disappear beneath the concrete and ground.
This is particularly important where that professional will ultimately be asked to provide certification or an opinion on compliance for the completed extension. Once the concrete has been poured, an important part of the construction is permanently concealed.
So, by all means look at where you can sensibly save money through your own labour but choose those areas carefully. If you decide that excavating the foundations is one of them, work from proper construction information, keep your overseeing professional involved and make sure the excavation is inspected before the concrete arrives.
I hope this provides some useful direction, and I wish you all the best with the hard work ahead.
Aidan McDonald is a chartered building surveyor and a member of the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland

title: Second cities are a capital idea this winter
description: Escorted tours in the shoulder season are a fantastic way to see unique sights while avoiding summer’s queues and excess heat
content:
Seasoning your winter with city breaks can make the dark months much more palatable. What’s more, as with all short breaks, you get much more bang for your buck because you feel like you’ve been away for longer than you have been, and with relatively little disruption to your day-to-day life.
A great way to explore a few cities in one short break is to take an escorted tour. Italian specialist Topflight, known for its winter ski holidays, also offers a range of escorted tours, some of which run through to October.
That includes its Taste of Tuscany and Umbria tour, a five-night programme which takes you to Perugia and Assisi, as well as the stunning Tuscan towns of Pienza and Bagno Vignoni. This last is on the Via Francigena, the historic medieval pilgrim route from Canterbury to Rome. The tour also includes a wine tasting stop in Montepulciano. Who needs city breaks when you’ve Tuscan hilltop towns to explore?
Topflight has recently expanded its escorted tour schedules to take in other countries too, including Portugal and Croatia. An October trip to Croatia sees you fly into Trieste before being transferred to the four-star Grand Hotel Adriatic in Opatija, known as the pearl of the Adriatic and a perfect base for exploring the coast. It has temperatures of 16 to 19 degrees in October, making it a lovely way to ease into winter.
Where previously there was a perception that escorted tours attracted an older demographic only, that is no longer the case, says Liane Coleman from Topflight. She sees first hand how much people of all ages appreciate the value of experiencing all the highlights of a particular region, while having all the logistics – from transport to entry tickets – sorted for them.
It’s why the company has been extending its escorted short options in Austria and France too, and has a terrific two-centre programme in Sicily which takes in Syracuse, Taormina, Cefalu and Palermo.
The months ahead are also a great time to visit top-tier cities that traditionally get very packed in summer, such as Rome, Venice, Florence and Barcelona.
It’s a particularly wonderful time to visit the Andalucian cities of Seville, Granada and Cordoba, giving you an opportunity to explore its mighty palaces and cathedrals without the endless queues or the relentless sun.
But there are plenty of great smaller cities to explore too, many of which are often overlooked. “As Italian specialists we have a lot of experience in smaller cities. Some of my favourites are Lucca, which is a great place to see everything, including Florence, and is really under visited,” says Coleman.
Ditto Sienna which, in the shoulder season, is a lot less crowded and much more atmospheric as a result.
In Sicily, many holidaymakers head straight to popular spots such as Taormina, she says, but she recommends they consider staying in Catania instead. “It’s brilliant, fun and vibrant, but close to Taormina and a great base from which to explore,” she says.
While cities such as Venice and Florence are year-round attractions, heading further down to the boot of Italy to some of its lesser-visited spots is also rewarding, particularly in the shoulder seasons. Matera, in Basilicata – think of it as the instep – is not your typical city break, as the Unesco World Heritage Site is famous for its cave dwellings, including hotels.
If even that is too busy for you, Gravina, a town built along a deep ravine in Puglia next door, features cave homes of its own, and is a quieter, less crowded alternative.
Out of season is also a lovely time to visit Alberobello, recommends Coleman, with its famous and fairytale-like conical houses. And while Ryanair flies to Bari until the end of October, she suggests a stay in one of her personal favourites instead, the quiet whitewashed town of Locorotondo.
For her own next city break she’s keen to get back to Salzburg, a city she recently stopped at en route to a ski resort. “It was early December and the Christmas markets had just started up and it was just enchanting, like a fairy-tale town. I can’t wait to go back,” she says.
If a major city is your preferred city break option, autumn and winter can be a great time to go. “Off season has its own charms,” says Mary Masterson of luxury travel company Oroko. You’ll get a much nicer experience not just in terms of overcrowding but less queuing for museums and restaurants too, she points out.
If you have Paris or Venice in your sights, there is certainly no more charming way to arrive than via the Orient Express. Having just alighted from the iconic train herself, she can confirm it is everything we might dream, and more.
“It’s got amazing staff, beautiful food, and is just spectacular,” she says, still smarting at having had to get off. She travelled from Venice to Paris and reckons it was a great way to do it. “The timings of the train mean you get a lot of beautiful countryside scenery during daytime hours,” she explains.
Most of her clients choose to go the traditional route, from Paris to Venice, and to ensure they don’t have to cope with the shock of stepping off this palace on wheels and back into real life alone, she arranges for them to be met at the station and transferred by luxury water taxi along the Grand Canal to equally salubrious lodgings while they adjust. Her personal favourite is the famous Cipriani, on Giudecca, as frequented by George and Amal Clooney.
While in the city, she will prepare a bespoke itinerary for guests, taking in glassware sites, churches and museums, including the Guggenheim, as well as foodie tours. “Venice is a wonderful city in terms of there always being something new to discover,” says Masterson.
Those arriving in Paris are whisked to the George V, a hotel with a three-Michelin-star restaurant, or the Grand Hôtel du Palais Royal, a favourite of her own situated just opposite the Louvre in the heart of the first arrondissement.
If you’re not quite ready to push the button on a ticket for the Orient Express just yet, Italy’s popular summer resorts can be a great option in the off season, she suggests, including Sorrento and all the little towns along the Amalfi coast. These are stunning at any temperature, as well as being close to the archeological sites of Pompeii and Herculaneum, which can be overcrowded in summer.
“And the nice thing about these Italian places is that they are all functioning places, not resorts,” she points out. It means you won’t get that off-season sense of tumbleweed when you visit. “Or of being somewhere that was built for heat, in the wrong season,” she adds.
It’s why she also recommends Athens, Greece’s capital, which has so much to offer in terms of culture and style but can be suffocatingly hot in summer. “It’s an amazing city and one of that is, still, less homogenous than other cities – with loads of individual artisanal shops,” she says.

title: Sunshine or snow sure? The winter escape choice is yours
description: Winter escape options for snow or sun in 2026
content:
To turn winter from a slog to a slay, or indeed a sleigh, check out the possibilities of a crisp Alpine break. Of course it’s all about the snow, but it’s not necessarily all about the winter sports.
“I have clients who just want to experience that winterscape, and there are parts of Europe you can do it, such as Finnish or Swedish Lapland, where you enjoy that lovely snowy experience, with snow mobiles, husky dogs and reindeer,” explains ski specialist Conor Magee from luxury travel company Oroko.
“But the vast majority of people who go to the mountains in the winter are looking to go skiing or snowboarding and for that, it’s all about the Alps, whether French, Swiss, Italian or Austrian.”
Here too there are horses for courses, he points out, with different resorts ticking different boxes for holidaymakers.
Some opt for high-altitude resorts such as Courchevel 1850 in the French Alps and Zermatt in Switzerland, as much for the locale as for the snow-sure skiing, he points out. “They want to soak up the atmosphere and go for long lazy lunches and do a bit of shopping in the high-end boutiques too,” he says.
For those focused solely on skiing, his first question is, what time during the season are they looking to travel?
“If it’s early in the season, like Christmas or new year, or late in the season, like Easter, then obviously, with the current world climate, we need to ensure we get our customers to as high an altitude as possible to ensure good quality snow cover and good quality snow,” says Magee.
“From a beginner’s perspective in particular, learning to ski in light, fluffy snow is so much easier than trying to ski in heavy, slushy snow, and altitude plays an important role in that.”
For experienced skiers, it’s all about the expansive ski terrain offered by locations such as the Three Valleys ski area in the French Alps, the largest interconnected ski area in the world with 600km of ski slopes and resorts such as Courchevel, Méribel, and Val Thorens.
Alternatively, there is Espace Killy, which connects the French Alpine resorts of Tignes and Val d’Isère, an hour’s drive away. Zermatt, another favourite, has 200km of ski runs on the Swiss side, and almost double that when combined with the Cervino Ski Paradise resort across the border in Italy.
Regardless of proficiency, the higher you go the more snow sure you can be but if you go in February, the height of the season, “wherever you go across the Alps you are going to get snow,” he says. That opens up a range of picturesque options such as Kitzbühel in Austria, Sölden in Austria, and Les Gets in the lower French Alps.
That matters because, when it comes to atmosphere, not all ski resorts are equal. While some can be quite utilitarian in appearance, others are straight off a Christmas card.
For sheer simplicity and ease, the ability to find a “ski in, ski out” property can’t be beaten, says Magee, particularly when travelling with kids.
For those travelling without children, the après ski scene is more of a factor. “It’s all about matching the criteria that each customer has, and no two requests are the same,” he says.
Ski specialist Topflight has a range of offerings designed to suit all manner of skiers, and budgets. This year it has expanded its ski programme in La Rosière in the French Alps.
“It’s a really gorgeous resort, close to the Italian border, so you can ski between France and Italy, which is really appealing. It also has loads of really good activities for kids and is really popular with families, with plenty of self-catering options to accommodate families staying together,” says Liane Coleman from Topflight.
As well as new resorts in Tignes this season, Topflight has also introduced a Cork to France route, in addition to its popular Cork to Austria route. “This is proving very popular so far for the season ahead,” says Coleman.
Topflight has always offered an extensive range of holidays in Livigno, one of Italy’s best ski resorts, known for an unusually long season from November to May, thanks to its high altitude.
This year the company has expanded its Italian offering with a new collection of resorts in the Dolomites, including Madonna di Campiglio, Val di Fassa, Val Gardena and Pinzolo.
“There’s been a lot of attention on the region following the Winter Olympics and we’re seeing that translate into real interest from Irish skiers. It offers fantastic skiing, but there’s also the scenery, food and Italian hospitality, so the appeal goes well beyond the slopes,” says Coleman.
Austria continues to perform incredibly well with the Irish market. “There’s a real affection for Austrian ski resorts and Zell am See remains particularly popular for us,” she says.
“I think part of that is because people are looking for the complete Alpine holiday – they want great skiing, but they also want atmosphere, good food, lovely hotels and a resort they can enjoy off the slopes too.”
Indeed, one of the biggest trends Coleman has seen in relation to travel has been the rise of multigenerational holidays, including winter breaks in which not everyone wants to hit the slopes.
That has helped drive demand for Zell am See, because it’s wonderful place to be even if you don’t ski. “It’s a great little town, really beautiful, right beside Lake Zell, with great shops and great restaurants,” she explains.
If the mere thought of snow makes you yearn for heat, that’s okay, there are plenty of great winter sun options out there too. Top of the pops for Irish winter holidaymakers, both for value and for weather, are the Canary Islands.
If you fancy a luxury Canaries option, check out the Ritz Carlton Abama, a luxury five-star cliffside resort located in Guía de Isora on the southwest coast of Tenerife, with a Michelin starred restaurant.
But even if the budget doesn’t stretch that far, and you feel you already know the Canaries inside out, the advice of a travel agent can be invaluable.
“Tenerife alone has 26 different micro climates and we know what those are,” says Mary Masterson, sun holiday specialist with Oroko. “When people have limits in terms of the times they can go, it’s really important to get it right.”
If you’re willing to travel further afield, the Caribbean should be top of your winter sun list. As befits a luxury travel operator, Oroko partners with luxury hotelier Belmond, paving the way to some seriously sumptuous breaks in the region.
That includes the elegant beachfront resorts of La Samanna on St Martin and Cap Juluca on Anguilla. “Both are fabulous hotels on beautiful beaches with outstanding food, and you can stay in one and then take a short hop by boat or plane to the other,” says Masterson.
For value, a Caribbean cruise can be a surprisingly good option for winter sun, she points out, particularly over the Christmas period. “It’s a time of year that is peak season for hotels, but cruises typically don’t put their prices up for those couple of weeks,” she says.

title: When it’s cheaper to extend than upsize, here’s how to create your ideal home
description: Modular homes, energy upgrades, interiors, outdoor living, lifestyle and wellbeing are top of the agenda for home shoppers in 2026
content:
Unsurprisingly, there’s been a surge in interest in modular homes since planning exemption regulations were announced by the Government last July. Irish homeowners can now build detached habitable modular units of up to 45sq m in their gardens, without planning permission, provided they meet specific criteria. It’s a practical way to create independent accommodation for an adult child or an ageing parent, without extending or altering a house, but modular homes could also be used to earn additional income.
Budget 2027, due to be announced on October 6th, is expected to ratify earning up to €14,000 per year tax-free for renting out a modular home, once you register with the residential tenancy board.
Which modular home should you buy? How much money should you pay for it? And how long will it take to build? At the PTSB Ideal Home Show visitors can see a range of modular homes first-hand and find out more about costs, construction methods and build times.
“In fact, a modular home can be built in as little as three days,” says Caitriona O’Connor, director of the PTSB Ideal Home Show. “There will be a selection of different types of modular homes on display and visitors can compare designs and construction options and speak directly with companies about what’s suitable for their property and their budget.
“Those featured will be produced in Ireland with an emphasis on sustainable materials that suit the Irish climate,” she adds. There will also feature a selection of garden rooms which are also increasing in popularity as the planning exemption for such structures has increased from 25sq m to 30sq m.
The interest in both modular homes and garden rooms are part of a general trend of home investment. “A few years ago, the emphasis was on saving money on household energy bills, but now people are less likely to sell their home. Instead, they are investing in their homes and making them as comfortable as possible,” explains Caitriona. “That could be in the form of a modular or a garden home, but equally they could be making energy-saving upgrades, such as installing solar panels or doing a home energy retrofit.”
At the Electric Ireland Superhomes Home Energy Upgrade Pavilion, a range of experts will offer advice on upgrades, available supports, and how to go about it. “With the new SEAI grants you can now have your windows upgraded for example because there’s an awareness that you should start with the fabric of the building,” says O’Connor.
Despite the rise in the cost of building materials and labour in recent years, it’s still cheaper to extend a house than buy a new one, and the show caters for this by acting as a hub for experts on all things renovation related.
“The expert advice is always a big draw,” says O’Connor. “At the PhoneWatch Ask an Expert Hub you can avail of free one-to-one consultations with architects, garden designers/landscapers and interior designers from leading professional associations and get personalised advice tailored to your own home or project. There’s a lot to be said for meeting people in person too, and the fact that you can do it all under one roof is a big advantage.”
Another trend in home improvement, which will feature at the event is outdoor living. “Most new-builds now have a designated wellness area in the garden which is in line with an increased interest in health and wellbeing and an attempt at work life balance,” she says.
“There’s also been a rise in the number of people installing outdoor kitchens, saunas and ice baths, perhaps because recent summers have seen above average temperatures, and with global warming, it’s a trend that will likely continue.”
For the same reason, and after a summer of higher than normal temperatures, interest in air conditioning is on the rise. There will be experts on hand to answer questions and give advice on this too.
If you’re looking for interior design inspiration, you’ll want to attend some of the talks by top designers, scheduled to take place over the course of the weekend. The Dulux Heritage Interior Design Hub will feature a curated roomset designed by Charlotte Bradshaw Interiors, along with design consultant Jane Witter and a team of colour consultants on hand to advise you on paint colours and up-to-the-minute trends. Visitors are encouraged to bring photographs and samples of material from their homes to receive tailored advice.
Hazel Burton of The Home Reset will offer tips for organising your home, while quantity surveyors, Shay Lally and Patricia Power, will share practical advice on planning house projects and how to manage the costs.
As always, a number of Irish celebrities will be making an appearance. The former professional rugby player, Peter O’Mahony, and his wife, Jessica O’Mahony, will be promoting their new garden and homeware brand søw-sé.
On October 17th, architect Dermot Bannon will join experts from Mitsubishi Electric for a talk on home heating, giving advice about heat pumps, ventilation and energy-efficient heating systems. While Diarmuid Gavin will be talking all things Hampton Luxury Greenhouses later that day with OutdoorLiving.ie.
With Christmas on the horizon, Dunnes Stores will be using the occasion to showcase their festive homeware, gifts and interior decor. Designer Helen James will share her festive tablescaping and interiors ideas; hotelier Francis Brennan will provide tips for five-star hotel quality touches in the home, and designer, Carolyn Donnelly, will show her Christmas designs for the brand. William Costelloe, son of the late Irish designer Paul Costelloe, will also be creating personalised sketches for visitors.
In addition, there will be live cooking demonstrations from the team at Saba, and celebrity chef Neven Maguire will be launching his Simply Better Christmas pudding and Christmas cake. Donal Skehan and Brian McDermott will also be cooking up a storm.
“The PTSB Ideal Home Show is about helping people make informed decisions about their homes,” says O’Connor. “Whether you’re planning a renovation, an energy upgrade or simply looking for new ideas, you can meet leading brands, discover the latest products and solutions, and get practical advice from experts who are among the best in their fields.”
The PTSB Ideal Home Show runs from October 16th to 18th at RDS Simmonscourt, Dublin. Find out more at idealhome.ie , and Irish Times readers can get their free tickets here

title: Mary and Padraic Colum - Lives and the Dream: Bringing a singular literary duo back to life
description: Margaret Kelleher seeks to introduce new readers to the work of this successful intellectual couple
content:
On April 10th, 1925, the day The Great Gatsby was published, F Scott Fitzgerald observed to the literary editor Max Perkins: ‘I’m sure anyhow that at least two critics Benét & Mary Colum will have heard about the book. I’d like her to like it – Benét’s opinion is of no value whatsoever.’
That Fitzgerald valued more the opinions of the fiercely independent-minded Irish critic over that of her fellow reviewer, William Rose Benét – editor of the influential Saturday Review of Literature – was testimony to Colum’s high standing in the American literary scene at the time.
Margaret Kelleher, in this joint biography of Mary and Padraic Colum – wife and husband for 45 years – explores the nature of posthumous reputation, suggesting that the cruellest fate for writers is to be remembered not for who you were or what you wrote, but for whom you knew.
And between their sojourns in Ireland, France and the United States, they got to know just about everybody, from Patrick Pearse and Roger Casement to Eugene O’Neill, Ernest Hemingway and Sylvia Plath. In her revealing account, based on significant new material, Kelleher wants to bring new readers to the Colums’ work, rescuing their achievements to more than merely walk-on parts in the lives of others.
If Padraic Colum is still remembered, it is by an older generation of school-goers, for poems such as An Old Woman of the Roads and A Drover. For contemporary readers, he is largely unknown, although music fans might be familiar with Sinéad O’Connor’s rendition of Colum’s version of the Donegal folk song, She Moved Through the Fair.
Mary Colum has slipped even further from popular memory, and her remarkable memoir, Life and the Dream (1947), is no longer in print. The daughter of an RIC sergeant in Sligo and a mother whose family had known better days (such as when two of her ancestors, the Gunning sisters, were painted by Joshua Reynolds), Mary Colum née Maguire was a precocious child who excelled at her studies in St Louis’ convent school in Monaghan. She went on to study Modern Languages and Literature at university level and was one of the first graduates from the National University of Ireland Dublin in 1909.
A background in European languages was crucial to her repeated insistence on adopting a comparative perspective on writing. In a later work, From these Roots (1937), a study of the roots of literary modernism, she stresses the European dimension to the Irish Literary Revival, discussing the influence of Baudelaire on Synge and engaging in a contrastive analysis of the work of Joyce and Proust.
Mary Colum has slipped even further from popular memory, and her remarkable memoir, Life and the Dream (1947), is no longer in print
As a poet and dramatist, Padraic Colum was of course intimately involved in the revival and its key players. Dublin being such a small place, such intimacy was not without its drawbacks. WB Yeats, for example, gave evidence in court against Colum’s father, who was charged for his part in the riots against the Abbey Theatre’s staging of Synge’s Playboy of the Western World.
[ Classical echoes – An Irishman’s Diary on Padraic Colum and Homer Opens in new window ]
What was true for literature also obtained in politics. Thomas MacDonagh, for instance, was an intense rival of Padraic’s, having proposed to Mary before the Colums’ marriage. When she turned his proposal down, in a fit of pique, MacDonagh threw the ring into the fire – only for it to be retrieved by Padraic, returned to its owner, to end up on the hand of Muriel Gifford, whom MacDonagh ultimately married in 1912.
Mary Colum was an active member of the Irish Women’s Franchise League and a founding member of Cumann na mBan. Both she and Padraic were unstinting in their support for the national cause and, upon relocating to New York, continued their advocacy for Irish independence.
This was not without professional consequences, where criticism of British policy was increasingly seen as a pro-German stance in a country preparing to enter the war on the Allied side. Intending to go to the US for only a short period in 1914, they would not return to Ireland before 1922, and only for a visit. Apart from periods in France in the 1930s and intermittent stays in Ireland, they would spend the rest of their lives in the US.
A lifelong advocate of the work of James Joyce, when such a position was neither popular nor profitable, Padraic Colum was unfailingly loyal to friends and family
Mary Colum would go on to establish herself as one of the most formidable post-first World War literary critics in the US, but in later years, due to a combination of poor health, difficult relationships with publishers and the increasingly ideological polarisation of criticism, her work met with less receptive audiences. She passed away in 1957, and the only remaining material trace of her presence in Ireland is her gravestone in St Fintan’s Cemetery in Sutton.
Padraic Colum, in addition to his involvement in a number of leading US literary magazines, would develop a very successful career as a writer of children’s literature. He was three times recipient of the prestigious Newbery Honor Book prize. A lifelong advocate of the work of James Joyce, when such a position was neither popular nor profitable, he was unfailingly loyal to friends and family. Towards the end of his life, his poetry would undergo something of a rebirth under the aegis of Dolmen Press.
[ Lives and loves: the sexual side of the Rising Opens in new window ]
Margaret Kelleher, with a fluency and captivating style already on ample display in her Maamtrasna Murders (2018), has brought this singular couple back to life and shown how, in matters of intellectual courage, tenacity and depth of feeling, they demand to be our contemporaries.
Michael Cronin’s latest book is Ireland: Why it Matters to Be an Island (Royal Irish Academy)

title: Beckett is bleak only to those with no sense of humour
description: In a Word ... Distress
content:
The works of Samuel Beckett are not for everyone. He presents a bleak, boring, meaningless world in which not a lot happens. For instance, this is the opening sentence of his novel Murphy: “The sun shone, having no alternative, on the nothing new.” Bleak and boring but what a great line – perfectly balanced, rhythmic.
His most famous work, Waiting for Godot, was described by critic Vivian Mercier in a 1956 review for this newspaper as “a play in which nothing happens, twice”.
It was more subtle than that suggests. What he said was that Beckett had “achieved a theoretical impossibility – a play in which nothing happens, that yet keeps audiences glued to their seats. What’s more, since the second act is a subtly different reprise of the first, he has written a play in which nothing happens, twice.”
Mercier was a huge fan of Beckett’s work and wrote an acclaimed book on him, Beckett/Beckett, published in 1977.
The tragedy for Beckett, if that is the word, is that many of his interpreters are so awestruck they miss out on, or disregard, elements in the work they feel are beneath him, then misinterpret these.
This applies particularly to the humour, which some academics and theatre directors feel has no place in Beckett. But Godot is laced with humour, as brought out so effectively in the terrific 1988 Gate Theatre production with actors Barry McGovern, the late Johnny Murphy and Alan Stanford.
Another was Druid Theatre’s 1976 production of Happy Days, with Marie Mullen and the late Mick Lally.
I think Irish actors and directors have an innate advantage in dealing with Beckett. They get his humour.
Beckett himself could be dismissive of “bleak” criticisms. He recalled how “an English intellectual – so-called – asked me why I write about distress. As if it were perverse to do so! He wanted to know if my father had beaten me or my mother had run away from home to give me an unhappy childhood. I told him no, that I had had a very happy childhood.”
Beckett “left the party as soon as possible”. In a taxi later there were signs seeking help for the blind, for orphans, for refugees. Distress, he said, “is screaming at you, even in the taxis of London”.
Distress, from Latin districtus, for “draw apart, hinder, anxiety, hardship”.

title: FAI president Paul Cooke defends handling of Israel v Ireland game
description: ‘I haven’t heard anybody say that this decision was taken by the football community, which is what it was’
content:
The Football Association of Ireland ( FAI ) president, Paul Cooke, has defended the handling of the build-up to the Nations League clash with Israel in Hungary, saying the week “went as well as could be expected in the face of unprecedented coverage”.
Heimir Hallgrímsson admitted after Ireland’s 3-0 win in Debrecen that he believed at one point yesterday that the game would not go ahead, and was visibly emotional as he described the build-up as the most difficult experience of his career.
Gavin Bazunu’s withdrawal from the Israel matches on Saturday morning led the Irish players to reconsider their own positions on fulfilling the fixtures, with players eventually voting among themselves on whether to proceed with the match. The FAI said the players voted with a “significant majority” to fulfil the game, but have declined to specify the result of the vote.
“I think we’ve handled the week quite well,” said Cooke. “I think, first of all, before we even get into that, I think if you look at the courage, the performance, the way they conducted themselves, everybody that was here tonight, those 20-odd players, they’ve as a nation, a country, as a football organisation, we should be so proud of them in the face of the difficulties that they encountered.
“I think the week went as well as could be expected in the face of, I would say, unprecedented coverage and the way some people conducted themselves. And I’m not referring to anybody in the camp.”
[ Ken Early: Ireland beat Israel in a bleak farce that leaves everyone feeling betrayed Opens in new window ]
Asked to whom he referred, Cooke rounded on the media.
“I am referring to the way some of you have behaved in some respects,” he said. “The pressure, the way some stories have been chased. I’ve worked in media for 35 years. I thought journalists were meant to be balanced and reflect two sides of an opinion. I haven’t seen that. That’s just my personal gripe.”
Cooke also took issue with what he saw as insufficient coverage given to the reasons why the FAI was fulfilling the games, saying it proceeded with the matches to safeguard the future financial interests of Irish football. He also pointed to the result of an EGM vote earlier this year, at which delegates passed a motion committing the FAI to fulfilling all Nations League games by a 68 per cent majority, saying the decision had been democratically endorsed by the FAI’s members.
[ Ireland fulfil fixture against Israel, but pressure to cancel return game will not let up Opens in new window ]
Cooke said at no point did he personally feel the Israel games should not be played, pointing to the unknowns around what Uefa’s potential sanctions would be in the event of a boycott.
“They are, but I don’t know what they are,” said Cooke of the unknown sanctions. “But equally, the other sanctions are serious. Let’s not forget that. Two 3-0 defeats. They are serious as well. And the consequences of going down to League C. But equally, as I said, I haven’t heard anybody say that this decision was taken by the football community, which is what it was.
“There’ll be a thought process from a lot of people in the country that the decision isn’t just about what should be good for football.”
[ Allegation of racism by Israel fans towards Ireland’s Adam Idah will not be investigated Opens in new window ]
In illustrating the potential impacts of unknown sanctions, Cooke pointed to Southampton’s punishment in the Spygate controversy of last season, which saw them kicked out of the Championship play-offs.
Cooke also said he did not give an opinion to the players during yesterday’s long meeting as to whether the game should be played, and that the decision to proceed with the game was left up to the players’ vote.

title: House price inflation slows as demand falls
description: Buyers cautious about bidding high for homes, figures show
content:
House price inflation slowed last month as demand for homes fell, prompting speculation that uncertainty is making buyers cautious about bidding for properties.
Prices rose 3 per cent in the year to September, about half the rate of inflation a year earlier, according to a report from property website Daft.ie.
The average Irish home sold for just short of €445,000 in the three months to the end of September, the report says, while the price at which houses were listed was 44 per cent above pre-Covid pandemic levels.
The prospect of interest rate hikes and the global uncertainty sparked by the US-Iran war could be making buyers more cautious about what they offer for homes, the report’s author, Trinity College Dublin economist Ronan Lyons, said on Sunday.
Demand for homes appears to be easing, but supply has not increased, Lyons said, with Daft.ie’s figures showing that buyers are reining in what they offer for properties.
A year ago, he said, people bid between 6 and 7 per cent more than a home’s listed price when trying to buy a property, but this has now fallen to between 2 and 3 per cent.
Lyons said it was not possible to say if the trend would continue or if it was a more short-term pattern.
However, a fall in employment in key industries that generate foreign earnings could ease house price inflation in the longer run, he said. “Otherwise, it could just be that people are taking stock.”
Homes are also taking longer to sell, with the number of properties taken off the market down by 3 per cent in the year to August.
[ Tax cuts in Budget 2027 for renovating vacant properties ‘could boost housing supply’ Opens in new window ]
While demand for new properties increased slightly outside Dublin, sales of new and second-hand homes fell in the capital. “That is the clearest sign of genuinely softer demand and a signal to watch in the coming quarters,” Lyons said.
The report shows that the number of homes for sale in the Republic has not increased. On September 1st, close to 13,800 second-hand houses were for sale, up 12.5 per cent on a year previously, but still around half the pre-Covid average.
Close to 52,700 second-hand homes were put on the market in the year to August, the same as last year and in 2024, the figures show.
In the three months to the end of September, the average three-bedroom semidetached home sold for €635,000 in Dublin – 2.7 per cent more than during the same period last year.
In Cork , the same type of property sold for €431,000 – an increase of 5.7 per cent. Prices in Galway rose 5.8 per cent to €618,000, in Limerick they increased 5.8 per cent to €376,000, and they surged 11 per cent in Waterford to €313,000.

title: Energy costs hitting hiring and expansion plans
description: Companies stall investment as bills rise following US-Iran war
content:
High energy costs are forcing businesses to stall plans to hire workers and delaying investment in expansion, according to a new survey.
Irish energy bills are among the highest in Europe, with businesses and homes having endured increases this year following the outbreak of the US-Iran war .
Seven out of 10 business managers say increased energy costs are at the head of their list of concerns going into the winter, according to accountants Azets Ireland .
Almost half of those surveyed by the firm say the problem has prompted them to delay investment plans, while 54 per cent have stopped hiring new workers in the face of the increased cost.
Irish businesses face “significant cost pressures” as they enter the final months of the year, said Azets Ireland chief executive Neil Hughes.
“Rising energy prices, economic uncertainty and continued geopolitical volatility are making it much harder for firms to plan and grow with confidence,” he said.
“The findings highlight the real-world impact these pressures are having.”
He warned that many small and medium-sized businesses are absorbing big cost increases while trying to protect razor-thin profits.
However, close to nine out of 10 firms are optimistic that they will grow over the next year, the Quarter Three Azets Barometer shows.
[ Business optimism on the rise despite interest-rate and geopolitical fears Opens in new window ]
The firm questioned 150 companies across Ireland in July and August for the survey.
Azets Ireland is part of the international Azets group, which has operations in eight countries. The firm focuses on small and medium-sized businesses.

title: Standoff continues near Drumcree as Orange parade blocked from accessing Garvaghy Road - as it happened
description: NI Secretary: ‘I don’t think there is a single person’ who really wants to go back ’28, 30 years and relitigate everything and dismantle the Good Friday Agreement’
content:
Follow along tomorrow for more rolling coverage.
Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Chris Bryant is set to face fresh demands to block any possibility of the Orange Order being allowed to march down Garvaghy Road, writes Ireland and Britain Editor Mark Hennessy in Portadown.
The stand-off between Orange men at Drumcree seeking to march down the road – a Catholic estate in a largely Protestant town – follows two days of rising tensions that raise questions over the ability of Northern Ireland’s Stormont institutions to survive.
The legal permission won by the Orange Order after lengthy court battles on Saturday to march from Drumcree Church of Ireland to its headquarters in Portadown expired at midnight.
The order now requires a fresh application to the Parades Commission to see if its march is legal under 30-year-old legislation.
Secretary of state for Northern Ireland Chris Bryant told the BBC “we haven’t got a solution yet” after holding discussions with all the main political parties separately.
“There’s a few ideas around about things we might be able to do and I’m happy to explore those and I’ll continue those conversations tomorrow,” he said.
He said he has spoken twice with First Minister Michelle O’Neill on Sunday evening.
“I have made it very clear that I think it is important that we get to a resolution and we need to find some kind of compromise so that people are able to go home.”
He urges “everybody to keep calm” and says it is “very important that people co-operate with police” both at Drumcree and across Northern Ireland.
When asked by a journalist about the DUP leader Gavin Robinson’s comments that her presence at the protest was unlawful, Michelle O’Neill said: “I stand with the people of the Garvaghy Road today and every day.”
St John the Baptist’s College in Portadown will also close on Monday.
In a post on Facebook, the school said, “in the interest of everyone’s safety and the escalating situation on the Garvaghy Road this afternoon, the decision has been made to close the school, tomorrow”.
SDLP leader Claire Hanna has said the situation on the Garvaghy Road “urgently needs to be de-escalated”.
Speaking ahead of meeting secretary of state Chris Bryant on Sunday evening, she urged him to “use every avenue available to him to stop this parade and take this dispute off the street and into a structured process of dialogue”.
“The extraordinary courtroom drama of the past 48 hours should give nobody confidence that this situation is as straightforward as some have suggested,” she said.
“A High Court judge made clear that the concerns of all parties needed to be properly heard. Whatever the legal position, there remains an important distinction between what can legally happen and what should happen.
The priority, she said, must be on de-escalation.
“Dialogue must replace stand-off, light must replace heat, and political leaders need to think carefully about their words and actions as we navigate the days ahead,” she said.
“The answer is not, and never has been, to collapse Stormont.”
Marie-Therese Murray approached police lines on Portadown’s Garvaghy Road at 7.40am on Sunday morning holding a placard of her child who died nearby 30 years ago, reports Northern Correspondent Seanín Graham .
Behind her, thousands of protesters linked arms in torrential rain to block a planned Orange Order march from Drumcree church.
“Please, please stop this for the children of both communities ... we don’t want no more violence,” Murray pleaded, sobbing.
There is no sense for now that anything will kick off at the Drumcree side tonight, reports Ireland and Britain Editor Mark Hennessy .
There are plenty of supporters but equal numbers leaving, and zero tension so far.
Numbers at Drumcree church are steady, in the low hundreds, with constant replacements.
The PSNI have removed the officers who were on duty at a country road leading up to the church. However, the PSNI could not confirm why this had happened for now.
There are no signs that there will be any attempt to breach the PSNI lines.
Gerry Adams visiting local residents at the Drumcree Centre off the Garvaghy Road. Sinn Féin stands with the Garvaghy Road residents in rejecting supremacist orange marches which have no support in this community. pic.twitter.com/SSGtDEpmyL
In a post on X, Sinn Féin shared that Adams had visited the Garvaghy Road on Sunday.
“Sinn Féin stands with the Garvaghy Road residents in rejecting supremacist orange marches which have no support in this community,” the post read.
DUP MP Carla Lockhart said, after leaving party’s meeting with secretary of state Chris Bryant, that he is “in no doubt about the urgency” of the situation.
“He has 24 to 48 hours to ensure the rule of law is upheld and the parade proceeds in line with the Parades Commission’s determination,” the MP for Upper Bann said in a statement posted on Facebook.
She said the consequences will be “profound” if the parade is not allowed to go ahead.
The party, she said, remained “four square” with the Portadown Orangemen and “the rule of law”.
“Mob rule cannot defeat the rule of law,” she said.
Addressing supporters on the Garvaghy Road, First Minister Michelle O’Neill thanked those for staying on the road and “going the course over the last day and a half”.
“This march cannot go ahead, and the reason that it hasn’t went ahead is because of your determination, is because you have stood on this road with these people, and we will continue to stand on this road,” she said, standing beside Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald.
“We will not let those aggressive forces drive us backwards.
“We will not let people bring us back to the harder times and the dark days of the past. We will keep driving forward.
“The reason that the parade has not come down this road thus far is because you are here, and we need you to stay the course.
“We need you to stay here ‘til 12 o’clock tonight at least.
“Do not give up at this stage; we have come this far.
“The people of Garvaghy Road need us to stand with them tonight,” she said.
St John the Baptist PS Bunscoil Eoin Baiste, an Irish-medium primary school located on the Garvaghy Road, has made the “difficult decision” to close the school on Monday, September 28th, “in the interest of everyone’s safety and due to the continuing situation on the Garvaghy Road”.
In a post on Facebook, the school said: “The safety and wellbeing of our pupils, families and staff must always be our first priority and we feel that closing the school is the most responsible course of action in the uncertain circumstances.
“We appreciate that this decision may cause inconvenience for families and sincerely apologise for the short notice. We thank you for your understanding and co-operation.”
It said it will “continue to monitor the situation closely and will keep parents informed of any further developments or arrangements”.
Reports that Scottish police were deployed at a controversial parade in Northern Ireland on Sunday have been described as “deeply concerning” by the Scottish Greens, who called for the agreement underlying it to be reviewed.
The party’s justice spokeswoman, Maggie Chapman, said the Orange Order march on Garvaghy Road in Portadown was “designed to spread tensions and hatred”, and that the Parades Commission was “utterly wrong” to allow it to go ahead.
She said Scotland should not provide policing resources for events that “inflame tensions”, and called for the Scottish government to review the policing agreement to ensure officers were not deployed to such events in future.
The North East Scotland MSP also said she had raised the issue in a letter to justice secretary Neil Gray on Friday but had not received a response.
Chapman said: “This march was designed to spread tensions and hatred and to intimidate the community and families who are trying to get on with their lives.
“The organisers knew exactly what they were doing, and the Parades Commission was utterly wrong to allow it.
“It is deeply concerning that Police Scotland officers were deployed to support policing around a march that caused such fear and division.
“The Scottish Government must be transparent about what role Scottish officers played, what resources were committed, and whether they think this agreement is appropriate.
“Scotland should not be providing policing resources for sectarian events like this that are called to inflame tensions.
A Scottish government spokesperson said: “The deployment of police officers on mutual aid is an operational matter for the chief constable.
“Mutual aid arrangements between forces are a longstanding feature of policing, which help to ensure that all forces are equipped to respond to major incidents or to cope with particular periods of high demand.”
Police Scotland has been approached for comment. - PA
PSNI vehicles block the road at the bottom of the hill down from the church on the way to Garvaghy Road, less than half-a-mile from it, reports Ireland and Britain Editor Mark Hennessy .
A DUP delegation led by party leader Gavin Robinson has arrived at Hillsborough Castle to meet the secretary of state, Chris Bryant, about the developing stand-off at Drumcree, the BBC reported.
Alliance Party deputy leader Eóin Tennyson and North Belfast MLA Nuala McAllister have also gone inside Hillsborough Castle for their meeting with Bryant.
The SDLP MP Colum Eastwood has called on Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant to “step in” and end the Garvaghy Road parade crisis.
Bryant said on multiple occasions on Sunday that he does not have the power to call off the parade without a request from the PSNI chief constable, Jon Boutcher.
Eastwood claimed there could be a route for Bryant to intervene decisively with the “risk of disorder”, which is now present “in every town” in Northern Ireland, providing him with a potential legal underpinning for the secretary of state.
Bryant cut his participation in the Labour conference in Liverpool short on Sunday to go to Belfast, immediately calling for “compromise”.
Eastwood said: “I have personally, forcefully, said to Chris Bryant today ... and last night, and most days this week, that he has to step in. This decision [by the Parades Commission] is wrong, and he has a responsibility to take the heat out of this and just say we’re going to deal with this properly.”
He said Bryant had a “tough job”, but it was the one in “front of him”. - Guardian
Orange Order members seeking to march down the Garvaghy Road should follow the example of a Belfast lodge that unilaterally decided to abandon a march down Belfast’s Falls Road 60 years ago, Sinn Féin’s former director of publicity has said, writes Southern Correspondent Barry Roche .
Danny Morrison said the claim by the Portadown District Loyal Orange Lodge that members were entitled to march from Drumcree Church down Garvaghy Road to Corcrain Orange Hall as it was the historic route did not stand up to scrutiny, as the order’s traditions have changed over time.
“I lived on the Falls Road before I moved to Broadway in Belfast in 1963 and the Orangemen were still marching on the Falls Road then,” he said. “They used to march from Sandy Road up Broadway to the Broadway Presbyterian Church on the junction with the Falls Road.
An SDLP member of Northern Ireland’s assembly has said she is concerned that the Stormont executive will collapse amid escalation of tensions over the Drumcree parade.
“I don’t know if it will last until the end of the week,” she told a panel at the Labour party conference.
The MLA, from Derry, said the parade crisis had already raised the temperature across Northern Ireland with helicopters out in her city for the first time in a “long, long time”.
She described the ruling to allow the march as “senseless” and “abhorrent” and said it was “irresponsible” of unionism not to have walked the Orange Order away from the parade.
She questioned whether their “game plan” was to bring down the executive.
“At the minute, this instability and insecurity is in real danger of bringing down those institutions and the people at least can afford that are the people that are living in poverty in our communities and delivering living without proper public services,” she said. - Guardian
The 35 members of the Orange Lodge permitted to march on Garvaghy Road by the courts left the Drumcree church shortly before 6pm, but they were refused permission to go more than a 100 yards by the Police Service of Northern Ireland, who told them that they could not allow the marchers to go further on public safety grounds, reports Ireland and Britain Editor Mark Hennessy .
The marchers, led by Portadown No 1 LOL’s Worshipful District Master, Nigel Dawson, returned quietly to the church and went back into the church hall.
Dawson told The Irish Times that they may well do again this evening in a bid to keep up pressure to march on Garvaghy Road, which has not been allowed for nearly 30 years.
“We were attempting, as we did this morning at 8 (am), to exercise our rights given to us by the court, the High Court.
“The police have once again said the road is not available to us and that we can’t proceed because he wants to protect our safety, and that is fine.
“We’ll stay here until the police tell us it’s safe to go home,” said Watson.
Repeating his conversation with a senior PSNI commander, Dawson said he had been told: “He’s saying it’s public order. That’s what he said. Well, if we were to let you go down the road, we can’t guarantee our safety and therefore he has the legislation to say, ‘In order to protect you, I’m not letting you cross’.”
Asked if the lodge would follow through on the pledge made on their behalf earlier by Loyalist influencer and lawyer, Jamie Bryson, that they would “wait an hour, a day or 10 days” to exercise their court-ordered right to march, Watson said they had said repeatedly that they would “give space” to the PSNI to cater for the parade.
The Methodist Church in Ireland said the developments on the Garvaghy Road “threaten a return to tribal politics, division and unrest”,” in a statement.
“Over the last number of years we have seen many across society take significant and sacrificial steps to build a lasting peace. These last days threaten a return to tribal politics, division and unrest.
“It is a time for calm and measured voices.
“For the sake of the generations to come, we urge all parties to work to find a way forward which respects the traditions and identities of all.
“We make this call aware that this may involve sacrifice for the sake of the common good.
“We record our gratitude to the Police Service of Northern Ireland.
“We call on Methodists and all people of faith to recognise the image of God in everyone; to pray for others, especially when we differ; to work for peace, reconciliation and a society in which all know they are respected.”
The UK government’s secretary of state for Northern Ireland declined to say whether First Minister Michelle O’Neill had broken the law by participating in a protest.
Chris Bryant was asked about DUP leader Gavin Robinson’s earlier claim that O’Neill had broken the law.
Bryant said: “I just want to make sure we have fully functioning, as normal as possible, executive and assembly, functioning, working, trying to deliver public services for the people of Northern Ireland.
“It’s not my job to decide whether somebody has or hasn’t broken the law; that’s a matter for others.
“All I would say is that everybody should be co-operating with the police at the moment. That is everybody.”
He added that those in public office had a “particular onus upon us to try and calm and bring temperate language to everything”. - Guardian
For a generation of politicians, journalists and others, the Drumcree parades crisis of the 1990s was a bitter, often deeply unpleasant chapter that had been filed away, often as a bad memory best forgotten, writes Ireland and Britain Editor Mark Hennessy .
But it was never forgotten by Loyal Orange Lodge No 1 on Carleton Street in the town, which still carries many of the divisions of the Troubles.
Each Sunday since 1998 they held a token protest at Drumcree church on the hill to complain about being barred from marching on the Garvaghy Road.
Each year, the lodge submitted an application to march on the Sunday before the Twelfth of July on their traditional route from the church to Carleton Street. Each year, it was refused.
“Nobody wants to go back to 28 years,” said Chris Bryant, the UK government’s secretary of state for Northern Ireland.
“I don’t think there is a single person involved in politics in Northern Ireland that really wants to go back 28, 30 years and relitigate everything and dismantle the Good Friday Agreement,” he told reporters in Belfast.
“I’m very determined that we will do everything to maintain that, but we need to make sure that we have resilience in the political system here.
“I think it’s all the more important that we have a Parades Commission that is fully functioning. Of course, these issues were litigated in court at length yesterday afternoon and through into the night.” - Guardian
The PSNI chief constable Jon Boutcher said: “So whatever’s been happening, by whatever party, we’ve been gathering the evidence of what they’ve been doing.
“So we’ll deal with that at the right time.”
He said a successful conclusion to the current situation would be that “not one hair on one head gets harmed”.
He wants everybody to find “a place that they can, with dignity, walk away from the current situation”.
He said there needs to be a “longer-term conversation, which involves politicians and the people involved in what we’ve seen in the last 24 hours, trying to find a space that they can resolve these issues”.
The UK Government’s Secretary of State for Northern Ireland has said he has spoken to the Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs several times today, as a stand-off continues on the Garvaghy Road.
Christ Bryant arrived in Belfast this afternoon, having left the Labour Party conference in Liverpool early as tensions over the scheduled Orange Order parade through a largely nationalist area of Portadown, Co Armagh intensified.
While certain unionist politicians have called on the PSNI to investigate demonstrators gathered on the road intent to block the parade, Bryant said it is “not my job to decide whether somebody has or hasn’t broken the law”.
“All I would say is that everybody should be co-operating with the police at the moment,” he said, adding that “those of us who are in elected office have a particular onus on us to try and calm and bring temperate language to everything.”
“If there’s a way of finding a way through this, we want to be able to put ourselves at the service of others to be able to achieve that,” he continued.
“It is only compromise that is going to get us through these difficult moments,” he went on, adding “the resilience of the political system in Northern Ireland is really important, we’ve made so many strides, I feel so frustrated.”
While he said he feels “so frustrated” over the ongoing dispute, “we can get through this. There are decent people of good faith on every side of this argument.”
The Catholic and the Church of Ireland Archbishops of Armagh have issued a joint statement calling for an “inclusive and reconciling initiative” to be introduced urgently to find “a way through this current crisis.”
“Too much is at stake,” said Archbishop Eamon Martin and Archbishop John McDowell, who said they “feel deeply the concerns of the people of Drumcree and the wider community that we serve.”
“As our community faces the crisis in Drumcree today, in which so many sincere views, painful histories and important issues are at stake, we cannot think of any time in the last 30 years when this simple message needs to be more urgently heard,” they said.
“How can we be good neighbours to each other? What can we do to patiently, constructively and positively build on all the sincere and generous efforts over recent years to foster mutual trust and understanding among our different traditions?”
The archbishops said respect for the rule of law and the use of peaceful and democratic processes “are vital to a stable and democratic society, even when they are difficult and challenging”.
“We are willing to do all that we are asked to guide the feet of all, in the name, and after the example of Jesus, on the way of peace, and the building up of a better future for all. We call for the urgent creation of a constructive, inclusive and reconciling initiative to patiently find a way through this current crisis. Too much is at stake.”
Senior Sinn Féin politicians, including First Minister Michelle O’Neill, should face investigation and prosecution for encouraging an illegal protest to block the Orange Order’s parade in Portadown, Ulster Unionist Party leader Jon Burrows has said.
“The PSNI must investigate what happened and follow the evidence wherever it leads, including to those in the most senior positions. Where offences are established, those responsible should face prosecution,” he said.
Burrows has called for “cool heads and calm language” as the stand-off continues. The UUP leader has up to now tried to separate himself from the more incendiary language used by the DUP over the blocked march by Orange Order members.
“Two things can be true at once: those who broke the law must be held to account, but we also need an urgent off-ramp to create space to resolve this situation. A prolonged confrontation risks damaging our peace, our economy and our stability, and putting police officers in harm’s way,” he said.
Burrows, a former PSNI officer, said he had spoken to Chief Constable Jon Boutcher and offered his full support as the force deals with an “exceptionally challenging situation”.
The ruling of the Court of Appeals, which in the early hours of Sunday granted the Orange Order permission to march, “should be respected lawfully” and “anyone with an issue should take it to court”, he said.
“The procession was permitted under a lawful determination, tested in court and upheld hours before it was due to take place,” he said.
“Blocking the road to prevent it is disgraceful and the apparent unnotified protest must also be investigated. For 28 years the Orange Order abided by determinations restricting its route. Had its members defied those determinations, they would rightly have faced the consequences. The law must apply equally today.”
Ulster Unionist Party politician and Northern Ireland’s Health Secretary Robbie Butler has called for “everyone to take a step back, lower the temperature and allow the PSNI to do its job”.
“We cannot afford more instability,” he said, adding “despite its flaws, devolution really does matter.”
“Politicians of every shade should be focusing on the budget crisis, not opening up another one and inflaming tensions over parading,” he said.
