title: Donald Clarke: The anger Meryl Streep and Greta Gerwig have triggered over Narnia is biblical
description: There’s nothing wrong with their upcoming film Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew featuring a female Aslan. Jesus wasn’t a lion either
content:
W e should have seen this coming. It was reported as long ago as April of 2025 that Meryl Streep was in talks to voice Aslan, the lion, in Greta Gerwig ’s upcoming Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew for Netflix . There was some rolling of eyes. Then the story went away again.
Now, four months before the film is scheduled for cinema release, Gerwig confirms Streep will indeed be taking over voicing duties most recently carried out by our own Liam Neeson.
We are used to nerds complaining when some actor is deemed insufficiently magnificent to play their favourite superhero. But the anger this week was biblical. The aggrieved were nailing their numbered objections to church doors in Wittenberg. (Not really, but you get the idea.)
Jenna Ellis, a conservative lawyer and former adviser to Donald Trump, was having none of it.
“Greta Gerwig cast Meryl Streep as the female Aslan in her new ‘adaptation’ of Narnia, profaning Christ with the divine feminine,” she thundered .
“It’s an act of creative vandalism pretending to be artistic sophistication.” L David Fairchild, a pastor from Texas, elaborated .
As you will probably be aware, Aslan is not just a talking lion in the sense that Dorothy’s cowardly friend in The Wizard of Oz was just a talking lion.
CS Lewis’s The Chronicles of Narnia, written between 1950 and 1956, propels earthly children into a magic realm of white witches, amiable fauns and gloomy “marsh-wiggles”.
Readers and critics have puzzled over Christian readings of the text ever since. Lewis, raised in Belfast, denied the sequence was an allegory but made no secret of its religious underpinnings.
“What might Christ become like, if there really were a world like Narnia and He chose to be incarnate and die and rise again in that world as He actually has done in ours?” he wrote. Aslan is that figure.
[ How CS Lewis’s Irish childhood influenced the Chronicles of Narnia Opens in new window ]
The controversy, if it can be called that, comes at a time when the recreationally offended are on alert for anything that reeks of gender swapping or trans accommodation.
Just cock an ear to the yelling about Elliot Page’s appearance in The Odyssey a month or two ago. Jesus Christ was a man. Casting a woman, even one so exalted as Meryl Streep, is, the argument goes, an act of blasphemy (or something).
If my memory of Sunday school serves, Jesus wasn’t a lion either. Indeed, his humanity was a pretty big deal. “But look! He has a mane in the stills!” the originalists yell. Well, sure. But is that supposed inconsistency any more egregious than the fundamental absurdity of a talking lion?
Once you let an animal speak, it requires little more of a leap to have him pilot a steamboat (like Mickey Mouse) or sell breakfast cereal (like Tony the Tiger).
At base, the current kerfuffle is, for all the bashing of Bibles, not much different from 100 other furies about film-makers not kowtowing to the sacred principles of faithfulness.
There was a similar rumble this week when Florence Pugh, who plays the psychotic Cathy Ames in Netflix’s imminent adaptation of John Steinbeck’s East of Eden, dared to suggest the series doesn’t try to make the character “a monster”.
The release of images from The Magician’s Nephew, the first in a new Narnia imagining, to accompany a feature in Empire magazine provided the purists with a wealth of ammunition.
[ Florence Pugh on getting her way: ‘I was very sassy. I cornered a few people’ Opens in new window ]
We already knew Gerwig was having fun with the chronology. The Magician’s Nephew was the sixth of the seven novels to be published, but it is set before the time frame of The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, the first book to emerge. It had not, however, been made clear that she was taking promiscuous influence from 1970s rock opera.
“David Bowie saved my life. Paul McCartney saved my life. David Gilmour saved my life. Pete Townshend saved my life,” the director told Empire.
Cue more hysterics about not remaining true to the source material.
[ Saoirse Ronan says she was meant to be ‘a weird Barbie’ in Greta Gerwig’s film Opens in new window ]
Here’s the odd thing. In cinema and television, ardent fans, many just wishing to show off they’ve read the book, get in a tizzy at the tiniest deviation from their beloved tome. Just watch how they are already poring over stills from the upcoming Harry Potter series.
Yet, over the past century (and before), theatrical producers have worked the most imaginative liberties on Shakespeare to only the mildest of objections. Would anyone now blink an eye if you staged Macbeth as kabuki or Coriolanus on an aircraft carrier?
If the screen originalists had their way, all Hamlets would play out in doublet and hose while banners flapped over the cardboard ramparts of Elsinore. How unspeakably dull.
I have no idea how The Magician’s Nephew will turn out, but I praise Gerwig for her willingness to experiment.
East of Eden streams on Netflix from Thursday, October 1st; Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew is due to be released on Friday, February 12th, 2027

title: Irish artist Donald Teskey at 70: ‘There’s a lot of history – of baggage – to painting’
description: Donald Teskey couldn’t find a way to make his paintings say what he wanted them to. Then he spent time on residencies, both with other artists and alone
content:
A rtists can be more susceptible than most to the subtleties of their surroundings, but environment affects us all. This is something for planners to consider as they mark the routes of roads and draw out the boxes that will both shelter and inflect the passage of our lives.
These questions have come to mind in the company of Donald Teskey , who turned 70 this year. The acclaimed Irish artist is talking from his newish studio in rural Co Mayo ; he moved from Dublin two years ago.
Teskey turns his screen to show, via Zoom, his works in progress, so that I can watch this new location seeping into his art. On tables and benches is an array of paints and brushes, papers and cloths. An apron that has clearly seen plenty of art action hangs from a hook. There are canvases nearing completion on the white walls. One shows the rugged scene where the nearby estuary widens to meet Blacksod Bay.
You read in art-history books about an artist’s “mature period”, so how does Teskey feel, at 70, about his own progress? “I guess you can count 70 as mature,” he says with a thoughtful smile. “It’s a lot to me. Otherwise I’d have to live quite a long time to reach my mature period.”
He laughs. “But I think it’s more when an artist really finds themselves, and that can happen much younger.”
He dates his own moment to 2005, and his Tidal Narratives exhibition at Limerick City Gallery of Art. “The largest canvas was 14ft by 8ft. Being able to work in that scale, that was a kind of benchmark – that moment in a career that takes it to another level.”
During the boom Teskey’s level was dizzying. His exhibitions at the Rubicon Gallery, in Dublin, would sell out, his work then frequently flipped at auction for multiples of the original price.
His work is still in strong demand, both on the primary and the secondary markets. He has said that the memories of those times prompted both excitement and discomfort; but he has also remarked that “it’s better when it’s slower”, as it means he’s “not quite as anxious”.
He doesn’t necessarily know how a painting is going to turn out. Our virtual studio tour shows one smaller canvas, colour-washed in a stony ochre, while another pair of paintings, side by side, are all gestural swirls of grey.
“This is me just starting. I put these two together to see whether I’m going to go with it. Now it’s a mass of turbulent underpainting. But it’s kind of lovely,” Teskey says, as if in surprise. “I love the way the paint just kind of sits.”
A level of experiment is going all around. In an adjacent work, the scene is a local view that had begun with a similar grey underpainting.
“With this one I’ve upped the texture and the amount of paint within the body of the paint.”
It starts to sound like a sort of esoteric alchemy. In another canvas, water glows, as if lit from within.
“I have no idea yet what that’ll be,” Teskey says, pausing at the ochre underpainting. “Sometimes it’s to try and spark an idea.”
He will take his sketchbooks on his walks, and a sketch and an underpainting may suddenly seem made for one another. The paintings are not direct representations of what he sees. Instead they’re spaces where serendipities of connection, and of thoughts, feelings, sights and memories – even the sounds and scents held in the land, and in the unconscious – can come to the fore.
In person Teskey has the reserve you often associate with a deep thinker, and he has a seriousness about him, but these characteristics are then belied by his warmth as his reserve drops, and he has moments of honesty and of irreverence that make me wonder how hard won his calm might be.
As he talks through his most recent works, describing hikes in Wild Nephin National Park , and bike rides to the shores of Blacksod Bay, we find ourselves in an interesting time shift, as the subject at hand is elsewhere, at Castlemorris Woods, as explored in his pair of new exhibitions. Running in Dublin and New York, both are drawn from the artist’s year at the Tony and Jane O’Malley Residency, quartered in the late Tony O’Malley’s childhood home in Callan, Co Kilkenny.
Based there for a year, between 2022 and 2023, Teskey began to explore the nearby woods, where he discovered hills and trails, native trees and the solitude he had come to require.
“It was so quiet. You’d hardly meet anyone. You’d wonder, Where is everybody? But of course they’re elsewhere, doing something else.”
That absence of other people haunts the work, as the dense trees, foliage and undergrowth, rushing rivers and calmer clearings have an added idea of the uncanny. There are still some places, even in Ireland, where we humans are not entirely at home.
This was a feeling Teskey had discovered, amplified, on a residency at the Joseph Albers Foundation, in Connecticut, in 2006. There, the vast forest had initially overwhelmed him.
“It was just like vertical bars, like a cage. I was making drawings, but I was really having difficulty getting into it.”
It took a conversation with a Canadian friend to resolve things.
“He knew all about camping, canoeing, walking the woods. He gave me the confidence to approach the woods. It’s like the ocean in a way. It has a power so immense; how people go out in it at all is amazing.”
It is this sense that exists within the trees in the works from that period. Maybe, as what passes for progress erodes and erases our wild and lonely places, art like this will become all we have to turn to. An image of the thing: glowing, contained, powerful.
“Residencies are what has really fuelled my work, and my drive to work,” Teskey says. “You get a period taking you out of your own situation, putting you in an environment where you’ve only got yourself, your thoughts and the world around you to deal with. I have always responded very well to being dropped into a situation like that.”
In this way you could see residencies as little bites at the taste of other lives, and track Teskey’s path from residency to studio and back through his work over time. From his early drawings and city paintings; to the seascapes from his time at Mayo’s profoundly influential Ballinglen Arts Foundation; to the Paris Journal pieces, made on residency at the Irish Cultural Centre in the French capital; to the lush abundance of butterbur painted along the banks of the Dodder near his former Dublin home during the pandemic; place truly takes place in Teskey’s work.
The backdrop of the Tony and Jane O’Malley Residency offers a nice counterpoint to this, as the nuances of place are writ large in the work of both the O’Malleys.
Having met in St Ives in Cornwall, the pair spent time in Ireland and the Bahamas, where the warm and dry climate was beneficial to Tony’s fragile health. With their bird’s-eye overviews of abstracted landscapes, form, in Tony’s paintings, can remain similar. But his Irish landscapes are cast in hues of blues and greens, often grounded in brown; while the paintings from the Bahamas dance with vibrant light.
[ Jane O’Malley obituary: Artist with an innate, impeccable aesthetic Opens in new window ]
Tony O’Malley died in 2003, and Jane in 2023. An exhibition marking the bequest of both artists’ estates to the Butler Gallery is currently running at the Kilkenny venue, where you can make the comparisons for yourself.
Born in Limerick, Teskey graduated from the city’s school of art and design in 1978, but he traces his desire to be an artist to a childhood memory from primary school, “when the teacher looked at my drawing on the wall and praised it. I look back now, and I feel it was the first time I was aware of myself as a person,” he once told me.
At first his work concentrated on drawing. “There’s a lot of history, a lot of baggage to painting,” he says, casting his mind back to the mid-1990s, when his work was starting to find success. “Every time I painted something, it felt like I wasn’t saying what I wanted to say. I hadn’t found the way of using paint that I was able to express myself correctly with.”
Ballinglen unlocked that. “My first visit was confined; my son was small, so I couldn’t stay too long. But I returned the following year, and that really connected me with the landscape. I had been a studio painter, and there were a few artists from America there. Seeing their work, their variety of ways of working in the landscape, this introduced me to landscape painting.”
He describes taking his sketchbook to the rocks at Downpatrick Head. “It’s so full of natural lines and shapes, it almost does the drawing for you.”
It also seemed to echo the architecture he had been exploring through his city drawings. “And then, of course, there was the sound of the sea. Everything was about the incredible sensation of noise, of sound.”
Teskey’s paintings of Ireland’s rugged landscapes and coastlines are well known, but you may be surprised to find that it wasn’t until the pandemic brought him to painting the banks of the Dodder river that he “discovered how to use green. It’s a funny colour. There are so many – not the cliche – but literally, in painting all those shades of green. You often use colours that are not green. You use blues and purples and greys to suggest green. A leaf can be tiny little slivers of green, the rest can be purple, and yet convey the sense that everything is green.”
The year in Callan brought another explosion of green to Teskey’s canvases. It also marked a turning point. He remembers both the paintings and the place. His personal life was undergoing a period of change, and he is now in a new relationship, “so it was important to be able to be there, and feel that weight lifting”.
Has the artist’s 70th birthday marked any more milestones?
“I think I had my stocktaking moment a couple of years ago,” he says. “I had some health issues, and I got over those. I think I’m fine.”
The new studio is in a converted double garage adjacent to his home. “It’s in one of the most remote parts of Mayo, which I adore.”
It is in one of those blessed spots that are quiet but not lonely, and Teskey describes a strong sense of community and friends. “August would be a busy time, but after that it turns to solitude.”
Donald Teskey: Castlemorris Woods, which was at Oliver Sears Gallery in Dublin in September, is at 92NY , in New York, until November 19th. Tony & Jane O’Malley: The Shared Studio is at the Butler Gallery , in Kilkenny, until October 26th

title: Four new films to see this week: Sense and Sensibility, The Lost Children of Tuam, Her Private Hell, Stupid August
description: Daisy Edgar-Jones, Caitríona Balfe, Monica Dolan and Andrew Bennett feature in a quartet of movies released in the week of September 25th, 2026
content:
Directed by Georgia Oakley. Starring Daisy Edgar-Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe, Frank Dillane, Herbert Nordrum, George MacKay, Fiona Shaw. PG cert, gen release, 132 min
Perfectly respectable, adequately acted new take on Jane Austen’s first published novel from the director of the acclaimed Thatcher-era drama Blue Jean. Edgar-Jones and Creed-Miles play the two elder Dashwood sisters. MacKay and Nordrum are their hopeful suitors. The new film – not a patch on Ang Lee’s famous 1995 version – feels frustratingly flattened. That is partly to do with the misty cinematography, the contained performances and the leisurely editing. But there is also a regrettable shortage of humour. And yet. The majestic clockwork ends up delivering the emotional embrace that all Austen fans expect and deserve. Not novel, but pleasant enough. DC Full review
Directed by Frank Berry. Starring Monica Dolan, Andrew Bennett, Ian McElhinney. 12A cert, gen release, 79 min
Berry, director of Michael Inside and Aisha, takes on Catherine Corless’s meticulous historical investigations into the former St Mary’s mother-and-baby home in the Co Galway town of Tuam. Dolan, as Corless, working alongside Bennett as her husband, remains astutely understated; it’s as if the actors want to stay out of the way of the research. Berry’s direction is similarly restrained. Kate McCullough’s plain and observational cinematography and Hannah Peel’s subdued score keep step. Berry has crafted a crucial entry in Ireland’s wider examination of its mother-and-baby homes and institutional control while keeping attendant horrors off-screen. TB Full review
Directed by Nicolas Winding Refn. Starring Sophie Thatcher, Charles Melton, Havana Rose Liu, Kristine Froseth, Dougray Scott, Diego Calva, Shiolo Kutsuna, Aoi Yamada. 16 cert, limited release, 110 min
Dreadful, supposedly transgressive tosh from the director of Drive and The Neon Demon. Her Private Hell is about so little it’s not even about nothing. A bevy of variously gifted actors position themselves around a city of abrupt angles and garish colours composed from boringly virtual sets. More than a few reviews have already compared the visuals to that of a perfume commercial, but I am not sure the scent magnates would tolerate this degree of ugliness. Think more a new-romantic pop video made before the boffins knew which buttons they should be pressing. Exhausting. DC Full review
Directed by Pádraig Trehy. Starring Kevin Barry, James Browne, Cara Jade Chapman, David Coon, Louis Lovett, Jean Law, Pat Egan. 12A cert, limited release, 89 min
The setting is 1960s Ireland, but the iris shots, maps with animated arrows and silent intertitled sequences are rooted in early-20th-century cinema. The heart of Stupid August concerns an exiled “world clown” whose “leftwing politics have recently caused controversy” yet remains a welcome figure on the west coast. A lifelong devotee of silent cinema, Trehy credits his film-making career to discovering Chaplin as a teenager. That performer looms large in Stupid August. Trehy’s latest feature marries silent cinema, expressionism and surrealism to create a historical fantasy that touches on clowns, Nazi hunters and Magdalene laundries. Unique. TB Full review

title: Hope amid the dangers of tech, magic, and bad breakups: this month’s YA recommendations
description: New books for teen readers from Máire Zepf, Kelechi Okafor, Elizabeth Acevedo and Catherine Doyle
content:
“Didn’t I tell her often enough / that the internet is full of bad people and / danger?” Fiona, mother to a teenage girl, rages. “Wasn’t I sick tellin’ her?” In He Loves Me (Not) (Little Island, €11.99), Máire Zepf delves into the fraught world of online predators.
There have been novels about this particular brand of stranger danger since the 1990s, and we are about to step into an era where it will no longer be plausible that the parents of teenagers did not themselves grow up with internet access ; it is a relief, therefore, that Zepf includes these familiar fears but also interrogates them.
Is Daisy, who narrates the first half of this verse novel (previously published in Irish; the prolific author for young people writes across both age ranges and languages), less sceptical of her new online friend than she could be? Yes, I would argue, and I suspect many teenagers will spot the red flags, but this friendship is taking place within the context of constant online messaging , where someone who claims to be from the nearby school may well be. The internet is no longer a niche space, as it was when these kinds of stories were first published; we cannot tell teenagers that everyone online is lying and dangerous when so many adults meet their spouses via dating apps.
And so, when Daisy’s best friend speaks up after something awful happens, it is important: “Why is it that when a girl / dresses in attractive clothes / we dress her in blame too?” she wonders. “It is no life,” she argues, “for a young woman / to be imprisoned in a / safe tower / like Rapunzel.”
The past cannot be undone; however, blaming teenagers for the actions of adults, of abusers, is not the path to preventing future incidents. Nor is it realistic. This stance moves this novel from cautionary tale (or out-of-touch lecture) into something more complicated and interesting; it will provoke discussion as well as keep readers turning the pages.
Speaking of the ways in which technology continues its seemingly inexorable march on our daily lives (and tech bros keep demonstrating they’ve misread all those dystopian novels as guidebooks), meet Dorcas, who is “trying to get her head around her entire life being nothing more than a storyline on the server network of a planet in another galaxy”.
Kelechi Okafor’s Are You Still Watching? (Scholastic, £9.99) takes us to the year 2032, to a small town where no one ever really gets out – they can, of course, but there’s a lot of red tape involved, and something always seems to go wrong – and where a teenage girl has just learned that aliens (who appear “like a pop-up ad” in her mirror) are watching her.
If she doesn’t become more active – become a more dynamic character, in other words – her very existence may be at risk. “More drama. More self-belief. The more exciting you are, the more we enjoy the show, then the higher the chance you have of survival.”
Okafor, who has previously written for adults and small children, uses her debut teen novel to explore the impact of reality television and surveillance on humanity, with a particular eye on the potential impact of AI in a still-racist world.
[ Castles, conspiracies and communism: thought-provoking back-to-school YA reads Opens in new window ]
The death of the fictional Sandra Taylor at the hands of robot police is a deliberate nod to the real-life deaths of Sandra Bland and Breonna Taylor in police custody; the narrator notes that even delivery drones seem to have trouble “not recognizing Black people” as human beings rather than objects.
Her depiction of the alien observers also draws on Yoruba cosmology, and their role in this story is fascinating, if perhaps a little underdeveloped. (Sequel, please?) If the idea that “the universe is just one massive advertising campaign” may seem a tad bleak at first, the reader is ultimately left with much-needed hope.
“My little sister is four and a half months old and already in her first courtroom.” Known troublemaker Lil is glad, sort of, that her whole family shows up to provide “visible support” at her hearing, and to be out of her “jailhouse uniform”, but returning to school on probation, with an ankle monitor, is not exactly ideal. She knows her “impulses are a problem ... most people have coffee bags of self-control, and I got at most a dusting of ground-down beans”, though is less supported in how to manage that.
Her family, too, resists talking about what’s going on with her older brother at college – the strangeness that seems to have taken over him, his conversations with people who aren’t there, the belief in conspiracy theories.
The ways in which neurodivergence, trauma, and mental illness collide with race and class are depicted deftly in Anger is Only a Shadow (Hot Key Books, £8.99), the latest novel from the acclaimed Elizabeth Acevedo.
Lil moves between prose and verse as she steps into her new reality, making new friends and trying to stay in control while being aware that “leashed things yank and yank until they break free or break their own neck”. It is impossible not to root for this girl “made of starred and studded things, more / than wild flesh / and bones and bits that break and get / locked up and can be crushed / behind clanging doors.”
[ Summer YA reads: from a Snow White who’d prefer not to to same-sex love-love on the tennis court Opens in new window ]
The world of Sarah Dessen is much more middle class, though no less emotionally charged. After a pause of several years, the iconic YA author is back with Change of Plans (Simon & Schuster, $21.99), in which high school graduate Finley’s summer plans are upended by first her usually businesslike mother (“She was all surface, gliding. Whereas I was always aware of my feet churning beneath me”) and then by her boyfriend of two years dumping her.
Summer as a liminal, transformative space has always been something Dessen does well; with care and nuance she brings us through Finley’s slow steps into becoming someone different, someone not in her boyfriend’s shadow, someone who might embrace the chaos of a new summer job and a busy extended family she comes to love.
It is a pleasure to see Dessen publishing again and a reminder that quieter coming-of-age stories are still a vital part of YA literature, belonging on the shelves along with the high-concept tales and latest trends.
Finally, Catherine Doyle concludes her bestselling City of Fantome trilogy with The Dragon and the Dove (Simon & Schuster, £18.99), in which her heroine struggles with the consequences of using her powers.
Sera, who “endured the violent shifting inside herself. The feeling that a strip was being torn from the very fabric of her soul”, considers that this pain is to be expected.
“Making saints was no small task. It was a rethreading of the tapestry of fate. Of course it was going to exact a cost. And what did it matter, so long as she could bear it in her bones?” After all, war is coming; her side need all the saints they can get.
This is a solid, satisfying end to Sera and Ransom’s story, with the kingdom changed forever by the final pages.

title: Appeal court overturns ban on Orange Order parade passing through Garvaghy Road
description: Parades Commission had on Friday granted permission for Protestant organisation to march through mainly nationalist area of Portadown
content:
A court in Belfast has allowed an appeal of the decision to bar the Orange Order from parading down the predominantly nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown on Sunday.
At 11.30pm on Saturday, at a sitting of the Court of Appeal, Chief Justice Siobhan Keegan said the Belfast High Court judge who granted an injunction against the march had “unfortunately erred in law”.
Members of the Orange Order had been banned from marching down the Garvaghy Road in Portadown after a judge granted a temporary injunction.
Residents of the largely nationalist area launched a legal challenge against the Parades Commission ruling permitting the Orange Order to walk down the Co Armagh street on Sunday for the first time in 30 years.
On Saturday, Judge Patricia Smyth blocked the commission decision, saying the “long-running dispute has the potential to escalate” across Northern Ireland.
The stand-off at Drumcree made headlines in the 1990s, with nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road opposed to the parade passing through the area, leading to violent clashes for several summers and political tension necessitating a major security operation.
The Orange Order has unsuccessfully applied for more than a quarter of a century to complete its 1998 walk along its traditional route.
On Friday, the commission reversed its long-running determination, to the welcome of unionist parties and outrage of nationalist and republican parties.
Delivering her ruling on Saturday, Smyth said: “The level of mistrust between the residents and the Portadown Orange lodge cannot be overstated.
“It’s also clear to me that this particular long-running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland.”
In the early hours of Sunday morning, Keegan was deciding whether the case can be remitted back to Belfast High Court for a further hearing.
Large groups of people began to block the Garvaghy Road in Portadown shortly before midnight on Saturday, within minutes of the Court of Appeal ruling.
“We’ve been rejected,” shouted one of the protesters angrily as he learned that the Orange Order had been given permission to march after a long day of hearings in Belfast.
Shortly after 12.20am, stewards told the protesters to “go back into the footpaths” as confusion emerged locally about the details of the late-night court ruling.
Earlier on Saturday, a large crowd gathered outside the High Court in Belfast in advance of the legal challenge.
Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, addressed the crowd, saying they were at court to “seek justice for our community in Portadown”.
“All of this depends on the support that we have, not just here, the support that we have in Portadown as you are probably aware, over the last number of days, coming from all of the six counties, and coming from the 26 counties – Ireland’s behind us,” he said.
Alongside Mac Cionnaith were Sinn Féin representatives John O’Dowd and Catherine Nelson, as well as SDLP leader Claire Hanna and MLA Justin McNulty.
DUP representatives Carla Lockhart, Jonathan Buckley and Diane Dodds were also present, as were representatives of the Portadown Orange Lodge and loyalist activist Jamie Bryson.
Smyth had earlier urged the parties in the dispute to “step back from the abyss” and “reach agreement for the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland ”. However, the Portadown District Orange Lodge declined a request to postpone the parade.
The judge noted the important date for the Orange Order is July 5th and therefore there was “no prejudice in adjourning for a short period to allow this case to be prepared by all parties”.
Smyth highlighted that there was “nothing special” about the date of September 27th and said she “hoped parties might agree some midway to hold the status quo” while legal issues were resolved. She also said that notification of counter protest needed “to be taken into account”.
[ Drumcree dispute overshadows last UUP conference before Stormont election Opens in new window ]
In its ruling, the Parades Commission said it understood “the genuine hurt experienced by many residents of the Garvaghy Road”. It said the determination was “not, and should not, be perceived as a victory for one side or a loss for another”.
It placed a number of restrictions on the procession, including limiting it to 35 participants. If the parade goes ahead, it will depart from Drumcree Church at 8am on Sunday, under the commission’s restrictions, and will be a silent parade with no bands. Members of the Portadown lodge had originally applied for a 60-member parade beginning at 1pm.
The PSNI has put in place a significant security operation for the parade, with officers from outside the region set to assist under mutual aid arrangements. – Additional reporting: PA

title: Ireland v Israel: Day of infamy exposes serious lack of leadership in FAI
description: Gavin Bazunu has been left brutally isolated as any semblance of squad unity has been utterly sundered
content:
N ot even the most pessimistic forecasts of the reality of playing Israel could have foreseen a day as abject and rancorous as this.
It began at 9.56am, when the FAI press officer sent a WhatsApp message to an Irish journalist to say Ireland’s press conference, due to start in 19 minutes, would be postponed by around two hours until after their 11am training session. Uefa’s match delegate learned about the delay at the same time as the media. At 10.40am, the Israel FA press officer told us that the Irish training session would be delayed, as he had been told that the Irish team had not yet left the team hotel.
The Irish players would not leave their hotel for another four-plus hours. They were holed up together in a fraught meeting, arguing about whether they should play Israel. The players met on Friday in Pristina to come to a collective stance as to what to do around the match. An eleventh-hour boycott was not on the agenda – instead they planned to air their views and come to a unified position around the prematch protocol such as handshakes. They planned to draft and publish a statement after the meeting, in advance of the Saturday morning press conference.
The meeting was tense and acrimonious, running so long that the FAI delayed the departure of their charter flight to Hungary. Saturday dawned and still the players’ statement had not been published. It needed unanimous sign-off, and unanimity did not exist. Gavin Bazunu declined to approve the statement when asked by the FAI to do so on Friday night, telling them he would talk to them on Saturday morning. Bazunu awoke on Saturday and sought a meeting with Hallgrímsson, and told him he did not want to be involved in the Israel game. Bazunu said he did not want to withdraw from the squad and would make himself available against Austria next Thursday, but his conscience would not allow him to face Israel.
Bazunu’s decision led some players to consider whether to withdraw with him. The total number of players who considered withdrawing is not yet known, with conflicting numbers emerging across the day. At 12pm, with the Irish squad still in their hotel, the Irish media abandoned the stadium to pitch up outside the team hotel. A few Israeli journalists came in tow.
TV cameras and microphone stands were assembled outside the hotel door, while the team bus stood outside, empty aside from its local driver, who looked bored and perplexed. At one point an FAI security guard came out to the bus driver, told him something, and returned to the hotel.
When we asked him whether the team would be going to training, he theatrically shrugged his shoulders to tell us he didn’t know.
Armed police outside the hotel erected a cordon in front of the assembled press, while FAI security smiled half in apology as they escorted hotel guests inside. A couple of local fans sat outside with sour faces, flicking listlessly through the Irish player photographs they had brought along in the hope they would get autographed. We looked at a glossy photo of Caoimhín Kelleher holding the Premier League trophy in a Liverpool shirt and told her that she had picked a bad day to go autograph hunting. An Irish fan hung in the background to the whole scene, wearing a white Irish jersey and a black-and-red cap bearing the logo of the Kosovan Liberation Army.
Journalists sweated beneath the fierce sun and sighed the strange sigh of weary disbelief that is the mark of people who watch the FAI for a living. We wondered whether the FAI would become the first sporting organisation in history to boycott something accidentally; not so much taking a stand as a stumble. Our phones rang with requests from international media outlets, asking what was happening and whether the game would go ahead.
Having met with chief executive David Courell and then among themselves, the players sat in meetings with Hallgrímsson and staff. At 1pm, the players emerged from their conclave, barely visible to us through the narrow gaps between partitions in the window. The players spoke with their families, friends and agents seeking their counsel as to what to do. Some asked how withdrawing from the game might affect their careers at club level. One source close to an Irish player said that the situation had become so difficult that the Irish Government should step in and make the decision for the players. Some turned on Bazunu, one of whom is understood to have abused him directly to his face.
Finally, at 2.20pm, an Israeli journalist yelled to us that the Israel FA had been told the Irish team would be training at the stadium at 3.45pm. After hours of ignored calls and messages, the FAI communications department confirmed this when we asked them, adding that the press conference would be held 15 minutes prior. They did not confirm whether the game would go ahead.
The media scrambled into Ubers back to the stadium where at 3.30pm, Heimir Hallgrímsson finally appeared. He was accompanied not by a player but by CEO David Courell and director of football John Martin. President Paul Cooke, the head of the delegation and the elected representative of the FAI’s General Assembly, was nowhere to be seen, consistent with his message to the Irish press back on Wednesday that it would be “unlikely” that he would do media this week. That no member from the FAI board on whom this decision rests appeared before the media is breathtaking.
Courell read from a prepared statement, apologising for the delay to the press conference. He explained that one player had said that morning that they did not want to be involved in the Israel match – he did not name Bazunu – and that this led to another round of talks among players as to what they should do. Courell described Bazunu’s decision as “a new variable that required time and deliberation among the squad.”
Courell said that at around 90 minutes earlier, the players balloted on whether to proceed with the game. He said there was a “a significant majority” in favour of playing the game, and so the game would go ahead. He persistently refused to divulge the precise result of the vote. When one journalist said he understood that the vote was 14 in favour and eight against and asked if that was true, Courell replied, “a significant majority can be open to interpretation.”
Courell also said the players would not be speaking to the media at all for the rest of the international window; would make a charitable donation that will be supplemented by the FAI; that the players would wear black armbands during the game in recognition “for all lives lost in the conflict”; and that they would refuse to shake hands with the Israeli players and coaching staff.
John Martin sat hunched and silent to Courell’s left, while Hallgrímsson sat to his right, looking wan and almost dissociated. The manager spoke in a low, abashed tone, and when harangued with questions by Israeli media, he was left alone to answer questions about Hamas and his decision to work in Qatar, and later about Ireland’s 1936 match against Nazi Germany.
None of Courell, Martin, nor the press officer stepped in. Hallgrímsson resiled from his use of the word genocide last week, saying he was echoing a slogan used by one of the boycott advocacy groups, “don’t play ball with that word.” His comments, he said, were intended to convey that playing against Israel did not endorse their politics. It was an excruciating scene, with Hallgrímsson at one point talking his way into an endorsement of some social reforms led by the late Emir of Qatar.
We asked Courell how the FAI had allowed it all to come to this, and whether he believes his position as CEO was still tenable. He launched into an epic filibuster – at one point explaining the concept of the FAI’s general assembly for the benefit of the Israelis present – before he eventually revealed the FAI had spoken to around 30 players in advance of the camp to gauge their feelings on playing Israel. They based this list on players’ recent record of caps, and Bazunu was not among the people to whom the FAI spoke.
Hallgrímsson then revealed that he had not spoken to Bazunu in advance of the camp after he was named in the squad. Hallgrímsson said last week that he had spoken to every player he called up and asked for their feelings on playing Israel, but now he said he had only spoken to the outfield players. So, extraordinarily, neither the head coach nor an executive at the FAI had a conversation with Bazunu in advance of this week to ask him about how he felt about playing Israel.
Shortly after the press conference ended, the Irish players appeared on to the pitch for training, five hours and 15 minutes later than billed. The Uefa match delegate asked the stadium staff to put the standard 15-minute countdown on the stadium screens to indicate the portion of the session to be open to the media, and then punched the air in relief.
Israel turned up exactly on time for their press conference at 6pm, with their head of communications reading his own pre-prepared statement. He said the FAI and the Irish players had belatedly come to the right decision, as “the separation of football and politics must be maintained,” adding that Uefa, the Israel FA, and the FAI had “stood together” to avoid the politicisation of football.
He said the Israelis would be offering their hands to the Irish players on Sunday night, and added an addendum that Israel has asked Uefa to reverse the sending off against Austria of their player Saied Abu Farchi, who got a second yellow card for grabbing the corner flag and making a gesture that some interpreted as mimicking a rifle. The Israel FA said he was actually pretending to make a snooker cueing action, “like the legendary Ken Doherty.”
The chief result of all of this is that Ireland will play Israel on Sunday night, but the ramifications of this abject day will be long-lasting, and the toxicity of the fallout may come to rival Saipan.
Bazunu has been left brutally isolated, any semblance of squad unity has been utterly sundered, the head coach looks bewildered, matchgoing fans are already voicing their disgust, and the FAI has been humiliated before the watching world.
There is genuine anger towards Bazunu by some members of the Irish squad and staff for his decision, as if his withdrawal was responsible for this chaos; that without his decision they would have arrived at a satisfactory compromise to continue the FAI policy of merely trying to get through this mess without too many mishaps.
[ ‘It would be wrong to participate’: Gavin Bazunu on decision to withdraw from squad for Israel match Opens in new window ]
But Bazunu is not responsible for any of this, because everything that happened across this day of infamy is a direct consequence of a serious lack of leadership from the Government, Uefa, and ultimately the FAI. All of these bodies allowed the most bitterly contentious news story of modern times to cascade down upon a group of players, forcing them to wrestle with their conscience and careers beneath a torrent of extreme public criticism and pressure, and all before the eyes of the world.
The FAI hoped to wing their way through this fortnight but today collided with its brutal reality. The fallout is only beginning.
Irish football has once again shown the world the importance of leadership by its unforgivable absence.

title: Clayton McMillan encouraged by Munster display despite defeat
description: Head coach said team showed character given an extensive injury list
content:
Although palpably frustrated and disappointed after a game that gradually and grimly got away from Munster , Clayton McMillan also expressed pride in his team’s performance despite an opening day loss at Thomond Park against Glasgow.
“I think it became a game of territory and possession and generating pressure off that,” said McMillan after seeing Glasgow overturn Munster’s 17-7 interval lead to win 26-20, leaving McMillan and his team with the small consolation of a bonus point.
“In the second half, definitely, they had the lion’s share of that and probably took away a little bit of our legs. But I was pretty proud. I think we made 100-odd tackles more than them. We kept bouncing up and going forward and fought right to the end. It wasn’t good enough, but some green shoots there.”
With JJ Hanrahan calling the shots and their Kiwi-reared Irish qualified scrumhalf Ben O’Connor a focal point of their attack, Munster unveiled a string of clever launch plays. Scoring two good tries, they had preserved their 17-7 lead thanks to some superb scrambling defence and a wonderful maul turnover by Fineen Wycherley to look well set at the interval.
“I think that last two or three minutes in the first half shows the character of the group,” said McMillan. “To hold out a team that scored more tries for fun last year. It was probably more disappointing in the first five minutes of the second half, where they scored a try off an error that I thought should have went our way. And then momentum swung and we became an arm-wrestle.”
McMillan was referring to the officials somehow missing a blatant Glasgow knock-on in midfield and wrongly awarding a scrum against Munster in a pivotal moment early in the second half.
“Yeah, I think it was a clear knock-on that should have went our way. And a couple of plays later they’re scoring in the corner on the far side.
“That’s going to happen and at the end of the day we make no excuses. They just had the lion’s share of possession at the right part of the field and did enough to keep the points on the board.”
Still, McMillan believed there were some encouraging signs in this Munster display, all the more so given an extensive injury list.
“Yeah, definitely. Early on in the game when we had our possession in the right parts of the field, we were able to stress them with our strikes and phase play.
“That’s a reflection of new guys coming in and being really clear about how we want to play. You guys would have got a little bit of an insight to that. Possession dried up a little bit, which we’ve already talked about, so we weren’t able to do a hell of a lot more in the second half. But that was nice to see.”

title: ‘It would be wrong to participate’: Gavin Bazunu on decision to withdraw from squad for Israel match
description: Goalkeeper released statement on social media after leaving Irish squad before Nations League game
content:
Irish goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu has released a statement on social media after his decision to withdraw from the Republic of Ireland squad before their matches against Israel in the Nations League .
Bazunu informed the squad on Friday that he did not wish to participate in the Israel games, tomorrow and on October 4th behind closed doors in Bačka Topola, Serbia.
“Representing my country means everything to me. I have the utmost respect for every single one of my team-mates, the manager, his staff and the Irish people,” Bazunu said.
“However I have reached a decision that I have not taken lightly. I am a man of strong faith and try my best to be a person of character and principle therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel.
“My decision is based purely upon my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong.
“It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community but against the atrocities in the region.
“There are few times where you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger and I strongly believe this is one of them.”
Ireland’s press conference and training were postponed this morning by several hours as the team discussed whether to proceed with the match against Israel.
The FAI chief executive David Courell said Ireland would proceed a “significant majority” vote in favour of playing by the Irish players on Friday afternoon.
Former Irish manager Brian Kerr said on Virgin Media that the vote was 14-8, without Bazunu’s vote, quoting his “sources and people close to the dressingroom”.

title: Performance of Munster’s young scrumhalf Ben O’Donovan a positive from Glasgow defeat
description: Glasgow’s superior quality off the bench counts as home side suffer disappointing defeat
content:
A point was better than nothing for Munster and a little like the outcome, despite the sense of anti-climax, the performance was not without its positives either.
There were clear signs that the employment of two attack coaches, with Jared Payne coming aboard to supplement Mossy Lawlor, has sharpened their launch plays and a striking feature of their strike plays, as it were, was the regularity with which Ben O’Donovan was employed.
The 21-year-old is quick over the ground and Munster’s strike plays availed of this by employed as a quasi-playmaker, often becoming the second receiver or getting a second touch further out.
O’Donovan is Dublin-born, with Irish lineage through both parents and a grandfather on his New Zealand-born father Daniel’s side, while his mother Ruth from Dublin. Some of his family holidays were spent in Timoleague, west Cork.
He was reared in Christchurch and played for the New Zealand Under-20s. O’Donovan looked an interesting signing when joining halfway through last season and, having been fast-tracked into the senior squad, looked an even shrewder acquisition in this full debut.
“He’s a kid that come through the New Zealand pathway, played New Zealand Under-20, so he’s a kid that’s actually got talent,” said Clayton McMillan afterwards, “and he probably just sat in New Zealand and assessed the people that maybe were blocking his pathway to professional rugby, and given that his Dad is Irish and he’s Irish-qualified, he took a calculated risk, a brave one I think for a young man to come over here and try his luck with and not only [earn] an academy contract, but he made every post a winner at the back end of last year.”
Munster’s head coach also believes there is much more to come from O’Donovan.
“I think he’s really benefited from having a full preseason, he would have come to us a little bit underdone last year. He’s a great acquisition, he’s level-headed and I think with more games under his belt we’ll start to see his running game come into play, which would have been one of his strengths back in New Zealand.”
Despite McMillan’s own vast knowledge of rugby in his home country, he admitted that this had little to do with Munster acquiring O’Donovan.
“To be honest, not really. He’s from Canterbury, so don’t pay too much attention to those blokes down at that end of the field. But one of my assistant coaches at the Chiefs would have coached him at Canterbury, so he gave us some pretty good intel around him, and, yeah, we’re just grateful that he’s here and he adds to a bit of depth around the nine position.
“We’ve got good young guys coming through, even young Jake O’Riordan, we think that there’s something about his game too, and with a bit more time out in the middle, they’ll continue to grow.”
On a weekend when the Irish summer tourists were still on the sidelines, including both Jamison Gibson-Park and Craig Casey, O’Donovan’s display suggested Munster have some depth in the position now and who knows what the future may hold for him.
After all, Gibson-Park also came through the New Zealand pathway and after moving to Leinster at the age of 24 was still second choice to Luke McGrath a couple of seasons into his time with the province. But he turned out okay.
