title: High Society director Rachel Kavanaugh: ‘Jukebox is often used disparagingly. But a jukebox musical can be brilliant’
description: Musicals are a formidably expensive business, and the jukebox variety offer a sense of security to both producers and spectators
content:
T he jukebox musical is “the cockroach of Broadway”, a prominent New York critic declared in 2018, reviewing another in the long line of theatrical tributes based on existing songbooks of popular artists.
If you were to look at the current offerings on Broadway and the West End, the cockroaches have well and truly invaded. From MJ the Musical to Moulin Rouge, Mamma Mia to &Juliet, big commercial theatres are more than well served by familiar scores drawn from a catalogue of popular song.
“Some music you know by heart”, goes the tagline for the award-winning Buena Vista Social Club Musical, based on the famous album by the Cuban ensemble, which will transfer from Broadway to the West End in 2027.
That show’s motto sums up the whole rationale behind the genre, which seeks to capitalise on an already existing audience. Musicals are a formidably expensive business, and the jukebox variety offer a sense of security to both producers and potential spectators.
The theatre director Rachel Kavanaugh has originated several jukebox musicals over her 30-year career, including A Knight’s Tale, which debuted in 2025, using hits by Queen, Robbie Williams and The Proclaimers to retell the story of the 2001 film, and Here & Now, which visited Dublin last autumn, plumbing the back catalogue of the 1990s pop band Steps to tell an original love story.
Given her production credits, Kavanaugh is well positioned to comment on how sniffy critics can be in their engagement with this dialogic art form. “Jukebox” is a funny term, she says. Although it just describes the genre, “it is often used disparagingly, and I don’t like that. A jukebox musical can be brilliant.”
Kavanaugh’s touring production of High Society, which originated at the Barbican, in London, this summer, might also be defined as a jukebox musical. A stage version of the classic film from 1956, which starred Bing Crosby, Grace Kelly and Frank Sinatra , it uses the songbook of Cole Porter to animate its comic romantic plot.
Porter created dozens of hits for Broadway revues in the first half of the 20th century, before anyone thought to try to make standalone stories out of them. If the critic’s tendency is to categorise the jukebox musical as an exploitative invention, High Society offers a counterpoint.
Kavanaugh points out that High Society “isn’t quite a jukebox musical” in the way her other jukebox projects have been. “There is an existing score with existing songs, most of which come from the movie score.”
But, as Porter stole several songs in the film from his own back catalogue, the origin material might well be described as partially jukebox from the beginning.
Still, Kavanaugh prefers to think of “our stage musical as an enhancement of the musical film’s score, with Cole Porter songs from other lesser-known movie musicals or from his catalogue of standalone classics. So while, technically, yes, you could call it jukebox, it’s a hybrid really.”
Kavanaugh’s work as a director falls broadly into two categories: creating new musicals in a commercial context – Clueless, A Knight’s Tale, Here and Now – and large-scale productions of classic musicals and Shakespeare plays.
High Society, she says, gave her an opportunity to work across both registers. While it is, in one sense, a classic musical, because of its unusual form it presents the challenges of working on new material.
“I have done a lot of Rodgers and Hammerstein , the classic narrative-driven musical,” Kavanaugh says. (The morning we speak, she has just opened a production of My Fair Lady at Chichester Festival.)
But although High Society was written around the same time as My Fair Lady, “it is a very different experience for me as a director. Because it was a movie before it was a stage show, there isn’t a definitive version of the stage musical, so what we set out to do – and what I hope we have achieved – is to make the definitive version. In that way, I needed to bring together both skill sets.”
Ironically, Kavanaugh found the key to unlocking the potential of the High Society musical lay in its jukebox form. The score she started with, she says, “was much more of a confection than a Rodgers and Hammerstein musical. It didn’t have the narrative heft of that kind of classic musical material. It was much lighter on story, and we wanted to find a way to bring as much emotional depth as we could to the characters.
“One of the great blessings is that we were given unlimited access to the Cole Porter canon to enlarge the existing script, and to put in a lot of songs that are not in the movie, to help us create a more convincing story that would work on stage.”
Kavanaugh worked with Stephen Ridley, the production’s musical supervisor, to enlarge the vocal score. “We listened to loads of versions of songs, and we were basically allowed to look at anything except the songs used in Kiss Me, Kate and Anything Goes, so we had a huge array of wonderful songs to mine, and some of them – Under My Skin and You Do Something to Me – are absolute bangers.”
Part of the appeal, Kavanaugh understands, is the familiarity audiences will have with the musical numbers, which also include Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, True Love and Well, Did You Evah?
“These songs have been recorded and rerecorded over the decades: they have become standards, and that is part of the joy. But we have also given them new vocal arrangements, and new orchestrations, to make the songs work for the way we want to tell the story.”
A lot of traditional versions of Porter songs fade away at the end, she explains by way of example. “They don’t have the big climaxes a musical theatre song might have – they don’t have what we call ‘buttons’ – so we have given a couple of the songs big finishes that allow us to give a dramatic drive to the story.”
Kavanaugh also got a thrill thinking of how Porter himself might have approved of their endeavour. “Porter was incredibly prolific, but he was also a great repurposer of music. He was incredibly practical: if something didn’t work in one context he would try it again somewhere else, so we are maybe in some way following in his footsteps, and that gave us confidence in making this version of the show.”
For the musical’s “dramatic drive” Kavanaugh plumbed her experience directing Shakespeare’s comedies, whose romantic storylines revolve, as High Society does, around confusion of identities, with the neat resolution of a wedding.
Kavanaugh says she was “absolutely conscious of the parallel” with her work on Shakespeare “all the way through. Working on the design with Tom Rodgers, I wanted the world to be like Midsummer Night’s Dream.
“Like all Shakespeare comedies, we have this move from an interior space to an exterior one – the court to the woods in Midsummer. In High Society the story moves from this enclosed space inside the house to the grounds of the estate. Just like in Shakespeare, this means the social norms and boundaries dissolve, before normality or harmony or balance is restored and everyone ends up with the right person.”
Also key to Kavanaugh’s vision were the touring prospects of the work, which were part of the brief from the get-go. “Our run at the Barbican was always only going to be just a part of [the production’s] life, so it was important that we would build a set that would fit into every theatre we are visiting, including the Bord Gáis , so no audience would be getting a pared-down or poorer version of the show.
[ Judy: End of the Rainbow review – Anna-Jane Casey’s voice soars as it conveys a heart almost ritually broken Opens in new window ]
“But we applied that logic to building the company too. We wanted [a cast] that would be there for the long term, the whole run – not where we would have a London version, with star names who would leave when we started touring – and that is relatively unusual.”
Kavanaugh found a terrific group of talented stars ready to commit. Some, like Helen George, who plays Tracy Lord, and Julian Ovenden, as her estranged husband, are stalwarts of the stage musical. Others, like Freddie Fox , who is known for villainous turns in TV dramas like Slow Horses and House of the Dragon, make their musical-theatre debuts. Fox gives a show-stealing performance as the romantic hero Mike Connor.
No matter where they are, Kavanaugh is delighted to emphasise, audiences will be getting the same “naughty and mischievous and playful” experience: a perfect escapist tonic.
High Society is at the Bord Gáis Energy Theatre , Dublin, from Tuesday, October 20th, until Saturday, October 24th

title: Mainie Jellett at Whyte’s auction: a unique marriage of cubism with religious and Celtic motifs
description: Two particular pieces mark the artist’s concerns: La Pietà and Nude by the Sea
content:
W hat a difference a year makes – Mainie Jellett painted her charming and delicate little watercolour, Gorse (€1,500-€2,000) in 1920. She, or less likely a subsequent owner, had liked it enough to put it up in her studio, arrayed to inspire. You can see the pin marks that make this piece even more alive to the mind. A year later, Jellett and her friend Evie Hone would be in Paris, studying cubism and exploring abstraction under the tutelage of André Lhote and Albert Gleizes.
As last year’s excellent exhibition, Mainie Jellett and Evie Hone: The Art of Friendship, at the National Gallery of Ireland showed, Jellett and Hone didn’t ditch realism entirely, but the modernism they returned to pioneer in Ireland was defining. Gorse features alongside some of Jellett’s abstract works in a sale at Whyte’s, viewing now and at auction on September 28th. Two particular pieces mark the artist’s concerns: La Pietà (€20,000-€30,000) was painted in 1928, the same year she was among the nine Irish artists representing Ireland at the Olympics, back when art depicting sport was a medal category. In it, cubism allies with religious and Celtic motifs, three pillars of Jellett’s unique style.
Was the religious element a Trojan horse to make her art more acceptable to home audiences, as has been suggested? Maybe, but it is more likely that her Christian convictions found a rich expression through her expanded artistic vision. Nude by the Sea (€90,000-€120,000) was made more than a decade later, and is a more secular work entirely. A magnificent arabesque of a painting, the nude figure appears to be made of the land, or is it that the land is made of her? Art historian Joseph McBrinn believes the work was one of just eight oil paintings in what was to be Jellett’s final solo exhibition in Dublin in 1941. If so, it had illustrious company in Achill Horses, now in the collection of the National Gallery of Ireland; and The Land, Éire, which sold at Whyte’s in 2019 for €110,000, having been estimated at €26,000-€40,000.
Barrie Cooke, who died in 2014, was perhaps most famous for his series featuring great Irish elk skeletons, discovered preserved under the boglands. But he was also a passionate champion of the environment, making paintings of algae bloom and, also at Whyte’s, the prosaically titled, Sewage Outlet, River Nore (€4,000-€6,000). A remarkable painting, the date alone should sober us up: 1982; how things don’t change. Three very nice pieces of minimalist abstraction by Cecil King are included in the sale too. All finely balanced tension, they prove you don’t need extravagant gestures to hold a page (€1,500-€2,000 and €3,000-€5,000).
What is the collective noun for whiskeys? A clutch? A sip? A spill? Dolan’s autumn art auction happens to have plenty of the Midleton variety, the oldest being 1998 (€750-€1,000). Or settle down with a series of them from 2021 to 2025 (€1,300-€1,600). On the art side, if you ever wondered what the cuddly toys do when you’re out, Susan Cronin’s Waiting €2,800-€3,500) has the answer: your bears line up at the window and watch for your return. The Dolan’s sale takes place on September 28 th from 6.30pm, and also includes works by Charles Harper, John Shinnors, Charles Harper, Mark O’Neill and Flora Mitchell.
As if you needed an extra reason to stay in such lovely spots as Sheen Falls, Ballyfin and The Montenotte, the hostelries have art in the offing too.
Gormley’s Art at the Falls sees works by the likes of Patrick O’Reilly, Debbie Chapman, Christine Bowen, Andy Warhol, Banksy, Salvador Dalí and Tracey Emin dotted about the hotel and gardens until October 18th.
The Victorian sunken gardens at The Montenotte feature the work of Mike Duhan until the end of this month.
“I want my work to be as timeless as the human condition itself,” says Duhan, adding that he hopes the 50 pieces displayed “don’t distract from those views”.
And Ballyfin continues its artist-in-residence programme in collaboration with Oliver Sears Gallery Dublin, and John Martin Gallery London. Sarah Iremonger will be on site October 19th-21st, while Samuel Walsh is at the hotel November 8th-10th, during which informal chats, exhibitions and cocktail hour conversations are the order of the day.
Alternatively, you can learn to do it yourself, as Blue Book member Coopershill House, Co Sligo, is offering an artist retreat week, led by Tracey Sweeney and Marian Garvey, and put together by Geraldine Benson Tucker. Running October 24th-31st, it includes seven nights’ accommodation, all meals, tuition, materials, talks, writing classes and other creative activities, at £2,995 (€3,439) per person.

title: Do you love good French sauvignon blanc? Try a white Bordeaux
description: Bordeaux tends to be known for its reds, but wine insiders have been admiring its whites for years
content:
When the word Bordeaux is mentioned, we tend to think of red wine. Most of the time we are correct; over 80 per cent of production is red wine, with the remainder being comprised of sweet, rosé, sparkling and white.
The dry white wines have been a Bordeaux insider secret for many years. Well-priced and usually well-made, they can offer great value. Those made from pure sauvignon blanc are typically aromatic and fresh with racy green fruits. Fans of Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé should enjoy them. Some producers blend in Sémillon grape, which lends texture, a waxy note and sometimes exotic fruit, and/or Muscadelle which adds floral notes of honeysuckle and acacia. Either way, the wines can be very good and often very reasonably priced.
The best come from the Péssac-Léognan subregion. Wines such as Domaine de Chevalier, Châteaux Haut-Brion, de Fieuzal, Pape-Clement, Smith-Haut-Lafitte and Carbonnieux are all very well priced compared to similar wines in Burgundy. Most of these wines also age very nicely.
At a less exalted level, there are plenty of well-priced white Bordeaux priced between €15-35. I feature three today. I also enjoyed the Le Dauphin d’Olivier 2023 (€33) and the Château Marjosse (€22), both from Whelehans. However, while there are plenty of inexpensive red wines, I was unable to find any white Bordeaux at €10 – strange given that Bordeaux is going through a crisis at the moment. I feature the Haut-Poitou sauvignon blanc from the Loire Valley instead.
A very tasty aromatic sauvignon blanc with lifted aromas and plump green fruits. This would make a nice aperitif or partner for light salads.
Fresh green apples with a touch of pineapple, some herbs and a crisp dry finish. This would be better with food; plain grilled white fish with lemon or goat’s cheese.
Avoca; Boxofwine.ie; MacGuinness Wines, Dundalk; Higgins Family Butchers, Dublin 13; Worldwide Wines, Waterford
Herbal aromas, vivid grapefruit and peach with a long dry finish. Great value for money.
WinesDirect.ie, Athlone, Mullingar, Co Westmeath
A dry wine from Sauternes producer Château Suduiraut. Rounded, lightly honeyed notes balanced nicely by some citrus. Try it with grilled black sole or scallops.

title: Eating in: It doesn’t get better than a movie night at home with classic, elevated snacks
description: Who needs a cinema when you’ve got loaded nachos with chilli beef and parmesan?
content:
T his week was inspired by a recent, rare trip to the cinema. Let me paint a picture for a moment. We are in the depths of the most beautiful chaos, with two under two, two businesses on the go and a furry animal walking around the house who thinks she owns the place. These are all good complaints, but many who read this will just “know”. So when the offer came to head off to the movies for the evening, it felt like something between winning the lotto and a week in Vegas – only better. Never mind Michelin-starred restaurants or fancy meals, the combination of a lavish seat, bucket of popcorn and surprisingly delicious, warmed nachos with tomato dip was luxury personified. For the record, it was The Odyssey, and, between my lack of sleep and crazed schedule, the dog scene reduced me to tears. But we are not here for a film reviews.
The experience got me thinking about food in film, and whether there were recipes to develop. Liver with a side of fava beans and a glass of Chianti came to mind but I thought it a bit too 1991 for the times. Perhaps a bowl of gruel and “Please, sir, I want some more”? Nope; my mind kept returning to the warm nachos with spicy dip. This week’s dishes are inspired by the potential of the cinema. Just imagine heading to the latest blockbuster and getting treated to loaded beef cheek nachos or a beautiful hot dog with Irish pork sausage. Well, you don’t have to. These are easy to re-create at home and can be premade, then left to reheat once everyone is settled in front of the TV. Sometimes, there’s nowhere like home.
The first recipe is a take on chilli con carne, but we have upgraded the mix to include beef cheeks and kidney beans. A simple taco sauce is just mixed together, while Parmesan brings a sense of luxury to proceedings. I make this in bulk and freeze it down to serve in batches. For tortilla chips, look no further than Nino Blanco, produced in Co Tipperary and packed with flavour.
The second recipe relies fully on the quality of the sausages, so source the best you can find. The jalapeño crème fraîche is a different and delicious alternative to the standard ketchup and mustard, while caramelised onions bring a sweetened edge. The saltier the sausage, the better this will be. All you’ll need after this will be a bucketful of popcorn and a captive audience. Tip of the week: when browning beef, make sure you get as much colour as possible. Don’t overload the pan and do it in batches if required. If there’s too much smoke, add more vegetable oil to the pan.

title: How to set your garden ablaze with autumn colour
description: It’s the season for trees and shrubs to steal the limelight through a process of radical transformation
content:
A t this time of year, a coterie of trees and shrubs begin to steal the limelight through a process of radical transformation, a metamorphosis of colour that ensures their elevation into the ranks of garden classics. I’ll always remember, for example, the first time I saw a Persian ironwood in all its fiery autumnal glory, its foliage a luminous blaze of crimson and gold. Ultra-resilient in the face of drought, waterlogged winter soils and even fierce cold snaps, a magnificent specimen of this large, deciduous, spreading shrub or tree greets visitors to the National Botanic Gardens in Glasnevin, where it grows just inside the main entrance. Suitable for bigger gardens, Persian ironwood’s autumn colour develops best when grown in full sun, but it will also grow in shade.
Famed for its elegant, palmate, finely lobed foliage and graceful growth habit, the large and very diverse species known as Acer palmatum or Japanese maple is equally prized by gardeners for its autumn colour. First introduced into cultivation in Europe in the early 1800s, the number of varieties now in cultivation is mind-bogglingly huge – as much as several thousand – and contains many that are garden worthy. But the variety most universally celebrated for its remarkable display of autumn colour is Acer palmatum ‘Osakazuki’, a bushy shrub or small tree whose leaves turn a brilliant shade of flame-red at this time of year.
Others Japanese acers that shine brightly in the autumn garden include Acer ‘Bloodgood’, a medium-sized upright tree with purple leaves that begin to flush bright red as winter approaches; and Acer ‘Sango-Kaku’, an outstandingly ornamental garden tree whose finely cut green foliage brightens to buttery shades of yellow and orange before they fall to reveal coral-pink young shoots.
For those of us with very small gardens, or with a soil not suitable for cultivating these lime-hating trees, container-growing is the way to go. Compact, slow-growing varieties of Japanese acer suitable for growing in a large tub or container and which offer a wonderful display of autumn colour include Acer palmatum ‘Garnet’; Acer palmatum ‘Dissectum’; Acer palmatum ‘Beni-Maiko’; and Acer palmatum ‘Orange Dream’. To keep them happy, make sure to give these containerised specimens a 50:50 mix of ericaceous compost and a loam-based John Innes compost, keep them regularly watered, and top-dress them in spring.
Japanese acers growing in the ground need a deep, humus-rich, moisture-retentive but free-draining neutral-to-acidic soil to thrive, and are excellent candidates for a slightly shady, sheltered garden where their delicate foliage won’t be damaged by spring frosts, icy winds or intense summer sunlight, or by gales that might bring their autumnal displays to an untimely early end.
Yet another woody species that brings a joyful burst of brilliant foliage colour to the autumn garden is Ireland’s very own native spindle, Euonymus europaeus, a gorgeous edge-of-woodland or hedgerow species that’s also prized for its highly decorative, long-lasting, lipstick-pink and orange fruits. This grows wild in my own neck of the woods in rural Laois, lighting up the hedgerows at this time of year with its foliage in fiery shades of russet-red and crimson. Ultra-hardy and happy in either full sun or shade and a damp soil, the spindle bush also happily tolerates a lime-rich soil. While naturally bushy, it can be easily crown lifted to form a very decorative small tree. Cultivated forms are also available, including Euonymus ‘Red Cascade’, which has gently arching branches, while for something suitable for a small garden, seek out its colourful cousin, the winged spindle or Euonymus alatus.
For gardens where growing space isn’t an issue, the magnificent sweet gum tree, Liquidambar styraciflua, has traditionally been considered one of the arboreal glories of the autumn garden on account of its stupendous size, star-shaped leaves and eye-stopping display of brilliantly colourful autumnal foliage.
A native of the US, where its popularity is now in steep decline because its sticky, prickly fruits are such a hazard, in Ireland this tree does best in warmer parts of the country where its wood can properly ripen. While the fruits aren’t always reliably produced on most Irish sweet gum trees on account of our cooler summer temperatures, it’s worth noting that this may not be the case for very much longer because of climate change .
A very fine alternative – some would argue finer – is the katsura tree, Cercidiphyllum japonicum. This majestic, deciduous, lime-tolerant tree is famed for its graceful growth habit and extraordinary display of autumn foliage colour as well as the sweet, butterscotch scent of its heart-shaped leaves as they fall. In ideal conditions it can eventually grow as tall as a beech tree, but is very suitable for coppicing to keep it much more compact. Best in a deep, rich, moist soil with shelter from icy winds and harsh frosts, one of Europe’s largest specimens – a champion katsura tree probably planted in the late 1800s and last measured in 2021 at 22m x 5m – grows in the gardens of Ashbourne House in Glounthane, Co Cork.
Plant Collectors, Exploration & Empire, a guided tour at the National Botanic Gardens: Sunday, September 27th at 2pm, Glasnevin, Dublin 9. Part of Dublin Festival of History 2026, prebooking essential via Eventbrite.
How to Start A Fruit Garden: Sunday, October 4th (2pm-6.30pm) at the Tilled Earth Project, Tonragee, Mulranny, Co Mayo. A half-day practical workshop and study tour with organic gardener and author Klaus Laitenberger. €80 including supper, greenvegetableseeds.com

title: Exposed – The Scandals that Shook the Irish State: Drawing a line from the past to today’s hot issues
description: Stories of envelopes exchanged in pubs and Mafiosi-like politicians are familiar, but they still shock
content:
Exposed, Scandals that Rocked the Irish State opens with a quotation from an unusual source. Veteran journalist Frank Connolly, whose work played a key role in exposing political, corporate and police corruption in the late ’80s and early 2000s, references a song by Gen Z darling CMAT .
Euro-Country is a threnody for the broken dreams of the generation who came of age during the recession, and in using it, Connolly makes his intentions clear. This work aims to draw a straight line from the scandals that categorised mainly Fianna Fáil-led governments for two decades to contemporary hot-button issues, from housing to climate protection and even Palestine.
Connolly’s reportage led to watershed moments in recent Irish history, culminating in the Mahon/Flood tribunals on planning and payments to politicians and the Morris Tribunal on police corruption. Looking at modern Ireland, with a housing crisis and a resurgent Michael Lowry, Connolly feels it’s time for a refresher course.
Stories of envelopes exchanged in pubs and Mafiosi-like politicians are familiar, but they still shock. Connolly’s forensic attention to detail and capacity as a storyteller translate complex graft into compelling reading. The Kafkaesque experiences of property developer Tom Gilmartin are particularly evocative. Hoping a donation to Fianna Fáil will move a project along, he writes a cheque and asks to whom he should make it out. “Don’t” comes the oily reply, “just leave it on the desk.”
Ultimately, this book is more effective as a historical treatment than as a diagnosis of modern Ireland. Planning corruption is one thing, but the connection between P Flynn and the “current complicity in ... genocide” requires more than just stating it. Connolly also leaves some of the most interesting questions unanswered. What was it about the Ireland of the time that allowed corruption to become so endemic? And, perhaps more optimistically, how far have we come since?

title: Ukrainian Lessons - Art in a Time of War: A plea about a conflict in the here and now
description: Guardian’s chief culture writer offers Ukrainian art as something happening now, not work to be interpreted later
content:
“If it has no culture, Ukraine does not exist.” These are the words of Paulo Makov, one of many Ukrainian artists Charlotte Higgins meets over the course of her three years visiting the country. He highlights an often forgotten aspect of the Russian invasion : the war is about identity, and therefore, culture.
For all the media talk of culture wars in countries experiencing relative peace, Higgins’s book emerges as a stark reminder that there is a much more tangible culture war going on – one in which missiles are being fired and lives lost by the day.
Higgins, chief culture writer for the Guardian , did not set out to become a war reporter. However, her visit to Lviv to cover a literary festival in 2022 convinced her to return to the country, drawing her much closer to the war than she ever anticipated. She meets a legion of artists all responding to the invasion, documenting the seeming contradictions of their emotional responses: cosmic, near-ineffable rage, debilitating compassion, a blend that Higgins argues has produced art that will last. As Kateryna Iakovlenko puts it, “My love is born in grief and sorrow, … and thanks to my rage, it becomes stronger.”
To write about bombs is simple, Higgins argues. The ever-quickening news cycle is not built, however, for the nuance of the poem. Higgins writes with skill about the writing produced in the rubble, the songs sung over air-raid sirens. The case for a book-length project is clear – no newspaper has the room for a study like it. Higgins puts war-formed art in its rich context, and one of the highlights of the book is the connections she draws between Greek myth written in and about wartime, British novels of the 1940s, and contemporary Ukrainian writing.
Higgins offers Ukrainian art as something happening now, not as a body of work to be interpreted later, with the disinterest of decades. In her book, time and space become almost synonymous, and she quite brilliantly exemplifies how a war taking place elsewhere can be as distant to foreigners as a conflict safely consigned to the past.
[ How culture became one of Ukraine’s most powerful weapons against Russia Opens in new window ]
This is the ethical heart of the book, a plea that echoes the artists of the country: “Ukraine’s war is not far away, it is now.”
Andrew Cunning is the author of Clara and Christina

title: John Banville reviews On the Equality of All Things by Carlo Rovelli
description: The Italian theoretical physicist’s most ambitious work so far is marvellous, insouciant and liberating
content:
It is a misconception widely entertained, even by some of its cleverest practitioners, that science is engaged in the pursuit of ultimate, foundational truths about the nature of reality. Science, unlike art, has rigour, and makes rigorous pronouncements on the nature of things. An equation cannot be gainsaid. So it is believed.
This delusion is a relatively modern phenomenon. Even at the height of what we call the Renaissance, scientists – or natural philosophers, as they were called then – did not imagine that they were figuring the world and the heavens as they actually are. Rather, they were content to “save the phenomena”, as they put it, that is, to devise systems that would agree with the evidence presented to them by the physical world. To know how things really are was God’s business, certainly not ours.
With the Renaissance, with the Enlightenment, with the industrial revolution, human arrogance, not to say hubris, inexorably set in. Isaac Newton (d.1747), one of the greatest minds our species has produced, and one of the most unappetising personalities, discovered, or better say invented, a set of laws governing the mechanics of the quotidian world, laws that are still valid, in the quotidian world, at our scale, despite Einstein’s theory of relativity, despite quantum theory, and despite whatever mind-boggling theory is to come next.
We live in a Newtonian world. The table we eat at is made up of a countless number of unimaginably tiny particles, yet it stoutly sustains our plates, our knives and forks, and our elbows. As Carlo Rovelli writes: “We are in the world. We are here. And we are home.”
But are we content, here at home? Do we not, in what the poet Wallace Stevens called our “rage for order”, still hanker after simple, stable, incontrovertible proofs of the world’s workings? Indeed we do. But Rovelli is here, gently, to dash our hopes: “Respectful of all philosophies, but a humble devotee of the so-called exact sciences, I find it wiser to abandon the goal of certainty altogether, in all aspects of knowledge.” Read that sentence again, and feel the foundations of our most cherished and most aspirational beliefs crumble to dust.
And do not imagine that Rovelli is some new age guru urging us to chill out and stop worrying about ultimate truths. Born in Verona 70 years ago, he has had a brilliant career as a theoretical physicist, doing his main work in the field of loop quantum gravity, as well as being one of the most stimulating popularisers of science and the philosophy of science. His books include Seven Brief Lessons on Physics, The Order of Time and Reality Is not What It Seems: The Journey to Quantum Gravity. He is emeritus professor at the Centre of Physics Theory in Marseilles, and works at the Western University in Canada and the Santa Fe Institute in New Mexico.
On the Equality of All Things is his most ambitious work so far. It is written in clear, crisp prose studded with gems of poetic insight, and ventures deeply into the realms of western and eastern philosophy, quoting as freely from the great second-century Buddhist teacher Nāgārjuna and the 19th-century American pragmatist Charles Saunders Peirce, as from Ludwig Wittgenstein and Martin Heidegger.
Significantly, the book was written in response to an invitation to deliver a series of lectures, or “lessons”, as Rovelli calls them, to the Department of Philosophy at Princeton University late in 2024. One might imagine it would have been discomforting for a physicist to be thrown into such an arena, but if Rovelli was daunted he certainly hides it well. His tone is sure, his assertions are bold, and he has not the slightest hesitation in taking an occasional swipe at what he sees as the complacency, and in some cases the plain stupidity, of professional philosophers. They must have been lively, those couple of months in Princeton, when this obstreperous savant – Rovelli was a student activist in the 1970s – was rattling the branches in that venerable grove of academe.
It would be a disservice to the reader to pretend that this is an easy book, but the labour we are required to give to it is amply rewarded by the excitement of the venture, by the richness of the lessons we are offered, and by moments of pure aesthetic bliss, when this or that knotty concept is suddenly, silkily unravelled for us by the ever-accommodating Prof Rovelli. For the nervous ones among us, such as this reviewer, it might easiest to read the very short preface and jump straight to the afterword, take a breather, and then tackle the main text, which begins with the cheering observation that “We are united by our curiosity.”
[ From the archive: Carlo Rovelli on Schrödinger, God and physics being ‘better than LSD’ Opens in new window ]
However, we are united too, even the brightest of us, by our stubbornness and complacency, and scientists are no exception. For instance, from the very beginning, when mankind began to take the measure of the skies, it was held as axiomatic that the orbits of the planets trace out perfect circles, if for no other reason than that God cannot abide imperfection. This mistaken belief led many of the ancient cosmologists into awful muddles.
One of the most influential of those ancients was Claudius Ptolemy, born in Egypt in the second century AD. His astronomical treatise Almagest sought to solve the puzzle of the planets – and save the phenomena – by adding to their orbits a juggler’s bagful of epicycles, that is, small circles on larger circles, and smaller circles on the small circles, like Jonathan Swift’s little fleas upon the backs of bigger fleas. Even Copernicus (d.1543), in devising his model of a sun-centred planetary system, had to preserve the Ptolemaic pieties. Then along came Johannes Kepler (d.1630), who among many doubts and after deep heart-searching, announced to the world that in fact the planets move in elliptical orbits. Had the world been listening harder, he might have been burnt at the stake for such an outrageous notion.
This is how science works, now in slow accretions, now in fits and starts, now in blind conformity, now in sudden breakthroughs. Always the fog persists, though shafts of light strike through it here and there, and now and then. Rovelli quotes from a speech by Max Born, whom he believes to be the true creator of quantum mechanics, on the need for us to curb our grand notions of ourselves and of our ability to know for certain the nature of reality:
“I believe that ideas such as absolute certitude, absolute exactness, final truth, etc are figments of the imagination that should not be admissible in any field of science ... This loosening of thinking seems to me to be the greatest blessing modern science has given to us. For the belief in a single truth and in being the possessor thereof is the root cause of all evil in the world.”
And it is not just in science that we should show humility. Like Wittgenstein, like the Danish quantum theorist Niels Bohr, like the poet Reiner Maria Rilke, Rovelli not only acknowledges but celebrates the ambiguity of language in which we frame scientific concepts, the ambiguity that “allows [us] to express ever more subtle things in the infinite process that has given rise to the vastness and richness of language and culture”.
But why is Rovelli so much concerned with verbal language, when science has the language of numbers – mathematics – in which to address nature’s secrets? It was Niels Bohr (1885-1962) who recognised that many of the problems encountered in quantum theory derived from the imprecision of the language spoken by quantum scientists. “We must never forget,” Bohr cautioned, “that ‘reality’ too is a human word just like ‘wave’ or ‘consciousness’. Our task is to learn to use these words correctly ...” But note: “correctly” is not the same as “unambiguously”.
To some, and not just scientists, Rovelli’s ideas will seem subversive, even anarchic. Are we to have no solid scientific ground on which to set our feet? No, we are not, and a good thing too; if there is nowhere to stand, we shall just have to fly. Rovelli writes: “To say, as I often hear, that if we know the world’s fundamental physical equations then we know everything about the world, is, I believe, nonsense ... Physics is overrated.” And later he adds: “Even thunderstorms are not yet completely understood.”
The Equality of All Things is a marvellous, insouciant and liberating book. It celebrates our extraordinary ingenuity – we invented agriculture, we flew to the moon – and at the same time turns a sceptical eye upon our grand claims to be the lords of the universe. In closing, Rovelli quotes Milton’s image of Adam and Eve, having been driven out of Paradise, but with “the world all before them”. And he adds: “We are still like this.”
John Banville’s latest novel is Venetian Vespers

title: John Boyne: ‘Wilde was gay, he went to Trinity, he went to England. That’s me, me, me’
description: The Irish author’s new novel is an alternate history in which Wilde lives a long life. It has been on his list of books to write for years, he says
content:
What if Oscar Wilde hadn’t sued the marquis of Queensberry for branding him, typo aside, a “posing somdomite” on the infamous calling card he left at the Albemarle Club in London in 1895? What if Wilde hadn’t set in motion the events that led to his imprisonment and the decline in health that hastened his death at the age of 46?
In his new novel, The Weight of Angels, John Boyne has imagined exactly this. Boyne’s Oscar writes plays the real Wilde never got to write. He meets people – writers, politicians, Hollywood royals, actual royals – he never got to meet. And he eventually strives to push for gay rights, living long enough to see legislative change.
“This one has been on my list for many years, waiting for its moment for me to think, yeah, this is the time,” Boyne says. “I’ve always liked the idea of one moment deciding how your life goes, and I feel he had that moment that night in the Albemarle Club.
“That decision to sue, instead of just saying ‘Sod it’ and waking up the next morning and getting on with his life, was the beginning of the end for him.”
“I do, for a couple of reasons. When I was in my late teens and early 20s, and starting to write seriously and think about Irish writing, I didn’t feel it with Joyce, who I could never really make head nor tail of, to be honest, and I didn’t feel it with Seán O’Casey . Those war plays just didn’t really do it for me. I felt it with Oscar Wilde.”
He lists what they have in common. “Wilde was gay, he went to Trinity, he went to England to study there. That’s me, me, me, as well. He achieved success early in life; I did as well. I was in my 20s when I was published for the first time,” Boyne says.
“We both went through the wringer a little bit as well. I can’t compare myself to somebody of that level of genius, but I would certainly feel more connection to him than I do with other great writers in the canon.”
So, across a zippy 610 pages, Boyne tries to give Wilde “the second life that he didn’t get”. Indeed, his Oscar reaches the grand old age of 98, well past the average life expectancy of the era – “That’s one of those things where I’ve used a little bit of poetic licence” – before dying shortly after the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, in 1953.
‘I think I’m just a writer who happens to be from Ireland. I think Oscar was as well’
Wilde would not have thrived in the real 1960s, he says. “I don’t think it would have been his era at all. I can’t see Oscar with The Beatles or the Stones, or [the Look Back in Anger playwright] John Osborne or someone like that. No, I think I get him out at around the right time.”
As for the social-media age – Boyne is no stranger to the vagaries of X – he thinks Wilde could have been a witty early adopter, “like Stephen Fry”, who played him in the 1997 biopic. “Then he would have eventually said something that brought it all down about his ears,” he says, laughing. “If not Reading Gaol, literary jail, shall we say?”
His Oscar is a man of flaws. “It’s not about making him perfect, not about making him a saint, because none of us are, and he certainly wasn’t. And if I was to write a novel where I just polished his halo all the way through, I don’t think it would be very good.”
So Oscar hurts Gus, the fictional partner Boyne invented for the book, who is “just this normal, decent person who has the measure of Oscar and is pretty much the best thing that’s ever happened to him”.
Oscar has stabs of conscience about his treatment of the young boys he hired for sex but leaves it to Gus to vocalise disgust at the actions of his friend André Gide, the writer, a self-declared pederast. He tells Emmeline Pankhurst he will help with the suffragette cause, and he does to an extent, but “he’s not really willing to dig in there” – a sense of self-preservation kicks in.
Boyne’s Oscar also causes havoc for EM Forster by accelerating the publication of his gay novel Maurice so that it emerges in the 1920s, not posthumously in 1971. “He recognises the brilliance of Maurice and how important it is that a book like that should be published. But he is not willing to publish one himself. He wants someone else to do it.”
The real Wilde “probably did” advance the cause of gay rights, Boyne believes. “Within about 15 years it was looked back on as outrageous and a tragedy and the loss of somebody of real genius,” he says. But he wanted his Oscar to be instrumental in bringing forward the decriminalisation of homosexuality in England.
In reality, this did not begin until 1967, but the book notes an “Oscar’s Law” passed in 1953 with the aid of Winston Churchill. “By the time Oscar gets to Churchill, it’s years after he’s not done for Emmeline Pankhurst what he wants Churchill to do for him, which is to use his voice and help. I could be wrong, but I felt Churchill would.”
Royal events are used as a marker of 20th-century history throughout. “I felt Oscar would be sort of mocking of those coronations but would give his left arm for a ticket as well,” Boyne says. He is “one of those people” who reads a lot about the royals. “You can get some good comedy out of it, some good drama.”
Does he follow the current lot as well? “Oh God, yeah. I’m fascinated by the current lot.”
The Weight of Angels at times leans into the playful improbability of the alternative-history genre, notably when Boyne’s what-if version of Wilde’s lover Bosie (aka Lord Alfred Douglas, the marquis’s son) is jailed and goes on to write The Ballad of Reading Gaol – the exact same one the real Wilde wrote.
But as for the life and career trajectory of his Oscar – he wins the Nobel Prize in Literature and an Academy Award and affects not to be overly fussed about either – it feels to Boyne “like a reasonable concept of how he might have turned out”.
One of the most obviously fun scenes in the book is a conversation Oscar has in 1909 with WB Yeats and Lady Gregory in the Long Hall pub in Dublin about what it means to be an Irish writer.
“I wanted Oscar to question whether he was an Irish writer or just a writer who’s from Ireland. In the same way, are you a gay writer or are you just a writer who happens to be gay?
“And I think I’m just a writer who happens to be from Ireland. I think Oscar was as well. But then he also feels, when he’s talking to them, a sense that he’s not included.
“Sometimes it’s nice to be on the outside while not feeling that you’re excluded from the inside. Maybe that’s how he feels. Sometimes, in chapters like that, I’m asking those questions for myself.”
Boyne researches as he writes because he tends to “get a bit panicky” if he isn’t getting a first draft down. For The Weight of Angels, the research included a trip with his partner, Jake Moriarty, to the Paris hotel where Wilde (or Bosie in the book) died.
“Not a chore,” he says. “The room itself where he died is now the bar downstairs, but we stayed in the Oscar Wilde suite, which has a lot of memorabilia on the walls.”
He also spent about a year reading “every word” Wilde wrote, “not just the obvious things”, to help him capture his voice. The book is peppered with invented epigrams. “I spent a long time just making up as many Oscar-type lines as I could and then finding ways to get them in – the best of them anyway.”
One character interrupts Oscar mid-flow and tells him the lines are “boring”, not “terribly witty” like he thinks.
“Yeah, you do want to throttle him sometimes,” Boyne says. “I also didn’t want to have every line be a joke, because nobody can get through life like that. So there are moments of introspection, humour, selfishness, narcissism. I think anybody in that sort of position probably has all those traits. I probably have them myself.”
As a “novelist at heart”, Boyne identifies Wilde’s only novel, The Picture of Dorian Gray , as the work of his that means the most to him. Throughout the 18-month writing process, he was continually struck by how young Wilde was when he died, and the works that were never written as a result. “I still feel young, and I’m 55. I still feel like I’m only starting out.”
What was he referring to when he said he also “went through the wringer a little bit”? “I was 23 or 24 when I told my parents I was gay, and obviously he didn’t have that experience. He wasn’t really able to say what he felt and who he was until he was in the dock.”
He had it easier than Wilde, a century later, but it was still “a little more difficult” than it is today. “It wasn’t decriminalised in Ireland until I was in third year in Trinity, so my early sexual experiences, theoretically, were illegal.
“When that happens, when you’re 18, 19, 20, whatever, if you know what you’re doing is theoretically illegal, it does mess with your head a little bit. It makes you feel that everything should be conducted in subterfuge and under cover of dark, and it’s obviously not the healthiest way to begin one’s romantic life.”
The lighter side of The Weight of Angels appealed to him because he was “exhausted as a writer” after the two years he spent working on the four abuse-themed novellas – Water, Earth, Fire and Air – that make up The Elements, winner of two top literary prizes in France last year.
“They were all so dark, you know. Barely a joke between the four of them. By the time I finished the last one, Air, I was so drained by the sadness of those four books that I needed to start something big and broad, with jokes,” he says.
He doesn’t need to be so prolific. “I have 28 books, and they’ve sold all over the world and the royalties come all the time. So, no, I don’t have to, not financially, but it’s how I want to live my life. When I die there’ll be a Mystery of Edwin Drood – you know, the unfinished Dickens novel – on my computer.”
As a writing-every-day kind of novelist who has “pretty much become a one-a-year guy”, Boyne is astonished by successful authors who leave long gaps between books. “I don’t know how they fill their days. I genuinely don’t,” he says.
He gets “antsy” just waiting three or four weeks for the editorial notes to come back after he’s handed something in. “Everybody works differently, and good luck to them. If they bring out a great book every eight years, that’s great. But, for me, I need to be every year. Dickens was every year. Philip Roth was every year.”
Boyne plans to spend time over the Christmas holidays and in the spring writing at his new place in Spain, just outside Malaga. He likes the sun and is “doing well” so far in his bid to learn Spanish via Duolingo.
He has already delivered his next novel to his publishers. “It’s an out-and-out comedy. A pure comedy,” he says. “It was time to lighten things up a little bit.”

title: AK Blakemore: ‘The best historical fiction is comfortable living with the sheer weirdness of the past’
description: The author on new novel Doom Painting, the parts of English history that are ‘intentionally minimised’, and her memories of 2005 bombings of London
content:
It’s an hour-by-hour retelling of the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381.
A “doom” was a type of medieval devotional art, usually a church mural illustrating Judgment Day. But the concept of a “doom” wasn’t so unequivocally negative to the medieval mind – it meant an ending, not necessarily a bad one. I wanted to evoke the idea of the imagined future.
The revolt is conspicuous by its absence from most overviews of English history, and is generally interpreted – if it’s interpreted at all – as merely illustrating the invulnerability of the institutions it set itself up against. But figures like Wat Tyler and John Ball have been immensely important helping to define countercultural and later revolutionary English identities for figures like Milton, or William Morris. The radical, utopian thinking of these first common insurgents is a sort of substrate that everything afterwards has been built up on. A glimpse of a different kind of England.
Enormous question! If I’m honest, I think there are some elements of escapism there. Not in the sense of romantic escapism, necessarily, but – speaking as a godless, quite coldly rational person – of a desire for a world that feels more charged with meaning, and more sacred than the modern world. I also love and relish the challenge of imagining myself into shoes so far removed from my own as those of a 14th-century heretic priest, or Witchfinder, or 18th-century French army surgeon.
I think a common difficulty for writers of historical fiction is the desire to make the past relatable to the modern reader – but I think the best historical fiction is comfortable living with the sheer weirdness of the past, and the alienating aspects of moving through it, imaginatively. I never want my characters to feel like modern people in ruffs and pointy shoes.
Yes – “accuracy” is a phantom target. I want the seams to be visible!
I don’t really feel qualified to answer that question. But I would say that some widely held historical misconceptions feel indicative of a certain myopia ... I think the English national identity is so bound up with ideas of infallible continuity, tradition and political stability that the revolutionary epochs that I enjoy writing about are often intentionally minimised as part of the national narrative.
The Manningtree Witches is a fictionalised account of the Essex witch trials of the 1640s, and the ascendancy of Matthew Hopkins, who later became notorious as “the Witchfinder General”. He began his career hunting a local “coven” of women in the town of Manningtree, about 60 miles from London.
The cottage we live in is part of what used to be a 17th-century pub, and the mantel beam in our livingroom shows evidence of apotropaic burn-marks, also commonly known as “witch marks”. They’re sometimes scratched images, or else burn marks made in the wood of a beam with a candle.
We don’t know loads about why or how people would make them, historically, but it’s commonly thought they were a sort of simple charm or spell meant to ward your home against fires (which is why they’re often found near fireplaces or chimneys). They’re more common than you’d think. Keep a lookout for them in old houses!
The Glutton is about Tarare, a French showman, sometime spy and soldier in the revolutionary army. He was known for his prodigious appetite and bizarre public bingeing performances. His life, to read of it, was sad, short and strange, and I suppose the novel I wrote about him is those things also. I suppose I’ve always been interested in darker themes and writing bodily extremity. I’m fascinated by the novel as a sort of engine of empathy, and how far a reader’s empathy can be pushed.
I think writing – and reading! – poetry helps you understand the power of ambiguity, and how, sometimes, meaning has to cut a weird channel through language. I find writing prose far, far easier ... I’ve never been able to simply discipline myself into producing a poem without some initial spark of inspiration. Whereas hard graft will get a novel most of the way to where it’s going, in my experience.
I think so. As I said earlier, “historical accuracy”, in as much as it exists, isn’t totemic for me. And I like using all the colours in the box (so to speak).
Two-hundred words every day isn’t very much, but it adds up fast.
Universal basic income seems like an unambiguous good?
What Am I, a Deer? by Polly Barton is a brilliant novel. I thought Curry Barker’s Obsession was a neat little film. As for podcasts – This Guy Sucked, hosted by Dr Claire Aubin, in which historians discuss the guy that sucked most in their research area.
I was a schoolgirl in London when the 7/7 bombings happened – I remember the fear and uncertainty of that day very vividly.
Probably the Monreale Cathedral in Sicily. Breathtaking.
I’m not very attached to things – but I love my Tessa Metcalfe engagement ring.
I’ve had a battered old copy of Brian Froud and Alan Lee’s Faeries for as long as I remember ... Froud’s illustrations are totally, skin-crawlingly eerie and lovely at the same time. I often find myself leafing through it when the world isn’t feeling quite enchanted enough.
I suspect a lot of my favourite writers would be truly awful company. But Proust seems like he was a laugh and Christopher Marlowe would have some interesting stories? I’ll round things off with Oisín Fagan and Catherine Lacey because they’re both geniuses but also sound.
The best thing about north Essex is the big, painterly skies; the worst thing is Nigel Farage’s Reform.
“Me and my friends would’ve killed ET with hammers I can tell you that much” – @HelloCullen on Twitter (back when it was still Twitter, and ruled).
Doom Painting is published by Granta Books

title: Connacht fall to defeat against dominant Stormers in opening match
description: Irish province punished by Stormers side who wore them down with strong pack
content:
The expectation surrounding Connacht as Stuart Lancaster heads into his second season in charge was not matched by the performance on the field and they were punished by a Stormers side who wore them down with a dominant pack.
It was a bitterly disappointing performance on a night when they honoured the players who won the PRO12 title in 2016, many of those players and head coach Pat Lam back at the Sportsground for the first time since the €40m redevelopment of the ground.
Two late tries wrapped up a big win for the Cape Town side but there was no disputing their dominance throughout.
Connacht were without the seven players who were on duty for Ireland during the summer while the Stormers were missing a dozen players on Springboks duty in Australia.
Connacht led 12-10 at the end of an opening where they were in difficulty in the scrum and guilty of a lot of poor handling in a game which struggled to come to life on a blustery evening.
The Stormers opened up a 10-0 lead by the end of the opening quarter and looked set to extend their lead as they pounded the home line coming up to the interval.
But an intercept a few metres from his own line and a clearance which ended up deep in the other 22 set in motion a remarkable few minutes for Connacht when they hit the Stormers for two tries.
Mack Hansen, back for his first game for Connacht in eleven months, delivered the first one after 38 minutes after Niall Murray won a lineout. Centre Cathal Forde took him up and when he was stopped a few metres from the line, Hansen picked at the base and dived over. Sam Gilbert added the conversion from the left.
And they punished the Cape Town side for failing to clear their lines with the clock in the red with Hansen again going close before a recycle saw outhalf Josh Ioane made the line for an unconverted try.
That good the home following on their feet and ignited a contest which up to then the South Africans had an edge with fewer mistakes.
Hansen’s first action on his return was to spring back and deny centre Ruhan Nel after an intercept from deep, but a couple of phases later outhalf Jurie Matthee got them off the mark with a penalty.
The opening try came after 20 minutes after good pressure from the Stormers with scrumhalf Andre Warner threading a grubber which his fullback Warrick Gelant finished behind the posts.
Flanker Seán O’Brien did well to get back and deny Matthee after a good break before Connacht sorted out their scrum with debutant loosehead Francois van Wyk and Finlay Bealham getting on top.
It took a great triple effort from Hansen, Gilbert and John Devine to prevent winger Seabelo Senatla in the right corner three minutes after the restart before Matthee missed a penalty from 35 metres in front of the posts.
Gilbert extended Connacht’s lead with a 52nd minute penalty from the 22 but a yellow card to captain Paul Boyle for coming in from the side saw the Stormers strike for their second try, mauling their way from distance before replacement tighthead Sazi Sandi got in under the posts with the conversion making it 17-15 to the South Africans after 57 minutes with impressive No.8 Hacjivah Dayimani leading the charge.
Connacht had to saturate enormous pressure but defended stoutly with replacement scrumhalf Caolin Blade, despite limping when he came on after Ben Murphy took a knock, executing a turnover when it seemed the pressure would pay off for the South Africans.
Replacement Yaqeen Ahmed had a try scratched six minutes from time for crossing but the reprieve was brief when debutant Vernon Paolo rumbled over from close range.
And the Stormers secured a bonus point and denied Connacht a losing one when replacement Ezekiel Ngobeni chased a clearance to score in the final play as Connacht’s season got off to a disappointing start.

title: Shelbourne and Galway United cannot be separated for fourth time in a row
description: Jimmy Keohane penalty kick was cancelled out by a Mipo Odubeko’s strike in Galway
content:
A Jimmy Keohane penalty kick was cancelled out by a Mipo Odubeko second-half strike, as Galway United and Shelbourne shared the points at Eamonn Deacy Park on Friday night.
Incredibly, Galway and Shels have now drawn all four of their league encounters against each other this season, 1-1.
The result sees the north Dublin men remain in sixth place in the league table, two points above Galway.
This was a scrappy and physical clash, which was exemplified when United defender Wasiri Williams was forced off with a nasty facial injury just 10 minutes into the contest. Minutes into the second period, his replacement Al-Amin Kazeem was also forced off through injury.
The contest was played at a frantic pace at times, with both teams happy to play direct.
In a game of few chances, it was Shels who had the first real attempt at goal, but Evan Caffrey saw his header into the Dyke Road end crash off the crossbar.
Two minutes later, Anthony O’Connor saw his acrobatic effort just go wide for Galway, to the relief of the away dugout.
On the stroke of half-time, John Caulfield’s charges hit the front, when Keohane converted from the penalty spot. The westerners were awarded the spot kick after Clare native Lee Devitt was fouled by Jack Henry-Francis.
To their credit, the Dubliners responded well, and they levelled matters with just over 30 minutes remaining. Following some good play by Milan Mbeng down the right flank, the ball fell to Odubeko who finished well with his left peg, from just inside the penalty area.
For the remainder of the contest, both sides went in search of a winner, as they both introduced a number of attackers for the final stages.
The best chance over the remainder of the second half fell to Francely Lomboto in injury-time, but Conor Walsh dealt with his effort well.
Backed by a large following, the Tolka Park outfit will feel they possibly deserved all three points on the balance of play, but they had to be content with a point.

title: Ulster’s late comeback not enough against Edinburgh in URC opener
description: Only a madcap second 40 allowed Ulster get in range after they trailed by 29 points
content:
Ulster failed to open their URC account with an expected victory in a crazy game which saw them trail 34-5 early in the second half.
Only a madcap second 40 allowed Ulster get in range and though they did manage to collect two points from this reverse, there was little consolation to be had for Richie Murphy.
Edinburgh, who started by putting together some neat phases, had the opening chance for points though James Grayson hit the uprights and Ulster were able to clear after Jamie Benson secured the ball.
Ulster continued to live dangerously, Michael Lowry charged down near his line and then shortly afterwards it took a lineout steal by David McCann to again allow the province take play out of their 22.
It remained scoreless until the 19th minute when Ulster opted to throw a lineout in near their own line over the back and the ball was picked off by Harri Morris. Soon afterwards, Edinburgh sealed the gift presented to them when Freddy Douglas burrowed over. Grayson converted too and Edinburgh led after 19 minutes.
It was added to shortly afterwards when Ulster were pinged for not rolling away and Grayson bisected the uprights again.
The Irish province rapidly responded though, giving the ball air through Robert Baloucoune’s hands, allied with those of Jack Murphy and Jamie Benson, which saw Michael Lowry scuttle clear.
Murphy missed the extras but Ulster were off the mark. From the restart, Grayson made use of the penalty conceded by the hosts stretching the Scots’ lead to 13-5.
Matters didn’t improve for Ulster and the half ended with Edinburgh scoring their second try. This time the ball was moved left off a scrum and a kick through – a familiar tactic from the visitors – took a cruel ricochet and in doing so the ball fell to flanker Liam McConnell who had no one near him.
He surged towards the line and though Lowry caught him, the ball was offloaded to the supporting Malelili Satala and he raced clear.
Grayson converted and though Ben Carson went on a charge down the right flank with time nearly up, Ulster could do no more as Edinburgh showed them how to win a long throw over the top near their line, Grayson kicking the ball dead to end the half with the Scots leading 20-5.
After two minutes Edinburgh had try number three, Magnus Bradbury and Satala combining to send Hector Patterson away for an easy enough score which Grayson converted again.
Ulster then nearly collected an opportunistic try for David McCann only for him to be put in touch.
The Edinburgh bonus point duly came when O’Conor got on the end of Patterson’s pass and ran in at the posts. Grayson converted and Edinburgh now led 34-5.
Staring down the barrel, Ulster scored for the first time since the 25th minute, Zac Ward getting through after Henry Walker was held short. Murphy converted but Ulster had a mountain to climb.
But they now had the momentum. McCann crossed just after the hour and Murphy kicked a superb conversion from the touchline.
McCann came close again only for Keynan Knox to claim the bonus-point try. Murphy was again accurate off the tee and Ulster had the bit between their teeth.
With seven minutes remaining Ulster won a penalty after O’Conor hit Ward high and Murphy slotted the kick prompting a crazy endgame but no result for the hosts.

title: Garvaghy Road residents to seek last-minute halt after Orange Order granted permission to march
description: ‘Fuse has been lit’ by Parades Commission decision to allow first march since 1997
content:
The Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition will lodge a legal challenge in an effort to stop an Orange Order parade going ahead in Portadown on Sunday.
About 200 people gathered outside the High Court in Belfast on Friday evening in support of residents ahead of the emergency judicial review application, which will be heard on Saturday morning.
Earlier, the Parades Commission granted permission for 35 Orange Order members to march along the mainly nationalist road in the Co Armagh town.
It will be the first time the Protestant organisation has walked the route since 1997, in what has historically been one of the most contentious parading disputes in the North .
Breandán Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition rounded on the commission, saying its determination had “set this community back 28 years”.
“There’s shock and complete and utter disappointment with the commission,” he said.
“But that shock is slowly turning to anger. A fuse has been lit here that I don’t think anybody’s going to be able to put out.”
The ruling will not only affect Garvaghy Road, “but all those other places where people thought the marching issue had been resolved”, he said.
“This is going to have a snowball effect right across the North and I think that’s why there’s so much anger and frustration.
“It’s 28 years since the last march went down Garvaghy Road. That was at a price too.
“We’re always conscious of the fact that 21 people were murdered over Drumcree between 1996 and 1999.”
The Orange Order parade will depart from Drumcree Church at 8am on Sunday, under the commission’s restrictions.
It will be a silent parade with no bands.
Members of the Orange Order’s Portadown lodge had originally applied for a 60-member parade beginning at 1pm.
No supporters are to accompany the parade or congregate along the route and it must disperse from Carleton Street Orange hall before 9.30am, the commission has ruled.
[ Orange Order march could ‘reawaken old animosities’, Drumcree residents warn Opens in new window ]
About 200 police officers from Scotland are to be deployed to Portadown under a “mutual aid” agreement, in what is expected to be a significant security operation.
The commission’s ruling has drawn widespread anger from nationalist politicians, with Sinn Féin president Mary-Lou McDonald describing it as “utterly reckless”.
But DUP MP Carla Lockhart insisted that residents have “nothing to fear” from the parade.
The Orange Order argued it was an opportunity to right a historic wrong.
In a statement, the Government said it is “very concerned” by the ruling, adding it is conscious of the “very difficult and traumatic history associated with parades on the Garvaghy Road”.
“The Government does not want to see a return to the divisions of the past. That would be a retrograde step.”
In its ruling, the commission said it understands “the genuine hurt experienced by many residents of the Garvaghy Road”.
The body’s determination “is not, and should not, be perceived as a victory for one side or a loss for another”, it said.
“It is the outworking of the application of the legal framework to the facts available to the commission.”
Violent clashes during the Drumcree stand-off made international headlines.
The dispute began in 1995 and ended in 1998 following the murder of three Catholic children.
Brothers Richard, Mark and Jason Quinn were killed when the UVF petrol-bombed their Co Antrim home.
On Friday, UK prime minister Andy Burnham appealed for leaders to “work calmly” through the weekend.
He said it was a matter that had been “independently determined” and it was not for him to cut across the commission.
Stormont Justice Minister Naomi Long also urged those in leadership against sending a signal that there is no “justification for anything other than peaceful protest”.
The High Court hearing is at 11am tomorrow.

title: Pope Leo’s family secret: a birth in a mother and baby home
description: The pope’s French surname, Prevost, was an invention to conceal a birth outside of wedlock
content:
A lone and fleeing scandal, a 23-year-old gave birth in a Catholic mother and baby home close to the US border with Canada in the summer of 1917.
She named her little boy “Jean” and chose “Prevost” for his surname: the maiden name of the mother she had left behind in her native France two years earlier, when she boarded a ship from Le Havre to New York.
That decision, at the Our Lady of Victory Infant Home in Lackawanna, reverberated down the decades, ultimately determining the surname of her grandson, Robert Francis Prevost, now Pope Leo XIV .
“To the best of our knowledge, the pope’s grandparents were never married,” said Sean Daly, a US-French genealogist with France’s family history website Geneanet, whose name reflects his own Irish roots.
Daly was among a group of people who set about solving the mystery behind the Prevost surname when the pope was elected in May 2025.
“Prevost is a French name. But this is weird,” he remembers he and his colleagues thinking. “Because we can’t find a marriage certificate; in fact, we can’t find anything about his grandparents.
“It’s because the pope’s grandpa was already married to someone else.”
The family secret has been pulled into the spotlight as the pontiff visits his grandmother’s native land of France this weekend, drawing hundreds of thousands to masses at Notre Dame and on the Champs-Élysées before travelling to Lourdes and Metz.
Leo probably didn’t know the circumstances of the birth of his uncle Jean in 1917, and his father Louis in 1920, before his election as pope unleashed the curiosity of genealogists worldwide.
Researchers at Geneanet soon established that Leo’s French grandmother used two names: Fabre, an assumed name, and Fontaine, her real surname at birth.
She was a baker’s daughter, born in the port city of Le Havre, Normandy, in 1894. She had migrated to the United States in 1915 and lived at the Catholic-run Jeanne d’Arc Home for Friendless French Women in New York, where she was listed as a governess.
But who was the father of her children, Jean Prevost, and why was he strangely absent from records?
Daly discovered that other genealogists had been digging into the same mystery on an online discussion group, The Genealogy Discord.
There, some researchers had a theory. The pope’s grandfather Jean Prevost, a language teacher, was associated with the “Riggitano-Prevost School of Languages” in Chicago.
Just as the name Jean Prevost began to appear in archival documents, the name of the school’s renowned founder Salvatore Giovanni Riggitano faded out.
Some researchers had a theory: were Riggitano and Prevost the same person?
The answer was provided by the discovery of two forms filed by Leo’s grandparents in 1940, when the introduction of the Alien Registration Act required all non-US citizens to register with the government.
“I entered the United States under the name Salvatore Giovanni Riggitano Alioto” reads the form filed by Leo’s grandfather, which is signed “John Riggitano Prevost”.
He emigrated to the United States from Sicily in 1903, aged 27, in search of opportunities he felt he was blocked from accessing at home.
Salvatore Riggitano became known as a prominent teacher of languages, celebrated in Chicago society for his knowledge of European culture.
In 1914 he married Daisy Hughes, who was described in a later news report as being “of Irish parentage”. Riggitano was 37, and his bride was 38.
It is unclear when and where Riggitano met a young French governess who was 18 years his junior.
However, in March 1917, the Quincy Daily Herald of Illinois ran a story with the headline “Riggitano in triangle”.
The newspaper reported that Riggitano’s wife Daisy had accused her husband of being “mixed up improperly” with “Suzana Fountan”, and that the accused lovers had both been arrested.
Adultery was a crime in Illinois; it remains on the statute today, though unenforced.
When released on bail, Fontaine fled to Canada, skipping a court date that had been scheduled for April.
“The pope’s grandparents were in a jam. She was pregnant, and at the court appearance a month later, she would be visibly pregnant,” Daly said.
“They hatched a plot: you’re going to go off to Canada, where no one can find you, and then you’re going to give birth to the child somewhere where nobody knows us.”
Fontaine crossed back into the US from Canada in May, US entry records show, and then travelled to the Our Lady of Victory Infant Home in Lackawanna, not far from the border.
Her baby Jean Prevost – the pope’s uncle – was born in the “Infant Home” on July 23rd, 1917, according to a birth certificate that Daly wangled from a civil registrar.
“This document shows the parents using their made-up names for the first time. Salvatore Riggitano becomes Jean Prevost.”
The couple had another son three years later, in 1920: Louis, the pope’s father.
By then, Suzanne “Fabre” was living in Chicago with her children. According to the 1920 census, Riggitano was still living with his wife Daisy at the other end of town.
“The conclusion is that the pope’s grandpa led a double life for a few years,” Daly said.
Riggitano eventually left his wife Daisy, but there is no evidence they ever divorced. Daisy died in 1939, still calling herself Mrs Riggitano.
Mother and baby homes in the US do not always come with the same connotations of trauma that they do in Ireland.
The founder of the Our Lady of Victory Infant Home, Fr Nelson Baker, is fondly remembered for his initiatives for the poor and was posthumously given the title “Venerable” by the Church in 2011, a step on the path to sainthood.
However, a Facebook page, Our Lady of Victory Infant Home Adoptees, is full of the familiar, painful stories of people seeking family members and struggling to find records.
“I was in Father Bakers home for unwed mothers in 1971. I gave birth to my son on November 5th 1971 at our lady of victory hospital. My parents would not let me bring him home as I was only 17,” one post reads.
“In Jan 1972 I turned 18, I called the home to tell them I was coming for Christopher. That is when they told me he had been adopted out. I have been searching for him ever since then.”
Genealogists published their findings after the pope’s election and, in August 2025, Leo met the host of a popular US genealogy television show.
Harvard professor Henry Louis Gates Jr made a presentation to the pontiff about his diverse ancestry, which includes both enslaved black people and slave-owners, and remote connections to Canadian nobility.
Christopher White, author of Pope Leo XIV: Inside the Conclave and the Dawn of a New Papacy, says it is “hard to imagine that he hasn’t” reflected on the experience of his grandmother and uncle. Both lived until the then-Robert Francis Prevost was well into adulthood.
Leo has not made any public comment on his family story, but a future visit to Ireland could be the moment he does.
“I think the pope will visit Ireland. He’s got Irish connections,” White said.
“I think it could be a moment of deeper reflection for him, to reflect on his own personal story and tie it to the real wounds and suffering that exist in Ireland and beyond.”
