title: ‘Mom and Dad’? ‘Mary and Gearóid’? What you call your parents says a lot about your family
description: It can be hard to equate calling a parent by their first name with a healthy and intimate filial relationship. It seems unfeeling, distant
content:
I n an episode of The Simpsons , Bart addresses his dad as Homer. “Call me Daddy!” he orders. But when Bart persists, Homer falls into his usual exclamation of “Why you little...!” before throttling him in exasperation. Bart had tickled a curious nerve.
The way we address our parents can say a lot about family dynamics.
I remember a poster that so many of my generation had on their bedroom wall when I was a kid. Bart on a skateboard. “Eat my shorts, Man!” read the caption. By using his dad’s name he was able to undermine his authority.
When I recently heard a colleague refer to their father by his first name, I was startled. It can be hard to equate this form of address with a healthy and intimate filial relationship. It seems unfeeling and distant. Yet, a 2022 survey by iReach found that 4 per cent of Irish adults call their mothers by their first names. One can infer that a similar number do the same with their dads. This means that more than 150,000 Irish adults call their parents by their actual names – instead of Mum or Dad.
[ Co-parenting: ‘We always put our children’s needs before our own, so we could see the bigger picture’ Opens in new window ]
“I can’t remember exactly when I started to call my parents by their first names,” says Mia Sherwood, a 25-year-old writer and historian from Dublin. “Early in secondary school, I started to exclusively call them Barbara and Paul.”
But is it the child or the parent who makes the change?
Sherwood says her parents always signed her birthday cards using their given names, rather than “Mum” or “Dad”.
For Eamonn O’Tierney (no relation to this writer), a 62-year-old Irish man living in England, it was his own proclivity that pushed him to use his parents’ names. “It was something I started doing when I was about 13 or 14,” he recalls. “I had a very difficult period in my early teens… maybe it was precocity, maybe it was about not giving them the deference that (they) thought they were due.”
There are many tools at the disposal of a teenager who wants to undermine a parent, but creating distance by removing the intimacy of “Mum” or “Dad” is a pretty powerful one. “It was also about wanting to have a more adult relationship,” says O’Tierney.
On other occasions, the way we address our parents can offer insight into a more egalitarian family dynamic. Consider the character of Atticus Finch in Harper Lee’s To Kill a Mockingbird. His children, Jem and Scout, call him by his first name. This would have been unusual in the Deep South of the 1930s, but Lee uses it as a literary device to show how Finch has fostered a parent/child relationship based on trust and equality.
Sherwood’s experience has something of Harper Lee’s sentiments too. “My parents always had a more relaxed parenting style than some of my friends’ parents,” she remembers. “Barbara would always tell me I had her trust until I broke it, and then I wouldn’t have it back. So I was never under the level of scrutiny I feel some of my friends were under. I was kept on a long enough tether, growing up.”
Neil Kavanagh, an audio producer from Dublin in his early 40s, had a completely different experience. “You know that thing where you’re pestering your parents and they’re not answering you because they’re engaged in something else?” he asks me.
Him and his brother devised a cunning plan. They soon realised that if they called their mum by her actual name, they would instantly get her attention.
“She didn’t really have much of a negative response to it,” he says. “She got used to it. And fast forward 30 years… I still call her Maeve.”
‘They didn’t ask me not to. They gave the impression of being surprised and disgruntled. But they accepted it’
For Gavin Keogh, of Wines Direct in Co Westmeath, a company founded by his parents, there was always a pragmatic reason why he chose to call his father by his first name. “It’s a complex one. I used to work with Dad when he was alive. He was ‘Paddy’ in work and ‘Dad’ at home.”
This reminds me of a recent episode of the hit police procedural Boston Blue. When Marcus Scribner’s character, a rookie cop, addresses the district attorney (who happens to be his mother) as “Mom”, she quips: “Don’t call me ‘Mom’ at the office.”
When family members work together, the use of more formal naming conventions can help draw a line between work and domestic settings.
A certain family dynamic, and indeed how we perceive our roles in a family, often determines the form of address we use for each other. A few years ago, the singer Grimes (real name Claire Elise Boucher) revealed that her son calls her by her first name. In an interview with Vogue she stated: “Being a mother feels weird to say. For some reason, I don’t identify with that word. Maybe he can sense my distaste for the word ‘mother’.”
[ ‘I am often called in during rows between my daughter and my wife’ Opens in new window ]
For Eamonn O’Tierney, his parents were confronted by a teenage boy who no longer addressed them by their familiar titles. Did they try to change his behaviour? “They didn’t ask me not to,” he explains. “They gave the impression of being surprised and disgruntled. But they accepted it.”
Sherwood understands that using a parent’s first name is unconventional. “It was unusual, I remember classmates and teachers commenting on the fact I used their first names. Even though I’m 25 now, some people still find it funny that I use their first names.”
While using a parent’s given name can seem cold and remote to some, the interpersonal dynamic that Sherwood describes between her and her parents suggests the opposite. “I’ve always liked hanging out with my parents, so the parenting dynamic might not have been as much to the fore.”
Despite choosing this system of address for his own mother, Kavanagh doesn’t want to repeat it with his own children. “I don’t think I’d like it,” he admits. “Because it’s a privilege to be a parent. You feel like you’ve earned it. To me, the best sound is hearing your child say “Dada” or “Daddy”.
[ Young parents: ‘A lot of them would suffer social anxiety and isolation’ Opens in new window ]
The innate propensity for using intimate forms of address with our parents is hard to overcome, despite all efforts to the contrary. Sherwood recalls a particular incident where this came to the fore.
“The only time I called Barbara ‘Mom’ in recent years was when I rang her after I collapsed – just shows your mammy is always your mammy, regardless.”

title: Five homes on view this week in Dublin from €325,000
description: New to the market in Harold’s Cross, Rathmines, Howth and Churchtown
content:
This four-bedroom end-terrace artisan house of 125sq m (1,345sq ft) occupies an excellent location within walking distance of Harold’s Cross, Rathmines and Dublin city centre. St Stephen’s Green can be reached on foot in about 30 minutes. The accommodation comprises four good-sized bedrooms and a large livingroom and a light-filled kitchen. The property has high ceilings and retains much of its original period detailing. Ber C.
Located within a secure, gated development in the heart of Rathmines, this one-bedroom (50sq m/538sq ft) apartment comes for sale in excellent condition following a full renovation that includes a new, fitted kitchen, bathroom suite and new flooring throughout the property. The apartment is own-door and has a double bedroom with an open-plan living, dining and kitchen area and its own parking space. Ber E1.
On View: By appointment at Kelly Bradshaw Dalton.
This semidetached four-bedroom, three-bathroom home is generously sized at 247sq m (2,658sq ft) and is arranged over three levels. The accommodation is in walk-in condition and has a contemporary finish. The kitchen and livingroom open out into a large, wraparound conservatory that overlooks the landscaped communal grounds of this gated development. Ber C.
On View: By appointment at Sherry FitzGerald.
Built in 1953, this large, four-bedroom semidetached house has been brought right up to date by its current owners and is presented in move-in condition. The accommodation, which extends to 157sq m (1,690sq ft), is bright and has a C1 Ber rating following the installation of new insulation, triple-glazed windows and solar panels. The house has a large, landscaped rear garden that stretches to 21m (70ft) in length and ample off-street parking at the front. Ber C1.
Positioned within a short walk of both Rathmines and Ranelagh villages, this two-bedroom midterrace redbrick of 45sq m (484sq ft) comprises a bright, open-plan living/dining and kitchen area at ground-floor level and two double bedrooms upstairs. There is on-street permit parking available for residents and the Luas Green Line stop at Ranelagh is just a 12-minute walk from the property. Ber E.
On View: By appointment at Sherry FitzGerald.

title: Patrick Freyne: Lola Petticrew, a bearded grump and Siobhán McSweeney’s sneaky Irish: My top TV shows of 2026 so far
description: Brilliant Irish actor Lola Petticrew (just a normal Irish name) stars in Elizabeth Meriwether’s Disney crime drama, Furious.
content:
W hen I was a boy, they had not yet fully eradicated smallpox, and we would spend our time, as a family, watching the cube in the corner (a television, not my brother David). Now, we have our own portable viewing machines, and none of us has shared a livingroom in years.
Nonetheless, we still have television “shows” in which Americans, Britons and worse (Dubliners) dramatise reality for us, which we then harvest from the sky using the arcane magic of our enchanted pocket rectangles.
Indeed, as an old Elizabethan, I still like to watch these oldfangled entertainments despite the fact that most people prefer Instagram microdramas, having anxiety and recreational laughing gas. Here are my favourite programmes so far from the year of our Lord 2026.
Two seasons into The Pitt (Sky and Now) and I’m pretty sure I can do operations now. I’ve bought my own scrubs and scalpel. You’ll often find me down at A&E, asking the nurses if I can “have a go”. (They’re pretty understaffed, so they often let me.)
The Pitt differs from its medical-drama predecessors (including ER, in which Noah Wyle, its star and executive producer, once featured) in its hyperrealistic real-time depiction of an over-run Pittsburgh emergency room.
It prioritises this over medical love affairs or dramatically obscure ailments. You see a lot of close-up operations on necks and heads and eyes and guts.
The characters are great, the politics of US medical funding are presented in all their grotesquerie, the pace is frenetic and the operations are really easy I reckon, and I should definitely be allowed to do them. Just give me a go.
I tuned into these popular dramas on Disney+ and Now to learn about (a) the economics of regional TV broadcasting in the 1980s, and (b) ice hockey, because I am, as you’ll know from the previous paragraph, a gifted polymath.
I was shocked and appalled to learn that the attractive characters/actors in both shows spend much of their time engaged, not in regional TV broadcasting/ice hockey, but in rumpy-pumpy, jiggery-pokery, the Chatt-awooga Choo-Choo, Mammy and Daddy’s special bedtime exercises, the fishwife’s prerogative, Dr Feelgood’s Goodtime Remedy and, also, riding.
[ Heated Rivalry: This hugely bingeable erotic filler at least dares to be different Opens in new window ]
I’m speaking euphemistically because of The Irish Times’ large child readership. Both shows are heartfelt filth. 10 out of 10.
We all love teensy freaks with squeaky voices and mad hair. But enough about guest star Sabrina Carpenter. I can’t believe Disney+ only brought The Muppet Show back for one special episode. It should have inaugurated it as a weekly happening, ideally instead of the news.
The revived show was overseen by the Fraggle-voiced human Muppet Seth Rogen, and Carpenter, the Carry On sex poppet, was an ideal choice to bounce off Miss Piggy, the programme’s resident amphibian amorist. Indeed, there were times I looked from starlet to Muppet and Muppet to starlet and couldn’t tell which was which.
A bearded grump who’s up to something in his suburban shed? I’m a bearded grump! I have a suburban shed! I’m often up to something! Mackenzie Crook’s gentle BBC comedy features tiny weird humanoids, much like The Muppet Show, except these are intricately animated, kept in big jars and can prophesise the future.
This is a fantastically mundane, and mundanely fantastical story about grief, love, magic and friendship. I love it. It’s funny and odd and beautiful. Another series is coming soon.
It’s clearly the season of messy, bearded old weirdos. (We have so little and we give so much.) This Disney+ series stars Ethan Hawke as a crusty old investigative journalist/bookshop owner who gets lured into an investigation linked to historical injustice and contemporary racism in Tulsa, Oklahoma.
It’s dark and funny, and it comes from the pen and camera of Sterlin Harjo, the creator of Reservation Dogs. It somehow manages to be an uncynical sunlit noir, which kind of defeats the point of noir, I guess, but I’m too dazzled by Hawke’s excellent cowboy shirts to care.
I’m just happy to see Siobhán McSweeney flounce magnificently around a castle flanked by Irish wolfhounds . In my view, giving her a castle is a form of reparations for what was done to Cork by its ancient enemy (Dublin), and everything else is just a bonus.
She is also here to oversee the native Irish, freed of the shackles of the capital, all engaged in their favourite pastimes: gossiping and rooting out traitors. I believe there’s a row of shallow graves out back.
RTÉ’s version is better than the BBC’s, because being a colonised people makes you sneakier.
[ The Traitors Ireland: What makes this intoxicating show so utterly gripping? Opens in new window ]
It’s about time Mary Bennet from Pride and Prejudice got a spin-off . It has only been 213 years, and Mary is the most overlooked and least man-crazy of Jane Austen’s Bennet sisters. (Pride and Prejudice was originally called Man Crazy.)
Other minor characters from other franchises were given a go long ago: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, from Hamlet; Velma, from Scooby-Doo; Robert F Kennedy jnr, from the Kennedy family; the more sluggish Kardashians.
[ The Other Bennet Sister on BBC One: A love letter to outsiders, introverts and people who don’t fit in Opens in new window ]
Based on a novel by Janet Hadlow, and starring the excellent Ella Bruccoleri and talented Corkonian hunk Dónal Finn, The Other Bennet Sister is a moving, funny and triumphant celebration of eccentricity and difference.
A weird town of insular, closed-minded busybodies besieged by arcane customs, eccentric shut-ins and grotesque freaks. And now I’m homesick. Widow’s Bay is a bit like Eerie, Indiana or Gravity Falls in that it’s about a small, isolated community experiencing unexplained paranormal phenomena, except, unlike those excellent shows, this Apple TV series is aimed at adults and has a prestige-TV budget.
It somehow transcends the horror tropes it very successfully pastiches to become legitimately scary on its own terms. It’s also very funny and charming. It deservedly won loads of Emmys, including one for the British actor Kate O’Flynn, who is brilliant and should be in everything.
I will have nothing said against my adult architectural son, Dermot Bannon. His quest for the perfectly transparent house continues. Its completion will signal that end-times are upon us.
Elizabeth Meriwether’s Disney crime drama is the best show of the year. Emmy Rossum, Quincy Tyler Bernstine and Scoot McNairy (just a normal US name) all play differently damaged lawfolk on the trail of a trafficked girl turned serial killer played by the brilliant Irish actor Lola Petticrew (just a normal Irish name).
It’s more than a crime caper. It’s also a story about institutional callousness and deficits in care, and it is, most importantly, a show about consequential female rage (hence the title). It is dark, complex and thought-provoking, and despite this, it’s also often funny and humane. I will be furious if it is not renewed.*

title: Sense and Sensibility review: Perfectly respectable Austen adaptation offers a pleasant afternoon out
description: Decent young actors ponder (among other things) the eternal tension between duty and desire
content:
Brave Georgia Oakley . The shadow of Ang Lee ’s 1995 take on Jane Austen’s debut novel hangs heavily over this perfectly respectable, adequately acted new take from the director of the acclaimed Thatcher-era drama Blue Jean.
The Lee film propelled Kate Winslet towards the A-list. It secured a second Oscar (this time as writer) for Emma Thompson. It fired an early shot in the millennial Austen boom that has still not gone away.
How has the mood changed? The influence of Joe Wright’s Pride & Prejudice, from 2005, should also be noted. That film allowed a bit of exterior dirt into Austenland. Like many literary adaptations since, the 2026 Sense and Sensibility thinks itself closely in touch with nature. Autumnal light is forever breaking through damp foliage. There is a sense the attractive costumes have endured the odd snag on the odd thorny bush.
Yet all that only goes to emphasise the quality of the dentistry and the abundance of hair conditioner. Maybe the key player is Working Title Films. This is Regency reality as the defining British studio of Cool Britannia understands it: honed, wispy, unthreatening.
None of which makes the film any less easy to digest. A decent group of young actors have come together to ponder (among other things) the eternal tension between duty and desire.
Caitríona Balfe bravely steps up to play the formidable Mrs Dashwood. When her husband dies, she and her three daughters are nudged towards what counts for poverty in this world. Their estate has passed to the girls’ half-brother, and they have been forced to make the best of a cottage in Devonshire.
Daisy Edgar-Jones, late of Normal People, plays the responsible Elinor Dashwood. Esmé Creed-Miles, daughter of Samantha Morton, is the more romantic Marianne. The rising Bodhi Rae Breathnach, from Limerick, brightens up the frame as young Margaret.
This is literally and figuratively a less colourful Sense and Sensibility than the Lee version. Greg Wise’s cad in that film had the breadth and posture of a surly mountain. In contrast, Frank Dillane, so good in the recent Urchin , makes an introverted slope-shouldered neurotic of John Willoughby. Hugh Grant was, in the Lee film, all stammery charm as Edward Ferrars, Elinor’s suitor. George MacKay is more of an enigma here.
It is, of course, unfair to stress comparisons between this and any other version, but the contrast does clarify how approaches to period adaptation have changed. There is a greater sense of youth and near-youth in panic here than there was in the earlier, more stately film (if only because young people now look younger than they used to).
There is a clearer feeling in Oakley’s film of how narrow the marriage window was for a woman just out of adolescence.
The new film does, however, often feel frustratingly flattened. That is partly to do with the misty cinematography, the contained performances and the leisurely editing. But there is also a regrettable shortage of humour.
[ Fiona Shaw on working with Phoebe Waller-Bridge: ‘She’s like a daughter I wish I’d had’ Opens in new window ]
No blame attaches to the indomitable Fiona Shaw , who, as Mrs Jennings, risks slipping a disk with her endless batty enthusiasm. Few other actors are invited to embrace Austen’s famous comic potential. This is a sedate work much impressed by its own seriousness of purpose.
And yet. The majestic clockwork ends up delivering the emotional embrace that all Austen fans expect and deserve. There is, perhaps, nothing hugely novel in Oakley’s approach, but a professional team behind and before camera allow the immortal characters one more chance to end up where they belong.
[ Sarah Moss on Jane Austen and 250 years of undermining the romantic novel Opens in new window ]
“To wish was to hope, and to hope was to expect,” Elinor muses in the book. One can expect a pleasant afternoon out from this Sense and Sensibility. That is no small thing.

title: Stupid August review: Irish film marries Charlie Chaplin with an analysis of nefarious alliances
description: Pádraig Trehy’s latest feature marries silent cinema, expressionism and surrealism to create a historical fantasy
content:
The setting is 1960s Ireland, but the iris shots, maps with animated arrows and entirely silent, intertitled sequences are rooted in the cinema of the early 20th century.
Stupid August, funded by the Arts Council of Ireland’s Authored Works programme, is about an exiled “world clown” whose “left-wing politics have recently caused controversy”. He remains a welcome figure as he holidays on the west coast.
Characters are introduced swiftly in vignettes – the Nazi commando, the government minister, the Roman fixer – to build a story about an amnesiac who, following the trauma of the second World War, cannot remember the bank details that would allow him to access family gold.
He finds kindly allies among the marginalised, including the Travelling community and the unfortunate women enslaved by nuns. He conversely finds adversaries among wanted war criminals and those who harbour them.
The simplicity of Pádraig Trehy’s dialogue-free storytelling belies a larger analysis of nefarious alliances and realpolitik. Or, as the film puts it, “What follows is a fable … but some things remain fact.”
Trehy is a Cork-based film-maker, writer and educator whose three-decade career comprises documentary, experimental cinema, theatre and visual art.
From his earliest credit as a floor runner on War of the Buttons to his feature-length exploration of the relationship between James Joyce and the tenor John McCormack, in Shem the Penman Sings Again , his work has blended history, literature, music and formal playfulness.
A lifelong fan of silent cinema, Trehy credits his film-making career to discovering Chaplin as a youngster.
Chaplin, as an artist and historical figure, looms large in Stupid August. In common with Andrew Legge’s steampunk mockumentary Lola , Trehy’s latest feature marries silent cinema, expressionism and surrealism to create a historical fantasy.
As anyone who has watched the rare remaining footage of The Day the Clown Cried in From Darkness to Light, the Jerry Lewis documentary from 2024, parachuting a clown into a movie warzone is a fraught business. Against the odds, Trehy finds a way.
At Triskel Arts Centre, Cork, from Sunday, September 27th

title: A car show that speaks to everyone
description: See every type of electric vehicle under one roof at the Nevo EV show in partnership with Bank of Ireland at the RDS this November
content:
Electric cars have never been more popular. They now account for 26 per cent of the Irish car share market, ahead of regular petrol hybrids at 24.6 per cent, petrol cars at 20.4 per cent, plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) at 14.5 per cent and diesel cars at 12.5 per cent. With this in mind, you could say the timing of the fourth edition of the Nevo Electric Vehicle show at the RDS, Simmonscourt, on November 7 and 8, has never been better. “The momentum behind electric vehicles in Ireland has never been stronger and the Nevo EV Show 2026 will reflect just how far the industry has come,” says Nevo managing director, Simon Andreuceutti. “This year’s event is significantly bigger in every respect, with more vehicles, more brands, more live experiences and more opportunities for consumers to learn about electric mobility.”
Nevo is Ireland’s home of electric motoring, with a single mission to make electric simple and exciting for everyday drivers. Nevo.ie provide EV reviews, easy-to-follow buying guides, and every choice of electric car all in one place. Now in the fourth year, Nevo have replicated everything they do online into a physical event, which is now Ireland’s largest motor show in the calendar.
Sponsored by Bank of Ireland , the Nevo EV show 2026 is not just for those with a knowledge of electric vehicles but also for the EV curious. In fact, you can go along knowing nothing about electric motoring and walk away with a wealth of information.
Susan Russell, CEO, Retail Ireland, Bank of Ireland: “We are proud to sponsor the Nevo EV Show for the third year running. As our partnership with Nevo continues to grow, it reinforces our commitment to making sustainable transport more accessible and supporting the transition to a lower carbon future for communities across Ireland.
This year’s Nevo EV Show promises to showcase the best in class of electric vehicles and will act as a showcase to demonstrate the sentiment towards the EV sector.
In line with demand for electric vehicles, our recently launched Electric Vehicle Marketplace, in partnership with Nevo, is building on that momentum, giving customers the tools, knowledge and financial support to make the switch with confidence”
The event will showcase 140 electric vehicles, all of which are plug-in models, from over 40 of the world’s leading automotive brands. “It’s the only venue where you can see every type of EV on the market and the only motor show focusing solely on EVs to ever take place in Europe,” adds Andreuceutti.This year, the electric vehicle (EV) manufacturer, Leapmotor is joining as the official vehicle launch partner and will be debuting several EVS that have never been seen here before. “There’s now an EV to suit everyone, whether you’re looking for a family car; a small city car; an SUV; or a luxury car,” he says.
What’s more, electric vehicles have come down in price in recent years. “According to research Nevo carried out this year, the top selling EV is actually €2,500 cheaper than the average equivalent in a same size petrol or diesel vehicle,” says Andreuceutti. “The mid €25, 000 mark is one of the fastest growing segments in the EV space, however you can buy an electric car for a little as €18,000 .” Commercial use of EVs is also growing and there will be a wide selection of EV commercial vans at the Nevo event too.
At the ESB Live Demo Area, 14 brand-new electric vehicles models will be showcased across the two-day event. Hosted by Derek Reilly, EV expert with Nevo, there will be demonstrations, providing information about the latest innovations and emerging technologies in electric motoring. You can also try out an electric vehicle for yourself, by signing up in advance at the new myenergi Driving Experience which has a range of electric cars to be test-driven over the weekend. “We’ve mapped out a specific 20-minute route in Ballsbridge and participants will drive the car with a representative from the brand.”
(L-R); Simon Andreucetti (managing director, Nevo), Mark Brennan (marketing manager, Leapmotor Ireland), Stephen McGrath (brand manager, Leapmotor Ireland), and Derek Reilly (content and pr director, Nevo).
Buyers can claim a Sustainable Energy of Ireland (SEAI) grant of up to €3,500 on new battery electric vehicles (BEVs), plus €300 towards a home charger and the SEAI will be at the show providing information on this. For those with questions about electric vehicles, a new section called ‘Nevo x Bank of Ireland Meet the Experts Lounge’ will have brand experts and representatives from Bank of Ireland and leading Automotive brands to answer them. It will feature a panel where visitors can put questions to experts and find out about available finance packages for EVs, as well as interactive audience discussions and panel debates, covering a range of topics including home and public-charging, battery technology, running costs and how to choose the right electric vehicle.
The benefits of driving an EV will also be explained. Obviously they’re better for the environment because they don’t produce tail pipe emission and use energy more efficiently then petrol or diesel cars. Electric vehicles also need less servicing than a standard car. “With an EV, there are no spark plugs; there’s no timing belt; and there are hundreds of fewer parts which would typically need to be replaced or repaired in a petrol or a diesel vehicle.”
The event aims to do away with common misconceptions about electric vehicles, for example the belief that the battery of an electric car needs to be replaced after just a few years. “It’s like saying that if you drive too many miles in a petrol or a diesel vehicle, you’ll have to replace the engine. In fact, it will cost no more than a regular car,” he says. There’s also a belief that the cost of charging is prohibitive. “The only situation that could be pricey is when you’re doing fast-charging which is not for a daily commute,” says Andreuceutti. “It’s only for occasions when you’re out and about and in need of power.”In such cases, you don’t need to charge the vehicle to 100 per cent. “The technology in the car will tell you by what percentage charge you need according to your driving behaviour. You might only need 20 to 30 per cent for example, and it’s still considerably cheaper than traditional fuel,” he adds. There are ways in fact to keep the cost of charging down. For example, electric vehicles can be charged at home with the use of solar panels. “There are owners who are actually paying zero expenses to run their EV because they’re using smart energy,” he says. “Or by signing up to one of the apps you get an automatic discount.”
Nevo is a free event which attracts women as much as men. “People used to go to motor shows because they wanted to know about horse power and the size engines etc. but it’s not about that anymore,” he says. “We expect men, women, couples, families with young children, and business owners. This is a car show that speaks to everyone and it’s one everyone will enjoy.”
Since launching on 15th August, more than 19,000 tickets have been registered for the two-day event at the RDS Simmonscourt, Dublin on 7th and 8th November. Register for your free ticket today at www.nevo.ie

title: Women film-makers deserve greater recognition in history of Irish movies
description: Ireland’s most talented film-makers included women long overlooked - academic and archival collaboration is setting the record straight
content:
Most people have never heard of Flora Kerrigan, even though she was one of Ireland’s most innovative and talented film-makers during the late 1950s and early 1960s. Her award-winning animated and live-action films were broadcast on RTÉ and screened at international film festivals, yet she and her work, like that of many other gifted female film-makers of the era, have largely disappeared from Irish film history.
That glaring omission is being rectified thanks to the work of Sarah Arnold, associate professor of media studies at Maynooth University, and Kasandra O’Connell, head of the IFI Irish Film Archive, who have been collaborating on a number of projects examining overlooked women film-makers and developing new approaches to documenting their contribution to Irish film history.
“Women’s creative work has historically been underreported and under-recognised, making it difficult to document and catalogue accurately,” Arnold explains. “This challenge is particularly acute in amateur and non-professional film-making, where records are often incomplete and women film-makers can become effectively invisible within the historical record.”
Through a Research Ireland New Foundations project, Arnold and O’Connell are combining academic research with archival expertise to improve how women’s creative contributions are identified, catalogued and contextualised within local, regional and national archives. The collaboration forms part of wider efforts to ensure women’s film-making history is better represented within Ireland’s cultural record.
“When you read about history of Irish film, it’s mainly about the success of setting up a commercial Irish film industry after the establishment of the Irish Film Board,” says Arnold. “Irish amateur film-making is often not included. It was as if the period from the 1910s until the 1990s was the dark ages. There was lots of interesting activity during that time, but it doesn’t fit the narrative because it wasn’t commercial film-making.”
Part of the reason for this is a certain disdain or snobbery towards amateur film-making. “People think amateur is not very good, but some of it was extremely good,” Arnold says. “Some of these film-makers were doing amazing stuff with Super 8 and so on. The Irish Film Society was cofounded in 1930 by novelist, playwright and critic Mary Manning and its members were making very good films, but they are considered amateur because there wasn’t an industry around it.”
Home movies tend to be derided and undervalued, she adds, but films by people like Margaret Currivan provide a valuable record of life in Ireland at the time. “She was a member of the Dublin Cine Club. Her family owned a chemist, so she had access to materials. Her films are really interesting and quite accomplished. She was interested in storytelling, and she used family and neighbours and local area as props to tell those stories. These films are a rich archive of daily lives.”
The Flora Kerrigan story is even more interesting. “She is so different, she almost upends what we know about film in the 1950s and 1960s,” says Arnold. “We were told that nothing was happening, that there were no amateurs, but we have this really interesting and exceptional film-maker who has somehow disappeared from the record. But people like Flora and Louis Marcus were doing really interesting film-making down in Cork. It wasn’t this stagnant period. We had a really vibrant film culture with really interesting and bold film-making.”
Kerrigan’s film-making star shone brightly but briefly before she left for London in the mid-1960s where she became a highly innovative poet. During her time in Cork, she sent films to festivals in Australia, Yugoslavia and other countries. “They are abstract, surreal and told very interesting stories. One of Flora’s animated films has cutouts of shoes representative of people interacting with controlling and coercive relationships portrayed by different sized feet.”
Another of her films, The Seventh Day, illustrated the concept of time and explored our understanding of it. “In another the Earth is anthropomorphised as a face with rockets and other things coming out of it,” says Arnold. “It illustrates the cold war, among other things. Dream Maker explores sensuality between women. A Hard Day’s Night was inspired by The Beatles movie in some ways. It is film about chess players; the chess players turn into people and a white pawn turns into a queen and the male player gets frustrated because he’s no longer in control of her.”
Kerrigan puts her own introductions in some of the films. “She is quite playful, saying things like ‘you’re never going to see this because of what’s in it’ or ‘if you understand this you must be a psychopath’. Amateur film-makers could do almost anything because the censor was never going to see it. Our aim is for Flora and others to be written back into history and that will transform what we think about that time.”
The films are being put up on the Irish Film Archive player ( ifiarchiveplayer.ie ). “This is not geo-blocked so anyone from anywhere in the world can look at the Flora Kerrigan collection.”

title: Sole Seafood & Grill review: I’m in shock – €35 for chicken supreme using non-free-range Dutch chicken
description: Many dishes in this lavishly refurbished Dublin spot are good, but it’s hard to get past the sourcing
content:
I am one of those people who if you turn them around, doesn’t know where they are. Actually, I don’t even need to be turned around for confusion to set in. And the newly refurbished Sole Seafood & Grill in Dublin is just the place to put this to the test, because, rather than moving to new premises , as I mistakenly thought, it has simply doubled in size within the original building and moved its entrance from South William Street to the far busier Drury Street, right beside Ciss Madden’s.
Sole is part of the EHL group, owned by seasoned operator Padraic O’Kane and Bord Bia chairman Larry Murrin . The hospitality group includes Fire Steakhouse and The Round Room at the Mansion House and Sally Mac’s Pub & Kitchen.*
After checking in at reception – serious exclusivity vibes – we are guided up a sweeping staircase through a warren of dining areas, past some tables for two in what amounts to a corridor, and finally reach the dramatically decorated bar area of the restaurant. It feels more escape room to me. I have no idea of the way back out, so I sit tight in my seat for the evening, rather than risk the need to send out a search party.
There’s a three-course table d’hote menu for €69, but as it includes farmed sea bass (from Spain, Greece or Turkey, €35 on the a la carte), it narrows my options. I discover afterwards that the Cajun chicken is Polish and not free-range, and the chicken supreme (€35 on the a la carte) is made with Dutch chicken that is not free-range either. The Guinness smoked salmon is farmed in Scotland (€16.50 on the a la carte), and the tiger prawns in the chowder are farmed and block frozen in Bangladesh. Considering Sole claims that its “food philosophy is one honouring seafood sustainability and local Irish producers”, this is not a good start. In its defence, the cod for the fish and chips is landed by Irish boats and the rib-eye steak is Peter Hannan’s excellent salt-aged beef.
But I really want fish to be the focus of my meal, so the a la carte menu it is. It leads with oysters and then goes on to caviar – €59 to €178 – followed by the Sole seafood towers – €85 to €137.50. A 500g lobster, €95, is catch of the day. Clearly, I’m in a room of well-heeled diners; I see towers winging their way like drones around the room.
[ Osteria Nove review: I expected more from Oliver Dunne’s new Dublin spot Opens in new window ]
Rock oysters are €7 for two, and there’s a choice from four Irish producers. David Keane’s Connemara oysters are sweet and creamy while Kelly’s oysters are slightly smaller, tasting of a fresh day by the sea. They are delicious with a squeeze of lemon, a splash of Tabasco and a glass of Picpoul de Pinet Cap Cette (€45 for a bottle) from a safe list that is strong on whites. Reds top out at €1,800 for the 2016 Château Latour.
Dingle brown crab claws (€19.50) are succulent, sautéed in butter and served with a delicious lemon beurre blanc, scattered with samphire.
There is a bit of theatre around my main course. Sole meunière (€59.50) arrives whole on the bone, golden around the edges, and is skilfully filleted tableside. It is sweet-tasting and beautifully cooked, served with melted butter and a wedge of lemon. The side dish of green beans is crunchy and perhaps a little heavy on the garlic.
[ Ómós review: Faultless cooking already at two-star Michelin level. Get in before prices rise Opens in new window ]
Fish ’n’ chips (€29.50) arrives as two large chunks of beer-battered cod, the fish deliciously moist inside a crackling batter, the chips golden and crunchy. The accompaniment of peas is a minted purée, oddly soupy.
Dessert is mango mousse (€12.50), refreshing after a feast of fish, accompanied by passion fruit and mango salsa and chunks of toasted coconut meringue.
[ Letter to the Editor: Tipping culture in Ireland and the US Opens in new window ]
Sole is a well-oiled machine with some notably good dishes on the menu using freshly landed fish and seafood: oysters, Roaring Water Bay mussels, Dover sole, cod, monkfish and lobster. But there is also an over-dependence on frozen seafood: squid from southeast Asia, Vietnamese yellowfin tuna, Bangladeshi and Argentinian prawns – even the Dublin Bay prawns and Dingle crab claws are frozen. It is not unusual for a restaurant to use frozen seafood – it allows more control over stock – but a restaurant that positions itself as a place where seafood sustainability and local Irish produce are at the forefront merits more in-depth scrutiny. The Polish and Dutch non-free-range chicken diminishes the case further. EHL might have allocated some of that €4.5 million expansion spend on better sourcing.
Dinner for two with a bottle of wine was €180.
The Verdict: Sole’s sourcing does not always match its claims.
Food provenance: Fish and frozen seafood, Kish Fish; scallops, Mourne Seafood; beef, Peter Hannan and Dawn Meats; Dutch and Polish chicken from La Rousse, Keelings vegetables.
Vegetarian options: Limited. Burrata with fennel, orange and beef tomatoes; pappardelle with basil; vegetable side dishes.
Wheelchair access: Fully accessible with an accessible toilet.
Music: Barry White, Bill Withers and lounge music.
*This article was amended on September 24th.

title: ‘Price growth is moderating’: Irish estate agents give their views on new homes market in 2026
description: Selling agents give their views on the current new homes market and prospects for the year ahead
content:
It has been a particularly busy year to date in the new homes market . Demand is strong, driven by continued economic growth and the underlying strength of the labour market along with favourable demographics, including continued strong net migration. Affordability supports are also continuing to support new homes demand and sales activity.
The fact that supply is increasing is also a key positive factor. New housing completions were up 10.8 per cent in the first half of 2026, compared to the same period in 2025 (with a total of 16,679 units delivered to the market). While total completions for the year will not exceed 40,000 units, the market is expected to deliver a similar amount as in 2025 (at just over 36,000 units). First-time buyers continue to lead activity, and this trend will continue for the rest of the year and into 2027.
The improvement in supply is beginning to have an impact on the level of price growth. After a number of years of exceptional price increases, the rate of price growth is moderating. This is evident in both the second-hand and the new homes markets. New homes prices continued to increase throughout 2025 and the first half of 2026.
The pace of growth in new home prices moderated to 6 per cent, however, at the end of the second quarter from 6.4 per cent at the end of quarter one. This is a trend that we forecast will continue, largely driven by increased supply and by the level of price increases that have already been absorbed by the market. Buyers will still see new home prices increasing, but this will happen at a slightly slower pace than in recent years.
Activity is set to remain strong into 2027, with more choice for first-time buyers in the form of an increasing supply of urban and commuter-location apartments, alongside options for buyers trading up as Ireland’s big developers increase their delivery volumes.
As we approach the last quarter of 2026, DNG has experienced robust levels of activity both locally and regionally across Ireland. According to figures released by the CSO covering the first half of 2026, 16,679 new dwellings were completed, representing an increase of 10.85 per cent year-on-year. We likewise saw a jump in apartment completions in the first half of 2026 compared to 2025 with an increase of 4.6 per cent.
We have seen a number of measures implemented in the areas of planning reform, VAT reductions on new apartments, the Housing Infrastructure Investment Fund, the Housing Activation Office and the Critical Infrastructure Act. These measures and initiatives have all helped to increase the level of housing delivery. There has been a decisive approach across the board to create the right conditions for sustained housing delivery through investment, the provision of infrastructure, and home ownership supports.
Government supports such as Help to Buy (HTB), the Starter Home Purchase Scheme (formerly the Local Authority Affordable Purchase Scheme) and the First Home Scheme (FHS) have played a pivotal role in sustaining purchaser demand and making home ownership a reality for many. DNG’s 2027 Budget submission calls for the level of HTB to be increased and for regional FHS price ceilings to be reviewed to ensure the scheme remains effective.
DNG has seen strong demand for mixed-tenure housing. This has been driven by a combination of these schemes’ quality design and their well-connected locations. The Croí Cónaithe scheme is helping to unlock apartment delivery and support prospective owner-occupiers in securing these apartments. It’s a new form of housing supply that is being well received in the market.
Demand for new homes in Ireland by owner-occupiers is at an all-time high, with first-time buyers accounting for a large proportion of this. The population is growing and our economy continues to perform strongly. But while the supply of housing is increasing steadily, it’s yet to grow at a pace that’s sufficient to meet the Government’s targets or the needs of homebuyers.
First-time buyers remain the key cohort when it comes to the demand for new homes, and they continue to be supported in this by both the Help to Buy and First Home schemes. In the case of Help to Buy though, the €500,000 price threshold is now 10 years old and pitched at too low a level to be of benefit to those looking to buy in Dublin and its commuter belt. The price threshold now needs to be increased if it is to keep pace with build costs and inflation.
The ongoing conflict in the Middle East is adding to construction costs and having a knock-on effect on the supply of new homes as developers are forced to constantly reassess the level of risk to their projects. Regulatory costs are also mounting up, putting pressure on house prices and reducing delivery viability, especially for higher-density development. These costs include the imposition of the concrete levy, the payment of carbon tax, the increase in Part V social and affordable housing provision to 20 per cent and the payment of the water levy.
The building industry has been playing its part in increasing supply through the acquisition by developers of new sites, where available, and through seeking planning permission in a difficult regulatory environment. Large sites are being developed on at speed, and the homes being built on them are of superb quality. All of this is happening against an ongoing backdrop of insufficient zoned land, infrastructure deficiencies and planning delays.
Separately, both the affordable purchase and Croí Cónaithe (Cities) schemes are proving to be very successful. Apartment living is increasing in popularity as a result.
As of September 2026, demand for new homes remains very strong across the market, particularly from first-time buyers. The Help to Buy and the First Home Scheme initiatives continue to support market activity, but affordability is being tested by current new-build pricing, higher household costs and the gap between Government scheme price thresholds and current market values in Dublin and the commuter belt. In our view, the HTB price cap should now be reviewed and brought into line with current new homes pricing levels.
The market is delivering more homes, and visible activity on the ground has improved. However, Ireland is still carrying the weight of a long-running supply deficit, and current output is not yet where it needs to be.
High-density apartment delivery is crucial, but remains the most challenging sector of the market. The 2025 VAT reduction was very helpful in regard to viability, but much of that benefit has been absorbed by higher construction and funding costs (driven by the conflict in the Middle East).
Croí Cónaithe (Cities) can improve viability for high-density schemes, but only if payment timing can be accelerated, and implementation can be simplified, to give more clarity and confidence to developers and their funders.
Many mid-size builders want to grow and have the capability to do so, but access to well-located land, lack of planning certainty, infrastructural deficits, and a limited availability of equity funding remain real constraints. This is especially relevant in the east and midlands, where demand is deepest and serviced land is still limited.
In our view, the Government must continue to focus its efforts on addressing infrastructure bottlenecks, unlocking viable sites, improving Croí Cónaithe payment certainty, supporting mid-tier builders to scale, and keeping purchaser supports (Help to Buy in particular) aligned with current market values.
The autumn selling season traditionally follows a summer lull, with builders and developers typically waiting until after the holiday period to launch new homes. Summer 2026 broke this pattern, with a significant volume of new homes coming to the market, and sales remaining strong.
Encouragingly, supply is gradually increasing, supported primarily by apartment delivery through the Croí Cónaithe (Cities) scheme, which continues to support activity in the new homes market.
[ Should planning rules for one-off housing be relaxed? Opinions for and against Opens in new window ]
On the ground, buyers have welcomed the wider range of homes released for sale. The strongest demand has been for attractively priced, well-located apartments – both with and without parking – town houses with terraced or courtyard gardens, and highly energy-efficient homes, including passive houses and apartments.
Energy-efficient homes are particularly attractive to buyers conscious of both running costs and environmental impact. Trading buyers moving from older housing stock are especially conscious of this, valuing the greater comfort and lower running costs a new home can offer.
The wider mix of property types on offer is giving buyers more choice across a range of price points, and we will see more activity this autumn, with upcoming releases including one, two and three-bedroom apartments, duplex apartments and town houses, alongside traditional terraced, semidetached and detached houses.
Although affordability remains a challenge, this variety offers more options for first-time buyers, including those using government incentives. It also gives trading buyers options, particularly where they can use equity from the sale of their existing home.
As we enter into the final quarter of the year we see the outlook for new homes as being positive overall. While demand remains high and continues to outstrip supply, there is a growing sense that this situation will balance itself out over time. There has been an unlocking of lands that once were unavailable for development and this should give prospective buyers more choice in 2027.
But there are still other factors that are holding the new homes market back. The main ones are a lack of infrastructure and affordability. Higher interest rates directly impact the purchaser with higher monthly payments giving people less capacity to borrow which makes it that much harder for people to make that first move.
First-time buyers are always more vulnerable when it comes to upwards interest-rate movements. The Government’s Help to Buy scheme remains in place, however, for those that are eligible. Sustainability, meanwhile, has now become intermingled with the issue of affordability. Green mortgages for new homes which are customarily A-rated for energy usage are good for people’s pockets in terms of the amount paid to the mortgage lender, and in the lower amounts paid to utility companies once the new homeowner is in situ.
A growing trend we have seen in 2026 is that of “right sizing”, or downsizing. More people are looking at whether their homes are still the right fit for them. This trend is beginning to increase the number of larger family homes on the market, and this movement of property is good for everyone.
The new homes market and general house-building sector has demonstrated strong resilience in the face of a lot of challenges this year. Forecasts approaching 40,000 completions are to be welcomed and are across all tenures with only around a third of completions coming for sale to the private market.
Within the home building industry, the Government’s housing plan Delivering Homes Building Communities has been broadly welcomed. It’s not yet a year old and there is a lot that’s yet to happen. From a housing delivery and business perspective, we are focused on two of the key priorities: zoning sufficient and serviced land and creating the right environment for investment.
The scorecard for the great rezoning is mixed and momentum has perhaps drifted, with different local authorities showing greater or lesser ambition. It’s an onerous and technical process that needs local authorities to be equipped with sufficient technical ability to prepare appropriate development plans. The push for higher densities can be a double-edged sword and in the wrong location density can result in heavy subsidy and greater reliance on the State. Development plans need flexibility to deliver what’s viable and affordable as opposed to what is aspirational from an urban design perspective. Simply put, to have more plans, we need more planners.
Big decisions were made around creating the right environment for investment to include the changes to Rent Pressure Zones and VAT reduction. In the face of a rising interest rate cycle, however, and with much heavier construction inflation, the impact of these changes have been somewhat negated. With yields moving outwards, it’s incredibly important that current State interventions are maintained and enhanced in the absence of alternatives.
For the past number of years our internal theme has been “Tenures and Typographies” and in 2026 we have seen meaningful progress following compact settlement design changes and many more apartments coming to the market supported by the Croí Cónaithe scheme. Both the Land Development Authority and various local authorities have been preparing projects to bring to market and we are seeing much more evidence of this in recent months.
Maintaining momentum is really important in a high-inflation environment, and in this regard, the zoning and infrastructure agenda is going in the right direction. We just need to ensure we’re consistent when it comes to delivery.

title: Youth: This might be the best art-imitates-life show Sharon Horgan has attempted
description: Television: Now, in her 50s and divorced, she is once again wrenching chuckles from her life via looking‑for‑love‑in‑middle‑age dramedy
content:
S haron Horgan might not take it as a compliment, but her new HBO comedy Youth confirms her status as the Woody Allen of her generation – a writer of sad, brittle chortle-fests that serve as a sort of comedic autofiction, blurring the divide between creator and their character.
She’s done this before – Pulling was informed by her experiences as a thirtysomething Irish woman dating in London, while Catastrophe captured the messiness of a situationship with legs, which is how her marriage, by all accounts, began. Now, in her 50s and divorced, she is once again wrenching chuckles from the fabric of her life via looking‑for‑love‑in‑middle‑age dramedy Youth ( HBO Max from Monday).
It’s perhaps the best thing she has attempted – wry, unsparing and featuring a breakout performance by Aran Murphy (son of Cillian) as the moody student son of Horgan’s character, Alex. Forget Adolescence – Youth is one of the most realistic portraits you will see of a young man adrift in a world all too ready to think the worst of him.
As with her previous work, Horgan is brave enough to make her character unlikeable. Alex is a self‑obsessed literary agent who sees other people’s problems as a mirror in which she can behold her own reflection and ask why she can’t have it all. Or, if not have it all, then at least aspire to a functioning love life before 60 strikes and she turns into “old me”.
But as writer, producer and star, Horgan is equally merciless about the other characters. Alex’s ex, Lorcan ( Owen McDonnell ), is a self‑involved man‑boy actor who expects the world to bend to the demands of his ego, while her current love interest ( Rupert Friend ) is a smarm onslaught in nice‑guy’s clothing.
The only place where Youth really stumbles is when it tries to fill in the blanks of Alex’s family life. One of the things Horgan wants to address is the pressure of the Sandwich Generation as they juggle growing kids, a potentially troubled marriage (or no marriage at all) and ageing parents. But because Alex is an Irish woman in London, the show demands that her entire family – including an ailing mother and father and a sister – be a) Irish, and b) based in the UK ... which makes no sense.
Youth isn’t the first show to try this wheeze of an Irish person living in the UK with a fully Irish extended family on their doorstep. This was also attempted in the thriller Unforgotten , when Sinéad Keenan joined the cast, and in Siobhán McSweeney ’s Disney+ series Extraordinary . Of course, if the goal were to give an Irish character a family network, the logical thing to do would be to ... set the entire show in Ireland. But you suspect that the idea of locating an urbane comedy where people have fancy creative‑class jobs in ... shudder ... Dublin, would cause craniums at HBO to implode.
[ Sharon Horgan on suddenly being single in your 50s: ‘Will I just attract weirdos and freaks?’ Opens in new window ]
That huge distraction aside, Youth whizzes by on snarky energy and earns bonus marks for its realistically unsentimental depiction of the mother‑son relationship and its honesty about how shouty and disconnected from reality teenage boys can be. But amid all of that, it never forgets the giggles, and if this is to be the final chapter in Horgan’s “Dear Diary” trilogy, then it brings things to a close with perfectly apportioned quantities of tears and laughter.

title: Budget 2027 should mark the beginning of tax simplification, says KPMG
description: Successive budgets have added complexity, increasing cost for taxpayers, says Brian Brennan, tax partner at KPMG in Ireland and president of the Irish Tax Institute
content:
As Ireland prepares for Budget 2027, due to be announced on October 6th, the economic backdrop is more challenging than many expected 12 months ago. Conflict in the Middle East, the war in Ukraine and continued uncertainty in international trade are testing an economy that remains highly exposed to global developments.
Growth forecasts have softened, inflation has re-emerged and energy prices are again a significant concern. Annual inflation reached 3.3 per cent in June, while energy prices were 10 per cent higher than a year earlier. These pressures affect household finances, business investment decisions and the public finances alike.
In light of these pressures, Budget 2027 should not be judged by the number of measures it contains, but by whether it responds effectively to Ireland’s economic challenges and strengthens the foundations of sustainable growth. With tax revenues to the end of August at €66.3 billion, up more than 6 per cent on last year, the key question is how Ireland uses its strong public finances to address immediate pressures while investing in productivity, economic strength and the ability to withstand future shocks.
The Summer Economic Statement provides for an €8.5 billion package, comprising €1.5 billion in tax measures and €7 billion in additional expenditure. While this represents a significant intervention, the available fiscal space is more limited than the headline figure suggests. Choices will need to be made, with priority given to measures that expand Ireland’s productive potential.
Ireland’s labour market remains resilient, with approximately 2.79 million people employed in the first quarter of 2026. However, employment growth has slowed, and the employment rate has eased from 74.7 per cent to 73.3 per cent. The challenge now is not simply creating jobs, but increasing participation, improving productivity and ensuring work continues to pay.
Budget 2027 should increase the main tax credits and standard-rate income tax band in line with wage growth to limit fiscal drag and protect workers’ purchasing power. Combined with reform of PRSI thresholds, these measures would ease the burden on workers and employers, strengthen incentives to participate in the labour market and support productivity.
Reform of share-based remuneration schemes and enhancements to the Special Assignee Relief Programme would also improve Ireland’s attractiveness for highly skilled workers and support investment decisions by internationally mobile businesses.
Ireland’s appeal as a business location is often discussed in terms of tax rates. In reality, businesses increasingly assess jurisdictions based on certainty, administrative efficiency and ease of doing business.
Successive budgets have added layers of tax legislation, filing obligations and compliance requirements. While each may have had a valid policy objective, the cumulative effect is increased complexity and cost for taxpayers.
Simplification would reduce compliance costs, improve certainty for businesses and enhance the overall efficiency of the tax system. Clarity and ease of doing business and administration are critical factors in attracting FDI.
‘The Government’s Housing Infrastructure Investment Fund is a welcome step, but tax policy should also support additional supply’
Budget 2027 should mark the beginning of a comprehensive programme of tax simplification. Reforming the taxation of interest and foreign branch profits, streamlining corporation tax and VAT compliance obligations, and eliminating reporting requirements that duplicate information already held by the State would make Ireland a more efficient and attractive place to do business.
This work has become even more important as international tax reforms continue to reshape the global landscape. With the OECD Pillar Two framework and related reforms changing how multinational groups evaluate investment locations, Ireland will increasingly compete on certainty, skills, infrastructure, administrative efficiency and the quality of its overall business environment.
Housing and energy are often viewed through a social policy lens, but they are now fundamental economic issues.
Housing shortages affect recruitment, labour mobility, business expansion and the ability of individuals to access employment opportunities. Housing has become one of the most significant constraints on Ireland’s economic growth potential.
The Government’s Housing Infrastructure Investment Fund is a welcome step, but tax policy should also support additional supply. Measures that encourage office-to-residential conversion, improve the taxation of rental investment and facilitate employer-supported accommodation could complement direct public investment and help accelerate delivery.
Energy resilience deserves similar attention. Temporary measures such as excise reductions and carbon tax deferrals could provide short-term relief, but they do little to address Ireland’s underlying exposure to energy price shocks.
Budget 2027 should therefore focus on measures that support investment in energy security, energy efficiency and the green transition. Reducing exposure to imported energy would lower business costs and leave the economy better equipped to absorb future price shocks.
Ireland’s success in attracting foreign direct investment has transformed the economy and remains one of the country’s greatest strengths. Corporation tax receipts reached €32.9 billion in 2025, with foreign-owned multinational groups accounting for the overwhelming majority of those revenues.
Maintaining Ireland’s attractiveness as a location for international investment must therefore remain a priority. However, a more balanced economy also requires a broader domestic enterprise base.
A stronger cohort of Irish-headquartered businesses would diversify sources of growth, employment, exports and tax revenue, while reducing concentration risks within the economy. Budget 2027 should help more Irish businesses invest, scale and compete internationally.
‘A successful budget will not seek to do everything; it will focus on the measures that can make the greatest difference to Ireland’s future prosperity’
Priorities should include reform of the capital gains tax regime, enhancement of Entrepreneur Relief, improvements to the Key Employee Engagement Programme, extension of start-up reliefs and simplification of the Employment Investment Incentive Scheme. Reform of succession rules would also support the long-term sustainability of family-owned businesses and farms.
Budget 2027 comes at a time when Ireland holds the presidency of the Council of the European Union.
The presidency provides an opportunity for Ireland to advance a European competitiveness agenda focused on simplification, investment, productivity and reducing administrative burdens for businesses. These priorities align closely with wider EU efforts to improve economic performance, enhance energy security and deepen the single market.
Ireland has long been regarded as a pragmatic and credible voice on economic policy. Progress at European level on competitiveness and simplification would directly benefit Irish businesses and strengthen Ireland’s position as a location for investment.
Budget 2027 will require a difficult balance between supporting households facing higher costs and investing in Ireland’s future economic potential. The Government will be tested on whether it can look beyond short-term pressures and use the public finances to reward work, improve the business environment and unlock investment in housing, energy and Irish enterprise. A successful budget will not seek to do everything; it will focus on the measures that can make the greatest difference to Ireland’s future prosperity.

title: Apple continues to dominate Irish Top 1,000 rankings with €209bn in revenue
description: Pharma company Eli Lilly makes the top 10 for the first time, while CRH ranks as the largest indigenous company
content:
Big technology companies continued to dominate the Top 1,000 rankings of companies published by The Irish Times on Thursday, with Apple once again way out in front in both turnover and profits.
The California-based iPhone maker recorded revenue of €209.3 billion in the year to September 27th, 2025, with profits of €72 billion. The tech giant’s profit was roughly double that of the rest of the top 10 companies combined and has been a key factor behind the surge in Irish corporation taxes .
Reflecting the recent trend of jobs cuts in the tech sector, Apple’s headcount in Ireland reduced to 5,575 last year from the near 6,000 reported in the Top 1,000 survey a year earlier.
The top four spots in the rankings are once again the preserve of Big Tech, albeit that Microsoft and Meta swapped places.
Google retained second spot with revenue of €86.6 billion, while profits rose by roughly a quarter to €4.5 billion. The company had 4,882 staff here last year.
[ CEO pay in Ireland in 2025: One executive earned $237m Opens in new window ]
Microsoft’s profits rose by about 16 per cent to €4.65 billion while turnover rose by 11 per cent to just under €83 billion, but it slipped from third to fourth spot.
It was overtaken by Meta, with the Mark Zuckerberg-led tech giant recording profits of €2.9 billion on revenue of €85.3 billion. The company trimmed its headcount here during the year to 1,738 from just under 2,200 a year earlier.
Pharma giant Eli Lilly makes the top 10 for the first time with revenues of €40 billion, displacing rival Pfizer to secure fifth place. Pfizer posted a profit of €6.4 billion on turnover of €35.7 billion in the period. Both of these figures were reduced on a year ago.
CRH was the largest indigenous company – it remains headquartered and tax domiciled in Ireland even though its shares are listed in New York. Led by Jim Mintern, the building materials company recorded a profit of €4.2 billion on turnover of €33.3 billion.
[ Explainer: Why it may take years for Google to pay its latest Irish fine Opens in new window ]
As the world’s biggest packaging group, Smurfit Westrock made it into the top 10 this year, up from 11th spot a year ago, with revenues of €27.7 billion.
Medtronic and Johnson Controls (a “world leader in smart buildings”) rounded out the top 10, with power management systems manufacturer Eaton Corporation and DCC, which is soon to delist from the London stock market following a takeover, slipping out.
In assets, Citibank was the largest financial institution at €186.5 billion, with the Central Bank of Ireland slipping from first to third place this year.
Among the retail banks here, Bank of Ireland was ahead of AIB in assets but the Colin Hunt-led lender posted higher profits.
[ What top CEO pay and gender pay gap reporting tell us about Irish business Opens in new window ]
Revolut was 11th in the table of banks, with assets of €35.4 billion. The fintech, which says it has 3.4 million customers in Ireland, made a profit here last year of €278 million, just more than double that of a year earlier.
Others to note in the top 20 are Guinness maker Diageo in 14th, Ryanair in 15th and gambling group Flutter in 16th.
Energy group ESB was the largest State-owned entity, posting a profit of €750 million on revenue of €6.7 billion.
You can also find the full list of this year’s Top 1,000 companies in The Irish Times ePaper .
