“Thankfully it didn’t come to that, they stuck with me. But I was confident I’d a good enough training block, would always back myself going into a Grand Tour.
“I’ve honestly lost track of all the crashes now. For most of them, there’s nothing you can do, you’ve no control over them. It’s weird, I just seem to find myself on the wrong side more than others. But I’m thinking more about the stage win, that’s important, because mentally and physically, all the accidents do take a toll.
“And I’ve love to go back to the Tour de France. Especially the way it ended last year, I feel I’ve a bit of unfinished business there. Just go there in top shape, be competitive in stages, maybe make it to finish in Paris the next time.”

title: Leaving Dublin to build a new home in a Wicklow village: ‘The drama is just part of the process’
description: Remote working made a move home feasible for this family - their architect drew on ring-forts and expansive views on-site when planning the property
content:
Whether it’s at home or on holiday, we all want a room with a view. So, when architect Gareth Brennan of Brennan Furlong architects saw the site where his would-be clients wanted to build their home, he knew the vista would be an important element to the project.
Located on the outskirts of the village of Grangecon, which is on the Kildare- Wicklow border, the site was relatively flat, but the views extended a 60km distance across the plains of Kildare, and southwest towards the Slieve Bloom mountains.
The extended views are due to the low-lying nature of the wider landscape. Brennan’s clients, who were building on family land, wanted to relocate from Dublin to a rural location. His brief “called for a modest, understated, traditional facade to the public roadway”, while the rear would “make the most of the afternoon sun and the views towards the mountains”.
“The clients came to us, as one of them [a graphic designer] had previously done work for us,” he says. “When we first visited the site I was struck by how far you could see in all directions – the flat landscape made the mountains and sky feel really prominent. I have done a lot of reading on Irish ringforts, many of which present today as subtle anomalies in the landscape. So I wanted the house to have that sense – a subtle ‘object in the landscape’, as it was going to be centrally placed in the site, not adjacent to any pre-existing structure or feature.
“Inside, they wanted an open-plan kitchen/living/dining area, which would wrap around the external terrace, and be the hub of family life. Then at the other end of the house, they wanted a quiet, calm, secluded livingroom – and given the relatively flat site and surrounding countryside, they wanted a terrace off the main bedroom at first-floor level, which would afford them views across the landscape.”
Design work on the project began at the firm, which was established in 2015 by Brennan and Séamus Furlong, in the autumn of 2022. A planning application was submitted in the summer of 2023, and full planning permission was secured by the end of that year.
The project started on site in early 2024. Altogether it took roughly three years, from design stage to completion, which was just a few months over its expected finish date – with the homeowners moving in “just in time for the start of the 2025-2026 school year”.
“The house is just over 200m² in area, with a 30m² detached garage,” says the Clontarf-based architect. “And along with the open plan area and separate living area on the ground floor, there is also a guest bedroom on the same level and a further three bedrooms upstairs – one each for their two children, and a main bedroom suite. Also, the kitchen is supplemented by a large utility, as our client is a keen baker.
“We worked closely with the client on the interior fit-out, particularly the internal floor finishes, a ‘top-coat’ polished concrete throughout, and the stairs and landing balustrade. They had very clear ideas on the fit-out of both the kitchen and the bathrooms in particular, with fittings and tiling all selected by them. But we used 3D models of the house which evolved and developed throughout the build process to test various finishes before they were selected.”
The outside wasn’t forgotten, with landscaping a collaborative effort between the architects and the client. The patio areas, which Gerry Brennan Concrete worked on, were core to the original design of the house, with the clients working with Elma Fenton on designing, selecting and sourcing the soft landscaping and planting to the wider site.
Having a good relationship with the clients from the outset was very instrumental to ensuring the project went to plan. This was tested when, after a request to rework the designs, Brennan visited the homeowners to talk them through the new workings, only to find that he had left the plans behind at the office. However, he acted on his feet – and a mutual trust was confirmed.
“I offered to sketch the updated designs for them there and then,” he recalls. “They were sceptical, to say the least, but I sat down and proceeded to draw out the revised layouts in front of them as we sat at their kitchen table, explaining the ideas and rationale behind the plans as I drew. They realised that I wasn’t making it up, and were much more comfortable with the updated designs.
“Then as soon as I got back to the office, I scanned in the original hand-drawings I’d done in preparation for the meeting and mailed them over. The clients were very much reassured and encouraged by the evolution of the design, and the process moved much more smoothly from there. Even though the appearance of the design changed radically from the first iteration, the rationale and the arrangement of spaces in the final design still owes a lot to those original ideas.”
Some notable features of the project include the splayed window reveals, which were a contemporary interpretation of a traditional detail; the use of two complementary yet contrasting render finishes – both smooth and dashed; the curved stairs balustrade; the colour selection for the windows; and delivery of the subtle metal framing of the entrance door, which was constructed by Metweld Fabrication.
The end result is down to the collaborative effort between architect and client.
“I think they appreciated that we were thoroughly invested in delivering a special home for them, and I like to think this is borne out by the end product.”
Brennan Furlong has won awards for its work and has exhibited abroad, but when it comes to fulfilling a specific brief, how the homeowner feels about their new space is the most important thing. Suffice to say, the Kildare family were delighted with the outcome.
One of the homeowners grew up in the Wicklow village, “but the idea of living there simply wasn’t practical when working in Dublin. But after the pandemic, remote working became more feasible, so this opened up the option of moving back, as we thought it would give us a better quality of life and would allow our children to grow up closer to their grandparents, which is very important to us.
“We had a few ideas of what we were looking for, but we didn’t want to be too rigid and wanted to allow Brennan Furlong to bring their own ideas and perspectives – and I think Gareth and Paul delivered exactly what we wanted. Also, we were fortunate that our builder, Johnny Wynne of Dublin Carpentry, had worked on other family members’ houses – so there was already a relationship there, which put us at ease.”
Delighted with their new build, they advise that anyone thinking about building a house should “not lose sight of the end result”.
“There will inevitably be days when it feels like nothing is going right and it will never be done but, as any home building TV show will tell you, the drama is just part of the process,” the homeowner says. “I would advise taking the time to get to know your builder and architect and being open to suggestions and alternatives. An architect can see something a builder won’t, and vice versa, which can catch problems before they happen or make a design tweak for the better. Also, push back when your gut tells you to, because, at the end of the day, you’re the one living in the house.
“Also, try to stay two steps ahead and have fittings and finishes decided and bought early – because although the house may seem to be just block work, suddenly you need to have your sanitary wear ready to make sure everything lines up. There’s nothing like having to think about tiles on Friday when you’ve just been told the tiler is coming on Monday. But don’t lose sight of the goal and why you are building in the first place.
“From our own perspective, the end result was a house that feels made just for us, exceeded our expectations, and is a credit to everyone involved in making it happen.”

title: Living with breast cancer: ‘I’ve possibly had one of the best years of my life. I’ve got rid of anything that didn’t matter’
description: A farmer tells of how astonishingly beautiful seemingly ordinary things can be after a hellish year coping with cancer
content:
I’m not fortunate enough to live in the wild – not yet, anyway – so when I’m home in Dublin, I take in whatever slices of the natural world I can find. In the evenings, I walk my dog through the local park, past trees whose familiar shape and presence I depend on. In all the nights I’ve walked these paths, one venerable tree – a knotty oak, of course – has lodged its way into my life. When I pass, I cannot shake a feeling, mad as it sounds, that it sees me.
On clear nights, the few stars that make it through the city’s haze of light pollution become visible. It’s relaxing, staring up. And then something moves at the edge of my vision, and I think it’s a shooting star, until I realise it’s something entirely unmagical: one of Elon Musk’s SpaceX satellites in orbit. He’s recently applied to put a million of them up there – the Muskification of our night sky has only just begun.
I walk up to the old oak and have an improbable feeling of recognition. The poet Mary Oliver wrote that her work was mostly “standing still and learning to be astonished”. Attention, she said, is the beginning of devotion. And so, with Oliver on my mind, I stand under the oak, letting myself love what I love, and never feel alone.
A few weeks ago, I spent time with Hannah Page Fox on her sheep and Christmas tree farm in Grangecon in Wicklow. Until last spring, her life was normal, with her husband and three daughters. There had been a few health issues the previous year, signs that might have been missed, but nothing that added up to anything. Then an acute bout of sickness landed her in A&E, and she was told she had stage four lobular breast cancer , with tumours that had spread and wrapped around her stomach. Six weeks in hospital followed, with months of nil by mouth, unable to swallow. She is still on treatment, and always will be.
We walked through an old rusted gate into a stubble field of harvested corn, up towards a ring fort, one of two on the farm, which has never been ploughed or touched. Many farmers still don’t plough ring forts, or fairy forts as they’re called. Page Fox and her husband Andy built a series of wood-fired saunas from old horse boxes and antique bathtubs pulled from the hedge, where they’d once been drinkers for the cattle, now fed by a spring. A woman who talks to fairies told her that the fairies wanted the land healed before they’d accept the sauna. The challenge? Walk the perimeter of the farm.
It’s a farm with no neat borders. Page Fox set off with a friend and two dogs. She walked through brambles, across streams, through ditches. It took three hours. Her dogs gave up and wandered home. She was still very sick, and it took everything she had. But she told me, “I have never laughed so much in my life”.
She had not known or noticed what was around her before. She saw a mushroom shaped like a fried egg – sunny side up – which she had never seen before. She stopped and realised how astonishingly beautiful it was. The perimeter walk, she said, was the turning point of her hellish year, marking the first time she really laughed. “I had forgotten how to live in it,” she says of the farm. “I was just living on it.”
I asked Page Fox whether it was too insensitive to ask whether some part of her tough year had also been a gift. “I’ve possibly had one of the best years of my life, because I’ve got rid of anything that didn’t matter,” she said. What went was the tidy house; what she wants is to be outside. She spent this March in the lambing sheds helping her brother, which she hadn’t had time to do in years, and she got out for the Christmas tree harvest. At night, she goes out and looks at the stars.
‘There are days where the tears still flow. There are days where I wonder what the future holds for my children’
Lobular cancer is the second most common type of breast cancer, but it doesn’t behave like the kind so many of us are warned about. It often doesn’t form a lump at all. “It acts like a spider’s web,” Page Fox says. It threads through tissue rather than balling up, which can make it close to invisible on a mammogram. It’s particularly invisible in dense breasts. In one survey of breast radiologists, only a quarter said they were confident they could catch it on a screening mammogram in a dense breast. Roughly four in 10 women of screening age have dense breasts, yet BreastCheck does not currently measure density, record it, or tell you yours.
[ New figures show thousands of people not getting timely access to cancer care, TD says Opens in new window ]
Her days aren’t all serene. “There are days where the tears still flow,” she said. “There are days where I wonder what the future holds for my children.” But she’s been more hopeful lately than in a long time. On October 13th, she’ll travel to Leinster House with the #TellMeMyBreastDensity beingdense.com campaign for women to be told their breast density after a mammogram. “I love life. I love nature. I love being in this world,” she told me. “I’m not ready to leave it. Not for a long time.”

title: Gurriers singer Dan Hoff: ‘I try to talk about my mental-health issues the same as a common cold’
description: Postpunk band are upfront about having accumulated hard-won wisdom since they formed in 2020 before lockdown
content:
The most agonising nine hours in Pierce Callaghan’s life was a drive in a tour bus from Prague to Vienna that he experienced through the business end of a biblically crippling hangover.
“I remember coming home from a tour that we did. It might only have been, like, a week, week and a half. And I genuinely think I had alcohol withdrawal,” the drummer with Gurriers recalls in the shellshocked tones of someone recalling their time in the trenches.
With a shudder, he describes staying up all night drinking in Prague hours before Gurriers were due to drive across central Europe for their next gig. When the group assembled in their tour bus the following morning, his bandmates immediately clocked that he was in the horrors – and found his predicament hilarious.
“There is a distinct lack of sympathy in all directions. I’m a complete wind-up, like; then, when I’m in the position where I’m a little bit tender, I’m getting it from every direction. I deserved it,” he says, laughing.
The incident was born of youthful exuberance shortly after the release of Come and See , the debut 2024 album from the acclaimed Dublin postpunk band, when they were heralded as heirs to Fontaines DC ’s crown.
“When we went on the first big tour after we released the first record – at one stage we did eight, nine shows in a row. The last one before a day off, we played in Prague,” Callaghan says.
“A load of my mates came out for the weekend. I remember going out afterwards and getting pissed; got into the hotel at probably, like, 7am, had my bag in the van at 9am. We were driving to Vienna – driving for nine hours. And I was hanging.”
[ Irish postpunk band Gurriers: ‘Everyone asks about the Dublin music scene. It’s not just Dublin any more, it’s everywhere’ Opens in new window ]
The anecdote gets a laugh from his bandmates, who are dialling in from various locations. As they join the Zoom call, it’s immediately obvious that the group, so raw and furious on record, are in an upbeat, even jolly frame of mind before the release of their second album, Nobody’s Coming to Save You.
But they’re also upfront about having accumulated a lot of hard-won wisdom since they formed, in 2020, when they held their first rehearsal weeks before lockdown. They’ve learned to curb their partying, appreciating that excess is a fast track to burnout.
They’ve become increasingly mindful, too, of their emotional health – something they need to look after in an industry that is notoriously tough on mental wellbeing.
That process includes showing kindness towards one another and, self-inflicted hangovers aside, being aware of their bandmates’ frailties, Dan Hoff, the band’s singer, says. He has taken mental-health breaks from Gurriers when he has felt the need to decompress from touring. Self-care is something he’s mindful of, having left his previous band because of the anxiety he experienced at the time.
“It’s about complete honesty,” he says from his flat in Dublin. “I’m on medication. I’m going to go to therapy. I try to talk about my mental-health issues the same as if I have a common cold.”
Attitudes towards mental health have come a long way, but there is still a stigma to it, Hoff says. “If the people around you are more educated about what is wrong – well, not wrong with you, but what you have – the easier it is to navigate things.”
Come and See was a big hit with critics, and Gurriers could have easily cranked out a facsimile.
But they were determined to go out on a limb, and so, while their second album replicates the storm and fury of its predecessor, it also takes a risk by introducing a punk-funk element, resulting in new songs that have the feel of a riot at a discotheque. They may no longer drink their way through tours, but creatively they’re still living on the edge, pushing things to the limit.
“We could have very easily pigeonholed ourselves and made a Come and See II,” Hoff says. “But if you want to be in a band and you want to prove to yourselves and to your audiences that you can evolve and push the envelope further, why not take risks and go for it?”
What hasn’t changed is the political element in Gurriers’ writing. Just as Come and See addressed the rise of the far right in Ireland (Approachable was a viciously humorous takedown of the National Party), so Nobody’s Coming explores subjects such as the war in Sudan and the slaughter of innocents. (“We wash this blood off of our hands,” Hoff howls on the band’s single Party Lines.)
They feel strongly that musicians should stand up for what they believe, and were proud to withdraw from the South by Southwest (SXSW) in Austin, Texas, in 2024 after Kneecap’s manager, Daniel Lambert, told them the event was sponsored by the US military and defence contractors connected to the war in Gaza.
The drama started the day before Gurriers were due to play at the influential festival, by which point they were already in Texas and ready to go.
“I remember getting a phone call off Dan Lambert the night before. We were playing on the Monday, and he rang me on the Sunday night, saying, ‘We’re not [participating in SXSW].’ They’d been in America and they were coming home,” Callaghan says.
“We spoke to the other bands and took the decision to all pull out. We had the governor of Texas tell us we should all leave Texas.”
‘We’ve had our share of free margaritas. I’m not going to tell a younger musician not to go out and enjoy themselves’
But if they remain fervently political, Hoff insists they aren’t trying to preach to anyone – and they don’t pretend to know how to solve the world’s problems. He recalls a review of Gurriers that criticised them for “saying so many political things but having no answers”.
“How the fuck am I going to have the answers?” he says. “We don’t have the answers. Nobody does.”
He believes the last thing a band should be is dogmatic. He recalls a youthful infatuation with the firebrand atheism of the scientist Richard Dawkins and the late journalist Christopher Hitchens . It ended after he decided they were as doctrinaire in their convictions as any Bible-thumper.
“I would always find them to be very preachy. Very dogmatic – which is what they’re fighting against. They’re creating their own religions, almost – Hitchensism, Dawkinsism. It made me feel betrayed by these men. I never want to be preachy. I want to tell you how it is: here are the facts, that’s how I feel about it.”
Gurriers also don’t pretend to have any answers to the thorny issue of whether the Irish music industry is doing enough to support home-grown artists. With Fontaines DC, they’re part of a generation of Irish bands that are acclaimed in Britain, where they receive much of their airplay on BBC 6 Music.
There’s an argument that British radio is far more supportive of Irish artists than RTÉ or Today FM is; look at how 6 Music championed CMAT at a time when she hardly got a look-in on daytime playlists back home.
There’s an obvious temptation to write off Irish radio as hopelessly behind the times and still trapped in a mindset where, if you don’t sound like Hozier or Dermot Kennedy , then you’re not getting on the radio. Gurriers say that the truth is more nuanced – and that comparing RTÉ or Today FM to a behemoth such as the BBC isn’t necessarily illuminating.
“This is not me creating excuses for RTÉ, but you’re talking about two countries of massively different sizes and massively different budgets,” Callaghan says.
“The BBC doesn’t do everything perfectly. But 6 Music have carved out a little space for alternative music, and the infrastructure is there and the support network is there from the wider BBC. When 6 Music was created you had people like John Peel.”
He believes that left-leaning voices in Irish radio were siloed off and never given any real power or influence.
“The pioneers of alternative music on Irish radio, they never got their own little thing. You think of, like, Dave Fanning – the idea that 35 or 40 years ago Dave Fanning could have been given his own radio station and that it could have developed into its own thing. It could have been an amazing thing, but it didn’t happen.”
Gurriers’ frustration with the challenges of operating a band from Ireland has resulted in the biggest change since Come and See: the band’s decision to relocate to Manchester. Hoff remains in Dublin, but his bandmates have all crossed the Irish Sea to the home town of Oasis , The Smiths and The Stone Roses – a city where the rent is comparatively affordable. There was no burning desire to up sticks, they say; the motives were largely practical.
“There’s this classic case of Irish artists, particularly Irish bands, making the move to London,” Mark McCormack, the band’s guitarist, says from his parents’ home in Castleblayney, in Co Monaghan, to which he has returned for a flying visit. (He and Callaghan grew up in the town and met at school.)
“We’re making a little bit of money – and the emphasis is on ‘a little’. Let’s not blow the whole thing on a house in London that we’re not actually going to be in.”
Manchester seemed like the best compromise. “There’s great community. It’s not too big, and serves the purpose of having a base in the UK now. The whole purpose of living in the UK is that we drive everywhere, as opposed to flying and then getting a van there. We have a van in the UK. We all pile in, we go to Calais and then we go where we need to go.”
They’ll be back on the road shortly as they gear up for a tour that will include not only a return to Texas but also a number of dates in different venues in Dublin soon, and in Belfast in October.
“We’ve had our share of free margaritas,” says Callaghan. “I’m not going to tell a younger musician not to go out and enjoy themselves. But I think you ultimately have to look after yourself and the people around you if you want to keep the show on the road.”
Nobody’s Coming to Save You is out through Pias Recordings on Friday, September 25th. Gurriers play the Grand Social, Dublin, on Thursday, September 24th. They are then at Ulster Hall, Belfast, on Wednesday, October 28th; Vicar Street, Dublin, on Thursday, October 29th; and 3Olympia Theatre, Dublin, on Sunday, November 1st

title: Trespasses author Louise Kennedy: ‘I lived on adrenaline all my life from kitchens’
description: The author on her new novel, Stations, moving south from the North, and how she ‘hired’ Gillian Anderson
content:
‘My granny was in a bomb explosion when I was four. She was on her way from our pub to the bank to make a lodgment when a bomb exploded and a big piece of glass cut her jugular vein. An off-duty British soldier saved her life. One of my uncles didn’t recognise her, because her face was blown open. He went back to the pub and said there’s some poor woman up there in a terrible state, dead.
“She’d lost a lot of blood, her heart kept stopping and she had all these surgeries and skin grafts, maybe 400 stitches. And she woke up with some wee man standing over her, saying ‘Missus, what was in your handbag?’
“He said that they nearly had to break her arms to get the handbag off her because she wouldn’t let go of the money. She used to tell that story really proudly.
“She was very glamorous. She was wearing a fur coat, so that kind of protected her body. She had a line and loads of little nicks, but they did a brilliant job on her face.”
Louise Kennedy is a born storyteller, with a particular gift for finding the saving grace of humour in the midst of trauma – the traumedic art.
Like Róisín, the protagonist in her new novel, Stations, she left the North when she was 12, moved with her family to the South but never truly settled before emigrating to London for a spell. She has lived in Sligo for 20 years and is happy there but will forever be a blow-in. “I don’t know how to be in the world except as an outsider. My home place doesn’t exist any more.”
Sligo and its hinterland served as the backdrop for most of The End of the World Is a Cul de Sac , her brilliant short-story collection, from 2021. Her native North came alive in her award-winning, bestselling debut novel, Trespasses , from 2022, a Troubles love story made into a Channel 4 series starring Gillian Anderson.
Stations, which is her second novel, starts off in a Kildare town much like Naas, where she moved from Holywood, Co Down, after one loyalist attack too many on the family pub. But it quickly shifts to London, where Kennedy lived long enough as a young woman to capture its essence.
Stations is a love story, too, albeit an unrequited one, but it is as much about family and friendships, shadowed by abuse and addiction yet leavened by wit and warmth. It also proudly takes its place alongside If I Could Read the Sky, by Timothy O’Grady and Steve Pyke, and The Grass Arena, by John Healy, both namechecked in the text, and JM O’Neill’s novels Duffy Is Dead and Open Cut as part of the London-Irish story. “I am operating in some kind of tradition,” Kennedy says.
‘There was a lot of anxiety in our house. The phone would ring, and it might be that a bomb had just gone off in the pub’
The Grass Arena’s opening line – “My father didn’t look like he would harm anyone” – echoes chillingly through Stations.
Starting in 1982 and spanning 25 years, it tracks the relationship of Róisín and Red from their schooldays in Kildare to a London squat and beyond, sometimes estranged but always entwined.
There are many autobiographical elements in Stations – jobs Kennedy has done, places she has lived, meals she has cooked. “I couldn’t imagine a character just moving through some kind of bland space. I need to put them in a place I know to be able to generate it or for anything to happen.”
There are definitely parallels between Róisín’s background and hers, Kennedy says. “She lived in a town near the sea, like I did, and moved to the South at 12 in 1979, like I did, and was spectacularly unpopular in school, like I was.
“But they left the North because her father was in the RUC, so I actually think I need to get a T-shirt made that says, ‘My dad was never a peeler’. He was an accountant in a firm on the Newtownards Road, the only Catholic in a very large workforce, so he had to look under his car for different reasons.”
The book’s title is suggestive of the transport hubs where key scenes play out but also of social standing and the depiction of Christ’s Passion.
“Róisín is certainly getting ideas above her station, going to Henley regatta, so there are class things and maybe something about mobility or aspiration as well. And I guess there’s that thing about the Stations of the Cross, stumbling and falling and keeping going. The book was called Red for a while, and the German publisher is going to call it Red.”
Kennedy has a degree in social studies from University College Dublin, and Pierre Bourdieu’s concept of cultural capital is a ghost at Stations’ feast. Róisín’s love rival Octavia turns up with Christmas leftovers, culinary capital in the form of rich crumbs from the table of her Tory-MP father. Róisín, on the other hand, conjures up delicious meals from base ingredients: grey mince and ketchup for want of tomato puree – rags to rich ragu.
[ Louise Kennedy on her career change: ‘At 45 I thought I was finished' Opens in new window ]
Kennedy spent almost 30 years as a chef, training alongside Irish Sloane Rangers at Alix Gardner Cookery School, then working at Bon Appetit in Malahide and Elephant & Castle in Temple Bar, opening Garravogue in Sligo for Jay Bourke and Eoin Foyle, then starting her own place there with her husband, Stephen, The Silver Apple, named for the Yeats verse – “notions, even then”.
She worked at Hodges Figgis in the 1990s for a couple of years and used to cater for book launches. ) “One party ended up being so mental there was wine spilled all over the till. I think we might have got in trouble for that, because I don’t think it was supposed to have been that much fun.”
After we talk, Kennedy treats me to a delicious home-made lunch: quiche with bacon, scallions and Coolattin cheddar with orzo, tomatoes, pesto and Cnoc Liatroma goat’s cheese, followed by raspberry-and-almond cake.
“My dream would have been to be a charcutier in Lyon. I used to get these organic ducks delivered and would use every single bit. I’d render the fat, make confit, take the breast off the bone, keep the hearts and put them on rosemary skewers and grill them, duck liver pate. I made rillettes with whatever was left on the carcasses and stock. I had grease up to my elbows.”
‘I am not one of those people who’s managed to carry people with me for years and years’
But cooking was also a way of dealing with anxiety by living on her nerves.
“I used to get really bad panic attacks. Some of it maybe went back to how awful it was in [secondary] school, but I started having sleeping problems when I was about seven or eight.
“There was a lot of anxiety in our house. The phone would ring, and it might be that a bomb had just gone off in the pub. If there was a loud noise you’d go to pieces.
“No one ever used the word ‘trauma’ then. I was really interested in food, and cheffing gave me a way of being able to support myself. You just turn up with your uniform and bag of knives and either you were shite or you weren’t.”
So it’s little wonder that food enriches Kennedy’s writing. The dinner party in Trespasses is a standout scene. In Stations there is great poignancy when Róisín is given “a few Golden Wonders. The ones your father set”, which she offers to cook for a friend.
“I didn’t know if I’d got away with that. I just wrote that and was bawling and crying and then I thought, Jesus Christ, what are they going to think, getting very emotional about the spuds?”
Does Kennedy ever laugh when she’s writing as well? “So okay, a lot of the response to this has been, ‘I am devastated, crying my eyes out.’ I’m going, ‘Does nobody think it’s funny?’ Because I was roaring laughing at certain times.”
For the record, I laughed when Róisín said her father “would be best represented by a pint of Tennent’s and a letter from the Child Support Agency” and, later, “I can’t say a good word about him, it’s like a form of Tourette’s”. And the description of Barry’s girlfriend, who “looked like a postulant but roared ‘Slap me, hai’ as she came, a demand that carried all over the house.”
Another significant reference in Stations is the Rake’s Progress series of satirical paintings by William Hogarth, which chart the downfall of Tom Rakewell, and which Róisín and Red see on a visit to Sir John Soane’s Museum, one of Kennedy’s favourite places in London.
“It’s magic, but you’d have to be in the whole of your health to go there, because there’s just so much stuff.”
Is there an obvious parallel between Tom Rakewell’s decline and Red’s? “I think so. It starts off kind of beautiful. Maybe he’s having a premonition of what might happen to him.”
Stations spans a quarter of a century. How challenging was it to handle the passage of time?
“It was murder. The first couple of drafts I had too many scenes. I was carrying a lot of backstory. My editor said, ‘Just put a date on each chapter.’ That meant I didn’t have to use any backstory, and I hoped that it would be okay just to drop the reader in and it’s, like, you leave off in 1989 and then it’s 2007. I didn’t want to have passages like, ‘In the meantime, Róisín did this and she got divorced.’”
A funeral scene helps because a lot of characters gather for it.
Is there an argument for letting the reader do a bit of work?
“I think so. People aren’t stupid. I sometimes get resentful when things are explained to me too much. The really hard bit was trying to age Róisín. She starts off in her teens, and there’s a big jump to where she’s, like, 40, and she can’t be slamming doors. I guess maybe my curiosity was, has she learned anything? Is she still fighting with everybody? Is her head still up her backside, blaming other people for things that she had a hand in as well? Does she regret anything?”
One thing that surprised Kennedy was the reappearance of Barry, a peripheral character who becomes central. “Barry was maybe the biggest surprise to me because he was so real to me. It was really weird. Like, I was walking around for about four months thinking I was having an affair. He was so vivid to me. It was really ridiculous.”
Kennedy’s husband needn’t worry, though. “Barry is still a bit of a dose.”
‘I have any kind of mental or emotional stress, or when it’s really warm, I can’t function at all’
Like Kennedy, Róisín is an outsider at school too. She first appeared in Belladonna, a story in Kennedy’s debut collection.
“I liked the voice and the fact that she was smart, but not as smart as she thought she was. Children in an adult world just don’t really get it. I liked her character because she’s not really that likable. So I guess this is her, maybe a year or two later, and I gave her a friend.
“I am interested in relationships, not just romantic ones. I’m interested in families, in friendships. I think maybe I find that fascinating because it’s something that eluded me for a lot of my teens, like I have one friend who I knew in secondary school. I am not really in touch with anybody from primary school. I am not one of those people who’s managed to carry people with me for years and years.”
The second strand, which Kennedy wrote in the year that she started writing, features practically unchanged in Stations, a poignant scene where Róisín is about to head home from Victoria coach station when she meets a much older Irish immigrant in a bar. Not every Irish writer can as credibly set their work across the Irish Sea.
“I did live in London, but I think it’s just about paying attention. I think I also have a really good memory. I have a sister who’s got an even better memory than me who was with me in London at the same time.”
Kennedy was diagnosed with melanoma and had surgery in 2019, the same year she was shortlisted for the Sunday Times short story award. She was shortlisted again the following year. In 2021 her debut collection was published and the cancer returned, now stage four, “so they had to bring out the big guns: immunotherapy”.
In January 2022, four months before Trespasses came out, Kennedy was hospitalised after a severe reaction. “In about four days I’d gained 5kg, all fluid. I’d my head in a basin of ice water to reduce the swelling. My skin was like marzipan, itchy, coming off like paste. My pituitary gland had exploded. I hadn’t produced any cortisol for 10 days.
“That damage is permanent, so I have to take steroids every day and carry a syringe. But if I have any kind of mental or emotional stress, or when it’s really warm, I can’t function at all.
“It made it really hard to write the book. I lived on adrenaline all my life from kitchens. I was just brilliant at producing that burst of energy. It’s probably not very good for you, but I can’t do any of that now.”
When Kennedy started writing, did that replicate the buzz? “No. I think that was a different thing, probably the complete opposite. I’m probably using a different part of my brain, mucking about with language.”
Kennedy has a dry, deadpan wit and a refreshing frankness, so it’s no surprise to learn that when, at a dinner party, she found herself sitting beside Gillian Anderson, who told her how much she liked the mother in Trespasses, the writer asked if she’d play the role.
“I was full of wine,” Kennedy says, but also serious illness is a good antidote to razzmatazz. “I think maybe I was very lucky in that I was either doing things like that or I was in Galway on a public oncology ward. Because there were two very extreme things going on, I didn’t really think a lot about it. Maybe also I’m a bit too old to be really impressed by that stuff.”
Until her friend Niamh Mac Cabe, author of the recent short-story collection Four Night Seas, dragged her to a creative-writing workshop run by the Irish-American author Una Mannion in 2014, Kennedy had no notion of becoming a writer, despite having worked in bookshops in Naas and Dublin and then as a librarian after she was burned out as a chef. Except, as is so often the case, a good teacher had planted a seed that lay dormant for decades.
“Miss McKenna used to do really amazing things. No child had a lot of cultural capital in this wee Catholic primary school in Holywood. One day she played a Mozart horn concerto and got us to write something. Another time she pinned Monet’s poppies to the blackboard and she was wildly encouraging.
“Years later she told me I had written something that was lovely. I remember thinking, maybe really briefly, God, I’d love to be a writer. I probably thought it was like something magical. Must be f**king mental, actually, is what I think now.”
Kennedy did a PhD in creative writing at Queen’s University Belfast, which included a dissertation on the writer Norah Hoult, whom she had discovered in Sinéad Gleeson’s anthology The Long Gaze Back. She singles out two books as “really extraordinary”: Hoult’s debut short-story collection, Poor Women, and There Were No Windows, a novel set in London during the Blitz.
[ Why has Norah Hoult been overlooked? Opens in new window ]
She had a lonely life, Kennedy says. “I cried a lot going through her archive,” the bulk of which was a 40-year correspondence with an English writer and literary editor.
“There was an identity thing as well, where she didn’t feel that Irish and didn’t feel very English either.”
“Over time I did, because she was kind of on my shoulder to an extent when I was writing the short stories, some of which were part of my PhD.”
Despite her stellar start as a short-story writer, Kennedy feels that form is behind her.
“I find short stories so hard now. And nobody buys them. Who is going to give you a decent contract for short stories?”
She is a bit behind schedule – “Last year nearly killed me, trying to finish Stations” – but is seven chapters into her next novel, “set in a coastal place in the west in 1994, the summer of Riverdance and also the ceasefire. It’s about a glamorous Irish-American couple landing into a village and the unsettling effect they have on the locals – and one woman in particular.
“Something started to happen with the short stories. Some shouldn’t have been short stories – like definitely In Silhouette could have been a novel; there’s enough in there. Certainly the last story in the collection, Garland Sunday. I wrote 60,000 words for it, not linear but still. It wasn’t until I had written a novel that I thought that should have been a novel.”
Belladonna was never going to be a novel – it’s probably the shortest story in the collection – but she saw the potential to develop not the plot but its central character, Róisín.
I did a Q&A with Kennedy when Trespasses was published, and I was struck by how steeped her answers were in the North for someone who had moved south in 1979. The public event that affected her most was that year’s trial of the Shankill Butchers. The most beautiful book she owns is her grandfather’s copy of Ernie O’Malley’s On Another Man’s Wound. Her favourite fictional character is Joe Logan, in Jennifer Johnston’s Shadows on Our Skin. The books that made her laugh were anything by Sam McAughtry, and the book that moved her to tears was Bear in Mind These Dead, by Susan McKay .
[ Louise Kennedy Q&A: ‘I made a ghost of the Troubles in my head and imagined a life for him’ Opens in new window ]
“I think there’s maybe something about the age that I was when we moved. There were things that I had become very aware of when we lived in the North.”
If the North was a cold house for Catholics, who were treated like a despised minority, the South’s Ber rating for refugees was not so hot either.
“I do think there was a suspicion and sometimes hostility for northerners in the 1970s and 1980s. When Tiede Herrema and others were kidnapped, our house and other houses of families from the North would always have been searched first.
“There was that suspicion at an official level, but there was also the day-to-day stuff, like the day that Bobby Sands died. A girl from the year ahead of me came up to me at break and said, ‘I wish the rest of you murdering northern bastards would starve yourselves to death as well.’”
Kennedy’s mother was 19 when she had her, and in 1981 she went into labour the day Sands died.
“I was tormenting her to call [my brother] Bobby, and she wouldn’t. I wrote a short story about it called Hunger.” He was instead named John, after their father.
Kennedy lost her accent a long time ago, but her inner voice is northern. She is also a gifted mimic.
“I think writing kind of settled something in me, because the voice in my head is completely northern. So I feel like myself when I write in a way that I probably don’t when I’m speaking in my southern accent.”
Stations is published by Bloomsbury Circus on Thursday, September 24th

title: ‘It was like Moses coming down from the mountain’: John Coltrane and the creation of A Love Supreme
description: The jazz great John Coltrane was born 100 years ago next week. Musicians around the world are marking the saxophonist’s centenary
content:
Even for a musician who was famously restless, and tireless in his search for new forms of expression, 1964 was a busy year for John Coltrane .
Known for his obsessive practising and compulsive dedication to his craft, the jazz saxophonist, who turned 37 that year, embarked on a series of studio recordings, lengthy New York club residencies and extensive tours of the US and Canada with his celebrated quartet.
He had also recently separated from his wife and was living with the pianist Alice McLeod and her four-year-old daughter. In July they bought a house in a semi-rural suburb out on Long Island; the following month their first child, John jnr, was born.
Shortly afterwards, taking some rare time off, Coltrane secluded himself in an upstairs guest bedroom with little more than a pen, some manuscript paper and his tenor saxophone. Five days later he re-emerged. “It was like Moses coming down from the mountain,” Alice later recalled. Coltrane told her, “This is the first time that I have received all of the music for what I want to record.”
As the music writer Ted Gioia has observed, “Note that word: received. He didn’t say composed. He didn’t say created. It was a gift from something larger than himself.”
Three months later, in a single four-hour session at Rudy Van Gelder’s legendary studio in New Jersey, Coltrane recorded that new composition: a four-part suite titled A Love Supreme, which has become one of the most acclaimed and beloved albums in jazz and beyond – a timeless testament to music’s ability to move the heart and soul.
Created with one of the greatest groups in jazz – Coltrane’s nonpareil, near-telepathic quartet of McCoy Tyner on piano, Jimmy Garrison on bass and Elvin Jones on drums – A Love Supreme was conceived as an ecstatic song of praise, a devotional prayer of gratitude to God for his life and music.
An unexpected commercial success, selling 500,000 copies by 1970 alone, the album is now regarded as Coltrane’s masterpiece, the acme of his gifts as an improviser, composer and innovator, and a peerless example of music as sublime and spiritual practice.
“How to praise God and be honest?” Bono asked himself on first hearing the album, which he subsequently referenced in the U2 song Angel of Harlem. “I don’t know how, but I was listening to someone who did.”
Patti Smith concurred, saying that it “fulfils people’s need for prayer, and has a feeling of moral authority in the most humble and spiritual way”. As the jazz writer Cormac Larkin has put it, A Love Supreme is a “recording that transcends language, genre, time – even music itself”.
“I used to think of the suite as being almost untouchable,” says Ronan Guilfoyle , the 68-year-old bassist, composer and educator, who has played many of Coltrane’s compositions over the years. “For me it has the same emotional atmosphere I get from Béla Bartók’s music – an intensity, a grasp of a particular kind of human condition, a knowledge of something indefinable that is powerful and deep. It never even occurred to me to actually play it.”
Over the past decade, however, Guilfoyle has performed A Love Supreme with various quartets about a dozen times; this month, with Michael Buckley on saxophone, Leopoldo Osio on piano and Darren Beckett on drums, he will present the album in full in Limerick and Dublin.
“It’s both a privilege and an immense challenge – and like nothing I’ve experienced in jazz,” Guilfoyle says. “Every time I’ve played the suite, there’s a total silence before we hit the opening flourish. Most fans of the music know every single note, but they’ve probably never heard it live, so you can really feel the audience expectation.
“It’s as close as jazz gets to a classical-music performance – like the thrill of that moment before you hear a famous piece by Shostakovich or Beethoven.”
In Limerick, as part of the city’s enterprising annual jazz festival, Guilfoyle is going one better: he and the band are playing A Love Supreme on September 23rd, the actual centenary of Coltrane’s birth.
As such, it is part of a large number of special concerts and album releases, reissues, compilations and box sets, as well as books, music videos and merchandise, celebrating Coltrane’s life and work, many of them falling under the year-long global umbrella of Coltrane 100.
[ 3 Shades of Blue. Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Bill Evans and the Lost Empire of Cool: an eloquent elegy Opens in new window ]
There are even plans, after many years of preservation and renovation, to open John and Alice’s home on Long Island, and its “A Love Supreme Room”, to the public for the first time.
One of 2026’s more compelling tributes is the all-star, multigenerational touring group put together by the US master saxophonist and Coltrane aficionado Joe Lovano, which comes to the National Concert Hall in November.
An international quintet featuring Lovano and the Chilean rising star Melissa Aldana on saxophones, plus the South African pianist Nduduzo Makhathini, the Malaysia-born bassist Linda May Han Oh and the US drummer Jeff “Tain” Watts, the band will present the radical sweep of Coltrane’s art, a body of work that is by turns tender and turbulent, sorrowful and seductive.
It’s music with an ever-widening arc that, in just 12 years – from the mid-1950s, when Coltrane joined Miles Davis ’s First Great Quintet, to 1967, the year he died of liver cancer, at the age of just 40 – moved through multiple forms.
Those styles and approaches included hard bop, so-called sheets of sound (torrents of tumbling notes over increasingly complex chord changes), the blues, modal jazz, harmonic and rhythmic expansion, spiritual expression, engagement with non-western traditions, and free and collective improvisation. Coltrane challenged himself at every turn; playing his music is a dizzying and demanding dare.
“I was quite overwhelmed at first,” Aldana, who is 37, says from her apartment in Brooklyn; her most recent Blue Note release, Filin, has Coltrane’s 1963 album Ballads as one of its inspirations.
“Not just because we’re doing the full frame of Trane’s work, the whole journey, right up to the deep and, in a way, scary late period. But also because I’m playing alongside Joe Lovano, an elder I admire so much. Then Joe said to me, ‘It’s not about copying Trane or trying to recreate what he did. It’s an invitation to create in the spirit of John Coltrane and to be yourself.’ That helped.”
[ John McLaughlin: ‘I tell my hands how beautiful they are. Now I have no pain at all’ Opens in new window ]
Aldana acknowledges that, like every jazz musician since the mid-1960s, especially those playing tenor and soprano saxophones, she has had to define her relationship with Coltrane – by both embracing and reacting against such hallmarks as his colossal technique, his fearless desire for continual reinvention and the utter authority of his imploring legato and all-consuming sound.
It recalls what the American literary critic Harold Bloom famously called “the anxiety of influence”.
“Yes, I recognise that, but John Coltrane also opened so many doors, for all of us,” she says. “Way beyond his incredible hard work and virtuosic playing are lessons about discipline and going deeper into the music; about studying different cultures, religions and philosophies; about how far you can push and find things, how you can tell the story of who you are. He was also trying to find that universal vibration that connects us all as human beings.”
It is that universality, and the sense of total artistic freedom and commitment, that has inspired countless musicians and creators – and meant that, over the past 60 years, Coltrane’s stature and significance have only expanded.
He is a touchstone that has shaped generations of improvisers, while reaching far beyond jazz into rock (Santana, Sonic Youth ), hip-hop ( Kendrick Lamar , Flying Lotus) and minimalism ( Steve Reich , Philip Glass ), as well as film ( Spike Lee ), literature (Amiri Baraka) and dance (Alvin Ailey).
“In the same way Picasso did beyond 20th-century art, Coltrane’s name has transcended the boundaries of the jazz world and gone into the wider culture,” Guilfoyle says.
Coltrane’s personal journey and spiritual quest have even inspired religious observance. Uniquely, there has been a variously named Church of St John Coltrane in San Francisco since 1969, its congregation celebrating his “conversion” from 1950s heroin addict to 1960s visionary, and staging performances of his music as acts of worship.
“We honour Saint John Coltrane as a spiritual guide, artist and prophetic musical voice,” the church website reads , “whose work points toward divine love and higher consciousness.”
Those latter two qualities were foundational to Alice Coltrane, who was integral to her husband’s later more experimental and expansive music. (The couple married in Mexico in 1965; later that year, after McCoy Tyner left the group, Alice became Coltrane’s pianist.)
“She was one of the greatest piano players, and she had a whole thing going before she and John met,” Aldana says. “So Alice was a very important part of the whole equation of Trane’s music in his last few years; she knew what he was going for.”
Alice continued their transcendental journey after John died, releasing a series of albums in the late 1960s and early 1970s – including Ptah, the El Daoud and Journey in Satchidananda – that are now considered the ur-texts of a transporting and trance-like music that has become known as “spiritual jazz”.
She would later devote much of her life to spiritual practice, travelling in India, establishing an ashram in California and largely withdrawing from conventional music-making; Alice died in 2007.
Since then, especially over the past decade, there has been a remarkable reassessment of Alice Coltrane’s music, recognising her contribution not just to her husband’s art but also her pioneering role in the use in modern jazz of the harp, an instrument she largely taught herself to play, and her synthesis of improvisation and Indian devotional music.
“In many ways, she was too advanced for that time period,” Aldana says.
[ Sonny Rollins: ‘Genius’ saxophonist was one of the most inventive jazz musicians of his generation Opens in new window ]
The Coltrane 100 year has also created a further platform for this vital reappraisal. Indeed, as well as Cosmic Music, the recently published first full-length biography of Alice Coltrane, the National Concert Hall will next March present Translinear Light: The Music of Alice Coltrane, a celebration featuring her and John’s second son, Ravi Coltrane, on saxophones, and the much admired Brandee Younger on harp.
In keeping with his wife’s continuous search for self-improvement and spiritual growth, John Coltrane once said, in Tokyo in 1966, “This is my belief: that I am supposed to grow to the best good that I can get to.”
Aldana says she takes inspiration from the idea, both musically and personally.
“Yeah, absolutely. Keep pushing. Keep questioning. What Coltrane means to me is: the possibilities are endless and you can always become a better self, a better version of yourself.”
Ronan Guilfoyle will perform A Love Supreme at Dolans Upstairs, as part of Limerick Jazz Festival , on Wednesday, September 23rd, and in two shows at Arthur’s Blues and Jazz Club , in Dublin, on Thursday, September 24th. Coltrane 100: Both Directions at Once is at the National Concert Hall , in Dublin, on November 14th; Translinear Light: The Music of Alice Coltrane is at the same venue on March 4th, 2027. Cosmic Music: The Life, Art and Transcendence of Alice Coltrane, by Andy Beta, is published by White Rabbit. You can find out more about Coltrane 100 album releases, the photography book Coltrane: The Definitive Visual Celebration of the Legend and more at johncoltrane.com

title: Catherine Zeta-Jones hates her children being called nepo babies. Chris Pine has the answer
description: Have some sympathy for the children of movie stars who follow their parents into the business
content:
“This horrific phrase ‘nepo baby’ is horrible because these kids didn’t ask to be born into this,” Catherine Zeta-Jones said last week. “They’re finding their own way in life.”
It would be easy to snort. Dylan Douglas and Carys Zeta Douglas, her children with Michael Douglas , are moving, respectively, into acting and directing. No sane person would deny they do so from a position of advantage.
Their father knows something about that. As the son of Kirk Douglas, he entered the business draped in ermine appropriate to the glitziest Hollywood royalty. People knew who he was. Some doors were already open. But (hear me out) such privilege has its downsides.
“I remember earlier on as an actor where you’re trying to create your own identity and they’re all saying, ‘Oh, that looks just like your father,’” he said in 2024. “‘Oh my God, you sound just like your father.’”
The language may be a tad overheated, but (please, do hear me out) Zeta-Jones really does have a point here. Have some sympathy for the children of movie stars, and other creators, who follow their parents into the business.
It doesn’t matter much if an eventual Oscar winner emerged from the loins of working actors in Birmingham rep, but, if the paternal line features two Douglases, and the maternal strand includes Velma from Chicago, you are going to hear about your parents for the rest of your life.
I think back to 2009 and my first meeting with Duncan Jones . Having entered the world as Zowie Bowie, son of David , the director of such fine films as Moon and Source Code knows no interviewer will resist asking him about the late Starman. There is always a chance someone such as me will wonder why no reply arrived to the letter he wrote Bowie in 1978.
“I’ve got a letter for you here, actually,” he said, laughing . “Look, I was prepared for this and I understand it. One of the reasons I waited so long to make my first film was that I wanted to build up a thick skin, so I could deal with it.”
Jones, whose latest feature, Rogue Trooper, will be with us soon, continues to be realistic about his father’s legacy. Then again, though Bowie did make the odd film, the two men were essentially in different businesses. That makes things easier.
As long ago as 1973, an entrant to the New Stateman’s weekly competition, asked to come up with an unlikely book title, settled upon Martin Amis : My Struggle. That sarcastic quip hung around. Martin arguably became as celebrated as Kingsley Amis, his novelist father, but it was the older man who eventually won the Booker Prize.
Though the younger always dealt amiably with questions about “the King”, it can’t have been fun to cart that legacy into your 70s.
[ Domhnall Gleeson on nepo babies: ‘I’ve been so lucky. It’s important you can acknowledge it. Otherwise you’re lying to yourself’ Opens in new window ]
It is, however, in the entertainment business that the words “nepo baby” have been most often brandished. It is not hard to see why. A recent article in The Economist reports that more and more working film professionals have relatives in the business. “Nepo babies are commanding more roles and more lines,” the piece explained. “In 2000 they made up 6.6 per cent of appearances by young actors, but by 2025 that share had more than doubled, to 16.3 per cent.”
Over the same period it has become harder than ever for working-class performers to break into the business. In the UK, actors from the poshest public schools have never been more in evidence at the top of the tree. “It’s very difficult for anyone without any money to get into drama school,” Bill Nighy, himself from a working-class background, told me in 2024. “Therefore it’s very difficult for them to become actors.”
[ Meet the nepo parents Opens in new window ]
All of which is to clarify that, yes, the people who most need our sympathy are those talented folk who, without money or connections, cannot get a foot near the lowest rung on the ladder. Work to challenge that injustice.
We can, however, still spare a thought for actors forever accused of profiting from their elder relatives’ renown. Zeta-Jones is right to have sympathy for her offspring. The best possible solution is to become more famous than Dad or Mum. Chris Pine , whose craggy father, Robert Pine, was in the TV show CHiPs, can probably make that claim (though best not at Christmas dinner). Robert Downey jnr ’s fame long ago eclipsed the that of his dad, the avant-garde director Robert Downey snr.
[ Eve Hewson on finding her own fame: ‘Some people have no idea of the connection or don’t even care. It’s a nice feeling’ Opens in new window ]
The nepoboost gives an actor a start, but, to hang around decade after decade, you really do need some combination of talent and charm. Life is not fair. But the unfairness takes you only so far.

title: What climbers grow well in a shady city courtyard garden?
description: Small urban courtyard gardens are easily transformed into lovely leafy spaces with the right selection of plants
content:
The good news is that small urban courtyard gardens like yours can be easily transformed into very beautiful, tranquil, atmospheric, leafy spaces, just so long as the selection of plants used is really carefully edited.
Suitable climbers that will make full use of the sheltered growing conditions as well as the plentiful vertical growing space available include the evergreen jasmine-like Trachelospermum jasminoides and its cousin, Trachelospermum asiaticum. Although they’re more floriferous in sunnier growing conditions, both are tolerant of light shade and will produce their scented white flowers in generous quantities throughout the summer months.
Climbing hydrangeas are another option. The slow-growing, shade-tolerant, deciduous Hydrangea petiolaris is always a welcome addition to any garden, although you’ll have to wait a couple of years for it to take off. Not as well known is Hydrangea seemannii, which has the added virtue of being evergreen. It produces its large, greenish-white, lacecap flowers in summertime. Again, it’s typically slow to establish but once it does, it’s a wonderfully elegant plant that can be used to light up even a shady north wall so long as it’s protected from low temperatures and icy winter winds.
To extend the season of interest, also consider growing a selection of clematis, a huge and useful genus of climbing plants. Suitable varieties include the evergreen Clematis ‘Winter Sensation’; Clematis ‘Freckles’; Clematis ‘Avalanche’; varieties of the spring-flowering Clematis alpina and the late summer-flowering Clematis viticella.
Training decorative shrubs against the wall is another option well worth considering, in which case you could consider Azara microphylla, or its white-and-green variegated form, Azara microphylla ‘Variegata’ and Chimonanthus praecox.
Lastly, before you stick so much as a single plant in the ground, first prepare it really well by removing any builder’s rubble or compacted subsoil that may have found its way into the beds. Adding plenty of well-rotted organic matter will make a huge difference to the quality of the soil as well as to healthy, vigorous plant growth. Bear in mind also that you’ll need to install a series of horizontal training wires along the walls on to which you can then tie any young growth.

title: Four great wines made from a mix of grapes
description: John Wilson: It’s worth branching out to try wines made from more than one grape variety
content:
Many consumers prefer to buy wines with a grape variety on the label. I can understand why. It gives you a good idea of how the wine will taste, and moving to other wines can require a whole new level of knowledge. Yet it means missing out on a lot of very good wines.
Many wines are blends, a mix of several varieties, regions or even vintages. Blending is done to improve the quality of the wine. You may be drinking a blend without knowing it, as it doesn’t always have to mention it on the label.
Bikavér, which translates as “Bull’s Blood”, is made from an almost bewildering array of local and international varieties : 60 per cent kékfrankos; 20 per cent merlot; 9 per cent cabernet franc and sauvignon; 8 per cent kadarka; and 3% syrah. It works beautifully.
The Pepe Mendoza featured below is made from a blend of viognier, macabeo, merseguera, and moscatel. According to the label : “The wine reflects the sea, the mountains, the character and all the magic of the Mediterranean.”
The full name of the wine below is Bonkers Zombie Robot Alien Monsters from the Future ate my Brain (sur lie) V2. It is made by the talented half-Irish team at Sugrue South Downs in England. Bonkers is a still white chardonnay made from a blend of three vintages – 2022, 2023 and 2024.
Made from a classic Rhône blend of 54 per cent grenache, 39 per cent syrah and 5 per cent mourvèdre, this is a delicious, rounded, full-bodied red that would go nicely with red meats and firm cheeses.
A beautifully crafted, elegant wine with light, succulent red cherry fruits, good acidity and gentle spice. Roast chicken, pork or duck.
Pinto, Dublin 9; BaRossa Wines, Dublin 4; Blackrock Cellar, Co Dublin; Delgany Wine Cottage, Co Wicklow; Lennox Street Grocer, Dublin 8
A very seductive wine with herby aromas, textured red apples and vivid lemon zest. Try it with grilled fish, or seafood paella.
Avoca Ballsbridge, Dublin 4; Baggot Street Wines, Dublin 4; Blackrock Cellar; Jus de Vine, Portmarnock, Co Dublin; Red Island Wine, Skerries, Co Dublin; Neighbourhood Wine, Dublin 2 and Dublin 4
A wonderful complex wine filled with textured ripe peaches, grilled nuts, cut through with a rapier-like acidity. Try it with grilled scallops with lemon and butter, or a slice of Comté.
The Counter Deli, Letterkenny, Co Donegal; Fallon and Byrne, Dublin 2; Fíon Eile, Dublin 7; Sweeney’s D3, Dublin 3; Searsons, Monkstown, Co Dublin

title: Four new films to see this week: Bad Apples, Resident Evil, Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? and The Degenerate
description: Saoirse Ronan, Austin Abrams, Jarvis Cocker and Andy Milligan feature in a quartet of movies released in the week of September 18th, 2026
content:
Directed by Jonatan Etzler. Starring Saoirse Ronan, Eddie Waller, Nia Brown, Jacob Anderson, Rakie Ayola, Robert Emms, Sean Glider. 15A cert, general release, 100 min
Ronan excels as a primary school in the English west country who, constantly harassed by a troubled student, eventually cracks and chains him up in her basement with nothing but a bucket for company. Plausibility becomes an issue when the film, hitherto naturalistic, takes that surprisingly dark turn. But film-makers find queasy comedy in even the most troubling plot turns. Ronan channels the panicked desperation of a classic screwball heroine – but sadder, and with less chance of a happy ending. It ultimately takes on the tone of a fairy tale or a grim fable. DC Full review
Directed by Zach Cregger. Starring Austin Abrams, Zach Cherry, Kali Reis, Paul Walter Hauser. 16 cert, general release, 93 min
The director of Barbarian and Weapons tackles the venerable zombie franchise and, against the odds, the result is an absolute blast. Abrams plays a medical courier who gets caught up in the undead mayhem while transporting a package to Raccoon City. Fleshed out with elaborately vile body horror whose lineage passes through the source content and back to John Carpenter’s The Thing, Cregger’s shameless romp, though smallish in scale, feels like the best Resident Evil film in the franchise’s long history. All that “lore” baloney is abandoned for straight-up yucks. DC Full review
Directed by Garth Jennings. Featuring Jarvis Cocker, Nick Banks, Candida Doyle. No cert, limited release, 90 min
Following on the heels of the box-office smash Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger, this scrapbook meets concert film is a keen reminder that the alchemy of a band such as Pulp cannot be replicated. As a dependably droll Jarvis Cocker recalls, the changing line-up was determined by people he bumped into in pubs. The film’s most affecting passage steps away from the spectacle, with a stripped-back performance dedicated to Steve Mackey, their bassist, who died in 2023. Four musicians, little ornament and no bells and whistles do more than the arena fireworks to explain why Pulp still matter. TB Full review
Directed by Josh Johnson and Grayson Tyler Johnson. Featuring John Borske, Alex DiSanto, Gerald Jacuzzo, Hope Stansbury, Jimmy McDonough. No cert, Shudder, 109 min
Andy Milligan made crude, rushed and spectacularly cheap movies, yet their peculiarities and darkness have kept them in circulation. As one commentator notes in this wildly entertaining doc, the lo-fi auteur was never as distinguished as famous schlockmeisters such as Herschell Gordon Lewis; if they were the bottom of the barrel, the Irish-American Z-movie master was below the barrel. His best-regarded films include Nightbirds, a UK production; his more disreputable efforts include The Ghastly Ones, of which the contemporaneous promoter says, “Well, it was ghastly, and it had ones.” Watch and learn. TB Full review

title: New poetry: ‘The most horrifying, exquisite and staggering poems I have ever read’
description: Mícheál McCann reviews Milk & Moon-water by Milena Williamson; Real Estate by Mark Ward; Landscape with Question by Leeanne Quinn; and 48kg by Batool Abu Akleen
content:
How we can revivify the wisdom of the past occupies Milena Williamson’s Milk & Moon-water (The Emma Press, £7.99) which is, at heart, playful translations of Anglo-Saxon charms, lullabies, spells and counterspells, which the poet then uses as springboards into an entirely contemporary “remixed” poem.
The opening Charm for Unfruitful Land opens the book with an expectedly antiquated cadence – “Cut a piece of sod […] Mix oil, honey and yeast […] Turn sunwise three times” – which establishes the enormous swathes of time the poet is trying to cross, arriving in the modern day with Charm for Unfruitful Land (Remixed).
I shirk a little from the adjective remixed, mainly as these poems signal their modernity well enough: “I walk on the earth while there is still time and sprinkle seeds / on riverbanks, lawns and graveyards. The smoke pours”.
This book is a very neat act on Williamson’s part of throwing a lifebelt of connection between the distant past and the contemporary present. The Old English translations function mainly as companion pieces, shackled a little by the poet’s necessary adherence to metrical demands, to the excellent and, often, tour-de-force original poems. In the brutal and excellent Charm for Miscarriage (Remixed), the poet memorably announces, in ode-like fashion, “O ovum, O snorkelled pearl, O anarchic grain of rice”.
There is a striking balance of tenderness and fury in these poems that never becomes unwieldy: “These revolutions make me the angriest flower”. Other standouts, Charm for Tumours “Remixed” (“My mother finally takes a shower. My brother researches what / the biopsy means.”) and Charm for Loss of Land “Remixed” (“If they are good landlords, she is a good landbaby”) recall to us that Williamson is, above all, a skilled lyric poet, her next collection worth anticipating.
In a housing-crisis-ridden country, a person’s perception of home, the estate of one’s self, and where we feel safety and communion with others will shift profoundly. In Mark Ward’s Real Estate (Salmon, €14), “home”, understood as a place of stability, shape-shifts in surreal, mind-bending poems into uncanny other places.
In Apathy, the speaker finds their own powers of perception challenged by a mirror house: “You feel for the exit, / wandering through a carnival / of other yous”. There are erotic poems aplenty in this book, often with transitory settings, like In the Air, where a mid-journey hookup concludes with an unexpected bank of clouds descending, transforming the scene into “a Super Mario world where the world / theoretically exists below us”. This is a good paradigm of how a poem only about sex is uninteresting, but a poem where perception of said encounter is somehow changed, very much can be.
Fog as a visual metaphor recurs often throughout the book (“Your emotions are a fog, slowing the car / due to low visibility”) and the nothingness of a fog bank accentuates the diminishing sense of secure space. Absence, or missing certain people, is consolidated in the opening poems as an orbital theme to this collection. In Icarus Dreams of the Future, an aching Icarus plummets through the air and notices “Daedalus is / nowhere to be seen”; the unforgiving speaker of Creation Myth is alienated by the boisterous family – “The fishwife and her screaming / children surround me” – and tries, against their better instinct, to believe that “it’s all music”. The best poems are narrative ones, where Ward has the capacity to take in the action and energy of entire cities or families, such as the concluding Guided Tour: “Enough to see shapes. A washer and dryer stacked. Stuff piles everywhere.”
Landscape with Question (Carcanet, £12.99) by Leeanne Quinn achieves what few books manage: to engage in the abstract in a way that is not befuddling to read.
Quinn’s third collection emerges out of years of dedication and interest in the celebrated Irish painter Nano Reid, who in interview often gave incorrect dates of birth. Quinn takes this mysterious act as her structuring principle.
Each section begins with an impressionistic poem based on a supposed birth year of the artist: “on the day of my birth was not captured the rain / fell in a sort of slant before it hit the pavement / and drew us in I must have been looking”.
Reid’s expressionist and oblique artworks somehow perforate Quinn’s poems themselves with an engaging sense of mystery, as in Landscape with Daffodils, which opens with a spliced sentence that equally baffles and intrigues: “Since I survived the winter, since I was so happy, / and it was already March, the first warm day / of the year.”
My first thought was that the poems make little effort to orient the reader, when it occurred to me that Quinn’s speaker is often half-hearing conversations, not quite understanding what is at work in these places, split between Drogheda and the urban visual landscape of Europe, themselves disorientated. The Bullring exemplifies this brilliantly: “I could hear words indicating / absence but didn’t blame them as I too saw the town / in past tense.”
Quinn has instanced something wonderful – a genuine act of exegesis that the reader can follow along with. Quinn’s poetic voice is the central achievement here – unassuming, beguiling, it moves with agility and without judgment, and with an enormously generative inquisitiveness: “The dream of the tree looks the same / at the beginning as it will the end.”
When Paul Celan published Todesfuge in 1948 about his incarceration in a concentration camp, it was impossible to imagine how he was able to filter his horrific experiences through the formal conceit of a fugue. The same thought occurs reading 48kg (Penguin, £10.99) by Batool Abu Akleen, who writes about the genocide unfolding in Gaza in the most horrifying, exquisite and staggering poems I have ever read.
Akleen notes in the introduction that when she wrote these poems in Arabic: “I was afraid of death, afraid that my body might be torn apart without there being anyone there to recollect it … but when I started to translate this book, I made peace with death.”
[ Fiction in translation: Yang Hao an exciting new voice in Chinese – and Irish – literature Opens in new window ]
The titles of these 48 poems decrease in weight across the book; Akleen, in diminishing typeface and ink, has created a terrible symbolic connection to the starving population of Palestine. In 47kg, Akleen writes “I’m roaming through the alleys of the refugee camp […] I get two bags of flour, lentils, chickpeas, oil, tinned food, sugar. / Elation …” The emotional weight embedded in a simple list of dried and tinned goods is unbelievable.
The poems are laced with Old Testament allusions – “Sijjil stones from every direction” – and deftly explore ideas of senseless punishment. In 23kg , a litany concludes the poem: “I want my hand back, oh Lord / I want my hand. / I want the person I once / belonged to / I want my person back”, and as the weight decreases the speaker’s/character’s spirit diminishes. At 7kg , Death is addressed directly: “O death / I won’t have to wait for you anymore” […] “If you don’t kill grief // O death / then who will?” This essential poetry of witness stares into the abyss, and we must look in the direction it looks.
Mícheál McCann’s new collection is Lives of the Saints (Gallery Press)

title: In a Word ... Population
description: Within 75 years, the issue worldwide will be depopulation
content:
It seems unlikely now that Ireland’s population will ever exceed pre-Famine levels. According to the 1841 census, there were 8.17 million people on the island. By 1845, when the Famine began, that number was approximately 8.5 million, dropping to 6.5 million by 1851.
Over recent years, it has been forecast that the island of Ireland would soon exceed that 1841 figure. By 2022 the population of this island was approximately 7.2 million (5.35 million in the Republic, according to the 2022 census, and 1.91 million in Northern Ireland, according to the 2021 census).
Since then, all has changed. Between 2015 and 2025, births on the island of Ireland fell 18.8 per cent, with a drop of 17.9 per cent in the Republic and 21.3 per cent in Northern Ireland.
In the Republic, births fell from 65,909 in 2015 to 54,125 in 2025. Fertility rates on the island are now 1.5, well below the replacement level of 2.1. We are not unique.
Worldwide, more than half of all countries show fertility rates below the replacement level of 2.1 births per woman, with 198 out of 204 countries projected – in an analysis by British medical journal The Lancet and the United Kingdom’s Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation – to be below replacement levels by 2100.
So, within 75 years, the issue worldwide will be depopulation. Whatever happened “the population explosion” and all the alarms that went with that? “Stopped short, never to go again,” like Johnny Cash’s grandfather’s clock.
And the trend has been there for decades. According to 2024 figures – from the UN World Population Prospects – growth in global population peaked six decades ago. In 1963 it was more than 2 per cent per year. It had dropped to less than 1 per cent by 2020.
UN researchers expect growth rates to continue falling until the end of this century, leading to a decline in growth rates and a shrinking global population – the first global decline in population since the Black Death of the 14th century.
Meanwhile, the world’s population will grow at an average 0.4 per cent per year. That’s another estimated two billion people before there is a decline, or a 25 per cent increase on the world’s current population, to more than 10 billion people.
Population , from Latin populus , for “a people”.

title: Meet the Irish-American TV star bishop who is about to be beatified
description: Fulton Sheen turned from proselytising to providing a reassuring message for Americans of all faiths, drawing on his Irish roots
content:
At 8pm on February 12th, 1952, a strangely clad figure walked across the stage of the Adelphia Theater in New York City and into thousands of American livingrooms.
Dressed in full episcopal regalia, complete with a purple cape, a zucchetto skullcap, and a pectoral cross given to him by the pope, Bishop Fulton Sheen proceeded to hold forth extemporaneously for the next half-hour.
Behind him, conspicuously placed within the camera shot, was a statue of the Virgin Mary that would soon be known as “Our Lady of Television”.
Sheen’s show, Life is Worth Living, featured a one-way conversation in which the host cited ancient philosophers and medieval intellectuals to assuage the fears of contemporary American listeners.
Whether addressing the threat of Stalinist communism or home-grown concerns about the rise of “teen culture”, the charismatic Sheen offered the reaffirming message encapsulated in his programme’s title.
