“We love Howth and the community so much. We definitely want to stay within walking distance of the village,” they say.
Number 9 Abbey Street is now on the market with Sherry FitzGerald, seeking €1.15 million.
A walnut staircase leads up to the open-floor living area. You arrive straight into the kitchen which has fitted cream units on both sides with granite worktops. There is an island in the centre with a sink, lit up by bronze pendant lights at night and a Velux window by day.
There are steps up to the living area which has a vaulted ceiling and doors out to a large deck and terraced garden beyond.
Glass doors at the opposite end of the kitchen lead into a separate dining/livingroom. This room was the original part of the house, with three sash windows overlooking Abbey Street below and the ruins of the old Abbey church. There is a gas fire with marble surround, as well as the original corner tiled fireplace. Lastly on this level is another bathroom with the original enamel roll-top bath.
The dramatic landscaping at the back of the house happened by accident, when the owners had a gardener take a look at the lower area outside the house.
“He went up to the top of the back garden to have a sandwich one day, which was absolutely wild territory at the time. He called down to us to come up and have a look at the sea view, so that is when we changed the plan completely.”
The multi-tiered garden now has a stepped path that climbs up to a decking area with views of the village and harbour, where the owners love escaping to for a glass of wine at sunset. There are also various seating areas at other levels and on the ground level there is artificial grass with planted beds and a storage shed.
The B-rated home has Howth’s best cafes, restaurants and bars, including the renowned Abbey Tavern, just minutes away, as well as the Dart station. The H3 bus route goes through the village and there is space for two cars in the front driveway.

title: Catherine Corless: ‘I was always a bit determined. I was teased a lot growing up’
description: The historian on her difficult upbringing, how it feels for your life to be adapted for the screen, and why Trump’s visit to Ireland made her angry
content:
I was born in 1954, and there was a big gap between me and my siblings. I’m fifth in my family’s birth order and I have four siblings. There is a four-year gap between my sibling before me and there are bigger gaps beyond that. I was teased a lot growing up. They usually say that the baby in the family is spoiled and all that kind of thing, but it wasn’t so with me. I was teased a fair bit by the elder siblings when I was a child, and sometimes it turned into a bit of ridicule. I kind of grew up with teasing and that was because I think I was very different from the rest of the family and my siblings. I was always a bit determined and maybe a bit obstinate at times because I was kind of fighting my way. I felt I never really fitted in with my family in that kind of a way. I was different and especially compared to my sibling before me, my older sister. My sister was quiet and she was perfect all around, and I could not fit in with that. I was always fighting to be myself and not to be changed. I think that fight and the way I grew up is why I have been able to do what I have done in the last few years in my work. I felt I had to fight for the little ones that had no voice and I just felt that I never really had a voice in the household so that is how it has really defined me as a person.
My name is Catherine Patricia, and I never liked either name. I was born in March in 1954, so my name probably had something to do with St Patrick and St Patrick’s Day. My father’s name was also Patrick. There are Patricks everywhere in my family. I think I just did not want to be called that, and I really didn’t like it.
The last time I got angry, to be honest, was probably last weekend because of Donald Trump’s visit to Doonbeg, Co Clare. Donald Trump being there was bad enough, but when I saw all the people in Doonbeg, well not everyone, but most of them, clapping and cheering for him. That is what really got to me. It’s bad enough that the Republican Party and Americans are cheering for him and cheering him on the whole time, but we all know the facts here. I know what Donald Trump is, and I know what he has done, and that is what really got me going recently.
Probably my teenage years. You have better health and you have more energy, and that is never coming back.
The drive from Clifden into Leenaun in Co Galway. It is just spectacular. I love the mountains and nature and all that. I always think of that drive between Clifden and Leenaun and we really try to get down to there as much as we can.
I remember I was in hospital as a child and I was maybe about six years old. At the time. I needed eye surgery and I remember, I’ll never forget it, I woke up after the surgery, and I was so terrified. I thought I had gone blind, because there were these bandages all over my eyes. I was trying so desperately to take off the bandages. I remember a nurse came in and gave a whole thing to me about leaving the bandages on and how I should not touch them again. It was very frightening, it was all so dark, and I did not know what was happening. But everything was fine once all the bandages were off.
I would say I was happiest when I met my husband in my teen years. We met just through friends of friends when we were younger, meeting after school and things like that. We became soulmates, and he listened to me, really listened to me, and he appreciated me. He appreciated me more than my family did, and it was a new life, it was a new awakening for me. I’m happy to say that we are still soulmates, even though we’ve been through a lot of turbulence. But me and him were very alike, and that was when I found him, through the turbulence.
Well not what the church is preaching to us. I think that is a fairy tale. The body evaporates and we go into molecules and all that, but I do believe that whatever goodness we have within us, whatever kindness, has to live on somewhere, and has to turn into something new, that’s my belief.
The actor Monica Dolan has played me in The Lost Children of Tuam this year, and it is out there now, and I must say, she was such a great choice. She is really fantastic, and she played me as a character so well. She just played me as I was and truly showed my want for the truth to come out, I have always wanted to stick with the truth, and she plays that very well. It is surreal though seeing yourself on screen, because [the idea for the film] came around about 10 years ago and it was just all surreal for our family. The film coming out is just so wonderful for us and the children and our grandchildren are in the film. My husband, Aidan, has even got a small part to play also. So it really is a huge deal for us in the family really and it’s going well so far. I wasn’t involved in the production of the film. I left it all to themselves.
[ ‘Would you believe I got a call from Liam Neeson?’: Catherine Corless film premieres in Galway Opens in new window ]
I really do not think I have any personal regrets. I was just thinking on this the other day and we all have regrets. Small, tiny regrets. Maybe there are small, tiny regrets every single day, but we get through them and we put them behind us.
The Lost Children of Tuam, produced by Liam Neeson and starring Monica Dolan as Catherine Corless, is in cinemas from Friday, September 25th, with a gala screening taking place in Dublin this evening .

title: An Irish voice in Beijing’s debate on the new world order
description: At China’s Xiangshan Forum, an Irish general argues that a multipolar world can only be stable if smaller states’ sovereignty is respected
content:
T he session was supposed to be about “major-country relations and strategic stability”, but its attraction lay in the panellists, who included former Ukrainian foreign minister Pavlo Klimkin and Olga Alexandria, dean of the faculty of world politics at Lomonosov Moscow State University. Attila Demko, a former Hungarian diplomat and security expert who sat between them, remarked on the novelty of it.
“It’s very rare now that on one side you have a minister from Ukraine and sitting on the other side, somebody from Russia . There is no such thing in Europe, and this is the real importance of this forum,” he said.
The Xiangshan Forum, Beijing’s annual security conference, is unique in its ability to bring together representatives from both sides in some of the hottest conflicts in the world. An earlier session was marked by fiery exchanges between speakers from Saudi Arabia and Iran over Tehran’s attacks on targets in the Gulf.
Prince Turki al-Faisal, chairman of the King Faisal Centre for Research and Islamic Studies, accused Iran of failing to respect the sovereignty of Arab states with “aggressive and unlawful attacks” on their territory. Mohammad Taghi Osanlou, an Iranian general who is deputy for operations at the army’s general headquarters, said Tehran’s attacks were aimed only at American assets in the region.
“We have not attacked any Arab countries or their territories. We only attacked US military bases in Arab countries,” he said.
“We not only targeted Saudi Arabia. We launched strikes against US military bases in Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar, not just those in Saudi Arabia. Our target is the United States, not other Arab countries.”
The later session was less heated, not least because Klimko and Alexandria each looked straight ahead while the other spoke, but there was nothing close to a meeting of minds. Klimko said he could foresee negotiations towards a ceasefire, but there was no prospect of a peace deal, much less of a broader agreement on Europe’s security architecture.
Alexandria described the war as a failure of strategic stability and suggested that, while a post-ceasefire agreement could deal with issues like borders and military forces, a more ambitious strategic agreement was needed to make the next war less likely. Demko, who said the Russian invasion of Ukraine was unjustified, suggested that it was time to talk but with limited expectations.
“What we need now is to extinguish the fire and keep it down. We cannot rebuild the house,” he said.
The panel in an earlier session about the trend towards multipolarity in the international order included Timothy O’Brien, an Irish general who is director of cabinet for the chairman of the EU’s military committee, former Defence Forces chief of staff Seán Clancy.
O’Brien said that, if the EU was focusing more on military affairs than before, it was because of the changed circumstances it faced.
“We are not becoming a more military organisation. However, we live on a Continent in Europe ... where conventional war has returned by Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine,” he said.
“The war in Ukraine is an illegal act of aggression against one of our partners. And therefore, that is why you hear defence being discussed now, by European leaders, both leaders of the institutions and the prime ministers of the member states, because that’s the reality we’re living in. War has returned to our Continent.”
O’Brien said that there was no doubt that the world was becoming multipolar, but the question surrounded what kind of multipolarity was most desirable. He said the EU favoured a multipolar world that envisaged more voices, greater representation and stronger participation in international decision making.
“Multipolarity alone does not necessarily produce enhanced stability. Several centres of power can co-operate, but they can also compete, divide the world into spheres of influence and leave smaller states caught between them. That is why the European Union believes that multipolarity and multilateralism must be brought together,” he said.
“If a multipolar world means that several large powers each require a privileged sphere of influence around themselves, then we have not created greater equality. We have simply redistributed a hierarchy. The sovereignty of smaller states must carry the same fundamental meaning as the sovereignty of a major power.”

title: The Hibernophile holding France’s purse strings at a critical moment
description: Finance minister Roland Lescure, whose Irish wife has given him a close view of Ireland’s transformation, is trying to keep voters and bond markets on side as fuel prices surge
content:
O ne topic looms large over French politics in the febrile build-up to a presidential election with populist forces on the rise both left and right: the price of fuel per litre.
The issue dominates press questions to the government, fishermen have blockaded ports in protest, and hanging over the country is the prospect of the return of the “ gilets jaunes ”.
The grassroots “yellow vests” movement paralysed France with protests between 2018 and 2020, beginning with a call for lower fuel taxes before spiralling into a broader expression of discontent.
As diesel prices neared a record high over the last two weeks, calls for protests in cities across France on October 17th went viral online.
By Wednesday, president Emmanuel Macron was telling government ministers he wanted “total mobilisation” to drive down prices and ensure supply.
Amid it all, international bond markets are watching closely: this time last year, opposition to a budget that aimed to address France’s large debt pile brought down the government, and the political turmoil rattled bond markets.
[ French minister wants Ireland to share its technology tax billions Opens in new window ]
French minister have to square the public demands for fuel price subsidies, pressure from the international markets to cut debt, and fierce opposition in parliament to cuts – with the government desperate to avoid collapsing once again before the election in April.
Yet all is calm for now in the office of the man in the hot seat, finance and economy minister Roland Lescure, who looks out over a panoramic view of the Seine from the imposing office blocks of his ministry, known for short as “Bercy”.
The first details of the proposed budget are set to be announced in the event.
“I think we’ve balanced it rightly,” Lescure tells The Irish Times. He insists that the subsidies are “targeted” and “transitory”.
“We have been helping the people at the front of the crisis: fishermen, farmers, lorry drivers and people who use their car to work ... without doing blanket-wide measures that would help everyone, including people who don’t necessarily need it.”
“They’re very costly. They’re not efficient. To be fair, we did that during the Ukraine crisis. It cost us an arm and a leg then, and I’m not sure it was very helpful, including politically.”
That suddenly familiar turn of phrase – “to be fair” – speaks to Lescure’s backstory. His wife is Dublin native Susie O’Reilly. The two met in Brussels, when Lescure was a trainee at the European Commission working on the creation of the EU single market.
They went through three years of a long-distance relationship before marrying in O’Reilly’s ancestral Donegal in the summer heatwave of 1995.
“The French loved it, and they all enjoyed the beautiful view on Horn Head. We had a great wedding,” Lescure remembers. On the honeymoon, he followed in the steps of Charles de Gaulle to Connemara’s Cashel House Hotel.
After a career as a civil servant and in the finance industry in France and Canada, politics in Paris beckoned.
“I decided to jump in the pool of political life when Emmanuel Macron called for people from the civil society to join him,” Lescure recalls. O’Reilly works as a yoga teacher in the city, and the family returns to Ireland often.
“Susie comes from a family of nine, so the family gatherings at Christmas you can imagine imply a lot of people,” Lescure says. Their son, a teacher in London, has Irish citizenship.
Irish people don’t give themselves enough credit, he believes.
“I think Irish people should be aware ... of what has been achieved in the last 35 years. I’ve seen it first hand,” Lescure says.
“I’ve seen a quiet revolution occur in Ireland. Obviously economically, from one of the poorest countries in Europe to one of the richest now, but also socially.”
[ Starting gun fires on Europe’s make-or-break election in France Opens in new window ]
“I saw the referendum on divorce, I saw the citizen convention on abortion, I’ve seen same-sex marriage being adopted by referendum as well. I have been impressed by the ability of the Irish people to address complex issues, to debate them without too much drama,” he says.
France, in contrast, “sometimes loves the drama, and doesn’t like compromise”.
Is there a risk of a return to the jittery autumn of 2025, when bond markets focused on France and there began to be whispers of a return of the euro zone debt crisis?
“Obviously, we’re faced with a difficult international environment. The Strait of Hormuz , the war in Ukraine, global interest rates on the rise because of global indebtedness, public and private,” Lescure says.
He hopes that the budget will show that “despite the political uncertainties of France eight months before an election” the government is “consolidating public finance, reducing public deficit, but also favouring growth”.
“We’re going to be very adamant about keeping the fiscal environment for companies stable, and to make sure that France keeps on growing while stabilising and reducing the public deficit next year,” he adds.
People in Ireland sometimes admire France for the high standards that the public demand from their government, and their willingness to protest when they are unhappy, I tell the minister.
“Well, I’ll tell you one thing,” he replies, letting slip another Hibernicism. “The grass is not always greener on the other side ... the grass is very green in Ireland. Keep it that way.”

title: New detached four-bed in boutique development in Kilcoole
description: Chestnut Grove home extends to 210sq m, with luxury finish throughout
content:
Those of a certain vintage will know Kilcoole in Co Wickow as the setting for Glenroe, the long-running soap. The show ceased to air 25 years ago, but the “Welcome to Glenroe” sign remains. House-hunters squeezed out of the Dublin market, however, will know Kilcoole as a viable alternative to nearby Greystones and Delgany , with new housing developments under way in the area.
Chestnut Grove is a high-end boutique development of contemporary homes in a quiet cul-de-sac just off the Sea Road in Kilcoole, designed and built by Ambihouse.
Number 5 Chestnut Grove extends to 210sq m (2,260sq ft), with four bedrooms. With an A Ber, it is now for sale through DNG, seeking €1.1 million.
The developer has focused on optimising space and light and using high-quality materials at the development. The layout of these homes blend luxury style with practical everyday living, ensuring that each house meets the needs of a busy family in this commuter-belt location.
Outside, the contemporary aesthetic is apparent from the dark-grey zinc portico with timber slats and the large corner window in the livingroom, to the modern oriel window jutting out from the main bedroom to the side.
Inside, the entrance hall is laid in herringbone flooring, and to the right is a bespoke built-in bench, boot drawer, coat-hanging area and cloak cupboard. A generous understairs cupboard is one of several storage areas cleverly placed around the house.
Off the hall is a large utility room, with a washer and dryer that are included in the sale. The plant room housing the air-to-water heating system is tucked away here. There is also a guest loo with half-panelled walls and leaf-patterned wallpaper.
The herringbone flooring moves to plank flooring for the livingroom and the open-plan kitchen/dining/living area. The large corner window brings in light and offers views out from two sides, while leaving plenty of wall space for furnishings and a media centre.
The L-shaped kitchen/dining/living area is designed as the hub of the house, with bespoke cabinetry and shelving, and large glass sliding doors opening out to a wide side patio.
The kitchen revolves around a large central island, with cabinetry in a warm grey and elegant stone worktops. A large concealed pantry provides all the storage needed to keep the kitchen uncluttered.
A back door leads from the kitchen to the rear garden, laid in lawn with wooden fencing lined with new plants. A wide patio-style path leads from the main patio at the side to another patio outside the kitchen.
Upstairs are four double bedrooms, with the main bedroom overlooking the back garden. Thanks to the oriel window, however, the main bedroom also has a view to the front. It has a large walk-in wardrobe with shelf, drawer and hanging space, and an en suite shower room with twin hand basins.
The other three double bedrooms have fitted wardrobes, also in grey, and soft carpeting. The large family bathroom has a bath and separate shower and is laid in a tasteful blend of dark and light tiling.
There’s off-street parking for several cars to the front, with provision for an electric gate and electric car charger. There’s also no shortage of on-street parking on this peaceful cul-de-sac.
Two more homes are set to be launched at the scheme soon.
The area around Kilcoole is well served with schools and shopping and leisure facilities, not to mention coastal walks and other outdoor activities by the sea. Dublin Bus services run from the village, while Greystones Dart station is just under 6km away.

title: Outsurance’s Irish chief: ‘In Ireland everyone wants to tell you insurance is too expensive’
description: Aussie Peter Broome on launching the South African insurer into Ireland, AI and extreme weather’s impact on pricing
content:
Peter Broome spent the summer holidaying in Ireland. As well as enjoying the exceptionally dry and sunny period, the Brisbane native used his time to take up fly fishing.
“I got all the gear and had no idea and just started,” he says. “I’ve been fishing with different guides around the country and meeting people and it’s enjoyable.”
The boss of Outsurance’s Irish insurance arm has also been casting out for new customers.
The fly-fishing trips have proven to be inadvertent market research opportunities.
“I tend to find if you’re in a pub talking to people because you’re travelling and they find out you’re in insurance, they always want to have a chat,” he says.
“They all want to tell you that it’s too expensive.”
Broome laughs as he recalls some encounters.
He says he enjoys “educating” people on why insurance premiums work the way they do - but also that Irish customers are among the savviest in the world. It is that cohort his business has been trying to win over for the past two years.
From its Irish base in Cherrywood, south Co Dublin, Outsurance has employed more than 200 people and has concentrated on cracking the Irish motor insurance market.
Its TV ads and online media spots have sought to use “real” customer testimonies and feature a distinctive paper-man character who consists of random sheets of paper and bundled-together office supplies.
Broome is under no illusion about the challenge. “I can say to you, probably tens of thousands of customers have now joined us. We’re still very small.”
With the considerable backing of its parent group – the multinational Outsurance Group in South Africa - Broome says the Irish business should begin to make proper inroads.
“We’re still going to be well in the lowest, lower single digits when it comes to market share at this stage of the game,” he adds. “And, and you know, that’s fine because it takes time to build trust with consumers.
“You can’t just come in overnight and think you’re going to run some ads and get a big book. Because I mean, the Irish have got long memories as well and so they’ve seen in the past where insurers have come and then gone.
“You need to build a little bit of confidence with the market that you’re here to stay for the long run. As we earn those stripes, they’ll join us at much higher rates.”
Broome is alluding to the troubled past of Ireland’s insurance market.
Quinn Insurance’s collapse in 2010 still haunts the minds of Irish consumers. Until this year, every non-life insurance customer here was paying a 2 per cent levy that essentially covered the cost of the Quinn administration. It was reduced this year to 1 per cent.
In the years that followed the Quinn debacle, more than one international insurance brand looked at Ireland and turned its nose up.
Outsurance’s arrival proper in 2024 was welcomed by the Government as a watershed moment - and recognition that the fundamentals underpinning the insurance sector had been significantly improved.
A new Book of Quantum had been established, which was designed to bring down the high cost of personal injury payments, and moves were made towards a more efficient and less costly way of dealing with claims.
Reform of the Personal Injuries Assessment Board sought to increase the use of mediation and ultimately bring down insurance premiums by limiting the use of solicitors and the need to go to court.
This was “all very positive”, says Broome, but more needs to be done.
“There’s plenty of data out there, as you’ve seen around the quantum of bodily injury payout, in comparison to the UK it is still higher. So I think there’s still probably work to do there.
“We need to drive as much through the Injuries Resolutions Board [formerly PIAB] as we can. I think in terms of mediation, you want a fair outcome for the customer – that’s a must.
“Sometimes the legal route can take you years, whereas if we can try and keep that process with the Injuries Resolution Board to a shorter process, it costs less and still ends up with a very fair outcome for the consumer.
“The more those numbers look the same, the more people will transition towards the resolution board.”
While the insurance market is arguably more attractive now than it was a few years ago – offering the promise perhaps of cheaper premiums in the future – there are new trends that may mitigate any big reduction in costs.
The increase of more technologically-advanced electric vehicles on the road poses new types of claims for the industry.
“With the ADAS [driver assistance] systems that were coming in and more automation of vehicles coming through, that always comes with increased technology, which inevitably comes with more costs in repair,” says Broome.
“The other side of that coin is it can come with lower frequency of accidents because the alarm systems are telling you you’re about to back into something, rather than the old days where we had to just use the mirrors.
“So it can help reduce your frequency, but it does tend to lead to it being a more expensive repair in the long run.”
Key to bringing down the costs of repairs, he says, is an increase in the availability of parts. With more of these cars on the road the pressure on new parts should lessen over the next few years.
For now, it is the motor insurance market that Broome is largely occupied with.
The company has yet to venture seriously into home insurance. According to Broome, this is to be expected.
“When you’re a new entrant into the market, consumers will try you with their car and give you an opportunity to price on that and to cover them for a year and they’ll see how your service is,” says Broome.
“And if they can trust you and then as that trust builds, they’ll then trust you with their larger assets. So that’s not an unusual thing.”
He has watched as severe weather events in Ireland have begun to change the reckonings for many customers and their insurance providers. It was a horrendous winter for many homeowners around the country due to flooding.
The Central Bank of Ireland estimates that around one-in-20 homes struggle to get cover due to being located in an area that has already flooded or is deemed to be at risk of flooding.
Just last month the industry’s representative body, Insurance Ireland, published proposals to close what it called Ireland’s “flood insurance protection gap”.
Among them, the establishment of a “sustainable” flood insurance fund that would extend cover to vulnerable properties.
Broome says Outsurance has been part of drawing these up. “The house that was built in a spot decades or hundreds of years ago, is now exposed in a way that it never was back then,” he says.
“They could never have imagined at that point in time that that home would be exposed to consistent weather events. And it’s exactly the same worldwide.”
He refers back to his home country where severe weather is now a simple fact of life. As an example, he talks about houses on the Brisbane river in Queensland that are now expected to be flooded-out every “seven to 10 years”.
“It’s very hard to insure your way out of that because the cost of it is massive,” he says.
He says the insurance gap in Ireland isn’t as large as some other countries, and he is optimistic that it will be addressed.
No conversation with a senior business person these days would be complete without the inevitable mention of artificial intelligence.
Surely the insurance industry would be well placed to take advantage of what AI offers - particularly when it comes to automating claims and detecting fraud?
“We take a softly, softly approach with AI,” he says. “It could be an excellent tool for assisting humans in doing their job. But I think it’s quite important for us to be a bit slower in adoption in terms of making sure that it’s not making decisions.”
The company has not, he says, deployed AI when it comes to pricing risk or new policies.
“There’s a million companies that would be quite happy to sell us their AI model tomorrow,” he says. ”We certainly don’t think that at this stage it’s costing us anything from a competition point of view.”
But at the same time it is watching this area “quite closely”.
Might this mean, in future, a reduced headcount in Cherrywood?
“We don’t want to replace people,” he replies. “Irish consumers, if there’s something going on and they want to pick up the phone and ring somebody, they want to get you on the phone and have it sorted out fairly quickly.”
He says the 240 staff there are part of a “service level commitment” to answer 95 per cent of all calls in 20 seconds.
“And that’s by a human being, not by the IVR (Interactive Voice Response) or an automated message saying, yes, you’re in the queue. That’s actually picked up by a human who can help you.
“That, to us, is quite a pivotal piece.”
Broome saysOutsurance aims to have 300 people on the payroll by the end of the year. The Irish market, he believes, is different to others in that customers here want to talk about their policies with other human beings.
“You need to be there to take that call. And that’s why chatbots and things like that, those [things] can be quite frustrating. We’re still a bit old school in our service offering.”
In terms of pricing, it has been a tough decade or so for consumers here - with persistent claims of price gouging on premiums.
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) has instigated investigations in the past into “price signalling” - a practice where providers make public statements about what they intend on doing with their premiums, allowing the rest of the industry to price accordingly.
Understandably, Broom says he has to “keep his cards close to his chest”.
“We are constantly monitoring on a daily basis … as to how the numbers track and we have brought prices down quite intentionally,” he says.
“My team put through another base rate decrease here just in the last couple of weeks. Which again, I shouldn’t be telling you. But you know we are proactively looking at price and trying to make sure that we’re matching as much [of] those numbers [that] will add up to stay competitive.”
Ultimately, he says, the business has to be profitable. And how is that working out?
“[There’s] ... always a long tail in insurance,” he says. “So when you start out, it’s always going to be a costly exercise to set up the business.
“We’re lucky to have such a supportive group in Outsurance that’s very committed to the business and stumped up the capital for us to get started. We’re well capitalised and in a very good position and the business plan is going quite well.”
Broome plans to see more of Ireland over the coming years having already taken in “Malin to Mizen”. The increasingly “savvy” Irish customers he encounters on his travels are likely to provide more real-world research and selling opportunities.
“That’s why the chats are always quite interesting, depending on how many pints I’ve had.”

title: Urbanite David McCullagh’s baptism of fire at the National Ploughing Championships
description: Radio: Radio 1 host’s broadcasting mettle is tested by his visit to farming jamboree, while Anton Savage shows his bite
content:
H e has hosted crunch general-election debates, gone toe to toe with Russian ambassadors and tangled with taoisigh on a regular basis. But as seasoned a broadcaster as David McCullagh is, little can have prepared him for the blistering baptism of fire that is helming a live chatshow at the National Ploughing Championships .
Presenting Wednesday’s edition of Today with David McCullagh (RTÉ Radio 1, weekdays) from the annual agricultural jamboree in Screggan, Co Offaly, the host is as wry and inquisitive as ever. But from the off McCullagh also seems somewhat unsettled by his alien surroundings, finding himself on the back foot when talking to the Independent Ireland TD Michael Fitzmaurice about State support for the farming sector.
Asked by the host for his take on the situation, Fitzmaurice praises those working in agriculture as “the salt of the earth” before decrying the “farmer-bashing” aimed at the sector. “Where do you see farmer bashing?” McCullagh asks sharply. “You’re pretty good at it yourselves in the media,” Fitzmaurice replies jauntily, to cheers from the spectators in attendance.
Stung by the politician’s (all-too-predictable) riposte, the host responds slightly tetchily – “You’ve got the hometown audience with you there” – only to walk into another palpable hit by his guest: “Yeah, I rented a crowd.”
Populist that he is, Fitzmaurice certainly knows how to work this one, what with the subject and the setting.
This one-sided sparring contest eventually settles into a more even-handed and factually grounded discussion, but after his initial bruising McCullagh doesn’t really sound comfortable.
It’s an uncharacteristically astringent moment, however. Otherwise, the host is in tune with the good-natured festival atmosphere of the ploughing, though he still betrays his ingenu status at times. During his conversation with Michael and Aoife Ruddock, father and daughter contestants in the senior and junior brown-bread competitions, a more relaxed McCullagh samples the baked goods with relish: “It tastes fantastic!”
Even this triumph is fleeting, however. McCullagh then compliments Aoife for wearing an Offaly jersey, only to be corrected that it’s actually the Leitrim strip. Cue much ribbing from the audience. “I’m going to have to apologise after that,” the host sheepishly admits.
At other times McCullagh seems to revel in being the confirmed Dubliner in the rural environment. Talking to the RTÉ reporter Brian O’Connell, the host is upfront about his lack of familiarity with the vast enterprise: “Thanks for filling us in on what is really happening at the ploughing, because it’s a mystery to me.”
Not all his on-air mishaps arise from urbanite blind spots, though. His interview with the chairwoman of the Road Safety Authority, Anne Graham, is prefaced by a clip of the host being strapped into a rollover simulator, to his evident discomfort.
“I’m beginning to regret having that full Irish this morning,” he splutters while enduring the sensation of a car flipping over. Afterwards, he drily wonders why he was subjected to such buffeting: “That was mainly done for the entertainment of my production team.”
Maybe so, but it adds to the gaiety of listeners too. And, for all his scrapes, McCullagh actually emerges with his credentials enhanced: his Screggan expedition makes for great radio.
It’s in keeping with a good week for the presenter. Having been light on meaty political interviews of late, McCullagh hosts not one but two heavyweight encounters on Monday’s show.
He first speaks with Mary Lou McDonald, the Sinn Féin leader, focusing on Donald Trump’s bombshell endorsement of a united Ireland, a development she guardedly welcomes while decrying Taoiseach Micheál Martin for discouraging a Border poll.
[ Irish unity rather than protests the focus of US coverage of Trump visit Opens in new window ]
McCullagh also interviews the Taoiseach himself, who for his part prizes constitutional caution over rushed unification referendums, while excoriating Sinn Féin for its IRA past.
For all their spiky talk, it’s fairly rote stuff from both Martin and McDonald, but their presence adds topical ballast to McCullagh’s programme.
Not everything is as absorbing, however. Tuesday’s chat with the EU agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, is as exhilarating as one would expect from a Eurocrat outlining official policy in intricate detail, with the host rarely intervening.
He may have had the odd sticky moment at the ploughing, but McCullagh is better when he gets stuck in.
Even as rural life is exuberantly celebrated elsewhere, over on Newstalk Breakfast (weekdays), Anton Savage hears how the differences between city and country are narrowing, in some respects anyway. On Tuesday he speaks to the journalist Jacqueline Hogge, who describes how cocaine use is commonplace among younger farmers: “It’s becoming a norm now for young people in the farming community.”
While this might come as a shock to some – “There’s still a perception in parts of rural Ireland that drugs is an urban issue,” Hogge says – it doesn’t surprise Savage, who notes the ubiquity of cocaine throughout the country.
Even so, the countryside coke trade comes with a uniquely unwelcome twist, with Hogge reporting suspicions among agricultural contractors that new operators are using drug money to fund their business.
Savage’s item gives an unexpected, if dispiriting, glimpse into the changing nature of rural society in Ireland. Even so, with his knowing mien and smooth delivery, the presenter is emphatically not a horny-handed son of the soil; the closest he gets to the ploughing is a phone interview with (the on-site) Minister for Agriculture Martin Heydon.
Not that it matters. With its brief items and zippy style, Savage’s show is tailor-made for the studio, allowing him to pivot seamlessly from ministerial encounters to health advice, as when he speaks to the dentist Caroline Robins about bruxism, aka teeth grinding. Robins, a self-confessed “clencher”, attributes the condition to everything from stress and sleep to drink or dementia, while suggesting the most effective treatment for nocturnal gnashing is a mouthguard.
Savage is dubious about the idea of wearing such a device overnight. “My only experience of gumshields is looking forward to half-time, so I could briefly take them out,” he remarks.
Flippant though this comment seems, it’s also strangely apposite. The host’s item on bruxism is, in its own way, incisive; for all his sly irreverence, Savage’s approach is far from toothless.
Sartorial questions prevail on The Hard Shoulder (Newstalk, weekdays) when Shane Coleman asks the public-relations guru Terry Prone (aka Savage’s mother) if people have lost the art of dressing up, particularly in work settings.
Prone is firmly of the first-impressions-last school – “Whether we like it or not, clothes and fashion are semiotics” – and bemoans the decline of formality in the workplace, albeit in slightly convoluted form: “The suit and tie is now pretty much dead, but we make a big mistake if we think it’s a permanent deadness,” Prone says, conjuring up images of besuited zombies.
But a bigger jolt comes when Coleman wonders whether his guest is driven mad when she sees TV presenters in casual clothing. “You’re asking the wrong person, Shane, because I don’t watch television,” Prone coolly replies.
Even in the digital era, for a legendary PR figure to admit she ignores the telly sends out an odd signal.

title: Farmers in the Dáil
description: Eyebrows would be raised if a minister for education were running a grind school on the side
content:
Sir, – The symbiotic relationship between the Government and farming is revealed in the excellent investigative article by by Cormac McQuinn and Killian Woods (“ The Oireachtas farmers: who are the largest landowners in Leinster House? ”, Investigation, September 15th). It reveals the Dáil is top heavy with farmers, with 15 per cent of the total having significant interests in the sector. It is unequivocal that this mutualism is influencing Government policy and the result is more cows, polluted rivers and lakes, food insecurity and a huge carbon footprint (accounting for 38 per cent of Ireland’s greenhouse gas emissions). So much for the Paris Agreement 2030.
A spokesman for Martin Heydon said there could be no conflict of interest between being a farmer and minister for agriculture, citing the example of a teacher being a minister for education. It is a hard to believe that eyebrows would not be raised, however, if a minister for education was running a grind school on the side.
I believe we should follow the lead of the Danes and abolish the minister for agriculture and instead appoint a minister for nature and animal welfare, someone who would advocate for animals and the environment, and the benefits would be felt by all of us. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I think most farmers would agree there is no conflict of interest between Martin Heydon, the Minister for Agriculture, receiving Cap payments and being part of the negotiations for the EU budget 2028-2034. He will receive future Cap payments according to a clear, transparent and formulated system along with 120,000 other farmers in Ireland.
However, I think most farmers would welcome the Minister delivering more support to the sector, given national and international issues of the last year.
His response to a drought in half the country this summer has been to promote a national fodder survey and a promise of earlier Cap payments. Most farmers are well aware of how many round bales are in their yard. A targeted plan to get more bales in the affected areas or imported into the country is instead required. Similarly, earlier Cap payments will only help cash flow, they will not reduce costs or find the required fodder.
His response to record fertiliser prices, now double what farmers were paying five years ago, has been nonexistent, even though the annual window for spreading fertiliser has now closed for this year.
The consumer is suffering and will continue to suffer with ongoing food inflation. Hopefully the Minister will negotiate, secure and distribute sufficient funding to ensure food security and low inflation. – Yours, etc,

title: Ten top trends in Irish staycations
description: Sauna raves and chilli festivals are among the hot trends in Irish holidays this year, writes Thom Breathnach
content:
A new travel season means new trends, new openings and fresh festivals. So what’s literally hot for autumn 2026? From country house escapes, gourmet croissant hauls, sauna raves, and yes, chilli festivals, here are ten trends you can expect to feature on your staycation calendar.
You can’t talk about autumn in Ireland without showboating Halloween. And being the ancestral home of the ancient festival of Samhain, it’s great to see a celebratory renaissance of those traditional roots year on year. Discover Ireland have unveiled seven hubs for celebrations for 2026 with an eclectic line-up of atmospheric events around the country.
The City of Tribes will host Gaillimh Ah-Boo! (cliste!) featuring its annual Macnas parade and dark history tours, while in Ireland’s Ancient East the Púca Festival with headline happenings in the Boyne Valley while the Lú Festival of Light will illuminate the town of Drogheda. Nearby in Longford and Westmeath, the counties will be hosting the likes of the Fire & Shadows procession and An Tairseach Samhain, while in North County Dublin, the Fingal Festival of Fire will be setting the skies alight while Limerick’s Harvest Festival will be taking place at the popular Milk Market.
In The Kingdom, Samhain Ciarraí will mark a fortnight of colourful events while food lovers can make tracks for Savour Kilkenny, taking place at the city’s iconic castle. And don’t forget about Derry’s magical festival as an option too.
Sweet treat craze, anyone? It doesn’t seem long ago that heading out for food on a weekend morning meant a fix of eggs Benny or avocado toast, but now there’s a growing rise (pun intended) in our grá for every baked good from almond croissants to chocolate cruffins. With that bakery tourism is emerging as a new travel mainstay where consumers can now experience accessible luxury produce in trendy, artisanal bakers rather than splashing out on an extravagant meal. There are a whole plethora of options to enjoy from The Grumpy Bakers in Cork to Scéal Bakery in Dublin. Perhaps we can look forward to some tasty seasonal specials too?
As wildlife tourism evolves like all niches, there’s a growing appreciation that you no longer need to embark on an epic safari to get a thrill from wildlife. A simple “twitch” will do the trick. Trending slow birding, for example, celebrates low-impact, low-mile wildlife watching closer to home and appreciating some of our lesser sung avian delights. Autumn is a great time to pull out the binoculars, with migrating visitors such as Brent geese on the island as well as the likes of skuas and shearwaters along the south coast. For a great day out, pay a visit to the RSPB centre in Belfast, North Bull Island in Dublin or Harper’s Island in Cork. To make a night of it, the family-run Castle Hotel in Macroom offers excellent dining breaks and sits just a kilometre, as the heron flies, from the tranquil Gearagh bird sanctuary. Keep an eye out for giant egrets!
Is there anything more inviting than a country house stay in autumn? Benefit from lower off-season rates and a wonderfully inviting atmosphere whether curling up alongside a roaring fire, or even retiring by the pool if we’re treated to an Indian summer this year. Ireland is blessed with a whole host of hideaways, with collections from Ireland’s Blue Book properties and Hidden Ireland to independent gems peppered across the countryside. Fancy a whole-house takeover for friends or family? The Irish Landmark Trust also offers characterful historic properties which make for excellent value, particularly when there’s a gang to divvy up the costs.
South Korea seems to be the new Japan when it comes to leading TikTok travel trends and now glowcations is just one of the latest. The trend, where consumers travel for skin care and wellness is on the rise, not only for women but also for males who previously may have given the cryotherapy a skip. You don’t need to travel to Seoul either … how about popping Tipp in your wellness diary. The Horse & Jockey Hotel in Thurles features a great spa and excellent value autumn wellness and dining breaks for anyone chasing a value wellness getaway. Pair a treatment with a walk along the Littleton Labyrinth which reaches the majestic ruins of Derrynaflan Church.
Forget Finland, saunas have become such a mainstay feature of the Irish coastal experience, it’s hard to image sea swimming without them. But with their proliferation, how can they stand out from the crowd? A rave sauna, no less. Adding a new musical element is taking the experience next level, by providing outlets for those not wishing to spend their nights (or at least all of it) in a pub, and increasing wholesome community levels too. Coastal Cabins located on Garryvoe Beach in East Cork are one such operation, where you can sweat, plunge and throw shapes while overlooking Ballycotton Lighthouse in the bay. Keep an eye out for their popular full moon sauna sessions too.
A literal hot trend alert. There’s been an exponential global rise in the appeal of chillies, hot sauce and spicy food in recent years, not least thanks to viral YouTube shows like Hot Ones, where celebrities are interviewed while tackling increasingly spicy rounds of chicken wings. That online obsession has spilled into real life, driving a surge of chilli festivals not only in prime Tex Mex country but in Ireland too. Marina Market in Cork just hosted a chilli festival while this September, head to Co Down for its family-friendly chilli festival on the grounds of Bangor Castle.
Ireland has become a nation obsessed with staycations, particularly since the post-Covid era, and as our familiarity with the island grows, so does the appetite to find somewhere at home which is just a little bit more undiscovered. With that, expect counties like Monaghan, Longford and Tyrone to grow in popularity as visitors trade well-trodden hotspots for quieter nooks, with the added bonus of far fewer tourists around. The new addition of Ómós is expected to see a lot of travellers heading to Co Laois too.
Pining for a forest getaway? This year brings a whole new range of cabin breaks for those looking to reconnect with mother nature. Cabü in Co Cavan has launched a new collection of barn-style houses, with USPs of their own private deck hot tubs, while Glamping Under the Stars in Co Laois has added three new properties to its site this year. Meanwhile, Cape Clear Glamping in West Cork has unveiled a whole new fleet of designer cabins set against a spectacular coastal backdrop. For families, Killarney Glamping’s brand-new site at Killarney Racecourse offers a great all-weather base to nestle down in.
One thing that always strikes me as a travel writer and an Irishman is just how many people across the island have never actually travelled to the six counties. It’s always pretty much top of my list when it comes to a staycation tip with its energy, people and landscapes always guaranteeing a memorable trip. The Harrison in Belfast is a great pick for a stylish city break, while Co Armagh aka the Orchard County is the most idyllic spot to celebrate for autumn’s cider season, while for a unique self-catering break, the Old Kiln in charming Bushmills is one of my favourite finds of the year.

title: The case for camping: Sites where even the rain won’t ruin your holiday
description: Love the great outdoors? Jennifer Sheahan offers a personal selection of memorable Irish camping destinations
content:
There has been a lot of talk this summer about what it costs to holiday at home; €2,000 per week seems to be the going rate for a house near a beach in Kerry, if you can get one at all. Hotels are scarce and dear, and a fair few seaside ones have closed altogether.
The argument doing the rounds is that Ireland is missing an entire tier of accommodation - hostels, and properly serviced sites for campervans and tents - scattered around the country the way they are across much of the mainland.
I have a vested interest in that argument. I have been touring Ireland in a micro-camper for the past few summers - a converted seven-seater Nissan Serena with a fold-flat bed, a narrow kitchen unit, an electric shower in the boot, and a drive-away awning. There’s nowhere better than Ireland on a sunny day and when you combine that with a good campsite, it’s the best holiday you could have. Although, when the weather is bad and the campsite is worse, you can find yourself sitting bored in a damp car park re-installing the Ryanair app.
I am not a tent person. My tent-camping career peaked at Witnness music festival (yes, I am that old) and now extends only as far as a glamping yurt at All Together Now. So my camping experience is exclusively campervan-based. That said, the experience itself is widespread. I have toured France and Spain in my micro-camper, along with a fair amount of Ireland, so my baseline for comparing campsites is quite high.
They know how to do it on the continent, and while we could do with more, we have some fantastic campsites right here. Here are three sites that earned that title. They are not ranked, they are just the ones I keep going back to.
Mannix Point sits right on the water’s edge just outside Cahersiveen, nestled prettily in grassy banks against a hilly backdrop. The pitches terrace down towards the sea, with Valentia Island in front of you and a harbour behind, and the whole thing is arranged so that almost everybody gets a view rather than just the people who arrived first.
The basics are all there and all well minded - hot showers, a communal kitchen, laundry, and a location you can walk into town from for dinner. The staff are warm and helpful. But that is not what earned it its place on my list.
What puts it on my list is the living room. There is a fire lit on wet evenings, games to play, and instruments left out for anyone to pick up. Guitars, a bodhrán, and a piano. Nobody organises anything, it’s just all there for you to entertain yourself as you dry off by the fire. I don’t know if anyone remembers the storms of July 2025, but I was so grateful to escape the thundering in the campervan. I passed a very happy evening singing songs and playing piano and listening to a fabulous guitarist sing better songs, and we all had a roaring evening while the rain poured.
Book early - it is small, it is popular, and word has got out. campinginkerry.com
Connemara does not need any help from me selling itself. Acton’s Eco Camping is tucked into the dunes outside Clifden, and rather than the usual open field with numbered sites, you find yourself pitching among hilly dunes and tall marram grass. The effect is that the campsite can be full to capacity and you can still feel like you have the place to yourself. The grass does the work of a windbreak too, which in that part of the country is not a small thing.
The beach is a hop, skip, and a jump away. So are the walks, the swims, a barrel sauna, and some of the best coastal scenery in the country.
I’m a Galway native by birth and by university, and there are a million things I love about the county, not least of which is the seafood. A local fisherman rowed up onto the campsite beach one evening and sold us fresh fish straight off the boat, which we cooked over the charcoal an hour or so later. It was divine - nearly as good as the excellent fare you can get in Oifig an Fish a few miles down the road.
It books up fast, and it helps if the owners like you, so be sound. clifdenecocamping.ie
This one is different, because I’ve been going to Keel long before I ever had a van (or a driver’s licence).
Keel Camping sits right on the beach in the middle of the village, which is about as central as most Irish campsites get. My aunts and uncles have descended on Achill every summer since long before my cousins and I were born, and one aunt kept a caravan there back in the nineties when we were little. Two of them have since bought homes on the island, so we are all still regulars, only now we are bringing the next generation with us.
The routine hasn’t changed much. Paddling with the littles in Keel Lough. Swimming and surfing at Keel, Keem and Dugort. A walk around the Deserted Village on the slopes of Slievemore. The aquarium for a wet afternoon, which never fails to delight the children. Coffee in the Beehive. And a pint in Lynott’s with my cousins, which remains one of my favourite activities of all time.
Last summer we camped there with my cousin and his wife, their baby, and our three dogs between us. We swam, dozed in the dunes in the afternoons, and watched my cousin surf while we ate 99s, which feels like a fair division of labour. It is busier than it was thirty years ago, of course it is. But the magic of the place has not been diluted one bit. keelcamping.ie
The weather is the whole game. Not the rain itself - you get wet, you dry off - but whether there is anywhere warm and dry to retreat to afterwards. A campsite with a communal room and a fire is worth twice one without, especially if your camper is lacking in living space, and this is exactly the sort of thing that a national investment in serviced sites would fix.
Sand gets absolutely everywhere and there is nothing you can do about it, so stop fighting it. Hose everyone off at the back door when you get home.
Barbecue smoke is my personal underrated misery of Irish camping. It sticks in the hair and the clothes, and stings the eyes no matter where you sit. That said, I’d never pass a night without a barbecue or a campfire. Just check which way the wind is going before finding your perch for the evening.
And bring the dog. Mine has been to all three of these sites and many more besides. I recommend a frisbee to wear them out on the beaches.
Prices vary by season and I’d recommend phoning first, though all three sites have good websites. Wherever you end up going, check the dog policies, barbecue requirements, and opening dates before you travel. Remember to be sound and have fun.

title: Former Paddy Power chief calls for draconian tax on online casinos
description: Stewart Kenny says online slot machines and casino games pose danger to young people and serve no public good
content:
The co-founder and former chief executive of Paddy Power bookmakers has called on the Minister for Finance to levy a 40 per cent tax on online gaming and casino businesses, which he said posed a “significant danger”, particularly to young men, and served “no public good whatsoever”.
In a letter, co-signed by several addiction specialists, Stewart Kenny described online slot machines and casino games as “the crack cocaine of gambling ”.
These games were being heavily marketed here as “harmless fun” when they were anything but, Kenny said, while claiming that international gaming companies were taking advantage of Ireland’s “lenient” tax regime.
The UK government recently increased its remote gaming duty, which applies to profits from online gaming, from 21 per cent to 40 per cent.
Ireland takes a different approach to taxing these companies, applying a 23 per cent VAT rate to their gross gambling yield.
“As an absolute minimum, it is necessary that the Irish Government immediately follows the example of the UK and introduces a new minimum levy of 40 per cent on gross gambling yield for online casinos,” Kenny’s letter said.
“We believe in subsequent budgets the online casino taxes should be raised further to mirror taxation levels on tobacco, which are close to 80 per cent.”
Kenny was chief executive of Paddy Power from 1988 to 2002. He resigned from the board in 2016, accusing the company of profiteering from gambling addicts online. Since retiring he has become a critic of the gambling industry’s tactics.
Paddy Power’s parent company Flutter , which also owns Betfair in the UK and FanDuel in the US, is the world’s largest gambling and online gaming company.
[ ‘World’s largest’ betting website closed to Irish users after regulator action Opens in new window ]
Kenny’s letter is co-signed by Prof Colin O’Gara, clinical professor of psychiatry at University College Dublin; Dr Frank Houghton, principal investigator of the Tobacco, Alcohol and Gambling Research Group at Technological University of the Shannon; and Niall McNamee, a former Offaly county footballer and recovering problem gambler.
There is growing evidence to suggest that gambling companies are using traditional sports betting “as a Trojan Horse or a gateway, to lure gamblers from sports betting to their more addictive online casino and slot machine operations”, the letter said.
Online slot machines and casinos are much more profitable than traditional forms of gambling such as horse racing as they require little or no manpower and can operate 24 hours a day, it added.
Gaming and gambling sites have proliferated in Ireland over the past 10 years with the gambling spend and online advertising rising in tandem.
The letter was accompanied by a report from Dublin City University economist Tony Foley that examined the evolution of onling gambling in the UK, which it concluded was fast “becoming a reality in Ireland”.
The UK gambling market is now dominated by online casino games and slot machines, with an estimated £84 billion (€97 billion) a year gambled on online slot machines alone.
“Put simply, Ireland has become a magnet for these online casinos who concentrate marketing spend here rather than in other, higher-tax markets,” Kenny’s letter said.
“Online casinos pose a significant danger especially to younger men, who often do not fully understand the risks of actions they take,” it added, while noting that that there was growing evidence that gambling addiction is now a major cause of suicide and self-harm.

title: Affordable wines: a Spanish alternative to sauvignon blanc and a red wine to drink with lamb
description: Verdejo makes aromatic wines with fresh green fruits and good acidity – sound familiar?
content:
This week, we feature two Spanish wines from Tesco . Both are made from local Spanish grape varieties.
Verdejo has been grown in the Rueda region of Spain for centuries. Most of the wines are aromatic with racy acidity and fresh green fruits. If you enjoy sauvignon blanc, I suspect you will like verdejo too.
The red wine comes from Ribera del Duero, a region that has enjoyed great success in recent years. The most popular grape here is called tinto fino, which translates as “fine red”. It is the same grape as tempranillo, the Spanish variety used to make rioja and a host of other wines. In Ribera del Duero, it tends to produce robust full-bodied wines.
Fresh floral aromas, lemon peel and green apple fruits with a dry finish. Enjoy on its own, with lighter salads or maybe a seafood paella.
A powerful wine with plenty of ripe dark fruits and vanilla spice from a short ageing in oak. Locally, they would enjoy it with roast lamb, but any red meat, pork or firm cheese would do nicely.

title: How can you make your home more sustainable? For most of us, it’s one step at a time
description: Advice, support and practical solutions from Electric Ireland are guiding customers towards a more sustainable and cost-efficient life
content:
For many Irish households, the challenge of living more sustainably isn’t a lack of willingness. It’s knowing where to start.
Over the past few months, severe weather events have made climate change feel immediate, while the impact of geopolitical issues such as conflicts and tariffs brings energy matters home to us in a very real way.
Electric Ireland ’s head of net-zero strategy and sustainability, Ellen Diskin, understands this completely, both in her professional capacity and as a single parent to two young children, trying to make the best energy decisions for her own household.
“As an organisation, Electric Ireland is committed to reaching net zero by 2040. But a really important part of our culture is making sure we don’t leave customers behind. The energy transition needs to work not just for the environment, but for households and families too.”
Ireland is making significant investments in renewable generation, including wind and solar power, helping reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.
But for consumers, the transition becomes real through everyday decisions in their own homes, whether that’s moving to a smart-meter tariff, installing solar panels, upgrading heating systems or switching to an electric vehicle.
“The challenge for many people isn’t motivation,” says Diskin. “It’s understanding what action makes sense for them, and what step they should take first.”
But such steps cost money, and decision making around them can feel overwhelming.
Electric Ireland sees its role as helping make those decisions easier.
“It is our role to help make those decisions as easy and accessible for people as possible, working with government and other organisations to make sure that people are not left on their own to make them,” she says.
“People shouldn’t feel like they’re navigating this alone. We want to help customers understand their options and make informed decisions that suit their household, lifestyle and budget.”
People shouldn’t feel like they’re navigating this alone. We want to help customers understand their options and make informed decisions that suit their household, lifestyle and budget
This is even true of her own family choices. For Diskin, sustainability is as much a personal consideration as a professional one.
“So for my household the easiest thing to do right now was to go on to a smart-meter tariff and start making small changes to when and how we use energy.”
“With the Electric Ireland app you can get smart-meter insights on your phone. It gives you a breakdown of what appliances are using energy and generates tips for savings. For me, the big one was waiting to do the washing and drying until after peak time,” she says.
“Cooking is another big energy user for me but one I can’t really move around – when the kids get in from school and have homework to do, I have to feed them. But the Electric Ireland app gives suggestions on ways to reduce energy usage, such as slow cooking, batch cooking at weekends, or using an air fryer or microwave, which just use so much less energy.”
It’s a simple example of a wider reality about sustainability. The journey to net zero is not “one big bang retrofit”, she points out.
“For most people it’s about doing it bit by bit over the years. That might mean moving to a smart meter tariff today, investing in solar panels in a few years’ time, or considering an electric vehicle when it’s time to replace the current car,” she says.
Results from the most recent Electric Ireland Sustainability Index, a survey conducted among 1,005 consumers in Ireland, bear this out. It found 36 per cent of people want to live more sustainably but just don’t know how.
For Diskin, that’s an important insight. Consumers are aware of the big climate questions, but they want to understand the practical solutions for their life.
“What they want to know is, if the radiator starts to leak, what should they replace it with? Is there a grant available? And how can they be sure the replacement will be ready for a heat pump down the line?” she says.
Some 87 per cent of us would take such actions if we had confidence they would work.
That peace of mind is something else Electric Ireland can help with. “We are an organisation that commits a lot of time and expertise into making sure the solutions we make available will work, help you manage your costs, and help you reduce your carbon footprint,” says Diskin.
That is also reflected in the Electric Ireland Sustainability Index findings. “People who put solar panels on their roof report seeing perceived savings of on average of about €58 per month, and households that have gotten a heat pump – and if you’ve got a relatively new home, it may be heat pump-ready from the outset – are reporting savings of €77 every single month on their heating bill,” she says.
“Those who have electric chargers are saying they are saving on average €91 a month on fuel costs.”
And wherever you are on your sustainability journey, Electric Ireland ensures the path ahead is clearly defined.
Increasingly, consumers are looking for more than an electricity supplier, but for trusted advice that helps them understand their energy use and make informed decisions for the future.
To support customers in their sustainability journey, Electric Ireland has transformed itself, becoming not just an energy supplier but a trusted provider of expert guidance and effective solutions too.
Not alone is it committed to completing its own journey to net zero, but it is supporting its customers, both businesses and residential, as they make the transition too.
Whether through smart meter tariff plans, energy management solutions, or products such as solar panels, EV chargers and batteries, Electric Ireland is enabling customers to better understand their energy use and make more informed decisions.
“For the journey to a more sustainable life to work, it has to work for the household, for the family, for the business. That’s where we focus our attention, helping people take the next step with confidence,” she concludes.
For more information on the steps you can take in your journey to Net Zero, visit the Electric Ireland Net Zero hub

title: Wonderful Waterford: Taking in the delights of the Déise
description: Waterford is a hidden gem that you will keep you coming back year after year, as Mimi Murray discovers
content:
There are two counties in Ireland that have it all, but don’t get the attention of heavy hitters such as Galway or Kerry, Garvan Cummins from The Greenwayman Bike Hire in Dungarvan, Co Waterford, tells me. I know one of them is going to be his home turf, but when he also says Sligo, I’m not surprised. I agree with him. I’ve been visiting these coastal counties since a young age and instantly fell in love with both and return often. With mountains, sea cliffs, clean sandy beaches, a decent sized city or town close by, rich countryside and a warm welcome, they both tick a long list of requirements for a memorable staycation. I am happy to wax lyrical about my summers on Mullaghmore beach or Clonea Strand with someone who feels as strongly about them as I do.
Cummins has been instrumental in putting Waterford squarely on the map in recent years, having been heavily involved in the opening of the Greenway in 2017. The 46km route from Waterford city to Dungarvan has grown in popularity with cyclists and walkers in the past nine years. Lots of cafés and restaurants have sprouted up along the path, with Coach house Coffee at Kilmacthomas offering a wide selection of lunch options, while the cakes at The Railway Cottage are homemade and a feast for the eyes as well as the belly.
But the views of powdery stretches of sandy beach below as you make your way from Durrow, past Clonea Strand and into Dungarvan, passing through the Ballyvoyle tunnel makes the long but manageable cycle worth it. On a recent trip to the sunny southeast, we hired bikes from Greenwayman and Cummins gave us an interesting history lesson on the area as we strapped on helmets and took to the bike path.
My kids have also been going to Waterford since they were babies and have a deep love for the Déise. Their paternal grandmother is from Dungarvan, and every time we visit there is always something ‘more’ to discover in the county of Mores. We stayed in Comeragh pods at the foot of the Comeragh mountains, a perfect spot to base yourself.
The brainchild of Tracy and Padraig Quinlan, the couple has put six glamping pods and a spa area including outdoor hot tub and sauna overlooking the unspoiled mountains and the Tay river close by. It’s rustic but with everything needed to make a stay less arduous than actual camping – a win for a tired mum who really doesn’t want to have to sleep on a blow-up bed in a tent.
The kids took to paddling in the river in rolled up jeans and making smores over the gas lit coal fires as the sun went down. We threw the devices to one side and tried our hands at a couple of the board games that are available in the communal area before chilling out in our pod with a movie. A breakfast basket is provided by the owners in the morning.
Before leaving the Dungarvan area check out Cookhouse 360, with a vast menu that will suit both adults and kids, it’s unfussy, tasty food with excellent service in pleasant surrounds.
Along the coast to Dunmore East, a gorgeous town of thatched cottages, secluded coves and buzzy food spots and places to have a pint. East Pier was set up by Elaine Power in 2019, who previously worked with Rick Stein in his Padstow restaurant.
A selection of the freshest fish including oysters, hake, lobster and prawns, as well as white fish caught close by for your classic fish and chips make this menu a fish lover’s dream, or nightmare, the choice a hellish conundrum. We narrowed it to crab brioche, scampi and fries and the most delicious fish tacos on a bed of corn and coriander salsa. With plenty of outdoor seating and some indoor, munch on your takeaway while quaffing a Rose or even a snipe of Moet. Chips and champagne, a classic combo.
Dunmore East Adventure centre is a must if travelling with kids, there is an inflatable aquapark (that they deflate and bring to shore each evening), kayaking, SUP as well as an excellent indoor adventure area including climbing wall, Ninja course, Laser challenge and archery which is perfect for grey, drizzly days.
One of their instructors, Andy took me on a tour of the coastline by kayak, while the kids were busy bouncing and sliding on the water. He told me a little of the history of the area, pointing out Hook lighthouse in neighbouring Wexford, and showing me Smugglers Cove, a charming swimming spot.
Back in Waterford city and a Viking virtual reality experience awaits that is as interesting for the adults as it is fun for the kids. Put on headsets and get transported to longships raiding monasteries and watch as Reginald, grandson of the legendary Ivar, returned to Waterford where he built a fort and became king in 917 AD. You also get to inhabit a recreated Viking hut, constructed just as it would have been, in the ruins of Baileys New Street’s ancient friary. Learn what it meant to be a Viking and how they cooked, kept warm, slept and passed the time over 1000 years ago.
Close by on Greyfriars Street in the heart of Waterford’s Viking Triangle, the Irish Museum of Time is housed within a restored Gothic-style church. A highlight of the trip and the real reason for visiting this time around is to see the recently opened Black Forest Cuckoo Clocks exhibition, which is believed to be among the finest collections in the world.
I’ve always been transfixed by the cuckoo clock; a great aunt had one when I was a child and I would impatiently wait for the clock to strike the hour and the little mechanical bird to appear, as if by magic.
This new gallery brings together hundreds of exceptional pieces, from miniature works to much larger pieces inspired by woodland scenes. Originating in southwest Germany, cuckoo clocks uniquely showcase a blend of craftsmanship, artistry and engineering. A standout feature is a rare century-old fairground organ that plays it’s tune as you sit listening in a mini theatre.
The museum also showcases the oldest Irish-made grandfather clocks, table clocks and watches, as well as featuring rare timepieces from across Europe and beyond, including Switzerland, England, Germany, France, Italy, Austria, the Netherlands, Russia and Japan.
Finish with lunch at Grow HQ, an award-winning café on the outskirts of town with an organic kitchen garden, farm shop, education centre and working farm. We enjoyed delicious salad and frittata as well as homemade ice cream, the perfect way to end a relaxed summer staycation.

title: How will Irish Rail keep trains running after firing company behind new signalling system?
description: Irish Rail, having fired Indra, wants to directly award contract to Siemens Mobility
content:
J ust after 8.30am on May 29th last, Irish Rail warned passengers via its social media channels they were going to face significant delays to train services across large parts of the network.
There was, the State-owned rail operator said, a “major signal fault across the suburban network”.
For about 30 minutes during the morning rush hour, rail services were suspended, affecting the Dart in Dublin as well the busy northern commuter line from Drogheda and trains using the Phoenix Park tunnel linking the city and west Dublin and Kildare, along with the Rosslare and Sligo routes. The disruption was caused by a fault at the Irish Rail control centre at Connolly Station in Dublin city.
The train network relies not just on tracks and carriages. Signalling is crucial to control the movements of trains carrying hundreds of passengers, particularly on the congested routes into Dublin city and on large portions of the network where there are only single tracks.
Irish Rail had been working on updating its system for controlling train movements for years as the existing system was considered to be on the brink of obsolescence.
Irish Rail chief executive Mary Considine told the Oireachtas Committee on Transport in June that the central traffic control technology in use at the facility at Connolly was “life-expired” and no longer supported by the developer.
The rail operator had been working on introducing a new traffic management system (TMS) that would integrate signals, communications and other systems on the railway network for more than a decade but the project experienced extensive delays.
The problems experienced on May 29th showed, albeit for 30 minutes – the disruption that could be caused by an ageing control system. Considine told the committee the planned new control system would not now be in place for the foreseeable future.
Irish Rail and the Department of Transport have interim plans to shore up the existing arrangements, particularly to cover the busy Greater Dublin Area in the absence of a complete new system.
[ Dispute over failed Irish Rail IT project could end up in court Opens in new window ]
Irish Rail insists safety is its priority. Considine said if serious control problems emerged, it would shut down parts of the network affected.
“There would be interruptions to services but safety would not be compromised,” she said.
Passengers would face potential significant disruptions, Paul Hendrick, director of capital investments at Irish Rail, told the committee. “If the system goes down, it will pose a challenge in terms of service levels. We may have to operate in a degraded mode. We would not be able to run our normal, full timetable. It is more of an operational impact on the services we offer to customers.”
Less than a fortnight before the system fault on May 29th, the long-running saga over the replacement control system essentially reached the end of the line. Twelve years earlier, Irish Rail had approved a €500,000 budget for a proposal to update its then central traffic control system. The IT project, known as a traffic management system (TMS) was to be a subset of a new overall national train control centre at Heuston Station, which was approved by the government in 2019.
The contract for the design, supply, installation and commissioning of the new system and control equipment was agreed with Spanish multinational IT company Indra Sistemas in 2020. The project was expected to cost €19.5 million including VAT, with a target that the new TMS would be commissioned by June 2024.
However, the project was beset by delays and cost overruns. The final straw for Irish Rail came in April when the company maintained the latest software delivered by Indra failed a number of key tests.
On May 6th, the board of Irish Rail wrote down by €50 million the value of its investment in the national train control centre, due to the problems with the TMS. On May 18th, the company sent its accounts for 2025 to Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien. A note in the accounts said Irish Rail, informed by the test results to date, “does not have confidence that the asset in the current state can be deployed for use on the network”.
Three days later The Irish Times revealed details of the €50 million writedown, leading to fury on the part of the Dáil Public Accounts Committee (PAC).
