It emerged that Indra had received about €28 million from Irish Rail for its work on the TMS. However, in addition the rail company had also spent about €20 million on third-party costs and other project supports, including a significant amount on external consultants.
The board of the National Transport Authority (NTA) – which provided the funding for the TMS – commissioned consultants EY to investigate what had gone wrong. Quickly it became clear that Irish Rail and Indra have different versions of the background to what PAC chairman John Brady of Sinn Féin described as a “ national scandal ”.
Considine told the Oireachtas Committee on Transport that six years after the contract was signed and two years after the original commissioning date for the TMS, “Indra still does not have a developed product fit for deployment on our rail network, and it remains in a product development cycle”.
[ Irish Rail fires IT firm behind much-delayed project and prepares to seek damages amid €50m writedown Opens in new window ]
The board of Irish Rail had been told by management that it could be the summer of next year before the first phase of the project – covering the Dublin-Rosslare line – would be introduced and that it could be well into the 2030s before the full system was operational.
Indra, for its part, has blamed Irish Rail for how it has handled the project.
In a lengthy statement to The Irish Times, it said Irish Rail had depended too heavily on external advisers, mainly from abroad.
Indra also said that critical knowledge about the unique characteristics and limitations of the Irish Rail network had neither been comprehensively documented nor systematically shared with the project team. It said key Irish Rail personnel who would use the planned system had not been actively involved in the project until its fifth year.
“Indra was required to design the solution without visibility of infrastructure behaviours that materially affected system performance,” it said.
Indra said it had made every effort to deliver the project.
“Irish Rail did not or was unable to collaborate on the implementation of the TMS in a way that would be considered standard for operators in other countries. For the first five years of the contract, the absence of effective sponsorship from Irish Rail coupled with its failure to appoint and empower suitably qualified internal technical experts to assume leadership of the project created a significant governance and oversight gap,” Indra said.
The statement came as The Irish Times was about to reveal that the board of Irish Rail had fired Indra.
In late June, following a meeting of its board, Irish Rail management wrote to the NTA seeking approval to end the contract with Indra. This was accepted by the NTA on July 13th and within a few days the rail operator told Indra it was invoking provisions in the contract to terminate the arrangement “for convenience”.
However, Irish Rail has also been working on plans to sue Indra, leaving open the prospect or likelihood that the dispute over the TMS will end up in the courts.
With the Indra software now seemingly off the pitch, there is a growing focus on what should happen next. Irish Rail, the NTA and politicians all agree that a new control system is needed.
The NTA told the PAC that €20 million over three years may have to be spent to shore up the existing control systems in Dublin. This will be in addition to the €50 million writedown on the TMS system that Indra was to have delivered.
“As a result of delays in the delivery of the TMS, the Minister for Transport has approved additional signalling works ... this year that will deliver additional signalling resilience on the busiest parts of the network around the Greater Dublin Area and mitigate the risk of a big failure of the existing central traffic control system at Connolly Station. An additional benefit of this investment is that it will ensure that envisaged future Dart+ services will be able to come on-stream in the coming years regardless of the delayed delivery of the TMS,” the NTA said.
“These resilience works envisage reducing the load of the current train control centre system by migrating a number of ‘desks’ controlling parts of the network on to an alternative control system in the National Train Control Centre [the new facility at Heuston Station]. This will provide the additional control capacity needed for those particular parts of the network.
“Expenditure on these resilience works is estimated at €5.7 million in 2026, €9.8 million in 2027 and €4.3 million in 2028,” the NTA said.
The NTA also warned of other potential costs, particularly in relation to planned developments in Cork.
[ Spending on rail expansion plans could be hit by costs of failed €50m IT project Opens in new window ]
“The current planned date for commissioning the new signalling system in Cork is August 2027. In advance of this signalling system being commissioned, it will be necessary to have developed a suitable TMS for the signalling to feed into. If there is a delay to the commissioning date for the Cork signalling system, this could lead to additional costs on the project including contractor delay claims and internal and external project management of up to €800,000 per month,” the NTA told the PAC.
In parallel with terminating Indra’s contract, Irish Rail decided to look to another company, Siemens Mobility, to deliver a control system. But this needed the backing of the NTA.
Irish Rail told the NTA it wanted to publish what is known as a voluntary ex-ante transparency (VEAT) notice to the market. This would set out its plans to award a direct contract to Siemens Mobility to deliver its system, known as Westcad, across its network without going through a procurement competition.
The timing of NTA approval was important for Irish Rail’s strategy, in particular for dealing with Indra.
There would be a 30-day window for any challenge to the VEAT notice. The company wanted to have this out of the way before it proceeded to issue a default notice regarding Indra’s performance. Irish Rail believed this had to be done by the middle of October.
However, the NTA initially sought more information and then in July rejected the application by Irish Rail to publish the VEAT at that time. In August there was more correspondence between Irish Rail and the NTA.
The NTA wanted more details surrounding Irish Rail’s plans. The rail operator was increasingly concerned that any breach-of-contract case against Indra had to be issued by October 15th. It was worried that Indra could challenge the VEAT notice about the contract to Siemens.
Irish Rail considered it was essential the VEAT notice be issued by the first week in September to allow it to initiate its action against Indra in mid-October.
In a statement this week, the NTA said Irish Rail had submitted an approval request in relation to proposed delivery arrangements for an alternative train control system.
“This is currently the subject of engagement between Irish Rail and the NTA and involves a legal assessment of the procurement proposals. That process is ongoing.”
While the forthcoming EY report is expected to deal with what happened in the past about the TMS project, in Leinster House there are concerns also about the future.
The chairman of the Oireachtas transport committee, Michael Murphy of Fine Gael, said Ireland needs a modern, reliable TMS.
“Urgency cannot become an excuse for simply moving on without establishing what went wrong. Approximately €50 million has already been written down on a system that was not delivered. We need to understand when it became clear the project was in serious difficulty, why expenditure continued despite repeated missed deadlines, and what lessons have been learned,” Murphy said.
“My concern is that the failure of the previous TMS project cannot now be allowed to create a further bottleneck for the wider rail investment programme. I want clarity from Irish Rail and the NTA on what impact the failure and subsequent delays could have on Dart+ and other planned investments, and what measures are being taken to ensure those projects remain on track.”

title: The best places to view the night sky in Ireland
description: With three DarkSky International-accredited areas on the island, astro-tourism is on the rise
content:
Oscar Wilde once mused that everyone was in the gutter, but the lucky among us had our gaze fixed firmly on the stars. And as an Irishman, the witty scribe knew a thing or two about the magnificence of our skyscape.
In fact, our Stone Age masterpiece, Newgrange, whose passage and chamber are aligned with the rising sun around the winter solstice, is one of many reminders that the Irish people have long maintained strong celestial connections.
Today, the island of Ireland holds a trio of DarkSky International accreditations: Kerry International Dark Sky Reserve, Mayo Dark Sky Park and Tyrone’s OM Dark Sky Park and Observatory. This coveted status, which recognises the absence of light pollution in their night skies, was achieved through years of careful monitoring.
To the delight of rural communities, Ireland’s astro-tourism is seeing a surge in interest, not only at these three locations but also in remote spots across the island, especially between September and April when nights are longest and darkest. As a bonus, our northerly position means that during periods of strong solar activity, stargazers might even glimpse the aurora borealis.
“Plan your observing session because knowing which planets, meteor showers or nebulae are visible is key,” Caoimhe Lyons from Blackrock Castle Observatory suggests. She also recommends finding out “what the moon is up to”, as its light can obstruct your view of the stars and other objects in the sky.
“Software like Stellarium is brilliant for mapping what will be in the sky,” Caoimhe adds. “Binoculars and small telescopes can go a long way if you get your timing right. Also, being somewhere elevated or on a beach means it’s less likely that trees, buildings or other structures will obstruct your view.”
Whether you’re an expert stargazer or a novice, or are simply drawn to these sanctuaries of tranquillity to escape the chaos of modern life, this guide offers insights into the best places to witness the wonders overhead.
And despite Mr Wilde’s claims, none of them involves any gutters.
In 2014, South Kerry became the first place in the Northern Hemisphere to be designated a Gold Tier International Dark Sky Reserve. In addition to a coastline of cliffs, coves and beaches, the reserve extends inland to Ballaghisheen, with many archaeological sites scattered across the landscape. Standing alongside a Neolithic or Bronze Age site on a starry night offers the perfect way to connect with our ancestors.
Constellations closest to the Pole Star, such as Ursa Major and its well-known asterism, the Plough, are visible all year round here. Orion, the iconic constellation, is visible from late September to April, and in the summer, the Milky Way dazzles.
Kerry Dark Sky Tourism participates in several events throughout the year, including the Skellig Coast Archaeology Festival in October and Heritage Week in August. kerrydarkskytourism.com
Local intel: “The Kerry Dark Sky Reserve feels far from a city and closer to the stars,” says archaeologist Aoibheann Lambe, co-owner of Kerry Dark Sky Tourism, which offers stargazers immersive astronomy and heritage experiences.
“It reminds us that we are tiny and part of something greater than ourselves. We are, after all, made of stardust. The dark skies connect us to everyone, past and present, who has ever looked up.”
Where to stay: The historic Royal Valentia hotel is a convenient base. Their Dark Skies Package runs on selected dates from October to March. royalvalentia.ie
Where to eat: For over 60 years, Waterville’s family-run Lobster Restaurant and Bar has been impressing travellers on the Ring of Kerry with award-winning seafood. thelobsterwaterville.com
By day: Located on Valentia Island, the Skellig Experience Visitor Centre is dedicated to the Unesco World Heritage Site of Skellig Michael. Alongside boat tours (weather permitting), the centre brings the magic and mystery of these famous rocks to life through film presentations, reconstructions and soundscapes. skelligexperience.com
As the sun fades, Wild Nephin National Park transforms into Mayo Dark Sky Park, where views of the Milky Way, meteor showers, planets, stars and, on occasion, the aurora borealis await. The site, named International Dark Sky Place of the Year in 2024, is free to access at any time. There are also exhibits to admire at the Ballycroy Visitor Centre.
Wild Nephin National Park is twinned with Yosemite National Park, and they have extended this connection to protect their nocturnal nightscapes and biodiversity under the tagline, ‘Two parks, one sky’.
At different times throughout the year, the park hosts free events, including weekly walks. The annual Mayo Dark Sky Festival is soon to celebrate its tenth anniversary, with an exciting programme of events running on October 30th and November 1st. Other meteor showers include the Geminids in December and the Lyrids in April. mayodarkskypark.ie
Local intel: “Mayo is working towards becoming an International Dark Sky Reserve, which will encompass the whole county, further protecting the dark sky park as its core and darkest centre,” says Georgia MacMillan, Mayo Dark Sky Park development officer.
“The future reserve will provide further access to peripheral sites across the county, including the north coast of Mayo for the aurora views, and island communities such as Inishturk at the edge of the Atlantic.”
2. Claggan Mountain Coastal Trail car park
A short drive from Ballycroy Visitor Centre is the four-star Mulranny Park Hotel, a firm favourite with locals and tourists alike, thanks in part to its majestic views of Clew Bay. mulrannyparkhotel.ie
Where to eat: Ginger and Wild is a light and airy café next to the Ballycroy Visitor Centre. The homemade food is crafted from locally sourced produce and its gallery showcases Irish artwork. gingerandwild.com
By day: The Céide Fields Neolithic Site contains the world’s oldest known stone-walled fields, dating back nearly 6,000 years.
OM Dark Sky Park and Observatory, the only one of its kind in Northern Ireland, is a truly special destination for stargazers. Its name honours the sound of the universe while also referencing Ogham, our ancient alphabet, both of which perfectly encapsulate a visit here; connections to our past and present abound.
OM organises events all year round, depending on what the night sky reveals. They offer hands-on telescope sessions as well as naked-eye observing.
Local intel: “We have a range of night-time experiences available to book if you would like to join us on one of our night-time adventures,” says Roisín Doyle, duty manager at OM Dark Sky Park and Observatory. “From the darker nights to the brighter days, our skies are always offering us something special to see.”
1. The on-site Ceoldán — an enormous statue imbued with celestial and mythical symbolism
2. The park has viewing platforms near the building with special red lighting
Where to stay: Ardtara Country House, a member of the prestigious Bluebook collection, is a 30-minute drive from the park in neighbouring Derry. ardtara.com
Where to eat: OM has an on-site grab-and-go café serving hot and cold drinks and snacks. For something more substantial, try Millwheel Bar & Restaurant in nearby Dunamore.
By day: The Sperrin Mountains, particularly Davagh Forest, teem with surviving megalithic monuments, including the incredible Beaghmore Stone Circles, comprising seven mystical circles, 10 rows of stones and 12 cairns, all carefully arranged.
It may be known as the Forgotten County, but a stargazing experience in Donegal will surely be remembered long after your stay, thanks to its remote northwestern location, which brings clear skies and low light pollution. For those interested in the Northern Lights, winter and spring offer the best chance of seeing them. govisitdonegal.com
Local intel: “When the aurora borealis is visible, the best place on the entire island to witness the phenomenon is undoubtedly Malin Head in Inishowen, Ireland’s most northerly point,” Shane Smyth from Donegal Tourism explains.
“However, in more recent displays, it has been visible in many parts of the county and as far south as Sliabh Liag, Ballyshannon and Bundoran.”
Where to stay: The four-star Redcastle Hotel stands sentinel on the rugged Inishowen Peninsula. On-site leisure facilities include a swimming pool, gym, spa and a nine-hole parkland golf course. redcastlehoteldonegal.com
Where to eat: Seaview Tavern is a firm favourite on Malin Head. The seafood is sourced from the local pier and from nearby Greencastle Harbour, while Ronald Boggs, a butcher in the town, supplies the meat. seaviewtavern.ie
By day: Rising 600m above the waves, Sliabh Liag is one of Europe’s highest sea cliffs and served as a Christian pilgrimage site for over 1,000 years.
With its limestone terrain, Co Clare’s Burren National Park is undoubtedly one of Europe’s most unique regions, and it also makes a perfect base for stargazing. In addition to its remote location, the rocky, expansive landscape contrasts beautifully with the sparkling skies, making it popular with photography enthusiasts. burren.ie
Local intel: “The Burren is home to some of Ireland’s darkest and most pristine skies,” says Niamh Farren of the National Parks and Wildlife Service, which, together with its partners, including Clare County Council, is committed to keeping the skies above the Burren naturally dark for present and future generations to enjoy.
“Generally, the best viewpoints are at altitude, in areas free from or with little light pollution, and with good views of the southern sky.”
Where to stay: The four-star Doolin Inn blends the relaxed charm of a country house with the professional service of a hotel. The property’s staff are happy to share their knowledge of stargazing and other local experiences. doolininn.ie
Where to eat: Housed in a charming Victorian property, The Wild Honey Inn is Ireland’s only Michelin-starred pub, specialising in bistro-style cooking with a twist. wildhoneyinn.com
By day: After admiring the dark skies, turn your attention underground to Doolin Cave, home to the Great Stalactite, one of the world’s longest known free-hanging stalactites.
The many writers, poets and artists who have found inspiration here all agree that Connemara has something otherworldly about it. Maybe it’s the deep connections with the Irish language and culture. Or perhaps it’s the unique landscape that unfolds towards the dramatic coastline.
Whatever the reason, this undefinable energy enhances every stargazing experience. With its long, crisp nights, November to April is the best time to visit, and if the gods are on your side, you could spot shooting stars and even the northern lights. connemara.ie
Local intel: “I’m incredibly fortunate to call Connemara home, as it’s one of the best places to experience the magic of the night sky,” says TG4’s long-serving weather presenter Fiona Ní Fhlaithearta.
“What’s more, the vast open horizons, framed by mountains, lakes and the rugged Atlantic landscape, create the perfect setting for creative photography.”
1. Connemara National Park (Diamond Hill)
Where to stay: The Connemara Coast Hotel is located at the gateway to Connemara, where the dark skies can be admired from the grounds. connemaracoasthotel.ie
Where to eat: Perched in the heart of the Ceardlann Craft Village, Spiddal’s Builín Blasta is many things at once — a café, bakery, gourmet grocer and takeaway. The queues outside at lunchtime attest to its enduring popularity. builinblasta.com
Nearby is the famous Standún Department Store, which serves hot refreshments and cakes in its café. standun.com
By day: Killary Fjord is the only one of its kind on the island. Killary Fjord Boat Tours offer a 90-minute trip departing from Leenane, with uninterrupted views of the spectacular scenery. killaryfjord.ie
Co Cork holds a special place in the hearts of astronomy enthusiasts interested in the planets, stars, the wider universe and space exploration. The region is home to many sites dedicated to or inspired by its dark skies. These include Blackrock Castle Observatory and the Wild Sky Dome in the Mealagh Valley, Europe’s first dark-sky-approved lodging. Elsewhere, at the Liss Ard Estate, is the Irish Sky Garden, created by the renowned American artist James Turrell.
Local intel: “While there are a few sites relatively close to Cork City, such as Rockey Bay, Nohoval Cove and Corrin Wood, for really dark skies you need to travel further from the city,” says Declan Foley, secretary of Cork Astronomy Club, which is set to celebrate its golden anniversary.
“The ideal places are by the coast, with any light pollution behind you. Looking out over the sea gives you a great southeasterly, southerly and southwesterly horizon.”
Where to stay: Esk Mountain, a 270-acre nature restoration project near Glengarriff, offers unique studio apartments that blend indoor and outdoor living. eskmountain.com
Where to eat: The delightfully named Fishy Fishy Restaurant in Kinsale is an award-winning restaurant run by the husband-and-wife team Martin and Marie Shanahan. The kitchen follows an ethos of cooking local, fresh and seasonal fish, served in an informal setting. fishyfishy.ie
By day: While Gougane Barra is another favourite spot for stargazers, the glaciated mountain valley — home to the oft-photographed St Finbarr’s Oratory — is also popular with hikers.
Despite its proximity to Dublin, the Royal County of Meath offers some of the darkest skies in eastern Ireland, blending peaceful rural landscapes with Brú na Boinne’s ancient monuments, which have been linked to the night sky for millennia.
On the outskirts of Oldcastle, the mighty Loughcrew Cairns are widely regarded as the county’s best stargazing spot. At over 5,000 years old, Loughcrew is a focal point for visitors during the spring and autumn equinoxes, when the rising sun illuminates the inner chamber of the Cairn T passage tomb. Stargazers also plan their trips around meteor showers in August, October and December. discoverboynevalley.ie
Local intel : “Sitting atop the county’s highest point, Loughcrew offers panoramic views, dark skies and a unique connection to Ireland’s ancient astronomical heritage,” says Sarah Farrell from Loughcrew Cairns Megalithic Centre.
4. Rathbeggan Lakes (a popular spot for the Meath Astronomy Group)
Where to stay: Open seasonally from March to October, Loughcrew Megalithic Centre invites visitors to bring their own campervan or tent, or to opt for glamping in one of the cosy yurt. loughcrewmegalithiccentre.com
Where to eat: Nelly’s Café is the on-site tea rooms at the Loughcrew Megalithic Centre. It is open daily from 11am, serving a range of beverages alongside homemade cakes and treats.
By day: Every stargazer visiting Meath should arrange a trip to the world-famous Neolithic monument of Newgrange, which, among other purposes, served as a scientific instrument, recording the solar year. It’s also an early example of a sundial and a calendar. The nearby sites of Knowth and Dowth are also worth a visit.
Birr Castle is home to the Great Telescope, once the world’s largest, which helped reveal the spiral nature of galaxies. Designed and built in the 1840s by the Third Earl of Rosse, the 72-foot-long feat of engineering drew visitors from around the world to observe the stars.
Today, the Great Telescope sits at the heart of the castle’s demesne, while the Historic Science Centre demonstrates how the extraordinary telescope was constructed. birrcastle.com
Dublin’s Dunsink Observatory has been a centre for astronomical research since 1785 and has been associated with many of our most renowned scientists, including Sir William Rowan Hamilton. The historic facility is open to the public for select, family-friendly events throughout the year, particularly during winter. dunsinkdias.ie
Armagh Observatory and Planetarium is a leading centre for astronomical research and education. Its extensive grounds, which include Astro Park, offer opportunities to get closer to nature and space.
In the Planetarium’s dome theatre, visitors can explore the night sky, while the exhibition area celebrates the region’s rich celestial heritage. Ireland’s largest meteorite is also here. Elsewhere, the observatory features several historic telescopes and, although an active research facility, is open to the public for limited, scheduled tours. armagh.space
On the outskirts of Cork stands the 16th-century Blackrock Castle. Its original role as a watchtower has evolved into a place for observing the wonders overhead, and it also serves as a science centre featuring the new Ireland in Space exhibit.
In the working observatory, a team from the Munster Technological University searches for new planets around distant stars using telescopes both within the castle and abroad. A ‘behind the scenes’ guided tour brings the past, present, and future together.
2. Phone, camera, tripod and portable charger
3. Red torch light (helps you see in the dark without spoiling night vision)
4. Charts, maps and apps like Stellarium, SkySafari and Mobile Observatory
5. Warm clothing, including a hat, thick socks, fingerless gloves and good, old-fashioned long johns
7. Snacks and thermos with hot beverages
3. High humidity or sharp temperature changes can scatter light and affect how crisp your view of the sky is
4. There are plenty of websites that provide detailed weather forecasts for stargazers. For casual observers, something like AccuWeather is simple and reliable.

title: God’s own dining spots
description: From train carriages to country estates, we take a look at some of the Irish dining spots worthy of a celestial visit. Words by Mimi Murray, Deanna O’Connor and Marcus O’Laoire
author_name: Mimi Murray, Deanna O'Connor, Marcus O’Laoire
content:
First up on God’s food trail is recently opened Ómós in Abbeyleix, a visionary concept by chef Cuan Greene, formerly of Noma in Copenhagen and Bastible in Dublin. The fine dining restaurant is just part of the overall experience at this restored Victorian estate, its neutral tones, stone and wooden interiors a lesson in relaxed refinement.
It’s hard to believe this estate had fallen into ruin before it was bought by Irish tech billionaire John Collison in 2022. He and a handful of other investors have allowed Greene the time, creative space and money to pull together a unique addition to the Irish travel and food scene.
The 13-course tasting menu with wine pairing, or a thoughtful non-alcoholic option, is a joy from start to finish. Its summer menu begins with tomato pie, topped with anchovy brought to the table by one of a large team quietly working away in an open-plan kitchen that exudes calm. No thrown pots or kitchen hysterics here, just a love for the produce and in creating an exceptional meal for guests.
Dishes include dry-aged hamachi with rhubarb dressing and magnolia condiment, an Irish summer salad (reimagined rolled ham and egg) line caught fish as well as a snail dumpling that evokes more nostalgia by way of old school chicken Kiev that arrive one after another. Tables at Ómós are mainly held for residents, but some are made available to those not staying. — MM
Look out onto the empyrean sight of Douglas Firs, Corsican Pines, Giant Redwoods and Atlantic Cedars from your table at Sika restaurant in Powerscourt estate. The eight-course tasting menu is thoughtfully compiled by executive chef Cormac McCreary and each new course is a triumph. Start with canapés that comprise tuna tartar with ponzo, Coolattin cheddar gougère, brioche feuilleté and Guinness and treacle bread paired with a glass of Perrier-Jouët Grand Brut NV. An assortment of tastes bursting with flavour, this is an exciting start to an exceptional meal. Next tuck into foie gras parfait with peach, native lobster, tomato and parmesan followed by sole Viennoise, broccoli, sudachi and smoked Dashi Sauce, an elegant dish excellently paired with a Trimbach Riesling. Things switch up a gear with the final savoury course and Wicklow lamb with Baba Ganoush, Romesco and Polenta. — MM
Kick off eight divine courses with nibbles and a glass of Billecart Salmon aboard The Pullman restaurant which is presided over by head chef Angelo Vagiotis. Stunningly located aboard two decommissioned Orient Express carriages on the grounds of Glenlo Abbey and overlooking magical Lough Corrib, Vagiotis’ ethos is to be ever-changing with the seasons. This Michelin-star meal starts with cheese puffs (hastily eaten in one bite), Flaggy shore oysters and Guinness bread, deftly followed by Bonito, topped with caper and raisin, hazelnut and cucumber. The bouquet salad, a signature dish and on the menu since day one is an example of the best use of seasonal ingredients from farm and garden. Fragrant, simple and delicious. A tomato consommé with pea ravioli, red prawn and lovage is followed by Atlantic perch, a new dish that got its first outing the evening we visited. Paimpol beans, the most delicate baby octopus and Luciana top the fish, which is expertly paired with a Spanish Albarino. Service and atmosphere is as good as how I imagine it aboard the Venice Simplon Orient Express and if that is on your bucket list, like mine, The Pullman isn’t to be missed. — MM
Head out around the Slea Head drive and just after the wholesome frolics of the Hold a Baby Lamb (does it get more Godlike?) experience, you will find Éalú at The Stonehouse. On a sunny day there is nowhere finer to sit outside admiring the glistening majesty of the Atlantic spread out before you, with a glass of bubbles expertly chosen by wine buff Clíona Moriarty. With her chef husband Kallam, they took the lease on the restaurant in this unusual stone building and turned what could have been a very standard tour bus café stop-off into one of the Dingle Peninsula’s must-visit foodie destinations. Try some sharing plates of baked Cavanbert or some juicy Nocellara olives, pick a small plate like a lobster bisque, or go for a more substantial elevated take on a seafood chowder. But make sure to leave room for dessert. Kallam’s patisserie skills are of a level rarely seen outside Paris. — DO’C
The ethereal magic or Ard na Sidhe hits you full force as you pull into the driveway and the vista of Caragh Lake down below takes your breath away. The old house, all stone, sits unobtrusively, complementing its surroundings. It still has the feel of an exquisite country home, rather than a hotel. The welcome is warm, and whether you come for the famed afternoon tea or stay on for dinner, you are guaranteed to feel entranced. On the menu is fine dining paired with a surprisingly reasonably priced wine list. The pan-fried duck breast with cherries and smoked beetroot is a standout flavour combination, while the excellent hake served with a courgette and parmesan puree, mussels and spicy chorizo is another delight. After a bottle of Gruner Veltliner with our meal, very generous serves of Sauternes dessert wine sent us off to enjoy the cosy lounge with a very warm glow. — DO’C
Mara is somewhere to contemplate, be mindful. The tiny restaurant with just six tables is a far cry from the site’s original incarnation – vegetarian café Haricots. Today, the experience is elevated but relaxed – you can choose between a la carte and an 11-course tasting menu (pre-booking essential). The menu changes seasonally but is inspired by chef Luis Martin’s Spanish roots, paired with the best of local produce, with an emphasis on local organic and foraged ingredients. The highlight for me perhaps was the appearance of padrón peppers as a side to my steak – to my mind a perfect pairing. Gaston, front-of-house, is on hand to advise on perfect wine pairings, with lots of vegan and biodynamic options. — DO’C
An open crab Sandwich in O’Sullivan’s on a sunny July day is a simple but sublime experience.
The crab itself, simply bound, dressed and allowed to sing sweetly and delicately, is the stuff of legend, both local and further afield. But it’s the setting that makes this a one-of-a-kind place to eat and a must on God’s foodie road trip. In a world of complicated dinners, this is on my list for its simplicity, for the way the sea breeze acts as a seasoning and the sound of herring gulls and kittiwakes lapping over waters providing a celestial soundtrack to the food. — M’OL
There is a very understated decadence to the upstairs dining room in Mamó. It’s not just to be found in the walls, fine stemmed glasses or the tablecloths, the true pleasure of the room comes from a deep generosity on the pass and the plate. Allow your palette to be kicked into gear by a Buffalo Ray wing and a signature cod chip - one sharp with cayenne-spiked vinegar against a soft nugget of ray wing meat, the other a masterclass in coaxing nostalgic magic from a spud. Two bites that will stay wedged in your hippocampus for a long time to come. If you’re lucky, and the boats have come in, you may be treated to a whole Turbot to share, and if you’re enjoying it as part of a Sunday lunch, there may be a moment where the sun shines in and casts a halo in the slick, sticky, collagen-rich jus around the fish, blurring the lines between heaven and earth in a single bite. — M’OL
Being able to see the water from which your Kenmare Bay pot prawns were plucked a few hours earlier is a glorious thing, and The Landline at the Park Hotel, headed by chef James O’Sullivan, is a sublime restaurant. Kerry is a place of otherworldly natural beauty, with produce to match. Mountain lamb, incredible seafood and a million other ingredients make this one of the most special places to dine in Ireland for me. The food itself is considered, fresh and delicious, hyper-local in a way that doesn’t feel like a box-ticking exercise, cooked with a level of confidence that’s rare and exciting to see. Eating in the Landline, looking out at the clouds rolling over the infinite shades of brown and green in the hills leading down to water gives a context to what’s on the plate in a way that feels like a full-circle moment. What you’re eating in the Landline is Kerry itself, and it’s never been better. — M’OL

title: Dublin’s history: from the great Liberties whiskey fire to the remarkable story of Neary’s pub
description: Also reviewed: histories of the Navan Road, Milltown, Dalkey, Mount Jerome Cemetery and industry
content:
As a teenager in the late 1980s Louise East got to know Dublin by osmosis, walking around the capital for hours, becoming familiar with the streets, squares and general shabbiness of the city. On Dublin: Reflections on the Irish Capital (The Little Museum of Dublin, €24.99), with photographs by the American Deanne Fitzmaurice, is an extended essay that captures the genius loci.
East, who refers to herself as a “lapsed insider”, now lives in Berlin. More than three decades on, she looks back at the city she knew well, whether walking or cycling around, and switches her focus to the present by talking to strangers. Once you know where to look, she writes, evidence of the city’s watery past is everywhere. The intangible changes, she decides, are a great deal more positive, “not least the long-overdue pivot away from a civil discourse and moral code dictated by the Catholic Church in lockstep with the Irish State”.
The text is accompanied by striking colour photographs reflecting the reshaped skyline filled with cranes, as well as gatherings at ukulele and trad sessions, Smithfield Horse Fair and Moore Street market. Portraits include Alice Leahy, who set up a trust in the Liberties, tour guide Emma Moohan, the former senator and scholar David Norris and actor Ronan Wilmot.
One of the main Dublin arteries, the Navan Road – initially part of the townland of Greater Cabragh – is the subject of an in-depth exploration that includes not just its built heritage and boundaries but numerous other subjects. Navan Road: An Illustrated History 1700-1960 (Eastwood, €25) by Enda Finnan, comprehensively traces the social and economic history of the suburb, which reflects Ireland’s wider journey.
When turnpike trusts were set up, they were financed by charges, and in 1729 the first toll was established for the Dublin to Navan road, although at this point the modern Navan Road had yet to be built.
During the 19th and 20th centuries the development of the road was vital to the cattle trade. The Prussia Street cattle market – a mile to the east – which ran from 1863 to 1973, was central to the economy. This was reflected in a description by a former cattle-market sales master, Joe Barry, who referred to Ireland in that era as being “little more than one large cattle ranch”.
The path of transformation of the Greater Cabragh townland into the suburban parish of Navan Road took place during the middle decades of the 20th century.
The process began in 1935, when new roads were laid out with a St Patrick-themed run of streets, a customary practice in post-independence Ireland. The book ends in 1960, at which point transport connections, residential housing and local amenities were well developed. The suburb was booming, and although it still retained an enduring rural element, prices for a “Superior House” at Kinvara Avenue started from £1,680.
In The Greens of Medieval Dublin: A History of the Rights of Commons (Liffey Press, €24.95), Michael Cregan delves into the story of five principal medieval greens that have received little attention from historians. They are: St Stephen’s Green, Hoggen (College) Green, The Steine, Abbey Green and Oxmantown Green, as well as Fair Green adjoining Dublin Castle and Kilmainham.
Their primary use was for grazing draft animals, but they were also places of recreation, celebration and military training. Population growth and changes in agricultural practices led to their demise by the beginning of the 19th century, and the loss of greens meant the city was seriously lacking in open spaces. Today there is an awareness that carefully planned public areas contribute to the attractiveness of cities, and the author suggests that the city’s greens may have been ahead of the times by offering a variety of overlapping functions.
Dublin’s Latin Quarter: A History and Guidebook (Mountjoy Publishing, €25) by Brendan Lynch researches the cultural history, geography and stories of those who lived and worked in this south Georgian enclave. The area runs along an axis from Pembroke Road and Upper Baggot Street to St Stephen’s Green, and west along the Grand Canal to Leeson Street Bridge.
Eighty brief biographies include, among others, the writers Samuel Beckett and Elizabeth Bowen, artists Francis Bacon, Roderic O’Conor and Mainie Jellett, and composers Charles Villiers Stanford and Michael Larchet. The guide pays overdue tribute to the intrepid women artists who left to study in Paris in the early 1900s.
Dublin’s Latin Quarter may not have had the same illustrious and bohemian pedigree as its Parisian namesake, but it was unquestionably a vibrant place brimming with artistic energy and creative inspiration.
The final resting place for many prominent Dublin citizens is the focus of Mount Jerome: Dublin’s Victorian Cemetery (The Old Dublin Press, €24.95) by Maurice Curtis. Eleven chapters consider the cemetery’s early history and walks within the grounds. The cemetery, at Harold’s Cross, is divided into old and new parts. The old part, surrounding a Gothic-style Victorian Chapel, is lined with rows of impressively decorated tombstones, temples, monuments and mausoleums, a hallmark of the affluent and influential Anglo-Irish gentry, as well as the merchant classes.
Notable burials include the novelist William Carleton, Sir Richard John Griffith, author of Griffith’s Valuation, the brewer and philanthropist Benjamin Lee Guinness, journalist and poet Susan Mitchell, writer and activist Charlotte Stoker, and the renowned former Irish Times editor R M “Bertie” Smyllie.
Killester: From medieval manor to garden suburb (Four Courts, €17.95) by Joseph Brady and Ruth McManus describes the development of the northside suburb. Its history stretches from the early days as Killester Demesne – with a watercolour of the mansion house by Harold Leask – through its 20th-century evolution as a garden suburb for ex-servicemen up to the emergence of today’s community.
On the other side of the city, Dalkey: An Illustrated History (Eastwood, €20) by John Martin explores the area from the earliest settlement about 5,000 BC to the present. Urban development during the 19th and 20th centuries considers housing, transport and services with charts, maps, engravings and photographs.
Pen pictures in two final chapters appraise people who helped shape the development of Dalkey, while the other focuses on notable residents. These include Maeve Binchy, Hugh Leonard, Lennox Robinson and Frank O’Flanagan, the self-styled “Recorder of Dalkey” who lived on Sorrento Road and whose passion was the promotion of the town and preservation of its heritage.
Tallaght: A History of its Nobility and Gentry (Tallaght Free Press, €15) by Éamonn Maloney delves into the lives of landowners in the Parish of Tallaght throughout the centuries. Profiles are presented of those who gained ownership through a variety of ways such as Grierson, Lentaigne, Luttrell and Wharton.
Dr Evory Kennedy was one of the most eminent medical men in 19th-century Ireland and established his Co Dublin residence at Belgard Castle in 1853. He presided at the coroner inquest in Tallaght Courthouse into the death of Stephen O’Donohoe, who was killed at the Battle of Tallaght in 1867. On leaving the courthouse, Dr Kennedy gave O’Donohoe’s widow a financial contribution towards her husband’s funeral. Poems and songs were written in memory of O’Donohoe, including Song of Tallaght.
Ghosts of Old Dún Laoghaire (Eblana Forum, €20) by Breasal Ó Caollai focuses on the 200-year-old history of the Eblana Lodge, alongside aspects of local life. The Eblana Club, a place where people of all religions and none socialised together, is today the centre of local community activities. Stories of important historic events are included, such as the sinking of the Holyhead mailboat Leinster in October 1918 at the end of the first World War.
In July 1898 the first wireless radio broadcast of a sporting event was made from Dún Laoghaire. The Italian radio engineer Guglielmo Marconi sent telegraphed reports from the Kingstown Regatta. His invention also improved sea safety and rescue. One of the town’s most famous sons was Ronnie Drew of the Dubliners, who died in 2008. Locals have campaigned for a lasting memorial to him but the author states that their efforts have been “constantly ignored”.
Milltown: A History (Eastwood Books, €45) by David Costello is a large-scale study of the suburb, although the author states frankly that not everyone knows where Milltown is. He helpfully pins it down as straddling the river Dodder in the modern postal districts of Dublin 6 and Dublin 14, falling under the jurisdiction of Dublin City Council and Dún-Laoghaire Rathdown County Council.
The book spans 4,000 years of social, economic, political and military history. The impact of the Famine, the Fenian Rising, the first World War and the War of Independence is analysed. The book also recovers the stories of an old village community. The volume is lavishly illustrated with maps, plates and photographs and is particularly strong on the history of Milltown House, a mid-18th century villa of high-quality craftsmanship.
Under the Rainbow: Observations and recollections of Skerries and other places (Monument Media, €15.95) by Hugh Fitzgerald Ryan brings together more than 100 short pieces drawing on eight decades of the author’s memories of growing up, getting married and raising a family in Skerries. There are recollections of wider events and news stories as well as opinions on books and films. The full text is available at the author’s blog: hfryan.wordpress.com .
The Great Liberties Whiskey Fire (Eastwood Books, €12.99) by Las Fallon is a detailed account of a fire in 1875 that broke out in a whiskey warehouse in the Liberties. The blaze quickly escalated as barrels of whiskey ignited, sending rivers of burning alcohol through the streets and posing a serious challenge to firefighters. The author is a veteran of the Dublin Fire Brigade and has researched this story, bringing to life a little-known historical event and combining it with an understanding of the legacy.
In A Little History of Neary’s (The Little Museum of Dublin, €9.99) Daryl Hendley Rooney uncovers the remarkable story of one of the city’s best-known pubs. Since 1887 Neary’s on Chatham Street has been a mainstay of cultural and convivial social life. Its diverse clientele has included balladeers, thespians, writers, office workers, street traders and tourists.
The bar’s facade is inspired by architectural design elements ranging from Romanesque to red brick. At the front door two elegantly crafted iron lamp brackets are designed as a pair of human arms grasping glazed lanterns emblazoned with the pub’s name – beacons of light that, according to the author, “have guided generations of visitors to a place of warmth and hospitality”.
Dublin’s Industrial Heritage: From Sandymount Strand to Crumlin Road (Wordwell, €17.99) by Rob Goodbody is the first in a three-volume series of illustrated books. This one covers a specific geographical area of southeast Dublin, exploring the transformed south Docklands and sites along the Dodder, the Poddle and Grand Canal, as well as locations in the south city centre. Among the topics discussed are mines and quarries, land reclamation, watermills and windmills, light and heavy industry, transport, communication, military installations and utilities. The next two volumes will consider southwest Dublin and north Dublin city and suburbs.

title: Taoiseach to become first foreign leader to visit UK prime minister Burnham at No 10 North
description: Irish-UK relations and post-Brexit reset to be on agenda for first meeting in Manchester
content:
Taoiseach Micheál Martin will become the first foreign leader to visit No 10 North when he attends a bilateral meeting with UK prime minister Andy Burnham .
One of Burnham’s first acts as prime minister was to establish an office in Manchester as a counterbalance to No 10 Downing Street in London .
Burnham said he wants to rebalance power and control in the country and having a prime ministerial office in Manchester is part of that change.
Friday’s meeting will be the first between the Taoiseach and UK prime minister since Burnham took office in July. They have met previously when Burnham was mayor of Manchester.
There will be a private tête-à-tête between the pair and then a wider bilateral with officials.
The agenda will include Irish-UK relations, Northern Ireland and the long-delayed EU-UK reset summit which is due to take place before the end of Ireland’s presidency of the EU.
[ Trump asked President Connolly if Irish unity would be ‘resolved’ during her lifetime Opens in new window ]
The meeting comes after US president Donald Trump ’s comments last weekend that he was in favour of a united Ireland and also the agreement between the leaders of the Scottish National Party, Plaid Cymru and Sinn Féin calling for independence for Scotland and Wales and the reunification of Ireland.
The Taoiseach has already said publicly that legacy is a priority. He has also called on the British government to set out the circumstances under the terms of the Good Friday Agreement in which a Border poll could be called.
The next UK-Ireland summit will take place in the UK next year.
