title: Social media age limits: Von der Leyen hits on control-shift alternative
description: Providing proof of age will present big obstacle to EU plan
content:
Y ou can tell when Ursula von der Leyen lands on a turn of phrase she likes. She’ll repeat it in speeches and add the same flourish of emphasis each time.
The European Commission president found one a few weeks back when talking about a possible EU-wide age limit on social media .
The debate shouldn’t be framed around when young people should get access to the platforms, she said. Instead, it’s a question of “when social media has access to our children and teenagers”.
The German head of the EU’s powerful executive body, which churns out regulations, has been under pressure to take a big step on online safety for children.
Von der Leyen rarely agrees to sit-down interviews with the press, instead favouring speeches to get her message across.
Months, yes months, of work went into crafting the one she delivered yesterday in Strasbourg, which the EU executive calls the president’s “state of the union” address to the European Parliament (a tradition since 2010).
For several weeks, the European Commission had a countdown running on its website to tick off the days, hours, minutes and seconds until Von der Leyen stood up to deliver her big speech.
One of the points widely trailed beforehand had been a proposal to prohibit children under the age of 13 from accessing social media.
[ Europe is entering a new phase. Ireland may lose out Opens in new window ]
“Platforms will have to prove that they are safe, because it is not about our minors accessing social media, it is about when and how do we allow social media to access minors,” she said.
The proposed new rules, which must pass through the lengthy Brussels policymaking ringer, envisage teenagers gradually being allowed on to Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat and the rest.
Between the ages of 13 and 15, teenagers could have “mini accounts” set up and supervised by their parents, with restricted features and screen-time limits. Tech giants would be required to provide “safer” feeds for the accounts of 16- and 17-year-olds, under the commission’s plans.
Not content with nicking the state-of-the-union theme for the set piece policy speech, the commission has fallen into the very American habit of naming new legislation after a vaguely relevant “backronym”. Hence, the EU Kids Act, or its full title, the Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy Act.
The proposed regulations will surely trigger a fresh row between Brussels officials and Big Tech firms, who fiercely resist having to make changes to their products and have already been waging a fightback against EU guardrails.
It looks like large chunks of separate legislation EU justice commissioner Michael McGrath had been preparing – the Digital Fairness Act – to regulate infinitive scrolling and other addictive features will instead be wrapped into the EU Kids Act.
Von der Leyen’s thinking has been shaped by an expert group. Its report, published this summer, went heavy on this idea of making social media “safe by design” for children and young teenagers.
[ EU to bring in minimum age limit of 15 to set up social-media accounts Opens in new window ]
Rather than EU regulators launching lengthy investigations to prove certain features are harmful and handing out fines, the companies would have to demonstrate their platforms were safe for minors before being allowed on to the European market. The threat of hefty fines will remain on the table.
Irish Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan has been making a lot of noise calling for an EU-wide social media age limit. However, France, Greece and Spain have led the charge. National legislation tabled by those governments put Brussels under pressure to do something to avoid member states going off in different directions.
The big issue will be proving someone who opens a social media account is 14, 16, or 23. “A harmonised EU age restriction to access social media and other digital services cannot be enforced without an age verification ecosystem that can be used to prove the age of minors,” that recent expert report said.
The commission wants to use an age verification app it is developing alongside an EU “digital identity wallet” scheme already in the works.
A person will upload a photograph of their passport or other identity paperwork once, so their smartphone or device “knows” how old they are, without a copy of the document being retained in the app.
[ EU to curb teenage access to social media but stop short of outright ban Opens in new window ]
The wallet has been thought up as a secure, but voluntary, way for people to store a digital record of important documents and an authentication tool when applying for public services online.
It will be politically very fraught for Brussels or national governments to make signing up for the digital wallet scheme, or uploading sensitive documents to an age verification app, an effective requirement for creating a social media profile. That’s where this proposed age ban may run into the most trouble.

title: Diary of a CEO host Steven Bartlett: ‘This is new ground, frankly, as a podcaster’
description: The Diary of a CEO host, who has faced criticism over spreading fringe claims, is building a one-stop shop for other creators
content:
O ne thing Steven Bartlett will not be doing if The Diary of a CEO becomes the world’s most subscribed podcast on YouTube this year is celebrating with a glass of wine or two.
The British podcaster, who fronts the show that is closing in on the top-ranked The Joe Rogan Experience, caused an internet furore this summer after a clip was circulated of him complaining that even two or three glasses were enough to ruin the next few days.
For his critics, this was a moment to pile on Bartlett, whose podcasts have featured guests pushing some of the more fringe ideas in the cult of aspirational wellness and self-optimisation.
But Bartlett seems as relaxed as one would imagine the author of a book entitled Happy Sexy Millionaire to be, despite the roasting he took from friends and the mockery he draws from waiters bearing down with wine lists. “You’d be shocked to see how little time I spend on the internet,” he says.
The popularity of such content has helped make The Diary of a CEO the second-biggest podcast on YouTube, with 19.5 million subscribers and combined listens and views per month that regularly exceed 100 million. If its current growth continues, it is on track to overtake the US influencer Joe Rogan’s 21.1 million YouTube subscribers this year.
But Bartlett’s aspirations are fixed on a longer and more ambitious goal: building the world’s leading creator media company. “What you’re seeing now [are] the foundations of what I believe will be the definitive company in this industry over the next 50 years,” he says.
He is in talks for a fresh fundraising, which he says will exceed the $425 million (€368 million) valuation established for his holding company, Steven.com, in a round last year, which left him owning more than 90 per cent. “I’ve designed the business ... so that I can maintain ownership and board control for the next 50 years. Because, essentially, this is my last dance.”
For a youthful-looking 34-year-old, it feels like Bartlett has been in the online world a long time – he started working on his first online business idea when he was 18. Since then he has ridden out questions over the value of a business after it merged with a German company in 2019, and complaints about how he has promoted products he invests in. His podcast has prompted concerns from health experts about whether he takes enough responsibility for the more questionable claims made by guests on topics such as Covid and cancer and has faced some criticism for giving a platform to more niche parts of the online community, such as guests who have been associated with the manosphere.
Bartlett does not claim to be a journalist and says the podcast has become better at fact-checking and now appends notes to clarify or correct wrong claims on screen. “This is new ground, frankly, as a podcaster, because there isn’t necessarily a blueprint here of how you increase rigour within the medium. But hopefully, we’ll help to create one.”
He says he is working with an AI company that will further analyse transcripts for accuracy and provide on-screen context. “Packaging things in a way that will deliver reach while also making sure that they are as accurate as they can be.”
His London office feels like an encapsulation of the Bartlett brand: sleek and modern, and centred around a two-storey metal rocket ship as befits a social media start-up in trendy Shoreditch.
There is plenty of natural light to help cortisol levels – a wellness hack much loved by some of his guests – while air quality in his studio is optimised for alertness. Supplement drinks such as Cadence (“to elevate daily discipline, performance and recovery”) are in the fridge alongside Perfect Ted matcha lattes. Both count Bartlett – one of the “dragons” in the BBC’s hit show Dragons’ Den – among their investors.
The office is the hub for the Delaware-incorporated Steven Holdings, which Bartlett aims to build into a one-stop shop for other creators, spanning production, technology, representation, events and brand work.
“We see that when creators get to a certain size ... they are pulled to have a book agent, and a publisher, and a content team, and a tour provider,” he says. “[We have it] all in-house.”
He is working with popular creators including Davina McCall and Paul C Brunson and Bartlett says more big names are imminent. His Flightcast platform hosts about 435 podcasts.
“Central to our platform are technology and data, and helping creators ... pull their audiences into owned environments [such as their own events and deals], not rented environments [on social media platforms],” says Bartlett.
Businesses within the holding group have been consistently profitable and are growing strongly, according to the company, but no overall numbers are made public. More than 80 per cent of revenue comes from The Diary of a CEO, but Bartlett wants this percentage to fall quickly as other parts grow.
On Monday, he will announce the latest move in this strategy – a joint venture with US group Authentic Brands which will work with creators to build media companies and brands.
Bartlett dropped out of university in Manchester to focus on business, and credits Social Chain, the social media marketing company he launched in 2014, with teaching him about platforms and algorithms that determine whether content lives or dies online. Even now, he gives a heartfelt plea for listeners to subscribe at the start of his shows. His team edits and tests formats relentlessly to eke out as many viewers and followers as possible.
“I didn’t know the rules of podcasting at all ... [but] because I had a background in the commercialisation of media ... and because I had spent a long time in social media, that naivety with a little bit of experience in adjacent things created a different type of more vertically integrated business.”
Even he seems taken aback by the growth of his show in a fiercely competitive market. “I think I’m the most surprised. I started on my kitchen table in London not that long ago. I had many dreams in my life, and podcaster was never one. But here we are.”
Despite The Diary of a CEO ’s top ranking in US and UK business podcast charts, there is still a large cohort of businesspeople who would struggle to say what it does. Its content has evolved beyond business to feature lifestyle and wellbeing tips. But among discussions about aliens and AI threats, Bartlett also attracts big names such as Michelle Obama, JD Vance, Kamala Harris and Jürgen Klopp.
Bartlett characterises his audience as “strivers” who “want to have their mind expanded”.
He sees the podcast – whose episodes tend to run long and often feature him doing little more than looking quizzical – as giving people the space to open up. He points to a recent interview with WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann, who discussed childhood trauma. “There are periods where I didn’t interrupt him for 15 minutes. That’s my style of interviewing.”
Creators have not historically had “the same rigour and experience and training as a lot of real journalists”, he concedes. “This is something that, as my platform’s grown, I’ve thought more and more about.”
Bartlett admits he has timed his ventures well but also puts his business’s growth down to an obsession with detail and experimentation – the 1 per cent marginal gains, as he calls them, that add up to something bigger. Even studio CO2 levels are monitored to stay below 1,000 parts per million, which is when, he says, “your cognitive performance will change ... your ability to answer questions or ask them will shift”.
The optimised life extolled in his studio crosses over to his portfolio of investments, which include Zoe, a health-testing company, and Huel supplements. This has led to trouble at times with the advertising regulator. In 2024, the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) found a Huel advertisement featuring Bartlett misleading because it did not disclose he was a director. The ASA also upheld a complaint about a Zoe ad carrying Bartlett’s endorsement that omitted to say he was an investor.
“I think we’ve done a really good job over the last couple of years making sure that whenever there’s a commercial relationship with particular brands, we declare it, and we have a really great editorial process now,” he says. “If I mention Whoop [the fitness tracker] ... the team will either remove that or they’ll ask me to do a pickup, just saying that I’m an investor.”
Bartlett is certainly an enthusiastic endorser of fitness and wellbeing products, although he admits to being most influenced by whoever he last had on the podcast. Referring to advice shared on a recent episode by a neuroscientist, he says: “I got out of bed today ... and I was like, right, where’s the pint of water?”

title: Watching The Gentlemen, I have an urge first to doff my cap, then to head an angry mob
description: Posho dressed as a pearly king Guy Ritche offers up more cartoon geezer yarns
content:
“Wotcha, mate. It’s me, Guy Ritchie, genuine geezer and Madge’s old pot [and pan: man; Madonna’s ex-husband]. I’m doing the Lambeth Walk up from me ol’ kite [and spool: private school] with nothing but my barrel of bees [and honey: money] to whisper a jack [-anory: story] into your King [Lear: ear] on the Liza [Minnelli: telly]. Lawks! Is them the Bow Bells I hear? Gawd bless his majesty,” etc.
The Gentlemen ( Netflix ) is a yarn about an aristocratic family who go into a criminal enterprise with a gritty crime family (in fairness, all aristocratic families started out as crime families) so their estate can return to its former feudal glory. The gist of the story is, once again: “We’re not so different, you and I … Have we not both, in a sense, pulled off a heist on the people of Britain?”
Writers like Guy Ritchie are wedded to a notion of “authenticity” that celebrates both aristocrats and salt-of-the-earth types for knowing their place (with a class-mobility dispensation for the entrepreneurial criminal element) and sees aspiration and social mobility as illusory.
This is all, of course, coming from a posho dressed as a pearly king. It sells the same ideology, ultimately, as Downton Abbey, which is aimed at a different demographic but written by Guy Ritchie’s spiritual twin, Julian Fellowes . And what is that ideology? “Property is theft (and what of it?).”
The middle class barely register in the Ritchieverse. This is because the middle class, annoying as they might be in their rush to tax-cut themselves out of existence (the writer gazes ruefully at the Irish Times readership), can only exist in countries with social mobility and a functioning social-security net.
Britain funded those things by taxing the hell out of aristocrats after the war, something that is depicted in the opening of the second episode of the second series as a terrible shame altogether.
At this point our anti-hero Eddie, the duke of Halstead (Theo James), gives a speech in which he laments the era of aristocratic guilt and vows to get his ancestral lands back. I have an urge to doff my cap at this point, followed by an urge to head an angry mob.
What are you at, Freyne? This is pure entertainment, not a political polemic. You’re breaking a butterfly upon a wheel (or, in terms Ritchie would understand, boffing a posh moth on a hoop).
Guy Ritchie is just the Tex Avery of his day. This is like doing a Marxist analysis of Quick Draw McGraw. A poststructuralist critique of Pepé Le Pew. A Lacanian dissertation on Alvin and the Chipmunks.
Yeah, well, I’m no fun, and I’m happy to do them too: Quick Draw McGraw legitimises the westward theft of the American continent; Pepé Le Pew needs to be me-tooed for several decades of consequence-free sexual harassment; and Alvin and the Chipmunks are clearly narcs.
[ Continuity Top Gear: Three men cosplay as an early 2000s trio who recall rationing, old money and petrol’s purpose Opens in new window ]
I’m not saying The Gentlemen isn’t fun. In the new series Eddie and his criminal foil, Susie Glass (an excellently deadpan Kaya Scodelario), are leveraging their big marijuana business into something bigger with the help of some murderous Italian mafioso types and, at one point, a silent, torture-prone Asian assassin. (Ritchie seemingly never saw a stereotype he didn’t feel was absolutely fine.)
In the first few episodes they watch an associate being fed to a tiger, they chase a motorcycle gang in pursuit of a Botticelli painting and they pimp out one of their associates to a lecherous member of the House of Lords played by Downton Abbey’s Hugh Bonneville. (He probably thinks he’s a real aristocrat at this stage.)
In episode one the brilliant Irish folk musician John Francis Flynn can also be found playing to a barn full of flatcap-wearing servants, as is the lot of the travelling Irish minstrel under colonisation.
Vinnie Jones plays a faithful retainer who says things like “anything for you and this family”. Ray Winstone plays himself (I think) and rarely leaves the sauna from which he runs a crime empire, has mystical visions and says things like “I ain’t paying that posh c**t another shekel”, which reminds me a little of pay negotiations here at The Irish Times.
Here are some Guy Ritchie projects I am pitching for future television seasons (I’m happy to executive-produce):
I’ve Got a Luverly Bunch of Coconuts: Everyone in the House of Lords receives a head injury and now thinks they’re a cockney.
Top Geezer: Jeremy Clarkson, James May and Richard Hammond race cockneys around like horses.
Mumsy’s Gone Kray Kray: Reggie Kray and the queen mum go on a cocaine-fuelled crime spree (with Vinnie Jones and Ray Winstone as Kray and the queen mum, respectively).
The whole high-concept premise of Dark Matter (Apple TV) imploded towards the end of the first series. A show in which the main characters travelled between dimensions, it ended with dozens of identical versions of a physicist named Jason (Joel Edgerton) trying to return to his wife, Daniela (Jennifer Connelly) in their home dimension.
The multiples occur for sciency reasons that are subsequently shown to be, at the very least, inconsistent. At a certain point you just have to accept it.
The question is, can you have too many Joel Edgertons? “No”, says my brother, and “No”, presumably, says Joel Edgerton’s agent. “Yes”, says I, because I’m finding it very, very confusing.
[ TV & Radio Call My Agent! actor Camille Cottin on the star-studded celeb satire: ‘All the stories were true’ Opens in new window ]
Not only is it hard to know which Joel Edgerton is which, and not only does the faux-science quickly fall apart, but the moral logic also crumbles, because Daniela choses the “Jason” we’ve been following all along instead of the others, seemingly on a first-come-first-served basis.
Subsequently the family become relatively blase about the violent deaths of numerous other Jasons before hopping dimensions once again for more adventures.
The moral stability of our hero is also under question, given how easy it seems to be to make some of these near-identical doppel-, troppel- and quadroppelgangers go “evil”.
“We’re not bad people,” Jason Number One says to a policeman after Daniela murders yet another lookalike in the first episode of the new series.
If you’re explaining you’re losing. If you ever see me saying “we’re not bad people” to a tied-up policeman please step in and say something.
I’m also pretty sure that if a dozen or so Joel Edgerton corpses turned up in an American city they would forgo a big investigation and say: “Best leave it.”
And then, instead, they would choose to investigate the much cooler, less existentially-troubling crimes committed by Guy Ritchie characters who speak in cockney rhyming slang and/or posh.

title: Pulp - What Do You Do for an Encore? review: Alchemy of such a band  cannot be replicated
description: Cultural trove charts outfit’s improbable passage from woodchip wallpaper to Britpop royalty
content:
Another week, another concert film featuring iconic 1990s folk. Following on the heels of Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger , Pulp : What Do You Do for an Encore?, a scrapbook-meets-concert film, is a keen reminder that the alchemy of a band such as Pulp cannot be replicated.
It’s certainly not a question of musical virtuosity. As a dependably droll Jarvis Cocker recalls, the Sheffield band’s changing line-up was determined by people he bumped into in pubs. Their long-serving drummer Nick Banks, as Cocker recalls, turned up for his audition with a dog that had followed him from the bus stop, and then spent his try-out attempting to contact the dog’s owner. He got the job without hitting a skin.
Garth Jennings, the director of the hugely successful animated Sing franchise, returns to his musical roots with a film Cocker rightly describes as a “jumble sale”. In an overture, Cocker and Jennings banter during a car journey that traces their relationship back to the 1998 promo for Help the Aged.
Circling the grand occasion of their show at the O2 in London in 2025, which was staged around Pulp’s first album in 24 years, More, Jennings lightly skips through the decades, finding grainy television appearances, photographs, home movies and an occasional Milk Tray advert, a cultural trove that charts the band’s improbable passage from woodchip wallpaper to Britpop royalty. A replica Dalek fashioned by Cocker’s grandfather is an unmissable family memory.
The effect is less a conventional rockumentary chronology than a fond, handmade collage of a kind that might be projected at a wedding anniversary or GAA club.
Cocker, always good chat, provides the connective tissue, narrating with the dry, self-deprecating wit that has defined Pulp’s lyrics. He didn’t lick it off a stone; in a snippet featuring his mum, Christine Connolly, she deadpans in the recognisable family style: “If your second name is Cocker, it’s important that your first name isn’t Everhard.”
Disco 2000, Babies and Common People arrive with the expected communal charge, while the newer material sits surprisingly comfortably among later entries.
The film’s most affecting passage steps away from the spectacle: a stripped-back performance dedicated to Steve Mackey, their bassist, who died in 2023 .
Four musicians, little ornament and no bells and whistles do more than the arena fireworks to explain why Pulp still matter.
In cinemas and on Mubi from Friday, September 18th

title: The Degenerate: The Life and Films of Andy Milligan review – below the bottom of the barrel
description: Raucous doc about Irish-American Z-movie master and his misanthropic milieu is wildly entertaining
content:
Andy Milligan made crude, rushed and spectacularly cheap movies , yet their peculiarities and darkness have kept them in circulation.
As one commentator notes in the wildly entertaining The Degenerate: The Life and Films of Andy Milligan, the lo-fi auteur was never as distinguished as famous schlockmeisters such as Herschell Gordon Lewis; if they were the bottom of the barrel, the Irish - American Z-movie master was below the barrel.
Directed by Josh Johnson and Grayson Tyler Johnson, this lively documentary assembles actors, collaborators, critics and academics to delve into a career that seldom dovetailed with conventional film-making practice. Milligan would write, direct, shoot, edit, design and costume his own productions. Scripts, he insisted, should be written within three days.
Working on New York’s 42nd Street circuit – an insanely profitable district allowing for erect nipples during the Hays Code era, when Hollywood policed its own films for unacceptable content – Milligan made plenty of money for his producer William Mishkin, a former perfume promoter.
His best-regarded films include Nightbirds, a UK production; his more disreputable efforts include The Ghastly Ones, of which the contemporaneous promoter says, “Well, it was ghastly, and it had ones.”
Milligan, who started out directing Tennessee Williams plays at Cafe Cino, an off-off-Broadway launch pad, moved into live 1950s TV drama, and acted opposite Leslie Nielsen and James Dean before drifting into no-budget film-making. His peers and fans included Andy Warhol and Sam Shepard.
A fashion designer on the side, he found expression in recycled horror conventions, grotesque props, improvised performances, cramped camerawork and dialogue that veers from melodrama into outright abuse. The 29 films he completed between 1965 and 1988, some of which are lost, include Tricks of the Trade, The Naked Witch and The Rats Are Coming: The Werewolves Are Here.
His recurring archetypes include domineering men, damaged women, grotesque outsiders and families seemingly organised around cruelty. “You have a filthy dirty mind to go along with your filthy dirty body,” is standard dialogue. His own mother, an abusive and obese woman who insisted that young Andy clean her feet, casts a dark shadow across his misanthropic milieu.
His biographer Jimmy McDonough emerges as an important and entertaining voice in this raucous, fascinating portrait of a difficult man, even as the documentary approaches its tragic ending. Milligan died in 1991 from Aids-related complications. The film-maker was broke and was buried in an unmarked pauper’s grave.

title: Renovated Mountpleasant Avenue Victorian with bright kitchen in Ranelagh
description: Four-bedroom end-terrace homes with charm and character close to D6 amenities
content:
Number 49 Mountpleasant Avenue Upper is a renovated four-bed Victorian that is now on the market with Mullery O’Gara, seeking €1.295 million.
The owners bought the 145sq m (1,560sq ft) end-terrace property in 2021 and got stuck into it as a renovation project, updating the bathrooms, decorating all the rooms, sanding the floors and installing a new extension. The Ber rating is E1.
Set back from the road behind a neat beech hedge, the entrance hallway is painted a fresh green, and red and green stained glass surrounds the front door.
To the left is the main reception room, which has retained its original charm and character. The room showcases new double-glazed sash windows in the box-bay window and restored pine floors. Overhead is an elaborate ceiling rose and ornate cornicing complemented by period fittings such as chandeliers and gilt over-mantel mirrors, which fit the room perfectly.
To the left off the hall is a sittingroom with plenty of built-in storage. This room connects to the new extension that houses a kitchen and dining area. There’s also a guest loo under the stairs at the end of the hall.
To make the most of the southerly aspect of the De Barra kitchen, a sliding, Crittall-style door was installed which opens to the courtyard garden. The space, with its sloping roof to which the owners added rustic beams, was always here, but was closed in by a flat roof. When they took that away, they opened up the space and incorporated the warmth of an old brick wall above the units. A dining area sits in the corner with banquette seating.
Outside, the courtyard garden is paved and faces south. There’s a small shed fixed on to the side of the house for bike storage and an EV charging point – the gates slide back and a car can be reversed in for charging.
On the return is a bedroom with an unusual layout: as well as being roomy enough to take a small double bed, a cot, plus a built-in wardrobe, it also has a free-standing, claw-foot bath. The owner explains this was originally a bathroom and they converted it back to a bedroom but kept the bath, which was useful with young children.
A small bedroom to the front of the house is used as a study. The main bedroom is beside that so there is potential to knock through and incorporate the study as a walk-in wardrobe. There’s another fine double bedroom on this level – both it and the main bedroom have good, tall, built-in wardrobes either side of the fireplaces and a modern bathroom, tiled in a stone-effect tile.
Moving on to another renovation project, the owners have loved the area as it’s about midway between Rathmines and Ranelagh, and is close to shops, schools, sports clubs and restaurants.

title: Twenty-four hours in Dublin: A city break written in history
description: For a short city break, The College Green Hotel has the capital on its doorstep
content:
There is something rather appealing about having Dublin to yourself for 24 hours. For those of us who live outside the capital, a trip to Dublin can often mean a day of appointments, shopping, a concert or a family occasion before heading home again. But with autumn and winter approaching, there is another option: make a proper night of it.
Dublin in the autumn and winter months has its own particular atmosphere. The evenings arrive earlier, Georgian streets glow beneath the street lights and the city’s museums, galleries, theatres, restaurants, cafes and bars become destinations in themselves. It is a time of year when Dublin feels less hurried and more suited to wandering.
For a short city break, The College Green Hotel has the capital on its doorstep. Trinity College is directly opposite the hotel, while Grafton Street, St Stephen’s Green, Dublin Castle, the National Gallery and the city’s cultural quarter are all close by. It means you can arrive, leave the car behind and spend the next 24 hours simply exploring.
Start with breakfast at the hotel before heading out into the city. From College Green, there is plenty to see without needing to plan every minute. Walk across to Trinity College, take a stroll towards Grafton Street and St Stephen’s Green or spend some time in the National Gallery. For those who know Dublin well, it can be surprisingly enjoyable to see the city again without the pressure of having to be somewhere.
And if the weather turns, there are plenty of places to duck into. Dublin’s galleries, museums, cafes and shops provide an easy excuse to take things at a slower pace.
Come evening, the city’s cultural life comes into its own. Theatre remains an important part of Dublin’s identity, with the Abbey Theatre, Gate Theatre and Bord Gáis Energy Theatre offering an eclectic programme throughout autumn and winter.
The College Green Hotel building has more than 200 years of history behind it, beginning as the Royal Irish Institution before later becoming the headquarters of the Bank of Ireland. Its past is still evident in the architecture and character of the hotel.
The former Banking Hall remains one of the most impressive spaces, while the old bank vault has been transformed into The Mint Bar, a hidden speakeasy serving award-winning cocktails and dining in an intimate setting.
Then there is the Atrium Lounge, the hotel’s striking five-storey space beneath a glass roof. It has long been at the heart of the building, bringing natural light into its centre and providing a setting for breakfast, afternoon tea or simply taking a break from the city outside.
This November, the Atrium Lounge will begin a new chapter following a complete transformation and renovation. The aim of the reimagined space is to retain the character and heritage of the building while elevating it as a destination for afternoon tea.
This September marks 25 years of The College Green Hotel. That silver anniversary sits within the building’s much longer history and offers an opportunity to celebrate both the hotel and its connection with Dublin. To mark the occasion, the hotel partnered with Irish silversmiths Silverworks to create A Silver Legacy, an experience centred on Irish craftsmanship and creativity.
Guests taking part can visit the Silverworks Atelier and choose between a private ring-forging workshop or a Claddagh ring-forging experience. Working alongside an Irish silversmith, guests create their own piece to take home. The experience also includes Champagne on arrival and a curated guide to Hidden Dublin.
There is something particularly appropriate about celebrating 25 years through the tradition of making something by hand. Silver may mark the anniversary, but the idea of Irish craftsmanship goes back much further to generations of makers creating objects with meaning and stories of their own.

title: Mamó in Howth, Co Dublin review: Why does this fabulous Howth restaurant not have a Michelin star?
description: Crisp white linen, relaxed service and ambitious cooking make this seafront spot a joy to visit
content:
I sometimes question how I feel about formal restaurants . It’s what happens when you visit rather more of them than a normal person would – not expecting sympathy here – and there is a danger of developing a jaded palate, an occupational hazard. They are restaurants you would typically visit once a year for a special occasion. The important thing for a critic is not to get bored because it is yet another tasting menu. Each restaurant has to be judged with fresh eyes. The danger is dismissing something simply because you’ve seen it before.
But then I walk into Mamó on a Sunday afternoon in Howth , escaping the traffic where tempers are at south of France levels – yes, people lepping out of cars and fighting over parking spaces – and enter the bright upstairs diningroom where every table is clad in a crisp, white linen tablecloth. It feels fresh and assured rather than formal, in the way that French and Italian bistros do. And there is no tasting menu, nor restrictions on ordering.
There is one non-negotiable on the menu of three nibbles, four starters, four mains and two desserts, and that is the cod chip (€9 for three). Perfect with a glass of champagne if you’re celebrating – champagne with fish and chips is a thing – but we instead go with a glass of Telmo Rodriguez ‘Gaba do Xil’ Godello (€14) and Château de Bousval ‘Gouttes d’O’ (€16.50), a Belgian Chardonnay, from an inspired list compiled by a true wine lover.
The cod chip has been on the menu since Jess D’Arcy and her husband, chef Killian Durkin, opened Mamó in 2019 , which I think qualifies it for legendary status. Confit potato is pressed, cut into fingers and deep-fried until crisp and golden, then seasoned with salt and vinegar and topped with lightly whipped taramasalata. It is the best fish and chips you’ll eat, steaming hot and crisp, with a sharpness from the vinegar.
Translucent slices of IPA-cured langoustine carpaccio (€19) sit beneath a Niçoise salad: frisée, haricot beans, crisp croutons and a breaded quail’s egg, cut in half so the runny yolk spills out. Capers and fresh anchovy add punch. There are quite a lot of flavours involved here, but it all works together, mopped up by a slice of very good sourdough slathered in whipped brown butter.
Summer tomato tart (€15.50) sounds simple, but once you bite into it, all you want to do is sit back and eat it slowly, relishing every bite of the Coolea sablé. It’s the crumbliest, cheesiest pastry imaginable, forming the base of the tart. Tomatoes are cut into ribbons and wound into flowers; ricotta, tiny basil leaves and finely sliced strips of chive bulb add creaminess and freshness, and black garlic brings a deeper note. I want to eat this so much again, it pains me to write about it.
Lobster linguine (€19), on as a starter special, works as a small main course for me. The house-made pasta, with generous pieces of lobster, is tossed in a light, buttery lobster bisque and dusted with Espelette pepper. It is delicious, although tiny bits of preserved lemon are a bit strident and surplus to requirements.
Hake is the market fish (€37), served off the bone and finished under the grill. It comes with a courgette flower stuffed with Morteau sausage, sitting on a very good courgette purée, and a side dish of gnocchi, girolles, tiny courgettes and pearl onions in a beautiful light broth.
Something fresh is required to clear the palate after all of this fish and the “pavlova” with passion fruit and lime (€14) sounds like just the thing. Initially, I am disappointed when I see that it comes in deconstructed mode, with flat shards of lime-flavoured meringue standing in for a marshmallowy base, but as I dig in, there’s frozen passion fruit mousse underneath, cubes of lime jelly, passion fruit pulp and piped, fluffy coconut cream. It is a wonderfully refreshing dessert.
Mamó is a joy to visit. The room is crisp, the service is friendly and professional, the food is playful and original and the wine list is one you want to dig into. Durkin has a light touch and, even though some of the dishes have numerous elements, there is a harmony here, with nothing over-laboured. The restaurant is listed in the Michelin Guide but has no star. Perhaps it’s time for a return visit.
Lunch for two with two glasses of wine was €144.
The verdict: Playful, original cooking that deserves Michelin’s attention.
Food provenance: Fish, Kish Fish and Glenmar; meat, Higgins Butcher; Redmond’s Fine Foods and La Rousse.
Vegetarian options: Cheese beignets, tomato summer tart, Cáis na Tire agnolotti, and sides.
Wheelchair access: Fully accessible with an accessible toilet.
Music: Unobtrusive, ranging from St Germain to Bill Withers to Air.

title: UCD in the world’s top 100: A university growing in global influence
description: From research and education to public life, business and culture, UCD’s growing global standing reflects the achievements of a university community whose influence extends far and wide
content:
University College Dublin (UCD) begins the new academic year ranked among the world’s top 100 universities. The latest QS World University Rankings recognise the growing strength of UCD’s education, research, reputation and global community. For UCD alumni, it is a shared achievement.
Every day, UCD graduates carry the university into the world: through the organisations they lead, the discoveries they make, the businesses they build, the communities they serve and their contribution to public life, culture and society in Ireland and internationally.
“These outstanding achievements reflect the excellence and ambition that define UCD,” says UCD president Prof Orla Feely. “They are also a reflection of our outstanding graduates, who make an impact across the world.”
UCD’s top 100 position is part of a wider picture of international recognition.
The university is ranked among the world’s top 50 for sustainability and remains firmly within the global top 100 for employment outcomes – important recognition of both UCD’s contribution to an increasingly more sustainable future and the value employers place on its graduates.
Research is another big source of UCD’s growing international influence. UCD is Ireland’s leading university for securing Horizon Europe research funding and is among the top 20 universities in Europe for funding secured under the programme. Its researchers are working across disciplines and borders to address some of the defining challenges of our time.
“Pioneering research with societal impact continues to be one of UCD’s greatest strengths,” Feely says. “Our researchers and innovators are breaking the boundaries of existing knowledge and engaging creatively across disciplines to address challenges in areas such as climate, health, sustainability and AI (artificial intelligence).”
The university is also establishing a UCD AI Institute, bringing together researchers and educators from diverse disciplines to advance research, education, innovation and responsible leadership in one of the defining technologies of our age.
The physical university is changing too. UCD’s campus continues to evolve to support new generations of students, researchers and educators. The O’Connor Centre for Learning, officially opened in March at Belfield, represents a significant investment in the future of teaching and learning.
“This marked the start of a new era of teaching and learning that is already enriching the student experience,” Feely says.
Yet UCD’s future is inseparable from its history. In 2026, the university marked 100 years of agricultural education, recognising the profound contribution UCD graduates, researchers and partners have made to agriculture, food systems and environmental sustainability. UCD also celebrated 20 years of its Clinical Research Centre, where more than 25,000 patients have accessed new therapies and enhanced medical care through clinical research.
The university marked the 170th anniversary of the UCD Literary & Historical Society, founded by St John Henry Newman.
“His vision of a university education that develops the whole person continues to inspire our mission today,” Feely says.
Together, these milestones tell a larger story: generations of UCD people applying knowledge beyond the university itself.
That influence is particularly visible in Europe. UCD graduates have played remarkable leadership roles in European institutions. Seven of Ireland’s 14 European Commissioners are UCD alumni, while Catherine Day became the European Commission’s first woman secretary general.
As Ireland takes on an important European leadership role, UCD will continue that tradition by bringing leaders and thinkers together at Belfield for important conversations around AI, innovation and democracy.
For Patricia Reilly, a UCD veterinary graduate and member of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s cabinet, the connection to UCD remains deeply personal. “I am a very proud UCD graduate,” says Reilly, “and I made precious, lifelong friendships with people who mean a great deal to me.”
‘I am proud of the global reach and impact of the UCD community, and the enduring relationship between the university and our alumni’
Across the Atlantic, another UCD graduate is leading one of America’s great civic institutions. David Leonard, president of Boston Public Library, the oldest large municipal library in the United States, studied philosophy and mathematics at UCD. His career demonstrates the enduring value of a university education in preparing people not simply for their first job, but for lives and careers that evolve in unexpected directions.
“That’s the beauty of a good university education,” Leonard says. “It gives you a foundation and helps you find the things you care about, but that doesn’t mean that’s where you’re going to end up. If you’re learning about something you’re passionate about, then you can apply that in any field.”
The UCD community grows every year. Throughout 2026 new graduates joined an international network of more than 350,000 alumni spanning 183 countries, many professions and generations. Reunion celebrations brought others back on campus, reconnecting former classmates with each other and with their university that has continued to change since they graduated.
Feely has also met UCD graduates at events around the world. “I had the pleasure of meeting many graduates who continue to speak with such affection for their time at UCD and the friendships and opportunities they found here,” she says. “I am proud of the global reach and impact of the UCD community, and the enduring relationship between the university and our alumni.”
That relationship between UCD and its alumni matters in both directions. The standing of a university is built over generations. Every graduate carries something of UCD into the world, and every achievement, contribution and connection strengthens the university for those who follow.
UCD’s standing reflects the collective strength of a university community: its students and faculty, its researchers and partners, and generations of graduates whose influence reaches far across the globe.
“UCD alumni exemplify the qualities that have long defined University College Dublin: ambition, creativity and a commitment to making a positive difference in the world,” Feely says. “At a time of profound global change, these values have never been more important.”
UCD has reached a new level of global recognition. The opportunity now is to build on that momentum; extending its contribution, its connections and its influence even further.
Connect with the UCD alumni community and discover more about UCD’s global recognition at ucd.ie . UCD Connections accompanies The Irish Times on Friday, September 11th, with the digital edition also available through the UCD alumni website

title: Connecting Irish employers with Europe’s skilled workforce
description: Eures combines digital recruitment tools with free expert guidance to support employers facing skills shortages
content:
As Irish employers continue to face recruitment challenges and skills shortages across a range of sectors, Eures Ireland (European Employment Services) is helping businesses access a wider pool of talent from across Europe. Through a network of more than 900 Eures advisers, employers can avail of a free European recruitment service. Eures connects businesses with suitable candidates through targeted recruitment campaigns, advertising vacancies in any EU/EEA country, presenting job opportunities at European Job Fairs and providing access to financial supports such as the Targeted Mobility Scheme integration grants or relocation grants for eligible recruits.
For more than 30 years, Eures has supported the free movement of workers, helping employers to source skilled candidates across all EEA countries and Switzerland. As a powerful European collaboration network, it brings together public and private employment services to make cross‑border recruitment smoother, fairer and more transparent.
The Eures network of advisers provides essential information to jobseekers and employers through personal contact. Eures Advisers are trained specialists who provide the three basic Eures services of information, guidance and placement, to both jobseekers and employers interested in the European job market. They have specialised expertise in the practical, legal and administrative matters relating to mobility at national and cross-border level. They work within the public employment service of each member state, or within other member or partner organisations in the Eures network.
Since it was first established, Eures has evolved and expanded the network, continuously adapting to more modern recruitment methodologies and labour market trends. Eures has introduced various technical innovations, establishing its unique position in European employment services. These include a sophisticated job matching engine on the Eures portal , which has more than one million registered CVs, more than three million job listings and a European Job Days (EJDs) recruitment platform which has so far hosted 364 EJDs.
This year marks the 15th anniversary of EJDs, a platform service that has become a cornerstone in connecting jobseekers with employers across the European Union, the European Economic Area and Switzerland. Both employers with skill shortages and jobseekers or job-changers looking for new roles can benefit from Eures services and its online EJDs. As a free European public service, the EJDs platform is designed to make transnational and cross-border recruitment simple, transparent and accessible. By combining a dynamic digital platform with expert human support across 31 countries, EJDs offer far more than a typical online job fair. In addition to matching employers with suitable candidates, it provides practical information on living and working in specific countries, enabling jobseekers and businesses to explore new opportunities and build meaningful connections across Europe from wherever they are.
Eures Ireland is hosting its next European Job Day event, Boost Your Career with Eures 2026, on October 20th
EJDs are organised by Eures organisations across Europe and showcase employment opportunities in a wide range of sectors, including IT, engineering, healthcare and hospitality. Each year, more than 35 European Online Job Days are hosted on the platform, giving Irish employers the opportunity to participate in any event that aligns with their recruitment needs. Eures Ireland is hosting its next EJD event, Boost Your Career with Eures 2026, on October 20th. This online event offers Irish employers a unique opportunity to promote vacancies in technology, life sciences and engineering to jobseekers in Ireland and across the EU/EEA. Jobseekers will be able to apply for roles and schedule interviews in advance through the platform’s interactive features. A range of recruitment services will be available to employers, including publishing vacancies on the event’s website, automatic matching, interview scheduling and conducting interviews through the EJD platform. The event will be streamed live and will feature employer presentations, online interviews and public and private chat sessions, enabling direct engagement between employers and jobseekers.
Since its launch in 2011, EJDs have moved countless careers and companies forward. EJDs have translated European co-operation for employment into tangible results. Nearly 400,000 jobseekers have participated in 364 EJD events, engaging 14,000 employers from 32 countries and sectors such as tourism, IT and healthcare. According to official data, EJD participation has contributed to support the publication of 25,000 job vacancies, generating a total of circa 250,000 job applications, underscoring the platform’s positioning as a trusted and unique tool for providing fair European jobs.
This EJD initiative underscores the important role of Eures in fostering European and cross-border recruitment, showcasing the extensive benefits of its network services to jobseekers and employers in Ireland and across Europe.
Whether you are an employer seeking skilled workers or a jobseeker looking for your next opportunity, Eures offers the expertise, network and support to make it happen. Discover how connecting with Europe could open up new possibilities for your business or career at euresireland.ie . Or find your job in Europe at europeanjobdays.eu

title: Irish fashion and beauty brands attracting global attention
description: Some of Ireland’s leading fashion, beauty and lifestyle brands have showcased the sector’s unique offering at an event in Switzerland
content:
The burgeoning international success of the Irish fashion and beauty sectors was showcased to a key overseas audience at the Enterprise Ireland Irish Fashion & Beauty Showroom in Zurich’s historic Zunfthaus zur Meisen guild hall on September 2nd.
The showroom featured a carefully selected group of Irish fashion and lifestyle brands including Celtic Tweed, John Hanly & Co, Landa Leather, McNutt of Donegal, Moon + Mellow, Ted 1942, O’Neil of Dublin and Urban Aran. Also featured were leading Irish beauty and wellness brands including Inis, Hildun Beauty and The Smooth Company.
Designed as a high-quality sourcing and networking event, offering buyers direct access to founders, decision makers and products in an intimate and commercially focused environment, the event enabled meaningful conversations, hands-on product discovery and the opportunity to identify brands with genuine potential for growth within Switzerland and across Europe.
“For retailers seeking brands that combine authenticity, sustainability, craftsmanship and innovation, Ireland is increasingly becoming a source of exciting opportunities across both fashion and beauty,” says Enterprise Ireland market adviser Kenny Legg.
“The showroom showcased exceptional products as well as telling the wider story of modern Ireland, a country where heritage and innovation work hand in hand, creating brands that are winning recognition from consumers, retailers and industry leaders around the world.”
Switzerland has been a relatively untapped market for Irish fashion and beauty brands until now, according to his colleague and fellow market adviser Jane Greene. “Swiss consumers are very discerning, with high spending power, and there is definitely potential for these companies to win new business and build partnerships in the market. The showcase helped us bring these brands to a new audience who appreciate design and strong heritage.”
During the two-day visit to Zurich, the companies received expert advice on how to sell into Switzerland along with a “retail safari” tour of key department stores and boutiques. The showcase, held on the second day, attracted dozens of buyers, stylists, distributors, retailers, influencers and industry professionals who were provided with a unique opportunity to discover emerging and established Irish brands that are successfully competing on the global stage.
The showroom was highly successful, according to Legg. “We had great support from the Irish embassy in Bern in organising the event. We had buyers from leading department stores, as well as the Maison Gassmann multi-brand fashion boutique and luxury fashion boutique Quaglia Zurich in attendance,” he says. “Typically, these buyers would go to Milan or Paris. It was a wonderful opportunity to be able to put Irish brands in front of them in Zurich and help them bring something new and exciting to their customers.”
Ireland is “very much on trend at the moment”, says Legg. “For example, PKZ, the leading independent fashion house in Switzerland, with 40 stores across the country, featured Ireland in its stores this summer.”
This reflects the resurgence of Irish fashion, says Greene. “Some of the industry’s most influential creative voices now hail from Ireland, including Jonathan Anderson, creative director of Dior, Simone Rocha, and Seán McGirr of Alexander McQueen,” she adds. “Alongside them, a new generation of Irish designers such as Róisín Pierce, Michael Stewart of Standing Ground and Robyn Lynch are attracting international attention through their distinctive creative vision and commitment to craftsmanship.”
She also points to another trend: “Fashion brands across Ireland are rediscovering and reimagining the country’s rich textile heritage. Drawing inspiration from centuries of expertise in wool, linen and tweed production, Irish brands are transforming traditional techniques into contemporary luxury collections that resonate with modern consumers. Today, quality, authenticity and craftsmanship have become increasingly valuable attributes, positioning Irish fashion brands at the intersection of heritage and innovation.”
The international spotlight on Irish fashion continues to intensify, says Legg. “Dublin will host Dior’s first-ever runway show in Ireland in December 2026, a milestone expected to attract global media, buyers and fashion leaders while underscoring Ireland’s growing influence within luxury fashion.”
Alongside fashion, Ireland’s beauty and wellness sector has emerged as one of the country’s most dynamic consumer industries, Greene points out. “The sector is building an international reputation for combining scientific credibility, high-quality ingredients, sustainability and authenticity,” she says.
“Ireland’s beauty and personal care market now exceeds €1.2 billion, with much of its growth being driven by independent entrepreneurs who have built brands around purpose, innovation and customer needs.
“These businesses are proving that global influence is no longer limited to multinational corporations. Instead, founder-led brands with compelling stories and effective products are establishing loyal customer bases far beyond Ireland’s shores. From internationally recognised fragrance collections and specialist beauty products to viral social-commerce success stories, Irish beauty brands are increasingly attracting attention from retailers seeking differentiated products that align with evolving consumer expectations.”

title: ‘Incomprehensible to sit on cash pile as global economy undergoes rewiring,’ says new Ibec president
description: Maureen Walsh calls on Government to ‘immediately release’ €2 billion National Training Fund surplus
content:
Support for Irish businesses to embrace artificial intelligence (AI) and develop future-focused skills can make Ireland a net beneficiary of the new technology, according to Ibec’s newly elected president, Maureen Walsh.
Walsh, who is managing director of DeCare Dental Insurance Ireland, also identifies infrastructure investment, including housing, energy, transport and digital connectivity as key to enabling continued growth in all parts of the country.
Looking back to her early years in DeCare and the near panic surrounding the so-called Y2K bug, she says the current technological shift “makes Y2K look like an administrative glitch”.
“Artificial intelligence is no longer a futuristic concept; it is here, and it is going to rewrite the rules of how we work, how we live and how we compete,” she continues. “Just as we prepared then, we must strategically, confidently and deliberately prepare now. The world is navigating a profound reordering of the global trading system. Public policy must once again actively pursue growth rather than passively expecting it.”
Against this backdrop, Walsh says the focus of her presidency will be on three core policy themes: equipping the workforce for the AI era, creating a fairer ecosystem for entrepreneurs and delivering on balanced regional development.
“We are entering a once-in-a-generation period of technological change and opportunity that has the potential to transform our labour market and make Ireland the home of the world’s most competitive AI native workforce,” she says.
However, she points out that while Ireland consistently ranks as having one of the most highly educated workforces in the world, the country is not moving fast enough on structured lifelong learning.
“We have a clear solution at our fingertips,” Walsh contends. “We must immediately release the €2 billion surplus currently sitting untouched in the National Training Fund. We must deploy this funding to rapidly expand programmes like Skillnet Enterprise-led networks and Springboard+. It is economically incomprehensible to sit on a cash pile while the global economy undergoes a fundamental rewiring. The best way to shape the future is to invest in the people who will build it.”
Calling for greater backing for Irish entrepreneurs, Walsh says “we must support the risk-takers. Small indigenous businesses are the vital lifeblood of our local communities and a dynamic force within our broader economic ecosystem. They are even more than that. They are the creators, the innovators and the disrupters. They have proven themselves on an Irish and global scale.”
Irish business owners are “currently facing a perfect storm of rising operational costs and dense regulatory administrative burdens. We must move beyond taxation alone and tackle the dense administrative burdens weighing down our founders.”
And there are ways to do this, she says. “We must commit to radical regulatory simplification through an expanded ‘SME Test’ to protect scaling firms from disproportionate red tape. Our entrepreneurs must be able to secure the external investment necessary to turn vision into reality. We must simplify the access to, and take-up of, critical taxation support measures and grant schemes to support growth requirements.
“By dismantling these financial and administrative barriers, we empower business owners to do what they do best: innovate, secure the investment they need to scale and create the high-quality jobs of the future right across the country and indeed globally.”
Turning to infrastructure, Walsh says resolving regional deficits in transport, energy, water and housing is crucial if businesses across Ireland are to maintain productivity, compete for talent, and trade internationally.
“Speaking as a business leader in the west, I see daily that the resourcefulness of our workforce remains our true competitive edge,” she says. “But to safeguard existing enterprise and convince the next generation of foreign direct investment to choose our regions over competing global markets, that human potential must be backed by high-capacity utility and connectivity networks – because ambition for our regions without world-class infrastructure is just noise.”
She calls for capital spending to be prioritised above all other fiscal demands. “That means protecting budgets in real terms, rebalancing the planning system to put the common good first, and streamlining processes to accelerate project delivery on the ground.”
Long-term thinking and commitment are required, she concludes, calling on the Government to “look past the immediate political cycle, to clear the regulatory quagmires holding back our entrepreneurs, and to bring an unapologetic focus to building an economy that can withstand whatever comes next to ensure continued growth and prosperity.
“We want to look back 10 years from now and say that this was the moment Ireland chose to back its risk-takers, the family business that invested in the next generation, the start-up that created jobs we had not yet imagined, the multinational that chose to reinvest here as part of their growth strategy.”

title: Event guide: Dublin Theatre Festival, Denise Chaila and the other best things to see in Ireland in the week ahead
description: September 19th-25th, 2026: Our pick of music, art, theatre and more coming your way this week
content:
Taking over the city for 18 days of world-class theatre, this year’s Dublin Theatre Festival features more highlights than we have space for. Be prepared for the gamut of experiences: some things will soothe you, some will shock you, according to artistic director Róise Goan. The festival opens with the world premiere of Radio Bette (Gaiety Theatre, September 23rd-27th), which was to have starred Ruth Negga . Inspired by a rare rehearsal recording of a 1951 Bette Davis radio broadcast, it now features Marcus Amaglo as Davis, who is herself playing Margo Channing, the ageing star of All About Eve. Other highlight include Erica Murray’s new play, Meredith (Gate Theatre, September 25th-October 11th), Druid’s production of A Moon for the Misbegotten, by Eugene O’Neill (Gaiety Theatre, October 1st-4th), and the late Sarah Kane’s 4.48 Psychosis (Project Arts Centre, October 6th-11th).
Denise Chaila has been away for a while, dreaming it all up again, no doubt, but the charismatic songwriter and singer steps into the spotlight again for a brief Irish tour, a “reintroduction”, she says, and “a small glimpse into the subterranean work” she has been busy with for the past year or so. These shows will feature music we know, notably from Go Bravely, Chaila’s 2020 Choice Music Prize-winning album, as well as songs from an album due for release next year. Also, Saturday, October 3rd, Set Theatre, Kilkenny, 8pm, €27.50, set.ie
Farewell, Saint Etienne. After 35 years as one of the most consistently imaginative (if never significantly commercially successful) English pop groups, they have decided to put their microphones into storage. With a back catalogue of 13 studio albums (the most recent of which is last year’s International), there will be no shortage of sparklers for the dedicated long-term fan. Take a bow, Sarah Cracknell, Bob Stanley and Pete Wiggs.
Laura Veirs might be best known for her collaboration with Neko Case and KD Lang on the trio’s acclaimed self-titled album from 2016, but the American singer-songwriter’s solo work has long been admired by fans of artful and subtle alt.country/folk. With 14 albums to her name, she has no shortage of back-catalogue songs to pull out of the bag, as well as material from Temple Songs, her most recent record.
Presented by Sounds from a Safe Harbour and hosted by Lisa Hannigan, Sirens focuses on the authority and character of the female voice. Through original material by Hannigan, Anna Mieke, Kate Stables, Angie McMahon and Amanda Bergman, as well as imaginative versions of songs by other female songwriters, the performances aim to highlight the themes of creative give-and-take, combined energy, and harmony. Choral arrangements are by Theodora Byrne. Also, Saturday, September 26th, NCH, Dublin, 7.30pm, €40/€34, nch.ie; Sunday, September 27th, Opera House, Cork, 8pm, €41, corkoperahouse.ie .
In what is surely a first, six Co Cavan pubs welcome a touring theatre company – the Cavan-based Livin’ Dred – with a production of Poguemahone, Pat McCabe’s epic verse novel from 2022, which he refers to as “an insurgent, psychedelic folktale”. Livin’ Dred Theatre’s artistic director, Aaron Monaghan, features, and Padraic McIntyre directs. Also, Saturday, September 26th, Bridge Inn, Mount Nugent, 8pm, €16; Thursday, October 1st, Bridge Tavern, Canningstown, 8pm, €16; Friday, October 2nd, Stables, Swanlinbar, 8pm, €16; Saturday, October 3rd, Jenny’s Bar & Lounge, Mullagh, 8pm, €16.
Public interviews, readings, poetry and workshops, with a fishing village on your doorstep? We can’t think of a more picturesque environment for a boutique literary festival. Complementing the scenery are events that aim to stoke the imagination and intellect; highlights include Richard Ford and John Banville (Friday, September 25th, St Peter’s Church, 7pm, €35, sold out), Carlo Gébler and Sinéad Gleeson (Saturday, September 26th, Stella Maris Centre, 5.30pm, €15) and Neil Jordan and Pat McCabe (Sunday, September 27th, St Peter’s Church, 2pm, €15).
A cornerstone of the Irish Film Institute’s annual programme, the festival presents 13 features, including Try! (Thursday, September 24th, 6.10pm), Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie (Friday, September 25th, 6.15pm) and Acting (Sunday, September 27th, 4.10pm). There are two shorts programmes, IFI & DCU: Masters of Documentary (Saturday, September 26th, noon) and IFI & Galway Film Fleadh: Small Corners, Whole Worlds (Sunday, September 27th, 1pm). Festival guests include Sophie Feinnes, Jackie Fox and Iryna Dovhan.
This year’s Kavanagh Weekend investigates the Monaghan poet’s links to the beat generation through a series of multidisciplinary events curated by the actor Adrian Dunbar and the musician Nick Roth. The programme includes the US poet and cultural activist Anne Waldman, the comedian and actor Tommy Tiernan, the novelist Liz Nugent, the poet Victoria Kennefick and the musician Jinx Lennon.

title: The Pathless Walk by Tim Hannigan: Why has Ireland the worst countryside access in Europe?
description: To find answers the author, originally from Cornwall, sets out on a 678km diagonal walk across Ireland
content:
The raison d’être of Tim Hannigan’s travel book is to unravel the mystery of why so much Irish countryside is inaccessible compared with England and Wales, where footpaths stretch across fields and moors. Why, he wonders, has Ireland never had a similar network of paths and now has the worst provision for countryside access in Europe?
To find answers, Hannigan, originally from Cornwall and now living in Co Galway, sets out on a 678km diagonal walk across Ireland, choosing an arbitrary route from Dunmore Head on the Dingle peninsula to the Ards peninsula. As he crosses mountain ranges, bogland and open countryside – frequently camping overnight – his quest is the search for paths.
The author’s bête noire is walking on tarmac roads, which leads to blisters, throbbing feet, stinging toes and aching heels, impeding his progress. But he perseveres, meeting a cross-section of people in chance encounters, which often prompt digressions. The book extensively covers in explanatory detail historic events including the Cromwellian settlements, early years of the Ordnance Survey in Ireland, the Famine of 1845-52 and the post-1880 Land Acts.
Hannigan’s desire line eventually brings him to Burr Point in Co Down, the most eastern extremity of Ireland. He feels that the northern countryside is “ever so slightly less hostile to a walker” since he discovers many waymarked paths. However, he finds it extremely difficult to prove the existence of an old right of way in Ireland, no matter how long people have been walking on it. And while it remains a vexed question, he brings considerable light to bear on what is a complex topic that raises passionate feelings.
Several times he breaks his journey to meet his family, or to attend meetings of Keep Ireland Open, while also delving into conversations with others who illuminate the subject. On one occasion, at what he calls an “unconference” of informal discussion on the theme of “legacy” issues about countryside access, a woman informs him: “The English have always had their land … so maybe it doesn’t matter to them if other people walk all over it. But we had it taken away from us and we had to fight to get it back, so it’s different here.”
Paul Clements is an author and travel writer

title: Probiotics claims: ‘Over 60% of supplements off the retail shelf failed our test’
description: Ali Winger has founded Cork-based Key2Biotics to bring laboratory-grade product development to probiotic brands
content:
D r Ali Winger is a life scientist with more than 20 years’ experience in biotechnology, probiotics and product innovation with some of the biggest names in the business, including Leo Pharma, Deerland Probiotics and Enzymes, Novozymes OneHealth and Novonesis.
Her career has spanned both scientific and commercial roles at a senior international level, and she could easily have spent her entire working life in the corporate sector and been well remunerated for it.
Instead, she decided to take the plunge into entrepreneurship, and in 2025 she set up Key2Biotics, which specialises in developing formulations for probiotic and gut-health supplement brands.
“Having spent almost a decade working in probiotics and supplements within two of the world’s largest biotechnology companies, I became convinced that much of the best in health innovation was being held back by the lack of access to the right development capabilities,” Winger says.
“The large nutraceutical companies typically have sophisticated scientific, formulation and quality teams supporting their products, but that infrastructure is largely inaccessible to the rest of the industry, whether that’s established brands and ingredient companies looking for external innovation, emerging brands or academic spin-outs.
“Key2Biotics was founded to bridge the gap and provide a similar depth of product innovation capability to the wider market. Our level of expertise is rarely found within traditional contract manufacturers.
“Anyone can come up with an idea for a supplement, but if it’s going to work and survive a shelf life of maybe two years or more, it needs to be backed by science. It’s not just about what’s in it.
“Many of the larger players are also ingredient suppliers, so they’re often tied to a specific list,” Winger adds. “Key2Biotics is ingredient-independent. This means our scientists can select from the latest clinically researched probiotics and other ingredients to create truly differentiated, efficacious and compliant products for our customers.”
[ Feed the ‘rainforest’ in your gut Opens in new window ]
Winger is from New Zealand, where she initially studied biochemistry. Her PhD is in mitochondrial biology and proteomics, and she earned her postdoctoral research stripes with universities in France, Australia and South Africa before moving to Ireland in 2014 to join start-up company Monaghan Biosciences. There, she led the team developing novel organisms and enzymes for use in industrial applications.
“I came to Ireland as a single mother with an 18-month old in tow and knew no one,” Winger says. “But it was a really cool job, and that’s what attracted me. I thought I’d stay a few years and then go back to New Zealand, but 12 years later and I’m still here, married to an Irish man and living in Cobh.”
Being Cork-based is a happy coincidence given the company’s focus on probiotics, as Prof Ted Dinan from University College Cork is a world-leading authority on the gut-brain axis, and some of the most significant research in this area has been carried out by academics at UCC.
“Because the big companies are focused on their own product development, the powerful and innovative research coming out of the universities, especially in Cork, has nowhere to go,” Winger says.
“Knowing the industry from the inside, I knew this wasn’t going to change any time soon, something I found deeply frustrating as a scientist. I kept feeling: this isn’t right. The science needs to get to the consumer because they deserve access to supplements that stand up to scientific scrutiny. The idea for Key2Biotics basically grew from there.
“Having built product development pipelines and set up processes and lab capabilities from scratch before I knew I could do it again,” says Winger, whose previous scientific roles included director of R&D and clinical trials with Deerland and global head of product development with Novozymes OneHealth.
From the outset Winger decided that Key2Biotics would be a niche player. “We are not a generic vitamin and mineral product development house, but if a product contains a probiotic, then we will get involved because probiotics are live organisms and have to be properly handled. You can’t just take it and put it into a capsule like you can with a vitamin or a mineral because it simply will not survive,” she says.
“Recently, we’ve taken a number of supplements off the retail shelf and tested them in our lab. Over 60 per cent did not meet the number of live probiotics stated on their label. Our expertise lies in getting the strain intact into a supplement so it provides the health benefits shown by the clinical data.”
Key2Biotics already has paying customers in the EU, the UK, North America, Asia-Pacific and Turkey, and it charges according to the service required. Its customers are global and include healthcare brands, functional food and ingredient companies, biotechnology companies, academic spin-outs and start-ups.
“We work with those looking to develop new products, translate novel science into commercial applications or access specialist probiotic and microbiome development capabilities without building them in-house,” says Winger, whose company employs six people, including three PhDs in microbiology.
“We also work with practitioners to help people with IBS [irritable bowel syndrome] or Crohn’s disease, for example, and we provide technical and commercial consultancy as well as testing services to check shelf life or if the probiotic in a product is still alive.”
External investment in the business to date is around €200,000 with support from LEO South Cork and the Enterprise Ireland pre-seed start fund. Early customer revenues have also been reinvested to build out the scientific team and the laboratory infrastructure, which comprises three labs and a clinical trial product manufacturing suite.
“We’ve bootstrapped to date but are now looking to raise a seed round of €1 million to accelerate our development,” Winger says. “We’re building something unique and have big ambitions to scale it to a global level. Our scientific platform is really strong, and we can see from customer pull where we need to go next. I’ve been in the industry for a long time, so I have good contacts, but we don’t have visibility with the supplement brands yet. Getting that is my aim for now.
“Without question finance has been the hardest part of starting the business,” Winger adds. “Building a science-led company is capital intensive, as you need specialist people and laboratory infrastructure before you can fully scale the commercial opportunity.
“The biggest challenge has been balancing the ambition to build the business properly and quickly with the reality of conserving capital at an early stage. We have achieved a huge amount with relatively limited investment so far, but access to growth capital is critical to accelerating what we can build.”

title: More children missing school today than before Covid pandemic, says ESRI report
description: Boys and girls are more likely to miss school if their parents have a harsher parenting style and if there is a lack of routine at home
content:
More children are missing school now than before the Covid pandemic, especially those from socially deprived areas and those who do not like school, new research from the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) has found.
The report used data from the longitudinal study Growing Up in Ireland to identify patterns of absence among children aged nine to 13 years old.
It compared two sets of children a decade apart – those who were born in 1998, and those who were born in 2008. There are almost 20,000 children in both of these cohorts, though not all of those would have been the correct age for this study.
Over a fifth of primary and post-primary students have chronic absence levels, that is missing 20 days or more over the school year.
The ESRI report uses longitudinal data to identify the reasons underlying this trend and whether particular groups of young people have increased absence levels.
The headline finding is that there are higher rates of school absence in Ireland since the pandemic, as has been found in many other countries.
There are also greater socio-emotional difficulties among young people now than a decade earlier, and this increase “has played an important role in driving a growth in absence levels,” the report said.
Not liking school is also more strongly predictive of absence than previously, according to the research.
[ School refusal: Parents and experts call for compassionate approach to classroom anxiety Opens in new window ]
The analysis found school absence rates were higher among unskilled manual and non-employed families, families experiencing financial strain and lone-parent households.
It also found young people with a disability are much more likely to miss school than their peers, as are those experiencing adverse life events such as bereavement or addiction in their homes.
Young people are also more likely to miss school if their parents have a harsher parenting style – for example, shouting at their child rather than explaining things – and there is a lack of routine around bedtimes and breakfast, it said.
In terms of the types of school these students attend, there are higher absence rates in DEIS schools, due to the concentration of socio-economic disadvantage in these areas.
Schools that involve students to a greater extent in decision-making tend to have lower absence rates, while absence rates are higher among young people with negative attitudes to school.
[ Chronic absenteeism from school has worsened since Covid and must be tackled Opens in new window ]
