Argentina have been dealt significant injury blows ahead of the Nations Championship, with two players ruled out and another in doubt for their game against Ireland at the Aviva Stadium next Friday week.
Felipe Contepomi has lost his brilliant utility back Santiago Carreras and prop Thomas Gallo, while Toulouse centre Santiago Chocobares is in doubt after suffering a head knock at the weekend.
Carreras, who has 70 Test caps, limped off in the 13th minute of Bath’s 23-5 defeat to his former club Gloucester on Friday and watched the remainder of the match on crutches.
The Argentina international is due to undergo a scan to determine the extent of his lower-limb injury, which appears serious.
His place in the squad has been taken by Mateo Soler, who made his Test debut off the bench against the Wallabies last month.
Gallo, capped 39 times, has also been withdrawn from the squad because of a wrist injury sustained playing for Lyon away to Bayonne on Saturday, with Dragons prop Rodrigo Martinez, who has four Test caps, called up as cover.
Chocobares, capped 31 times, missed Toulouse’s win over Perpignan last Saturday after suffering a head injury in their Champions Cup win over Exeter a week previously. Matías Moroni has been placed on standby should Chocobares be ruled out, potentially giving the experienced centre a chance to reach 100 Test caps.
Moroni is currently on 99 caps but was initially left out of Argentina’s squad for the November internationals. The 35-year-old has not played for the Pumas since suffering a facial injury against Australia in August.
Argentina have arrived in London ahead of a demanding run of fixtures against Ireland on November 6th, Italy on November 14th and France on November 21st, followed by the Nations Championship finals weekend.

title: Sharks captain André Esterhuizen ruled out for URC clash against Munster
description: Prop Phatu Ganyane sustained an elbow injury, while centre Jurenzo Julius will miss out through a hamstring issue
content:
André Esterhuizen is one of three injured Sharks players who have been ruled out of Saturday’s URC game against Munster at Thomond Park (kick-off 5.30pm), with replacements already in situ with the rest of the squad in Limerick.
Esterhuizen injured his right ankle and was forced off after less than a minute of the Sharks’ bonus-point 36-21 victory over Cardiff at the Arms Park last Friday night. Prop Phatu Ganyane sustained an elbow injury, while centre Jurenzo Julius is also nursing a hamstring problem.
The trio will undergo scans and consult specialists on their return to Durban to determine the severity of their injuries.
The squad has been bolstered by prop Cameron Dawson, winger Litelihle Bester and outside back Suleiman Hartzenberg, who joined the team on Sunday.
JP Pietersen’s team sit fifth in the URC table on five points, with Munster in ninth on 10 points, and although Clayton McMillan will be without his Ireland squad duo of Tadhg Beirne and Craig Casey, he is optimistic that summer signing Will Harrison will be fit to make his debut and likewise Edwin Edogbo for what would be his seasonal reappearance.

title: Man arrested after woman (40s) found dead in Finglas
description: Suspect (50s) located at a retail premises elsewhere in Dublin about seven hours after body discovered in Melville Terrace
content:
Gardaí investigating the killing of a woman in her 40s in Finglas, north Dublin , have arrested a man.
An area in the Melville estate has been sealed off, with gardaí searching undergrowth for evidence.
The man (50s) had left the scene and was not detained until seven hours after the woman’s body was discovered.
Gardaí were alerted and arrived at the scene on Melville Terrace shortly after 4.30am on Monday, where they found the woman’s body.
The Irish Times understands the woman, who had come from abroad to live in Ireland, suffered stab wounds in the attack.
The crime appears to have been a spur of the moment incident, rather than pre-planned, and investigating gardaí suspect the killer left behind forensic evidence that will link him to the fatal assault.
The arrested man, who was known to the woman, had fled before being tracked down by gardaí at a retail premises. Gardaí carried out searches in the estate, which is on the outskirts of Finglas, off the Melville and Jamestown roads, in an attempt to locate any items he may have discarded.
In a statement confirming the woman’s death, the Garda said: “The scene has been preserved for forensic examination by the Garda Technical Bureau. The coroner and the Office of the State Pathologist have been notified and a postmortem will be arranged in due course.
“This investigation is being co-ordinated from an incident room at Finglas Garda station under the direction of a senior investigating officer. A family liaison officer has been appointed to support the family of the deceased.”
The man was located at about 11am and taken to a Garda station in west Dublin for questioning. He is being detained under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984, which allows for gardaí to hold suspects for up to 24 hours without charge.
Gardaí were harvesting CCTV from the area around Melville area on Monday and conducting house to house inquiries, blocking off a large section of the estate.
They have appealed for witnesses to come forward and want to speak to anyone who was in the Melville Terrace area between midnight and 5am on Monday.
The force has also appealed to anyone in the area who was recording video footage, including dashcam, to make that available to the investigation team.

title: Leinster’s Tadhg Furlong cited for alleged incident against Munster’s Gavin Coombes
description: Citing follows complaint by Munster’s number eight that he had been grabbed in his groin area
content:
Tadhg Furlong has been cited for an alleged incident that occurred in the 37th minute of Saturday’s URC game between Leinster and Munster .
The Leinster prop’s citing follows a complaint by Munster number eight Gavin Coombes during the game that he had been grabbed in his groin area.

title: Séamus Power beaten in sudden-death playoff in Bermuda by Austin Smotherman
description: Playoff was scheduled for Monday after play was suspended on Sunday due to inclement weather
content:
A third career win on the PGA Tour slipped away for Séamus Power in the Butterfield Bermuda Championship on the paradise island in the Atlantic, where Austin Smotherman won in sudden death on the third playoff hole of a tournament reduced to 54 holes due to high winds.
Power’s cap was off his head and in his hands, aware of his fate as Smotherman lined up a three footer for par on their return to the par 3 16th – the signature hole used for all three playoff head-to-heads – where a handshake of congratulations to his conqueror brought a conclusion to the duel.
Yet, even in defeat, the 39-year-old Waterford man could focus on the positives after a runner-up finish that changed the entire shape of his season.
Outside the top 100 who secured their full playing rights when the FedEx Cup finished in August, Power has made the most of his second chance in the so-called FedEx Fall Series with two top-10s in three outings so far as this runner-up propelled him from 103rd up to inside the top 60 on the updated order of merit and guaranteed a full tour card on the PGA Tour for 2027.
“It gets me back to like full status again, which was frustrating this year playing, not really knowing when you’re in, when you’re not in. So, that’s nice. That was a big goal for the fall (autumn) was to get a top 100 locked up. Now I’ll have a look at the list and see if I can maybe move into that top 60 or 70, whatever that cut-off is for the first couple elevated events (in 2027).
“But made big strides for me forward in the fall, three events, two top-10s, almost winning here, so a lot of good stuff,” said Power, who will aim to take that momentum with him into back-to-back weeks in Mexico, starting with this week’s Mexico Open and next week’s World Wide Technology tournament.
Sunday’s final round was abandoned in its entirety due to high winds with Power and Smotherman – tied on 16 under – returning on Monday for the playoff, which was confined to the par 3 16th hole in conditions that had winds gusting up to 37mph.
The first playoff hole was halved in threes (with Smotherman getting up and down from greenside rough) and the second time of asking again halved in pars (with Power getting up and down from a greenside bunker, holing an eight footer to continue the fight).
With the flag location changed to the front of the green for the third playoff, Smotherman’s tee shot finished 25 feet from the hole while Power again missed the green left but finished in thick Bermuda rough from where he barely cleared the sprinkler head and managed to find the green some 30 feet away. He missed the par putt, and Smotherman two-putted for his par and the win.
“I had a chance this morning, wasn’t able to do it, which is disappointing, but overall a great week, and I can’t complain too much. I hit some good shots in the playoff, just didn’t quite judge the wind right, but that’s golf sometimes. I’ll move onwards, a lot of positives from the week,” said Power, who earned $654,000 for his runner-up finish to Smotherman who banked $1,080,000 and moved up to 51st on the FedEx Fall standings.
It was the second runner-up finish of the week for an Irish player, after Darren Clarke came up short to Rory Sabbatini – who closed with a 62 – in the Stifel Charity Classic on the Champions Tour, the first of three playoff events on that seniors circuit.

title: Man released after questioning over fatal arson attack on family’s home in Waterford city
description: Philip and Kim English and their children Callum (12) and Jayden (9) died in the fire in Birchwood estate on October 13th
content:
A man arrested in connection with a fatal arson attack on the home of the English family in Waterford city earlier this month has been released without charge.
Philip and Kim English, and their children Callum (12) and Jayden (9), died in the fire.
Two other children – a girl (14) and a boy (6) – were rescued from the house and taken to hospital in a critical condition.
In a statement on Monday, An Garda Síochána said it continues to “investigate the multiple murder” that occurred in Birchwood, Waterford city, shortly on October 13 th .
It said a man (20s) arrested on Thursday had been released without charge and a file would be prepared for the Direction of Public Prosecutions (DPP).
On Saturday, a man in his 50s and two women in their 30s were released without charge after being questioned in connection with the fatal fire. The Garda said files would be prepared for the DPP.
Two others have been charged and appeared before the courts in connection with the arson attack. Jessica Dalton (31), with an address in Waterford city, and Cian Stacey (21), of no fixed abode, are in custody after being charged with causing criminal damage to the English family’s home at Birchwood Avenue on October 13 th .
A Waterford drugs gang is suspected to have ordered the attack. Gardaí suspect that Philip English was being pressured to pay a €20,000 drug debt owed by a man he knew.

title: Pilot fatigue risk badly managed in Ireland, says international survey
description: Trade union calls for greater oversight after Republic trails European peers in latest study
content:
Trade unionists want greater Government and regulatory oversight of pilot fatigue after a survey showing the Irish air travel industry performs poorly relative to the rest of Europe in managing the problem.
European safety rules limit the hours that pilots can fly and allow them to stand down if they feel fatigued.
But most Irish pilots say the issue is poorly managed here while a significant number say they do not report fatigue to their employers as they fear “punishment” or “reprisals”, according to a survey by trade union group, the European Cockpit Association.
The Irish Airline Pilots’ Association (Ialpa) called for greater oversight of the issue in the Republic, in response to the survey.
Capt Nicola Hughes, the trade union’s international director, said Minister for Transport, Darragh O’Brien, should appoint employment inspectors to ensure that airlines comply with the law and allow pilots to exercise their safety responsibilities without fear of punitive consequences.
The report, which does not name any Irish airline, shows that 71.5 per cent of Irish pilots say fatigue risk is “not well managed” or “mostly not well managed”.
In the last such survey in 2023, the number was 61.7 per cent.
“Ireland is at or near the bottom across a range of critical fatigue-management and reporting measures, and in several areas the position has deteriorated rather than improved,” said Hughes.

title: AI firm Anthropic begins countdown to IPO with prospectus filing
description: Investors expect company to seek IPO valuation of $1.5-$1.75tn, down from $2tn projection in August
content:
Anthropic has fired the starting gun on one of the largest-ever initial public offerings, unveiling its pitch for a listing that is set to be the biggest test so far of investor appetite for the artificial intelligence boom.
The developer of Claude published its highly anticipated prospectus on Monday, detailing for the first time how it plans to sustain the exponential growth that propelled the company from a $183 billion (€163.5 billion) valuation just over a year ago to $965 billion in its last private funding round in May.
The group recently told backers that its third-quarter revenue had jumped nearly 50 per cent on the previous three months to $16.8 billion and that the company was profitable on an adjusted basis.
The nearly 240,000-word prospectus showed that in the first half of the year, Anthropic’s net loss was $81 billion, with more than $72 billion related to changes in the value of convertible notes as the company’s valuation increased.
The bulk of the remaining losses come from a near-$9 billion outlay on computing power and infrastructure.
The document also said that Anthropic plans to aggressively increase its spending in the years to come, with commitments totalling close to $800 billion over the coming decade.
Goldman Sachs was listed as having secured the coveted “lead left” role in Anthropic’s IPO.
Anthropic’s founders said AI could “raise productivity across every sector of the economy” but also warned its models “have become better able to circumvent” systems designed to make sure they act as intended. It added that it has documented cases where models “manipulate or subvert” monitoring.
The company also pointed to risks stemming from a small number of high-value clients that account for a large slice of its revenues. While it noted that “no single customer” represented more than 10 per cent of its revenue in the nine months to September, Anthropic said that a quarter over the period came from its “top five” clients.
The San Francisco-based group is pressing ahead with the IPO at a critical juncture for the AI industry, as a furious debate rages over the safety of the technology and concerns grow over whether the increasingly debt-fuelled investment boom will pay off.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 has fallen just over 7 per cent from a record high touched on October 6th.
In a sign of the more testing backdrop, existing Anthropic investors expect the company to seek a valuation of between $1.5 trillion and $1.75 trillion. In August, several of Anthropic’s backers had said they expected the group to list at a valuation of $2 trillion or more.
In its prospectus, the company’s founders said the advice they had received from multiple partners was: “Never let your company be worth a dollar more than it is actually worth.”
The publication of the prospectus puts Anthropic on track to list after the US midterm elections on November 3rd, in which the benefits and costs of the AI boom have emerged as a central issue for voters, but before the Thanksgiving holiday on November 26th.
Disclosing the prospectus is likely to ease the nerves of investors who feared that Anthropic’s window to go public was rapidly closing. It is rare for companies to list between the Thanksgiving holiday and the end of the year.
Anthropic has emerged from the shadow of arch-rival rival OpenAI this year, surpassing the creator of ChatGPT in revenues and traction with business customers.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a group of seven former OpenAI researchers and engineers after they became disillusioned with the approach to AI safety at Sam Altman ’s AI lab.
Chief executive Dario Amodei and other AI leaders including Altman and Elon Musk have called for a slowdown in AI research to ensure the technology does not run catastrophically out of control.
Investment banks including Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs will fix Anthropic’s valuation following conversations with investors over the coming weeks.
Anthropic said it would issue five different classes of shares, including Class T shares that would give its long-term benefit trust the right to appoint the majority of its board and class F stock that would hand its seven founders 50.1 per cent of the voting power. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Whiskey distilleries attract over one million visitors, industry group says
description: Irish Whiskey Association survey reports 20% jump in visitor spending, even as one-third of visitors decline tasting
content:
More than one million people visited whiskey distilleries across Ireland for the second year running, according to the Irish Whiskey Association (IWA), with tourists from the United States representing the largest national cohort.
The number is up 30,000 on the previous year, the industry group said. The 1,040,00 visitors between June 2025 and June 2026 spent approximately €50 per person on average, up around 20 per cent “as more visitors choose premium distillery experiences”, the IWA said.
The Jameson Distillery in Dublin city centre remains the most popular whiskey visitor centres followed by the Old Bushmills Distillery in Co Antrim and the Teeling Whiskey Distillery , also in Dublin city centre, according to the IWA. The Midleton Distillery Experience in Co Cork and Leitrim’s Shed Distillery , where numbers jumped 20 per cent, were also popular with visitors.
“Distillery experiences and visitor centres have become an established part of Ireland’s tourism offering” the findings from its annual survey confirm, the association said, with numbers and spending outpacing general growth in the tourism sector.
“Distilleries are drawing people interested in Ireland’s heritage, culture and craftsmanship, as well as those seeking a tasting experience”, the IWA added, noting over a third of sightseers do not consume alcohol during their visit.
Irish people represented the second highest nationality among distillery visitors after Americans, followed by Britons, Germans and French.
“Reaching one million visitors for the second year in a row shows that Irish whiskey tourism has real staying power, and that is down to the innovation and resilience of our distilleries and visitor centres,” said Eoin Ó Catháin, director of the Irish Whiskey Association.
“Visitors are spending more and travelling further, bringing that value into rural communities across the island,” he said. “Since we launched the Irish Whiskey Way last November, it has given visitors a new way to discover our distilleries”.
“With continued support from Government, State agencies and our tourism partners, Irish Whiskey can play an even bigger role in growing tourism in every region of Ireland,” Ó Catháin said.
The IWA promotes an Irish Whiskey Way, a route of 28 distilleries open to visitors across Ireland, divided into five separate regions.

title: José Mourinho left Camp Nou a manager reborn after Real Madrid’s stunning Clasico win
description: Kylian Mbappe’s late clincher breathed new life into a season that was in danger of going stale
content:
Thirteen years later, José Mourinho led Real Madrid into the Camp Nou as one team and then out again as another having secured the kind of late victory he loves and which opens up a whole new world. With just three minutes and the final reserves of energy remaining, a wonderful moment of skill from Jude Bellingham found Eduardo Camavinga and set them on one last run. Camavinga sprinted free, skilfully slipped Pau Cubarsí and pulled back for Kylian Mbappé to provide the finish. A little bit of history was written.
“The world that loves football will have stopped to watch this and they won’t have gone disappointed; this was two teams that played to win,” Mourinho said. It had been an intense, breathless ride, a proper battle, and it was his team who won it. Arriving right on time, Mbappé scored his second to make it 2-1, the Camp Nou falling quiet and their team given no time to react. They had drawn level after Mbappé’s opener – Raphinha scoring the equaliser – but could not do it again.
In the corner, Madrid’s players piled on. This was the Frenchman’s 10th goal against Barcelona but none felt quite like this. Not only was this the first time Barcelona failed to win in the league this season, their record-equalling run halted at nine; it was the first time they had failed to win any game since returning here a year ago.
“I’m not going to let them have their heads on the moon,” Mourinho said, but he knew what this meant. So much for a struggling side heading to an inevitable fall; so much for Barcelona going nine points clear, the title race run before November. There is life in Madrid and in this league. Life in their manager too: this was expertly planned and executed, the rivals who were running at 4.3 goals per game reduced to just one. Those certainties, misplaced, seemed a long way away now. A season starts here instead.
In the beginning, the ball was all Barcelona’s but no sooner had they lost it than the first shot was Madrid’s, Pedri’s startlingly loose pass allowing Arda Guler to break and fire over on four minutes. That felt like a pattern set, a portrait of the way both teams would likely approach this. So too did the way Marc Cucurella went for Lamine Yamal, the Madrid full-back seeking a way under the winger’s skin – a task in which, it had to be ­concluded, he was successful.
The impression, though, was deceptive: Madrid willing to step on to the front foot and apply a pressure with which Barcelona were not comfortable, Pedri and Rodri unable to fully settle. Where they could, they played too, Bernardo Silva included alongside Aurélien Tchouaméni.
They were also, naturally enough, ready to run. In those early phases, Fede Valverde was opening the pitch with long diagonals. From one, Mbappé went dashing up the left, leading to Joan García scooping away ­Guler’s shot. This was frantic and Madrid were finding it to their liking, as Mbappé and Yan Diomandé always looked a threat.
The hosts tried to impose control but could not. That said, they too enjoy flying into space, and from a Pedri run Raphinha shot over. Then Anthony Gordon bombed through and produced a neat back-heel for Raphinha to curl wide. The Brazilian would have another shot wide soon after, although the openings were often lost to an insistence on playing (and ­wasting) one last pass or, conversely, to snatch at shots. The half’s best opportunity came when Guler’s gorgeous ball was volleyed over by Mbappé. Back and forth it went, Gordon drawing a sharp save from Andriy Lunin.
In the midst of it all, the Camp Nou roared in indignation with each increasingly intense Cucurella challenge on Yamal, before silence fell on 41 minutes. Cucurella released Diomandé, so often the destination, who pulled across low and hard. Gerard Martín got there first but could only hit it against Mbappé and in. There was fortune there, but it had been worked for, not simply found. And when Yamal had a wonderful chance to level he wasted the opportunity, scuffing wide at the near post, a picture of a night that wasn’t his.
Barcelona came back at Madrid in the second half. The tackles around the box were racking up: Tchouaméni and Bellingham, Dean Huijsen and Ibrahima Konaté. The threat never went away, Martín ended one ­Bellingham break, but the match had tilted. On the hour, Barcelona were level. Yamal took a corner short to Pedri who slipped a clever angled, reversed ball into Raphinha to strike low into the net.
The noise rose. Raphinha was denied at one end. García saved from Guler at the other. And, Barcelona back again, Lunin made an astonishing stop from Martín’s header. Barcelona had taken a grip but not entirely, leaving them exposed to every break and leaving the game, the players and the entire place on edge. Mbappé ran at Barcelona, Pedri ran back again, leading a move that concluded with some neat footwork and a shot just wide. Huijsen then dived in to stop Frenkie de Jong and stopped a Yamal shot with his face, laying him out. The chance had been laid on by Gordon.
Barcelona insisted. Madrid, tired now, resisted. But there was still some fight in them, and still some finish too.

title: Ageing Aaron Rodgers may yet get his Super Bowl farewell
description: Pittsburgh Steelers quarter-back is not at his peak level, but a strong defence gives them a chance
content:
Aaron Rodgers is nowhere near this season’s MVP conversation. At times in his second season with the Steelers, the almost 43-year-old has shown glimpses of the player he was in his prime, slinging the ball with zest and precision, able to suss out any coverage. Other times he has looked like, well, a guy in his 40s playing a young man’s game.
Rodgers looked more like prime Rodgers in the Steelers’ gritty 16-10 win over the Saints in Paris. He was not satisfied with his side of the ball, telling reporter Molly McGrath, “I don’t think we played very good on offence today.” But Rodgers did enough to secure the win, including a 51-yard strike to DK Metcalf in the second quarter. He later scrambled for a first down on third-and-six to secure the win.
Sure, there were points left on the table – the Steelers had several stalled drives and only scored one touchdown in four red-zone trips – and 16 points against a two-win team is not impressive. But the Steelers left France with a win, a 5-2 record and a ton of upside.
So here’s a crazy thought: Could Rodgers win a Super Bowl in his final NFL season?
When you consider the parts around Rodgers, perhaps it is not so crazy. As competent as Rodgers was against the Saints, the defence stole the show. They smothered Saints quarterback Tyler Shough, and shut down the Saints run game as Steelers linebacker Patrick Queen had predicted.
This Steelers run defence is punishing and only improving. In Weeks 1-4, they allowed 4.5 yards per carry. Over the last three weeks, it has dropped to 2.8 yards per carry. All told, Pittsburgh’s defence has allowed just three touchdowns in the last 15 quarters. That is some 2025 Seahawks-level domination.
Offensively, Rodgers is no worse than Sam Darnold was last year when the Seahawks won the Super Bowl. He’s thrown 13 touchdowns and five interceptions for 1,699 yards through his first seven games this season – Darnold had 12 TDs, four picks and 1,754 yards over the same span in 2025. Saints linebacker Kaden Elliss likened Rodgers to a point guard, noting the advantage he has over other NFL quarterbacks. “Even though he’s up there in age, I think that’s an advantage to him, his mind,” Elliss said after Sunday’s game. “And I think he used that today.”
Maybe Rodgers’s football IQ could catapult Pittsburgh to a deep playoff run in the AFC. Yes, there are the perennial Super Bowl contenders like Kansas City and Buffalo, but no AFC team this season is a winning machine like the Patriots in the Brady-Belichick era.
And, after a ho-hum Super Bowl from a star power perspective, a Rodgers return to the big stage would set off fireworks.
Of course, Rodgers comes with plenty of baggage due to his commitment to his “own research” during Covid, his ridiculous antipathy towards Anthony Fauci and his habit of calling out coaches and team-mates.
Recently, though, he appears to have realised keeping his opinions to himself is probably the best course of action. His worst take over the weekend was appearing to think Peaky Blinders was set in France rather than England. He’s not exactly likable, but considering what he’s said in the past, his recent behaviour seems like progress.
Not that he is completely quiet. In Paris, when asked about the International Series, he let it be known that team owners had considered a 16-game schedule with an entire international week, where teams play all over the world and two byes. Instead, according to Rodgers, they opted for the 17-game schedule to rake in extra cash. Rodgers added that the league “may be a little tight on money,” a refreshing level of shade that will win him some fans.
Realistically, Rodgers and the Steelers will need a good deal of luck to make it to the Super Bowl this year. But that’s the case for plenty of teams. A run to the title game would send Rodgers’s smugness of the charts, but you have to admit that his final game coming on Super Bowl Sunday would be interesting.
Joe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals. Down 13-0 at the half, the Bengals looked destined for an infuriating loss, an art they specialise in. They had mustered just 49 passing yards, and were struggling to sustain drives. Meanwhile, the supposedly retooled Bengals defence could not get the Ravens off the field. At the half, Baltimore, led by a backup quarterback, had dominated the time of possession 22:20 to 7:40. Yet again, Cincinnati looked like a fringe playoff team not meeting their full potential. And after locking up star receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins for Joe Burrow in his prime, being a fringe playoff team is not acceptable.
Joe Burrow took over in the second half, throwing 4 TDs as Cincinnati scored 35 unanswered points. 22/30, 292 PASS YDS, 4 TD, 0 INT vs Ravens Is this finally the year Burrow wins MVP? pic.twitter.com/sf1sTJ2d0J https://t.co/fop5e5gOCb
Chase’s half-time team talk seems to have worked. “I told our offence [that] we can’t look at our defence the whole time. We’ve got to step this shit up and make something work,” he said after the game. Burrow, who is chasing his first league MVP, duly played out of his mind. He was essentially perfect after the break, dicing up the Ravens secondary for four touchdowns on four drives with 243 yards and an 89 per cent completion percentage. Burrow made it look effortless as he tends to do at his best.
Bucky Irving put the team on his back 💪 🏈 11 touches on 14 plays 👏 47 rushing yards 🙌 1 touchdown 📺: #TBvsCAR on FOX pic.twitter.com/zfBBLQ2JLs
How do the Bucs win a game 43-13 when Baker Mayfield only throws 64 passing yards? They faced a Panthers team who were a walking comedy of errors. Mayfield only threw 11 passes in his first game back from dislocating his thumb, and did connect with Tez Johnson for a score. The damage unsurprisingly came on the ground – Tampa rushed for 258 yards and three touchdowns, including two from Bucky Irving, who eclipsed 100 yards. The Bucs also strip-sacked Bryce Young and returned it for a touchdown. Imagine the score if Mayfield was slinging the rock.
Bo Nix came into Sunday’s game with just 37 rushing yards all season. So when the Broncos quarterback nearly doubled that total in one play – a 62-yard touchdown run that gave Denver a late second-quarter lead over Arizona – hell yeah, he was going to add a flourish.
BO NIX 62-YARD TOUCHDOWN RUN DENvsAZ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/sxC4uWF33r
The spin move at the goalline may not have been necessary, but it must have been cathartic. Nix has been criticised for not providing an offensive spark, even though Denver came into the game at 4-2 after negotiating one of the league’s toughest schedules. But Nix looked far more comfortable – and at times electric – in Sunday’s 30-16 win. He finished with the one long rushing touchdown, and 222 passing yards. – Guardian

title: Status-yellow wind warning for 11 counties to come into effect this afternoon
description: Strong and gusty south to southwest winds set to sweep across Ireland again as some continue to deal with impacts of Storm Boelo
content:
A status-yellow weather warning covering 11 counties will come into effect on Monday afternoon, with strong and gusty south to southwest winds set to sweep over Ireland again.
The Met Éireann wind warning, which comes after storms Austen and Boelo, covers counties Carlow , Clare , Cork , Donegal , Galway , Kerry , Kilkenny , Mayo , Waterford , Wexford and Wicklow from 5pm until midnight.
The forecaster said the public should be aware of potential impacts including difficult travel conditions, fallen trees and branches, and large coastal waves.
The UK met office has also issued a yellow wind warning for Antrim , Down and Derry from 3am until midnight on Tuesday.
A status-yellow rain warning for Cork and Kerry, which advised of the potential for localised flooding, expired at 9am.
More than 40,000 homes and businesses were left without power on Sunday morning following Storm Boelo, with ESB Networks crews restoring power to the majority of these over the course of the day. The northwest and west regions were hardest hit.
“There are a number of homes, farms and businesses still without electricity as a result of Storm Boelo in the northwest of the country,” the company said in a statement on Monday.
“ESB Networks crews, including teams from other parts of the country, have been deployed since first light this morning to restore power to all remaining customers.”
[ Further weather warnings issued as thousands remain without power after Storm Boelo Opens in new window ]
Monday morning will start wet and breezy with widespread rain and drizzle along with moderate to fresh and gusty south to southeast winds. The rain will clear from southern and eastern areas during the afternoon, but another spell of rain will move in from the southwest during the late afternoon and evening, becoming widespread by early night. Highest temperatures will be between 14 and 17 degrees.
Tuesday will be a blustery day with fresh to strong southwesterly winds, veering westerly through the day. A mix of sunshine and showers throughout the day, with some turning heavy and the chance of isolated thunderstorms. Highest temperatures will be between nine to 12 degrees.
Wednesday will be mostly cloudy at first with lingering patches of light rain and drizzle. It will brighten up through the morning and afternoon with sunny spells developing and just isolated showers. Highest temperatures will be between 13 and 16 degrees.
Patchy light rain and drizzle will clear on Thursday morning to sunny spells and scattered light showers. Cloud will again build from the west through the afternoon, followed by rain and drizzle. Highest temperatures will be between 12 to 15 degrees, in moderate to fresh south-easterly winds.
Met Éireann said Friday is expected to be another dull and breezy day with rain spreading eastward. However, current indications suggest it will turn more settled next weekend.

title: Andy Irvine pays tribute to Dónal Lunny: ‘The first 18 months of Planxty were the most joyous of my life up to then’
description: Irvine – a founding member of Planxty – was thrilled by Lunny’s empathy, both as a friend and as a musician
content:
I am devastated by the loss of my great friend and brilliant musician, Dónal Lunny . It has taken me a few days to even begin to get used to the fact that he is no longer with us . I wanted to pen my own early memories of our friendship.
We met first in the 1960s; I was looking for somewhere to live and had an appointment to view a bedsit in Grosvenor Road in Dublin’s Rathmines . I rang the bell and the door was opened by Dónal, who lived there. He would always tell the story that I stood there “festooned” with musical instruments. We had a cup of tea and the owner arrived. I did not get the bedsit unfortunately (musicians were viewed with suspicion in those days).
In 1970, after I came home from eastern Europe, Dónal and I began to play together. Seán Mac Réamoinn , the famous broadcaster and journalist, was involved in the Irish-Soviet Friendship Society and asked both of us – independently – if we would play for half an hour to entertain Russian guests at a forthcoming meeting.
Dónal and I arrived and had about half an hour to work up a programme, having never played together before. It was then that I got my first taste of his brilliance. The speed with which he got a grip on the three or four songs I had planned to play thrilled me, and we became close friends and played together for the next 54 years.
I had brought back a Greek bouzouki from my Balkan travels and Dónal discovered it one day, lying in a pile of other instruments in my room. He picked it up and started learning his way around it. After about an hour, he had made such progress, even though he was left-handed and it was set up for a right-hander, that I just gave it to him.
[ Dónal Lunny obituary: Innovative musician who leaves indelible mark on Irish folk and traditional music Opens in new window ]
We formed “The Mugs Gig” together after that, downstairs in Slattery’s of Capel Street (later, we managed to move upstairs to the bigger venue where Planxty – even before it got its name – made its debut in early 1972).
Dónal and I played concerts in The Exam Hall in Trinity and recorded for Shay Healy ’s radio programme. I was thrilled by his empathy, both as a friend and as a musician. He had the wonderful ability of playing the perfect accompaniment to my songs. Later, musicians of all kinds would discover this same ability.
Christy Moore , who was a long-time friend of Dónal’s, asked us, and Liam O’Flynn , to play on a recording he was planning, which later became Prosperous. It was quite a hit and Christy asked me would I be interested in forming a band.
This took me by complete surprise and I said, “Well, who would be in it?” He said Dónal and Liam.
[ Andy Irvine on Dónal Lunny: ‘He glued Planxty together and made the structure work’ Opens in new window ]
I said: “But surely Liam wouldn’t be interested.”
He said: “Oh yes he is, very interested.”
That left me only one option. The first 18 months of Planxty were the most joyous of my life up to that point. Off stage – and often even on stage – Dónal and Christy were like a comedy double act. They had us all in stitches as we rolled around the country in our Transit van. We were popular, we were full of humour, we loved each other and ... we were loved.
Dónal’s music is an inspiration and though he is no longer present, his name and all he stood for will be remembered for all time.

title: Marathon runner gets back on track after robotic surgery for ‘neobladder’
description: Brian Lenihan getting ready to race again after successful procedure at St Vincent’s hospital in Dublin
content:
It was July 2025 when Brian Lenihan first noticed blood in his urine. It began as a small amount, but the then 44-year-old became concerned when it increased to alarming quantities, which prompted him to see a doctor.
“I was diagnosed with bladder cancer. I remember being in complete shock. That was the worst minute, hour, day of the whole journey. When you hear the word cancer, you just wonder is this going to be terminal?” he said.
Lenihan, a keen marathon runner, began chemotherapy and immunotherapy in September of that year.
For many people, bladder cancer surgery means having a bladder removed and living with a stoma bag – a small, soft, waterproof pouch that attaches to an abdominal opening to collect waste from the body.
The Limerick man, who now lives in south Dublin, was offered an alternative: a neobladder.
In this procedure, a team at St Vincent’s hospital in Dublin performed robotic surgery to remove his bladder and replace it with a new internal pouch created from a segment of his intestine. Following rehabilitation, it now operates like a normal bladder.
“You wouldn’t know unless I told you. The incision for the surgery was so small as well,” he said.
Dr Nikita Bhatt, a urological surgeon who specialises in robotic surgery and who led the operation, said Lenihan was one of the first patients in Ireland to have this surgery done robotically.
“If you get your bladder out, obviously you need a way to remove the urine through either a stoma bag or a neobladder, which is when a new bladder is formed from your bowel.”
However, Bhatt said until now the vast majority of neobladder surgeries have been done through open surgery, which has a high risk of complications.
“Recovery is very prolonged. But since they’ve been doing robotic surgery, it’s much better because people can go home. His operation took eight hours, it was completely keyhole and was able to start using his neobladder within three weeks,” she said.
Bhatt has done three of these surgeries this year so far and has another one scheduled next month. She said for Lenihan it means he doesn’t have a bladder, but his body operates as if he does.
“A stoma bag is very obvious. It carries a certain level of stigma,” she said, adding that bladder cancer is increasing in younger ages and alternative options are better to improve a person’s quality of life after cancer.
The shorter recovery time was something for which Lenihan was particularly grateful.
[ Irish researchers discover how cancers evade chemotherapy by entering ‘zombie-like state’ Opens in new window ]
“I was in hospital for eight days and then I was released home under what’s called the virtual wards. So I had an iPad and I checked in twice a day with my vital signs. That was great, it really helped my recovery because it’s just impossible to relax and sleep in a hospital,” he said.
“For four weeks, I was told not to lift the kids, and to do absolutely no heavy lifting because there was lots of internal trauma. Two months later, I was able to go back out for a run. Recovery isn’t linear; there are great days and some you feel crap. But those days are now less and less.”
[ At 49 I was a mum, a wife, a runner and constantly tired. Then one day I collapsed at work Opens in new window ]
Lenihan’s hope after surgery was to run this year’s Dublin marathon, having ran 13 others in the past.
While he made the decision to skip Sunday’s run, it was more from a competitive point of view than due to his ability to run the 26 miles.
“I was quite a competitive runner – 10 months before my diagnosis I ran Dublin in 2 hours 32 [minutes]. But I just felt like my energy wasn’t there, that I would have to walk some of the last 10km, and I didn’t want that,” he said.
“For me, running the 42km wasn’t the difficult part. It was to run for a specific time that was more difficult. But I’ll be on a marathon starting line very shortly. Dublin only happens once a year, but there are lots of other races.”

title: Sweden’s Centre Party leader hands task of forming government back to parliament speaker
description: Andreas Norlen could decide ‌to schedule ⁠new parliamentary vote for prime minister
content:
Swedish Centre Party leader ‌Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist said on Monday she was handing the ‌process of forming a government back to parliament speaker Andreas Norlen, ​as widely expected, after he tasked her a week ago with trying to do so.
An election in Sweden last month gave the centre-left ​bloc a narrow majority in parliament , but while all four opposition ⁠parties favour Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson as ‌prime minister, ‌they ​do not agree on who should be part of a new government.
⁠Ringqvist told ​reporters on Monday ​there was no majority for a centrist government. “There ‌is a clear demand for ​solutions that can bring together a broader majority,” ⁠she said. “However, the ⁠parliamentary ​situation makes it difficult at present to translate that support into a government.”
Andersson earlier this month lost a parliamentary vote to form a government.
Norlen could now decide ‌to schedule a ⁠new parliamentary vote for prime minister regardless, or hand the task of government-formation to ‌the leader of another party.
[ The Irish Times view on the Swedish election: tightest of wins for the centre-left Opens in new window ]
The centre-left opposition won 176 seats to 173 in ​September ​for prime minister Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing bloc. – Reuters

title: Meta plans $95bn stock offering to bankroll AI expansion
description: Chipmakers Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom will act as cornerstone investors
content:
Meta is planning to raise $95 Billion (€85 billion) in a stock offering to fuel its massive artificial intelligence infrastructure spending, backed by chipmakers Nvidia , AMD and Broadcom, who will act as cornerstone investors.
The parent of Instagram and WhatsApp last week reported a 26 per cent jump in sales in the third quarter, ahead of analysts’ estimates, and projected capital spending of up to $145 billion this year, as it warned investors it would need to raise “hundreds of billions of dollars” over several years to fund its bet on AI.
The news sent shares in Mark Zuckerberg ’s social media group tumbling by 7 per cent on Thursday.
Meta kicked off that fundraising process on Monday with a plan to raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings. It also plans to raise a further $60 billion via an “at the market” programme.
“AI is creating significant opportunities for Meta across its core business and new products and services,” the Silicon Valley company said. “Meta’s AI investments are already generating tangible returns through increased engagement, improved advertising performance and increased monetisation.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: UCD professor of chemical engineering leaves estate worth €3.6m
description: Equestrian trainer Pamela Kerr leaves estate valued at €2.78 million
content:
Jim Walsh, a former head of the department of chemical engineering at University College Dublin (UCD) , left an estate valued at more than €3.6 million when he died in January, probate documents show.
Walsh, who was aged 93 when he died, had a long career at UCD. He worked on the design of wind tunnels and the drying and thermal degradation of biological materials in his early years and later moved into the area of atmospheric pollution.
He became the Irish national delegate on the European Commission committee on Physico-Chemical Behaviour of Atmospheric Pollutants, and was a consultant to the OECD on the teaching of Applied Mathematics in Irish engineering schools.
Walsh was also a member of the Royal Irish Academy ’s National Committee for Theoretical and Applied Mechanics, and served as a long-term member of the UCD governing body’s Computer Policy Committee.
Outside of his professional life, he was a very active member of local community walking groups such as Let’s Walk and Talk, where he frequently led educational and social walks around UCD, Blackrock, Sandymount and Dún Laoghaire.
Patricia Martin Farrington, an actor with an address at Brighton Terrace, Dublin, left an estate valued at €1.429 million when she died in January 2025, papers published by the Probate Office in Dublin show.
Martin Farrington was primarily a theatre actor who performed in independent and local theatrical productions across Dublin throughout the mid-20th century.
She was the wife of the late Conor Farrington , a well-known actor, playwright and member of the RTÉ Players, who died in 1996. Before her marriage to Farrington, she was married to Sean Martin.
Martin Farrington’s notable creative ties lay behind the scenes and within collaborative circles. She frequently supported, performed in and collaborated on regional dramatic workshops, independent stage readings and local arts productions.
Equestrian trainer Pamela Kerr, aka Pam Horan, left an estate valued at €2.78 million when she died in August 2025, probate papers show. She was based at Broomfield Equestrian Centre in Tinahely, Co Wicklow.
Through her work at Broomfield, Kerr spent decades training and breeding ponies and running pony camps. She was known for her horsemanship and teaching skills, and dedication to local hunting, riding, and hunter trials.
She dedicated much of her life to guiding, training and championing her daughter, Kate Kerr-Horan, who became a Paralympic equestrian .
When Kate was four years old, she survived a near-fatal riding-related incident that left her with deep physical challenges and required her to relearn how to walk and talk.
Under her mother’s guidance, Kate returned to the saddle to win at the Dublin Horse Show aged seven. She grew up to become an international Para-Equestrian dressage rider representing Ireland.
Senior Counsel George Brady, of Donnybrook, Dublin, left an estate valued at €1.788 million when he died in September of last year.
He was a known for dedicating time to helping younger, junior barristers to master complex cases involving competing wills, missing title deeds and land law.
He was married for 56 years to Margaret Brady (née Lysaght), who was among the first 100 women called to the Irish Bar.

title: ‘This is a symbol for Europe’: Joy on streets of Belgrade after Vucic election defeat
description: Student movement ousts Serbian strongman from power, ushering in a seismic political shift in Balkan country
author_name: Ana Milosavljevic in Belgrade, Ashifa Kassam
content:
Standing on the streets of Belgrade, as passing cars honked excitedly and revellers high-fived police officers, Sara (24) gestures to her surroundings to explain just how much things had changed for Serbia’s student-led movement.
Moments earlier, the country’s long-standing president, Aleksandar Vucic, had conceded defeat to the student movement , ushering in a seismic political shift in the Balkan country.
It was a surreal reversal of fortunes for the hundreds of thousands of people who had spent nearly two years peacefully protesting against a ruling power that had become increasingly authoritarian.
“It’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors,” says Sara.
The realisation saw people pour into streets across Serbia to mark the incredible trajectory.
[ Brazil and Serbia show that progressive forces can defeat the far right Opens in new window ]
In Novi Sad – where the protests had begun in November 2024 following the deadly collapse of a train station roof – thousands gathered in celebration after Vucic conceded that the Students’ List movement had likely won between 135 and 140 seats in the ‌250-seat parliament, while his rightwing SNS party had 105, citing preliminary results.
In Belgrade, tens of thousands of people flooded the city’s main boulevards, chanting euphorically, waving flags and setting off flares against an unrelenting backdrop of honking car horns.
“Oh my gosh, I don’t know how to explain it,” says Tamara (35). “I’m so happy and excited.”
Sunday’s results would ultimately set Serbia on a path towards “freedom and hope for a better tomorrow”, she says. But she was under no illusions that it would come easily.
“I know we have a tough period ahead of us, I do,” she adds. “But even so, it’s a huge relief and gives us energy to keep going.”
The tremendous task of reversing the country’s drift towards authoritarianism and deeply entrenched corruption now falls to the list of 250 candidates, which includes more than 160 doctorates, as well as a sprinkling of farmers, athletes and others.
[ EU warns Serbia over funeral for ‘Butcher of Bosnia’ Ratko Mladic Opens in new window ]
Adding to the challenge is the fact that the students’ policy platform downplayed some of the country’s more divisive issues: the question of future EU membership has been left to a referendum, and the fact Kosovo is claimed as an integral part of Serbia.
On Sunday, however, many were simply thrilled to celebrate the end of a government that had become known for routinely threatening its critics and chipping away at press freedoms.
“The people have won!” says Nebojsa Cosic. “The people defeated a dictator! The people will lead Serbia!” he says, as those in the street linked arms to dance the traditional Serbian folk dance, Kolo.
The crowds were also swift to descend on the central park in Belgrade where Vucic’s loyalists had camped out for more than a year, joyfully tearing down the fences and tents that had blocked off access to the park.
Vucic had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party in the election in hope of returning to the post of prime minister, which he had left in 2017 .
Duško Suvajac (52) points to the broader implications as the elections kicked off 10 pivotal days of ballots across the globe in which the authoritarian right is facing off against pro-democracy forces.
“This is a symbol for Europe and the world,” he says. “It’s a demonstration of how freedom can defeat evil.”
As he spoke, those around him hugged, kissed, cried and screamed with joy. For many, it was a singular moment to reclaim the same streets where the student-led call for change had been met by police wielding batons and tear gas and even a suspected sound cannon.
“It’s simply the realisation of our dream,” says Sara. “We will remember this moment for the rest of our lives.” – Guardian

title: ‘Turnout has sort of drained’: Democrats battle to mobilise Georgia’s black voters
description: Rev Al Sharpton warns of an epidemic of ‘amnesia’ over the struggles of the civil rights generation
content:
Big Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church, grey-stoned and imposing, has been a fixture on Sweet Auburn Avenue since the 1880s, and its historical range of speakers has encompassed everyone from president William Taft, in 1911, to Nelson Mandela.
On Sunday morning, the congregation listened to a sermon from Rev Al Sharpton, who took an early flight to the city as part of a concerted effort to encourage early voters in the city’s Fourth Ward. Sharpton stuck around for the day, attending a lunchtime class on AI education held in Bishop Hall before participating in a leg of the Souls to the Polls initiative that ferried people from the necklace of African Methodist Episcopal (AME) churches around Auburn to the polling sites and home again.
“The entire purpose of the early voting period here in Georgia is to make sure people have an opportunity to exercise their franchise,” pastor Jay Augustine explains before accompanying Sharpton on a walk through Auburn.
“There have been challenges, and threats of challenges and threats of more challenges, so we have to encourage people to not wait until election day but to take advantage of the early voting period. We knew enthusiasm would be high because of economic conditions across the country. People vote with their pocket so we knew there would be good turnout. But predictably turnout has sort of drained in the past couple of days. You have to finish strong.”
Atlanta sits in Fulton County, the potent symbol of Donald Trump ’s persistent and debunked allegation that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. It was to Fulton County Jail that Trump voluntarily presented himself in August 2024 when he was indicted, by grand jury, on racketeering charges, emanating from his notorious call to Brad Raffensperger, the Georgia secretary of state, on January 2nd, 2021, when he told the official of his need to “find 11,780 votes” that would flip the state into a Republican victory. His mug shot was quickly repackaged and branded on Trump merchandise during his election campaign.
The case was dropped following Trump’s return to the White House.
In January 2026, the FBI conducted an early morning raid on a Fulton County election hub, seizing 2020 election records for examination.
“We are very cognisant here in Fulton County of the price that has been paid in the past for the exercise of the franchise,” Augustine says.
“And we are also very cognisant of the fact that there was a seizure of ballot boxes here. It doesn’t make sense that years and years later we still are litigating and talking about and contemplating fraud-no-fraud from that number of years ago.
“There’s been investigation after investigation and allegation and there has been no credible evidence found that there was any fraud whatsoever with respect to the 2020 election here in Fulton County. But we continue to talk about that because of one person’s ego.”
That recent history has formed the backdrop to the persistent message by Jon Ossoff, the incumbent in the Georgia senatorial race against Mike Collins. In his message to mark the Souls to the Polls initiative, which has roots in the city’s civil rights tradition, Ossoff said that the Georgia Democratic vote will represent a “mobilisation so massive and with a defence of voting rights so fierce that no plot against the franchise can foil the will of the people”.
A year ago, Republican s eyed Ossoff as a potential vulnerability in the midterms. But his formidable campaign fundraising and withering repudiations of Trump’s administration during his televised debates with Mike Collins have belied all expectation. Now, Ossoff is regarded as a strong fancy to retain his seat, with an eight-point lead in the latest polls, and his performances have elicited speculation about a presidential candidacy.
“Would I be surprised?” says Diane McCoy, who stopped to speak after voting.
“I hadn’t given him much thought as a presidential candidate. But I wouldn’t be surprised. I do like senator Ossoff. I feel like he has the interests of Georgia in his heart and mind. He wants to see housing, groceries lower and he wants the things that as a Democrat I feel that I am interested in.”
A native Atlantan, McCoy says she hasn’t noticed the impacts of the Trump administration on her city so much as a general pessimism among her friends when it comes to the political landscape.
“I think African-American people are discouraged – when Obama was president it felt more hopeful and more like the country was going in the right direction. So especially among my friends we are starting to feel discouraged by things we see and hear. I mean some of the dialogue and the language coming out of the White House ... if I had said, my parents would have slapped me! It’s gone really horrific. The language and the things that are acceptable. I do have conservative values when it comes to how grown-ups and our elected officials should conduct themselves. And I’m appalled.”
McCoy decided to vote on Sunday on the assumption that the voting centre would be quiet only to arrive upon the Souls to the Polls jamboree taking place outside. But footfall on what is a gorgeous Sunday afternoon is slow.
Sharon Trasher, who worships at Bethel AME, had come along to participate, although she has already cast her vote.
“I was there at noon on the first day,” she says during the bus trip across the city before explaining why she believes these midterms will be so consequential.
“I almost broke the machine, actually. I think if you value your freedom across the world – not just in Atlanta, Georgia – but in Ireland, in Sweden, everywhere ... if you value your freedom and your children’s freedom, wildlife, the oceans, nature ... then you will vote against what they are calling the right-wing takeover.”
But Trasher worried about what her ears and eyes have suggested at a lack of engagement among young people.
“From what I’m hearing, listening to news and talk radio – APR, BBC World Service – the younger voters are not engaging as they should be. Did you notice that too? It’s really sad because they are the ones who stand to lose the most.”
We talk for a while about the relative obscurity of the midterm elections on the street in comparison to the incessant media coverage. Apart from the Souls to the Polls mobilisation, the streets around Auburn are Sunday-sleepy. The city’s parks, like Piedmont and Grant, are a different story.
Next week will be a crowded week for the city, whose women’s basketball team, Atlanta Dream, is locked in a riveting WNBA finals series against Golden State Valkyries.
Former president Barack Obama will be here on Wednesday to hold a rally with Ossoff and Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic candidate for governor and a former mayor of Atlanta. Her race, against Rick Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive of the company he founded, is a near-dead heat in the polls.
When Sharon Trasher thinks back to when she cast her first vote at 18, she wonders if today’s first-time-voter generation has become blase about that right.
“I don’t know ... I sometimes think when you are too privileged, you forget about what others have suffered for you to get where you are today.”
I suggest that maybe younger people don’t have enough time to go through the series of down-ballot elections in every state. It’s an idea to which she gives short shrift.
“Well, you better make time – because social media can’t pay your bills.”
Her point echoes that of Al Sharpton’s when he spoke to the Big Bethel congregation on Sunday morning, warning of an epidemic of “amnesia” among the generation of black Americans who do not have living recall of the struggles of the civil rights generation.
Meanwhile, the president continues to pummel voters with warnings about the Democratic threats, and sweeteners. He visited Georgia as recently as Saturday, announcing during his rally that German car manufacturer Audi has plans to build a $4 billion factory in Georgia, creating 4,500 jobs. The agreement, Trump said, was a direct consequence of the tariffs policy. During his speech, he also denounced Ossoff as a “far-left extremist that votes to destroy everything Georgia values”.
All indicators point to a successful night for Ossoff and the Democrats, but on the streets, the late push to reach voters continued.
“I was literally with him last night and that was one of the points he was making,” pastor Augustine said.
“This cannot be a small distinguishable margin of victory. We need to send a resounding message to make sure that this administration understands its policies are unpopular. It’s got to be a landslide margin of victory to shut down doubters.”

title: Cinntí muiníneacha Shinn Féin do thoghchán an Tionóil
description: Tá sé i gceist ag Sinn Féin triúr MP reatha a chur san iomaíocht do shuíocháin i gCnoc an Anfa in 2027
content:
D’fhógair Sinn Féin an tseachtain seo caite go mbeidh triúr MP dá gcuid ag seasamh i dtoghchán an Tionóil i mí Bealtaine na bliana seo chugainn agus súil dháiríre acu suíocháin a bhaint. I gcúpla cás acu sin is bua stairiúil a bheadh i gceist don pháirtí agus don phobal náisiúnach ó thuaidh trí chéile.
Le cúpla seachtain anuas, tá Sinn Féin i ndiaidh láithreacht láidir a chur in iúl sna meáin maidir le seasamh an pháirtí ar cheist Dhroim Crí agus ar roinnt ábhair eile, agus iad ag súil anois le torthaí níos fearr a fheiceáil sna pobalbhreitheanna agus, níos tábhachtaí, i dtorthaí an dtoghchán don Tionól agus do na Comhairlí Áitiúla a bheidh ar siúl ar an bhliain seo chugainn.
Fógraíodh go mbeidh Chris Hazzard, atá ina MP don Dún Theas i láthair na huaire, ag seasamh i dtoghcheantar Loch Cuan agus é ag iarraidh suíochán a fháil sa Tionól. Agus athruithe curtha i bhfeidhm ar theorainn an toghcheantair le déanaí, creideann Sinn Féin gur féidir leo suíochán a bhaint amach ann den chéad uair riamh. Ní raibh MLA náisiúnach i Loch Cuan i stair an Tionóil riamh, agus mar sin de bua ollmhór a bheadh ann dá n-éireodh leo.
Ní raibh MLA náisiúnach i Loch Cuan i stair an Tionóil riamh, agus mar sin de bua ollmhór a bheadh ann dá n-éireodh leo.
Bhí Hazzard ina MLA sa Dhún Theas ó 2012 go 2017, agus bhí sé ina Aire Bonneagair ag Cnoc an Anfa ó 2016 go 2017 nuair a thit an Feidhmeannas. Toghadh é i dtoghchán Westminster in 2017, an chéad bhall de Shinn Féin chun suíochán a bhaint sa Dún Theas, a bhí i lámha an SDLP le fada an lá go dtí sin.
Is é Paul Maskey an t-iarrthóir nua in Iarthar Bhéal Feirste. Is ag Sinn Féin atá ceithre shuíochán amach as na cúig cinn sa toghcheantar, agus súil ag an pháirtí na suíocháin siúd ar fad a choinneáil. Fógraíodh nach mbeidh an MLA reatha Aisling Reilly ag seasamh mar iarrthóir sa chéad toghchán eile de bharr cúrsaí sláinte, agus is é Maskey anois a bheidh ag seasamh ina háit. Tá Paul Maskey ina MP ó 2011, agus leis an chinneadh seo tá próifíl ard ag gach duine den cheathrar iarrthóirí a bheidh ag Sinn Féin sa rás seo.
Cé go bhfuil Sinn Féin an-láidir in Iarthar Bhéal Feirste, seans go mbeidh sé dúshlánach go leor acu na suíocháin uilig a choinneáil agus an SDLP, PBP agus DUP in iomaíocht chun suíochán a bhaint amach sa toghcheantar chomh maith.
I dtoghcheantar Bhéal Feirste Theas agus an Dún Láir, is í an MP reatha do cheantar Fhear Manach agus Thír Eoghain Theas, Pat Cullen, atá le seasamh ann. Is de bhunadh Thír Eoghain í Cullen ach tá sí ina cónaí i mBéal Feirste le fada an lá. Bhí sí ina Príomhfheidhmeannach ar Choláiste Ríoga an Altranais sa Ríocht Aontaithe le blianta fada sula ndeachaigh sí isteach i saol na polaitíochta nuair a sheas sí i dtoghchán Westminster in 2024.
Beidh Cullen ag seasamh don pháirtí in éineacht le Deirdre Hargey, atá ina MLA don cheantar ó 2020 agus a bhí mar Aire Pobal ag pointe amháin. Sprioc iontach uaillmhianach atá ann don pháirtí an dara hiarrthóir a chur isteach sa toghcheantar seo, go háirithe agus an SDLP agus Páirtí na Comhghuaillíochta ag súil le tacaíocht láidir a mhealladh sa cheantar chomh maith. Is é seo an cás is dúshlánaí as na trí cinn maidir le MP ag aimsiú suíochán sa Tionól. Tá próifíl ard ag Hargey i mBéal Feirste Theas agus níl raibh an páirtí fiú cóngarach don dara suíochán ag an toghchán Tionóil deireanach.
Má éiríonn leis an chur chuige seo, spreagfar fothoghcháin do na suíocháin Westminster a bheadh folamh, agus dúshlán as an nua a bheadh sa mhéid sin do na páirtithe uilig. Go deimhin, dá dtarlódh siad, bheadh seans maith ann go mbeadh na toghcháin seo ag titim amach sa tréimhse chéanna ina mbeadh Feidhmeannas úr ag iarraidh a chosa a aimsiú agus Clár Rialtais a chur le chéile. Ach straitéis uaillmhianach atá ann chun cuid de na polaiteoirí is aitheanta atá ag Sinn Féin ó thuaidh a bhogadh chuig an Tionól, áit a mbeadh siad níos feiceálaí agus ar fáil le bheith ceaptha ina n-airí amach anseo chomh maith.
Cuirfidh na cinntí seo imní ar an SDLP agus ar Pháirtí na Comhghuaillíochta ach go háirithe. I mBéal Feirste Theas agus sa Dún Láir, tá dhá shuíochán ag Páirtí na Comhghuaillíochta agus is ón fhoinse sin a mbeidh Sinn Féin ag súil le tacaíocht a mhealladh. Mar an gcéanna i dtoghcheantar Loch Cuan, beidh Sinn Féin ag meas gur féidir leo an bua féideartha stairiúil a úsáid chun vótóirí Pháirtí na Comhghuaillíochta agus an SDLP a tharraingt chucu féin.
Gan amhras, tá Sinn Féin ag bogadh i dtreo dearfach le tamall anuas agus borradh ag teacht faoi fhuinneamh an pháirtí arís i ndiaidh cúpla bliain dheacair, ó tharla gur chuir deacrachtaí san Fheidhmeannas bac ar an pháirtí spriocanna a bhaint amach. Ach léiríonn na cinntí toghcháin seo go mothaíonn an páirtí an-mhuiníneach faoi na deiseanna atá rompu sa bhliain seo chugainn.

title: Brazil and Serbia show that progressive forces can defeat the far right
description: Lula’s stunning election win came after a massive mobilisation of the voters with most to lose from a Flávio Bolsonaro presidency
content:
Lula’s dramatic comeback to win Sunday’s presidential election in Brazil has put a halt to the right-wing advance across Latin America. It offers hope and a lesson to progressive movements around the world.
By the time Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva began his speech at a victory rally in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday night, his voice was hoarse from campaigning and he was chugging from a water bottle. After a few sentences, he handed the microphone to his vice-president, Geraldo Alckmin, a political centrist with strong ties to Brazil’s business community.
Alckmin will be a crucial figure in Brazil’s efforts to calm financial markets that were betting on a win for Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-winger whose margin of victory in the first round appeared to make him unstoppable. Bolsonaro had promised to cut taxes for the rich and slash welfare spending for the poor, an agenda that warmed the cockles of investors’ hearts.
Focusing Brazilian voters’ attention on Bolsonaro’s austerity plans was part of the key to Lula’s success in turning a 2.2 million vote deficit three weeks ago into a winning margin of four million votes on Sunday.
But Lula’s 51.8 per cent to 48.2 per cent victory was chiefly the result of a massive mobilisation of the voters with most to lose from a Bolsonaro presidency, led by the young and the less well-off.
When Lula took the microphone back from his vice-president, much of his acceptance speech was devoted to thanking those who helped him, among them a man in a football jersey standing next to him. This was André Janones, a 42-year-old lawyer and federal deputy who led a social media campaign that transformed Lula’s strategy between the first and second rounds.
The digital campaign mobilised millions behind pro-Lula demonstrations on social media platforms and on the streets, even persuading the president to get his first smartphone and to make short videos. The surge of campaigning energy behind Lula contrasted with the complacency that appeared to take hold of Bolsonaro as he prepared to coast to victory aloft a wave of fear, greed and defeatism.
Thousands of kilometres away in Serbia, voters on Sunday were also demonstrating the power of campaigning as candidates backed by student protesters defeated former president Aleksandar Vucic in a parliamentary election. Vucic, who had resigned as president to seek the position of prime minister, conceded defeat on Sunday as projections pointed to the Student List winning between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-member parliament, compared to his list’s 105.
Two years of protesting, organising and campaigning that began after the collapse of a railway canopy in Novi Sad in November 2024, facing police violence and state repression, have brought the student movement this far.
The Student List has promised a free media landscape, anti-corruption legislation and the safeguarding of judicial independence as well as better education, healthcare and access to housing.
Lula’s upset victory in Brazil has important geopolitical implications in halting the spread of right-wing governments across Latin America and challenging Donald Trump’s ambitions in the region.
But Brazil and Serbia also reminded the world on Sunday that progressive forces can defeat the far right and dislodge entrenched power but if they wish to do so, they must organise.
