title: Na sráideanna beannaithe
description: Ba le daltaí scoile a thosnaigh na léirsithe is déanaí sa bhFrainc
content:
Is é dícheall an staraí scríobh faoin aimsir chaite le haon chruinneas. Go deimhin, dá bhféadfaí sin bheadh go leor acu ar aon fhocal agus ar aon tuairim, rud is annamh. Is deacra go mór is go fada, áfach, trácht go beacht ar a bhfuil ar siúl inár dtimpeall i láthair na huaire, ar urlár leathan fairsing an lae. Tá cabaireacht gan chríoch ó na hilmheáin agus tráchtaireacht go farrabachall agus tuairimíocht saor le fáil ó thaobh na dtaobhanna níos mó ná mar a bhí riamh, agus teacht ag an ngnáthdhuine sa tsráid nó i ndoircheacht a bhotha féin air go dtí go bhfuil bolg a chloiginn stuptha le hiomad eolais. Is í an cheist go dtéann dínn a réiteach le siúráil ar bith, ná cad is brí leis seo go léir, cá bhfuil an domhan agus an daonnacht ag dul?
Bheadh sé furasta go leor a áiteamh nach bhfuil sna círéibeanna a bhí agus atá ar siúl sa bhFrainc le tamall anuas ach gníomh sealadach. Is de dhual is de dhúchas na mac léinn a bheith ag agóidíocht, ag cur in aghaidh na bunaíochta. Bheinn thar a bheith míchompordach mura mbeadh. Dá mba go rabhadar sásta ar nós uain bheaga dheasa ag dul chun an tseamlais ba mhó ba chúis bhuartha é sin.
Is fíor, leis, gur mhinic iad ag aithris ar a chéile, ionas go bhféadfaí a chur i gcás nach raibh sna círéibeanna agus léirsithe a tharla le déanaí san Iodáil agus sa Bheilg ach faisean. Ina choinne sin thall bhí trioblóid sráide sa Spáinn tamall roimhe sin mar gheall ar an tslí ar díbríodh seanbhean as an teach ina raibh sí ina cónaí ar feadh breis agus trí scór bliain de dheasca ardú cíosa. Deargfhearg in aghaidh na héagóra ba ea sin, agus an léirthuiscint ag fás gur ag lucht an airgid atá an chumhacht agus gur lag é guth an duine, nó cearta daonna féin, nó bunbhá leis an té atá buailte i bhfarradh leis.
Ach féach leat gur thosnaigh suaitheadh na Fraince, ní leis na mic léinn, ná le léirsitheoirí ag cur i gcoinne chostais ataithe na beatha, ach le daltaí scoile. Is í an tsamhail choiteann den dalta gurbh fhearr leis a bheith na céadta míle ó gheata na foghlama agus doicheallach aon chuimilt a bheith aige le scoil ar bith. Dealraíonn, áfach, gurbh iarratais réasúnta go leor a bhí á ndéanamh acu: oideachas níos fearr, foirgnimh shlána, breis múinteoirí, péint gan a bheith ag sileadh ó na ballaí. Níorbh aon phinn órga a bhí acu á n-éileamh, ná strufal dubh Périgord le haghaidh an lóin, na cúisíní maotha faoina dtóin. Is é sin, níorbh aon réabhlóidithe teasaí faobhracha de chuid na heite clé ba bhun leis an treabhlaid, ach daoine ar cás leo an aimsir atá amach rompu, mar is ceart.
Tá an chuma air, agus táim ag iarraidh a bheith faichilleach anseo, nárbh iad a bhuail an chéad bhuille, má caitheadh buille ar bith, ach na póilíní, an péas, an Gendarmerie nach bhfuil cáil na cneastachta orthu. Níor chúrsaí iontais é go dtiocfadh daoine eile amach ar an tsráid d’fhonn tacaíocht a thabhairt do na daltaí agus chun a ngráin a léiriú ar na húdaráis ar fearr leo an dorn iata iarainn ná leathchluas féin le héisteacht.
Níl ach mothú, braistint lag ag dúiseacht ionam, cigilt bheag i gcúl na hintinne go bhfuil an bhearna idir an pobal mór - an dream go dtugaimis an chosmhuintir orthu fara an mheánaicme mheasúil féin - agus rialtais tofa lucht cosanta caipitil agus margaí ag dul i méid. Is iad na sráideanna beannaithe an chéad áit a léirítear sin agus ní ar an bpáipéar ballóide.

title: Brazil’s electoral phenomenon Lula stages unprecedented comeback
description: Leftist veteran stages unprecedented comeback to defeat far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s election
content:
Already the greatest electoral phenomenon in his country’s history, Brazil ’s president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva saved his best for last.
Just two days shy of his 81st birthday, seeking a fourth mandate in his seventh presidential campaign, 37 years after his first run, the leftist veteran staged an unprecedented comeback win to defeat far right-senator Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s election.
In doing so he breaks a string of victories in recent years for the hard right across Latin America and deals a blow to US president Donald Trump ’s ambitions to exert greater influence over the region.
When Lula unexpectedly lost to Flávio by 2.22 million votes in the first round on October 4th, most analysts wrote off his chances. Never before in Brazil’s electoral history had anyone who came second in the first round gone on to win the runoff.
[ Lula wins fourth term as Brazil’s president over Flávio Bolsonaro Opens in new window ]
But at ten past nine local time on Sunday night a chorus of fireworks and car horns in cities across Brazil greeted the confirmation by the country’s electoral court that Lula was the victor in what he insists is his last campaign.
In an astonishing performance, he added more than ten million votes to his first round total to beat Flávio by 4.4 million votes, or 51.8 to 48.2 per cent.
The turnaround followed a massive mobilisation by the left on the country’s streets and online after its first-round defeat. This transformed a race marked until then by indifference.
Energised, Lula’s campaign focused relentlessly on Flávio’s character, his links to organised crime and the array of corruption allegations against him. This scrutiny allied to warnings about how he was signalling to the financial sector that he would make deep budget cuts helped Lula orchestrate his come-from-behind win.
In a victory speech to ecstatic supporters in São Paulo Lula promised to change his method of governing, a nod to the high levels of dissatisfaction with his administration that cost him the first round.
“This election has taught me many things,” he said.
Flávio’s defeat ends his hopes of freeing from detention his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro. He is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after he lost his re-election bid to Lula in 2022.
The plot included plans to assassinate Lula and his vice-president Geraldo Alckmin. Now instead Flávio faces the prospect of joining his father in jail. When he leaves the senate at the end of January he will be without parliamentary privilege for the first time since 2003.
With various investigations into his activities ongoing his legal jeopardy will likely increase significantly.
In his first public comments after the result he refused to recognise his defeat, citing a supreme court decision to extend voting by two hours after allegations that bolsonarista-controlled municipalities had sought to suppress voting by restricting public transport.
“What happened is inexplicable ... I will call for an annulment,” he told supporters in Brasília. But the result was confirmed by the head of the electoral court – a supreme court justice appointed by Flávio’s father – who said the extension made no difference to the outcome.
This latest display of authoritarian petulance by the Bolsonaro clan will be just one of many challenges facing Lula as he prepares for a history-making fourth term in office. The opposition dominates the new congress, the supreme court has lost all authority after a string of scandals and investors were already worried about the budget deficit even before Lula made lavish spending promises as part of his re-election bid.
But Sunday night was about securing the future of Brazilian democracy from the authoritarian far right. And with a second victory over the Bolsonaros in four years Lula might just have done it.

title: An Irish documentary on a relatively obscure American figure can illuminate so much
description: The success of You Can See Everything shows people are looking for something deeper
content:
S inéad O’Shea is one of Ireland’s finest documentary-makers. Her last film was a compelling documentary on Edna O’Brien, called Blue Road . Her latest, out in Irish cinemas this Friday, is All About the Money.
In it, she follows the US communist activist Fergie Chambers . Chambers is from the billionaire Cox family, and a few years ago, he cashed out. In recent years, he used some of his money to establish a collective in Massachusetts, donate to humanitarian causes in Gaza , invest (if you want to call it that) in a Tunisian football team, move to Ireland, and occupy a contradictory space in culture some cannot make sense of: a member of the one per cent who is avowedly anti-capitalist. Last July he was arrested in Spain, and is now awaiting extradition to the US in a case many characterise as politically motivated.
All of this is fascinating, a strange tale of our times. But O’Shea’s approach to her subject and her craft tells us a bigger story, one that lives not in conclusions and certainty, but in complexity and nuance.
After a preview in Dublin last week, she spoke about truth: “It has become quite political to be truthful. It’s not seen as a neutral space. Reporting what you see leads to accusations of bias.” Her words stayed with me because that’s not just about a film, but where we are in all sorts of discourse; political, social, cultural, digital.
Documentary-making can be a lens through which we witness the broader world, literally. But what happens when you don’t render issues or people as right or wrong? What happens when nuance and contradiction is favoured over partisanship? It’s not just the story O’Shea tells that illuminates complex times, it’s her approach to staying in the truth of things rather than leaping to easy answers for the purpose of entertainment or attention-hooking.
As an avid consumer of documentary film I will watch pretty much anything, although I’m not big on true crime. But if there’s a doc out there on a long-retired NFL quarterback, a country musician I’ve never listened to a song of, an arcane subculture or forgotten scandal, I will watch it. So much of this stuff is of course hagiography bordering on propaganda, one of heroes and monsters, successes and failures.
Watching All About the Money, you can almost see another film hiding in the distance, a lesser film, one with the flashy animated graphics, corny voiceover, whiplash twists, stacked cliffhangers that stretch the story over several hours begging the viewer to not even wait for the next episode to buffer, all wrapped in the algorithmic structure that plagues contemporary documentaries in the streaming age.
This sort of form is what is “binged”. When we talk about “bingeing” streaming series, we rarely talk about the aftermath of the binge, which, like all binges, renders the consumer addled yet spaced out, full yet empty. What’s also relevant is how truth is sacrificed in the pursuit of attention.
And yet something else is happening in documentary-making that is unseating this culture of short, sharp and simple. Suddenly, people are searching for something deeper.
You Can See Everything – Nathan Fielder’s documentary on the disgraced Elizabeth Holmes , who rose to power and wealth on hubris, delusion and, ultimately, fraud – is being lauded as the film of the year. It may even become the first documentary nominated for Best Picture at the Academy Awards. It is also just under three hours long, and audiences are going wild.
Musk, Alex Gibney’s latest documentary on the tech oligarch and man responsible for dismantling USAID, with devastating consequences, is three hours and 45 minutes long. The consolidation and politicisation of media power has infused its promotion, with YouTube, Meta and TikTok all restricting its advertising and then reversing that, citing “errors”. Who knows what the truth is?
The second installation of Julia Loktev’s, My Undesirable Friends, which follows independent Russian journalists in exile, clocks in at close to six hours. The first part, which follows the journalists while still in Moscow in the run-up to and in the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine , is five hours 25 minutes long. Its immersive length is justified, because the time spent with the film’s subjects is essential to capturing the relationship between time and how the repression of free speech escalates.
Speaking to O’Shea the day after the screening, she discussed what is being lost right now, which is truth. “Truthfulness is sort of out of fashion. Documentary making is one thing, but everything has become a giant football match. Everything is so partisan. The truth is much more nuanced, and that’s almost not conventional at the moment.” This isn’t just about filmmaking, it’s sort of about, well, everything.
Misinformation, disinformation, conspiracy, censorship, lies, pretences, propaganda, denials, vested interests, the growing struggle to determine what is “real” in the age of AI – all of this has created a great untethering across politics, culture and social discourse.
It’s interesting that an Irish documentary on a relatively obscure American figure can illuminate so much. What it tells us is that when one makes a decision rooted in journalistic integrity, not the pursuit of commercial gain, the truth does actually out. There’s a lesson in that that goes far beyond a single film.

title: Méadú agus mealladh Oireachtas na Samhna
description: Cuirfear tús oifigiúil le mórfhéile na nGael i gCill Airne Dé Céadaoin
content:
‘Fágann chuile Oireachtas a oidhreacht féin.”
Sin a dúirt Máirín Nic Dhonnchadha, ceannasaí ar fhéile iltréitheach na nGael, Oireachtas na Samhna, agus í ag caint le Tuarascáil roinnt laethanta roimh thús fhéile na bliana seo i gCill Airne.
“Tá súil agam go bhfágann an tOireachtas oidhreacht ar an gceantar ina mbíonn sé ar siúl ann ach freisin, is cinnte go bhfágann chuile cheantar marc ar an Oireachtas,” a dúirt sí.
Bhí Oireachtas na Samhna i mBéal Feirste anuraidh den chéad uair le beagnach tríocha bliain, agus b’fhianaise é an tsuim a chuir pobal na cathrach ann ar thábhacht na féile do chultúr agus do phobal na nGael.
D’fhreastail sluaite móra ar chomórtais damhsa, agallaimh beirte agus amhránaíochta ar an sean-nós, chomh maith le léachtaí, seimineáir, ceardlanna agus go leor eile.
…tá borradh ‘as cuimse’ tagtha ar chomórtas na n-agallamh beirte freisin: bhí 78 n-iomaitheoir ann anuraidh, ach tá 106 cláraithe i mbliana.
“An rud is mó ar thug muid faoi deara ná an méid cainteoirí Gaeilge a bhí thart timpeall orainn an t-am ar fad,” arsa Nic Dhonnchadha. “Agus muid ag siúl na sráide, bhí Gaeilge agus canúintí as chuile cheard den tír le cloisteáil i ngach áit.
“Déarfainn gur chuir sé iontas ar an dream s’againne a bhí i mBéal Feirste den chéad uair le fada go raibh an oiread sin Gaeilge le cloisteáil ar na sráideanna, agus le feiceáil ar na comharthaí.”
Creideann sí “gan dabht ar bith” go dtreisíonn féile Oireachtais na Samhna agus an pobal Gaelach a chéile.
“Tá muid dóchasach go bhfuil pobal nua leanúna ag an bhféile de bharr Oireachtas na bliana seo caite. Ní féidir a rá nach raibh tionchar thar a bheith dearfach ag Oireachtas na bliana seo caite ar chlár na féile i mbliana.”
D’iompair Oireachtas na Samhna lasóg phobal na Gaeilge agus na Gaeltachta le fada an lá agus is láidre atá sí agus na healaíona traidisiúnta anois dá bharr.
Tá méadú tagtha ar líon agus ar raon na gcomórtas i mbliana agus thug maoiniú breise deis don eagras tuilleadh foirne a fhostú.
I dteannta na gcomórtas sean-nóis, ceoil agus scéalaíochta, tá comórtas rapcheoil, comórtas cóir agus comórtas in onóir don amhránaí agus gníomhaí Albert Fry ar chlár na bliana seo.
Tá 1,200 iomaitheoir cláraithe i gcomparáid le beagán breis agus míle duine anuraidh. Beidh 54 chomórtas ar siúl don aos óg agus 21 chomórtas don aos fásta, agus tá méadú tagtha ar líon na n-iomaitheoirí ar fud an chláir.
Beidh 198 nduine faoi 18 mbliana d’aois ag iomaíocht i gcomórtais amhránaíochta ar an sean-nós i mbliana agus tá borradh “as cuimse” tagtha ar chomórtas na n-agallamh beirte: bhí 78 n-iomaitheoir ann anuraidh, ach tá 106 cláraithe i mbliana. San iomlán, tá súil go mbeidh breis agus 14,000 duine, idir chuairteoirí agus iomaitheoirí, ag déanamh aeir ag an Oireachtas i mbliana.
Creideann Nic Dhonnchadha gur imir rannpháirtíocht phobal agus eagrais áitiúla Bhéal Feirste tionchar ar an ardú sin.
Bhí go leor eagras, scoileanna agus grúpaí pobail rannpháirteach sna himeachtaí, agus baineadh leas as árais lena n-áirítear Áras Mhic Reachtainn agus Cultúrlann McAdam Ó Fiaich.
Dar le Nic Dhonnchadha go bhfuil sé ríthábhachtach go mbeadh caidreamh mar sin idir an tOireachtas agus na heagrais Ghaeilge, cuma cá bhfuil an comórtas á reáchtáil.
“Tá a phobal féin thart timpeall ar chuile cheann de na hárais sin agus chuir sé sin go mór leis an bhféile,” a dúirt sí.
“Ceapaim, leis an leagan amach a bhí ar an bhféile anuraidh, an spás a bhí ann do na comórtais, gur thug sé deis dúinn i bhfad níos mó lucht féachana a bheith againn in go leor de na comórtais agus gur spreag sé sin an t-ardú.
“Má fheiceann gasúir gasúir eile ar an stáitse, tugann sé sprioc dóibh é a dhéanamh iad féin má tá spéis acu ann. Osclaíonn sé an doras dóibh é a dhéanamh iad féin.”
Ar ndóigh, is cabhair mhór a bhí sa maoiniú stáit €4 mhilliún a leithdháileadh ar Oireachtas na Gaeilge dhá bhliain ó shin dá Phlean Gníomhaíochta Náisiúnta, chun ealaíona na Gaeilge a fhorbairt agus a chur chun cinn.
Tá ochtar déag ag obair ar chroífhoireann an Oireachtais anois i gcomparáid le seisear dhá bhliain ó shin agus tá siad sin ag obair i réimsí éagsúla sna healaíona teangabhunaithe.
“Tá scéim againn ar a dtugtar Ar Bharr do Theanga a thacaíonn le scoileanna agus le clubanna teagascóir a fháil isteach le cuidiú leo ullmhú do na comórtais nó amhránaíocht a dhéanamh i lár scoile, sa seomra ranga, nó sna clubanna,” a dúirt Nic Dhonnchadha.
“Tá níos mó agus níos mó scoileanna ag baint leas as an scéim agus is léir go bhfuil tionchar á imirt aige.”
Tá comhpháirtíocht nua le hOllscoil Notre Dame le seoladh i mbliana freisin a bhaineann le drámaíocht na Gaeilge agus reáchtálfar comhdháil, i gcomhar leis an Oireachtas, i mí Feabhra na bliana seo chugainn.
Osclóidh an tUachtarán féile na bliana seo in Airéine Óstán an Gleneagle i gCill Airne Dé Céadaoin.
Dar ndóigh, is cur chuige mór é imeacht ar scála Oireachtas na Samhna a reáchtáil agus luann Nic Dhonnchadha an buíon oibrí deonach a thugann cabhair chuile bhliain.
“Ní fhéadfadh muid é a reáchtáil gan iad,” a mhíníonn sí.
“Tá muid thar a bheith buíoch díobh agus tá an t-ádh linn go dtagann siad ar ais bliain i ndiaidh bliana.” Luann sí an 20 teicneoir fuaime agus físe a thugann cabhair freisin chomh maith le foireann an INEC i gCill Airne agus foirne na n-óstán.
“Tuigeann siad muid, tá siad cosúil le teaghlach. Tá siad ar nós na gcol ceathracha nach bhfeiceann tú ach uair sa bhliain.”
Nós seanbhunaithe atá ann go gcuirtear tús le mórfhéile na nGael agus na Gaeilge ar an gCéadaoin deiridh i mí Dheireadh Fómhair ach de bharr an fháis atá tagtha ar líon na n-iomaitheoirí agus líon na gcomórtas i mbliana tá roinnt imeachtaí seachtracha ar siúl níos luaithe sa tseachtain ná mar a bhíonn de ghnáth.
“Ciallaíonn sé sin go bhfuil an pobal ag triall ar an bhféile níos túisce sa tseachtain ach is tarraingt iontach é freisin go bhfuil Uachtarán na hÉireann, Catherine Connolly, le bheith i láthair, agus gurb ise a bheidh ag seoladh na féile go hoifigiúil.”
Dar ndóigh, is iad na comórtais taibhealaíon, cultúr agus traidisiún na Gaeilge croílár na féile. Cuirtear fáilte roimh chách agus is iomaí deis atá ag daoine nach bhfuil sáite sa phobal páirt a ghlacadh sna himeachtaí.
“Is ag na seisiúin bheaga neamhfhoirmiúla is mó a mbíonn spórt ag daoine acu, go háirithe nuair a thagann siad orthu gan choinne,” a deir Nic Dhonnchadha.
“Tá an t-uafás ócáidí plé ar siúl, bíonn seimineáir ag Conradh na Gaeilge chuile bhliain, arís i mbliana tá cúrsaí tithíochta á bplé, tá ollscolaíocht lán-Ghaeilge ar an gclár freisin á plé ag mic léinn.”
Tá neart eile ar siúl chun daoine a mhealladh - “craic agus spraoi, drámaíocht, léitheoireacht filíochta agus próis, club na féile, agus míle rud eile.”
“Tá súil againn tús spleodrach a chur leis nuair a bheidh an tUachtarán ar an stáitse, tráthnóna Dé Céadaoin,” a dúirt sí.
Beidh Oireachtas 2026 ar siúl i gCill Airne, Co. Chiarraí, ón 28 Deireadh Fómhair go dtí an 1 Samhain 2026. Beidh aip an Oireachtais ar fáil ón Máirt ar chostas €5. Tuilleadh eolais: onas.antoireachtas.ie .

title: Cork, Dublin, Galway, Limerick: Which are Ireland’s cheapest and dearest cities?
description: We compare the cost of living in Ireland’s capital with Cork, Galway and Limerick. The result is not what you might expect
content:
L ife in capital cities across the world tends to come with a hefty premium. If you want to settle in London you’ll pay more than if you live in Birmingham or Liverpool, while the day-to-day cost of Parisian living is considerably higher than in Marseilles or Strasbourg.
But what about closer to home? It would be easy to assume our capital is a much more expensive place to put down roots than other cities around the State, and while dear old Dublin does live up to the moniker in some respects, Galway , in particular, runs it far closer than you might expect.
When it comes to deciding where is the cheapest place of all, socialising, public transport , childcare and a host of other things have to be considered, as well as average wages.
But there is one thing that stands alone: a home . The cost of putting a roof over your head is obviously the biggest drain – whether you are buying or renting.
While Dubin is – as you might expect – the dearest place to rent, Galway is within touching distance, although just how close it is depends on the measure you use.
The most up to date data from daft.ie puts the average cost of renting a two-bedroom apartment in Dublin at a pretty eye-watering €2,634 a month.
Galway city is in second place with monthly rent currently standing at €2,336 although it does fall to €1,559 across the county as a whole.
Limerick is in the bronze medal position with a two-bedroom home in the city likely to cost around €2,244. The self-styled real capital, Cork, is the most accommodating when it comes to accommodation, with the monthly rent averaging €2,168. Across the county as a whole, rents were a more modest €1,700.
For our purposes we will confine ourselves to city living and if we were to look at the average annual costs, a person renting a two-bed apartment in Dublin will spend a sobering €31,608. The annual cost in Galway comes in at €28,032 while in Limerick it is €26,928 and in Cork it falls to €26,016, according to the daft.ie figures, a full €5,592 less than in Dublin.
And at the risk of stating the obvious, for many people that will be an after-tax figure, which means someone living in Dublin will have to earn in excess of €10,000 a year more than their Cork counterpart just to be in the same place financially.
But of course not everyone wants to rent so we should also look at the cost of buying and, just as it did with renting, Galway City runs Dublin closer than you might think.
The average price of a three-bedroom semidetached house in the capital is €635,000, according to daft.ie, while the average price in our rainiest, most western city is €618,000. Cork city is a long way off the pace, with prices said to be averaging €431,000, while Limerick was further back on €376,000.
But the daft figures are not the only measure and other sources suggest a degree of conflict.
The Central Statistics Office (CSO), for example, estimates the average price paid for a similar property in Dublin in the 12 months to August was €598,677 while MyHome.ie, which is owned by The Irish Times, puts the median price in Dublin at €585,132. It also puts the median price in Galway – covering both city and county − at €375,000, with the price in Cork €360,000 and in Limerick €290,000.
But while different sources reveal different prices, the rankings are the same, with Dublin and Galway considerably ahead of the rest.
Outside of housing, many of the costs people have to pay are the same no matter where in the State they live.
Generally speaking, the Lidls in the west charge the same for groceries and blow torches as they do in the east and the south, while milk and bread in Dunnes in Dublin are the same price as in a Dunnes in Limerick.
There is also no premium paid for electricity supplied to homes in Dublin when compared with homes in Dingle – although many rural homes – 700,000 of them, in fact – are expected to rely on home heating oil, which has soared in price over the past 10 months. But that is a whole other story.
Health insurance is also the same no matter where you live.
But there are discrepancies in other areas.
Numbeo is a price-conscious website that describes itself as “the world’s largest cost-of-living and quality-of-life database, combining millions of crowdsourced reports with automated market-data collection and statistical validation to produce reliable global benchmarks”. It says it covers “cost of living, housing, crime, healthcare, transport, and other key indicators used by individuals, researchers, and organisations worldwide”.
[ Grocery price inflation hits nearly 5%, latest data shows Opens in new window ]
It is entirely unofficial but still a useful resource when working out where is the cheapest of them all.
It puts the estimated monthly expenditure for a family of four in Dublin at €3,864, excluding rent, while the estimated monthly costs for a single person in the city are said to be €1,088, again excluding rent.
In Cork, the monthly costs for the notional family of four are €3,654 or €210 less than in Dublin. The estimated monthly costs for a single person are €1,025, a modest saving of €63 on the capital.
Excluding housing, the estimated monthly costs for a family of four in Galway are €3,618 with a single person likely to spend €1,015. Limerick is the cheapest of them all and the estimated monthly costs for a family of four there is €3,437, with a single person able to get by on €943.
The site has a whole lot of granular detail about the cost of things.
A meal for two in a Dublin restaurant is put at €90 while a one-way bus, tram or train ticket is €2 with a pint said to cost €7 – it’s actually 500ml, according to Numbeo, but we will round up. It also puts the monthly cost of private childcare at €1,136 for one child.
Eating out in Cork, meanwhile, is priced at €80, with a pint costing €6.50. A single journey on local transport is said to cost €1.45, while a month in private childcare for one child is said to be €963.
The cost of eating out in Galway averages a fairly hefty €100 with a pint “of local beer” priced €7 and a local bus journey averaging €1.90. Childcare costs €900.
Spread out over the course of a year, then, Numbeo’s figures suggest that a person living in Dublin will spend €13,056, with someone in Cork likely to need €12,300 and a person living in Galway set to spend €12,180. Someone living in Limerick, meanwhile, will manage to get by on €11,316 or €1,740 less than a Dublin resident.
And again, that is an after-tax figure, which means a Dublin person will need to earn around €3,500 more than someone living in Limerick to be in the same financial position.
The CSO has county-level earnings and its most recent tranche of data, published on October 6th, suggests that the median salary for people living in Dublin is €848 per week, which, when annualised, amounts to a salary of €44,099.
The comparable figure for Cork is €796, while in Galway it is €765 and in Limerick it is €773. The annualised figures are €41,832, €39,758 and €40,197.
So, if someone in Dublin earns €44,099 and someone in Galway earns €39,758, the former is €4,341 better off each year.
They do spend €948 more on day-to-day living each year, according to Numbeo, which closes the gap to €3,376.
If the Dublin resident is paying for half of an apartment in the city, their monthly rent is €1,317, which works out at €15,804 over the course of a year. The Galway renter, paying for half an apartment, will have to fork out €14,016 over the course of a year, €1,788 less, which closes the gap still further to €1,588.
[ There’s no cost-of-living crisis for Ireland’s quietly prosperous class. Who are they? Opens in new window ]
Relying on all the averages and medians and crowdsourced prices, then the Dublin resident is left with an additional €132 a month when compared with someone living in Galway city.
But numbers only tell one part of the story and away from statistics are the experiences of real people.
Niamh Delmer is in her late 20s and lived and worked in Dublin for several years before returning to her home place of Galway. How does she think the two places compare from a cost of living perspective?
“Day to day, Galway is definitely not a cheaper place to live,” she says. “The cost of coffee, the cost of lunch, the cost of public transport and the cost of going out at weekends are all very much in line with Dublin.”
There is one area where she makes savings – rent.
“We are a couple and renting a two bed apartment in Oranmore. It is about €300 less a month than what we were paying in Dublin for a two bed, so it is not a huge amount but you are saving a bit.”
When it comes to working and socialising, she says she spends most of her time in the city and it is not cheap. “I was out on Saturday and paid €8.10 for a pint in a popular place on Eyre Square that is full of Galway people,” she says. “The night out between food, drinks and transport to and from her home cost her around €150. “If I did that all the time I’d be smashed but even if I were to go for a few pints it would be around €60.
“I went for a flat white this morning and it was €4.20 and that is decent value. It was a lovely cup of coffee from an independent coffee shop. I bring in my lunch almost every day but if I am having lunch it is around €10 to €13 for a toastie or a salad bowl.”
Delmer says she is “a bit older now so I am not going out as much as I used to when I lived in Dublin, and that means I am saving more and I am saving every single month. Do I have more disposable income? I don’t think so but I am putting more away. Life in Galway is a bit quieter so I am able to put more money away. I don’t go out for food or drinks as much.”
She suggests that while day-to-day living is comparable “we don’t have the same facilities as Dublin. We don’t have the late buses and generally our public transport isn’t as good. For most of the four years I lived in Dublin I did not have a car and I tried to live without one in Galway. I lasted eight months. The bottom line is I am spending the same amount day to day but I am not benefiting from Dublin’s amenities.”
Delmer says that, like many people, she has become “desensitised to how expensive things are because everything is so dear now” but moving back to Galway has changed one thing about her outlook.
[ Ireland is richer and spending more than 30 years ago but is it making us happy? Opens in new window ]
“When I lived in Dublin I felt that buying a house was so far out of reach but now, living in Galway, I am saving and it will still be three years away but I feel like it is something I can do. Galway city is out of the question, for sure. I won’t be able to buy a house in town but looking at Oranmore or Athenry it is definitely something that will be attainable. That is kind of why I moved out of Dublin. That is a goal I want to achieve and I don’t think it was possible in Dublin.
Nollaig O’Sullivan is also in her 20s and, like Delmer, relocated from Dublin to her home place in Cork.
“I think a couple of years ago there was a bigger difference in the cost of living in both places and there was this perception that Dublin was a lot more expensive than Cork and you would definitely notice it but now it is much of a muchness,” she says.
Her rent in Cork is “pretty much the same: but she admits that “some of that is down to luck because when I was in Dublin I was paying €636 for a double room and I knew people who were paying upward of €1,000 for the same thing.”
She says costs can be better managed by those who know where to get the best value. “If you’re starting out in Dublin and don’t have a good social network it can be a lot harder and a lot more expensive until you find your groove. When you know where to go for things like a coffee and a pastry you can pay €6 compared to a tenner in a place around the corner.”
She says in both Cork and Dublin eating out is equally unaffordable. “A sit-down meal would be only on birthdays or special occasions and otherwise. If I go and meet a friend we’d be getting a slice of pizza and a pint because it’s extremely expensive to just go out for dinner.
Like Delmer, O’Sullivan says that while the prices are the same, the infrastructure outside Dublin is not as good. “I live in Midleton and I’m lucky that I have the train that gets me up and down to the city in 20 minutes but there are rarely buses and even in the city itself the buses are very unreliable, If you go out for a night out the taxis are extortionate. The last bus leaves the city at 11pm and before that they only go once an hour so you really have to be co-ordinated or else have someone around who can give you a lift,” she says.
[ Ireland is no country for young people. It will stay that way until houses are affordable Opens in new window ]
And, like Delmer, she says one of the main reasons she has more disposable income now that she is living in Cork rather than in Dublin is as a result of limited options for spending. “When I was living in Dublin I was doing a lot more, I was going out more and that is because there’s more to do, more events happening on weekdays. In Cork I tend to meet my friends and go for a walk on the beach or for a coffee so I’m spending a lot less here.”
Ultimately, it comes down value for money and on that score, Delmer has no doubts.
“I definitely feel like Galway gives me my value for money. We have loads of really nice coffee shops, we have loads of lovely pubs and lovely restaurants. You are not going to be able to go out every weekend or go for dinner every week but when you do it is a real treat. And walking around Galway on a Saturday morning, I realise how lucky we are. It is beautiful, it is small and we have a good community so there are a lot of perks to being here. And what Galway is really special for is there are loads of local businesses and it is easier to support them.”

title: The IT knits: Winter warmers that pack plenty of personality
description: Practical but stylish, knitwear offers a cosy quick fix against the cold and a handy styling hack
content:
W hen it comes to autumnal dressing, coats do most of the heavy lifting as temperatures drop, but knitwear is a close second. With transitional weather so unpredictable, knits are proving their mettle this season: a cosy quick fix against the cold, they can also add a pop of colour to an outfit or serve as a handy styling hack, wrapped around the shoulders or knotted at the waist.
Practical but stylish, this season’s knitwear is far from a supporting act or just something to slip under your coat for extra insulation; it is becoming a foundation of an outfit, adding personality, colour or a fun print and making a statement in its own right.
And if the autumn catwalks are any guide, there’s no better time to add a fun, fuzzy knit to your wardrobe and warm up those cold, dark days. After seasons of pared-back purls and quiet-luxury woollies, fashion has returned to more-is-more, and knits are getting a maximalist makeover too – think bold colours, playful prints, motifs and texture.
Cosy knits appeared on the catwalks in an array of bright shades at Prada , Celine and Miu Miu. An instant mood lifter and outfit energiser, you can temper the bold shade knit with deeper autumnal tones, like slipping a red style under black leather or chocolate brown suede, or pairing cobalt with grey or burgundy.
At Ralph Lauren , moody florals bloomed across chocolate, strong-shouldered knits. Elsewhere, heritage prints got a catwalk airing, with windowpane checks, argyle and Fair Isle getting a fashiony fresh spin, reimagined by designers like Moschino and Khaite.
To keep traditional prints from feeling too countryside chic and give them more edge, opt for modern styling, like leather midi skirts or utility trousers, as seen styled at Dries Van Noten. Meanwhile, Victoria Beckham and Lanvin leant into more geometric patterns in a restrained, monochromatic palette, proving statement sweaters don’t have to be too intimidating.
If you prefer understated but don’t mind making a statement with silhouette, embrace the bold-shoulder trend this season, like boxy or exaggerated balloon shoulders, as seen at Tory Burch and Carolina Herrera , and structured silhouettes with shoulder pads that give the simplest jumpers a sculptural, architectural feel. Balance the shoulder volume with tailored trousers, straight-leg denim or a streamlined midi skirt.
Funnel-neck knits add some drama too, and the exaggerated neckline means you can skip the scarf.
Texture is another way to adopt the statement sweater without leaving the neutral palette territory.
Opt for chunky cable knits, fuzzy mohair or brushed finishes to add interest to simpler outfits. Have fun playing with textures: contrast tactile knits with smoother, sleeker finishes; think silk, satin, leather and glossy patent leather.
The trick to making a personality knit work for the season is to let it take centre stage and breathe new life into your wardrobe staples. A patterned, fun jumper can freshen up your favourite denims, while a chunky cable cardigan can refresh a dress. Consider your new knitwear a practical purchase with a personality punch.

title: Squirrel-proof bird feeder my eye. This squirrel is getting fatter and bigger on the bird food
description: Thuggish magpies, hummingbird moth tourists and a Latin American butterfly: Your notes and queries for Éanna Ní Lamhna
content:
This grey squirrel is not deterred by what is laughingly described as squirrel-proof bird feeder . It is getting bigger and fatter on the food we are putting out for the birds. Derek Brady, Terenure, Dublin
This one is certainly thriving and will continue to do so all winter at the expense of your garden birds because, of course, squirrels don’t hibernate. Your only hope is that it will get too fat to squeeze through the bars. Squirrel-proof bird feeder my eye. You could try lacing the nuts with a hefty dose of strong chilli powder if you prefer to be feeding the birds. They won’t taste this, but the squirrel will.
I saw this spider on the wood frame of a mini greenhouse in a suburban garden on June 22nd in Galway city. Do you have any idea what it is? Éimear Lavelle
This is the candy-striped spider Enoplognatha ovata . Although your image is somewhat out of focus, there is no mistaking this form of the species, which has a broad red band covering most of its back. It is a very small (5mm), long-legged spider that can be found on low vegetation in open habitats. There are several Irish records, including two for Galway city.
I came across a big butterfly recently in Annascaul. I found it again the next day but it was dead by then. I attach the scaled photo I took. I believe it was a Blue Morpho butterfly. Anna Moriarity, Annascaul, Co Kerry
Sometimes Google is actually right, no matter how preposterous the identification seems to be. The Irish butterfly expert, Jesmond Harding, confirms that it is certainly not a European or North African species so there was no way it could have reached our shores unaided. The Blue Morpho lives in the tropical forests of Latin America from Mexico to Colombia. It is possible to purchase tropical pupae online to hatch the adults and that is likely what happened here. It is far from Annascaul it was reared as an egg and caterpillar.
Attached is a picture of what we think is a hummingbird moth, a frequent visitor to our salvia plant. We first saw these insects in Puglia, Italy in June this year I have heard they are migrating north due to warming climate here . Thomas O Doherty, Ashbourne, Co Meath
I have been sent a huge number of questions and images of hummingbird hawk moths all summer and indeed I wrote about it in this column on June 6th. But for all the new readers since then, this is what I said. This is a day-flying moth that is a summer visitor to Ireland. It arrives from further south in Europe during hot weather. It feeds on nectar from flowers. It can breed here too but it is too cold yet for it to overwinter. So, they are not migrating north as such – they are still just warm weather visitors here.
I rescued this guy who was being badly mauled by a magpie in our garden. There was damage to its chest and legs, but it did eventually fly off. Brendan O’Sullivan, Connemara
This guy is a female sparrowhawk, most likely a young and still inexperienced one. They are the top avian predator in gardens, catching small birds at the feeder by swooping up over the wall and grabbing one. In fact the larger female can even catch, kill and eat magpies which are bigger than them. But magpies can hunt in groups, so maybe the sparrowhawk was set upon by a gang of thuggish magpies looking for a fight.
Please submit your nature query or observation, ideally with a photo and location, via irishtimes.com/eyeonnature or by email to weekend@irishtimes.com

title: ‘My son has a first-class honours degree, but he has no job offers’
description: Graduate demand seems to have been affected by AI - what advice would you give highly educated people with no interest from employers?
content:
My son recently graduated with a first-class honours Business degree and anticipated starting his career journey, as many previous graduates have, with one of the big four consulting firms – Deloitte , PwC , EY or KPMG .
Sadly, the demand for graduates seems to have been affected by the advances in AI, which seem to be resulting in significant cuts in graduate recruitment.
What advice would you give those who find themselves with top-class degrees and no job offers after four years of study?
The employment market for all graduates and school-leavers is changing daily, and traditional employment tracks have been completely transformed – at a breathtaking pace. Many high-level employers are now asking a simple question: when a function needs to be filled, can AI meet our needs or do we actually need to employ a human being?
The World Economic Forum (WEF) in their Future of Jobs Report 2025 identified 10 key skills that employers are seeking in people they recruit. Graduates who are seeking employment positions following completion of their undergraduate education need to present or fine tune their competencies in these 10 areas.
AI can already leave human beings in the dust when it comes to processing data of any nature, and in solving mathematical or scientific questions that we as humans have yet to unravel.
AI technological literacy is rapidly outpacing our capacity to control its actions, giving rise to a debate as to whether we need to slow the technology’s development before we lose the capacity to slow it.
Employers still need graduates who are expert in scientific, mathematical or other fields of data, so that humans can still discern the accuracy of the outcomes of AI’s endeavours.
[ ‘Be curious, ask questions’: Industry professionals advise graduates on how to approach a new career Opens in new window ]
But employers also need humans who can think analytically about problems within their organisation. They need people who can respond with resilience, flexibility and agility to the daily challenges that our ever changing world presents.
The human mind has the unique capacity to think creatively in every area of human endeavour, from the arts, literature, fashion, design, sport – in fact in every area of human interest.
We also have a unique ability to develop our sense of self-awareness and self-motivation which has over millenniums created the world we live in. We can also hone the skill to nurture motivation in others in our team, showing leadership skills through this process.
[ Ten organisations in Ireland offering paid graduate programmes Opens in new window ]
Humans are also unique in our capacity to actively listen to the often subtle messages we transmit in our daily words and actions, and to respond empathically, thus winning the trust and loyalty of those we encounter in our professional and personal lives.
Some of the greatest advances in human knowledge and insight, which have brought humanity and the world to their current state of development, have come about through curiosity and our constant striving to unravel the unknown within our fields of interest.
Leadership and management are central to all human advancement and success, and that ability to harness the talent within a team or organisation is uniquely human.
The final core skill that the WEF identifies s our capacity to be service-orientated and skilled in meeting the needs of our customers, in whatever sector of the economy we find ourselves operating.
The challenge to any graduate today is to select a field of employment in which they have an innate interest and a level of expertise and knowledge, and to benchmark themselves against the 10 key competencies identified by the WEF and seek to actively develop and hone them in living out their daily lives.

title: As my children plead with me not to bring them to creche, my heart is stretched thin
description: Since becoming a mother, I have not yet reconciled my two identities
content:
I t’s just gone 8am and I have decided I can no longer go to the job I am ready and dressed for.
I must give it all up and attend full time to the needs of my two young children. I am in the hallway of our house, then the kitchen. My eldest trails behind me, groaning. My daughter follows closer, weaving in between my legs so that I can no longer walk without picking her up.
It began with one of them, then the other, every emotion between them contagious in their population of two. They are pleading with me not to bring them to creche .
I am repeating the words my partner and I have been soothing them with all morning. I name the people they will see, the games they will play, how we will collect them as early as we can. I remind them that they love it there – and it’s true, they do. And we love it too; their teachers are caring and kind. They teach and entertain them in ways we never could. Our children have friends the same size as themselves, and they play all day with them in a safe and loving environment.
And still, I am grounded by the immediacy of this moment, my heart stretched thin across my chest as my body withstands the impact of their protestations.
It’s impossible to leave. I cannot stay.
[ The motherhood penalty: ‘Once they’re in bed, you log back on at 9pm or 10pm and work’ Opens in new window ]
My partner and I both work full time, out of financial necessity and also because our careers are something that we have worked hard to build. They have been forged, over many years, by the brute force of our labour, the sweat of our efforts. I worked in politics all through my twenties and early thirties. It was a job that demanded the complete subjugation of self. At any given moment, at any time of day or night – weekend, holidays or otherwise – there was never any greater priority than whomever was on the other end of the phone.
It’s one thing to wilfully disregard your own wellbeing for an extended period of time, but once becoming a mother, such reckless behaviour is no longer feasible. The opportunity cost of overwork is staring me in the face: it is asking me for a drink; it wants me to sit down and play with it. When I was pregnant with my son, I worried constantly about how I would maintain momentum around my career once he arrived. My ambition was a barely leashed animal that I was already struggling to hold on to. Role models for content, successful mothers in the workforce were few and far between. This, among the obvious concerns around the health of the baby, preoccupied me entirely.
[ Loneliness in early motherhood: ‘I can’t keep calling my mum up here every day’ Opens in new window ]
I knew better than to confide these worries in friends, many of whom were struggling in one way or another with fertility or career progression. I felt ashamed of myself for thinking this way, for feeling unable to reconcile the trade-offs necessary in a life of such abundance.
Even now, several years on, it is still something I struggle with. Since becoming a mother, I am completely transformed and yet, I am exactly the same person. I have not yet reconciled the two, arguably inconsistent identities. Instead I attempt to hold both at the same time. I am checking emails and reading newspapers before the children wake in the morning. My partner and I are on our laptops at the kitchen table when they are asleep, the two of us, fitting our old selves into the margins of our new ones.
[ The case for flexible working: ‘We lose one-third of women in their child-rearing years’ Opens in new window ]
I squat down to face my son. My partner is putting socks on his feet, then his shoes. He is a child; a baby really. This I forget sometimes. My daughter is still attached to my body like a front-facing backpack. I straighten up and she tightens her floppy noodle arms around my neck. Her tears are hot on my hand as I wipe them away.
I am at my desk, in the calm of an office environment when I receive a message from my partner informing me they went in okay. I have seen it myself, how quickly they move on, leaving behind the wreckage of their parents .
When I finish work and travel to collect them, they do not want to leave. My son is standing in front of a better collection of Lego than we have at home, avoiding eye contact with me. His teacher is telling me he had a great day. My daughter is in my arms and there is sweat prickling the back of my neck as I hold her. It is staining the silk material of my blouse, which will now need to be dry-cleaned.
My son is whispering to his friend; he is suggesting to her that they play hide and seek.

title: Women weary of being ‘exported’ when medical profession unable to meet vital healthcare needs
description: GPs should pause to ‘reflect, review, rethink’ when woman shows same symptoms three times in 12 months
content:
Women are “sick and tired of being exported” every time the health service is unable to meet their “essential healthcare needs”, and the necessary specialist care should be in place in the State.
Social Democrats TD Jennifer Whitmore railed against the treatment of women by the medical profession, whom she claimed are “gaslighting” female patients. She called for a “cultural shift” in the approach to women’s health problems and said this “has to come from Government”.
The Wicklow TD also called for a system adopted in the UK to be implemented here where if a woman presents to her GP three times in any 12-month period with the same symptoms, the doctor would “reflect, review and rethink” the case.
She acknowledged the investment in women’s healthcare and endometriosis by Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill . In October last year, however, €16 million funding was announced for endometriosis care, but “as of September, only one of those staff was in place”.
The Wicklow TD highlighted the experience of some of the 300,000 women here suffering from endometriosis, the debilitating and chronic illness where tissue similar to the lining of a woman’s womb starts to grow outside the uterus.
The figure represents one in seven women, but “many in the medical profession seem to have barely heard of it. How else can we explain why it takes a woman an average of 14 years to get a diagnosis?” she asked.
Raising the issue in the Dáil, she referred to last week’s “harrowing” Virgin Media documentary – Health Hysteria: Are Women being Gaslit? – which featured women “who spent years in excruciating pain before eventually being diagnosed with conditions like endometriosis and premenstrual dysphoric disorder”.
Their healthcare concerns “were repeatedly dismissed or minimised by doctors”, and women had to travel abroad for surgery because specialist care is not available in the State.
She also highlighted the recent RTÉ Prime Time programme featuring Dr Rachel O’Connor, who had to take out a large loan to travel to Poland for surgery. “She was told if she had not had that surgery, she would have died.”
The Minister admitted it is a “shame on me and everybody else that a doctor in our health system used her HSE salary and a loan to get emergency surgery in a different jurisdiction”.
[ Health staff face sweeping promotion restrictions under spending controls Opens in new window ]
Surgery abroad is being funded on an emergency two-year basis, but “we are trying to develop longer-term surgical pathways”, including a relationship with a specialist clinic in Bordeaux.
Irish surgeons are being trained abroad, and there will be a “continual series of fellowships for surgical training and endometriosis”. In the interim, “we are trying to recruit specialists as best we can”.
She acknowledged the “medical gaslighting” and said women have been treated differently in the system, with research on men sometimes applied inappropriately to women.
Carroll MacNeill said the chief executive of the HSE and she wrote to “every single GP to try to raise awareness that this impacts one in seven women”.
A programme was introduced to fund emergency surgeries abroad, and in the last quarter of 2025, 143 surgeries were conducted in the State, as the health service builds a specialist surgery system here.

title: Garda vetting and child safeguarding can  involve multiple processes
description: Surely, if I am Garda vetted to work with children in one sporting club, this vetting could apply to other clubs too
content:
Sir. – I volunteer with a couple of sporting clubs in which my three children are involved.
To volunteer to coach children in any club, one needs to complete a child safeguarding course and apply for Garda vetting. I have no issue with this; however, I cannot understand why I need to complete both processes for each club with which I volunteer. Surely, if I am Garda vetted to work with children in one sporting club, this vetting could apply to other clubs too?
Also, if I complete an approved child safeguarding course for one approved sporting body why can that training not also apply to all approved sporting bodies?
Having just spent two hours attending an online safeguarding course that was nearly identical to another one I recently attended, I am at a total loss. – Yours, etc,

title: TG4 overcomes run of bad luck at Dublin Marathon as Manchester United hit latest hurdle
description: From battles to burial sites, cheerful presenting team deliver highly entertaining and informative commentary
content:
N ot to be unkind, but TG4’s coverage of the Dublin Marathon started a little like Manchester United ’s season has gone thus far: pear-shaped. Anything that could go wrong insisted on doing so in the opening stages of the first televising of the event in 15 years, to the point where you wondered if the production team had been struck by clock-change confusion and were still at home in their beds.
But, in time, the glitches were ironed out. And after the channel hit the wall they dusted themselves down, sprinted towards the finish line and all was well with the world.
And anyway, the marathon must surely be one of the trickier sporting events to cover considering the scale of it. TG4 had to keep an eye on 20-ish-thousand runners stretching over 26.2 miles, whereas Sky largely only had to monitor the scoreboard and Bruno Fernandes ’s face at Old Trafford on Sunday. Granted, there are usually around 26.2 miles between United’s midfield and attack, so there’s that to cover too, but, generally, in comparison football-broadcasting is a piece of cake.
Watching the marathon called to mind Owen Hargreaves’s observation about Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki the previous day. “He’s literally created in a lab.” You’d imagine that’s not literally true, but sometimes you can be so in awe of sporting people, you’ve a notion that they were engineered rather than born.
This thought occurred all through the race, but particularly when those 20-ish-thousand lined up at the start line on a morning into which you wouldn’t put a polar bear. And some of them were actually smiling. As was TG4’s Máire Treasa Ní Dhubhghaill, who somehow remained jolly while interviewing folk about the place despite, presumably, suffering from hypothermia.
Our host Gráinne McElwain was at least indoors, with former international athletes Rory Chesser and Mary Cullen for company, as were Ronan Duggan and Olympian Michelle Finn in their enclosure; the pair at first looking a little like hostages reading a script written by their captors encouraging their government to release 500 political prisoners in return for their release.
They relaxed, though, the ransom possibly having been paid, and went on to provide a highly entertaining and uber-informative commentary on the race. If the cameras picked out, say, runner 12,382, they’d tell you his/her life story and inside leg measurements in a nanosecond.
And if you ever want a guided historical tour of Dublin, Ronan is your man. Especially if you want to know where famous dead people are laid to rest (“we’ve gone just by St Patrick’s Cathedral where Jonathan Swift is buried ... we’ve just gone left at Christ Church where Strongbow is buried”).
And also where you can find a rhinoceros outside a pub. “It’s a metal rhino, not a real one,” Ronan reassured us as we passed The Dropping Well, the runners possibly fearing they were hallucinating as they jogged by. “You should probably have stressed the ‘metal’ bit,” said Michelle.
[ Dublin marathon: Family rivalry, lengthy friendships and a group of lads ready to go ‘wild’ Opens in new window ]
Ronan even successfully linked 1916 with the winner of the men’s race, Abay Alemu Lesa, and the runner-up, Ebba Tulu Chala.
“The Battle of Mount Street Bridge was between a thousand British troops and a handful of Irish Volunteers. The odds were a thousand to one for those soldiers back in the day but these two were the most likely winners in our betting odds at the start.”
[ ‘What’s next? I really don’t know’: Manchester United boss Michael Carrick on the brink Opens in new window ]
Meanwhile, “what are you going to do to celebrate?” Máire Treasa asked Patrick Monahan, the winner of the wheelchair race. “Probably go back to bed,” he said. A wise man. Judith Storm had rowdier plans, though. How was the first Irish woman finisher going to celebrate? “A drink. I’ve been teetotal for the last few months, so a wee glass tonight.”
Owen Hargreaves came to mind again when we heard Judith’s story.
“He’s a Swiss army knife – he can do everything, he’s literally everywhere,” he said of Geneva-born Johan Manzambi. Judith’s literally a bit of a Swiss army knife herself. “With triplets and another child, it’s probably far easier to deal with the latter stages of the marathon than her normal everyday life,” as Rory put it back in the studio.
“I’ll ride it while it’s going,” she said. “I’m nearly 40 so I know I’ll probably go downhill.”
There’s no probably about it, Judith, but until then, enjoy that wee glass. You earned it. Literally.

title: Sick of fans phoning it in, Borussia Dortmund take action against in-game distraction
description: Bundesliga club hope new incentive will help wean supporters off their devices during matches
content:
That’d be the one announced by Borussia Dortmund , who are trying to encourage their supporters to watch their actual games rather than spend a chunk of the 90 minutes looking at their phones.
So, if the Dortmund faithful activate a thingumajig called Fan Mode in the club’s app, it will track how many times they unlock their phones during games. The fewer times they do it, the more points they will earn – and points can be exchanged for goodies in the club shop.
Oddly, perhaps, Vodafone have teamed up with Dortmund on the initiative, when you’d imagine they’d quite like people to be glued to their phones. But according to Reuters, the company carried out a survey that found 63 per cent of spectators frequently use their phones during games, a source of severe annoyance for the other 37 per cent. Among the most irritating habits was fans taking selfies.
Mercifully, selfie sticks appear to be less of a thing these days, but if Dortmund could create an app that gives an electric shock to anyone still using one, we’d all be grateful.

Undoubtedly, Paul Merson’s take on the first 35 minutes of the Champions League game between Bayern Munich and Arsenal . After Eberechi Eze gave Arsenal the lead, Merse, on Sky Sports News duty, held out little hope for the Germans’ chances of getting back in the game.
“So comfortable, Arsenal . So, so comfortable. Absolutely putting on a performance. Their movement, their passing, they have been by far the better team. At the moment, you can’t see any way back for Bayern Munich. But they do score goals, you’ve got to be careful, but at the moment . . . absolutely brilliant . . . it’s 1-1.”

title: Leinster bragging rights after defeat of Munster muted in wake of Coombes’ allegation
description: Winners move on to another provincial derby away to Connacht next Friday, when side will be without 17 Irish squad members
content:
Some of the gloss has been taken off Leinster ’s hard-earned 24-18 bonus-point win over Munster last Saturday at the Aviva Stadium due to Gavin Coombes’ allegations.
That cloud will also hang over Leinster as they move on to their next assignment, another provincial derby away to Connacht next Friday night when they will be without their 17 Irish squad members.
Granted, Connacht will also be without their eight-strong Irish contingent and the pity is that this derby has been denied two fully loaded sides, including a Ciaran Frawley-Sam Prendergast duel at outhalf.
But the points will be of the same value and a packed Dexcom Stadium will afford the back-to-back URC champions a warm welcome after Connacht’s consecutive home wins over Saracens and Zebre.
“Exciting, isn’t it?” suggested Leo Cullen. “It’s a new challenge, a completely different challenge next Friday. Today is to finish out that sequence of games and off they [the Ireland internationals] go into camp, which creates an amazing opportunity. Connacht are riding high right now, particularly when playing at home, so it’ll be a proper challenge.”
The game was notable for, among other things, a silky return to blue after an eight-year absence by Joey Carbery, while the Leinster and Ireland captain Dan Sheehan added another string to his bow with an 80-minute outing at number 8 in which he was the game’s leading carrier with 17.
“I thought he was very, very good in carrying the fight in the game, which is getting his hands on the ball in attack and being hungry to make hits defensively as well. Because when he’s playing 8, he’s in the middle of the field a lot more. Quite often the hookers end up on the edge quite a bit. I thought Dan was excellent there.”
Cullen said that this is “definitely a live option” for Ireland as well “whether that’s in game, in how you have your bench”.
Munster defied expectations by deservedly taking a 13-0 lead inside half an hour thanks to another superbly worked try, finished off by Shane Daly. After Leinster’s four-try salvo (three of them created by Jamison Gibson-Park), the visitors at least had the final say through Ben O’Connor’s try to earn a bonus point.
Although Munster head coach Clayton McMillan is too much of a competitor to “take any satisfaction out of being gallant losers”, he admitted: “They’re a significantly more experienced and cohesive side and we know that if you want to get a win down here you’ve got to come and throw your best shot.
“Patches in games is not going to be good enough and there’ll be some great learnings for our young squad out of the game tonight. So it is what it is.
“We’re happy with our cattle. We know we need to get better. There’s lots of young guys that are getting thrown into some pretty big occasions and from where I’m sitting a lot of them are doing a bloody good job.”
Munster, in ninth, host the in-form Sharks, in fifth, at Thomond Park next Saturday and McMillan hopes to have Will Harrison and Edwin Edogbo available.
“They warmed up with us today. Probably just didn’t get through enough training to be genuinely considered for today’s game.
“Forwards-wise, we’re probably looking quite healthy. Not too sure about the two looseheads [Jeremy Loughman and Michael Milne], probably touch and go at this stage. It’s in the backs we’re running pretty thin,” added McMillan, after Daly was forced off with a head injury. Sean O’Brien has a groin issue, while Tadhg Beirne and Craig Casey will be in Ireland camp.
“We’ll see what washes up after the medical clinic ... But it’s a huge game for us. We’ll just lick our wounds and then get back to work on Monday.”

title: Letters to the Editor, October 26th: On renewable generation, that consent ad and little things mean a lot
description: Individually, these resources are relatively small
content:
Sir, – Ireland is investing heavily in renewable generation, grid infrastructure and large-scale battery storage. Yet substantial quantities of available wind and solar are being curtailed because the electricity network cannot accommodate it.
Before committing consumers to further expenditure, we should be asking whether we are making the best possible use of the resources we already have.
One option could be using our 1.9 million households to become part of a distributed energy network, combining rooftop solar, domestic batteries, smart meters and intelligent electricity controls.
Individually, these resources are relatively small. Co-ordinated through an aggregator, they could collectively absorb surplus electricity, reduce demand during peak periods and ease pressure on weaker parts of the network.
The Netherlands is already exploring how smartly controlled household batteries can reduce local grid congestion.
Ireland has also begun developing flexibility services, but where is the ambitious national strategy to assess what could be achieved if domestic energy resources were co-ordinated on a much larger scale?
Unfortunately, the cost of batteries remains prohibitive for many. A Government-funded pilot could help overcome this barrier while testing the contribution domestic storage could make to the wider electricity system. Rather than simply subsidising installations, participating households could be rewarded for making some of their stored energy available when and where the grid needs it.
Such a programme would require compatible equipment, smart controls and safeguards to ensure households retain the electricity they need.
There is also an immediate resilience benefit. Ordinary grid-connected solar panels shut down during a power cut, even when sunlight is available. With previous storm-related outages highlighting our vulnerability, should the Government not also examine grants to equip existing solar installations with the necessary backup technology?
This would allow households to maintain essential electricity supplies during outages while making better use of investments already made in renewable energy.
None of these measures would eliminate every grid constraint or remove the need for large-scale storage and network upgrades.
But they could help defer some infrastructure expenditure, reduce household bills and make better use of renewable generation.
The question is whether the Government has properly compared the costs and benefits of distributed energy with those of additional centralised infrastructure.
Powerful industry stakeholders have commercial interests in expanding generation, storage and transmission, but those interests should not overshadow alternatives that could deliver better value for consumers.
With a significant proportion of planned offshore wind capacity intended to supply data centres through private connections, isn’t it time Government gave greater priority to the needs of domestic consumers?
Before asking the public to pay for more infrastructure, it should establish how much more we could achieve by making better use of the renewable electricity and energy resources already available to our homes and communities. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I was interested in Finn McRedmond’s column citing Harold Wilson’s 1974 memo “Little Things mean a Lot”. I wish the Government here would consider a few little things to make our lives a little bit better.
Such as: a half hour free parking in small towns when one wants to do a quick message, for every one hundred new houses built on the outskirts of town build an additional 50 car parking spaces at train stations or bus depots, allow more seating outside cafes and restaurants to encourage more use and social activity, after every dental visit get a free toothpaste, not the sample size. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I can understand why some people had a knee-jerk reaction. Obviously grandparents love their grandchildren and want to show them affection but the video’s message was simple – a child’s body belongs to the child.
Many of us can remember receiving sloppy kisses from a family member at a family gathering, and the discomfort of knowing we had no choice in the matter.
Too often, adults, grandparents included, assume love entitles them to a child’s affection, but it doesn’t.
As a parent of two small children, I have already been teaching my three-year-old that she has full autonomy over her body, and that other people have autonomy over theirs. She asks others “Do you need a hug?” and knows to say “I need space” if someone is encroaching on hers.
Many parents are starting this early so that children understand they have control over their own bodies, and that if a grandparent asks “Can I have a hug?”, it is okay to say no.
A grandparent who asks before hugging is not being demeaned, instead what they are doing is modelling respect. That early understanding becomes the foundation for everything children later learn about consent.
It is a shame the DRCC felt it had to take the video down. I think this episode shows how far we still have to go as a country in understanding consent. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I fully accept the necessity of educating our children about the importance of consent. However, the recent controversy about hugging is just a step too far. The video in question is wrong in so many ways.
I am a daughter, sister, wife, mother and grandmother. Hugging has always been a big part of my life and that will never change. There is little to beat a warm hug – it is a term of endearment.
It is very sad to think that grandparents might have to stop themselves from hugging their grandchildren or worse still that they might have to ask permission. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I see Irish Rail has written off €50 million of (our) public money regarding a failed IT project. (“F irm contracted by Irish Rail had never delivered a traffic system ,” October 23rd). Did it not occur to Irish Rail to consult any other rail company in Europe to find out what IT system they use?
Coinciding with a planned increase in public transport fares, the public is again left to cover the costs of incompetence for which there never seems to be any responsibility taken. –Yours etc,
Sir, – I am wondering has climate change affected our autumn colour which is different from previous years. On returning from a visit to Vermont in the USA where the autumn colour was exceptional due to the many trees, I was amazed that our autumn colour here lacked the intensity of previous years.
I remember 2023 when the whole country was a kaleidoscope of colour and was comparable to Vermont.
Autumn is nearly over now and we have not seen anything to equal it. It seems to me that climate change is having a big impact on the autumn colour as well as our weather. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Your coverage of “Irish doctors in Australia” made me smile, but it told only half the story (Letters October 19th). Having worked in Australia for seven years, I could add a chapter about Irish nurses
Australian hospitals are very much aware what Irish nurses bring to a team. Just like doctors, employers recognised the skill, resilience, compassion and a genuine warmth at the bedside that patients and families remember. Humour was front and central in our days’ work – the busier you were the more humour you would find in the most mundane things.
Some of my colleagues suggested that humour was as much a part of our Irish training as any clinical skill,
We were present in all areas of clinical practice from emergency departments to neonatal units. I always felt valued, respected and appreciated which was a foreign concept to me. This recognition mattered. It is respect, appreciation and fair remuneration that made staying a real choice. Pay reflected our responsibility and role and let me have a quality of life, a home, savings and a potential future.
I thrived during my stay but for family reasons I chose to come home and change my career path. The real question is why so many of us left (and continue to leave) in the first place?
Why did I have to emigrate to experience this supportive working environment and what would it take for the next generation of nurses/ doctors to want to come home? – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I read with interest your article of “ Psychotherapy group files complaint to EU against Minister for Health over sector standard s.” (October 12th).
The assertion by Coru that concerns about the potential difficulties Irish-trained psychotherapists might face practising elsewhere in Europe are inaccurate, and that the opposite is true, deserves closer scrutiny.
Coru appears to conflate statutory recognition of a profession in Ireland with the recognition of professional qualifications across Europe. These are not the same thing.
EU legislation facilitates professional mobility, but it does not guarantee automatic recognition of qualifications, particularly where significant differences exist in education and training requirements.
Several European countries already regulate psychotherapy and have established demanding standards concerning the duration and depth of training, supervised clinical practice and personal psychotherapy.
If Ireland adopts substantially lower requirements in these areas, on what basis can Coru confidently assert that this will improve the mobility of Irish-trained psychotherapists?
Has Coru undertaken a comparative assessment of its proposed standards against those of other European countries? If so, the findings should be made public.
The European Association for Psychotherapy has worked for decades towards greater coherence in psychotherapy training and professional recognition across Europe, while respecting the diversity of psychotherapeutic approaches.
Regulation should strengthen professional standards and facilitate mobility, not merely establish a statutory title. Without evidence of comparability, Coru’s assertion risks confusing legal recognition with the substantive professional formation necessary for recognition elsewhere in Europe. – Yours, etc,
Vice-President of the European Association for Psychotherapy (EAP)
Chair of the European Training Standards Committee (ETSC) of EAP
Sir, – There have been several letters complaining about pedestrians and cyclists going through red lights.
Based on my daily commute, I would add that many motorists seem to consider a light that has gone red within the last few seconds to be little more than a suggestion – only a little bit red, perhaps.
While everyone should obey the rules of the road, it seems obvious that motorists, who are among the most dangerous and least vulnerable road users, should be held to account first and foremost.
The blind eye that our car-dominated society turns to the bad behaviour of motorists also goes some way to explain the reaction of letter writer Frank J Byrne to cyclists on the footpath.
There’s a reason they’re not in the road with the cars. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Motorists, motorcyclists, e-bicyclists, cyclists, etc. should all read the RSA’s Rules of the Road, currently available in all good bookshops – fiction section. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Further to Norman Croke’s letter (October 20th) about the need to meet the requirements of the EU directive on adequate minimum wages – whereby in countries where collective bargaining coverage falls below 80 per cent an action plan must be established to increase it – there are aggravating circumstances in Ireland as a result of the financial crisis in 2008-2009.
One of these, which fell entirely on private sector workers, was the decision to impose a levy on private sector pension funds equivalent to 5 or 6 per cent of their value.
Inevitably this was passed on to the recipients of those pensions.
There was no Fempi-type provision for these cuts to be reversed when the State’s finances recovered, any more than there was for private pensions to be adjusted in line with those regularly awarded to public servants in negotiations with the public services committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions.
The EU directive does, however, provide for alternative means of addressing this shortfall. It could most effectively and equitably be done through the creation of a universal pension scheme, introduced incrementally, to which all employees and employers contributed, and from which all pensioners would eventually benefit. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – What an interesting article on the “ school meals initiative” (Friday, October 23rd).
The way in which school meals has been introduced is clearly not working. I’d suggest it’s not tighter controls we need but a completely different approach.
It’s hard to believe that ¤232 million was spent in the 2025/26 school year, especially when we’ve been made aware that it was spent largely on high sugar and high fat food, with very little nutritious content.
In France and most continental countries, school meals are cooked in the school kitchen. Local ingredients are used, local staff are employed.
Why can’t we build kitchens in our schools? I’d imagine you could build a lot of kitchens for ¤232 million.
Our children deserve better. – Yours, etc,

title: Ken Early: Flighty Manchester United executives have pandered their way into a corner
description: Fans are fickle and easily swayed, while executive club management has proved to be serial failures
content:
A goal didn’t look on when Lewis Cook hit it forward early into Manchester United’s half. Senne Lammens was rushing out and would surely get there first ... but the wind god had other ideas. The ball held up in the breeze and Evanilson nipped in to prod it beyond the keeper. Now he was well wide, but he hit the shot the only way it ever goes in from out there: with total conviction.
Seeing Evanilson’s finish, many of the home crowd at Old Trafford will have thought of Mark Hughes’s famous goal against Barcelona in the Cup-Winners Cup final in Rotterdam. A memory from a time when their club was animated by a different spirit.
This was United’s third 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth, under a third different manager, in three years. The game had the usual pattern: Bournemouth compact, organised, sharp, United shuffling around in an apparent fugue state, mystifyingly unable to execute the simplest tasks.
