The unusual thing was that this time some of United’s biggest and best-paid stars were watching from the bench due to recent differences of vision with the coach: Bruno Fernandes, Lisandro Martinez, Matheus Cunha.
When Martinez did come on in the second half, he was promptly overrun by Rayan, who should have scored. Bruno, United’s player of the 2020s, was left to stew on the bench, watching Michael Carrick introduce players like Joshua Zirkzee and Shea Lacey ahead of him.
Before the third goal, the noise at Old Trafford had all been coming from the Bournemouth fans: “Sacked in the morning”; “You’re going down with the City” and so on. But in the last 25 minutes the home crowd found their voice. The collective commentary they offered left no doubt as to who they blame for the current mess.
“You can stick your new stadium up your arse”, “We want Glazers out”, “Jason Wilcox, you’re a w****r”, “Sell United and f**k off home”, and a new entry “Best In Class – you’re having a laugh”.
The boos at full-time quickly gave way to Carrick’s song: “It’s hard to believe it’s not Scholes, it’s Carrick you know”. As Carrick walked apologetically down the tunnel, the song gave way to furious boos for the players who were following behind him.
It is worth pausing to reflect on what a remarkable scene this was – the supporters saluting their failed, about-to-be-sacked manager, while screaming their contempt for everyone else associated with the club.
Afterwards Carrick kept saying that hearing the reaction of the fans had given him “mixed emotions”, though he didn’t say what those emotions were. It was obvious enough that sorrow was one of them, but the unmentionable emotion he was also feeling was relief. Relief to know that in the end (and this surely was the end), the supporters don’t actually blame him for this. And maybe also relief that this scene would finally ensure his escape from the nightmare his position has become.
Imagine you’re one of the players walking towards that tunnel behind Carrick, hearing the crowd salute him, seeing him wave his thanks and acknowledgment – and then hearing the same fans round viciously on you.
It’s clear that quite a few of them don’t rate this coach. Fernandes’s interview after the Como debacle last week made it clear that he didn’t think Carrick’s tactical preparation was good enough. Martinez’s interview after the defeat to Atlético Madrid made it evident that he didn’t believe Carrick was a very important factor in club affairs. You simply don’t speak that way about a coach you respect.
Fernandes had also said in Como that United “focus too much on the past ... Everyone at the club has to understand that it’s not the same any more, we’re not in the past any more and we have to look to the future. We have to create something different in the present.”
Then Carrick came out for his press conference on Friday and delivered a five-minute homily on the historic values of Manchester United that name-checked Ryan Giggs, Wayne Rooney, Sir Alex, Sir Bobby and Sir Matt.
That stuff goes down well with the fans, who yesterday unfurled a banner featuring the faces of Eric Cantona, Bryan Robson and Roy Keane over the word “STANDARDS”. But is “you are nothing compared to those who came before you” a message that is likely to inspire these young United players?
We like to think of the fans as being the collective repository of the deep wisdom of the club, but in reality crowds often display terrible judgment. The United fans swept Ole Gunnar Solskjær into the job on a wave of jubilation. They shamelessly hero-worshipped Cristiano Ronaldo when that circus rolled back into their club in 2021. They rallied so ferociously behind Erik ten Hag when he won the FA Cup in 2024 that the club decided not to sack him and to renew his contract instead. Carrick, too, was transformed from interim to permanent by the alchemy of popular acclaim.
Of course, it’s not the fans who are ultimately responsible for those regrettable decisions, but the weak executives who pander to them. Unfortunately for United chief executive Omar Berrada and sporting director Jason Wilcox, they appear finally to have pandered their way into a corner. The terrible results and the falling-out with Fernandes have left them with little choice but to sack Carrick this week. But a third midseason sacking in three seasons would leave them dangerously exposed.
“Why are this pair of ex-Manchester City officials running Manchester United anyway?” is a question an uncomfortably large number of people are now asking. For Jim Ratcliffe, their City credentials meant “best in class”, but the recent independent commission findings indicate that illegal owner funding from Abu Dhabi was playing a rather more significant part in Manchester City’s success than anything Berrada or Wilcox were doing.
Their record since joining United reveals that, rather than working according to clear and well-thought-out principles, they are always ready to throw out their plans according to what seems popular in that moment. Renew Ten Hag, sack Ten Hag, believe in Amorim, sack Amorim, make Carrick permanent, sack Carrick. The best thing they could do for United would be to pander to the crowd one last time and follow Carrick out the door.

title: This will be my sixth year trick-or-treating. Here’s what I’ve discovered
description: Halloween offers up a portal for neighbours to connect – even if it is only once a year
content:
Having only come to trick-or-treating late, as a parent, I’ve been thinking about how this centuries-old tradition opens up something that’s missing in our modern lives.
As a country kid, my Halloween nights looked inward. We would pull the curtains tight on the encroaching darkness outside. I’d scrunch my eyes closed, preparing for the cold, and hold my breath before dunking my whole face in a basin of water. Sometimes I’d emerge victorious – with a golden 20p coin caught between my teeth. (You’ve got to love 1980s health and safety.)
But for my townie friends, Halloween brought them outwards, wandering the roads and paths of their streets and estates. They roamed in packs, wearing their not-so-firesafe plastic bag costumes and old-school masks tied with string. As well as trick-or-treating from friendly neighbours they already knew, they would prise open the squeaky gates of those they rarely saw, with shaking fingers pressing the doorbell. When the doors opened they would peer inside the porch, hoping for apple drops not apples. And grabbing before running. There were no adult chaperones – it was safety in numbers.
Raising townie kids of my own, I was horrified the first year my husband suggested we bring them knocking on our neighbours’ doors asking for sweets.
We live in a well-heeled Dublin suburban town. And we are both blow-ins. You nod at your nearest neighbours. You might even chat when there’s a crisis – like an electricity outage or an annoying alarm. You only knock on their door when a delivery driver has left a parcel. But beyond the occasional comment about the weather, it’s strictly business. As for those more than three doors away – they may as well live in the next county.
This is not the world many of us grew up in. There were cups of tea in neighbours’ houses, staring up at the light around their sacred heart pictures, wondering when the adults will ever stop talking. We were sent next door to borrow a lawnmower or a big ladder. And there was always time to stop for a chat or to gladly take a digestive biscuit and a glass of orange squash.
Perhaps the difference is the way of today’s family life for many of us urban-dwellers. When both parents work full-time, days feel full to the brim with swimming, martial arts, homework, birthday parties and school events. The minutes in between are filled with emails, WhatsApp messages and more late-night doomscrolling than I care to admit. There is barely enough left in the week for us to enjoy hanging out as a family, and rarely do we get to meet our own friends. So who in the world has time for cups of tea and chinwags with random neighbours?
Thus the thoughts of knocking on the doors of neighbours in those fancier houses on the next street with the big gates and long front gardens made me feel like a travelling salesman.
[ Fashion Irish childrenswear just got a whole lot more interesting Opens in new window ]
But like any good door-to-door seller knows, you put your shiniest product first. And so I pushed my very cute children/ monsters to the door, pressing the bell they couldn’t reach and stepping away.
This year will be my sixth trick-or-treat. After pressing dozens of doorbells and banging all sorts of knockers and successfully filling many buckets of sweets, here’s what I’ve discovered. My children are almost always met with big smiles. And enormous baskets of sweets and crisps, some thoughtfully prepared in hand-painted bags. There’s nearly always a kind word, a question about school, an “ooh” and “ahh” for their costume. And there’s a wave and a little chat with Mammy – who has now taken to wearing a spooky hat or headband for the occasion. We’ve met delighted toddlers, nostalgic parents whose teenage children have grown out of trick-or-treating, elderly people missing their grandchildren abroad and a group of giddy nuns only delighted that my atheist children rang on their doorbell.
[ Why Halloween pumpkins are smaller this year, and three viral hacks to carve them Opens in new window ]
And as a naturally nosy journalist, I do like to get a peek inside the hallways: from designer glass tables to Ikea shoe cupboards, polished concrete floors to linoleum and seeing which multimillion Victorian house is so cold the owner is wearing layers of woollen jumpers.
But the insight I mainly love is getting to meet the people who live in my wider neighbourhood. There is something reassuring about getting to see the goodness and kindness in the people who have randomly purchased or rented homes near my house. And for my excited children, it’s one of the highlights of their year. And it’s not just the mountainous sweet haul.
For thousands of years Halloween or Samhain has been celebrated as a portal. The one time of year when the boundary between the living and the dead grows thin, when ghosts and ghouls fly around our mortal world.
Trick-or-treating feels like a different sort of portal. When the sun rises on November 1st, the distant neighbours in my south Dublin suburb will return to being strangers. We will not knock on their door for a chat. They will not stop my kids in the street to ask them how their school day was. We will, like my 1980s rural Irish Halloween, return to looking inward, keeping ourselves to ourselves.
But every Halloween night I wonder. What would it be like if the trick-or-treat portal stayed cracked open just a little bit? If we stopped and smiled and had a little word about our day and the weather, would our overscheduled insular lives really collapse with the weight of it? Or would we all feel just a little more connected.

title: Bus and rail fares to be reviewed annually, NTA chief tells Minister
description: Move could mean passengers set to absorb 15% price hikes in January face increased fares in future
content:
Bus and rail passengers face higher charges in the years ahead, with reviews of fares set to take place annually.
Bus and rail fares are already scheduled to increase by 15 per cent from January, ending a period going back to 2018 marked by fare reductions.
Official papers released by the Department of Transport show that the new fare increases came about on the back of strong pressure from the Department of Public Expenditure.
It argued there had been a deal with Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien 12 months ago that fare reductions put in place in 2022 would be reversed by the middle of this year, as part of an overall €940 million exchequer allocation to subsidise non-commercial bus and train services.
The Department of Public Expenditure maintained the reversal of the 20 per cent cut in bus and train fares introduced in 2022, as part of a Government cost-of-living package, was to take place by June.
The Department of Public Expenditure told the secretary general of the Department of Transport on April 24th that it was concerned and disappointed to learn that this initiative was not to be progressed as scheduled, and that August was being considered as a date for any fare rise.
The Department of Public Expenditure also maintained it had learned that, rather than the full reversal of the 20 per cent fare cuts, consideration was being given in the transport sector to a rise of 10 per cent.
The minutes of an official oversight group reviewing State funding for bus and train routes, dated April 20th, state that the Department of Public Expenditure believed fare revenue should pay for the delivery of new services.
The minutes of the group, which includes the Department of Transport, the Department of Public Expenditure, the National Transport Authority (NTA) and New Era, the agency that provides advice to Ministers about commercial State companies, state: “If new services are funded solely through fare revenue this would require substantial additional fare revenue to sustain into following years.”
The NTA has said available funding has been primarily directed towards maintaining existing services.
On August 28th, NTA chief executive Anne Shaw told O’Brien of a planned 15 per cent fare rise to be announced in September.
Shaw said that to support the long-term sustainability of the State subsidised routes – known as public service obligation (PSO) – and provide greater certainty in funding, it intended “to undertake an annual review of fares”.
Shaw said the NTA recognised that fare increases may be of concern to some passengers. However, she said PSO fares had not increased since 2018, despite rising inflationary operating costs over that period. “Even following this determination, many fares will remain below the levels that would have applied had fares increased in line with inflation since 2018.”
Shaw said a consistent theme of talks involving the departments of Transport and Public Expenditure had been “the need to place PSO services on a more sustainable financial footing, with fare revenue making a greater contribution. These fare adjustments are an effort towards rebalancing the critical equation in how we fund PSO public transport nationally.”
Shaw said that while there had been a substantial increase in exchequer funding for PSO services this year, “continued inflationary pressures have increased the cost of operating public transport services”.
She said available funding had primarily been directed towards maintaining existing service levels.
The Minister has maintained that about 140 new and enhanced transport services will come on stream next year.

title: ‘Catholics seem to see the Orangeman as the bogeyman. They have this visceral hatred’
description: Orange Order veteran Noel Liggett says Drumcree was ‘moment of clarity’ for unionist community
content:
N oel Liggett’s days of marching in Orange Order parades are long behind him, following a football injury decades ago that has left him now with severe arthritis. But the order still means everything to him.
“In my knees, it is. Now I can’t walk, I need to sit down all the time,” the former baker tells The Irish Times in his sittingroom, “but I’m still out four or five nights at lodge meetings.”
“I first walked the Ormeau Road when I was age four. In 1969, on the way back from the old field up at Finaghy – after my ma got sick and tired of listening to me saying I wanted to walk,” he goes on.
Liggett is the District Master of Ballynafeigh Loyal Orange Lodge, No 10, whose Orange Hall stands on the Ormeau Road in south Belfast – once one of the most contested Orange routes.
Last December, he was awarded an MBE award for demonstrating “outstanding determination, tenacity and drive in promoting good relations and community cohesion in south Belfast for 30 years”.
The last time the Ballynafeigh lodge marched the full length of the Ormeau Road to mark the Twelfth of July, including the sharply-contested lower stretch of the road, was in 1998.
From 1999, the Parades Commission formally banned the lodge from crossing the Ormeau Bridge into the Lower Ormeau, a restriction that has been followed every year since.
“After 2000, we really couldn’t solve the parades issue. We had a decision to make: that we basically retreat behind our doors of the Orange Hall, or we go out and be part of the wider community.
“We decided to go out. We had various people in. We do a tour of the Orange Hall, we explain the history of the Orange Order, and then we let them ask any questions that they like.”
[ Jamie Bryson: Northern Irish unionists ‘must go on the offensive’ Opens in new window ]
“There was even a pensioners’ group from the Garvaghy Road that came up to visit us,” Liggett says, chuckling.
The Ormeau Bridge confrontations in the 1990s, like those in Drumcree , had drifted into history, but the core of the issue had never been dealt with: “Everyone believed the Ormeau Road’s been settled. It’s never been settled.”
Between the course of the Troubles and today, the Ormeau Road area has gone from being overwhelmingly Protestant to being majority Catholic, he says.
“The Protestant community on the road is now very clearly in a minority. Every other group on the road can enjoy its rights to the full, bar the Protestant community,” Liggett says.
In addition, the area has gentrified and many “middle-class Prods” look down on the Orange: “Some of our main problems now is with the middle class who believe they own the Ormeau,” he goes on.
“If you drive down the Ormeau Road in a bit of sunshine, you’ll see the coffee shops, all the guys sitting sipping their coffees. The older Prods will be down the side street, not really taking part. They look on us with contempt.”
[ Culture wars in the North Opens in new window ]
Now, the Ormeau is in the headlines because the Belfast Walkers’ Club, which represents Apprentice Boys members of the Ballynafeigh lodge, has sought permission to march over the bridge on November 7th, in advance of Armistice Day.
However, the application is the same one lodged for the last 15 years that has been refused by the Parades Commission, so “it has nothing to do with Drumcree”.
“Because of what happened in Portadown, people are scouring the internet and the Parades Commission website and will start reading into it a lot more ... ” Liggett goes on.
Questioned about Drumcree, Liggett shrugs, exasperated: “Boil Drumcree down, it was about 35 elderly men on a road. Yet it met with a universal response from the nationalist republican community, north and south.”
“Two communities suffered. Is there a hierarchy of suffering? I was never involved in that, unlike others on the other side. There, there are convicted bombers who set out to kill people. There’s nothing in my record.”
Pointing to the MBE that sits proudly on a shelf, a parchment copy of his citation from the British king Charles and a book holding letters of congratulations, he says: “I don’t like being in the spotlight, but, yes, I am very proud.”
Uncomfortable with questions about Portadown, he says he does not want to talk about matters that should be best left to members of the lodge in the Co Armagh town who are closer to the details.
[ Leo Varadkar thinks we should apologise to northern nationalists for partition. Why? Opens in new window ]
However, he has a wider criticism of the Orange Order itself: “And this is not specific to Portadown; we have allowed this to be portrayed as an institution against a poor, suppressed community.
“When in essence, it’s one community with two different parts in it, and it’s about what rights they should be able to enjoy – two communities that [have] been dumped on for years by others, yes.”
He had, he said, thought for a day for a word to describe the impact of Drumcree this year on the Protestant community. Not wanting to sound pompous, he says he believes the word is “clarity”.
“It’s a moment of clarity for the unionist community. The whole nationalist republican community in the North, and the Taoiseach, political parties, cultural figures in the South all came together,” he said.
Questioned about the belief of many that the Orange Order is a bitter, sectarian organisation, Liggett is perplexed: “It’s an organisation for Protestants. Does that make us sectarian? The Catholic Church is an organisation for Catholics. Does that make them sectarian?
“I don’t believe there’s anything wrong in having societies for the benefit of the community it represents. But Catholics seem to see the Orangeman as the bogeyman.
“They have this visceral hatred of the Orange Order, thinking that we spend hours thinking, ‘how can we annoy Taigs?’ Well, we’re not. Half the time we’re worried about where we’re getting our sandwiches on the Twelfth, or our sore feet.”
[ PSNI feared gun use by dissident republicans if parade went down Garvaghy Road, court told Opens in new window ]
This year’s Drumcree controversy will cast long shadows, he believes: “No unionist will look at any assurances that will be offered by the South, or by Sinn Féin and say, ‘maybe, it’s worth considering’.
“There was a lawful decision that the parade could take place. There were lawful decisions in past years that said it could not take place, and that was accepted by the Orange.”
In time, he believes sharper people in Sinn Féin will realise that they went too far at Drumcree: “There must be some thinking that. If your aspiration is truly a united Ireland, this is not the way to go about it.”
Despite their talk, he does not believe the people in the Republic, in their hearts, want anything to do with either community in Northern Ireland, and they certainly do not want to pay for it.
[ Many loyalists are desperate to leave – the only thing stopping some is a £5,000 ‘exit fee’ Opens in new window ]
In any event, they do not see a place for unionists in such a unified state, he believes: “One of the things I took out of a trip to the Dáil years [ago] is that Irish history basically starts in 1916. There’s 700 years missing.
“You can’t peddle this line that Irish history starts in 1916, and if you don’t buy into that then you’re not Irish. I’m Irish. But I’m British and an Ulsterman, and Orange.”

title: Plan for 70 houses and apartments on Dublin 4 site beside Muckross all-girls school
description: The Dominican religious order sold the land, including its former convent and chapel, for more than €8 million in 2021
content:
Up to 70 houses and apartments have been proposed on the site of a former convent and chapel in Donnybrook, Dublin 4 that was owned by the Dominican Sisters, documents recently filed to Dublin City Council show.
The developers have sought permission to construct a new five-storey complex with 29 apartments as well as various refurbishments and partial demolitions to existing structures, some of which were built nearly a century ago and hold protected status.
The partial demolition and complete refurbishment of Muckross Park House, a former convent that housed 12 nuns some five years ago, has been proposed. This would provide for 25 apartments, the refurbishment of the religious order’s former chapel for 10 apartments and the construction of six houses within the adjoining walled garden.
The application was submitted to the council earlier this month by Muckross Park Developments, a subsidiary of a McGreevy Investment Holdings – a Dundalk-registered company owned by Arthur and Sean McGreevy. The company generated €29 million in turnover and €7.9 million in pretax profits in the year to the end of November 2024, its most recently filed financial accounts show.
The proposed housing development on Marlborough Road is equidistant to Donnybrook in Dublin 4 and Ranelagh in Dublin 6, and would back on to Dominican College, Muckross Park (often referred to simply as Muckross), a prominent all-girls school that is one of the few non-fee paying schools in the area.
Past pupils include judges on the High Court and European Court of Human Rights, an RTÉ presenter, and author and Booker Prize finalist Emma Donoghue.
Some 709 girls currently attend the school, while 587 boys and girls attend the neighbouring St Mary’s National School, according to the Department of Education. Both border the site of the proposed development.
Documents submitted to Dublin City Council as part of the planning application indicate street access to Marlborough Road is shared with the secondary school, although it makes provisions for “alterations to the existing vehicular, pedestrian and cyclist access arrangements”.
While Muckross Park House is a “protected structure”, meaning any proposed alterations to the building must comply with additional regulations, the developers do not propose demolition to the most historic parts of the house.
The Dominican Sisters bought the property in August 1900, opening primary, secondary and collegiate level schools for girls later that year.
As the school community expanded, the order built a boarding house for pupils, residences for novice nuns and a modern concert hall between the late 1920s and early 1930s.The convent was built in 1928 and the chapel was blessed in 1945, according to the secondary school’s website.
They sold the site for €8.4 million in total through two separate sales on the same day in September 2021. A property called “Veritas House, Dominican Convent” was sold for €4.9 million, while “Dominican Convent, Muckross Park” was sold for €3.5 million, according to the Property Price Register, the State’s official database for residential property sales.
The properties are not listed on Táilte Éireann, the State’s official land registry, and thus further exact details of its ownership and size are not publicly available.
A one-bedroom apartment in Veritas House is currently listed to rent for €2,000 per month.,

title: What makes someone a murderer? Irish-born philosopher believed she had the answer
description: NAZA lays bare the horror of AI-enhanced war but there is a glimmer of hope
content:
I n 1956, an unconventional Irish-born philosopher staged a one-woman protest against the then US president, opposing plans by her university to award the man – whom she believed to be a mass murderer – an honorary degree.
The philosopher was Elizabeth Anscombe , the president Harry Truman , and the charge against him: the intentional killing of civilians in Hiroshima and Nagasaki in Japan.
Anscombe’s stance at the University of Oxford 70 years ago challenged a general consensus among western political leaders that using nuclear weapons to end the second World War was justified. She set out her thinking in a pamphlet still referenced today in moral philosophy: Mr Truman’s Degree.
“Choosing to kill the innocent as a means to your ends is always murder,” she wrote.
Anscombe wasn’t a pacifist. Killing innocent civilians “is not necessarily murder”, she said, “even if you know as a matter of statistic certainty” that such deaths will take place as a downstream effect of military force. What qualifies as murder is the intent to kill innocent people.
While Truman might argue the nuclear attack hastened the end of war and spared further loss of life in combat, there is no escaping the fact that the US set out to kill men, women and children indiscriminately. It is estimated that between 120,000 people and double that number ultimately perished.
Anscombe’s essay is highly relevant to modern discussions on the limits of legitimate military action. And it came to mind after watching NAZA , a chilling and impactful documentary on the Israel Defense Forces ’ (IDF) bombing campaign in Gaza that began after the Hamas terror attack of October 7th, 2023. The film comprises interviews with 24 anonymised soldiers and intelligence personnel exploring the IDF’s policy on “collateral damage”, or NAZA as it’s known militarily (short for nezek agavi in Hebrew).
Shocking claims are made that the IDF uses artificial intelligence (AI) to help select targets, using crude formulae to decide how many civilian casualties are permitted in each airstrike. Some interviewees testify that “20 NAZA” – killing 20 civilians in order to target one suspected Hamas member – is routinely allowed. One veteran claims a strike endangering 500 civilians was approved to target a single Hamas member. The IDF denies this and other allegations in the film, while Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu has branded NAZA’s Israeli directors as enemies of the state.
The documentary strengthens the case for hauling Netanyahu before a war crimes tribunal. But, strangely, it may weaken the case for describing what has been happening in Gaza as genocide by the strictest, legal definition of that word. Under international law, to constitute genocide there must be “proven intent” to exterminate a specific population. However, none of those interviewed testified to deliberately trying to kill civilians.
If they are representative of IDF thinking then it suggests what lies at the heart of the Israeli war machine is not so much murderous intent as callousness, inhumanity and a sickening indifference to the scale of Palestinian suffering.
[ Naza: Why Israel doesn’t want the world to see this movie Opens in new window ]
Some will recoil at this line of thinking, and it feels distasteful to be mulling over the meaning of words when more than 74,000 people in Gaza lie dead, according to local estimates. However, Anscombe insisted on clearly defined moral concepts, without which, she believed, ethical reasoning would collapse altogether.
Anscombe was born in Limerick on March 18th, 1919. Her father was a captain in the British army posted to Munster during the War of Independence so the family didn’t stick around Ireland long. In academic stints at Cambridge and Oxford, she established herself as one of the greatest moral philosophers of her generation and became a close confidante of Ludwig Wittgenstein . The two endlessly discussed the limits of morality and linguistics – and when Wittgenstein moved to Dublin in 1948 to recuperate from illness, Anscombe joined him for a fortnight in Ross’s Hotel (now the Ashling Hotel) on Parkgate Street where he had lodgings.
Anscombe, who was Catholic, continued to work on the idea of intention for decades. Establishing intent is far from straightforward, and it is beyond the scope of this column to settle the argument in the case of Israel. At least one IDF insider interviewed for NAZA supported the argument that Israel’s actions amounted to genocide. And there are numerous examples of innocent civilians being killed by the IDF as a means to an end (for example, the end of creating a security buffer zone) – which is the definition of murder in Anscombe’s book.
[ ‘You hack her phone, then you kill her’: What Israeli intelligence officers told Naza director Yuval Abraham about their tactics in Gaza Opens in new window ]
Crucially, Anscombe emphasised that evil impacted on your character irrespective of its wider consequences. Truman could not escape the fact that he was a murderer – and he had to live with that knowledge, Anscombe insisted – no matter how he tried to justify his actions.
A striking aspect of NAZA was how many of the interviewees were struggling to marry an instinctive loyalty to Israel with an awareness of the nature of their actions. It was like watching in real time what psychologists call cognitive dissonance – the mental discomfort that comes from holding two incompatible beliefs.
Tellingly, one contributor said it was better that AI selected the targets in Gaza since it would be difficult for him, or any other human, to sanction them.
There is horror in that realisation, but also hope.
The hope is that a moral conscience lost in midst of war can yet be found.

title: Ireland urges greater efforts to save nature at global biodiversity summit
description: Cop17 in Armenia taking place against backdrop of ‘vast decline in nature’ on global scale
content:
Irish wildlife champions are among thousands of politicians, officials, academics, campaigners, conservationists, industrialists and finance chiefs attending the Global Biodiversity Summit – or Cop17 – in Yerevan, Armenia .
Their task at the global summit, which started on October 19th and runs until next Friday, is to examine how a commitment made four years ago to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030 is playing out. Following on from this, they will aim to put in place supports to ensure it can be realised.
That commitment came 30 years after the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro produced the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). Under the convention, the world undertook to protect nature and use its resources sustainably and fairly.
In the three decades that followed, those promises were broken repeatedly, universally and disastrously.
So what has happened since 2022 when a renewed effort was pledged?
A World Wildlife Fund report published just before Yerevan put the loss of wildlife populations at 73 per cent in 50 years and said the “vast decline in nature at a global scale” was continuing.
The secretariat of the CBD said similar in their pre-summit report.
“Many of the critical elements of progress, including finance, capacity, co-operation and data are still missing in action,” UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres remarked.
“Nature won’t thrive on good intentions,” he warned.
Ireland can’t hide from those remarks. An assessment last year showed 90 per cent of protected habitats – and the plants and animals dependent on them – were unhealthy.
But the Irish government – when the Green Party was part of it – led the charge in a tough battle for the European Parliament to pass the landmark Nature Restoration Law in 2024, establishing aims that mirror the global 2022 agreement.
Ireland then became the first member state to submit its mandatory national Nature Restoration Plan to the EU .
So can Ireland and the EU hold their heads high at the Yerevan negotiations?
Fintan Kelly of the Irish Environmental Network is there with representatives of Fair Seas, the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group , BirdWatch Ireland , the Irish Wildlife Trust and Streamscapes. He acknowledges the good intentions but holds the same fears as Guterres.
“The EU will arrive to the table and say, ‘look, we’ve got this world-leading law, we’re in the process of implementing it, member states have their national plans so trust us, we’re doing this’. But we’re there to point out this isn’t the full picture,” he said.
Kelly cites the ending of the EU’s LIFE projects, which have been critical for localised nature restoration. He also criticises the lack of funding for environmental protection in the new Common Agricultural Policy package and the proposed weakening of environmental assessment requirements in the Birds and Habitats Directives.
The next seven-year EU budget currently under negotiation also proposes cuts in funding for the environment and there is no EU-wide, or Irish, fund to support action under the Nature Restoration Law yet.
“We want to set up meetings with MEPs and point out we’re really concerned about the direction of travel,” Kelly said of the campaigning opportunities the Irish organisations hope to grab while in Yerevan.
Jane Stout, professor of ecology at Trinity College Dublin, has just returned from Yerevan and describes the first week of negotiations as “a mixed bag” of positivity and concern.
“The positivity is around the fact that all the governments are there and the reach of the CBD is expanding,” she said. “When it was first ratified back in 1992, for example, private businesses were not even mentioned and they were seen very much as the problem. Now they’re seen as part of the solution, so there were lots of sessions on business and biodiversity .
“On the one side, that’s positive and hopeful because it’s bringing more people into the conversation. On the other side, it’s a reflection of the fact that they’re starting to worry that this isn’t just an environmental problem.”
Stout is referring to the belated realisation that once water becomes too polluted to use and soils too depleted to grow anything, once pollinators disappear and oceans stop supporting marine life, almost every industry loses its raw materials and the vital services that nature provides.
Wrangling finance out of industry and the richer countries to support a turnaround in nature’s fortunes is a key focus of the summit.
Minister for Nature Christopher O’Sullivan is in Yerevan and acknowledges Ireland has yet to put its own money where its good intentions lie.
“I have been working with colleagues across Government to establish a dedicated nature restoration fund for a number of months,” he said, adding he hoped to “be in a position to share more information soon”.
On the wider issues, he said his approach to the talks would be to emphasise what is at stake.
“We’re not on track to meet our 2030 targets, [which is] putting people, the economy and the wider environment – as well as wildlife and habitats – at risk of significant consequences,” he said.
“What we’re saying, as both the EU and as Ireland, is that we can’t give up. We need to do more. We need to work together to change this awful trajectory and protect the diversity of life on this amazing planet.”

title: Dublin City Council outbid in sale of Martello tower in Sandymount
description: Monument was purchased in excess of its guide price of €1.5 million, a cost described as ‘excessive’ by a council official
content:
A bid made by Dublin City Council ( DCC ) below the guide price of €1.5 million to purchase Sandymount ’s Martello tower in Dublin 4 was unsuccessful, with the monument instead being purchased by a private individual.
The protected structure and recorded monument, which has lain vacant for more than two decades, has recently been sold.
A private individual purchased the tower for more than the guide price of €1.5 million, according to a source familiar with the details of the sale.
Several councillors had called for the council to buy the structure after it came on the market, with council officials also eager to acquire the tower, saying it was an “important bit of heritage in the city”.
Before making the unsuccessful bid, options outlined by the council and seen by The Irish Times detailed three potential uses, including retaining it as a historical monument, which would see its 1980s three-storey extension demolished.
Another option was the refurbishment of the tower and its extension for use as tea rooms, while a third possibility would have seen it retained as a historical monument with stand-alone new-build tea rooms and a “possible link to the tower”.
Council officials inspected the tower earlier this summer, describing it in internal correspondence as an “iconic structure”, though a Dublin city valuer warned the extension would require “complete modernisation or demolition”.
This was something he believed the previous owner was “not prepared to take on”, adding that it would cost a “fortune” to bring it to current building standards.
The valuer also believed the guide price was “excessive”, correspondence obtained through the Freedom of Information Act shows.
[ ‘Very heartbreaking’: The Cedar Tree, Ireland’s first Lebanese restaurant, set to close Opens in new window ]
In an update in June, the city valuer told DCC chief executive Richard Shakespeare the council had made what it considered to be a “very fair and reasonable offer, if somewhat below the guide price”.
However, estate agent Colliers advised that three bids had been made and the council’s was “unsuccessful”.
The structure was one of 28 defensive towers built between 1804 and 1805, stretching from Bray to Balbriggan, to protect against the threat of a French invasion during the Napoleonic wars.
Sandymount’s Martello tower became a popular cafe in the 1960s, before an extension was added two decades later, the large windows of which have been covered by shutters for years.
Property developer Robert Noonan had plans for a restaurant at the site, hoping to partner with Peter Langan, the Irish restaurateur behind Langan’s Brasserie, a celebrity hotspot in London.
Langan died at the age of 47, weeks after suffering injuries in a fire at his UK home in 1988, and the project never came to fruition after his death.
[ Owner of €2.5m ‘uninhabitable’ house in Dalkey seeks its demolition Opens in new window ]
Until recently, it was owned by Michael Doyle of the Doyle Hotels family. He sought to convert the space into a microbrewery, though he failed to secure planning permission in 1999.
Green Party councillor Hazel Chu , who was one of several councillors to call on both the State and the council to purchase the site for public use, said it was a “large missed opportunity”.
“It’s a piece of our heritage and a piece of our history. We really should be keeping it for public use,” she said.
When the site went on the market, Minister of State Emer Higgins said the Office of Public Works, had “no plans” to buy the tower, though Chu argues the State “should have stepped in to buy it”.
“There’s always a ‘we’ll leave it to someone else’,” she said.
“It’s not something the State couldn’t have afforded. It wasn’t a price tag of €20 million. €1.5 million is a lot of money still, but it wasn’t a large price tag for something that could be put back into use.”

title: An Irish documentary on a relatively obscure American figure can illuminate so much
description: `Truthfulness is sort of out of fashion’, says Sinéad O’Shea, maker of film about communist activist Fergie Chambers
content:
Sinéad O’Shea is one of Ireland’s finest documentary makers. Her last film was a compelling documentary on Edna O’Brien , called Blue Road. Her latest, out in Irish cinemas this Friday, is All About the Money. In it she follows the American communist activist Fergie Chambers .
From the billionaire Cox family, a few years ago he cashed out. In recent years he used some of his money to establish a collective in Massachusetts, donate to humanitarian causes in Gaza , invest (if you want to call it that) in a Tunisian football team, move to Ireland, and occupy a space in culture that can come across to some as contradictory: a man hugely wealthy thanks to a family fortune but who is avowedly anti-capitalist.
He was arrested in Spain last July on foot of an extradition request from the US and accused of money laundering, in a case many characterise as politically motivated.
All of this is fascinating, a strange tale of our times. But O’Shea’s approach to her subject and her craft tells us a bigger story, one that lives not in conclusions and certainty, but in complexity and nuance. At a preview in Dublin last week, she spoke afterwards about truth.
Her perspective is this: “It has become quite political to be truthful. It’s not seen as a neutral space. Reporting what you see leads to accusations of bias.” Her words stayed with me because that’s not just about a film, but where we are in all sorts of discourse; political, social, cultural, digital.
Documentary making can be a lens through which we witness the broader world, literally. But what happens when you don’t render issues or people right or wrong? What happens when nuance and contradiction is favoured over partisanship?
It’s not just the story O’Shea tells that illuminates complex times, it’s her approach to staying in the truth of things rather than leaping to easy answers for the purpose of entertainment or attention-hooking.
As an avid consumer of documentary film I will watch pretty much anything, although I’m not big on true crime. But if there’s a doc out there on a long-retired NFL quarterback, a country musician I’ve never listened to a song of, an arcane subculture or forgotten scandal, I will watch it. So much of this stuff is of course hagiography bordering on propaganda, one of heroes and monsters, successes and failures.
Watching All About the Money, you can almost see another film hiding in the distance, a lesser film, one with the flashy animated graphics, corny voiceover, whiplash twists, stacked cliffhangers that stretch the story over several hours begging the viewer to not even wait for the next episode to buffer, all wrapped in the algorithmic structure that plagues contemporary documentaries in the streaming age.
This sort of form is what is binged. When we talk about binging streaming series we rarely talk about the aftermath of the binge, which like all binges, renders the consumer addled yet spaced out, full yet empty. What’s also relevant is how truth is sacrificed in the pursuit of attention.
And yet something else is happening in documentary making that is unseating this culture of short, sharp, and simple. Suddenly it appears people are searching for something deeper. You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder’s documentary on the disgraced Elizabeth Holmes who rose to power and wealth on hubris, delusion, and ultimately fraud, is being lauded as the film of the year. It may even become the first documentary nominated for Best Picture at the Academy Awards. It is also just under three hours and audiences are going wild.
Musk , Alex Gibney’s latest documentary on the tech oligarch and man responsible for dismantling USAid leading to hundreds of thousands of deaths, is three hours and 45 minutes long. The consolidation and politicisation of media power has infused its promotion, with YouTube, Meta, and TikTok, all restricting its advertising and then reversing that, citing “errors”. Who knows what the truth is?
The second installation of Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends, which follows independent Russian journalists in exile, clocks in at close to six hours. The first part, which follows the journalists while still in Moscow in the run up to and in the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, is five hours 25 minutes. Its length is justified because the time spent with the film’s subjects is essential to effectively capturing the relationship between time and how the repression of free speech escalates.
Speaking to O’Shea the day after the screening, she discussed what is being lost right now which is truth. “Truthfulness is sort of out of fashion. Documentary making is one thing, but everything has become a giant football match. Everything is so partisan. The truth is much more nuanced, and that’s almost not conventional at the moment.”
This isn’t just about filmmaking, it’s sort of about, well, everything.
Misinformation, disinformation, conspiracy, censorship, lies, pretences, propaganda, denials, vested interests, the growing struggle to determine what is “real” in the age of AI – all of this has created a great untethering across politics, culture and social discourse.
It’s interesting that an Irish documentary on a relatively obscure American figure can illuminate so much. What it tells us is when one makes a decision rooted in journalistic integrity, not the pursuit of commercial gain, the truth does actually out. There’s a lesson in that that goes far beyond a single film.

title: Israeli election will have profound implications for Jewish state and Palestinians
description: Binyamin Netanyahu’s hold on power is in the balance as neither his far-right coalition nor the opposition is forecast to win a majority
content:
F or the past four years, Salim Slebi has watched Israeli settlers seize hilltop after hilltop in the occupied West Bank , as Binyamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition has overseen the biggest expansion of outposts in the Palestinian territory on record. But he never expected the same thing to happen in Israel.
Then, one day in September, it did. On a ridge overlooking Majd al-Krum, an Arab town in northern Israel where Slebi serves as mayor, a group of settlers pitched tents and hoisted an Israeli flag on land owned partly by the Jewish National Fund – and partly by Arab landowners.
After mass protests from locals, the settlers eventually left. It later emerged that the fund had only given permission for grazing on its land.
But Slebi doubts their departure is the end of the matter. The settlers arrived just days after Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s ultranationalist finance minister, set out a plan to “Judaise” the Galilee and the Negev, two parts of Israel where the majority is Arab rather than Jewish, if his party is part of Israel’s next government.
“It was very clear to us that they are trying to transfer what they are doing in the West Bank to the Galilee,” says Slebi. “They don’t have any limits ... it is only a matter of time before they come back.”
Smotrich’s plan – to which he gave the tagline “Yes. We’re Judaising!” – is part of a suite of hardline proposals put forward by members of Netanyahu’s coalition in advance of an election that many in the country regard as the most important in Israel’s near 80-year history.
Tuesday’s poll is the first since the catastrophe of Hamas’s October 7th, 2023 attack. For many Israelis, the vote will be a reckoning with that day and the failures that preceded it. But it is also a choice between two radically different visions of the country’s future.
In the year before Hamas’s attack, a bitter feud over the very nature of the Israeli state split the country into two camps. One, nationalist and religious, was led by Netanyahu’s coalition and the other, more secular and politically heterodox, was represented by the opposition.
That same fault line underlies Tuesday’s vote. Members of Netanyahu’s coalition, widely regarded as the most rightwing in Israeli history, are touting ideas that are, if anything, more radical than anything they have done so far. These range from emptying Gaza of Palestinians to the resumption of a controversial judicial overhaul that sparked months of mass protests before the Hamas attack.
[ Protests across Israel call for October 7th inquiry on third anniversary of attack Opens in new window ]
The opposition is pledging to undo this legacy, with the judicial changes that have already passed into law among the things it plans to roll back. But its members are also promising measures the government refuses to countenance: ending the blanket exemption from military service for Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community and holding a state inquiry into the failures of October 7th.
Polls suggest the race is on a knife edge. Neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition, centred around former general Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, is forecast to win a majority. Whether either can form a government is likely to depend on post-election horse-trading, which could last for months.
But analysts say the fundamental choice is as stark as any put before Israeli voters. Even if it takes further rounds of voting to reach a decisive outcome, the implications will be profound for the fabric of Israeli society, for the Palestinians and for Israel’s position in the world, with even traditional allies threatening sanctions over the government’s hardline policies in the West Bank.
For opposition voters in particular, the sense of jeopardy is acute. “Israel is moving culturally, religiously, in a certain direction, where the people who want Israel to remain a western liberal democracy connected to universal ideals feel under threat,” said Shmuel Rosner, an Israeli pollster.
“[The choice in this election] goes to the very core of Israel’s identity as a country.”
At the heart of the choice facing Israelis is Netanyahu. The veteran prime minister has led Israel for 19 of the past 30 years, dominating its political scene like no other leader. He also has become an intensely polarising figure, with corruption charges, which he denies, and a series of fallings-out with erstwhile allies limiting his political options.
At the previous election in 2022, with several parties refusing to enter a coalition with him, Netanyahu returned to power by allying with the ultra-Orthodox and two of the country’s most extreme-right parties. He insisted he would have his hands “firmly on the steering wheel”. But his coalition’s policies have been heavily influenced by his ultranationalist allies. Most observers expect that, were his coalition to return to power, the same dynamic would play out again.
Netanyahu has sought to cast the election as a choice between his bloc, which would stand up for Israeli interests, and an opposition that would capitulate to international pressure. No opposition party is proposing the establishment of a Palestinian state. But the campaign motto of Netanyahu’s Likud party portrays the vote as a simple choice: Yamin o Falestin – the right, or Palestine.
The party has repeatedly said it will thwart a Palestinian state. In August, it said that if the coalition were re-elected it would maintain its “historic momentum in the settlement” of the West Bank, where it approved more than 100 new settlements – which are illegal under international law – during its term.
Netanyahu’s allies have gone far further. Last month, the ultranationalist Jewish Power party, headed by national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who was previously convicted of incitement to racism against Arabs, set out a plan for removing 1.86 million Palestinians – nearly 90 per cent of Gaza’s population – from the Palestinian enclave over the next seven years.
He is not alone. Ofer Winter, the head of a new right-wing party seeking to join Netanyahu’s coalition, also backs what he and Ben-Gvir both call “voluntary” emigration from Gaza. Moshe Feiglin, an extremist whose Zehut party is running on a joint slate with Smotrich, has said he wants to see Gaza “empty”. “Occupation, transfer all, all the Arabs. I don’t care. They cannot stay there after what they did,” Feiglin told the Jerusalem Post this month.
Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have both said Israel should also “encourage” the emigration of Palestinians from the West Bank. Smotrich, who has long advocated annexing that territory, said last month that Israel should also annex the more than half of Gaza it already controls, as well as land up to the Litani river in southern Lebanon.
[ Israeli government orders army to prepare for full closure of West Bank Opens in new window ]
Among an increasing share of rightwing Israelis, such messages are vote winners. “There are a lot of places in Israel that belong to us but the Arabs claim they are theirs,” said Yosef, a 32-year-old who owns two stalls in Jerusalem’s Mahane Yehuda market, and is planning to vote for Ben-Gvir. “If we want to win, we have to take back what belongs to us.”
For Arab Israelis, who make up a fifth of Israel’s population, and more leftwing Jewish Israelis, the gradual mainstreaming of ideas such as population transfer that were once beyond the pale is horrifying. “These are eliminationist policies,” says Diana Buttu, a Palestinian-Israeli lawyer and analyst. “This is existential.”
Others worry about the international implications. In recent months, several countries, including the UK, France, Canada, Spain and the Netherlands, have announced or imposed sanctions on goods from settlements in the West Bank in protest at their relentless expansion and the Israeli government’s refusal to rein in spiralling settler attacks on Palestinians, which the UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband recently branded “ethnic cleansing”.
“If anybody was holding anything back [in terms of sanctions], another three or four years of this government will trigger anything and everything the international community can think of to express their deep distaste and revulsion for this Israel,” says a senior opposition official.
“And the argument that there is an alternative, there is another Israel ... just falls flat if we cannot replace this government.”
For many Israelis, the election is defined by domestic politics. Perhaps the most immediate question is whether Israel will finally launch a state commission of inquiry into the failures that allowed Hamas’s October 7th attack, widely regarded as the worst security failure in Israeli history.
Netanyahu and his allies, on whose watch the disaster occurred, have resolutely opposed establishing such a commission. The opposition has pledged to do so as one of its first moves in power.
But two other issues will have an even more far-reaching impact: the coalition’s determination, if re-elected, to return to its judicial overhaul and the opposition’s pledge to end the ultra-Orthodox exemption from military service.
Before it was engulfed by the war in Gaza, Netanyahu’s coalition’s push to rein in the powers of the judiciary was the dominant issue in Israeli politics. For many on the right, the drive was a long-overdue corrective to years of judicial over-reach. Opponents saw it as an attempt to undermine the already weak checks on Israeli governments and to allow Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox and extreme-right allies to impose their worldview on society.
The overhaul was eventually frozen by months of protest and the outbreak of war. Three years on, Netanyahu’s allies are eager to put it back on the agenda. Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party and Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power have put forward various proposals, including allowing parliament to override Supreme Court decisions, limiting how the court can be petitioned, and ousting the attorney general – one of the main checks on government power – and splitting up her roles.
[ The Irish Times view on the Israeli election: the battle to unseat Netanyahu Opens in new window ]
The proposals are more radical than the relatively limited changes the government managed to achieve in its first term. But the stakes of any overhaul are raised by the fact that up to 10 new judges are due to be appointed to Israel’s 15-strong Supreme Court over the next four years, meaning that the next government could determine the political balance of the court for years.
Yohanan Plesner, head of the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem-based think-tank, says that, if implemented, such changes would “shape the nature of Israel’s democracy for many years to come”.
“It will be a change of Israel’s democratic regime in a way that concentrates all governing power in the hands of the political majority. And that power will be practised by ministers and political appointments with virtually no constraints,” he says.
Others put it more bluntly. “If we lose, Israel will stop being a democratic country,” says Yaya Fink, a candidate for the leftwing Democrats. “We succeeded in the last four years, with millions of people on the streets protesting, in keeping Israel a democratic state. But this guarantee is not forever.”
No less far-reaching is the question over the future of the complex relationship between the Israeli state and its fastest-growing demographic group: the ultra-Orthodox community, known in Hebrew as Haredim.
The exemption of Haredi religious students from military service, the result of a 1948 deal between Israel’s founder, David Ben-Gurion, and the ultra-Orthodox community, has long been a source of frustration for other Jewish Israelis. But the strain of the war in Gaza – Israel’s longest-ever conflict – on its reservist-dependent military has catapulted the topic up the political agenda.
The two ultra-Orthodox parties in Netanyahu’s coalition – Shas and United Torah Judaism – both said last week they would not join a new government with Netanyahu unless it enshrined the exemption in law, after the Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that the existing arrangement had no legal basis.
The opposition parties have made drafting the Haredim a central part of their platforms, proposing sanctions for those who do not serve that range from the loss of benefits to the loss of the right to travel and vote. Some, such as Yashar, are even proposing criminal charges for draft dodgers.
[ Trump’s backing fails to lift Netanyahu as Israel heads for defining vote Opens in new window ]
On both sides of Israel’s political divide, the issue is seen as fundamental. Aryeh Deri, who heads Shas, said this year that the election boiled down to a choice between Jewish traditions and teachings and “the rule of the attorney-general trying to erase every spark of Torah and Judaism”.
Rosner, the pollster, says the sense of urgency is even greater among opposition voters, as the growth of the Haredi community means it will become increasingly hard to outvote. Due to high birth rates, the Haredi share of the population is forecast to rise from an eighth today to a quarter by 2050.
“On the centre left there is a realisation that ... the opposite camp is growing and maybe 10 years down the road it will be too large to be defeated,” he says, adding that this fear relates not just to Haredi conscription but also to a broader feeling that Israel is moving inexorably to the right.
“That’s why people feel this sense of urgency. That’s why so many Israelis are coming back from abroad to vote,” he adds.
For now, opinion polls suggest that even the returnees may not be enough to tip the balance either way. Both Netanyahu’s bloc and the Zionist opposition centred around Eisenkot are forecast to fall well short of the 61 seats needed to form a government. And key players in both blocs have ruled out coalitions with Israel’s Arab parties that could get them over the line.
[ Fintan O'Toole: Zionism is not racism, any more than Irish nationalism is sectarianism Opens in new window ]
Israel’s President Yitzhak Herzog, who will oversee the coalition-building, has said he wants the election to deliver a new government and will push parties to do everything to avoid falling into a cycle of repeated votes, as happened between 2019 and 2021. But even if he fails, the fundamental choice facing Israel will remain.
“The election is incredibly consequential, the most important in our lifetimes,” says a second opposition official. “Even if it isn’t decisive on election day and even in the unlikely scenario of a second round it will be settled one way or another, and [that choice] will be very dramatic.”
