title: Official papers reveal budget deal to reverse 20% fare cuts by June this year
description: Department of Public Expenditure voiced concerns timeline would not be met as transport sector considered 10% rise
content:
On October 8th last year, announcing a then-record €940 million Exchequer subvention for bus and rail services, Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien said future fare rises were not off the table. He pointed to the need for a “sustainable” funding model.
Newly released official documents show that five days earlier – October 3rd, 2025 – the Department of Public Expenditure (DPER) believed a deal had been reached that would see an effective 20 per cent price rise take effect from June 2026.
By spring of this year, however, DPER was worried the transport sector seemed to be moving away from this agreement.
The vast bulk of public transport services are not run on a commercial basis. Instead, they rely on State subsidies to keep going. Over recent years, there have also been a series of measures to make public transport more attractive and affordable.
[ Bus and rail fares to be reviewed annually, NTA chief tells Minister Opens in new window ]
The last general fare rise was in December 2018. In 2022, then-minister Eamon Ryan reduced fares by 20 per cent . In recent years, free travel for children aged between five and eight was also introduced, and the Young Adult Leap card was extended to those up to 25. People over 70 with a free travel pass could nominate a companion to accompany them.
While revenue from fares fell, staffing and fuel costs increased, leaving the Exchequer with a larger bill at a time when the Government was coming under pressure to expand and enhance services. By Budget 2026, the Exchequer subvention was over €900 million and it will rise to €1.042 billion next year.
DPER officials maintained that the deal with O’Brien and his officials stipulated Ryan’s 20 per cent fare cut would be reversed by early summer. By April, however, they were concerned the timeline was slipping and the transport sector was talking about a 10 per cent increase.
On April 21st, DPER officials told the Department of Transport they had been assured, as part of the deal the previous October, that “an implementation date of 1 June 2026 would allow for the necessary preparations to be made”.
“There seems to have been a significant delay in communicating [this] to the National Transport Authority, which has left us in a situation, regardless of the ongoing geopolitical situation, whereby they would not have been ready to implement the increase on the agreed date.”
Two days later, the Department of Transport said it remained committed to the budget deal, but added “it must be acknowledged that the implementation of a fare’s adjustment in the context of the ongoing geopolitical situation has become much more challenging”.
On April 24th, DPER wrote to the secretary general in the Department of Transport, Ken Spratt. The correspondence stated it had been informally advised that it could be August before any increase was introduced and consideration was being given to a 10 per cent rise.
“On the basis of the information provided to us, a 10 per cent increase implemented in August would yield only c.€17 million in 2026, leaving a shortfall of approx €40 million against the budgeted position."
DPER said such an outcome would “be very difficult to accommodate”, particularly in light of a Government decision the previous week to moderate expenditure growth.

title: Jones Engineering eyes record €1.9bn turnover on back of data centre boom
description: Irish contractor specialises in large-scale engineering projects for tech and life sciences sectors
content:
Dublin-headquartered Jones Engineering expects to achieve a record €1.9 billion turnover this year as it capitalises on the boom in data centre development.
According to its most recently filed accounts, the company generated a turnover of €1.6 billion in 2025, up from €1.28 billion the previous year.
Operating profits rose by 65 per cent to €170 million, giving the business a margin of 10.6 per cent.
“The results reflect the continued growth and diversification of the business, with international operations making an increasingly important contribution to overall performance,” it said.
The company, which specialises in building large-scale engineering projects for the tech and life sciences sectors, said the momentum had continued into 2026, “with turnover projected to exceed €1.9 billion, supported by a strong pipeline of work extending into 2027 and beyond”.
The company generates more than half of its revenue from overseas.
In the accounts, the directors note the company faces inflation pressures associated with macroeconomic conditions.
“Our global operations are exposed to heightened geopolitical tensions, with ongoing conflicts across the world affecting lead times on certain materials,” they said.
“In addition, we are seeing this impact currency markets with significant fluctuations seen over the recent year.”
[ CRH set for earnings boost from early closing of $8.5bn Arcosa deal Opens in new window ]
Founded in the 1890s, Jones Engineering was acquired by US group Cathexis Holdings in 2022 for an undisclosed sum. The deal saw the group’s longstanding chairman and majority shareholder Eric Kinsella exit the business.
Cathexis is a privately owned holding company, run by billionaire chief executive William Harrison. It is based in Houston, Texas, and holds investments ranging from property and energy to private equity.
The latest Jones accounts indicate the company employed 2,741 staff in 2025, up from 2,501 the previous year. Wages and salaries amounted to just under €243 million.
“2025 was another strong year for Jones Engineering, with increased turnover reflecting the continued growth of our international operations,” chief executive Stephen McCabe said.
“While we remain the market leader in our sector in Ireland, our business continues to evolve and diversify, with international markets making an increasingly important contribution to our overall growth.
“Our focus remains on building on this progress, delivering complex, high-value engineering projects and continuing to expand our presence across Ireland, UK, Europe and the Middle East.”
McCabe said he was “encouraged by the strength of our pipeline, with work extending into 2027 and beyond, and remain confident in the opportunities ahead”.
The global data centre boom is being driven by soaring demand for artificial intelligence (AI). Investment in AI infrastructure will hit a record $31.6 trillion through to 2050, according to baseline projections in PwC’s recent global data centre outlook report.

title: Allianz threatens to sue pro-Palestine campaigners who asked schools to cut ties with company
description: Insurance giant accuses campaigners of making ‘grave allegations’ in emails to more than 100 schools
content:
Allianz has threatened to initiate legal action against pro- Palestine activists who contacted more than 100 schools, encouraging them to drop the insurance company due to its alleged links to Israeli companies.
Campaigners earlier this month emailed the boards of management of secondary schools run by the Catholic Education, an Irish Schools Trust (Ceist), asking them to review their relationship with Allianz and explore “suitable alternative providers”.
The email, seen by The Irish Times, said “severing ties with Allianz would enhance” the reputation of Ceist’s schools.
It referenced a report published by United Nations special rapporteur Francesca Albanese last year that said Allianz had invested “large sums in shares and bonds implicated in the occupation and genocide”. Allianz and a number of other companies named in the report denied the allegations made against them.
“Educational institutions should, in best practice, adhere to international law to ensure that human rights inform their procurement policies and strategic decision-making,” the email said.
“Parents and guardians expect schools to adhere to International Humanitarian Law. Acting as exemplary role models for our children and youth is of paramount importance for schools in every aspect of their work.”
John Dolan, Allianz’s company secretary and in-house legal counsel, on October 19th wrote to campaigners to inform them that the organisation was considering legal action over claims made in the email.
“You have made grave allegations against our company, circulated them to our customers and urged those customers to terminate their contracts. The responsibility for substantiating those allegations rests with you,” the letter said.
Dolan said the company required “a substantive written response within seven days” and “will consider further action as appropriate following your response”.
[ Palestine supporters such as Sally Rooney are demonised like apartheid opponents, says Mary Robinson Opens in new window ]
“Allianz plc expressly reserves all rights and remedies available to it under applicable law, including in respect of defamatory statements and any resulting reputational or commercial harm,” the letter added.
Niamh Bonner, a well-known pro-Palestine campaigner, was among those to receive the legal letter. She accused Allianz of trying to “intimidate” activists, but said they would not be deterred.
Bonner said if Allianz initiated legal action it would be a strategic lawsuit against public participation – a meritless civil lawsuit filed by a person or organisation to intimidate or financially hurt critics.
“It’s very wrong that a multinational company would send a letter like that to people who are just trying to defend children and stop the massacre in Palestine.”
Bonner said campaigners are seeking legal advice.
A spokeswoman said Allianz Ireland “fully respects the right to peaceful protest, freedom of expression and legitimate scrutiny of corporate conduct”.
[ Zionism and supporting Palestine Opens in new window ]
“Allianz has repeatedly and unequivocally rejected the allegations contained in the July 2025 special rapporteur’s report and we have explained publicly and in detail why we consider those allegations to be fundamentally flawed,” a statement said.
“Allianz operates in accordance with applicable law, its fiduciary duties and internationally recognised human rights and sustainability frameworks.
“Allianz categorically rejects the suggestion that lawful, indirect participation in global financial markets constitutes complicity in the actions of governments or third parties. Such an argument has no coherent limiting principle and would, taken to its logical conclusion, implicate institutions across the global financial system simply for conducting lawful business.
“Seeking factual substantiation of serious allegations directed at our customers is entirely legitimate and should not be confused with an attempt to suppress public debate or peaceful protest.”
Two Allianz executives spoke at Ceist’s annual conference last week. A spokeswoman said Ceist “has no comment at this time”.
Campaigners have also called for other organisations to cut ties with Allianz. Last December, the GAA decided to retain the company as a sponsor .

title: ‘There are other ways to live if it doesn’t suit you’: The two sides to life on Inis Mór
description: Locals facilitate waves of tourists for half the year before navigating periods of solitude when the sun is gone
content:
It is a bustling tourist attraction, where for six months each year any number of cosmopolitan languages can be heard between the limestone walls that line every road and field on this, the largest of the three Aran Islands.
But a change comes over the Co Galway island in late October. As the weather adopts a much more serious disposition, the tourists slow to a trickle and finally stop.
With each passing day, the waves on Kilronan beach reach a little higher as the seas become choppier. Each October the island slowly reasserts its dominance over the tourist resort.
For Noel Seoighe, metalwork and math teacher at Coláiste Naomh Éinne and owner of the Bláthín cafe, winter is the best time to live on the island.
But he admits that it takes a certain kind of person to survive it.
“We kind of live two separate lives. You are going flat out, seven days a week in the summer months and you are getting really tired when September comes, so you can’t wait for October to roll around so you can take a break,” he says.
“You need to be content to live here. It takes a special person to last a winter when things really quieten down.
“For me, I think that it is magical in the winter months when you have the island to yourself. It’s then when you feel what real island life is like, especially when a storm is brewing. It’s the end of November let’s say, the wind is coming up and you go to the pub for a pint and a chat with the locals. In the summertime, we are so busy we don’t get a chance to even look at each other.”
Born and raised on the island, Seoighe couldn’t wait to leave when he finished secondary school. He spent a year driving heavy machinery in the US state of South Dakota before training as a schoolteacher and spending four years working in Dubai with his Tipperary-born wife Tess.
“We were living the high life out there. But something clicks for you after a while and you realise that you need to go back home. So we came back here to build a house and start a family,” he says.
Life on the island “goes both ways,” he says. “You know every person but you know every person’s business as well – whether you want to or not.
“There is an absence of an age group on the island during the winter, people from 18 up to their mid-20s. They have gone away to get a bit of life experience.
“It’s different when you are young. I can see it in my own children, they really can’t wait to turn 18, finish their Leaving Cert and get out of here for a while. But when you go away and experience life elsewhere, you realise that life here is not that bad.”
During the summer months, Inis Mór is serviced by more than 12 ferries each day bringing about 2,000 tourists from Rossaveel, Doolin and Galway City.
By early November, the number of ferries has dropped to two a day, and in stormy conditions the island may be completely cut off for several days.
“You try not to take things too seriously [during storms] and you have to be prepared. You always have a freezer full of food if you live on the island, especially during the winter months,” says Seoighe.
“So if the shop is closed for a day or two or the cargo ferry doesn’t make it, you’re not too hungry.
“I guess we are resilient out here, more than other communities.”
Self-proclaimed “city slicker” Gearoid Browne left his home in Galway city to work for his family business on Inis Mór in 1987.
When the salmon smoking company closed in 2008, he made the decision to stay on Inis Mór permanently and make a life for himself on the island.
After what he describes as an “unsuccessful spell” working in the Inis Mór Supermac’s , when he gained more than two stone in weight, he eventually set up the Man of Aran cafe and crafts shop.
“I love mixing with the tourists, having the craic with them, taking the mick out of them. It’s all go during the summer. But we will be closing the day after Halloween and that will be us for the year,” he says.
“Things slow down a lot then. What I do for myself at that stage is that I start baking cakes. I bake porter cakes. That keeps me occupied up until the Christmas.”
Browne says he started baking years ago when he had no money.
“It was after we lost the business [Aran Salmon] and I wanted to do something for the family, to give people a present, but I had no money to buy anything, he says.
“At this stage I make a good number of them coming up to the Christmas each year. I do it, more or less, to keep the mind occupied. I like to be doing something, but I don’t want to be working. We work hard from March to October; we work really hard. I like the down time after, but I don’t like to be sitting on my arse doing nothing.
“So that takes me up to Christmas, and after the Christmas it is nearly time to start getting the shop ready for the new season – varnishing floors, preparing.”
In recent years Browne has become a season-ticket holder with Connacht Rugby , and he values his trips on to the mainland every second weekend.
“It is hard to keep the social side of things going in the winter. It is quiet. People are not going out as much. But I like to cook and so do a few of my friends, so we have dinners together,” he says.
“You have to be able to make your own fun. We try to organise a few things. There are things in the hall, they have different functions on. So we support them and that is something we can go to.
A few of the locals have Connacht season tickets so they head into Galway for matches.
“That gives us a social outlet. We get to go into Galway every second weekend over the winter,” he says.
“There were some friends that I have known for years [in Galway City] and I felt I was losing touch with some of them. It’s a small thing in a way, but the season ticket has helped me to re-energise those friendships.”
Aran farmer, Fionn Ó Flaithearta and his partner Maírín Ní Chonceannáin left their jobs on the mainland in 2023 and returned to make a go of living full-time on the island.
Having recently opened Minnie’s Café and the Cipín Sauna, the couple are extremely busy during the tourist season and welcome the break that comes with October.
“Up until a few weeks ago [when it started to get quiet] we hadn’t really left the island since April. It is six months solid of working flat out. But that is the island life, and there are other ways to live if that doesn’t suit you,” Ó Flaithearta says.
“I am all right personally during the winter. The farm keeps me busy, you have to go out and see the cattle even when it is blowing a gale and the rain is coming at you sideways.”
Ó Flaithearta is also a carpenter and spends time in his workshop, though in the winter he has his own schedule.
“If I want to have a lie-in on a Wednesday morning, I can do it,” he says.
“But this time of the year is my favourite. The calm days in October, you have lovely light, you get to appreciate the island for what it is. If you go up to [stone fort and sea cliff] Dún Aonghasa this time of the year, you almost have it to yourself,” he says.
“I really enjoy the off season. You can catch up on your jobs. People can come up and see you and you have time to talk and catch up.
“In the middle of summer, you can’t see why people are coming here. But this time of the year, the waves are rolling in, the sea is getting a bit rough, it’s getting cold so you throw on your jacket and go out into it. That is when I understand why thousands of people are coming here every day throughout the summer.”
The population on Inis Mór grew dramatically this October, with two new babies being born to islanders in just one week.
For a community with just 800 full-time residents, this is a recent and significant trend. More people seem to be coming to Inis Mór to start a family.
“We have had a mini baby-boom going on all right, which is fantastic to see,” says Ó Flaithearta.
“At least for now, more young people are deciding to make life for themselves on the island, which is really fantastic.”

title: Photo story: Surveying Ireland’s seas aboard the RV Tom Crean
description: Our photographer joined scientists and technicians on a voyage to recover Ireland’s M5 weather buoy and carry out marine research
content:
Launched in 2022, the RV Tom Crean is Ireland ’s newest research vessel, dedicated to maritime science and ocean resource management. Operated by the Marine Institute , the ship and its larger counterpart the RV Celtic Explorer form the foundational pillar of Ireland’s national marine research infrastructure.
Surveying Ireland’s exclusive economic zone, the 53m Tom Crean conducts crucial oceanographic, hydrographic, geological and fisheries surveys. The vessel is a deployment hub for advanced maritime equipment; it manages an array of weather buoys, deep-sea observational networks and remotely operated underwater vehicles that monitor the North Atlantic. Most years, the ship operates for almost 300 days at sea; individual surveys last seven-21 days, each carrying up to 12 scientific and 12 ship’s crew.
In early August, the ship installed a replacement M5 weather buoy, a critical five-tonne offshore monitoring station anchored in the Celtic Sea roughly 30 nautical miles south of Hook Head, Co Wexford. The buoy is jointly managed by the Marine Institute and Met Éireann.
Scientists on board took the opportunity run a battery of experiments: testing underwater noise pollution on wildlife, modelling ways to locate lost fishing nets and studying the marine wildlife that grows on buoys or otherwise lives in the area, such as the elusive Risso’s dolphin.
“Being able to research the environment you live in is an important thing,” said Atlantic Technological University researcher Jamie Roche, stressing the benefits of knowing about the marine environment around Ireland and assets it contains.
“It’s something you need to continue doing. And considering the size of our land mass to our economic zone, there’s huge benefit in actually doing the research, and coming out here to the sea and doing this sort of work.”

title: Dún Laoghaire artist Johnman’s cancer story: ‘I’m a big man and I’m used to being strong’
description: The spray-paint artist on why he decided to share his health updates on Instagram
content:
“Y ou can’t stare death in the face and not feel sad about it. But I’m determined to remain upbeat and positive,” says John Green (49), aka Johnman, the spray-paint artist who is documenting his cancer journey on the Instagram account, @johnmansjourney.
“I see it as cathartic. Sharing my journey with a community of followers on Instagram allows me to get things off my mind,” says Green, who was diagnosed with glioblastoma, a malignant aggressive brain tumour, in March.
The English-born artist lives with his wife, health economist Siobhan Browne, and their 10-year-old son Sam in Blackrock, Co Dublin . He says he first started recording videos on the social media account following extensive surgery to remove the tumour at Beaumont Hospital earlier this year.
“I’d wake up early and go into this little family room at the hospital. I needed to talk because my mind was so active from being on steroids. It was my way of letting my family and friends know about what was going on as I didn’t have the time or energy to engage with them one-to-one on a personal level,” says Green.
He had already built a couple of thousand followers on his @johnmanspraycan Instagram account to promote his art so the platform was not new to him.
Over the last six months or so, he has shared unpleasant details of setbacks (including a blood clot in his lung that resulted in immediate hospitalisation while on holiday in Galway ), but he also shares his efforts to find the right balance of taking it easy and having a good quality of life.
“The only time I get really emotional and struggle is when I think about Sam,” he says. “I’m at peace with myself. I look back at my life and I feel it has been f**king brilliant. I’ve been blessed. My life has been full of fun, love and positivity.”
Green says his main motivation to record his cancer story is not to have a super-strong social media presence, but to leave something behind. “I hope that it will be a legacy for Sam to see how I coped and be inspired by that,” he says.
As a self-taught artist, Green first started creating spray-paint art as a side hustle when living in Devon. “I was working in fresh food produce and then food manufacturing at the time. I took on the pseudonym Johnman in 2011 when it was popular in urban art to have one,” he explains.
Green studied at university in Bristol, and the city’s street artist Banksy has always been an inspiration to him. “Anyone who works with hand-cut stencils and spray-paint is inspired by him,” he says.
In his artwork, Green turns digital black-and-white shaded images into hand-cut stencils which he embellishes with vivid primary colour spray-paint.
[ Davina McCall reveals new health battle against cardiovascular disease Opens in new window ]
He had a solo show in London’s Graffik Gallery in 2014 and has participated in the Art Osaka contemporary art fairs in Japan. In Ireland, he has sold his work at the annual Art Source fair in the RDS in Dublin, on the railings at St Stephen’s Green and, recently, in a pop-up art shop in Dún Laoghaire Shopping Centre. He plans to have a stand at Art Source in the RDS next month.
Residents in Dún Laoghaire will be familiar with his striking murals, namely Crimean Cannon on Patrick Street and Saol agus Grá on Musgrave Street. He also painted three outdoor traffic signal boxes: Embrace the Rain at Stillorgan Shopping Centre, tigers on Mount Merrion Avenue and a leopard on Leopardstown Avenue.
Green met his wife at their best friends’ wedding – her best friend was the bride and his the groom – and they started seeing each other when Browne was on a secondment in the UK. One of the first gifts he gave her was a collage of overpainted train tickets from their journeys to meet up. Overpainted train tickets were one of his first commercial successes.
Green moved to Ireland in 2014 and the couple married in 2017. When Sam was two, they were struggling with their work/life balance and didn’t want their son to be in a creche full-time.
“I gave up my job in 2018. I wasn’t happy and I wasn’t coping so I took redundancy. I wanted to give my art a go. I knew that I’d never make the same money but I’ve been infinitely happier and have never looked back,” he says. Initially working in a shed behind his parents-in-laws’ house, he installed a studio in the garden of their home last year.
The sudden death of his father on New Year’s Day in 2023 was a big blow to Green and he says he found it hard to be inspired to do his art for some time afterwards. He has similarly lacked inspiration to do visual art since his cancer diagnosis. “I took up the guitar again after my dad died and I have found that it has helped me again more recently. Also, I have some poems I want to write.”
Since his cancer diagnosis and radiotherapy and chemotherapy treatment, Green hasn’t had the same physical stamina as before. “It’s a grind. I’m a big man and I’m used to being strong. The physical deterioration is difficult. And as the tumour grows, I know it will impact me in ways I can’t control.”
He also says that since his hair has grown back, it’s less obvious that he’s sick. “I’m conscious that you wouldn’t know anything was wrong with me but I’m quite frail. I’m not able to lift things. I struggle with stairs and I can’t stand up on the bus,” he says. He has also been prohibited from driving since his surgery.
Green recently got a Hidden Disability badge and a Jam (Just A Minute) card, which people show to transport operators, shop assistants or service providers to indicate that they need a little more time to complete tasks in public.
Green says his priority remains to be an inspiration to his wife and son. “My number one priority is to spend quality time with my family and that they are put through the least trauma possible [by my illness]. If @johnmansjourney is an inspiration to people, that’s great too.”
Art Source is at the RDS November 13th-15th
Follow John Green @johnmansjourney and @johnmanspraycan

title: Unlocking inspiration remains sport’s final frontier that can’t be bought
description: In a landscape of endless statistics and data mining, the ability to motivate on a human level remains priceless
content:
In sport, inspiration is one of the last mysteries. Almost everything else has been reduced to explanations. Winning and losing are no longer left in peace: there must be an investigation. The data points must join the dots.
Inspiration is different because nobody can be sure of its source, or how it will fly. Words have an infinite number of arrangements, but which ones will work? In what order? At what temperature? Are you trying to reach their heads or their hearts? Can it arrive at both places?
A couple of weeks ago, the jockey Saffie Osborne gave a brilliant interview to Nick Luck on his Sunday morning show on Racing TV. Last month, Osborne crowned her best ever season by winning the St Leger for Joseph O’Brien , becoming the first female jockey to ride the winner of a British classic.
But halfway through the season she hit a bump. She was criticised for a losing ride in one of the biggest races at Royal Ascot and subsequently lost the ride on the horse. “I spent a few weeks feeling like people were looking at me and thinking I wasn’t good enough,” she said.
Osborne had been in this slump for a while when, one day, her father sent her two long text messages. The first was full of tenderness and love.
“My humble advice,” he wrote, “would be just enjoy it for what it is, a fun, short part of your long life. You have freedom to do whatever makes you happy at any time – but now is the only time you can do this part of your life. It is frivolous and unimportant but fun. You’re a great rider, I mean that, a really great rider. You’ve already left your mark on the sport. Don’t get hung up on what other people are doing. Just enjoy what you do. You do it so well and I’m so proud.”
As Osborne read out the texts in the Racing TV studio it was clear how powerful they had been, even now, months later. In her mind, it had been the turning point in her season.
When her dad chose those words and picked that moment, though, he had no idea how the messages would land. Her eyes might have glazed over. The messages might not have pierced her skin. Every attempt at giving inspiration carries that risk. There is no halfway house.
You wonder if it is harder now than it used to be. More complex. In dressingrooms, the pre-match talks and half-time talks used to exist on a short spectrum. The emphasis was on machismo and emotion and confrontation and fear and threat and fiery eyes and flaming tongues. If you were not aroused by any of those stimuli, you were left to your own devices.
But the pursuit of high performance is a much more nuanced and sophisticated business now. Finding the right frame of mind is never left to the last minute. Sports psychologists are involved or performance coaches or mental skills coaches. Elements of it are personal. On every team bus going to a game, some players will hunker down behind their ear buds and listen to whatever they need to hear.
But before the players run down the tunnel, somebody will stand up in the middle of the dressingroom and reach for something they hope will cut through the fog of nerves and adrenalin and land as something inspirational. In that moment, all that guides them is instinct.
When it goes wrong, there is a sickening thud. In his autobiography, Every Single Ball, Brian Corcoran tells a story from the Cork dressingroom before the 1992 All-Ireland hurling final. The Cork coach, Canon Michael O’Brien, was known for his dressingroom oratory, but this time he misread the room and lost his audience.
“Just before we went out, he went down on one knee and called us in [around him],” writes Corcoran. “Outside, the stewards were banging on the door, while inside fellas were after banging every wall with their shoulders. So, we gathered around and looked down on the floor. Then, after what seemed like an eternity, he looked up with tears flowing from his face, and in the softest voice we’d ever heard from him said, ‘Lads, do it for me’.”
But it is not unusual for inspirational team talks to have a performative element and sometimes it works. At half-time in the 2002 All-Ireland football final, Joe Kernan, the Armagh manager, showed the players his runners-up medal from the 1977 final, which he had nailed to a wooden plaque. Armagh were losing at the break and as he finished his half-time speech, Kernan smashed the plaque against a wall in the showers and walked out of the dressingroom.
With that “inspirational rant”, wrote Oisín McConville in his autobiography, “he wrote himself into the history books”.
It had clearly been premeditated and Kernan had made a calculation on the risk. With a stunt like that, there are no each-way bets: boom or bust.
Before Munster beat the All Blacks in 1978, Tom Kiernan, the Munster coach, took one of the most audacious risks in the history of team talks. Kiernan booked a restaurant in a Limerick city-centre hotel for a team meeting, a couple of hours before the match.
He rose from his chair at the top of the room and in various poses, he looked at the players in silence for 15 minutes, forcing them into a meditative state. “No one was moving. Some were breathing so deeply it was as if they were gasping for air,” wrote Alan English in his seminal book on that match, Stand Up and Fight.
“He just stood there, still crouching, motionless. He had planned the silence, but it was a risk. He couldn’t be sure how they would react. What if one of them laughed, as one of the lads at Cork Constitution had done when he tried the same thing years before?”
Part of the mystique of the most inspirational team talks is that word breaks from behind the curtain, just enough fragments to fire the imagination. But in recent years there have been so many fly-on-the wall documentaries about football teams, especially, that we no longer need to wonder so much. How many of those dressingroom speeches have made your heart race? Fewer than you expected.
There are exceptions. Three years ago, the BBC Scotland cameras were allowed into the dressing room of Darvel, a team from the sixth tier of Scottish football, before their Scottish Cup match against Aberdeen.
Their manager, Mick Kennedy, spoke for seven minutes and 23 seconds without once raising his voice or uttering a profanity or touching on a tactical point. Instead, he spoke about them as people and about the bonds that tied them and their values as a group and the place they represented and people who cared for them. Without knowing him or anybody in the room, everything he said felt authentic and overwhelmingly empowering. Like every piece of great dressingroom oratory, it was designed for their heads and their hearts.
They beat Aberdeen 1-0. Whatever else has changed in sport, inspiration never loses.

title: Irish in LA: ‘Irish people are really good at calling out bull in US corporate life, there’s a ton of it’
description: Micheal Sheehy says ‘Irish people are really good at calling out bulls**t and in American corporate life there is a ton of it’
content:
W hen Micheal Sheehy stood in the Nasdaq stock market in New York ringing the closing bell five years ago, he pictured his 17-year-old self standing in the school hall in Dingle CBS wondering, “What the heck am I doing here?”
This moment, which saw an image of Sheehy and other executives from financial service firm Payoneer beamed on to a billboard in Times Square was “huge, a big deal”.
But the Irish man in Sheehy was hesitant: “I’m like, I can’t post this on Instagram. Everyone at home will think I’m an a**hole.”
It points to, as the Los Angeles resident sees it, a key difference between Irish people and Americans in the business world. “Irish people just don’t do a good job of self-promotion. It feels uncomfortable. And we’re really quick to point [out] when someone has notions.”
Self-advocating is something Sheehy has had to learn over the past decade in LA, although it felt “really uncomfortable at the beginning”.
As chief compliance officer with Payoneer, Sheehy is part of the executive team navigating a proposed $2.75 billion acquisition with Nuvei.
He feels one of the strengths the Irish bring to the business world is: “We’re really good at, like, calling out bulls**t. And in American corporate life there is a ton of it.”
“I use a lot of humour and I’ll be like, ‘Are you serious?’”
[ London is a city where Irishness gets shouted out, rather than smoothed over Opens in new window ]
Born in the UK to an Irish father, Sheehy moved back to Dingle, Co Kerry when he was 11. “It was great to live in a place where everyone can pronounce your name straight away,” he says.
Growing up in two-channel TV Ireland, with a lot of American programmes, the United States was “very much the promised land” in his younger mind. “I just always wanted to come here. It was just a fascination of mine.”
After studying business and law at Dublin City University , Sheehy got a job in banking in Dublin: “I just was never a corporate fit kind of guy,” he says. “I just didn’t really fit the banking environment.” He grabbed an opportunity to transfer to Boston.
Although he found the east coast city “quiet and not much craic”, the move played a central role in his life, because it’s here he met his now-husband, a Bostonian. “His father is Irish, so he grew up in very similar circumstances to us ... feeling Irish,” he says.
Just a couple of months into dating, Sheehy got a job opportunity in Ireland that he couldn’t pass up. His then boyfriend moved with him. “He definitely had an identity crisis. He got to Ireland and he was seen as an American. He was like, ‘No I’m not American, I’m Irish’ ... People were calling him Johnny the Yank. We always laugh about it.”
[ A message for Ireland from one of the lesser-known Irish-American Kennedys Opens in new window ]
Although his husband loved Ireland, after nearly four years he needed to move back. “Some Americans can live anywhere,” Sheehy says. “Most Americans can only live in America because they can’t adjust to other things.” Not wanting to return to the east coast, Sheehy got a job in Los Angeles. He now spends much of his time in LA, travelling to New York regularly for work.
After a decade of LA living, returning to Ireland gives him a “short sharp shock to reality”.
“You get spoiled with convenience in America,” he says, noting how in LA he gets his dry cleaning picked up and returned to his house, or if he needs a blood test his doctor will get them taken in his home.
“My mum and my sister are mortified at the way I carry myself sometimes when I’m back in Ireland,” he says, laughing. He recalls looking for a takeaway coffee at 8am in Co Cork on a Sunday morning, and ending up in the petrol station where the coffee machine wasn’t even turned on. He can see the funny side of his LA habits.
But the biggest differences are a lack of ice and air-conditioning. “I was in Ireland in July ... There was no AC. I was almost hanging around the grocery refrigerator section. I can’t sleep without AC all year round – I need the noise and the breeze on my face.”
He finds himself miffed in Ireland when he’s handed a warm coke and two cubes of ice in a glass. “As soon as you sit down at a table in America, someone will hand you an arctic cold glass of ice water. You don’t even have to ask for it.”
The City of Angels has firmly become home. “I remember the first time when we landed in LAX and I said to my husband ‘Thank God, we’re home’. It was a moment for me.
“Life here is really nice. It changes your mindset. When you wake up every day and the sky is blue and the sun is shining, it’s easy to be positive.
“It took a really long time to be okay with it being sunny outside, but sitting on my couch doing nothing. There’s the guilt. I can still hear my parents in my head being like – the sun is shining, get outside.”
One downside to LA is the lack of a large Irish community. “I always joke that it’s me and Colin Farrell are the only two Irish people here,” Sheehy says.
“I miss the rhythm and the way [in] which, like, Irish people communicate. It feels so genuine, even just with strangers,” he says with a smile.
“One of the hardest things about being an emigrant is the way that Ireland changes,” he says. “You don’t want anything to change in Ireland, and when I return I want everything to stay exactly as I left.”

title: Handsome two-bed redbrick within short walk of Dublin’s docklands
description: East Wall
content:
At the start of the 1700s, Dublin was plagued by severe harbour silting. At high tide, the water reached as far inland as modern-day Townsend Street on the south side, and as far as North Strand on the north.
In the 18th century, however, large-scale structural reclamation was carried out to wall in the river Liffey . A large stone barrier – the original East Wall – was erected by the then Dublin Corporation to protect the reclaimed land from the sea and, in the 1820s, the East Wall area, including West Road, was established.
In the early 20th century, a series of redbrick Victorian houses were built on this reclaimed land. One of these, 56 West Road, a two-bedroom, end-terrace house, was constructed circa 1923.
It now extends to 70sq m (754sq ft) with a C Ber rating and is for sale through Sherry Fitzgerald seeking €475,000.
When its current owner bought it in 2021, paying €400,000 according to its entry on the Property Price Register, it had been extended and had an open-plan layout downstairs. “Most of the walls were red or purple, which made it very dark and gloomy,” he says. “My plan was to repaint them and bring as much light in as possible.”
With that in mind, he created openings in the wall between the hall and the sittingroom, producing the desired effect.
He also replaced all the flooring with manufactured wood. In addition, he installed new units in light grey, a splashback and a counter in the kitchen.
The house’s windows were replaced throughout while the brickwork was repointed two years ago.
Upstairs, there’s a bathroom with a wardrobe with sliding mirror doors.
In both bedrooms, he retained the Victorian fireplaces and removed the built-in wardrobes to create space. In the main bedroom, wooden slats were installed on the wall behind the bed. “Both rooms are very bright now when the sun shines,” he says.
A tall tree overshadowed the south-east-facing back of the house when he first moved in. It was cut down, and a paved courtyard was created. The walls were painted blue and potted plants now line the borders.
The house is close to the city’s financial district in the north docklands and the IFSC, and is about a 40-minute walk to Grafton Street and St Stephen’s Green. It’s also a 12-minute walk to Fairview Park and about a 10-minute walk to the East Road Cafe, a popular spot with locals.

title: French stocks: ‘Buy when there’s blood in the streets’?
description: Bank of America’s fund manager survey shows a record number plan to underweight French stocks over the next year, but other market adages are available
content:
“Buy when there is blood in the streets” is one of the oldest maxims of investing . France , where riots have sent shopkeepers counting the cost of looting and investors worrying about spiking bond yields, is currently putting it to an unfortunately literal test.
Right now, there’s no shortage of investors willing to wait for the blood to dry. Bank of America ’s latest monthly fund manager survey shows a record number plan to underweight French stocks over the next year.
Barclays says French shares are now some investors’ biggest short position, as they bet on further declines.
French shares have lagged for years. Global equity indices have roughly doubled since the bull market began in October 2022, notes investment strategist Ed Yardeni, but the MSCI France index has risen just 36 per cent.
Down 5 per cent in 2026, France’s CAC 40 is on course for its biggest annual underperformance against the broader European market since 2010, having lagged for three consecutive years.
Political risk is not the only driver – luxury stocks like LVMH and Hermès account for a significant chunk of the index, and they have struggled amid weaker demand for high-end products – but it is an important one.
Goldman Sachs estimates around half of France’s underperformance against other European indices in recent years is explained by political risk.
Given that only around 16 per cent of CAC 40 revenues are generated in France, the sell-off might tempt contrarians. Yardeni notes the French index’s price-earnings ratio has fallen from 16 in February to 13, even as corporate earnings have hit record highs.
Analysts have raised their 2026 earnings growth forecast to 24 per cent.
[ European stocks extend slide as French unrest rattles investors Opens in new window ]
“French earnings have decoupled from the French economy”, says Yardeni. French banks “warrant a discount; the multinationals don’t”.
Of course, cheap stocks can also get cheaper. With the 2027 presidential election looming and France’s fiscal problems unresolved, cautious investors may prefer to ignore the advice to buy when there is blood in the streets and heed another market adage instead: don’t try to catch a falling knife.

title: Across-the-board pay rise will do little to help fill key public sector posts
description: Public sector pay deal won’t attract workers to areas where posts have been hard to fill, such as in the Naval Service, special care, and IT
content:
U ntil the early 1970s, the Civil Service was a very traditional organisation that had changed little over time. There was limited movement between departments, and almost none between the public sector and the private sector.
Most people joined straight after school, there were few graduates, although many ambitious civil servants, like TK Whitaker, studied for a degree at night. Unless they were women who married [and who were effectively fired as a result], civil servants were likely to stay until they retired. Men progressed slowly through the ranks, based on seniority.
My first boss in the Department of Finance told me that when he joined it in the 1950s, he had calculated, based on the seniority rule and his colleagues’ ages, that he would spend most of his career as an assistant principal before, in the final three years before retirement, being promoted in rapid succession as a principal officer and then assistant secretary. In the event, he served as secretary general of the department for seven years.
Joining the EU meant quite a number of Irish civil servants left to work for the European Commission. The marriage bar ended in July 1973. Gradually, other reforms led to much more fluid movement across the public service.
The wider public service included graduate roles such as secondary teachers, doctors and local-authority engineers. While less than a third of public servants held third-level qualifications in 1970, those who did constituted more than half of the Irish graduate workforce.
All of this made public sector employment rather different from that in the private sector, with limited parallels in terms of pay. To a large extent, public and private sector employers were not competing to attract the same workers.
The advent of mass third level education in Ireland changed things. Few now enter the public sector straight from school. Primary teachers and nurses now have graduate qualifications. Today, three quarters of public sector workers have a third level qualification, but only constitute a third of graduate workers.
There is also greater choice, and substantial movement, between jobs in the public and private sectors. The security of a public sector job does not have the same allure when there is full employment. So the State as an employer needs to compete to attract and retain talent. That means the public sector must pay competitive rates, or some of the most able and ambitious teachers, civil servants, nurses or physiotherapists will seek better pay elsewhere.
[ Are public sector workers all as badly off as strikes might suggest? This is what the data says Opens in new window ]
In the run-up to the 2008 economic crash, average pay in the public sector had reached 50 per cent more than in the private sector – an excessive gap.
Following the collapse in the public finances, all public sector workers experienced painful cuts in pay. Over the subsequent decade, public service pay rose more slowly than the private sector. However, over the past few years the relationship has stabilised.
Public service workers are paid, on average, about 30 per cent more than the private sector, but this largely reflects their higher average qualifications.
The Government now needs to deliver a pay increase for public service workers, not because prices are higher but because most other workers are seeing their pay rise. Failure to keep pace with the private sector would see skilled employees leave.
The Department of Finance forecast that average pay across the economy will rise by around 4 per cent this year and next. The budget arithmetic provided for a 3 per cent public pay rise next year, so any higher pay deal will need additional funding.
The expected rise in private sector pay sets a guideline for any public sector pay agreement. If public sector workers are offered significantly more, that could push up taxes, and have knock-on effects on other pay. But if offered significantly less than their private sector counterparts, there could be an exodus of skilled staff for better pay elsewhere.
[ A public pay deal will be done – and here’s what it will look like Opens in new window ]
While this sounds fairly straightforward, things are, of course, more complex. Private sector pay deals are generally contingent on increased productivity. That, too, should be the case in the public sector.
Across-the-board pay increases in the public sector won’t address what’s needed to attract workers to some key areas where posts have been hard to fill – in the Naval Service, in special care, in some IT roles.
While a private employer would simply pay more, public pay agreements cannot easily handle such differentiation, but need to find a way to do so. The alternative of filling key roles by outsourcing to consultants is not an ideal one.

title: How to avoid communication issues during a home renovation
description: Sort It: Setting clear expectations can help avoid unnecessary difficulties during a building project
content:
When renovating a home, things don’t always go according to plan. Unexpected problems arise, budgets get squeezed and decisions sometimes have to be reconsidered. But often the problem itself is not what causes the most frustration. It is how the problem is communicated, or sometimes that it hasn’t been communicated at all.
Here are four areas where clear communication can help avoid unnecessary difficulties.
It might seem obvious that the more information you give your architect or designer, the better. But surprisingly, some homeowners are reluctant to reveal too much about what they want.
Occasionally, clients say they have a fairly clear idea of what they would like but don’t want to share it because they want to see what the architect comes up with on their own. They worry that explaining their preferences might somehow limit the designer’s creativity.
While the intention may be to give the designer a free hand, withholding information rarely leads to a better result. An architect’s job is not to guess what you want. It’s to understand how you live, what you hope to achieve, and then use their expertise to deliver it in the best way.
Be open about your ideas and share your likes and dislikes. The more your designer understands about you and how you live, the better equipped they will be to create a home that genuinely works for you.
One of the most important pieces of information you can give your architect or designer is your budget. Yet it is often the very thing homeowners are most reluctant to discuss.
A surprisingly common belief is that if you tell an architect or builder how much you have to spend, they’ll find a way to spend it all. As a result, some homeowners deliberately understate their budget, believing they’re being financially prudent.
[ Why planning is so important for your home renovation Opens in new window ]
In reality, this can be counterproductive. A budget isn’t just a limit on what you can spend. It is one of the most important factors informing the design process. Alongside the brief, it helps determine the scale of the project, the materials that might be appropriate and where the money will make the greatest difference to how you live.
The aim isn’t to spend every euro available. It’s to make sure the money you do spend delivers the greatest possible improvement to your home and your quality of life.
Discovering well into the design process that a client has considerably more to spend than originally indicated can be frustrating, not because there’s more money available, but because different decisions might have been made from the outset.
Your neighbours might not be directly involved in your renovation, but they will almost certainly be affected by it. Even a relatively straightforward project can involve months of noise, dust, deliveries and disruption. If you’re extending or making significant alterations, there may also be concerns about overlooking, loss of light or the impact on neighbouring properties.
Understandably, homeowners might be reluctant to raise the subject, particularly if they’re worried about objections to a planning application. But avoiding the conversation rarely makes things easier.
You don’t need to ask for your neighbours’ permission, but explaining your plans before submitting a planning application gives them an opportunity to raise concerns and can help prevent misunderstandings.
Of course, not every neighbour will be happy about building work next door, regardless of how considerate you are. But approaching the situation openly and respectfully gives you a much better starting point.
[ Five decision-making strategies to make your renovation less daunting Opens in new window ]
And communication shouldn’t stop once planning permission has been granted. Let neighbours know when particularly disruptive work is planned, be considerate about deliveries and access and make sure they know who to contact if there is a problem.
A little consideration can go a long way toward maintaining good relationships with the people you’ll live beside long after the builders have gone.
Once building work gets under way, it can be tempting to leave everything to your architect and contractor. But even with an experienced team managing the project, homeowners still have an important role to play.
Renovations involve countless decisions and not all of them can be anticipated in advance. Unexpected problems arise, materials become unavailable and sometimes you need to reconsider things once work is under way. Being available to discuss these issues and make decisions is essential to keeping the project moving.
Regular site meetings are a great opportunity to see how things are progressing, ask questions and address any concerns. Equally important is making sure you’re talking to the right people. It can be tempting to have a quick word with a builder or tradesperson on site about something you’d like changed. But these side conversations can lead to misunderstandings, unexpected costs, and work being carried out without the wider team’s knowledge.
[ A Dún Laoghaire barbershop transformed into a modern home: ‘I used to get my hair cut here as a kid’ Opens in new window ]
Make sure any changes or instructions go through the agreed channels so everyone knows what’s been decided and any implications for the budget or timeline are understood. This is also why it’s so important to choose an architect and contractor you feel comfortable talking to. You need to feel able to ask questions, raise concerns and have honest conversations, even when something isn’t going to plan.
Being involved doesn’t mean micromanaging the project. It means being available, staying informed and making sure everyone is on the same page. Good communication won’t prevent every problem during a renovation, but it can make an enormous difference to how those problems are resolved.

title: With EU presidency, Ireland has chance to implement digital identity wallet by end of year
description: Citizens should not be repeatedly asked by governments or multiple agencies for information already available
content:
The priorities for Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the EU have been wide in scope across various sections of society, different sectors within the economy, along with competing national or common interests.
Some of those will resolve in due course under the current term, while many will either stall or progress as it passes onto Lithuania and then Greece through 2027.
One long-standing objective and policy priority that falls directly during our watch is the provision for an EU Digital Identity Wallet for all citizens and businesses by December of this year.
This is part of the wider Digital Decade Policy Programme (DDPP), which is the EU’s framework for achieving digital transformation by the end of the decade.
It includes targets in relation to digital skills, digital infrastructure, the digitalisation of businesses, and access to digital public services.
That last (but not least) area essentially involves all key public services being available online with citizens’ digital identity and ability to access services working seamlessly throughout the EU.
The practical applications are complex but the “only once” principle applies throughout, where citizens should not be repeatedly asked by governments or multiple agencies for information already available.
With progress being made on all fronts to various degrees, this is now a defining period for Ireland to help push the digital public services agenda forward for citizens, businesses and State services. Interoperable data should flow freely enough to support everything from mortgage approvals to healthcare records and planning applications.
The main challenge is one that often falls on European or cross-border projects. It comes down to collective co-ordination and consensus. Twenty-seven member states, with as many starting points, governance structures, all building toward the same targets along separate paths that sometimes fail to intersect.
The issues to be resolved don’t solely lie within policy, legal or technological constraints. It is often social where the connectivity falls down. How do people, who each hold a piece of a public problem, find one another, build trust, and produce outcomes that outlast a ministerial photocall or presidential term? The EU and the Irish Government have invested heavily in the building blocks that are needed for this journey. The digital identity wallets, data spaces and cloud platforms already exist.
What is missing is the right people coming together from different corners, knowing how to assemble these blocks in the right way.
Practitioners who have the ability and mindset to move between a Brussels regulation and a rural county council’s operating reality, without treating the two as separate jobs.
Ireland’s role in this during its EU presidency is reflected in a new initiative that will gather the necessary stakeholders to generate those collective solutions for the next phase of Europe’s digital public services roadmap.
To break the roadblocks and unlock the capabilities that can advance these future services, we need to first go back though to an age-old practice. Before internet technology, quantum computing or artificial intelligence were even imagined, Ireland had meitheal.
This was among our oldest social networks and was based on reciprocity, trust and shared responsibilities. Its approach was replicated in similiar forms in different countries: Norway’s dugnad, Finland’s talkoot, Lithuania’s talka, Hungary’s kaláka and the Balkan moba.
Each European tradition reflects the same civic principle that complex problems can be solved when communities pool effort, skills and responsibility. It activated to do work that no single person or household could manage alone.
The main rule being that help given would be returned. This created a social infrastructure and self-enforcing system for dedicating skills exactly when and where they were needed. That practice and principle may be what is needed now to push forward on Ireland and Europe’s digital public services programme.
On November 19th and 20th, Ireland will hold the first Meitheal Digiteach that will bring policy makers, community groups, data designers, delivery practitioners, architects and engineers into the same room to work through the shared challenges, while looking to create practical solutions and connect the diverging tracks on the new Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) rails.
The gathering will not work like a regular conference with the usual panel discussions, keynote addresses and firesides or roundtables. This will be a hands-on exercise for participants with no hierarchy and no spectators.
It is due to be held at a fitting location within the Drogheda Civic Offices which, since its relatively recent refurbishment, now represents a suitable blend of heritage with modern design and functionality. The call is for like-minded citizens and groups to get involved in building the next level of digital public services.
I’d encourage all who have a role to play to join us, as Ireland’s meitheal provides a mechanism that can be passed on to the next custodians of the EU presidency and the subsequent phases of our shared digital public services programme.
Gar Mac Críosta is digital advisor strategy & architecture at the HSE, and co-founder of Meitheal Digiteach 2026

title: Jerry Fish: ‘I have lost pretty much everything. It was one of the best things to happen to me’
description: Jerry Fish is a musician, songwriter and singer
content:
I save when I can, and I spend when I can. I like to have something put aside for the rainy days, but I am acutely aware that you only live once. I am generous with my money; my family and I live simply and are grateful for what we have. My experience is that once you start worrying about money, it dries up. As a musician, my finances are always up and down.
I have been working since before the age of 10. My first job was a paper round in south London. I can’t remember how much I got paid, maybe a couple of quid, but I know I told my parents that I no longer needed pocket money any more as I was now a man of independent means. I was young, too, when I started serving my time as a painter and decorator with my father in Dublin.
A bargain is not necessarily a bargain just because it’s cheap. I like quality because it lasts longer and is often better value than cheap stuff. I like things that are well made by properly paid craftspeople. It’s like food cooked with love – it tastes better.
My most extravagant purchase must be the home I bought with my wife for our family. Not sure you can call that an extravagance, but it cost €550,000. On the other hand, I bought a vintage caravan for €1,000 and spent another couple restoring it to its former 1970s glam glory.
The vintage caravan. I love it. It’s my home and office at Electric Picnic, where I go on holiday every year to Fish Town.
[ Jerry Fish: ‘I’m a London-born Dub but I discovered most of my DNA is from exactly where I now live’ Opens in new window ]
There is plenty I regret spending money on, but that’s the price of an education, in life and the music business. You live and you learn.
Not regularly, but it can be fun. I spent time with Bedouins in the Sinai in the 1980s, and they taught me how to haggle. I love the odd bric-a-brac antique, so you’ve got to haggle sometimes. Also, I am a survivor in the music business, and we have to hustle for a living.
Nah, I can’t get my head around cryptocurrency. I miss cash.
I have a pension from some money I got to squirrel away once, when I was flush, but it’s been through a financial crash and a pandemic, so it’s not much. I don’t plan to ever retire, though. I have a job that I love doing, and I know I’m very lucky to be doing what I do. I want to keep on working as a full-time day-dreamer and entertainer until the day I die.
A trip to Cadiz to hang out with an old and dear friend. You can’t put a value on friendship or making memories, because they are priceless. Friendship is surely the most precious commodity.
Yes, I’m pretty good at knuckling down to get something if it’s something I truly want. I am aware there are many things I can’t afford, but I believe everything starts with a dream. You have to visualise the things you want, then strive and work hard to get them.
I have lost pretty much everything I had. Strangely, it was one of the best things to have ever happened to me. I think once you survive a fall, it makes you stronger, less concerned or worried about the road ahead. Losing money isn’t the end of the world. Sometimes you need to let it go, look around at what you have and be grateful.
[ Camille O’Sullivan: ‘I’m terrified of being out of money’ Opens in new window ]
The biggest gamble I ever took was returning to the music business after the birth of my first child, and it is also my biggest win. I’m lucky to have made a success of doing the thing I love with the support of a beautiful wife and four wonderful children. As far as I’m concerned, that’s winning at bingo!
My best and worst habits when it comes to money are quite possibly the same thing: my generosity, giving away my money. I believe in the karmic effect of giving, in that what you give comes back to you multiplied. I have travelled a lot in my life, and I have always managed to hold on to my fare home, usually hidden somewhere on my person.
Everybody knows that cash is king. I have €70 on me.
Jerry Fish performs as part of Puca Festival, Trim Castle Hotel, Saturday, October 31 st . pucafestival.com

title: What my most embarrassing job interview taught me
description: Job hunters should not have to disclose their pay history or guess what salary is on offer
content:
T he other day, I was chatting with a friend about how we got into journalism when I suddenly remembered my most disastrously embarrassing job interview.
It happened years ago, not long after I arrived in London and spotted an ad for a deputy news magazine editor. The advert was highly detailed. Applicants had to send in an assessment of the publication outlining what worked and what did not, along with compelling cover story ideas.
Having recently edited a national news magazine in Australia , I was full of thoughts. But there was one question in the advert that stumped me. What was my preferred salary?
I asked two other journalists I knew in London, both men, for advice. Each told me to ask for what I had been paid in Sydney, plus more for the abysmal exchange rate and the cost of living in London, which I did.
To my delight, I got an interview. A team of people politely listened as I went on about their magazine, whose editor then took me off to a side room for a further chat. He loved my application, he said, but there was just one thing. How wedded was I to that salary I had mentioned? “Because it’s a lot more than what I’m paid.”
At the time, I was mortified. My face burned. What an idiot I had been to name such an outlandish figure. Why hadn’t I done a better job of researching the going rate for deputy magazine editors?
Today, though, I recall that moment fondly. Women are always being told they cement the gender pay gap by asking for too little in pay negotiations, and there was my younger self, gormlessly doing the opposite.
I also think of how much easier it would have been if that advert had simply listed the salary on offer. That way, I would have known if it was worth my while to apply and everyone else, inside and outside the magazine, would have had a better idea of whether their pay was fair, or if they should demand more. This is, of course, precisely why so many employers do not spell out salaries in public.
For similar reasons, job hunters are often asked to disclose their salary history, even though this is an excellent way to bake in the lower pay endured by so many women, ethnic minorities and others.
[ Workplace conflict is said to be costing Irish firms €239m annually. What can be done about it? Opens in new window ]
It’s tough to ask for £50,000 for a job, no matter how well qualified you are, if you have just revealed your last role paid £35,000, which it might have if you had been doing the same work at, say, a charity.
Women were told for years to just “lean in” and become savvier negotiators. Thankfully, this approach is fading as research shows the benefits of policies aimed at fixing the practice of negotiations, instead of fixing the women.
This is why the EU has brought in a directive requiring employers to do two things: tell job seekers about starting salaries or pay ranges, and stop asking them about their pay histories. A number of US states already have such measures, which can help to shrink a gender wage gap that averaged 11 per cent across OECD countries in 2023.
The deadline to put the EU directive into national law was June 2026, but unfortunately many countries have yet to get there. They include Germany , the bloc’s largest economy, where Indeed data shows that less than 15 per cent of job advertisements include explicit pay information. That number plunges for sectors such as banking and finance, which typically have far worse gender pay gaps.
No wonder thousands of women are supporting outfits such as Female X Finance, a five-year-old start-up that aims to help boost women’s careers in the financial industry. Its Dutch co-founders just published their second annual survey of the salaries – and bonuses – being paid in investment banking, M&A, private equity and other fields in the UK and the Netherlands.
[ HR bosses predict AI will not cause ‘significant reduction’ in employee numbers Opens in new window ]
How I wish this type of information, and those pay transparency laws, had been around when I answered that magazine advert all those years ago.
If you’re wondering, I never did get the job. It went to an insider, which is probably just as well. I’m sure they did a far better job than I would have done, but I would still like to know how much they were paid. – The Financial Times

title: Niamh O’Sullivan on Carmen’s Habanera: ‘It’s scary. She’s straight in with the most famous aria in the opera’
description: The mezzo-soprano has sung Bizet’s title role in English, in Calixto Bieito’s version. Now she’s to perform the original version for Irish National Opera
content:
T he Salle Favart, home of the Opéra-Comique in Paris, is where the first performance of Georges Bizet’s Carmen took place, in 1875.
The theatre, which regarded itself as a family venue, was also known, and often pilloried, as a place where marriages were arranged. Parents seated a daughter at the front of a box, where, during the interval, prospective husbands could be interviewed.
Adolphe de Leuven, one of the theatre’s directors, pleaded with one of the librettists, Ludovic Halévy, not to have Carmen die on stage. No character, he said, had ever died in a show at the theatre.
The first Carmen, Célestine Galli-Marié, invested the sultry factory worker with a sensuality and independence that triggered an entirely different chorus of objections. When the opera finally entered the repertoire of the much larger Palais Garnier, in 1959 (no, the date is not a typo), Jane Rhodes launched her international career through the title role, in a lavish production that was sexy enough for her to be called “the Brigitte Bardot of opera”.
Irish National Opera’s new Carmen is the Cork mezzo-soprano Niamh O’Sullivan. She was contracted for the role after she appeared as Carmen’s friend Mercédès in INO’s 2022 production, at the Bord Gáis Energy Theatre, in Dublin.
“It’s crazy how far in advance we’re booked,” she says. “Some opera houses book five years in advance. I kind of know my schedule right now up till the end of 2029, which is great. I feel very lucky and honoured that that’s the case. Fergus Sheil” – INO’s artistic director – “knew it was a role that was coming soon in my career, so he said, ‘You’ll have done it already. Why not try it at home?’”
Is she at all like Carmen? “I think yes. With every role I do, I try to find a bit of me in them, so it doesn’t seem completely far away from me. I’ve been thinking about her and her independence. I feel I’m a very independent person. As an opera singer you kind of have to be. We’re alone a lot, and most of our lives we spend on the road on our own.
“I’m also very passionate, I’m also sensitive, and this is one of the things I try to get across when I play Carmen: I try to find that other side to her. She’s just a human being at the end of the day as well.
“So, yes, I do find a lot of similarities between us. Feeling closer to her, and relating to her a lot more, makes it much easier as an actor to bring that across to an audience.”
Does the independence cross over into wilfulness?
“The whole thing is about her wanting to be free and stay free. That’s the bottom line for Carmen. She won’t be controlled by anyone. No matter what, she will get her own way in the end, even when she knows she’s going to die. So there is an absolute wilfulness with her.”
Carmen’s Habanera, one of those numbers known to millions even though they wouldn’t be able to put names to them, was one of the first arias O’Sullivan studied.
“It’s the scariest aria, I would say. Because there is nothing else before it. She’s just straight in with the most famous aria in the opera. I knew it and I always wanted to sing it, but I thought maybe I was too young and hadn’t lived life enough yet to sing it. So I sang it a lot in concerts, and then I started to study the role with Ronnie – my teacher Dr Veronica Dunne .”
In 2025 O’Sullivan sang Carmen for English National Opera, in a revival of Calixto Bieito’s 1999 production (which the now defunct Opera Ireland also presented at the Gaiety Theatre in Dublin in 2002).
ENO presents opera in English. Has it been difficult to wipe the English from her head?
“Honestly, having it in my head has been very helpful. Because everything is so fresh in my head in my native language, it was very, very easy to slip into the French.
“I mean, it was much harder to learn the English, because I had already done La Tragédie de Carmen, the shortened version of Carmen [by Peter Brook] in Buxton. So my first learning of the role was in French. Going into the English was quite tough.
“In a way, I treated it like a different piece altogether. Even though it was the Calixto Bieito production, such an iconic production, I did have the French in my mind, although La Tragédie de Carmen doesn’t have any of the ensembles, just all the numbers for Carmen.”
What comes first when she starts to work on a new role?
“I’d love to say text, because that’s what everyone says: start with the text, then go to the music. But if it’s a new role for me I will straight away listen to it.
“It’s the most exciting thing hearing what it’s like, what it’s going to sound like in the voice, if it’s going to suit me, if it’s not. How high it goes, how low it goes.
[ Niamh O’Sullivan: ‘I am obsessed with singing. I couldn’t imagine myself doing anything else’ Opens in new window ]
“I’ll always try to find a good version on YouTube or on Spotify or wherever and have a listen right through with the score. When I accept, then I’ll start looking at the libretto separately, then go back to the music, once I kind of know what I want as an arc for that character.
“When I have it pretty well learned I’ll bring it to a coach, and then they will correct rhythms or language or give me some other interpretations or suggest different colours.”
A lot of singers lean more heavily on their coaches.
“I’m a very quick learner. Sometimes that’s not great, because I can get lazy and learn things too quickly. But I tend to do most of the work myself. If I feel a little bit insecure about a role I’ll bring a section of it to my current teacher, and I’ll go to a coach if it’s brand new and I need someone else to hear it on the piano.
“I find I’m kind of the best judge as well. I think we’re the best judge of ourselves as singers. And I don’t let myself get away with anything. So the bulk of the work is usually done in my apartment, just me and the piano.”
I offer O’Sullivan a time-machine trip to meet Carmen – not the Carmen of Prosper Mérimée’s original novella but that of Bizet and his librettists.
“I would commend her for being so brave and would ask her how she got to the place of being so independent, so focused on living and loving on her own terms. It’s really inspiring to work through this role of someone who is so independent and so secure.
“I’d ask if she could tell me a little bit more about that, about how I could take a leaf out of her book in those terms. And I guess I’d ask her if she was ever truly in love, if it has always just been lust and passion or if she ever actually did have someone in her life who she really did want to belong to.
“I can’t imagine her in a relationship. I can’t imagine her settling down with someone.”
That’s a real fascination for O’Sullivan, “because there was such a long part of my life where I also thought that about myself in that way. I thought, ‘Oh, I can never be in a relationship, because I just am too obsessed with this life I’m living.’
“Not to be vain, but I’m so obsessed with singing that I couldn’t imagine anyone who’d be able to understand that. I thought maybe this would be a life on my own and I would be okay with that. But now that I have a partner I’ve realised I couldn’t do that.”
Irish National Opera’s production of Carmen is at the Bord Gáis Energy Theatre, in Dublin, on Monday, November 2nd, Wednesday, November 4th, Friday, November 6th, and Saturday, November 7th

title: Let rural and Gaeltacht communities build
description: The money and the know-how are there
content:
Sir, – David McWilliams (“ From dereliction to Airbnb, the Gaeltacht is being destroyed by the housing crisis ”, Opinion, October 17th) and Donncha Ó hÉallaithe (“ Minister for Gaeltacht has power to alleviate housing crisis in Irish-speaking areas ”, Letters, October 20th) are right: if young Irish speakers cannot find an affordable home in the Gaeltacht, the Gaeltacht will not survive. Yet the means to build those homes already exist.
Cost rental, introduced by the Affordable Housing Act 2021, sets rents that cover only the cost of building and maintaining homes. However, almost nine in 10 cost-rental homes advertised to date are in Dublin and its commuter belt; none have reached the Gaeltacht town or village that needs 10 or 20 homes.
Community-led co-operatives can fill that gap, and the finance is in place. Some 40 per cent is available through the Housing Agency’s STAR cost-rental investment scheme and about 50 per cent through low-cost lending from the Housing Finance Agency or the Council of Europe Development Bank.
The remaining 10 per cent or so comes from co-operative members or support organisations. The expertise to deliver exists in Ó Cualann and more widely across the Approved Housing Body sector.
What is needed now is the will to proceed and a solution to the question of allocation. Cost-rental homes are allocated nationally by lottery, but a local co-operative cannot be built that way.
Homes must go to people with a genuine link to the locality and, in the Gaeltacht, to Irish speakers. At present, the Minister can approve such an allocation plan only in principle at the outset. Few families will commit years of effort and their savings without certainty that they can move in.
