Gibbons’ journey to Finland began more than 20 years ago when he went on an adventure from Delgany to Australia (“working in IT for a bank believe it or not”) and met a Finnish woman, now his ex-wife. They moved back to Rovaniemi where he built a house and they had a son. The city in the Arctic Circle is known as the official home of Santa Claus and indeed tourism is its economic backbone.
Gibbons moved an hour south to a tiny village after his divorce where he was able to buy a house for €32,000 that was in move-in condition.
“Houses up here can be bought for absolutely nothing. After the second World War Finland built houses called rintamamiestalo, which are were simple, cheap and easy with a wood fire stove and a well in the garden.”
If there was “some kind of apololypse” Gibbons posits he would be “grand for a while” if he had potatoes and firewood, because the house is so self-sufficient.
This may sound like a fantasy, but it’s not beyond the bounds of reality when sharing a border with Russia (closed since 2023). The region has become a strategic location for Nato during the Ukraine war.
Despite the threat from the east, Finland has been named happiest country in the world nine times in a row in the UN-backed World Happiness Report, and Gibbons can see why.
“Where I live there is no crime. There’s a real summer and a real winter ... it’s a magic place, it really is”
“Anywhere in Lapland, within 10 minutes I can go to a river, a lake or a forest and there’s not a soul near you. You can pick berries, you can go on hikes.”
He also loves the people. “They have a reputation for being unfriendly but you just have to get to know them. They’re very much like the Irish, there is mighty craic to be had ... you don’t meet many a**h**es up here.”
His first Finnish winter was on a building site 200km north of the Arctic Circle, where they only stopped work when temperature hits -25 degrees.
But working for large building company focused on speed wasn’t for the Delganyman, and Gibbons embraced a slower approach to his craft.
He started his own traditional woodworking company three years ago ( Arctic Carpentry ), after doing a college course in logbuilding, which added to the carpentry and joinery apprenceceship he completed after finishing school in Greystones.
“You can’t really rush traditional carpentry, There’s more enjoyment to it and it takes time and a lot more skill.”
“I build log cabins and it’s you’d be fairly confident that the frame is still going to be standing in 100 or 200 years ... can I say the same for modern houses I built?”
Gibbons lifts all the logs by hand, makes smaller single-room traditional wilderness cabins. He describes his “handcrafted cabins” as a “niche market” when there are cheaper kit cabins at a fraction of the price. But his customers understand that it takes time to make it this traditional way.
He loves the ownership: “I’m responsible for everything, every aspect and every decision. That’s me.” And Gibbons loves the chance to use his axe skills: “It’s the most simple and basic of tools, but to use it properly requires an insane amount of skill and concentration.”
More recently Gibbons turned to a Finnish-style project but back in Ireland, designing and building a sauna for a client. These hot rooms are an essential part of Finnish homes and ingrained in culture but have exploded in popularity across Ireland.
“The Finns have perfected the sauna. To have a one room log sauna with a Finnish stove, you can’t get better.”
“It’s nice to see that it’s finally making its way back to Ireland ... but with the climate I wonder what took so long.”
In Ireland, Saunas can be pricey and are aimed at people with “a few bob”, says Gibbons. But what he loves about the sauna culture in Finland is they are the “great leveller”.
“You could have the president of Finland and a binman both sitting there in the sauna. There is no upper level, they’re equal.”

title: Soft toy ban among new restrictions for roadside crash memorials in south Dublin
description: Victims’ group says memorials at crash ‘black spots’ can contribute to driver awareness and behaviour change
content:
Soft toys, illuminations, large-scale floral tributes and “highly conspicuous materials” will be banned from roadside memorials to crash victims under a new policy covering much of south Dublin .
Shrines and monuments to those killed in collisions have for decades been erected at the side of roads across the State by bereaved families. Most often, however, they are informally installed without consultation with councils or road authorities.
The Department of Transport and Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) last year issued regulations to local authorities banning such memorials on motorways and dual carriageways and directing they “should not be permitted” on roads with a speed limit over 60km/h.
Local authorities were also directed to develop their own roadside memorial policies that would conform with government road safety strategies. However, the department and TII were not prescriptive as to the type or appearance of memorials that could be permitted in any local authority area.
Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council ’s draft roadside memorial policy, to be presented to councillors for approval on Monday, outlines the department and TII regulations, but also includes a list of “prohibited elements” which cannot be used in memorials specifically in the south Dublin area.
These include reflective, fluorescent or “highly conspicuous materials”, illumination “of any kind”, floral tributes exceeding an area of 1sq m, “large permanent physical structures”, and “soft toys”.
The memorials cannot exceed 60cm in height, should be “modest in scale” and “shall not resemble gravestones or burial plots”.
The council said it reserves the right to “remove excess or deteriorated tributes where a safety concern arises or where reasonable complaints are received”.
Existing memorials will “generally not be affected by this policy unless they give rise to road safety concerns, obstruct maintenance activities, or require replacement”.
[ Damning findings of report on Garda roads policing ‘heartbreaking’ for victims’ families, campaigners say Opens in new window ]
The council said it “recognises and respects the deeply personal and emotional significance of roadside memorials for families and friends wishing to commemorate loved ones as a result of road traffic collisions”.
However, it “also has a statutory duty to manage and maintain public roads in a manner that prioritises the safety of all road users”, it said.
“This policy seeks to balance compassion for bereaved families with the council’s responsibility to safeguard road users and those who may visit or maintain roadside memorials. The safety of all road users, including pedestrians, cyclists, motorists and council staff, is the overriding consideration in the assessment of roadside memorials.”
Applications for memorials can be made to the council, and “road safety considerations shall be the determining factor in all decisions”, it said. “Unauthorised memorials erected without prior written consent may be removed by the council.”
[ Mayo council tells dead man’s family to remove roadside memorials Opens in new window ]
Alternatives to permitted roadside memorials could also be considered by the council, including tree planting and donations to road safety charities, it said.
In a submission to the council, the Irish Road Victims Association said it “fully acknowledged that memorials placed in unsafe locations, or which introduce hazards to road users, cannot be supported”.
However, it said roadside memorials “can, when appropriately managed, contribute to greater driver awareness and behaviour change. This reflects how accident ‘black spots’ have historically been recognised, where the location itself becomes part of road safety awareness.”

title: Six months into the Iran war, stock markets are still well ahead
description: The cliche ‘buying on the sound of cannons’ appears to have held up once again
content:
“Stock markets plunge amid fears of prolonged war in Iran”; “Stocks plunge, oil prices up 20% since start of Iran war”.
The headlines at the outbreak of the Iran conflict were not exactly conducive to calm.
Back then, bulls countered that this would be a short conflict, that we’d get a Trump “taco” (Trump always chickens out), and the US president, conscious of November’s midterm elections, would surely bring the war to a quick conclusion.
Six months later, the conflict is unresolved. Oil prices are again above $100. Inflation has been felt around the world, with food and energy prices spiking.
And the S&P 500? It’s up 13 per cent, and stocks around the world have enjoyed a similarly sunny time.
Back in March, this column quoted BCA Research’s Marko Papic, who noted that “buying on the sound of cannons” had historically been a winning strategy.
Creative Planning strategist Charlie Bilello makes the same point. Wars end, says Bilello, while economies and corporate earnings, even when temporarily impaired, have tended to grow over the longer term.
They certainly have in 2026. S&P 500 earnings grew a “historic” 52 per cent in the latest quarter, notes Bilello, doubly exceeding expectations.
Net profit margins hit a record 17 per cent, while full-year earnings growth forecasts have more than doubled to 34 per cent.
For all the talk of geopolitical risk, investors have had a very decent six months, with the market behaving much as history would suggest.

title: Can I request a price reduction if a property’s floor area was incorrectly advertised?
description: Is it generally accepted as ‘approximate’ marketing?
content:
I encountered a significant discrepancy between the advertised floor area of a property and the area stated in the Ber certificate and subsequent measurements.
I appreciate that there are different ways to measure, such as internal versus external, and that floor plans are often labelled as approximate, but this difference feels material in the context of Irish pricing and my expectations as a buyer.
In your experience, how are such discrepancies typically treated in Irish practice? Is it generally accepted as “approximate” marketing, or can it be grounds for a price reduction or withdrawal without penalty? What is the best way for a buyer to raise this with the selling agent?
The situation is different depending on whether or not contracts have been exchanged (ie signed by both parties and a contract deposit paid). I presume you viewed the property in person before bidding? On the basis that you have not yet signed contracts and paid the contract deposit, all negotiations are on a without prejudice basis and therefore neither you or the seller are legally bound to the transaction and either party can walk away from the deal without recourse.
Fundamentally, though, I can see your point. Price per square metre is indeed a reference point metric, but only one. In reality, price is determined by several factors including demand, location, condition and decor, amenities and so on. While the floor area of the house is somewhat smaller than you were led to believe, it may not necessarily result in a proportionate reduction in price.
The standard basis for the measurement of a residential property for sale is gross internal area (GIA), which is measured inside of the outside walls and accounts for liveable space, therefore attics are excluded.
Ber ratings, however, can take into account non-compliant attic conversions, where they may be excluded from the standard GIA measurement. I’m somewhat surprised that a stairs void is generally not excluded from GIA. My point is, that there can be genuine reasons why there is a discrepancy between stated measurements.
To set out the position, the legal basis of property purchase in Ireland is “caveat emptor” or “let the buyer beware”. In other words, it is up to the buyer to carry out whatever due diligence they deem appropriate before entering into the contract to purchase the property. Yes, have your professional advisers, but once you’ve signed the contracts, any problems will be your own.
[ My elderly mother’s neighbour has blocked access to the side of her home. What can we do? Opens in new window ]
Furthermore, and material to your query, the matter of a purchaser relying on a selling agent’s statements was dealt with in the case of Walsh v Jones Lang Lasalle Ltd (2017). In that case, the Supreme Court overturned a High Court decision and decided a selling agent did not owe a duty of care to a buyer and, therefore, was not liable to the buyer for errors and misstatements in the sales brochure. So, in a situation where contracts have been signed and exchanged, I’m afraid there is very little you can do.
To get back to your query, it was only when you saw the discrepancy in the floor area that you began to question the price, it was not because something fundamental to the sale or property arose after you went sale agreed. That is not to minimise the discrepancy. The floor area should be correct, and you are quite entitled to seek at least an explanation of the difference in measurement.
I would advise that you raise the issue directly with the agent. I think a phone call is best, followed up with a brief email setting out your position. The success or otherwise of your request will be dealt with by the agent in discussion with his client, but I imagine the outcome will depend very much on demand for the property and their likely success in finding another buyer as opposed to offering a straight price per square metre reduction on the price.
Even if the outcome for you doesn’t change, it is far better to deal with your concern before signing contracts.
Ed Carey is an estate agent and member of the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland

title: ‘I’m picturing Galway’: introducing Cork to a teenager in 48 hours
description: Even a leg injury doesn’t dampen enthusiasm for Cork’s easy-to-navigate charm
content:
“I’m picturing Galway,” says my teenage daughter when we’re about halfway to Cork on the train from Dublin – me settled in with a novel, her with many TikToks still to absorb. The Galway reference is not as wild as it seems; she has been to the west many times but was not old enough to register the delights of Cork the last time she visited.
This two-night trip is aimed at changing that, with travelling by train rather than car designed to reduce stress for all involved. Thus, we step out at Cork’s Kent Station at midday on Friday with the weekend mood already upon us, the sun helpfully lighting our path up MacCurtain Street to our home for two nights, The Metropole Hotel.
To get the most out of our stay sans car, we have designed a teenage-friendly itinerary where everything spins out from this location between the station and Cork’s Patrick Street area just across the river. We’re checked in at the Metropole, a charming grande dame, about 15 minutes after getting off the train and just over four hours after leaving our home – so far, so efficient. But here enters the glitch.
A few days before our trip my daughter sprained her ankle, and is now sporting an unstylish support boot. She’s mobile, but not in the best state for extensive walks (shopping is curiously still very manageable) – so earlier plans to fully explore Cork on foot are slightly curtailed. We will, however, be helped by the relatively petite nature of the city centre that lies before us.
Hungry and with Cork’s deep culinary heritage at the front of at least one of our minds, we orient ourselves with a short stroll across St Patrick’s Bridge for a restorative lunch at casual Med-style cafe/bar Orso, where we agree the mussels are wonderful. A quick tour around the English Market later, we’re ready to embrace the friend of less mobile and time-poor tourists – a hop-on/hop-off (we won’t be doing a lot of hopping) bus tour run by Cork City Tours (€22 for an adult, €9 for a child).
Stops include all the Cork biggies – the Shandon Bells in St Anne’s Church, St Fin Barre’s Cathedral, University College Cork (UCC), the Butter Museum, and more – and it’s up to the passenger to decide where or when they want to alight and investigate further. In our case, the boot means we take the approach of an aged Floridian on a cruise ship and view most of the attractions from the choppy waves (or from the bus as it weaves through the teensy, hilly streets) and just one or two in the flesh.
We agree on the Butter Museum in Shandon, which is located next to the derelict Cork Butter Exchange, aka the largest butter market in the world in the 19 th century. The museum looked small and achievable on paper and is possibly even smaller and more achievable in real life – a huge boon for a teenager not known for a love of museum life who is basically indulging her mother by even considering walking through the door.
Reflecting later on our purchases and the quality of our short first day in Cork, we’re both impressed with how much we got to take in, even before dinner
The set-up is charming and quaint, showing retro videos on Ireland’s masterstroke invention of Kerrygold in the 1960s (featuring Tony O’Reilly, who would soon be master of the universe, and whose name is over the building) and the kind of butter churning that would make a tradwife question her commitment to the skill. There’s also a chance to print your own butter wrappers and you can even taste some soda bread spread with… you’ve guessed it… butter.
Out of 10, and taking account of the museum’s compact nature, the sprain-afflicted teenager says she gives it 11, but her tone may not be entirely sincere. At my end, some points are lost for the narrowness of the souvenir range; maybe a butter dish or butter knife could be added, perhaps a keyring? We suddenly feel compelled to get our retail fix in some actual shops instead.
[ Cork Airport named best regional airport in Europe for third time Opens in new window ]
For the record, Cork shopping gets a genuine 10 out of 10 from both parties, with the displays in the fish section of the English Market contributing a couple of marks on their own.
If you want to combine your retail extravaganza with a little history, try taking in the pedestrianised Huguenot quarter around French Street and Carey’s Lane, where you’ll get echoes of this group of persecuted French Protestants who took refuge in Cork in the 17 th century. Particularly compelling amid the commercial bustle is the tiny 1733 Huguenot Graveyard, with its still-visible gravestones and poignant air of calm. From the end of 2028, you’ll also be able to take in some art alongside your make-up counters when the nearby Crawford Art Gallery reopens after refurbishment.
Reflecting later on our purchases and the quality of our short first day in Cork, we’re both impressed with how much we got to take in, even before dinner. For this, we choose the stylish and buzzy Market Lane on Oliver Plunkett Street, where everybody in Cork seems to be out celebrating something, both indoors and on the terrace. The outdoor Friday night vibe builds as we make our way back to the hotel past crowds of happy revellers on MacCurtain Street, not even close to reaching its crescendo.
On Saturday, we turn away from the city centre and use our Leap cards to take the 25-minute train trip to historic Cobh. The topography of this pretty maritime town is not ideal for sprained ankles, so we take in its jauntily coloured, daintily perched houses and domineering cathedral from below as we wait for the boat to Spike Island, one of the area’s premier tourist attractions (return ferry, guided tour and other attractions cost €27.95 for an adult and €14.95 for a child).
Having stopped at the cheery Seasalt Café and the lively Saturday Cobh farmers’ market for picnic lunch provisions, the bleakness of “Ireland’s Alcatraz” is a little jarring, in an instructive way. Best known for its past as a military fortress (both British and Irish) and a prison of various eras, the island is just 10 minutes away from the action in Cobh, with the suggested visit time about 3.5 hours. This includes time to hike around the island on your own.
The pedestrianised lanes off Patrick Street (or Pana as we now call it) show brilliantly how space filled with people walking and mixing together in the open air of a bright evening can be a joyous thing
We visit the chilly and eerie prison punishment block, where 1850s prisoners were locked up in the poorest of conditions, and take in glorious, elevated views of Cork Harbour from the back of the 104-acre island. The highlight for both of us, however, is the section on the 1985 prison riot, which saw a group of “young offenders” then held there break out of their dorms and take control of the whole island. It was a major event at the time, with the story very effectively told through various contemporary media reports, and colour added by the tour.
Back in Cork city, the Saturday evening atmosphere is even livelier than it was on Friday, with the pedestrianised lanes off Patrick Street (or Pana as we now call it) showing brilliantly how space filled with people walking and mixing together in the open air of a bright evening can be a joyous thing.
[ Dublin and Cork shortlisted for European Capital of Smart Tourism award Opens in new window ]
On Sunday, the sprain again enters the picture, with earlier plans to tour the UCC campus and follow a recommendation for lunch in Léa’s at The Glucksman gallery unfortunately abandoned. Instead, we join the hipsters (or whatever the hip word for hipsters is now) in Priory Coffee for very good coffee and scones near our hotel before heading back to Kent Station and home.
Summing up our trip as we pull back into Heuston, the teenager puts strolling around the city (even in a boot) as her highlight, with the museums a good bit further down the list. Overall though, would she recommend a weekend in Cork to her friends? Definitely, yes.
Úna McCaffrey was a guest of Visit Cork: purecork.ie/experiencecork

title: First term resolutions to live by for a peaceful and happy new school year
description: Avoid overparenting, set aside some time for yourself and, like Elsa, learn when to let it go
content:
T wo weeks back at school and only one school jumper lost so far. This must be some sort of record at chez Hogan. But then again, I haven’t checked the Twistables or pencil situation yet.
And now that I think about it, one child definitely left for school this morning wearing last year’s shoes.
Welcome to September. The season of new beginnings. A new school year, a new you, my walking buddy has suggested, if not in so many words. What she actually suggested is joining a gym because it’s getting darker, colder and a lot rainier than it was during the summer.
Now I’m not sure if she realises I own a walking pad – I must not go on about it enough – and a pink 2kg kettlebell, which sits in the corner of my room, a bit like the brick in Father Ted. This is mostly because I don’t know what I’m supposed to do with a kettlebell, but I bought it when they were all the rage. And also it’s pink. So I’m practically a gym bunny already.
Anyway, I’m ready to embrace the new school year, new me theme. If not least because January resolutions seem a tad pointless when we all know parents live by the school calendar anyway.
So in that vein, here are some other resolutions to live by, in the interests of a peaceful and happy parental new school year.
There is a real temptation to do anything and everything for our kids because (a) sometimes it’s easier and (b) because we are such a time-poor society that we don’t want to waste precious family time making our kids do things they don’t want to do. And we don’t necessarily want to have to hear about them doing it either.
Overparenting means we’re depriving them of the opportunity to build life skills and develop resilience. But we also end up unloading the dishwasher more, doing all the vacuuming, completing their school projects and spending way too much time in the class WhatsApp groups asking about homework. What happens if you forget to take down your homework or bring home a book? Learning of a different kind.
Religiously. Because when those after school activities and training sessions come knocking again, and they will, you will find your time swallowed up completely, pointing the car in the direction of some field, hall or other, while also preparing to surrender your entire weekend to standing pitch side in the wind and rain as you embrace the joy of children’s team sports, music, drama and the special hell known as the swimming pool changing rooms.
And when you’re overheating in a cubicle definitely not made for families with squirming, half-showered children, you may find yourself questioning all your life choices. If, of course, it wasn’t for that one hobby or outlet that you’ve carved out to keep you sane. Please note personal care, such as showering, does not count as either me-time or a hobby. Meeting up with friends can.
Hobbies should be at the very least weekly. If you don’t have time for this at any stage of the week, your children are probably overscheduled. And you may be struggling with point 1.
Go full Elsa. The comment that’s irritated you in the class WhatsApp group. The homework that wasn’t finished that evening. The training run that may actually push you over the edge. Some days don’t pan out as hoped. Such is life. So cut yourself some slack and make a decision on those days that suits the family – without berating yourself for the rest of the week for your choices.
Make life easier for yourself – buy the cakes in the supermarket and pass them off as your own at the school cake sale. (Or, failing that, I have an excellent Rice Krispie buns recipe over on my Instagram page).
You don’t have to have the same values, expectations or even commitment to dress-up day as other parents. Know what you want your children to get out of school and let that be your guide, rather than the distraction of the competitive parent battle cry.
But if your priority is academic and sporting achievement over happiness and inclusion, perhaps have a word with yourself. For all our sakes.
So you can see where everyone should be. But delegate the responsibility of filling it out because you’ve done your bit in putting it there.

title: Housing supply won’t increase simply because councils set higher density targets
description: Homes will only be delivered at scale if planning, infrastructure and development economics are aligned
content:
I rish housing policy often presents a false choice between affordability and viability. In reality, neither can exist without the other.
Homes that are unaffordable fail households. Homes that are unviable won’t get built. If Ireland is serious about solving its housing crisis , it must place viability at the heart of the planning system while ensuring the benefits of increased supply flow through to purchasers and renters.
Minister for Housing James Browne ’s comments in his recent Business Post interview highlight this challenge.
He described Ireland’s housing market as “dysfunctional” and acknowledged that apartment development currently struggles to survive without substantial State support.
Direct State interventions through subsidies, schemes and tax measures are estimated to reach almost €12 billion this year. While these measures have supported apartment delivery in the short term, the Minister is correct to ask how Ireland can eventually move towards a market that stands on its own feet.
There are encouraging signs. Reforms to the rental sector and last year’s VAT measures for apartment development have helped restore confidence among international investors. Investment capital is gradually returning to the Irish residential market.
However, finance alone will not solve the problem. Homes will only be delivered at scale if planning, infrastructure and development economics are aligned.
This is where Ireland can learn from continental Europe. Across countries such as Denmark, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, Spain and Sweden housing viability is not treated as an afterthought. Instead, it is built into the planning system from the outset.
[ Ireland would do well to pay close attention to differing housing policies in Spain Opens in new window ]
Local authorities typically prepare detailed plans supported by infrastructure programmes, development agreements and delivery strategies. Before land is released for development, authorities assess infrastructure requirements, servicing costs, development phasing, affordable housing obligations and overall deliverability.
The objective is not merely to maximise theoretical housing numbers. It is to ensure that plans can actually be implemented.
Ireland’s discretionary planning system has historically taken a different approach, which makes it a European outlier. Development plans often identify ambitious growth targets and density objectives without demonstrating how they will be financed or delivered.
Infrastructure commitments frequently lag behind zoning decisions. As a result, housing viability becomes a problem to be resolved at the planning application stage, long after land has been purchased and expectations set.
The consequences are becoming increasingly apparent.
Recent debates around apartment delivery have highlighted the tension between density policy and development economics. While medium-density, low-rise housing remains viable in many locations, higher-density development often requires apartment-led schemes. These projects can face substantial challenges arising from construction costs, financing costs, regulatory requirements and infrastructure burdens.
The lesson is not that density is undesirable. Rather, it is that density objectives must be aligned with deliverability. Planning policy should be grounded in the realities of the market, not in abstract aspirations.
A more effective approach would make viability a statutory requirement of plan-making. Development Plans, Urban Area Plans, Priority Area Plans and Urban Development Zone Masterplans should all be required to demonstrate how proposed housing targets can realistically be achieved.
This should include infrastructure cost assessments, housing typology analysis, viability testing, delivery projections and implementation phasing.
The central question should be simple: can this neighbourhood actually be built under current market conditions?
Such a framework could distinguish between three levels of growth. The first would identify deliverable sustainable density based on current market conditions. The second would identify target density achievable through public investment and policy support. The third would identify longer-term aspirational density that could emerge following major infrastructure investment. This would create more realistic housing projections and improve public confidence in the planning system.
Viability should also be considered when national policies are developed. Ireland routinely assesses the environmental, transport and flood-risk impacts of planning proposals, yet rarely undertakes systematic viability assessments of these proposals. In addition, before introducing new apartment standards, sustainability obligations, infrastructure levies or affordability requirements, Government should examine their impact on housing output. If additional costs reduce supply, compensating measures should be introduced simultaneously.
Most importantly, Ireland should move towards a genuinely infrastructure-led European planning model.
[ What would happen if Ireland followed Vienna by designing housing with women in mind? Opens in new window ]
Many successful European cities identify growth areas, fund major infrastructure, prepare detailed three-dimensional masterplans and establish development frameworks before housing applications are submitted. This reduces risk, increases certainty and encourages investment. Developers can focus on building homes rather than navigating uncertainty around servicing, transport or utilities.
Ireland has too often followed the reverse discretionary planning sequence, granting permissions in areas where infrastructure arrives years later or, in some cases, not at all.
The path to affordability ultimately lies in increasing housing supply at scale. But supply will not increase simply because planning authorities set higher density targets or announce more unrealistic housing targets for selected sites. It will increase when land, infrastructure, planning and economics are aligned.
That is the real lesson from European planning systems. The countries that deliver large numbers of homes do not ignore viability. They embed it within the planning system from the beginning.
If Ireland wants fewer housing subsidies, greater private investment and more affordable housing, the solution is not to choose between viability and affordability. The solution is to recognise that one depends on the other.
By creating a planning system that prioritises viable deliverability, Ireland can build more homes, more quickly, and ultimately make housing more affordable for the people who need it most.
Tony Reddy is chairman of Reddy A+U and Property Industry Ireland

title: Reconstructions: A Room for Mike Kelley review – A thoughtful, generous exhibition
description: Mary McIntyre and Robert Anderson’s Belfast show is equal parts installation, re-creation and speculation on the performance participant’s status
content:
It’s a familiar scenario: you’re attending a performance, a concert, a reading or a gig, yet the primary spectacle before you is a sea of phones. We’re living in an age of documentation when little to nothing evades the lens.
In the final decades of the 20th century the camera was distinctly less pervasive, which adds a wonderful fugitive aura to the handful of existing photographs that capture the seminal early performance works of Mike Kelley .
An American artist of immense sensitivity who died by suicide in 2012, Kelley produced, over five decades, a remarkable body of work characterised equally by playfulness and pathos. His practice ranged from sculpture to video and installation, but his earliest works, from the late 1970s and early 1980s, primarily took the form of performances where he utilised both found and self-made objects.
Working from fleeting images of these early performances, the photographer Mary McIntyre and the sculptor Robert Anderson have collaborated to produce a thoughtful and generous exhibition that is equal parts installation, re-creation and speculation on the status of the performance participant.
The Mac’s sunken gallery space features a precise reconstruction of one of Kelley’s studio environments. It is minimal in appearance, an irregular life-size plywood room with a desultory rug on the floor and a replica of Kelley’s smiling diamond face banner leaning in the corner.
In another, larger galley space a series of objects are presented on a snaking angular plywood workbench construction. These are re-creations of a selection of Kelley’s idiosyncratic wooden performance props: birdhouses both conventional and unconventional, with perspectively skewed proportions, and a cartoonish bullhorn (Kelley called it a perspectaphone) stamped with the words “near” and “far” on each end.
Around the walls are a number of carefully composed photographs of studio interiors strewn to various degrees with prop objects. A small, flat display cabinet presents original catalogue documentary images of Kelley’s performances. The exhibition is rounded out by a room devoted to further reading and study materials.
Conspicuous within the entire presentation is the absence of figures. Nowhere in McIntyre’s and Anderson’s reconstructions do we see people appear or use the objects, either as Kelley did or otherwise.
This is of course by design, as the artists ask us to consider exactly what it is that the presence both of the artist and of the spectator brings to such work.
In posing this question in the particular manner they do, however, McIntyre and Anderson run the risk of fetishising the objects that Kelley created for his performances, detaching them too much from the lived context in which they appeared and rigidifying them into discrete sculptural pieces.
In the end, the inclusion of another of Kelley’s banners in the show is telling. A white sheet with gold tassel fringing, yellow paint spilling from the empty eyes and mouth cut in it, it’s like a strange, comic Shroud of Turin pointing in some way to the ghost or the residue of Kelley himself. The artist is present, even when he is absent.
Reconstructions: A Room for Mike Kelley is at Metropolitan Arts Centre , Belfast, until Sunday, October 18th

title: Make time to talk
description: Valuable advice
content:
Sir – Well done Sarah O’Toole on her advice on interrupting the suicidal thoughts of a friend, family member or colleague ( Letters , September 10th).
Instead of advising people who feel hopeless to “talk to someone”, let us as humans talk to those we feel or know are having a hard time. People often feel alone or sad these days, and with many working remotely, people are not always around to talk or don’t have the time.
We will all be challenged some days, those that feel suicidal are not a different species. – Yours, etc,

title: ‘Juliette Binoche brings a tour de force of emotional energy. You have to get out of its way and let it happen’
description: The director Lance Hammer on making Queen at Sea, his new film, with the French actor, Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall
content:
L ance Hammer, an American film-maker of great rigour, has made just two features in nearly two decades. His first, Ballast, set in the Mississippi Delta, won the directing award at Sundance in 2008 and was widely regarded as one of the best American films of that year. It even made the late critic Roger Ebert cry.
Hammer’s second, equally powerful feature is Queen at Sea, starring Juliette Binoche and Tom Courtenay , which has already earned worthy comparisons with such powerful depictions of later life and dementia as Gaspar Noé’s Vortex and Michael Haneke’s Amour .
It has been worth the lengthy wait. But where has he been?
“I wanted to make something that in the creative process itself gives me meaning,” Hammer says. “In America you can’t make money making independent films, so the creative process is my payment.
“At a certain point I just felt, like, if I can’t make the kinds of films I want to make, then I’d rather do something else. I had to make a living doing regular stuff. I was an architect by training. So I did a little architecture. I worked in investment and lived a regular life, but I kept writing things all this time.”
When the idea for Queen at Sea first came to him, Hammer was reluctant to tackle the thorny subject matter.
“I thought, I don’t want to make a story about the elderly,” he says. “I don’t want to make a film about dementia. I don’t want to do this. But it just kept coming out easily. I really wanted to finish the screenplay at that point, just for my own exercise.
“This is really challenging subject matter, and if you’re going to tell it, you have to tell it truthfully. You can’t make it a redemptive, sentimental story, because that’s not true. That’s not how it works.”
Hammer’s uncompromising film opens with a desperately sad dilemma. Amanda (played by Binoche) walks in on her mother, Leslie (Anna Calder-Marshall), having sex with her stepfather, Martin (Courtenay). Amanda immediately scolds Martin: Leslie has advanced dementia, and Amanda believes her mother is no longer capable of giving consent to her doting husband and carer.
She then calls the police – this is clearly an ongoing dispute – which bring Martin and the family into a bruising series of encounters with the law, medicine and social services.
“It’s not my own story or my family story,” Hammer says. “But my father is 88 years old, and there’s a lot of dementia around in his friend group. I’m close to my father, so I’ve been hearing and witnessing what’s happened to some of his friends.
“I think my radar started going up somehow. Then I came across a story that dealt with the sexual-consent component with dementia. And that was really fascinating to me, because the moral questions around it are different than for the cognitively intact. You have to rethink the rules. There are no easy answers.”
The film-maker has been a huge fan of Binoche, his first choice for the lead role, since Three Colours Blue.
“You feel something watching Juliette,” he says. “There’s this magnetism, this aura, this powerful life force. The pathos in her is amazing. She’s technically a master. She was the first person on the project, and we were on it together alone for a long time.
“She was actually a producer – a development producer – although she didn’t want to take that credit. And together we scraped it off the ground several times when it fell apart.
I really believe in this workshopping process where you start with the foundation of something ... You find actors that really want to work this way. And you cast actors that have the unique ability to bring their own souls and emotionality to a character
“But the thing I most admire about her is her commitment to artistic integrity. She thrives on the creative process. She’s addicted to it. Nothing can compromise it. And I feel very much that way myself.”
Courtenay and Calder-Marshall, who were jointly awarded the Silver Bear for best supporting performance at this year’s Berlin film festival, have been friends since playing Hamlet and Ophelia in a celebrated 1968 stage production.
Courtenay, famed for his defining performances in the British new-wave films The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner and Billy Liar, has twice been nominated for an Academy Award: for Doctor Zhivago, from 1965, and for The Dresser, from 1983.
Calder-Marshall, who also played a famous Cordelia opposite Laurence Olivier’s King Lear in a television production, has remained an extremely familiar face from series such as Morse, Poirot and, opposite her son Tom Burke, Strike.
That longevity and experience proved useful in the making of Queen at Sea.
“They’re incredibly powerful machines of artistic talent,” Hammer says. “I loved Tom as an actor, but then with Tom came all this other stuff, including his history. And with that history came this incredible real-life relationship, which translates to the screen between Tom and Annie.
[ Willem Dafoe: ‘I wasn’t a man about town. I was a kid trying to make theatre in a tiny company’ Opens in new window ]
“It feels like absolute luck. I did not plan it. I had no idea it existed. I couldn’t write it. They brought it, and we captured it. The same with Juliette. She just brings a whole tour de force of emotional energy. You have to get out of its way and let it happen.”
With Ballast, Hammer was less interested in dialogue or conventional storytelling than in the texture of life in the Mississippi Delta: its winter light, its soundscape and its unhurried rhythms. He recruited nonprofessional actors, giving them situations and loose instructions rather than conventional dialogue, allowing their responses to shape the film.
Queen at Sea was similarly fashioned from a skeletal story. Some scenes, notably Martin’s account of meeting his wife at a Tchaikovsky recital, were improvised by Courtenay, recorded by Hammer and subsequently written into the script.
“I really believe in this workshopping process where you start with the foundation of something,” the director says. “You’re not starting from scratch. You find actors that really want to work this way. And you cast actors that have the unique ability to bring their own souls and emotionality to a character.
“Not everybody can do that. I’m asking for the real person. I want the real Juliette Binoche. I want actors – usually Juliette – who say, ‘I would do this differently,’ or, ‘I wouldn’t react that way.’ Tom really invented a lot of his language to make the film not only British but his own way of seeing the world. That’s where the real truth comes from.”
A parallel plot involves puppy love. While Amanda, Martin and the authorities argue over care arrangements, Amanda’s teenage daughter, Sara (played by the Bridgerton star Florence Hunt), roams around north London and finds romance with a local boy.
This narrative counterpoint required an intimacy co-ordinator.
“We wanted to make sure that everybody was comfortable,” he says. “The first step is to show that, as in production, you’re not trying to create any exploitative moments.
“I never worked with an intimacy co-ordinator before, so I was worried that I would be told to do things with the script or the story. But in fact Jenefer Odell really protected our story. She was a great creative collaborator. We all sat down and figured out what blocking felt comfortable.”
Although Hammer spent a month rehearsing the material, he never discussed the film’s central moral quandary with his cast.
“I didn’t want to put my finger on the scales,” he says. “When I watched Tom and Juliette’s characters at loggerheads, I was curious to see if I could decipher what their actual positions were morally. But everybody kind of kept it close to their chest. I still don’t really know what they think.”
Queen at Sea is in cinemas from Friday, September 18th

title: John FitzGerald: How can we get the measure of an Irish economy that defies conventional metrics?
description: It would be helpful if CSO explained underlying reasons for surprising GDP numbers on publication
content:
I n the 1970s, as a junior official in the Department of Finance working on economic forecasting, I learned about the complexity of measuring Irish output and income, and related economic growth. A meeting with the Central Statistics Office in 1973, concerning a tricky national accounting issue, taught me that in the real world there was a need for suitable accounting compromises to reflect the underlying reality of what was really happening in the Irish economy.
The State-owned Irish Shipping company had ordered a large bulk carrier, which was built in a shipyard in Glasgow. When it was finished in 1973, because of its size and its specialised function, on its maiden voyage it would not come to Ireland, and might never have visited an Irish port.
According to the CSO , accounting rules meant that, because it would never dock in Ireland, it could not be counted as an import. However, it was undoubtedly part of Irish investment for the year.
The result would have been a rise in investment that would not have been offset by the import of the ship, adding to output measured by GDP, despite the fact that the output, the building of the ship, took place in Glasgow.
After some debate about the accounting rules, a compromise was reached. If the ship sailed through Irish territorial waters on its maiden voyage, the CSO would count it as an import. The ship duly sailed within 12 miles of the Irish coast and Irish GDP was untainted.
In the subsequent half century, the growing complexity of the Irish economy has posed many greater challenges for the CSO and economists alike. Today all economy watchers in Ireland know that GDP, the standard international measure of national income, is a very inaccurate reflection of the income of the people of Ireland.
Instead we have developed a series of alternative measures, GNI* and modified domestic demand. These two measures strip out the activities of multinational enterprises in Ireland that affect GDP but have no impact on the welfare of those of us living in Ireland.
The OECD has suggested yet another measure for use in international comparisons of welfare, net national income. This takes out all depreciation – capital that is used up in a year. If this measure were used, comparing Ireland with other countries would be straightforward.
[ Noisy headline data underlines uselessness of traditional measures for Irish economy Opens in new window ]
However, there is strong resistance within the EU to using this alternative measure as some countries have enshrined GDP in legislative rules relating to fiscal policy. As a result, GDP will be with us for the foreseeable future.
While we in Ireland use other measures of national income and economic welfare, the problems with Irish GDP are sufficiently large that it makes the interpretation of euro zone economic activity difficult using GDP. For this reason, the European Central Bank, when looking at national income in the euro zone, excludes Irish GDP, using an alternative measure, modified domestic demand.
Over the past year there have been exceptional gyrations in Irish GDP each quarter, with very noticeable knock-on effects on euro-zone GDP. In the first quarter of this year Irish GDP fell 5.6 per cent on the previous quarter, reducing euro-zone GDP by 0.2 percentage points. It then rose in the second quarter by 11.5 per cent, adding 0.4 percentage points to euro-zone GDP.
Using a more appropriate measure of activity in Ireland, there would have been very little impact on euro-zone GDP.
While the ECB understands what is happening, many others watching the European economy are not aware of the distorting effects of observed very large changes in Irish GDP on the euro zone as a whole. One central banker from a large euro-zone economy whom I met this summer had very strange ideas of what was going on in Ireland as a result of the antics of Irish GDP.
The recent extreme changes in Irish GDP occurred because of fluctuations in the export of pharmaceuticals. In the first quarter of 2026 exports were down but, as a counterpart, continuing production increased stocks. However, because the stocks are valued at a fraction of the sale price, it appeared as a fall in output. This was reversed in the second quarter, with significant exports coming from stocks.
The CSO knows this was what happened and it would be helpful if it explained the underlying factors causing surprising GDP numbers at the time of publication. This would help outsiders watching not just Ireland, but the wider euro zone.
Life was much easier when diverting a ship sorted out all the accounting problems.

title: ‘US business people buy properties in Ireland because they love everything about it’
description: Westmeath-born, Palm Beach-based Desmond Keogh, president of the Irish Georgian Society in the US, owns Oakley Park House in Co Meath
content:
W estmeath-born businessman Desmond Keogh is the first Irishman to become president of the Irish Georgian Society in the United States .
Now based in Florida , he took up the office in April. Keogh grew up on the 120-hectare (300-acre) Ballinakill Farm on Lough Derravaragh, Co Westmeath , and is passionate about Irish country houses. He bought Oakley Park House, outside Kells, in 2023.
“I had been searching for a house in Ireland for three years. I wanted somewhere about half an hour from my mother’s and a reasonable distance from Dublin Airport,” he says.
We are sitting in the drawingroom of the late Georgian country house that his wife, Cristina, an interior designer, has transformed into a comfortable, airy space, decorated with historical paintings, urns, Georgian furniture and a large elk head facing the fireplace.
“I like moving. I like houses. It’s my comfort zone. It’s really fun,” she says. The couple have five children, aged 11 to 26.
In the diningroom across the corridor, the Keoghs have installed a large, oval-shaped dining table with chairs upholstered in French fabric and practical, modern, American side cabinets. The kitchen at the back of the house has modern, fitted cabinets, the original Aga cooker and a sizeable table to accommodate visiting family and friends.
“I like mixing everything up, being practical with a bit of character. I don’t want the house to look like a museum. I want people to come and use it, and for it to be exciting, comfortable, with nothing too precious,” she says. The five bedrooms upstairs have yet to be given a makeover.
Keogh has an eight-phase restoration plan for the late Georgian country house estate. “We did emergency work on the roof and the valleys. The exterior wasn’t in bad shape,” he says, as he shows us where he has uncovered the dilapidated basement, completely abandoned by previous owners who also knocked down a much larger older house to the rear of Oakley Park House.
Keogh’s long-term plans include work on the main house and the basement, restoring the steward’s and coachman’s houses and other buildings in the extensive farmyard, replanting and repairing the walled garden and another sunken garden on the estate.
He regularly returns to Ireland to join the Irish Georgian Society spring and autumn tours of country houses across the 32 counties.
“We bring 14 to 16 people on these tours from America. We stay at the private houses, have lunch and dinner with the owners,” he says. Keeping numbers low is key to giving the visitors an up-close-and-personal sense of life in the 18th- and 19th-century country properties.
Keogh expresses astonishment at the number of Irish country houses that remain intact, considering that almost 300 were burned down between 1919 and 1923 and many more were demolished or allowed to go to ruin in the mid-20th century.
Although interested in architecture and drawing from a young age, he first got involved with the Irish Georgian Society in the US in the 1990s. “Now we have events at the Beach Club in Palm Beach [Florida], where I am a member, and dinners in New York, Boston and Chicago in the autumn,” he says.
[ A Wicklow mansion rescued from ruin by seven people: ‘I felt sorry for the house’ Opens in new window ]
During his four-year tenure as president, he would like to expand the presence of Irish Georgian Society scholarship programmes to other US cities with strong Irish-American connections, such as Atlanta, Philadelphia, Dallas and San Francisco.
“I’m looking for universities with good architecture and history of art programmes, so that we can bring Irish students there, build relationships and open chapters of the Irish Georgian Society in these cities,” he says.
A member of the US Republican Party since he “landed” in the US, Keogh has many connections and on his recent visit to Ireland, popped in to see the current US ambassador, Edward Walsh.
He was also friendly with the late US businessman Fred Krehbiel, who bought and restored the five-star Ballyfin Demesne hotel in Co Laois. The hotel is now run by his sons, Jay and Liam Krehbiel. Tommy Quick, president of the Ireland Funds charitable network, is another Palm Beach resident with whom Keogh associates.
Keogh says American business people buy properties in Ireland because “they love everything about Ireland”. “They also feel that they get incredible value and enjoy fixing them up and putting money into restoring them.”
The Irish Georgian Society in the US counts several wealthy business people among its members, including the late Wall Street financier Beth Dater Jennings, whose donations to restoration projects in Ireland have been significant.
These included a donation of €1.5 million towards the mid-2010s restoration of the City Assembly House, the Irish Georgian Society headquarters in on South William Street in Dublin 2, and, more recently, support for restoration works on the Sirius Arts Centre, the former yacht club building in Cobh, Co Cork.
The Irish Georgian Society in the US is currently considering which new projects to fund. “I’ve looked at five projects, from Tipperary to Cork to Waterford, that I’ll bring back to the board,” says Keogh.
Keen to promote the Irish Georgian Society at home and in the US, he says, “people think the Irish Georgian Society is elite and stuffy but it’s a really fun and interesting organisation to be in. It’s not expensive to join and you don’t have to own a Georgian house to enjoy the parties and tours.”
His own back story is an example of how some Irish people successfully built their lives from scratch in the US. While studying at Multyfarnham Agricultural College in the 1980s, Keogh spent two summers in the US playing Gaelic football. While there, an encounter with an American businessman who invited him to his winter home in Palm Beach changed the trajectory of his life.
“I just loved the architecture and the climate. I thought, when I finish college, I’m going to go back there and have a business there,” he recalls. And, so he did.
Working first for a Maryland businessman who imported stone and tiles from Europe for the neoclassical mansions of south Florida, Keogh fell on his feet. “I had £300, no green card, no credit card but I started working for Stuart Cronin and I stayed with him and his Roscommon-born wife and eight months later, I bought my first house,” he says.
Designing and selling glass tables with a marble base as a side business, he then began restoring marble for wealthy homeowners in south Florida and beyond. This led to his current businesses, Haifa Limestone and Haifa General Contracting, which deal with high-end clients throughout the US.
“I import stone to the US from 21 different countries. We do all the architectural drawings, the global sourcing, the fabrication, the installation and the finishing work, so the buck stops with us,” he says. He named his business Haifa, after the Israeli city, because he had a lot of Jewish clients.
[ From the archive: Dublin needs a Georgian house museum worthy of its rich heritage Opens in new window ]
When he is in Ireland, Keogh loves nothing more than joining the Meath hunt and he also hunts with the Palm Beach hounds in Florida. “I grew up with horses and I now host the Meath hunt in the first week in January,” he says, proudly.
He is also avidly researching the history of Oakley Park House, keen to explore every angle that presents itself.
He recounts how when he was under contract to purchase the property in 2023, he began looking into the Bomford family, the original owners of the property. And he was chuffed to find one of the last surviving family members, Jim Bomford, retired in Longwood, Florida.
“He had the [American] civil war medals, gun and sword of his great, great-grandfather Augustus Bomford, who was disinherited from Oakley Park because he fell in love with a Catholic girl and went to New York in 1861,” Keogh says.
As the 84-year-old retiree didn’t have any children, he gave the military memorabilia to Keogh, who now has them displayed in the front hall of Oakley Park House.

title: From financial support to study abroad, higher education can take you further
description: Funding, guidance and global opportunities are available to help students get the most from their time in higher education
content:
Higher education can take people further than they ever expected. Sometimes that’s because the right support is there at the right moment, helping someone stay on track when finances are tight. Sometimes it’s because a door opens that they never expected to walk through, such as the chance to study abroad.
For many students, the journey into higher education begins with questions about costs, support and settling in. Yet many are unaware of the range of opportunities and services available, from financial assistance and disability supports to international experiences through Erasmus+.
Financial concerns are often the starting point. What financial supports are available to me? Who can I speak with about accessing supports? Where can I find out more information?
One of the key sources of support is the Student Assistance Fund, provided by the Higher Education Authority (HEA) on behalf of the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science. The fund helps full- and part-time students experiencing financial difficulty with costs such as books and class materials, rent and utility bills, food, essential travel, childcare and medical expenses.
While it does not cover tuition or registration fees, it can provide valuable assistance when it’s needed most. Students who find themselves under financial pressure should contact their higher education institution’s access office to learn more about the help available.
The HEA also administers the Fund for Students with Disabilities on behalf of the Department. The fund helps higher education institutions provide the necessary support and equipment students with disabilities may need to access, participate in and successfully complete their studies.
This can include assistive technology, transport costs and academic learning supports. Students are advised to register with their access or disability office to ensure they can avail of the assistance available to them.
Students preparing for higher education can consult studentfinance.ie , which provides clear information on the financial assistance schemes available. The website explains eligibility criteria, application processes and other sources of support, helping students, families and teachers navigate their options with confidence.
At the heart of this support network are the access offices found in every higher education institution in Ireland.
Access teams aim to remove barriers to education by providing information on entry routes, answering questions about financial assistance, and helping people navigate their higher education journey. Anyone attending, or considering attending, a higher education institution should contact its access office for information on the services available.
For many students, this guidance is the first step towards higher education. It can also open the door to opportunities they may never have considered. An Erasmus+ experience can be one of those opportunities.
Erasmus+, the EU’s flagship mobility programme, has transformed the lives of more than 16.7 million people. In Ireland alone, around 200,000 people have benefited from the programme.
The experiences take many different forms. A year spent studying abroad is the image a lot of people have of Erasmus+. That remains a popular option, but today’s programme is far more flexible than many realise. Alongside semester and year-long exchanges, participants can complete traineeships or take part in blended intensive programmes (BIPs), which combine online collaboration with a short period abroad, from a few days to a few weeks.
University of Limerick student Ciaran Kelly chose a BIP in Spain while completing his master’s degree.
“It combined an international and virtual experience with a topic directly relevant to my future career as a language teacher in Ireland,” he says. “The shorter format also suited my master’s, as it allowed me to gain an international perspective without being away for an entire semester.”
For students balancing work commitments, family responsibilities or intensive courses, this flexibility can make an international experience feel much more achievable.
“Making higher education accessible is not only about helping people get through the door. It’s also about ensuring they can take full advantage of the opportunities that come with it. One of our priorities is making sure international opportunities are accessible to all students. Financial supports, inclusion funding and flexible options are helping more students take part and benefit from Erasmus+,” says Sheena Duffy, head of international at the HEA.
Erasmus+ opportunities are not limited to Europe. Depending on the institution and course, participants may study or train in destinations ranging from Japan and Canada to South Africa and New Zealand.
Funding is available towards travel and living costs, with additional support available for students who may face financial, health-related or other barriers to taking part. This includes students in receipt of SUSI, those with disabilities or ongoing health conditions, carers, lone parents, care-experienced students, members of the Traveller and Roma communities, and refugees. Participants also pay no tuition fees to their host institution and their studies or training abroad are fully recognised as part of their Irish degree.
“More people are now able to take part than ever before. In Ireland, the proportion of Erasmus+ participants from backgrounds that have traditionally been less likely to participate in international mobility increased from 6 per cent in 2014 to 31 per cent in 2024, reflecting the programme’s growing reach and accessibility,” Duffy says.
The benefits continue long after graduation. Research shows that graduates who studied abroad are more likely to find work quickly, have higher levels of employment, and often earn more than peers who stayed at home. Employers value the skills that come from living and working in a different environment.
While research points to the long-term professional benefits of Erasmus+, participants often speak first about the personal impact.
Royal Irish Academy of Music student Grace Mercer remembers setting off for Finland, not quite knowing what lay ahead.
“My biggest worry was the unknown, moving to another country where I knew no one,” she says.
Her year abroad completely changed her perspective on what she was capable of.
“I can now put myself in unfamiliar situations and trust that I’ll be able to figure it out. I found that it became easier and easier to try new things and go new places. What struck me the most was how I could walk up to a group of new people and introduce myself without feeling socially nervous at all.”
The opportunity to study alongside musicians from around the world was equally transformative.
“I’ve been so lucky ... being surrounded by so many talented people has helped me grow and become more open-minded as a musician.”
Looking back, it’s the independence she gained that stands out most.
“I’m no longer nervous to travel by myself ... now it’s just no big deal. It’s like, ‘pop on a plane, be grand’”
Ciaran experienced similar growth. “I learned a lot about myself and how I communicate. The BIP helped me develop communication and collaboration skills that hadn’t been tested before.”
He encourages students that may be unsure to take the leap. “I know some students worry about money and language, but there are so many supports available. Just apply. Feeling nervous is normal, and confidence often comes from taking the first step.”
Financial assistance, disability supports and opportunities such as Erasmus+ may initially seem like very different things. But, in reality, they all serve a shared purpose at the HEA: helping people participate fully in higher education and make the most of everything it has to offer.
For information on the Student Assistance Fund, Fund for Students with Disabilities, and other supports, students should contact their institution’s access office or visit studentfinance.ie .
Those interested in Erasmus+ should speak to the international office at their institution, where staff can provide guidance on destinations, funding, application processes and deadlines. Further information is available at erasmusirelandhe.ie

title: Compelling and unsettling: The Last Years of Edna O’Brien by her son Carlo Gébler
description: The memoir powerfully evokes O’Brien’s rage against ‘hideous’ dying
content:
On July 27th, 2024, Edna O’Brien died in London at the age of 93. Over subsequent days, her funeral Mass in Tuamgraney, Co Clare, and burial afterwards on Holy Island, Lough Derg, received widespread media coverage; this newspaper published a four-page special literary supplement on Monday, July 29th. “She was a speaker of truth,” said her funeral celebrant, Fr O’Meara, a “remarkable woman” who “held up a mirror for us in a very narrow time in Ireland”.
This memoir, by her older son Carlo Gébler , covers the final years of Edna’s life, beginning in May 2020. It is, for a number of reasons, a surprising book; any expectations that this will be a “tell it all” account of what it was like to have a famous author mother are quickly dispersed, and the chronological coverage is somewhat jagged and uneven.
Interested readers will find some of the wider familial story in Sinéad O’Shea’s recent documentary Blue Road: The Edna O’Brien Story, featuring memorable interviews with O’Brien filmed not long before she died, as well as contributions by her two sons.
Instead, what is offered here is a quiet, unflinching and moving reflection on watching a loved one age; a book that tells, in close-up focus, what it feels like to watch a parent weaken and to learn what “no one tells you” before.
In his preface, Gébler recounts how the knowledge of his mother’s impending death began to feel “like a sore tooth to which the tongue keeps darting: it wouldn’t let me alone” and so “I decided I should stick with the sore tooth. I would write about my experience of my mother’s death. It was what I needed to do. Solipsistic of course, but it had to be done.”
[ Carlo Gébler on his mother Edna O’Brien: Coming to the end Opens in new window ]
That solipsism is also an act of narrative generosity. The emotions he describes are familiar to very many, and his acknowledgment of them a source of solace. They range from helplessness to anger, through anxiety and worry, back to rage. And even more powerfully, the memoir evokes O’Brien’s rage against dying: “She would testify to the brutal truth and she did and terrible as it was to hear, it was also bracing. She wouldn’t baulk; she would resist; she would cavil. Wasn’t that the better way to face extinction, to say loudly over and over and over, ‘No, no, no, it’s hideous.’”
The hideousness of dying notwithstanding, Gébler’s account of his mother’s final years also brings some welcome humour. Reading lines like these – in which Edna O’Brien’s voice is still powerfully sharp, and thankfully so – one feels like cheering out loud: “I hate emails, I fucking hate emails. I want them out of my fucking life. I want them abolished. I never want to see another fucking email for as long as I live, which won’t be long. God grant me this wish – no more fucking emails for the time remaining.”
Not only a narrative about a son and mother, this is definitely also a book about two writers and about the vital power of writing as a life force for them both. The early chapters feature some fascinating depictions of Edna O’Brien’s writing process. This is one example: “When she worked with someone, she either read from handwritten sheets, changing what she had written as she read, or made it up on the spot without the aid of notes. She could dictate off the cuff and when she did, her voice had a strange, tranced, otherworldly quality.”
Other details convey the continuing impact of practical reality, including financial worries and the precarity of being a 90-year-old tenant, as well as O’Brien’s remarkable work ethic. Even in her last months she struggled to complete a book on TS Eliot.
For the writing son, the last years have been times of watching – his mother and himself – and of painful learning: “Death, in this case (or do I mean her case?) I was coming to understand, was less an event than a series of incremental reductions, with one capacity after another being taken away until at last, you came to the end – extinction. And like some wretched formula I needed for an examination but could not keep hold of in my mind, I had to keep relearning this, again and bloody again.”
In February 2023 O’Brien had a terrible fall, one consequence of which was that she could no longer live at home. Recounting the story of her fall to her son, she vigorously protested that “No one warns you about old age” and “No one tells you that your body falls apart”. In retrospect, he realises that the world’s seeming failure to warn her adequately also left her free to rage against it. Now, his own decision to speak the truth, to warn and tell, makes for very compelling, if unsettling, reading.
Margaret Kelleher is Chair of Anglo-Irish Literature and Drama at UCD. Her biography of Mary and Padraic Colum is published this month by UCD Press

title: Auto-enrolment brings jump in private pension numbers – but widespread worries remain
description: Just two in five people are sure of good standard of living in retirement, watchdog research shows
content:
The number of people with private pensions has risen significantly over the past year, but less than half believe they will be able to afford a good standard of living in retirement, new research from the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) suggests.
A report published today reveals that pension ownership has risen by 17 per cent since 2025, with the jump coming in the wake of the introduction of the Government’s MyFutureFund auto-enrolment scheme earlier this year.
However, confidence in retirement outcomes remains low, with just two in five sure their pension will provide a good standard of living in retirement. Only one in three are optimistic that their pension savings will be able to keep pace with inflation.
The research also highlights a significant gender gap in how men and women prepare for and think about retirement.
All told, 24 per cent of women have no retirement arrangements in place, compared with 17 per cent of men. Meanwhile, fewer women than men said they understand pensions. A total of 49 per cent of women told researchers they had an understanding of pensions, compared to 63 per cent of men.
Women are also more downbeat about their future prospects, with 32 per cent lacking confidence in the standard of living they will have in retirement compared to 23 per cent of men.
“Our research shows that consumers avoid reviewing their pension statements and too often are not confident that their pension will allow a good standard of living in retirement,” said the CCPC’s director of financial education and Ireland’s first financial literacy ambassador, Gráinne Griffin. “We are encouraging consumers, particularly women, to review their pension, and remind them that they don’t need to do it alone.”
[ More than 29,000 Irish workers opt out of pension auto-enrolment during two-month window Opens in new window ]
She acknowledged that pension statements can be long, complicated and hard to understand and noted that it can be “very easy to just avoid them”.
However, she stressed that consumers do not need to “become an expert”, and can instead “book a short review with a financial planner or a financial adviser to check that your pension arrangements are suitable for both your current budget and your future hopes and dreams”.
The study shows that as has been the case in previous years, almost two-thirds of consumers have never had a one-to-one conversation with a financial adviser about retirement, and among those who did seek advice, just under one-third did so through their employer.
The research also highlights a low level of understanding of pension fees and charges among private pension-holders, with one-quarter reporting limited knowledge and 6 per cent unaware there were any charges associated with their pension at all.
[ Big Irish employers plotted to undermine pension auto-enrolment, says Government paper Opens in new window ]
“Employers also play a powerful role in their employees’ financial wellbeing,” Griffin said. “For those consumers who have sat down with a financial adviser and discussed their retirement plans, our research shows that they’re most likely to have been connected to that financial adviser by their employer. Also, employers that offer to match higher pension contributions make employees much more likely to increase their own level of investment in their pension.”
The chief executive of the National Automatic Enrolment Retirement Savings Authority (NAERSA) , Dermot Griffin, welcomed the jump in numbers of those with a private pension. “This is great news for workers in Ireland and reflects the positive impact since the introduction of MyFutureFund in January 2026,” he said.

title: The Traitors Ireland: Host Siobhán McSweeney comes across as a bit fed up
description: Television: The series has come down with a severe case of difficult second season syndrome
content:
T he Traitors Ireland ( RTÉ One, Sunday, 9.30pm) has come down with a severe case of difficult second season syndrome and two weeks in there is little indication that it has captured the public’s imagination. Part of the issue is the lack of a breakout character such as series one’s Paudie Moloney or the bromantic tag team of Nick and Ben.
The other problem is that nobody involved this time around looks like they’re having fun – certainly not host Siobhán McSweeney , who mustered an enjoyable villain shtick last year but now comes across as merely a bit fed up and ready to move on to something new.
The contestants seem disgruntled also. There are tears at the round table at the end of Sunday’s instalment as Dave is condemned as a Traitor even though he is very obviously a Faithful. His expulsion follows an uncomfortable flashpoint as an upset Janet is accused of traitorous carry-on by Pete because she didn’t burst into tears upon hearing that Sam had been murdered.
“I’m saying I’m having a human moment,” she says, adding that Pete is “going to look like a horrible person” if he has his way and she is voted off as a Traitor.
But in the end the momentum is against Dave who is condemned because of verbal slips which make it seem he’s up to something. He makes mistakes right to the end, such as when he refers to the “other Traitors” but, even allowing for that, he is so affable and incredulous that you can tell he’s a Faithful.
It’s not nice seeing him go and there’s no tension as the Faithful then all dissolve into tears and self-recrimination. Meanwhile, the actual Traitors, Carla and Páraic, lack the maniacal quality you need for a good back-stabber. They’re obviously not having any fun plotting in the shadows – and if even the Traitors are a bit over the whole thing, how are the rest of us supposed to feel?

title: As Shane Lowry watches on, Donald Trump reinvents himself as champion of all things Irish
description: The secret service needn’t have worried – the biggest danger at Doonbeg was an Irish golfer with a red-hot putter
content:
True to form, even on a weekend when his golf course was hosting a record-breaking native winner, Donald Trump still managed to dominate the headlines.
His unerring instinct for self-promotion survived even the fraught moment when he had to present Shane Lowry with the crystal trophy for winning the Irish Open .
Before doing which, he first raised a glass of a different kind, or at least the subject of it.
Somehow upstaging the man who had just won the event by an unprecedented 11 strokes, Trump announced that in response to intense lobbying the night before, he had decided to lift his tariffs “on Irish whiskey” .
But then Shane Lowry was only a golf champion. Whereas the US president had reinvented himself – if only for the weekend – as a champion of all things Irish and repeatedly voiced support for a United Ireland.
As he and Lowry strode separately to the first tee on Sunday afternoon, some in the international media teed Trump up to modify or retract his suggestion in Dublin on Saturday that a unified state was inevitable and would be “a great thing”.
Was he aware of the “backlash” his comments had caused in the UK, an ITV reporter asked. “I love my comments,” said the president, smashing the issue up the middle of the fairway, just as Lowry would shortly do the ball.
Minutes later, Lowry was mastering the green. Trump, meanwhile, was wrapping himself in it.
