In an impromptu press conference, he expanded on his Hibernophilic feelings (despite an aside in Dublin when he had also noted that some of us were “vicious bastards”).
“I’ve always loved the people of Ireland and it just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland and it would seem to me one of the naturals of all time is [to] put them together.”
The president stopped short of leading a chant: “What do we want? A United Ireland. When do we want it? Now.” Later again, asked if he had a “timetable” for unity, he refused specifics.
But in keeping with the traditions of the Banner County, he was determined to fly this one, timetable or no. Trebling down on the main theme, he repeated: “I think it should happen.”
As Micheál Martin, who joined him in Doonbeg on Sunday, will know, this part of Ireland has form in setting the political agenda, most famously when Éamon de Valera won a by-election here in 1917.
Whether the latest New York-born Irish patriot will have the same staying power remains to be seen. In the meantime, as he faces his own midterms, Trump’s West Clare pre-election pitch certainly made a stir.
His secret service detail, at least, will be glad to see the back of Doonbeg. Links courses in general must be a presidential minder’s nightmare, composed as they are of a series of grassy knolls.
The one opposite the Doonbeg resort’s VIP suite, overlooking the 18th green, added greatly to their concerns on Sunday, as it became a gathering point for media and a curious public alike.
[ Golf Shane Lowry distils the mania around him as Donald Trump and Clare Force One hit the course Opens in new window ]
Framed by “Golf Force 1” (the President’s reinforced golf buggy) on one side and a scaffold-tower for snipers on the other, the resort’s side entrance was the subject of intense scrutiny all morning and afternoon.
At the behest of the secret service, gardaí evicted the public from the hill at one point and made a half-hearted attempt to evict reporters too.
In the event, the media held firm and were rewarded when Trump finally emerged to dismiss the buggy and walk past us to and from the first tee, answering questions all the way, and even signing golf hats, to the concern of paranoid minders.
They needn’t have worried. The biggest danger on the course was Lowry, whose putter was so hot it was a fire risk. Leading by four shots overnight and with a course record 62 already on his card this week, he razed the course again with a 63 to beat the previous record-winning margin: Bernhard Langer’s in 1987.
Many of his supporters were wearing Offaly GAA jerseys. But on a weekend when Trump narrowed the gap between the American and Irish brands of republicanism, he could have been forgiven for thinking all the green, white and orange colours were for him.

title: Trump scraps tariffs on Irish whiskey ‘on behalf of the United States of America’
description: US president praises Irish hospitality he experienced during weekend visit
content:
US president Donald Trump made the surprise announcement that he would remove tariffs from Irish whiskey at the end of his two-day visit to Ireland.
It came shortly before he presented golfer Shane Lowry with the winner’s trophy after he triumphed in the Irish Open tournament at Trump’s golf resort in Doonbeg, Co Clare .
Irish whiskey was impacted as part of wide-ranging tariffs the Trump administration imposed on imports from the European Union and elsewhere.
Those on Irish whiskey were as high as 15 per cent last year, but that was subsequently reduced to 10 per cent.
It is understood Taoiseach Micheál Martin raised the issue with Trump during their meeting at Farmleigh on Saturday.
As he wrapped up his address to the crowd at the Irish Open, Trump said: “I want to mention one thing [the] Taoiseach and I talked about it, and Shane [Lowry] talked about it.
“Everybody’s been bugging me. They’re saying, ‘Will you do me a favour, it’s so unfair what’s going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey?’
“And I said, on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off.”
The Irish Whiskey Association (IWA) quickly welcomed the announcement. Director Eoin Ó Catháin said: “Nothing exemplifies the US-Ireland trade relationship better than Irish whiskey.”
Exports to the US were worth €450 million in 2025, he said, while Irish distillers purchased €80 million worth of US whiskey casks.
“This relationship represents thousands of jobs and millions in investment on both sides of the Atlantic, and the return to tariff-free trade for our Irish whiskey distillers will strengthen this success and lead to further growth and investment.”
Tanaiste Simon Harris said the announcement was of economic significance and reflected the importance of the economic relationship between Ireland and the US. Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke said the US was a “vital market for our many quality local distillers across the country”, and the move would protect jobs.
At the post-tournament press conference, Lowry was asked about Trump’s remarks that the golfer had been among those with whom he had discussed whiskey tariffs. Lowry joked: “Irish distillers better be sending me a cheque soon. That must be worth a few quid to them.”
Meanwhile, the Taoiseach defended the manner in which he raised the issue of Gaza with Trump, including how he had not referred to what had happened in the Palestinian enclave as genocide.
People Before Profit TD Paul Murphy accused the Taoiseach of an “abject failure to challenge Trump” on the issue. Sinn Féin MEP Kathleen Funchion – who joined protesters near Trump’s golf resort in Doonbeg on Sunday – argued that the Irish people “would have liked for Micheál Martin to be a lot stronger” on Gaza and the “upholding of international law and accountability for Israel”.
Martin said his main focus was “accelerating getting more aid to Gaza” and that this was the “key issue now for the Palestinians”. He said he had received a thank you message “immediately afterwards” from the Palestinian ambassador.
Martin also mentioned Ireland’s intervention in the International Court of Justice (ICJ) case taken by South Africa alleging genocide by Israel in Gaza and said: “I took that decision with the Government some time back and we have been very consistent as a country in relation to the Middle East and in relation to the Palestinian question.”
He said the US president “undertook to do everything he possibly could to get aid into Gaza and particularly the Irish contribution in respect of that.”
Asked whether he told Trump that what was happening in Gaza was genocide, Martin said: “No, I didn’t use that term specifically,” while denying he had changed his language on the issue when meeting Trump.
The US president’s whirlwind visit to Ireland ended on Sunday. Trump praised the hospitality of the Irish people he had experienced, while also remarking that some were among the “most vicious bastards” he has done business with during his two-day visit.
He said Irish-based medical companies had “fleeced” the US by not paying taxes there.
Following his arrival in Ireland on Saturday, Trump first visited the Phoenix Park, where he met President Catherine Connolly in Áras an Uachtaráin and then the Taoiseach in Farmleigh House. Afterwards, he spoke at an event in the residence of the US ambassador Edward Walsh at Deerfield, also in the Phoenix Park.
The president then flew on Air Force One to Doonbeg, where he watched the final two days of the Irish Open.

title: ‘It all clicked this week’: Shane Lowry’s Irish Open win a reminder of his golfing genius
description: Offaly man slays sporting demons with emphatic, record-breaking display in Doonbeg
content:
The stars have a habit of aligning for Shane Lowry when it really matters. And if demons have been swirling around in his head for much of the season, he slew them unequivocally – his golf reaching otherworldly heights – to capture the Amgen Irish Open at Trump International in record-breaking fashion and add another famous chapter to a storied career.
This was a true statement of Shane Lowry being Shane Lowry, the best version of himself, in closing with a stunning 63 for a total of 23-under-par 257, which gave him an 11-shot winning margin over runners-up Patrick Reed and Joaquin Niemann.
What did this do for Lowry? It gave him a pay-day for €878,529. It moved him to 40th on the official world rankings, which will earn him another Masters invite come the end of the year. It jumped him to 17th on the Race to Dubai rankings. It moved him to the top of the Ryder Cup rankings for next year’s defence against the USA at Adare Manor.
And yet more valuable that any of those statistics or monetary gain, the win and the manner of it propelled Lowry – who won the Irish Open in 2009 as an amateur, who claimed the Claret Jug in 2019 at Royal Portrush, and who retained the Ryder Cup for Europe in heroic fashion at Bethpage – to a new awareness of what his golfing genius can attain.
There were times this year when Lowry doubted many things about himself. His game. His mental strength. He changed caddies, switching back to his old bagman Dermot Byrne after the US Open in June. He got his team together – coach Neil Manchip, fitness coach Robbie Cannon – for a recalibration week in Florida after missing out on the final stages of the FedEx Cup playoffs and all of that resulted in a re-energised Lowry arriving to Co Clare and putting it all into practice.
“It all clicked this week. I felt mentally I was in an amazing place this week, as well. I felt like I went out and went after it. I felt like I played somewhat carefree-golf, when I wasn’t worried about making mistakes. I wasn’t worried about the outcome of anything,” said Lowry.
And those demons, which had stemmed from losing late leads in the closing rounds of the Dubai Invitational and the Cognizant, and also of not contending in the final round of the Masters, most notably.
“Dubai was difficult. Cognizant was pretty hard. But the Sunday of the Masters was especially difficult for me this year, and I feel like after that, a lot of wind went out of my sails. I feel like I was playing great golf, and even after that I felt like I was playing decent and finishing 25th, 30th, 40th, just doing nothing every week and it was very, very tough,” he said.
“And in that stretch, I played like 11 out of 13 weeks or something. So it was quite hard. And then the more you kind of keep trying to play through it, the harder it can get sometimes. So, to take a few weeks off and kind of reset, was nice.
“What do you do? First of all, I went and looked at my stats. They were pretty good. Not bad. Not amazing but not horrendous. So that kind of gives you a glimmer of hope. So, right, I need to keep trying to put myself in position, and that’s probably the only way I’m going to get through it. Put yourself in tough positions and try and fight through it. Believe in what you’re doing with your team. Believe in what you’re doing with the people around you. I feel like I’ve done that.
“And today was a big day for me. If I didn’t win today, I don’t even want to think what I would have been like for the next while. It would have been hard.”
In an Irish Open unlike any other, where ultimately golf was the winner, Lowry was the poster boy.
And while Lowry was the star of the show in Doonbeg, Leona Maguire also had much to celebrate as part of the Europe team which defeated the United States in the Solheim Cup by 15-13 in the match at Bernardus in the Netherlands.
[ Leona Maguire loses singles match but Europe win back Solheim Cup Opens in new window ]
Playing in her fourth Solheim Cup appearance, Maguire – who lost her singles to Lauren Coughlin by 2&1 on Sunday – emerged with two points from her four matches and again played an important role.
“My main goal this week was if everyone can leave Sunday knowing that we’ve all done our best, but you’re going to have lifelong friendship and memories from this event, and I think we succeeded. I think we surpassed all of that, so I’m really proud of the girls,” said Europe captain Anna Nordqvist.

title: ‘As obvious as it gets’: Michael Carrick fumes at VAR call on Erling Haaland’s derby winner
description: United manager adamant Enzo Fernández interfered with play in the build-up to controversial winning goal
content:
An unhappy Michael Carrick expressed concern over Erling Haaland’s winner in Manchester City’s derby victory against Manchester United not being ruled out for Enzo Fernández interfering with play when in an offside position.
Haaland’s 60th-minute strike at Old Trafford on Sunday came after Joško Gvardiol’s cross hit Patrick Dorgu’s boot, passed Fernández and United defender Lisandro Martínez and was finished by the Norwegian striker.
After the goal was ruled out initially for offside, the video assistant referee decided Fernández was not interfering despite Martínez marking the Argentinian midfielder. This left Carrick discontented and confused.
“At the time I hadn’t totally seen it. But the explanation I got was he wasn’t interfering with play, so I just don’t get it,” the United manager said. “I can’t understand how they’re trying to help referees and putting so many layers behind them with so many people, screens, and so many whatever offices they are to try and come up with the right decisions.
“If that’s how the rules are interpreted, that you’re not interfering with play because you’ve thrown yourself at the ball six yards from goal and pretty much nearly touched it, which then Lisandro has to react from – it’s worrying if that’s really how the game’s seen by those who are officiating it.”
Carrick was asked if an apology from the official body, Pro Ref, would be welcome. “Yeah, that’d be great, that. Yeah, I can’t wait for that one,” he said. “I don’t really know how you go and get another explanation on that one. I think we all understand what that rule means [regarding interfering with play], and it’s pretty obvious. It’s as obvious as it gets.”
Enzo Maresca , though, was adamant that Fernández was not interfering. “Yeah – and the fourth official said Erling is onside,” the City manager said.
The 199th Manchester derby’s other controversial decision was Phil Foden’s 22nd-minute red card. The forward kicked Bruno Fernandes in the stomach, but only after United’s captain had kicked him. Maresca backed Michael Oliver’s red card but also suggested the referee should have sent off Fernandes also.
“Phil Foden red card is a red card, but I also think it is red card from Bruno,” City’s manager said. “Reviewing the action, it is a clear red card for Phil because it is a reaction but you can also see Bruno’s [action].”
City now have 12 points, second only to Arsenal on goal difference, while United have only four points and are 13th. “We will get there, I’m convinced of that,” Carrick said.
“We haven’t got as many points as we wanted and we should have. We’ve got to accept that and take that. It doesn’t change us moving forward and our hopes for the season and what we can achieve as a team. We’ve made really good strides over a period of time and we will continue to do that.” – Guardian

title: Mark English runs personal best to finish sixth in 800m final at Ultimate Championship
description: Rhasidat Adeleke misses out on 200m final
content:
It was the race to decide the best 800m runner in the world, and in the end Mark English could have no complaints or regrets about his sixth-place finish. Not when he ran another personal best of 1:42.78, a month on from winning the European title, against suitably revered company.
On the closing night of the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, the eight-man final brought together the best of the best. Despite unleashing another furious finishing kick down the homestretch, English couldn’t quite get himself into contention to claim the $150,000 prize for the new ‘ultimate champion’, the largest first-place prize in the history of the sport.
Instead, it went to Algeria’s Djamel Sedjati, who moved from third to first in the last 50m to take the victory in 1:41.91, blasting past former World champion Marco Arop, while Olympic champion Emmanuel Wanyonyi was third.
Sedjati, the 27-year-old who won silver at the World Championships last year and Olympic bronze in Paris, is a renowned tactician, but English ran a near-perfect race too, ultimately caught only for raw speed.
“I think I probably ran the perfect race for the shape I’m in this year,” said English, who collected $14,000 in finishing sixth. Every athlete to compete in Budapest walked away with some part of the record $10-million purse on offer across the weekend.
“It’s a very high standard. World finals are always quick, so I’m happy. I ran a PB, and you can never not be happy when you run a PB. It was cool to be a part of, to be honest. Sedjati did well to get the win, he runs well in all the championships, so that’s not a surprise. It’s nice we’re all so condensed, it shows the depth in 800m running right now.”
Arop took the race out from the 200m mark, the bell lap passed in a fast 49.68 seconds, with English sitting back in sixth. With no let-up in the pace, the Donegal man found it hard to make up ground, remaining in sixth to the finish. Francesco Pernici held on for fifth, running an Italian national record of 1:42.67, with the top seven finishers all coming in under 1:43.
“My plan was to just run how I feel, and make sure I could run an even-paced race as much as I could,” English added, Budapest representing his 16th 800m race this season. “It’s been a really good season, and to be doing this at 33 years of age, I don’t take it for granted. To be running those times and finishing in those places is a real privilege. But as years go, this has been my best year.”
Earlier, Rhasidat Adeleke was run out of a place in the 200m final, visibly disappointed after finishing a tired-looking fifth in her semi-final.
Adeleke had Olympic champion Gabby Thomas and World champion Melissa Jefferson-Wooden for company, but a surprisingly slow start left the Dubliner chasing them from the gun. Adeleke’s time of 22.81 seconds was short of her 22.28 national record which she set when winning silver at the European Championships last month.
Adeleke finished strongly to blast past Jamaica’s Lavanya Williams, but couldn’t scrape her way into a top-four finish needed to make the evening’s final. Switzerland’s Fabienne Hoenke took the last qualifying spot of the first semi-final in 22.72.
Adeleke was ranked 10th of the 15 finishers with the second semi-final run, earning her $8,000. Shaunae Miller-Uibo from the Bahamas was disqualified for a lane infringement having qualified for the final, bumping Adeleke up a place.
Jefferson-Wooden won the final in 21.48 seconds, the third fastest time in history, to complete a sprint double for $300,000. Her fellow American Kenny Bednarek also completed the sprint double, winning the 200m in a lifetime best of 19.52.
Adeleke is set to race the 200m once more this season, taking to the track in London next Friday for the all-women Athlos meet, where the winners will bank $60,000.
After scored a stunning 5,000m win on Friday night, Jakob Ingebrigtsen was a non-starter in Sunday’s 1,500m final, clearing the way for Josh Kerr. The Briton produced a devastating kick over the last 200m to win in 3:29.35, holding off the challenge from Australia’s Cameron Myers, who finished second in 3:29.68.
The Ultimate Championship, set to take place biennially, certainly lived up to its billing of being the ultimate season finale.

title: The Irish Times view on the Trump visit: diplomacy takes second place
description: The US president’s comments on a united Ireland grabbed attention
content:
In a couple of hours in the Phoenix Park on Saturday morning US president Donald Trump opined, with varying degrees of coherence, on a dizzying range of topics.
The Government will be content that the visit passed without any major rows and with Trump expressing his confidence about the future of the relationship between Ireland and the US.
His support for a united Ireland – which he said he would “love” to see – did spark headlines and ruffled some feathers in London and among the unionist community in Northern Ireland. Were a statement such as this made by a previous US president, it might have been seen as a significant indication of US policy.
From Trump, prone to giving freewheeling opinions on anything and everything, it was still notable, even if his motivation was unclear and Taoiseach Micheál Martin said he had expressed similar views in the past.
It hardly signifies any real change in policy in Washington – US involvement in Northern Ireland is much less significant now than under some previous administrations and there has long been bipartisan support for the Belfast Agreement. And in a later comment Trump did make the point that “no matter what you say or how you say it, there is no good answer”.
Trump is, of course, in electioneering mode and may have had an Irish-American audience in mind. Certainly, the main focus of many of his remarks, delivered in a long and rambling address at the US ambassador’s residence, related to domestic politics ahead of November’s midterm elections. It was not the kind of speech a US president would traditionally make on an overseas visit. But Trump is no respecter of tradition.
The two key meetings, with President Catherine Connolly and the Taoiseach, appeared to pass off smoothly. Trump seemed in no mood to pick a fight. President Connolly said in a statement that she had conveyed the view of the Irish people that “the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted”. Thousands marched in Dublin in opposition to the visit and there were also protests in Doonbeg and Shannon.
Trump chose not to react in public to Connolly’s statement and to swat away questions about protests. The main reason for the trip, after all, was to visit his property in Doonbeg to watch the Irish Open golf tournament and promote one of his investments. Diplomacy took second place.
The Government will be broadly satisfied by the visit. The promise to remove US tariffs on Irish whiskey was welcome. And Trump has clearly taken on board one of Dublin’s talking points – the extent of investment by Irish companies in the US. But no one should mistake the weekend’s events for anything resembling real politics. Expect tensions over foreign policy, trade and regulation of the technology sector to resume.

title: The Irish Times view on the West Bank: Israel’s increasing isolation
description: The move is a qualitative stepping up of attempts to rule out a two-state solution
content:
Israel has bridled at British foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s accusation of “ethnic cleansing” against Palestinians in the “illegally occupied” West Bank. But ethnic cleansing is what it is.
Last month Israel announced contracts for tenders for the building of 1,200 Jewish housing units in the West Bank’s E1 area. Meanwhile, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that so far this year Israeli troops (IDF) and illegal settlers had demolished 1,078 Palestinian homes and displaced over 4,000 people across the West Bank. There have been over 1,400 settler attacks against Palestinians this year.
The E1 settlement project would forcibly displace over 18 more Bedouin communities in the area and in effect divide the West Bank in two. It would thus make the establishment of an independent contiguous Palestinian state impossible.
This is not just another of the 104 new settlements approved by the country’s government since taking office, but a qualitative stepping up of attempts to rule out a two-state solution and to advance a creeping annexation of the West Bank.
Miliband’s welcome announcement last week of a UK ban on trade in goods from the occupied territories and sanctions against those abetting settlement expansions echoes previous moves by Ireland and Spain, and was joined by a total of 12 states, including France and Canada. The EU as a whole should follow suit, as Kaja Kallas, its foreign policy chief, said in an interview with The Irish Times.
Milliband rightly described settler violence, often encouraged by ministers, passively overseen by the IDF, and assisted with government cash, as terrorist in nature. He also committed to recognition of a 2024 opinion of the International Court of Justice deeming the Israeli occupation illegal.
The willingness of more countries to break with the US over Israel is an important moment that will further isolate the government of prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu internationally, ahead of vital elections next month.

title: Trump departs Ireland following two-day visit
description: On day two of his visit, Trump said he is going to ‘take the tariffs off’ Irish whiskey
author_name: Sarah Burns, Karl McDonald, Ronan McGreevy
content:
The Government will reflect on two days that went as well as expected if not better.
Trump was on good form throughout and showed considerable stamina for a man of 80.
President Catherine Connolly was able to get her point across to him without causing an international incident.
Trump’s support for a united Ireland has caused consternation among many British politicians and especially unionists in the North.
Balanced against that, Trump has a long history of saying the first thing that comes into his head about geopolitical issues like wanting to make Canada the 51st State or annexing Greenland.
He may well be winding up the British government which he has accused of being less than helpful about the Iran conflict.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin said there had been an “overreaction” to Trump’s comments and that they should not come as a surprise given that he said something similar during the St Patrick’s Day events in Washington this year.
Trump claimed that he planned to go back to the United States this morning, but decided to stay to present the trophy to the eventual winner Shane Lowry.
His announcement that he was lifting tariffs on Irish whiskey raised a big cheer from the crowd at Doonbeg after Lowry’s victory.
Trump had been lobbied by the Taoiseach and by Shane Lowry who quipped that the whiskey industry should be sending him a cheque for his intervention.
Trump now heads back to the United States with a net approval rating of minus 26 and a battle to hold on to the House of Representatives and Senate in the mid-term elections.
Thank you for tuning into our coverage today.
Air Force One has just departed Shannon Airport at 8.10pm flying west to Washington D.C.
The airplane flew into a beautiful orange sunset on its way back to the United States.
The Government will be pleased that the two day visit went without a hitch.
Trump’s comments about a united Ireland will be the most memorable thing about the visit, but it is hard to see it having long-term consequences.
Trump’s announcement at the end that he is lifting tariffs on Irish whiskey will endear him to that sector at least.
Trump is now posing for photographs on the runway with his Eric and family. He’s also saying goodbye to the US ambassador to Ireland Ed Walsh and to the Irish ambassador to the US Geraldine Byrne Nason. He’s finally got on the plane and Air Force One is about to take off.
🚨 President Trump signals he will NOT be attempt to intervene in the Lindsay Clancy case, despite her attorney's pleas for him to do so "There is NO WINNER there. There's no win no matter what you do. 3 children are DEAD." "That's something THEY have to work out." pic.twitter.com/ibzyaKkQi5
Trump is saying that he intends to give US voters $5,000 each if Republicans win the mid-terms.
Trump is extemporising at length on the tarmac at Shannon Airport.
“Would anybody like to be press secretary,” he asks the assembled press corps in reference to Karoline Leavitt who recently resigned from the position.
Trump has been asked about the proposals by the UK government to impose sanctions on Israeli settlers in the West Bank.
His response appears to suggest that he hasn’t given it much thought yet.
He is due to have a call with the UK prime minister Andy Burnham on Monday or Tuesday.
He’s also being asked about various mid-term elections and also the prospects of JD Vance being the 2028 Republican presidential nominee.
President Donald Trump has just got out of Marine One and is approaching Air Force One.
His son Eric, Eric’s wife Lara and their two children are on the tarmac to greet him and to form a guard of honour before he embarks on the Aircraft.
He appears to be saying a few final words to the press, but we’re not sure what he has said yet as the RTÉ feed isn’t audible.
The impromptu press conference appears to be going on longer than many had expected.
Marine One is just taxiing to its stand beside Air Force One at Shannon Airport.
Air Force One is on the tarmac waiting to fly the president back to the United States.
Conservative foreign affairs spokesman Tom Tugendhat has become the latest British politician to express his displeasure at Donald Trump’s comments about a united Ireland.
“I knew Trump was a Republican, but I didn’t know he was that kind of a republican,” Tugendhat told Sky News.
“That’s not how we expect allies to behave. We all agree that the people of Northern Ireland have the right to choose their own future.
“That’s the agreement we came to through the Good Friday Agreement and the Americans were the brokers of it.
Donald Trump has said that he will take tariffs off Irish whiskey.
As he wrapped up his address to the crowd Trump said: “On behalf of my son Eric and the whole Trump family this is an honour. We’re so proud.
“We own Doonbeg and frankly Ireland itself has been so incredible, so inviting, and we’re very honoured by presenting you with a great course. It’s been great.”
Then he added: “I want to mention one thing the Taoiseach and I talked about it and Shane [Lowry] talked about it and everybody’s been bugging me. They’re saying: ‘Will you do me a favour, it’s so unfair what’s going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish Whiskey?’”
“And I said on on behalf of the United States of America I am going to take the tariffs off.”
Donald Trump has just presented the American Crystal trophy for the Amgen Irish Open to Shane Lowry.
A raucous home crowd has been singing football chants and cheering as Lowry lifted the trophy into the air.
“Golf has been quite difficult this year. I just kept fighting through it. Little did I know I would do something like this,” he said.
“I’m happy that I put on a show for everybody.”
He was about to sign off on his post-win interview, but he jumped in to thank Trump who was standing beside him.
“Thank you Mr President for coming to this amazing golf tournament and thank you for this amazing golf course,” he told him.
Lowry’s father Brendan didn’t see the final round. He went home to watch Clara being beaten in the Offaly senior football championship.
Today is Grandparents Day in the United States and the White House is making sure the rest of the world knows about it.
The White House has posted a picture of President Donald Trump speaking to one of his grandchildren.
“To the world, he’s the President. But to some, he’s still just Grandpa. ❤️Happy Grandparents Day!” the White House official X account posted.
Luke Trump is one of the US president’s 11 grandchildren. Luke is the son of Eric and Lara Trump.
Lara posted on X: “No better way to celebrate being 9 than in Ireland with Grandpa! 🇮🇪🎂🤗 HAPPY BIRTHDAY, LUKE! 💛”
Shane Lowry just holed the last with a huge putt and he’s won it by 11 shots.
President Donald Trump watching from the balcony is unlikely to see a display of golf quite like it. Lowry just carded a 63 today to win the Amgen Irish Open for the first time in 17 years.
Lowry is quite emotional about it and dedicated to his wife and daughters who are living back in Florida.
“My daughter keeps asking me when I’m going to bring a trophy home, now I’m bringing it home,” he said.
“This year has been quite difficult for me. I had a few chances to win. I have had very tough times.
“I don’t do things by half-measures. A lot of things went right to me.”
The crowd are now singing The Fields of Athenry and, of course “óle, óle, óle”.
CNBC has live footage of the presidential cavalcade on its way to Doonbeg to pick up Trump.
The US president will present the trophy to home favourite Shane Lowry and then depart immediately for Marine One to be taken to Shannon Airport where he will fly back to the United States tonight.
The crowds are now approaching the 18th green to see the very popular Lowry win the Irish Open for the first time in 17 years.
Trump is on the balcony looking down at a masterful display by Lowry and the crowd are starting to chant the Irish sporting anthem “ole,óle,óle”.
President Donald Trump’s endorsement of a united Ireland could hardly be more timely and inconvenient for the British government.
It has now emerged that Trump’s comments weren’t off the cuff or off the top of his head. They were calculated to inflict maximum damage on a British government whom he accuses of doing nothing to help him in the Iran war.
Coincidentally, the leaders of the three devolved Celtic “nations”, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are meeting on Monday to sign a memorandum of understanding pushing for referendums in their respective countries.
The trio will meet in their capacity as party leaders, rather than as officials in their respective governments.
Michelle O’Neill cannot sign the memorandum of understanding as first minister as she does not have the permission of the deputy first minister Emma Little-Pengelly to do so.
Nevertheless, the three leaders SNP leader John Swinney, Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth and O’Neill will see the MOU as the starting gun in a likely protracted campaign to get independent referend a on the table.
Shane Lowry’s on fire. He’s just holed a 60 footer from the edge of the 15th green to go ten ahead. This is exhibition stuff. He almost scored another birdie on the par three 16th hitting the flag with an attempted chip in. The pressure’s off. He’s romping home.
Shane Lowry just scored his sixth birdie of his final round of the Amgen Irish Open.
Lowry birdied the 14th and is nine shots ahead of the field.
He is cruising to victory and a rendezvous with President Donald Trump who will present the trophy to the winner in about a half an hour’s time.
Lowry won the Irish Open as an amateur in 2009. He last won a tournament in 2022. What a return from the proud man from Clara, Co Offaly.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin has spoken to the media about his lunch with US President Donald Trump and outlined how the US President asked about the economic issues and Northern Ireland as well as discussing golf courses. It comes as Trump separately on Sunday stood over controversial comments he made about Irish unity.
Martin said it has been a “fantastic Irish Open” and “we’re all hoping that Shane Lowry can pull it off which I think would be fantastic icing on the cake of what has been a fantastic four days of golf.”
He said the tournament has put Doonbeg and west Clare “on the map” adding: “The Trump family made a huge investment here over many, many years. #
“I met with Eric Trump [Donald Trump’s son] earlier today and he was taking me through his own experiences of Ireland and how familiar he is with Ireland and their deep commitment and affection for this course.”
Martin also spoke of his lunch with the US president.
“I had lunch with President Trump, Mary and I, and our respective ambassadors”. He set out how there was conversation about golf and that Trump was “was curious about many issues in terms of Ireland both economically and also in terms of the North.
“He was asking me lots of questions about the North-South and relationships and so on like that.”
Trump was doorstepped on the golf course as he went out to watch the final rounds.
He reiterated what he had said many time previously that the UK needed to start drilling in the North Sea again.
“If the UK is going to open up the North Sea, the UK is going to be rich. If it doesn’t open up the North Sea, the UK is going to be bankrupt,” he told reporters.
Aberdeen, he said, would be the “unbelievable capital” of the oil industry in the UK again.
Earlier this year the UK government banned new oil and gas exploration licences in the North Sea though existing licences will continue to operate.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin has been in attendance at the Irish Open at Doonbeg for much of the day, Cormac McQuinn reports.
It is understood that Martin and his wife Mary had lunch with US president Donald Trump.
Topics of discussion included the Doonbeg resort, the Irish Open and the performance of golfer Shane Lowry.
Not getting into the details on Irish unity, it seems.
Donald Trump continues to address wider issues on his trip to Doonbeg, though the focus here has been largely on his thoughts on domestic matters – and the golf.
In those Doonbeg remarks to reporters he also addressed:
“We should be paying the ⁠lowest interest rate ⁠in ​the world, regardless of their formulas,” he said ahead of the US federal reserve’s policy meeting.
Rate rises have returned to the agenda across the world recently, with the European Central Bank raising rates already and the UK, Japan and the US all considering next moves.
The situation in the energy market amid the conflict in the Gulf has contributed to higher-than-target inflation. But Trump has consistently opposed rate rises, central bankers’ main tool for tackling inflation, for any reason.
Trump said the United States had “the best credit in the world. We make other ‌countries rich. We ⁠can turn that off in two minutes.”
Asked whether he had spoken to Volodymyr Zelenskiy, Ukraine’s president, after a recent conversation with Vladimir Putin, he said: “Mr Zelenskiy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia.
“Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel fuel.”
He said “very ‌negative forces” are bringing things up about AI that won’t happen and said that he wanted to make ​sure that the United States remains the industry leader.
“We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins ​AI wins,” he told reporters when asked if the AI industry ⁠should slow down or be more regulated.
“We could put guardrails. We can ‌do ‌this ​and that. But I think you have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be ⁠bringing it up and ​they’re bringing up things that won’t happen.”
Further thoughts from Donald Trump on the question of unification, per the White House pool:
“I’ve always loved the people of Ireland and it just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland and it would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is put them together... many people agree.”
“I made what I considered to be a fairly routine comment, I have had so much support on that.”
Trump said he would “say nothing” about Scottish independence, stating he will “save that for another day”.
Two Co Galway women have appeared in court over alleged public-order offences on the seventh green at Trump’s Doonbeg golf course as the US president’s Marine One helicopter was in the air preparing to land on Saturday afternoon.
At a special sitting of Ennis District Court on Saturday night, two pro-Palestinian activists, Emma O’Grady (41) of Inis Oírr, Co na Gaillimhe, and Áine Ní Thréinir (35) of Cúirt na Trá, Salthill, Co Galway, appeared in connection with the alleged offences at the golf course during the Amgen Irish Open.
US president Donald Trump has stood over his controversial comments on Irish unity as he attended the Irish Open golf tournament in Doonbeg on Sunday.
Asked by reporters if he had a timeline for Irish unity, he said: “I think it should happen.”
It came after he said on Saturday that Irish unity would be a “great thing” in comments made alongside Taoiseach Micheál Martin at Farmleigh in Dublin.
The remarks caused eyebrows to be raised north and south of the Border and in London, but they were subsequently downplayed by a spokesman for the Taoiseach who made it clear that Ireland’s policy on the North had not and would not be changing.
A spokesman for British prime minister Andy Burnham said there was no majority support for a referendum and that one will not be held until that changes.
At Doonbeg Trump was asked about the reaction from Downing Street and he initially responded saying: “I don’t know what he [Burnham] said.”
When it was put to him that Downing Street said there would be no referendum until the majority of people in Northern Ireland supported it, Trump replied: “Everybody says that and then the things happen.
“By the way, I’ve spoken to him [Burnham]. I think he’s a very nice guy. He tends to be on the liberal side unfortunately. the one thing he is going to be doing I think he’s going to be stopping the stupid windmills and he’s going to be drilling in the North Sea.”
Earlier, while he was walking from the hotel down to the golf course Trump was asked if he realised the backlash his comments on Irish unity caused, he said: “I love my comments.”
Meanwhile, Trump was asked by one of the Irish media, a Press Association reporter, if he had seen any footage of the protests in Dublin and what he made of that opposition.
Trump did not address the question but said: “You know you remind me of somebody. An Irish singer who passed away recently. Do you know who that is?
“Sinéad. You look like Sinéad O’Connor. That’s a compliment. She sang beautifully.”
For those of you looking for live updates on the actual golf, you can find them here .
US president Donald Trump has been asked if he realised the backlash of his Irish unity comments, to which he responded: “I love my comments.”
Asked if he had a timeline for Irish unity, he said: “I think it should happen.”
During his visit to Dublin on Saturday morning, Trump said Irish unity would be a “great thing” in response to a reporter’s question.
The comments, made alongside Taoiseach Micheál Martin at Farmleigh, caused eyebrows to be raised north and south of the Border and in London, but they were subsequently downplayed by a spokesman for the Taoiseach who made it clear that Ireland’s policy on the North had not and would not be changing.
A spokesman for British prime minister Andy Burnham said there was no majority support for a referendum and that one will not be held until that changes.
US president Donald Trump has emerged from his hotel and headed out to the golf course at Doonbeg followed by a large entourage.
US President Donald Trump has emerged from his hotel and headed out to the golf course at Doonbeg followed by a large entourage and his ‘Golf Force One’ armoured buggy pic.twitter.com/8El4UQCqi9
US president Donald Trump’s remarks in support of Irish unity reflect the “broad north American sentiment”, former Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams has said.
Adams has welcomed Trump’s comments but said that Taoiseach Micheál Martin had “put himself outside this positive attitude” towards holding a Border poll.
On Saturday, during a meeting with Martin and in response to a question from a reporter, Trump claimed Irish reunification was inevitable, adding it “may as well happen now”.
He said: “I think it would be a fantastic thing.
“Now the UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”
During a subsequent engagement at the US ambassador’s residence in Ireland, Trump did not back away from his earlier answer, stating Irish unification would be “a very cool thing”.
Adams, who was the Sinn Féin leader when the Good Friday Agreement was signed in 1998, delivered a speech in Dublin on Sunday reflecting on the peace deal.
Adams said Sinn Féin had disagreed with US administrations since 1998 on a number of issues “particularly the Middle East and other conflicts”.
He added: “Yesterday’s remarks by president Trump on the issue of Irish Unity are welcome, even though we profoundly differ with him on many other matters, as we did with his predecessors.
“They reflect the broad north American sentiment towards Irish unity and particularly the Irish diaspora towards Irish reunification.
“And this is increasingly reflected in mainstream dialogue.
“Micheál Martin has put himself outside this positive attitude to Irish unity in Ireland and the diaspora. He needs to correct this and play a leading part in this process.”
Adams said no Irish government has ever “produced a strategy” to give effect to Irish unity.
“The absence of Irish government planning, almost 30 years after the Agreement, is indefensible and incredibly short-sighted,” he said.
“There is no excuse for this. What is needed is the full implementation of the Good Friday Agreement, including setting a date and planning for the referendum on the future.
“This requires inclusive discussions about the future to ensure that not only do citizens take informed decisions but that the new Ireland which emerges when the union ends is one in which everyone is valued and social and economic rights are upheld.
“The Irish government should establish a Citizens’ Assembly or series of such assemblies to discuss the process of constitutional change and the measures needed to build an all-Ireland economy, a truly national health service and education system and much more.”
Gardaí policing the visit of US president Donald Trump to Ireland have made just three arrests, all at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg, Co Clare.
Two of those arrested are known anti-war activist, who staged their protest on the course as Trump was arriving there on Saturday, Crime and Security Editor Conor Lally reports.
The Irish Times understands the two women arrested on the course on Saturday, while play was unfolding, are known to gardaí for their links to protesting against the presence of US war planes and troops at Shannon Airport.
Both of the women - in their 30s and 40s - appeared to emerge from the crowd at the seventh green on the course at the same time the Marine One helicopter carrying Trump was landing at the Doonbeg golf resort.
The women were wearing clothing with anti-Trump slogans and when they made their protest as the US president was landing they were arrested.
They were detained on suspicion of committing a public order offence, it appears because they had made an incursion into an area on the course where they were not permitted.
On Friday evening, another woman, in her 20s, was arrested at the golf course on suspicion of trespass. After the course had been closed and was being checked by Garda members and US security personnel the woman was discovered.
It is understood she refused to leave, though the course was not open to the public at the time, and she was detained.
Garda Headquarters has confirmed the arrests, adding the three women appeared before a special sitting of Ennis District Court on Saturday evening.
While here have also been protests at Shannon Airport, and a large event in Dublin city centre, with several thousand people, on Saturday, no arrests took place.
The White House Press Pool news feed reports that US president Donald Trump spent Saturday evening at his hotel where he was photographed celebrating his grandson’s birthday and was greeted with cheers when he appeared at Doonbeg’s hotel bar.
It also reported that a White House official confirmed that Trump had dinner on Saturday night with some of the players at the hotel. No update as yet on when Trump will be seen at the Irish Open tournament on Sunday.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin has arrived at Doonbeg golf resort in Co Clare where he has entered one of the Irish Open viewing pavillions.
Britain’s shadow foreign secretary has said Donald Trump’s expression of support for a united Ireland is “unhelpful”.
Tom Tugendhat told Sky News that it was “a shame that he’s playing games”.
The Conservative MP for Tonbridge said: “It is unhelpful because US presidents have traditionally supported the right of the people of Northern Ireland to determine their own future. That’s how we got to the Good Friday Agreement.
“I suppose I knew he was a Republican, I didn’t know he was that kind of a Republican.”
US president Donald Trump started Sunday at his golf resort in the south-west of the country as it hosts players including Rory McIlroy and Shane Lowry for the Amgen Irish Open.
It is anticipated Trump will hand over the winner’s trophy at the Trump International golf resort in Doonbeg, Co Clare, before flying back to the US at the end of a two-day itinerary.
While the president restricted himself to watching the golf from a balcony over the 18th green on Saturday evening, it is anticipated he could traverse the course on Sunday.
A major security operation is continuing for the visit, with An Garda Síochána liaising with the Defence Forces and US Secret Service in the area around the resort.
Trump’s presence sparked protests in Dublin and Clare – but Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said there would be “no tolerance” for public disorder or attempts to impact “critical movements” of the US president.
US president Donald Trump and Taoiseach Micheál Martin are due to be reunited later on Sunday at the Irish Open in Co Clare.
Martin is to attend the final day of play at Trump’s golf resort in Doonbeg alongside the Minister for Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media Patrick O’Donovan and the Minister of State for Sport Charlie McConalogue.
It is understood they will feature when Trump awards the Irish Open trophy to the victorious golfer.
No formal meeting is scheduled between Martin and Trump.
Britain’s housing secretary has brushed off Donald Trump’s backing for a united Ireland, saying the UK remained committed to the Good Friday Agreement.
Angela Rayner told Sky News’s Sunday Morning programme: “Donald Trump is Donald Trump, and the president will say what and speak his mind as he sees it.
“But look, we’re really serious about the Good Friday Agreement.
“We’re very proud of our history there and working with Ireland to make sure that we implement the Good Friday Agreement and we continue on that path.”
Video has also emerged of US president Donald Trump walking through a bar in his hotel in Doonbeg to chants of “USA, USA” and “four more years” from the crowd who also sang The Fields of Athenry.
Irish golfer Rory McIlroy has said the sight of Air Force One flying-by the Irish Open tournament is “not the experience we’re used to”.
He added: “That was pretty cool to sort of see all that going on. I was trying to avoid making doubles at that point so I was trying to concentrate on my own stuff as well.”
McIlroy made the remarks in an interview with sports reporters on Saturday evening after US president Donald Trump arrived at his golf resort in Doonbeg, Co Clare where the tournament is being held and play will resume this morning.
He dismissed a suggestion that the aircraft was a distraction as he searched for a ball saying: “I don’t see what a plane at 10,000ft got to do with looking at a ball on the ground.”
While McIlroy has had a disappointing tournament, fellow Irish golfer Shane Lowry is leading going into the final day.
He said: “There’s a great buzz around the tournament because Shane’s up there and leading.”
McIlroy also confirmed he would attend the dinner for Trump at Doonbeg on Saturday night.
Trump also batted away any suggestion that planned protests indicated the desire of many Irish people that he stay away and he said that he was unaware there were protests happening.
“It can’t be a very big one because we’ve been all over Ireland today already but I haven’t seen any protest.”
Thousands gathered in Dublin city centre and in Co Clare to protest against the US president’s presence.
During his visit to Dublin on Saturday morning, Trump said Irish unity would be a “great thing” in response to a reporter’s question.
The comments, made alongside Taoiseach Micheál Martin at Farmleigh, caused eyebrows to be raised north and south of the Border and in London, but they were subsequently downplayed by a spokesman for the Taoiseach who made it clear that Ireland’s policy on the North had not and would not be changing.
A spokesman for British prime minister Andy Burnham said there was no majority support for a referendum and that one will not be held until that changes.
DUP leader Gavin Robinson said Northern Ireland’s constitutional future “will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington”.
The US president’s flying visit to Dublin passed off without further controversy.
After brief meetings with President Catherine Connolly and the Taoiseach, Trump addressed a crowd including business leaders, politicians and cultural figures at Deerfield, the US ambassador’s residence. All three engagements took place within the Phoenix Park in Dublin.
Good morning. US president Donald Trump continues his visit to Ireland on Sunday.
A significant policing and security operation remains in Co Clare, with Trump staying at his hotel in Doonbeg where the Irish Open is taking place.
He is due to fly out of Shannon Airport on Sunday evening and return to the US.
Follow irishtimes.com for updates throughout the day.

title: Shane Foley’s Champion Stakes ride slammed as ‘brutal riding’ by Donnacha O’Brien
description: O’Brien supplies Billy Loughnane with first winner in Ireland as Comanche Brave lands Flying Five in style
content:
Shane Foley won’t appeal against the 11-day suspension he picked up for careless riding in Saturday’s dramatic 50-1 victory for Hotazhell in Saturday’s Royal Bahrain Irish Champion Stakes , although it appears that he may have ground to make up with some of his rivals.
Donnacha O’Brien labelled Foley’s riding as “brutal” on Sunday following the previous day’s €1.25 million Leopardstown feature where the disgruntled trainer’s A Boy Named Susie, ridden by Oisín Murphy, was one of three horses checked by Hotazhell in the closing stages.
The Leopardstown stewards took a dim view of Foley’s riding and handed him an 11-day ban, taking into consideration that it was his third offence for careless riding in the last six months, as well as the “prolonged and continuous nature of the offence”.
O’Brien, a former champion jockey, who rode alongside Foley for some years, landed Sunday’s Bar One Flying Five in some style with Comanche Brave. But he was still clearly fuming with the jockey widely known as Dusty and how A Boy Named Susie wound up “wiped”.
“I thought it was brutal riding from Dusty, to be honest. If a claimer did that, you’d give them a bollocking. That’s racing and I’m sure he’d know that himself.
“Paddy [Harnett] hit a horse one extra [strike] in Cork the other day and got a similar ban to what Shane got, so it’s frustrating. Oisín thought he was coming to win; he thought he was going better than the winner at the time,” O’Brien said. A Boy Named Susie finished fifth, beaten less than three lengths.
“I think he had the quickest second last to last furlong and then he obviously just got wiped. He’s a good horse and he seems okay afterwards, so it could be worse.
“It’s so hard to get horses that good and to get them right on the day. To get to a race like that with a chance is so hard that it is frustrating,” he added, before confirming A Boy Named Susie to be “A1” afterwards.
Foley’s ride on Hotazhell was also criticised by some prominent pundits, with Ruby Walsh reviewing the race on RTÉ on Sunday and claiming there was “nothing careless about that”. His colleague Fran Berry described it as “almost a win at all costs ride” and suggested he would have swapped victory in such a valuable race for an 11-day ban.
Foley was judged to have ridden improperly at Naas in June and suspended for nine days. However, on appeal the jockey had the penalty reduced to six days as the appeals panel judged he was guilty of the lesser breach of careless riding.
It was a third Group One victory for Hotazhell, who could have a final career start in next month’s Champion Stakes at Ascot. Magical in 2019 pulled off the double. Jessica Harrington’s star is a general 12-1 shot in antepost betting for the Champions Day highlight.
A Boy Named Susie could be campaigned more globally, with the Breeders’ Cup and the Hong Kong carnival in December on his radar.
Comanche Brave will be on his travels too after giving Billy Loughnane his first winner in Ireland.
On course to be crowned champion jockey in Britain this season, it was a typically high-flying feat by the 20-year-old prodigy who established his Group One credentials this season with a Group One hat-trick on the retired Bow Echo and landed the July Cup on Comanche Brave.
O’Brien’s colt made light of dropping in trip for a first try at five furlongs and was much too good. Briefly looking like he might struggle to get a run, the 5-2 favourite ultimately swept through to win by over a length.
“He’s getting better, Billy said five was definitely his trip. I was worried about the ground today, but obviously that wasn’t any problem. He’s just a very, very good, fast horse,” O’Brien said.
“I think there is a chance he might stay in training again next year, which would be great as well. I think he’s a horse that is getting better the whole time. He’d be a really nice one to have. He ran in Abu Dhabi, Hong Kong and Saudi and he still has his passport so I’m sure we’ll travel this winter,” he added.
There was a fourth Britain-based winner of the €5 million weekend when Tom Marquand brought the 7-2 favourite Coul Angel through for a smooth victory in the opening Bold Lad Handicap.

title: Taoiseach downplays ‘overreaction’ to Trump’s call for united Ireland
description: US president raised his support for a united Ireland during private discussions with Catherine Connolly
content:
There has been some “overreaction” to Donald Trump ’s remarks on prospects for a united Ireland, according to Taoiseach Micheál Martin , who said the US president’s view was that he believed unity was “the logical way for the island to be configured”.
Martin made the remarks as he attended the final day of the Irish Open at Trump’s golf resort in Doonbeg, Co Clare .
Also speaking at the tournament, Trump stood over his controversial comments. “I think it should happen,” he said.
Trump had said on Saturday that Irish unity would be a “great thing”, in comments made alongside Martin at Farmleigh in Dublin.
The remarks caused raised eyebrows North and South of the Border , and in London, and a backlash from some quarters.
A spokesman for British prime minister Andy Burnham said there was no majority support for a referendum, and that one will not be held until that situation changed.
That position was put to Trump at Doonbeg, and he responded: “Everybody says that – and then the things happen.
“By the way I’ve spoken to him [Burnham]. I think he’s a very nice guy. He tends to be on the liberal side, unfortunately.”
In a social media post, Trump ally and Reform party leader Nigel Farage wrote: “Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom. The people of Northern Ireland neither want a referendum, nor unification. I disagree with President Trump.”
Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch was also quick to reply, accusing the US president of “shooting from the hip” and describing his remarks as “deeply unhelpful”.
“President Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state,” she posted online. “This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension.
“Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom. At a time when separatists are in power in Scotland, Wales and NI, we need a Government that will defend the union clearly and confidently.”
Later on Sunday, the Taoiseach said he belived it was Trump’s view. ”That’s his take on Northern Ireland , the Republic.”
Asked about the response from some unionists and British politicians, and whether Trump’s remarks were causing difficulty in relations on the island and between Ireland and Britain, Martin said: “I think some of the reaction is an overreaction.”
He said Trump’s position should not be a surprise and that “he takes a different sort of perspective on things”.
From his conversations with Trump at Doonbeg, he noted that the US president was “looking at it from a perspective of looking in on the island of Ireland and logically saying: ‘To me it seems inevitable that it should be unified’.”
Earlier, the Taoiseach was asked whether, on the back of Trump’s comments, he would raise the possibility of a border poll with Burnham. He is to meet the prime minister this week, but said the meeting would be about legacy issues and reform of Northern Ireland’s political institutions.
Martin said Trump’s position was ”not a particular surprise to me”, noting remarks by the president during the most recent St Patrick’s Day festivities in Washington when Trump asked about a “merger” in Ireland.
The Taoiseach said: “In fact President Trump has memories of the violence of that 30 years and the extraordinary murder and mayhem and killings that took place. So I think in that context, that will be an important part of our meeting with prime minister Burnham.”
It emerged on Saturday that Trump had raised his support for a united Ireland as a central theme in private conversations with President Catherine Connolly , as well as with the Taoiseach.
A number of people with knowledge of what was said during those meetings, but who wish to remain anonymous, have confirmed he raised the subject, unprompted, during his meeting with Connolly . He said he was in favour of unification, and also mentioned the border poll.
In her statement, Connolly confirmed that Northern Ireland had been discussed.
Trump’s comments during his Saturday media conference had prompted a swift response in the UK and from unionists in Northern Ireland.
“I know he’s a Republican president, I didn’t realise he was that kind of a republican,” said the Conservative party ’s foreign affairs spokesman, Tom Tugendhat.
Trump, he said, was “completely wrong” in his view. “I would say he was... being incredibly unhelpful to peace in Northern Ireland.”
Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson dismissed the remarks, saying the future of Northern Ireland would not be decided by voices from outside.
Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said: “The onus is on the Taoiseach to begin planning,” she said. “Our national journey is now reunification.”

title: Shane Lowry distils the mania around him as Donald Trump and Clare Force One hit the course
description: Doonbeg was rowdy with giddy adulation as crowds clambered over dunes in pursuit of Offaly man’s every shot
content:
The morning breeze around Doonbeg was gentle but still it carried murmurs about Donald Trump ’s intentions. Some thought he would rise early to see off Rory McIlroy , others swore he’d be out to see Brooks Koepka less than an hour later. Media gathered opposite the hotel door, their backs to the 18th green, waiting for another chance to open a diplomatic tinderbox and hand the president a match.
But Trump didn’t stir until lunchtime, which made him Shane Lowry ’s problem. Eric Trump arrived at the first tee box at 1.47pm, quickly followed by Taoiseach Micheál Martin and his wife, Mary. Eric talked up the golf course during small talk while the White House snappers and TV crews went into position with precise choreography. A sniffer dog bounded along, straining at the end of its leash, briefly starting for a marshal before veering away. “Good job I don’t have the rashers in me pocket,” he said with a laugh. We chose not to ask the man in what scenario he usually carried rashers in his pockets, lest we draw any unwanted attention from the Secret Service agents.
Next we heard a “G’wan Donald” shouted from the grandstand. It emerged with such a guttural roar that we thought Trump had just shouldered a corner-forward out over the endline. The American president had just stepped out of the bulletproof golf buggy that had driven him the 200-odd metres from hotel to tee box. The buggy has been stoking fascination all week, nicknamed Clare Force One.
Trump strolled to that tee box in that usual languid slouch of his, telling us he hoped we had a good day. He was given a cheer by the grandstand and raised his fist in return. His roar, however, was several decibels lower than the crescendo of throaty roars that met Lowry’s appearance. Lowry first had to skirt by Clare Force One, which was plonked in his way, and then walk through a thicket of gardaí, armed agents, marshals, journalists, politicians and Trumps to get to the tee.
Having navigated all of these absurd hurdles, the tournament leader now needed only to get out of his own way.
He fumbled the Dubai Invitational on the final hole at the start of the year and then threw away a three-shot lead on the final three holes of the Cognizant Classic to fall into a slough of form from which he was unable to clamber out. This would be his first solo title in exactly four years, since winning the BMW PGA at Wentworth. That event was shortened to 54 holes. The last time he won a solo, 72-hole title was the 2019 Open in Portrush. On Sunday, just as on that glorious day seven years ago, he held a four-shot lead overnight.
And so Lowry distilled all of the mania around him into one pure hit of adrenaline that sent his tee shot 349 yards down the fairway. He strode off with his caddie and Donald Trump turned around to the media to return to his elephantine diplomacy.
While the president withdrew, Eric Trump followed Lowry down the fairway in the middle of a scuttling ring of secret service agents; his angular figure and long-limbed walk looking like a series of Quentin Blake illustrations coming alive in a flick picture book. “Trump’s son can’t be that old,” gasped one kid in the crowd when his father told him who he was looking at.
[ Shane Lowry laps the field to win a stunning second Irish Open by a record 11 shots Opens in new window ]
If there were any anxieties niggling at Lowry across the morning, he dispelled them all by rolling in a birdie putt from 16 feet on the first hole. It was a calling card. This was not the Shane Lowry that can let tournaments slip through red mist and sweaty palms. No, this was the steely-eyed version of Lowry that absorbs the whirling energy around him and lets it flow without distraction through him; as if it rolls down his loose shoulders and is returned to the crowds through his deft hands.
This was the unflappable Lowry of last year’s Ryder Cup, but where Bethpage convulsed with hostility, Doonbeg was rowdy with giddy adulation. The crowds clambering over dunes in pursuit of his every shot looked like rivers of lava; rope lines were treated as little more than suggestions. Crowds burst from cross walks and rushed up fairways, shuffling a couple of feet from the secret service agents encircling Eric Trump.
One marshal had to reconcile himself to vague threats to keep a group of fans from sprinting around a dune along the fourth fairway, telling them they couldn’t pass that way as it was designated a “country walk.” The biggest security operation in the history of the State, propped up by the phrase “country walk”.
Eric Trump whipped out his phone to record the crowning moment. The stage was the fifth green, with thousands of fans lassoed around vast, towering dunes as the Atlantic waves gurgled and crashed in the background. Lowry drained a birdie putt to go seven shots clear.
Trump the Younger left the action on the sixth tee, clearing space for Lowry’s procession. When he sank a putt for yet another birdie on the seventh green, Lowry raised his right arm and pointed to the sky, pumping his fist in what marked a brief parole from his locked-in focus. The next jailbreak came on the 15th, when he poured in a birdie from 45 feet. He threw his arms in the air and surrendered to the grin that broke across his face. The 18th fairway burst at the seams, a stampede of people charging after their imminent champion.
Lowry rolled in a final birdie putt to secure the record winning margin while he was at it. He beat his chest and roared a cathartic roar into the teatime sky. Amid the mass of humanity ringing the final green, it was possible for just a moment to forget that the American president was one among them. Such is sport’s confounding, restorative power. The copyright of this tournament was taken by the Trump Organisation, but its legacy belongs to Shane Lowry.

title: Irish Open: Shane Lowry claims title with emphatic final round in Doonbeg – as it happened
description: Offalyman finishes 11 shots clear with final round of 63
content:
That’s all from me, thanks for following along.
Keep an eye on The Irish Times website for more from Doonbeg, but I’ll leave you with the happy sight of two Irish champions − Irish Open winner Shane Lowry, and Solheim Cup winner Leona Maguire.
“In sport, those with the killer instinct don’t hold back or wait for any favours,” Philip Reid writes from Doonbeg. “Such was the mindset Shane Lowry brought into the final round of the Amgen Irish Open, where the 39-year-old Offaly man started with a four-stroke lead and mercilessly stretched his advantage stroke by stroke, hole by hole so that his second win in a tournament so close to his heart came as a ceremonial procession.
“This was Lowry at his imperious best, transforming a season of ifs, buts and maybes with a display of controlled shot-making and utter calm as he fired a closing 63 for a total of 23-under-par 257 to seal the deal.
“Lowry’s 11-stroke winning margin over Patrick Reed, the number one on the Race to Dubai order of merit, and Joaquin Niemann constituted a new Irish Open record, eclipsing that of Bernard Langer, who won by 10 at Portmarnock in 1987.”
[ Shane Lowry laps the field to win a stunning second Irish Open by a record 11 shots Opens in new window ]
“Leona Maguire surprisingly lost 2&1 to Lauren Coughlin,” Ewan Murray writes from Bernardus Golf in the Netherlands. But it matter little in the long run as Europe dominate the final day of the Solheim Cup to beat USA 15-13.
[ Leona Maguire loses singles match but Europe win back Solheim Cup Opens in new window ]
Philip Reid’s report from Doonbeg will be with us shortly.
Shane Lowry is introduced as the 2026 Irish Open champion.
Trump hands over the trophy, making the most of the not-so-quick photo op.
After a few handshakes with the Irish politicians standing by, Lowry FINALLY gets to hold the Waterford Crystal trophy aloft.
Seems we may have spoke too soon. They’re doing a second trophy presentation.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin says a few words first and then hands over to the weekend’s host, US president Donald Trump.
Trump says he was supposed to leave Ireland this morning, “but I said I’m going to stay and watch Shane win”.
He adds, after a chat with Lowry, he’s promised to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey.
Here’s Lowry’s reaction on the 18th immediately after his win:
An emotional Shane Lowry talks his Katie Taylor moment, breaking records, fighting demons and winning in front of his mother at the Irish Open. "My daughter is always asking when are you bringing a trophy home. I'm bringing one home." pic.twitter.com/Blk02mYoH9
We’ll have more reaction from Doonbeg shortly.
Not that Lowry will much care, a win by whatever margin was all that was on his mind, but his 11-shot victory is an Irish Open record.
Bernhard Langer’s 10-shot victory at Portmarnock in 1987 previously held the top spot.
For those who missed it, here’s Lowry’s the final birdie on the 18th:
Shane Lowry finishes it in style, with one last birdie, for a 63 and a second Irish Open title. It's a record victory by 11 shots for Lowry. https://t.co/rNppWIEdQJ pic.twitter.com/6gYDmv9k5S
In the biggest shock of the day, it’s not Donald Trump who hands over the trophy to Lowry. Not sure how Amgen wrangled that one back.
Shane Lowry, the 2026 Amgen Irish Open champion 🏆 #AmgenIrishOpen pic.twitter.com/BYTHN7E0VM
A happy Shane Lowry on the 18th is always a special sight.
Seventeen years after claiming the Irish Open title at County Louth, Shane Lowry has done it again, and what a way to do it.
“I can’t believe I’ve just done that, and that way I done it,” he says on the 18th green.
The crowd in Doonbeg is in full voice for our champion. Even Trump is smiling.
Lowry lines up the birdie but it’s a mammoth task.
Olesen gets the support of the huge crowd around the 18th but can’t manage his first attempt on the green.
He goes again to leave Lowry to finish solo. And he sinks it for a round of 73.
Lowry holds his putter in the air as his shot finds the 18th green. He begins the walk to his birdie putt, soaking it all in.
He has a fair bit to go to the pin, just over 29 feet out, but he doesn’t seem to care now. He’s already smiling from ear to ear.
On the 18th, Olesen has put himself in the bunker. Just about sums up his day.
Lowry is 169 yards to the pin after his tee shot. He finds the green to the delight of the eager crowd swarming after him. The olés have already begun.
Even Lowry’s magic putting can only go so far. His first attempt at the 17th pulls a shade left. He taps in for par.
It’s par also for Olesen, who rather oddly puts the golf ball in his mouth afterwards. Not sure about that one. He’s in tied-fifth, with McKibbin and Gregorio de Leo for company. It’s just not been his day.
That’s Tom McKibbin’s final round all wrapped up. The Northern Irishman signs for a three-under 67 for 10-under after four rounds.
Paul McGinley’s having a natter with Donald Trump overlooking the 18th. It’s certainly looking like the US president is sticking around to hand over the trophy, à la the World Cup.
He pitches down on to the 16th green, reading the slopes perfectly to put it on track for the hole, but the ball curls around the rim.
No matter, par will do at this stage, and he has a laugh at just how magic a birdie it would have been.
He sinks the putt for par. Just two holes to go now.
No doubt as to who this crowd are shouting for:
SHANE LOWRY TAKE A BOW. He makes a 44-foot putt on the 15th to extend his lead yet again. Incredible.
Good man Olesen, he follows it up by making his first birdie of the day. Smiles all round.
The stroll to victory continues as Shane Lowry moves an incredible nine shots clear at the Amgen Irish Open with four holes remaining. 📺 RTÉ2/RTÉ Player 🖥️ https://t.co/rNppWIEdQJ pic.twitter.com/QC6XYdO0vd
Tom McKibbin’s tipping away nicely, back in a share of seventh. He birdied the 15th, his fourth of the day, for an overall 10-under.
Also on 15, Lowry’s first shot went to the rough, but even that played in his favour. He finds the green of the par-four with his second shot.
You’d feel for Olesen. He can’t buy a birdie here, settling once again for par on 14. His day has been made all the more frustrating by the form Lowry’s showing alongside him.
And there’s another birdie for Lowry! He goes to 21-under, five-under for Sunday.
The leader is utterly locked-in coming down the back nine.
Lowry sends a beauty towards the Atlantic from the 14th tee, giving himself another chance of a birdie, but he hardly cracks a smile. This is one lead he doesn’t want to see slip away.
Olesen and Lowry both make par on the 13th. Lowry’s happy with that one, great save after finding the bunker.
Olesen gives the flagstick a rattle with his third shot on 13. He’s looking a frustrated figure.
Lowry is taking all the luck of their pairing. He gets out of the bunker without a bother, leaving himself a handy putt for par.
McKibbin’s putt on 14th goes low of the hole. He stays on eight-under overall in a share of ninth.
Olesen and Lowry are on the 13th fairway. The Dane pulls his pitch well left of the green, and Lowry follows by finding the bunker. It’s a tricky par-four, but they can both still recover.
Tom McKibbin manages a solid drive from the 14th tee to land just over eight feet off the pin.
On the 15th, Patrick Reed’s birdie putt goes inches shy. He’s on six-under for the day, eight shots adrift of Lowry overall.
The birdie putt alludes Lowry again, and he’s looking a bit miffed by it, but he remains eight shots ahead of Patrick Reed in second.
And Olesen continues his birdie-less run. He overshoots the pin and has to settle for par.
Lowry finds himself in the middle of the 12th fairway. No hassle for him to find the green, giving himself another good shot at a birdie.
His playing partner Olesen, now in tied-fourth, also has a chance to pick up a shot which would give him a share of second.
Lowry fails to make the birdie putt on the 11th, tapping in for par. It’s a frustrating, but not fatal, one for the leader.
The last singles match has wrapped up at the Solheim Cup so Europe can now truly get their celebrations started. Rose Zhang took the last point on offer, beating Celine Boutier, but it went Europe’s way overall, 15-13.
My god, Lowry is on fire. From the 11th tee box he puts it right on the green. He’s four feet off the pin on the par-three.
In second, Patrick Reed was unlucky not to make the birdie on the 13th, his putt pulling slightly left to leave him on six-under for Sunday, 12-under overall.
And there’s the birdie, Lowry’s fifth of the day.
He’s back to eight shots clear on 20-under after 64 holes.
The AWS stats put Lowry’s probability of winning at 83.9 per cent.
With that, his eagle putt attempt leaves him three feet off the hole. Another birdie is looking on.
Lowry’s put himself into a nice spot to go for another birdie on the 10th. He managed it yesterday.
His second shot off the fairway lands 11 yards from the pin.
Over in the Netherlands, Leona Maguire took a 2&1 defeat against Lauren Coughlin. Not to matter, Europe had already claimed the Solheim Cup at that stage, and the Cavan woman played her part across the weekend.
Just one match remains in play, USA’s Rose Zhang currently 1UP against Celine Boutier thru 16. It’s 15-12 to Europe.
THE MOMENT TEAM EUROPE RECLAIMED THE SOLHEIM CUP! 🇪🇺🏆 #TeamEurope | #SolheimCup pic.twitter.com/BrytRplVdc
And here’s Lowry’s putt for a birdie on the eighth:
SHANE LOWRY. EIGHT SHOT LEAD 🤯 #AmgenIrishOpen pic.twitter.com/JwTqFReh7C
Lowry drops his first shot of the day, his putt for par just short on the ninth.
Gavin Cooney has an update for us from Doonbeg:
Shane Lowry is dealing with several different pressures today: his own recent struggles to convert from winning positions; the bedlam of the crowds breaking rope lines to follow his every shot, and the absurdity of the Trump factor, with Eric Trump and a group of secret service agents walking the fairways behind him. That he has increased his lead to seven shots across his first nine holes is extraordinary.
Here’s Lowry’s birdie putt on the seventh:
SHANE LOWRY. EIGHT SHOT LEAD 🤯 #AmgenIrishOpen pic.twitter.com/JwTqFReh7C
That’s 20-under for Lowry! He sinks his birdie putt on the eighth to extend his lead.
Patrick Reed is up to a solo second, now on 12-under after three straight birdies from the eighth to 10th.
Liam Nolan has just finished up his final round. The Galwayman signs for a one-under 69 for three-under across the four days.
Huge battle going on behind Lowry. Italy’s Gregorio de Leo is up in a share of fourth now, seven birdies adding him to the mix.
