If we could somehow meld the New Yorker’s attitude to summer with what used to be the Irish version of that inconvenient season then the country would (for my team, anyway) become an infinitely less irritating place to dwell.
Anyway, it will soon be over for another eight months. Or will it? Tell me we’re nearly there.

title: ‘Hey, it’s not that hard to grow your own spuds’: how Portnoo in Donegal spawned a social media star farmer
description: Barrie Quinn of Portnoo Market Garden has 780,000 followers hanging on every update from the chemical-free farm he started on family land
content:
“L ife is good when you grow your own food ” is the philosophy of Donegal man Barrie Quinn, one that has drawn more than 780,000 followers to his Instagram account , where he shares snippets of his life as a regenerative grower. For more than six years, he has told the story of Portnoo Market Garden, a small, chemical-free farm on the west coast of Donegal, as well as sharing candid chats, helpful videos and tell-all food tales. Now, he has put it all down on paper in a part-memoir, part-how-to book called Homegrown.
Over a video call on a late summer afternoon, Quinn offers a look at the spectacular south-facing hillside farm that started it all. He points out the house where his father grew up, where his uncle now lives, and the shed where his grandad worked as a blacksmith. This land has been in the family since the 1800s, when his great-great-grandparents first set up home, but Quinn’s is not a simple farm-being-handed-down story. When he was young, he had no real interest in growing and was working as a plasterer when, in 2009, he headed to Australia. While there, he ended up harvesting iceberg lettuce for one of Australia’s biggest supermarkets.
“It was my first taste of farm work – and it was awful,” says Quinn. But a seed was planted for him – it was the first time he had really thought about agricultural chemicals. “I became aware of names like glyphosate and Monsanto, and started to dig into it.”
Along the way he met his now-wife Yuka Quinn, from Japan, and together they started paying more attention to what they were eating. Weekends in Brisbane were spent tracking down organic produce and shopping at local butchers. By the time he moved back to Ireland in 2016, Quinn was hungry for better food.
“I had it in my head that I wanted to grow. Three days after I got off the plane, I was in my mam and dad’s greenhouse,” he says.
And so, Quinn grew, he read and he gave food away to neighbours, learning that he wanted to be able to produce food in a way that allowed him to be sure of “exactly where it had come from”.
He still had the day job, though, which at the time was fitting PVC windows. Then the Covid pandemic hit and work became precarious.
“I was cracking up,” says Quinn. “I was really suffering with my mental health.” Against this backdrop, he found solace in the garden, deciding to put everything into growing, and seeing results as early as August 2020.
“I had a huge amount of cucumbers and tomatoes and apples. I took photos in the back garden and posted on Facebook and said, ‘Anyone want to buy a box of veg?’ There was a bombardment of messages, and I sold everything. That was the point when I said, ‘I’m going to go fully in on this.’ That was the day Portnoo Market Garden was born.”
Quinn started to transform two acres of the family land that hadn’t been touched in decades. With YouTube tutorials and help from family and friends, he cleared land, learned to drive a digger and found a water source. Trees were cut, ground levelled and 2,000 bags of firewood hauled away. He googled polytunnels.
“There was so much work involved, I wouldn’t do it again,” he says, recalling blacking out from exhaustion while planting beetroot. “I went down on my knees to take a breather, and my face hit the dirt. It took my dad to say to me, ‘Barrie, you’re going home. You’re going home right now,’ otherwise I might have gone back to the beetroot after I’d come round.”
That first year in the garden Quinn planted about 28 different vegetables, but not everything sold. He realised rainbow chard was not a big seller in Portnoo, but soon the standout products became obvious, and now he does a strong trade in lettuce, kale, tomatoes, cucumbers, French beans, scallions and garlic.
One plot, now abundant with potatoes, did not start out like that. Quinn tried cabbage there first, but it didn’t take, and spinach was no better. When he tested the soil, he found toxic levels of copper; it turned out his uncle and dad had grown potatoes there decades earlier, spraying copper fungicide against blight every year, and that copper had sat in the soil ever since.
He presumed the fungicide had ruined the ground and so he covered the beds, until he read how sunflowers can take metals out of soil. “So I planted 250 sunflowers in there and pulled them out the next season. It’s meant to take two years to change the soil, but we tried it after one, and we got a massive crop. They had cleaned the soil; it was unbelievable. We grow potatoes there every year now, and they have been fantastic.”
[ The rural Dublin family farm where the best chefs in Ireland source their produce Opens in new window ]
Every crop and every corner of the garden tells a part of his story. John’s Tunnel is a polytunnel his late friend John McCole, who taught him how to grow tomatoes, left to him. “It’s a really special part of the garden. I made a video of it a few years ago, and I started bawling crying when I was making it.”
Quinn’s social media videos have played a huge part in the business. He started out posting photos of the garden, then began talking to camera. “Initially, I thought if I just tell people how I’m growing things, it will help sell them. This is how I grow, this is how I do things.”
But his breakthrough came with a video about a scallion shortage in Ireland, caused by a hurricane in Mexico. “I think it really struck a chord with people because scallions feel so Irish. That was my first video that went big – 100,000 views, I think. Then I was like, hang on, people want to hear this stuff, and I had loads of it in my head.”
Six years on, he still shares plenty of shocking food stories, but he’s also wary of catastrophising too much. “I also want to talk about, ‘Hey, it’s not that hard to grow your own spuds.’ I always come back to that – growing your own, and how to do it.”
That balance runs through almost everything in his garden. Overgrown corners that might look neglected are essential, the building blocks that let him grow without chemicals. “We are always trying to rebalance the ecosystem. What people don’t realise is this is pest control. I’ve never seen so many ladybirds in the garden this year, and this is where they live. Then they come out on to my lettuce and eat any greenfly.”
[ Study of ‘forever chemical’ in European foods finds highest level in Irish cereals Opens in new window ]
Quinn says he gets most questions about slugs. “I have a long answer and a short answer. The short answer is using things like copper tape and sheep’s wool, but the long answer is to balance out your garden, not using chemical sprays, creating a water source, building habitat. Leave grass to grow the way it should. A pile of old sticks, a pile of rocks. It can be anything. They all work together. So nothing gets out of whack, and there’s never too many of anything.”
Quinn credits the land itself, too. “The soil was pretty good when I came here. It’s a very unique place. There’s a section with incredible topsoil, and all I can come up with [to explain it] is the trees. Oak, rowan, all this plant life growing on this hillside for centuries, building up and down, growing.”
He shows me heads of lettuce planted stripe by stripe, colour by colour, for no real reason other than that it looks great. Lettuce is his biggest seller, which he finds ironic: after that first job in Australia, he swore he’d never look at another head again. In a tunnel bursting with tomato vines, he plucks one and wraps it in a basil leaf growing beside it, smiling widely. “This is a little perfect moment. Almost every day I’ll do this. There’s nothing like it. I take people in here just for that. It’s an experience. So fresh, oh my God.”
The only time he smiles more is when talking about his two children, aged four and seven. “It’s like a playground to them. Then they say, ‘I’m hungry, Daddy,’ and I’ll say, ‘Go down there and get yourselves a cucumber,’ and they’ll be munching away.”
Outside the tunnel, a slide made from water pipes leads down to another tunnel; it’s used for birthday parties, and for the tour groups who make the trip to Portnoo to meet Quinn.
“We have people from all over – gardening groups from Ireland, Scotland, England. People that follow me on social media. We do school tours too. I wish we could do more, but they’re time consuming.”
He admits to having hosted a few super fans: “Some people get overwhelmed when they get here, but a walk around the garden always sorts that out.”
Quinn says a book had been in his head since he started the garden, but he didn’t want it to just be a how-to; he wanted to tell the story behind it too. Some writing days were hard. “There was so much emotion. I had tears on the keyboard writing about my friends that passed, my dad’s upbringing. I didn’t think I’d have all those feelings writing about fruit and veg.”
He knows not everybody has a garden and that not everybody can grow, but he would still love us all to pay more attention to where our food comes from. That’s what he tries to teach at home. On Sundays, the kids pick nettle tops for an omelette made with their own hens’ eggs. At dinner, it’s “there are your spuds, Daddy, and that’s Cathal’s beef”. His kids know the names behind their food, and that’s a philosophy he would love to see spreading in the wider world.
Homegrown by Barrie Quinn is published by Gill Books. Follow Quinn on @portnoomarketgarden

title: Fiction in translation: Hafni Says by Danish writer Helle Helle is close to perfection
description: Plus new works by Pirkko Saisio, Felix Hartlaub, Karim Kattan and Angélica Gorodischer
content:
“You aren’t given power. You take it.” The Red Book of Farewells (Penguin International Writers, £14.99), in a sparkling translation by Mia Spangenburg, is the final volume in Pirkko Saisio’s hugely acclaimed Helsinki trilogy.
It continues, as with previous works Lowest Common Denominator (childhood) and Backlight (teenage years), the non-linear story of the coming of age of an artist and queer woman in oppressive 1970s Finland, a time when homosexuality was criminalised.
Now, the ultimate break into adulthood occurs as Saisio leaves home, shaves her head “her bald head is big and angular, free, and unmistakably modern” and begins theatre studies (despite its socialist ethos, Saisio and her “clown-eyed” girlfriend are bullied under officialdom at theatre school).
Saisio moves irrepressibly between first and third person, past and present in this auto-fiction, a careful construction of her manifesto of becoming. Appearing on the surface fairly spontaneous – the prose is dreamlike, delivered in short bursts – in its detail and immediacy the whole trilogy is exact and wrought. Most pertinently it is a joy to witness Saisio’s apprenticeship and progress as a writer.
In true auto-fiction style the book’s opening is simultaneously devastating and mischievous – it is 2002, on a summer boating trip to a remote island and Saisio makes a discovery of a dead seal. During a subsequent phone call from her publisher the writer casually reveals the loss of a manuscript entitled The Red Book of Farewells, which she now has to recreate.
“The book I’ll write all over again, will be different” she states, a poetic tribute to selfhood, personal reckoning and the many facets of a human life.
In his introduction to Felix Hartlaub’s Notes from Führer HQ (Pushkin Press, £10.99), translator Michael Hofmann describes the author’s life as “short and strangely weightless.” Hartlaub, a former humanities PhD student, who, following an unremarkable stint in combat, was assigned as a historian with the German army during the second World War, disappeared without trace in Berlin in May 1945 as part of the chaos and upheaval following the Allied victory in Europe. He was 32, and would officially be declared dead in 1955.
What remains of him are the scrupulous archival notes and journals he termed “word-etchings”. They certainly paint a vivid portrait. Pushkin has also published Clouds over Paris, in which Hartlaub depicted the Nazi occupation of the French capital, during 1941); now his attention is turned to the eastern front, to the fields and soldier camps of Ukraine, and then on to Hitler’s own command post, his eyrie Kehlsteinhaus (Eagle’s Nest) high in the Bavarian Alps.
[ Fiction in translation: How trauma interrupts the flow of a life, to devastating effect Opens in new window ]
Reading them now, Hartlaub’s extraordinary eyewitness observations place the writer centre stage, but in his own time he was purely incidental; one tiny unknown cog in the vast machine of war, recording war’s mundane brutality and eventual futility.
“Time here follows its own rules, it’s more like eternity than ordinary time … this day last year is no further away from us than yesterday, or, if you’d rather, they’re both equally remote. The dry leaves you tramp through on the way to lunch are a constant, the morning hoar frost on the lattices shimmering in blue and pink, the bitter smell of moonlight in the evenings and the smoke from the ashbox outside the sauna that’s a little addictive. And you still feel the grim silence of yore …”
“What do you do when you see your country disappearing?” Karim Kattan has followed up his debut novel, the beautiful and much-praised The Palace on Higher Hill, with Eden at Dawn (Foundry Editions, £13.99), translated from French by Jeffrey Zuckerman, a gay love story set in an almost mythical Jerusalem “a bombed out ... city of the nation of humans”.
We follow his two young protagonists Isaac and Gabriel, through time and space, under the thrill and terror of a sandstorm biblical in its intensity and force. The whole is overseen by a narrator whose commentary is sagacious and expansive. “You will notice that they hail from an occupied people in an occupied country. They did not mention it because one does not harp on what makes the stuff of our lives.”
Time collapses under the weight of both men’s individual histories then comes sharply into focus again as the lovers experience not simply their own here and now, but many lifetimes and even forms – “as much as six or seven thousand years”.
Their last life together, which is the plot of the novel, and culminates in a dangerous journey to the West Bank, occurs at a centrifugal point: “in this place they never had any chance of escaping”. Kattan employs an intense lyricism undercut by a wincing brutality: he isn’t going to sacrifice reality for whimsicality, there’s no time for that, in a book that for all its urgent messaging of political and environmental catastrophe, seems utterly atemporal.
Hafni S ays , by the wonderfully named Danish writer Helle Helle (Akoya Publishing, £12.99), in an exquisite translation by Martin Aitken, is, like They, its predecessor in English, slow fiction. Helle sets her deliberately unhurried novels (tantalisingly, about everything and not very much at all) in rural Denmark, where the author herself grew up.
They are conversational, acerbic, melancholy and also so full of everyday truths and observations that it is difficult to resist the urge to underline every phrase. Hafni, the protagonist, is on a road trip across Denmark in an attempt to discover parts of the country she has never seen. She also appears to be running away from or running towards something we can’t quite see. And, as is the case with wayward odysseys, she comes unstuck.
A month after her departure, she makes a call – to whom, we don’t know – explaining exactly what has gone wrong, why she is weeks over schedule and what has been happening. It is with this phone call that the novel itself begins. Helle works rather like an artist in miniature.
As with They (in which Hafni appears almost anecdotally, as a minor character), she begins abruptly, as if the reader is already fully cognisant of her people. There’s the title of the book and then the first chapter opens with the line: “that she’s getting divorced. She’s pulled into a lay-by not far from Ringe. There’s a field across the road, and an ancient burial mound. She might pay that burial mound a visit, if the field isn’t too claggy. The beech is well into leaf now, green is the hedge of spring. When was the last time we spoke? she says, it must be thirteen years ago. Just before the millennium.”
A stream of consciousness from one woman, travelling forward, but looking back on her life: “it’s such a long way from sixteen to twenty, from thirty to forty-eight.” Hafni Says is close to perfection.
Angélica Gorodischer (1928-2022) is finally getting her due as one of Argentina’s foremost writers of speculative fiction. Her fantastical novel from 1983, Kalpa Imperial: The Greatest Empire That Never Was (£10.99) has now received the Penguin Classics treatment, with the added kudos of using the 2003 translation by Ursula K Le Guin, that late, great maker of alternative worlds.
Notably written at the time of right-wing dictatorship across Latin America, Gorodischer’s fabulist literature rewards the reader with a legion of storytellers, its 11 chapters relating tales of an empire built and lost and built again – each on the ruins of the last, mimicking the act of mythmaking itself. Borges and Calvino are the obvious comparisons here, but Gorodischer has an earthy humanity and philosophy all her own, self-contained though far removed from the constraints of icy logic.
“Many years have passed and many emperors have lived and reigned, but the mountain city is still the capital of the Empire … it’s a splendid capital, beautiful, mysterious, charming, old as the capital of an old Empire should be, solid, wealthy, built to last thousands and thousands of years. And yet, I wonder …”
The book’s epigraph, “the twentieth century oppresses me” is attributed to one Trafalgar Medrano – a name that happens to be the title of another work by Gorodischer, a satisfying touch ensuring this labyrinthine creation comes full circle.

title: Rite & Reason: ‘He was only 88’: There is a cosy familiarity to Irish funerals
description: Rite & Reason: The Irish do funerals well. It’s a cultural phenomenon, writes journalist Molly O’Reilly
content:
H ave you ever craved a funeral sandwich? Or better yet, the soup that is handed to you in a mug while your neighbour runs around with a saucepan of tea waiting for someone to accept a cup?
The Irish do funerals well. It’s a cultural phenomenon, if you haven’t experienced it first-hand.
As Catholicism’s rigorous routines slowly disintegrate, I still feel guilt about eating meat on Good Friday. And I still appreciate a good Irish funeral. I am always taken aback when I speak to someone of my age and they let me know they have never been to a funeral, or have attended very few.
“We have been on this earth for so long, what do you mean you haven’t been to an extensive amounts of wakes?”
There is a strict routine when it comes to Irish funerals. They might look different, depending on the county, but they follow the same pattern. The women land into the kitchen – this is where those fabulous funeral sandwiches come into play. There are mountains of cakes, tarts, bread with sugar sprinkled on. (Not really, but there’s a lot of sweet things). By the third day you can’t look a Pat the Baker sliced pan in the eye.
It’s parallel to an Irish wedding: three days of drinking, three days of eating food that will sit in your stomach for weeks and three days of polite small talk to extended family members you may never see again.
The local men help dig the grave. If there are grandchildren they must be on standby for errands: tea-pouring, hotting of the whiskey. Otherwise there is little parental supervision. Someone will quietly criticise those smoking inside (“I thought she quit?”)
Once, at a funeral, I saw children playing funerals. Pringles were the Communion. This was the pre-tablet age, back when children had pure imaginations. (I was one of the children.)
[ We’re not bouncy castle Catholics – we’re the incense and eulogies kind Opens in new window ]
The three days of wake, removal and funeral, can bring nuanced feelings. The rooms are full of laughter, nostalgia and, simultaneously, even despair. “He was only 88.”
You practice your prayer of the faithful, intrigued by the gifts to be placed on the coffin and then, of course, the eulogy, when hankies are grabbed out of sleeves and even the most stoic of men just can’t keep it in any more.
There is the awkward walk as you slither into the chapel trying not to trip on the overly long skirt you keep just for these morbid family occasions, scanning the pews to see who came, while also trying to avoid eye contact so you don’t have to smile. It is either freezing to the point where your jaw starts to tremble and your breath is visible, or you’re sweating like you’re on a walk in peak July Tenerife.
“Someone get me an antihistamine quick and get this jumper off me now.”
The sympathising starts – such a beautiful thing, community coming together. (I hope I don’t pick up something shaking all these hands. ) “I am so sorry for your loss,” they say as they shake your hand, and then: “God, I remember when you were yea high.”
You shuffle out behind the gorgeous oak coffin and ponder the impermanence of the past several days. The men walk shoulder to shoulder. I say my thanks that I will never have to do that part, but there is also disappointment I will never have to do that part. Or maybe I will. It is 2026. Who is to say I can’t shoulder a coffin, especially since I have started the gym?
[ Edwards syndrome: ‘How many siblings do you have?’ I once had two and now I have one Opens in new window ]
There is a pressure that accompanies these events, such as the feeling I am hosting a family member’s entire life in the good sittingroom. But mostly it’s a great excuse to see everyone. You hear mumbles from locals trying to suss out who you are. “She’s his daughter – went to Dublin, full of notions,” someone will say.
I am privileged I don’t have to measure up to the same ideologies past generations in my family have had to.
Do I appreciate an Irish funeral or is it the familiarity of rural Ireland’s cosiness?
One day, you reach an age where you no longer are playing funeral at a funeral. You are in the kitchen ensuring the butter is spread evenly on the sandwiches. Before long, checking Rip.ie becomes an evening ritual. And then you arrive at the stage where you are grateful that it’s been a while since you had to eat a funeral sandwich.
Molly O’Reilly is a journalist with considerable experience of funerals in rural Ireland

title: I heard some terrific news the other day: ‘The happiest men over 40 are 25lbs overweight’
description: ‘If you’re 61 and you have washboard abs, you’re making a big sacrifice for that’
content:
I heard some terrific news the other day: “The happiest men over 40 are 25lbs overweight.” So said Prof Arthur Brooks of the John F Kennedy school of government at Harvard University in the United States, more commonly known as the Harvard Kennedy School.
He lectures on human happiness. Only in America!
“It’s not because of the gentlemanly paunch. It’s because they are relaxed about their lives,” he said. “If you’re 61 and you have washboard abs, you’re making a big sacrifice for that. And that sacrifice might not be a healthy sacrifice for you. That’s important to keep in mind,” he said.
What’s not to like! Mirror, mirror on the wall, mind your own business. You’re invading my privacy.
Brooks highlights the nonsense that, to be happy, you “have to optimise across more than one variable. You’ve got your abs, joy in your relationships, spiritual transcendence, the way you serve your community.”
Mad or what? Noting the ludicrousness of this, he said. “It’s as if you do this one thing and your whole life is going to fall into place. Wrong!” Idiot, leave those pounds alone (my translation).
More generally, he says, research has shown again and again over the past 30 years that a higher number of people are unhappy with their lives. Happiness, he said, “comes from faith/philosophy, family, friendship, and work” and that “all four have been getting more and more dysfunctional” in this 21 st century.
People now are less likely to practise a religion or have a coherent life philosophy. They’re less likely to be married and have children, less likely to have friends, or say their work is a source of meaning.
“My belief is that the big problem with depression and anxiety, especially for people under 30 today, is they don’t know the meaning of life and they don’t even know where to look,” he said.
Plus ça change. The meaning of life has been a challenge for every generation of homo sapiens since time immemorial, yet some academics still have a capacity for presenting this as highly original and with the excitement of a Columbus arriving in the Americas, convinced he was in a different place and incorrectly naming the natives, Indians.
Was it ever otherwise, dear professor? (I was under 30 once).
Paunch , from Latin panticem , for belly.

title: Guimarães and Saka fire Arsenal to win at Sunderland
description: David Raya denies Enzo Le Fee from the penalty spot for a clean sheet
content:
As the final whistle blew Bruno Guimãraes wore a mischievous smile, Enzo Le Fée was a study in dejection and Arsenal ’s immaculate start to the season remained unblemished.
Two minutes after David Raya had, rather majestically, saved Le Fée’s second half penalty, Guimãraes delighted both his new north London, public and plenty of old friends in Newcastle by sending a shot curving past Robin Roefs.
Yet no one should be deceived by the emphasis lent to the scoreline by Bukayo Saka’s stoppage-time penalty and Reinildo’s sending off, this was the toughest of tests for Mikel Arteta’s team. If Sunderland can keep playing like this, Régis Le Bris’s players will surely enjoy more good days than bad.
That penalty miss aside, chapeaux off to Le Fée who has, deservedly, made Zinedine Zidane’s provisional France squad for the forthcoming Nations League matches. Sunderland’s attacking playmaker knew another good performance here could only enhance his chances of moving from long list to shortlist and he did not take long to draw a foul and win a dangerous free-kick.
Arsenal’s former captain Granit Xhaka delighted in curling the meanest of dead balls in Dan Ballard’s direction but the home central defender, a one-time Gunners youth captain, could not quite connect.
There had been a similar reprieve for Le Bris’s rearguard when Saka failed to make the most of Declan Rice’s fine early delivery following more stellar work from Christos Tzolis.
Yet, bar a Gabriel Magalhães shot from distance that whizzed just wide of Roefs’s goal, a Kai Havertz shot on the turn saved smartly and a low 20 yard effort that Le Fée dragged fractionally wide of an upright, that was pretty much it in terms of first-half goalmouth action.
Arteta’s side were taking their time to establish a settled passing rhythm. If Sunderland’s superb organisation hardly assisted the visiting cause, Arsenal looked a little fazed whenever the excellent Nordi Mukiele – surely another candidate for the France squad – advanced from right-back.
Ezri Konsa, meanwhile, did not appear to be either relishing, or winning, his extremely physical contest with Le Bris’s ever combative centre forward, Brian Brobbey.
If a packed Stadium of Light enjoyed that little subplot, the roof was nearly lifted off by the roar of approval that greeted Reinildo’s full blooded early challenge on Martin Ødegaard.
One constant was Arteta’s excursions outside his technical area and eventually the referee, John Brooks, responded by jogging over to the touchline and waving a yellow card in the Arsenal manager’s face. While that booking was hardly unmerited, it seemed a shame that Brooks was turning a blind eye to some persistent shirt pulling from both sides at corners.
With the match even, Arteta replaced Myles Lewis-Skelly and the hobbling Ben White at the interval with Bruno Guimarães and Jurriën Timber. The Brazilian’s past as Newcastle’s captain ensured Guimaraes’s every touch was booed, while Sunderland started the new half strongly with Brobbey continuing to bully Konsa.
A penalty area encounter with Ballard at a throw proved no more welcome and when Konsa grappled the defender to the ground, Brooks had no hesitation in pointing to the spot. Up stepped Le Fée but there was a fairly lengthy delay and Sunderland’s normally ultra-reliable penalty taker looked uncharacteristically nervous. He attempted to squeeze his kick just inside David Raya’s left upright but the goalkeeper guessed correctly and tipped the ball, quite brilliantly, on to the woodwork and away.
Then, two minutes later, and very much against the run of play, Arsenal broke from another Sunderland throw and Guimarães curled a sumptuous shot beyond Roefs from the edge of the area.
As the scorer celebrated Arteta made a point of congratulating Raya, while Le Bris instructed Wilson Isidor to prepare to replace Nilsson Angulo. Sunderland duly shifted to 4-4-2 and a temperature that had already risen perilously closing to boiling point when Xhaka was booked for a powerful sliding challenge on Guimarnães continued climbing.
With no option but to take risks, Le Bris sent on Malick Fofana, newly-signed from Lyon in place of Thomas Meunier, and the Belgian’s first advance into Arsenal’s penalty area prompted rare defensive chaos among the visitors.
Although it took Roefs, who saved superbly from Saka, and Ballard, with a header off the line, to keep Le Bris’s side in the game, while Timber had a headed “goal” disallowed for offside, Arteta had reason to look slightly nervous. Sure enough, Mukiele volleyed a Le Fée corner just over the bar and, with Xhaka now reigning supreme in central midfield, an equaliser beckoned.
Arsenal, though, are not Champions for nothing and when, deep in stoppage time, Reinildo felled Saka in the area another penalty was awarded. Sunderland’s left-back, who had already been booked, was shown another yellow and then a red card and trudged off. Roefs touched but could not hold Saka’s kick from 12 yards. – Guardian

title: Venice Golden Lion goes to Woman Unknown, postwar film about ‘female body as battleground’
description: Saoirse Ronan misses out after premiering directorial debut at festival
content:
May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown, a European co-production set in the aftermath of the second World War, has, in a marginal upset, won The Golden Lion – the top prize – at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival . The film, well reviewed on premiere, concerns a young nanny preparing for marriage into a wealthy Copenhagen family. El-Toukhy, a Danish-Egyptian film-maker, was hitherto best known for the 2019 drama Queen of Hearts.
“To me personally, Woman Unknown is about the female body as a battleground,” she said from the podium. “At the same time, the film tells the tale of women who are invisible, unseen and voiceless.” The award from a jury headed by the actor Maggie Gyllenhaal feels pointed following complaints that only two films by women had been selected for the main competition.
John Malkovich won the Volpi Cup, the best actor prize, for his performance as an incorrigible older CIA operative in Martin McDonagh ’s Wild Horse Nine. The latest work from the London-Irish film-maker and playwright, which co-stars Sam Rockwell in a tale set on Easter Island before the 1973 Chilean coup, is packed full of sharp dialogue and telling political asides.
“I am humbled to be chosen for this award, which has been given to so many wonderful actors over the past 83 iterations of the Venice Film Festival,” Malkovich said on a video relay. “Thank you to the jury for bestowing this honour upon me, and thank you, Martin McDonagh, for writing this lovely screenplay and for your superb directing of it, and for gifting me with this fantastic role.”
Malkovich, who is both fragile and sparky in the picture, is hereby installed as current favourite for the best actor Oscar, but will receive strong competition from Irish actor Andrew Scott in Simon Stone’s Elsinore, which premiered to raves at the Telluride Film Festival in Colorado as the Venice event was playing out.
Mathilde Arcel won the Volpi Cup for best actress for her lead role in Woman Unknown. “This is my first lead role in a in a movie, and it’s my first time at a film festival, and my first time to win a film award,” she said, happily dumbfounded.
Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s NAZA, a documentary, co-produced by The Guardian, concerning the Israeli Defense Forces’ assault on Gaza, was many punters’ tip for the Golden Lion, but ended up with a Special Jury Prize. Added late to the programme and screening towards the close of the event, the film, which is principally concerned with the mass killing of Palestinian civilians, was received with huge enthusiasm at its premiere on the Lido. Abraham and Szor, both from Israel, have already shared the best documentary feature Oscar for their work on No Other Land from 2024 and will surely compete for next year’s Academy Award.
“Thank you to the jury, and we are both very grateful to be here,” Abraham said. “It’s honestly not very easy to stand here, thinking of all the people, the Israeli politicians, the journalists back home who are now attacking this film, denying it, without even seeing it. And so much is being done as to not look at reality. The reality is that, since this festival started, just over these 10 days, Israel killed six Palestinian children in Gaza.”
The Grand Jury Prize went to Lee Chang-dong for Possible Love, a hugely long pondering of current infelicities in the economy of South Korea. “I made this film to ask what cinema can and should do in times like these,” the director said. “I take this award as a sign that you want me to keep asking these questions.”
Saoirse Ronan was on the Lido to premiere her directorial debut, a touching vignette titled Paper Plane, but that film lost out in the Orizzonti short films competition to A Few Moments of Happiness by Moroccan-Lebanese film-maker Shaden Safieddine Tazi.
Founded in 1932, Venice International Film Festival is, after Cannes, easily the second most significant festival on the cinematic calendar. In recent years, the event has premiered a large number of Oscar contenders – including best picture winners such as The Shape of Water and Nomadland – but the 2026 edition saw fewer submissions from the American studios. Golden Lions for lifetime achievement were, this year, presented to veteran actors George Clooney and Ellen Burstyn during the festival.

title: Eddie Dunbar crashes out of Vuelta, day after claiming stage win
description: Corkman suffers shoulder injury and potential broken collarbone in penultimate stage
content:
A day after taking a brilliant stage win at the Vuelta a España , Eddie Dunbar suffered brutal luck when he crashed in the penultimate stage of the race.
The Corkman was part of a group chasing the breakaway during the early part of Saturday’s 186.8km route from La Calahorra to Collado del Alguacil, but the crash forced him to abandon the race.
His team, Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling, later confirmed the 30-year-old was taken to hospital for assessment. He has since been diagnosed with a fractured left collarbone, and will undergo surgery.
The incident adds to an unfortunate run of injuries for Dunbar. In March, he withdrew from the Paris-Nice stage race after sustaining a fractured rib in a crash, and then suffered an ankle injury when he was hit by a scooter having returned to his base in Monaco.
Having spent three months away from the bike on account of those injuries, he was hailed for his resilience in winning Friday’s 19th stage in Peñas Blancas.
[ Eddie Dunbar powers to stage victory in Vuelta a Espana Opens in new window ]
Meanwhile, Enric Mas all but ‌secured victory in the general classification, refusing to crack alongside challengers Primoz Roglic, Felix Gall and Richard Carapaz in baking conditions on the slopes ​of the Sierra Nevada mountains.
The 31-year-old Spaniard extended his advantage at the finishing, pushing two minutes 15 seconds clear of four-time Vuelta champion Roglic.
With only Sunday’s ceremonial stage around the city of Granada remaining, Mas is set to become the first Spanish rider to win the Vuelta since ‌Alberto Contador 12 ⁠years ago.
In an added celebration for the home crowd, Mikel Landa powered up the Collado del Alguacil to ​take the stage victory, his ​first stage win in seven years.

title: Shane Lowry shows his steel to extend Irish Open lead
description: Presidential distractions in Doonbeg do little to put Offalyman off his title charge
content:
In a strange day, when the whirring blades of Marine One and its escort of Chinook helicopters brought a notable visitor to the Irish Open, the show simply went on for Shane Lowry. Demonstrating his own brand of steel, he retained his lead heading into the final round of the €5-million DP World Tour tournament, four-shots clear of his nearest challenger.
Lowry’s low-scoring streak at Doonbeg continued, adding a 65 to his previous rounds of 67 and 62 for a 54-hole total of 194 for 16-under. Denmark’s Jacob Skov Olesen sits second on 12-under, with Chile’s Joaquin Niemann third on nine-under.
“An insane day,” said Lowry, referencing the goings-on surrounding US president Donald Trump’s arrival at his Co Clare course. But the Offalyman kept his focus, leaning heavily on his scrambling and his putter, recording nine single putts for the first time in his career on the homeward run.
On his magical spell with putter in hand, Lowry added: “I’m normally the one watching other people do it, so why not me sometimes? I’m seeing my lines well and starting the ball where I want and they’re going in and hopefully it stays that way for another 24 hours.”
The 39-year-old started the third round at Trump International with a three-stroke advantage over his two playing partners, Olesen and Haotong Li. His fight to hold the lead was evidenced by both his pursuers rolling in eagle putts on the Par-5 eighth.
To Lowry’s credit, he played the role of observer to the two eagle putts – which briefly moved Olesen into a share of the lead on 12-under – before walking to his own 12-foot birdie putt. Olesen birdied the ninth to catch the leader.
But Lowry’s stellar play with the blade on the back nine proved instrumental in re-establishing and ultimately extending his advantage. On the 18th, a poor drive down the left hit a spectator, preventing it going into heavy rough, and Lowry then hit his approach left to under the hospitality unit where some members of the Trump family were watching the green. He again made a brilliant par save, chipping to eight feet and holing the putt.
A winner of the Irish Open as an amateur at Baltray in 2009, Lowry will aim to win the Irish Open for the first time as a professional in what would be his first individual win on the DP World Tour since claiming the BMW PGA Championship in 2022.
“I’m going to try to not think about it,” said Lowry. “I’m going to talk to people around me, have a nice evening, hopefully get some sleep and get out there tomorrow afternoon.
“Hopefully the crowd gets on my side and I can put on a good show for them again and shoot a good score and do what I’m supposed to do.
“I‘m leading my home tournament and it would mean the world to knock this one off. I’m just going to have to put my head down, get back to work whenever my tee time is tomorrow, and give it a run.”
Lowry will go in the final pairing with Olesen at 2.05pm on Sunday.
Tom McKibbin moved into the top five with a 68 for seven-under. However, a disappointing finish in which he bogeyed two of his closing four holes slipped him back.
“A bit of a benign finish,” said McKibbin. “That bogey from the middle of the fairway on 15 was frustrating and then obviously that putt on the last was very annoying. I’m definitely looking to go as low as possible tomorrow and finish off a very good week.”
And Trump’s arrival during play didn’t prove too disruptive. “I see it all the time in Palm Beach,” Rory McIlroy quipped of the helicopters coming in to land near the seventh hole.
[ Golf momentarily takes backseat in Doonbeg as Trump touches down at Irish Open Opens in new window ]
Indeed, such matters were the least of McIlroy’s concerns as he struggled to a 74 for two-over to plummet down the leader board. His problems began with a double-bogey six on the third, where he lost a ball, followed by a second double on the sixth.
“Two doubles in the first six holes wasn’t the way I wanted to start it, obviously,” he said. “A couple of wayward drives. I took a chance on three, trying to hit driver there and get it close to the green and hit it out of bounds or lost ball, either/or.
“Then same thing on six – I tried to get it up close to the green, had to take an unplayable and made another one there. So, no momentum early, and then it was a tough enough day. I Just just couldn’t quite get it back after that.”
Liam Nolan, the 26-year-old Galwayman playing on an invitation, continued his impressive first appearance on the DP World Tour with a 68 for two-under, moving him into a share of 26th.
“I was very happy after I finished yesterday. Making the cut, getting to play four rounds at my first Irish Open is pretty special and I’m happy I was able to play some good golf today and get my name up there a bit closer to the top of the leader board,” he said.

title: Liffey Swim winner ‘surprised’ as annual race becomes focal point of new Liffey Festival
description: This year’s swim is part of the inaugural Dublin City Council Liffey Festival, running over the weekend
content:
“I am really surprised. There were better swimmers in this race than me,” Bruno Delmonte, winner of the men’s race in the 106th year of Dublin’s Liffey Swim , said on Saturday.
Cheering crowds lined the quays between Rory O’More Bridge and Custom House Quay, making the most of the sunshine, as the swimmers, visible only as a shoal of elbows, arms and hats, raced downriver.
In front of the Custom House, tables were placed across the temporarily pedestrianised road as merry-go-rounds, ice cream stalls, face painters and many colourfully dressed, marine-themed “animators”, some on stilts, some on roller skates, vied with each other for attention.
Olivia Octopus and Dan the Diver were among those who wandered among the crowds, posing for selfie pics with children.
“Turn! Turn! Turn!” shouted a garda on Butt Bridge as he tried to get the attention of a wandering swimmer in the men’s race. Head down, the swimmer appeared to be heading for Liberty Hall as the guard urged spectators to call out to him. “Right of the pillar, quick!” the guard shouted as the male swimmer looked up at the last minute.
At Custom House Quay there were cheers and whoops of joy as “the man from Delmonte” – Bruno Delmonte from Crumlin – was declared the winner.
“They are actually my togs. I could never win the Liffey Swim, but at least my togs did,” said a passing swimmer as The Irish Times spoke to Delmonte.
Originally from Argentina, Delmonte trains three times a week with Templeogue Swim Club but said he was still surprised when he won the Liffey Swim. “I am really surprised. There were better swimmers in this race than me. I just enjoyed it, I didn’t really set out to win,” he said.
Delmonte had a handicap of three, which meant he had to wait three minutes after the “off” to start his race.
Not happy with the handicap system in their race, however, were swimmers Claire Griffin, Trudy Carty, Bronagh Carey and Doireann Ní Ghrioghair. “The men get better handicaps,” said Griffin, pointing out that some women were given handicaps in the region of 13 to 17 minutes. Ní Ghrioghair agreed, saying men and women swimmers at similar levels did not get the same handicaps. “You can put that in the article,” said Carey firmly.
Paul Gallagher, chief executive of the Irish Hotels Federation , emerged from the river hoping he was in the first 10. A keen open water swimmer and a member of Glenalbyn Swimming Club, he was, in fact, placed seventh in the race, according to officials.
Winner of the ladies’ race Sadhbh Byrne, from the Tallaght Masters Swim Club, said this was her first Liffey Swim and she was delighted to win.
This year, the swim is part of the inaugural Dublin City Council Liffey Festival, taking place this weekend from noon to 6pm daily. Visitors are being offered the chance to get out on the water in boats, to try a new sport, step aboard visiting ships, join walking tours and watch spectacular aerial and jet pack displays. The Pelican of London tall ship is also visiting for the festival and is moored at Sir John Rogerson’s Quay.
On Sunday, the river becomes the main stage for the Liffey Festival Flotilla. Local boats, rowing clubs and community vessels will gather at Custom House Quay before travelling together along the Liffey towards Dublin Port, with Glasshouse Ensemble providing an eight-piece orchestral and vocal backdrop.
The festival is free for all to attend, with a small number of fee-paying activities, some of which can be booked in advance at dublinliffeyfestival.ie

title: Frustrated Liverpool fail to take chances as Fulham claim deserved first point
description: Organised Fulham end losing streak at Anfield
content:
In the not-so distant past when they were vying for a right-back role with Spain, Andoni Iraola often lost out to Álvaro Arbeloa. The points were shared at Anfield but the Liverpool head coach was thwarted by his old adversary once again as Fulham deservedly claimed the first Premier League point of Arbeloa’s tenure.
The visitors belied their lowly position and a run of three successive league defeats to take a point from a Liverpool side that represented a pale imitation of their Champions League selves against Atlético Madrid on Wednesday.
Whether it was the after-effects of the win over Diego Simeone’s side, with a quick turnaround between fixtures, or the three changes that Iraola made from the European game, hardly a significant amount, the deterioration in Liverpool’s performance was dramatic. The hosts were sluggish and sloppy in possession – Florian Wirtz and Kostas Tsimikas both put simple passes straight out of play in the first half – and Fulham bypassed their midfield repeatedly. Tsimikas’s return to the starting line-up lasted all of 45 underwhelming minutes.
Another factor in Liverpool’s subdued performance was Fulham’s confidence on the ball and defensive organisation. For a team arriving at Anfield with only defeats to their name in the Premier League this season, the visitors’ belief and willingness to attack was hugely impressive. With more conviction in front of goal, Arbeloa’s side could have capitalised on Liverpool’s slow start.
Bradley Barcola created an early, difficult chance for Alexander Isak with a measured pass behind the Fulham defence. Liverpool’s number nine just missed the far post from a tight angle. Victor Muñoz went closer still with a glancing header from a Dominik Szoboszlai corner. Bernd Leno, the Fulham goalkeeper, reacted superbly to claw the ball away from just under his crossbar. But that was the sum total of Liverpool’s enterprise in the first half, with an attacking quartet that cost almost £400 million.
Fulham were gifted a glorious opportunity when Alisson played a ridiculous pass to Ryan Gravenberch when he was under pressure from Sander Berge on the edge of his own area. The loose ball fell to Josh King, catching the eye yet again in the visiting attack, who was sent flying by the Liverpool keeper but the referee Thomas Bramall played a good advantage as Gonzalo García took over. Garcia had time to pick his spot only for Jérémy Jacquet to block his shot in front of the goalline.
The visitors prospered down their left and Oscar Bobb missed another good opening when, unmarked and 18 yards out, he mis-controlled Alex Iwobi’s pinpoint delivery. Jacquet came to Liverpool’s rescue once again seconds later when preventing García breaking through with an excellent challenge. Antonee Robinson would head wide before the interval from Bobb’s right wing cross.
Liverpool were deserving of a few home truths during the break – chiefly, you would have been slaughtered for this last season under Arne Slot – and did perform with greater intensity and purpose in the second half. But not with any more threat. The introductions of Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and Milos Kerkez brought a measure of improvement but Fulham continued to contain the hosts comfortably. Calvin Bassey in particular had a commanding game against Isak.
The visitors remained dangerous on the counterattack and Alisson pushed away a King effort that was heading for the top corner after the forward had cut inside Jacquet to create space for himself. His replacement, Rodrigo Muniz, also let a decent chance run away from him inside the area and the substitute Kevin dragged a shot wide from 18 yards.
Isak finally escaped Bassey’s attentions in stoppage time to flick Szoboszlai’s corner wide of the far post from close range. There was still time for one more Liverpool raid when Jeremie Frimpong escaped down the right and crossed through the heart of the Fulham box. The ball struck Rio Ngumoha and sailed over, leaving Liverpool with a third draw from four league games at the start of Iraola’s reign.
Elsewhere, Keith Andrews’ Brentford took a 2-2 draw at the Vitality against Bournemouth, as was the case for Hull against Chelsea, with Mohamed Belloumi on the double for the visitors at Stamford Bridge. A late goal from Igor Jesus sealed a 2-1 for Nottingham Forest at Aston Villa, and a first-half red card for Axel Disasi left Crystal Palace with too much to do against Ipswich, Dara O’Shea’s side coming away from Selhurst Park with a 3-2 victory.
And over at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Ireland defender Jake O’Brien came off the bench for his first appearance for Everton in their scoreless draw against Roberto De Zerbi’s side. – Guardian

title: Solheim Cup: Jennifer Kupcho produces stunning finish to leave US and Europe level for Sunday singles
description: Leona Maguire earns point for Europe alongside Esther Henseleit in foursomes before four-ball defeat
content:
Jennifer Kupcho summoned a pair of superb last-gasp putts to drag the United States back all square at 8-8 after a riveting second day of Solheim Cup , while it was a mixed day for Ireland’s Leona Maguire , winning alongside Esther Henseleit in the morning foursomes before a 3&2 defeat with Nastasia Nadaud in the four balls.
Europe had built a two-point lead after Saturday’s foursomes at Bernardus Golf in the Netherlands and the hosts looked strong favourites to retain that advantage as the final quartet approached the closing holes.
But Kupcho had other ideas, draining a birdie putt from 91 feet on the 17th to bring her and team-mate Lindy Duncan level against Carlota Ciganda and Celine Boutier going to the 18th.
Ciganda had been the hero of the opening day for Europe when she emerged from the rough to somehow secure a half on the final hole and ensure the two teams would be locked at 4-4 overnight.
But she failed to repeat the feat on Saturday, missing a birdie putt to keep Europe’s hard-earned lead intact, before Kupcho produced another mighty putt from the edge of the green to snatch an improbable victory for the US pair.
Europe had made a big move in the morning session, with Maja Stark and Linn Grant teaming up to beat Allisen Corpuz and Nelly Korda 3&2 before Maguire and Henseleit won two of the final three holes to claim another point for Europe.
A third home point came from Mimi Rhodes and Nastasia Nadaud, who dominated Andrea Lee and Auston Kim 4&3, but the woes of Europe’s high-profile pair Charley Hull and Lottie Woad continued as they crashed 6&5 to Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin.
Questions may be asked about European captain Anna Nordqvist’s persistence with Hull and Woad as a partnership after they also fell in the four balls, losing 1UP to Yealimi Noh and Andrea Lee.
With Rose Zhang and Kim beating Maguire and Nadaud, what turned out to be Europe’s only point of the afternoon session was carved out by Stark and Grant, who beat Megan Khang and Lauren Coughlin 2&1.
Attention swung to the increasingly dramatic finale being played in the remaining match, and Kupcho’s pair of monster putts that sent her team-mates dancing across the green in celebration.
Maguire will face Coughlin in Sunday’s singles matches, teeing off as the fourth last pair at 11.46am.

title: Dearbhaile Brady adds bronze for Ireland on closing day at World Para Swimming European Championships
description: Ireland finish with seven medals in Turkey
content:
Dearbhaile Brady took her tally of medals at the World Para Swimming European Championships to four on the final day of the event in Turkey, winning bronze in the 100m breaststroke final on Saturday.
Added to Róisín Ní Riain’s haul of a gold and two silver, Brady’s result brought Ireland’s total to seven medals in the championships.
The Derry swimmer set a lifetime best in the morning’s heats and shaved almost three additional seconds off that mark in the final. Brady came from fourth at the turn to take bronze, adding to her three silver medals from earlier in the week.
“I’m happy with a bronze, it’s not one of my best events,” said Brady. “It’s been a good week, I’ve learned a lot to take into next year, a lot of positives. It’s about putting the head down and taking it day by day.”
Ní Riain finished fifth in her last event, the 400m freestyle. While she was disappointed with the placing, she was happy with her week’s work, highlighted by the successful defence of her 100m backstroke title.
“I would have liked to end if on a little bit of a better note, but I have to be happy coming away from this week,” she said.
Limerick’s Ellie Lynch finished seventh in the 100m backstroke final on her European debut, while Luke O’Donoghue clocked a personal best to take eighth in the 100m backstroke final.

title: ‘The only people on the streets are here to oppose him’: Thousands protest Trump visit
description: Breakaway group burns US flag before setting off firecrackers and chanting against US troops in Shannon
content:
Palestine, Iran, paedophilia, racism, misogyny, transphobia, corruption, climate destruction – there was a placard for all.
The crowds that gathered in Dublin to protest the visit of Donald Trump had a pick ‘n’ mix assortment of grievances to air.
“I have friends who volunteer for the Rape Crisis Centre ,” said one protester, who wore a satirical T-shirt depicting Trump’s friends in despotic places, and a badge saying: “I believe her.”
“I’m here in solidarity with women and I just hope it makes a statement,” said the protester, who asked not to be named in case it affected his job.
“I think it does. When [Barack] Obama was here in 2011, 50,000 came out to College Green to hear him. With Trump, the only people on the streets are here to oppose him.”
Holly Eustance carried a poster declaring: “Manatees Against US Imperialism”, a nod to the social media meme featuring the docile marine mammals said to love just about everything. So anything they don’t love must be really bad.
“It’s for all the species on the verge of extinction and threatened by Trump’s policies,” she said.
“War and climate change destroy so much, and the economic systems Trump supports prioritise money for genocide, money for rockets to space and the interests of billionaires – not people or our planet.”
Thirty political, protest and campaign groups and trade unions came together to organise Saturday afternoon’s demonstration.
They put the number attending at 25,000 though it was likely much less. The crowd spread across more than a kilometre as they walked from the Garden of Remembrance to the Dáil.
People Before Profit , the Social Democrats , Labour, Sinn Féin and the Green Party were among the banners carried while many marchers waved Palestinian flags and others held home-made placards.
Trump may have brushed off questions from reporters about protests earlier in the day − musing that they were probably “friendly” – but the sentiments expressed were anything but.
Many placards were profane, darkly humorous, or both, but their messages were deadly serious.
One woman in a floral face mask asked not to be named for fear of repercussions.
“I’m an American citizen with an American pension and I’m concerned about facial recognition software,” she said.
A returned emigrant, she said she no longer recognised the United States she had grown to love and could not imagine returning to live there.
“I hope the Irish Government hear what people are saying. I hope the American people somehow get to hear it too,” she said.
“It feels important to stand up and say, Trump, you are not welcome here.”
A group called Anti-Imperialist Action (AIA) were masked, with black clothes and dark glasses completing their uniform.
As the main group of marchers reached Molesworth Street and songs and speeches were delivered from a platform outside the Dáil, the AIA group raised a US flag and burnt it before setting off firecrackers and chanting loudly against US troops in Shannon.
Their action caught other groups and non-affiliated protesters by surprise but they dispersed quickly and attention returned to the speakers.
Labour TD Ciarán Ahern lambasted the Government for “sycophancy” in facilitating the Trump “circus”, in return for US investment, describing its behaviour as “brown envelopes on a global scale”.
Senator Alice Mary Higgins, a founder of the Irish Neutrality League, said Trump’s trip was a “grotesque pantomime that seeks to normalise his assault on decency and democracy”.

title: Donald Trump backs Irish unity in comments during Dublin visit
description: Catherine Connolly raises ‘normalisation of war and genocide’ in ‘respectful’ meeting with US president
author_name: Conor Pope, Freya McClements, Katie Mellett
content:
US president Donald Trump said Irish unity would be a “great thing” in response to a reporter’s question on his visit to Dublin.
The comments, made alongside Taoiseach Micheál Martin at Farmleigh, caused eyebrows to be raised north and south of the Border and in London, but they were subsequently downplayed by a spokesperson for the Taoiseach who made it clear that Ireland’s policy on the North had not and would not be changing.
A spokesman for British prime minister Andy Burnham said there was no majority support for a referendum and that one will not be held until that changes.
DUP leader Gavin Robinson said Northern Ireland’s constitutional future “will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington”.
“As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic,” he said.
Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald acknowledged the remarks, but focused in her statement on calls for the US to “stop facilitating the genocide of Palestinian people”.
The US president’s flying visit to Dublin passed off without further controversy.
After brief meetings with President Catherine Connolly and the Taoiseach, Trump addressed a crowd including business leaders, politicians and cultural figures at Deerfield, the US ambassador’s residence. All three engagements took place within the Phoenix Park in Dublin.
Trump told reporters at Farmleigh he had discussed Northern Ireland with Connolly during their private meeting in Áras an Uachtaráin and said it was a topic that was of great interest to him.
[ Beauty queens, corporate titans and Michael Flatley gather for Trump’s meandering address Opens in new window ]
Almost immediately he was asked for his views on a united Ireland.
“I’d love to see it unified. It is going to happen eventually. You have the right man over here to get it moving,” he said, gesturing to Martin.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing. I think the UK would have something to say about it but I think it would be a great thing. How could it be bad?”
He also batted away any suggestion that planned protests indicated the desire of many Irish people that he stay away and he said that he was unaware there were protests happening.
“It can’t be a very big one because we’ve been all over Ireland today already but I haven’t seen any protest.”
[ ‘The only people on the streets are here to oppose him’: Thousands protest Trump visit Opens in new window ]
Thousands gathered in Dublin city centre and in Co Clare to protest against the US president’s presence.
Trump had met Connolly, who has been vocally critical of him in the past, for slightly longer than the allotted 10 minutes scheduled and the handshakes before the meeting appeared cordial.
Trump described it as “a very nice meeting”, adding that he had considered it “respectful”.
In a subsequent statement, Connolly said she had “conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted” and “emphasised the unique insight which Irish people can bring to the resolution of conflict”.
The Taoiseach spoke of links, both economic and sporting, between the two countries in their joint press conference.
After the two semi-official events, Trump delivered a speech at the residence of the US ambassador Edward Walsh.
“This country is a fantastic,” he said as he hailed the hospitality of Irish people.
“You know they say you can’t generalise about groups of people, countries, but you can. People love coming to Ireland. You know why? Because they love you. They love the people. There’s a friendliness,” he continued before pausing ever so slightly.
“There’s also a viciousness and a toughness. Let me tell you, you are some of the most vicious bastards ... but when you want to be nice there is nobody nicer.”
After the speeches, he travelled by motorcade back to Dublin Airport where Air Force One was waiting to fly him and his entourage, including several family members, to Shannon from where he travelled on to Doonbeg to attend the Irish Open golf tournament.
On Saturday evening, three women appeared at a special sitting of Ennis District Court following their arrests.
On Friday evening, a woman in her 20s was arrested for trespassing on the golf links in Doonbeg, gardaí said. Two other women, aged in their 30s and 40s, were arrested for public order offences on Saturday on the links.
[ Pat Leahy: Ireland keeps good relations and Trump talks golf. Both sides get what they want from visit Opens in new window ]
Gardaí said no other arrests have been made.
A significant policing and security Operation will continue in Co Clare on Sunday. Members of the public were told to expect ongoing restrictions on traffic and movement in West Clare, particularly in the environs of Doonbeg and Trump International Trump International Golf Links and Hotel.

title: Trump’s focus turns to Doonbeg as thousands in Dublin and Clare protest
description: Following earlier engagements with President Connolly and Taoiseach Martin, Trump has landed at Doonbeg
content:
That is all for today on our live coverage of Trump’s visit to Dublin and Doonbeg.
Follow along tomorrow for more rolling coverage.
Rory McIlroy had a 1.08pm start for his third round at the Irish Open and one of the marshals assigned to follow his round arrived with a minute to spare, panting for breath, writes Gavin Cooney .
He had been held up en route by a mass motorcade of around 30 vehicles; an obsidian black chain of armoured Cadillacs, Mercedes’ saloons, ambulances and, incongruously, a bus bearing the name of Spain’s Coach Hire.
The convoy did not include the US president - it was merely a rehearsal event for the delivery of Donald Trump to the front door of his hotel. Further down the course, one fan was so rapt by the convoy that she didn’t hear golfer Joe Dean yell fore from the third teebox. His ball thwacked her on the back.
Trump stepped off the stage at the US ambassador’s residence about 40 minutes before the announcer at Doonbeg welcomed McIlroy to the first tee.
That whole speech distilled the extent to which the world is being governed as if it’s a country club.
First, the Irish ambassador praised Trump as an “amazing golfer”, then calling him an “amazing man” and repeated one of Trump’s favoured fantasies in heralding him as a winner of 41 club championships.
The comments by the US President today on the future of the island of Ireland show how much the conversation about a unified island is advancing at home & abroad. It shows the importance of political parties engaging in a constructive, informed & evidence based way.
In a post on X, Tánaiste Simon Harris wrote, “the comments by the US president today on the future of the island of Ireland show how much the conversation about a unified island is advancing at home and abroad.
“It shows the importance of political parties engaging in a constructive, informed & evidence based way.”
He also added, “as you know I made it clear that Fine Gael would produce a blueprint for a unified island.
“That work is progressing well and we will produce our output and next steps at our Ard Fheis in November.”
Well-known poet Sarah Clancy was among protesters that assembled in the village of Doonbeg near US president Donald Trump’s Co. Clare golf resort, reports Political correspondent Cormac McQuinn .
While Trump spent much of the afternoon watching The Irish Open tournament there were around 40 protesters present at any one time in the nearby village with another 200 or so at Shannon Airport.
Clancy was a supporter of Ireland’s own first citizen Catherine Connolly during last year’s presidential election and featured during one of the independent candidate’s campaign rallies where she read out one of her poems.
Meeting Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin was Trump’s first port of call after he arrived in Dublin on Saturday morning.
She released a statement afterwards saying she conveyed to Trump “the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted.”
So how does Clancy think Connolly did during her meeting with Trump earlier in the day?
“I’m kind of sorry for her that she had to meet him at at all,” she said but added that Connolly “was very clear to all of us during the campaign that Catherine does things by the letter of the law.
She’s a barrister and she would have examined exactly what the role of the president was so she was quite clear that she would do what was required as president.
“And so it is required to meet the president of another country when they come.”
Asked about Connolly’s statement on her meeting with Trump, Clancy said: “Those would be exactly the things that we need her to say. It takes a much better leader to build peace than it does to build war.”
Clancy took part in the Global Sumud Flotilla aiming to bring aid to Gaza last year before they were detained by Israeli authorities.
On her reason for protesting in Doonbeg she said she is a community worker in Clare “so I just didn’t want to leave it that the person who is funding and arming and fomenting all of this warfare would come unremarked”.
Clancy said demonstration is “not a protest about the people of Doonbeg” adding: “It’s very strong in my mind that we have seen village after village in Gaza, villages just like this wiped out, people murdered or forced to move over and over again, villages just the size of Doonbeg”.
She said that war “could have been stopped at any single point during that war if Donald Trump acted to say he was withdrawing funding or arms for Israel.”
Clancy argued: “the people in Ireland do not want this visit from Trump. We don’t like him, we don’t want him here”.
People Before Profit TD Paul Murphy said Taoiseach Micheál Martin “engaged in a demeaning performance in front of the nation and the world” while speaking with Donald Trump at Farmleigh House in the Phoenix Park.
“Trump has armed and continues to arm Israel’s genocide to the teeth, but when asked about Gaza the Taoiseach’s response was an abject failure to challenge Trump.
“The Taoiseach failed to utter a single word of condemnation or even concern about US actions.
“Instead, the Taoiseach spoke in support of Trump’s so called 20-point peace plan for Gaza that is to be implemented by a board with Trump as president and including the likes of Tony Blair, Jared Kushner and Marco Rubio.
“These are self-appointed colonial viceroys, appointed without anything resembling a democratic process and without any consultation with the people of Gaza.
“It’s obvious they intend to carve up Gaza to serve Israel’s interests and enrich themselves and their cronies. Shame on the Taoiseach for failing to challenge Trump and for endorsing this modern colonialism,” he said.
It was, as one senior SDLP figure put it, “quite a moment, to have the American president saying that,” wrote Northern editor Freya McClements .
The “that” in question was Donald Trump’s endorsement of Irish unity, delivered when answering questions from the media after his arrival in Ireland on Saturday.
“I’d love to see it unified”, Trump said; it would be “a fantastic thing ... a great thing” and even “a very cool thing.”
At the SDLP conference, taking place in a south Belfast hotel as Trump was speaking in Dublin, they were already talking unity.
President Trump's endorsement of a united Ireland is welcome. The Good Friday Agreement states that this is a decision for us on the island of Ireland to make on our own - north and south. That does not mean that outside opinions and advice cannot be offered. Going back to… https://t.co/wQV4xRX6Cv
In a post on X, former taoiseach Leo Varadkar said “president Trump’s endorsement of a united Ireland is welcome.
“The Good Friday Agreement states that this is a decision for us on the island of Ireland to make on our own - north and south.
“That does not mean that outside opinions and advice cannot be offered. Going back to independence and before, America has always had a special role to play in our national story,” he wrote.
On day three of the Irish Open, Trump can be seen applauding the action as he looks across the 18th green as well as waving to spectators.
He arrived at Shannon Airport before making his way to Doonbeg following earlier meetings in the Phoenix Park in Dublin with President Catherine Connolly, Taoiseach Micheál Martin and US ambassador Edward Walsh.
Among the crowds lined out to watch professional golfers, such as Rory McIlroy play at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, a US flag can be seen featuring a portrait of Trump.
The Taoiseach’s senior officials need to possess a variety of skills and abilities, writes Political editor Pat Leahy .
Among them is the ability to show a poker face in meetings with foreign leaders. Never was that ability more tested than today, when Donald Trump threw in his tuppence worth about the desirability of a united Ireland.
Trump’s comments are likely to cause at least temporary consternation in the Irish and British governments, and a longer-term unease among unionists.
His remark that Micheál Martin was “the right man over here to get it moving” are also likely to be deeply unwelcome on the part of the Taoiseach, who has faced criticism from the pro-unity lobby – and from some quarters within his own party – for not being more enthusiastic about the prospect.
⚠️ Phoenix Park has reopened. Please be advised that all gates and roads at Phoenix Park have reopened and normal access has resumed. #PhoenixPark pic.twitter.com/99KVV3AzBi
Gardaí said, in a post on X, the Phoenix Park re-opened after 4pm.
The Phoenix Park was closed to the public to accommodate president Trump’s visits to Áras an Uachtaráin to meet with President Catherine Connolly, Farmleigh House to meet with Taoiseah Micheál Martin and Deerfield, the US ambassador’s residence in the park.
All gates, including pedestrian gates, were closed during this period.
They were due to re-open at 6pm this evening.
The Office of Public Works said the closure was in place for “operational reasons” following a request from An Garda Síochána.
Is it ever too early in the morning to listen to YMCA? Apparently not, writes Political correspondent Jack Horgan-Jones .
By the dawn’s early light at Deerfield, the US ambassador’s residence in the Phoenix Park, the Village People’s signature tune belted out as they tested the PA system inside the large marquee set up to receive guests, and eventually, US president Donald Trump. It was half past six in the morning.
Air Force One was inbound across the Atlantic as the invited guests began to troop in, bleary-eyed and flocking towards the embassy’s coffee and pastry table.
The lawn at Deerfield was soon crowded with the great and good - plenty of past and present TDs and Senators (Fine Gael had a particularly good attendance), as well as high flyers from the corporate world, with Amazon, Meta, Google, Stripe and many more represented.
Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom. The people of Northern Ireland neither want a referendum, nor unification. I disagree with President Trump.
In a post on X, the Reform UK leader said “Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom.
“The people of Northern ireland neither want a referendum, nor unification.”
The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the US president of “shooting from the hip” and describing his remarks as “deeply unhelpful,” in a post on X.
She said, “president Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state.
“This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension.
“Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom. At a time when separatists are in power in Scotland, Wales and NI, we need a Government that will defend the union clearly and confidently.”
Trump has been photographed watching over the eighteenth green during the third round of the Irish Open taking place at Doonbeg Golf Course.
The US president and his son Eric spoke with American golfer Brooks Koepka.
Following his earlier engagements with President Catherine Connolly and Taoiseach Micheál Martin, he has since removed his tie and instead is wearing a white cap with “USA” written on it in gold letters.
Trump will stay overnight at Doonbeg and present the Irish Open trophy before returning to the US tomorrow.
The Government’s facilitation of Donald Trump is “brown envelopes on a global scale,” Labour TD Ciaran Ahern has told the Dublin protest, reports Climate and Science correspondent Caroline O’Doherty .
He said the Trump visit to Doonbeg was officially welcomed to allow the US president make more money so that be might be kinder to Ireland in trade talks.
The trip was a “circus” and the Government were “sycophants” for supporting it.
“We believe in politics of hope, not hate, and we are disgusted to see the red carpet rolled out by the Government for this fascist,” he said.
I was very pleased to welcome President Trump to Ireland, particularly for the Irish Open. With college football recently and the Ryder Cup next year, the sporting ties between our two countries continue to grow. 🇮🇪🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/ItkAHKApwx
Taoiseach Micheál Martin said he was “very pleased to welcome” president Trump to Ireland, “particularly for the Irish Open”.
“With college football recently and the Ryder Cup next year, the sporting ties between our two countries continue to grow,” he said in a post on X.
A view from above on Air Force One, flying over Doonbeg, Ireland. ✈️🇺🇸🦅 pic.twitter.com/nNzvl6QMpt
Deputy chief of staff at The White House, Dan Scavino has shared this video on X, showing the view onboard the Air Force One, flying over Doonbeg.
While Trump has arrived at Doonbeg, a protest is ongoing at Shannon Airport.
Protester Jean Moran described herself as “anti-Trump, anti-everything that he stands for.”
“He’s a total tyrant, he’s like a dictator, he’s ruining democracy, he’s ruining the world and he’s funding genocide.
“He’s everything that I hate in the world at the minute.”
Johnny White described Trump as an “enabler of genocide” and called him a “fascist.”
“I just think we shouldn’t be as friendly and as welcoming to him. We’re only welcoming him for financial reasons.”
“I’m here in solidarity with the world today because it might be great for the parish but it’s not great for the world,” said Laura Mulcahy.
Marine One has landed at Doonbeg Golf Resort. Shortly afterwards a motorcade - with President Trump presumably in one of the ‘Beast’ armoured cars - headed towards the hotel pic.twitter.com/YRG7iFKCCG
Shortly afterwards a motorcade - with President Trump presumably in one of the ‘Beast’ armoured cars - headed towards the hotel, reports Political Correspondent Cormac McQuinn .
The Marine One helicopter carrying US president Donald Trump has landed at Doonbeg Golf Club.
At Shannon Airport, Trump disembarked Air Force One, shook hands with ministers and waved to the cameras before hopping aboard Marine One, the presidential helicopter, for the journey to Doonbeg.
Gardaí await the arrival of US president Donald Trump at his golf resort in Doonbeg on day three of the Irish Open.
Firecrackers have been set off and a large US flag burnt by a group taking part in the Dublin protest, reports Climate and Science correspondent, Caroline O’Doherty .
While the main part of the crowd filled Molesworth Street and listened to songs of peace and protest from a platform erected outside the Dáil, a group called Anti-Imperialist Action staged their own action.
Dressed all in black and wearing masks and dark glasses, they unfurled the US flag and set it on fire before launching firecrackers into the air.
They chanted mainly against US troops in Shannon but also shouted repeatedly, “tiocfaidh ár lá”.
One of the group said they hid their identities “for security” and to avoid recognition by “Gardai and the far right”.
Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said, “at this time of very significant global challenge, Ireland seeks to promote our values of peace, neutrality, disarmament, upholding international rule of law and strengthening the pursuit of justice and the protection of human rights.
“The Irish peace process and the role of the United States in this are an example of successful diplomacy and foreign policy where the US has been a critical partner over three decades.
“We want to see president Trump apply the same approach to Palestine and promote a global agenda for peace.
“This means that the United States must stop arming Israel. The United States must stop facilitating the genocide of Palestinian people. Israel must no longer be allowed to act with impunity.
“We are absolutely prepared to offer our continued support and solidarity and to lend all our experience to this end.”
She also acknowledged Trump’s comments on the reunification of Ireland.
“The conversation on Irish unity has shifted and the onus is on the Taoiseach to begin planning.
