“We have secured peace and as we approach the thirtieth anniversary of the Good Friday Agreement our national journey is now reunification, which is organised, planned and a peaceful transition,” said McDonald.
Some spectators at the Irish Open have turned their attention from the sporting action to the helipad with President Trump expected shortly pic.twitter.com/n7qcoZGBtZ
Reporting from Doonbeg, Political Correspondent Cormac McQuinn , said some spectators at the Irish Open have turned their attention from the sporting acton to the the helipad with president Trump expected shortly.
A spokesperson for Taoiseach Micheál Martin said, president Trump’s comments on a United Ireland should come as a surprise to no one, reports Political Editor Pat Leahy .
Over the years the president has been consistent in his view that he sees unity in Ireland as the optimal outcome.
On the last two years in the White House he expressed this to the Taoiseach, and on Capitol Hill this year.
The Taoiseach told the president that he leads a party that supports Irish unity.
He also outlined the work of the Shared Island initiative and the importance of creating stronger communities and shared experiences on the island.
The Taoiseach highlighted Ireland’s significant experience in conflict resolution as a result of the peace process, and that this experience could be brought to bear in the Middle East or other conflict areas.
President Trump was very aware of how violent the conflict in Northern Ireland was, and of the importance of peace, said the spokesperson.
The Taoiseach paid tribute to successive US governments for their role in the peace process and in helping bring about the Good Friday Agreement.
The Taoiseach outlined the three sets of relationships that underpin the Good Friday Agreement; The British-Irish relationship, The North-South relationship and the relationship between the two traditions in the North.
He stressed that both the British and Irish governments working in tandem together was a key factor in bringing peace about.
Back in Dublin, Climate and Science correspondent Caroline O’Doherty has the latest from the protest which has now swelled to many hundreds of people stretching from O’Connell Street to Dawson Street.
It’s lively and loud but peaceful and an anticipated counter protest at the GPO did not materialise, she reports.
The marchers are chanting in support of Palestine and with demands for Trump to be jailed.
In recognition that Trump brushed off mention of protests earlier, saying he hadn’t seen any, marchers are seeking the ear of Government, chanting: “Micheál Martin, can you hear, we don’t want warmongers here.”
Irish Times photographer Bryan O’Brien captured Trump’s Air Force One flying in over Shannon before landing.
Trump’s Dublin departure was captured by the DAA with the authority only delighted to hand over responsibility to the folk down in Shannon.
President Trump has departed Dublin Airport after his short visit to the capital. Over to you @ShannonAirport ✈️ 🇺🇸 🇮🇪 pic.twitter.com/Qlk3jQwdF4
Back to Clare for now where we are still waiting for Trump to land in Shannon but something quite dramatic has just happened.
Air Force One has done a fly-by of President Donald Trump’s golf resort at Doonbeg en route to Shannon Airport. Trump is due at the Irish Open tournament later this afternoon pic.twitter.com/YMIXbvzw2p
The Taoiseach Micheal Martin and the Government should capitalise on President Donald Trump’s wish for an eventual united Ireland by using the comment to pressurise the British government to be explicit about the criteria for when a Border poll can be held, Aontu leader Peadar Toibin has urged.
Gerry Moriarty i s at the party’s think-in in Derry and reports that Tobin said he understands “that Trump makes comments off the cuff on a regular basis but first of all most of the progress we have made as a country in terms of independence has been with the help of Irish-America.”
He said he was in no doubt that the comments “are aimed at Irish-America as well with eight weeks to the mid-terms. But it is significant that we have an American president making this intervention now and I think that if I was in the Irish government I would use a little of the momentum created by this statement to try to engage with the British in terms, at the very least, of crystallising what exactly is the threshold for a referendum to be called.”
Under the 1998 Belfast Agreement it is for a British Northern Secretary to determine when and if a Border poll should be called although it is not exactly clear what specifically are the criteria for calling such a plebiscite. Last month Andy Burnham on his first visit to Northern Ireland upset nationalists by saying a Border poll was “off the table”.
Toibin said the “major disingenuous element” of the British approach to the issue was “keeping that threshold opaque”.
He said the government in the wake of Trump’s remarks should pursue this issue with the British Labour government because if Kemi Badenoch or Nigel Farage ended up as British prime minister it was unlikely such clarity would be provided.
“The British are reneging on their responsibilities to an international treaty not to crystallise what that threshold is. We should be using Trump’s response as a platform to push harder in relation to that,” “added Toibin.
People are continuing to gather in Dublin for a protest against the visit of Donald Trump. More than 1,000 people have gathered at the Garden of Remembrance and are marching down O’Connell St in the direction of the Dail.
The crowd is stretching from the Garden of Remembrance to the GP0.
According to the news wires this was one of the key chants. “Donald Trump, can you hear? We don’t want you here.” I can’t help but think they might have workshopped that a bit more. Rhyming hear with here is pretty poor, whatever about the actual sentiment. It is awful You just can’t rhyme hear with here.
Caroline O’Doherty has just been on to say the chant has been changed to: “Say it loud, say it clear. Donald Trump’s not welcome here.”
President Donald Trump’s comments in support of a united Ireland have reached the SDLP conference in Belfast.
Northern Editor Freya McClements reports that in her speech to the conference, SDLP leader Claire Hanna acknowledged the US President’s presence on the island and reassured delegates “don’t worry, we’ve checked. He’s not coming here. It’s his turn to boycott us.
"It turns out that he isn’t as orange as he looks." SDLP leader @ClaireHanna reacts to Trump's comments on Irish unity. "I'm not sure if anybody has checked on the DUP. I suspect they're burning those Trump flags as we speak." pic.twitter.com/2IEcohIviv
“Donald Trump, in the last hour, has announced that he is in favour of united Ireland,” she said. “Turns out he’s not as orange as he looks,” she said, in an allusion to the Orange Order, to laughter from those listening.
“I’m not sure if anybody’s checked on the DUP,” she said. “I suspect they’re burning those Trump flags as we speak.”
Trump’s comments underlined “as clearly as anything that change is happening, whether some parties here want to acknowledge it or not,” she said, in a reference to Northern Ireland’s unionist parties.
In a speech in which she emphasised her party’s commitment to Irish unity, Hanna said it was “becoming clearer by the day that the future of this island is changing” and “more and more people are talking about our constitutional future.
“Don’t just take it from me, take it from the leader of the free world,” she said.
Always liked him https://t.co/gXjFoQjD2J
Several hundred people have gathered at the Garden of Remembrance in Dublin for a protest against the visit of Donald Trump.
Groups represented include the Irish Anti-War Movement, Ireland Palestine Solidarity Committee, Militant Left, the Green Party and Palestine Action but many non-affiliated protestors have also gathered, writes Caroline O’Doherty.
Claire Doherty from Dublin said she came to join in because: “There’s no point sitting at home giving out.”
She said she was not just protesting against Trump but at his “enablers”.
“What’s coming behind him is worse,” she, fearing that future Republican administrations may accelerate Trump policies.
The protestors are due to march through Dublin city centre to the Dáil.
The president Catherine Connolly has issued a statement outlining what was said at her meeting with the US president.
“As President of Ireland, I am very conscious that Ireland and the United States of America are bound by strong ties. This is a deep connection, built over centuries, which allows us to speak openly to one another.
We are in a world facing the existential threat posed by war and climate change, both of which are inextricably interlinked.
I conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted.
As a country which has suffered famine, colonisation and the violence of the Troubles, but also the importance of the long and challenging road to peace, I emphasised the unique insight which Irish people can bring to the resolution of conflict.
I highlighted to President Trump the strong commitment which the Irish people have to international relations, to the importance of the United Nations, including the pride which Irish people feel in Ireland’s contribution to UN Peacekeeping since 1958, and to the obligations contained within Article 29 of our Constitution towards the peaceful resolution of international disputes."
I assured President Trump that the Irish people would strongly support all those who have the strength to build a shared peace in all those parts of the world currently suffering from such horrific war and violence.”
During his speech in Deerfield House, Trump went through some of his greatest hits including the “rigged” 2020 presidential election, the failings of Joe Biden, immigration and how he has single handedly made America great again.
“We had a rigged election, as you know, because I won three times. I didn’t win twice. I won three times,” he said.
He also boasted about the power of the US army and its laser weapons. He mentioned lasers quite a few times.
He also told the gathering that the US would become the number one supplier of oil and natural gas in the world. .“We’re bigger than Saudi Arabia now,” he claimed. “Saudi Arabia and Russia combined,” he said.
On Venezuela he said the US had “won the war. We worked it very well with the people that are now running it and millions and millions of barrels of oil every single day.”
And he talked about migrants coming into the US in the most disparaging of terms.
The unionist parties in Northern Ireland have strongly criticised President Trump’s comments in support of a united Ireland, writes Northern Editor Freya McClements.
The DUP leader, Gavin Robinson, said Northern Ireland’s constitutional future “will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.
“As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic,” he said.
The deputy leader of the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), Robbie Butler, said “Presidents are entitled to their views” but “they don’t get a vote in Northern Ireland” and accused those “now cheering him” of “cherry picking.
“One sentence about a united Ireland and he is apparently a statesman of rare vision,” he said, adding that under the Belfast Agreement the people of Northern Ireland were “the only people whose consent counts.”
The leader of the Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV), Jim Allister, said Trump was “not the first US president to meddle in affairs which don’t concern him.
“You attend to your own affairs and we will attend to ours.
“Northern Ireland is not a pawn in Trump’s fall out with the UK. Our constitutional future does not depend on him or any other foreign dignitary,” he said.
President Donald Trump’s declaration that he “would love to see” a united Ireland and that he believes it will be established eventually has been criticised by Unionist politicians.
Mark Hennessy r eports that Ulster Unionist Stormont minister, Robbie Butler said US presidents “are entitled to their views, but they don’t get a vote in Northern Ireland”, since this remains a matter for voters in Northern Ireland.
“I note the sudden conversion. For years we have been told this President is beyond the pale: his character, his conduct, his position on Gaza. Some of those now cheering him boycotted the White House over it.
Mocking the support by pro-unity individuals on social media, Butler said: “One sentence about a united Ireland and he is apparently a statesman of rare vision. It seems his judgement is sound only on the one subject where it happens to suit.
“The cherry picking is at least consistent. Principle is a funny thing when it changes according to whether you like the words being spoken,” said Butler, who serves as Stormont’s Minister for Health.
“The President was at least candid enough to accept that the United Kingdom would have something to say about it. So would the people of Northern Ireland, who under the Belfast Agreement are the only people whose consent counts.”
Former Ulster Unionist leader Doug Beattie said Trump “also wants the Gulf of Mexico called Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America, if Trump is anyone’s measurement on a United Ireland I’d say the Union is safe”.
However, Alliance Stormont MLA, Stewart Dickson mocked the previous efforts made by Unionists to curry favour with Trump during St. Patrick’s Day visits to the White House: “So, this is what Unionist get for sucking up to him.”
The British ‌Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s position on Irish ‌unification remains unchanged, a spokesperson for his ​office said this morning.
Responding to questions from ‌MPson Wednesday about a possible border ⁠poll ​in Northern Ireland, Burnham ​said: “I am not aware ‌that there is ​majority public support for another referendum, ⁠and until ⁠that ​changes, there will not be one.”
A spokesperson for Burnham’s office said on Saturday the prime minister’s remarks still stood after ‌Trump told ⁠reporters after a meeting with the Taioseach Micheal ‌Martin in Dublin that unification would ​happen eventually and would be a “great” thing.
We will come back to the speech - which was clearly intended for his domestic audience, there won’t have been many in the audience who care too much about crime rates in Washington DC - in a bit but right now the motorcade is heading through the Phoenix Park towards the Infirmary Rd entrance after which he will go straight on to the M50 and then on to Dublin Airport. Once they he will fly to Doonbeg which is probably where he wants to be.
Trump has finished speaking and there is a lot to parse.
He finished with a bit about Ireland that probably has most relevance.
“This country is a fantastic it’s just a fantastic place. I love it. I have investments here but that’s not why I love it I like it because it’s special people you have unbelievable people in Ireland.”
He hailed the hospitality of Irish people
“You know they say you can’t generalise about groups of people, countries, but you can. People love coming to Ireland. You know why? Because they love you. They love the people.There’s a friendliness.
“There’s also a viciousness and a toughness. Let me tell you you are some of the most vicious bastards... but when you want to be nice there is nobody nicer.”
Earlier in the speech he said the Irish unity would be “a cool thing” which might have been his way of rowing back his comments earlier when he said it would be “a great thing”.
Donald Trump is speaking at the US ambassadors residence right now.
He has covered Kamala Harris’s failings, military successes and the stunning economic recovery he has been responsible.
He is also talking about oil and how much " there is oil popping up" all over Venezuela.
Protesters who have gathered in Doonbeg have accused US President Donald Trump of supporting genocide in Gaza and of “disrespect for women.
Cormac McQuinn reports that by mid-morning a group of fewer than 20 protesters had gathered in the Co Clare village near Trump’s golf resort where the Irish Open tournament is being held.
Trump is due to arrive at the golf course by helicopter from Shannon Airport later today.
Sarah Clancy took part in the Global Samud Floatilla aiming to bring aid to Gaza last year before they were detained by Israeli authorities.
She said she is a community worker in Clare “so I just didn’t want to leave it that the person who is funding and arming and fomenting all of this warfare would come unremarked”.
Clancy said demonstration is “not a protest about the people of Doonbeg” adding: “It’s very strong in my mind that we have seen village after village in Gaza, villages just like this wiped out, people murdered or forced to move over and over again, villages just the size of Doonbeg”.
She said that war “could have been stopped at any single point during that war if Donald Trump acted to say he was withdrawing funding or arms for Israel.”
Clancy argued: “the people in Ireland do not want this visit from Trump. We don’t like him, we don’t want him here”.
She added: “we really want no part of this. It’s vulgar and also he’s causing authoritarian toxicity all over the world at the momemnt. And so I’m delighted to be here even if it makes me a little bit unpopular where I live and work.”
Another protester Caolann O’Dwyer said: “I’m here because when I want to think about this in the future I want to know that I was on the right side of things.
“I don’t want Ireland to be a place that just accepts and welcomes someone with open arms who actively is supporting genocide”.
Grainne Carr, who was holding sign that read “Stop Killing Children” said “I’m here because I feel that Ireland shouldn’t be supporting people who are contributing to genocide in other countries. I’m here because I feel there’s far too much taxpayers’ money going to safeguard and provide security for a man who is supporting genocide, supporting child murder and I think it’s entirely wrong.”
Jessie Phillips, originally from the US, but living in Co Clare said she was protesting: “Because I just want my opinion out there about Trump. It’s not positive.
“I still have family over there obviously. We moved here, we’ve been living here for seven years.
“I still pay my taxes over there and I just don’t like anything he represents, the wars and what he’s done to the economy, his disrespect for women and I have two grown daughters over there and my grandchildren are growing up over there and it just makes me sick.
“So I just want to be able to say how I feel about him.”
A spokesman for Taoiseach Micheál Martin has been asked if Trump’s comments about a united Ireland would make any difference to Government policy. “No, our Good Friday Agreement and Programme for Government commitments remain,” was the somewhat terse response.
The US President Donald Trump also covered a range of other topics during his Farmleigh press conference and expressed optimism about resolving a trade war with Canada.
He told reporters that a deal could come “fairly soon”.
He was asked Saturday whether he intended to have the US leave the US-Mexico-Canada Trade Agreement but womdered if right here right now was the best time to ask such a question.
He did say that Canada wanted to reach a deal with Washington and that he was seeking better terms for US farmers.
“Canada has to treat our farmers better, and they can’t charge our farmers tariffs. They’re charging our farmers 400 per cent tariffs and many other things, so when those things go away, they’re willing to get rid of it all. You’ll probably see a deal with Canada fairly soon.”
The third event of the morning is about to get underway at Deerfield House in the Phoenix Park
The Taoiseach has arrived and is exchanging pleasantries with Dermot Desmond and the Irish ambassador to the US, Geraldine Byrne Nason, reports Jack Horgan-Jones, who will be our man on the ground for the next part of the visit.
Trump was pressed on the nature of his conversation with Connolly and the questioning prompted the US Chief of Protocol Monica Crowley to step in briefly.
“The President had a very constructive conversation with President Connolly today about a whole range of issues including energy and European supplies of energy.”
Nessun Dorma was playing as the Beast pulled into Deerfield House, reports Jack Horgan-Jones . “We will be waiting another little while before Trump joins the reception - word is he is having a round-table inside with some VVVIPs from the business world beforehand.”
Trump is now on the way to Deerfield House where he is to deliver a speech to hundreds of politicians and business people and other invited guests.
We will have more on that extraordinary press conference presently.
Trump and Martin have just finished their press conference and it was longer than expected. And it was certainly freewheeling.
Trump said the conflict in Gaza was not the main thing on the agenda any more after he had “put out the fires”. He also suggested Iran was two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon when the war started in February and he said he would “love to see” a united Ireland and suggested it would “happen eventually”.
The Taoiseach started by referencing 9/11 and said Ireland was “thinking of all Americans”. He highlighted the “deep impact” the terror attacks had in Ireland.
He said he was “particularly pleased” that Trump made it over for the Irish Open.
Referencing the economic relationship between the two countries he said Trump would “meet hundreds of Irish business people who have investments in America, who are employing American people”.
He acknowledged the numbers of people employed by American companies here but stressed that “they get access to the European market from their bases here and the Asian market and they do particularly well, so it’s a very strong, old relationship”.
Trump said the Irish Open was “a very big event in Ireland and frankly all over the world” and he talked about the role he played in developing the golf course.
He said the war in Iran would be over soon and said Iran was “ trying to hold out as long as they can to complicate the election but I think people are wise to it because Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. It’s very simple, this is a very simple thing Iran cannot have.”
He claimed Iran was “ two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon [and] if they had it they would have blown up Israel, they would have blown up the Middle East.”
He said they would have targeted Europe too.
When asked how he responded to suggestions that the US was facilitating genocide in Gaza and also facilitating Israel around the illegal occupation of territories in the West Bank he said “ we put out the fire and we got all the hostages back. There’s very little happening right now in Gaza. That’s not the place that people are talking about actually.”
He was also asked about protests in Ireland today and said “I didn’t know there was a [protest] . It can’t be a very big one because we’ve been all over Ireland today already , it’s early in the morning… but I haven’t seen any protest, It’s a friendly protest.”
He said he had “ a very nice meeting ” with Catherine Connolly. “We had very respectful meeting.”
And then there was Northern Ireland. “I always find it to be a very interesting and we had a very interesting discussion”.
He was asked for his view on Irish unity.
“I’d love to see it unified. It is going to happen eventually. You have the right man over here to get it moving,” he said, gesturing to Martin “I think it would be a fantastic thing, I think the UK would have something to say about it but I think it would be a great thing. How could it be bad?”
He also suggested that a united Ireland would be “ a feather in everyone’s cap”.
Trump has now arrived at Farmleigh and a bugler from the Irish Defence Forces school of music is standing by to greet him.
He shook hands with the Taoiseach Micheál Martin (and it has to be said it was a good long handshake, close to 10 seconds by our reckoning).
The Taoiseach and his wife Mary have now gone into Farmleigh House with Trump who has been followed by his entourage.
Trump has now left Áras an Uachtaráin and he is heading to Farmleigh. If our knowledge of the geography of the park is anything to go by, he should be there in less than three minutes.
The US president stopped briefly for questions before entering the Beast.
When asked about the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, he replied: “Everything will work out fine.”
Trump deflected when asked about Irish consumers paying high prices for home heating oil, replying: “If they open the North Sea it will help, but they haven’t done that.”
He did not respond when asked how his meeting with President Connolly went.
That's a wrap on the Áras an Uachtaráin leg of Trump's visit. He stops briefly for questions before leaving in the Beast. pic.twitter.com/rq5gRbk6XX
The meeting between Connolly and Trump seems to be running longer than expected. The Beast is ready to go with the engine running but no sign of Trump, James Cox reports.
So, the courtesy call between the two presidents is ongoing and a few hundred metres away at Farmleigh House the Taoiseach Micheál Martin is standing by. That meeting is likely to be short enough and after that Trump heads across the road to the US ambassador’s residence where he will deliver a speech. Apparently we are running 10 minutes behind schedule as of now. But, and I can’t stress this enough, Trump has not started speaking publicly yet. His speeches are known to go on a bit so that could throw the schedule off by a bit. We will wait and see.
Members of Trump’s family have arrived as have the Secret Service. And just now the US president has pulled up and the meeting is getting underway.
The US president arrived and briefly shook hands with our president and then they disappeared from view.
It all seemed pretty friendly. The rest of the entourage - including Don Jr and his family - are right now standing outside the Áras. Thank heavens it’s not lashing.
Donald Trump had arrived at Áras an Uachtaráin pic.twitter.com/Cq3WfrgLpw
Time for the national anthems now, staring with the American one. You might be interested to read that Natalie Harp is on the red carpet alongside the Trump family.
Amhrán na bhFiann has just been played and at a fair old clip it must be said. We’ll have a clip of that presently.
Just by way of a quick update, Trump’s motorcade has arrived at Áras an Uachtaráin. He made it from Dublin Airport to the park in less than 20 minutes, surely some class of record?
Simon Harris has been speaking out at Dublin Airport. He said he was “pleased to be here on behalf of the Irish government to welcome the president of the United states and also some of his family”.
He said he had talked briefly to Trump”at the foot of Air Force One [and] we had an opportunity to recall previous conversations we had. Indeed I had phoned President Trump on his election as president of the United states.
“He’s very much looking forward to getting to Doonbeg. He’s a man who obviously loves golf and he’s very proud of his Doonbeg golf course and is looking forward to getting down there.
Harris said he was “also conscious of my conversation with the president and indeed his daughter in law that this the president’s grandchildren’s first time in Ireland and I know there’s great personal excitement in relation to that.”
He said that “alongside the politics, alongside some of that pageantry of a US President arriving in Ireland there’s also the a reminder of those deep interpersonal links between our two countries.
He added that as “finance minister I’m very conscious of the economic benefit of the relationship. Hundreds of thousands of people in this country are employed in US firms [and] people in every single state in the United states are employed in Irish owned firms and that two way bilateral relationship matters [and] transcends any individual office holder.”
So what is going to happen next? Well Trump will be in the Phoenix Park shortly and will be greeted outside Áras an Uachtaráin by the president Catherine Connolly.
There will be a few moments for video and pics after which the two presidents will go inside for a brief conversation - that is expected to last no more than 10 minutes.
Interestingly, there will be no video record of that meeting and we will have to wait for around 90 minutes for a statement to be issued outlining what was said.
A crowd gathered from the early hours at a nearby viewpoint to get a glimpse of Air Force One’s landing, reports Jack White.
Trump travelled to Ireland on the controversially gifted luxury $400 million Boeing 747-8 that was given by the Qatari royal family.
Before the new plane came into use in July, two Boeing 747s had been used since the 1990s to transport US presidents, one of which landed at Dublin Airport shortly before the new aircraft, with Trump saying they were “pretty old”.
The red, white and blue jet is serving as an interim Air Force One aircraft until new Boeings, which have faced long delays and are not expected to be delivered until after Trump’s term ends, are delivered for US presidential use.
The gifted jet was hastily retrofitted at a cost at a cost believed to be in the hundreds of millions.
Unveiling the retrofitted plane in June, he said it was “considered the world’s most luxurious plane. When it was built, it was built at a level that will probably never be seen again,” he said.
Trump’s arrival to Ireland onboard the jet marks the aircraft’s second international flight since Trump began using it on July 1st, after he travelled to a Nato summit in Turkey in July.
However, he did not depart Turkey on the aircraft due to intelligence received on a potential threat from Iran.
The new jet lacks the defensive countermeasures, such as advanced antimissile capabilities, that are typical of other Air Force One jets, the New York Times previously reported.
Trump recently told reporters the aircraft is going to be taken out of service for security upgrades.
The US media broadcasting from the Phoenix Park have just been heard describing the Trump visit to Dublin as a “brief swing-by” with the main focus being his golf tournament.
Trump has disembarked the plane and has been greeted by the Tánaiste Simon Harris and Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee.
He was then given a quick Captain’s Escort of Honour from the Irish Defence Forces before hopping into the Beast ahead of a quick spin to the Áras.
Footage from the airport suggests that he is travelling via motorcade. He will travel down the M50. We can only hope it s not its usual carpark.
Trump being greeted to Ireland by Tánaiste Simon Harris and Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee pic.twitter.com/bVnCzfQGGD
Just ahead of Trump making his first appearance on the steps of Airforce One, it might be worth recalling a previous visit he made to Ireland, way back in 2014 when he came to have a look at his new golf course in Clare. It was then, is now and always will be mortifying for all concerned.
The US president Donald Trump’s plane has landed in Dublin Airport ahead of his two (ish) day visit to Ireland.
Air Force One has landed pic.twitter.com/h2VsRZh7zJ
We have Jack White out in Dublin Airport and he is reporting that Air Force One is on its final approach now.
We have list of the confirmed delegations for the Áras an Uachtaráin reception from James Cox.
Irish Delegation: Orla O’Hanrahan, Secretary General to the President; Geraldine Byrne-Nason, Irish ambassador to the US, Beibhinn O’Connor, adviser to the President; George Burke, Deputy Secretary General; Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly; Lieutenant General Rossa Mulcahy, chief of staff, Defence Forces.
US Delegation: Edward Walsh, ambassador to the US; Lynn Walsh, wife of ambassador to the US; Richard Walters, assistant to the President and WH deputy chief of staff; Daniel Scavino, assistant to the President and WH deputy chief of staff; Donald Trump Jr; Bettina Anderson, Donald Trump Jr’s wife; Donald Trump III (17), grandson; Spencer Trump (13), grandson; Chloe Trump (12), granddaughter
The DAA - the authority that runs Dublin Airport - has just said the US president Donald Trump will be landing in the next couple of minutes.
Donald Trump is expected to land at Dublin Airport soon pic.twitter.com/XiFZZdGK8E
Probably not as many as you think. While many people here like to talk up Ireland’s very special relationship with the US, only eight presidents have come here while they were resident in the White House.
The first, of course, was John F Kennedy who came to the auld sod in June 1963. He spent four triumphant days travelling the country visiting Dublin, Wexford – from whence his family came – Cork, Galway and Limerick. He also became the first US president to address the joint houses of the Oireachtas.
Richard Nixon came here on a State visit in 1970, stopping off in Dublin, Limerick and Timahoe. It was a decidedly less celebratory affair for many reasons.
Then, in 1984 it was the turn of another Republican, Ronald Reagon. He came in June 1984 and as well as Dublin visited Galway and Ballyporeen where his roots were said to rest. He also addressed the Oireachtas.
Bill Clinton - riding on the crest of the Peace Process wave - came on three separate occasions. He was here for the first time in December 1995 and then again in September 1998 and for the third and final time as president in 2000.
George W Bush was in Ireland twice while in the White House. He flew into Shannon and travelled to Dromoland Castle for an EU-US summit in June 2004 and then popped in in February 2006 to meet US troops in Shannon.
Barack Obama’s visit in May 2011 had much more of a celebratory feel to it. He visited Dublin and Moneygall, from whence his great-great-great-grandfather came.
Donald Trump was here once before - back in 2019. It was a flying visit then too and equally focused on golf. He stayed for one night only, again at Doonbeg.
And then there was Joe Biden. He came to Ireland in April 2023 and it had a homecoming feel akin to Kennedy’s visit 60 years earlier. He visited Dublin and Louth, addressed the Oireachtas. He also went to Mayo where he talked about the Saw Doctors and expressed his hope that Sam would one day be coming home.
As you might expect, there will be rolling road closures near Dublin Airport and Phoenix Park today as well as around Shannon Airport on Saturday afternoon and Sunday evening.
The airports will remain open throughout the visit but those travelling have been advised to allow extra time for their journeys.
Access to the areas of Doonbeg village, Trump’s hotel and the “wider west Clare environs will be restricted” for much of today and tomorrow.
There will be “no tolerance” for public disorder or attempts to impair US president Donald Trump’s movements during his visit to Ireland the Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly has said, with water cannons deployed if necessary.
Speaking to the press yesterday he described the visit, which has been declared an “extraordinary event” by An Garda Síochána, as one of the biggest policing and security operations “in the history of the State”.
Kelly said it “goes without saying” there would be protests during Trump’s visit, adding that “most people” are expected to do so in a peaceful way.
“On the flipside of that, we have invested extensively over the last number of years, particularly since the Dublin riots, in equipment around public order,” he said.
“We will have water cannon on standby for this weekend,” he said. “We hope we don’t have to utilise that, but if we need to, that’s what we have it for.” Two water cannons were bought by the force in the wake of the 2023 Dublin riots.
Kelly said gardaí were doing “everything we can to minimise disruption to the public but during a visit such as this, it is inevitable. So I would ask for people’s patience this weekend, particularly in Dublin and Clare.”
We have a guestlist of sorts for the Deerfield House event.
It has been “gleaned from the names on the seats set up facing the rostrum,” reports Jack Horgan-Jones .
Alongside those who you would expect - like Micheál Martin and former Taoisigh Enda Kenny and Bertie Ahern - there will be Denis O’Brien and Dermot Desmond and Michael O’Leary and builder Sean Mulryan.
Other names on the backs of seats include Michael Flatley, former Tánaiste Simon Coveney, Irish ambassador to the US Geraldine Byrne Nason and former cabinet minister Mary Hanafin.
There are also seats for the Secretarys General of the Departments of Defence, of Transport, of Enterprise, Foreign Affairs and of Energy, and Lt General Rossa Mulcahy Chief of Staff of the Defence Forces
Eddie Hobbs has a seat, as does Niamh Uí Bhriain of Gript.ie and conservative activist Laoise de Brún.
There there are ambassadors from other countries and figures from companies including Meta, Amazon, Google, Ornua, Intercom, Glanbia, Stripe, Coca Cola, Amgen and Diageo.
I am writing this Live Story from just outside the Phoenix Park so I am in a position to offer a fairly reliable weather update. The grim and grey start to the morning has been replaced by blue skies over Dublin with Air Force One around 90 minutes from the city.
We have more from Jack Horgan-Jones in the Phoenix Park.
“We have our first TD. And it’s Cork East’s James O’Connor (Fianna Fáil), who is pressing the flesh already as the first bus of proper guests seems to have arrived.
“And he’s joined from Seanad Éireann by Gerard Craughwell. Well done James and Gerard.
“Update on the music: they are now test running the introduction of US ambassador Edward S. Walsh, and we can reveal his entrance music will be ‘God Bless the USA’ (Also known as “Proud to be an American”, the 1984 classic from Country & Western star Lee Greenwood).
One of the advantages of confining Trump’s events in Dublin to the Phoenix Park is how easy - comparatively - it has been to shut it off to protestors. And it has been widely accepted and advertised that there will be protests today.
The entire park has been closed to the public since Thursday night and no-one is being allowed in either on foot or in cars.
That has seen the biggest of the Dublin protests scheduled for the city centre for lunchtime.
The Irish Neutrality League’s No Welcome for Trump protest will start at the Garden of Remembrance in Dublin city at 1pm, with protesters set to march down O’Connell Street and towards the Dáil. Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday, Irish Neutrality League convener Sara O’Rourke said the group hopes thousands of people will turn out.
Our man in the Park (one of them) is Jack Horgan-Jones and he was up before dawn’s early light to get the best of the seats at Deerfield House.
“You couldn’t quite call it a crowd yet at the US ambassador’s Phoenix Park residence, but there’s at least a growing gaggle of officials and journalists mustering before the reception for Donald Trump, who is expected here around 11am.
“We also spotted Eddie Hobbs at one point. There’s a stiff breeze testing the large marquee set up in the garden for guests, where a rostrum has been set up for himself to speechify from later. And as we write this, they are testing the sound system… and yes, that is the opening bars of YMCA reaching our ears.”
The White House Press Pool is covering the visit from the American side and we have a breakdown of Trump’s time in Ireland (the capital letters are all theirs).
9:10 AM: THE PRESIDENT participates in an Arrival Ceremony
9:20 AM: THE PRESIDENT participates in a Courtesy Call with the President of Ireland Áras an Uachtaráin.
10:10 AM: THE PRESIDENT participates in a Bilateral Meeting with the Taoiseach of Ireland Farmleigh House
11:35 AM: THE PRESIDENT delivers Remarks to US Embassy Personnel and Business Leaders Deerfield Residence
(At this point the precise timings stop, presumably because no-one has a notion how long the aforementioned “remarks” will take.
THE PRESIDENT departs Dublin, Ireland en route Doonbeg, Ireland
THE PRESIDENT attends the 2026 Amgen Irish Open Doonbeg,
This weekend promises to be like no other with the US president Donald Trump arriving for a two-day visit to Ireland that – it is safe to say – is not universally popular.
One of the Air Force Ones – the new one, we are told - will be touching down in Dublin in couple of hours, with Trump set to be greeted by the Tánaiste Simon Harris at what promises to be a grey, damp and blustery Dublin Airport.
He will then be whisked away in a motorcade to the Phoenix Park before 9.30am where a busy (ish) morning awaits.
First he will meet the President Catherine Connolly, a fierce critic of Trump in the past and not just because he once mistakenly referred to her as a man.
After what might be a frosty enough courtesy call, he will make the short journey to Farmleigh House to meet the Taoiseach Micheál Martin, after which he will pop in to Deerfield House where the US ambassador Edward Walsh lives.
The marquee is already up there and crowds are gathering (but more of that anon).
From the Park he will travel to Shannon and then on to his golf course at Doonbeg, where he will stay overnight, before watching more golf on Sunday ahead of his return to Washington.
And that should be that. Nice and calm. No drama.

title: Jessica Harrington beats the odds with Champion success for Hotazhell
description: Saffie Osborne becomes first woman to ride an English classic winner as Highwayman leads Joseph O’Brien 1-2 in St Leger
content:
Jessica Harrington ha defied the odds so many times during her groundbreaking career, but rarely as spectacularly as her 50/1 shot Hotazhell landing the Royal Bahrain Irish Champion Stakes at Leopardstown .
Having won almost every big National Hunt race since starting her career almost 40 years ago, the 79-year-old trainer from Moone, Co Kildare has transformed herself into a major player at elite level on the flat over the last decade.
That status was underlined in remarkable style in the €1.25 million highlight of the first leg of the 13th Irish Champions Festival.
Ignored by punters, Hotazhell and Shane Foley plotted a dramatic route through one of the deepest Group One fields of the year to hold the 33/1 Wimbledon Hawkeye by the minimum margin of a nose in a desperate finish. The 11/8 favourite Constitution River was third.
“I know he was an outsider, but I knew he was better than that and I dared to hope,” said Harrington.
However, there was a sting in the tail for Foley, whose stretch drive saw him pick up an 11-day suspension for carless riding. It was his third similar riding offence in the last six months.
Despite Hotazhell’s SP, Harrington was a popular winner less than 90 minutes after a groundbreaking moment at Doncaster.
A new page was turned in the 250-year history of the Betfred St Leger as Saffie Osborne became the first woman to ride the winner of an English classic.
The 24-year-old daughter of trainer Jamie Osborne struck on Joseph O’Brien’s Leger second-strong Highwayman, an 11/1 shot, who proved two-and-a-half lengths too good for his stable companion Enceladus. Aidan O’Brien’s 22/1 outsider Amelia Earhart filled the frame.
Largely dwarfed in profile terms by Leopardstown’s leg of the Irish Champions Festival, the old race conspired to serve up a milestone for the sport. O’Brien was at Leopardstown, although it hardly mattered as Osborne was firmly centre stage.
It was a first Group One success for the Englishwoman, whose services were snapped up the previous Monday. The glut of top-flight racing had O’Brien scrambling for options. Billy Loughnand got the prized spin on Enceladus but it was ultimately Osborne’s day.
“I don’t think I’ve ever been speechless in my life, and I didn’t have this on the bingo card for this week,” said Osborne. “I didn’t have a ride in the race on Monday morning, let alone one with a chance, and I can’t thank so many people enough.
“Firstly, Joseph and his team for putting their faith in me, it won’t change Joseph’s life, but it will change mine. My agent Tony Hind, I would be nowhere without him, and I know it’s cliched but my mum, dad and whole family.
“This means the absolute world. As I crossed the line, I was in shock. I just can’t believe it and it just doesn’t feel real. I was more forward than I anticipated, but he was travelling so well into it, I couldn’t believe it.”
Rachael Blackmore enjoyed a pioneering riding career over jumps, but Osborne is joining select company. It’s four years since Hollie Doyle won the French Oaks on Nashwa. In 1993, Julie Krone landed the final leg of the US Triple Crown, the Belmont Stakes, on Colonial Affair.
Harrington has been a trailblazing figure for longer than all that, and her readiness to dream big paid off in spectacular style once again.
Hotazhell, a Group One winning juvenile as a two-year-old, endured a blank 2025, including finishing fourth to Delacroix in last season’s Irish Champion Stakes. He only regained wining form in a Group One in Munich in July.
Any snootiness about German form got blown out of the water on home ground as he defined the odds with grit to match his speed under a determined Foley.
“I didn’t think he deserved to be 50-1,” said Harrington. “He’d won a Group One in Germany last time and came here in good form. If you look up all his form from last year it was on ground that was too quick for him. He kept on trying, he got his conditions today and he went and did it.
“Shane is very strong, but the horse is very tough. He knows where the winning post is and he put his head down on the line.”
Foley’s ride was penalised by the stewards after appearing to lean into Oisin Murphy, who was trying to launch a run on A Boy Name Susie outside the furlong pole. A concertina effect looked to result in the Ballydoyle pair, Hawk Mountain and Lambourn, being snatched up. A Boy Named Susie also looked to suffer interference closer to home.
The big disappointment of the race was Item, winner of the Juddmonte International, who never looked at ease on his first trip outside of Britain, failing to land a blow in sixth.
It was an unexpected reverse for Colin Keane, who still enjoyed a lucrative 32nd birthday with another Group One victory on Blue Bolt in the Coolmore Matron Stakes. He also landed the day’s opener on another Juddmonte filly, Maire Rua.
“It was an easy watch to be honest,” trainer Andrew Balding said of his odds-on winner. “You just have a little bit of jitters when you’re expected to win but, watching the race, we never really had an anxious moment. Colin was always in the right place. It was run at a true gallop and she looked very good.”
English jockey James Doyle was also on the double, first aboard Quddwah in the Group Two Sononaway Stakes and made all to score for Godolphin on the supplemented Arabian Crown in the Group Three Kilternan Stakes. Keane could finish only third on Purview. Maire Rua’s trainer Ger Lyons quickly followed up with Krasimir in a handicap.
Classic colts such as Auguste Rodin and Australia have won the big juvenile contest on Day One of the Irish Champions Festival on route to Derby glory at Epsom and Darkness Falls is a new 7/1 favourite for English racing’s ‘Blue Riband’ after beating his HKJC Golden Fleece Stakes by over four lengths.
Newly promoted to Group One status, and lengthened to nine-furlongs, the stamina test looked ideal for Darkness Falls who justified strong market support as an evens favourite. The impact was such that even the inscrutable Ryan Moore admitted to loving him.
“Ryan said the trip is going to be no problem, a mile and he’s going to get a mile-and-a-quarter next year. He’s just has a lot of class,” said Aidan O’Brien.
“It’s an unbelievable race to have on here at this time. It’s a lovely first running of it. It’s going to be a very important race and all the good horses were there, all the good type middle-distance horses.
“It’ll be hard for a classier Derby-type horse to come out than this, the way he did it the last day and the way he did that today. It was a proper gallop, there was nowhere to hide out there. He has a lovely nature, which makes him really special. He’s very exciting,” he added.
The official attendance at Leopardstown for the opening day of the Irish Champions Festival was 11,516, marginally up on last year’s corresponding figure of 11,354.

title: Mark English reaches 800m final in emphatic style at Ultimate Championship
description: Huge pay-day on offer in Sunday’s final in Budapest
content:
Another magnificently timed effort by Mark English secured him a spot in the men’s 800m final at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, winning his semi-final in 1:43.74.
Just as he did when winning the European title in Birmingham last month, the Donegal athlete bided his time to the last 100m before unleashing his finishing kick to take the win.
The top four from both semi-finals progressed to Sunday’s final (6.41pm), with $150,000 on offer to the winner as part of an $10-million purse across the weekend.
Running in the second semi-final, English was in complete control as he kicked past three rivals down the homestretch. Italy’s Francesco Perncici held on for second in 1:43.80, with Canada’s Marco Arop third and Algeria’s Djamel Sedjati fourth.
“This year is one of big progression for me,” English said afterwards. “I have never made a final before on the global stage, that is why everything from this moment onwards is going to be bonus territory.
“It’s a big stepping stone for me, because the quality of the 800m has skyrocketed through the roof. Thankfully it worked out nicely today and I’m looking forward for tomorrow’s final and I hope to do even better.”
The first semi-final was won by American Brandon Miller in 1:43.86, also with an impressive finishing burst, while Olympic and World champion Emmanuel Wanyonyi took fourth in 1:44.43, seemingly keeping something in reserve.
The last-place finisher in Sunday’s final will receive $10,000. Any place inside the top four on would mark the biggest pay-day of English’s career, coming four months after he pocketed $20,000 with his Diamond League win in Shanghai.
In Saturday’s opening final, Olympic and World champion Marileidy Paulino won the women’s 400m in familiar style, powering down the homestretch to win in 49.07 seconds. Unbeaten this season, the result completed her sweep of titles, having also won the Diamond League final last weekend.
In the men’s 400m final, the similarly unbeaten Collen Kebinatshipi blasted off with sub-43.03 in mind for a new world record, but the 22-year tied up in the last 50m, clocking 43.39.
Rhasidat Adeleke will race in the women’s 200m on Sunday, drawn in lane two in the first of the two semi-finals (5.44pm), with Olympic champion Gabby Thomas and World champion Melissa Jefferson-Woodenin for company.
Adeleke’s national record of 22.28, set at the European Championships last month, is the fourth fastest time this season of the 16 athletes in the 200m, so a spot in the final may be within her reach.

title: Golf momentarily takes backseat in Doonbeg as Trump touches down at Irish Open
description: Third tee provides prime viewing spot for US president’s arrival in West Clare
content:
Rory McIlroy had a 1.08pm start for his third round at the Irish Open and one of the marshals assigned to follow his round arrived with a minute to spare, panting for breath.
He had been held up en route by a mass motorcade of around 30 vehicles; an obsidian black chain of armoured Cadillacs, Mercedes’ saloons, ambulances and, incongruously, a bus bearing the name of Spain’s Coach Hire.
The convoy did not include the US president - it was merely a rehearsal event for the delivery of Donald Trump to the front door of his hotel. Further down the course, one fan was so rapt by the convoy that she didn’t hear golfer Joe Dean yell fore from the third teebox. His ball thwacked her on the back.
Trump stepped off the stage at the US ambassador’s residence about 40 minutes before the announcer at Doonbeg welcomed McIlroy to the first tee. That whole speech distilled the extent to which the world is being governed as if it’s a country club. First, the Irish ambassador praised Trump as an “amazing golfer”, then calling him an “amazing man” and repeated one of Trump’s favoured fantasies in heralding him as a winner of 41 club championships.
The American writer Rick Reilly wrote a book Commander in Cheat debunking Trump’s various golf claims. In it, he explained one of his tactics was to build or renovate a course, play the inaugural round alone, and then simply declare himself a club champion. Reilly also said Trump earned the nickname Pele for his habit of kicking the ball onto the green. Trump used this formal occasion to tell the crowd “it’s not that I wouldn’t cheat,” but that the 250 Secret Service agents now detailed to guard him during a round of golf don’t allow him to get away with it. Perhaps this is power being held to account.
Trump left the stage with a leaderboard update from Doonbeg - “Shane is leading and Rory is doing very well” - but we wonder whether the golf course owner in him would have enjoyed watching Lowry slice it apart with Friday’s 62. There is a story doing the rounds of the media tent in Doonbeg about Trump’s attendance at this year’s LIV event at his Washington DC course. The US president was allegedly so miffed at the easy scoring that he visited the tournament office and changed some of the pin locations himself.
Shortly after Trump stepped off the stage, Jim Gavin was spotted walking around Doonbeg with Paul McGinley. The mind wandered to the alternate version of history which would have seen Gavin greeting Trump at Áras an Uachtaráin.
The third tee was the prime viewing spot for Trump’s arrival, with the helicopters due to touchdown on the vast, steel-reinforced helipad in an adjacent field. McIlroy’s drive from the third went right, and so he hit a provisional ball to the middle of the fairway. As McIlroy and his caddie Harry Diamond went foraging for their ball in a dune, they heard a rumble overhead. They picked up their heads to see Air Force One arcing ostentatiously across the sky, on its way to Shannon Airport.
McIlroy double-bogeyed the third to end his interest in the tournament. Everyone else’s interests were already suspended. Journalists and photographers clambered to the top of a dune behind the third tee overlooking the helipad, backs to the second green. That same green thudded intermittently with flighted golf balls, to which everyone remained exquisitely ambivalent. Robert MacIntyre made birdie and yelled up: “Must be a sweet spot up there.”
The crowds swelled and a put-upon marshal had the job of shooing fans down the dune on which the media were perched. “Excuse me, out!,” she barked before turning around to tell us with a mortified grin that she hated having to talk so stridently. But we were all putting our stern faces on for the Americans.
The motorcade reassembled along the narrow road that split the golf course from the helipad, Spain’s Coach Hire still among them, sticking out like the fan who wears a GAA jersey to the Masters. A secret service agent ushered each vehicle to pull in tighter to the vehicle in front; another agent came along a few minutes later and asked each vehicle to angle themselves outward a few inches. Perhaps this was skittishly done for the sake of doing something to pass the time.
Eventually, at 2.47pm, a pair of chinook helicopters appeared as distant specks in the sky, advancing towards the agog masses like the scene from Apocalypse Now. Agolfalypse Now.
The trio of golfers at the third teebox laid down their clubs and whipped out their phones once they heard the whump-whump of the helicopter blades. The chinooks disgorged the journalists and assorted staff within them as the first of the presidential helicopters touched down.
While all of this was happening, Shane Lowry and his group hit their shots into the second green. Next time you hear a professional golfer complain about the click of a camera phone or a murmur in the crowd, know that some can play their way through a quartet of military helicopters landing in the field next door.
We looked around to see Lowry standing on a dune behind us, putter in the crook of his elbow, watching Marine One touch down in Doonbeg. Trump landed at precisely 3pm, and seven minutes later he was whisked away by motorcade to his hotel a kilometre away.
At 3.22pm Trump emerged with his sons on a balcony overlooking the 18th green. He waved to the half-empty grandstands and pumped his fist at Brooks Koepka, leaning over the railing to exchange a few words. Koepka made bogey to fluff his lines before his president.
These surreal two hours in Doonbeg were an exercise in making sure nobody in Ireland could be accused of doing likewise.

title: ‘Not as orange as he looks’: NI parties weigh Donald Trump’s united Ireland comments
description: DUP says future to be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not in London, Dublin or Washington
content:
It was, as one senior SDLP figure put it, “quite a moment, to have the American president saying that.”
The “that” in question was Donald Trump’s endorsement of Irish unity, delivered when answering questions from the media after his arrival in Ireland on Saturday.
“I’d love to see it unified”, Trump said; it would be “a fantastic thing ... a great thing” and even “a very cool thing.”
At the SDLP conference, taking place in a south Belfast hotel as Trump was speaking in Dublin, they were already talking unity.
The “direction of travel” towards constitutional change was “clear”, the SDLP leader Claire Hanna told the party faithful in her speech. Addressing the recent assertion by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, that a Border poll was “off the table”, Hanna responded: “A new Ireland isn’t just on the table, it’s on the move.”
Then the US president weighed in. “ Donald Trump , in the last hour, has announced that he is in favour of united Ireland,” she said. “Turns out he’s not as orange as he looks,” she added, in an allusion to the Orange Order.
Her audience laughed. “I’m not sure if anybody’s checked on the DUP,” she continued. “I suspect they’re burning those Trump flags as we speak.”
But, she said, Trump’s comments underlined “as clearly as anything that change is happening, whether some parties here want to acknowledge it or not”.
On Saturday, those unionist parties disagreed, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) and Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) all issuing swift statements essentially telling Trump to keep out of it.
“ Northern Ireland ’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington,” was how the DUP leader Gavin Robinson put it.
UUP deputy leader Robbie Butler took a swipe at “those now cheering” Trump, accusing them of “cherry picking.
“One sentence about a united Ireland and he is apparently a statesman of rare vision,” he said.
The former SDLP leader Colum Eastwood, a long-standing critic of the US president, had his own tongue-in-cheek response, posting a video of Trump’s comments on social media with the caption: “Always liked him.”
“I think it’s a sign of the times,” Eastwood told The Irish Times. “We had the former British prime minister Gordon Brown last week saying he thinks a united Ireland will happen, now we have the current president of America saying he thinks a united Ireland will happen.
“I think there is a recognition around the world that, after Brexit, the direction of travel was clear, that we’re heading towards Irish unity.
“That doesn’t mean that those of us that want to see it don’t have to work very hard to make sure it happens.
“Whatever about all the conversation and the distraction about criteria and dates, there is going to be a Border poll, we are going to win it, and Ireland’s going to be united ... so it’s good to see that the American president, even though I don’t agree with him very much, understands that reality.”
As Hanna said in a statement later on Saturday, “when even Donald Trump has clocked that Irish unity is no longer some distant or theoretical prospect, it tells you something about just how far this conversation has shifted”.
Or, as she put it in her speech earlier, it was “becoming clearer by the day that the future of this island is changing” and “more and more people are talking about our constitutional future.
“Don’t just take it from me,” she said. “Take it from the leader of the free world.”

title: Lando Norris shocks himself with F1 Spanish GP pole
description: Reigning champ pips Kimi Antonelli by one-hundredth of a second
content:
Lando Norris took the first pole position at Formula One ’s newest circuit, the Madring, for the Spanish Grand Prix. The McLaren driver saw off a spirited assault by Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli, who was second, with a superb lap at a circuit that has proved challenging to master and punishing on the slightest of errors.
Red Bull’s Max Verstappen was third with Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc in fourth and fifth for Ferrari and George Russell sixth for Mercedes.
McLaren had not appeared to have the car where they wanted right until the final lap of the final session when Norris put it on top for the first time, one-hundredth of a second clear of Antonelli. “I’m shocked and a bit surprised,” he said.
McLaren have now denied Mercedes the top spot three times this season, with Norris taking pole and wins in Hungary and Zandvoort. It is Norris’s second pole at the Spanish GP, having taken the top spot for the race in Barcelona in 2024, but it is a race he has yet to win. It is the 19th pole of his career.
The Mercedes duo of Antonelli and Russell went out first on the opening hot runs in Q3, but going into the final session Verstappen looked to be in good form, having been quickest in Q2. Antonelli opened strongly with a 1 min 32.140 sec lap. The Ferraris were quick in his wake and Hamilton was immense to grab the top spot with 1:32.079. Verstappen followed, but could not nail the final sector and Hamilton remained on top.
The final runs, with the track offering the most grip, kept all in the balance. Mercedes were out first again, followed by Ferrari, with Verstappen once more at the back. Antonelli had the edge in the first sector and then once more quicker in the final sector, a full two-tenths up. Hamilton was not improving, but with his best lap of the weekend Norris had all but come from nowhere with an immense lap, including a slight kiss on the barrier at the final corner, to claim pole in 1:31.824.
After his outstanding victory from 19th on the grid at the last round in Monza, Antonelli leads Russell by 66 points in the championship, with Hamilton 76 points back in third place.
It was a suitably tense, dramatic show for the first race here, which proceeded without incident despite there being some major crashes. The 3.365-mile circuit had been designed to be fast and a spectacle, but it is a challenging and, as some have intimated, dangerous test. Quite how unforgiving was demonstrated in final practice when the session was red-flagged after Hamilton went into a wall. He hit the barriers nose first at the final corner, a sharp right-hander. He was unhurt and able to restart his car and made an effort to return to the pits before pulling over on the side of the track.
After a long stoppage for repairs, Britain’s Oliver Bearman also took a massive hit having spun and slewed side-on into the concrete barriers at turn 10, wiping out the left side of his car. He was unhurt, but the damage was so bad his Haas team were unable to rebuild the car in time for qualifying.
The pole may prove vital for Norris. The Madring is described as a street circuit, but it is made up of public roads and purpose-built track. It does, however, conform to street circuit norms of being narrow with walls looming over most of the lap.
Its layout produces high speeds, but there have been real concerns from drivers that overtaking will be difficult, especially with braking zones angled into corners, which make passing tricky and raises the risk of a procession on Sunday. Leclerc said after practice he felt overtaking was “extremely difficult or impossible”.
Strategy will probably play a crucial part, as will calls made under yellow and red flags, with the latter almost certain to be a factor given the likelihood of stoppages to deal with the results of any driver errors or mechanical failures. It will also be informed by a high-grip, but also high-degradation, surface, which will improve as it rubbers-in more. Multiple pit stops will play their part too. – Guardian

title: Exuberant Leinster make winning return to the RDS against Zebre
description: Leo Cullen offers opportunities aplenty in preseason friendly
content:
It’s safe to say that the RDS, specifically the Laya Arena, has never looked so resplendent for a rugby match.
“It’s good to be back,” said Leinster chief operating officer Guy Easterby in agreement with some Leinster fans before kick-off as the corporate boxes in the new €50-million Anglesea Road stand glistened in the sun.
They were the most commonly words heard at a low-key, preseason game to return Leinster to their true home after two long years away. Somehow, it really did feel more homely.
Leinster were content with an attendance of just under 7,000 for their dry-run ahead of the official opening when Cardiff come to Dublin in the URC on October 10th.
Head coach Leo Cullen also took the opportunity to use 29 players as the province prepares for a two-match trip to South Africa, facing the Lions and Sharks in the opening rounds of the URC.
It was particularly encouraging to see Ryan Baird back and fully fit after such an injury-disrupted campaign last season. He really could be a point of difference for both province and country, and all in all, Leinster look better primed this time around than they did at the same juncture last season.
It’s also safe to say that even in the depths of winter the Laya Arena will enjoy more full-blooded and captivating affairs than this, but a young and exuberant Leinster side put on a show, dotting down eight tries to Zebre’s two.
As was the case in Leinster’s previous preseason game in Lyons, Josh Ericson’s strong carrying caught the eye. He’s continuing to prove his inclusion in the Leinster academy, coming off the back of his AIL form with Old belvedere, was well deserved.
Fintan Gunne looked sharp in all he did, scoring two of the home side’s eight tries, and pulled the stings alongside fellow Terenure half-back Caspar Gabriel. The gifted Austrian-born outhalf didn’t overplay his hand and is making the most of his opportunity, so much so that he looks the likely choice at 10 against the Lions.
Charlie Tector also had a spell at outhalf as Cullen juggled his resources, but his decision to move to inside centre again looked a shrewd positional switch as he provided much of Leinster’s go-forward momentum.
The one-sided nature of the game was set within 40 seconds of Gabriel’s kick-off. Andrew Osborne availed of a mistimed Zebre lift to gather the kick. Tector and Max Deegan carried hard before Penny did well to claim Gunne’s long skip pass, leaving Niall Smyth to burrow over.
The second Leinster try came in the fourth minute when ex-Newbridge College fullback Todd Lawlor latched on to a Zebre knock-on and made 40 metres upfield before finding Gunne in support.
A third soon followed, Tector putting Leinster on the front foot with his carry off a lineout, and Gunne orchestrated until Gus McCarthy powered off with a good line from the scrumhalf’s pass.
Leinster became a little loose thereafter, and one wayward move too many led to Lorenzo Citton forcing Lawlor to concede a five-metre scrum with his cleverly angled kick. Outhalf Giovanni Montemauri outflanked the Leinster defence with ease, crosskicking for winger Simone Gesi to score.
Normal order was soon restored when Penny’s break off a lineout in midfield led to Tector providing the link for Gunne to score his second from another trailing scrumhalf line. Gabriel landed his fifth conversion to make it 35-5 for the break after Ericson scored when the pack went to work from a close-range tap penalty.
Amid the stream of comings, goings and positional switches, Tector moved to outhalf and took Hugh Cooney’s pullback to send Cormac Foley over before adding the conversion.
The steady flow of Leinster tries was interrupted by a second for Gesi, who skilfully regathered his own chip up the left touchline to finish neatly, but Leinster responded in kind, Josh Neill and Alan Spicer adding the province’s final tries of the afternoon.
SCORING SEQUENCE – 1 min: Smyth try, Gabriel con 7-0; 4: Gunne try, Gabriel con 14-0; 13: McCarthy try, Gabriel con 21-0; 21: Gesi try 21-5; 27: Gunne try, Gabriel con 28-5; 40+1: Ericson try, Gabriel con 35-5; Half-time 35-5 ; 51: Foley try, Tector con 42-5; 56: Gesi try, Montemauri con 42-12; 65: Neill try, Gabriel con 49-12 71: Spicer try, Gabriel con 56-12

Replacements: A Mullan for N Smyth (35 mins), S Smyth for McCarthy, P Dooley for Usanov, R Baird for Deeny, O Coffey for Osborne, C Foley for Gabriel (all ht), J Neill for Penny, A Soroka for Ericson (all 45), J Deegan for Gunne, H McLaughlin for Lawlor, D McNeice for O’Tiernaigh, C Molony for Cooney (all 52), A Sparrow for Mullan, A Spicer for Deegan (both 57), Gabriel for Tector, Osborne for Mangan (both 65), Ericson for Neill (70).
