She was drawn to India, just a decade into its independence, by the legacy of Mahatma Gandhi. She had won a Chester Bowles Asian fellowship to study there, but she quickly abandoned her classes. Wearing a sari, she walked through southern India with followers of Gandhi, absorbing lessons about “talking circles” and grassroots organising.
After returning to the United States, she spent a year in Cambridge, Massachusetts, as a director of the Independent Research Service, a non-profit educational foundation that recruited and provided government support for US students to attend communist-run youth festivals in Europe. The magazine Ramparts subsequently reported that the foundation had been partly funded by the CIA, and Steinem came under criticism from the left. She dismissed the entire venture as harmless, telling The New York Times in 2016 that no one in the CIA had ever told her what to do or say and that she had never reported to the agency.
She moved to New York in 1960 and began working as a freelance journalist. At the time, women were not taken seriously as writers; she wanted to cover politics but was stuck with celebrity profiles and fashion.
Still, she was prolific. Her articles appeared in Vogue, Cosmopolitan, Esquire, Family Circle and Life, among other magazines. She was a contributing editor at Glamour and New York.
At the same time, Steinem moved comfortably in the sophisticated milieu of New York’s intelligentsia and dated powerful men.
In 2000, Steinem overlooked her antipathy toward marriage and wed David Bale, a social justice activist born in South Africa (and the father of actor Christian Bale). She was 66. She initially denied rumours that she had married him because he needed a green card, but years later conceded that this had been the case. The marriage lasted three years before he died in 2003, at 62, from brain lymphoma.
Steinem had faced her own recurring battle with cancer (of the breast), starting in 1986, after which she suffered from total exhaustion and depression and underwent psychoanalysis. She then spent several years writing and rewriting Revolution From Within: A Book of Self-Esteem.
It was her first long public look at herself, and it disappointed some feminists, who saw her introspection as a retreat from much-needed social activism.
Revolution From Within wasn’t the only time that she disappointed her natural allies. In an opinion column in the Times in 1998, she defended president Bill Clinton against numerous sexual allegations, saying that his advances toward various women had not been unwelcome or coercive.
Steinem devoted much of her life to writing. One of her best-sellers was Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions (1983), her first collection of essays. Other books included Marilyn: Norma Jean (1986), a sympathetic portrait of Marilyn Monroe, and Doing Sixty and Seventy (2006), a reflection on women and ageing.
Steinem is survived by what she called her “chosen family” – her close friends. Her mother died in 1981, and her sister, Susanne Steinem Patch, in 2007.
Ms. magazine reached its peak circulation in 1989, with 540,000 subscribers, but its finances were constantly in peril. In less than a decade, its circulation fell to 200,000, and the owner threatened to close it.
Cobbling together a group of venture capitalists and entrepreneurs, Steinem formed Liberty Media for Women, which acquired Ms. for $3 million. In 2001, the Feminist Majority Foundation took over and kept the magazine alive. The magazine now publishes quarterly.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: Lara Marlowe: We need leaders with the courage of a Kennedy or a de Gaulle
description: Contrast their bravery with the behaviour of the Irish Government, which has refused visas to 97 Palestinian students, makes excuses about Aughinish and will today welcome a convicted felon
content:
T he times we live in require extraordinary courage of every citizen, but especially of political leaders.
It sometimes feels like heroism is a thing of the past. Researching a speech for the Kennedy Summer School in New Ross, Co Wexford, two weeks ago, I read John F Kennedy ’s Pulitzer Prize-winning 1956 book, Profiles in Courage.
In her introduction to the book, Kennedy’s daughter Caroline told how the small, motorised Patrol Torpedo boat commanded by Lt Kennedy in the Pacific during the second World War exploded after it was rammed one night by a Japanese destroyer. Two sailors were killed. A third was so badly wounded that he could not swim. Clenching the strap of the man’s life jacket in his teeth, Kennedy – who was himself wounded – swam three miles in darkness to the nearest island where he and surviving crew members hid from the Japanese. On subsequent nights, the future US president swam through shark-infested waters until he secured rescue by Australian forces.
A new biopic about Gen Charles de Gaulle was the surprise hit in French cinemas this summer. How many contemporary politicians would be capable of the moral clarity and determination demonstrated by de Gaulle during the second World War? The film depicts how de Gaulle was twice abandoned by Winston Churchill, his sole supporter, because Franklin D Roosevelt insisted he be replaced by a more pliant ally. “I embody everything the Americans hate,” de Gaulle says in the film. “I am weak, and yet I stand up to them.”
Like today’s Ukrainian armed forces, the French Resistance experienced the despair of fighting a brutal and tyrannical invading army with inadequate weapons. Like de Gaulle, Volodymyr Zelenskiy has been forced to plead for weapons from capricious allies.
The political courage of Kennedy and de Gaulle was commensurate with their physical daring. While police attacked civil rights protesters in the US south with dogs and fire hoses in 1963, president Kennedy deployed the National Guard to ensure that two black students could attend the University of Alabama.
Contrast that with the behaviour of the Irish Government, which has refused student visas to 97 Palestinian students , according to Trinity’s University Times. 52 are from the Gaza Strip, as Irish academic Emma Stokes wrote here recently . It took immense courage for those students to continue studying, to obtain admission and scholarships to Irish universities as Israel destroyed the Gaza Strip around them.
While barring qualified Palestinian students from entry, the Irish Government will on Saturday welcome a convicted felon who has been found civilly liable for fraud and sexual abuse.
[ ‘Very significant resources’ for policing Donald Trump visit, Taoiseach says Opens in new window ]
Irish Government policy regarding the Russian-owned Aughinish Alumina factory in the Shannon estuary has been characterised by wilful ignorance and evasion. Swedish tax authorities concluded that “Putin’s favourite oligarch” Oleg Deripaska, a staunch supporter of Russia’s assault on Ukraine, retains control of the Aughinish parent company Rusal.
The Irish Government has repeatedly cited “commercial sensitivities” in refusing to divulge information about Aughinish. It is protecting a Russian company which provides raw materials to companies which supply Russian weapons manufacturers, rather than protecting the Ukrainians it pledged to support “for as long as it takes”.
Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee summoned Russia’s ambassador, Yury Filatov, to protest the foiled Russian drone attack on Leipzig airport last month. Has it not occurred to the Irish Government that the drones used in Leipzig, or those which flew over Dublin Bay last December, could have been built with aluminium that originated in Co Limerick? The prediction attributed to Lenin that the West would sell the Soviets the rope by which to hang them has never rung truer.
Ukrainians are being killed every day by Russian drones and missiles which are made from aluminium. Aughinish Alumina now exports an average of 70,412 tonnes of alumina, from which aluminium is extracted, to Russia every month, up from 64,665 tonnes last year.
Aughinish Alumina has threatened job losses and diminished gas and electricity supplies in Ireland if EU sanctions are imposed. Ireland is succumbing to blackmail and excusing it with the claim that it does not know what happens to the metal once it reaches Russia.
Courage implies uncertainty, risk and often solitude. Canada’s brave prime minister Mark Carney has risked his country’s entire economy – not just 475 jobs in an alumina plant – to reject Donald Trump’s attack on Canada’s economic sovereignty.
The audience at the Kennedy Summer School applauded criticism of Government policy on visas for Gazan students and Aughinish Alumina. I hadn’t realised how strongly Irish people feel about these issues. There is a sense, at home and abroad, that this Government has lost its moral compass. The Italian MEP Pina Picierno, who is vice-president of the European Parliament, wrote to the EU Commission saying it was “unacceptable ... that a Russian-owned company operates undisturbed within a member state, supplying the Kremlin’s military industry”.
Organisers of a planned conference on Palestine at Maynooth University next month decided to postpone after academics withdrew in protest at Government policy. Earlier sessions took place at the University of California, Princeton, Cape Town and the Western Cape. “A policy of visa denial in the midst of genocide is both immoral and cruel and will be an enduring cause of shame to the Government and the individuals that impose it,” said a letter of protest signed by international academics.

title: TV guide: the best new shows to watch, starting tonight
description: September 13th-18th highlights: including The Late Late Show’s return, Forever Home and The Random Driving Test
content:
Extraordinary stories are told in this four-part documentary about the lives of people who have come from other countries to make Ireland’s offshore islands their home. In this first episode, for example, we meet Ukrainian refugees Krystyna and Diana, who speak about finding sanctuary on Tory Island. Across 12 months, from January 2025 to January 2026, the filmmakers met immigrants from Ukraine, South Africa, Nigeria, France, Scotland and Germany and followed as they built new lives on Arranmore and Tory Island in Co Donegal and Sherkin, Bere and Dursey Islands in Co Cork. Remarkably, some participants had never even been on a boat before moving to these remote locations. We’ll discover many perspectives on migration, identity and belonging in this new series, which should hopefully help to encourage empathy for the many people who have chosen Ireland as their new home.
There was some scepticism when it was announced earlier this year that the legendary long-running Saturday Night Live show on NBC was going to have a British version on Sky. Critics wondered if the humour would be sub-par, and if the gang of young comedians would really stoke up enough laughs. Well, the show ended up being a surprising success, and the buzzy comics demonstrated that they certainly have the chops to create something very interesting on the fly each week. Now they’re back for a second series, with a new weekly guest host, live sketches and a musical performance. Hosting tonight is Jeff Goldblum, and the musical guest is our own queen CMAT .
Children’s programming these days is all about ensuring every child watching feels seen. So hurrah for Pablo Next Level, a Belfast-made animated series with an autistic child called Pablo as its star. Tonight is its second episode after its debut last week on RTÉ Kids and CBBC. The show is aimed at ages five to eight, and focuses on Pablo’s experiences and adventures in primary school. With a nifty comic streak, this explores the perspective of an autistic child while introducing young children to his world. The 40 episodes are written and acted by young autistic talent, including 10-year-old Alexander Myles from Ballycastle, Co Antrim, as Pablo, while comedians Aoife Dooley from Dublin and Carol Walsh from Co Kildare helped write the show.
There are still many questions remaining about the horrifying Jeffrey Epstein sex abuse scandal after his death awaiting trial for sex trafficking. In this Panorama special, journalist Darragh MacIntyre looks at some of these questions, including how Epstein became so powerful, how he befriended such powerful people, and where the money came from that facilitated his abuse of girls and women. MacIntyre picks apart the money trail to find out the answers.
How does Graham Norton do it – present the hugely popular Graham Norton Show and write five bestselling novels? If he’d share his time-management tips with us, that would be great. At least he can presumably have a bit of a breather when his books are being adapted for telly, and the latest (after ITV’s 2022 adaptation of Holding) is Forever Home. The 2022 novel has been turned into a six-part drama for 5. Its story is focused on divorced teacher Carol Crottie (Amy Nuttall), who falls for older man Robert (Douglas Henshall), but the pair face an early-onset Alzheimer’s diagnosis that leads Carol to wonder how much she really knows about her new partner.
There’s something so poignant about following the story of real people throughout their lives, as this series has been doing since 1964. Back then it was aired by ITV’s World in Action strand and called Seven Up!, and aimed to look at whether the class a child was born into determined their future. That turned into a long-running series where the documentary team checked in with the children at seven-year intervals. 70 Up is – sniff – its final season, and sees the award-winning film-maker Asif Kapadia (who was behind acclaimed documentaries Senna and Amy) take over from the original director Michael Apted. Kapadia will direct a two-part finale that will include the surviving participants, including Charles, who had initially dropped out. We can also expect tear-jerking moments like a tribute to the participant Lynn, who died in 2013, and a final interview with Nicholas, who died in 2023.
If you had to sit your driving test again tomorrow, would you pass it? Oh, and would you give it a go if it meant the chance to win up to €1,000 cash? That’s the conceit behind this new show, which sees host PJ Gallagher ask drivers across the country if they’re willing to redo their driving test for the sake of our entertainment ... I mean, to put their road knowledge skills to the test. He visits 12 different driving test routes around Ireland, while the man ensuring the participants are getting a proper test is former senior Road Safety Authority tester Brian Harnett. Each driver starts with €1,000 and for every fault, they lose €100. After nine faults, they fail and leave with nothing. In the first episode, Pilates instructor Prajakta in Wicklow town and hairdresser Jason in Naas put their driving skills to the test.
There had been some speculation earlier this year that Patrick Kielty wasn’t going to be returning to the presenter’s seat for the next season of The Late Late Show. But he confirmed in July that he had signed a new three-year contract, which allows for up to 30 shows a season. The Co Down comedian is well settled into his role after three years, but can we expect something new added into the mix, to bring a frisson of excitement to a staple of the RTÉ schedule? We shall wait and see – all the broadcaster is divulging right now is that we can expect celebrity guests, a live studio audience, and “the stories that have Ireland talking”.
If you can’t head out of the house to enjoy Culture Night, let RTÉ bring it to you. Culture Night Live, supported by the Arts Council, will bring viewers at home a selection of live performances from across the country. Presenters for this year’s bilingual show will be Carla O’Brien and Doireann Ní Ghlacáin live from Kilkenny and Katja Mia live from Killarney. There will be performances from musician and composer Jamie Duffy, Galway five-piece trad band Clada, 2FM Rising artist Jessica Doolan, Mick Flannery and Susan O’Neill, and Cork Mezzo soprano Niamh O’Sullivan accompanied by concert pianist Gary Beecher. Plus, author Michael Harding will explore if Gulliver was a Cavan man as part of the county’s 300th anniversary celebrations of Gulliver’s Travels. Then actor and podcaster Norma Sheahan will visit the delightful Butter Museum in Cork, and presenter Brendan Courtney, alongside architectural historian Emma Gilleece, will pop into the office of the Attorney General, which is open for the first time to the public for Culture Night. Oh, and there’ll be giant puppets, fire dancers and poetry. Talk about a jam-packed night.
The acclaimed espionage drama returns for a sixth season, and Jackson Lamb, Gary Oldman ’s slovenly spymaster, still hasn’t bothered to darn his socks – or perhaps even wash them. At Slough House, MI5’s dumping ground for agents who have screwed up their assignments, his Slow Horses find themselves being targeted. Lamb and his team will have to find a safe house and find out who’s behind the attacks. Kristin Scott Thomas returns as MI5 director general Diana Taverner, with Jack Lowden back as agent River Cartwright. Saskia Reeves, Jonathan Pryce , Hugo Weaving and Olivia Cooke also star. Kevin Courtney
Fans of Jack Reacher will know Frances Neagley as the resourceful private investigator who has helped him crack many a case. A former protege of Reacher’s in a US army special-investigations unit, Neagley has some very specific skills, and while she may lack the lumbering brawn of her mentor, she has no shortage of brains and tech savvy to burn. This Reacher spin-off series starring Maria Sten begins right after the fourth series of Reacher ends. The big guy himself, played by Alan Ritchson, will be making a few guest appearances. (You’ll spot him easily: he’ll completely block out everything else on screen.) Mostly, though, Neagley will have to fend for herself as she investigates the murder of an old friend. KC
The Harrigan crime family are back for more mayhem in the second season of Guy Ritchie ’s explosive series, but are their fortunes about to take a downturn? Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren return as Conrad and Maeve Harrigan, the ruthless bosses of London’s most powerful criminal clan, with Tom Hardy as their fixer Harry de Souza. He has some bad news for Conrad and Maeve: their enemies are getting more powerful and more ambitious, and their empire could soon crumble around their greying temples. The only thing for it is to hit back hard, but it’s not long before Harry’s loyalty to the Harrigans is sorely tested. Joining the carnage for this new season are Paddy Considine, Emmett J Scanlan, Johnny Flynn, Janet McTeer and Toby Jones. KC

title: ‘There’s a really strong learning culture and supportive work environment’
description: Patrick Marron has been on the Vodafone graduate programme for a year and hopes to stay with the company
content:
I’m from a small parish outside Naas called Eadestown. For college I went to Maynooth and studied psychology through science. I chose to study that because I was really interested in people, and when I first chose it, I didn’t really know where I wanted to go with it. But I knew I was interested in how people think, how they interact in different social scenarios. So as I worked more through college, I found that I really wanted to use my degree in a business setting rather than the typical psychological route.
Through their attraction campaign. I saw it on LinkedIn, because I was scrolling one day, and I thought it would be a cool opportunity. I knew somebody who had done it before, so I reached out to them, and they said it was great.
I knew that Vodafone was market leading. I think what attracted me mainly was reading into it and seeing the different things that they offered. I found that there’s the rotational element of the Vodafone grad programme, in which you’ll do one placement for nine months in one team, and then a second placement for 12 months in a different team. It gives you that sense of versatility of experience, of being in different business units and seeing how different teams work.
It’s been amazing. There are so many great things that the graduate programme offers. I mentioned the rotational element and how you get different experience across teams, but as well, there’s flexible working, so you get to be in two days a week and work three days from home. I come in a bit more because I think it’s great to talk to people and be in the office.
There’s a really strong learning culture and supportive work environment. It’s one thing I noticed in comparison to some internships I did during college: Vodafone was just so welcoming. Everyone was so happy to support you and help you, and everyone knows that you’re there to learn.
There’s so many opportunities within the grad programme for improving yourself and development. We have a specific learning platform that I help work on, and it has loads of courses that you can upskill yourself in, whether it’s AI or if you want to move into a different kind of business aspect, such as finance or HR.
One cool thing about the graduate programme is, after 12 months of being on the programme, you’re eligible to apply for full-time roles. So I’ve just about crossed that mark and it’s something I’m looking at. I just know I want to stay at Vodafone.
I had a bit of impostor syndrome, thinking that I couldn’t do it, but from going through it, my advice would be just to be yourself. Be confident in what you can bring to a business like Vodafone. There’s such a wide-ranging, diverse group of people working here that everyone has something to bring, and it’s about shaping what you can bring to Vodafone.

title: Integration is the only way for GAA to level the playing field
description: Association needs to reflect the communities it serves
content:
Sir, − A recent letter writer states: “The men’s game generates by far most of the GAA ’s revenue” ( Letters , September 11th). Kieran Doyle justifies the GAA putting the brakes on integration in economic terms. But this ignores the realities.
The GAA only provides hurling and football for men and boys. Their games are regularly promoted and showcased in Croke Park and on TV. The women’s games are in Croke Park once a year at the grace and favour of the GAA. The rest of the year they are scrambling for facilities. The miracle is that thanks to the trojan efforts of those who run camogie and LGFA the games do as well as they do.
This is the economic result of the glaring inequality between the organisations. Integration is required to level the playing field and give women an opportunity to participate as equals and allow the GAA to truly reflect the communities it serves. – Yours, etc,

title: Trump’s divisive policies are having a profound impact around the world
description: Women’s rights have been particularly affected while his record on climate change has been abysmal
content:
Sir, – Donald Trump ’s inhuman and divisive policies are having a profound impact, not only in the United States but around the world.
The dismantling of USAid and sweeping cuts to foreign assistance have placed millions of people living in poverty and conflict at greater risk. They have had a devastating human impact, with fewer health services, less humanitarian assistance and diminished support for communities already struggling to survive.
Women’s rights are particularly affected. A 2025 UN study showed that an estimated $78 billion in global aid cuts is forcing women’s rights organisations to reduce or close life-saving services, halt prevention and empowerment programmes, and curtail advocacy work.
Trump’s administration has also restricted international funding for organisations working on sexual and reproductive health and rights. All of this puts decades of progress on gender equality at risk.
Trump’s record on climate change has been abysmal. Shockingly, he has said climate change is “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world”. He has withdrawn the United States from the Paris Agreement, promoted fossil fuel expansion and undermined the international co-operation urgently needed to address a crisis to which people who have contributed least are suffering most.
It is countries such as Nepal, crippled by the impact of global inaction, that will pay the price for these dangerous views.
His disregard for the lives and dignity of the people of Palestine and his support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza and the terrorising of civilians in the West Bank demonstrate a profound contempt for international law, human rights and the fundamental principle that every human life has equal value.
Trump’s administration has pursued mass deportations in the US, restricted asylum and rolled back protections for trans people. The consistent pattern is one of targeting those with the least power.
ActionAid Ireland will be joining the No Welcome for Trump protest on Saturday at the Garden of Remembrance, Dublin. We invite you to join us. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – While President Catherine Connolly finds herself obliged to meet and “greet” Donald Trump on his courtesy visit to the Áras this weekend, it would be wrong for the Irish nation to extend a céad míle fáilte to this most inhumane, dishonest and egotistical US president.
We must raise the placards and let the wider world know that we have no truck with Trump, or anything in his hold. Let him enjoy the golf in Doonbeg and then be off. Good riddance! – Yours, etc,
Sir, – US president Donald Trump’s offer to give a $5,000 “dividend” to every adult citizen if Republicans win the US House and Senate in November’s midterm elections raises deep philosophical questions.
German philosopher Immanuel Kant said that “everything has either a price or a dignity”, meaning that human beings have an intrinsic moral integrity that cannot be bought or sold. The November midterm elections will reveal a great deal about the dignity of the US electorate.
The same applies to those willing to roll out the red carpet for Trump this weekend, in Doonbeg or Dublin. – Yours, etc,

title: Ian O’Riordan: Josh Kerr and Jakob Ingebrigtsen’s heated rivalry to reignite in Budapest
description: This weekend’s Ultimate Championship will climax with women’s 200m, possibly featuring Rhasidat Adeleke
content:
I t can be hard sometimes to drum up much interest or excitement in any newly staged athletics event. One of the first people I spoke to about this weekend’s Ultimate Championship in Budapest responded by asking was that the one where they could take a load of drugs.
I could hear the marketing people at World Athletics shuddering deep down inside – and maybe the organisers of the Enhanced Games (who do allow the drugs) having a laugh. Another person responded by assuming it was some new breakaway division of the UFC. Which may or may not be even more insulting.
Anyway, by dangling a historically hefty $10 million prize purse – including $150,000 to each new “ultimate champion”, the single largest first-place prize the sport has ever seen – World Athletics has attracted most of its superstar names on the track and field. Or, in its own words, “the very best of the best”. This is not just about the taking part. It’s mostly all about winning.
Fortunately for World Athletics, perhaps, some of those superstars aren’t content to let their running do all the talking. Nowhere is that more evident than in the men’s 1,500m, where, in Sunday evening’s straight final, Josh Kerr and Jakob Ingebrigtsen are set to renew their now-heated rivalry..
“I wouldn’t like to race me right now,” Kerr said during the week. “I’m not going to lose. If you want to make it fast, if you want to make it slow, you’re going to be in trouble either way.”
Exactly the sort of ego-driven bragging that’s sure to fire up Ingebrigtsen – who loves to give as good as he gets. The Norwegian only returned to racing at last month’s European Championships in Birmingham, winning the 5,000m just six months after undergoing surgery on his Achilles tendon. After that he also rekindled his gentle trash-talking of Kerr, who skipped Birmingham, when saying “it is ruining the sport if we are not participating ... but I could never see myself in that position.”
In fairness to World Athletics, it bent its own rules to make sure this latest rematch could happen. No one I know is complaining. Kerr hasn’t raced over 1,500m so far this year, the British runner instead focusing his efforts on breaking the 27-year-old world record in the mile. Which he duly did, clocking 3:42.66 in London in July – before adding a Commonwealth Games mile title to his name a few weeks later.
This meant neither Kerr nor Ingebrigtsen were entitled to any of the automatic invites to Budapest. One place had been set aside for “exceptional invitations”, although in this case World Athletics agreed on two, saying “this race could not in good faith be considered a full line-up of the greatest athletes on the planet without the inclusion of both Kerr and Ingebrigtsen”.
So here we go again. They haven’t raced in each other in more than two years, and even though Ingebrigtsen holds a winning edge of 11-3 over Kerr across all distances, Kerr won three of their last four meetings – including gold at the 2023 World Championships, also staged in Budapest, then silver at the 2024 Paris Olympics, where Ingebrigtsen finished fourth.
At last weekend’s Diamond League final in Brussels, Ingebrigtsen’s lack of racing seemed to show when he only managed fourth in the 1,500m. After that he called out some of his rivals as “losers”, who “acted cowardly” given the way they ran. He has since apologised for the “losers” part, but still said, “if you’re not allowed to show a bit of passion after a race, you should find a sport that doesn’t want an audience.”
[ Ultimate Championship: What Irish athletes are competing in new $10m event, and where can you watch? Opens in new window ]
Given all the talk this week about equity and equality between men and women in our own Gaelic games, it’s worth noting the absolute parity for both when it comes to World Athletics, including the Ultimate Championship. Better still, the women’s 200m final on Sunday evening, possibly featuring Rhasidat Adeleke if she can get through her semi-final, is the climax to the entire weekend.
The race most people are probably anticipating is the women’s 800m, with that final set for Saturday evening. As a matter of fact, no event has evolved more dramatically this season, thanks in part to the sensational running of Audrey Werro, the 22-year-old from Switzerland who became only the third woman in history to run under 1:54.
The last woman to do that was Jarmila Kratochvílová, from the former Czechoslovakia, when running her world record of 1:53.28, back in 1983. That remains the longest-standing world record in the books, men or women, and whatever about its legitimacy, Werro is now coming within touching distance, improving her best again to 1:53.70 in Zurich last month.
In between, Werro also won the European title in Birmingham, beating Britain’s Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson in the process. Hodgkinson had also started her season by breaking the indoor world record for 800m, which had stood since March 3rd, 2000, the day Hodgkinson was born.
Also closing in fast on both Werro and Hodgkinson is Dutch superstar Femke Broeders-Bol, who has defied all expectations in her first season of two-lap racing, having moved up from the 400m hurdles. She finished just 0.06 behind Werro in last weekend’s Diamond League final in Brussels, and has run 1:54.71, itself a debut-season record.
No need for any gentle trash-talking here. Werro has adopted a sort of lion’s roar gesture as her signature post-race celebration, as if unleashing her own fierce competitiveness. But unlike Kerr and Ingebrigtsen, they’ve all faced each other several times already this season, with their egos a lot more contained.
Hodgkinson did miss the Brussels showdown through injury, and when asked this week was she 100 per cent recovered, she replied with a cheeky smile, “none of your business”.
Maybe these three 800m women do prefer to let their running do all the talking, and no harm in that. Still, there is something irresistible about this latest Kerr-Ingebrigtsen showdown, given only one of them can ultimately aspire to Muhammad Ali’s old claim that “it ain’t bragging if you can back it up”.

title: Makhlouf stays on the fence on future rate hikes
description: Central Bank governor reiterates path on interest rates not set, but inflation is now a big problem
content:
I t’s almost a tradition now that the day after the European Central Bank (ECB) makes a move on interest rates, the various members of its governing council make public statements justifying the decision and looking at what may come next.
As the governor of the Central Bank of Ireland, Gabriel Makhlouf is no exception. In a blog post published on Friday, he outlined his support for the move, describing the 0.25 percentage point hike as “a measured response” to spiking inflation.
“Energy prices have not faded and, if anything, are proving stickier than previously thought,” he wrote.
For mortgage holders and investors alike, perhaps the most important part of Makhlouf’s post looked at what comes next. He maintained that there is “significant uncertainty to the outlook” for the European economy, and that is almost entirely because of the continuing uncertainty in the Middle East.
He rightly described the Iran war as “a geopolitical driver more than economic one”. Nevertheless it is the key driver and as long as it continues, energy prices are likely to remain high. Brent crude oil topped $107 (€92.16) per barrel on Thursday and remained close to $105 on Friday.
That means higher inflation, but experts traditionally warn to be careful hiking when it’s all because of energy prices and not excessive consumption. Doing so could strangle the economy, especially if it hasn’t been thriving up to now.
That is clearly a concern right now and according to Makhlouf the ECB is “already seeing a tightening of financing conditions”. That’s central bank-speak for the economy is slowing down already. Not good if prices are going to keep rising. That opens the door to stagflation – something of a nightmare scenario for central bankers and anyone who remembers the 1970s era of no growth and runaway prices.
Markets appear to have made up their mind and have priced in three hikes over the next year, with ECB officials reportedly seeing the next one coming as soon as October.
[ Energia dual-fuel customers to be €230 worse off after price hike announced Opens in new window ]
Still, Makhlouf remains publicly on the fence. There is “no pre-commitment” to a move on rates, he wrote, while he will watch closely “the persistence of the energy price shock, and the extent to which it is showing up in consumer prices, both directly and indirectly; on wage dynamics; and on the transmission of previous moves”.

title: Coolmore and Juddmonte superpowers face off in Irish Champions Festival
description: Controversial French jockey Pierre-Charles Boudot has handful of Ballydoyle rides on just second time to ride in Ireland
content:
The air around flat racing’s elite is rarefied anyway, but this weekend’s Irish Champions Festival is conspicuously exclusive with the competitive pay-off for everyone in economy class of two days of the sport at its very best.
A total of over €5 million in prize money is spread around 17 races at Leopardstown on Saturday and the Curragh a day later, including seven Group One highlights.
It is the 13th edition of Irish racing ’s signature event and although the reality is that both venues are likely to be barely over half-full of racegoers, once again it will have a lucky global audience, many of them betting into the lucrative World Pool each day.
Despite the scale, it’s no stretch to tee up Saturday’s action as essentially a heavyweight clash of two bloodstock superpowers.
Having dominated much of the summer in Europe, Aidan O’Brien and Coolmore are on home ground with 31 weekend runners. The Juddmonte team has just seven. But they include a pair of Andrew Balding-trained stars that are the form picks for Saturday’s biggest prizes.
Item upset the International pecking order in York last month when running down Almaqam with O’Brien’s star three-year-old Constitution River only third. The trio provide a mouth-watering repeat prospect in the €1.25 million Royal Bahrain Irish Champion Stakes.
Just over an hour beforehand, Colin Keane teams up with another Balding star in Blue Bolt. She has won Group Ones in France and England on her last two starts and goes for a tripartite hat-trick. Both times she beat Ballydoyle’s Precise and they clash again in the Matron Stakes.
Although not represented in the newly promoted Group One HKJC Golden Fleece Stakes for two-year-olds, Juddmonte’s Purview will be a banker for many in the Group Three Kilternan Stakes while Maire Rua is a leading player in the opening Ingabelle Stakes.
It gives Keane an enviable hand although how he plays it tactically will come under scrutiny. Pacemakers and team tactics have been a recurring topic during the summer with Ballydoyle’s use of multiple entries coming under the spotlight.
Constitution River is O’Brien’s number one hope of a record-extending 14th Champion Stakes success, amid widespread presumption that both Hawk Mountain and Lambourn will try to cut out a hard tempo to help prevent a repeat of Constitution River’s free-running York performance.
It is an intimidating depth of resources should that be the case. Hawk Mountain is a Futurity winner and runner-up in the French Derby. Lambourn won both the Epsom and Irish Derbies last year.
Item is drawn in the middle and in the circumstances maybe Almaqam’s wide draw might work in his favour. So too would a wet forecast for Saturday. Kieran Shoemark’s mount has a head to find with Item who chinned him on the line in York.
Blue Bolt is drawn nine of nine in the Matron and Keane has long believed Leopardstown’s mile around a bend will be ideal for a filly who has taken her performance to another level this season.
Ryan Moore sticks with Precise rather than the other O’Brien Guineas winner True Love. She will be ridden by former French champion jockey Pierre-Charles Boudot, one of a handful of Ballydoyle rides on Saturday for the controversial rider.
Boudot (33) returned to racing in June after a five-year police investigation in France was dismissed. He was cleared of all charges relating to allegations of rape made by two women.
During his lengthy suspension, Boudot spent some time as a work rider in Ballydoyle and has a record of success for O’Brien, including a shock 73/1 victory on Order Of Australia in the Breeders’ Cup Mile. He also won the 2020 French Oaks on Fancy Blue for Donnacha O’Brien.
[ Racing needs will to implement the rule book when it comes to pacemakers Opens in new window ]
With Wayne Lordan and Ronan Whelan in Doncaster on St Leger duty for O’Brien, Boudot has been drafted in for what will be just his second time riding in Ireland. He was unplaced on his subsequent Arc winner Waldgeist in the 2017 Irish Derby.
Christophe Soumillon, who stepped in for the injured Ryan Moore to such affect last autumn, and won the Champion on Delacroix, appears to have slipped on the Ballydoyle pecking order. He rides twice for O’Brien on Saturday but is on the supplemented English hope Wimbledon Hawkeye in the big race.

title: Leinster have grounds for optimism but key exits could leave them rowing against the wind
description: While RDS return is a bonus for the province, chasing down the Champions Cup looks a tall order
content:
Leinster retained their URC title last season with a hat-trick of home wins over South African sides and their display against the Bulls in the final was arguably their best of the season. That was after a first-half blitz by Bordeaux-Bègles in Bilbao, which had decided the Champions Cup final by half-time. So, any season that includes a trophy cannot be considered a failure? Right?
Retaining their URC title was unquestionably a bigger achievement than any of their nine triumphs in that competition’s previous iterations. Leinster also reached a sixth Champions Cup final under Leo Cullen.
Yet after doing what was necessary to make their way to another final, Leinster were emphatically beaten by half-time in the decider. Maybe that was a heat and humidity-affected one-off. But maybe the scars have left baggage and an uber-demanding defensive game compounds the energy required for their multi-phase attack.
Perhaps partly because of the so-called ‘Leinster tax’, imposed by David Humphreys, as well as the much-reduced attendances for last season’s knock-out matches, Leinster’s outgoings also significantly outnumber their incomings. In addition to the western exodus to renew acquaintances with Stuart Lancaster – much to Cullen’s evident irritation – there has been a notable loss of stardust in Rieko Ioane and James Lowe. RG Snyman also begins the season sidelined, as does Caelan Doris. Luke McGrath’s departure after 13 seasons leaves a clear void.
They need one or more of Conor O’Tighearnaigh, Josh Ericson and Caspar Gabriel to energise their season. Big impacts from Fintan Gunne and Joey Carbery would also help.
Ioane wasn’t as lauded as Jordie Barrett but his impact was significant. Wrongly blamed for a defensive system error in Bilbao, it’s hard to envisage how Leinster would have coped without Ioane, for he started 16 of his 18 appearances after arriving in December, while scoring six tries and providing several assists.
Finding another A-lister was unlikely in a pre-World Cup season, and nor does it suit the needs of Team Ireland , but this looks another tricky juggling act for Cullen in his farewell season.
The strain of being bulk suppliers to Ireland and the Lions, and indeed the other provinces, is perhaps taking its toll. The return to the RDS and the new Laya Arena is timely, not least as the grand unveiling in round three against Cardiff is a week before their opening European trip to Clermont Auvergne, who will have played six games by then.
Leinster then host Munster and visit Connacht ahead of the Nations Championship hiatus, after which they regroup away to the Ospreys before Glasgow (home), Munster (away), Ulster (home), Pau (home) and Leicester (away). And the Six Nations will invariably leave a mark on Leinster.
There are encouraging auguries though. Cullen captained Leinster to their 2011 Heineken Cup, and in the last two pre-World Cup seasons Leinster reached the finals in 2019 and 2023, while winning the Pro14 in 2019 before losing a home semi-final to Munster three years ago. That was one of only three defeats in 28 matches that season. Alas, one of the others was against La Rochelle in the Champions Cup final at the Aviva Stadium.
In: Joey Carbery (outhalf, 30, from Bordeaux), Peter Dooley (prop, 31, Connacht), Stephen Smyth (hooker, 22, promoted from academy), Conor O’Tighearnaigh (lock, 23,promoted from academy), Josh Kenny (winger, 23, promoted from academy)
Out: Rieko Ioane (centre, 29, to Blues), Luke McGrath (scrumhalf, 33, Perpignan), Jerry Cahir (prop, 25, Connacht), Will Connors (backrow, 30, Connacht), Ciarán Frawley (outhalf, 28, Connacht), James Lowe (winger, 34, Tokyo Suntory Sungoliath), Rabah Slimani (prop, 36, Toulon), John McKee (hooker, 26, Scarlets)
Today sees a soft opening for the RDS in the shape of a preseason friendly against Zebre in front of about 8,000. The return to the renamed Laya Arena after the €59 million completion of the new stand and an absence of over two years cannot come soon enough.
Beginning with a full house of 20,500 for the visit of Cardiff on October 10th, it should be a boost for fans and squad. Aviva Stadium fatigue had contributed to the sharp decline in attendances, with last season’s five home knock-out ties in the Champions Cup and the URC (save for the final) drawing a total of 103,724 spectators, compared with 214,397 for the equivalent five fixtures in 2023-24.
Leinster have ‘earned’ 22 home knock-out fixtures in the last four seasons compared to Munster’s two ties, and maybe their fans have become spoilt. Yet even allowing for last season’s far-less-glamorous ties, that is still an alarming decline in attendances.
Cullen is entering his 12th and final season, with Felipe Contepomi the strong front-runner to succeed him for what will be a challenging first, post-World Cup campaign. Cullen’s legacy should be secure after leading Leinster to 13 finals, while also remaining bulk suppliers to Ireland. The seven trophies accumulated include winning their last six finals in the Pro 14/URC. Yet he, the organisation and fan base would dearly love to add one more Champions Cup triumph in his tenure.
For all the narrative around Jacques Nienaber’s defence, it’s worth noting that Leinster again scored the most tries in the 18-game URC regular season (77 as against 79 the season before) and added another 16 in three knock-out games.
Luke McGrath remained second-choice scrumhalf until the very end but his departure leaves the door ajar for Fintan Gunne , Cormac Foley and Oliver Coffey. Although Gunne is 23, he only has 33 appearances to his name. All but seven of those have been off the bench, and only once has he played in the Champions Cup. He has a very complete all-round game and is strong and brave, so if he is to have a breakthrough season, this should be it.
In theory, this coming season should be a doddle by comparison to the last one. While some of their 18 Irish summer tourists will most likely miss the opener against the Lions, they will be free to play against the Sharks in their opening trek to South Africa. But Ireland will have another four Nations Championship matches in November as well as the Six Nations. Although recent history suggests otherwise, the proximity of the World Cup could impact Leinster’s customary end-of-season hunt for silverware.
Finishing first and winning a third URC title in a row would be a serious achievement. While they could again go deep into the Champions Cup, a fifth star still looks elusive as beating Bordeaux-Bègles and/or Toulouse will be a tall challenge, especially as the final will effectively be another away tie in Lyon on May 22nd.

title: The problem with retrofitting: cost
description: Another obstacle is the rigidity of the criteria required for installation of a heat pump
content:
Sir, – While I would love to retrofit my 1952 home and install a heat pump, it would not be cost effective as the outlay is substantial in comparison with the grants received.
Therein lies the main problem with getting many people to retrofit: the cost involved. At my stage of life, I just couldn’t justify spending that kind of money for little return. Maybe if I live another 20 years, I’ll be able to get it done for free!
Another obstacle is the rigidity of the criteria required for installation of a heat pump. A close relative refurbished and insulated a 1950s home four years ago. They recently paid a whopping €900 for a suitability survey to be carried out. Believe it or not, the answer was no. Why? The insulation was not thick enough! – Yours, etc,

title: Joseph O’Brien set to underline rising status as his father’s main rival
description: Aidan and his son have six of the 11 runners in world’s oldest Classic at Doncaster
content:
Joseph O’Brien’s rapidly rising status as his father’s main rival is stamped all over this weekend’s Group One action.
Ahead of Sunday’s Irish Champions Festival action at the Curragh, the 250 th renewal of the world’s oldest Classic, the Betfred St Leger, is dominated by Aidan and Joseph O’Brien, who have six of the 11 runners between them.
O’Brien snr is chasing a ninth Leger, including in 2013 when his son rode Leading Light. He is also chasing four-in-a-row in the Doncaster Classic. O’Brien jnr became just the second person to ride and train a Leger winner after Galileo Chrome scored for him in 2020.
This time he has snapped up Billy Loughnane to ride likely favourite Enceladus, while Saffie Osborne has a chance to become the first woman to ride an English Classic winner on his other hope, Highwayman. Enceladus will carry first-time cheekpieces.
Up against them is a Ballydoyle quartet topped by the Derby winner Christmas Day. No Derby winner has doubled up in the Leger since Reference Point in 1987. Ronan Whelan is again on his “blue riband” winner, although Wayne Lordan travelling to ride Pierre Bonnard rather than staying at home for Leopardstown’s action is noteworthy.
Both of those jockeys will be on duty at the Curragh on Sunday with Whelan on board the top-class Jan Brueghel, who is nevertheless a Ballydoyle second-string to Scandinavia in the €500,000 Comer Group Irish St Leger.
Just seven line up in the Curragh highlight, with Aidan and Joseph O’Brien each triple handed. The sole interloper is the English outsider Arabian Force. Only Robson De Aguiar upsets a family affair in the earlier Moyglare Stud Stakes and both O’Briens have five of the eight contenders for the Goffs National Stakes.
Such big race numbers underline the growing influence of the 33-year-old O’Brien throughout the sport. His prize money tally of over €3.2 million in Ireland so far this season is a million behind his father. No one else has yet to reach seven-figures.
It is an astonishingly rapid rise since first taking out a licence 10 years ago and among his 15 runners at HQ on Sunday are the Epsom Oaks heroine Thundering On, who returns to action in the Blandford Stakes, and Star Of State in a lucrative sales race.
The O’Brien family can also call on Donnacha, who supplies the likely favourite Comanche Brave for the Bar One Flying Five.
[ Racing needs will to implement the rule book when it comes to pacemakers Opens in new window ]
A rare blot on Joseph O’Brien’s horizons is the unavailability of champion jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle. His recent Bellewstown spill rules him out of the most lucrative weekend of the campaign.
Declan McDonogh comes in for Trustyourinstinct in the Leger, although plenty will believe everything else is competing for place money behind the outstanding Scandinavia.
Winner of the Doncaster Leger exactly a year previously, the son of Justify has been faultless in four starts so far this season. He’s rated among the very elite of Ballydoyle stayers in Aidan O’Brien’s three decades at the helm there. That’s a bar that this opposition will find tough to scale.

title: Overspending health regions to be asked to slow hiring after headcount surge
description: Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill said there had been ‘extraordinarily high’ recruitment in the HSE
content:
Overspending health regions will be asked to slow the pace of hiring for the rest of the year after a “staggering” surge in headcount.
Two senior Coalition figures agreed there would be pressure to get the pay budget back to balance before the end of the year in four of the six regions that are to lose day-to-day spending autonomy amid growing political frustration at the scale of the overspending.
One of these figures said the growth in hiring since June was “staggering”, while the second said there would be “much greater restriction on headcount” after some regions hired more people already this year than approved for the whole year.
“Anything more will require much greater evaluation and justification,” they said.
Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill on Friday said there had been “extraordinarily high” recruitment in the HSE .
Speaking during the Fine Gael think-in ahead of the resumption of the Dáil next Wednesday, she told reporters there were 5,000 new people in the health service than this time last year.
“There has been extremely large recruitment. We have 3,000 people in the health system just in the first few months of this year,” she said. “So there has been extraordinarily high recruitment.”
Earlier this week, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said four HSE regions would be losing power over day-to-day spending .
Asked about the projected deficit for the year, Carroll MacNeill declined to give a figure as she was not accepting HSE estimates.
[ Bouncy castle play linked to largest outbreak of common superbug in Ireland Opens in new window ]
“I don’t accept the projections because they imply continued hiring in a way that isn’t appropriate at this stage of the year,” she said.
The Minister said hiring had to be “balanced up” in the final four months of the year, “as it was not in the first four months”.
She said she nonetheless had confidence in the leadership of the HSE regions, describing the spending as an “in-year challenge” which had been managed better last year.
“I have to take a sort of longer-term perspective on it,” she said. “It is necessary that we bring that pay bill back in each of those regions. That’s what the taxpayer expects.”
The Minister said the HSE “does not have a mandate from Government or from the Oireachtas to overspend its budget”.
Despite the overspend, the Fine Gael TD said she still expected to have money to fund new services and service expansion next year.
[ Spending on pay being monitored amid ‘extraordinarily high’ HSE recruitment, says Minister Opens in new window ]
Government sources said the overspend across the HSE grew in August, with a “cash deficit” in the region of €700 million at the end of the month – €110 million of which was driven by hiring, according to one senior government source.
While Coalition figures said the deficit was not directly comparable to the overall deficit at the end of July – which stood at €577 million – it nonetheless provided an indication of the trends since then.
These trends, they said, led to a significant escalation from the Coalition and a decision to further centralise spending control from the worst-performing regions.
In a statement, the HSE said it does not report a “cash deficit” and that at the end of July its overall deficit was €578 million on services funded by the Department of Health.
It said it drew forward €270 million in August to meet payroll, supplier and grant payments falling due in the month, which it said did not add to the deficit.
The HSE said the rate of spending growth had slowed since the spring, with year-on-year growth down from 10.9 per cent in the first quarter of the year to 8.5 per cent in July.
It said the HSE had approved 2,889 new roles since June 22nd, of which 1,274 were conversions of agency workers to permanent posts, which reduced cost.
Approvals slowed to 363 posts in the four weeks to September 4th, while net workforce growth in July was 249.

title: HSE doing the same thing but expecting a different outcome
description: Why is the definition of insanity being once again flaunted?
content:
Sir, – Due to the failure of various regions to control expenditure, budget control will be centralised in the HSE (“ Four HSE regions to lose power over day-to-day spending ”, Politics, September 10th”).
Surely a pertinent question is whether the poor financial control has been any worse than in the preceding 10 years when the HSE budget was centralised. If not, why is the definition of insanity (doing the same thing and expecting different outcomes) being once again flaunted? – Yours, etc,

title: Michael O’Leary says he won’t apologise for rapists comment
description: Ryanair chief executive has been criticised by the head of the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre for ‘trivialising’ rape
content:
Ryanair chief executive Michael O’Leary , who has come under criticism for characterising his airline rivals as “high-fare rapists” , has rejected the claim that his remarks “trivialise” sexual violence.
Rachel Morrogh, the chief executive of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre , a charity that supports victims of sexual and gender-based violence, said on Thursday “the words of high-profile individuals can contribute to trivialising and tolerating sexual violence in our society”.
“And for many survivors of rape, his words will be deeply hurtful and angering to hear,” she said and later signalled her intention to “write to Mr O’Leary to offer him training on how the trivialisation of rape is so harmful”.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday outside the airline’s annual general meeting, O’Leary said customers were “desperate to get to Ryanair’s low fares because they can’t afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe,” and named Aer Lingus, Lufthansa and British Airways.
He went on to repeat the “high-fare rapists” comment and, when asked by a reporter if this was an appropriate use of language, he responded: “Absolutely.”
Morrogh described these as “lazy and uninformed comments”, adding O’Leary had “no regard for how they may affect people”.
In a letter responding to Morrogh, seen by The Irish Times, O’Leary wrote: “I certainly did not trivialise the crime of rape as you wrongly claim.”
He continued: “I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape. I will certainly not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training.”
[ Ryanair boss Michael O’Leary criticised over ‘high-fare rapists’ comments Opens in new window ]
He wrote that Morrogh’s letter “wrongly claims” that he “dodged a question about whether it was offensive to victims of rape”.
“I was asked what I thought of rape, and answered that it was a heinous crime. I could not have been clearer,” he continued, adding: “I was also asked if describing high-fare competitor airlines as high-fare rapists somehow trivialised the crime of rape, and I was clear in my view that it did not.
“You are entirely free to hold a different opinion and we are free to disagree,” he wrote, before stating Morrogh’s view that his remarks “perpetuate dismissive attitudes to the survivors of rape” was “both false and defamatory”.
O’Leary has been criticised by politicians on both sides of the Irish Sea. Tánaiste Simon Harris described his remarks as “clearly an inappropriate use of language”.
“I also think he knows exactly what he’s at,” Harris said. “We’re all here talking about Ryanair – it is free advertisement.”
Heidi Alexander, the minister for transport in the British government, said: “Women who have been raped and who have been subjected to such appalling violence, I’m not sure they’re going to be rushing to book tickets with him, let’s be honest.”

title: Going through the motions: Did anyone learn a whole heap from party think-ins?
description: The think-ins organised by Fine Gael, Fianna Fáil and Sinn Féin this week showed Irish politics is static right now
content:
I t has been a long week of thinking in Irish politics. Fine Gael concluded its two-day think-in in Gorey Co Wexford on Friday, while the Green Party confined its thinking to one day in Dublin. Earlier in the week, Fianna Fáil brainstormed in Tullamore, while Sinn Féin and People Before Profit each held cerebral events in Dublin.
Labour got its thinking out of the way in Galway last week. Aontú is gathering in Derry on Saturday, while the Social Democrats cogitations take place in Dublin next week on the eve of the Dáil’s return on Wednesday.
It would be hard to say that all the thinking has brought a new clarity to Irish politics or policymaking. But the week’s events offer the parties – or more accurately, their leaders – the opportunity to opine on a variety of subjects to the travelling press pack. Maybe that is the real point.
In Tullamore, Fianna Fáil leader Micheál Martin outlined his thoughts on a wide variety of subjects in media encounters. They included but were certainly not limited to the budget, the unsettled international situation, the impending Trump visit, disabilities, childcare, migration, a possible future Border poll, child poverty and the evils of vapes (“nearly worse than cigarettes”), which he would like to ban, though has no immediate plans to do so.
In Gorey, Fine Gael leader Simon Harris addressed subjects as diverse as Michael O’Leary’s comments comparing other airlines to “rapists”, President Catherine Connolly meeting US president Donald Trump, child safety, GAA integration , the budget, the cost of living, the prospect of a united Ireland,and sundry other topics.
Labour’s Ivana Bacik, Sinn Féin’s Mary Lou McDonald, People Before Profit’s Richard Boyd-Barrett and the Green Party’s Roderic O’Gorman all had their own opportunities to unburden themselves of the fruits of their thinking. Really, though, did anyone learn a whole heap from any of it?
But the week of thinking did serve to underline some things about the state of Irish politics right now.
With a budget in sight, resources at its disposal and a cost of living squeeze getting tighter for people, the Government will spend as much as it can, consistent with its own fiscal limits – or, more likely, a bit more than those limits.
There will be tax cuts, spending increases and – perhaps – further relief on fuel costs. The one common thread among all the think-ins was the rising cost of living is by far the most important agenda for politics right now. It follows that the Government will respond to that in the budget.
The only criticism of the Opposition is that the Government is not spending enough – a criticism heard throughout the week and, undoubtedly, across the weeks to come between now and the budget.
[ Government protecting a broken system because it’s the easy thing to do? No change there Opens in new window ]
The constituency for prudence, as advocated by most economists and also by the Government’s own budgetary watchdog, set up in order to avoid a repeat of the last disaster in the public finances, remains largely unrepresented in our political debate.
While the Opposition is united in its demands for more spending by Government, the think-ins showed little other sign of left unity – and considerable signs of disunity. This is one of the other things to note about the state of Irish politics right now.
While the frenemies of Government, Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael, manage to rub along together despite occasional tensions, there is no sign that the left unity that brought Connolly to the Áras less than a year ago has translated to the Dáil or to the more keenly competitive world of actual power politics.
Bacik insisted that she wanted to see co-operation on the left and pointed to joint stances in the Dáil, but McDonald bluntly admitted that an “electoral pact ... is not on the horizon”.
McDonald does want the other left-wing parties to row in behind a Sinn Féin-led government, though. Poor Boyd-Barrett was reduced to complaining that he had emailed the other parties “several times” about a left-wing alliance for government, but they hadn’t got back to him. Have they not replied to you, he was asked. “Not really, no, to be honest,” he confessed.
[ Here’s a radical idea for the Government: start telling us the truth Opens in new window ]
It is, of course, a long way to the general election, a point Harris explicitly advised journalists to note on Thursday evening in Gorey. And this fact underpins the third thing that the think-ins made clear: with no election on the horizon, there is a sense of uneasy stability about Irish politics right now. It seems kind of static.
Within Government, there is fierce activity in advance of the budget, as Ministers wrestle with the parsimonious Department of Public Expenditure – and its commendably unyielding minister, Jack Chambers – for the best deal for their departments. His determination – so far anyway – to reduce the rate of increase in government spending is making him unpopular among his colleagues. That goes with the territory. It is also a familiar pre-budget refrain.
Much time and energy are being consumed by the European presidency. There is a bit of sniping between the partners in government, but no more than usual. And as was clear from the Fianna Fáil gathering, the question of the leadership has been put off until next year.
On the Opposition side, there is no urgency or sense of anticipation. Everyone is kind of going through the motions.
It’s times like this, of course, that something unexpected usually happens.

title: Falling standards are falling standards
description: Irish teenagers getting lower maths and reading scores is a negative thing and deserves an appropriate headline
content:
Sir, – In response to Annette Quinn’s letter (September 11th), which takes issue with your paper’s headline on declining reading and maths scores, I must submit I think your approach is correct (“ Irish teenagers getting weaker at maths and reading ”, News, September 8th).
It is factually accurate to say that reading and maths scores have declined among Irish teenagers. That the decline in Ireland is less severe than in other countries does not make it a success or an achievement of our teachers and students. Falling standards are falling standards, and are still a negative and deserve an appropriate headline. – Yours, etc,

title: Senator’s travel expenses
description: Many people in Ireland are struggling every day to make ends meet
content:
Sir, – It is appalling that a member of the Oireachtas was allocated €16,000 for expenses they never incurred (“ FF Senator paid €16,700 in travel expenses while sick at home for eight months ”, News, September 11th).
Members of the Seanad are paid €83,000 a year, which is more than many people in Ireland. They receive reimbursement for expenses for travelling to and from work, and for any overnight accommodation expenses incurred.
Senator Imelda Goldsboro has said she was working in “the constituency” in Tipperary. Her party has stated that “she is more determined than ever to get back to Leinster House and fight for the people of Tipperary”. Both responses suggest neither she nor her party understand her job.
Senators do not represent geographic constituencies. A senator’s job is to represent all of Ireland in the Seanad and attend at Leinster House regularly to do so.
Many people in Ireland are struggling every day to make ends meet, filling their cars with expensive fuel just to get to and from work, and commuting long hours. – Yours, etc,

title: Children and young people need offline support as well as online protection
description: Budget offers chance to deliver meaningful investment in youth services and youth work
content:
Sir, – A conference on online safety for children and young people took place at Dublin Castle this week as part of the State’s presidency of the EU Council . But with all the focus on social media bans, online safety and what children and young people are being exposed to online, what consideration has been given to the infrastructures and architecture that should be in place to support young people offline?
Mis- and disinformation, harmful narratives and hate speech have created toxic online environments, which steadily creep into the real world. Youth workers are supporting young people experiencing greater pressures and issues; issues that require time, skill and stability to address effectively.
Meaningful responses to online harms and supporting young people to be safe online cannot neglect, or ignore, safe offline spaces. Youth work cannot continue to be underfunded but expected to deliver more and meet increasing, more complex demand. The ability to support young people is undermined by the lack of multiannual funding, lack of recognition of the funding deficits that services find themselves in and demand consistently outpacing supply.
In under a month, the Minister for Finance and Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation will deliver a budget that will test the Government’s commitment to young people: if protecting them online is truly a priority, this is the moment to demonstrate it through meaningful investment in youth services and youth work. National Youth Council of Ireland has called for €27.3 million additional investment, of which €13.5 million would be a direct uplift to services, clubs and programmes where it is needed now. – Yours, etc,

title: Moving the goalposts on citizenship rules is deeply unfair
description: Proposed regulations ignore contributions made by those already resident for many years
content:
Sir, – I am writing as a general practitioner and an Irish citizen in response to the new proposals on citizenship (“ New rules for Irish citizenship: How will they work? ”, News, September 7th).
The issues raised are close to home. My husband is also a general practitioner serving our community and is experiencing a lengthy wait for a decision on his citizenship application despite meeting the residence requirements set out by the Department of Justice .
I am concerned about the proposed requirements, which may come into effect as early as Christmas. From what I understand, these changes could have a substantial impact on healthcare workers who were recruited from overseas to work within the HSE .
People such as my husband, as well as many overseas-born friends and colleagues, have dedicated years of their lives to caring for patients in Ireland and building their futures here. They play a huge role in supporting an already understaffed and overstretched health service.
During the Covid-19 pandemic, many of these same healthcare workers put their own health and lives at risk to care for patients in Ireland. They worked through extraordinary uncertainty and pressure, often while separated from their own families and support networks. Some healthcare workers tragically lost their lives during the pandemic. Their contribution and sacrifice should not be forgotten now, particularly when decisions are being made about their right to build a secure future in the country they served at a time of national crisis.
Many came to Ireland in good faith, worked continuously, paid taxes, established homes and families, and fulfilled the residence requirements expected of them. It would be deeply concerning if the goalposts were now moved while they are waiting for their applications to be processed, particularly when delays within the citizenship system are outside an applicant’s control.
Introducing more restrictive criteria risks sending a damaging message to the people Ireland urgently needs to retain. Ireland is competing internationally for doctors, nurses and other skilled healthcare professionals. Countries such as Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom are also actively seeking these workers. If Ireland’s citizenship and immigration system becomes perceived as unnecessarily uncertain, slow or unfair, we should not be surprised if highly skilled professionals begin to consider building their lives elsewhere.
At a time when our health service is already under enormous pressure, Ireland should be doing everything possible to retain the healthcare professionals who have chosen to make this country their home. We should recognise their contribution, provide certainty to those who have fulfilled the existing requirements, and ensure that any changes to citizenship policy are fair, proportionate and do not retrospectively disadvantage people who have already invested years of their lives in Ireland. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – The proposal to increase the period of residence required for Irish citizenship from five to eight years raises a fundamental question of fairness: should people who are already legally resident in Ireland be subjected to a new rule that did not exist when they made the decision to build their lives here?
Applying such a change to people who are already resident in the State is retroactive legislation and may be subject to being annulled by judicial review.
For Ukrainians in particular, this issue deserves special consideration. Many have now spent several years establishing new lives here and it is grossly unfair to extend their residency period to achieve Irish citizenship from five to eight years. – Yours, etc,

title: Doctor jailed for sexual assault in UK was subject of complaint in Dublin 20 years ago
description: In 2006, Muhammad Iqbal was the subject of a sexual harassment grievance from younger colleague
content:
A doctor who was jailed for sexual assault in Britain in August was the subject of a complaint alleging sexual harassment of a younger colleague in Dublin 20 years ago.
Muhammad Iqbal (64), of Julianstown, Co Meath, was jailed last month for 18 months at Newcastle Crown Court in relation to separate incidents in Darlington and Sunderland in 2023. He was also placed on the sex offenders register for 10 years.
The women at the centre of the incidents were attending physiotherapy sessions arranged by their insurers following road crashes and were assaulted by Iqbal during examination.
Iqbal worked for St Michael’s House in the Republic, an organisation which provides a range of services and supports to adults and children with disabilities, for 22 years. His employment ceased the week his British court case concluded.
The Irish Times has established that in 2006, Iqbal was the subject of a complaint which alleged sexual harassment of a younger colleague who worked with him at the organisation.
It is understood the allegations related to unwanted touching of the leg, an incident of unwanted kissing on the cheek and hand, behaviour described as “flirtatious”, questions about her personal life and requests for her personal phone number.
The complaint also referred to Iqbal allegedly telling the colleague that he knew where she lived, it is understood.
A spokesman for St Michael’s House said: “While the matter referred to was 20 years ago and the available information is limited, we can confirm that the organisation’s procedures were applied.
“To the best of our knowledge, there is no record of any subsequent allegation or complaint since 2006.”
It emerged during the British court case that during the assault of one patient, Iqbal had grabbed the woman’s breast, and that in the second, he had pretended he needed to examine her breast, saying he was checking for lumps, although that was not the reason for the examination.
Iqbal had denied the offences but was convicted following a trial, said the British police force.
After the court case, a spokesman for St Michael’s House said it implemented all safeguards and requirements communicated by the Medical Council as the prosecution case against him progressed.
“St Michael’s House is aware of the outcome of court proceedings involving Dr Muhammed Iqbal. The safety, welfare and dignity of the people who use our services are our primary concern at all times,” he said.
“Throughout this matter, St Michael’s House acted in accordance with the requirements of the Medical Council and complied with its obligations as an employer.”
The Irish Medical Council’s register of doctors states that Iqbal’s registration is suspended until “steps or further steps are taken” under the relevant legislation.
He is prohibited from practising medicine at this time, according to the register.
Outside court after his trial, detective constable Charlotte Naisby, of Durham Constabulary’s complex safeguarding team, said: “Iqbal preyed on these women during a very vulnerable period in their lives ... The women should have felt safe being examined by a certified GP, but instead Iqbal not only assaulted them but breached their trust in the most horrendous way and we are glad to see he is now behind bars.”

title: Building tycoon Maurice Regan buys Meath castle that was former home of Duke of Wellington
description: New York and Clonmel-based billionaire acquired castle in deal to buy developer Gerry Gannon’s debts from Nama
content:
Construction tycoon Maurice Regan has bought a castle in Co Meath and its surrounding 236 acres of land that was formerly owned by builder Gerry Gannon .
The purchase by Regan of Dangan Castle , the childhood home of Arthur Wellesley, the Duke of Wellington, came as part of Regan’s €250 million buyout of developer Gannon’s loans from the National Asset Management Agency (Nama) in 2024.
Land records show that Gannon bought Dangan Castle in 2008 and there were two charges placed on the property from AIB . Those charges were replaced by a charge placed on the historic property by Stolensky Ltd, a Regan company, on December 17th, 2024.
Regan became its full owner in June 2025 and there are no charges on the property now.
The property was offered for sale for €3.1m in 2023 . The 18th-century castle is in a ruinous state and it is understood the New York-based Regan is exploring what work is required to prevent further degradation of the large Georgian country residence.
The castle has a five-bay, two-storey facade above a vaulted basement. It was the childhood home of the Duke of Wellington, who famously went on to defeat Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.
[ Historic childhood home of the 1st Duke of Wellington for sale at €3.1m Opens in new window ]
It is understood Regan primarily sees the property as a farm. In 2023 it had 50 acres of grassland, 115 acres of tillage and 70 acres of forestry. It is located 2km from the village of Summerhill.
A spokesman for Regan said: “As part of our relationship with our partner developer Gerry Gannon, we acquired in a portfolio the Park2Travel car park at Dublin Airport and tillage and forestry land in Co Meath.”
As part of his purchase of Gannon’s Nama debts, Regan took over his Dublin Airport car-parking site that has capacity for 6,000 cars. It now operates under the Park2Travel brand and is managed by Apcoa. Airport operator DAA was previously blocked from acquiring the parking facility due to a ruling from the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission .
Born in London but raised in Kerry from the age of 10, Regan became wealthy through building up JT Magen, a New York construction firm that includes Netflix and a number of data-centre companies among its range of clients in the United States. In Ireland he owns the Mercantile Group of pubs whose bars include Whelan’s, Cafe en Seine and The George .
Regan has extensive farm interests in Tipperary centred on his base in Newtown Anner Stud outside Clonmel . He is due to acquire the 751-acre Barne Estate for €22.25 million after Coolmore ’s John Magnier failed in a High Court case to enforce an earlier handshake deal he agreed with the owners to buy it for €15 million.
[ John Magnier mystique unmasked in continuing conflict with Maurice Regan Opens in new window ]
Regan and Magnier are locked in an ongoing competition case that is before the High Court, with Regan claiming that Coolmore has used its power to block Regan’s stud from using the Fethard Equine Hospital and Coolmore’s stud services. Coolmore has denied breaching any laws and has said the hospital is free to treat Regan’s horses. It has accused Regan of threatening to “destroy” Magnier .

title: Remembering Frank McDonald
description: He was a lovely, charming man; a blithe spirit indeed
content:
Sir, – I knew Frank McDonald well from the early days of the Temple Bar development. For all his radical and sophisticated urbanism, a part of his spirit remained rooted in suburban northside Dublin, where he grew up, a true 1960s Christian Brothers boy.
He was a lovely, charming man; a blithe spirit indeed. We are reduced by his going.
May his gentle soul rest in peace. – Yours, etc
Sir, – The late Frank McDonald once memorably described the St Stephen’s Green Shopping Centre as a “ Mississippi riverboat ”.
