title: Ryanair investors say yes to Michael O’Leary’s €150m pay deal
description: Your view on O’Leary’s pay probably depends on where you stand
content:
Is Michael O’Leary worth more than €150 million?
Yes, according to Ryanair shareholders, who approved the CEO’s controversial new pay deal at Thursday’s annual general meeting, despite opposition from proxy advisers ISS and PIRC.
The figure is the potential value of a share option package, and depends on O’Leary remaining at Ryanair until 2032 and hitting performance targets.
Some might say no one is worth €150 million, although even O’Leary’s detractors would admit Ryanair’s growth would have been unthinkable without him.
Since 1994, he has transformed a loss-making minnow into Europe’s largest airline by passenger numbers and created enormous wealth for shareholders.
[ Ryanair boss Michael O’Leary criticised over ‘high-fare rapists’ comments Opens in new window ]
Still, it’s fair to ask if O’Leary is being rewarded in the right way. The sheer size of the potential reward could encourage excessive risk-taking, cautions ISS.
It also questions the €42 share-price target because O’Leary could benefit from a rising market or a broader recovery in airline shares, even without Ryanair outperforming its peers.
This is the classic “pay for luck” problem, one long recognised in the academic literature. If airline shares rise as oil prices fall, should a CEO get a huge reward? What if they plunge when oil spikes? Is that O’Leary’s fault, or Donald Trump’s? Surely incentives should reward what managers can control, as opposed to what they can’t?
There is also the fact that O’Leary gets the award if Ryanair’s profits exceed €4 billion in any one year through 2032. It does not have to sustain that performance, ISS noted.
And the defence? Well, the targets are demanding, O’Leary must stay until 2032, and Ryanair estimates that hitting the share-price target would create around €16 billion of additional shareholder value. His potential gain would represent less than 1 per cent of that.
Indeed, Barclays went further in a recent note, saying the pay proposal strengthens the investment case for the stock. “No other airline has incentives structures like these”, said Barclays, praising the “very strong” alignment between management and shareholders.
So is €150 million too much? That largely depends on whether you see an unusually powerful incentive as a flaw, as ISS does, or a virtue, as Barclays does.
For Ryanair shareholders, Thursday’s vote suggests the latter view won the day.

title: Plant, mulch, move: essential garden jobs as autumn closes in
description: Everywhere in the garden are unmistakable signs of seasonal shift, from trees heavy with fruit to spiderwebs silver-beaded with dew
content:
L ike a lot of people I try my best at this time of year to ignore the fact that autumn has arrived while winter is fast approaching. But of course, this head-in-the-sand approach only ever works for so long. Instead, everywhere in the garden are unmistakable signs of the seasonal shift, from trees heavy with fruit and spiderwebs silver-beaded with dew, to shades of gold and nutmeg in the hedgerows. Much as we might wish summer to linger a little longer, the year is inexorably turning, a signal to us gardeners that it’s time to take stock as well as to plan ahead.
Any recently emptied vegetable and cut-flower beds, for example, should be covered with a thick organic mulch of well-rotted manure, responsibly foraged seaweed or home-made garden compost to prevent weedy growth from quickly colonising all that bare ground, bearing in mind that nature abhors a vacuum.
Or if that seems like too arduous, time-consuming or expensive a chore, then the alternative – a good one – is to sow a green manure such as winter vetch, grazing rye, white mustard or winter field beans to nourish and protect the soil (seed stockists include fruithillfarm.com , quickcrop.ie and giy.ie ). Failing that, cover any emptied beds with a layer or two of brown cardboard or strong black plastic sheeting weighted down with stones, or with the edges neatly trenched into the ground.
Just make sure to strike while the iron is hot. Now that heavy rains have refreshed thirsty soils and the latter are still warm from repeated heatwaves, conditions are ideal for optimal germination and quick growth. But they’re less likely to be so in a month’s time.
Which is not to say that there aren’t any very useful overwintering food crops that can still be sown or planted over the coming weeks. For example, it’s well worth leaving some growing space uncovered to sow or transplant varieties of hardy winter salad leaves such as mizuna, mustard, pak choi, tatsoi, claytonia and corn salad (stockists include greenvegetableseeds.com and brownenvelopeseeds.com ), as well as to plant spring cabbage (these as young transplants) and overwintering varieties of onions (these as sets). Hardy varieties of garlic and broad beans can also be sown or planted next month, all crops that will prove their worth next spring.
If you sowed seed of hardy flowering biennials such as foxgloves, Canterbury bells, wallflowers and honesty earlier in the summer, move these young transplants into their permanent growing positions as soon as possible so that they can establish decent root systems before growth slows.
That same window of opportunity will also soon close for sowing seed of decorative hardy annuals for flowering next summer. So grab the chance while you can to sow seed of orlaya, ammi, cornflowers, snapdragon, larkspur, Chinese forget-me-not, Argentine forget-me-not and marigolds for the reasons outlined above. Most of these will happily survive an average Irish winter outdoors without help, but in cooler parts of the country where harsh frosts are likely, they’ll benefit from either a protective layer of fleece or being overwintered in an unheated glasshouse.
At the risk of being shot for mentioning the C-word so outrageously early in the year, mid-September is also the cut-off point for planting Christmas hyacinth bulbs in time to force them into bloom for the festive season. Just make sure to use bulbs that have been specially treated for this purpose (try mrmiddleton.com ).
Speaking of flowering bulbs, this is the time to start getting most kinds of spring-flowering bulbs in the ground or into pots, from narcissus, fritillaria, camassia and crocus to scilla, alliums and snowdrops. But hold off from planting tulips until late autumn or early winter to minimise the risk of disease.
To avoid accidentally introducing the latter into your garden, it’s always worth paying that bit extra for large, plump, firm, high-quality bulbs free of obvious blemishes and sourced from a reputable supplier. Along with most of those mentioned above, recommended stockists include most good Irish garden centres and peternyssen.com .
Make sure to plant these bulbs to the correct depth (typically roughly three times their own height), which helps protect their fleshy structures from temperature extremes and prevents them from drying out before they’ve had a chance to plunge their roots into the ground.
In gardens where raiding squirrels are a serious problem for freshly planted bulbs, it’s best to plant them in informal groupings and then place a protective layer of fine-gauge chicken wire over them (13mm-25mm openings, using the larger size for larger bulbs) before backfilling with soil. The same technique can be used for pots. Alternatively, make a small protective cradle of chicken wire to contain the bulbs before planting them to the correct depth.
Meanwhile, if you delayed doing so last month because of concerns about the negative impact on plants of this summer’s drought and intense heat, be reassured that beech, hornbeam, thuja and Leylandii hedges can all be given a final clipping so long as it’s completed by the middle of the month. So too can privet, yew and Lonicera nitida hedges.
September is also the ideal time to move or transplant conifers and other evergreen shrubby species. But it’s always a good idea to use a wind-filtering meshed fabric such as Bionet to protect the young plants against desiccating winter winds until their root systems establish, a process that will take at least until next spring.
Finally, consider planting up some containers using a mix of handsome evergreen and bulbous species for an eye-catching display that will give valuable interest through winter and into spring. Suitable evergreen species include grasses such as Carex buchananni, Chionochloa rubra and Carex testacea; ferns such as Polystichum setiferum and Polystichum polyblepharum; shrubs or sub-shrubs such as fatsia, Euphorbia wulfenii, camellia, skimmia, pieris, pittosporum and culinary bay; plus trailing ivy. Winter might still feel a very long way away, but when the days shorten and the temperatures begin to bite, your future self will thank you for it.
Keep deadheading dahlias to prolong their display and to protect emerging flowers from damage and disease.
Reduce watering of glasshouse and polytunnel crops such as tomatoes, aubergines, peppers and cucumbers to a minimum and remove any dead, damaged or decaying leaves or fruit to maximise productivity and plant health.

title: Art and Antiques: Collection of rediscovered Irish painter at deVeres
description: Dublin-born Frank Phelan was at the centre of the 1960s and 1970s international art movements
content:
From time to time, auction houses handle the sale of works from a studio of a recently deceased artist. Such is the case with deVeres ’ auction of the studio of Frank Phelan (1932-2023) on September 16th.
Born in Dublin, Phelan worked as a draughtsman in the capital city before emigrating to Canada with his father and brother. In the 1960s he worked in set design in London. He soon became involved with the group of artists based in St Ives in Cornwall, including Kilkenny-born Tony O’Malley. Citing Francis Bacon as his biggest influence, Phelan developed an abstract expressionist painting style and had shows in Scotland, England and Ireland. He continued to paint until his death aged 91.
“He was an interesting painter who flew below the radar at auction, and not many of his paintings came to the market,” says Rory Guthrie of deVeres. Landscape (€1,500-€2,000) and Calypso (€600-€900) are good examples of the work for sale. With more than 100 paintings for sale, going to see the work in situ is particularly worthwhile for any prospective buyer. Many of the paintings have estimates of €300-€500, which gives new collectors an opportunity to buy at reasonable prices. Works in The Studio of Frank Phelan will be on view at deVeres, 35 Kildare Street, Dublin 2, every day until the auction at 2pm on September 16th.
Elsewhere, there are a few auctions of Irish art on this weekend and early next week that offer enthusiasts a wide variety of work by artists from the 19th century right up to the early 21st century.
Sheppard’s Important Irish Art auction on September 15th – with in-person previews on today, tomorrow and Monday, September 14th – is an example of one such auction with landscapes, cityscapes and still-life paintings spanning the late 1800s, the 1900s and early 2000s.
The auction includes some interesting works by artists born in the 19th century, such as James Humbert Craig (1877-1944), William Conor (1881-1968) and Flora H Mitchell (1890-1973).
James Humbert Craig’s The Farm in the Glens (€5,000-€8,000) is one of a few pieces in Sheppard’s auction by the prolific Belfast-born painter, whose work sold for much higher prices in the early 2000s.
William Conor, another Belfast-born artist, was renowned for his portrayal of working-class life in Ulster, and several of his crayon and watercolour pieces are in the permanent collection of the Ulster Museum. Conor’s The Violin Player, in watercolour, ink and charcoal (€2,000-€3,000), is in Sheppard’s auction, as is Shawlie with Children, Quay Street, Skerries (€8,000-€12,000).
Flora H Mitchell is most widely appreciated for her watercolour, pen and ink sketches of the streetscapes of Dublin. Her drawing of Dame Street, Dublin (€2,000-€3,000) at Sheppard’s auction, captures the rich intact 18th-century architectural detail, including Jurys Hotel, which was at 6-8 College Green, just at the start of Dame Street, from 1839 to 1973. The hotel was demolished in 1980 to make way for the Central Bank, which was more recently moved to a new building on North Wall Quay. Mitchell was born in Omaha, Nebraska, and her 1966 book, Vanishing Dublin, with 50 coloured plates of her paintings of Dublin streets, is a valuable record of Dublin’s disappearing streetscapes.
Enthusiasts of still-life paintings should take a look at Norah McGuinness’s Still Life with Fruit (€4,000-€6,000) and Colin Stack’s Still Life of Flowers in a Vase (€600-€900).
Finally, enthusiasts of historical portraits, watercolours and drawings might be interested in donating towards a new publication by St Patrick’s Cathedral, Dublin. In an effort to make a durable record of the art associated with the cathedral over the past 300 years, the cathedral has commissioned art historian, Dr Paul Caffrey to catalogue what is one of Ireland’s most important ecclesiastical art collections. To help with publication costs, Dean William Morton of St Patrick’s Cathedral is asking subscribers to donate €250 in return for an invite to the launch and a free copy of the book, St Patrick’s Cathedral and the Deanery: Catalogue of the Collection of Portraits, Watercolours and Drawings. Those interested should email marketings@stpatrickscathedral.ie

title: Not a Rioja or albariño in sight: How to pick a more unusual Spanish wine
description: John Wilson: From light whites to robust reds, there’s plenty more to Spain’s wine offering than the most popular options
content:
Eat Spain Drink Spain 2026 began this week and will continue for the next two weeks. A celebration of Spanish food and wine, there will be events in shops, bars and restaurants all over the country. See foodswinesfromspain.com for details.
We are big fans of two Spanish wines in Ireland: albariño from Rías Baixas and Rioja. I have nothing against either of these, but Spain offers a huge range of other wines, from the lightest fine white wines to robust reds, as well as Sherry, one of the world’s great wines.
This week, we feature four wines, all made from Spanish grape varieties, three costing less than €20, and not an albariño or Rioja in sight!
Readers will doubtless be familiar with the devastating fires that hit Spain in August . For a number of wine producers, the fires were a disaster, burning down swathes of old vines, some a century or more old. The loss is irreparable, although the team from top producer Comando G posted that it could have been even worse. Apparently, in some places the vineyards acted as firebreaks, as they have more humidity and are planted further apart.
Medium- to full-bodied with plenty of spicy plum fruits and a lightly tannic finish. Locally, they would drink it alongside roast lamb or pork.
A very seductive, light, refreshing white wine with pear and apple aromas and vivid green fruits. Very good concentration and length. Drink by itself, with nibbles or with lighter fish dishes.

title: It’s blackberry season: here’s how to recreate those classic childhood desserts
description: It’s a humble fruit but the flavour a blackberry can bring to your table is spectacular
content:
A recent visit to The Old Spot Pub in Dublin 4 reminded me of the arrival of one of my favourite ingredients and, by default, seasons. After a long summer of sunshine, sweat and suncream stinging my eyes, autumn is here. With it comes an abundance of brilliant produce and wild food. I might only be speaking for myself, but as a chef, I start to get excited when September rolls around. But back to The Old Spot, where I managed to nab the last portion before it was scratched off the blackboard: “Steamed blackberry pudding with pistachio crumble and milk ice cream” – yes, please. Blackberries have graced our hedgerows with their presence in abundance over the past few days. A cousin of the raspberry, they have a deep purple colour with a lovely balance of sweetness and acidity. Fascinating fact: blackberries retain their tough core when picked, while raspberries kindly leave it behind on the stem at their departure. This means blackberries often require prior cooking to soften or remove the core if picked too early.
This week’s recipes celebrate the humble autumnal fruit without any fuss or faff. The first dish is a nostalgic warm rice pudding that, while simple in appearance, has a knack to it. The key to cooking sweet rice for pudding is to firstly wash off any excess starch to avoid a glutenous finish and second is to bake it in the oven under a sheet of parchment. The blackberry compote is as simple as it gets, involving cooking it out with sugar, lemon juice and some cinnamon. If you have a bumper crop, this can be bulked up and either frozen or stored in the fridge for an extended period of time. Toasted almonds are the make or break of the dish, adding texture and their signature caramelised flavour.
The second recipe is, yet again, a classic that has a hundred different iterations – this one focuses on the details. The compote of apple and blackberry is cooked in advance, as is the crumble topping. This gives you control over both the texture and flavour of each, meaning you just have to warm it up when the guests arrive. I have seen too many recipes over the years that assemble the crumble in its raw form and expect the oven to turn it into a masterpiece – it just doesn’t happen. These can also be assembled ahead of time and kept in the fridge ready to be heated and served up with a classic crème Chantilly on the side, although ice cream works just as well.
Tip of the week: if you are making rice pudding, rinse the rice to remove excess starch before baking it in sweetened milk and cream in the oven. This will avoid the mix turning to baby food.

title: Exit Party author Emily St John Mandel: ‘I cannot overstate how stressful the US is at the moment’
description: The bestselling Canadian writer returns with a near-future vision of the world – well, two of them
content:
E mily St John Mandel knows “it sounds deranged”, especially given everything she has just been saying about the political devastation of the United States , but Exit Party, her new novel , is “a hopeful book”, she feels. “Who will you be at the end of the world? I think of that as the book’s central question. It does imply that you’re going to be something and that things will go on. There is hope and art.”
The Canadian author, best known for literary phenomenon Station Eleven, is at her standing desk in Queens, New York – “That’s the East River out the sliver of window” – and explaining the genesis of Exit Party, in which she explores two distinct visions of the near future, both of them nightmarish, yet ameliorated to some degree by human resilience, connection and a Mandelesque belief in the beauty of the world.
“An idea that I’ve been fascinated with for a long time is this notion of the counterlife, the life you didn’t live,” she says. “I think about the way I would be a somewhat different person if I’d remained in western Canada, say, instead of coming to New York City when I was 22.”
She started writing her seventh novel in the spring of 2022, well before the reelection of Donald Trump, but even then there was a sense of brokenness in the country in which she has lived most of her adult life. “I cannot overstate how fractured and stressful this country is at the moment.”
She cites The City and the City, China Miéville’s speculative fiction novel, in which the citizens of two cities occupying the same geographical space are trained not to see the other city. They have two completely different understandings of reality. “That notion has seemed less and less fantastical to me with the passage of time,” she says.
Mandel does not write to a plot outline, preferring not to know exactly where she’s going to allow for “the possibility of weirdness”. But as she started to write the “A-side” of Exit Party, which opens in an unstable, violent and militia-ridden version of 2031 not long after a second American civil war and the collapse of the United States, she began to think about the flipside, or the “B-side” as it is demarcated in the book.
Mild spoiler ahead. In this counterlife, there is no Republic of California, no Republic of Ohio, but a singular, authoritarian United State, in which total compliance is secured by surveillance technology and the enforcement powers of a Stasi-like “Service”. Events such as “the last of the pro-democracy demonstrations” are recalled as distant history.
“I had this fairly chilling experience of struggling to stay ahead of the news cycle on the B-side. All of a sudden, with the Ice [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] raids in American cities, the idea of masked secret police sweeping up civilians and disappearing them into unmarked cars was suddenly not at all fictional.”
‘I feel much more in common with people in, say, London or Paris than I do with people in upstate New York’
Enter Ari Waker. It is not necessary to have read Mandel’s second novel, The Singer’s Gun, to read Exit Party, but a villain from that earlier novel returns as the central protagonist this time. Newly released from prison, Ari goes to a party in a chaotic, tent-filled Los Angeles, where a stranger – who seems to have a twin – mysteriously calls her by her unused legal name, Ibari. The host, Kareem, goes missing. Later, Ari encounters a woman who looks exactly like her old flatmate Gloria, only this version has no scar.
The idea of doppelgängers as “the physical embodiment of the counterlife” has been on her mind since she was a kid. “I had a nightmare about doppelgängers when I was quite young that kind of stayed with me. It’s just such an unsettling idea.”
What’s more unsettling, the idea that there’s a worse version of you out there somewhere, or a better one? “Neither is great, honestly.”
With Ari, who thinks of herself as a reformed character but still retains her ruthless edge, Mandel wanted to examine “the essential components” of a person’s soul and how this might be shaped by their world. “I love the idea that the thing you don’t like about yourself might be one of the things that keeps you alive.”
The act of parenting is also key to the novel in a way it didn’t tend to be in Mandel’s writing before she had her daughter in 2015. “I didn’t know enough about parenting to put it into my work before I was a parent, which is not to imply in any way that an author who isn’t a parent couldn’t write about those themes. For me, personally, it took being a parent to understand some of those nuances.”
She has always liked writing books that span genres. “I think of [Exit Party] as literary fiction, but then it does absolutely have that speculative element to it, and I think what that can give to us is a way of thinking about the present moment that’s bearable. A realist novel about the rise of nationalism and the fracturing of countries might feel quite unbearable.”
There are Mandel touches aplenty in Exit Party. Guilt manifests in the form of a ghost. A capacity for premonitions isn’t as useful as it might seem. Just as a graphic novel passes down the generations in Station Eleven, art is a recurring focal point in the form of Swan Dive, a painting by Lucas Alkaitis, an artist character from her novel The Glass Hotel.
“I’m interested in the way a work of art moves through time, and the way multiple people across decades, even centuries, can have quite intense relationships with it that truly mean something to them. I love that idea,” she says. The more practical benefit is that an object like this can be “helpful for cohesion” when writing a multi-stranded novel.
Although Mandel’s books are all stand-alone, the links between them have prompted fans to muse about the Mandelverse. “I love that term,” she says. It’s less of a mouthful than the Emily St John Mandel Cinematic Universe, another one she’s heard. And she’s always had a penchant for dropping in these callbacks to earlier books. “There’s some pleasure for me in trying to create these connections and some semblance of order in a chaotic universe. I love the idea that every story can kind of glance off of another story, and there’s a whole other drama unfolding just out of sight.”
Exit Party sees the return of the climate-controlled domes that featured in her last book, Sea of Tranquility. One over Paris, to which the action shifts, looks like “a series of giant soap bubbles”, with the buildings on the other side of its semi-transparent wall “faded out like ghosts”. The domes are “a terrible solution”, she says. “I don’t even know that they’re feasible from an engineering standpoint. But, you know, it’s a science fictional trope for a reason.”
Starting with her first novel, 2009’s Last Night in Montreal, Mandel’s cities – and not only her futuristic ones – have been skilfully rendered. She feels “very at home in large cities”, she says. “It feels to me like there’s a greater cultural connection sometimes between cities than there is between, say, the city and the countryside in a given country. I feel much more in common with people in, say, London or Paris than I do with people in upstate New York.”
Born Emily St John Fairbanks – St John, her middle name, was her grandmother’s maiden name – in 1979, Mandel grew up in the “absolute opposite” of a city in British Columbia, first on Vancouver Island, then on Denman Island. “It’s the same size and shape as Manhattan, but with a thousand people. It’s just trees. It’s a lot of trees.”
[ Sea of Tranquility by Emily St John Mandel review: Original and eerily prescient Opens in new window ]
She found this beautiful, but “a bit claustrophobic in that very small town way”. A trained ballet dancer, she moved to Toronto at the age of 18 for a conservatory programme in contemporary dance. From about eight or nine years old, she had written short stories or “fragments of short stories”, thinking of it as “just this odd little hobby” she enjoyed.
“Then, when I was about 22, I realised I didn’t want to be a dancer any more, and I thought, well, I could take this more seriously and try writing a novel.”
Last Night in Montreal was published when she was 30, then came The Singer’s Gun and The Lola Quartet, before a big step forward in her career in 2014. Station Eleven, her story of how civilisation slowly rebuilds itself after a deadly flu has killed most of the population, was an immediate hit, with Mandel winning both the Arthur C Clarke Award for best science fiction novel and legions of new fans. It has now sold more than 1.5 million copies, boosted by the second wind of Covid and a 10-part HBO Max adaptation – commissioned in 2019 – that presented her ultimately comforting, even uplifting, take on a post-apocalyptic society right at the time when people needed one.
While promoting The Glass Hotel in 2020, Mandel found she kept being asked about Station Eleven, and she put this experience into 2022’s Sea of Tranquility in autofictional form through the character of Olive Llewellyn, a 23rd-century author of a bestselling pandemic novel.
The pandemic also wound up being a catalyst for change in Mandel’s working life. Although she wasn’t involved in the Station Eleven series, she started working on television scripts during this time, including a planned adaptation of Exit Party, and she now divides her time between New York and Los Angeles.
“The pandemic was so solitary and I had this feeling afterwards that I don’t think I want to just work by myself alone in a room any more. To be clear, I do love that, just not all the time,” she says. “[TV writing] is such a collaborative experience, and it’s also health insurance.”
[ The best new books to look out for in autumn 2026 Opens in new window ]
She got divorced from her husband in 2022, which she bizarrely had to “prove” to Wikipedia editors by arranging a media interview to confirm it – the droll Slate.com headline was “Emily St John Mandel is divorced, Wikipedia” – and last year she married photographer and director Laura Barisonzi.
As we segue from talking about her childhood writing to recent alarm about declining literacy rates in the US, she once again offers an optimistic counterpoint.
“My impression of Gen Z is that they love books. It’s kind of extraordinary. My wife and I had this really lovely experience recently. We had some time to kill in midtown Manhattan, and we wandered into Bryant Park, which is a really lovely little park right next to the flagship location of the New York Public Library, and we stumbled upon this kind of strange scene where there was an outdoor stage, and a man was playing meandering, dreamlike piano music. The lawn was covered with people of I’d say a range of ages – but young people were very well represented – reading quietly on their picnic blankets.
“Then a man got up on stage and said, ‘Good evening, readers. You’ve reached the two-hour mark of our New York Public Library reading party. Please take a moment and go to the next blanket and discuss your books with each other.’ I thought, Oh my God, it’s a reading party.”
Part of the backlash against AI is “this longing for something real”, she says, and that includes the physical object of the book. It’s not something she would have predicted a decade ago but it seems to her that, for people in their 20s, books in the year 2026 are “kind of cool”.

title: Anita Brookner: Art & Life by Hermione Lee – A loving, careful and worthwhile biography of an evasive life
description: Is this biography so much about the books because there’s little to say about the life?
content:
“I have no private papers,” the English novelist Anita Brookner told an interviewer in 1995. “I shall leave no trace. That’s the ideal.” Appearing early in Hermione Lee’s biographer of Brookner, this quotation reads like a shot across the bows of the reader, alongside a quote from Brookner’s novel from the same year, Incidents in the Rue Laugier, which appears here as an epigraph: “The dead, perhaps even more than the living, have a right to their mysteries.”
Don’t expect big revelations, Lee seems to be saying. For the close observer, this was obvious even before opening the book, from its size: fitting the life into 450 pages (plus appendices), it’s half the length of Lee’s biographies of Tom Stoppard and Virginia Woolf. What is there to say about a writer who, it seems, spent her time teaching, then writing, lived alone and travelled little?
The trace that Brookner – who was born in 1928 and died in 2016 – did leave is in the books: as well as works as an art historian, she wrote 24 novels, mostly published at yearly intervals. If it hadn’t been for her winning the Booker Prize in 1984 with her fourth novel, Hotel du Lac, she would probably be even more of a minor interest than she is: according to her agent, Bill Hamilton, most of her books sell “very few indeed: between 20 and 80 a year”.
If Brookner’s life was – to adopt the phrase of Philip Larkin’s biographer Andrew Motion – not “much diversified by event”, that matches the popular perception of her novels. They were, goes this misreading, dull and quiet and unambitious. Even her Booker winner was controversial: it was “an unexpected choice”, said Melvyn Bragg, who hosted the TV coverage of the prize that year. The book was “insipid”, said Jeanette Winterson, and its win “typical of the way the establishment ... rewarded women who are compliant”.
Lee’s job is not just to tell the life but to rehabilitate the work. Not that this is necessary for anyone who has read Brookner’s work with any care. Brookner is “a deeply romantic and passionate writer,” says Lee, “whose armour is an austere, controlled manner, a dry, often formal vocabulary and a scathing wit”.
In her analysis of her characters’ thoughts, there is a Jamesian depth of qualified emotion as well as a cool detachment and analytical rigour more reminiscent of European modernism than much traditional English literary fiction. The books had recurring motifs, which she was well aware of. She would tell her friend Julian Barnes, over their annual lunch, that she had just written a new book. Dropping her voice, she would add, “It’s about ... a lonely woman.”
The rich understanding of people’s passions – those of lonely women and others – that her novels exhibit may have been sharpened by the way Brookner preferred, in life, to observe them from a distance rather than get too close.
Stories of her unique way of putting herself about in the world – not so much antisocial as asocial – abound in Lee’s account. One comes from her own experience, when Lee attended the Times Literary Supplement party and chatted to Brookner for a few minutes as they made their way in. Very soon after, Brookner came out again. “But Anita, you’ve only been here for five minutes!” cried Lee. “To which she replied, with perfect courtesy, ‘And I’m so glad that three of them were spent with you’.”
[ Anita Brookner: Author of elegiac novels labelled the ‘mistress of gloom’ Opens in new window ]
Hilary Mantel had a similar experience: “I saw her ‘attend’ the Spectator party by walking in at the front door, down to the end of the garden – smiling guardedly and nodding – and walking back – and out again.” To Julian Barnes she wrote, “I put in my usual ten minutes at the Spectator party but failed to see you there, no doubt for that reason.”
Brookner’s background was from a family of Polish Jews, and Jewish exiles feature in some of her best books, including Family and Friends (1985), Latecomers (1988) and The Next Big Thing (2002). Her father, who came to England in 1908 aged 16, changed the family named from Bruckner to Brookner, which his daughter later observed, with typical dry wit, was “like calling yourself Batehoven”.
She didn’t make it easy for her future biographer even in her youth, throwing away childhood photos, “wishing to silence the ‘clamorous voices’ they evoked”. At school she was “one of the brainy ones”, which was more a curse than a blessing: her mother, she told her friend Carmen Callil in a rare moment of self-exposure, “wanted me to be another kind of person altogether. I should have looked different, should have been more popular, socially more graceful, one of those small, coy, kittenish women who get their way”.
Her manner of getting her own way was to exert absolute control over her life, by letting few people get close. She never married, and Lee has been unable to uncover firm evidence of any romantic relationships, though she does her best to speculate about possible paramours.
The publisher Christopher MacLehose, for example, discounts any suggestion that he was the model for the charismatic lover of the heroine in Brookner’s 1982 novel Providence. The strongest evidence we get is that she told several friends that in the 1980s she and the Jewish philanthropist and property tycoon Max Rayne were lovers. “He fucked like a navvy,” she told one friend, in a distinctly un-Brooknerian cadence.
Before she became a novelist, Brookner was a highly respected art historian at the Courtauld Institute in London, where she worked with Anthony Blunt, who was subsequently disgraced when unveiled as a Soviet spy. His exposure left Brookner “shaking” with “absolute outrage”. Before that she lived for a time in Paris, but once again Lee is stymied.
“What happened to the young Anita Brookner, set free in Paris, city of possibilities? It’s a mystery.” Whatever it was, it informed her work: repeatedly in her novels we come across characters who think longingly of a period of youth in Paris, and struggle against the strictures of life back at home.
Back home for Brookner, for most of her life, was flat number 6 at 68 Elm Park Gardens in Chelsea, London, which had “an atmosphere of neutral austerity” – one visitor described her flat as “a machine for living in”. She offered tea to visitors, and biscuits: “shortbread, perfectly arranged, two vertical and then, on top, two horizontal”.
The minutiae of this detail is evidence of the issue that bubbles up regularly in the biography: that Lee is having to fill space. In the absence of big life events – all Brookner’s nonroutine travel is dispatched in one paragraph – what else is there?
This need to make bricks without straw is most obvious when Lee turns to the novels themselves. She passes 10 pages analysing the plot, characters and themes of Brookner’s debut, A Start in Life (1981); 11 on Hotel du Lac; 10 on Family and Friends; nine on Latecomers. Not all the novels are given such in-depth treatment, and Lee’s reading will provide a permanently valuable resource for future Brooknerites; but it does give the sense that the biography is so much about the books because there’s little to say about the life.
Brookner repeatedly spoke in interviews of her regret at not having children. “If I were happy, married with six children, I wouldn’t be writing,” she said to one interviewer. “That’s why I write ... because I have no children,” to another. Lee suggests that reasons may have included “that she couldn’t bear the thought of sharing her well-organised, self-sufficient existence with anyone else”.
In the absence of lovers or children, the book comes most alive in Lee’s account of Brookner’s friendships. We get lively accounts of her friendships with MacLehose, Callil and Barnes (whose friendship with her was “a kind of love story”) as well as rare openings of her heart. When she wrote a tribute to Ben Nicolson, who had been her beloved editor at The Burlington art magazine, she crossed out her closing line – “I miss him still” – in favour of a line ostensibly less effusive but for Brookner more meaningful, “He was a true friend”.
Her wit, so often overlooked in appreciations of her novels, was there in the person too. “What do you think of my new hair colour, Anita?” asked one of her neighbours. “Don’t worry,” she replied. “I’m sure we’ll get used to it.” But she could be challenging too. When historian Roy Foster was seated next to Brookner at a dinner, he told her how much he admired her novels. “I should prefer not to talk about this, please,” came her reply. “I do not like people to talk about my fiction. It has brought me more unhappiness than you can know.”
Yet the books brought much happiness to other people, even if they have been underappreciated in recent years. This book might, with luck, begin to reverse the trend. When Brookner died she left an estate worth £2.4 million. At her request there was no funeral; just two people attended her cremation. She was as evasive in death as she was in life. “How she would have hated having a biography!” Lee writes. But if she must have one, it’s hard to imagine one more loving, careful or worthwhile than this.
A Start in Life (1981) Brookner’s debut is a perfectly formed and surprisingly funny portrait of a woman whose “life had been ruined by literature”. Dr Ruth Weiss finds that “in books, great trials were undergone. At home there was no change”.
Hotel du Lac (1984) A perfect distillation of Brookner’s themes of love and regret. The heroine, a romance novelist, rejects the fable of the hare and the tortoise. “Aesop was writing for the tortoise market. Hares have no time to read. They are too busy winning the game.”
Lewis Percy (1989) Not a lonely woman for once, but a lonely man (“he came from a short line of dead people”), who marries, regrets and flirts with adultery. Meanwhile “the life of action, which he could not quite visualise, remained out of reach”.
The Next Big Thing (2002) A late masterpiece, where the title – meaning death – Is a typical Brookner joke. Julius Herz has too much time on his hands in retirement – but getting obsessed with his young neighbour is probably not a good idea.

title: Agrippa by Robert Harris: Augustus’s best friend tells all in his fictional memoir
description: The master of historical fiction reveals why Marcus Agrippa was so devoted to his friend’s grand design for ancient Rome
content:
Viewers of HBO’s Rome may recall Irish actor Allen Leech playing Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa. In the TV series he is just entering his 20s and embarking on a dangerous adventure with his best friend, Gaius Octavian (played by Max Pirkis). Sadly, the show ended before fans could witness how they would change the world together.
His full but foreshortened life story is told in Robert Harris’s new novel, Agrippa. Now aged 50 and facing his own imminent death, Marcus Agrippa hurriedly writes his memoirs. He has much to reflect on, and the wisdom to make sense of it.
Agrippa begins with his birth in 64 or 63 BC. Roman texts tell us that Marcus had a “difficult birth” (aegre partus in Latin), which was conflated into the nickname Agrippa. Being born feet first was widely seen as so unlucky as to blight a man’s entire life. Yet Marcus bore his name proudly.
His luck turned when he befriended Octavius (the form used in the novel) just a few years before Julius Caesar’s assassination in 44 BC. For Harris’s hero, defying the odds is Agrippa’s motivation, the common thread through his life of derring-do and awesome achievements.
Agrippa marks Harris’s return to the world of ancient Rome. As in the Cicero Trilogy and Pompeii, politics and engineering feature prominently in Agrippa. In siding with Caesar’s legal heir and posthumously adopted son, Octavius, Agrippa becomes a revolutionary, enabling the overturn of the corrupt system that had suppressed the Roman people. In investing the spoils of civil and foreign wars in public baths and parks, Agrippa becomes a socially aware benefactor to ordinary Romans.
The Agrippa of history wrote a memoir of his time as commissioner of public works in Rome, a post he held from 33 BC. Its existence is known from facts about Agrippa’s aqueducts and fountains cited by Frontinus (who later took on the job) and Pliny the Elder (the Roman encyclopaedist). The autobiography itself is lost. Harris here recreates it. Imitating the style Agrippa was reputed to prefer, the language of the novel is unembellished and matter of fact. The result is a man of deeds rather than feelings.
The great mystery of Agrippa’s life is why he was so loyal to his friend when he could have seized supreme power for himself. Harris has an answer (I will not reveal the plot twist) and says he got the notion from FA Wright’s Marcus Agrippa: Organizer of Victory, published in 1937. While pure conjecture, it suits the needs of fiction.
Being Octavius’s best friend comes with both benefits and burdens. He puts his life at risk when fighting to remove his friend’s political enemies. He travels exhaustively around the world, quashing rebels in the provinces and providing administrative talent, to ensure peace in his name. He marries three times, divorcing twice at his friend’s request. The two boys of the last marriage to his friend’s daughter, Julia, are adopted in a symbolic sale so that Octavius might have heirs.
Yet, by collaborating with him, Agrippa enjoys fame and fortune that an unlucky man might not have achieved. From humble origins, Agrippa rises to become the second most powerful man in the Roman world.
Positioning the novel, the publisher asks rhetorically, “When it comes to power, does friendship exist at all?” Through civil wars and in their aftermath, Agrippa facilitated Octavius in becoming princeps, “First Man”. It gave him the right to convene and speak first at meetings of the Roman senate. Acclaimed by its members as Augustus (“Revered” or “Venerable”), he assumed national leadership, and with it control of the army.
While imperium (power) was centred on him, Agrippa shared the same powers and workload, lacking only his influence. He did so willingly and selflessly. He rejected triumphs, the coveted reward for victories in war, instead accepting a unique rostral crown and a blue pennant for his flagship. Yet after he died in 12 BC, Augustus made scant reference to Agrippa’s contributions in his Res Gestae, the official account he wrote of his deeds. Imperium was what mattered to Augustus. A pragmatist, Agrippa understood that. In death, he leaves everything to his friend.
I am delighted that Harris chose Agrippa as the subject of his latest novel. I must declare an interest: the author and I met last summer and discussed our shared fascination for the man. He invited me, as the author of Marcus Agrippa: Right-Hand Man of Caesar Augustus, to read the draft manuscript, and I checked it for errors.
Where I, as a historian, try to capture and interpret the past from known facts, the historical novelist has some licence for speculation, short cuts and rearrangements to make a compelling story. Applying his practised craft as storyteller, Harris brilliantly succeeds in bringing alive the man I recognise from the texts, statues and coins of Ancient Rome.
Lindsay Powell is a historian, writer and f ellow of the Royal Historical Society

title: Hinterlands: Journeys through Europe’s Unfinished Frontiers – A bleak but revelatory dispatch
description: A blend of history, travelogue and geopolitical analysis that traces the faultlines of a 21st-century cold war
content:
‘A great European war will come one day,” Otto von Bismarck is said to have prophesied in 1888, “all because of some damned foolish thing in the Balkans.” Time was to prove Germany’s Iron Chancellor right. But what if that same region and its neighbours are sparking international conflict all over again and the West has barely woken up to it?
This is the troubling question posed in Hinterlands, a discursive blend of history, travelogue and geopolitical analysis by British journalist Hannah Lucinda Smith. For 15 years she has reported from disputed territories around the eastern Mediterranean and Black Sea, “grey zones” cut off from global banking systems where Google Maps goes haywire and Amazon won’t deliver.
These fringe areas of Bosnia, Moldova, Crimea and other old empire outposts, Smith declares, are rapidly becoming the faultlines of a 21st-century cold war. In particular she charges Vladimir Putin and Recep Tayyip Erdogan with fuelling separatist tensions there, an axis of upheaval that uses criminal technologies and propaganda to exploit the EU’s weakness.
Smith is a resourceful and empathetic observer, always concerned about the pawns on this chaotic chessboard. Her 1,000-mile journey includes encounters with northern Cypriots still piecing together skeletons from the ethnic cleansing that followed Turkey’s invasion in 1974.
She tiptoes “like a ballerina” through the plains of Nagorno-Karabakh, where Azerbaijani scientists send light-footed gazelles to detect landmines planted by Armenian troops. She interviews budding revolutionaries and disillusioned veterans as well as nationalist politicians such as Kosovan prime minister Albin Kurti, a “professional pain in the ass” who is presumably happy that so many men born after the 1999 Nato intervention are named Tonibler (an Albanianised Tony Blair).
“Damascus in 2011 was the equivalent of Sarajevo in 1914,” is Smith’s slightly melodramatic conclusion, arguing that the Syrian civil war, which she witnessed, has effectively created a new world order. She skilfully traces the links between Putin backing cryptocurrency mining operations in Transnistria, building Russian Orthodox churches in Republika Srpska and digging military trenches in Ukraine. “History tells us that the small tremors in these places,” she warns, “are the first rumblings of something much bigger.”
A bleak but revelatory dispatch, Hinterlands urges western strategists to readjust their centre of gravity before another Balkan-like powder keg explodes. Bismarck’s ghost can only sympathise.

title: The Bridge by Colm Tóibín: A painful chronicle of relationships in collapse
description: In his latest work to be set in Catalonia, Tóibín’s men pour their deepest tenderness into their animals while their human connections fail
content:
Miquel is a young gay man in Franco’s Spain whose mother’s death in a blizzard was the subject of Colm Tóibín ’s brief masterpiece A Long Winter.
Tóibín’s short novel The Bridge begins with a new bridge that promises to connect Miquel’s remote Catalan mountain valley to the outside world. It introduces temptations: electricity, smuggled contraband, strange men with whom to have encounters. When catastrophe occurs, the hurt, rendered with the author’s plainly worded reserve, is acute.
Perhaps The Bridge is painful because it opens with hope. Summer is approaching; Miquel is more sexually confident. Even the decision to relocate – to his dead mother’s childhood home – is cautiously optimistic. “It gave Miquel some comfort that this house was where his mother had been born; it was where she had been brought up, where she had been returning on the day of the sudden heavy snowfall.”
In Miquel, Tóibín makes us privy to the inner workings of a man not prone to profound introspection. Miquel dwells in moments, like a kiss “by the wall of the church, like lovers in some old song”. His dreams are both vast and plebeian: “He would do anything in his new life – he would cut stones, dig the road, work in a bar, drive a taxi.” But his father’s keenness for smuggling is unwise, and eventually lands them in prison.
Critical things are left unsaid, as one bleakness is heaped upon another. When Miquel’s brother Jordi returns from the military, no one has told him that both his mother and his dog are dead. When his father sells Miquel’s donkey to be butchered, Miquel mourns. Tóibín’s men pour their deepest tenderness into their animals while their human connections fail.
[ A Long Winter, and Ship in Full Sail by Colm Tóibín: A brain of serious range Opens in new window ]
At its heart, The Bridge is about what rends us apart, a chronicle of relationships that have been in collapse even before Miquel’s mother walked into the snow. “Obviously,” Jordi fumes, “she didn’t want to be here in this house with you, with either of you.”
After his lover Manolo visits him in prison, Miquel thinks, “He [Manolo] could wander back into the world, walk on whichever side of the street he wanted … He didn’t have to put much thought into where Miquel would go, how he would sleep, who would share his cell.”
His father has ruined him; his cellmate dotes upon and controls him. But Miquel is a mild man, and like Tóibín, without judgment. The Bridge may be steeped in sadness, but it is Miquel’s gentle spirit that makes his story, for the reader, difficult to bear.
Mei Chin is a writer from New York City living in Dublin.

title: Richard Osman: ‘My cats are the first thing I would save from danger. Apart from my wife of course’
description: The TV producer and author, whose latest novel is We Chase Shadows, is a fan of David O’Doherty, Patricia Highsmith and Palm Springs
content:
No. I thought when I was writing the first one that you just finish the novel because I’ve always been a writer. I’ve done sitcoms, TV and journalism. I did it without telling anyone. I had no expectations because you can’t when you are writing a novel. Even before the first one came out, Steven Spielberg bought the rights to it. That gave me some hope.
In the UK, definitely. I thought if I gave them the final draft, I could look them in the whites of the eyes. We sold the rights in Germany before the UK. Obviously, there and in the US and China, they don’t know me. I get to see what the books do on their own merits in other territories. So, I can compare and contrast.
Yes, although if the first one had gone badly then I’d be telling you that it was supposed to be a one-off. I always think if I read a book, I want to read those same characters again. I had that with the Thursday Murder Club . It hit so big and I had an immediate follow-up because I wanted to talk about the same characters again. That comes from TV. If you have a good idea in television, you don’t just want it to be one season. I love how Agatha Christie had Marple and Poirot. People love characters.
What audiences really want is two books a year, which is impossible. I do a book a year because if you have an audience and a loyalty, that’s a two-way street. It’s the least I can do.
The fun thing about Rosie is she’s much more like Jackie Collins. She’s got 1970s, 1980s money which is helicopter money, private jet money. She comes from a very different place to me, but there is stuff in We Chase Shadows, about some of the things she’s expected to do and some of the interviews she’s expected to do that comes from real life. I know the publicity hoops she’s having to jump through.
[ Richard Osman: ‘Having a hit in Ireland is one of my great joys’ Opens in new window ]
We are developing it for Netflix as a series. It doesn’t matter where you set it. It will be in the back lot of Pinewood before you know it.
The podcast is three hours a week. I can do it off the top of my head. I’m not working nine to five. I’m not working the late shift at the A&E. Doing the book is a different part of the brain.
I’ve just started the next Thursday Murder Club book, which is a nice place to be psychologically. That will be out next September.
[ Thursday Murder Club review: The weak link here, sadly, is the greatest James Bond of all Opens in new window ]
If I read a book with a sense of place, I always just immediately want to go there. I just finished reading an amazing book called No Name (1862) by Wilkie Collins set in 19th-century London and loads of it is set around Vauxhall Walk. So I thought I’d have a little wander down there and when I got down there it was full of serviced offices and Tesco garages.
Get it done. Stop going back, changing every sentence. Go back to the beginning because then you know what your story is. Get it done and get it good, but get to the end.
People who use their strengths to protect people rather than exploit people. My grandfather is who I always think about when I think about masculinity. He was a police officer in the 50s and 60s in Brighton and was very tough but he would look after you if you were in any sort of trouble. That’s what real masculinity really looks like.
I think that we would solve almost all problems in the world if everybody was allowed just five opinions a year on social media or anywhere else. If you use them up on January 1st, we don’t need to hear from you for the rest of the year. If you can find me somebody who has more than five useful opinions a year, I’d be very surprised.
Book: When the Cranes Fly South by Lisa Ridzén, which my mum recommended to me. It’s beautiful, heartbreaking but life-affirming. Film: The Ballad of Wallis Island starring Tim Key and Tom Basden. Who wouldn’t love that film? It’s so charming and funny. Podcast: I really love What Did You Do Yesterday with David O’Doherty and Max Rushden.
[ ‘It’s the first compliment I’ve got in 48 years.’ David O’Doherty and his dad’s familial jam isn’t overly sweet Opens in new window ]
I’m 55 and I was 10 or 11 when the SAS stormed the Iranian embassy in London and they had a breaking news thing which came on when the world snooker final was on. The first bit of breaking news I ever remember in life.
A couple of years ago, I went to Palm Springs for the first time in America. It became this big Hollywood place when Frank Sinatra and Dean Martin and Bob Hope all moved out there, And they signed a contract with the studios. In the 30s, with the Hollywood studios, you had to have a home base that was within two hours of the studios.
It looks like a 50s theme park with this incredible architecture of motels and diners and the neon. And yet in the middle of the desert you’re surrounded by mountains. This was the America of my imagination in the 1970s.
I guess my cats, Lottie and Liesel, but do you ever really own cats? They are the first thing I would save if my house was in danger. Apart from my wife of course.
When Thursday Murder Club really took off, and we sold our first million copies, I bought John le Carré’s Call of the Dead. On the first page he tells you about Smiley. It’s a perfect introduction. It’s a first edition and very precious to me.
I would love Patricia Highsmith even though anything I read about her tells you that she hated absolutely everyone, but that might be fun. Definitely, John le Carré, I would have George Eliot and then maybe Larry McMurty, who wrote Lonesome Dove, and then maybe Douglas Adams for levity
It’s one from my grandfather. “If you’re ever in a pub make sure you’re second through the door.”
Tom Ripley is awful, but you still want to root for him and you really love him. How has Patricia Highsmith pulled that off?
Jonny Sweet’s The Kellerby Code. It’s a bit like Saltburn, but very funny. Towards the End of the Morning by Michael Frayn is one of my favourite books of all time and that’s set in Fleet Street in the 1950s.
When the Cranes Fly South by Lisa Ridzén. You are crying in such a way that you are saying, “Oh, my God life is so awful and yet it is wonderful.”

title: Switzy by Emma Cline: A remarkable act of imagination and empathy
description: Novel beautifully humanises dementia and the often-polarising debate about assisted dying
content:
In Ireland the Assisted Dying Bill 2024 proposed to legalise assisted suicide for individuals under specific circumstances. The Bill lapsed without legislation, but the subject remains one of the most complex ethical and legal debates of our time.
In Switzy , bestselling US author Emma Cline allows the reader to consider the subject not as an abstract idea but through the lived reality of one man. David Hastings, an affluent 70-year-old with a dementia diagnosis, is on a final pilgrimage to an assisted dying facility in Switzerland. His life of wealth and privilege means all his material comforts are provided for; his concerns are purely existential.
Cline does not explicitly concern herself with morality questions in relation to assisted dying. David has already reconciled himself to his choice and so that becomes moot. This is where the power of art reveals itself; the novel is not an act of legislation, but one of imagination and empathy.
David travels by private plane from New York to London to visit his oblivious daughter, and reunites with an old friend in France, before landing in Zurich. He is cognitively sound enough to know the purpose of his trip, but not to handle the logistics, and so he is accompanied by an assistant. David’s mind is fragmenting. Memories are crystallised but in the present things have become “unbearable; meaningless”. He lives with “fear which lacked a shape” as if “someone else redacted his sentences”.
The oscillation between the darkly comic innovations of the mind in a quest for understanding and the devastating consequences of its profound unravelling is deftly handled. The prose is hypnotic but also full of a surprising narrative tension.
There are times, however, when the spell is broken by jarring shifts in perspective. Is it possible to pluck from our long-term memory details that were never retained in our short-term memory? David can, for example, recall now the three words – rose, ache, chair – that he was asked to remember but could not on the day of his dementia test months before. As such, there are moments when the functionality of his brain feels massaged in service to the narrative, in ways that feel discordant to what we understand to be his authentic cognitive state.
Overall, however, Cline does a remarkable job of articulating a fractured human consciousness that humanises beautifully both the alienating mystery of dementia and an often-polarising debate. Longlisted for the Booker Prize, this is a worthy candidate for the win.
[ Booker Prize 2026: Irish debutant features on longlist alongside Marlon James, Douglas Stuart and more Opens in new window ]
Helen Cullen is the author of The Truth Must Dazzle Gradually and the forthcoming Iseult

title: The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State by Jill Lepore: Courageous book offers visceral wake-up calls
description: Author charts dire consequences of our machine age, then takes an inspired turn to literature to reawaken us to a deeper reality
content:
At the beginning of The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, historian Jill Lepore recalls Hannah Arendt ’s reaction to news coverage of the launch of the first artificial satellite Sputnik 1 in 1957. According to Arendt, reporters described Sputnik’s launch as “the first step toward escape from men’s imprisonment to the earth”. Arendt found this language astonishing.
Throughout the remainder of Lepore’s deeply intelligent, insightful and humane analysis, she recounts how what was for most of human history a nightmare scenario has today become a fever dream pursued around the world with messianic zeal.
That fever dream is for humanity, through the development of ever more advanced robotics, human cryogenics, AI and space technology, to become “free” from entanglement not only from place – village, city, nation, Earth – but also free from the constraints of our physical bodies, with our minds uploaded to cyberspace allowing us to “live” forever.
[ Hitchhiker’s Guide offered glimpse of a future where technology would mediate almost every interaction Opens in new window ]
The insanity of the project and the terror that this is indeed the path we are on are just two of the visceral wake-up calls in this important and courageous book. Lepore traces the origin of this journey, from nightmare to 21st-century technological arms race, back to the rise of science.
Beginning in the 16th century, the scientific age introduced two radically new ideas into the governance of human affairs. The first is mechanical philosophy, the idea that everything is a machine that operates according to deducible laws, rules subject to quantification, calculation, and prediction. The second is technological determinism, the idea that technological development, despite its tendency for “creative destruction”, inevitably leads to betterment and progress.
Today these pseudoscientific dogmas everywhere shape our world. They can be seen in our belief that the more machines a country has, the more developed its people; in China and India’s breakneck “development” aimed at not only having more machines but also becoming the world’s leader in machine manufacture; in the United States’ use of its economic might to try to ensure that it remains the world’s number one machine nation.
Lepore charts the dire consequences of our machine age, including changes to the Earth’s climate, pollution, deforestation, and the eradication of wildlife species and habitats. In describing the adverse impacts on democracies, she quotes political theorist Langdon Winner, writing as far back as 1988, that so far “current developments in the information age suggest an increase in power by those who already had a great deal of power, an enhanced centralisation of control by those already prepared for control, an augmentation of wealth by the already wealthy”.
[ ‘The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy’: 40 years on Opens in new window ]
Part 2 takes an inspired and inspiring turn to literature to reawaken us to a deeper reality. Lepore begins by reminding us that the idea of creating an artificial man dates back to the earliest historical records and to humanity’s earliest stories. Prometheus fashioned humans out of clay. Mechanical men made of pure gold appear in the Iliad. And a wooden man created as a gift to a king appears in a Chinese story from the third century BCE.
Today these stories are found mainly in science fiction, to which we will return. But Lepore places another genre of literature, in which animals have the human abilities to speak and think, as a precursor to science fiction. Mark Twain’s A Dog’s Tale, Anna Sewell’s Black Beauty and Hugh Lofting’s Dr Dolittle are all examples of this genre. All were written, Lepore reminds us, as rejoinders to the then scientific orthodoxy that animals are essentially machines.
Escaping the artificial state will not simply require progress in science and greater machine ‘intelligence’. It requires that we imagine a different future
Lepore then charts how science fiction took up the mantle. In her overview she is at pains to point out that the stories contained therein were more often than not cautionary tales warning against hubris rather than fantasies of a better future.
She describes, for example, how Douglas Adams’s The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy punctures techno-optimism’s galactic conceit with humour. The novel’s anti-hero Zaphod Beeblebrox is the only human ever to have survived entering the Total Perspective Vortex. Entering the vortex gives you a total perspective on your place in the universe whereby you discover you are galactically insignificant. But not Beeblebrox, who discovers himself “to be the most important being in the entire universe, something he had hitherto only suspected”.
The fall of the artificial state is, Lepore believes, fore-ordained. “The artificial state can neither deny the laws of nature nor escape natural limits: an artificial world cannot survive without the natural world any more than a newborn can survive without milk or a forest without sunlight.”
But escaping the artificial state will not simply require progress in science and greater machine “intelligence”. It requires that we imagine a different future, Lepore urges, by listening again to the stories once whispered by firesides and read together at bedtime.
Ian Hughes is a senior research fellow at the Sustainability Institute, University College Cork. He is author of Disordered Minds: How Dangerous Personalities are Destroying Democracy

title: The Great Dictator by Matthew Sweet: Great gossipy nuggets about Barbara Cartland
description: The author makes excellent use of unprecedented access to the late romance novelist’s vast archives
content:
Picture a woman in a hot-pink chiffon gown lying on an overstuffed couch, talking incessantly. A second woman, one chosen for “her quietness, her stillness, her capacity to suppress a sneeze”, sits nearby, transcribing her employer’s words in impeccable shorthand. (If you’re now visualising Matt Lucas’s Little Britain Barbara Cartland-inspired character Dame Sally Markham, I suspect Matthew Sweet intends you to.)
Cartland dictated up to 7,000 words per afternoon. Between 1925 and 1997, she published 723 books, including 23 in 1976 alone. She maintained her literary output, Sweet writes, “with the zeal of a tractor factory during Stalin’s first Five Year Plan”. Only Shakespeare and Agatha Christie surpass her 750 million sales, yet you would have to look hard to find her novels in a shop today. Her books were written quickly, consumed quickly and discarded.
She came of age during the first World War into a society depleted of men, a “hidden wound” she shared with her contemporaries and readers. She returned to certain themes repeatedly: the misfortunes of her parents, the failure of her first marriage, the boyfriends whose passions she feared (she had 49 marriage proposals before accepting her first husband).
Cartland had three biographers during her lifetime but, as Sweet drily comments, she “seduced or nobbled all of them”. She once circulated a 46-page dossier to newspaper obituary writers called How I Want to Be Remembered. Her aim was to ensure the “untrue and unpleasant things” written about her and her daughter Raine (Princess Diana’s stepmother) would not be repeated in her death notices. But, as Sweet notes, “the record bulged with unpleasant things”.
Sweet had unprecedented access to Cartland’s vast archives and makes excellent use of the material he unearthed. He does a great trade in gossipy nuggets, such as the novelist Isabel Allende being sacked from her job translating Cartland into Spanish after being caught changing the text to make the heroines more assertive.
Part satire, part biography, part social history, The Great Dictator is not intended to send new readers to Cartland’s enormous back catalogue. Rather, it is a sharply enjoyable portrait of a changing society and how one intelligent, vexatious woman broke out of the role expected of her class – and made a fortune by doing so.

title: Andoni Iraola believes Florian Wirtz’s worth ‘should not be measured by numbers’
description: New manager is not worried by German’s lack of goals as he gets used to new attacking set-up
content:
Andoni Iraola has said Florian Wirtz should be judged by his influence on Liverpool rather than statistics and believes the playmaker’s impact will increase as his rapport with a new-look attack develops.
Wirtz impressed in Liverpool’s defeat of Atlético Madrid on Wednesday, having also produced some of his best performances last season in the Champions League. But he has also come in for criticism this term for the amount of times he has conceded possession. The £116 million Germany international has one assist and no goals in the Premier League so far but Iraola insists Wirtz’s contribution should not be measured by numbers.
The Liverpool head coach explained: “Flo played very well against Atlético Madrid and I also think he has been unlucky. I remember the ‘goal’ he scored against Nottingham Forest: they gave it live and then VAR disallowed it. He could have had very good assists but we haven’t finished them. That is why you cannot just play because of the numbers.
“Whether a striker scores a lot of goals or he doesn’t, you have to look at the performances. Does he help us to play well? Yes. Well, someone will score the goals and someone will give the assists. I am not too focused on numbers.
“Nowadays everything is about numbers, everyone tells players you have to assist, you have to score goals. For me, you have to help us play well. Someone will score the goals and I don’t care if it is the midfielders like it was the other day. Someone will score the goals if we are doing well collectively.”
Wirtz created an excellent chance for Bradley Barcola against Atlético and Iraola believes his “number 10″ will exert a greater influence as his understanding with the France international, fellow new signing Victor Munoz, Rio Ngumoha and Alexander Isak improves.
“There is an argument to make that the wingers have changed more than anywhere else,” Iraola added. “Now we have new weapons we can use with Bradley and Victor. With Florian, he is key for us.
“I am not worried because he will quickly learn where Victor prefers the ball or where Bradley prefers the ball. And, also, Bradley in just his second game you could see they already had a good association. I am not very worried.” – Guardian

title: St Pat’s knock Shamrock Rovers back at Richmond to blow title race wide open
description: Stephen Bradley’s side offer no reply to first-half home goals
content:
First-half goals from Jay McClelland and Aidan Keena delivered St Patrick’s Athletic a telling victory over champions Shamrock Rovers in a pulsating Dublin derby to blow the title race wide open.
Having knocked holders Rovers out of the FAI Cup last month, Stephen Kenny’s Saints followed it up at Richmond Park, avenging their three league defeats to Rovers earlier this year.
St Patrick’s can now go top of the Premier Division table on goal difference should they beat Dundalk at Oriel Park on Monday night, though Rovers, who were 10 points clear at the summit five weeks ago, will have a game in hand.
That, however, is against rivals Bohemians, who are also now just three points behind after recovering from 2-0 down to beat Galway United 3-2 at Eamonn Deacy Park.
Starting with intent, St Pat’s were in front from their first attack after just four minutes. Anchor midfielder Jamie Lennon was the architect, working a long-range one-two with Ryan Sheridan, the 17-year-old making his full league debut, to arc a superb cross to the far post.
McClelland arrived to find the net off the underside of the crossbar with a side-foot volley for a stunning first league goal of the season.
Rovers played their way into the game and enjoyed a good deal of the ball, patiently probing for openings as Saints, with the best rearguard record in the league, defended tenaciously, pinned deep in their own half.
It was 24 minutes before Joseph Anang was worked between the St Pat’s post, the Ghanaian springing down to his left to bat away one-handed from Hoops’ skipper Roberto Lopes’ flick after Jack Byrne had recycled a corner.
Despite having been on the back foot for a sustained period, St Pat’s struck to double their lead on the counterattack on 33 minutes.
Zach Elbouzedi was given time and space on the right to cross. Aidan Keena spun adroitly to get his shot away off his right foot to beat Ed McGinty.
Remarkably, it might have been 3-0 a minute later. A slip by Lopes, just yellow-carded for a foul on Ryan Edmondson, gifted Sheridan a run in behind. McGinty stood up well to make the save.
Befuddled to find themselves two goals down, Rovers kept passing the ball, St Pat’s captain Joe Redmond making a telling block on Michael Noonan just yards from goal.
A fifth Byrne corner to nil then presented Dylan Watts with a chance he shot straight at Anang as the visitors went to their dressingroom for the interval nonplussed at the scoreline.
With Adam Brennan on for Tunmise Sobowale, the one-way traffic from Rovers resumed from the restart, though Watts again did not worry Anang from a free kick.
It was McGinty who soon had work to do at the other end with saves on Keena and Lennon as St Pat’s remained a major threat in transition.
Rovers continued to press to get back into the game, substitute Jake Mulraney and Dan Cleary narrowly off target with shots from distance.
But St Pat’s defence, as it has done for much of the season, held firm to secure a rousing win.
