Register for free to attend WorldSkills Ireland 2026 via worldskillsireland.ie .
A coordinated visit to both the WorldSkills event (RDS Simmonscourt) and the Irish Times Higher Options event (RDS Main Hall) is more than possible with morning and afternoon bookings available; however, separate registrations are required for both events.
Once registered, make the most of your visit by downloading the checklist activity sheets from the website, which will guide you to events and exhibitors.
Familiarise yourself with the event floor plan as this will help you navigate the venue. With 31 live national competition finals, 60 exhibiting stands, virtual skills to try, and the MTU challenge, with amazing prizes to be won, you won’t want to miss anything.
Over three days, WorldSkills Ireland will encourage discovery, experimentation and creativity through live competitions, interactive skills, and VR demonstrations. With opportunities to speak with experts, educators and recruiters, young people will be met with their future in one location offering insights into various trades and skills.
The live national competition finals will see more than 160 finalists compete across 31 competitions to be in with the chance of representing Ireland in the WorldSkills Olympics in Japan in 2028.
The Heroes Stage is an exciting feature with multiple panel discussions running each day covering a range of skills-based industries, from construction and hospitality to ICT and automotive. Visitors will get up close and personal with how apprentices worked their way up the career ladder in their industry, and current apprentices will discuss how their career journey has been developing since they left school. The timetable for the Heroes Stage is available on the WorldSkills website.
The #ThisIsFET Zone allows visitors to get hands on with the opportunities available. Here visitors will meet instructors and training providers and explore real technology and equipment. There is so much to do from discovering the technology behind advanced manufacturing, going behind the scenes in film and technology, and the magic behind movie prosthetics. Visitors can also step into the world of AR and VR, consider building a sustainable future, discover the skills involved in working as an arborist or horticulturist, or pick up the tools and have a go at thatching a model cottage roof.
“WorldSkills Ireland is a fantastic opportunity to showcase the breadth and quality of further education and training (FET) and apprenticeship pathways available across the country,” says Laura Pakenham, assistant communications manager at Solas, the Further Education and Training Authority.
“As more school leavers consider a range of options beyond direct entry to university, events like this allow them to experience different careers first hand, explore their interests and see the exciting opportunities that FET and apprenticeships can offer. Through our partnership with the education and training boards and ETBI , we are giving students the chance to try out real skills and make informed decisions about their future”
With 60 exhibitors in the Careers Zone, visitors can learn and ask questions about intriguing and creative careers that bring technology, skills, creativity and critical thinking together. “WorldSkills Ireland is a celebration of what young apprentices are doing throughout the country in their chosen professions,” says Mulhern. “Horticulture is the perfect discipline to showcase at the event as it encompasses creativity, technical knowledge and dedication to the craft that is horticulture.
“It is hands on, and that is what attracts so many young people to the event. We are currently in our fourth year of intake for the horticulture apprenticeship in Teagasc at the National Botanic Gardens and the course is in very strong demand.”
Sabrina Hynes, careers and data manager at the Society of the Irish Motor Industry (Simi) says WorldSkills Ireland is an inspiring showcase of talent, dedication and technical excellence in skills and apprenticeships. “This event brings together students, educators, parents, employers and training providers to exhibit the many career pathways available across Ireland’s industries,” she says.
“The Irish motor industry continues to evolve through new technologies and increasingly advanced vehicles, where developing the next generation of skilled professionals is more important than ever. Simi is proud to support the Automobile and Heavy Vehicle Technology category and to help showcase the exciting career and apprenticeship opportunities available across our industry.”
Parentline has been exhibiting at WorldSkills Ireland for the past four years and considers it to be a wonderful showcase for promoting the services and supports it offers.
“Over 30,000 parents, guardians and students attend the event,” says Aileen Hickie, chief executive of Parentline, the confidential helpline that offers parents support and guidance.
“The stand offers Parentline the opportunity to engage with parents, carers and teachers, many of whom are feeling stressed and uncertain about the future, and explain parenting programmes that help deal with childhood anxiety, school avoidance, anger and aggression, and any and all issues affecting parents in relation to their children.”

title: ‘I thought, why not study microbiology to know as much as I could about the pandemic’
description: Hannah Balda applied to VHI’s graduate programme
content:
I am from Vermont in the US, so if you’re a fan of Noah Kahan , Ben and Jerry’s – that’s me from there. I studied at the University of Vermont for my undergraduate degree, and that was during Covid. So I thought why not study microbiology to know as much as I could about the pandemic at the time. I basically watched what a poor response the US and the rest of the world had to a pandemic, and that led me to pursue a master’s in public health, and I did that at UCD.
I saw an ad on LinkedIn or Indeed, one of the job platforms.
It combines the aspect of healthcare that I really enjoy, and the ability to explore different areas of the business as well, because I didn’t know exactly what I wanted to do after my master’s. I figured it was a great opportunity to get involved with something that I do have an interest in.
In the first area I was working with some of our corporate members and co-ordinating health services for them. In the second part of the rotations I was in group healthcare, which really focuses on population health. One of the key things I’m sure all grad programmes want you to do is get a well-rounded education of the company and how it operates.
So from there I moved into HR, which we call people services here. I didn’t think I would enjoy it but I really liked it, and that was completely unexpected because I had no plans to get into people services. So that was super fun.
Honestly, the best part of the grad programme has to be the people, it has to be the culture here. Everyone is just the sweetest. We’ve got so many different organisations and clubs, and I’ve been involved in sports and social, our women’s network and our mental health group. The people in every aspect of the company have been a pleasure to work with.
I am a communications and change co-ordinator. That means I’m split 50-50 with the internal communications department and the change management of our company. That came up about two months ago, there was a role that opened up on the people services team, which I had worked with before and I really enjoyed it, so I figured I might as well apply.
I ended up getting the job, and it’s only been a couple of weeks that I’ve been here, but I’m really enjoying it. I’d love to see where this will take me in communications and change management, both are relevant to so many businesses.
Networking. I would say in-person is always better, it’s one of the best skills and lessons that I have learned and that I was never taught in school. People will always have your back if you can learn to build a relationship with them. Part of that is showing you’re willing to learn, it doesn’t really matter that you know something, it’s just that you can learn it. Whether or not you think you are qualified or capable, just apply anyway, you never know, honestly. Go into anything with confidence.

title: Dublin 2 office block with scope for conversion to residential seeks €5m
description: Feasibility study suggests property overlooking Grand Canal could accommodate 21 apartments
content:
Agent Avison Young is guiding a price of €5 million for numbers 11 and 12 Warrington Place in Dublin city centre.
The property, on the fringes of the city’s Georgian core, overlooks the Grand Canal and comprises an office block laid out over five floors from lower-ground level to third floor with a net internal area of 1,329sq m (14,305sq ft). The office accommodation is largely open-plan and sits alongside a three-bedroom apartment at third-floor level.
Developed in 1979, the building has a mock-Georgian facade, allowing it to blend into the surrounding area, and has 11 secure car-parking spaces located to the rear.
Numbers 11 and 12 are partially leased to three tenants, namely Fidelity Information Services (FIS), Co-operative Housing Ireland and Sentrio. The total passing rent is €409,820 a year with further scope, according to the selling agent, to increase the overall rental income by securing tenants for the vacant floors and the apartment.
Roger Keogh of Avison Young believes the property would be suitable for refurbishment and continued use as office, or alternatively, for conversion to residential use (subject to planning permission).
The subject property is zoned Z1 – Sustainable Residential Neighbourhoods under the terms of the Dublin City Development Plan 2022-2028. A feasibility study prepared in advance of the sale suggests there is potential convert the property to 21 apartments with car parking. A copy of the feasibility study is available from the selling agent on request.
Roger Keogh of Avison Young says: “Opportunities of this nature are rarely available to the market, and we anticipate strong interest from both investors and developers.”

title: Fine four-bed with space to extend in Ballsbridge
description: Nutley Avenue home with spacious garden offers lots of potential in prime location
content:
Nutley Avenue, a long avenue of detached houses built in the 1950s, lies parallel to Nutley Lane, and enjoys all of the benefits of this Dublin 4 location without the headache of the traffic of a main road.
All of the features that attracted growing families to the area are still present more than seven decades later: proximity to schools, large gardens, generous reception rooms and large bedrooms.
Newer additions such as the Merrion Shopping Centre at the end of Nutley Lane make the prospect of living here even more attractive. The proximity of St Michael’s College, with an entrance at the end of the road, and Elm Park Golf Club won’t harm interest either.
Number 41 Nutley Avenue is being brought to market by DNG Donnybrook, seeking €1.895 million. It’s a fine home, extending to 167sq m (1,797sq ft), with four bedrooms and two bathrooms. Some renovations have been done, but the property would benefit from a cosmetic refresh and an energy update, as it has a G Ber.
All of the Nutley Avenue houses are well set back from the road, and the garden in front of 41 is in immaculate condition.
The house is double fronted and the front door is under a small porch, and opens into a bright hallway, with white panelling running halfway up the wall and continuing up the stairs.
On the left of the hallway is the main reception room, a lovely, dual-aspect room with coving, spot lighting, an original tiled fireplace and art-deco-style French doors that open to the garden. A garage lies directly on the left of this long room, so it would be relatively easy to convert and expand what it is already a good-sized reception room further.
On the right-hand side of the entrance hall is a study, which could alternatively be used as a playroom or a den. There’s a guest WC under the stairs, and the kitchen is in its original position, at what would have been originally the back of the house, but it now gives a fine living and dining area thanks to an extension.
This room gives a great idea of what is possible with this house. It might make sense to flip the layout here, putting the kitchen in what is the dining area, having it open on to the garden and converting what is now the kitchen into a spacious walk-in pantry or a large utility room. The living area is attractive with warm, dark timber floors and the potential to break through the walls with French doors.
Upstairs there are four bedrooms and a bathroom, which has been tastefully renovated. There is scope to extend this floor simply by building up above the existing garage or going all in with a fresh extension, subject to planning permission.
There’s certainly space for a new extension, given the length of the garden, which is in superb condition and has been well tended over the years. It could also comfortably accommodate a garden room.
Overall, it’s a fine family home in a superb location, with St Michael’s at the end of the road, RTÉ’s Montrose campus at the top of the adjacent Nutley Lane, St Vincent’s University Hospital across the road and the Dart a quick stroll away.

title: Westlife in Dublin, Harry Styles in NYC: Ireland loses out as major acts favour residencies
description: For artists, residencies are a ‘much kinder way of touring’. For Ireland, the shift towards long runs in big cities presents a particular challenge
content:
F ans who want to see Westlife perform their greatest hits in Ireland this year have just two options: Dublin or Belfast. The band, who are about to begin their 25th-anniversary world tour, will take up a residency at 3Arena for 13 nights, followed by a total of seven at the O2.
Westlife’s decision to hold court borrows from the new playbook for top-tier artists, who are reversing the mechanics of a traditional tour and asking fans to come to them instead.
In the past, the artist’s tour bus rolling from city to city for months on end was seen as a sometimes glamorous, sometimes gruelling but essential part of a musician’s lifestyle. Now it’s fans who bear the expense of travelling to see their favourite artist, potentially booking flights and accommodation, as well as factoring in other expenses.
Harry Styles ’ schedule is one of the best examples of how this trend has evolved in recent years. During his 2022 Love on Tour run, Styles’ North America leg consisted of 42 shows in five cities. In 2026 he’s performing in just one North American venue for his Together Together tour, taking over New York’s Madison Square Garden for 30 consecutive nights.
For Irish fans who wanted to see Styles perform this year, travelling to London for one of his dozen shows at Wembley Stadium was their nearest option. Similarly, Irish fans wanting to see Shakira in 2026 will have to fly to Madrid for her European Residency, a 12-night stadium run in the Spanish capital.
The growing popularity of this new approach could have particular implications for Ireland, whose smaller population makes it harder to compete with big European capitals for big residencies, and the cultural and economic windfall they bring.
Hosting residencies in megacities such as London and New York makes sense for artists, as the infrastructure is already there to support an influx of fans, and the location itself doubles as a draw for fans looking to make a holiday of the trip.
But the choice of where to perform can also be personal and very artist-specific.
“Rather than aiming for the biggest cities, some artists are turning their focus to where their biggest fans are,” says Olivia Jones, a music analyst at Midia Research, citing the example of Bad Bunny’s Puerto Rico residency last year, which built on the cultural theme of his latest album and aimed to uplift his community and the fans there.
The idea of a residency was first established in the 1940s in Las Vegas and revitalised by Céline Dion in the Nevada city in the early 2000s. Why are they experiencing such a boost now?
Music-industry veterans say it comes down to cost, comfort and production opportunities at a time when audience expectations are at an all-time high. There is an obvious saving in camping out in one location for 20 shows rather than visiting 10 cities to do the same; it simplifies logistics and maximises revenue. For artists and crew, it vastly reduces time spent in transit and offers a better work-life balance than a traditional tour ever could.
“It’s about the convenience for people of being able to go to half a dozen cities in the world rather than a hundred of them,” says Bren Berry, a musician and long-time music promoter with Aiken Promotions . “The costs of touring are so expensive, particularly now with fuel prices; it’s a lot to move stuff around the world at the moment. There’s obviously a huge saving to be made in setting up camp in one place.”
Berry cautions that Westlife’s 3Arena run isn’t necessarily a residency but more a band with mass appeal in Ireland selling out as many arena dates as they can. The vast majority of Westlife’s world tour outside Ireland consists of one- or two-night stops.
For artists with enough star power to draw fans to wherever they are, there are serious benefits to them of not moving city and country every night. They can get into a routine, get a good sleep and ultimately put on a better show.
“It’s a much kinder way of touring,” says Sarah Yeoman, who has worked in the music industry for 30 years, most recently as backstage manager on Kylie Minogue ’s worldwide Tension Tour. “For everyone involved, from wardrobe to catering, it’s logical. It gives people more time, which is so precious to us.”
From a production perspective, a set-up that can remain in place over multiple nights gives the crew more time to assemble and disassemble, and offers the opportunity to employ more high-tech staging. With conventional touring, it doesn’t matter how innovative current technology is if it can’t be set up and taken down again in a few hours.
Steven Douglas, a lighting designer who has toured extensively with The Killers , says a residency format allows for more creative options, as the show can be built for the venue.
“In a residency show, for the most part it will get built and then stay in place for a longer period of time, so building things that have to be disassembled quickly isn’t as big of a concern.”
For a Las Vegas show that lasts years rather than nights, production can be highly specific, says Douglas, who worked on Aerosmith’s Deuces Are Wild Vegas residency, which ran from 2019 to 2022 and hosted 55 shows at the Park MGM. For that show the set designers used a walkway that emerged from the roof, allowing the band members to get very close to fans in the venue’s highest seating.
There is also the potential for artists to create better branding and a buzz around their show in person and online if they stay in one city for longer.
Christian Tierney, a tour photographer favoured by A-listers such as Hozier and Niall Horan, says staying put gives the tour a chance to create bigger, more impactful content that is relevant to their chosen city than if they are moving constantly.
“What comes to mind straight away is the content that was made around the Oasis tour last year, where they were doing a few nights in each place. It wasn’t necessarily a residency, but it was a few gigs in big cities rather than a big long tour of a million different cities.
“They could go out during the day and do pieces based around the city they were in,” Tierney says. “If you’re somewhere for two weeks you can make a bigger piece of content there than having to try and make 90 pieces of small content.”
For promoters the shift is bigger than simply introducing a cheaper way to put on concerts. If fans are willing to travel, the concert itself becomes part of a wider tourism economy. In late September Live Nation , the world’s largest promoter, is hosting a tourism summit in New York to “explore how live events are changing the way people travel”. It is billing fan travel as the “next chapter of global tourism”.
For Ireland the shift towards residencies presents a potential challenge and means Irish fans could miss out on seeing their favourite artists locally.
Some big artists have already been leaving Ireland off their touring schedules for years, despite the demand. Beyoncé has not played here since 2016, leaving Ireland out of her Cowboy Carter stadium tour. Olivia Rodrigo, who brought her Guts world tour to the 3Arena for two nights in 2024 and played a headline gig at Marlay Park in 2025, has no dates set for Ireland in 2027, but she will play 11 nights at the O2 in London for her Unravelled Tour.
Live Nation’s plans for a new 20,000 seat-facility at Brick Yards, in Dublin’s docklands, could strengthen the capital’s position, giving artists another large-scale option as the industry streamlines towards fewer cities and longer stays.
But there is still a limit to how far the residency model can go, and for whom. “I don’t think a band going on tour is going to become a thing of the past any time soon,” says Steven Douglas. “People still want their favourite band to come to their town and play.”
Westlife are at 3Arena in Dublin from Thursday, September 10th, until Saturday, September 26th, and at the O2 in Belfast between Tuesday, October 27th, and Friday, November 6th

title: Pressure: Andrew Scott is brilliant in this intense D-Day drama
description: He plays James Stagg, who had pivotal role in second World War, with Kerry Condon as Eisenhower’s secretary
content:
Supporters of Maureen Flavin Sweeney , the Irish postmistress whose meteorological reports helped save D-Day from stormy catastrophe, have already been muttering in the wings about the focus of this effective, exciting tribute to heroes with barometers.
Fear not. Sweeney is mentioned. But, based on a play by David Hague, the film is chiefly concerned with a quiet, intensely professional Scot named James Stagg.
Anyone who has sat through the renowned 1970s documentary series The World at War will remember his sturdy contributions to the D-Day episode. As chief meteorological officer for Operation Overlord, Stagg, played brilliantly here by Andrew Scott , really did make a significant contribution to the success of the operation during the second World War .
As Pressure tells it, he found himself at odds with Irving P Krick (Chris Messina), the chief American meteorologist, when evidence seemed to suggest a storm was due on the planned date of the Allied forces’ mass landing on the north coast of France at Normandy.
A delay of a day or two would be significant. Any greater wait could be disastrous, as the required tidal and lunar circumstances would not again coincide for another two weeks. How much longer could the details of the plan be kept secret?
Anthony Maras, the Australian director of the eventful Hotel Mumbai, coats the film in nostalgic browns as Volker Bertelmann’s busy score heightens the building tension. There is throughout a sense of the headquarters operating on one huge collectively held breath. The tension is palpable even though we all (one has to hope) know the landing was ultimately a success.
Scott is unimprovable as Stagg. There is a sense of a near-religious devotion to the scientific method at odds with Krick’s less rigorous reliance on precedent. Towards the close a conciliatory gesture confirms that, beneath the stony carapace, a generous heart beats.
Kerry Condon enjoys herself as Kay Summersby, Gen Dwight D Eisenhower’s Corkonian private secretary. Damian Lewis, though maybe not quite eccentric enough, fills big rooms with mad bluster as the British general Bernard Montgomery.
Brendan Fraser is, alas, a little too fragile as the bullet-headed Eisenhower, but he still gets across the charisma of a big man with unimaginable responsibilities.
None of the film-making breaks new ground, but this is a tense, professionally made dad flick that will play handsomely on bank holiday afternoons forever. There are worse things.
In cinemas from Wednesday, September 9th

title: Fall 2: Deadpoint review – Sequel to a pleasingly silly survivalist horror is thin gruel
description: The actors work hard to enliven pastily written characters with insane motivations
content:
Released to a flurry in 2022, the pleasingly silly Fall has found a devoted following in the streaming afterlife. A high-concept yarn featuring two women stranded at the death-defying summit of a rusty, soon-to-be-demolished TV tower, the survivalist horror was powered along by vertiginous views from 625m up and compellingly corny twists.
It’s impossible not to think of Weekend at Bernie’s II – an over-reaching 1980s comedy sequel that required voodoo resurrection and congo lines as plot points – while watching the hurried opening section of Fall 2: Deadpoint. Wait: so the sidekick in the last film had an estranged sister? And they argued right before her death?
Enter Jax Hunter (Harriet Slater), weedy younger sister to Fall’s thrillseeker Shiloh, who is persuaded by a mysterious friend (Arsema Thomas) to take on Mount Hua’s plank walk in a stomach-churning traverse along sheer cliffs, across narrow wooden boards suspended roughly 2,000m above the valleys below.
Except, somehow, the entire plank walk has been relocated to the US ally Thailand. And then there’s rain. And then there’s a rockslide. And then there’s a revelation.
IP reigns, regardless of how preposterous any spin-off might be. But this story, as cooked up by Scott Mann (who directed the original Fall) and Jonathan Frank, is thin gruel. Set your watch by the beats: there’s no signal; oh, wait, there’s one bar. A loosey-goosey attempt to replicate the soapy plot twists of the first instalment results only in a firm shrug of the viewer’s shoulders.
Peter and Michael Spierig, directors of Predestination and Jigsaw, make the most of the urge to not look down. (But – oh, no – you just did.) Harriet Slater and Arsema Thomas work hard to enliven pastily written characters with insane motivations. Why are they going up this crazy, unsurvivable mountain? No idea.
The dire penalties for drug trafficking in Thailand are flagged early, so we’re primed for some scattershot, similarly themed development.
Higher does not necessarily mean better. The view from the top, aided by Mann’s AI-enhanced SFX company, remains appropriately sickening. It’s enough to paper over the movie’s crazy canyons and vast gaps in logic. But it’s nothing like the real thing.
In cinemas from Wednesday, September 11th

title: ‘I knew from day one I wanted to work in the music industry’
description: ‘I knew from day one I wanted to work in the music industry,’ says Kathryn Mason
content:
Throughout the morning and afternoon sessions at Higher Options , a number of talks will examine the various career opportunities that can follow different study choices. Each talk will feature a panel of guests at various stages of their careers and studies, who will share their experiences, insights and advice.
Here are a couple of the speakers attendees won’t want to miss.
Kathryn Mason is the managing director of Mason PR. She studied a business diploma specialising in music management.
“I knew from day one I wanted to work in the music industry. And it’s quite niche, so it’s very hard to get into,” Mason explains.
Nonetheless, she managed not only to forge a career in her preferred industry, but now owns her own PR firm that remains firmly connected to the music business, albeit in a different way.
Mason began her career working for record labels, before taking a break for a couple of years, moving abroad and becoming a ski instructor. “Because that’s what you do,” she says jokingly.
When she returned to Ireland , Mason was certain she wanted to continue working in the music industry, but to also broaden her line of work.
Her role means she is dealing not only with those who work in the music business, but also with people across the many forms of media. This gives her insights into, and experiences of managing, two sectors that often overlap.
One of Mason’s clients is the IMRO Radio Awards and she set up the All-Ireland Podcast Awards. “When people think media is dead, it’s not dead. It’s anything but dead. It’s just a different way of working it. That’s the difference.”
Sandi Ndebele is a chartered principal process engineer at Eli Lillyand Company. He didn’t necessarily realise at the time of studying that this was the branch of engineering he wanted to pursue, but he enjoyed his modules in chemical engineering and, after a few internships in the industry, he figured this was the path for him.
“Being a process engineer translates really well with all the stuff they try to teach us at college,” says Ndebele. “And the further up you go through the degree, the more it makes sense.”
Few paths, of course, are completely straight, and Ndebele has tried his hand at other things. Including being a trivia quizmaster.
During a career break, he travelled to Australia and while out there, found a new way to make some money. “For six months, in a different bar in Melbourne, I would host a quiz, go home, repeat,” he explains. It was an experience he could have, knowing that he could return to his company once his travels were complete.
And no skill is ever a wasted skill – Ndebele puts those quizmaster talents to good use for charity purposes, on occasion.
He is a recent convert from rave-music enthusiast to metalhead, in case you were wondering what kind of music a process engineer might enjoy. “It helps me concentrate,” he says.
One of Ndebele’s goals in life is to figure out what his cat’s meows mean. “I think we’re starting to understand each other. He knows what he wants. And I can tell he knows what he wants. I just have to go through different options.
“There’s a lot of engineering to be done, but we’ll get there,” he adds.

title: Arab Strap: Half-Told Tales review – The beautifully bleak Scots’ finest album since the 1990s
description: Aidan Moffat and Malcolm Middleton paint a fascinating portrait of middle age
content:
Back in the 1990s Arab Strap were the grumpy old men who gatecrashed Britpop. The Scottish partnership of Aidan Moffat and Malcolm Middleton were still only in their late 20s, but in a world of cheeky chappies in Adidas tracksuits their commitment to gut-wrenching, things-can-only-get-worse miserabilism was commendable – a vision laid out in songs that filtered Moffat’s spoken-word soliloquies through Middleton’s tortured indie-pop.
Thirty years and one lengthy hiatus later, the duo have returned with Half-Told Tales, their finest album since the 1990s. Seeing them square up to middle age like boxers readying for a final bout, it reconnects with the wistful ferocity of their early curmudgeonly classics.
Arab Strap have always been grouses with a trick up their sourpuss sleeves – which is that, when the mood takes them, they can write heartbreakingly beautiful songs about being in love, emotionally tormented and off your face. If it’s possible to be all three at once, then so much the better.
That was the secret fuel that sustained the brilliant Trippy, from 1998, a song about taking bad mushrooms that burned itself out in a shoegaze Götterdämmerung, and, even more so, The First Big Weekend, the best track ever written about being a skint twentysomething with nothing to do but get twatted with your pals.
Half-Told Tales opens with a kick in the form of I Get Noise, where Moffat wends his way through a typically bleak spoken-word monologue about his need to distance himself from a toxic influence (“you overshare and overbear”). Middleton chimes in with the sort of it’s-cheesy-but-I-like-it sax solo not witnessed from an indie band since peak Boomtown Rats.
The feral, frantic energy is a declaration that you’re never too old to get hot and bothered about the condition of the world
The challenge of topping that explosive intro is easily bested with You You You, where Moffat delivers a heartfelt valentine over a pogoing metal-disco beat: it’s like crashing a poetry recital while Metallica soundtrack Saturday Night Fever in the flat upstairs.
None of this is what you’d expect of two grouchy songwriters who were spiritually haggard before their time and who, in their early 50s, are wading into the trenches of midlife. But this is nonetheless an extraordinarily vigorous record that sees Arab Strap upgrade their familiar war chest of jagged, brooding guitars with hair-metal riffs and lashings of saxophone.
But the old melancholy has not gone away: it surfaces on the tender Be a Man, an address by Moffat to his son as he prepares to head into the world under his own steam, to face not just the random cruelty of the universe but also the poison of the manosphere.
“No one else will miss you like I will / no one worries quite like I can,” he croons. As he does so, he captures the poignant pain of watching your children grow up and leave – a universal feeling seldom expressed in music.
Arab Strap paint a fascinating portrait of middle age with this album – one that acknowledges the inevitable rubbishness of getting older but also explores the joy of still having traces of your old joie de vivre left.
That’s the message of the LP’s strongest moment, Fighting for You, a takedown of the far right (whoever they fight for, it isn’t “us”), which sounds like The Prodigy trapped in the quiet carriage of an Irish Rail service and struggling to keep their destructive tendencies to themselves.
The meaning of the song is political, but the feral, frantic energy is a declaration that you’re never too old to get hot and bothered about the condition of the world.
It’s full of zest and zing, but, as with a great night out once you reach a certain age, there’s a price to be paid. And that’s the subject of the record’s comedown track, Beats per Minute, where Moffat reels off the lifespans of all creatures great and small: the robin that dies after two years, the jellyfish that lives forever. He concludes by accepting that all things must pass, even miserable indie bands from the 1990s.
That sense of encroaching darkness ensures that an often exuberant album finishes with a bittersweet ache. He isn’t raging against the dying of the light so much as using what time remains to steady himself and then make one final leap into the mosh pit, all too aware it might be his last.

title: Cleared for career take-off: ‘Just go for it’ is trainee air traffic controller’s advice
description: Nathan Roberts applied to Airnav’s Student Controller Programme, and hasn't looked back
content:
I am 20 years old and from Dublin originally. I am living in Bunratty at the moment, just outside of Shannon , really close to where I work. I actually didn’t go to third-level education. I completed my Leaving Cert and did pretty okay. I got exactly what I needed to get into ATC [air traffic control] college, which I’m in now, which is two subjects with a H5 or above, and overall I needed to pass five subjects.
So it’s not a huge ask, but I did that, and then I went on to work in the fitness industry for around 18 months and then, as of last September, I got into Airnav’s Student Controller Programme .
It was a childhood hobby. I had such a big influence from aviation, because of where I live. I live pretty close to the airport, so I could always see planes to and from, so I always wanted to know more about aviation. And then when I started seeing it crop up on Instagram and social media platforms and on the radio, I said, I’m going to look into this. As time went on, I wanted to really pursue it.
Really, really good. It’s been intense, but extremely enjoyable. I started last September, and you do a couple of different stages in your training. At the moment, I’m in my units endorsement, so that’s basically the final stage of training. But you start off with the basics, which is a lot of theory and an introduction into the simulator environment, and then you do another part called the rating training, which is more theory, but it’s a little more emphasis on the simulator side of things.
Then you progress into the unit endorsement, which is the location you’re going to work in – for me, that’s going to be Shannon. You basically do everything that you [do] in real life; the only thing is, you don’t talk to real pilots. You still talk to a simulator pilot on the other side of the room, but you’re working off the same airspace, the same rules and regulations and the same equipment as you would in real life.
I’m going to be guaranteed to work in Shannon once I get my training completed here. It’s based on the demand of the company and the demand of the location between Dublin, Cork or Shannon. They would say, designate students to locations, and I’ve been designated Shannon because of the demand here in Shannon. So after my 18 months are finished, I’ll be based as a high level controller in Shannon En-Route Centre.
My advice would be just to go for it – what is there to lose? If it’s something that you’re interested in, why not pursue it? And if it doesn’t go well, then that’s your answer; you know then for the future. But my number one tip would be just go for it. Don’t look back.

title: Partnerships breaking down barriers to the arts take centre stage at the 2026 Business to Arts Awards
description: From classrooms and concert halls to workplaces and communities, this year’s winners are making the arts more accessible, inclusive and engaging
content:
Accessibility and inclusion are defining characteristics of this year’s Business to Arts Award winners. Across Ireland, creative partnerships are widening participation in the arts, ensuring that geography, disability, age or circumstance are no longer barriers to cultural engagement.
This year’s winners demonstrate that meaningful participation begins by designing programmes around the needs of audiences. By bringing performances to new audiences, introducing children and young people to the arts, embedding creativity within the workplace or extending cultural opportunities into communities across the country, these partnerships demonstrate that meaningful access strengthens not only the arts sector but society as a whole. They show that participation begins by meeting people where they are and creating opportunities for everyone to engage with creativity.
The small arts partnership award recognised basis.point and The Gate Theatre for bringing a nationwide livestream of POOR, Katriona O’Sullivan’s acclaimed stage adaptation, directly into secondary school classrooms across Ireland. More than 22,000 students in 337 schools across 29 counties experienced the production, many encountering professional theatre for the first time.
By overcoming geographic, financial and social barriers, the partnership created a scalable model for widening access to theatre while supporting conversations around resilience, empathy and personal potential. It demonstrates how digital technology can extend the reach of live performance without compromising the shared experience at its heart.
The Irish Times long-term partnership award was presented to ESB and the National Concert Hall for Quavers to Quadratics, an innovative Steam (science, technology, engineering, arts and maths) programme that uses music to inspire curiosity and learning in science, technology, engineering and mathematics. Since 2020 the programme has reached more than 10,000 students nationwide, with a particular focus on Deis schools and underserved communities, while workshops delivered through Irish have expanded participation in Gaeltacht regions.
By combining music and science in a shared learning experience, Quavers to Quadratics encourages creativity, confidence and critical thinking while opening new pathways into Steam subjects. The partnership demonstrates how collaboration between business, education and the arts can create opportunities that extend well beyond the classroom.
The creative access award recognised Specsavers Limerick and University Concert Hall for Panto for All, a programme developed to make live theatre more accessible to vulnerable and marginalised children and families across the midwest of Ireland. Between January 2025 and January 2026, more than 920 children and family members attended performances through the initiative, many experiencing live theatre for the first time.
Relaxed performances, Irish Sign Language interpretation, captioning, sensory supports and complimentary tickets created a more welcoming theatre experience for neurodiverse audiences, deaf communities and families facing barriers to participation. By embedding accessibility into every aspect of the production, the partnership demonstrates how inclusive design can enrich the experience for audiences of all ages.
The creativity in the workplace award recognised Connected Hubs and the Contemporary Irish Art Society for their project, Art in the Hubs, which brings contemporary Irish art into workplaces across Ireland while creating new opportunities for artists beyond traditional gallery settings. Since 2022 the programme has placed 70 artworks by 70 artists across 40 Connected Hubs, introducing new audiences to contemporary art while helping remote working hubs become more engaging cultural spaces.
The Irish Times €5,000 arts award was presented to Music Network for bringing migrant and local families together through music, creativity and cultural exchange in Clare and Kildare. Weekly workshops explored lullabies in English, Irish and 16 additional languages using a trauma-sensitive approach. Their programmes address isolation, language barriers and limited access to cultural opportunities while strengthening confidence, wellbeing and community connection, demonstrating the capacity of shared creative experiences to build stronger, more inclusive communities.
Across these partnerships, access takes many forms: digital innovation, interdisciplinary learning, inclusive performance, workplace engagement and community participation. Together, they demonstrate that widening participation depends not simply on opening doors, but on creating experiences that respond to the needs of different audiences and enable more people to engage meaningfully with the arts.
At Business to Arts, we work to build meaningful connections between the corporate and cultural sectors, creating opportunities for businesses to support the arts in ways that deliver lasting value. The partnerships recognised in this year’s awards show how collaboration can expand access, deepen participation and ensure that more people can experience the benefits of creativity in their everyday lives.
To learn more about developing a creative partnership or becoming a member of Business to Arts, please visit businesstoarts.ie

title: The Disappearers by Marlon James: A horrifying and exhilarating portrayal of men queer and straight
description: James is honest and generous in his shifting perspectives on an attack on eight gay men in Jamaica
content:
Marlon James, born and raised in Jamaica, and long-time resident of the US, is probably best known for his 2015 Booker Prize-winning novel, A Brief History of Seven Killings .
Described by the Booker judges that year as “startling in its range of voices and registers”, it spins a bloody tornado of violence and intrigue around the attempted assassination of Bob Marley in 1976. Spanning decades and continents, and recruiting the voices of more than 70 characters, it cemented James’s reputation as a writer of extraordinary talent and ambition.
Big literary prizes sometimes have the unintended consequence of keeping writers from their work, but James has been productive: he published Black Leopard, Red Wolf in 2019, and its follow-up, Moon Witch, Spider King in 2022; his TV crime series, Get Millie Black, aired last year. Now he’s back with his sixth novel, The Disappearers, longlisted for the 2026 Booker Prize.
We’re in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1988, where eight gay men arrive at a dilapidated mansion house, answering a casting call for a local production of Fortune and Men’s Eyes, by John Herbert. Some of them have come because they have nowhere else to go; others are more intentional about wanting to “stage a battyboy revolution” by staging “a gay play”.
Either way, they’ve taken an enormous risk just by showing up, because to be gay in Jamaica is to live with an ever-present threat of violence. Over the course of the next month, as they rehearse, friendships blossom and their confidence grows, but their happiness is not to last. A mob descends, armed with crowbars and cricket bats; by the time the attack is over, one of the men is dead, another is blinded, and the rest are deeply traumatised. The bulk of the novel deals with the fallout from this horrific event, tracing threads of consequence across the following 20 or so years.
[ Marlon James: It’s bullsh*t to say there is ‘high’ and ‘low’ literature Opens in new window ]
If you’re new to James’s work, be ready for a challenging read, but one that will be well worth your time. His style is expansive and freewheeling, a mash-up of forms, perspectives and genres. The novel’s opening section, titled The Play, is told via a series of diary entries by one of the eight men, 18-year-old Eddy Porteous.
Recently out of high school, he proudly keeps a tally of the number of men he has slept with, tries to get his hands on gay porn magazines and worries that he’s getting too old for his X-Men comics. Eddy misses rehearsals on the night of the attack, and he only realises that something terrible has happened when he sees the yellow crime-scene tape and police cars outside the mansion house.
In the next section, The Blackjacks, the perspective changes abruptly. Now, we’re with the attackers, all 12 of them, identified by abbreviated names like Corporal T, Jah Q, and Dat Nigga J. We get snippets of live-action reporting / stream of consciousness: “High time now we cap some batty bitchez.” “Rounding them up like cows, yo.” And, perhaps most poignantly, “Kill it in them, kill it in me.” The episode is played out from intention to bloody climax in violent, graphic detail, the narrative bouncing between the attackers like players moving a ball towards a hoop.
The continuous shifts in form and perspective are both dizzying and exhilarating – later sections arrive as partial interview transcripts and letters – but the original eight men in the play remain at the heart of the story. Two of the men go missing, and others try to track them down: along the way, one begins plotting revenge on the attackers, “turning himself into battyboy Robin Hood”.
James calls the novel his most autobiographical to date, and his great accomplishment here is his generous and honest portrayal of men, both queer and straight: their anger, fear, isolation, confusion and longing; their moments of tenderness, camaraderie and melodrama; the journey to self-acceptance; the delight in discovering new forms of sexual pleasure.
Yes, it feels like the world is against you, James seems to say, but you have more power than you realise, and life – beautiful life – is full to overflowing with possibility.
Claire Adam’s latest novel, Love Forms, was longlisted for the Booker Prize 2025

title: US says Iranian tankers destroyed after ballistic missile attacks on American warship
description: US Central Command says targeted tankers are part of a ‘multibillion-dollar shadow network’ that funds Iran’s Revolutionary Guard
content:
The US military on Tuesday said it had destroyed multiple Iranian tankers, after Iran ’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) twice attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles.
US Central Command (Centcom) said the warship evaded both attempted attacks, and no American personnel were injured.
US forces struck the tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Iran’s Kharg Island, Centcom said in a statement, adding that American forces “directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck”.
Centcom said the targeted tankers were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies”, though the military did not provide further details.
Remarking on the latest strikes, Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, said the US would not let Iran’s attacks to go unanswered.
[ Iran threatens US with new ‘economic warfare’ and missiles as Houthis attack Saudi Arabia Opens in new window ]
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers. And I think you’ll see that again today,” Rubio said, responding to reporters’ questions about the attack while on a trip to Colombia.
The strikes followed an earlier dispute over a US underwater drone in the strait of Hormuz, which the IRGC claimed its naval forces had seized as part of a “complex intelligence and operational action at dawn”, according to Iranian state TV. In a statement provided to Iranian state media, the IRGC said images of the vessel would be released shortly.
However, the US military said the unmanned submarine had “malfunctioned” more than a day earlier.
In a statement, US Navy Capt Tim Hawkins, a United States Central Command spokesperson, said the submersible was “defective” and an older model “that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment”. Operations in waters in the area continue, he said.
Iran has maintained a blockade of the strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about one fifth of the global oil and gas shipments, since the outbreak of the war more than six months ago, while the US has imposed its own blockade of Iranian ports.
After a month of relative calm in August, Iran and the US have resumed exchanges of fire, sending ‌global oil prices back up to levels last seen in July.
US president Donald Trump has struggled to end the unpopular war, which has claimed the lives of 18 US service members.
Iranian authorities have previously put the overall death toll from US and Israeli strikes in the thousands, figures that outside observers, including US-based monitoring groups, have broadly corroborated. – Guardian

title: Financial services sector lacks professionals to tackle fraud, warns Compliance Institute
description: Compliance Institute warning comes as value of fraudulent transactions increased year-on-year
content:
More than half of compliance experts believe the financial services sector lacks “sufficiently qualified” professionals to meet “the developing challenges around financial crime”, according to a new national survey.
A further eight in 10 firms reported this lack of skilled workers is “increasing regulatory and operational risks” across the industry, the institute found in a survey of 125 senior compliance experts in the State’s financial services sector.
Institute chief executive Michael Kavanagh described it as “concerning” that “the overwhelming majority” of compliance experts believe this qualification shortfall is increasing risk.
“Financial crime is increasingly digital in nature, faster to execute and more complex to detect”, he said, adding that artificial intelligence (AI) “has made the task of tackling financial crime even more challenging.”
The Central Bank of Ireland released on Friday its annual payment fraud statistics, revealing that almost €180 million was reported in fraudulent transactions in 2025, a 27.2 per cent increase in the amount of money stolen compared to the previous year, with a notable rise in the average value of fraudulent transactions conducted through e-money institutions.
The bank’s deputy governor for consumer and investor protection, Colm Kincaid, said: “All actors in the system from financial firms to technology companies need to continue to improve their systems and controls to reduce the likelihood of these frauds occurring.”
But 56 per cent of respondents to the institute’s survey said they do not believe the Irish financial services sector is developing enough compliance and financial crime talent to meet future demand.
Only 8 per cent “fully” believe the sector has enough properly qualified compliance professionals to deal with the issues at hand, while 41 per cent believe so “to some extent”.
Meanwhile, a further 41 per cent believe moderate shortages exist and 10 per cent say these are significant.
“The results of our survey suggest that skills gaps in the Irish financial services sector mean that many organisations may be already finding it hard to find people with the right skills to combat financial crime,” Kavanagh said.
He continued: “The overwhelming volume and pace of regulatory changes often puts significant pressure on compliance teams in the sector. The sheer breadth of regulations demands a significant allocation of time, expertise, and operational focus, often stretching teams to their limits.
“Firms of course need to take steps themselves to ensure their staff are adequately trained and have the know-how to combat the regulatory and operational risks faced by the Irish financial services sector.
“But there also needs to be a concerted effort by the Government and industry to invest more in talent so that the Irish financial services sector can truly prosper and navigate all the challenges that come its way.”

title: LIV Golf files for bankruptcy with stars such as Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau owed millions
description: CEO Scott O’Neil says ‘process is designed to build a stronger and more sustainable future for LIV Golf’
content:
Less than five years after it held its first event and created ‌a schism in professional golf, LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in New Jersey on Tuesday.
The filing - a ‌rare window into the league’s financial state - estimates assets between $100 million and $500 million, with liabilities between $500 million and $1 billion.
Most notably, ​the filing listed several star golfers as creditors still owed millions in unsecured claims. Spaniard Jon Rahm has the largest claim among players at $7.5 million, followed by Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7 million), Dustin Johnson ($5.5 million), Cameron Smith of Australia ($4.8 ​million), Tyrrell Hatton of England ($3.4 million) and Brooks Koepka ($1.7 million). Koepka left the league at the start of 2026.
LIV Golf ⁠was bankrolled by the Saudi Public Investment Fund from its inception in 2022 until this ‌year, ‌when ​the sovereign wealth fund decided to step away. LIV’s decision to file for bankruptcy is not a sign that it is dissolving, ⁠but rather a step toward restructuring and ​continuing the PGA Tour competitor under a new ​business plan.
CEO Scott O’Neil published a letter to fans addressing the filing.
“Now it is time ‌to enter the next phase of ​LIV Golf,” O’Neil wrote. “Today, we took an important step forward to get there. LIV Golf ⁠has entered a court-supervised restructuring process ⁠that provides us ​with the time and framework to address previous financial obligations and complete a transaction that will make the League’s next phase a reality. Put simply, this process is designed to build a stronger and more sustainable future for LIV Golf.”
O’Neil went on to say LIV intends to continue staging events in some of its more popular international destinations - Australia, South Africa, Mexico, Hong Kong and England among them. The league ‌also will seek to ⁠continue playing in the United States.
“The next phase of LIV Golf will be built around a sustainable business model and deeper alignment between players and the ‌League, with team golf at its core,” O’Neil wrote. “Players will have the opportunity to share directly in the value they ​help create, while teams will be positioned to grow into enduring ​global sports businesses. And fans will remain at the center of everything we do.”
LIV has an agreement in place with BC Partners Advisors for restructuring support.

title: Air traffic control issue that led to dozens of Irish flight cancellations ‘resolved’
description: Nats, which provides services to 15 UK airports, apologises for disruption and says it is working to clear the ‘backlog of flights’
content:
A technical issue that affected air traffic control services at many UK airports, resulting in the cancellation of hundreds of flights, has been “resolved”, according to the provider.
Dozens of flights in and out of Dublin Airport were affected, with airport operator DAA saying airlines had cancelled 43 outbound and 30 inbound flights on Tuesday.
Nats, which provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports, said its recovery from the technical issue, which forced the cancellation of more than 400 flights, had “taken longer than we had hoped” but is “resolved”.
“We are operating normally and working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights,” it said in a statement at 7.30pm. “We are truly sorry for the ongoing flight disruption. We know this is hugely frustrating and apologise unreservedly. Passengers should continue to check with their airline.”
Passenger Update - 17.00 Due to air traffic control issues in the UK, some flights in and out of Dublin Airport are subject to delays this evening. As of 5pm, airlines have cancelled 23 outbound and 21 inbound flights. Further disruption is possible as the evening goes on.… pic.twitter.com/G6OCMOWRXg
Tens of thousands of passengers faced disruption as a result of the outage, which had led to about 425 flights to and from UK airports being cancelled as of 5pm. Airports including Heathrow, Gatwick, Edinburgh and Stansted were impacted.
Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been disrupted and it had cancelled more than 50 scheduled flights.
British Airways said it was forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights on Tuesday which had impacted “tens of thousands of customers”.
ℹ️ Technical issue We have identified that the issue was in our flight processing system. Our engineers are on site and working urgently to resume normal operations as quickly as possible. We recognise the ongoing disruption to travel, for which we sincerely apologise. (1/3) https://t.co/T9tF7j31e1
Budget airline EasyJet said some of its flights were “unable to operate” following the issue which was causing delays to flights across Europe.
[ Ryanair cuts winter capacity as unhedged jet fuel costs bite Opens in new window ]
In a post on X, UK transport secretary Heidi Alexander said she was “seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job” following the disruption. She said she gave her “huge thanks” for those working to “get people moving”.
Nats chief executive officer Martin Rolfe, who was asked on Sky News whether he accepted responsibility for the incident which caused chaos for so many passengers, said: “I always accept full responsibility.”
He said: “I am the CEO of a piece of critical infrastructure, so it is my job to take responsibility for that. What I absolutely take responsibility for is keeping people safe and delivering the best service we possibly can on a day like today.
“You will understand my focus is entirely about how we actually resolve this issue, get things back to normal, help our airlines, our airport customers and the travelling public.”
Neal McMahon, Ryanair chief operating officer, called on Rolfe to resign, saying: “How many more failures do passengers have to suffer before overpaid failure Nats CEO Martin Rolfe accepts responsibility for his repeated mismanagement and resigns?
“Over three years after Nats’ catastrophic 2023 system meltdown, it’s clear that nothing has changed, with UK passengers once again suffering avoidable ATC (air traffic control) delays of up to eight hours today due a critical Nats ATC system failing.”
Travel journalist Simon Calder said the knock-on effects on Wednesday are “going to be horrible”.
He told Sky News: “There are going to be dozens of cancellations in the morning of flights coming into Heathrow because, basically, the flights didn’t go out tonight.”
Heathrow suspended arrivals from 8pm for the rest of the day on Tuesday “to ensure the safety of our passengers and colleagues”. Additional reporting: PA

title: Ex-60 Minutes head says dismissed journalists had ‘refused to be accomplices’ in show’s destruction
description: Guy Campanile says facts ‘increasingly treated as items in a buffet, chosen depending on specific appetite and ideological tastes’
content:
The former managing editor at 60 Minutes, who was fired in May with several other top correspondents, has spoken out about the ouster, saying he and his colleagues were dismissed because they “would not compromise our principles or reputations by jamming unverifiable notions or White House talking points into our reporting”.
Guy Campanile, who worked at CBS News for 34 years, said in a private Facebook post obtained by the Guardian on Tuesday that he had held off on commenting about his dismissal right away, having decided it was “wise to remain quiet when emotions are raw”.
But “after some time and deep reflection, I am now comfortable and prepared to talk about it”, he wrote in the post.
Campanile said he, Tanya Simon, Draggan Mihailovich, Matthew Polevoy, Scott Pelley, Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega “refused to be accomplices in the destruction of the most prestigious news programme on American television”.
The firings took place after the new management of CBS News booted them as part of its overhaul of the venerated show.
[ Anderson Cooper to leave 60 Minutes amid turmoil at CBS News Opens in new window ]
Of himself and his former colleagues who departed, Campanile wrote: “We would not compromise our principles or reputations by jamming unverifiable notions or White House talking points into our reporting. We objected when told to conduct interviews arranged by the administration.
“We insisted on asking the most challenging questions to business and political leaders without fear or favour. We did what reporters worth their salt do – we questioned authority… including our own bosses. That’s how the best newsrooms work.”
[ Anderson Cooper to leave 60 Minutes amid turmoil at CBS News Opens in new window ]
He continued: “To be clear: we were told to leave because we insisted on doing our jobs. What has happened recently at 60 Minutes – where I believe editorial independence has become a casualty of corporate priorities and ideological intrusion – was tragic. But it was part of an inevitable progression in the cascade of afflictions that have devalued our most trusted sources of news.”
Campanile said “information has become commoditised in the attention economy” and that “facts are increasingly treated as items in a buffet, chosen depending on specific appetite and ideological tastes”.
He wrote: “Journalism, especially on television, is now largely an exercise in presentation rather than examination: lead with weather because policy can be complicated. Hype everything to a point where it’s hard to tell what is really important. Protect yourself and keep the public distracted by focusing on the ‘what’ rather than the ‘why’. Showcase anchors with shallow experience but blessed with exceptional haircuts. Broadcast sweeping deductions from sealed studios rather than speaking directly to the people making history or pummeled by events.
“Making matters worse is the cadre of self-described influencers and online opinionists who market themselves as ‘journalists’. Some have been given control of our most precious reporting institutions – including CBS News. Many of these newsroom managers have never been exposed to the depths of poverty, the ravages of war or the heartbreak of disaster. Yet these dilettantes and their enablers make critical programming decisions based on what might trend online over the next few hours.”
[ ‘We were lucky’: Stephen Colbert marks end of The Late Show with emotional finale Opens in new window ]
CBS News also fired longtime journalist Scott Pelley, telling him he was being let go for “cause” due to his behaviour in a meeting with the show’s executive producer and network’s managing editor.
In this meeting, Pelley criticised Bari Weiss, the former opinion writer who is now CBS News editor-in-chief. Her appointment has spurred backlash from numerous network staffers who have voiced concerns about her impartiality.
“She’s murdering 60 Minutes,” Pelley remarked of Weiss. “She does not love this place. She was brought in to kill it and is doing exactly that.”
CBS was contacted for comment. – Guardian

title: Troy Parrott scores winner on Champions League debut as Real Betis sink Lille
description: Dubliner bags the winner for Spanish side in 3-2 away victory
content:
Republic of Ireland international Troy Parrott was in goalscoring form again for Real Betis , netting on his Champions League debut as the Spanish club claimed a 3-2 win away to Lille.
Ayasa Ueda put the hosts ahead early with his 12th-minute strike, but Marc Bartra scored his first equaliser of the evening on 33 minutes.
Alexsandro restored Lille’s lead minutes later, but Bartra would again find the net on 49 minutes to pull Manuel Pellegrini’s side back level.
On 53 minutes, Parrott, making his second start in his fourth appearance for his new club, capitalised on some poor defending by Nathan Ngoy to put Betis ahead.

A red card for Ethan Mbappé soon added to the home side’s woes and Parrott threatened again late on, hitting the woodwork with a long, curling effort in the last play of the game as Betis held on for the win.
It comes after the Dubliner scored his first goal for his new side last time out , netting what proved to be the winner in their La Liga meeting with Real Madrid on Friday.
“I’m very happy for Parrott,” Pellegrini said of the 24-year-old’s effort against Madrid. “He made a mistake against Levante,” he added, referencing their 5-2 defeat on Parrott’s first start for Betis on August 29th, “but [on Friday] he had the instinct to score that goal.
