The second talk, involving four separate application options, will outline the various progression routes students can apply for following their Leaving Cert.
While most Leaving Cert students will submit a CAO application, many will also add options in Northern Ireland and the UK through UCAS, Post Leaving Cert (PLC) courses or Tertiary degrees initially through their local Further Education college with the option of progressing on to university, and university options through English in Continental Europe.
Students who widen their range of options put themselves in the strongest position to select the most appropriate one in late August 2027, when they have to decide on their post second-level progression route.
The benefit to school-leavers of this unique event depends entirely on each student’s level of preparation beforehand. This preparation will have been ongoing over the previous two years through career exploration activities in transition year and fifth year. School guidance counsellors provide students attending the event with a comprehensive preparation document to help them plan their engagements throughout the day. By working through this document, students maximise the benefits of attending the expo.
Careful planning and an understanding of what they need to accomplish at Higher Options will hugely enhance the long-term value of attending. Guidance counsellors will provide students with details of various talks at the event, covering every conceivable topic relevant to progression to higher or further education, both in Ireland and abroad.
The WorldSkills Expo is taking place simultaneously in the RDS alongside the Higher Options exhibition. This event will provide extensive coverage of opportunities on offer through apprenticeships both in the traditional construction trades, where there are huge deficits of qualified tradespeople, and in the many 80-plus apprenticeships co-ordinated by Solas.
Any student attending either event should also compose a series of written questions they wish to tease out with the representatives on the stands. Each college will, of course, present the most positive picture possible of the various options their organisation offers.
Students should engage systematically with each one and after the event sift the information received to enable them to move their career-planning process on to the next stage.
Stand-holders will not expect students to make a final decision concerning their future career options based only on attending a talk or following a visit to the stand and a conversation with a representative at Higher Options and WorldSkills. But, for those who plan their activities in advance, these interactions will help set the agenda for each student as they consider their first step beyond second-level education in the months and years ahead.
If they have done their homework, many students will have developed very clear course preferences by the time they attend the Higher Options event in the coming days.
Some might learn they are not likely to secure the high points required for their preferred course or are not taking the subjects necessary to meet the minimum requirements for entry.
This is where the Higher Options event can be of real value. Rather than feeling downcast and abandoning dreams of their preferred career, they will have the opportunity to interact with other stand-holders, where they will learn about other options that might enable them to achieve their dream course by another route.
There are hundreds of high-points CAO programmes across all disciplines that are now accessible through further education (FE) one-year level five programmes.
Many students do not realise that CAO colleges reserve up to 20 per cent of courses, creating thousands of places each year for graduates of such programmes, where your Leaving Cert points results are not relevant.
At the beginning of August each year, more than 6,500 offers are made, based mainly on students’ performances in their FE programme. Many of these FE colleges will be present at Higher Options this year, so seek them out and find out which courses in the CAO link to their FE courses.
Alternatively, while CAO points requirements are very high for many programmes in Ireland, European universities have a different admissions system. They often simply require two H5s and four passes to gain entry to many courses that require more than 500 points in Ireland. Again, these colleges from all over Europe, where lectures are delivered through English, will be present at Higher Options.
In eastern European universities, fees for programmes in medical and paramedical programmes can range from €10,000 upwards. In many western European universities, fees can be modest to non-existent.
Once a student’s interest has been heightened by an interaction at Higher Options – consolidated and strengthened perhaps by a close reading of the literature published by the college – the next step should be to find out when the college is planning its 2026-2027 on-campus open days.
Many colleges will take your email details at their stand to notify you when such events are occurring. No Leaving Cert student should seriously consider deciding at this stage which college to attend without engaging with the institution in question and soaking in the atmosphere of the place at some stage before course choices are finalised next June. Remember, choosing a course commits you to far more than just a set of lectures and exams over several years.
[ A parent’s guide to helping your children start college life Opens in new window ]
Choosing a course or college is like committing to a long-term relationship and it commits you to a lifestyle and a range of social and extracurricular activities offered by the institution in question.
Every student is different in both personality and interests. Some will revel in the cut-and-thrust of very large colleges, while others may prefer smaller institutions where everyone gets to know each other very quickly.
Students who select their course choices based solely on the details of the course itself without considering the context within which it is delivered can often find very quickly that they have made a bad choice.
Having attended the Higher Options event for more than 20 years, it has become clear to me that a proportion of students attend each year without having given any serious thought to why they are there.
They drift around the RDS complex for a few hours, become bored and wander up Anglesea Road with a plastic bag full of prospectuses, which is regularly dumped as it becomes too heavy to carry. Don’t sell yourself short and pass up this opportunity to inform yourself.
As a fifth- or final-year second-level student you will never get so many education/training providers in one place ready to support your career journey. This experience has the potential to be the most productive three hours of career exploration you will spend this year, in clarifying your future options.
Use it wisely and build on it in the weeks and months ahead.

title: Heather Humphreys and sectarianism
description: ‘As the daughter of a Rector of the Church of Ireland from a line going back five generations ... I am still referred to as a ‘Brit’ or a ‘prod’
content:
Sir, – I was saddened to read Heather Humphreys’ piece about how her standing for the presidency seems to have awakened a latent sectarianism in Irish public life ( I don’t regret running for president , Opinion, September 5th).
I have the highest respect and regard for Humphreys and she stands in a noble tradition of the minority participation in independent Ireland from the foundation of the State to present times. From Lord Mayo and Horace Plunkett in the first Senate to current public representatives, the Protestant and formerly unionist minority joined in State-building despite, in Edna Longley’s phrase, having to work their passage to Irishness, as distinct from just being, like Catholics, born Irish.
The story of the Protestant minority in the Free State and the Republic in the early years is one of largely living within stockades, with occasional forays out into the wider world. But it is a positive story. If a sort of closet royalism continued into the second half of the last century, it was combined with an acceptance of, and even allegiance to, the new regime.
As Nora Robertson wrote in 1960: “In respecting new loyalties it had not seemed incumbent upon us to throw our old ones overboard.” Exactly. The southern Protestant journey from independence to now has been one of the “gradualness of inevitability”. Its gentle pace allowed the minority to come to terms with changes that were often distasteful and distressing. But eventually things bedded down.
There is a lesson here for the current debate on the political unity of the island. Leaving aside the economic hurdles, based on the southern minority’s experiences since 1922, two conditions need to be satisfied before unity has a snowball’s chance in hell. Forget a headlong, sudden rush into a 32-county socialist republic. As in the Irish Free State, there will have to be some sort of British belonging that northern Protestants and erstwhile unionists can still identify with. Cultural colonisation of the new minority will have to be avoided – a trivial but everyday example would be traffic light sequencing. The second condition is compromise on symbols, with a tacit, if tactfully undeclared, acceptance that things may develop in the future. Just as the Free State morphed into the Republic.
Heather Humphreys ends her article with a plea that we should be “brave enough to make room for every tradition on this island”. I would finesse that slightly, to make rooms for every tradition on this island. – Yours, etc.,
Co-editor, with Ida Milne, of Protestant and Irish: the Minority’s Search for Place in Independent Ireland (2019).
Sir, – I was deeply moved to read such a powerful account by Heather Humphreys of her toxic abuse by fellow Irish citizens in her bid for the presidency of Ireland.
I so get how she must have felt trying to make sense of being Irish, but then not if you do not fit the so-called criteria!
As the daughter of a Rector of the Church of Ireland from a line going back five generations of rectors in the South of Ireland and both sides of the family going back 1,000 years on the land – I am still referred to as a “Brit” or a “prod”, but when it comes to honouring Yeats or Oscar Wilde or even Wolfe Tone an enormous amount of people can be so proud of them being Irish and overlook the fact they were prods.
Heather Humphreys, by all accounts, was a wonderful TD and was put forward for the job out of honour and respect for her many skills and talents.
I do so hope she will continue to contribute to public life in Ireland for the benefit of us all. – Yours, etc

title: Farewell to Sarah Moss’s column
description: Her writings on identity have resonated with me
content:
Sir, – I was very sorry to read that Sarah Moss had written her last column for The Irish Times (“ Being hated on the internet has begun to tint my life, sleep and thoughts ”, Weekend, September 5th).
I have very much enjoyed her writing, and the column led me to read her books, which I have also found thought-provoking and illuminating. Her writings on identity have resonated with me, having a similar background to hers.
It is very sad that abuse on social media should have brought Sarah’s column to an end. As an elderly white male who generally found myself in agreement with her views on food, transport etc. I regret its ending, and wish Sarah all the very best in her future works. – Yours, etc,

title: In search of Pietro Bossi: The Italian craftsman shrouded in the mystery of his life in Dublin
description: Examples of the stucco worker and marble inlayer’s pieces can be found in Áras an Uachtaráin and Hugh Lane Gallery
content:
Having spent an extremely enjoyable evening at the new Conor McPherson play, The Brightening Air , in the Gate Theatre on Friday, I made my way the following morning to Avondale in Co Wicklow for a visit to the ancestral home of Parnell.
I had long planned to visit the house and do the Treetop walk there, but I was also hoping to identify the part of the historical estate where a series of football matches had taken place in 1886.
The wonderful guide who brought us on a hugely informative tour of the house was aware of the matches but was unable to tell me exactly where the location was. In an unusual turn of events however, he opened up another avenue of curiosity, one that I was blissfully unaware of before my visit to Avondale.
As we made our way through the various rooms in Avondale House we passed through the drawingroom. This was the space to which the ladies retired for their after-dinner tea and gossip, leaving the men to their cigars and cognac in the diningroom.
The focal point of the drawingroom is a fireplace designed by the famous Italian artisan Pietro Bossi. On first view, the ornate fireplace features the image of a bowl of fruit but which on closer inspection could also be some people in a boat. The design of a bowl or urn seems to have been a common motif of his, but here the ambiguity of the image is undoubtedly an intended optical illusion.
Not being a connoisseur of ornate fire surrounds however, I was intrigued by the work and its creator. For someone whose work adorns such famous Irish houses as Avondale, Áras an Uachtaráin and the office of the Taoiseach, surprisingly little is known about the man.
As Bossi worked in privacy behind a closed door, a curious Lady Belvedere peeped through the keyhole to see how the work was progressing
Apparently descended from a family of renowned stucco workers near Lake Como in northern Italy, he arrived in Ireland towards the end of the 18th century, probably around 1784 when he established his workshop in Dublin. Describing himself as an “Inlayer in Marble and Stucco Worker”, several sources cite his place of work being firstly at 22 Fleet Street in 1785 and at 38 Fleet Street from 1787-98.
Bossi specialised in the use of stucco and scagliola, a process where he applied a coloured paste inlay on to a white marble background. Apart from fireplaces, Bossi also designed and crafted Etruscan-style tabletops, one of which is located in Charlemont House or as it is more commonly known nowadays, The Hugh Lane Gallery.
For someone who now enjoys a big reputation for his work, very little about Bossi’s origin or indeed what became of him is known. Despite years of working in Ireland, no receipts or accounts for his work have been found. It is possible he married in Dublin and had a child here, but the date and place of his death is still unrecorded and his work appears to have come to an abrupt end in 1798.
In an essay on Irish Architectural and Decorative Studies in the Journal of the Irish Georgian Society, Conor O’Neill suggests that Bossi may have one of many itinerant craftsmen who plied their craft in Italy, Germany and Britain at that time. Bossi was reputedly very secretive about the way he went about his work and the techniques he used to achieve his results.
O’Neill relates an amusing anecdote about the time when Bossi was engaged in work in Belvedere House. As Bossi worked in privacy behind a closed door, a curious Lady Belvedere peeped through the keyhole to see how the work was progressing. Sensing her presence, Bossi blew powder through the keyhole which caught her in the eye causing her some discomfort.
Having exited Avondale House at the conclusion of our tour, the guide pointed out The Great Ride – a vast expanse of tree-lined meadow which sweeps down to the banks of the Avonmore river at the far end of the estate.
The undulating terrain, over a kilometre in length, was where the Parnell family rode out their horses but reading the account of the matches played in 1886, the description in the Freeman’s Journal of a tree-lined pitch on slightly rough ground adjacent to the Avonmore river was reminiscent of the scene there today.
The beautiful treetop walk through the estate provides wonderful views of the house and the surrounding Wicklow countryside. The walk culminates with a 38m-tall viewing tower which is accessed by a circular ramped boardwalk.
The viewing tower also contains another more modern great ride where a slide returns you the 38m to terra firma in a matter of seconds.
Unfortunately, the queue for this adventure was slightly too long and I took the more sensible option of retracing my steps back down the boardwalk.

title: Snipers and signal jammers: Inside the ‘most complex’ security operation for Trump’s Irish Open visit
description: Sources say securing the US president at golf resort in remote coastal location, with tens of thousands of spectators present, ‘a nightmare'
content:
Spectators attending the Irish Open at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg , Co Clare, will face significant security checks in an attempt to ensure no weapons or sinister items are brought on to the course while the US president is present.
Precautions for what one source described as one of the “most complex” security operations to ever be take place in the State are expected to include signal jammers, which disrupt the use of drones and other devices.
Instructions issued by An Garda Síochána on Monday to the tens of thousands of people expected to travel to the golf tournament later this week include advice not to rely on satnavs in their vehicles due to road closures.
US military Chinook helicopters were spotted in the sky over Dublin on Monday, flying from the UK towards the Irish Air Corps base at Baldonnel. It is understood they were transporting equipment for the US side of the security operation surrounding Trump’s visits to Dublin and Doonbeg.
About 4,000 Irish and US security personnel, including from the Garda, Defence Forces and US Secret Service, are expected to be deployed, mainly in Clare and Dublin, according to sources familiar with the operation. This includes about 1,000 US personnel and 3,000 Irish, mainly from the Garda.
The two-day visit has been declared an “extraordinary event” by Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly, meaning Garda leave and rest periods can be curtailed, and a longer working day can be imposed.
Garda and Defence Forces teams will be deployed, using new anti-drone ground technology to neutralise any encroachments from the sky. There will be a significant armed presence among the Garda and US security staff, including snipers.
However, the key concern relates to possible efforts by protesters to stage what one source described as “a spectacular incursion to try to embarrass” the Irish and US security forces.
A number of Garda sources told The Irish Times that securing the Doonbeg venue, a golf course with beach access in a remote area, would be “a nightmare” and “one of the most complex challenges ever” for Irish policing.
[ Irish Open at Doonbeg: Tee times, TV details, when is Donald Trump going to be there? Opens in new window ]
While Trump visited the course and resort in 2019 during his first term as a president, he did so to play a round of golf rather than to watch a tournament expected to be attended by 75,000 people between Thursday and Sunday.
The policing and military demands of hosting Trump come while the State holds the Council of the European Union presidency, which has been placing its own demands on security services.
Trump will visit Dublin on Saturday, meeting Taoiseach Micheál Martin at Farmleigh and President Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin, both in the Phoenix Park, before travelling to Doonbeg for the Irish Open. He is also expected to attend an event at the US ambassador to Ireland’s residence, also in Phoenix Park. The park will be closed to the public from 11pm on Thursday until Saturday evening.
Garda command centres have been established in Dublin and Clare to co-ordinate the policing response, under the name Operation Far Sunrise. This involves the deployment of armed members of the Special Detective Unit, which combats terrorism, and armed teams from the Emergency Response Unit and Armed Support Unit.
Other resources – such as the Army’s bomb disposal teams and the Ranger Wing – are also available. The Garda’s public order resources will be on standby and have been strengthened significantly since the November 2023 Dublin riots.
However, sources said the traditional tactics of combing areas for threats, declaring them safe and then using personnel to hold those areas until Trump has left, or passed through, is the bedrock of the ground operation.

title: Dara Ó Briain: ‘I don’t think anyone put an argument in favour of Brexit on Mock the Week’
description: Irish comedian reflects on Mock the Week’s past iterations ahead of revival and the material inspiring his next tour, Re:Creation
content:
D ara Ó Briain is still having photos taken when I arrive at the studio in west London .
Shoot over, he ditches his jacket and we walk up the road to find a quiet corner in a pub. There’s a new season of Mock the Week, the topical satirical panel show that ran for 17 years on BBC Two until 2022 and has now been reborn on the free-to-air channel TLC. A roster of comedians make up two teams and compete in a faux gameshow, ostensibly to answer questions about the previous week’s news, but really just to be funny.
Ó Briain (54) has hosted it since the start. In the first iteration, regular guests included Hugh Dennis, Frankie Boyle and Ed Byrne, but up-and-coming comics were often included too.
“It became a kind of debutante’s ball for people who’ve gotten to the top at Edinburgh and are ready to go on screen,” Ó Briain explains, not without pride.
When Mock the Week was on the BBC, there were accusations that the mockery was directed to the right from the left. Ó Briain, who describes himself as “centre left”, says that had a lot to do with what was going on in Westminster: “For the vast majority of that time, there was a Tory government – Conservative PM after Conservative PM – so obviously we were looking at them.”
But he also admits there was probably something to those accusations. “I don’t think anyone put an argument in favour of Brexit during the whole thing; nobody on Mock the Week was going: ‘Well, maybe sovereignty or whatever ...’ ”
The show featured the right-leaning comedians Geoff Norcott and Simon Evans, but the right isn’t as well represented in British comedy. Ó Briain isn’t sure why – perhaps because “the direction in which you punch matters or people don’t warm to it”, he says.
“I have seen comics do jokes about, say, nurses always asking for money, and the audience go: ‘No, I don’t think that, we’re not coming with you on that one’.”
But equally, he suggests, audiences don’t like it if you’re too far the other way – “too happy-clappy”.
The other accusation aimed at Mock the Week was that it was vicious, mean and male – a bear pit of a show on which macho comedians elbowed each other out of the way in order to get their jibe in. Jo Brand didn’t like it when she went on.
Again, Ó Briain says the criticism was fair. “It was generally seven men around the table: they were trying to find themselves; there were elbows.” But he points out that the programme started more than two decades ago, when this was the culture of shows of this kind (see also Never Mind the Buzzcocks). Ó Briain says he wouldn’t have liked to be a contestant.
“I would have found it too staccato; I like to build up a head of steam on a piece of bullsh*t. But now it has become a lot more conversational.”
While there’s plenty to converse about in the average week, some topics are riper for mockery than others. Trump , for example, isn’t the gift you might assume he is.
“Particularly Trump 2, darker Trump. There’s not even the funny mistakes going on. Now, it’s self-parody, so utterly ridiculous that maybe it’s normalised the ridiculousness, to a certain extent. And you know, the joke’s already there – what are we adding to it? It would be like doing jokes about The Simpsons.”
“Awful. He did nothing and said very little.”
He means as a topic of discussion, rather than as a politician, although he wasn’t impressed with the way he ran the country, either. He’s not sure about Andy Burnham yet – they are still to mock one of his weeks – but he is amused by the process by which he came to power.
“Makerfield gets to pick the prime minister now, is that how it happens?”
So what or who is a gift to Mock the Week? Peter Murrell and the SNP expenses scandal, he says: “Not quite a victimless crime, because I guess the people who made donations to the SNP were victims. But the details were so perfect: the number of video consoles, the £2,000 salt shaker [Murrell spent £2,618.16 on Lalique Feuilles pepper and salt grinders], the fact Nicola Sturgeon bent over backwards to act like she didn’t know her in-laws suddenly had a 30ft camper van.”
They got some good mileage from that in the last season – more mileage than the camper van, which drove only from the showroom to the in-laws’ drive.
Now, freed from the shackles of public service impartiality and scrutiny, and with more women involved, including Sara Pascoe, Maisie Adam, Laura Lexx and Angela Barnes, perhaps Mock the Week is a nicer place, even if it has many fewer viewers (a little more than 1 million when repeats are included) than the 3-million-plus it averaged in its BBC peak.
Ó Briain wasn’t meant to be a comedian. He studied mathematics and theoretical physics at University College Dublin in the early 1990s. He says he was a shy and self-conscious teenager, but pushed himself to join the debating society at UCD. During one debate, he told a joke: “It got a laugh, and a round of applause, and I remember this whoosh of adrenaline and me going: oh hello!”
He still feels that whoosh, although the high isn’t so high and it might take a two-hour show, rather than one joke, to get there. But he loves the work and it takes him to cool places such as Athens, Barcelona and Stockholm (as well as Chatham, Dorking and Leicester). His two most recent tours have been less about the gags, more about the storytelling – and more personal.
‘We are currently cool, but I think people are getting a bit tired of it’
Born in Bray, Co Wicklow, Ó Briain was adopted into what he has described as “a stable home” and had a happy childhood. A few years ago, he decided to find out about his biological parents.
“The plan wasn’t that it should be a show, it was just this thing I should investigate, because of normal human emotions. I always knew there was this story waiting to be found out, and then the impetus was that none of us are getting younger. I know of people who have found parents and then met them in a nursing home and they’ve had Alzheimer’s.”
He realised the story wasn’t only about him after seeing the film Philomena. “I came out of the cinema with a sudden appreciation that this is actually not my story at all, I’m only a baby in it, but there’s a woman who got pregnant and went on this journey,” he says.
“It’s her story and I should probably at the very least make contact in order to close that circle for her and let her know it was great and I found a lovely family and all that stuff.”
It was hard – bureaucratically, emotionally – but he found her and they met up. It was awkward and strange. He got a bunch of new siblings. He told the story in his show So ... Where Were We?, which won best tour at the Chortle awards in 2023.
His next show, Re:Creation, which he’s been touring across Europe, tells the story of trying to track down his biological father. No spoilers (there are some dates left, plus it’s on Amazon Prime), but it contains less sadness and anger than the previous set.
“It’s a bit of a romp, with a twist towards the end that is delightful to deliver. Not quite The Sixth Sense, but kind of a gasp moment.”
[ Dara Ó Briain: ‘I’ve willingly taken on a 600% increase in family members’ Opens in new window ]
The problem now is what to do next. “Both stories just kind of emerge in a very tellable form. There’s no way of doing a third, no trilogy. Even as I’m doing it, enjoying telling the story, my head is going: ‘Yeah, next time, you’re going to actually have to do some work, write some jokes, because you’re not going to be gifted another parent to find, there isn’t another great family reveal’,” he says.
Well, there is one possibility, surely. Maybe not a parent ... He laughs. “Yes, the perfect thing would be a knock on the door and there’s a 25-year-old going: ‘I think ...’ And I would go: ‘Thank you so much!’ Because this would be the only way you could extend the trilogy – if I was the father of a child given up for adoption.”
“I’ve done the audit, run it backwards in my head going: was there any situation that could have … ?”
He adds quickly: “I mean, I’ve had my checkered history. But I feel it’s all accounted for.”
His TV career started as a children’s presenter on RTÉ, while he was doing his first standup gigs on the Irish comedy circuit. He came to prominence hosting the topical panel show Don’t Feed the Gondolas from 1997 to 2001. His big break on the other side of the Irish Sea came in 2003, when he hosted The Live Floor Show on BBC Two, which led to appearances on Have I Got News for You.
Since making his debut as Mock the Week’s host in 2005, Ó Briain has presented just about everything on television. Alongside the panel shows and the comedy, his interest in maths and physics continued. He has presented Stargazing Live from Jodrell Bank observatory with Prof Brian Cox; his hobby is astrophotography, which he does from his garden in London (“you can filter out all the light”); and he’s had many pops at bad science (hello, Gillian McKeith!) in his comedy.
Even when chatting, he’ll borrow analogies from science. He says X, formerly known as Twitter, has become a black hole: “It’s got sucked into this thing and created so much density that it’s actually going to collapse under its own gravity.” (He has abandoned the platform.)
The popularity of panel shows? They have their moments. “It’s like this graph of an extinction event: it goes back down again, but it never fully eliminates a small number of hard‑shelled animals who survive each time – the cockroaches who are the comedians at the bottom, never fully eliminated because they’re cheap and people like them, so they’ll come back.”
His own career, meanwhile, is more of a sine wave: “It goes up and down, but carries on.” Or is it a damped oscillation?
“If you don’t pay attention, it gets smaller and smaller, asymptotically, until there’s only a tiny little vibration right at the very end and I’m sitting in an olive grove in Spain going: ‘Buenos dias’.”
You’ll know, if you’ve seen him on stage or on TV, that Ó Briain’s delivery is superfast. Well, it doesn’t slow down over a quiet orange juice and lemonade. When he sets off on something, he’s like a rocket in space. I fire little thrusters (chip in with the odd question) in an attempt to steer the ship, but when something has that much momentum sometimes you just have to run with it.
We go to many other places – solar eclipses, the World Cup, what to do if there’s a medical emergency in the audience, Arsenal’s transfer window, Blankety Blank, whether or not it’s cool to be Irish in London, but there isn’t space here ... oh, go on then, just that last one. The answer is yes, but again it’s sinusoidal. “We are currently cool, but I think people are getting a bit tired of it, so probably it’s time for someone else to be cool for a while.”
Whether he’s cool or not, 90 minutes with Ó Briain is eye-opening, exhausting and delightful. He’s still talking when he gets into the car that has come to fetch him.
It’s something about Melania Trump, although I’m not sure if it’s the documentary or the woman. And then it’s too late when I realise: I forgot to ask if he ever feels as if he’s trapped in a box. – The Guardian
Mock the Week returns to TLC on September 13th at 9pm. Re:Creation is on Amazon Prime

title: Why are Irish people saving so much?
description: CSO has made significant revisions to data, but how are we putting so much money aside?
content:
S ome good news for those who are intending to provide options under the new State personal investment account : Irish households are saving even more than was previously thought. That means there should be plenty of spare cash ready to be invested following October’s budget .
The Government reaffirmed its roadmap on the new tax-efficient investment account last week, just days after the Central Statistics Office (CSO) published revised numbers for household savings.
CSO figures showed that Irish households are a European savings outperformer, with a savings rate of 19.1 per cent for the first quarter of this year. Almost one in every €5 of disposable income is now being saved. This puts us on a par with those renowned German savers.
It’s a significant increase on the previously published rate – of just 12.5 per cent – and also a far cry from the heady days of the Celtic Tiger in 2007 when the savings rate sank below 2 per cent.
So why did the CSO make the revision? Why are Irish people saving so much? And what might it tell us coming into budget season?
Going from a savings rate of 12.5 per cent to 19.1 per cent is a significant revision.
“It’s very sizeable, and it’s surprising the extent to which it was revised upwards,” says Dermot O’Leary, chief economist with Goodbody . “This new data is pointing towards Irish households having amongst the highest saving ratio in the euro area.”
The change has arisen due to a separate revision in the national accounts for the first quarter of 2026. In those accounts, income was revised upwards while expenditure was revised downwards.
“The combination of these two revisions going back several years, with both moving in opposite directions, has led to the change in the level of household saving,” the CSO says.
[ Personal investment accounts likely to engage 85 per cent of Irish adults – survey Opens in new window ]
The finding means the ratio has been revised all the way back to 2020. The average since the start of 2023 has now been considerably altered; it was previously recorded as 12.7 per cent, but has now been revised upwards to 18.5 per cent.
The savings rate measures how much households are saving, expressed as a percentage of total disposable income. It’s calculated as household disposable income minus household consumption expenditure.
So if disposable income in a period was €10 billion, and spending was €9 billion, the amount deemed to be savings would be €1 billion, or a savings rate of 10 per cent.
Of course, each household will have their own individual savings rate; some may save significantly more, and many significantly less.
Should we be worried at such a scale of the latest revision?
A spokesman for the CSO says such changes “are a routine feature of national accounts” and arise because estimates, especially for the most recent year, “are based on incomplete data”.
[ New Government investment scheme: Here’s what we know – and don’t know Opens in new window ]
They also arise because of changes in methodology. For example, the household income figures include new data, such as the most recent Revenue Commissioners microdata files for wages and mixed income, as well as updated data from Ireland’s Pensions Authority.
And on the spending side, one source for the revision was the inclusion of updated household travel survey data, which led to downward revisions to estimates of household spending outside the State.
One of the biggest impact of the revisions is how we stack up when compared with our European counterparts.
Until the update, Ireland was a nation – apart from a brief blip during the pandemic – of solid, but unremarkable, savers.
In 2024, for example, under the old figures, Ireland had a savings rate of 13.49 per cent (down from the pandemic high of 25.8 per cent in 2020). This put it firmly mid-table, and below the overall euro zone average of 14.9 per cent.
By comparison, the Germans were saving 20 per cent of their income at the time.
[ Key decisions on new Government investment account scheme deferred until Budget 2027 Opens in new window ]
Taking the revised numbers into account, however, we can see that the Irish are among the most assiduous savers in the euro zone, on a par with the Germans, and about a third above the euro zone average of 14.3 per cent.
We’re substantially ahead of the French (13.5 per cent), the Spanish (11.3 per cent) and the Greeks, who actually have a negative rate. We are also saving at more than double the rate of our neighbours in the UK, where the first-quarter savings rate was 8.9 per cent.
The revised rate may explain why we have €175 billion sitting in household deposits – an increase of 58 per cent over the last six years.
O’Leary says such a high savings rate does point, to some degree, to a relatively low level of consumer confidence. Households are choosing to put away higher amounts as a precaution at a time of global and political uncertainty.
Ongoing hostilities in Ukraine and Iran , the perceived threat to jobs and otherwise from artificial intelligence , political uncertainty in the US – all these are conspiring to make households hold on to more of their incomes.
“Consumers can dip into their savings if they come across more difficult times,” says, adding that such a high rate will provide “a buffer for household spending going forward”.
And it’s not just that; our recent financial past is another factor.
“A lot of it does come back to the impact of the financial crisis on households’ attitude to risk – 17 years ago at this stage,” says O’Leary.
“Not at the moment,” O’Leary says, adding that it could be seen as more of a personal financial risk for households in that they may not be getting enough of a return on their money by keeping it in low-paying overnight type accounts.
Plenty of money then, perhaps, to fund the Government’s new retail investment accounts, which are due to be launched after the budget.
The bigger question, however, is whether or not this revised savings ratio should feed into this October’s budget. If we have such a strong savings rate, indicating the financial strength and stability of households, is there any need, for example, for cost of living measures?
As O’Leary notes, the aggregate savings ratio doesn’t tell us anything about what is happening within income deciles; who is actually saving what. Perhaps it’s the richest households that are saving the most?
Possibly, although figures in the Central Bank’s latest household wealth statistics show that savings are not concentrated at the very, very high end, but rather, as O’Leary points out, spread out across the population.
In any case, O’Leary suggests that any cost-of-living measures need to go to those who are most in need, rather than broadly based incentives as has been the case until now.
“You need to make sure that they are targeted,” he says.

title: Felipe Contepomi should be next Leinster head coach, says Ian Madigan
description: Argentina head coach is tied to national team until after World Cup, but Madigan believes he’s worth waiting for
content:
Ian Madigan, the former Leinster outhalf turned respected pundit, has endorsed Felipe Contepomi as a successor to Leo Cullen after the latter steps aside from his role as the province’s head coach at the end of the season.
Noting Contepomi’s “exciting” style of play is in keeping with “the Leinster way and the Leinster brand”, Madigan says: “What he’s done with Argentina has been really impressive.”
Speaking in his capacity as a pundit with Premier Sports at the launch of their URC and Champions Cup coverage, Madigan added: “I’d be slow to measure him too harshly on Argentina’s recent results.”
Argentina have only won three of their last 11 Tests, and two of those were against Wales. . Citing the “logistical nightmare” of drawing upon players from all over the world, Madigan noted that Los Pumas generally improve from slow starts in international windows.
“But what I’d expect with Felipe is that there’s a grand plan in place and I think they’ll still be peaking come the World Cup. Even seeing them against Australia at the weekend, that was a good result against a side that’s very much on the way up,” added Madigan of the 28-28 draw against Australia in Mendoza.
Madigan, Leinster’s fourth highest points scorer, also said of the man who is second in that list: “He understands the ethos of the club. He’d have a very good understanding of the school system and the academy system, and a very good relationship with the likes of Andy Farrell, Johnny Sexton and Sean O’Brien. So, he certainly ticks a lot of boxes.
“The negatives would obviously be it (coaching Argentina) is going to take him up past the World Cup. So, you’re looking at nearly December by the time he’d be coming in but there’s enough quality within the Leinster setup for people to step up and fill that void and then look to get him back for probably round one or two of the Champions Cup.
“But when I heard the murmurs, my initial reaction was very positive. I thought ‘that would be a great fit’.”
In the interim, this will be Cullen’s 12th and last season at the helm. Sport is littered with examples of such a scenario leading to a slippage in standards.
“It definitely is a concern,” admitted Madigan. “I think the solution to that problem is it’s got to be player-led. It can’t be Leo driving and defining standards and telling people they aren’t scraping the plates properly or not picking up their tape or turning up late to meetings. That has to be led by the likes of Hugo Keenan and Caelan Doris.
“These guys are so hungry to win and for Leinster to be successful I’d expect them to step up to the plate. They’ve seen that Leo’s largely devoted his whole adult life to the club. I think that in itself is going to be a real driver for Leinster this year. And I think the players are smart enough now to know that the way you achieve those goals of winning trophies is by setting those standards on a daily basis. That’s always been the Leinster way.”
In addition to RG Snyman being sidelined, Rieko Ioane and Rabah Slimani have moved on, as has all-time leading try scorer James Lowe. With no incoming players apart from the returning Joey Carbery and Peter Dooley, the squad is lacking some overseas stardust.
Three players have also headed west to Connacht, with Ciarán Frawley and Will Connors reuniting with Stuart Lancaster. Luke McGrath’s departure to Perpignan has “left a huge void” at scrumhalf, which Madigan believes is “the most important player in that Leinster system”.
The “chasing pack” as understudy to Jamison Gibson-Park is led by Fintan Gunne, with Cormac Foley and third-year academy scrumhalf Oliver Coffey also in the mix to establish themselves as first-choice back-up.
“Once you’re in that position, it opens up other opportunities for you to go on to the national setup. So we could potentially see a bolter there coming out of that Leinster team.
“But if that doesn’t work out for Leinster and none of those guys step up to the mark, that is a significant problem for them. I expect that they will. But that’s an area I’ll be watching so closely.”

title: Leopardstown boss hopeful of good ground and a big crowd at Champions Festival
description: Going could decide the opposition Constitution River faces in the Champion Stakes
content:
New Leopardstown boss Mark Clayton is gearing up for his first Irish Champions Festival on Saturday, although the old weather-watch story may be front and centre beforehand.
Ground conditions at the Dublin track ahead of Saturday’s programme are “good”, with officials “reasonably optimistic” that a similar surface will apply on the big day.
That could prove crucial to the shape of the featured €1.25 million Royal Bahrain Irish Champion Stakes in particular.
Aidan O’Brien ’s Constitution River is an evens favourite with some firms to deliver his trainer a record-extending 14th success in the race ahead of Tuesday’s latest acceptance stage.
The going is likely to be important in determining the opposition he faces, particularly in relation to the two horses that finished ahead of Constitution River in last month’s Juddmonte International at York.
Item just edged out Almaqam on that occasion and Andrew Balding has already indicated his willingness to travel to Leopardstown with the Juddmonte colt. However, he has also said soft ground conditions are not ideal for Item.
In contrast, they appear to suit Almaqam, who earlier this year landed his first Group One in the Tattersalls Gold Cup at the Curragh. His trainer, Ed Walker, has indicated he may ultimately wait for next month’s Champion Stakes at Ascot for the horse.
Walker was in contact with Leopardstown’s new chief executive on Monday and it might not be the only call he makes to Foxrock this week.
Clerk of the course Paddy Graffin and Horse Racing Ireland’s head of racing, Peter Roe, examined the ground there on Monday.
“It’s good going and we’re happy with what we’ve got,” said Clayton. “As for the forecast, if I was to say sunshine and showers that would probably cover it. I think we’re reasonably optimistic that it will be very similar ground on the day. If you pushed us, it’s probably the easier side of good.”
The Englishman started his new role at the HRI-owned track in January and came through a baptism of fire at the Dublin Racing Festival later that month. Stormy conditions saw the first day of the National Hunt highlight postponed and moved to the bank holiday Monday.
The appeal of jumps racing was underlined when over 10,000 still attended that Monday meeting on the back of a near-full house of over 18,000 for Sunday’s card. A total of 34,400 were at the Dublin Racing Festival in 2025.
Those figures dwarf the official 11,354 attendance at the Leopardstown leg of last year’s Irish Champions Festival. That was a 12 per cent increase on the 2024 equivalent of 10,135. Poor weather hit the Curragh’s Irish Champions Festival leg last year and resulted in an official crowd of 8,361.
Deciding how best to boost public engagement with Irish flat racing’s shop-window event has been a conundrum for much of the festival’s 12-year history. But Clayton is confident attendance figures at Leopardstown will be up this weekend.
“The way it’s tracking, we are expecting a bigger attendance this year than we had last year. That’s a positive. It’s looking like a record UK challenge with runners coming across. That will whet the appetite of the Irish racing public.
“It’s real international racing. The Champion Stakes itself is looking like a very good renewal. In addition, we have the Golden Fleece, a new Group One. And in addition to that, we have Precise against Blue Bolt in the Matron.
“We’ve got music and entertainment and a little bit of razzmatazz that I’m really looking forward to seeing. Once I’ve seen it, then I think there’s something I can understand and build on."
Both days at Leopardstown and the Curragh are included in World Pool betting. Over €5 million in prizemoney will be up for grabs.
There is Listed action in Galway on Tuesday, where the Ardilaun Hotel Oyster Stakes features seven Joseph O’Brien runners in a field of 16.
They include Beset, who must concede weight but who should relish the prevailing soft ground conditions in Ballybrit. So, too, should one of her stable companions, Snapretend, who returned to action at Cork recently with a decent effort in the Give Thanks Stakes.
Wayne Lordan’s pick of the first-time blinkered City Of Gold in the opening maiden looks significant. Noble Exhibit’s Curragh debut effort was promising too, but Lordan has overlooked his claims. Lordan could also score in a later handicap aboard Purely. She might prove significantly better than her current lowly 65 rating based on a future Group Three entry.

title: Language test for Irish citizenship raises questions
description: All equal but some more equal than others?
content:
Sir, – I read with some irritation comments expressed by Bernie Cronin ( Letters , September 5th) in response to Peadar Tóibín, (“ Should new citizens have to pass a language test? ,” Opinion, September 1st).
I hold no strong views on this particular subject though I recognise the practical benefits of the acquisition of the English language regarding integration and the accessing if services.
However, the claim in the letter that the referendum of 2004, which culminated in the 27th Amendment to the Constitution limiting citizenship of those born in Ireland to children with at least one Irish parent, demonstrated the value the electorate placed on citizenship cannot be left unchallenged.
Less than 60 per cent of those eligible to vote did so and many of those who did, did so on the back of a despicable campaign based on fear of a fictitious tidal wave of heavily pregnant women arriving in Ireland in order to grant their entire extended families permanent residency here, and subsequently the right to travel to any country in the EU .
It sickened me then, and today it still sits uneasily with me, that not all of the teenage boys sitting in front of me in the classroom – nearly all born in Ireland to parents legally resident here – are equal in the eyes of our laws, regardless of how well they speak Irish, or play hurling or Gaelic, or do in their Leaving Certificate exams.
All equal but some more equal than others?
Sir, – Not content with insisting that prospective Irish citizens should be able to demonstrate proficiency in English, Peadar Tóibín of Aontú has now told RTÉ’s Morning Ireland that applicants for citizenship should be able to display a rudimentary knowledge of the Irish language.
Having been born in England, neither I, nor my husband and brothers, ever learned Irish. Should we be preparing for deportation?
On a more serious note, this seems to augur very poorly for any hopes of uniting the various traditions on this island, which Aontú would no doubt claim as an aspiration.
Populism is such a blunt instrument. – Yours, etc,

title: Eamon Ryan: Here’s something you don’t often see - an optimistic column on the climate crisis
description: Regardless of what politicians say or do, people are starting to demand and deliver change locally
content:
I t is all too easy to succumb to despair as warnings from climate scientists become ever more stark and while governments are increasingly unwilling to act. Some are even reversing what they previously agreed to do.
There were two further reversals in Ireland last week: public transport fares were increased and hints were given about a further deferral of carbon taxes in the upcoming budget .
It is as if politics everywhere has taken on a more reactionary course, as governments ditch climate commitments if they think it might stop voters going to more populist extremes. Political science trumps climate science at every turn.
Environmental writer George Monbiot argues there is still hope . He believes we can stop climate change if we reach a certain social tipping point, where people demand and deliver change in their local area, regardless of what their politicians say or do.
I still think we will need both top-down government decision-making and a bottom-up community effort – but in the absence of political leadership in the centre, then local action is where we have to begin.
Such a bottom-up approach is needed to get the design details right for new local infrastructure and to help speed up its delivery. It might also raise public support for action, which is the political capital that matters most to politicians in the end.
A movement to help deliver this approach will need people coming together in person, rather than online campaigns. Real-life encounters will become more valuable as artificial intelligence-generated content, pushed by social media algorithms, erodes trust. Face to face meetings generate their own positive energy.
Thankfully, there are some signs of such green shoots starting to emerge across Ireland as in other countries. On Tuesday and Wednesday next week, up to 500 people will attend a Climate Carnival at Ballintubbert House, Co Laois .
It is billed as like a mini-Electric Picnic, only focused on climate change. It is the second year in operation and the theme this year will be around breaking out of individual silos and embracing systems-thinking instead, matching the interconnected nature of our world.
The carnival is run by the Climate Cocktail Club, which was started in 2018. Tom Popple, one of the founders, says the aim was to get the climate debate away from what he describes as an “invitation-only, miserable grey conference room space”.
The cocktail name doesn’t just refer to the drinks – but also the mix of people. Popple says these events attract a generation who do not need to be told what to do, but who want to do things themselves.
In a similar vein, Climate Finance Week Ireland starts in Dublin next Monday. For the ninth year running, it will bring leading people in sustainable finance together to consider how the industry can help make the transition happen.
We are seeing a tipping point, in which global investment in a new renewable and efficient electricity system is now twice what is spent on the fossil fuel alternative.
Ireland could play an important role in this shift, as evidenced by the establishment of the United Nations Development Programme Sustainable Finance Hub here, which will be one of the focuses of the week.
A climate gathering will also be taking place on the island of Inishbofin, Co Galway , next week. Sixty people with backgrounds in climate science, the arts, spirituality, campaigning and government will come together to consider what new narratives might raise our collective will for action.
The Gathering will be held in a “fifth province” format, inspired by the philosopher John Moriarty, who depicted an ancient Irish tradition of using such a safe meeting place to resolve differences. Everyone comes as an equal, every view is respected and the use of creativity and a connection to nature adds to the dialogue process. Again the gathering is designed to have a broad mix of participants.
If a grassroots approach to climate change is going to work then it has to involve most of our people. We need a climate story that connects to science and to the humanities, belongs to both conservative and progressive political traditions and delivers for both the global north and south by bringing benefits home for every community.
Such stories will matter more than any new cost-benefit analysis or scientific report about what is happening in our atmosphere. We need our hearts and souls engaged in the issue and not just our heads. Once that happens the positive tipping points will follow.

title: Opinion: Patient records are a vital part of our history. Destroying them is wrong
description: DPC ordered the HSE to audit stored records and ‘safely destroy any containing personal data that are no longer needed’. But these records have immense value
content:
T he Data Protection Commission (DPC) has imposed a fine of €645,000 on the HSE for its failure to properly secure patient medical records.
The fine – which was widely reported last week – is a result of an inquiry the DPC began in May 2024 , following two personal data breaches. The breaches were notified to the DPC in October and November 2023 after people gained unauthorised access to two derelict former psychiatric hospitals and found boxes of patient files in appalling condition, damaged by water, mould and animal droppings.
A post shared by Jamie Robinson (@jamie08rob)
The commissioner ordered the HSE to audit the current conditions containing the records and “safely destroy any records containing personal data that are no longer needed”.
But though the personal data may no longer be needed, these records have value medically, legally and historically. And the imposition of a fine only removes further resources from the HSE, which already struggles with a lack of finances and expertise to properly take care of historic records under its care. What the HSE needs is not fines, but support and expert help in preserving historical records.
The issue goes back to the National Archives Act (1986), when the records of the health boards (and later the HSE) were not included. There is no legal requirement that it retains and transfers those records to the National Archives. It is not surprising these records became homeless once the institutions that generated them closed.
The records include the experiences of generations of patients treated in psychiatric hospitals, once the largest institutions of confinement in the State. In the 1950s, there were upwards of 20,000 patients confined on an annual basis. The rate of admission to psychiatric hospitals was the highest in the world, with 710 beds per 100,000 of the population. Without preserving institutional records, it is not possible to write a comprehensive history of the collective experience of mental healthcare in this country.
The recent Commission of Investigation into Mother and Baby Homes and Related Matters , which published its report in 2021, was built on the records preserved by religious orders and the State, as well as those generated by the Commission itself. The words of the women and children, who had been in the care of the religious orders and the State in these institutions, provided crucial oral testimonies on their experiences. When a decision was made to destroy those oral histories, there was outcry and a recovery process successfully implemented.
Yet once again, the answer to the question of what to do with sensitive historic records is to destroy them.
[ TikTok video revealing access to medical records spurs inquiry into HSE data breaches Opens in new window ]
Unlike Mother and Baby Homes or Magdalene laundries, the State is solely responsible for the management of public psychiatric hospitals. The two hospitals at the heart of the recent fine – St Conal’s (formerly Letterkenny District Lunatic Asylum) and St Loman’s (formerly Mullingar District Lunatic Asylum) – were built in the 19th century during a period of massive State investment in healthcare and welfare. From the outset, they were charged with keeping safe the records of those admitted to their care, as well as the records of the institutions’ administration.
The history of inquiries into institutional care in this country in the past three decades reveals the extent to which confined populations were vulnerable to abuse and exploitation. The McAleese Report into Magdalene laundries found women were forced to work in return for housing and healthcare that was minimal at best. All that Remains, a recent RTÉ documentary with Niall Breslin, revealed that the psychiatric hospitals could also be subject to similar concerns. From a legal point of view, the only way the psychiatric hospitals can be fully understood is if the records are preserved.
[ HSE fined €645,000 after rotting medical records found amid animal droppings and rubble Opens in new window ]
Communities, former hospital staff, historians and archivists have worked to preserve similar records in Killarney, Monaghan and Grangegorman and these records are now housed in local and the National Archives. Those records, and the wealth of creative and historic projects that have emerged from them, offer an insight into what will be lost to the communities in Donegal and Westmeath, and to Ireland, if the recommendation of the Data Commissioner is followed.
Recently, the State has invested large sums recreating the lost archive of the Four Courts via the Virtual Record Treasury of Ireland Project . It has preserved the testimonies of all those who fought for the creation of an independent Irish State through the Military Service Pensions Collection . Those records reveal the cost of that conflict for many individuals, and the cost, in archival loss, for the long history of the country.
Psychiatric records offer something unique. Rather than tales of guerrilla warfare and the creation of the State, each one is a story of some of its more vulnerable citizens, and their individual losses and heartbreaks. Doireann Ní Ghríofa’s recent stunning novel, Said the Dead, explores records of Our Lady’s Psychiatric Hospital in Cork and demonstrates the immeasurable value of those records – both in facilitating creativity and fostering empathy. Those who were locked away deserve the respect they were often denied in life by having their personal histories protected. The destruction of those histories would be a further insult.
This is not simply about preserving more records for privileged historians – it is about whose histories we value and whose stories matter. It is about resourcing organisations whose histories are crucial in the lives of the ordinary citizens of the state.
What does it say about us that we invest millions in the history of the political nation while shredding patient files of those who lived and died behind the high walls of psychiatric institutions?
Dr Georgina Laragy is assistant professor in Public History and Cultural Heritage and Trinity College Dublin and Dr Aoife Bhreatnach is a writer and independent researcher

title: Social media’s age of the follower is replaced by tyranny of the recommender machine
description: It’s easy to rage against the machine. It’s harder to propose a viable alternative
content:
T here has always been something a little creepy about the follower. From the earliest days of the social media era the word carried a faint whiff of the compound and the commune, of Charles Manson or Jim Jones. To follow, in ordinary English, is to trail behind someone, to defer, to obey. But an entire communications economy got built on the cheerful assumption that amassing followers was a wholesome ambition, a sign that you had something worth saying.
As the platforms grew in reach and scale, the follower count became shorthand for status and proof of influence. To this day you will see it deployed as evidence of raw power. A politician commands millions of followers, a pop star tens of millions, the figures presented as evidence of who matters most.
Despite all this, analysts have been predicting the end of the follower for years. The trends they describe are hardly new. Social media platforms that began as chronological timelines, orderly streams of posts from accounts you had subscribed to, have been steadily downgraded or replaced. Facebook and Instagram started weighting feeds by predicted engagement rather than recency more than a decade ago, with Instagram abandoning the purely chronological feed as far back as 2016. TikTok arrived and dispensed with the premise almost entirely, building its whole experience around a For You page that served up strangers rather than friends.
YouTube leaned hard into recommendation. One by one, the networks quietly demoted the people you had followed in favour of whatever their ranking systems judged would keep you scrolling.
It has taken a surprisingly long time for the implications to be fully grasped. It was Patreon co-founder Jack Conte who coined the phrase “the death of the follower” in a widely shared keynote at the South by Southwest festival in 2024. Conte argued that a follow no longer guaranteed you would reach the person who made it, and that creators should cultivate genuine supporters rather than chase vanity metrics.
Others took up the theme. At the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, researchers set out how these ranking systems actually work, while admitting that the wider research community is unable to observe or explain the feedback loops of human behaviour they set in motion.
The machines that now shape public attention gave rise to a cascade of social and psychological effects that are only imperfectly understood.
It is fair to say that these developments have not been universally welcomed, including among those who built their business models on the back of the old rules. The marketing industry spent 15 years persuading clients that followers were the goal. A recent trend report from US agency MDRN Logic, also titled The Death of the Follower (these things catch on quickly), counsels brands to stop hoarding followers and instead earn attention afresh with every post, cultivating a recognisable voice rather than mere volume and behaving more like a personality with a point of view. Some of may feel the last thing the world needs is more brands with a point of view, but that’s a subject for another day.
More broadly, the uneasy sense that we have lost control of our own feeds is curdling into a more existential sense of dread. That was visible in the debate following last month’s crash on the M9, in which five teenage boys died when their car was driven the wrong way down the motorway Kildare , seriously injuring the four occupants of a car travelling in the correct direction. A grim consensus quickly formed, running from gardaí to child psychologists, that recommendation engines designed to amplify whatever provokes the strongest reaction helped feed a culture of recklessness performed for an audience. The question of who is being served this material, and why, is belatedly being asked.
Some are trying to fight back. The steady drift of X/Twitter to the right since Elon Musk’s acquisition drove waves of refugees to the alternatives. Mastodon offers no algorithm at all, only the accounts you choose in the order they posted. Bluesky lets users select or build their own feeds, a deliberate rebuke to the opaque engagement machines of the incumbents. The pitch, in each case, is a return of agency to the person doing the scrolling. But it is far from clear that either platform is achieving critical mass, and Bluesky in particular has been criticised for creating a monoculture where ideological conformity is rigidly enforced.
[ M9 crash exposes limits of rules on social media giants when it comes to online harms Opens in new window ]
It’s easy to rage against the machine. It’s harder to propose a viable alternative. But there are advocates and activists who believe that agency can and should be returned to the individual human user. The most recent case for a more optimistic vision comes from Mark Little, the former RTÉ correspondent and founder of Storyful, whose new book, The Last Good Day on the Internet, published next week, argues that we are entering an “age of intention” in which ordinary people reclaim agency.
Little acknowledges that recommendation systems have been silently mining our subconscious desires for more than a decade, but retains a belief in the more open and egalitarian principles that animated much of the early years of the internet can be revived. I would love to share his hope but I fear it is misplaced. These decentralised havens and digital commons remain minnows beside the tech giants, and the oligarchs who run them have not the slightest intention of surrendering their power without a fight.

title: New investment scheme cannot be called regressive
description: Argument that money put into scheme is money taken away from poorer households is invalid
content:
Sir, – Emma Howard’s criticism of the planned Government savings scheme does not stand up. (“One in three can’t afford to benefit from Government’s regressive new investment scheme”, September 5th ).
The basic problem is the assumption that money put into a savings or investment scheme is money taken away from poorer households. That might be true if there were a fixed pot of money, with every €1 given to one group meaning €1 less for another. But that isn’t how public finances work. Tax treatment of investment returns, cost-of-living supports and capital markets policy are not necessarily competing for the same money.
That assumption also makes the “regressive” conclusion rather convenient. The article shows that people on lower incomes are less likely to benefit from the scheme. But that is not the same as showing that they are harmed by it.
The article even acknowledges that “it is difficult to fully evaluate how effective the proposed scheme will be”, before nevertheless declaring it definitively regressive and harmful. If its effects cannot yet be properly assessed, surely the same caution should apply to such a strong conclusion.
There may be good arguments against the scheme. But calling it “regressive” requires more than showing that some people are unlikely to benefit from it. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I read with interest Emma Howard’s article on the proposed Personal Investment Account. While the piece raises valid questions about scheme design, it overlooks some important realities.
It is often missed by commentators that any investment made through the scheme comes from income that has already been taxed, namely a household’s disposable income.
The proposal does not “take” money from anyone. It simply encourages citizens to invest their after-tax earnings. As investments grow, households benefit from compounding, while the resulting gains also generate tax revenues for the State.
Properly designed, this is a policy that can benefit both citizens and the exchequer. Over the long term, a growing pool of invested capital has the potential to generate far greater economic activity, tax revenues and household wealth than savings left in deposit accounts, where inflation steadily erodes purchasing power.
The real challenge facing Ireland is not that too many people invest, but that too few do. – Yours, etc,

title: Big pharma exports from Ireland an impetus to euro zone growth
description: Euro zone economy expands more than initially thought after a sharp upward revision in Ireland
content:
Not for the first time, the Irish tail is wagging the European Union dog. Euro zone growth for the second quarter has been revised up to 0.6 per cent (from 0.4 per cent), marking it the strongest quarterly acceleration in more than a year. Good news for Europe, which has been struggling with stagnant growth and high inflation for several years.
It also comes after downward revisions to gross domestic product (GDP) in France, Austria and Portugal. The upgrade was triggered by the Central Statistics Office (CSO) here, which last week revised the Republic’s headline GDP growth in the second quarter to 10.2 per cent, up from a previous estimate of 3.9 per cent, lifting growth for the bloc as a whole.
The CSO said the expansion was driven by a 22 per cent spike in output from the multinational-dominated “industry” sector here, which includes big pharma groups such as Eli Lilly and Pfizer.
Eli Lilly shipped $42.3 billion (€36.4 billion) of ingredients for its weight-loss drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound from the Republic to the United States in the first four months of last year.
This was initially put down to the company strategically front-loading product into the US to avoid tariffs, but it also related to the explosive demand for these drugs globally, which may have continued into 2026. The company has been launching its drugs in various countries.
Irish GDP is susceptible to large quarterly revisions because of multinationals using this State as a base for exports. Economists consider it an unreliable metric.
Modified domestic demand, seen as a better measure of underlying activity here, shrank by 0.8 per cent in the second quarter.
The positive euro zone growth number is the last data point before the European Central Bank’s interest rate decision later this week. The bank is expected to announce another quarter-point hike in response to the latest pickup in energy prices.
Despite inflation at a three-year high due to the Iran war and rising borrowing costs, and with the Republic’s GDP bulge, the outlook is marginally rosier for Europe as governments spend big on defence and infrastructure, a trend that is expected to boost growth.

title: Frank McDonald was Dublin’s greatest champion
description: Former Irish Times environment editor was in many ways the living embodiment of the capital
content:
Sir, – We have lost Dublin’s single greatest champion in the passing of Frank McDonald. (“Frank McDonald, former environment editor of The Irish Times , dies aged 76″, September 7th .)
It’s hard to come to terms with a Dublin without Frank. He was, in so many ways, the living embodiment of our capital – brimming with enthusiasm for its history and identity, reflecting its infectious and affable charm, with an added dose of sophistication. Frank was the trailblazing inspiration for countless younger people to get involved Dublin’s conservation and development, this writer included. He was the touchstone for almost everyone in the architecture, planning and conservation worlds, where a giant void has now opened up.
To his immense credit, planning – that most neglected of professions – was always at the heart of Frank’s focus. He recognised from an early point the immense power of the process and its potential to be harnessed as a tool against the public interest.
Right up to his last days, Frank was justly incensed at the recent dismantling of Ireland’s planning process, and the kowtowing to institutional property lobbying in reducing hard-won housing standards and coherent urban design principles. Frank was far from a Luddite: he was a well-travelled, progressive and pragmatic urban dweller – always seeking international reference points to advance a better future for Dublin.
In his passing, policymakers must take stock of Frank’s immense achievements, of which we have all been beneficiaries, and focus on adequately resourcing the State’s planning sector to manage a rapidly changing Ireland. It is also an imperative that Frank’s outstanding legacy to Dublin is marked by the city in a fitting memorial.
Frank McDonald was one of the most principled people in Irish public life. It is thanks to him that so much of historic Dublin, our vital patrimony, still stands for our appreciation today. Defending the public estate and civic values went to the core of his being. – Yours, etc,
In late August 1987 Frank McDonald and I sat in the sun on the steps outside my home, plotting what Irish Times readers could do to wake everyone up to growing marine litter and pollution issues. Frank’s editor was not raring to give it a go as a contribution to European Year of the Environment, but we persuaded him and the Irish Times printed a page of questions, inviting readers to bring these to their shore and record what they saw. Then they were to post the paper back to help produce an island wide shore audit. It was a risk taken by Frank as young reporter and The Irish Times which gave birth to Coastwatch.
In a few days’ time, it will be our 40th shore survey and I hope that volunteers going out will think of him our cofounder.
As the survey became an annual event and grew across Europe, Frank always took an interest as first results were emerging and we schemed how to turn information into action or how to expose and halt unsustainable practice. I can still see his googly eyes light up as we looked over surveyor comments of illegal dumps being eaten by the sea. “Ah, that’s brutal,” he would say. – Yours etc,
Sir, – Frank McDonald made an enormous contributions to public understanding of good planning and architecture, he understood the power of public participation, he was never afraid to exercise his constitutional right to judicial review, challenging the legal validity rather than the practical merits of a decision made by a public authority, corporate entity or board in planning and environmental matters and he understood the costs and risks involved.
His contribution made a difference, many buildings particularly in Dublin are still standing because he spoke up and made the case for their protection. – Yours etc,
I knew Frank McDonald in our student days in UCD, 1967-1970. Frank was a student activist and a leader in the students’ representative council. He gave voice to the need for political change and social justice, especially around poverty and the distribution of wealth.
Frank started early and for that we should all be grateful.

title: The Renovation by Kenan Orhan: Important and funny but it doesn’t quite land
description: The female protagonist, Dilara, feels like a bodiless mouthpiece being used to tell the story of Erdogan’s Turkey
content:
In The Renovation we meet Dilara, who, with her Alzheimer’s-suffering father and neurotic husband, lives in a small flat in Italy after fleeing Erdogan ’s increasingly constrictive regime in Turkey.
The novel begins when what was supposed to be a new bathroom is instead transformed into a cell in a women’s prison in Turkey. And so we’re given, with this tidy little legerdemain, the split-self experience of the exile. Dilara exists in two prisons, that of her life as an exile, and the actual prison she knows she would have ended up in had she never left.
This is skilfully aligned with the situation of Alzheimer’s, and of grief. It is so skilful, in fact, that the novel has that dizzying effect of seeming to be laden with too much understated meaning to be fully comprehensible.
Reading, I was put in mind of the political acuity and implied depths, all conveyed with featherlight dexterity, so characteristic of the contemporary American short story (only afterwards did I discover that The Renovation was expanded out of just that).
There’s no denying that this is a genuinely noble novel, worth reading for the political education it provides alone. It’s also extremely well-written, filled with crisp, clean sentences brimming with effective descriptions and insights that appear so insightful they’re momentarily bamboozling. It’s also funny, in a satisfyingly absurdist way.
So why this feeling of it not quite landing? The word “grotesque” is repeatedly so regularly I thought it was a fault of the translator. But no, this isn’t a translation (as I also discovered afterwards), but a novel written in English by a male Turkish emigrant based in Kansas. And, for me, that’s how it read; like a novel written about a Turkish woman’s experience of exile from Turkey, as imagined by a Turkish-American man who cares deeply about her plight.
I believe, unequivocally, that anyone can write anything in fiction – any place, gender or experience. But it must land. Trying to comprehend Dilara as a female character, I found a bodiless mouthpiece, one being used to tell the (again, important) story of Erdogan’s Turkey. Still, as a deftly composed, faintly magical-realist political agenda novel (with laughs), this is certainly worth reading.
Lucy Sweeney Byrne is the author of two short story collections, Paris Syndrome (2019) and Let’s Dance (2024), both published by Banshee Press. Her debut novel is forthcoming in September 2027

title: Leaving Cert maths gender gap discussion needs wider subject context
description: What is good for the goose should surely also be good for the gander
content:
Sir, – Dr Aoibhinn Ní Shúilleabháin raises a legitimate concern about the gender gap in H1 achievement in higher-level mathematics. She also points to the substantial gender imbalance in participation in applied mathematics. (“ Why I left the Leaving Cert maths reform group ”, Opinion, September 5th).
Both are worthy of examination. However, discussion of gender disparity in Leaving Certificate subjects should also consider the wider picture.
