“I bought a property down in Wicklow. Some people thought it was a listed building, so it was sitting on the market for ages. But we dug around, and it’s not. It’s a schoolhouse.
“I just had this dream of me going down and getting the tools and taking the place apart. And just doing something which I completely know nothing about. I can go back into student mode. My brother is very handy as well. So, I think, a bit of a family project.
“And, at the same time, start a family, spend time with my wife and maybe sit back a little bit. I’ve been hard at it now for 18 years.”
The User’s Guide to Being Human is released via BMG. The Script play 3Arena, in Dublin, on Friday, October 30th, and Saturday, October 31st; and O2 Arena, Belfast, on Monday, November 2nd

title: The Liberties musical Pretty Vacant: ‘It’s almost impossible to satirise what’s going on’
description: Dublin Fringe Festival 2026: Dereliction and greed are viewed through a surreal lens in this new show. But can anything top the ‘bizarre stuff’ that’s really happening?
content:
I t’s a new musical satire about greed, dereliction and “the battle for Dublin ’s soul” told through surreal humour and Europop bangers: Pretty Vacant, which will be performed later this month as part of Dublin Fringe Festival , intends to be as fun a 75 minutes as a piece of theatre about the Irish housing crisis possibly can be.
Written by Tom Swift and directed by Jo Mangan, aka the husband-and-wife team behind the production company Performance Corporation , the show, their first “proper” musical, is their preferred way to tackle the subject of hollowed-out cities and communities.
“It’s a big, heavy issue. So how do you approach a big, heavy issue? With the pen of a playwright who is embedded in the satirical world. There’s no point approaching it nose on, because no one wants didacticism. I’m certainly not interested in being preached at by the theatre I go to,” Mangan says.
Staged at Tailors’ Hall in the Liberties, Pretty Vacant centres on Carmilla, a failed former Eurovision entrant played by Ruth McGill, who is trying to sell her vision for the area on behalf of shark-like property developers. At a public consultation meeting, however, she is appalled to discover that the local community won’t simply go along with her plan to “set the Liberties free”.
“Carmilla’s Eurovision background just gives us licence for her to sing, and for others to break into song. Musicals are a funny thing, anyway, aren’t they?” Swift says.
“They’re totally wild. They make no sense,” Mangan says. “‘And now I’m going to sing a song!’”
Although the duo, working with the composer Ellen Cranitch, previously gave the operatic treatment to James Joyce’s The Dead, this is the first “straight-up musical” they have done.
Mangan sings a snippet of Carmilla’s Eurovision flop. “Re-re-re-re-Regeneration. Where does Regeneration go after that?”
“I don’t think Laura needs to know,” Swift says.
“She doesn’t need to hear our bad singing,” she agrees.
The Eurovision framing means Swift and Pretty Vacant’s composer and sound designer, Daragh Dukes, “can go anywhere musically”, so alongside dance numbers such as Regeneration and Living Apart (In an Apart Hotel), there’s a punk one called Vicious Circle, while Emmet Kirwan, playing a local socialist TD who’s really from Harold’s Cross, does a rap.
“We have a song called F**k You and the Horse You Rode in On. I don’t know if The Irish Times is allowed to publish that,” Swift says.
The production – which also features Alan Howley, Aisling O’Mara, Matthew Malone and Camille Lucy Ross – includes video work by Richie Power, the creator of the online project Chats in the Flats , as well as interviews with local people by Swift and Dukes.
“We go crazy and sing and dance, and there’s a whole big Eurotrash element to the piece, but then we hear the real voices of the neighbourhood, and it brings us to a real place,” Mangan says. “We want our audiences to have fun, but then ground them in the reality of the situation a little bit as well.”
Performance Corporation, now in its 24th year, is known for site-specific theatre. “The place always speaks to the work. Sometimes for us it starts the work, so we’re, like, ‘Okay, this is an amazing place, let’s do a piece of work in it,’” Mangan says.
Pretty Vacant wasn’t always going to be set and staged in the Liberties, however.
“The initial idea was all around the dereliction and vacant buildings that we see all over Dublin and all over so many towns around Ireland,” Swift says. “The question was: why? We’re in a housing crisis. Why aren’t these buildings being used? Why are they being knocked down for facilities for tourists, rather than facilities or housing for local communities?”
[ The fight to save Dublin’s Liberties: ‘It’s sadly dying, fading away’ Opens in new window ]
Having booked a room in the Digital Hub in the Liberties for a couple of days to develop the project, they started to look around the area. “We realised it’s a microcosm of all of those issues,” he says. So they “dug deeper”, and a walking tour with Anthony Freeman O’Brien, a local artist and activist who performs in Pretty Vacant, convinced them this was the right place. The search for venues began.
“We looked at a lot of large spaces that were in the churchy vein. We looked St Werburgh’s Church, we looked at St Catherine’s Church, but when we came across Tailors’ Hall we felt this was for us. It’s smaller, it’s more intimate,” Mangan says.
The piece is staged in traverse, with the audience sitting either side of the performance area and the walls used for decor and video projection.
Tailors’ Hall, situated on Back Lane, was built in 1706. It’s rich with history. Over the centuries it has been used by schools, charities and Freemasons, and in 1792 it was the meeting place of the Catholic Committee during its campaign against the penal laws, becoming known as the Back Lane Parliament. “It all seemed to tie in thematically to what we’re trying to talk about,” Swift says.
It is now run by An Taisce, the conservation charity, which will participate in a postshow discussion after a free (but ticketed) performance of Pretty Vacant on Culture Night, on September 18th. The event is also part of Home Ground, a Dublin Fringe Festival initiative aimed at the communities represented in fringe shows.
“People sometimes say people don’t come to things if they’re free. On the contrary, I think price point is a barrier for a lot of people in terms of engagement with the arts, so I’m always very keen on ensuring that we create access points to our work,” Mangan says.
Performance Corporation has won numerous awards. It first show, an adaptation of Voltaire’s Candide, won best production at the fringe in 2002.
“We’re really happy to be coming back to the fringe and connecting with, let’s be frank, another generation. We wanted to make this show for the fringe because we feel that the topics that we’re hitting are important for a younger audience,” she says. “It’s just remarkable the great swathe of dereliction and housing issues that everyone is dealing with.”
It’s a busy time for Performance Corporation. We chat, barefoot, in one of the studios in Dance House, off Talbot Street in Dublin, in late July during a lunchtime break from rehearsals for their August production, Tír an Traonaigh , an Irish-language play that brought its audience on a bus through the Mullet Peninsula, in Co Mayo.
[ Tír an Traonaigh review: As the sun breaks through the clouds, there are tears in the audience Opens in new window ]
“A rest” is lined up once Pretty Vacant concludes, though they’re also working on a large-scale version of Gulliver’s Travels. “Jonathan Swift is a distant relative of Tom’s, so we’re hustling something into existence on that,” Mangan says.
“I have an aunt who has done the research. We are talking a distant cousin many times removed,” Swift says. Still, it’s possible a penchant and aptitude for satire survived the generations. “I’d like to think that somehow there’s some small bit of a gene in there.”
These aren’t easy times for satirists. “After we would do a reading of a section Tom had written, Anthony would go, ‘That happened.’ Like, bizarre stuff. Tom would come up with something to be satirical, but it’s almost impossible to satirise what’s going on,” Mangan says.
“We’re definitely living in a world where satire is struggling to keep up with reality. It’s hard. Trump just makes everything redundant and ridiculous,” Swift says.
We talk about how communities can fight back against the forces of gentrification. “It’s very difficult. It feels like they’re up against a juggernaut, which is money writ large,” he says. “Corporate interests seem to be just ruling our world now.
“I don’t have the solutions, unfortunately. I suppose our role is to just point out the failures, and the dark humour in it all, the ridiculousness of it all. The solutions, hopefully, might come from people who go and see it.”
For Mangan there is something powerful in the sense of community identity in the Liberties. “There’s a lot of meitheal involved. There’s a lot of people working together to make things happen. It’s like a village in the middle of the city.
“To me it’s like places where my father is from, in Co Mayo, or my mother, in Co Galway, where everyone knows each other and everyone helps each other out.
“One can only hope that that sort of clinging on to neighbourliness, and minding each other and looking out for each other, will help the community survive.”
But will the old musical-theatre rule about leaving the audience in a better mood than when they arrived apply here?
“I don’t know how the audience will feel when they leave,” Swift says, laughing. “Hopefully they’ll be humming a lot of the tunes.”
Pretty Vacant is at Tailors’ Hall, as part of Dublin Fringe Festival , from Tuesday, September 15th, until Sunday, September 20th. The festival begins on Saturday, September 5th
The festival’s 2026 edition features 70 shows. Here are just half a dozen that have caught our eye.
Aimed at audiences of all ages, this Theatre Lovett production tells the story of how Franz Kafka rediscovered a fragile faith in the human spirit after consoling a girl who loses her doll. What follows is “an extraordinary act of imagination” told through letters detailing the doll’s odyssey.
Samuel Yakura’s new contemporary music-theatre, Soak, is billed as part concert, part confession, part reckoning. The show explores themes of masculinity, grief and inherited silence, inviting audiences on a journey of vulnerability, connection and healing.
Set in a children’s playground in Dublin, Thérèse follows a woman in the throes of grief for her brother, which opens up a portal to old wounds and past injustices. It’s a “theatrical homage to those who have been lost” that seeks accountability from those in power.
Inspired by Giovanni Boccaccio’s The Decameron, Dead in Here explores how it feels to be a young person who is hyperaware of the world’s problems but feels powerless to solve them. It’s a play about “love and death that interrogates our collective desire to escape reality”.
Bob is lost in an endless shop in this “journey through the aisles of existence”. It’s a surreal dance-theatre piece, choreographed by Diarmuid Armstrong Mayock, in which the inhabitants of the supermarket “move through a strange existence they do not understand”.
This new Irish-language musical (or ceoldráma) by Shauna Carrick was first performed at Galway International Arts Festival in July. It’s a summer Gaeltacht-set story of first love, freedom and the modh coinníollach. English-language access is available through the Sibwrd app.

title: Donald Clarke: Do Venetians see depictions of their city in film as we Irish see Micksploitaiton movies?
description: If fiction is any guide, Venice remains unchanged by the cinematic locusts who descend for its annual film festival
content:
O ne can hardly imagine a more 21st-century problem than being caught up in a broadband outage minutes before an online-booking session for Venice International Film Festival .
Such was the crisis last weekend. Like every other big film festival, Venice now requires visitors to have virtual tickets on their smartphone before entering the auditorium. You didn’t get that in Henry James or Thomas Mann . Or in films by Nicolas Roeg or David Lean.
Nowhere else on Earth has been so preserved in artistic aspic. Modernity is not supposed to happen here. Even the most contemporary films and TV series move about a city recognisable as the one that welcomed a sloshed Lord Byron.
But what about the tourists? Well, Byron was a tourist. The annoying visitors were featuring in stories about Venice when a doge still ruled the republic. “Though there are some disagreeable things in Venice there is nothing so disagreeable as the visitors,” James wrote in 1882.
In the same author’s dreamlike The Wings of a Dove a character seeks to escape the “amiable American families”. The addled, vain Gustav von Aschenbach, doomed protagonist of Mann’s Death in Venice, sees himself as being above the vulgar hordes sharing his Lido hotel.
Yet none of this dampens the romantic affection writers, poets and film-makers bring to their depictions of Venice. Federico Fellini set the seedy side of Rome alongside the glamorous one in La Dolce Vita. Many French film-makers have examined the social inequalities in Paris.
But when fictional crime comes to Venice, as in Patricia Highsmith’s The Talented Mr Ripley, it does so amid the accoutrements of the Renaissance. What psychopath could be unhappy living out his guiltless days amid such antique beauty?
Just think of the most famous films set there. Even those soaked in horror acknowledge the romance and wave away contemporaneousness.
The untouchable Don’t Look Now is a case in point. Adapted from a story by Daphne du Maurier, Nicolas Roeg’s film, from 1973, follows an architectural restorer and his wife as, visiting the city in cooler months, they encounter possible communications from their late daughter. Donald Sutherland is sceptical as the husband. Julie Christie, as the wife, is prepared to believe. It all ends in a confused, ultimately murderous pursuit through the city’s labyrinthine alleyways.
[ From the archive: Nicolas Roeg: the director who took the familiar and made it strange Opens in new window ]
Yet two or three generations of film enthusiasts have visited Venice in pursuit of the locations from Don’t Look Now. My very first time on the main island was taken up with a confused, apparently hopeless wander through narrow thoroughfares that constantly frustrated orientation. The hotel seemed inaccessible to anything other than fish.
After 15 minutes or so of this my friend and I inevitably began making jokes about imminent attack by (spoiler alert) tiny maniacs in red raincoats. Nothing seemed to have changed in the 50 years since Roeg shot Don’t Look Now. Little would have changed in the 50 years before that.
The most beautiful depiction of Venice in a feature drama is surely found in David Lean’s Summertime, from 1955. We are again among the tourists as Katharine Hepburn takes the train across the bridge connecting Venice to Mestre for (as it transpires) romance with the suave Rossano Brazzi.
Two years before Lean leaned into epic with The Bridge on the River Kwai, he conjured up a magically picturesque Venice in painterly Technicolor. The struggling postwar world is elsewhere. All is elsewhere.
[ From the archive: Five indisputably great David Lean pictures Opens in new window ]
For the attendee at Venice film festival, however, the key film is surely Luchino Visconti’s 1971 adaptation of Death in Venice. Not because I spend my days, as does Dirk Bogarde’s von Aschenbach, weeping in a deckchair while the make-up runs down my cheeks, but because, like the festival, much of the film takes place on the long, thin Venice Lido. There are motorcars. There are smooth, modern roads. There are many buildings constructed after the unification of Italy.
The creative antiquation of Venice that must so annoy the locals – do they see these films as we see sentimental Micksploitation movies? – no longer has any purchase here. No. Don’t Look Now and Summertime do not come to mind on the morning commute. This does summon up Anthony Minghella’s film of The Talented Mr Ripley.
[ Patricia Highsmith: a talented writer who always let rip Opens in new window ]
There is something else. We are at an international film festival. At Cannes and Venice, during the event, one feels cordoned off in a privileged space where little local colour intrudes. Everyone is huddled over their phone trying to grab that ticket they missed a week earlier. English is spoken by American, Brazilian, Japanese and German folk.
The cinematic locusts descend for a week or two, do their infernal business and then swarm elsewhere. If the films and novels are any guide, the city remains unchanged by our brief hermetic appearance.

title: Moving from Dublin to Kerry: ‘We really noticed the lack of any noise, apart from the animals’
description: Moving from Blanchardstown to the Beara Peninsula, where the landscape changes depending on the weather, has been a smooth transition for one family
content:
I f you are within walking distance of Blanchardstown Shopping Centre, then a cottage on the Beara Peninsula must seem like another world away. After all, it is more than 350km from the Dublin suburb and the nearest town, Kenmare, is a 20-minute drive away.
But it was precisely this remoteness that drew Dubliners Philip and Emma Joyce ( @jacobs.cottage) to the house.
“I’d been living in Blanchardstown all my life,” he says. In fact, they were so settled there that they had bought his childhood home in 2016 after his parents died.
“We had planned on staying around and I had thought of having a holiday home in the countryside, but then Covid came.”
When remote work became the norm during the pandemic, they began talking about leaving Dublin.
“Kerry has always been my favourite spot, and it just happened to be the place where this house came up.”
While he doesn’t have many family ties in Dublin, Emma does, so that was a major consideration when they began thinking about moving across the country. He is a software product designer, so his main concern was ensuring he had reliable internet so that he could do his job. Their son Noah was finishing primary school, and Emma had been considering a career break from the civil service, so the timing felt right. They moved into the four-bedroom cottage on an acre of ground in May 2025, naming it Jacob’s Cottage. This was in memory of their son who died when he was a baby, and it ensured he would be a central part of this new stage in their lives.
The house in Lauragh, on the road to the Healy Pass, was originally built in the 1800s. It was rebuilt on the same footprint by local builder Seán Healy of Lauragh Construction, so it looks identical to the original cottage from the front. He also added a flat-roof extension at the back for an open-plan kitchen and living area.
“The whole house was completely bare, so from a design point of view it was great,” Philip says. “We had to figure out what to do with each room and that’s still ongoing.”
They lived in the house for six months before their kitchen arrived. “Living off an air fryer and a little Ikea hob was our main source of cooking, but we survived and I am glad that we did that. When we renovated our Dublin home, one of the things I learned was that you should take your time living in the space, and figuring out how you naturally move towards certain areas.”
When planning their Kube kitchen, they were conscious that it should not take the focus away from the three-metre-long window that looks on to the Caha Mountains. There are no cabinets at eye level, and the rich green cabinets accentuate the various shades of green on display outside the window. The worktops from Stone Surfaces are silestone, an engineered quartz surface that is scratch and stain resistant and nonporous. The suspended Le Feu bioethanol fireplace in the living area is a work of art in itself, and gives the impression of floating flames. He sourced it in CA Design in Dublin, along with the Scandinavian-style kitchen stools.
Philip is a keen photographer, and regularly posts images of the house and surrounding landscape on his Instagram page @jacobs.cottage . They highlight his passion for good design. “My mantra is less but better – less things in the house, but getting the best you can afford, choosing things that will stand the test of time and avoiding trends.” He has been enjoying living in an area that is a magnet for creative people. “The great thing about Kenmare is the amount of artists and furniture makers that are so close to us,” he says. “We’ve already got a few prints around the home from local artists.”
They are now working with a local woodworker to design shelves, and a ceiling for a library and office that will replace one of the bedrooms. The final small bedroom will become a snug that can double as a bedroom when visitors come to stay.
He loves the contrast between the front part of the house, with the narrow hallway and dark bedrooms, and the large open-plan area at the back looking out on the landscape. “Not every room has to be completely filled with light, which is something I’ve learned over time.”
The landscape changes throughout the day depending on the weather, and they certainly experience a lot of weather on the Beara Peninsula. But he says they didn’t struggle during their first winter in Kerry. “It’s definitely windier than Dublin, but the rain is the same. No matter if you’re in Dublin or Kerry the winters are cold and long and wet.”
The house has a Ber of A2 and he says he has never felt cold, even on the stormiest of days. “The walls are so thick, and we have the heat pump and underfloor heating, so the temperature is very consistent.”
The next task will be the garden, “but that’s more of a future aspiration. We didn’t even have a back garden before, and now we have loads of space and loads of plans around how the garden should be laid out”.
Now that they’ve spent more than a year in Kerry, do they ever miss Dublin? Emma misses the convenience of walking to a cafe or the shops nearby, but Philip says “I could stay home for a week and not miss going out. Even driving from the house into town is different, no traffic lights, no roundabouts – it’s far more enjoyable than driving around Dublin. But from a practical point of view, you do need to plan around when you need to go shopping and stuff like that.”
A big setback came when he was laid off in November, but he has since got a new job. “That was the biggest challenge because obviously you have fewer options when you’re not in Dublin, because you are only able to do remote work or one day in the city.”
Such a dramatic change of lifestyle would not suit everyone, but they have no regrets. “We are more interested in a slower lifestyle and we are both very into nature and the landscape and it suits us. I wouldn’t change a thing.”
They have embraced the near total silence at night, after a lifetime of listening to the distant hum of traffic. “We really noticed the lack of any noise, apart from the animals. We are surrounded by sheep, cows and deer,” he says.
They were also struck by the night sky. “I was completely blown away by the lack of light pollution. It’s one of the clearest night skies I’ve ever seen. When you get a clear night, you are surrounded by stars. It is magical.”

title: Noisy headline data underlines uselessness of traditional measures for Irish economy
description: AI boom has put a gloss on Irish economic growth this year
content:
At the headline level, Irish economic data is so noisy and seemingly contradictory that it’s open to extremes of interpretation. A case in point: the second-quarter national accounts from the Central Statistics Office.
Looking at it through the lens of gross domestic product (GDP), the economy’s performance appears miraculous. After a precipitous 12 per cent quarterly fall in the first three months of the year, GDP expanded by more than 10 per cent amid a surge in exports.
As we know from bitter experience, however, GDP is an unreliable indicator. The decline in the early part of 2026 was due to the unwinding of a surge in pharmaceutical exports in 2025 as multinationals sought to get ahead of US tariffs.
Modified domestic demand (MDD), which removes large intellectual property-related and aircraft leasing transactions from the equation, is economists’ (and the Government’s) preferred metric. Through that lens, the economy has expanded by 3.1 per cent so far this year, despite a slowdown in the second quarter. That is roughly in line with the most recent full-year forecasts from the Central Bank and the ESRI, which both improved their MDD outlook slightly in June.
Those upgrades were informed by a boom in investment in information and communication technology equipment in late 2025 and into early 2026.
“This investment has been linked to the import of equipment for data centres, particularly those used to facilitate [AI],” the ESRI said at the time. It includes things like microchips, which have to be replaced on a very short timeline, meaning “there will not only be [capital formation] where new ones go ahead”, said ESRI economist Conor O’Toole in June, “but there’ll be high depreciation investment.”
There is some evidence that this trend stalled a bit in the second quarter. Overall, the decline in MDD was driven by a fall in investment, with new capital formation contracting by 5.2 per cent quarter on quarter, according to the CSO data.
It’s too early to say whether this is merely a dip or part of a larger trend. What is clear, however, is that even when the biggest distortions are stripped away, multinationals continue to fog the lenses through which we view the Irish economy.

title: Four new films to see this week: The Death of Robin Hood, The Incomer, Super Nature, Leviticus
description: Hugh Jackman, Jodie Comer, Domhnall Gleeson and Joe Bird feature in a quartet of movies released in the week of September 4th, 2026
content:
Directed by Michael Sarnoski. Starring Hugh Jackman, Jodie Comer, Faith Delaney, Murray Bartlett, Noah Jupe, Bill Skarsgard. 16 cert, gen release, 122 min
Revisionist study of Robin Hood’s final days featuring Jackman as the most heartlessly violent version we have seen for quite some time. There is a sense of the world coming to a desperate end. Which it nearly does. After the fighting is over, an injured Robin awakes under the care of nuns in the starkly attractive Priory of St Clement. His most conspicuous carer is Jodie Comer as the endlessly patient Sr Bridget. That shift has undone many viewers on US release. But the interactions between Jackman and Comer are nicely judged in their skirting of awkward truths. DC Full review
Directed by Louis Paxton. Starring Domhnall Gleeson, Gayle Rankin, Grant O’Rourke, Emun Elliott, Michelle Gomez, John Hannah. 12A cert, gen release, 102 min
Gleeson is back playing one of his trademark shy naifs – a council worker sent to eject two weird siblings (Rankin and O’Rourke) from a remote Scottish island – in a film that revels in Scottish weird. The three core actors bump against each other with admirable comic invention. The siblings are oddballs alone and (to this point) unmolested in their own oddball empire. Daniel is an oddball in a society that would prefer him to conform. The director can’t quite find a way out of the puzzles he has set for himself, but an arresting debut nonetheless. DC Full review
Directed by Ed Sayers. Featuring Ed Sayers. No cert, select release, 83 min
Here is a nature documentary made against the grain of a genre now characterised by drone shots and crisp digital precision. Instead of pursuing the immaculate, high-definition imagery familiar from National Geographic, Sayers curates his film entirely from vintage Super 8 footage, creating an episodic, arresting portrait of the natural world. Sayers’s careful editing and Alexandra Hamilton-Ayres’s score give the disparate material coherence. The effect is curative, but there is urgency among contributors protecting endangered species such as northern white rhinos in Kenya and turtles in St Vincent and the Grenadines. TB Full review
Directed by Adrian Chiarella. Starring Joe Bird, Stacy Clausen, Jeremy Blewitt, Mia Wasikowska. 16 cert, gen release, 88 min
This zeitgeisty horror, frequently cited with the similarly buzzy Obsession and Backrooms, follows two Australian teenagers whose emerging sexuality clashes with the strictures of their backwater Christian community. Producer and star Mia Wasikowska, revisiting the dark matriarchal energies of Club Zero, makes for a terrific fundamentalist mom. Bird gives his character a compellingly awkward, inward quality as he moves from sexual awakening toward attachment. Writer-director Chiarella ingeniously conjures horror off-screen, relying on atmosphere, shadows and the recurring device of an apparently familiar person behaving with unexplained menace. Puppy love has seldom seemed so terrifying. TB Full review

title: A stunning novel by T Geronimo Johnson is among this month’s best new crime fiction
description: The Occidental Book of the Dead reads like what you might get if Ishmael Reed and Walter Mosley had scripted Chinatown
content:
His first since 2015’s lauded Welcome to Braggsville, T Geronimo Johnson’s new novel arrives billed as “The Wire meets Colson Whitehead”. Over nearly 700 dazzling, dizzying pages, The Occidental Book of the Dead (Abacus, £25) shows why it’s attracted such heady comparisons.
The novel is largely narrated by George Washington Jonson, a veteran black cop in Atlanta who’s on patrol when his white rookie trainee shoots Anthony, a white teen. For Jonson and the reader both, that pivotal scene is viscerally chaotic and confusing. The consequences spin farther out of control with every passing day, leaving Jonson in grave danger. As one character warns with note-perfect Southern inflection, “Down here folks love everything about the Lord except him wanting to keep all the vengeance for himself.”
Jonson’s a terribly funny narrator, often with the acidic humour of a Gil Scott-Heron (whose work makes a crucial appearance). This very particular tone amplifies his experiences, which are at once infuriating, farcical and overwhelming, pointedly like the broader history of policing in the self-proclaimed “city too busy to hate”. Bouncing between past, present and future, Jonson’s account of his experiences fosters a pervasive dread about where the mystery’s going long before we know how it gets there.
This book’s sweep is hard to convey. A furious, sly postmodern mystery about a deeply corrupt society, it reads like what you might get if Ishmael Reed and Walter Mosley had scripted Chinatown. Challenging and enthralling in equal measure, The Occidental Book of the Dead is a stunning novel.
Cold Sunset (Penguin, £20) is the third in William Boyd’s stylish cold war series featuring travel writer Gabriel Dax. Gabriel has been an amateur spy since a few small favours for the UK foreign office led him to Faith Green, who ferrets out traitors from all corners of government. Four years in, his initial bemusement has waned: the money’s still good, but the increasingly complicated things Faith asks of him have come home to roost.
Gabriel’s sent to California to meet FT Falkner, a celebrated writer who’s near death and wants to share information about his war years at Bletchley Park. When Gabriel reports that Falkner identified fellow Bletchley member Angus Fairford as a Russian agent, Faith responds with “an unusual measure of outraged, almost destabilized, panic”, which should have given Gabriel pause.
But as with his perpetual plans to stop smoking his ever-present Gitanes, there’s significant distance between having a good idea and enacting it. This assignment quickly reconnects Gabriel to new and returning characters, including a CIA agent/lover (his spying makes for a spicy array of bedfellows), a vengeful gunman, a triple agent returning from Moscow and a resourceful locksmith who also knows how to dispose of a corpse.
Amid all that, Gabriel strives for a tidy existence. By the conclusion, however, “his unnerving, unwelcomed existence as Faith Green’s spy” reaches a crossroads, his path forward uncertain, at least until the next Dax novel.
Jo Spain’s Never to Be Found (Bonnier, £16.99) won’t disappoint her readers. Protagonist Veronica Page runs a specialised business: when someone wants – or needs – to vanish from their own life, she can help. She doesn’t ask too many questions, especially when a client’s easy, like Ben, whose abusive stepfather is intent on bleeding Ben’s inheritance dry. As soon as Ben’s of age, Veronica helps him disappear, taking his inheritance with him.
Though she eventually reveals a traumatic origin story, Veronica’s present life has all the trappings: meaningful work, a hot younger man who understands her wariness about commitment, a posh apartment. Until, that is, detective Seb Ashworth shows up.
Seb announces that Veronica’s instincts let her down a year ago, when she helped a depressed man escape his collapsing life. That man, Seb announces, was a fugitive who had brutally killed his wife and sister. Seb’s hunted him ever since and now demands Veronica’s help. Horrified by the idea she may have let a murderer escape, Veronica reluctantly works with Seb (who is, of course, quite fit). The catch: given her profession’s secrecy, she really doesn’t know the man’s new name or location.
As the novel speeds ahead, Spain folds in rich layers of twists and betrayals, past and present. Veronica’s real strengths are sometimes muted by this abundant plotting, but she has all the makings of a prominent series lead.
[ Jo Spain: ‘I rely on the next book, contract or TV show to pay that mortgage. I’ve no guaranteed salary’ Opens in new window ]
Former CIA agent Lily Sedako, the main player in Sara Paretsky’s Bad Company (Bedford Square, £20), shares a lot with Paretsky’s legendary Chicago private eye VI Warshawski. But the place that resonates most for Lily is Hayalistan, a former Soviet republic where she served decades earlier. When a New Yorker article about lithium mining there lands on her doorstep, Lily’s shocked out of retirement by its claim that some locals believe she was central to exploiting Hayalistan through a CIA-sponsored coup. She suits up for one final freelance op to learn who fed her to the journalist.
Lily’s CIA career ended unceremoniously after years of wildly successful results that made “younger, often male, agents look bad by picking up assets and intel they’d overlooked”. Now, she’s again a thorn in the side of CIA leadership, mostly characterised by their venal political agility in a presidentially weaponised intelligence service. The wiliness with which she outmanoeuvres the current CIA makes it clear their tech is no match for her old-school ears on the ground.
Paretsky lobs in a few espionage tropes – she’s particularly good at younger agents enthralled by (and older ones disdainful of) a legendarily troublesome spook – but Bad Company is never only about the agency. It depicts a professional woman’s third act, in which leaving on one’s own terms is quite clearly the Holy Grail. Paretsky impressively wraps all of that (and more) in a spy thriller.
Set in the same Pacific Northwest landscape as his phenomenal Coffin Moon, Keith Rosson’s Crone (Black Crow, £19.99) is a mystery in the very oldest, deepest sense.
Nearly blind and just 15, Hannah Lamp vanishes late one night, pulled into a van while walking along an isolated highway, leaving her friend Avery on the roadside. Thirteen years later, Hannah’s father Eli is still haunted by losing her. He’d been a cop, a good one, but after his wife Melanie died he fell into addiction, losing his hope, his career, and finally Hannah. Now he’s clean but under the thumb of local drug runner Dave, to whom he’s mysteriously indebted.
The plot escalates after local seer Vicki stumbles across a human heart bound in blackthorn, an unnerving work of witchcraft far beyond her particular powers. Dave then discovers his son Anton dismembered, conspicuously missing some organs, and orders Eli to catch the killer. At the same time, Avery returns to town, drawn back by vivid dreams of Hannah, whose fate hovers over them all. Eli, Avery and Vicki quickly begin finding some dark answers. As the title suggests, everyone learns those answers have roots deeper, more powerful and more supernatural than they could have imagined.
Although Rosson takes real storytelling chances here, his blend of horror and mystery delivers a memorable pay-off. Both brutally violent and deeply moving, Crone is a novel safest for broad daylight but one you’ll keep reading into the loneliest hours.
Brian Cliff and Elizabeth Mannion edited Guilt Rules All: Mysteries, Detectives and Crime in Irish Fiction (Syracuse University Press, 2020)

title: Elizabeth Wassell Montague: ‘My new novel was partly inspired by the mystery of eating disorders’
description: The writer on new novel At the Villa Celeste; her late husband, the poet John Montague; and the importance of ‘Call me Ishmael’
content:
The Villa Celeste is a lovely house in the made-up town of Ste-Agathe on the French Riviera. Between the two World Wars, it houses a clinic for people troubled in mind or who have TB. Florence, one of my main characters, is a patient there, and Clementine – the other main character, who lives in the present day – visits there also. The novel is set in Paris, New York and the Cote d’Azur.
Thomas Mann’s The Magic Mountain influenced me. That novel takes place entirely in a sanatorium, where the atmosphere is intensely charged, and the characters create their own eccentric society. I was influenced also by the life of Katherine Mansfield, who died of “consumption” at George Gurdjieff’s spiritual centre near Paris. My character Florence March is modelled slightly on Mansfield.
The novel concerns two women who struggle with anorexia. They are searching desperately for their true selves, and they fear their desires. But both women discover passion and purpose, and begin to realise that their real selves lie in the very things they feared.
I learned about Europe between the World Wars. It was a time of exhaustion and sickness, but also hope. Veterans were shell-shocked, families were consulting “spiritualists” to commune with their war dead, and lots of people sought help from mystics and philosophers. I learned about Varian Fry, a real-life war hero who appears in my book. I also learned more about downtown New York in the 1980s and 1990s, where Clementine lives after leaving her wealthy husband.
I think there must be a sense of urgency, a need to write. At the Villa Celeste was inspired partly by the colours and savours of the Cote d’Azur, but also by the experience of suffering and grace, and the mystery – a mainly feminine mystery, though not always – of eating disorders.
I love the stories of James Joyce, William Trevor, Katherine Mansfield and Chekhov. I cherish certain mid- to late-20th-century British novelists such as Margaret Drabble and Doris Lessing, for their style and intelligence. I adore contemporary Irish fiction: Christine Dwyer Hickey, Claire Keegan and Deirdre Madden, among others.
In At the Villa Celeste, Florence marries a much older man. Through this I explored what it means to love and be loved so deeply that age ceases to matter. John also influenced my practice of work. Work mattered more than anything to him. He asked not only me, but everyone he met, “How is your work going? What are you working on?” He himself worked tirelessly, even in the pub or at a restaurant table.
[ I still describe my day to my husband John Montague 10 years after his death Opens in new window ]
In both novels, food is ceremonial. Lily, in Sustenance, loves the formality of restaurants, and in this new book, both Florence and Clementine perform eating rituals.
Sleight of Hand centres on a Spanish Baroque painting that depicts the myth of Echo and Narcissus. Is this painting genuine or a counterfeit? Claire Browne, a young art historian who falls in love with a famous painter, tries to find out.
I’ve been writing short stories. My first collection of stories will be published next year by Mercier Press. Its working title is When New Gods Arrive.
Yes. Such places can be numinous, such as Wordsworth’s home among the lakes.
The first line of Moby Dick is “Call me Ishmael”. It’s vital to understand that it isn’t Ishmael who is speaking, nor is it the author. It’s the narrator. A novelist must create a voice to tell the story. That voice is the ether in which the story is suspended.
I pass a law that dogs are allowed into all pubs, restaurants and cinemas.
The election of Donald Trump. He had been just a thuggish real estate mogul until, suddenly, he was US president.
An illustrated Rough Field published by Maeght Editions.
Shakespeare, Siri Hustvedt, Henry James and Katherine Mansfield.
“In the prison of his days / Teach the free man how to praise.”
At the Villa Celeste by Elizabeth Wassell Montague is published by Vanguard Press

title: Northern Ireland has had several false dawns, but fleadh felt like a turning point
description: Rite & Reason: In a society where flags, emblems, religion and culture are at the heart of divisive politics, it was refreshing to see a number of loyalist bands parading in front of the Taioseach
content:
The much-acclaimed Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann 20026 has come and gone, but anticipation is already building in Belfast for an even bigger and better one next year.
Meanwhile, the impact of the fleadh in this city is raising important cultural, religious and symbolic issues which go far beyond the music, dancing and celebrations which 1.6 million people shared in the streets and big concert halls of the city, and in some of its churches. Traditional Irish music and dancing were not part of the cultural life of northern Protestants when I was growing up in the Border county of south Armagh a long time ago. It was made clear that all things Gaelic were part of the Catholic culture, but not for me because I was a Presbyterian, albeit by accident of birth.
However, my grandfather, Thomas McCreary, helped to challenge the stereotype. He was a practising Presbyterian, but he told me that he joined the Orange Order as a young man because it was the only social club in the rural Ulster of a then united Ireland.
He played jigs and reels on his fiddle at Orange Hall gatherings often until dawn, and he loved Irish music all his life. I am sure he would also have loved the fleadh in Belfast.
During the first World War he was a stretcher-bearer at the Battle of the Somme, and on his return home he joined the Civil Service. He regularly travelled to Crossmaglen, south Armagh, to help local republicans sign on for their dole money. Afterwards they all went to a local pub for more than a few drinks.
McCreary lived the practical south Armagh version of working between Orange and Green, until the advent of the Rev Ian Paisley, who asked people to “stand up and be counted”. And look where that led.
The scale of the success of the Belfast fleadh surprised everybody, including the organisers. There were visitors from around the world, and many thousands from all over Ireland, including Protestants from the North. Many of them attended the events to find out what they were like, and found themselves enjoying the fleadh immensely.
In a society where flags, emblems, religion and “culture” are at the heart of its divisive politics, it was refreshing to see a number of loyalist bands parading in front of the Taoiseach at the Titanic slipways at the Belfast Harbour, and also to observe the warm welcome given at the City Hall “gig-rig” to the Shankill Defenders Flute Band who were “overwhelmed” by the reception.
This could not have happened five or 10 years ago, and it is important to recognise the vision of the organisers, who invited the loyalist bands to join in as part of the “Scots-Irish” culture. It is equally important to recognise the courage of the band musicians who accepted that invitation, and gave of their best on stages and venues which they would never have dreamed of gracing.
Some Protestant churches in Belfast also became involved in the event, including the long-established First Presbyterian (Non-Subscribing) Church in Rosemary Street, Belfast, where Edward Harland, co-founder of the Harland and Wolff shipyard, once worshipped.
There was also an open-air performance by a large Irish music group, including harpers, outside St Anne’s Church of Ireland Cathedral and again in the presence of the Taoiseach. I was also fortunate enough to attend an excellent recital of traditional music by the lady choristers of St George’s Church of Ireland in nearby High Street.
[ Survivors experience Christian Brothers’ litigation strategy as abuse by other means Opens in new window ]
This is the church where Edward Bunting (1773-1843), the famous harpist and collector of Irish music, was the first organist, from 1817-1820. So often these details of important northern connections with the culture of the rest of the island remain unknown or forgotten.
DUP Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly made a warmly inclusive speech of welcome at the opening ceremony. No doubt, there are other unionists who may find excuses to criticise the fleadh by the time it returns next year. Nevertheless, in a province which can so easily tear itself apart, a cultural corner has been turned.
It is difficult to describe exactly what this means, but there is that kind of feeling in the air. Several of my “Protestant/unionist” friends who attended the event, some of them out of curiosity, have said: “Wasn’t it great craic!”
It’s almost as if part of the dark burden of history has been lifted off Belfast, and the charm and friendliness of this so often tough but remarkable city has made national and international headlines in the right way. Significantly, people on all sides here believe that this is not just now in the past, but that there is more to come.
As a veteran of so many brave but eventually false dawns in Belfast, I am aware, like many others, that it is important to rejoice in this new inclusiveness, but also to keep our feet on the ground. Perhaps it is a time to recall the words of our own Ulster man Seamus Heaney from his work The Cure at Troy and to feel that we could really “Believe that a further shore, Is reachable from here.”
Is it too much to believe also that some day even Heaney’s vision of the rhyming of “hope and history ” will indeed rhyme for all of us, across every Province of this island.

title: Loudon Wainwright’s simple, catchy tune that I always find impossible to shake
description: In a Word ... Worm
content:
I knew I was done for the minute I turned on the radio that morning. I could have turned it off but the worm was planted. The tune would haunt me for days. Too late to stop that, then.
Radio is my favourite medium. Back in the increasingly dim days of adolescence, my mother could not understand that I would study with the radio on beside me. Pop and rock as antidote to the ruthlessness of Macbeth, the indecision of Hamlet, the savagery of European history.
Even as I write this, the radio is on beside me, talk radio. The subject is murder mysteries. It’s as though there’s a sub-conscious layer to my mind that must be entertained before I can get on with a task in hand.
Besides, radio is great company. It is not as demanding as reading, scrolling or watching TV, leaving you free to do other things, such as write about how my day was usurped by a song that had wormed its way into my soul before I was even half awake. To be fair, it was not an entirely unpleasant realisation.
The “worm” was American Loudain Wainwright III’s The Swimming Song, a simple, catchy tune, with a simply catchy rhythm that I always find impossible to shake. “This summer I went swimming/This summer I might have drowned/But I held my breath and I kicked my feet/And I moved my arms around/I moved my arms around.” So it begins, and I am hooked.
Released in 1973, it became popular in Ireland when recorded by Canadians Kate and Anna McGarrigle 50 years ago, in 1976. The McGarrigles were popular in Ireland and Wainwright was then married to Kate.
I came across this and other Wainwright songs during happy, student Galway days. The Swimming Song was on his Attempted Mustache album which included I am the Way.
It went: “I can walk on the water and I can raise the dead (repeated). Don’t tell nobody but I kissed Magdalene (repeated). Every son of God gets a little hard luck sometimes (repeated)”, then “... Specially when he goes around saying he’s the way. I am the way (repeat).”
Belated happy birthday, Mr Wainwright, 80 yesterday.
Worm , from Old English wurm, variant of wyrm , for “serpent, snake”. In recent times used to describe “annoyingly unforgettable pop song”.

title: US and Iranian forces launch strikes on vessels in Tehran’s waters
description: Latest exchanges follow recent escalation that threatens to deepen months-long conflict in region
content:
US and Iranian forces fired at vessels in waters around Iran on Saturday, including three Iranian oil carriers struck by the Americans and three tankers that Iran said it targeted ​while on unauthorised routes in the Strait of Hormuz .
US Central Command said it struck the three Iranian vessels, including one off the coast of Kharg Island, near Iran’s oil export hub, after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two US navy ships.
“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of ​our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost – taking out three of yours,” said Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, which oversees the US military in ⁠the Middle East.
The IRGC responded by threatening intensified strikes against US military vessels in the region and said later it targeted the three ‌tankers ‌as ​well as three US-linked vessels in other areas.
“Do not be deceived by the ‘terrorist’ US military and refrain from any suspicious movement aimed at passing through unauthorised waterways,” the IRGC Navy said in a statement carried on Iranian state ⁠TV. “Otherwise, you will be targeted.”
Tasnim, the semi-official Iranian news ​agency, had reported that four US missiles hit a tanker in ​the area of Kharg’s anchorage. Tasnim quoted local sources as saying there were no casualties and the tanker’s crew was being evacuated.
No American personnel were ‌harmed, Central Command said.
The exchange of attacks followed an ​escalation in the past week that threatens to deepen a conflict that has continued since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran ⁠in February, disrupting global energy supplies and drawing opposition from ⁠a majority of Americans before congressional elections ​in November.
While US president Donald Trump ’s administration seeks to pivot toward an economic clampdown on Iran by widening sanctions, the president himself has kept open the possibility of military action.
On August 31st, Trump issued a one-line social media post accompanied by an AI-generated video depicting Kharg Island being “blown to smithereens”. Iranian authorities have vowed a strong response if Kharg is attacked.
Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and exported 90 per cent of its crude via Kharg Island before the war. Flows have been disrupted since a US blockade of Iranian oil exports began in mid-April.
Trump has spoken of an attack on ‌Kharg before. He said on June ⁠11th that he wanted to take over the island, but then said a US military operation there was off the table, days before Tehran and Washington signed an interim agreement aimed at ending the war on June 17th.
A US attack on ‌Kharg would further pressure Iran’s oil industry and its wider economy, which is already reeling from the US naval blockade.
The US imposed its blockade on Iranian ports after Iran effectively ​shut the Strait of Hormuz, an important waterway that carried one-fifth of the world’s oil supply ​before the war.
Brent crude futures closed at their highest level since July 24th on Friday, at $96.28 a barrel, as tensions in the Middle East drive global supply concerns. – Reuters

title: Eternal Katie Taylor does it her own way to the last as she defeats Pili in Croke Park farewell
description: Fans from all across Ireland came to see the boxer finish her career as the greatest to ever do it. She didn’t disappoint
content:
“Let me just look around,” she said, cutting the ring interviewer off at the knees. He wanted Katie Taylor to say something inspiring and momentous worthy of the night but instead, as she’s always preferred, she acted rather than spoke.
The lights went up and she drank in Croke Park , glistening now like a palace. Hers, finally and eternally.
She beat Flora Pili here, as expected, in one of the most straightforward fights of her career. The 29-year-old Frenchwoman landed a couple of good punches in the second round and had Taylor back-pedalling under the weight of some heavy blows in the seventh. But otherwise, Taylor’s last night of work in the ring was a spotless one.
The judges gave her a unanimous decision in the end, two of them calling it in her favour by 100-90 and one making it 98-91. She controlled the fight, keeping Pili at a distance of her pleasing, picking her off with ramrod left jabs and whipping her right to the challenger’s head at will. Pili was strong on her feet and aggressive in her advances. But it’s hard to hit a ghost.
Time and again, Taylor nipped in and out of Pili’s spaces, offering a target that was gone by the time the Frenchwoman’s glove got there.
It was like watching a live scrumping, with Taylor as a kid in an orchard whipping apples and leaving only a bouncing branch behind her. Pili did all she could but Taylor’s speed of evasion made it impossible to see her, never mind catch her.
All the while, the 80,000 crowd in Croke Park ate it up. She made it the perfect night for them, never once scaring them into thinking that anything other than the ending everyone expected was on the cards. They came to see her finish her career as the greatest to ever do it. She didn’t disappoint.
This crowd was all Ireland. You had families and couples and gangs of girls and bands of boys, all drawn here like pilgrims. You had Saturday night girlos in Saturday night hair, tottering down Jones’s Road.
Fellas in Yupbro tracksuits, dudes in chinos with jumpers knotted about their shoulders. Travellers and poshos, grannies and grandkids, Gah heads, rugby heads, soccer heads, all faiths and none. All here for Katie.
On a helpfully warm night, it all felt deeply surreal at times inside the stadium. People were running into each other and the first thing they’d do is gesture down to the pitch and up to the stands, as if they were all thinking the same thing.
Eighty thousand different versions of: “This is wild. Isn’t this wild?”
And it was. There was Westlife belting out a couple of tunes. There was Grace and Zombie and endless Olé, Olé, Olés. There were cans of G&T and Smirnoff Ice in the seats and the strongest smell of weed Croke Park has ever known wafting through the stands. It was a Saturday night in Dublin and the place felt alive.
[ ‘We’ll never get a woman like Katie Taylor again’ Opens in new window ]
The ringwalk was a Broadway show all by itself. Taylor was the only performer of the night to come in at the corner of the Hogan and Davin Stands, strolling along a KatieWalk all of her own.
By the time she reached the ring, the place was fizzing in every direction and fireworks were going off right around the stadium roof.
The thought did occur that this was all being presented as a fait accompli, as if defeat was so far out of the question as to be blasphemy to even suggest. It’s hard to remember a sporting event that ever had the fireworks display before the action kicked off. Were they tempting fate here?
From the ding of the opening bell, any of that kind of worry was washed away. Taylor won a cagey first round, never allowing Pili to enter her postcode, stitching her own shots when she wanted to.
Though Pili willed herself into the fight in the second, Taylor put clear water between them from the third to the sixth. Pili couldn’t land anything clean, so Katie knew she only had to find her range three or four times a round to take it.
She ended the whole thing laughing. By the 10th round, she was far enough ahead to enjoy herself and even then, it wasn’t until the final 10 seconds of her career that she took the chance of letting loose. She got in tight with Pili and, as if thinking she may as well be hung for a sheep as a lamb, indulged herself in one last tear-up.
The pair traded blows from there until the last bell, whizzing punches at each other as if somebody had suddenly pressed fast-forward. The final bell went and she burst out laughing, as if she had tickled herself pink by that one final flurry.
And that was that. All that remained was for them to announce the result, the stadium to explode one last time and Katie Taylor to ask for that one last look around. She gazed upon the spectacle she alone had conceived and created, no worlds left to conquer.

title: Katie Taylor brings curtain down on boxing career with historic Croke Park win over Flora Pili
description: Taylor retires with a wide unanimous decision win in front of more than 80,000 people at Croke Park
content:
Well folks, that’s all for tonight’s coverage of Katie Taylor’s final fight from Croke Park, and thankfully it was a big win for the Irish legend. She outboxed and outfought France’s Flora Pili to a wide unanimous decision victory in front of over 80,000 people, marking a successful end to one of Ireland’s greatest sporting stories.
Taylor only suffered one defeat in the pros, which she avenged months later and won undisputed world titles at two weights, fighting in some absolute thrillers along the way. As an amateur she brought women’s boxing to the Olympics, then won the gold medal, to go alongside her World and European titles. Taylor retires with a strong claim to being the greatest women’s boxer ever, the greatest Irish boxer ever, and even the greatest Irish athlete ever.
Thanks so much for joining us for this historic night at Croke Park. Here is Malachy Clerkin’s fight report . Goodnight and safe home to all who were in Croker tonight.
A superb montage from RTÉ to cap off an amazing night for Katie Taylor at Croke Park.
The end of an amazing career for Katie Taylor From the boxing club in Bray, to 80,000 people in Croke Park Ireland's greatest ever boxer #RTESport pic.twitter.com/Ka17LXoMjN
Anyone who’s stayed up late for other Katie fights over the years will know that this was one of the easier nights to be a fan. Compared to the Amanda Serrano, Delfine Persoon and Chantelle Cameron fights there was a lot less heart-stopping moments tonight. Still, those wins would rate as some of the best in the history of the sport, and tonight definitely ranks alongside them in terms of defining moments in Katie Taylor’s career.
Katie Taylor spoke to RTÉ in the ring after the fight and told them that this was the perfect way to end a 30-year career in boxing.
“I dreamed of this moment for years, it’s been absolutely remarkable. I’m looking around here at the stadium and seeing the 80,000 people here screaming my name; this is beyond my wildest dreams and I’m just so grateful. What a way to end this career. The people of Ireland gave me a dream ending to a dream career.”
There was so much going on in that final interview, but this is one big moment from it. The usually suave and cocky Eddie Hearn nearly melts completely, as he says farewell to one of the greatest fighters he has ever promoted.
Eddie Hearn pays his respects to one of the greatest fighter's he's ever promoted 🤝 #TaylorPili pic.twitter.com/C79hXTIxI8
Katie Taylor leaves her gloves down in the centre of the ring to mark her career finale, as her team surround them with her many, many titles. What a night for boxing in Ireland.
ICONIC! 🌟 A fairytale ending to the career of Katie Taylor ❤️ #TaylorPili pic.twitter.com/L9JZUHMfuF
Katie is having her moment, dictating her final career interview herself now, and taking the moment to appreciate everyone who played a part in her rise to stardom.
Katie Taylor wins the undisputed light welterweight title by wide unanimous decision victory.
Round 10: Katie Taylor’s coach, Ross Enamait tells her to go out and enjoy this final round, the final round of a historic career. Taylor tears into the fight against, sitting down on her punches and throwing flurries of hooks and straights at her opponent. Super right straight to the body from Taylor again. The crowd chant ‘olé’ and it looks like a brilliant end to a fantastic career tonight. One final flurry, and Taylor goes out swinging as she always did.
She gave everything until the very last second of her career 🙌 #TaylorPili | LIVE NOW on DAZN ▪️ pic.twitter.com/LUaG5jgMyP
Round 9: A bit of a quiet, tactical round, which suits Taylor perfectly now. Pili seems to have lost that impetus she had in round seven, but this was a fairly even round.
Round 8: Pili is really trying to push on now, getting in close and trying to land at close range. Suddenly, Taylor steps on the gas again and lands a great combination. Taylor lands two perfect straight right hands now, stopping Pili’s momentum. That round showed a lot of Taylor’s old-school amateur boxing skills.
Round 7: Taylor comes in with a combination, but Pili finally rallies back with her first big combination, knocking Taylor back for a second. There’s a little bit of bounce sapped out of Katie now and it’s been by far the best round for Pili.
Round 6: Another great straight right by Katie Taylor, and then a combination knocks Pili backwards; the best punches of the fight so far. Pili is pushing in, trying to force some success, but it’s giving Taylor opportunities to land cleaner shots. Great round for the home fighter.
Round 5: Pili’s corner are urging her to open up a little more, but the round begins with Taylor landing some quick punches, and making the French fighter miss with brilliant head movement. Somehow the 40-year-old has all the speed in the ring. Taylor ends the round with a signature left hook that cracks Pili on the side of the head and she pivots out of danger.
Round 4: Taylor opens up with some quick flurries early in round four, although most of the punches hit the guard. However, when Pili opens up a little, Taylor is landing in spots. The straight right lands clean once on Pili, and the speed difference is very evident. Not many clean punches again, but Pili’s activity is so low so far.
Round 3: Pili is starting to come forward a little more now, trying to hold the centre of the ring. Most of Taylor’s punches this round have been half-blocked by Pili, and the French boxer lands one clean left, but there’s not much activity from the away fighter.
Round 2: A super combination from Taylor early on, as she gets inside and lets three left hooks go, finishing on a right hook. Great work. Pili is more well known as a front foot fighter, but so far she’s drawing Taylor in. Even if it’s unsettled Katie a little, it isn’t really winning the early rounds.
Round 1: A tentative start from both, as Taylor gets on the front foot early. It’s the home fighter who lands the first real blow of the fight, sizing up her opponent early on. A nice opener for Katie Taylor.
As always, announcer David Diamante has an exhausting list of accomplishments to get through on Katie Taylor’s CV. That alone would give any opponent the shivers you would think.
An emotional ringwalk for Katie Taylor, who seems to be soaking in the atmosphere. Croke Park looks absolutely spectacular as fireworks and light shows go off for the Irish boxer.
Westlife is done, Grace and the national anthem have been sung, and now the challenger, Flora Pili, has made her way into the ring for the biggest fight of her career. She is 12-0 so far in her career, although this will be a far bigger test than anything she has faced yet.
Well folks, here it is, the main event of the evening; Westlife! Those white suits are blinding, but it seems to be going down a treat so far anyway.
Back to regular programming after that bizarre co-main event. Ronan McGreevy has been on the ground ahead of Katie Taylor’s final fight, soaking up the atmosphere and the thoughts of the fans around Croke Park.
[ ‘We’ll never get a woman like Katie Taylor again’: Fans look forward to Croke Park clash ]
My advice to Westlife tonight; don’t lean on the ropes lads!
No contest announced as the verdict of Thomas Carty v Dave Allen.
Malachy Clerkin reports from Croke Park: “The crowd don’t really know who to boo here – Allen for punching Carty in the back of the head or Carty for flailing full length out of the ring. Either way, Carty is getting oxygen and isn’t coming back. He’s walking down the tunnel here below us in the Hogan Stand. That was supposed to be the second biggest fight of the night and it’s over after one minute and 22 seconds. The fight is declared a No Contest. The crowd boo lustily and we get on with our night.”
If Thomas Carty thought he’d suffered a freak injury the last time then he didn’t know what was in store at all today. The replay clearly shows that Allen hit Carty on the back of the head right before the Dub flew out of the ring. The crowd boo loudly at that angle. This will either be a disqualification or a no-contest. What a shame for Carty though, the biggest night of his career by miles.
Another angle of one of the most bizarre ends to a fight we've seen in a long time 🤔 #TaylorPili | LIVE NOW on DAZN ▪️ pic.twitter.com/jQUzIvrV2x
Allen hit Carty with a couple of rabbit punches, but hardly enough to send the big Dublin man down. He fell like a sack of spuds there and that will surely be the end of the fight, as he hasn’t got back up.
Round 1: What has gone on there? Thomas Carty let off a nice combination and Allen leaned on the ropes, and when Carty followed in he tumbled through the very slack-looking ropes and right down on to ringside. I’ve never seen anything like that.
“No Carty, no party”, and the Dublin crowd respond to the home fighter. Carty has a record of 11-1, having sustained a freak knee injury in his only loss. Meanwhile, Dave Allen has been there and done it a lot more often, with a record of 27-9-2. His belly is protruding a lot more than it was at his best, but he’s still dangerous.
The co-main event is about to get under way at Croke Park, as Thomas Carty faces Dave Allen in a 10-round heavyweight clash.
And for anyone wondering if we might be flying through these undercard fights a little too quickly, don’t forget that there’ll be a special performance by Westlife on the way tonight.
Next up is a heavyweight fight between Phibsboro’s Thomas Carty and English fan favourite Dave Allen. Allen weighed in at nearly 280lbs yesterday, and has admitted to not quite being the most professional boxer ever in the build-up to this one. Gordon Manning reports on the back and forth between these two at the press conference earlier this week.
[ Before Katie Taylor’s farewell, the undercard fighters get their night at Croke Park ]
Round 4: It’s all over, as the doctor waves it off for a terrible cut on Tyrone McKenna’s eye that was spraying blood all over the ringside tables. That is probably Paddy Donovan’s best performance of his career, looking really patient, controlled and razor-sharp.
Paddy Donovan def. Tyrone McKenna by fifth round stoppage.
The fight is stopped due to a nasty gash on the face of Tyrone McKenna 🩸 A dominant display from Paddy Donovan nonetheless 👏 #TaylorPili | LIVE NOW on DAZN ▪️ pic.twitter.com/77h7XrDV8C
Round 3: Donovan’s trainer, former middleweight champ Andy Lee, tells him in the corner that he’s looking “sensational”, and he’s not wrong. His head movement looks particularly good in the third, slipping punch after punch. He’s winning this with his lead right hand alone right now.
Limerick’s former world title challenger Paddy Donovan is now boxing Belfast’s Tyrone McKenna, who is probably a few years past his prime. So far McKenna has been down in round two, but survived to reach the third.
Donovan puts McKenna down 💥 #TaylorPili | LIVE NOW on DAZN ▪️ pic.twitter.com/A9zQL3OyBP
Emmet Brennan is making his own way out of the ring now as the final result is read out. An incredibly brave performance from the Dublin man, but he was overmatched by Bevan. Fair play to the Southampton fighter too, who kept his celebrations to a minimum while the doctors examined Brennan after the knockout blow.
Round 6: The doctors investigate Brennan at the start of the sixth for a peculiarly long time, but he’s down from a body shot again as soon as it’s back on. The referee somehow decides to let it go again, and Bevan flattens him with a big left hook. That fight should have been stopped before that last punch.
Taylor Bevan def. Emmet Brennan by sixth round stoppage.
Taylor Bevan finally gets his stoppage after having the extremely tough Emmet Brennan survives 4 knockdowns 💥 #TaylorPili | LIVE NOW on DAZN ▪️ pic.twitter.com/kuY6LGw2TT
Brennan down for the third time at the end of the fifth from a lovely left hook to the body. He’s back up now and on the stool preparing for the sixth round.
Round 5: Fair play to Brennan, who not only survived but had a couple of good moments in the fourth. Still, he’ll have to go looking for only his second ever knockout if he wants a win.
Round 3: Emmet Brennan goes down heavily on a left hook from Taylor Bevan in the third round. He tries to get inside and smother the follow-up, but he’s caught and go down again. The bell saves him for this round, but it’s hard to imagine him surviving the fourth.
Two rounds into Brennan-Bevan, and the English fighter is getting the better of it so far. Brennan has a noticeable bit of reddening around the ribs, but has also had some success with his left hook upstairs. Eight rounds to go anyway.
Donald McRae charts his connection with Katie Taylor through the years, from her amateur days all the way through to the present day finale.
[ Katie Taylor: An emotional last night for a quietly defiant pioneer ]
Emmet Brennan, who grew up just around the corner from Croke Park, leads off the action on the main card tonight. The 6-0 super-middleweight and former Olympian makes his way to the ring to face the much-fancied Taylor Bevan, himself boasting a 9-0 record.
Although Katie Taylor is exiting the stage after tonight, there’s no doubt that her effect on sports in Ireland will be long-lasting. James Cox reports on the legacy of a pioneering fighter.
[ ‘I want to be like Katie’: In the shadow of Croke Park, Katie Taylor’s legacy is clear ]
Just to recap on what’s gone on so far tonight at Croke Park, as the preliminary action finishes up on the undercard. Prospects Bobbi Flood and Adam Olaniyan both won well early on, Liverpool’s Joe McGrail stopped Coleraine’s Matthew Boreland, and Katie Taylor’s cousin Molly McCann won a unanimous decision in her fifth pro boxing fight.
Paul Ryan def. Paddy Gallagher by unanimous decision.
Adam Olaniyan def. Matej Hudak by first round stoppage.
Bobbi Flood def. Jack Swallow by unanimous decision.
Joe McGrail def. Matthew Boreland by fifth round stoppage.
Molly McCann def. Sylwia Doligala by unanimous decision.
Before the main event tonight, it’s probably prescient to recap on how we got here. Malachy Clerkin gives the rundown on how Katie Taylor defied all the odds, helping to create the women’s boxing scene she has dominated for decades.

Hello and welcome to live coverage of Katie Taylor’s final fight as she draws the curtain on a legendary career tonight in Croke Park. Taylor will take on unbeaten French fighter Flora Pili for the undisputed light-welterweight championship of the world in front of a crowd of over 80,000. The fights will be broadcast on RTÉ from 8pm, and we’ll take you through the various Irish action on the undercard leading up to the main event.
