After moving to Ireland with his wife, Tatiane Esporte, seven years ago, he began supplying Brazilian savoury dishes to businesses in Dublin. “I said to Tatiane, ‘Why don’t we open a coffee shop?’ My dream was to create something like what my family had in Brazil, but here in Ireland.”
Tatiane had been a personal trainer in Brazil and was working as a childminder for an Irish family in Portmarnock when she noticed the empty premises nearby. The family she worked for encouraged them to take the chance. “I saw the ‘To Let’ sign and said, ‘Let’s try.’”
Their earliest customers were mainly local, with Brazilians taking longer to discover a cafe well outside the concentration of Brazilian businesses in the city centre. “We had great, great support from the locals,” Tatiane says. Word has since spread and they now have Brazilian customers travelling across Dublin and, on occasion, from as far away as Wexford.
Albert says he has no interest in making the cafe exclusively Brazilian, preferring to put foods familiar to Irish customers alongside things they might never have encountered. “We want Brazilian people to find flavours they recognise, but we also want Irish people to feel comfortable coming in and trying something new,” he says. For a first taste of Brazil he recommends a coxinha (a common street snack made of shredded, seasoned chicken wrapped in dough and shaped like a teardrop); pão de queijo (cheese bread) and chicken pie are among the most popular choices with Irish customers.
The business has already grown beyond the original space, with more tables outside and a larger kitchen upstairs. Other cafes have approached them about supplying food or teaching them how to make some of their products. Catering is also in the plans. “We have lots of plans and dreams for the future,” Tatiane says. “We love being here. We are living our dream.”
While the Brazilian food people leave behind can be reproduced in a Dublin kitchen, the professional lives they leave can often be harder to recover. Research commissioned by the Brazilian embassy found that 85 per cent of Brazilians arriving in Ireland had third-level qualifications, even though many spent their first years in Ireland doing work far removed from the careers they had trained for.
Paula Castro arrived in Dublin from Pelotas in southern Brazil in 2014 with a degree in English teaching and several years’ classroom experience. After completing the Cambridge qualification required by language schools here, she found work almost immediately, although her hours could range from full time one week to just two or three the next.
Seeking greater stability, she moved schools and rose from teacher to director of studies over four years, only for the pandemic to close the school three months after her promotion. She went on to complete a master’s degree in educational leadership at Trinity College Dublin, returning to a place she remembered walking through during her first weeks in Ireland more than a decade ago. “I remember thinking, ‘Imagine studying here one day,’” she says. After graduating and working at the National College of Ireland, she eventually returned to Trinity, where she now teaches and contributes to curriculum and assessment design.
“Now not only have I studied there, I’m employed there as well,” she says. “It’s surreal.” Her journey has made her wary of judging migrants by the work they do on arrival. “You meet engineers, veterinarians and other professionals working as delivery drivers or in hospitality because they’re starting their lives over again,” she says.
“Ireland offers many educational opportunities, and many Brazilians have built successful careers here. At the same time, access is not always equal.” The obstacles can include language, financial pressure, unfamiliarity with the Irish education system, visa issues, limited access to financial support and difficulty in having Brazilian qualifications recognised, as well as what she calls “the psychological impact of starting over in a new country”.
Paula became an Irish citizen in 2024, although she still describes herself as “90 per cent Brazilian and 10 per cent Irish”. “Maybe that percentage will grow over time,” she says.
“I’d like to see us continue removing barriers so that talent, ambition and potential, not a person’s country of origin, determine a person’s educational opportunities.”
[ ‘I work with a lot of Irish people around my age. Sometimes they ask me questions that are a bit weird’ Opens in new window ]
Louise Abrão first walked into Brazilian Aesthetics in Dublin’s north inner city carrying her CV. The salon had only recently opened and there was no position for her. “I’m so sorry I can’t give you an opportunity now,” owner Priscilla Becker told her, “but I’d like you to be on my team.”
Louise returned the following month as a customer and continued coming for treatments until, about 10 months after their first conversation, Priscilla called her. Louise now manages the salon.
Priscilla had worked in beauty in Brazil but began again in Ireland with babysitting and cleaning, eventually offering eyebrow treatments and micropigmentation from a room in Swords. When the room became too small, she chose to spend her savings on a salon rather than put them towards a house. Brazilian Aesthetics opened in December 2023; six months later she opened a doorway into the adjoining unit and rented that too, while a second branch has since opened in Portugal.
Irish, Spanish, Ukrainian and African customers now settle into the velvet-green chairs alongside Brazilians, while the staff have taken their work to Grafton Street, offering pop-up eyebrow treatments, haircuts and colour to passersby. “Our idea from the beginning was to bring Brazilian treatments and Brazilian beauty here, to make people feel better about themselves and also to make Brazilians feel a little bit at home,” Louise says.
The clientele has broadened as the business has grown, but inside the salon the Brazilian character remains strong. “We always say our team here is like a family,” she says. “We feel like we’re together and we support each other, both at work and outside work.”
Louise had not expected to find such a large Brazilian community when she moved to Ireland three years ago. “Especially in summer, I feel like I’m at home here,” she says. “Sometimes I literally feel like I’m in Brazil. It’s crazy because the community is so, so big.”
For her, the attraction of Ireland has always been as much about people as work. “I would say Ireland has its doors open,” she says. “It’s like a warm hug when you come in.”
Thais Gimenes Tambalo came to Dublin four and a half years ago with her Brazilian husband, having never lived outside Brazil and wanting, as she puts it, “another point of view on life”. Two years later the marriage ended, and because her immigration status had depended on her husband, she wrote to the Minister for Justice explaining that she wanted to remain.
“Even when I got divorced here, I never felt that I wasn’t home,” she says. “I never thought, ‘I need to go back to Brazil.’ I was already home. My life was here.”
She was allowed to stay and later met Burak Rencberoglu, who had moved to Ireland from Turkey. Their daughter, Melanie, was born in Dublin six months ago. Her experience of the Irish maternity system was entirely positive. “I would give it 10 out of 10. Everyone was very kind to me and I felt protected throughout the whole experience.”
After years working in hospitality, motherhood changed how she spent her time in the city. Summer days now involve picnics and playgrounds, while Melanie has Brazilian, Turkish and Irish friends. English has become the official language Thais and Burak speak to one another at home, although neither arrived in Ireland speaking much of it.
What Thais misses most is not Brazil itself but the family life she knew there. Her mother now lives in Portugal, but in the Brazil of her childhood grandparents and relatives shared the everyday work of bringing up a child.
“In Brazil, we tend to raise children together as a family,” she says. “Here, I feel very alone.”
Burak has been offered a job in Portugal and they are now preparing to leave Dublin. Thais hopes to look after Melanie herself until she is four or five, something she cannot see them affording comfortably on one income in Ireland.
“If my partner wanted to support the whole family here alone, he would need to work two or three jobs,” she says. “He would never see his daughter.”
“Ireland will always be the place that gave me an opportunity and showed me how big the world is and how much your life can change,” she says. “My daughter was born here, so I will always have good feelings about this place.”
She laughs and sounds, for a moment, unmistakably like a Dubliner: “I hate Dublin, but I love it too at the same time. That is the feeling.”
For Julio Cesar, the clearest measure of Dublin’s influence comes whenever he returns to Brazil. “Every time I go back, people tell me: ‘You have changed.’ I say: ‘Thank God I have changed. Imagine if I were the same person I was four years ago.’”

title: Ireland set to join EU-Nigeria ‘migrant returns’ pact
description: Five EU states plan to send migrants to offshore centres next year
content:
Nigerian migrants living in Ireland without status would be swiftly returned to their home country under a new European Union migration pact that the Government is set to sign up to.
Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan wants the Cabinet to agree to join a “readmission” agreement between the EU and Nigeria as part of a plan to prioritise returns to the west African country. Nigeria is consistently one of the main countries of origin for people applying for international protection in Ireland.
If approved by the Cabinet next week, the new migration pact would represent a much stronger returns arrangement than Ireland’s pre-existing 2001 agreement with Nigeria. This bilateral agreement was never formally ratified by the African country, though the Government believes there has been good co-operation from Nigerian authorities.
Following more than a decade of negotiation, the EU earlier this year signed a new readmission and returns agreement with Nigeria, which could see thousands of Nigerians who are either economic migrants or unsuccessful asylum seekers sent back to their country of origin. The deal, which will affect Nigerian nationals who no longer have the legal right to enter, stay, or reside in the EU, was agreed after Nigeria was offered greater access to the EU market and €288 million in healthcare funding. Nigeria will now be under fresh obligations to accept the swift return of their own nationals from EU member states.
The EU had said the agreement included safeguards on human rights, data protection, governance and monitoring. According to the agreement, both the EU and Nigeria will commit to protecting the rights of people returned under the agreement – which also facilitates the returns of EU migrants from Nigeria.
It is understood the Department of Justice expects the migration pact, if agreed by the Government, to speed up the enforcement of returns decisions against Nigerian migrants. It also expects the migration deal to encourage Nigeria to enhance their migration controls.
Ireland does not automatically sign up to EU justice and home affairs measures, but it has three months after such proposals are published to opt-in. The EU and Nigeria agreement was formally published on July 8th this year, giving Ireland until October 8th to agree to take part.
It comes as five EU states plan to sign deals this year to send migrants without legal residency to countries outside the EU. Though no countries have been named officially, Uganda and Rwanda are reportedly in talks.
[ Italy’s Giorgia Meloni faces a challenge from the right Opens in new window ]
Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands said they had agreed on concrete steps towards a deal with ​a non-European Union country on return facilities.
The countries, known as the “group of five”, did ⁠not name the nations they expect to host return centres.
Danish migration minister Morten Bødskov made the promise to have return centres up and running next year as he hosted his counterparts in Copenhagen on Friday.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin said in July that the Government had “no immediate plans” to join such a scheme and was instead focused on expediting asylum procedures in Ireland.
Notably absent from Friday’s meeting was Italy, in recent months a close partner of Denmark in robust migration responses. The Italian government is locked in dispute with the courts over the legality of sending migrants to detention hubs in Albania.
Though any final court ruling may differ, Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni said this non-binding opinion confirmed the “validity” of her government’s approach.
EU migration commissioner Magnus Brunner also attended Friday’s meeting. Though the commission is open to proposals for a common project in line with EU law and international standards, it has warned of considerable legal hurdles.
The five countries, all facing continuing pressure to reduce asylum numbers, say their project draws on powers provided by new EU asylum arrangements which came into effect in June.
But the idea of such facilities – variously called return hubs and exit centres – has been criticised by human rights groups. The Council of Europe, a non-EU body that promotes human rights and rule of law, said return hubs posed “considerable human rights risks”, including ill-treatment and arbitrary detention.

title: Changing Gender by Susan Stryker: A work of extraordinary energy, hope and emotional force
description: Through the seemingly dry framework of grammar, the author takes us on an intellectually stunning and thrillingly alive journey
content:
Trans theorist and activist Susan Stryker has long understood the radical possibilities of undoing simplistic narratives and redefining binary terms. Her seminal 1994 essay identifying with Frankenstein’s monster rejected reductive, stigmatising definitions and instead explored the monster as a figure of power, of possibility, of self-definition.
In Changing Gender, Stryker is still interested in how we create new forms of existence, but her tool is something seemingly much, much duller: grammar. She acknowledges the dryness of the framework – then immediately takes the reader on a journey that is not just intellectually stunning, but thrillingly alive.
Stryker begins starkly, noting how trans people in the United States are currently the victims of relentless, co-ordinated attacks, from bathroom panics and attacks on healthcare to the fixation on “gender ideology” – a phrase she describes as essentially vacuous, useful primarily for signalling hostility to gender itself.
But Changing Gender is determined to break open language itself and explore imaginative horizons far beyond the limited worldview of the transphobic. Moving through linguistics, anthropology, medicine, technology and trans history, she returns repeatedly to the idea of grammar: a largely invisible system through which we categorise things, establish relationships between them, and make the world intelligible.
Grammar is how we come to understand reality – and gender, she argues, operates similarly, encoding assumptions about which bodies, identities and relationships are possible, desirable, even thinkable. Change our understanding of language, change our understanding of gender, and we change what realities are possible.
This idea could be punishingly dense and intellectual, but Stryker makes it exhilarating. She is funny, irreverent and energetic, moving from analyses of Judith Butler and John Money to descriptions of nights drinking with academic friends and her emotional experience with psychedelics, noting how these substances – like language – encourage neuroplasticity, helping humans to perceive the world differently.
Her language itself is exciting and convention-breaking. Every time Stryker codas political analysis with poetry, layers awe on top of academia, marries the cerebral with the sacred, she cracks open new possibilities of understanding, and encourages us to see how grammar, of all things, could be revolutionary – something we can break open and reconfigure to imagine another way for the world to be.
It’s that feeling of possibility that gives Changing Gender its extraordinary sense of energy, hope and emotional force.
Stryker ends with an invitation that becomes a call to action, writing: “It’s time to breathe. To rise. To reassemble. To transform. Come with me? It’s never too late to live, however close to death we all might be. It’s not too late, but it’s definitely time to go.”
Roe McDermott is an Irish Times columnist

title: ‘Give them no hope’ – Rathwood messages show continued involvement of Keogh brothers
description: Internal messages at troubled retailer address which staff should be kept on and how business should be run
content:
The Keogh brothers, who ran troubled retailer Rathwood before it went into examinership last April, remain heavily involved in the company and are in regular communication with the new owners about the day-to-day running of the business.
The continuing involvement of James and Thomas Keogh comes after Rathwood’s sale to a consortium headed by Kevin Nolan, who runs a Cork-based corporate advisory firm.
An extensive series of internal messages seen by The Irish Times indicates the Keogh brothers have been involved in discussions about which employees should be kept on or let go and how certain creditors and the business should be managed in the wake of a dramatic fall from grace in recent years.
Complaints about Rathwood’s inability to fulfil orders first emerged in mid-2025, with Rathwood’s problems deepening last winter. In April the company went into examinership, after which it emerged that about 7,000 customers had bought products from Rathwood that were never delivered, with close to €3 million owed.
In July the High Court approved a €750,000 rescue scheme which saw Nolan and a consortium taking over. Customers owed money were promised refunds of just 0.25 per cent.
Confirming the scheme, Judge Rory Mulcahy said the manner in which the business had been managed before its examinership remained of “significant concern” and he noted liabilities of more than €21 million when it entered examinership.
Keith Farry, for the Keogh family directors of Rathwood, told the court his clients were undertaking not to act as directors of the company for a period of five years.
They have remained involved, however, and in one exchange between James Keogh and Nolan last month, Keogh suggested a redundancy package for some staff of €5,000 was a “clever” move. “Give them no hope, only 3 days a week or €5,000,” Keogh told Nolan. He suggested staff might simply choose to leave “if they know there is NO hope of the big pay-off”.
[ Rathwood receives more consumer complaints than Ryanair Opens in new window ]
In another piece of correspondence, James Keogh dismissed an employee suggestion that the retailer’s popular Christmas experience should involve local market stalls and craft markets and said such stalls were a “waste of time and never pay”. He dismissed “craft people” as “painful”.
Keogh also said employees were “scared” of the new chief executive, “which is ideal”.
In another sequence Keogh outlined how various staff should be treated, with “let go” or “really needs to go” appearing after some names.
In another exchange Keogh said a supplier was said to be “desperate to get back on track”.
In response Nolan said the desperation was “no harm, we keep it sweating until early next week. You get to play the Kevin card; ‘he’s not happy etc but you’re trying to get it sorted’,” which was answered with a “100 per cent” emoji from Keogh.
Many serious conversations, including some in which the Keoghs and Nolan discussed how little some creditors would be getting back as a result of the examinership process, were peppered with emojis including crying/laughing faces and devils.
In response to queries from The Irish Times Nolan said he had “drawn on the knowledge and experience of the inherited Rathwood management team, including James and Thomas Keogh, to understand the business and support its transition” and added that “given the complexity of the business and the circumstances in which it emerged from examinership, that was both necessary and commercially sensible”.
He insisted that since his consortium acquired Rathwood “the business has been under my full control” and he stressed that neither of the Keogh brothers had any “ownership, control or decision-making authority within Rathwood”.
“The fact that views or recommendations were expressed in private Slack exchanges does not mean those individuals made the decisions, nor should my failure to challenge every comment be interpreted as agreement with the language used. Decisions on staffing, suppliers and the operation and future direction of Rathwood rest with me,” he said.
He also said he rejected “any suggestion that seeking information and operational assistance from people with long-standing knowledge of Rathwood was contrary to the restructuring approved by the High Court. Evergreen owns Rathwood, I control the business and all material decisions are made by me.”
Both James and Thomas Keogh were contacted for comment.

title: I’m not really a ‘dog person’, but was I a ‘cat person’ either? I was about to find out
description: A week cat-sitting in my friend’s architecturally stunning house with poured concrete floors and a view of Dalkey Island was difficult to resist
content:
A friend asked me to do some last-minute cat-sitting because all her regular cat-sitters were unavailable. Would my family like to move into her home and mind Sooty for a week? I love my little North Strand terraced gaff, but the prospect of moving into my friend’s architecturally stunning house with poured concrete floors and a view of Dalkey Island was difficult to resist. I said I’d have to consult my family but in my head I was already sitting out on her terrace gazing at the have-yachts and trying to accidentally-on-purpose bump into Bono in Finnegan’s.
There were a couple of concerns. I had never been asked to mind a cat before. We’ve never had a pet ourselves as a family apart from a couple of hamsters (RIP) when the girls were much smaller. Taking charge of a cat felt like a serious responsibility. I consulted some friends, regular minders of pets, and they were mostly reassuring. One of them told me cats are much lower maintenance than dogs. Another friend, an avowed “dog person”, cautioned that cats were notoriously “difficult” and “sassy”. I’m not really a “dog person” myself, but I wondered if I was a “cat person” either. I was about to find out.
The other concern was slightly more worrying. One of my daughters is actively wary of cats. She has moderate, and I had to look this word up just now, ailurophobia. Very much not a “cat person”. When she spots neighbourhood cats roaming around on our back wall, she gets the big-time heebie jeebies. Funnily enough, when I showed her some pictures of my friend’s house – the outdoor sauna, the indoor fire pit, the sweeping sea views – the moderate ailurophobia seemed to miraculously recede. We were all off to Dalkey to mind a cat and live in luxury for a little while.
Sooty is, it soon became apparent, one very cool cat. She used to be a roamer, based in a house a few streets away, before she made my friend’s home her forever home five years ago. Sooty’s previous owner was fine with the transition, acknowledging that she seemed far happier in her adopted home. Sooty doesn’t roam any more and I can’t say I blame her. I barely left my friend’s exquisite house and garden for the week while I was cat-sitting.
I got to know Sooty over the first couple of days, feeling honoured when she’d come towards me, weaving around my legs. “You are a special lady, Sooty,” I found myself telling her. This was unusual for me. I generally resist making bonds with animals, which I think goes back to my heartbreak when our family mongrel Sam died in the 1980s.
With Sooty to take care of, we all got into a routine. A treat for her in the morning, her main meal at 3pm. At night I’d wait until she was ready to come in, then open the door when she’d snuggle up on her bed. On Day 2, my moderately ailurophobic daughter confessed to a fondness for Sooty, which was a wonderful and unexpected turn-up for the books. “We are completely slaying at this cat-sitting business,” I thought to myself. Which, naturally, is when it all went a bit wrong.
From around lunchtime on Day 3, there was no sign of Sooty about the place. When she didn’t come to the door that evening I began to seriously panic. I texted her owner, who was calm and reassuring. “She’s often very near, under a bush or hiding somewhere. You can call her? She’s very resourceful, clever and not afraid of foxes.” But then: “I’ve not known her to spend the night out.” Oh dear. I did not sleep much that night. Every couple of hours until dawn, I put on my Crocs and wandered into the garden calling “Sooty, Sooty”, but of Sooty, there was no sign.
In the morning, I put her treat in the bowl. I had scheduled an online exercise class that morning with Jason in Co Meath who has three cats. Instead of doing squats and other appalling things, I spent the entire session talking about Sooty. Jason thought she might be hiding or that maybe she’d got accidentally locked in somewhere like a shed. I went to check the outdoor sauna with a heavy heart but she wasn’t in there, thank goodness.
[ I’ve had many arguments with my husband - but this was the first wearing a harness Opens in new window ]
Sooty’s owner is a beautiful, generous person. We talked on the phone that day and she said she believed Sooty would turn up but that even if something catastrophic (sorry) had happened “it isn’t your fault and it’s just her time”. Then she went off to consult her pet psychic who had located a missing cat for her before.
We didn’t need the pet psychic in the end. Shortly after this chat, my daughters went to the car to get a hoodie and there, snuggled up in it, was Sooty. She must have snuck into the car when we weren’t looking. She was fine. Completely calm. Joy.
It turns out I am a cat person. Or maybe I am just a Sooty person. And now I am back in the North Strand, where the kitchen tiles are cracked and there is no sea view. And no Sooty. Turns out the hardest part of cat-sitting was leaving her behind.

title: ‘Babies in buggies are eating instant noodles. You never know what somebody is going through’
description: Research from last year found 9 per cent of the population were living in food poverty
content:
N ext time you’re in a crowd, take a look at the people around you. Chances are, more than you think have struggled at some point to afford healthy food.
Safefood research from last year found nearly half a million people in the Republic, or 9 per cent of the population, were living in food poverty.
Another recent study by a Dublin charity concluded that close to half of its catchment in Ballyfermot and Cherry Orchard had fallen into the category. The Society of St Vincent de Paul (SVP) said it received 112,772 requests for food assistance last year, up 8,548 since 2024.
Eilis Davenport, founder of Learn Local, a social enterprise bringing cooking skills into primary schools, says she works with many children who are living in temporary accommodation or family hubs.
“The babies in buggies are eating instant noodles at nine o’clock in the morning outside the school. You never know what somebody is going through. It’s so important to try and empathise on every single level,” she says.
A former fine dining pastry chef, Davenport grew up in Ballymun and left school at 16, when she was encouraged by her local youth club to enrol in a culinary skills course. She feels “lucky” that she had already learned much about cooking from her grandmother, who was an “incredible cook”.
Training in pastry, she worked in the fine dining world for several years but the evening hours became too difficult with children.“Once my children started at school I saw there was no education about food or cooking in schools, so I wanted to build something around that.”
In the Learn Local classes Davenport brings her cooking equipment (including hobs) into schools in the north inner city, Tallaght, Ballymun and Finglas. Most of the schools involved fall under the Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools (Deis) programme, so they receive extra State supports.
The classes start with a basic soup and bread recipe. Week two is eggs: scrambled and French toast. Later lessons include making spaghetti bolognese and a stir fry. The schools vary in what they can provide on site.
“I’m coming at it from a skills perspective. The health comes in then and the food literacy, but it’s about giving them the skills to cook,” she says.
The classes are funded via a mix of State funding, school payments and private business sponsorships.
“Deis schools really struggle with funding and they are the schools we want to be in. It’s about trying to lift children out of food insecurity. You’re trying to give those kids the skills so that when they are teenagers they can do a bit more for themselves, especially when maybe their parents can’t.”
Schools and parents have told Davenport that some children in her classes have become more vocal and developed stronger fine motor skills. Some have learned to use a knife for the first time.
Yvonne Fleming, senior manager for Crosscare Community Services on Dublin’s Portland Row, says she has seen an increasing number of working people who need food supports.
Crosscare offers a food parcel collection and does work in Finglas, Jobstown and Portland Row, where there is also a community cafe.
In the Crosscare cafe, open from Monday to Friday, clients can buy a three-course meal for €5. Last year the cafe served 12,500 low-cost meals.
“We have a range of people eating here; some are older and retired people who might come in from other areas as they have free travel with the bus pass,” says Fleming.
“We also are seeing younger people who are in jobs. They are coming in wearing lanyards ... We are dealing with more families with two incomes [who are] not able to make ends meet.”
Fleming says clients are assigned a case worker who assesses their income, outgoings, loans and energy payments, trying to find savings. The clients can access free food and household items, but the “aim is to get them back on their feet”.
“For some it’s a four-week relationship; for some it’s longer,” she says.
One father says he contacted Crosscare six months ago having already used food parcels for about two years. “My partner wasn’t able to work, and we had two small children in school. We were behind on rent, had a credit union loan, and struggled to afford necessities,” says the man, who does not want to be named. This put a strain on his relationships, but the provision of food and help with budgeting made a significant difference, he says. With Crosscare’s advice he switched energy provider, restructured loans, got a medical card and secured social welfare for his partner. “Within months, we could afford our own food shop. I can’t describe how much stress I was under at that time,” he says.
Anne Fitzgerald, chief executive of the Liffey Partnership community organisation in Ballyfermot, says the demand for food supports has “massively increased”, with people now living on less money.
Liffey Partnership, which delivers programmes aimed at reducing poverty and promoting social inclusion, conducted research into food poverty in the Ballyfermot and Cherry Orchard areas of Dublin in 2024 and 2025. It found a food poverty rate of 43.3 per cent, nearly five times higher than the State average. More than two in five people in the community said they were experiencing food poverty.
“We were shocked that in such a wealthy country people are choosing to heat their house or eat,” she says, adding that the research came before the war in Iran pushed up the price of fuel and energy. “We hear this phrase ‘heat or eat’ from many people, especially the elderly. And there’s a lot of worry about this coming autumn and winter.”
The Liffey Partnership study mapped the areas’ supermarkets, convenience stores, takeaways, food banks and services.
“In Cherry Orchard the research found a large proportion of people haven’t a supermarket within one mile of where they live. Many don’t have cars... They end up buying groceries in smaller convenience shops, which are much more expensive,” says Fitzgerald.
“There’s this narrative that if people knew better they would do better. But the truth is that more people just have less money; they are struggling and having to make choices.”
The Liffey Partnership and several other community groups recently formed the Dublin 10 Food Alliance, which has plans to open a community kitchen for cooking classes and shared meals. It is also looking at developing a community-owned grocery shop.
“We have some funding from HSE and other departments but we are in the early stages ...We talk about child poverty but no child has control over money; this is about family poverty and family income, which is not now enough to meet needs,” says Fitzgerald.
One client of the Liffey Partnership, who does not want to be named, says she began struggling after having a baby and having to stop work. “Food prices started going up and gas and electricity went up. I used to do prepay electricity. That was €20 a week and that went up to €50/€60,” she says.
The mother of two does one big weekly shop for about €100. “All the healthy food I find is really expensive. Meat has gone through the roof so I don’t buy that, but I get frozen stuff.“ She says it was hard to ask for help from a food bank. ”So many people are going through what I am going through. I don’t think the Government understands one tiny bit. They don’t see people struggling.”

title: Irish hopefuls racing for Premier League money at Kentucky Downs
description: Former Champion Hurdle winner Constitution Hill takes on stiffest flat task to date at Kempton
content:
Willie Mullins ’s Breeders’ Cup champion Ethical Diamond lines up in Grade Two company in Kentucky on Saturday night, although he and two other Irish hopefuls on the card are racing for Premier League prize money.
Ethical Diamond will have Ryan Moore on board in the $2-million Turf Cup at the Kentucky Downs track, just 40 minutes north of Nashville. The race is off at 9.56pm Irish time and will be shown live on Sky.
America’s only all-turf course has been snootily likened to a point-to-point, but thanks to Casino gaming terminals and local development funds it financially operates in a different league to most other tracks.
Seven days of action in less than a fortnight is worth up to $37 million. Saturday night’s highlight, the Grade Two Nashville Derby (off at 10.36pm Irish time), featuring Aidan O’Brien ’s Causeway and his son Joseph ’s Nil Bua Gan Dua, is worth up to $3 million. Only the Kentucky Derby is worth more in the US in terms of three-year-old races.
In trying to promote Kentucky-bred horses, the full prize funds are only open to horses bred in the Bluegrass State. It leaves the Irish-bred Causeway and Nil Bua Gan Dua to compete for $1.75 million. Ethical Diamond is also Irish bred, making the full $2 million out of reach, but Mullins still has his sights on the reduced $500,000 first prize, as well as confirmed entry into the Breeders’ Cup.
The action takes place over the US Labor Day weekend, with Kentucky Downs offering a staggering $18 million in purses over three days. However, Saturday’s proceedings could have a very Irish stamp.
Causeway is a local 5-2 morning line favourite. Moore rides the colt, who finished last in July’s Grand Prix de Paris but won Royal Ascot’s King Edward VII Stakes. Joseph O’Brien has booked US-based Irish jockey Ben Curtis for the Gowran Listed winner Nil Bua Gan Dua. Curtis shared the 2010 apprentice jockeys’ title with O’Brien and Gary Carroll.
Ethical Diamond is behind local star Burnham Square in the betting, although the combination of Mullins and Moore, riding at Kentucky Downs for the first time, could help switch that around.
“He’s coming right at the right time. We’re happy with how he’s travelled, and he’s training very well at Churchill Downs,” Mullins told local media. Not surprisingly considering the horse’s hurdling experience, Mullins isn’t worried about the undulating course either. “I think he’s very adaptable, the track doesn’t concern me. I thought the track would be an asset for him.”
Ethical Diamond will be Mullins’s first runner at Kentucky Downs, but it won’t be his first experience of the course. In 1990, he accompanied Grabel, trained by his father Paddy, to the venue when it was known as Duelling Grounds, with Tony Mullins guiding the mare to victory.
Closer to home, the mixing of codes will be front and centre at Kempton on Saturday, when the 2023 Champion Hurdle winner Constitution Hill has a third start on the flat. Winner of his two starts earlier in the year, the outstanding jumper whose jumping fell apart climbs several levels in quality for the Group Three September Stakes.
Such is the level of popular engagement with Nicky Henderson’s star that he’s been heavily backed to win a race won twice previously by Enable and top-notch flat talent in Giavellotto and Kalpana in the last two years. However, he’s holds an official rating of 101, the lowest of the seven runners, and is over a stone inferior to the German Group One winner Tornado Alert.
It means Saturday’s Group One highlight, the eight-runner Betfair Haydock Sprint Cup, is being elbowed for profile.
Last year’s winner Big Mojo will try for a rare double in the six-furlong heat, which is without an Irish runner. Royal Ascot winner Almeraq dominated the betting this week ahead of King Of Blue, who possesses an unwanted race double of his own having finished runner-up for the last two years.
Soft ground will be something of a novelty for these sprinters this season, and Marvelman’s proven seven-furlong stamina on testing conditions make him look a likely contender to be staying on strongly at the end for Irish rider PJ McDonald.

title: Pat Leahy: Your guide to the four basic camps in Irish politics
description: How these political forces negotiate the great tides of the age will determine the country’s future, for good or ill
content:
P olitics is inching its way back to business after the summer break. The Cabinet had its first meeting in a month, even if the agenda was less than jammers. Ministers are back at their desks, although Leinster House will remain quiet for another week and a half before the Dáil returns.
The European presidency is in full swing again, with meetings of EU ministers in Druids Glen on Tuesday and Wednesday, and in Dublin on Thursday and Friday. The think-ins have begun, with the Labour Party gathering in Galway on Thursday and Friday, an event graced by no less celestial a presence than Michael D himself. Fianna Fáil is in Tullamore next Monday; Sinn Féin in Malahide on Wednesday; Fine Gael in Gorey on Thursday; the Greens in Dublin on Friday. So, so much to look forward to.
Soon, those of us who watch politics closely will be buried in the day-to-day and the week-to-week ups and downs. But often the ebb and flow, the who’s up, who’s down of those episodes proves to be ephemeral, leaving little lasting impact or legacy. Big changes in politics tend to be the result of big forces. So it’s timely, perhaps, for some bird’s-eye-view consideration of the state of Irish politics and the disposition of its forces.
There are essentially four basic camps in Irish politics. How they conduct themselves internally, how they interact with each other externally and how they navigate the broader social, economic and political currents of the age will determine the future shape of Irish politics and who will turn out to be its winners and losers.
The first camp is the largest in Irish politics by some distance, and consists of Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael. They are assuredly different parties and will remain so (just ask their members). But they make up the same political force, largely agreeing on all big policy areas and sharing the same centrist, consensual, statist outlook.
They are also generally serious in their pursuit of power and their determination to retain it. They are in government together because they realised that this was the only way to retain power – by sharing it, rather than periodically swapping it. They are the largest camp because they have been successful in attuning themselves to the desires and tolerances of the Irish voter. This leads to the obvious charge that they are more interested in being in power than in using it.
They remain each other’s keenest electoral rivals and most willing coalition allies. It is a complicated relationship, and it is not at its most harmonious right now. But both parties know their most likely and congenial route to power remains with the other. For all the squabbling, they will not lose sight of that.
The second camp is Sinn Féin, alone. It is by far the largest opposition party, the largest party on the island and the only possible leader of a left-wing government. That is an important factor when so many voters favour an alternative to the status quo.
Unlike many other parties, Sinn Féin does not have natural coalition allies – see how the so-called Connolly coalition ( which elected the President last year) fell apart in the Dáil in the first half of this year. The centre-left is nervous of Sinn Féin’s turn to the right on immigration, and Labour, cursed with having a memory of Irish history, has residual doubts.
In 2024, having led the polls by a country mile for three years, Sinn Féin experienced an astonishing collapse in support before the local and European elections, unlike anything seen in Irish politics since the demise of Fianna Fáil in 2010. It is true that the party rebounded in the second half of 2024 and recovered a lot of ground in the general election. But it still came third. The awful sense that the party had blown a historic opportunity was unavoidable, and it is not clear if the party has really understood or learned from what happened. The party continues like it is 2019. But it isn’t.
The third camp is the rest of the left: Labour, the Social Democrats, the Greens, some independents. It is, to be sure, a disparate gang, but drawing largely from the same section of the electorate and so are each other’s deadliest electorate rivals, and most natural allies for government. They believe much the same things and want to achieve the same goals, but have proved incapable or uninterested in articulating a way to achieve them. In the post-election coalition scramble now inevitable in Irish politics, none of them seriously sought participation in government in 2024; Labour haven’t done so since 2011; the Soc Dems have never done it. That is probably no longer sustainable. Whether they can co-operate to govern remains an open question. But if they can’t, what’s the point of them?
The fourth camp is everyone else: independents who may or may not be available for government formation; Independent Ireland, Aontú, the far-right outside parliament and the radical left within it in the shape of People Before Profit. The last two bring energy and noise, but are not serious about being in government. They are over-represented in our political discourse and are the weakest of the four big camps. Although, they can influence the future direction of the country, for example, through the fuel protests, or on migration policy, or in the way that People Before Profit pushed Sinn Féin into opposition to water charges a decade ago.
How these political forces interact with one another, and how they manage to negotiate the great tides of the age – economic, political, military, social, demographic and climate – will determine the country’s future, for good or ill.

title: Exports of alumina to Russia must stop
description: We cannot condemn Russia’s bombing of Ukraine while supplying it with a strategic raw material
content:
Sir, – Ireland continues to export alumina to Russia while Russian missiles and drones rain down on Ukrainian cities. Remarkably, these exports have increased significantly since 2022. (“ Aughinish Alumina’s exports to Russia continue to rise ”, September 1st).
Alumina produces aluminium, a strategic material widely used in missiles, rockets and drones. The Government’s exercise in tracing holding companies, ownership structures and ultimate recipients bears little relationship to the reality: the alumina is going to Russia, where Ireland cannot control its ultimate use.
Meanwhile, Ireland bears the environmental cost of producing it, including vast quantities of potentially hazardous bauxite residue beside the Shannon Estuary.
We cannot condemn Russia’s bombing of Ukraine while supplying it with a strategic raw material. The Irish Government should stop these exports now. – Yours, etc,

title: At least Patrick Collison is trying to help in whatever way he can
description: He isn’t just patching it with plaster and praying it won’t go pear-shaped
content:
Sir, – Sinéad O’Sullivan queries Patrick Collison’s “democratic mandate” and criticises his attempt to help redirect the future of Europe’s political economy. (“ Europe does not need Patrick Collison to `fix’ it ”, Opinion, September 3rd).
One would think citizenship is a sufficient mandate to offer an opinion on Europe’s ills. When Collison’s successes in commerce and in providing employment opportunities are taken into account, perhaps, even if he does not have a “mandate” sufficient for The Irish Times, he is in a good position to offer opinions on Europe’s political economy, its ills and to suggest remedies.
A liberal democrat might debate the opinions offered rather than the contrived requirement of mandates. Otherwise, opinions from well-intentioned individuals can be strangled before birth. I hope Collison is not inhibited or prohibited from offering his opinions on matters that interest him in the future: surely not!
Indeed, pot and kettle come to mind if a mandate is a requirement for publishing an opinion. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Reading Sinead O’Sullivan’s article on Patrick Collison and the Rhine Group, I fundamentally disagree with the sentiment that “Patrick Collison has no democratic or institutional mandate, and yet here he is attempting to help redirect the future of Europe’s political economy”.
Our TDs and Ministers (who have a democratic mandate, and a duty to serve our citizens), whether domestically or within Europe, are pathetically failing to do anything but “kick the can down the road”. Their only concern seems to be being re-elected and rising to political greatness within their party (for those affiliated with political parties).
Over the past decade, since Ireland fully recovered from the economic crash, successive Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael led governments have failed to grasp the nettle and make tough and unpleasant political decisions to invest properly in infrastructure, leading to continuing and burgeoning crises in housing, health, transport, education, defence, climate, utilities and pretty much any other ministry you care to mention.
If any employee at Stripe looked after their responsibility as badly as our “democratically elected” officials (and in many cases, our senior civil servants who reflect “tone from the top”), they’d be fired without argument. At least Collison is trying to help in whatever way he can, rather than “patching it with sticking plaster” and praying it won’t go pear-shaped “on my watch”. – Yours, etc,

title: Pat Gilroy on the GAA’s future
description: ‘Interesting to note his scepticism towards modern and more scientific preparations’
content:
Sir – I read with interest in last Saturday’s Irish Times, Pat Gilroy’s views on the future of the GAA (Why are we so wedded to the county system – a British system: Pat Gilroy on the GAA’s future, Sports Weekend, August 29th). As one of the foremost thinkers within the association his observations were quite wide-ranging.
Among many talking points, it was interesting to note his scepticism towards modern and more scientific preparations now availed of by several club teams and the ensuing contribution to their development and success.
Having watched at first hand many games at varying grades over recent seasons, I have noted a vast improvement in the overall standards on display. Today’s players are fitter, more athletic and focused while possessing no mean level of skill sets when compared with their counterparts from even the recent past. They also have a life.
A higher standard of fare and entertainment now prevails. The sciences and the programmes they provide are having a positive outcome here. The present-day Junior B player (Gilroy’s term) no longer fits the old stereotype of a “have boots will travel” attitude.
If this cohort shows the same advancement at the administration table as they have shown on the pitch, then Gilroy’s fears for the future can be allayed. The leadership of Gaelic games will be in good hands. - Yours, etc,

title: Tenant ordered out of home after incident involving woman ‘dangling’ from balcony
description: Eviction notice and warnings issued over antisocial complaints included robbery at ‘knife point’ and breeding puppies
content:
A tenant has been ordered to vacate a property following a “serious incident” involving a woman who had been “dangling” from his apartment balcony in Dublin .
Tenant Myles Bryan was given 21 days to vacate the apartment at River Gardens, Glasnevin Hill, Dublin 9, after a Residential Tenancies Board ( RTB ) tribunal heard of various complaints of antisocial behaviour, including that he was “breeding puppies” at the property.
John Copeland, an employee for the owner management company and witness for the landlord, Focus Housing Association, told the tribunal that gardaí responded to a “serious incident” in September 2024.
Copeland said a woman was “dangling off the balcony” of Bryan’s apartment, claiming there had been a “violent argument with blood in various areas”.
The tribunal heard the woman was “trying to escape” from an upper floor window “only to be pulled back by a male occupant”, according to a tribunal report published this week.
Bryan said he had guests at his home that night who had been drinking. He said both he and a woman had been assaulted and his then girlfriend “tried to jump over the balcony”.
He said he tried to prevent this and his neighbours reported the incident. Bryan said he was arrested and brought to Ballymun Garda station and subsequently to the hospital.
Focus Housing Association issued a warning notice, giving Bryan 90 days to remedy antisocial behaviour. It ultimately served an eviction notice in November 2024 due to “ongoing” antisocial behaviour, giving him until December 12th to vacate.
The complaints on the notice related to an incident involving the “use of a weapon”.
Copeland told the tribunal a local shop had been “robbed at knife point” in October 2024. He said Bryan had been witnessed returning to the property afterwards, but was not seen again for several months.
Bryan told the tribunal he had left the apartment for a period “sometime after the robbery” and that he returned in July or August 2025.
During a hearing in April, Bryan accepted he had been involved in the robbery, saying he was “not in the right frame of mind” at the time. He told the tribunal he had a “difficult upbringing and background”.
Previous warnings had been made, including in 2023 when Copeland said he discovered Bryan had been “breeding puppies” in the apartment. He told the tribunal there was visible dog faeces alongside urine “seeping” through the floor to the apartment below.
Copeland believed the puppies were “dangerous” breeds, saying the Irish Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals ( ISPCA ) removed them.
He also described “a lot of partying” at Bryan’s apartment, resulting in noise complaints, alleging there had been a “general pattern of behaviour with the loud music, dog breeding and violence”.
Kevin White, Dublin housing manager at Focus Housing Association, said a colleague wrote to Bryan in August 2025 telling him he was overholding and that he continued to have a dog of a “restricted breed”.
Bryan told the tribunal he moved out of the apartment when the notice of termination was served but had retained the keys, which he said he did not wish to return.
He said he continued to pay rent and wished to return to the apartment, saying he had been “couch surfing” since.
The tribunal said it was satisfied that Bryan’s behaviour constituted antisocial behaviour and deemed the notice of termination to be valid.
Given he had been on notice of termination since November 2024, it gave him 21 days to give up vacant possession of the apartment.

title: ‘It’s only starting’: Richie Murphy committed to driving Ulster on to new level
description: Developing homegrown talent and staying true to the province’s roots key to Murphy’s goal
content:
Tall timber, the indigenous variety. Cormac Izuchukwu, Joe Hopes and Jude Postlethwaite climb in and out of cars. The imported kind. Ben Donnell, Irish-qualified, who recently arrived from Cardiff, can play either backrow or secondrow. Watching on, it’s a human version of a furling and unfurling process.
For a fleeting moment the land of Brobdingnag from Jonathan Swift’s Gulliver’s Travels springs to mind rather than the staff car park at the Affidea Stadium in Belfast . Relating the encounters to Ulster head coach Richie Murphy soon after, a chuckle escapes as he lists the heights and weights of his first-choice backline.
There will be few, if any, bigger/taller/heavier midfields in world rugby than Stuart McCloskey and Postlethwaite, while wings Rob Baloucoune, Jacob Stockdale and Zac Ward are outsize in stature, too. Hulking physiques are not a prerequisite as Jack Murphy and Mikey Lowry are also key constituents.
The snapshot in time offers a reminder of Ulster’s recruitment process during the summer, with an emphasis on bolstering the front five in the pack. Iain Henderson’s ongoing injury woe directed Ulster towards South African Eli Snyman, who has signed from Benetton.
The secondrow is a proven performer in the URC , a lineout technician who can assist in developing tyros Hopes, Charlie Irvine and Harry Sheridan. Tighthead props Argentinian Eduardo Bello and Keynan Knox, once of Munster, and Donnell, explosively quick and who can play across the back five of the pack, are other new faces.
James McNabney, who was due to tour Georgia and Portugal with Ireland last year before tearing his ACL in training, is back, while former Ireland under-20 hooker Henry Walker has been promoted to the senior squad following John Andrew’s departure. Martin Moloney, who spent time at Leinster and more recently Exeter, can cover all three backrow spots.
Scrumhalf Matthew Devine and wing Chay Mullins have joined from Connacht; Irish-qualified Jamie Benson will compete with Jack Murphy for the 10 jersey, even though the ex-Harlequins can play centre and fullback too, while Daniel Hawkshaw, who previously played under-20s for Ulster, has been recruited following Stewart Moore’s ACL tear. Aitzol Arenzana-King has progressed from the academy.
There is a new face in the coaching team: former All Black Clark Dermody takes over the forwards after Jimmy Duffy switched to Munster to be closer to his family in Galway.
“ Our coaching team had been very tight and very small. Most of us have worked together with the Irish 20s group,” says Murphy. ”There was an opportunity to bring someone in from outside, hear and see different ways.
“He’s [Dermody] been excellent, fitted in well, a good personality and a lovely person. If he doesn’t like something, everyone will know that he doesn’t agree with it. He’s a nice edge to him, an extremely strong forwards coach, [especially] around the scrum. Again, that’s an area of our game that we need to improve in. He’s been a good asset in that regard.”
Pushing the set-piece discussion of new personnel to one side, does Murphy feel that he’s changed as a coach from the one that presided over the most successful period in the history of the Ireland under-20s? He took the job on an interim basis in February 2024, before being appointed to the position that May.
He managed to work his way through the initial state of chaos, and, while there was some bruising along the way, he’s guided Ulster into a healthier, stronger position, even to the cusp of silverware, only to be denied by Montpellier in last season’s Challenge Cup final.
The team plays a hugely entertaining brand of rugby. “I don’t think I’ve changed a huge amount,” says Murphy. “If you look at the way our coaching team has formed, with Mark [Sexton] as attack coach, Willie [Falloon] as defence coach, Clark [now] looks after our forwards, Dan Soper fills a few holes around different areas as well as being our kicking and skills coach and helps with the transition of young players coming up. We’re very much a coaching team.
“I’m very collaborative in relation to how we do things. I don’t feel that I need to have all the answers. I’ve got experts in the room in their fields and what we do is bounce ideas off each other. That’s the way I did things with the 20s.
“I don’t think I’ve changed much in my personality. When I was with my 20s, I didn’t have to rule with an iron fist. It’s not my way. I think it’s important as a coach that you are who you are, because if you try to be someone different, you’ll get caught out pretty quick.
“It takes a little bit to get me angry, but if I do, I have a side to me that I can use that. We try to hold our players accountable for their performance, and for what they do during the week. Those conversations don’t need to be really harsh. They can be whatever way they need to be. I don’t feel like I’ve changed; what you see is what you get.”
He’s settled nicely in Belfast and recently moved to the Ballyhack area. He and his wife Steph still have a lodger. Murphy smiles: “You mean, Jack,” his son, Ulster’s outhalf. “Jack uses the house. We get a visitor every now and again from Connacht,” he adds, referencing his other son, Ben, capped for Ireland on the summer tour last year and currently contracted with the western province.
Murphy admits the dynamic is “hard for two games a year”, when Ulster player Connacht, “as you’re looking at your son and want him to do well.” But, he adds, “you want to beat the team that he’s playing for; make no bones about it. We talk all the time. Daily, mostly. If he’s having problems or he needs some support, he knows where to come and get some advice.”
Murphy is an inveterate watcher of rugby matches, not all strictly relevant to the job. “Like my poor wife understands, rugby is a huge part of our family. My uncle [Johnny Murphy] played for Ireland. My mum and dad would have followed me in rugby from when I was a kid. That hasn’t changed. Even in our extended family, rugby is a big part of who we are.”
Given a coach’s eye and an encyclopedic knowledge, what rugby trends does he anticipate in the coming season, and how does he want Ulster to evolve? “The game is getting looser, scorelines are getting higher, and I think we’re favouring the attacking team a little bit more.
“International rugby is slightly different from club rugby. The different leagues have different ways of playing. People are trying to make rugby more entertaining for the crowds.
“We want to lean on the game you’ve already seen. We’re not going to change everything. We were quite low in relation to our kicking game in URC. We will try and balance that out, try to become a little bit more unpredictable.
“Everyone talks about do you play through a team? Do you play around a team? Do you play over a team? The more problems you can cause for your opposition, the tougher you will be to stop.”
Murphy is self-deprecating and sees his role as a facilitator to enable the team and the players to be at their best. “I don’t worry about me; I worry about the team. I worry about our team performing at the best level they can. My importance within this organisation is minimal, in my opinion.
“My goal is to make sure that they’re improving and moving in the right direction. We want to be a smart rugby team. We want to play fast. We want to be dynamic. We want to have an air of abrasiveness around how we are in that contact area.
“I remember coming up to Ulster as a player, whether it be at club level or underage. You always felt when you played against an Ulster team that physically they were at it. We want to make sure that we keep that as part of the DNA and build on it.”
The development of young talent within the province is a priority. Murphy prefers players to work hard to filter through the system from provincial talent squads to national talent squads to the academy. It’s the application of pressure, but with support, a process that calcifies the potential.
Down the M1 in Dublin, there are superior numbers and greater depth of quality in that sector. But Ulster must continue to chip away, trying to ensure the best in the province compare favourably with their contemporaries elsewhere in the country. If there is a shortfall, then Murphy will draw from beyond the province.
“It’s important that we get the Ulster ones, but it’s also important that we have a vision that we’re a professional rugby team, one of four professional rugby teams in the country and that an Irish player doesn’t have to be born in Ulster [to play here].
“We have to spread our wings and make sure that we’re picking up the talent that we need in order to supply the senior team with the best players.”
Joe Schmidt will play a part in that process. He’s in week two of three in his block of visits in his role as a coach development advisor. “He’s been getting out into the different schools and looking at the age-grade system, trying to give us some recommendations in relation to what we can do.
“If you think about Joe Schmidt teams, what they tend to have is brilliant basics and there’s no magic pill for developing coaches or developing young players. It’s about doing the basics really well and he will drive that into the directors of rugby, who then will hopefully spread the gospel through the schools.
“Dan Soper is working in that area as well to make sure that the things that we’re talking about are done on a weekly basis. They’ll answer to him in relation to the Ulster way, and how we want to try and drive those schools. There is a decent connection being built. It’s in its infancy, but everyone has to start somewhere.
“Joe’s responsibility within that is to see, report back, come up with a plan about how we help develop those coaches so that you can spread the word a little bit better. Having Joe Schmidt here is also good for us as a coaching team because he’s got a really good, critical eye.”
Given the starting point, Murphy’s tenure has been laudable to this point. He claims it’s still early doors. He is ambitious, but Ulster is his priority and sole focus.
“I know what I want, but I’m very settled here in relation to this project that we’re building. It’s not anywhere near over; if anything, it’s only starting. Trying to drive this forward is my immediate and most important thing.
“My ambitions for where I want to get after that sit in the background. But I am ambitious; I want to be the best coach I can be.”

title: Schooling the Brits at taxpayers’ expense
description: Bewildering as to why we should be providing a publicly funded element of the secondary education of affluent British families
content:
Sir, - A number of British newspapers have reported that some private schools in Ireland are actively marketing themselves to British parents seeking to avoid the UK’s recently introduced VAT on school fees.
Indeed, one private school in Dublin states on its website that “Ireland’s subsidised education system allows us to offer a world-class education and premium facilities at less than half the cost of UK independent boarding schools”.
It is at best difficult to understand why Irish taxpayers should be providing a publicly funded element of the secondary education of affluent British families. At worst it is a scandalous use of public money. - Yours, etc.,

title: Disastrous consequences of climate breakdown right in front of us
description: You’d think encouraging public transport usage to reduce  gridlock would be motivating enough
content:
Sir, - After delivering business fuel subsidies and deferring tax increases earlier this year, the Government has now announced an increase in public transport fares.
At a time when the disastrous consequences of climate breakdown are already playing out in front of us, and the UN is issuing desperate warnings to encourage action, Ireland appears to have done a complete policy U-turn and is now in full reverse on tackling our emissions.
If preserving the safety of our own existence was not a sufficiently strong argument for Government to aggressively reduce emissions, you would think that encouraging public transport usage to reduce the sorry gridlock of our cities would be motivating enough.

title: Vaccine sceptics do not have ‘fringe beliefs’
description: Scepticism is, arguably, more important now than ever
content:
Sir, – Kathy Sheridan describes vaccine sceptics as having “fringe beliefs” (“ Spare a thought for families of Covid conspiracy theorists ”, Opinion, September 2nd). Not so.
When one considers the following quotes from present and former editors of prestigious medical journals, then one cannot consider vaccine scepticism as being a fringe belief.
Dr Marcia Angell, former editor of The New England Journal of Medicine in The New York Review of Books, January 15th, 2009: “It is simply no longer possible to believe much of the clinical research that is published, or to rely on the judgment of trusted physicians or authoritative medical guidelines. I take no pleasure in this conclusion, which I reached slowly and reluctantly over my two decades as an editor of The New England Journal of Medicine.”
Dr Richard Horton, editor of The Lancet since 1995, in The Lancet on April 11th, 2015: “The case against science is straightforward: much of the scientific literature, perhaps half, may simply be untrue. Afflicted by studies with small sample sizes, tiny effects, invalid exploratory analyses, and flagrant conflicts of interest, together with an obsession for pursuing fashionable trends of dubious importance, science has taken a turn towards darkness.”
Scepticism is, arguably, more important now than ever. – Yours, etc,

title: Adam Olaniyan: Jobstown heavyweight dreams of undisputed success and becoming a cowboy
description: The 20-year-old will fight on the undercard at Katie Taylor’s Croke Park homecoming
content:
Adam Olaniyan was just 13 when he won a European gold medal for the first time as an amateur boxer.
Instead of soaking in that feeling or bragging about it, he recalls being sat down by his father for a serious conversation about his future. “He sat me down and he said, ‘Look, you give your younger years to this game, you give your 20s and you’ll have the rest of your life to enjoy. What’s the point of going to parties, going out with friends and missing training, missing competitions and fights?’ I left that conversation and I asked myself: ‘Do I want mediocrity?’”
After that pep talk Olaniyan put his gold medal in a drawer and hasn’t taken it out since.
That’s a pretty heavy conversation and realisation for a 13-year-old kid, but now, at 20, Olaniyan is mature for his age, and has Irish, European and world amateur titles to show for his dedication.
The Jobstown heavyweight fights on the undercard of Katie Taylor ’s Croke Park homecoming on Saturday, his fourth fight as a professional, having won his first three by knockout.
It’s perfect for Olaniyan, who has always idolised Taylor and has a personal connection with her too. Taylor and Olaniyan share a manager in Brian Peters, and she accompanied him when he went looking for a professional gym, eventually settling on the Everton Red Triangle in Liverpool.
She also gave him a pair of gloves to mark the start of his professional career. “She took the gloves out of her bag and gave them to me and said, ‘I hope they serve you well’ ... She’s just a gem. She’s one of the best people ever, ever, ever.”
He also says she gives him little pieces of advice on his career, helping him to stay grounded. If Olaniyan needs grounding, though, he need only look back to his home community in Jobstown who have been supportive of him throughout his amateur days and now as a professional.
[ Before Katie Taylor’s farewell, the undercard fighters get their night at Croke Park Opens in new window ]
“When I go home after fights to see my parents, little kids from the area come up and ask for photos. I was that little kid at one point, when Robbie Keane would come back to Tallaght ... now I have young kids coming up to me asking for photos, asking me when I’m fighting.”
“‘I watched you on the telly,’ they go around saying ‘he’s on the telly’,” he laughs. “It’s the place that raised me, so I don’t want to forget it.”
Phone calls from schoolteachers are the last thing parents want, but his mam recently got a call from a former principal to say how proud they were of their former student.
Not that he would have been getting into much trouble back in those days anyway. He describes his schoolboy self as “very shy. Very, very shy.” Olaniyan now comes across as chatty, thoughtful and good-humoured in his interviews, and he knows he’s come on a lot since then.
“I hated speaking, I hated doing presentations, I hated all of that stuff. I don’t know where this has come from, but now I love speaking, I love talking to people, meeting new people.
“For the longest time I can remember, I was the shyest person, proper awkward,” he says, laughing again.
One memory of being a little more outspoken as a kid was thanks to the inspiration of boxing’s greatest icon: Muhammad Ali . Olaniyan will be the first heavyweight to fight at Croke Park since “The Greatest” and will also be wearing a specially designed Everlast replica of Ali’s kit from that night in 1972.
“I got the kit this morning, and it was a proud moment for myself. For me as a kid ... wanting to be just like him. I cut my hair like him, I’d go around saying ‘I am the greatest!’ I’d try and be like him as much as I could.”
One way he is hoping to differ from Ali is by having a shorter career, though. He admits to not having many hobbies, focusing his whole life on becoming undisputed heavyweight champion, but also says his ideal career path would be “five, six years. Heavyweight champion of the world. Live on a ranch in Texas.”
When pressed a little on this unusual dream, he says, “When I was a kid, I always said I wanted to be a cowboy. So when I retire from boxing, I’m going to get a ranch in Texas, a couple of horses, few cows, few dogs, few sheep – whatever’s on a ranch – big ol’ house, and just barbecue steaks every night.”
It’s certainly a unique goal for a prizefighter, but if Olaniyan can execute the first dream of unifying the heavyweight titles, it would put him alongside Katie Taylor at the top of Ireland’s boxing history.
Olaniyan faces Czechia’s heavyweight Matej Hudak on the undercard, who is 6ft 2in, with all six of Hudak’s wins coming by knockout in the first round.

title: McGuire vs Maguire: Who was the real Irish founder of America’s Labor Day?
description: A longstanding historical debate highlights the extent of Irish involvement in the American labour movement
content:
L abor Day will draw the final curtain on a historic New York summer in which the Knicks lifted their championship hex, and the World Cup circus came rumbling into town. After months of bonhomie, New Yorkers are afforded one final day of rest before the dreaded return to routine.
Unlike most of the world, which celebrates its workers’ holiday on the first of May, the US takes its repose on the first Monday of September – at the end rather than the beginning of summer. What may first appear to be another case of American exceptionalism, is in fact, rooted in the rich history of Irish labour activism.
As the US rapidly industrialised in the 19th century, the mass influx of immigrants helped shape its growing labour movement. While Germans, Italians and Jews often brought socialist and anarchist ideas, Irish immigrants tended to carry on the traditions of agrarian land activism that had been cultivated under British rule.
The infamous Pennsylvania coal strikes of the 1870s highlighted the strength of this connection, with as many as 20 alleged members of the Molly Maguires – a secret society that had originated in Ireland – later executed for their involvement.
Meanwhile, in the industrial cities Irish immigrants became a cornerstone of America’s working class. Irish workers helped organise unions and led mass walkouts amid the struggle for expanded labour protections.
However, the growth of the American labour movement coincided with the decline of the so-called Gilded Age at the end of the 19th century. The Panic of 1893, an antecedent to the Great Depression, had caused mass unemployment, leading to labour strikes and widespread social unrest.
In New York, Peter J McGuire emerged as a leading figure in the burgeoning labour movement. The son of Irish immigrants, he is credited with organising the first Labor Day parade in New York in 1882. More than 10,000 workers marched in solidarity, demanding expanded workplace protections in a demonstration of union power.
During this period of economic uncertainty the labour movement increasingly shifted towards more racially exclusive membership policies. Unlike many other union leaders, McGuire advocated for “fraternity among the working people regardless of creed, colour, nationality or politics”.
With the holiday approaching its 144th anniversary, American labour is enjoying something of a resurgence
The popularity of Labor Day spread quickly across the country, with US president Grover Cleveland eventually signing the holiday into federal law almost 12 years later. Staunchly anti-labour, he had been instrumental in suppressing strikes. Just days after signing, he deployed federal troops against demonstrators during the Pullman railway strike in Chicago.
While clearly no friend of the unions, Cleveland’s embrace of Labor Day aimed to distance the US from associations with the May Day movement, which was gaining traction among socialists and anarchists across the world.
Nonetheless, soon after Cleveland signed Labor Day into law, a New Jersey paper published an op-ed entitled “Honor to whom honor is due”. It claimed that another Irish labour leader, Matthew Maguire, was in fact the “undisputed author” of the holiday.
The debate centres around the organisation of the parade, with the New Jersey Historical Society claiming that Maguire headed the procession after having gathered many of the estimated 10,000 marchers. Meanwhile, the American Federation of Labor cites a resolution by McGuire from earlier in the year, in which he proposed a street celebration.
Dissenters argue that Maguire’s more radical politics denied him rightful recognition as the father of Labor Day. Having secured the vice-president nomination for the Socialist Labour Party of America, he contested the 1896 election – a move unlikely to endear him to the political establishment.
As the 20th century wore on, McGuire appears to have gained the upper hand in the struggle for posthumous recognition. In 1952 the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America erected a memorial in his honour in New Jersey, which remains the site of an annual Labor Day commemoration. Meanwhile, Maguire’s reputed contributions continue to go largely unnoticed.
Historical debates aside, both men paved the way for future generations of Irish labour activists. Before his involvement in the Easter Rising, James Connolly had emerged as a leading figure in the New York labour movement, establishing the Irish Socialist Federation in 1907. Decades later in 1966, Mike Quill from Kerry etched himself into New York labour history when he led a successful 12-day transit strike, having helped unite black and Irish workers.
With the holiday approaching its 144th anniversary, American labour is enjoying something of a resurgence. Though public support for unions now nears the highs of the 1950s, the US’s comparatively weak labour laws continue to obstruct organising efforts, particularly in the private sector.
Though Labor Day’s provenance remains worth investigating, the two men’s collective legacy outweighs the importance of any lingering historical dispute. All of which is to say: what’s really in a name?

title: Is Belfast Agreement deficient around the Border poll question?
description: Clarity required over ‘what the people are actually finally voting for’
content:
Sir, – UK prime minister Andy Burnham ’s recent pronouncement on the constitutional future of Ireland reveals the core deficiency and imbalance at the heart of the Belfast Agreement.
In 1998, as Irish citizens across the island, in good faith, voted for the Agreement, and the compromises and ambiguities it contained, the power to initiate constitutional change would continue to be invested in whichever British MP holds the office of Secretary of State for Northern Ireland.
While the principle of consent was accepted by the Irish government in the Anglo-Irish agreement, was enshrined in the Downing Street Declaration and underpins the Belfast Agreement, there has been no equivalent “principle of agency” to determine explicitly how and when citizens in the North can determine their constitutional future.
If the principle of consent established who will decide the future of Northern Ireland, then there is a need for a parallel principle of agency to give citizens the power of determining when.
All the lessons of the Brexit referendum suggest the “how” in the Belfast Agreement is deficient by defining a singular, ultimate Border poll as the mechanism.
It is easy to consider a more managed, phased process triggered by a simple majority vote in the Northern Ireland Assembly followed by:
Such a process could, necessarily, take years but delivers greater clarity of “what the people are actually finally voting for”.
Such a mechanism removes the power for determining the “when” from the British Secretary of State and gives it to the people of Northern Ireland.
It delivers a principle of agency to rank beside the principle of consent.
Such a proposal should be on the table. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Michael McDowell is wrong to support Andy Burnham’s ill-advised comment that “a border poll is off the table” (“Burnham is right: poll should be off the table”, Opinion, September 2nd ).
The point is there is no conflict between working for reconciliation, between Northern Catholics and Northern Protestants and between North and South, and working out what sort of united Ireland has the best chance of producing a harmonious united state, with sectarian divisions confined to the past.
