“By making a book and creating order you are soothing the unconscious. Here is something which is coherent and chronological and it’s finished and it’s done ... Just the actual business of doing it is of benefit. The pressure to do it is partially driven by bewilderment.”
Gébler describes in almost forensic detail the last four years of O’Brien’s life. Her house in Chelsea is burgled. An unattended candle sets fire to her diningroom, whence the loss of her Eliot manuscript. A family of foxes invade her basement, leaving a trail of blood, faeces and half-eaten books. At age 92, O’Brien is thrown to the pavement by a revolving hospital door. Her bank makes errors, counting deposits as withdrawals.
[ Edna O’Brien: ‘She could be so queenly and dominating, but then totally wounded by criticism’ Opens in new window ]
“Life should be a bit easier at 90,” O’Brien writes to her son, who lives in Enniskillen, Co Fermanagh. “Instead it’s far more difficult.” A pattern sets in: O’Brien tells Gébler of some new setback, then follows with a cheerful message attempting to quell anxiety over her problems. She is still asserting her indomitability and her determination to keep going. “Time after time into the abyss she fell, and time after time she pulled herself out again.”
Gébler comes to understand that death “was less an event than a series of incremental reductions, with one capacity after another being taken away until at last, you came to the end – extinction”.
Recovering from a bad fall, O’Brien rages: “No one warns you about old age. No one tells you that your body falls apart.” The quotation provided the title for Gébler’s book, and exemplifies our denial about what de Gaulle called the shipwreck of old age. Most of us prefer to believe we can defy the laws of nature.
Of course, she knew, Gébler thinks. Hadn’t she read and reread the Beckett trilogy, Molloy, Malone Dies and The Unnamable?
In earlier decades, Gébler reflects, the world seemed to make sense. But in O’Brien’s last years, it reverted to 20 th century levels of brutality and absurdity. Though O’Brien was dying, “her political ire was undimmed”, he writes. “She loathed Trump and dreaded his victory over Biden ... She was deeply exercised by the sufferings of the Ukrainians and the Palestinians. She hated Putin and the Russian army, and she hated Netanyahu and the Israeli Defense Forces.”
O’Brien was capable of infectious gaiety, but one always sensed an undertow of sadness. “No politically, socially and culturally alert human being could live through the 20 th century and into the 21 st century without experiencing profound unhappiness,” Gébler says. “This is what it is to be alive.”
Mother and son transformed personal sorrows and the world’s dramas into the stuff of literature. She taught him the importance of remaining in touch with one’s unconscious while also “dealing with the insanity flooding in”. The writer, Gébler says, must face in two directions, inwards and outwards, Janus-like.
[ Blue Road - The Edna O’Brien Story review: Was Ireland this dire? It really was Opens in new window ]
When Edna O’Brien divorced Ernest Gébler, her ex-husband was initially given custody of Carlo and his younger brother Sasha. O’Brien would take the boys to the cinema, then cry through the film at the thought of their imminent separation. She took her ex-husband to court. A judge ordered the boys to state in writing which parent they wanted to live with. Ernest punished them by breaking off contact.
One does not recover from such memories, Gébler says. “You cannot magic away experience, because experience has formed part of the geology of your psyche ... The material of hurt is an inexhaustible source of creative material and creative energy.”
O’Brien and Gébler jokingly referred to themselves as Stakhanovites, after the legendary, hard-working Soviet miner. She had an almost mystical vision of the writer’s vocation, saying she could not live without writing. Gébler credits writing with keeping her alive so long.
When Gébler’s publisher asked him for a modern-day version of Boccaccio’s tales, he says: “I did nothing but eat, sleep and breathe The Decameron; I spoke to no one, and contacted no one. I just wrote and wrote and wrote. This obsessively singular, focused manner of writing was something I had seen my mother practise.”
O’Brien always kept a spiral notebook and purple ink pens to hand. She wrote at the hairdresser’s, in taxis, while waiting in restaurants. “If she wasn’t in full creative mode or flow then she would do other kinds of work, non-fiction and journalism,” Gébler says. “She was very protean.”
[ A Cold Eye by Carlo Gébler: A vivid and arresting diary as memoir Opens in new window ]
Gébler inherited not only his work ethic but his anxiety from O’Brien. “She was highly, highly anxious and spent – which goes back to childhood – every waking moment in a state of hyper-vigilance as she waited for whatever blow or catastrophe was going to descend on her head,” he says.
Gébler and his British wife Tyga visited O’Brien in January 2023. O’Brien, then 92, made certain the champagne was chilled in an ice bucket, that there were linen napkins and proper fish knives for the smoked salmon. Had their conversation been recorded, Gébler writes, “viewers would, I think, have decided that here were people gathered who weren’t talking about what they knew they ought to be talking about. And we weren’t”. It was impossible to talk about O’Brien’s impending death, he says.
O’Brien created beauty around her and took pride in her appearance, even in her 90s. “She was one of these people who believed, who was absolutely certain that at every moment, every hour through the day, your job was to make the world more beautiful ... The frock you wore, or the way you put the flowers into the vase, or the way you laid the table, it was all part of the same process: beautifying, improving, aestheticising,” Gébler says.
The last time Gébler visited O’Brien in London, he studied his unconscious mother’s hands, to imprint them in memory. “I uncurled the fingers of both and turned them palm up. In childhood I had loved her hands. They were very beautiful, small and smooth, lovely and capable.” He enumerates the marvellous things his mother could do with her hands: the fluency and quickness of her writing, the way “she muttered under her breath the lines she was writing ... as if she were giving herself dictation”. He recalled the way she set tables and cooked. “There was no end to the brilliant things she could do with her very beautiful and brilliant hands. And looking at them now I saw they were still the small and soft and very shapely hands with the same lines on the palms that I remembered from childhood.”
Grief plays tricks on the mind. On returning home from his last visit to O’Brien, Gébler discovers a hedgehog outside his study, the first he has seen in a quarter century. He feels certain that his mother has died and returned “as this beautiful little animal”.
In 1960s and 1970s London, in what O’Brien called her reckless period, she entertained lavishly. Her sons carried champagne up from the cellar and waited on rich and famous guests. After her death, Gébler imagines he will see her again, walking towards him in the street, or at “a composite of all the parties”. Two years after her death, she is still “a live and vivid presence” to him.
A thread of coincidence run poetically through the book. On July 27 th , 2025, Gébler arrived outside the borrowed apartment in Belgravia where his mother had died at 4.20pm, exactly one year to the minute after she passed away. “The universe has gone to some trouble to organise this, I thought.”
Gébler believes that through coincidence, the universe invites us to pay attention to patterns of meaning we would not otherwise observe. “We spend most of our lives not being conscious, mainly dreamy, not focused, and actually what the universe is demanding is absolute presence in the moment. And when you are, you begin to notice these coincidences. You need to be attuned to the world.”
[ Carlo Gébler on his mother Edna O’Brien: Coming to the end Opens in new window ]
Paradoxically for a writer who put so much autobiography into her fiction, Edna O’Brien was an intensely private person who jealously controlled her public image. Gébler did not tell her he was writing a book about her last years. How does he think she would have reacted?
“She would have wanted more jokes,” Gébler says. “She always wanted more jokes, more laughter.” He says she would not have minded him divulging the difficulties of her last years. “This is a historical record,” he says. “It’s obviously inadequate, because no record is ever sufficient. But there’s nothing in it that isn’t true. It’s not a celebrity memoir. It’s a book about what the effect of death is, which is a thing that we ought to pay a lot more attention to.”
No One Tells You - The Last Years of Edna O’Brien by Carlo Gébler is published by New Island

title: Edmund van Esbeck obituary: Highly respected rugby writer with encyclopedic knowledge of his sport
description: Passion for rugby shaped career of former Irish Times journalist but he also covered golf, had a love of hurling and was a lifelong Arsenal fan
content:
In his time as Irish Times rugby correspondent Edmund van Esbeck enjoyed an unparalleled influence; his standing among the primary constituents of rugby in Ireland − administrators, coaches, players and supporters – meant he had a greater reach and rapport than any of his contemporaries.
Ubiquitously known as Ned, he was born in Tramore , the youngest of seven children to Louis and Mary Josephine (née Walsh) and spent the first two-and-a-half years of his life in the Waterford seaside town.
He had three sisters, Constance, Eileen and Bridget, and three brothers, Phillip, Frank and Danny who died in childhood from scarlet fever. There is conjecture as to exactly where the family name originated but the agreed narrative is that his antecedents came from “the Dutch-Belgian border”.
Ned was inadvertently responsible for a change in the spelling of his family name from van Eesbeck to van Esbeck. The person who hand wrote his details on his birth certificate dropped an “e” So when it came time to get a passport, he had to keep the spelling van Esbeck. This contrasted with his brother Frank, also a journalist with The Irish Times and later the Irish Press, who spelt his name, van Eesbeck.
The family moved from Tramore to Sunday’s Well in Cork and then to Douglas. Ned was initially educated by the nuns at St Aloysius’ up until his Communion, after which he attended Presentation Brothers College, Cork, going through its doors for the first time in September 1940.
[ Former Irish Times rugby correspondent Edmund Van Esbeck dies aged 94 Opens in new window ]
He enjoyed his schooldays, showing a particular affinity for history, geography, English, Latin and sport. While his passion for rugby would predominantly shape his professional career, he also covered golf for a time and had a love for hurling – he won a juvenile medal with Blackrock in 1948 – and soccer. Truthfully, all sports.
He could rattle off the names of the legendary Cork hurling teams of the early 1940s but, as he said in a podcast several years ago, if he could be granted one sporting wish it would be to see Waterford win another All-Ireland hurling title before he died. Just to put this in context, this from a man whose house in Churchtown was called Highbury in homage to his beloved Arsenal.
Injury denied him an opportunity to play senior cup team rugby at Pres. The death of his father, Louis, from pneumonia at age 55, while Ned was in the latter years of secondary school, was a huge blow for the family, emotionally and financially.
Frank, in second-year medicine at UCC – he was honorary secretary of the rugby club – had to drop out of college because the family did not have the funds to support his studies. Ned took the well-travelled path to London – the antidote to the rife unemployment in late-1950s Ireland − and got a job in journalism at the Exchange Telegraph in Fleet Street, or Extel as it was known, a rival to the Press Association.
[ Edmund Van Esbeck was a giant of journalism whose influence transcended the rugby pages Opens in new window ]
He covered soccer primarily including the 1966 World Cup final and several FA Cup finals and when clearing out the attic his son Declan came across one of his father’s old address books that contained the phone numbers of England manager Alf Ramsay and players like Bobby and Jack Charlton, Bobby Moore, Jimmy Greaves and Roger Hunt.
He was very good friends with Brian Moore, the ITV soccer commentator and host of The Big Match. London also provided him with an even greater love than Arsenal as it was there that he met Mary Treacy, at a Legion of Mary event, whom he subsequently married. The couple later welcomed three children, Declan, Mary Katherine and Geraldine.
Ned was teetotal and had a deep Catholic faith. It wasn’t unusual for him to inveigle a colleague or two to attend Sunday Mass on rugby tours. He was rarely seen without his pipe – he only gave it up aged 89 after a bout of pneumonia – or a cup of tea.
He took over the rugby position at Extel after the previous incumbent moved into the sports editor’s role, but it was a call from his brother Frank, to whom he was very close, that proved pivotal to his career.
Frank informed his younger brother that The Irish Times was looking for a number two to Paul McWeeney, the rugby and golf correspondent. He got the job and eventually succeeded McWeeney, writing on both disciplines initially before concentrating on rugby. He retained that role until his retirement in 1997 but continued to write a rugby column for several years thereafter.
His distinctive style of writing was underpinned by discipline, diligence and an encyclopedic rugby knowledge to sit alongside a contacts book that was the envy of his rivals. He lived those qualities. “I never went to bed without writing my report, so I wouldn’t be influenced by anything else,” his reference to covering a Saturday game with a Monday publication date.
Often seen as an establishment figure, a gatekeeper, it didn’t preclude him from being critical of the IRFU on occasion. No one broke more exclusive stories.
He was proud of rugby’s inclusivity and 32 county sport status during the Troubles, that aligned Catholic and Protestant for an afternoon in Lansdowne Road. He wrote: “Rugby is the only game where you will have the hard-case unionist, maybe from the Shankill, coming down to Lansdowne Road and roaring on the team shoulder to shoulder with the most rabid nationalist.”
He lamented the change in the sport from amateur to professional in 1995. A huge advocate for schools rugby, he covered hundreds of matches including provincial finals, his words and thoughts cut out and plastered over school notice boards the length and breadth of the country.
He covered 18 overseas tours with Ireland and the Lions, seeing Ireland win both Tests in Australia in 1979, the Lions triumph in South Africa in 1974 and 1997.
His favourite rugby memory was Ireland’s 2009 Grand Slam, Ronan O’Gara’s drop goal for a team coached by Declan Kidney: two Pres old boys. He named Jack Kyle as the best Irish player. Munster’s triumph over the All Blacks in 1978 was another cherished memory.
[ Late rugby correspondent Edmund Van Esbeck’s report on Paris victory was a career highlight Opens in new window ]
Among his Arsenal heroes were Joe Mercer, Liam Brady, Dennis Bergkamp, Tony Adams and Arsene Wenger. His season ticket for the Gunners has been passed down through the generations.
He had a love of American sport, especially baseball and the LA Dodgers, fostered by taking regular holidays in Manhattan Beach, California, to where his children will return in his honour.
He is survived by his wife of 65 years Mary, his children Declan, Mary Katherine and Geraldine, his grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

title: Meet the Limerick woman who won Edinburgh comedy newcomer: ‘Irish people are the funniest people in the world’
description: The ‘chill’ Limerick comedian last got irked when a male MC labelled her adorable
content:
When it comes to making art , I’m not agreeable. I’m very adamant about going by instinct. I’ve learned a lot from being a painter and a comedian for years and I think it must feel right and authentic. So you have to go with that and you need to stand firm and show people what’s inside your brain and what you believe in. But as a person in everyday things, I tend to go with the flow.
When you’re doing a club set , you have audiences that are there not just for you. You want people to come and have a good time with you all together, you’re trying to bring everyone in. But at the same time, you need to do what you’ve come to do. You can’t pander to everyone.
If you commit more, they’ll commit to you. Whereas painting is more standalone and you don’t know who’s going to appeal to someone in that quiet moment they’re looking at the work. Whereas in comedy, they’re getting kind of a 360 vision of you. So I think people connect to people more than something that’s hanging on a wall. It’s very different. But I think in both cases I would be very much like: “I’m here to do what I do.”
I have two middle names, Louise and Elizabeth. And when I was a kid, I thought my name was Marty Louise Elizabeth. My Confirmation name was Valerie, and I picked that just because of the TV show Sabrina the Teenage Witch. I wanted to pick Sabrina but they were like: “You can’t pick a witch name.” It was too pagan for them. So I picked Valerie because that was her best friend’s name on the show.
I have a soft spot for the Limerick School of Art and Design. I learned a lot there about creative thinking and myself as a person. The school was such a massive part of the show I did at the Fringe. I met so many other creatives there that I’m still friends with. They’re friends for life and my best pals.
[ Breakthrough Irish comedian takes prize at Edinburgh Comedy Awards Opens in new window ]
One of my favourite shows at the Fringe this year was when they all flew over. Half the audience was made up of them. The place was absolutely rocking. It was so much fun.
But in terms of the landscape of Ireland I love anywhere by the sea. It’s so wild at home and there’s nothing like the Atlantic. It’s just the smell of it and the energy of it. And the Cliffs of Moher, my God, they’re something else. Whenever I see them it makes me feel like I’m so small but also massive at the same time.
I’m warm, which is an Irish trait. That’s helped me a lot over in the UK, especially being a comedian. I think that helps you source other warm people because warmth responds to warmth. Secondly, I’m quite independent. I think I have to be in what I do. And I’m playful. I’m definitely very playful. I think it’s a good balance with being independent because it’s nice to feel like you’re on stage and your eight-year-old self is up there with you but she’s your equal and you’re both up there. So I’d say warm, independent and playful.
I don’t generally get angry, to be honest. But I recently got introduced on stage by a male MC as “adorable”. I just thought that was crazy. But that was probably the last time. I kind of let things slide unless I think it’s a situation where I should say something. I’m quite chill. If I’m in a rush I’ll get angry but just internally angry at myself.
I think when I was a little kid and I’d be playing with my cousins in the summertime in the grass. You could just smell the grass and you’re running around playing 40-40 or something and you all get sniffly noses because you’re absolutely tearing around the place and then going inside to watch a big movie. That night you’d be begging your parents to have a sleepover and then getting to stay up late and watch movies you maybe shouldn’t be watching, like Liar Liar, and we’d all be laughing together.
I’m the youngest of two so my sister is four years older than me. And she is very different. She’s an accountant. So I think our brains are different. She’s quite logical and I’m quite creative. Our parents just allowed us to follow the thread of what we were interested in because they had one of each, logical and creative. I think that’s how it defined me. I couldn’t do what my sister does and vice versa. So it’s just natural encouragement from our parents because of how different we are. I guess being the youngest maybe lets you do things that are a bit mad, like stand-up.
Probably my first time properly performing in Ireland. I did the Paddy Power Comedy Festival in this big tent and I hadn’t performed much in Ireland at all at that point. So I was quite nervous about it because Irish people are the funniest people in the world. I knew I kind of had to really show them what I was made of.
But also I was like: “What are people going to think?” But I got to be exactly who I am and just really bring it. And it was unreal. It was a crowd of like 300 people. The room was humming. It was this kind of surge of electric energy. I loved it. We’re talking about trying to sort an Irish tour now.
I think the biopic would have to be an animation. It has to be a cartoon. Maybe like Cartoon Network visuals, like Cow and Chicken and then I could do the voice. But if I had to pick someone else it would be a hybrid of different people. If there was a way of putting them into a machine and making it one person then it would be CMAT and Jack Black.

title: ‘I don’t give a damn, honk away’: Is this 105-year-old Ireland’s oldest driver?
description: Hugh O’Neill still drives his Citroën C5 to the shops and says he is a better driver now than when he was in his 20s
content:
H ugh O’Neill is older than the Irish State.
When he was born on September 7th, 1921, there were “still British soldiers on Grafton Street”, as he puts it, and the Anglo-Irish Treaty had not been signed.
He will be 105 on Monday. Birthdays, he says half in jest, are “old hat when you have had so many of them”.
“People always say to me: ‘What’s the secret to your long life?’ and I always give them the same answer: ‘I haven’t a clue. It’s the luck of the game.’”
According to Gerontology Wiki, an unofficial list of Ireland’s oldest people (there is no official list), O’Neill is the State’s third-oldest man, just behind Paddy Claffey from Co Offaly and John Albert Allen from Sligo, who were also born in 1921.
There’s no official list of Ireland’s oldest drivers, either, but there can’t be many older than O’Neill. He still drives his 2005 Citroën C5 to the shops and to his Mount Merrion Friendship Club in south Dublin every week.
“I’m a better driver than I was when I was in my 20s,” he says. “In your 20s, there wasn’t as much traffic. You weren’t as conscious of your surroundings.
“I’m a really meticulous driver. I drive at 25 miles per hour. I’m this guy that people behind me are honking at to get out of my way.
“I’d like to have a sign printed on the back of my car: ‘I don’t give a damn, honk away.’”
O’Neill lives on his own in Mount Merrion, reads The Irish Times on his phone and only uses his glasses for reading.
He has the usual aches and pains that come with a person of his vintage, but age has not diminished his sense of humour.
“I have such a quantity of accoutrements inside me that if I live long enough, I’ll be a robot,” he says.
O’Neill’s wife Diane, who was born in England and to whom he was married for 58 years, died in 2009. She was evacuated as a child during the Blitz and ended up living in Ireland. He still misses her.
“I’ve been on my own since then,” he says. “It’s not to be recommended, I can tell you. It’s not so much living on your own, but it’s the loss of someone you are still in love with.”
He is grateful to the Mount Merrion Friendship Club for the social outlet, but notes, in a group for the elderly, that he’s the oldest “by a long shot”.
O’Neill has lived a healthy lifestyle. He is a moderate drinker and quit smoking when he was 25, but others, he points out, have also lived healthy lives and not lived as long.
He thinks growing up on a farm in Lisronagh, south Tipperary, where the food was healthy and there was plenty of exercise, has been a factor.
“We always ran barefoot as a kid,” he says.
When his father died, he carried on farming before opting for a desk job at the age of 29. He eventually became one of the first public relations practitioners in Ireland, before retiring at 50 in 1971.
He then bought the Kiltimon fruit farm near Ashford in Co Wicklow, which he had for more than 30 years. At peak times 300 people would come through the gates to pick their own.
The biggest change in his lifetime in Ireland has been increased wealth. He grew up in an era when many more people were poor and poverty was more extreme.
“I remember young fellows hanging around the streets without the price of a packet of cigarettes wearing nearly ragged clothes,” he says.
“In general, the lives of the ‘have-nots’ have improved. There are very few people destitute and hanging around looking for jobs now, and there are all sorts of health payments and all that sort of thing,” he says.
“For the well-off, the ordinary wealthy people, your doctor, your solicitor, your accountant, your well-off shopkeeper, life has not changed for them as much. They all had a good life.”

title: Christine Casey obituary: Architectural historian an intellectual powerhouse with a wry twinkle
description: ‘Deeply caring’ internationally renowned scholar envisaged architecture as a social endeavour
content:
Christine Casey, one of Ireland ’s leading authorities on Irish and European early modern architecture , historical craftsmanship and the decorative arts, has died aged 65, following an illness.
Professor of architectural history at Trinity College Dublin ( TCD ) at the time of her death, Casey was an internationally renowned scholar, award-winning author of books on architectural heritage and inspirational teacher and mentor to a generation of architectural historians.
Her comprehensive book on Dublin’s churches, public buildings and streets for the Buildings of Ireland series (Yale University Press, 2005) remains one of the most authoritative books on the city’s architecture. She also co-authored an earlier book in the Buildings of Ireland series on North Leinster with Alistair Rowan in 1993.
Her more recent books on architectural decoration have enhanced the knowledge and understanding of the role of traditional building skills and materials in architectural expression and production.
These include Decorative Plasterwork in Ireland and Europe, edited with Dr Conor Lucey (2012), Making Magnificence: Architects, Stuccatori and the 18th Century Interior (2017) and Enriching Architecture: Craft and its Conservation in Anglo-Irish Building Production 1660-1760 (2023) edited with Dr Melanie Hayes.
In December 2025, her book Architecture and Artifice: The Crafted Surface in Eighteenth-Century Building Practice was published by the Paul Mellon Centre for Studies in British Art. A year of research as the Parnell Fellow in the Magdalene College in Cambridge University from 2021-2022 informed this book. Casey won Research Ireland’s Researcher of the Year award for 2024.
In a tribute to their late colleague, the Department of History of Art and Architecture at Trinity College Dublin said that rather than treat architecture as a paper exercise dominated by individual geniuses, Casey “focused on the communities, crafts and materials that made our lived environment”.
“She envisaged architecture as a social endeavour expressing the respect for materials and the human skills that went into its creation,” added Hayes, senior research fellow in the Department of History of Art and Architecture at TCD.
Any conference led by Christine was a hot ticket, a gift from the architectural gods, guaranteed to provoke, challenge and delight
Lucey, a former PhD student of Casey’s and now associate professor in architectural history at UCD said: “She had beautiful prose and wrote with a well argued, lucid, readable and literary voice.”
With funding from the European Research Council, the research project she led, Stone-Work explored the journey of stone from quarries to columns and chimney pieces, and the skills, techniques and supports inherent in the process. An earlier research project, Craftvalue focused on the contribution of craft to 18th century classical architecture.
Graham Hickey of the Dublin Civic Trust noted that Casey’s recent work on the relationship of architecture to decoration highlighted the vital role of craftspeople, builders and material suppliers and “upended views about the top-down building production by architects and clients”.
“Christine was an authority on stucco and stuccatori, tracing the long line from Ireland’s decorative plasterwork of the 18th century to the slopes of the Ticino and a pan-European craft tradition,” said Hickey.
Casey’s boundless energy and enthusiasm found expression in her public talks. “Any conference led by Christine was a hot ticket, a gift from the architectural gods, guaranteed to provoke, challenge and delight – her distinctive Louth accent enlivening the occasion, accompanied by an inimitable wry twinkle,” added Hickey.
As a university lecturer, Casey transmitted passion and curiosity for her subject to her students. Warm and engaging by nature, she showed great generosity and loyalty to her students, bringing them on field trips in Ireland and guided tours across Europe to forensically study the architectural details of historic churches and public buildings.
She regularly lay on the floor of churches with students to better study the decorative detail of their ceilings.
Dean of the Faculty of Arts, Humanities and Social Science at TCD Carmel O’Sullivan said: “Christine was an intellectual powerhouse, fearless, curious, creative and deeply caring ... She was a well-known presence around Trinity and Dublin, always bustling with purpose, always making time for others, and bringing energy, humour and determination to everything she did.”
But Casey did not confine herself to academic circles in the capital city. She mixed with friends and neighbours in the village of Annasgassan, Co Louth where she moved full-time with her husband, Michael Byron and their two children around 2010. Casey was a regular sea swimmer at nearby Salterstown pier. She was also a long-time member of the Co Louth Archaeological and Historical Society for which she gave talks, wrote articles and led excursions.
A member of the Royal Irish Academy and an honorary member of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, she also served as a trustee, board and committee member of national organisations of architectural heritage including the Castletown Foundation, the Alfred Beit Trust, the Irish Architectural Archive and the Irish Georgian Society.
Christine Casey grew up on Carrick Road, Dundalk, Co Louth, the eldest of four children of Des and Mary Casey. Her father’s work as a trade union official left her with a strong sense of the importance of trade and artisan workers.
She attended St Louis’ girls secondary school in Castletown, Dundalk for her second-level education and studied history and history of art at UCD. She completed a Master of Arts at UCD, followed by a PhD in TCD in 1992.
Casey then held roles at the National College of Art and Design and UCD before becoming lecturer in the Department School of Art History and Cultural Policy in UCD between 1994 and 2008, thereafter taking up a post at TCD as associate professor in architectural history. She was head of the Department of History of Art and Architecture at TCD from 2013 to 2016. In that same year, she was elected a fellow of the college.
In a lecture at the Royal Irish Academy in 2021, Casey spoke about how her interest in architectural heritage began early. “Since childhood I have been absorbed by the structures that human beings make in the world, from the kerbstones of Newgrange to the rubble walls of demesne, farmyard and field that frame and fragment the rural landscape,” she said.
She is survived by her husband, Michael, her children, Catherine, Michael Desmond, her sisters, Anne (West) and Máiread (Martin), her brother Páraic and her mother, Mary. Her father Des predeceased her.

title: Was this bird on our back porch one of the finch species?
description: Éanna Ní Lamhna answers readers’ queries about a bird, a moth and very small fly
content:
We saw this bird in our back porch in late August and wonder is it a finch species? Geraldine Woodgate, Kilkenny
It is a juvenile goldfinch. Young goldfinches just out of the nest lack the blood-red face, white chin and black top of the head that male and female adult goldfinches have. Their heads are completely pale brown. They will acquire their striking head colouration after their first juvenile moult, which happens about three months after they hatch. Goldfinches (among other finch species) can have two or three broods a year, which is why hedge cutting is banned until the start of September.
In May we spent a weekend at Lough Ramor in Virginia. My six-year-old pulled a rock out of the water’s edge and told me he’d found zebra mussels. We looked up pictures online and found a link to report sightings, which we did, as my son Niall insisted. We’ve since had an email back from the National Biodiversity Data Centre to confirm the sighting – it is the first report they’ve had of the invasive species there and their website will be updated in the coming weeks. It is so important for everyone to be made aware of the existence of this invasive species to try to limit further spread. Also, it’s great to have our young people vigilant and interested in our wildlife. Anna O’Gorman (on behalf of Niall O’Gorman, aged 6)
Citizen scientists like Niall contribute a huge amount of valuable scientific data to the National Biodiversity Data Centre.
This is a photo of a butterfly which was attached to my window at Sandyford. On closer look I do not now think it is a butterfly. The window and surrounding area had been power-washed the day before and I think we disturbed its sleep. Could you please identify it ? Helene Scott
It is not a butterfly but a moth – a swallow-tailed moth, Ourapteryx sambucaria. It is a common enough moth that flies at night in hedges and large gardens. It is often attracted to lighted windows. It sleeps during the day, so your power-washing must have rudely awakened it. Mated females lay scarlet-red eggs under the leaves of ivy and many other woody trees and plants. The caterpillars feed on the leaves until the following June. They hibernate as caterpillars in bark crevices in the trees they feed on. The adult you photographed will lose its lovely lemon colour as it ages.
I saw this beautiful demoiselle damselfly in Courtown woods in late July. It was one among five others flying around and landing on leaves. They also landed on my sun hat and dress. Rosaleen Power
This aptly named damselfly is typical of fast-flowing waters. The male, which you have photographed here, has a most beautiful metallic blue body and splendid dark wings with iridescent blue veins. The female is duller with dark brown wings and a green bronzy body. The males are territorial but will stray from their territory when seeking a mate. It is found commonly along the southern half of the country but there are no records north of a line from Clew Bay to mid Co Louth.
This lovely friendly little fly visited me, and I would like to know what it is please. Brigid Murtagh, Wicklow
This very small fly is called Minettia inusta. Immature specimens feed on decaying vegetation while adults feed on the fungal spores on leaf surfaces. Adults fly during the warmer summer months. Overwintering typically occurs in the adult stage, with individuals hiding in sheltered terrestrial microhabitats until spring when the females lay eggs on moist decaying vegetation.
