title: Ryanair’s earnings could get worse before the shares get better
description: Shareholders may have to wait for the bad news to play out before things start to improve
content:
Barclays thinks Ryanair is a buy. It also thinks its earnings are about to get much worse.
The bank has come up with various “quirky” reasons to be bullish on the airline. For one, Europe’s growing focus on competitiveness will likely lead governments to ease some costs imposed by green regulation, says Barclays.
Despite being one of Europe’s most fuel-efficient airlines, Ryanair’s low fares mean green costs take up a relatively large share of the ticket price, making any easing of the rules particularly valuable.
Barclays also likes Ryanair’s decision to bring more operations in-house, helping it maintain its formidable cost advantage. And it sees potential in the large customer base being built through MyRyanair accounts, which could eventually allow Ryanair to make more money from passengers by selling them package holidays and other services. However, there is also a catch.
Ryanair has just cut its passenger target for the year to March 2027 from 216 million to 214 million, partly to limit its exposure to expensive unhedged fuel during the loss-making winter months.
The move is expected to reduce winter losses by €70 million to €100 million.
Barclays is more worried about what happens after that. It has slashed its forecast for Ryanair’s 2028 profits, leaving it 42 per cent below the current market consensus.
Ryanair has only 15 per cent of its 2028 fuel hedged, compared with 80 per cent for 2027, leaving it heavily exposed if fuel prices remain high.
Despite shares falling over 20 per cent this year, Barclays reckons this weakness is not fully priced in, saying it has captured “some but not all” of the fuel-related pressure. It expects consensus 2028 estimates to fall “very significantly” when investors next focus on Ryanair’s results.
For Ryanair shareholders, in other words, the good news may have to wait for the bad news to play out.

title: ‘You’re looking at the artist’s mind working’: Marvels of the National Gallery’s works on paper
description: As well as showing treasures from its collection, the National Gallery of Ireland has made all of its prints and drawings available for individual viewing
content:
A ccording to Henri Matisse, “painting and drawing say the same thing”, but “a drawing is a painting made with reduced means”.
Is that true? Is drawing the undersung younger sibling of paint? If that’s the case, Rembrandt to Matisse, the exhibition of European works on paper at the National Gallery of Ireland , shows that perhaps drawing’s limelight moment has come.
Through lines on paper made with chalk, pastel, etching, ink and graphite, there is something enticingly intimate about a drawing. Those lines, the mind knows, were made by a hand, just like our own, and the sense of connection may be more believable than when looking at so many of art history’s highly polished paintings.
“It’s the initial idea of the artist, down on paper,” the exhibition’s curator, Niamh MacNally, says. “You’re looking at the artist’s mind working.”
Whereas history’s celebrated canvases tend to require a stepping back to assess them, drawing invites you in. And if colours continue to glow in oil paint across time, the ways in which men and women, angels and demons, castles and collapsing cottages can come to life through the gap of centuries, with little more than a clutch of lines and patches of shading, is almost more miraculous when looking at works on paper.
Take the transubstantive magic in silverpoint. To make a silverpoint etching, according to MacNally, you would have needed to burn animal bones to ash and mix them with glue, probably made with boiled horse hide and hooves.
Covering the page with this unpleasant-sounding and, most likely, unpleasant-smelling substance, you would then draw with a silver tip, perhaps using something as fine as a wire held by a wooden rod.
Initially your lines would be almost invisible, but as the silvered markings oxidised – a process that could take months – your image would emerge. So transcendent beauty comes about through the sense of belief required to make invisible marks in the very materials of life and death. It’s quite the metaphor.
That ethereal beauty of silverpoint, so at odds with the physicality of its ingredients, is definitely the case with Lorenzo di Credi’s A Female Head, in which the downcast gaze of a young woman is held in a few spare lines.
The resulting image is delicate and timeless, and it takes an imaginative leap to acknowledge that it was made in the 1480s, more than 500 years ago.
Di Credi trained in the same studio as Leonardo da Vinci, and you can see the elements of style that echo between the pair. Di Credi was clearly a prodigy; he would inherit the workshop of his master, Andrea del Verrocchio, when he was still in his 20s, although it is obviously Leonardo who is the best remembered of the old masters today.
A Female Head is among the 57 works on show, which MacNally selected from the National Gallery’s collection of more than 15,000 works on paper, which includes drawings, prints, photographs and miniatures, and which spans works from the 15th century to the present day.
The occasion of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union helped MacNally whittle the selection down a little, as she looked for ways to explore the work of Irish and European artists, and the artistic conversations, influences and cross-currents that have emerged since the earliest piece on show.
That work is Profile Portrait of a Young Man, from around 1470, by either Antonio or Piero del Pollaiuolo. “Early Renaissance drawings like this are rare,” MacNally says. “Many would have been seen as working drawings and would have been discarded. But they are invaluable for building our understanding of the development of drawing.”
Some were working drawings; some come from that vital tool for all artists: the sketchbook; others, such as Gaudenzio Ferrari’s The Virgin and Child with Angel Musicians, from about 1525, were made as cartoons for frescoes.
These full-scale drawings would have their outlines pricked with tiny holes. In a technique known as spolvero, or pouncing – pounce is a fine powder – the drawings would then be placed on to fresh lime plaster and dusted with chalk or charcoal, to leave the outline drawing on the wall.
Look closely at the cartoon and you can see those pounce holes. There is plenty of close looking going on at the exhibition – so much so that MacNally frequently pauses to rub at the glass that fronts the display cases.
Given their fragility and sensitivity to light, works on paper tend to be less often displayed, and some of these pieces are on exhibition at the National Gallery for the first time.
Indeed, the terms of its Henry Vaughan bequest of watercolours by JMW Turner, in 1900, stipulated that they could be shown only in January, when light levels are low. The gallery continues to honour that, and the annual new-year showing of the Vaughan Turners always feels like a special event.
[ Turner’s watercolours are at the National Gallery of Ireland for January. It’s worth seeing them in person Opens in new window ]
But time and technology move on, and since 2018 the Print Gallery series of rooms are fitted with special lighting and nonreflective glass that is so finely engineered as to be almost invisible; hence the finger and nose prints that MacNally is assiduously rubbing away.
“People really want to get close to works on paper,” she says, smiling, as we look at one of the gallery’s more recent acquisitions, Rembrandt’s Landscape with Cottages and a Hay Barn, dated 1641, and purchased in 2023.
“There’s such a network of tiny lines, and it’s surprisingly modern, with all the space of the sky, but people feel the need to get close and, say, spot that little figure that’s walking their dog along the Amstel river.”
How much of the almost magnetic pull of the piece comes from reading the label and knowing it’s a Rembrandt? MacNally points out how attributions can change over time, but should that change our appreciation of an artwork? We stop to look at a figure of St Catherine of Alexandria from 1513, exquisitely rendered in ink.
It is by either Albrecht Dürer or Hans von Kulmbach. Does Dürer’s monogram at the bottom right not seal the deal? MacNally says that the monogram was most likely added later, by someone else, but she adds that doesn’t mean it’s not Dürer.
Art is full of such mysteries and conundrums. So what’s in a name? The drawing is both remarkable and beautiful, yet the fame of an artist adds layers of story, as well as the weight of the value of all their other works.
Try as we might, it seems only human to want to understand things in context, however skewed that context may be. One of the most powerful things about great art is the way it can sit between the two, susceptible on one level but resolutely itself underneath it all.
Not all the works are studies or sketches, early workings for the bigger “real thing”. A pair of pastels by the Venetian artist Rosalba Carriera from the 1740s glow in their frames. According to the meticulous and intriguing catalogue notes, Carriera’s portraits were one of the must-buys for the wealthy on their Grand Tours of Europe. This pair once hung at Russborough House, in Co Wicklow.
If Carriera’s works were the souvenirs of the day, 18th-century miniatures were, arguably, the first selfies. Made as mementoes, betrothal tokens and love tokens, five of them are shown in this exhibition. Fascinating as they are, they are slightly out of kilter with the narratives of artistic development, conversations and influence that emerge through the rooms.
Those conversations include those taking place between a trio of works depicting dancers, from the Edgar Degas pastel of two ballerinas in a dressingroom at the Paris Opéra, from around 1880, via Pablo Picasso’s pair from the Ballets Russes, in 1925, to Henri Matisse’s Dancer Reflected in the Mirror, from 1927.
Working within the space of just a generation, and with their own distinct styles, they clearly have in common the physicality and strength of the female dancers they depict. These are athletes. They are also human and, caught pre- or post-performance, reflective, readying, supportive of one another, and tired.
From here the exhibition moves on to also encompass German expressionism, including, poignantly, artists such as Emil Nolde, who were declared degenerate by the Nazi regime and banned from making, exhibiting or selling their work.
Nolde and so many of his colleagues persisted, and his work from that period includes the haunting watercolour Rain over a Marsh, from 1938, on show here. Proving Matisse right, Nolde had turned to watercolour when ostracism limited his access to materials. Art will out.
The gallery’s prints and drawings collection is an extraordinary resource. And while the digitisation of museum collections accelerated during the pandemic, the experience of viewing art online underlined that however great the world’s digital archives are, they are no match for the real.
The National Gallery of Ireland’s collection of works on paper is too fragile to be part of the growing global trend of “visible storage” in museums (such as at the V&A East Storehouse , in London), but the collection is truly open access. Anyone, whether student, scholar, academic or any other interested person, can make an appointment to view individual works in person at the Prints and Drawings Study Room.
MacNally notes that you need to specify the piece you would like to see, and she cautions against expecting an instant appointment, but she and the Study Room team are justifiably proud.
“It gives people a real idea of how artists work, or how they worked at the time. I know when I was studying art history, these kinds of spaces were never open to us.”
Relatively small in scale, the Print Gallery is housed in just three (perfectly engineered) rooms, but this exhibition opens up a remarkable series of worlds, and a collection that is now available to us all. A truly remarkable thing.
Rembrandt to Matisse: A Celebration of European Works on Paper is at the National Gallery of Ireland until Sunday, December 6th. Admission is free. Accompanying events include a family drop-in workshop on French Village Collage, on Sunday, September 13th; a talk-and-tea session with Niamh MacNally on Tuesday, September 22nd; and a drawing workshop on Thursday, September 24th; booking is at nationalgallery.ie . Make an appointment to view a work from the Print and Drawings collection, or from the gallery’s wider archives of correspondence, manuscripts and photographs, by emailing drawings@ngi.ie

title: It’s National Cinema Weekend, which means movies for €4. Count me in
description: Films cost just €4 at most participating cinemas on Saturday and Sunday, marking a temporary break from ticket inflation
content:
C inemas will have a lovely time-travel vibe to them this weekend. Some are screening one of the most joyful films of my childhood, a fish-out-of-water classic in which a group of people from the 23rd century wind up in 1986, but that’s only one reason why. The other is that it’s National Cinema Weekend , and tickets for most screenings will cost €4. So retro.
Led by a cross-industry group called Cinema First, this weekend is an extension of the National Cinema Day initiative that has run in Britain and Ireland since 2022, and it’s a good thing, a great thing and not a sign of desperation at all.
Five stars from me, and let’s not worry about the fact that an increasing pool of people would rather watch free but glitchy, distraction-filled illegal streams than pay to sit still in a darkened auditorium for a couple of hours, as the gods of cinema intended.
Popcorn expenses are not included in this maths and, as ever, may require a small loan. But, at many cinemas, €4 represents just a quarter of the usual evening-time cost, meaning anyone in a position to cancel all other operations in their lives could go to see four films this weekend for the price of one and come away happy, if a little cold from the overly zealous air conditioning you get in cinemas these days.
Technically, Irish screenings were never €4 on a regular basis, as average prices had already edged past that sum by the time the euro was introduced, in 2002. It was the mid-1990s when prices were the equivalent amount in Irish pounds. That feels like a long time ago, and it is, but ticket inflation since the turn of the century is still staggering to contemplate.
[ Irish people are flocking back to the cinema. What’s going on? Opens in new window ]
Cinemas have edged up their prices so cleverly and consistently over the years that you forget what it used to cost. When I was at the Irish Film Institute last week I was struck by a promotion for its year-round offer of €5 screenings for holders of its 25 & Under card – an amazing deal – and spent a solid 10 minutes wishing I could have availed of prices that cheap when I was under 25. If only cinemas had felt a more urgent need to retain the custom of my generation, I thought.
My second thought was I’m so ancient that prices probably were about €5 when I was in my early 20s. Then I remembered I’m a hoarder and I can check. My box of old ticket stubs tells me I paid €5.25 to see a weekday matinee of “Sweet Hom” – Sweet Home Alabama – in December 2002 at UGC Cinemas, the site of what is now Cineworld Dublin.
At the same cinema I went to a morning screening of Bridget Jones: The Edge of Reason in November 2004 for a mere €4.50. In January 2004 I paid €7.50 for an evening showing of “Girl With” – Girl With a Pearl Earring – at the Screen Cinema (RIP), while as late as September 2005 I could still spend an afternoon indulging in “Pride & P” – the brilliant one with Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen – at Cineworld for €6.80.
[ From the archive: A farewell to Dublin’s Screen and the rest of the old-school arthouse cinemas Opens in new window ]
There was one outlier, datewise, in my collection. I still have a stub for True Lies at the Savoy (its glorious old Screen One, RIP) on a Sunday evening in August 1994. It was so popular we could only get seats right up the front and spent the film staring up. The price, according to the invoice-like paper my ticket is printed on, makes me want to weep. It was £2.50.
Today, special weekends excepting, cinemas actually make a virtue of high prices. I roll my eyes at chains that specialise in premium tiers that invite filmgoers to “upgrade” their seats to something vaguely comfortable.
But I am a sucker for those pricier formats. I will pay €19 to see The Testament of Ann Lee in 70mm at the Irish Film Institute. I will pay €20.94 to see One to One: John & Yoko in the Imax at Cineworld. I’m not so keen to pay €21.99 to see Spider-Man: Brand New Day in Cineworld’s “sensory cinema” 4DX format – I prefer nonvibrating chairs – but that’s what it costs for the pleasure.
This increasing focus on premium formats reveals the real challenge for the industry. It needs to offer experiences that can’t be replicated at home. It needs hype. And, somewhat alarmingly, it needs reminders of the very concept of cinemagoing. So all releases will be going cheap on Saturday and Sunday thanks to National Cinema Weekend.
I’ll be succumbing to nostalgia at the 40th-anniversary re-release of Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home, forgetting about my fantasy of a disposable income that keeps pace with the cost of living for a while, and laughing as I watch a 1980s-bound Kirk and Spock ponder the meaning of “exact change”.

title: Colour disrupter: how to position white flowers in your garden
description: White flowers can be a wow, but also a distraction
content:
A s a gardener as well as a florist, I’ve learned to be wary of white. Flowers in this colour are what you might call ‘shouty’, sometimes at odds with their neighbours and difficult to position well, especially in the hard, harsh light of a hot summer’s day. Adding to the challenge is the fact that there’s not just one but many shades of white, from warm creamy white to grey-white and icy-white. They don’t always get along.
Put a cool white right next to a warm white, for example, and it will look instantly jarring. Using white flowers in any kind of vibrantly colourful planting plan has a similar visually disruptive effect, drawing the eye and creating a full stop when one often isn’t wanted. Even just one single small white flower in a sea of vivid colour packs a visual punch that’s well above its weight, the harsh contrast transforming it into an attention-hogger that demands to be noticed.
Instead, white flowers almost always look their best when combined with lots of interesting foliage plants in soft shades of green and grey, a lesson the noted English gardener Vita Sackville-West famously taught the world when she created her white garden at Sissinghurst.
An essay in restraint, Sackville-West used what she described as “a low sea of grey foliage” – species such as santolina, artemisia, stachys, Cineraria maritima, and Achillea ageratifolia – to anchor the planting and allow its more ephemeral blooms – white-flowering varieties of regal lilies, irises, peonies, foxgloves, delphiniums, the giant Arabian thistle Onopordum arabicum – to rise above it, so that they softly glowed rather than loudly shouted.
Skilfully used this way, white flowers can add magic and mystery to the tiniest of spaces, especially if you combine them with formal evergreen hedges and well-executed hard landscaping details such as elegant paths and paving. Unlike richer colours that tend to recede or even disappear in low light, they’ll bring a shady garden to vivid life in the similar way that they’ll add a luminous quality to the garden at twilight. For the very same reasons, white flowers come into their own at this time of year as the days shorten and natural light levels begin to fall.
In my own country garden, for example, an intentionally late sowing of white cosmos has produced plants that are only now getting into their stride. Planted in soft drifts into gaps in a sunny border, this hard-working, easy-to-grow annual will continue to bloom until the first harsh frosts so long as I keep it regularly deadheaded. With tall stems of pure white daisy-shaped flowers and feathery foliage, it also makes an excellent cut flower to bring indoors. Of the many varieties available, my favourite is the reliably abundant Cosmos ‘Fizzy White’.
Another white-flowering, autumn-blooming plant I wouldn’t be without is Gaura lindheimeri. Easily grown from seed, this ultra-resilient, drought-tolerant, sun-loving, exceptionally long-flowering perennial produces clouds of delicate white flowers flushed through with just a hint of blush for months on end and combines excellently with ornamental grasses and other modern-style perennial species such as sanguisorba and echinacea.
I grow a creamy-white flowering form of the latter in the same sunny border, propagated from seed sourced from Jelitto , the German seed company that carries a huge range of seeds of garden-worthy perennials. Slow to emerge in spring, echinacea can be a martyr to slugs and snails, but if you nurse it past this stage then its large, elegant, daisy-like flowers with their central boss of dark golden disc florets are both highly ornamental and very long lasting.
Another white flowering perennial that’s providing a great display in my garden despite this summer’s punishing drought is the white-flowering form of goat’s rue, Galega officinalis ‘Alba’. This plant’s dainty pea-like, clean white flowers and graceful foliage belie the fact that it’s as tough as old boots, as well as exceptionally easy to raise from seed. Shade tolerant, white goat’s rue also makes a great cut flower – yet another reason to love it. A tall perennial, it forms a large spreading clump, so make sure to give it space towards the back of a border to accommodate it.
[ Should I weed my garden in a heatwave? Opens in new window ]
That’s not the case for the dainty Mexican fleabane, Erigeron karvinskianus, an invaluable, semi-evergreen, drought-tolerant perennial which forms low clouds of its long-lasting miniature daisy-shaped flowers for many months. Different named varieties are available, including some with a slightly mawkish hint of blue or mauve. But the species itself is lovely as it is, with a multitude of white to very pale pink flowers and an ability to seed itself gracefully about the place without ever being unwelcome.
As for white-flowering shrubby species for the early autumn garden, you can’t go wrong with Hydrangea paniculata ‘Limelight’. Much more drought tolerant than its thirsty, mop-headed cousin Hydrangea macrophylla, this deciduous shrub’s large cone-shaped flowers emerge in a shade of pale lime green and then gradually change to a warm shade of creamy-white. Impressively long-lasting, these have a near-magical ability to partner well with almost anything – the reason why this hardy shrub is the backbone of so many garden designers’ planting schemes.

This highly rated 10-month course takes place one day a month with expert gardener, educator, author, designer and plantaholic Jimi Blake, owner and creator of the gardens. Places limited. See huntingbrookgardens.com .

title: Irish fintechs face a tougher funding market as global concerns weigh on investors
description: Firms in the Republic raised €136m in first six months of 2026, says KPMG
content:
Irish and European financial technology companies have found it more difficult to raise money this year as political and economic instability continues to dent investor risk appetites, according to a new KPMG report.
The Big Four accounting firm’s latest fintech pulse report reveals that Irish companies raised $158.13 million (€136.32 million) across seven deals in the first six months of the year. That’s a more than 9 per cent decline compared to the same period last year.
KPMG said this year’s figure was “buoyed” by the $110 million that Dublin-based tax automation company Fonoa raised early in the summer.
That company announced in June it had closed a Series C funding round and also bought PwC ’s tax platform, Indirect Tax Edge, for an undisclosed sum.
KPMG said other “notable deals” in the first half of the year included Dublin -based Circuit’s $22 million fundraise, which closed in February; $11.83 million raised through acquisition by blockchain company True and $10 million raised by Cork -based transaction platform Trustap.
“Ireland’s fintech sector remains strong in 2026, despite a decrease in investment compared to the same period last year,” said Ian Nelson, head of financial services and regulatory at KPMG Ireland.
“There is still an appetite with investors for Irish fintechs that offer innovative solutions to real business challenges and demonstrate a clear path to scale.”
However, investor sentiment across the EU continues to be “weighed down”, KPMG said, by heightened geopolitical tensions, inflation arising from the US-Israeli war with Iran, and uncertainty around the trajectory of interest rates.
Against this backdrop, fintech investment in the Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA) region fell by around 37 per cent to $11.3 billion across 626 deals in the first half, compared to $18 billion invested across 753 deals in the same period last year.
Globally, deal volumes tumbled “below historic norms” in the first half of the year, KPMG said, although the value of deals is way up since 2025.
Often achieving lofty valuations, artificial intelligence-related companies have been at the top of the menu for investors this year, with a smaller number of mega-deals helping to inflate global deal values.
In total, AI helped fuel a 35 per cent increase in global merger and acquisition deal values last year. The New York Times reported that in the first half of the year, the global value of deals increased by a further 45 per cent compared to the same period in 2025 to $3.2 trillion.

title: Wines from Georgia and Armenia: four great bottles to try
description: This region was where wine was (probably) born, so they know what they’re talking about
content:
B oth Armenia and Georgia lay claim to being the oldest producers of wine in the world; given that there were no borders 6,000-8,000 years ago, both are probably right.
A recent visit to Armenia was fascinating. Under Soviet rule, Georgia and Moldova were designated as wine producers, while it was decided that Armenia would produce brandy instead. As a result Armenia still produces some excellent aged brandy that is well worth trying. One big producer is owned by French luxury goods group LVMH. However, like Georgia, Armenia also has hundreds of indigenous grape varieties, some of which produce excellent wine. I feature one below made from the very promising areni noir grape.
I haven’t made it to Georgia yet, but I sometimes feel as if I have after listening to John Wurdeman. Wurdeman is an American artist and collector of songs who arrived in Georgia to study Georgian folk music. There he fell in love with the unique wines, and founded a winery called Pheasant’s Tears in 2006, as well as several restaurants and a travel company. He also tours the world promoting the wines.
The tradition in Georgia, going back 6,000 years, is to ferment and age wine in qvevri, large clay amphorae, that are buried in the ground of the winery. Sometimes whole bunches of grapes are included for varying periods of time. Usually made from white grapes, the resulting wines have a deep colour and often some tannins too. This is the original home of orange or amber wine . As well as this week’s wines, I featured the excellent Chinuri from Iago Bitarishvili (Georgia, €30.85) in May this year .
Intensely floral with a complex mix of dried herbs, apricots and peaches with light tannins on the finish. A personal favourite of mine, this is a great introduction to orange wine at an exceptional price.
Light and refreshing with delicious tangy honey, orange peel and spicy, exotic fruits. Attractive grippy light tannins on the finish.
BaRossa, Dublin 4; Cappagh Stores, Galway; Delgany Wine Cottage, Co Wicklow; L’Atitude 51, Cork; Le Caveau.ie
Lively and fresh with pears, pineapples and tropical fruits; tangy and lightly tannic. Intriguing and very enjoyable.
Lightly spicy aromas with vibrant piquant red cherry and redcurrant fruits and refreshing acidity. Very different and very delicious.
64 Wine, Glasthule, Co Dublin; The Corkscrew, Dublin 2; Mitchell & Son, Glasthule and Hatch Street, Dublin 2; Woodberrys.ie, Galway; Wineonline.ie

title: My roses are underperforming. What can I do?
description: Mulch generously around the root systems in spring and prune as appropriate
content:
My roses haven’t performed well this year, which I suspect is due to the hot, dry summer we had. Is there any way I can help the plants so that they do better if we have another similar summer next year? Anna K, Dublin
Although roses enjoy warm, sunny conditions, these hardy shrubby plants also need a humus-rich, fertile, moisture-retentive, deep soil if they’re to flower well. This summer’s hot, dry conditions have tested them, especially plants growing in less-than-ideal growing conditions where their root systems may not have had access to sufficient water and nutrients.
To improve growing conditions, mulch generously around their root systems in spring, using well-rotted manure (Irish suppliers include Cork-based geeup.ie which delivers nationwide) or a commercial mulch such as enrich.ie
Pruning is also important to remove dead, damaged or diseased wood and encourage the production of lots of new, healthy, vigorous, flower-bearing young branches. Exactly how and when you should prune your plants depends on what type of roses they are. A hybrid tea rose, for example, needs a different pruning regimen to a climbing rose or a rambler. For detailed advice on this, check out the website of the RHS at rhs.org.uk
Working a slow-release organic fertiliser into the soil in spring will also help to supply important plant nutrients, as will regular liquid feeding during the flowering period. Deadheading is also important, as this prevents the plants from turning their energies to producing seed and instead encourages them to produce more flowers.
Also bear in mind that most roses like to have a little space around their root systems rather than be squeezed in tight with other plants. If, for example, perennials or other shrubs have been allowed to gradually encroach upon your roses, then consider gently cutting these back.
Lastly, no plant lives forever. While roses are more long-lived than most – they can typically live for 10-20 years, while climbing roses in particular can live for up to a century – plants naturally and gradually lose vigour over time and will eventually succumb to disease and old age. While you can slow this process down through careful husbandry as described above, as well as by collecting and disposing of any diseased material in early spring, you can’t prevent it.
If your plants are old, then they may be reaching the end of their natural life cycle. If this is the case, then consider the possibility of replacing them with young, vigorous roses, ideally choosing a vigorous, productive, floriferous variety known for having good disease resistance. But just bear in mind that a disease known as rose sickness or rose replant disease can sometimes cause these new plantings to struggle for reasons that aren’t yet fully understood.

title: Find romance and potentially a bargain with a 19th century Irish artist
description: Some Irish art from this period is selling for a fraction of the price of work by more contemporary artists
content:
R ather than investing in contemporary artists whose work is currently selling well, what if you decided instead to take a longer-term view and invest in the work of artists whose paintings aren’t making high prices at the moment?
There are a number of Irish artists born in the 19th century whose work is currently selling for a fraction of the price of works by more contemporary artists. Their somewhat romantic representation of the landscape is in stark contrast to more abstract landscape paintings of contemporary artists; but this gentleness has an appeal all of its own.
Arabella Bishop, independent art adviser, says there is a lot of good value in the period. “There were a lot of very talented Irish artists painting in the 19th th century who are often overlooked now,” she says. She mentions artists such as Sir Frederick Burton, Richard Thomas Moynan, Bartholomew Watkins, Andrew Nicholl and Daniel Maclise – all of whom have pieces in the National Gallery of Ireland.
In terms of work for sale at auctions, paintings by William Percy French (1854-1920) often come up. Roscommon-born Percy French began songwriting while studying engineering at Trinity College Dublin. He also became a prolific painter of landscapes in watercolour and considered art to be his true vocation, according the Cavan County Museum, which has a Percy French gallery. His painting Peat Stacks, Connemara (€1,500-€2,500) is for sale in Morgan O’Driscoll’s current online art auction.
Mildred Anne Butler (1858-1941) is another artist worth considering for anyone starting an art collection. One of Ireland’s first professional female artists, who exhibited widely, she sold well throughout her career. The gardens and fields of her family home in Kilmurray, Thomastown, Co Kilkenny were the inspiration for a lot of her paintings. Butler’s Garden at Kilmurray (€2,500-€3,500) is also in Morgan O’Driscoll’s current online art auction.
Roscommon- born artist Seamus Coleman, who died in January 2025, is a more contemporary artist who also focused on landscapes and countryside scenes, albeit with a more vibrant palette. Cutting Turf, Connemara (€600-€900), will appeal to anyone who remembers the back-breaking work of cutting turf for winter fuel, a common activity for decades in this country.
Dublin-born and Sligo based artist Sean McSweeney (1935-2018) was a self-taught artist influenced by artists including Jack B Yeats. His abstract landscape painting entitled Evening Bogland (2004) – also for sale at Morgan O’Driscoll’s art auction – is in stark contrast to the aforementioned more representational works by French, Butler and Coleman.
Letitia Marion Hamilton (1878-1964) is an Irish artist who worked and exhibited internationally. As with several artists from the period, landscapes, market and hunting scenes were the focus of her work. A small framed print, entitled Fair Day at Castlepollard, has an estimate of €100 to €150, and the sale includes two other prints at Lot 100’s current online auction of 20th and 21st century art.
The Lot 100 auction house, based in Lismore, Co Waterford, specifically aims to attract new collectors with its wide range of prints and affordable paintings.
The current online auction – which ends on September 15th – also has some fascinating pieces by Felix Faulkner, who is based in Cappoquin, Co Waterford. Faulkner’s vibrant work offers buyers a much more modern take on rural Ireland where tractors, sheds, containers and other paraphernalia are elevated simply by being chosen as objects for her landscape paintings. The piece, Clontarf St, Cork, with an estimate of €400-€600 is one such entry-level piece.
Finally, collectors of rare and vintage books should take some time to check the catalogue for Purcell’s upcoming books auction on September 16th.
The WB Yeats sale is mainly made up of the libraries of the late Prof Warwick Gould and his wife Deirdre Toomey, both of whom were prominent Yeats scholars. Australian-born Gould was the founding director of the Institute of English Studies at the University of London, and an internationally renowned scholar of Irish and English literature. He is best known for his work on the Irish Literary Revival and WB Yeats in particular. Toomey, also a Yeats scholar, co-edited The Collected Letters of WB Yeats Volume 2 1896-1900 with Gould and John Kelly. The couple were both frequent visitors to the Yeats International Summer School in Sligo.
As well as a vast collection of various editions of Yeats poetry books (some of which are signed by the poet), and two striking photographic portraits of WB Yeats by Alexander Robert Hogg from 1931 (€400-€800 each), the auction has other gems. These include the complete volume of the Letters of Virginia Woolf; a book on Irish lace-making by Eileen O’Connor (with pattern sheets); and the lesser known collection of Oscar Wilde’s fairy tales, A House of Pomegranates (1891) for €600-€900.
Book auctions such as this one are also excellent places to buy books to fill a new library. Purcell’s has up to 20 lots of mixed book collections, with estimates of €60-€120 per lot.
