It is to ask whether the podcast medium was ever a good development in the first place – as depth was sacrificed for breath, generalism encouraged over specialism, and I was given a hazy impression that Harold Wilson did say something about the pound in 1967 while not being able to offer you any further thoughts on what or in which direction. Is this kind of intellectual grazing bad for us?
It shouldn’t be zero sum, of course – I can read and listen to a podcast in the same day. And I would hesitate to blame the literacy crisis – excellently detailed by James Marriott (who is also a friend) in the just-now-released book The New Dark Ages – on podcasters. In fact, Dad Books would never catch my eye in the first place. I know more about Harold Wilson now than I ever would have done in the hypothetical podcast-free alternate reality. It is a small, barely perceptible win but if forced to pick a side, a win nonetheless. It will be worse than a tragedy if podcasts kill literacy. I am highly sceptical that they will.

title: ‘Sad to see him go’: Josh van der Flier wants to make Leo Cullen’s final season a great one
description: Veteran Leinster flanker admits he can barely recall a time when Cullen wasn’t involved with the province
content:
With an incredulous look, Josh van der Flier points out that he was five years old when Leo Cullen made his Leinster debut.
Cullen’s bow for the province came in October 1998 and, bar two seasons with Leicester Tigers, the Newtownmountkennedy man has been with Leinster ever since.
That run will end next summer. Leinster announced in June that Cullen’s 12th year in the head coach’s hot seat will be his last. It was right at the end of last term that Van der Flier heard the news from the man himself.
“I was surprised, yeah,” said the long-serving flanker. “I had a brief chat with him at the end of the season, just literally a couple of days before, and he kind of said that he was going to be finishing up. It would be sad to see him go.
“It’s mad. I was probably like five when he first got involved in Leinster. I’ve only known Leinster with him there as long as I’ve been there, obviously.
“He’s made a lot of brave calls, he’s brought other coaches in who have maybe taken over and done a lot more of the rugby side of things. He could have done it himself but he’s facilitated it very well.
“He will be missed and it’ll be a big change for whoever takes over then, but we have a year with him yet.”
Cullen has spent more than a decade carrying the responsibility of leading a team expected to win every week, and the weight of Leinster’s repeated Champions Cup disappointments has often landed on his shoulders. Another final defeat, against Bordeaux-Bègles in May , extended the province’s run to five since their last Champions Cup triumph in 2018.
Van der Flier has sympathy for his fellow Wicklow man, particularly because of the ease with which responsibility can be assigned from outside.
“Yeah, not fair,” said the 33-year-old, whose only Champions Cup final success came eight years ago in Bilbao. “I spoke to him a bit about it before. He doesn’t mind it at all. He’s used to it.
“I’ve talked to a few coaches about it. I’ve played in a lot of those finals, semi-finals, whatever. You lose them. You had a part in it, you tried your best.
“He’s probably prepared the team as well as he thinks he can. A drop goal goes over or doesn’t go over, someone drops the ball over the line and he’s the one to blame. He’s [not] on the pitch.
“In fairness to him, it must be a hard thing to do. But he’s always willing to put his hand up. Even if it wasn’t anything to do with him, he’s always happy to take on the pressure that way.”
While the Leinster players have yet to broach the subject collectively, the 48-year-old’s long goodbye will surely make the coming campaign feel different.
Van der Flier insists the squad is not approaching it as some kind of extended farewell tour for the first man to captain and coach a team to Champions Cup glory.
“We haven’t sat down and done goals or anything like that. The group just hasn’t been together yet in terms of everyone training together,” he explained.
“I think the goals are always pretty similar year to year, but there’s definitely added motivation. Obviously everyone has their own motivation, and the club itself, but with this being Leo’s last year, then it adds to it, for sure.”
And Van der Flier has already told Cullen what he hopes the players can do for him. “I was even saying to him, ‘we’ll have to make it a good year for him’,” he said.
“Not that we don’t give our best all the time, but [we want to] make it a good year for him, because he’s obviously been such a servant to Leinster. He’s done unbelievable things in his time here, playing and coaching. So, hopefully make it a good year.”
The clock is also ticking towards the 2027 World Cup, of course. Andy Farrell ’s Ireland will return to Australia next autumn, having played two Tests there in the summer.
Naturally, Van der Flier’s ambition for what he hopes will be his third World Cup is for Ireland to go further than before. For now, though, he is focusing on what comes before their latest tilt at breaking through the quarter-final glass ceiling.
That meant doing what he does every summer – analysing every part of his game to see where he can get better.
“The World Cup is an added motivation at the end of it,” he acknowledged. “There’ll be another period off, I assume, between the end of this season and the start of the World Cup, so perhaps I’m trying to not put that in the picture.
“But it’s obviously not too far away, so it’s definitely a major motivator, because everyone wants to play in World Cups. It’s one of those things you look forward to once the last one ends.
“You’re like, ‘I can’t wait for the next one’, so it’s definitely in the back of the mind. But I try not to think about it.”

title: Farmers blamed for carbon footprints while people fly around the world
description: Food producers blamed for damaging the atmosphere while someone just had his 54th flight of 2026
content:
Sir, – A correspondent ( Letters, September 1st ) tells us that he has just had his 54th flight in the first eight months of the year and that he knows his “carbon footprint is appalling”. I am in my 70s, and I have had one flight to India and five or six to the UK in my lifetime.
Before I retired, I was a small-time food producer, and I am now finding it hard to understand why it is the food producers (farmers) of this country who are being blamed for their carbon footprints, for damaging the atmosphere, and are now being paid to reduce food production in a world that is starving.
Surely the solution is for people to stop, or at least reduce, flying around the world as they are doing? – Yours, etc,

title: Pressure on frontline services
description: Without urgent Government action, rising demand will continue to place frontline services under increasing strain
content:
Sir, – Depaul ’s latest impact report, “Frontline Prevention – Shaping the Present, Looking to the Future” , shows that, while significant progress has been made helping people move out of homelessness and into long-term homes, the growing scale and complexity of demand is placing unprecedented pressure on frontline services.
Last year, 8,204 people were supported by Depaul across Ireland and Northern Ireland , including 2,574 children, a 12 per cent increase on the previous year. Demand from families rose sharply with 1,456 families supported, a 28 per cent increase in just one year.
Behind these figures are families and individuals facing homelessness alongside increasingly complex challenges, including mental health concerns and addiction . The pressure is particularly evident in mental health. Reported mental health concerns increased by 93 per cent in 2025, with 1,361 service users reporting support needs. Depaul team members also responded to 273 incidents of suicidal ideation and 129 incidents of self-harm.
At the same time, the report demonstrates what can be achieved when people have access to the right support and housing. In 2025, 914 households and 1,452 individuals moved out of homelessness and into long-term homes. This is a clear demonstration that homelessness is not inevitable.
In advance of Budget 2027, we are calling on the Government to maintain and increase investment in social and affordable housing, strengthen prevention, mental health and addiction supports, accelerate Housing First and provide sustainable funding for frontline services. We also need sustainable accommodation solutions for people in the international protection system, and a State-led approach to reducing reliance on temporary accommodation.
Prevention must remain at the heart of the response, ensuring people receive support before homelessness becomes entrenched. Those most vulnerable also need the right mental health, addiction and community supports to build stable lives, develop a sense of belonging and become part of thriving communities.
The progress made in 2025 shows what is possible. But without urgent Government action, rising demand will continue to place frontline services under increasing strain while more families, children and individuals risk being left without a secure place to call home. – Yours, etc,

title: Ireland’s services sector expands in August but employment growth stalls
description: Cost pressures intensify but remain below earlier peak, says AIB
content:
Ireland’s services sector expanded in August at its fastest pace since late 2025, despite a notable slowdown in hiring and an increase in inflationary pressures, AIB said on Thursday.
The bank’s latest services purchasing managers’ index (PMI) indicates that there was little change in employment levels across the wide-ranging sector last month after a flurry of hiring in July.
It meant that August was only the fourth month since March 2021 in which the sector did not add jobs, AIB said in the PMI report, which is based on a survey of around 400 services firms.
At 55.4, the headline index was up by 0.2 points from July, which the report authors said was the fastest rate of growth since November 2025. Any figure above 50 signals growth, while a number below that points to contraction.
Of the four main subsectors, financial services reported the fastest rate of headline growth, followed by technology, media and telecommunications. After a slow first half of the year, transport, tourism and leisure services activity levels expanded for the first time in six months.
Business services, meanwhile, registered the weakest increase in activity levels.
AIB chief economist David McNamara said the headline results were underpinned by growth in new business and improved sentiment among services firms about their prospects.
“New business continued to grow strongly following a dip in activity earlier in the year, while new export business also expanded on the month, albeit at a more modest pace than in July,” he said.
“Higher activity was driven by increased demand and new business wins. In that context, the volume of outstanding work rose steadily in August once again. However, despite a solid demand backdrop, employment fell marginally for the first time since March, following several months of rapid gains.”
Meanwhile, services businesses reported an increase in input costs in August for the first time in four months. However, while the rate of inflation “moved further above the long-run survey trend”, AIB said, it was still the second-weakest reading in six months.
Transport, tourism and leisure firms reported the most intense inflationary pressure in the month.
“On the inflation front, input cost inflation ticked up in August, but remains well below the 40-month peak reached in April and May, and broadly in line with the long-run survey average,” McNamara said. “However, cost pressures were driven by rising wages, fuel and transportation. The rate of increase in prices charged also picked up, and it remains elevated in a historical context.”

title: Donald Trump to meet Catherine Connolly and Micheál Martin in Phoenix Park
description: Doubts over separate stop by US president to turn sod at new US embassy complex in Ballsbridge
content:
US president Donald Trump is scheduled to meet President Catherine Connolly and Taoiseach Micheál Martin in separate engagements at the Phoenix Park during his visit to the Republic next week, before travelling to his Doonbeg golf course.
The logistical details of Trump’s brief visit and the significant security operation surrounding it are being finalised by officials.
The current schedule the Government has mapped out has Trump travelling to Dublin’s Phoenix Park where he will separately meet Connolly and the Taoiseach, according to three sources with knowledge of the plans.
Trump is also expected to meet US ambassador Edward Walsh, whose Deerfield residence in Phoenix Park is a short distance from Áras an Uachtaráin and Farmleigh House, where the Republican leader is to meet Martin.
The Government has not yet confirmed any details of the US president’s visit, or any official engagements in Dublin.
[ What will happen during Trump's visit? Opens in new window ]
Trump is expected to attend an event marking the anniversary of the September 11th terror attacks in the United States, before travelling to the Republic to attend the Irish Open golf tournament being held in his Co Clare golf course.
It is understood he plans to fly into Dublin Airport where he will be greeted by a senior member of the Government, possibly Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris .
Officials who have been working on the logistics of the Trump visit stress that the current plans could still change at a later stage. The Government is expecting Trump to arrive on Saturday, September 12th, however.
[ Inside the Doonbeg bubble where the locals and Trump have reached a deal of mutual benefit Opens in new window ]
According to the latest version of the schedule, which has begun to be firmed up in recent days, the US president will travel to Phoenix Park for a string of political and diplomatic engagements.
A separate stop to turn the sod on the site of the new US embassy complex in Ballsbridge had provisionally been listed on a draft itinerary as recently as last week. However, sources in Government have said that event may now not take place.
Following his meetings in Phoenix Park, the US president is due to fly from Dublin to Shannon Airport , possibly travelling by helicopter, to stay in his Doonbeg golf course and watch the Irish Open tournament, which will conclude on Sunday 13th. He is expected to depart later that day.
Connolly, who has been a vocal critic of Trump, said during the Irish presidential election last year that if required in the course of official duties she would meet the US president.
Anti-Trump protests are being organised by neutrality campaigners, Opposition politicians and other political activists to take place in Dublin and Co Clare, which will necessitate a significant security operation led by the Garda .
Last November it was confirmed Trump International Golf Links Ireland would host the 2026 Amgen Irish Open tournament, which will see Rory McIlroy defend his title in a field that will also include Shane Lowry, Brooks Koepka, Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton.

title: Average accountant’s pay tops €130,000 in Leinster amid high demand for services
description: More than three-quarters of accountants surveyed expect earnings to rise over next 12 months
content:
A chartered accountant working in Leinster will take home an average of €130,960 this year, down slightly from a record in 2025 but around one-fifth higher than the pre- Covid average.
The figure, which includes salary, car allowances and bonuses, is based on a survey of almost 800 accountants working in the region, conducted by Chartered Accountants Ireland’s (CAI) Leinster Society and accountancy recruitment firm Barden.
CAI said that while average earnings have moderated somewhat after hitting a record €131,654 in 2025, the overall trend is that accountants are earning “significantly more” than in pre-pandemic 2018.
The average salary for a mid-career accountant in Leinster this year is €89,759, down from €97,527 in 2025, but also up 20 per cent since 2018.
Meanwhile, newly qualified chartered accountants will command a remuneration package of €65,538 this year, which CAI and Barden said is substantially ahead of pre-pandemic levels.
“Average salary packages remain close to record levels, demonstrating the strength of demand for finance professionals and the continued value employers place on accountancy and finance expertise,” said Darren Holmes, chairman of CAI Leinster Society.
Separately, more than 88 per cent of accountants who responded to the survey said their total earnings have increased over the past three years. Some 21 per cent said their take-home pay has increased by more than one quarter, while 77 per cent said they expect to see it increase over the next 12 months.
Holmes said the survey also highlights the “stability of the profession”, with, ”with 93 per cent of respondents employed on a permanent basis and 37 per cent having progressed into more senior roles over the past three years”.
Elaine Brady, managing partner at Barden, said: “Despite the continued backdrop of macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty over the past 12 months, and the ongoing impact of US trade policy and tariffs , demand for accounting talent has held up across Leinster.
“The survey points to the resilience of the profession, with high levels of permanent employment, continued opportunities for career progression and salary packages remaining close to record levels. These findings underline the enduring demand for chartered accountants and the value organisations place on finance professionals who can help navigate an increasingly complex business environment.”
This story was updated on September 3rd to reflect that Barden is accountancy recruitment firm.

title: Bus and train fare hikes to be announced by National Transport Authority
description: Rising cost of State funding for public services has been a spending concern for some time
content:
Bus and train fares are to increase by about 15 per cent on average under new measures to be announced on Thursday.
The move is expected to see the Transport for Ireland 90-minute fare – which gives unlimited travel across eligible services in Dublin for €2 over a period of an hour and a half – rise to €2.30.
The changes, which are to be announced by the National Transport Authority , will see some fares for children and young adults fall. However, in other cases, specific fares may rise by about 30 per cent.
On average, overall fare prices will rise by about 15 per cent.
Free travel for all children up to age nine and for older people will continue.
The changes come at a time when the Government is already facing pressure from the Opposition, trade unions and campaign groups over the rising cost of living . It is also likely to be criticised by environmental campaigners who argue the State should be encouraging greater public transport use.
The exchequer this year provided €940 million to offset the cost of delivering what are known as public service obligation (PSO) routes that could not be operated on a commercial basis. However, it is understood that the Department of Public Expenditure has been concerned for some time about the rising cost in this area.
Speaking after the budget announcement last October, Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien said increases in bus and rail fares were not off the table. He said there must be a “sustainable” funding model for public transport systems.
Although the Minister said at the time there would be no fare rises following the 2026 budget, he could not rule out later price hikes.
“I’m not writing anything off because what I want is to expand on the transport network.”
According to the Minister, the Government had made “significant progress” in changing the PSO public transport budget.
“I think, for the last six years, the expansion of public transport services has been great, but we need the funding to back that up,” he said, adding that people had responded to the increased services across the country. However, he said that any fare system must remain “affordable”.
The rising cost of State funding for public transport services has been a concern in the Department of Public Expenditure for some time.
In briefing material prepared for Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers last year, officials said exchequer funding for PSO routes had increased by €350 million since 2019 and that more than €650 million had been provided in 2025.
“This is in part due to the introduction of fare initiatives over the period during which fare revenue decreased by 26 per cent despite increasing passenger numbers,” it said.
“There is limited evidence that the fare initiatives are effective in encouraging modal shift as the increase in passenger numbers has not kept up with overall population increases.”
It noted that network enhancement and new services were likely to have a greater impact on passenger numbers.
“A balance needs to be found between the exchequer annual subvention and the revenue raised by fares. This ratio has increased substantially since 2019.”
A spokeswoman for the Minister for Transport could not be contacted.

title: Investing in priorities on Achill Island
description: Tourist facilities are welcome, but investment in the village that supports them must surely come first
content:
Sir, – Keel in Achill is home to just 256 people, yet welcomes tens of thousands of visitors during the summer season. This year, the village endured a boil water notice through the height of that season.
Yet a €1.2 million watersports facility providing free year-round hot showers, toilets and changing rooms, all connected to that same public water network, is due to be completed by the end of this year.
Still absent are a pedestrian crossing, continuous footpaths, a dedicated beach warden and effective traffic management measures throughout the village. These are the basic provisions expected in one of Mayo’s busiest tourist villages.
The funding streams and responsible agencies may differ, but residents and visitors experience one village, and the collective order of priorities is difficult to understand.
Keel can apparently be prioritised as a place in which to provide free showers, but not yet as a village in which residents and visitors can reliably drink the water, cross the road safely or navigate the seasonal traffic with any degree of ease.
The answer to mounting seasonal pressure cannot simply be infrastructure designed to accommodate still more pressure.
Tourism is vital to Achill. Investment in tourist facilities is welcome, but investment in the village that supports them must surely come first. – Yours, etc,

title: South Dublin hospital gifted to State with plans for new HSE facility on site
description: Leopardstown Park Hospital in Foxrock opened in 1917 to care for first World War soldiers
content:
A south Dublin hospital with 12 acres of land has been gifted to the State, with plans to build a new 125-bed facility for older people on the site.
Leopardstown Park Hospital in Foxrock was established under a charitable trust in 1917 after Gertrude Frances Dunning donated the house and lands to provide care for soldiers injured in service of the British forces during the first World War.
The hospital began admitting non-military patients in the 1970s and is now a service provider for older people.
After obtaining approval from the Charities Regulator , the Leopardstown Park Hospital Trust formally transferred the hospital buildings and 12 acres of land to the HSE earlier this year.
It is understood the State had to cover the legal and professional fees involved in the transfer.
The entire site is almost 22 acres, and the charity plans to sell the other 9.6 acres to a developer.
The trust says this land has the capacity for 600 new homes and is beside the green line Luas Central Park stop.
“The existing mature woodlands offer the opportunity to establish a new pocket public park, opening up this valuable amenity to the local community for the first time,” the trust said in a statement.
“Opportunities also exist to restore a protected structure as a vibrant community hub and to provide a range of new local services and amenities for existing and future residents.”
The trust says it will use the proceeds of this sale to continue its work assisting ex-military veterans across the country.
The HSE secured planning permission for a new 125-bed healthcare facility on the site in January, consisting of more than 9,000sq m (96,875sq ft) of floor area.
Some buildings in the existing hospital, which are in need of modernisation, will be demolished and others will be refurbished and linked up with the new building.
Leopardstown Park House itself, a protected structure, will not be changed.
The facility, which will be owned and operated by the HSE, will provide residential and day-care services for older people, including rehabilitation, respite and supported living.
Almost 5,000 new trees will be planted on the site to mitigate the removal of 39 existing trees, and the relocation of five existing orchard trees into woodland, the planning file shows.
“The trust is proud to transfer the hospital and land to the HSE,” Larry Walsh, chair of Leopardstown Park Hospital Trust, said in a statement.
“The trust’s donation of the hospital and the surrounding 12 acres will enable the development of a modern, state-of-the-art healthcare facility to care for elderly people long into the future.”

title: Is it the HSE or the taxpayer being fined?
description: I’m suggesting a headline change
content:
Sir, – So the Data Protection Commission has fined the HSE for “profound disarray and neglect” in the storage of records in several locations (“ HSE fined €645,000 after rotting medical records found amid animal droppings and rubble ,” September 2nd).
I have been a professional archivist for more than 30 years, and may I assure you and your readers that such storage conditions are actually quite common, not just in the HSE but also in other public bodies. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Can I suggest the headline “HSE fined €645,000 after rotting medical records found amid animal droppings and rubble” be changed to say it’s the Irish taxpayer who is being fined? – Yours, etc,

title: Standing up for neutrality
description: Our neutrality surely should be a badge of honour
content:
Sir, – There is a growing sense that our Government is softly conditioning the Irish people towards abandoning our military neutrality. Support from visiting military figures and a variety of European interests suggests Ireland is defenceless.
They imply that Ireland should feel a sense of national inferiority for enjoying the membership benefits of the economic union of Europe without contributing to a collective military framework.
A senior Government Minister attending this year’s Munich Security Conference stated that “neutrality doesn’t mean standing apart from others”. Yet surely the legal and moral essence of a country’s neutrality means precisely that it stands apart from others?
If our leaders regularly witness the obscenity of global conflicts on their screens just as our citizens do, the question is why would they not want to stand apart? Our neutrality surely should be a badge of honour.
During Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the EU, much discussion on military security can be expected. However, distant observers in Moscow and Beijing may not appreciate the political nuances of Ireland aligning itself with and chairing European military security discussions.
The people of Ireland must protect our neutral status before it is quietly eroded or bargained away. Austria, Malta and Switzerland have preserved neutrality within their constitutions.
Given a rising threat of war and rumours of nuclear conflict on Europe’s eastern flank, the State similarly should take the initiative now for a referendum to permanently enshrine neutrality in the Irish Constitution. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Reports that Ireland is relying on foreign military hardware, including a Royal Navy warship and a British submarine-monitoring helicopter, to provide security during the EU presidency have raised many eyebrows, with security experts wondering to what extent Ireland is taking ownership of its own national security amid the turbulent geopolitical and security climate.
People Before Profit’s Paul Murphy, however, was moved to ask how this arrangement is compatible with neutrality, and to suggest that policy is undermined by Ireland’s “deepening military co-operation with Nato militaries”.
Given that we only hear from the Opposition on security and defence matters when it is to lambaste Nato, to undermine support for Ukraine in its war against Russia or to lament the (apparently spontaneous) “militarisation” of the European Union, I have to ask what alternative security arrangements would they put in place during the EU presidency?
Can they provide some detail on what threats they believe we should be concerned about, and what hardware they would use to monitor and deter them? Sinn Féin in particular must be uncomfortable with this arrangement, so what is their alternative? – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Ireland’s EU presidency has once again highlighted the pitiful commitment to our nation’s defence. Ireland must rely on Britain and France to provide cover for key meetings, as our own Defence Forces do not have the capability to do so.
The Minister for Defence, Helen McEntee, has recently boasted about how the Government is increasing expenditure on defence. Ireland’s defence budget in respect of GDP is approximately a 10th of our European neighbours.
McIntee’s proud announcements are akin to a person needing a garden wall and being delighted that they have bought a second brick. – Yours, etc,

title: Department withholds notes of discussions between Aughinish Alumina and top civil servant
description: Department of Enterprise secretary general held several discussions with Limerick refinery director while review into Russian exports was being finalised
content:
The Department of Enterprise has claimed it cannot release notes of recent discussions between its top civil servant and Aughinish Alumina management, citing a desire to protect “highly confidential information” shared in confidence by the company.
Declan Hughes, the department’s secretary general, and Ciaran Kelleher, managing director of the Co Limerick refinery, had a number of phone calls and a meeting between June and July, when officials were finalising a review into the company’s exports to Russia .
The department’s investigation was launched following reporting in The Irish Times that traced how alumina refined in Aughinish is being shipped in vast quantities to smelters in Russia, where it is made into aluminium that is sold to ASK, a Moscow trading company known to supply the alloy to Russian arms and missile manufacturers.
The Limerick plant’s exports of alumina to Russia have significantly increased since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and account for about half of Aughinish’s business.
Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke said the department’s investigation could not be published, as it contained commercially sensitive information. However, a copy was obtained by The Irish Times .
The report said Irish officials could not find evidence proving alumina exported by Aughinish was ultimately used by Russian arms producers. The finding was qualified by the fact the inquiry was unable to source information about the clients of ASK and had no means to trace Irish-refined alumina inside Russia.
The department has refused a Freedom of Information (FOI) Act request from The Irish Times seeking notes of meetings and phone calls between senior civil servants and Aughinish Alumina.
Hughes, the secretary general of the department, met Kelleher, the head of Aughinish Alumina, on June 12th. There were three phone calls logged between the pair in June and July, with notes of what was discussed written up afterwards.
The department refused to release notes of what was discussed, stating the records contain “highly confidential information shared by the company with department officials in confidence”.
A department spokeswoman said it applies an “unbiased and objective” approach when deciding to release or withhold documents under the FOI Act.
“Records are withheld only in instances where specific, legally defined exemption provisions under the Act, such as personal privacy or commercial sensitivity, strictly apply,” she said.
Aughinish Alumina separately lobbied Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport Patrick O’Donovan and Minister of State in the Department of Agriculture Niall Collins, earlier this year, records show.
A filing Aughinish Alumina made to the State’s register tracking lobbying of public officials disclosed phone calls to the two Limerick TDs, to highlight “risks to business and employment at Aughinish Alumina”. The calls were made between January and April this year, according to the submission to the lobbying register.
The company disclosed Kelleher made representations over the phone to Taoiseach Micheál Martin’s chief of staff Deirdre Gillane, on the same subject.
Revelations detailing Aughinish Alumina’s role in the Russian supply chain were published by The Irish Times, in co-operation with the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, in late March.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy has made repeated calls for EU-level sanctions to prohibit exports of alumina to Russia, claiming the material is aiding Moscow’s war machine.
The European Commission, the EU’s executive body that leads on sanctions, is weighing up whether to include alumina shipments in the bloc’s next rounds of proposed sanctions. The measures are intended to make it harder for Russia to sustain its war in Ukraine.
Aughinish Alumina has warned the Government that cutting off its ability to sell to Russia could force the plant to close, costing hundreds of jobs in the mid-west.

title: Speeding lorries on motorways
description: I see trucks driving at 100km/h and more on a very regular basis
content:
Sir, – Now that the Government has agreed to extend the fuel support scheme for a further two months, costing an extra €400 million, with the possibility of further extensions remaining on the table, would the Irish haulage industry, for their part, agree to drive within the speed limits and obey the rules governing the use of lanes, particularly on our motorways?
As a frequent user of the M50 and M1 motorways, I see trucks driving at 100km/h and more on a very regular basis. Official sources tell us that such high speeds in lorries involves significant additional fuel usage.
Abiding by maximum speed limits would make a critical contribution to reducing the cost of haulage for everyone’s benefit. It would also serve to acknowledge the taxpayers’ very significant assistance to the haulage industry at this time of high fuel prices, as well as being a valuable road safety measure. – Yours, etc,

title: Increase in number of childcare providers investigated for possible overcharging
description: Department of Children review team undertakes audits to ensure core funding requirements are honoured
content:
There has been a steady increase in the number of childcare providers under investigation for possible overcharging of parents since 2024.
It comes in advance of a new audit process designed to identify creches that might be flouting their core funding rules and charging parents more than their 2021 agreed fee freeze.
This September, for the first time, childcare providers will have to have their 2026/2027 fees approved by the Department of Children “to confirm adherence to the fee freeze as part of the core funding rules”.
Under a 2022 agreement with the Government, childcare providers who received such additional funding promised to freeze their fees at 2021 levels. Until now, no formal auditing of childcare fees had been done at Government level, and the Department of Children only became aware of childcare providers who may have been overcharging if, or when, a parent made a complaint.
Since 2024, a National Fee Review Team within the department has been tasked with investigating potential breaches of frozen fees following such complaints.
According to documents released under Freedom of Information, the number of such complaints has increased since 2024.
For the 2023/2024 year, there were only three such reviews, with just one finding a breach of core funding rules. The number of reviews increased to 17 in 2024/2025, with documents showing that at least seven childcare providers were caught overcharging parents.
Only two were found to have “no breach” of their core funding rules. Another three services closed entirely or dropped out of core funding, and five other fee reviews did not state whether a breach had been found or not.
The number of investigations increased to 20 in 2025/2026. No outcome had yet been recorded for these investigations.
One review, recorded in documents held by the Department of Children, stretched from 2023 to 2026 without finding a breach.
The department said that, since fee review investigations were first set up in 2024, there have been “59 fee reviews whereby an initiator has raised a potential breach of fee controls. In the last two years the number of reviews initiated annually has been relatively steady.”
A number of childcare providers have complained that the amount of Government funding they receive under the core funding arrangement is not sustainable and has not met inflation, prompting some creches to threaten to withdraw from the scheme so they can hike their prices .
Minister for Children Norma Foley had said that, as of the end of July, only five providers had left the core funding scheme in 2025/2026, while 15 had joined.
The department said childcare services that feel their fees “may not be sufficient to sustain their business can access other supports while remaining in core funding”.
“For example, eligible services could apply for controlled fee increases in 2024. A new process for controlled fee increases was recently announced,” a spokesman said.

title: A book without an index is an incomplete work, and AI won’t fix it
description: Sharing an author’s arguments and quotes is tricky without a good index to point the way
content:
A simple request: would the publishers of non-fiction books please go to the bother of including an index? Even in the age of digital domination and search functionality, a print index serves a great purpose. And I remain unconvinced AI will sort out this problem.
I can list numerous books published in recent years by scientists, naturalists and even biographers whose writings are undoubtedly significant – and sometimes outstanding – yet they come without an index. Some are household names. I won’t name and shame them but be warned – you’re in the last-chance saloon!
To explain: a journalist, researcher, fellow writer or commentator often needs to source material, to use a quote or echo a great thought or idea that needs sourcing reasonably quickly – if only to quote an author accurately. It can enhance an article that has to be written to a tight deadline. Recollecting that the needed quote is somewhere between pages 150 and 250 is not helpful.
I grew up in a household that regarded most books as sacrosanct. My mother felt that to adulterate the page with markings – such as crude indexing – was the equivalent of scrawling over the Bayeux Tapestry. Post-it notes emerged later, but they bulge out of a volume or become unsticky, with obvious consequences.
Give me an example of being shortchanged in this way, you ask. I would highlight the case relating to the intriguing history around the discovery of DNA’s double helix structure in 1953 by the unlikely duo of Watson and Crick. One of my afflictions in life is to acquire books on what is probably the most consequential breakthrough of the 20 th century. It is remarkable how new insights have emerged, even of late.
One excellent book of popular science emerged with a section that provided compelling context in the race to determine DNA’s structure. Unquestionably, it provided new insight – probably because the author is at the frontier of globally significant scientific endeavour. This was not an aside of a few paragraphs, it was a substantial and fascinating take. The book, however, came without an index.
In such cases, the offending volumes, which offer singular pleasure, remain on the shelf, barely dipped into; uncited, their message is blunted unless you have the patience to read large chunks of text again.
In the interests of compromise, I suggest that book publishers, if they are not inclined to provide indexes for reasons of being strapped for cash, should provide a searchable ebook free of charge to purchasers of hard copies. After all, it is not unusual for a hardback to cost a hefty €30 or more. I’m not aware of any progressive publisher doing so – though some in the academic space do through Open Access initiatives, grant funding or institutional library packages. Why not go mass market on this for the common good?
[ Top companies keep talking about AI – but can’t explain the upsides Opens in new window ]
Of course, there will be those who say AI will inevitably perform the task of creating an index, so why get into a huff? Anecdotal evidence online questions its effectiveness, however. As noted elsewhere, AI is almost a pejorative term in the indexing community. One indexer noted: “AI tools do a bad job of indexing: they tend to under-index, cannot bring together related material, cannot identify implicit topics, and introduce inaccuracies and errors. So you still can’t index a book with a chatbot – you need a human indexer for that.”
Nonetheless, I’m not a Luddite. The evidence suggests there are effective ways of integrating AI into the work of an indexer to speed the process along (and reduce the cost).
To divert a little: In 1982, I and some of my journalistic peers made up the first group of young mavericks to complete Ireland’s first third-level professional journalism training course in what was then NIHE, later to become Dublin City University .
Some things stand out from that time under the tutelage of journalism master supreme John Horgan. Firstly, getting a place on the course hinged on an interview and spelling test; the latter being trendy at the time; an indicator of precision and observation, considered essential for good journalists.
Secondly, there were seemingly endless lectures on public administration and communication theory, when we wanted to be out in the field. But there was one aspect of the latter that stayed with me – the concept of “unity” in print and graphic design. It can be best summed up by looking at a page and concluding it doesn’t look right; there is something jarring visually. It can equally apply to a newspaper as to a page of a book. It is the principle that ensures all visual elements work together to create a cohesive, harmonious and clear whole.
[ Teachers disliked the ‘homework helper’ app. But AI-powered cheating makes it look quaint Opens in new window ]
May I suggest the principle be broadened to include the non-fiction book. Put another way, the absence of an index makes such volumes incomplete. It is an egregious example of “disunity”.
Kevin O’Sullivan is an environmental commentator and consultant

title: ‘In Toronto, a call from Ireland surprised me. My mother had made a decision’
description: Months after the sudden loss of my father, my mother looked out her window at the car she never learned to drive
content:
M y mother’s phone call surprised me. More than two thousand miles of ocean and land separated the two of us and she had made a decision.
Months after the sudden loss of my father, she looked out her window at the car she never learned to drive. It was still parked outside, a mere 10-minute walk away from the Derry walls. “I got this idea in my head that I should book a driving lesson with John,” she told me on the phone. “You remember him, Maeve’s son.”
I moved to Canada in 1981, but as my mother’s only daughter, we still chatted on the phone every week.
She set me straight when I mentioned the learner licence. “I already took a taxi downtown and sorted that out.” After that I received updates on her progress during our weekly conversations. “John’s patient and I pay him.” There was pride behind those words from a woman who found her first job outside the home 30 years after marriage.
No one in our family had John’s skill in diplomacy. My mother had little tolerance for correction of any kind but there was never a harsh word or complaint about him. John told her that her driving was excellent. Her nerves were a bit of a problem, he admitted, especially when she was stressed. I would have paid good money to listen in on that conversation in the car.
In the months of lessons that followed I wondered from afar about his endurance. I had my own experience of driving with my mother on trips back home. “Dear God,” she would pray when we travelled along small country roads around Derry while oncoming cars passed by my small rental. She clutched the dashboard with both hands, her seat belt extended way beyond normal.
John assured her when she failed the test a second time that she was a really good driver. Their lessons continued on and off. I was proud of her, if a bit concerned. She did not offer to take turns in the car when I flew home to see her and although she loved to gossip about other people’s foibles, John escaped any such commentary.
On one of my visits home from Canada, I drove my mother to see her brother William, who lived across the Border near Carndonagh. We stopped at a checkpoint with ramps and barbed wire manned by soldiers in battle dress, their accents from across the sea. That afternoon I gave details of our journey to a soldier almost as young as my oldest son. Sadness followed me beyond the barbed wire and sandbag huts.
Moments later my mother spoke up. At that same spot she stopped the car on her way to visit her brother. “Each time I stall, one of the soldiers helps me out of the car. He takes off his hat and drives over the ramp for me.”
I drove away from the checkpoint, the guns and her story without saying a word.
Back home at my kitchen table in Toronto I thought about the times she drove along roads and across army ramps with the L plate on the car and no driver beside her. Who knew? Who did she tell? Then I remembered what we learned as children. Outside the house, say nothing.
[ From the archive: Refusing to say nothing Opens in new window ]
“I have decided to give the car to Colin,” she told me on the phone two years after the first driving lesson. I may have misread her tone. Was this a great gift bestowed on the only child who lived near her while the rest of us scattered far away?
I last saw the old grey car parked by the side of my brother’s house outside Letterkenny surrounded by trees and fields in the midst of remote calls from cows and sheep. A cat lay stretched out on the bonnet while a new pup scouted around the tires.
I looked through the driver seat window and remembered my father’s pride in the new car long ago. Only one driver I told myself. Then I remembered the second, my Donegal mother fearless and feisty at the age of 70.
Mary Curran moved to Canada in 1981. She is a retired educator from Derry who lives in Toronto

title: Pete Hegseth’s military purge comes at a risky moment for Pentagon
description: Global Briefing: US defence secretary’s campaign against ‘wokeness’ is causing unease among some Republicans
content:
Good morning, I’m Jack Power, Europe correspondent for The Irish Times based in Brussels, and filling in today for Denis Staunton while he is away.
Not content with waging an actual war in Iran , Pete Hegseth has busied himself fighting another battle inside the US military to reshape its leadership to better align with the Trump administration’s political outlook.
The chaotic tussle on the home front claimed another high-profile casualty this week. Dan Driscoll, the army’s top civilian leader, tendered his resignation, following months of tension.
Driscoll had clashed with Hegseth over the defence secretary’s decision to fire or sideline more and more battle-tested military officers and generals, leaving the army and other branches light on leaders as Washington struggles to prosecute its war in Iran.
Hegseth has led a campaign to purge what he says are “woke” tendencies in the branches of the US military.
That has manifested itself in bizarre outbursts at times, including a diatribe last year against “fat generals and admirals” working in the Pentagon, the headquarters of the defence department – or, in Trump-speak, the Department of War.
What has really worried the military brass is how Hegseth has blocked the promotion of several lower-level officers, often women and members of minorities, to the rank of one-star general and other posts, overruling assessments recommending their advancement based on their records of military service.
It is unusual for the Pentagon chief to intervene in such run-of-the-mill appointments and doing so brought Hegseth into conflict with Driscoll and senior generals. It has also caused unease within Republican ranks on Capitol Hill, which may cause him headaches down the line.
Hegseth hasn’t shied away from clearing house in the upper echelons of the military either. He sacked army chief of staff Randy George in April, a key position that has yet to be properly filled. Navy secretary John Phelan was fired around the same time.
[ Hegseth plans testosterone screening for US troops, including women Opens in new window ]
A former Fox News host, Hegseth was in jeopardy himself for a period. He had a rocky start and it appeared US president Donald Trump might cast him overboard, but his position is much more secure now.
The recent departure of Driscoll, the army secretary, had appeared inevitable for the last while. Driscoll brought his grievances to the White House last week and reportedly laid out his concerns about the state of the military under Hegseth, highlighting difficulties caused by the spate of firings and stops put on certain promotions by the defence secretary.
Driscoll had been keen for the army to embrace drone warfare and other emerging technologies. That ran up against Hegseth’s chest-thumping, back-to-basics vision for the US armed forces.
The Trump administration will have a tricky time steering picks to fill the vacancies left by Driscoll and George through confirmation hearings in the Senate, where Republicans hold a slim majority.
Two figures loyal to Hegseth, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell, and Christopher LaNeve, who is acting up as army chief of staff, have been mentioned as candidates for the respective top jobs.
The votes of Republican lawmakers who keep a close ear to the views of senior military leaders may be hard to win.
