Minaun Capital’s other retail park investments include Wellpark Retail and Leisure Centre in Galway which it acquired from a private investor in an off-market transaction for €20.5 million in 2023. Developed originally by Gerry Barrett’s Edward Holdings at a cost of €75 million, the Galway scheme has a strong tenant line-up that includes Woodie’s, Lidl, Homestore & More, DFS furniture, Petmania and Boots. It also has the nine-screen Eye Cinema complex along with a 550-space surface and basement-level car park.
In 2022, Minaun Capital made its first investment in the regional retail park market when it purchased Mill Retail Park in Gorey, Co Wexford, from MM Capital for about €4.5 million.

title: Netanyahu has new protector inside European Union
description: Israeli government has waged an intense campaign to dissuade governments from backing EU action over Gaza
content:
Good morning, I’m Jack Power, Europe correspondent for The Irish Times based in Brussels, and filling in today for Denis Staunton while he is away.
On the same day Janez Jansa’s populist right-wing government took office in Slovenia this summer, Israel announced it would be opening an embassy in the small central European country.
Binyamin Netanyahu was delighted to see the back of Robert Golob, the previous Slovenian prime minister whose liberal party was unseated this June by a conservative coalition.
Under Golob’s government, Slovenia sat in a camp of pro-Palestine countries pushing for the European Union to take a much firmer stance against Israel.
Netanyahu has described the centrist Slovenian politician as “just about the most hostile” prime minister in Europe.
Domestically, Slovenia banned trade coming from occupied Palestinian territories, halted the sale or transit of arms to Israel, recognised the Palestinian state and instituted a travel ban on Netanyahu and extremist ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
Slovenia, the Republic of Ireland and Spain comprised an initial trio pushing Brussels to hold Israel to account. That coalition grew as the death toll in Gaza mounted.
The change of government has enabled Netanyahu to gain a close friend inside the EU. Jansa has become one of Israel’s most ardent defenders and will likely block any EU sanction that needs the unanimous sign-off from all 27 governments.
Announcing the decision to open an embassy in Ljubljana, the Slovenian capital, Israel’s foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar said the Jansa government marked a new chapter. “We now have an opportunity to rebuild, strengthen, and deepen a real partnership … When Israel’s friends return to power, Israel returns,” he said via a statement.
It is a clear-cut case of Netanyahu employing the diplomatic carrot in what has been a sustained effort to head off political sanction from Brussels.
The Israeli government has waged an intense behind-the-scenes campaign to dissuade European governments from backing any joint EU-level action in response to what’s happening in Gaza and the West Bank.
According to diplomats and officials in Brussels, that often involves Israeli politicians insisting to allies, such as Germany, that they can effect greater change through quiet dialogue, rather than hard leverage.
The efforts helped to kill off a push to suspend an EU-Israel free trade deal in an “association agreement” governing relations.
It is understood Sa’ar spent considerable time on the phone with foreign ministers and the bloc’s high representative on foreign policy, Kaja Kallas, during periods when it seemed momentum was building to do something to restrain Israel’s actions.
The Israeli minister sold Kallas a deal last year promising to allow more humanitarian aid into Gaza, just when support to suspend Israel’s tariff-free access to the EU market was creeping close to a required qualified majority.
Kallas was outplayed by Sa’ar on that occasion. It was only a US-brokered peace agreement several months later that eventually enabled significant supplies of food, water and more into Gaza.
Current political chatter centres on a proposed EU-wide ban ending trade with illegal Israeli settlements in Occupied Palestinian Territories. Talk had been parked for August, but foreign ministers would have returned to the subject at an EU council meeting in Wicklow.
National capitals that were already on the fence will be reluctant to back an Occupied Territories trade ban before Knesset elections in Israel next month. Don’t hold your breath for the EU to take a decision soon.

title: La bonhomie is back: Macron arrives in Britain bearing gifts
description: Return of Bayeux Tapestry offers a symbolic backdrop to the warmest UK-French relations in years
content:
A ndy Burnham spent the summer striving to prove to the UK’s Labour Party that he will be a better, more empathetic general than his predecessor, Keir Starmer . But could he be a luckier one, too?
The timing this week of his first hosting of a world leader in London suggests that he might be.
Anglo-French relations are under the spotlight with the arrival in Britain on Wednesday of France’s president, Emmanuel Macron . He is in town to formally unveil the near-1,000-year-old Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum in London’s leafy Bloomsbury district, where it is on loan from the French government until next July.
The temporary relocation of the priceless 70-metre-long embroidery, which depicts the Norman conquest of Britain right up to Battle of Hastings in 1066, was championed by Macron in 2018 at the height of the Brexit negotiations with Theresa May , one of Burnham’s many recent predecessors as UK prime minister.
Macron saw his offer to loan the artwork, which hadn’t been on British soil for almost a millennium, as a way of buttressing his nation’s ties with the UK at a time when they were under strain due to messy geopolitics. The French had repeatedly refused to lend the Bayeux Tapestry to the British over the previous century or so.
Against the advice of many French experts, who feared the tapestry could be damaged, it was spirited into Britain overnight in July in a high-security, high-stakes operation. A single tear in the fabric, and Macron might be put in fear of France’s political guillotine.
The arrival of the historical embroidery has sparked giddiness in Britain and also a round of sentimental soul-searching in UK media over the country’s relations with its closest neighbour to the east.
Hélène Duchêne, France’s ambassador to Britain, was recently brought on to Sky News to discuss the tapestry’s arrival, where she mused with her hosts that the loan deal said much about Britain and France’s “past, but also about our future”.
The day after unveiling the tapestry, and after a short expected meeting with king Charles , Macron is expected to hold talks with Burnham in London on Thursday. He will be the first European Union leader to do so with the new UK prime minister on British soil, beating the Republic’s Micheál Martin , who may be in line for a visit to Burnham’s old stomping ground of Manchester at the end of the third week of September.
[ No more summer sunshine for Burnham as the real work begins Opens in new window ]
Macron will also be the first world leader of any sort to be greeted by Burnham at his new home of Downing Street (the UK prime minister briefly hosted Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskiy in July, but in Portsmouth).
This is where the new UK prime minister’s good timing comes in. Macron’s arrival comes just as Anglo-French relations reach their warmest point in years. Much of the spade work on the UK side was put in by Starmer, but that lucky general Burnham reaps the benefit.
For the past four or five years, Anglo-French relations have been viewed domestically in Britain principally through the prickly prism of migrant small boat arrivals. But recent deals done with the French under Starmer have stemmed the flow significantly.
July’s total number of arrivals was the lowest for the peak summer month since 2020. French police, with funding from London, stopped 60 per cent of small boat launches in the past three months. The British are paying to put 40 per cent more “boots on the ground” to patrol French beaches. The UK press has taken note.
Meanwhile, the two nations in effect jointly lead the “coalition of the willing” helping Ukraine in its fight against Russia; they recently co-operated, for example, on giving Zelenskiy’s government the blueprints for Storm Shadow missiles.
[ Starting gun fires on Europe’s make-or-break election in France Opens in new window ]
France and Britain are also joint linchpins in European discussions around upgrading the continent’s defences, while as two nuclear-armed permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they have also co-operated in self-perceived roles as geopolitical grown-ups in the dangerous age of US president Donald Trump.
Luckily for Burnham, this will do him no harm as he pursues closer relations with the European Union while, so far, offering little in return.
Meanwhile, the hype machine for the Bayeux Tapestry is cranking up. It opens for public viewing on Thursday next week but all tickets until December were snapped up in one day when they were released in July. Some people queued online for nine hours to get them.
The next tranche will be up for grabs online on October 21st. There has been some controversy, however, around private viewings for well-connected individuals, such as billionaire Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel .
There is a home-grown alternative for those who cannot secure a coveted ticket to view the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum. In the late 1880s, a group of women who were members of a Staffordshire embroidery club stitched a full-sized, faithful replica, which to this day is on display at a little museum in Reading, just west of London.
A faithful replica in all respects but one.
As it was stitched in prudish Victorian Britain, the Staffordshire ladies censored all of the warriors’ penises that could be seen in the original.

title: Nuns seeking €4.5m for 50-acre estate beside Wicklow’s Magheramore beach
description: Magheramore complex has served as international headquarters of Missionary Sisters of St Columban since 1957
content:
Having served as the international headquarters of the Missionary Sisters of St Columban since 1957, the order’s home and lands at Magheramore in Co Wicklow have been placed on the market through agent Bannon at a guide price of €4.5 million.
The “Motherhouse”, as it is referred to by the sisters, sits on 50 acres directly across the road from the entrance to the well-known Magheramore beach and is located within a short drive of Wicklow town, Brittas Bay and junction 18 of the M11 motorway. There are several buildings arranged across two clusters on the site, and these extend to a total area of 7,318 sq m (78,766 sq ft) of accommodation that includes 111 bedrooms.
The buildings include the original Magheramore period house. Built around 1870 and known originally as Seapark House, the property has a large extension that houses the complex’s main bedroom accommodation and a church, built in the 1960s. A nursing home, which operated until last year, has 24 en-suite bedrooms and interconnects with the main building. The Bobbio Centre, which consists of 12 en-suite bedrooms, a five-bedroom cottage and offices, is located in a separate area of the site and there is a gate lodge at the main entrance to the complex.
The original Magheramore House had been in use as a hotel before its acquisition by the Missionary Sisters in 1957. That may yet inform the plans of a future owner given the property’s location across from Magheramore beach. The 21-acre site immediately adjacent to the beach had been the subject in 2023 by its then owner, Paddy McKillen jnr and Matt Ryan’s company, Creatively Pacific, of a planning application for a boutique holiday resort and surf school. The plan, which was rejected by Wicklow County Council, attracted local opposition, with Sr Kathleen Melia of the Missionary Sisters of St Columban describing the “grandiose plan” as “the height of folly”.
Commenting on the sale of the Magheramore complex, Paul Doyle of Bannon says: “This property, set in the most tranquil environment, has served the Missionary Sisters of St Columban well for several decades. The opportunity now presents for a new owner to maximise its potential most likely by repurposing the existing buildings. Potential future uses may vary, dependent on the buyer, and may include an element of residential, education, care/rehabilitation, tourism/hotel and a range of hospitality uses such as a wedding venue, all subject to planning permission.”

title: Fully let south Dublin student accommodation scheme seeks €4.5m
description: Koula Rooms in Monkstown has 28 bedspaces and is generating net operating income of €307,000 a year
content:
Investors involved in the supply of housing to third-level students will be interested in the opportunity presented by the sale of Koula Rooms, a fully let student-accommodation scheme in the south Dublin suburb of Monkstown . The property, which comprises 28 bed spaces across two detached two-storey blocks, is being offered to the market by agent Colliers at a guide price of €4.5 million.
Koula Rooms generates income across the academic year and summer letting periods. The development’s gross income and net operating income stand at about €357,000 and €307,000 a year respectively.
The asking price of €4.5 million reflects a capital value of approximately €150,000 per bedspace and a net initial yield of approximately 6.53 per cent on the net operating income, assuming purchaser’s costs of 4.46 per cent.
Located on Abbey Road and within a short walk of the campus of the IADT (Institute of Art, Design and Technology), which has approximately 2,500 enrolled students, the subject property comprises eight self-contained three-bedroom apartments. Each bedroom benefits from its own en suite bathroom, accommodating a total of 28 student bedspaces across single and twin-occupancy configurations. The scheme extends to a total area of 511 sq m (5,502 sq ft) and has recently undergone a comprehensive refurbishment programme, including newly installed storage heaters, upgraded fire safety systems and modernised bathroom fittings throughout.
Apart from its proximity to the IADT campus, Koula Rooms is convenient for students looking to commute to UCD’s Belfield campus or to other third-level institutions including Trinity College and TUD. The property is well served by public transport, with several Dublin Bus routes providing regular access to and from Dublin city centre.
Michele McGarry of Colliers says: “Koula Rooms is a fully stabilised student accommodation investment in an established south Dublin location. The combination of strong demand for student accommodation, a comprehensive refurbishment and an attractive income profile should appeal to a wide range of domestic and international investors.”

title: Site of Dublin’s historic Ormond Hotel sold in off-market deal for €12m
description: Malaysian owners dispose of property which featured in James Joyce’s Ulysses after 13-year odyssey
content:
The long-awaited and much-debated redevelopment of the site of the former Ormond Hotel on Dublin ’s Ormond Quay Upper may have moved a step closer following the property’s sale to a group of Irish investors.
Having paid about €2.5 million to developer Bernard McNamara in 2013 to secure ownership of the Victorian-era hotel, which features in “the Sirens” chapter of James Joyce ’s Ulysses, Malaysian-based Monteco Holdings has sold the site in an off-market transaction brokered by agent CBRE for about €12 million. While the figure is a multiple of the price Monteco paid for the property, it is still far short of the €17 million McNamara splashed out on the hotel’s purchase a year after its closure, in 2006. The developer put it back on the market in 2009 shortly after his various businesses began to experience financial difficulty, with an asking price of €7m, but it failed to sell.
It remains unclear whether the Ormond Hotel site’s new owners, who are understood to be experienced hotel developers, will pursue the development of the hotel for which Monteco finally secured planning permission in 2017 or submit a new planning application of their own.
The current planning consent provides for the development of a 120-bedroom hotel, along with food, beverage and meeting facilities distributed across 5,850sq m (62,970sq ft) over seven floors.
Commenting on the completion of the Ormond Hotel site’s sale, Alexandra Sheeran of CBRE’s hotels division said: “This transaction marks a significant milestone and we look forward to seeing the positive impact the new hotel will bring to this prominent riverside site and the future development of the area.”

title: Citywest office and warehouse guiding at €6.85m
description: Offices at 2024 Bianconi Avenue are vacant while warehouse is fully let until December 2030
content:
Agent Knight Frank is guiding a price of €6.85 million for 2024 Bianconi Avenue at Dublin’s Citywest Business Campus .
The subject property comprises a two-storey office headquarters building of 1,777sq m (19,127sq ft), together with a self-contained warehouse extending to 2,813sq m (30,278sq ft). The property has 67 car-parking spaces.
The offices, which are vacant, have a flexible layout incorporating both open-plan areas and cellular offices/meeting rooms.
The South Dublin County Development Plan 2022-2028 permits office, industrial, science/ technology-based uses. Appropriately scaled commercial healthcare uses may also be considered for the property subject to further consultation, the selling agent says.
The warehouse has independent access and is let to Hevac Ltd (part of the Wolseley Group) until December 2030.
Number 2024 occupies a high-profile site extending to three acres (1.21 hectares), with frontage on to the N7. The subject property is located within a 10-minute walk of the Luas Red Line stop at Saggart.
Citywest Business Campus has long been regarded as one of Dublin’s key commercial hubs, with occupiers in the area including software and technology solutions provider SAP, semiconductor specialist AMD (Advanced Micro Devices) and healthcare services giant Uniphar.
[ Belfast’s five-star Fitzwilliam Hotel hits the market with €37m price tag Opens in new window ]
Tom McNamara of Knight Frank says: “We expect strong interest from both owner-occupiers and investors seeking value-add potential.
“The existing income from the warehouse generates short-term cash flow while offering potential for future asset management, regear or redevelopment, subject to planning permission. On a stabilised basis, following the letting of the office accommodation, we would anticipate a net return in the region of 10 per cent.”

title: Large landholding beside the K Club in Kildare seeking €2.25m
description: Lodge Park lands extend to 12 hectares and have 200m of road frontage and 800m of direct access to river Liffey
content:
The sale of a 12-hectare (30-acre) landholding just outside the village of Straffan in Co Kildare is expected to see interest from a range of potential purchasers. Located directly across the road from the entrance to the five-star K Club hotel and golf resort, and positioned along the river Liffey at Straffan Bridge, the lands at Lodge Park are being offered to the market by agent Sherry FitzGerald at a guide price of €2.25 million.
The subject property is zoned for agricultural use at present and comprises two large grass fields with mature boundaries and a substantial barn and two-storey farm building. The land has road frontage of approximately 200m from Straffan Bridge, facing the boundary wall of K Club to the resort’s entrance. It has direct access to the river Liffey along an 800m stretch running towards Castledillon.
While the subject property’s potential in the short to medium term is likely to remain confined to its current agricultural use, prospective purchasers will take note of plans being progressed for a nursing home and housing on nearby lands. The Lodge Park holding is positioned immediately adjacent to a 14-hectare (35-acre) holding previously owned by Gerry Gannon, the well-known property developer and former co-owner of the K Club.
The lands’ proximity to the K Club is expected by the selling agent to be a key driver of interest in the sale. Developed originally by businessman Michael Smurfit, the resort, which is now owned by nursing homes entrepreneur Michael Fetherston, extends to 220 hectares (550 acres) with two Arnold Palmer-designed championship golf courses surrounding a five-star hotel alongside a bespoke apartment scheme and gated community of high-end houses.
The K Club was the venue of the 2006 Ryder Cup, the first to be hosted in Ireland. Since then, the resort has been the location for 13 European Opens and the Irish Opens of 2016, 2023 and 2025. Last week, it hosted the 2026 KPMG Women’s Irish Open.
Bobby Lloyd of Sherry FitzGerald says: “The land at Lodge Park presents an opportunity for purchasers looking for a special landholding with exceptional road and river frontage in a village setting. Facing the world-famous K Club, it’s rare for land of this quality to come to the market.”

title: Fully let IFSC office investment for €10m offers buyer net initial yield of 8.45%
description: Proposed sale of 4 Custom House Plaza follows recent disposal of neighbouring blocks for €24m
content:
A range of Irish and international investors are expected to express their interest in the sale of 4 Custom House Plaza, a fully let office investment in Dublin’s IFSC . The property, which is multi-tenanted, is being offered to the market by agent TWM at a guide price of €10 million. Should a sale proceed at that level, the new owner would be in line for a net initial yield of 8.45 per cent, after standard purchaser’s costs of 9.96 per cent.
The proposed disposal of 4 Custom House Plaza comes 10 months after Irish family office Ardvest’s acquisition for €24 million of the neighbouring properties, numbers 3 and 5 Custom House Plaza. The two buildings extend to a total net internal area of 60,606 sq ft (5,631 sq m) and are generating €2,656,974 in annual rental income, with 50 per cent of the rent roll derived from Citco Fund Services. Other tenants include FlexiFi Europe Services, Companjon, Maxol and Device Atlas.
Number 4 Custom House Plaza extends to a net internal area of 1,811 sq m (19,500 sq ft) distributed over five floors, with 20 secure basement car-parking spaces. The building is fully let to five tenants and is generating overall annual rental income of €929,414.
The property is situated immediately adjacent to Connolly Station, which provides Dart, commuter rail and Luas services.
Kim Moran of TWM says: “This is an excellent opportunity to acquire a fully let office investment in the heart of the IFSC. We expect to see interest in this sale from both domestic and international investors.”

title: Kevin Rowland: ‘I wish I’d stuck to my guns more, not be influenced by people who didn’t get it’
description: The singer on growing older, figuring himself out, and what might be the last Dexy Midnight Runners album – which is full of love songs with a twist
content:
B eginning an interview by deliberating an ending is somewhat unusual, but Kevin Rowland has never been a man to play by the rule book.
We’re talking about Love, the new (and perhaps final) Dexys Midnight Runners album, which was recorded in Belfast with David Holmes . Rowland says he was clear when they were making it that it would be the swansong of the band that he has led in various iterations since 1978.
“Me and David got on great; it really worked,” he says. “And while I was over there he went, ‘This is f**king great. I want to do more albums with you. Let’s do more and more.’
“But I’d already decided that this feels like the last one, and I don’t really want to do another one. I mentioned that to the record company as well, and then they wanted me to promote it as the last Dexys album – but that’s when I said no, just in case I change my mind.”
“So never say never, but I haven’t got any inspiration and I haven’t got any desire to do another one at the moment, I must confess. But in three or four years, who knows? It might feel different.”
Anyone who has read Rowland’s excellent memoir Bless Me Father , which was published last year, will be aware what a complex character he is. A maverick both inside and outside the music industry , he had an often turbulent childhood in Wolverhampton and London, the son of Irish parents from Crossmolina, Co Mayo. (Yes, he confirms with a smile, he did celebrate their All-Ireland triumph.)
There were teenage forays into petty crime, his hard-fought success in the music business with Dexys and, later, a debilitating cocaine addiction and bankruptcy before a glorious comeback in the 2010s.
It’s a story for the ages, told without self-pity and in full acknowledgment of his flaws. I tell him it would make a great biopic, which he finds particularly amusing. “Who would play me?” he says, slightly horrified at the thought. “God knows.”
Dexys Midnight Runners was the first music I ever heard on headphones. They were the first band I ever saw live, and I was obsessed with them
Love is the first album since Don’t Stand Me Down, from 1985, to feature the full Dexys Midnight Runners band name. A conversation Rowland had with a younger neighbour, who didn’t realise that Dexys and Dexys Midnight Runners were the same band, inspired the reversal.
“I always like the idea of getting through to younger people,” Rowland says. “So it just seemed like a no-brainer.”
In many ways Love is a companion piece to Rowland’s memoir. The book provides context for certain songs about his proud Irish heritage (My Life in England), for example, while one of the most touching tracks is Once a Man, Twice a Child, written about his fractious relationship with his overly critical father, which he documents in painful detail in the memoir.
It was ultimately mended before his dad’s death, at the age of 102, when he had “turned into this sweet person, like a little child”, Rowland says. “And I never, ever could have imagined that, because he was such a tough bastard.”
As its title suggests, this is an album of love songs with a twist. Rowland is a grandfather – in fact a great-grandfather now – and the sweet, sprightly soul song You’re Alright (“You’re the most lovely people, and I’m so proud of you/Please know that I love you deeply, and I always will do”) was written for his daughter AJ, whom he didn’t meet until her teenage years, and his extended offspring.
Another song, Old Love, laments the passing of time with lines such as, “I hate getting old, it happened so fast, where did it go?/They don’t see me, they just see my age.”
[ Dolly Parton laid to rest in private Nashville funeral Opens in new window ]
We speak a few days before Rowland’s 73rd birthday, and he accepts congratulations with a grimace. “There’s not much to recommend [getting older], do you know what I mean?” he says. “You might have a bit of wisdom on a good day, but, you know, the body starts to deteriorate, and that’s not fun.”
Rowland has battled health issues in recent years, including problems with his kidneys. He became gravely ill while in Thailand in 2024, and made peace with the fact that he may not pull through. These days he is doing better; his kidney function is now at 50 per cent, up from the 20 per cent that almost led to him going on dialysis. “But five years ago they were 97 per cent or something.” He shrugs. “So it’s slow, but it’s going the right way.”
Perhaps it has been that newfound lease of life that led Rowland to try something relatively radical by making a connection with Holmes. It’s not the most obvious pairing, but the Belfast musician, composer and producer is an avowed Dexys fanboy.
“Dexys Midnight Runners was the first music I ever heard on headphones,” Holmes says. “They were the first band I ever saw live, and I was obsessed with them. And the fact that I have now played a part in what could be their final album is beyond.”
Rowland admits to being nervous about the partnership, as he had only met Holmes in passing over the years. “I didn’t know him, really,” he says. “And I thought, ‘What’s he going to do? Is he going to want to turn it into a remix or something?’”
He chuckles, noting there was some push and pull between them right from the beginning.
“I said, ‘David, the only way this is going to work is if we do it together. It has to be together.’ And I think he was a bit nervous as well; he said, ‘If you micromanage everything, it’s going to be difficult.’ And I just said, ‘Well, I’m not prepared to hand it over to anybody.’”
He shrugs. “But those conversations helped us get to where we’re going. He’s quite out-there. I had to get used to his way of working, but I’m really happy with it.”
This may well be the final Dexys album, but Rowland doesn’t mention whether that extends to another solo record, too. His last solo album, My Beauty, from 1999, featured his superb interpretations of songs that had seen him through his darkest hours, such as This Guy’s in Love with You, You’ll Never Walk Alone and The Greatest Love of All.
The press attention at the time was largely focused on the cover art, however, which depicted Rowland in make-up, a dress and stockings. (He admitted that he “battened down the hatches” after its unfair critical mauling, although the album has since been reappraised and was re-released in 2020 to UK chart success.)
The dapper Rowland has always placed huge importance on image and clothes, since the very first incarnation of Dexys Midnight Runners; but considering the way gender-bending artists and imagery is celebrated now, does he feel he was simply ahead of his time?
[ Irish rapper Reggie: ‘Dundalk’s on top of the world right now. The centre of the universe’ Opens in new window ]
“I’ve never thought that, really,” he says, shaking his head. “I don’t think I was ahead of my time in 1978 when we formed Dexys, and with the original flamboyant look of the band; I think the timing was right.
“I think the only thing is I wish I’d stuck to my guns more, rather than be influenced by people who didn’t understand what I was doing, who didn’t get it.” He shrugs. “That’s how it goes sometimes.”
These days he is a vegan tai-chi practitioner, still in an addiction-recovery programme. It may be poles apart from what his younger self might have envisaged, but he is grateful to have come this far.
After a lifetime of questioning who he is artistically, is he any closer to figuring himself out?
“I suppose so,” he says, “but it’s always changing. Everybody is. I do feel more at peace with it all. I’ve made a lot of statements about who I am and how I feel at a certain time, and I’ve done what I’ve wanted to do, largely.
“But, quite often, it’s something different to what it was two years ago. And I have to work on peace of mind daily, but it’s all good.”
If Love really is the final Dexys album, it’s a bookend to a remarkable career. Does he think about legacy much these days? Rowland tilts his head for a moment, thinking deeply.
“I don’t know if I can put that into words,” he says. “But I’ll tell you what I do think: it’s been a hell of a journey from Searching for the Young Soul Rebels to here, to Love.
“I think it’s a good body of work now, and I wouldn’t have said that before. And this new album, Love, is a pretty good way to end it, really. Because what else is there?”
Love is released by Heavenly Recordings on Friday, September 4th. Dexys Midnight Runners play 3Olympia Theatre , Dublin, on Wednesday, November 4th; Ulster Hall , Belfast, on Thursday, November 5th; and Black Box , Galway, on Friday, November 6th

title: Office rents must hit record €80 per square foot to justify new building, says HWBC
description: Broker sees headline rents topping €70 per square foot by end of 2026
content:
Rent for top-level office space in Dublin will need to hit a record €80 per square foot to justify the next round of new development in the city, according to HWBC .
So-called prime rents are set to top €70 by the end of the year, the broker said amid ever-increasing demand for space in the heart of the capital. That itself would be a new record. Rents for grade A office space in Dublin stand at about €67.50 at present.
“The outlook for the second half of the year remains positive, particularly for prime energy-efficient space in the CBD [central business district] as the supply of standing stock continues to be absorbed by corporate tenants,” said Paul Scannell, HWBC director of agency and business. “We expect recent developments will be substantially leased or reserved by year-end.”
Rents of €80 per square foot would be an unheard-of level for the Dublin office market. While some bespoke deals do go above the headline rate for the city, few, if any, have come close to €80. Rents peaked at about €65 per square foot during the Celtic Tiger years two decades ago.
Pre-lets – once a hallmark of the Dublin market – are likely to return, HWBC said, as businesses seek to guarantee space in favoured developments. About two-thirds of the 800,000sq ft of space under construction at present has already been rented out, with a new wave of building needed to meet demand.
While office availability in the city centre remains tight, companies are taking more space outside of what was traditionally seen as Dublin’s central business district. On Tuesday, US tech firm Klaviyo said it had signed terms to take space at One Le Pole Square near Ship Street in Dublin 8.
The surge in rents comes despite a wave of so-called grey market office space coming to the market as big companies that had taken on huge amounts of space in recent years seek to sublet or offload altogether at least part of their lettings.

title: Measures to keep young children from accessing online platforms failing, says report
description: Account creation on YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram still relies solely on self-declaration of age
content:
Measures to keep young children from accessing online platforms are failing to live up to expectations, a new report has found, with little impact on the number of underage children signing up for accounts.
The CyberSafeKids 10th annual report, The Year Little Changed, also found there was a rise in exposure to sexual content among 12 to 15-year-olds.
It found 70 per cent of children aged eight to 12 years old have accounts on social media apps that are designated for children aged 13 and older, a figure that is almost unchanged from the level recorded in July 2025.
[ Plan to set 13 as EU-wide minimum age for social media access to be discussed Opens in new window ]
Sixty-three per cent use YouTube, up slightly from last year’s figure, while Snapchat and TikTok accounted for 21 per cent and 20 per cent respectively.
This is despite new legal requirements designed to keep underage users off platforms, which CyberSafeKids said suggested age assurance measures are not functioning as intended on the platforms they use most.
Platforms use various methods to detect underage users, even among those who have given an incorrect age at sign-up to access the service, such as behavioural or content analysis and user reports. But with account creation on YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram still relying solely on self-declaration of age, children can still avoid triggering parental oversight features.
Among the children in the eight-to-12-year age group, 94 per cent have their own smart device, with tablets the most popular in this age group. More than half said they spend most of their time online gaming, with Roblox the top app.
However, 26 per cent of children said they had been bothered by something they had seen or experienced online, with more than half saying this had occurred on Roblox.
By the time children are aged 12 to 15, the most popular device switched to smartphones, with messaging app WhatsApp the most popular in this age group at 85 per cent. Sixty-seven per cent said they played Roblox.
A quarter of children in this age group said they had seen something online that bothered them, with 48 per cent saying this happened on Snapchat. The most common material reported was scams and fake information, with hate content following in second.
Older children were more likely to keep these interactions to themselves, while 29 per cent said they reported it online.
Fifteen per cent of those who were bothered by online content said they had seen or been asked for nudity or sexual things. That rose to 20 per cent in the older age category, while 24 per cent said they had accessed sexual content this year, up from 10 per cent last year.
Most concerning was that 22 per cent said the material was pushed to them and was not sought out.
Artificial intelligence (AI) use has also increased significantly among children. More than half of children under 12 said they used the technology regularly, with 59 per cent using it to look up information and 47 per cent asking it fun questions. Among older children, 76 per cent said they use it, with three-quarters using it to look up information.
Despite this increase in use, children say no one is talking to them about AI use, with only 50 per cent of eight- to 12-year-olds and 55 per cent of 12- to 15-year-olds having conversations about the technology.
“After a raft of new legislation in Ireland and at EU level in 2025, we had real expectations of change, but this report shows those expectations haven’t been met,” said CyberSafeKids chief executive Alex Cooney.
“We flagged concerns last year about children’s access to AI chatbots and the absence of regulation for this powerful new technology. A year on, little has changed on regulation, while children’s access has grown exponentially, without safeguards or protections.
“After 10 years of reporting on children’s online experiences, this year’s data shows little positive impact from regulation. The intense debate over banning under-16s from social media is missing the point. We’re arguing over whether to lock the door while the laws already meant to protect children inside go unenforced. We have to do better.”
The report makes a number of recommendations, including the implementation of the State’s online health taskforce recommendations, setting the default minimum age for digital products intended for use by children to 16 and the blocking of minors’ access to pornography in the Republic.
It also wants to see agreement between the European Parliament and Council on an EU-wide ban on marketing and using AI systems to create non-consensual intimate images, and the funding of initiatives to support parents and caregivers.

title: Electric Ireland solar panels transformed this remote Irish farm
description: Because energy decisions can feel overwhelming, Electric Ireland provides clear, practical guidance to build confidence and support you at every stage
content:
Finding the right energy solutions for your home or business can feel difficult. But it doesn’t have to be.
Electric Ireland helps you take control of your energy use and costs, supporting you to make informed decisions. The result is greater energy-independence and peace of mind. Solar installations start at under €5,300 including a Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) grant, but mid-to-large installations are becoming more common. For instance, a solar system of 14 panels on a south-facing roof in the east of the country may generate approximately 5,450kWh per year, which could mean over €1,400 in savings annually depending on your electricity plan.
As product manager at Electric Ireland, Anne Marie McArdle knows exactly how easy finding the right solutions can actually be.
For example, she recently worked with Tom, a sheep farmer in Carrickfinn, a beautiful and remote part of northwest Donegal.
“Tom’s is a working sheep farm in quite an isolated part of the country – the next parish over is the USA,” says McArdle. “But his family has farmed here for generations and he has a lot of relatives nearby, so he has deep roots in what is a very close-knit community.”
In many respects, Tom’s farm is a traditional one. Depending on the season, he will ferry his sheep out to a nearby island to graze – a scene to behold.
But farmers are forward looking too, with an entrepreneurial spirit, and Tom is no different, diversifying in recent years to raise cattle and pigs.
The whole enterprise is very much a family affair. Both his wife, a local teacher, and his young children, who attend the local Gaelscoil, pitch in to help.
“The family has a flock of chickens that roam freely and the children know all the secret places they lay, so they go around collecting their eggs,” says McArdle. “These are sold at the gate from an honesty box.
“As well as being a teacher, Tom’s wife has won many awards with her baking, which she sells through the honesty box at Lakeside farm. They also make soap from their jersey cows’ milk. They are a really industrious family.”
That matters because, while the farm is an idyllic family home, it is also a business. Like so many business-owners, Tom has had to cope with rising costs. Fertiliser, fodder and fuel for his tractor are among the rising expenses.
‘For some it’s because they want to live more sustainably and to know that they are doing their part. Others want to know that they are investing their money in something that they can see a payback for within a certain number of years’
While he can’t control every expense, he can make some more predictable, such as the cost of electricity, which is what first brought him to Electric Ireland’s online Net Zero Hub. It’s the place to find out everything you need to know about smart meter plans, solar energy, electric vehicle chargers and home retrofits.
In short, it guides you through all the steps you can take towards a low-carbon, net-zero emissions future.
The next step is to fill in the callback form on the solar landing page and request a callback from an Electric Ireland solar consultant.
Within a day or so, you run through high-level checks about your home and book a 30-minute consultation at a time that suits you. These can take place over the phone or online by video call.
This allows the experts at Electric Ireland to use an online platform to assess factors such as roof space, your home’s aspect and orientation, or shading from trees or other buildings, to find the best option for you.
Tom’s farmhouse has a south-facing roof, making it ideal for generating electricity all through the day.
You don’t have to be an Electric Ireland customer to avail of its solar installation services.
“Of course, we love it when people switch over to us, but it isn’t necessary. Hopefully they will consider us for their electricity plan and strong Microgen export rate based on their solar experience,” says McArdle. “One of the reasons for getting solar PV is typically to protect against price volatility, as well as the financial savings. Tom was finding that some of his costs were becoming a bit unpredictable, and was looking for ways to have more control.
“He knew that by getting solar in he could start to predict his costs a bit more accurately, as well as reduce his usage from the grid.”
The company also offers two payment options for Solar PV for homeowners. You can either pay the full amount upfront, or you can pay half after the survey, with the remaining balance due on the day of installation. The panels come with a 25-year warranty, for even greater peace of mind, and prices have come down too.
“Solar technology has improved over the years, improving the overall value for customers thinking of investing in solar,” she says. “It’s the same for the storage batteries. Their price has come down over the last couple of years, making it much more affordable.”
Generous grants are still available from the SEAI towards the cost. But in this case, cost wasn’t the only factor. “Tom’s farm and home are in an exposed part of the country that can experience weather-related power outages. As a result, he was keen to make his home as energy-resilient as possible,” McArdle says.
‘Most people opt for solar PV because of the savings but for others, it could be that they want to futureproof their house for the next generation, or increase its Building Energy Rating and resale value’
That’s because, depending on the solution you opt for, it is possible to use some of the energy generated by your solar panels to power key appliances, such as a freezer or wifi.
“Pharmacies use it for example to keep a fridge containing vaccines going,” she says.
A key part of Electric Ireland’s assessment process is to find out about each applicant’s needs and goals. That includes looking at their usage patterns, whether they wish to export excess energy to the grid or store it in a battery, and whether they are thinking of installing a heat pump too at a later stage.
At the end of the process, Tom opted to have 22 solar PV panels installed on his roof, and a weatherproof battery.
Electric Ireland’s expert team looked after his SEAI grant and deducted it from the price, saving him both time and money.
Depending on the time of year, the period from initial inquiry to installation can be just a few weeks. The installation itself normally takes less than a day.
The team took care of the NC6 paperwork, the residential microgeneration form, allowing Tom to earn export credits from day one.
In McArdle’s experience, the drivers of decisions on renewable energy are as varied as the people who make them.
“Most people opt for solar PV because of the savings, but for others, it could be that they want to futureproof their house for the next generation, or increase its Building Energy Rating and resale value,” she explains.
“For some it’s because they want to live more sustainably and to know that they are doing their part. Others want to know that they are investing their money in something that they can see a payback for within a certain number of years which, in the case of solar PV, is on average five to six years.”
And, just as he has innovated and diversified on the farm with great results, Tom is now keen to take more steps on the journey to net zero.
McArdle says, “He’s asking, what else can we do?”
For more information on the steps you can take in your journey to Net Zero, visit the Electric Ireland Net Zero hub .

title: Burnout and longer working lives leading to career changes at later stage, says recruitment firm
description: Work Q&A: Recruitment firm says there is a “growing trend” of professionals aged 30 and over seeking new career paths
content:
Burnout and longer working lives are increasingly prompting experienced professionals in their 30s and 40s to switch careers, according to Matrix Recruitment .
The recruitment firm says there is a “growing trend” of professionals aged 30 and over, particularly women, seeking new career paths.
“Professionals are no longer afraid to take a calculated career risk,” says Joanne Foley, recruitment manager at Matrix.
“They’re asking themselves a very honest question: ‘Is this career still right for me and do I want to be doing this for the next 20 or 30 years?’ Increasingly, the answer is no and they’re taking proactive steps to change direction.”
Although there are several factors behind the change, Foley says the Covid-19 pandemic gave workers time to stop and take stock of what is important to them.
“This has changed people’s attitudes to work,” she says.
[ Burnout: What can you do to avoid it? Opens in new window ]
“People are no longer willing to stay in a job that they are unhappy in or perhaps feel that they cannot progress in.”
Burnout and boredom are among the primary drivers behind career changes, according to Matrix, saying that after 10 or 15 years in the same field, excitement that once motivated some professionals can begin to fade.
“Often, when we speak to professionals looking to switch careers, it’s not an impulsive decision; it’s the result of a gradual build-up,” says Foley.
“Burnout is a major catalyst. We’re seeing high-performing senior professionals who are simply exhausted. Others are juggling demanding roles with parenting responsibilities and realising something must give.”
Given that people are working longer, Foley says workers have more time to move at later stages of careers, which is also feeding into decisions.
“If you’re in your mid-to-late 40s, you may still have another 20 years in the workforce. If you’re unhappy in your current profession, that’s far too long to remain stuck in a role that no longer aligns with your goals or wellbeing,” she says.
The trend is more prevalent among women, says Foley, while Matrix has seen most movement into roles in HR, supply chain and accountancy.
[ I took a pay cut two years ago and it wasn’t put in writing. Can I demand it be restored? Opens in new window ]
Job security and “fear of the unknown” are more likely to be concerns among those considering a career switch at a later stage, says Foley, rather than perceptions around age.
“Employers are more concerned with experience than age,” she says.
“Experienced professionals understand workplace dynamics. They’ve managed teams, budgets and deadlines. They know how to perform under pressure. These skills are hugely valuable to employers.”
Noting that hybrid working arrangements and increased flexibility have allowed people to retrain and upskill more easily, Foley says this has made transitions “more achievable”.
“Online learning and evening courses allow people to retrain well into their 50s and 60s, even while maintaining full-time employment.
“Hybrid work also gives professionals the flexibility to balance study, work and family responsibilities in a way that simply wasn’t possible 15 years ago,” she says.
If you have work-related questions, from how to deal with burnout to running your own business, The Irish Times Work Q&A column is here to help. You can use the form below to submit your question. Please limit your submissions to 400 words or less and please include a phone number. Your name and contact details will be confidential and only be used for verification purposes. Any details about your employer will also be anonymised.

title: Look inside: Light-filled duplex by the National Museum in Dublin 7 for €525,000
description: Two-bed home features double-height corner windows overlooking Croppies Acre Memorial Park
content:
The corner windows of 71 Collins Square, a two-bedroom duplex apartment on Benburb Street in Dublin 7 , look directly on to the Croppies Acre Memorial Park that sits to the front of the National Museum of Ireland at Collins Barracks.
The former military exercise grounds are so named as they are understood to have been a burial ground for casualties of the 1798 Rebellion. The Irish rebels were known as Croppies due to their short haircuts that emulated French revolutionaries.
Extending to 95sq m (1,023sq ft) over two floors, with a unique layout that prioritises natural light, 71 Collins Square is ideally located within a stone’s throw of the Museum red line Luas stop and a short walk from Stoneybatter and Smithfield, as well as Phoenix Park.
The owners also walk to work on the south side of the city in less than 30 minutes.
Now that they have a small child, the owners have decided to move to Laois to be closer to family, placing this impressive B-rated city home on the market with Owen Reilly estate agents, seeking €525,000.
You enter the duplex on the fourth floor of the building, sharing the hallway with just one neighbour. The entrance hall leads into the L-shaped livingroom where a glazed mezzanine looks over a dining area below and the corner windows look out to the memorial park.
A portion of the space by the window is in use as a study, with built-in bookshelves.
Next to the living space is the main bedroom, which features high ceilings, an en suite shower room and a private terrace, with space for a table and chairs. The main bathroom, with full bath, completes the floor.
Stairs off the livingroom lead down to the ground floor of the duplex. There is neat understairs storage in the hallway and space for a seating area. To the right the kitchen/diningroom is flooded with light thanks to the double-height south-facing corner windows that continue to the mezzanine livingroom above.
The mezzanine layout allows for plenty of space to have people over for drinks, the owner points out.
The kitchen is hived off in a corner of the space and features sage-green units and a white tiled backsplash. Beyond that is a second double bedroom, and there is further storage in built-in closets off the hallway.
The home comes with a secure parking space, although you would not need a car often, living in such a central spot.

title: Battle to halt global heating at 1.5 degrees is lost – UN
description: Focus must now switch to limiting extent of overshoot, says United Nations' climate report
content:
The battle to keep global heating from passing the agreed 1.5-degree threshold has been lost, United Nations environment chiefs have conceded.
In their most explicit forecast yet, they say the target being exceeded is “unavoidable” and some of the effects of this will be “irreversible”.
They say the emphasis must now switch from trying to avoid hitting 1.5 degrees to limiting the extent and duration of the overshoot. New policies and technologies will be needed to halt the rise and begin a rapid reversal to 1.5 degrees.
“The rules of the game are now changing,” said climate scientist Debra Roberts, one of the authors of the Limiting Overshoot report for the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
“We now have to reconfigure our policies for an exceedance of 1.5 degrees. None of our plans are prepared for that.”
The goal of limiting average global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial levels – before fossil fuel use accelerated – was set in the 2015 Paris Agreement, signed by almost all the world’s countries.
The year 2024 was the first the threshold was exceeded every month but until a long-term exceedance was recorded, the UN held that the agreement was not breached.
The limiting overshoot report says that exceedance is inevitable in the next few years, “pushing climate risks and impacts to increasingly dangerous heights”.
The overshoot is expected to last several decades, with the “most optimistic scenario” – if behaviours change immediately and dramatically – marking a temperature rise kept to 1.8 degrees. A reversal to 1.6 degrees could then be possible by the end of the century.
However, the report’s international team of authors warn most scenarios predict a rise of more than 2 degrees and a return to or below 1.5 degrees is uncertain.
“Even if a return to below 1.5 degrees is secured, many nations and communities will face irreversible losses and permanently changed conditions,” they say.
Worsening extreme weather, ecosystem destruction and loss of small islands and low-lying coastal cities are anticipated.
“Severe damage to human health, food security, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies is expected.”
Irreversible impacts include glacier loss, with more catastrophes such as the recent landslides in Nepal.
Permanent sea-level rise will also occur and disruption is expected to the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation , the currents that moderate weather in many countries including Ireland.
“There are no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5 degrees,” said UNEP executive director Inger Andersen.
She referred to the deadly heatwaves that struck Europe and large parts of Asia and North America this summer.
[ At least 35,000 excess deaths recorded in Europe’s back-to-back heatwaves Opens in new window ]
“Extreme heatwaves are already proving that climate impacts will strike faster, hit harder and last longer.”
Peter Thorne, director of the Icarus Climate Research Centre at Maynooth University , said the science in the report was not radically new. But it was expressed in a more “unfiltered” way than usual. And he said this was because the report was not subject to line-by-line approval by UN member states, some of whom had an interest in retaining fossil fuels.
“There wasn’t really anything [in previous scientific analysis] that kept us at 1.5 degrees,” he said. “We’re still warming at 0.2-0.3 degrees centigrade per decade; we’re still year-on-year – albeit more slowly – increasing global emissions.”
Thorne said that “even with the most optimistic scenarios of what might happen in terms of emissions, we’re passing 1.5 degrees”.
He added: “The question is how far past and for how long might we stay above that. It’s not looking good.”
UN secretary general António Guterres appealed to governments to step up climate action. “We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition.”

title: Danny Buckley: ‘Her last words to me were a plea to please get help for my ADHD’
description: ADHD Now is Ireland’s largest private ADHD assessment and treatment provider
content:
Danny Buckley is co-founder and director of ADHD Now, Ireland’s largest private ADHD assessment and treatment provider, offering clinically led diagnosis and ongoing care for children and adults across the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland.
Founded to tackle the chronic shortage of timely neurodevelopmental assessment, the company has reached approximately 60 per cent of the Irish private ADHD market.
The service spans both assessment and intervention, including therapy across psychiatry, speech and language, and occupational therapy.
What vision/light bulb moment prompted you to start up in business?
My late wife Simone told me she believed I had ADHD. I was in denial. Her last words to me were a plea to please get help for my ADHD. After losing her, I sought my diagnosis and experiencing first-hand the struggle to get access made me determined that the people who came after me could get answers in weeks rather than years. That is where ADHD Now began.
Describe your business model and what makes your business unique.
We provide private, clinically-led neurodevelopmental ADHD and autism assessment and treatment across Ireland and Northern Ireland, combining telehealth with in-person care. What makes us unique is scale paired with governance: we’ve reached roughly 60 per cent market share without compromising clinical standards, working with quality-assurance partners to keep diagnosis rigorous and patient-centred, supported by a team of over 100 clinicians across both services.
What is your greatest business achievement to date?
My proudest moment in business is deeply personal. From a place of pain, I was able to get assessed myself and experience first-hand the positive change that understanding yourself brings: a diagnosis, clarity and a plan on how best to support yourself moving forward. To then be able to build that experience into a service here in Ireland, offering quick access and a positive, supportive journey to thousands of others, and to see it work so well that it is now strengthening the public system alongside us, that is my biggest achievement in business. The commercial success matters, but it is the human impact that defines it.
What was your backs-to-the-wall moment and how did you overcome it?
In our early growth phase, demand for assessments far outpaced our clinical capacity. We had patients coming to us in their thousands, finally able to access help and we had a responsibility not to let them down. We had to move fast: going out to recruit further expert clinicians, building the supervision structures to support them properly, and putting the administrative backbone in place to allow them to focus on patients rather than paperwork. It was a defining period. We came through it because we refused to compromise on clinical standards, even under intense pressure, and it made us a far stronger organisation.
Self-funded and bootstrapped from day one. Profitable and reinvesting into growth.
How will your market look in three years and where would you like your business to be?
Demand for ADHD and autism assessment will keep rising as awareness grows and stigma falls. In three years, we expect a more regulated, more competitive private market. We intend to remain the clear market leader across the island, the trusted name patients and GPs turn to first and to have made meaningful inroads in new geographies
What is the single most important piece of advice you would offer to a less experienced entrepreneur?
Get the fundamentals right early: governance, compliance, contracts, quality. They feel like friction when you’re moving fast, but they are exactly what lets you scale credibly later. And beyond the commercial, know your “why”. Mine is Simone. When things get hard, and they do, knowing why you started is what keeps you going.

title: Castles, conspiracies and communism: thought-provoking back-to-school YA reads
description: Oran Doyle’s compelling debut Give Me ’Til Midnight is a refreshing take on the now-familiar time-loop plot
content:
What if Andie MacDowell had figured out Bill Murray was caught in a time loop? For 16-year-old Harmony, a recent dropout working in her mam’s cafe, it’s the first time she’s lived this Thursday in May – but she’s observant, and notices the swaggering way Liam moves through the world, like he knows exactly what’s going to happen. The rugby lad has proclaimed himself “King of Dublin”, embracing “the wonders of the loop” – which Harmony quickly diagnoses as him “throwing money around and acting the maggot”.
Oran Doyle’s compelling debut Give Me ’Til Midnight (Everything With Words, £8.99) is a refreshing take on the now-familiar time-loop plot, featuring a boy seemingly happy to stay stuck and a girl determined to set him free (it becomes, of course, more complicated than that).
Their wanderings around contemporary Dublin inspire commentary on its juxtaposition of glamour and grime, with an extra metaphysical edge: Harmony witnesses the gold-chained Lord Mayor mere moments after passing by a homeless person and thinks, “In some alternate universe he might be living in a tent himself.”
Immediately following up with “My brain is fried” allows this to be a relatable thought rather than a soapbox moment, letting the city be a well-rendered character in the novel without taking centre stage. The spotlight belongs to the two teens – figuring out how to make choices in a world that seems (and sometimes genuinely is) set against them. This is an absolutely terrific first novel from a writer we can hope to see more of.
There’s a different kind of exploration of autonomy and agency in Alan Carrigan’s Then We’ll Be Happy (Chicken House, £8.99), based on the author’s own experience of quadriplegic cerebral palsy . Sam is on the verge of legal adulthood, navigating his relationship with his mother, his current carer, while trying to advocate for himself in a school system that excludes him (“Sorry, Sam, I don’t know what to tell you; it’s not in the budget”).
Learning about “internalised ableism” and “the social model of disability ” through a new group of powerchair football friends provides hope without diminishing the genuine challenges of living with an impairment. As Sam puts it, “Sometimes it can feel like you’re expected to fall on one of two sides – either super depressed or super positive and inspirational. There’s no in between.”
Focusing on what you can control may be a cliche – but it is also true, and made relatable with this warm, funny debut.
“A gun did feel like cheating. It certainly didn’t have the elegance of an up-close maiming but needs must.” It would be wise not to get overly attached to any of the characters in Cethan Leahy’s Dead Teenager Movie (Little Island, €11.99), a Cork -set slasher horror. Leahy’s first-hand knowledge of filmmaking is evident in this twisty tale about a girl who understands “not to go into the basement or to read aloud the Latin from books covered in human flesh”. Wry commentary on familiar tropes and appalling rich people pairs well with a series of reveals about who is filming this deadly weekend away, and why.
The world of Russian ballet in the last days of communism is vividly evoked in Bluebird (O’Brien Press, €11.99), the first novel from former dancer and now psychotherapist Harriet Parsons. For Hope and her best friend Emily, ballet is an extracurricular activity they are excited to pursue more seriously when they are accepted to the school in Pavlovgrad. They soon learn that for their peers in Russia , “choice is ballet school or factory ... the chance to travel, to be an artist”.
[ A trivial comedy for serious YA readers, and more summer page-turners for teens Opens in new window ]
Convoluted queuing systems, food shortages and a lack of washing machines make their new home feel like stepping into a different era (although some of the living conditions which shock the middle-class girls would not be unheard of amid today’s housing crisis). For Hope, a Russian orphan adopted by Irish parents, it nevertheless is a place she yearns to belong to, and she is prepared to devote herself to the demanding discipline of ballet in order to succeed here.
The immersion in this strange, obsessive world compensates for the slightly meandering and sometimes implausible plot; dance lovers will appreciate the level of detail and respect given to their art form.
“Sometimes I think one of the reasons we dismiss this violence is because we can’t face the truth of how terrible it is. It feels too much.” It should surprise no one that Holly Bourne’s latest YA novel tackles a feminist issue; what is new about And Then We Screamed (Usborne, £9.99) is the setting. The British author uses a picturesque American small town – the sort of place where bad things aren’t supposed to happen – as the backdrop for an account of a strange epidemic in which teenage girls begin having screaming fits.
Five years on, a documentary crew investigates the strange incident, facilitating a range of voices aside from the two young protagonists – student journalists Clover and Brody – who narrate in real time. The device adds suspense but also smooths the way for expert opinions (along with the inevitable conspiracy theories about Satan, the HPV vaccine, and secret government poisonings).
It’s tricky writing about social contagion and psychogenic illness without it being read as undermining or dismissing teenage girls; Bourne uses the form to slip in reminders that male violence against women is also contagious, and that so-called “hysteria is a form of communication born out of desperation, for people who feel they can’t say what they want to through any other means”.
[ Summer YA reads: from a Snow White who’d prefer not to to same-sex love-love on the tennis court Opens in new window ]
A few too many Britishisms slip through, and it is depressing that in YA, a field with so much talk about diversity, an American setting is still regarded as the most marketable one. Nevertheless, I’ve never encountered a Holly Bourne teen novel I didn’t immediately want to press into the hands of young people, and her latest page-turner is no exception.
Fantasy settings so often allow for a thoughtful look at power – who holds it, how it is wielded, what might threaten it. Of one chaotic leader in the realm of Thaletal: “He lost the ability to sleep, and spent the nights roaming the battlements instead. He became savage and unpredictable. Nobody dared say it aloud, but he was losing his mind.” Imagine!
The beautifully weird world of Frances Hardinge’s latest novel, Traitors’ Nest (First Ink, €13.99), is inspired by medieval history but also very much its own universe, in which castles jump from location to location in a strange game understood by no mortal, its origins shrouded in myth. Fifteen-year-old Burr is part of a group of rebel farmers who take over one such castle, and are then faced with considering how to rule in uncertain circumstances: “the last thing he wanted to do was behead a monster and then grow a monster’s head himself”.
Much as I adore the swoony sea of romantasy we are now swimming in, it is a pleasure to explore what fantasy does so well: morality. The always-excellent Hardinge gently invites us to reflect on what it means to be good in an imperfect world, wrapping it up in some nifty magic and enchanting, though dangerous, creatures. What a gorgeous, thought-provoking, captivating read.

title: Would you buy this €35,995 French hatchback instead of a BMW?
description: France can sell €25,000 handbags, so why does it struggle to convince us to buy its premium cars like DS?
content:
There’s a question that hovers over the DS like a drone: is this a proper premium car or a case of fur coat and Penneys undies?
You get a good feel for the lure of a car in the shopping centre car park. There are some cars you could park across the doorway and they wouldn’t attract the attention of the local dog. Then there are those that act as motoring magnets.
DS leans towards the second category, thanks in part to the efforts of its stylists. The larger DS No 8, which set the new naming and design trend, proved to be a motoring magnet. Petrolheads in a BMW near Newry were so interested I feared we were about to get carjacked.
The No 4 is less eye-catching, but distinctive enough to lure in a local or two. “That’s pretty smart, is it Chinese?” was the first encounter. News that it was French and branded DS didn’t seem to clear things up.
A bit of a lurch into history and he recalled the old DS, but as the adage goes “if you’re explaining, you’re losing”. His questions had moved on to price before I had even got to the fact this was no longer a Citroën .
And here’s where the No 4 gets interesting. At €35,995, DS doesn’t have to persuade BMW and Audi buyers to defect. But it does have to persuade people to notice a brand many still don’t understand.
That’s getting harder. With the wave of new Chinese brands arriving, the noise of the motoring market is deafening and only set to get louder. Alongside this is the perennial problem of creating a genuinely premium French car brand.
This is a nation that can sell the world €25,000 handbags and perfume at €200 a drop and not bat a false eyelash, yet it can’t crack the luxury car market. Perhaps it’s down to preconceived stereotypes that associate France more with elegance than engineering nous.
But it raises a question for the Stellantis chief executive: aside from creating a car for the French president of the day, is there really any point in France investing in a premium car brand?
[ DS moves up a gear in its bid to pit French luxury against dominant German cars Opens in new window ]
Stellantis bosses have the cost-cutting shears out, so the clock is certainly ticking on DS proving its worth.
DS has done an impressive job with No 8 – even if its perfume-inspired naming convention is silly. Can it do the same with a hatchback?
An all-electric version is offered, with a claimed range of up to 450km, but our test car was the petrol hybrid variant. Its 1.2-litre hybrid petrol engine is mated to the 21kW electric motor to deliver a combined 145hp. That proves decently powerful and frugal, while remaining smooth and refined at motorway speeds.
The little electric motor is more than just for show. DS says it can run on electric-only mode for up to 50 per cent of the time in urban use, and in town, we certainly managed a lot of journeys in electric silence.
It’s even quite engaging through the bends, surprisingly so for a car that shares so much of its underpinnings with Citroën. It’s certainly much smoother and stiffer through the turns than the previous DS4. That’s down to the improved rigidity of the platform, which DS says uses almost 34 metres of structural adhesive alongside conventional welding.
On the motorway, the No 4 cruises comfortably, asking little of the driver. It’s got the ease of the larger No 8 and that poise that Citroën possesses in its better cars. Turn on to a national road and it threads its way neatly through the bends, though it does bottom out on the deeper potholes.
There’s enough initial softness in the suspension to take the sting out of poor surfaces, but it never falls foul of the floating sensation that afflicted so many older French cars.
Ask for a burst of acceleration and the three-cylinder engine makes its presence known, but once the six-speed auto transmission has settled into the right ratio, it fades convincingly into the background.
Most cars have a sweet spot, where all the elements work in harmony. Unfortunately, for some sports cars it’s at speeds only legal on the German autobahn.
Thankfully, the No 4’s sweet spot is around 75km/h. It’s here on your average national secondary road with sweeping bends that the DS feels most poised.
But this is never meant to be sold as anything close to the ultimate driving machine. Instead, its selling proposition is French design flair, elaborate detailing and comfort.
Inside is where DS tries to play its design hand strongest. You might be sitting on engineering shared with a mainstream hatchback, but this brand focuses its efforts on areas most others don’t. It’s bucking the trend of sticking a massive screen to the central console, hoping owners of these screens on wheels will be so distracted they won’t notice the spread of cheap and often shoddy plastics used elsewhere.
In contrast, the DS features a 10-inch touchscreen that sits snugly into the dash and is very clear and practical.
Yet the surrounding surfaces are like rough work sheets for a geometry test. And there are too many places clad with standard or less than premium plastics that serve to undermine the DS luxury pitch.
There are also points where design just gets in the way of functionality.
The line of metal buttons under the screen is a case in point. It’s great to see tactile controls return to a car’s interior, but the symbols on the silver-coloured buttons are white, so in daylight you can barely make them out.
Even when you can, the buttons control the fan speed, but to change temperature you still need to navigate the touchscreen.
Another example: there’s a small lip just in front of the transmission toggle. For the first few days, we were fixated on its function. It’s too short to support a phone, the car’s key is not a card.
Is there a bespoke piece of tech or kit, an optional extra that nestles in this spot and turns the No 4 into a nightclub? We finally cracked it: it holds your parking ticket or credit card. Smart thinking? Or comically prosaic?
Legroom is fine in the front but it gets a little cramped in the rear, which is a shame for a family hatchback in a market where EVs offer so much space these days.
That said, the boot is decent for this class, at 430 litres.
This DS is built on the Stellantis mid-sized platform, so is closely related to the Peugeot 308 and Opel Astra, sharing the same architecture and much of its hybrid hardware. That’s not a criticism – the Peugeot is a good car – but it means DS must find its premium credentials elsewhere.
Let’s remember, this isn’t an entirely new model. Originally launched as the DS4 three years ago, it was a smart-looking, comfortable hatch. But the price was wrong, starting at €40,000 in its base trim.
This revamped model starts at €35,995 for the Pallas version, a well-equipped entry-level grade.
It brings smart 19-inch alloys and an array of features that would normally require a lengthy visit to the options list, adding thousands to the price.
This is what allows the DS to credibly pitch itself against German rivals like the Audi A3 and BMW 1 Series.
Let’s be clear: both are better to drive. The 1 Series has sharper steering and better body control, while the A3 feels more polished when pushed on. The No 4 counters with a slightly softer, more relaxed driving demeanour that makes more sense in traffic or on a long motorway run. But you can’t ignore the DS at this price.
Had it been priced circa €45,000, we would have examined the plastics and the driving demeanour with a more jaundiced eye, asking whether this really was a premium car. At €35,995 with the specification level offered, those shortcomings matter less.
The No 4 is distinctive, comfortable and generously equipped, all for a price that’s comparable with mainstream alternatives. Sure, there’s a fur coat here, but DS is no longer charging Brown Thomas prices for it.
Power: 1,199cc direct injection turbocharged three-cylinder petrol engine combined with 21kW electric motor and a 6-speed dual-clutch automatic; 145hp and 230Nm of torque combined.
Verdict: Distinctive, comfortable and flawed, but at this price the No 4 makes sense

title: EV public charging price rises: can I save money by shopping around?
description: As with fuel prices, EV charging costs vary from location to location, but the differences aren’t massive
content:
Is it coincidence or just plain bad luck that the ESB announced price hikes – of up to 6c per kWh – for its public electric car charging points just as the Government was rolling out its ICE2EV scrappage grant?
The ESB’s prices are now as much as 73c per kWh for the fastest chargers, depending on whether you’re paying via the ESB e-Cars app, you have a monthly subscription, or you’re just tapping your contactless card.
We’re always told, when it comes to motoring costs – from insurance to fuel – to shop around for the best prices. That is, of course, our power as consumers. However, does shopping around for EV charging make much of a difference?
Can you truly shop around in the manner you can with petrol or diesel? Given the scarcity of public chargers as you move away from metropolitan Dublin, there’s no easy answer to that second question – because when you need a public charge, you generally really need it.
As a counterpoint, many in-car satellite navigation systems can now help you choose charging points on your route with the lowest possible price, but that requires a level of pre-planning on your part and, depending on your destination, there may not be much in the way of choice.
ESB e-Cars’ charging prices are now rising to 60c per kWh for chargers up to and including 50kW power output. For chargers between 50kWh and 350kWh, that cost is now going to be 72c per kWh.
That’s the pay-as-you-go rate. If you sign up for an ESB e-Cars membership, at €4.79 per month, then the rates are slightly lower – 55c up to 50kW power, and 67c for higher-power chargers.
If you’re paying with a contactless tap-and-go card – which is supposed to be the EU standard for EV chargers – the rates are 61c per kWh up to 50kW power, and 73c per kWh above that.
In those instances therefore, the bestselling Volkswagen ID.4 with its 77kWh battery will cost between €38 and €39 for a 10-80 per cent charge-up.
[ I want to buy a European electric vehicle. What should I buy? Opens in new window ]
Applegreen , the fuel forecourt operator, charges 68c per kWh for its fast chargers when using their app, which run at up to 350kW power. At that price, our notional ID.4 would cost €36 to charge.
Blink Charging currently costs 65c per kWh at any of its charging points, which are mostly slower chargers, and that would cost €35 to charge the VW.
Circle K chargers cost up to 69c per kWh for high-speed charging. The cost of charging our average VW would be €37.
