title: GP and elderly mother awarded €12,000 over Dundrum clinic receptionist’s ‘disrespectful’ conduct
description: Receptionist’s actions were ‘notably different to how Irish patients were treated’, WRC adjudicator rules
content:
A tribunal has ordered a medical diagnostic clinic to pay compensation totalling €12,000 to a south Dublin GP and her elderly mother over the “demeaning and disrespectful” conduct of a receptionist nearly three years ago.
It follows complaints under the Employment Equality Act 1998 against Affidea Diagnostics Ireland Ltd by Dr Shereen Gul and her mother, Mehr Un Nisa.
In decisions published on Tuesday, a Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) adjudicator recorded that Mehr Un Nisa was “a 75-year-old Pakistani lady who was visibly timid and frail” with “no English to speak of”.
She was in Ireland visiting her daughter, a general practitioner in Saggart in Dublin, when she went for a scan at an Affidea radiography clinic in Dundrum, the WRC heard.
There was “anxiety” on both sides after a mix-up about slotting Mehr Un Nisa in for a cancelled appointment the previous month led to a disputed interaction and the accusation that Gul gave “abuse” to clinic staff.
This was strongly denied by Gul, who had initiated defamation proceedings against Affidea when the WRC was hearing the case.
Gul said her mother was from a village in a tribal area in northern Pakistan where people traditionally use just one name.
On November 4th, 2023, she said, a receptionist, Karen Fitzpatrick, on seeing the name said: “Oh, what kind of a name is that and what is the surname?” Gul said.
She went on to say twice that the name “doesn’t make sense” when Gul tried to explain, and asked Gul to produce an identity document for her mother, the witness added.
Fitzpatrick then asked Gul: “Does your mom know any English?” and when told Mehr Un Nisa had only a few words, asked, “How come she has no English?” Gul said.
She was then told she couldn’t enter a changing area to assist her mother for “infection control” reasons. She had been let in on previous visits, and saw other patients enter with family members while she waited, she said.
The receptionist, Fitzpatrick, denied telling Gul that her mother’s name “didn’t make sense” but said she “needed to check the spelling”. She asked about English because there was a safety questionnaire to fill out, she added.
When counsel for the complainant Vincent Nolan, appearing instructed by Powderly Solicitors, put it to the witness that there she had “simply decided to be awkward”, Fitzpatrick said: “No, I was just doing my job correctly.”
Adjudicator Patricia Owens decided Fitzpatrick’s evidence was not credible and decided in favour of Gul’s account of the questioning about Mehr Un Nisa’s name.
Fitzpatrick was “demeaning and disrespectful” towards the women and went beyond what was required to identify her, Owens wrote. The receptionist’s actions were “notably different to how Irish patients were treated”, the adjudicator added.
Refusing to let Gul into the changing area was discriminatory on the same basis, she added.

title: Legal aid row pushing District Courts towards ‘Covid era backlogs’, solicitors warn
description: Minister for Justice urged to resolve dispute as withdrawal of services by criminal defence solicitors puts strain on system
content:
The District Courts resumed full hearings this week with no sign of a breakthrough in the bitter dispute over a new payment model for criminal legal aid work in those courts.
The impact of the withdrawal of services by criminal defence solicitors was underlined by Courts Service data. Figures show the number of new legal aid certificates plummeted since the new payment model came into operation on July 1st.
The 702 certificates granted in July, down from 10,344 in the same month a year earlier, shows the extent of the withdrawal of many solicitors from legal aid work under the new model.
As full District Court hearings resumed nationwide on Tuesday after the August break, more than 100 defence solicitors took part in a walkout at the Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin. Their action was replicated by solicitors in courts across the State.
The withdrawal of services, which began in June and escalated from July 1st, has led to the adjournment of thousands of criminal cases. This has affected accused people, witnesses, victims and prosecuting gardaí, as well as adding to delays and backlogs in the courts.
[ Dublin solicitors to continue withdrawal of services as courts prepare to return Opens in new window ]
The most controversial element of the new model is the flat fee of €520 per client, irrespective of the number of charges and court appearances. This replaced the previous system of about €239 for the first appearance and €60 for each subsequent appearance.
Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan maintains the changed model will lead to efficiency and cost savings, but solicitors say it forces them to work for free on complex or delayed cases.
In a statement issued on Tuesday, some of the solicitors who have withdrawn services said the model was imposed without “meaningful negotiations”. They are in favour of reform but want two changes to the Minister’s proposal which are “fair, reflect the work they actually do, and would see them return to work immediately”, the statement said.
They want the Minister to issue certificates for offences committed on separate dates, with a cap of five certificates per defendant, per court, per day. “As it stands, the Minister’s proposal means they would work for free once a case goes beyond what a single flat fee can reasonably cover,” the statement says.
They also want a further legal aid certificate once a case exceeds 10 court appearances. Fitness-to-plead cases (involving people with psychiatric or mental health issues), cases involving children and those with defendants remanded in custody often involve numerous court appearances, they said, which is driven by statutory and welfare rules and systemic delays.
Tony Collier, a partner in Ferrys Solicitors LLP, said solicitors want the Minister “to engage comprehensively and substantially” with the Law Society, their representative body, to resolve these matters.
He also called on the Taoiseach and Tánaiste to intervene “in order to bring this dispute to an end”.
“The criminal justice system is effectively grinding to a halt and we are going to see Covid era-style backlogs in court cases as a result of this ongoing dispute with the Minister,” he said.
“We want to be back at work but, as this dispute runs on, victims of crime are being left in limbo, defendants in the criminal legal aid system are going without legal representation and court cases will stack up more rapidly.”
In a statement, the Department of Justice said O’Callaghan “regrets the decision of some solicitors not to engage with the criminal legal aid panel”.
It referred to “ongoing engagement” since last October between department officials, O’Callaghan and the Law Society and Bar Council in relation to the fee model and to some adjustments made to that structure, including front-loading the payment of two-thirds of the €520 fee.
The further changes sought are “not compatible” with the objectives of the reforms introduced as they would “reintroduce the possibility of multiple certificates being awarded when the intention is to move to a single fee per case”, the statement said.

title: Shein shares slide as much as 10% in Hong Kong debut
description: Fast-fashion retailer completes long-delayed IPO at bargain-basement valuation
content:
Shein ’s shares fell sharply below their offer price on Tuesday as the fast-fashion retailer made its long-awaited trading debut in Hong Kong.
The stock fell as much as 10 per cent in the first minutes of trading before closing almost flat at 48.50 Hong Kong dollars (€5.33). The company had priced shares at HK$48.56, in the middle of its range, raising HK$13.6bn and valuing Shein at just over $26 billion.
Goldman Sachs, as the initial public offering’s “stabilisation manager”, is likely to have stepped in and bought Shein stock before the market close to support its price.
The lacklustre debut comes in stark contrast to other recent IPOs in Asia, with memory-chip maker CXMT and humanoid robot maker Unitree both soaring more than 400 per cent in their trading debuts.
“What the consumer sectors offer just doesn’t seem to be particularly compelling compared to technology at the moment,” said William Bratton, head of cash equity research for Asia-Pacific at BNP Paribas.
Shein’s IPO value represents a sharp fall from its peak. Pandemic lockdowns and social media hype from “Shein hauls” drew young consumers to its affordable fashion and earned the company a valuation of about $100 billion following a 2022 private fundraising round.
However, investor enthusiasm began to ebb later that year and the next fundraising valued Shein at $66 billion.
Its previous attempts to list in New York and London were derailed by opposition from politicians and regulators amid scrutiny of its Chinese supply chain. In July, Chinese regulators approved its application to list in Hong Kong.
The company is now one of the world’s biggest listed fashion groups, with a valuation roughly equal to Swedish retailer H&M, although both are worth far less than Zara owner, Inditex’s market capitalisation of about $213 billion.
Kenny Ng, a strategist at brokerage Everbright Securities International, said Shein had faced significant challenges in recent years. The company is battling trade investigations in the EU and US and lost a tax loophole that benefited its business.
“The market is adopting a wait-and-see attitude regarding the international trade policy environment and the recovery of global consumer sentiment,” he said.
Shein’s net profit fell to $2 billion last year after peaking at $3.4 billion in 2024, while net profit margins narrowed sharply to 4.9 per cent from 8.7 per cent over the same period.
The company reported a net loss of $99 million in the first quarter as it flagged the risks of US and EU trade tensions to its business. In May last year, Washington scrapped a tariff exemption for small packages that Shein had used to ship clothing directly to customers in the US. The EU has since closed a similar loophole. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: France bans phones in schools amid warnings of ‘intellectual crisis’
description: Rise of short videos has reduced people’s ability to read texts or watch long films, says French president
content:
It was back to school this week for French second-level students, but with a difference: a national ban on mobile phones.
The ban in lycées, attended by students aged 15-18, means that phones are now banned throughout France’s preschool, primary and secondary school system, as phones in school were already banned for younger ages since 2018.
The prohibition on phones in school is “absolutely essential”, education minister Édouard Geffray told journalists.
“We are facing a competition between screen time and learning time, to the detriment of the latter,” he said, adding that “all teachers” were noticing a gradual decline in students’ vocabulary and ability to understand texts.
“If we fail to reduce our young people’s screen exposure, we are heading toward an absolutely major health, intellectual, cognitive and even civic crisis,” Geffray said.
In practice, the ban means students must place their phones into collective boxes, lockers or pouches on arrival at the school and should collect them once classes end, according to the government.
There are exceptions for use for medical reasons including disabilities, and for phone use for educational purposes, such as in an IT room or under the supervision of a teacher.
Parliament voted for the ban in July and it came into force a week before classrooms reopened for the academic year, leading to complaints that not enough time was allowed to prepare for its implementation.
French president Emmanuel Macron had intended to combine the measure with a prohibition on social media for those aged under 15, but this was struck down by France’s top court in mid-August on the grounds that it went against freedom of expression.
On a visit to a school in southern France to mark the start of an academic year, Macron vowed to try to reintroduce the social media ban in a modified form.
Scientific evidence showed that “phones, screens, and even more so social media, detract” from being able to learn, he said, with particular harms for those aged under 15.
“They sap your attention span, as you’ve said, and the ability to be with one another,” he told students in a classroom of the Chaptal high school in the town of Mende.
Students could be seen “glued to their phones” at break time instead of interacting, and the rise of short videos had reduced people’s ability to read texts or even watch long films.
“After 20 seconds, we’re fed up,” Macron said.
“When I hold meetings at the Élysée Palace, I now ask people to put away their cell phones beforehand. Even at the Élysée, you have meetings with people, and they’re all on their phones,” Macron told the students.
[ Children now ‘struggle to grasp basic concepts’: Teachers’ views on screen time Opens in new window ]
“Because otherwise, we’re not fully present for what we’re doing. And that means we don’t get anything done.”
The Chaptal high school had voluntarily imposed a ban on phones in classrooms last year. Each student has to place their phone in a numbered pouch that hangs at the top of the classroom beside the blackboard.
It had stopped short of imposing a total ban within school premises, however, because the idea had been strongly opposed by students, members of the student council told Macron.
“There are strong arguments for limiting phone use: to improve concentration and student interaction, and to help those who struggle to manage usage on their own,” a student said.
“But the school was also pushing us to use phones and computers more and more,” for internet research, for school work, and to use school apps, she added, complicating the matter. The measure was also seen as “infantilising” by the teenagers.
“It’s not an easy subject, it’s been very controversial,” she continued, saying students needed to be won around. “It didn’t happen overnight.”

title: Gardaí hope postmortem provides answers into fisherman’s death off west Cork coast
description: Family of Michael Harrington (50s), from Beara, raised alarm when he failed to return from solo fishing trip on Monday night
content:
Gardaí hope the findings of a postmortem will establish what happened to a fisherman whose body was recovered from the sea off west Cork on Tuesday.
The man, named locally as Michael Harrington (50s) from Cahermore, Beara, went fishing alone on Monday on his 10-metre half decker, Sea Hunter, off Beara.
He was known to fish until night-fall, but when he failed to return home, his parents raised the alarm and neighbours began a search at first light on Tuesday.
Some neighbours spotted debris floating in the water off Black Ball Head, west of Castletownbere, at around 7.30am. Sea conditions were calm at the time.
The Irish Coast Guard Marine Rescue Co-Ordination Centre at Valentia tasked the Castletownbere RNLI all-weather boat, Annette Hutton, to the scene. Rescue 115, the Shannon-based Irish Coast Guard helicopter, was sent to assist the search operation, which also involved local fishing vessels and smaller craft.
The crew of a small punt located Harrington in the water at around 8.20am and notified the RNLI boat, which took him on board and returned to port at Castletownbere.
Harrington was pronounced dead on the pier in Castletownbere by a local GP. His body was transferred to Cork University Hospital, where a postmortem was due to take place later on Tuesday.
Gardaí hope the results of the postmortem will help establish what happened to Harrington, who was an experienced fisherman. He worked on fishing vessels in the 1990s, but had worked ashore for a number of years before returning to fishing last year when he bought the Sea Hunter.
There was no sign of the boat near where Harrington was recovered. However, local fishermen continued a search and noticed a diesel slick between White Ball Head and Black Ball Head.
The Sea Hunter was found sunken between the two headlands and attempts to lift the boat are expected to be made later this week.
The boat will be examined as part of an inquiry by the Marine Casualty Investigation Board, which will attempt to establish what happened in the lead-up to the man’s death.
Gardaí will also prepare a file for an inquest into Harrington’s death at Cork Coroner’s Court.

title: Transport body proposes greater access for pets on trains, buses and trams
description: Group of respondents to public consultation felt larger dogs should only have to be muzzled if among restricted breeds
content:
Small dogs, cats and other small animals are expected to be allowed greater access on public transport under proposals to relax rules covering the carriage of animals on trains, buses and trams.
The National Transport Authority (NTA) received 2,567 submissions during a public consultation held on the subject earlier this year, with most people supporting the proposal of pets being allowed on public transport.
Small dogs, cats, or other small animals that do not threaten the safety of other passengers would be allowed to travel on Transport for Ireland bus, rail and Luas services under the proposed policy.
The conditions included small animals being carried in a suitable container, not being allowed on seats (on owners’ laps or on the ground) and kept away from other animals.
The proposal would also allow larger dogs provided they are on a lead and have a muzzle, while they could be refused entry if the service is near capacity.
People responding to the consultation, which ran in February and March, were largely positive about the proposed changes.
Respondents were supportive of the proposals because they offered improved access for pet owners without cars, and easier travel to veterinary appointments and social destinations.
There was also a view that the Republic is behind European peers on this issue.
Many people also argued that the proposed policy is too restrictive for small dogs and that they shouldn’t need to be carried in a box.
Other respondents felt larger dogs should only have to be muzzled if they are restricted breeds.
Those opposed to changes cited allergies, fear of dogs, hygiene, safety in enclosed spaces, crowding and concern that existing rules would be difficult to enforce consistently.
A “small minority” opposed the proposal outright.
Owners would be responsible for their animals’ behaviour, while designated wheelchair space, buggy space and priority seats must be kept clear for those who need them.
The NTA will now work on draft revisions to its bylaws to allow for the proposed changes regarding pets on public transport.
It will also work with operators – in particular Dublin Bus, Irish Rail , Bus Éireann and Luas – to implement the necessary changes to their bylaws.

title: Dublin family’s former babysitter accused of armed burglary at  their home
description: Coolock woman denied bail over garda’s concerns of potential witness interference with victims
content:
A Dublin family’s former babysitter, who harboured a “long-standing animosity” against them, carried out a violent, armed burglary at their home, it has been alleged.
Sara Campbell (40) of Macroom Road, Coolock, Dublin 17, is accused of aggravated burglary at a residential address in the city’s northside last week.
Bail was denied at Dublin District Court after Garda Adrian O’Hanlon raised concerns over potential witness interference with the victims, a couple who both have health problems.
The garda cited the seriousness of the charge, the use of a firearm and an alleged assault that left a male occupant with blunt force head injuries.
Giving evidence, one of the victims told the court the incident unfolded at about 11.30am on Friday.
She recalled hearing a door open and seeing the accused standing there, initially feeling happy and moving to give her a hug because “she used to babysit for us”.
However, the witness said she then saw there was a man with the accused. The man began shouting and swearing at her husband before punching him, she said.
The woman claimed the man struck her husband twice in the head with a handgun before the weapon was handed over to the accused, at which point Campbell allegedly shouted: “Give me the gun, I’ll kill him, and then I will kill myself.”
The court heard that at one stage, the accused grabbed a kitchen knife and began swinging it around.
Meanwhile, the witness’s brother, who was upstairs, was put in a headlock and had €1,000 cash taken from him when Campbell rummaged through the rooms, it was alleged.
The witness also told the court her brother’s car was taken.
When he begged with the raiders to leave the keys in it, they agreed on the condition that the occupants did not call gardaí for 20 minutes, telling him they would leave the vehicle at a specific location.
The witness also told the court that the accused had demanded €10,000 in a text message sent some months prior.
Asked if any conditions could alleviate his concerns, the garda replied no, sustaining his objection because “the animosity and bad feeling” from the accused was “too strong”.
Pleading for bail unrepresented due to ongoing industrial action by solicitors over legal aid reforms, Campbell told Judge Mark O’Connell that she had a long-standing grievance with the family and “did not know what else to say” as she pleaded for bail.
She has yet to enter a plea and was remanded in custody to appear again next week.

title: Germany says Russia was behind last month’s attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
description: Minister for Defence Helen McEntee said Russia’s ‘attempted drone attack’ at Leipzig airport was ‘part of a clear trend’
content:
Germany has blamed Russia for last month’s failed drone attack in Leipzig and, in response, will close the Russian consulate in Bonn and a controversial cultural centre in Berlin.
Tuesday’s response to the Leipzig incident came hours after a failed rocket attack on a power station in Brandenburg outside Berlin.
While the perpetrators of that attack are as yet unknown, German authorities say they have no doubt who was behind last month’s Leipzig attack on Ukrainian military transporter planes.
“The federal government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack on August 4th,” said Alexander Dobrindt, federal interior minister at a press conference.
He said this assessment was based on police investigations, intelligence reports and a recurring pattern of similar attacks across Germany and Europe – with further attacks from Russia likely to follow.
Minister for Defence Helen McEntee said Russia’s “attempted drone attack” at Leipzig airport was “part of a clear trend”.
“I stand in full solidarity with Germany, and with all member states affected by Russia’s reckless and increasingly frequent hybrid attacks,” she said on Tuesday night.
“Russia is attempting to divide us and weaken our support for Ukraine. It will not succeed. Ireland stands ready to work closely with our EU partners to prevent, deter and respond to this malicious activity.”
On the evening of August 4th, a bus driver at Leipzig airport discovered a drone armed with explosives and a defective detonation mechanism near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft.
A second drone is believed to have collided mid-air with an airborne DHL aircraft. Last week, German media reported that a third explosive drone was also discovered at Leipzig airport, Germany’s second-largest air freight hub.
At a joint press conference on Tuesday, German foreign minister Johann Wadephul said Berlin’s “proportionate and measured yet resolute” response would be closely co-ordinated with other EU member states.
He said the attacks would not weaken Germany’s resolve in assisting Ukraine against its “defensive battle against Russian aggression” and that the first retaliation measures would not be the last.
He said he had ordered in the Russian ambassador for a meeting to discuss the closure of the consulate and cultural centre.
Immigration restrictions on Russian citizens will be stepped up, he said, as would observation of Russia’s so-called “shadow fleet” of ships.
“We will not allow our social cohesion to be divided by Russian attacks,” said Wadephul. “We remain ready to react along with our partners should the protection of our population require it.”
While Nato and EU leaders weighed in with their support on Tuesday, security experts in Germany and beyond are already debating whether, given the scale and frequency, the term “hybrid attacks” is now an unhelpful and inaccurate euphemism.
Pressure has been growing on Berlin to alter its course of restraint, with the conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine daily warning last week that the drone attack was a Russian operation and that “anyone who doesn’t say that out loud is playing Putin’s game.
Prof Phillips O’Brien, head of strategic studies at the University of St Andrews, wrote on X that the Leipzig incident was a “deliberate act of war, and it is important that Germans say that”.
Berlin’s shift on Tuesday ends a four-year standoff over the Russisches Haus cultural centre in Berlin, opened in the former East German capital in 1984.
As well as cultural events, the centre has been accused of operating as an informal espionage centre and abusing the terms of a 2011 bilateral agreement between Russia and Germany.
In response, Moscow is likely to now close Goethe Institut cultural centres in Russia.
Meanwhile, police in Brandenburg say at least a dozen improvised rockets were detected at a power plant in Turnow-Freilack near the Polish border.
State interior minister Jan Redmann said unknown attackers tried to fire the devices into the plant at 7:30am on Tuesday morning. Two rockets hit their target but caused only a short circuit and not a full outage.
Brandenburg officials declined to comment on possible perpetrators. Eight months ago a left-wing extremist group took credit for sabotaging a substation in Berlin and caused a major power outage in the capital.

title: Public service industrial action could be under way by month’s end, says Fórsa trade union
description: Any action would have ‘serious effects right across the public sector’, according to union chief Kevin Callinan
content:
Public service industrial action could be under way by the end of the month over the absence of a new pay deal, the general secretary of Fórsa , the State’s largest public sector union, has said.
Kevin Callinan said he expected it would be “a very long dispute” and “one that will have very serious effects right across the public sector”.
Speaking on Tuesday, after announcing that 96 per cent of Fórsa members who participated in a ballot had backed industrial action, he said it was likely the largest ever Irish trade union ballot on a potential strike.
Callinan said Fórsa’s leadership would meet on Wednesday to discuss the next steps. He said there would be talks on Monday with the leaders of Siptu , the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) and Irish National Teachers’ Organisation, which collectively make up the Irish Congress of Trade Unions public services committee, to co-ordinate wider action.
Siptu public sector members on Monday voted by 97 per cent to 3 per cent to back industrial action. Siptu and Fórsa have about 160,000 public sector members between them, more than a third of the total workforce.
Several unions have completed ballots that backed industrial action, while the INMO is to announce its result next week. The three teachers’ unions have said they will allow members to vote on the issue in the coming weeks.
In Fórsa’s case, 62,276 members voted to take action out of a total poll of 64,481. Callinan said the scale of the majority was a clear indication of the level of anger and frustration among public service workers who were seeing their earnings eroded by inflation.
He said the unions have not met anyone from the Government side to discuss the potential for a new deal for two months, but that when they had, it was made clear that public sector pay had fallen behind prices by at least 5 per cent since 2020 and that this would have to be taken into consideration in any negotiations.
Callinan, like other union leaders, has noted the Government’s failure to index tax bands in last year’s budget and the decision not to continue providing household energy supports as factors that hit ordinary workers.
He said the unions had argued that, on this occasion, it was essential to start the talks process “with how we were going to address the effects of the cost of living crisis” on people.
“What we wanted was a formula that would ... make good on the losses in a reasonable way,” he said.
“We didn’t, in response, get any firm commitment on that. We felt, in fact, they made it clear they wanted a repeat of what had gone before, and we are just saying, very simply, that that is not going to work on this occasion.”
Callinan said “there are no talks” at present and “nor do we expect that there will be talks unless there is a change in the Government’s position ... it does require a willingness on their part to recognise that there is a problem that needs to be addressed.”
He said the unions did not want to enter into a process “where they basically have decided what they’re prepared to spend and we have to suck it up. We’re not going to do that any more. So, unless we get a shift in that ... we’re probably in for a long haul, a very long dispute, one that will have very serious effects right across the public sector.”

title: Storm Evelyn a mixed blessing for Cusack: ‘It would be great if we got no storms at all’
description: The face of Irish weather forecasts for 40 years, Cusack shares the acknowledgment with former colleague Evelyn Murphy
content:
Evelyn Cusack has said she would be happy if Ireland “never got a Storm Evelyn”.
As the 2026/27 storm season started on Tuesday, Cusack – the face of Irish weather forecasts for 40 years – was reluctant to appear too happy about the naming of a storm in her honour. Storm Evelyn is also named after Evelyn Murphy.
Both Irish women are pioneering figures in the world of meteorology. Murphy was the first woman to work as a meteorologist in Met Éireann and became, in 1983, the first female meteorologist to present the forecast on RTÉ television. She went on to head the marine unit and led the creation of the Irish Marine Data Buoy Observation Network.
Cusack was the first female head of forecasting at Met Éireann and one of the longest-serving forecasters on RTÉ. She was a familiar presence on television and radio during weather events for decades before retiring in 2023 after 42 years with Met Éireann.
Storm Evelyn is the fifth name listed for the new storm season, which lasts for a year.
Cusack described being included on the list as a “mixed blessing”. She said it would not be accurate to call it an “honour”, but acknowledged that it was a way of marking Met Éireann’s contribution to Irish life over 90 years.
“I’d be just as happy if we never got a Storm Evelyn. Who wants to be associated with violent winds and the destruction of property? I’m not joking,” she told RTÉ Radio 1’s News at One.
“It would be great if we got no storms at all because they can be very destructive.”
However, she added if there was no Storm Evelyn, it could be the result of a prolonged period of high pressure over the winter, which could lead to further drought conditions.
“We’d like some rain and a little bit of wind, but not storms,” she said of the autumn and winter.
Cusack said she no longer watches the weather forecast on television as it is “triggering”. Instead, she looks at the 10-day forecast on the Met Éireann app.
There are 21 names proposed in total for the storm season, but no more than the first seven or eight are usually used in an average year.
There were five named storms last year – Amy, Bram, Claudia, Chandra and Dave. The most was 14 in 2024/25 and the least was four in 2022/23.
Met Éireann and the UK Met Office started naming storms in 2015, with the Dutch weather service KNMI joining them in 2019. Each weather service gets to name seven of the 21 storms.
Storm Austen is named after Austen Nagle, the first director of the Irish Meteorological Service. Despite its Irish name, Storm Finn was nominated by the UK Met Office after a mother who said her two-year-old son Finn was “wild”.
[ El Niño could cause Ireland to have unseasonably warm autumn Opens in new window ]
Storm Kilian is named after Kilian Rohan, who was director of the Irish Meteorological Service from 1978 to 1981. Storm Miriam is named after Miriam Lyons, the first woman to work in Met Éireann as an operational meteorological officer. She was also the first Irish woman to fly in a jet fighter when posted to Casement Aerodrome.
Eoin Sherlock, head of Met Éireann’s forecasting division, said it has been proven that naming storms makes it easier for people to keep track of weather events and safety-related information.

title: ‘In my heart until I die’: Argentina says a tearful thank you to Lionel Messi
description: The Argentinian’s decision to quit international football was met by an outpouring of affection from the country he led to World Cup glory in 2022
content:
Anyone who was present at Lionel Scaloni’s press conference immediately after the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina in New Jersey on July 19th and saw his tears, the sobs which prevented him from speaking while he got up and walked out, could tell this was a man weeping not because of defeat in a single match but because he was fully aware that what that particular group of men had been through for the past eight years had come to an end.
Messi’s announcement that he is retiring from international football , posted on Instagram on Monday complete with photos of three handwritten sheets of some anonymous yet corporate-looking headed paper and a Harry Potter Time Turner pen, to the soundtrack of Brindis sung by Soledad Pastorutti, instantly dominated the news and unleashed a barrage of homages, gratitude and joy from all corners. But it’s not exactly a surprise.
“How crazy that the day has come, dear Leo,” Cristian Romero posted, making it clear that this was expected in spite of the unexpectedness. “The day no one wanted to arrive has arrived,” echoed Giovani Lo Celso, who said he had “nine years listening to you, admiring you and learning by your side”. His international team-mates highlight how in their childhood they dreamed of meeting him one day, let alone actually play with him. Nico Paz says since he was four years old he “used to watch you play with my dad and we would calculate together whether I would be in time to play with you”.
It’s not just his team-mates who are expressing gratitude and nostalgia. On a Buenos Aires street corner someone put a red telephone on a table with a sign saying: “What would you say to Messi?” Passersby picked up the receiver and talked into it: “I’m 86 years old and you have given me the greatest joys in my life. You will be in my heart until the day I die,” one gentleman said. A young boy saw the news and “burst into tears even though I was at school”. A well-spoken woman said “we will miss you because you are an extraordinary being”, a little girl added “you’re the best and the greatest”. An old man signed off “bye, son”.
Influencers, journalists, artists, cultural commentators and psychologists all expressed their gratefulness for Messi being a great human being. “Messi led by example,” the veteran sportswriter Matías Martin wrote, while the coach and motivational speaker Matias “Coco” Gallo Bevegni posted that the World Cup winner “taught me more in defeat than in victory”.
The football pundit Morena Beltrán could not hold back the tears as she explained to her older colleagues that for her generation there is a sense of mourning and emptiness which can only be filled by gratitude, which maybe they have already experienced, because they have seen another God. Psychoanalyst Milagros Filgueras praised the decision to hand-write the note, saying some goodbyes need the body involved. The journalist Pablo Perantuono devoted his column to the “epistolary genre”, noting that a handwritten letter in this day and age is almost a counter-cultural act of originality.
The writer Andrés Burgo highlighted that in 10 of the past 12 World Cups, either Maradona or Messi played, so this truly marks the “end of an era in which grandparents, parents, sons and daughter and grandchildren enjoyed an incredible privilege during almost 45 years. The heir will arrive – we hope – but right now is a time of orphanage. And gratitude”.
Messi revealed that this letter was actually written two days after the final, a cathartic diary-like release, but that on Monday, after “[what happened with] my dad” he was more convinced than ever. The note said: “it’s a decision that hurt and continues to hurt,” but that he understands this is the moment. The poet Valeria Correa Fiz pointed out that he originally wrote “I think”, crossed it out and replaced it with “I understand”. Messi swore he always gave his all, not only these past few years when “everything was won” (he never says “I won”; it’s always “we” or “it” was won) but he has nothing left to give. He’s emptied.
The 39-year-old, however, scored four goals for Inter Miami at the weekend and continues his career at club level, where he clearly still has much to give. He is not retiring from playing football, the thing he loves most. He is retiring from Argentina.
With two international dates coming up and no rival agreed, no doubt the clarification that there will be no Messi in the squad will impact on the potential fixtures. And not unlike the time when he quit Argentina before, in 2016, the country’s football is in a bit of turmoil. The context and climate include scandals surrounding the Argentinian Football Association, the pressure by some lobbies to privatise football clubs, which are non-profit organisations, and the international furore ensued by several incidents during the World Cup which have seen Argentina landed with some hefty fines, sanctions and suspensions.
The heaviness of the Argentina flag which for so many years visibly weighed him down, turned idyllic when it became the cloak of victory, mattered very much to his father, Jorge. Messi said he wanted to win another World Cup for him. Perhaps his death has somehow freed him from that aspect of his Argentinianness.
And just like last time, the spontaneous visceral response from the Argentinian people is acceptance and relish at the good times lived. That inexplicable sense of pride that comes from being from the same soil as someone who is very good at something and whose magic is still untarnished by the sordid final match against Spain, or any of the criticisms directed at the squad and fans throughout the tournament. If anything, his final tears in front of the stands, like Scaloni’s tears at the press conference, are mirrored in a nation moved profoundly by the generations we have just lived through, perhaps not realising we were living through them.
The huge volume of emotive, sentimental outpouring is rather lovely, and amid it all an enduring image of three little boys walking down a Buenos Aires street with No 10 Messi shirts on their backs signals the way forward, towards a future unknown. – Guardian

title: Over one in four of all cars sold this year was an EV – Simi
description: More than 120,000 cars type have been registered in the State so far this year with Toyota the top seller
content:
Sales of electric cars have jumped 55 per cent so far this year, according to the Society of the Irish Motor Industry (Simi) .
Over one in four off all cars sold up to the end of August was battery electric. That’s just over 32,000 new registrations this year compared to some 20,600 in the first eight months of 2025.
Total new car registrations were up 5 per cent from last year, the trade association said, with 121,979 cars registered.
Electric engines accounted for 26.3 per cent of the new vehicle market share, with hybrid (petrol-electric) cars coming in a close second with 24.14 per cent.
Petrol-driven cars represented 20.09 per cent of all registrations in the first eight months of the year, with plug-in hybrids accounting for 14.95 per cent and diesel cars 12.56 per cent.
Toyota led the way as the top selling new car brand across all engine types so far this year, with Volkswagen , Skoda , Hyundai and Kia the next most popular. Among the most popular electric vehicle (EV) brands were Kia, Volkswagen, Hyundai, Skoda and Tesla .
Brian Cooke, Simi’s director general, said the market shift towards battery electric vehicles “is clearly evident, and it is crucial that the Government supports this trend with incentives that build on this momentum in what is still a developing market”.
He called on the Government to extend and retain current incentives, such as the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) grant, vehicle registration tax relief and the zero per cent benefit-in-kind threshold “that are vital in sustaining consumer confidence”.
“This would enable more households and businesses to make the switch, while also supporting our climate change goals,” Cooke added. “Now is the time to invest in incentives to drive change.”
“Additional targeted measures like the scrappage scheme, investment in high-powered public charging infrastructure and a focus on the business sectors can also help increase our national fleet and our second-hand BEV [battery electric vehicle] market,” he said.
Imported used cars have also seen a significant increase in sales this year to date, with just over 63,800 being registered so far, a 37 per cent increase on last year according to Simi.
The group added that the registration of light commercial vehicles, such as standard vans, had risen by 7 per cent to the end of August – to 29,600. However, when comparing on a monthly basis, sales were down 10 per cent this August compared to last.
While sales of heavy goods vehicles, such as trucks are down 1 per cent year-on-year, they were up 9 per cent last month compared to August 2025.
Bus and coaches have also seen a year-on-year increase in sales, with 457 registered so far in 2026, up 34 per cent from 340 last year.

title: Ferry that capsized off Cyprus, killing at least eight, had been subject of long legal row
description: Specialised Turkish navy vessel has joined rescue operation with 20 people still missing
content:
A search-and-rescue ship from Turkey has joined in the efforts to reach a ferry that capsized off Turkish-occupied northern Cyprus on Sunday.
At least eight people died when the vessel overturned shortly after leaving the port with 267 passengers and crew aboard. Twenty people are missing.
The ​Turkish navy rescue vessel has a remotely operated vehicle that can search the deep water where the ferry ⁠sank, about four nautical miles ​off the coast. The ferry had set off for the town of Tasucu in Turkey’s Mersin province only minutes before capsizing.
Survivors who scrambled to safety by clinging to part of the overturned hull were picked up by boats. Footage posted on social media appeared to show people still inside one of the compartments as others perched on the tip of the boat waited for help. Children are among ‌those missing.
The cause ⁠of the disaster is under investigation. Turkish Cypriot authorities said the vessel had a valid seaworthiness certificate.
The Turkish rescue vessel’s deployment coincided with the detention of the captain, crew, owners and port officials and their appearance in the district court.
The captain and crew testified that the ferry capsized after its bow was breached by high waves. They said the vessel had valid navigation certificates, and the weather was fine when the ship commenced its voyage to mainland Turkey. The ferry sank to a depth of 514 metres, significantly complicating the investigation and recovery operations.
The crossing had originally been scheduled for Saturday but was postponed due to a storm. Although the weather had improved on Sunday, conditions were difficult when the incident occurred, Turkish Cypriot newspaper Yeni Duzen reported.
The vessel was commissioned at the Iris Catamarans shipyard in La Rochelle, France on June 1st, 2001.
It was originally named Iris Jet and was owned by the manufacturer before being sold to the Spanish company Cape Balear SL, registered in Palamós, to operate in the Balearic Islands.
In 2003, Iris Jet was chartered by the Turkish company Meltem Denizcilik for limited sailings between Turkey and northern Cyprus. In 2003, it collided with a pier at Tasucu, a popular tourist resort in Mersin Province, but continued operating until suffering serious leakage.
Repairs at a suitable port were recommended, but these were not implemented before the ship’s condition deteriorated, leading to years of insurance and legal disputes.
The internationally recognised Republic of Cyprus said it was ready to offer resources and expertise for the search effort.
The north is cautious and can be hostile about accepting the republic’s help, but there have been exceptions. During two rapidly spreading wildfires in May 2020 in the villages of Diorios and Kormakitis, and in June 2022 in Kantara, the north asked for and promptly received aid, including firefighting aircraft.

title: ‘It is your round’: 20 embarrassing money conversations with pals – and how to deal with them
description: Financial realities and friendships together are often a minefield, so being smart and thinking ahead are key
content:
Socialising – from drinks to weddings to group holidays – can get expensive. Suddenly you start noticing those friends who don’t pay their way. Or the ones who splash the cash and make you feel cheap. In fact, there’s a host of annoying money-related habits that can cause tension among friends. Here are 20 common sources of financial frustration – and how to resolve them.
Pub etiquette seems simple: in a group of friends, everyone takes it in turns to buy the drinks. In practice, it is a minefield. There’s always someone who hangs back in the hope it won’t come round to them; someone who orders half a lager when it’s their turn to pay and a double G&T when it’s yours; couples who see themselves as one entity when it comes to paying, but not when it comes to the actual drinking.
Ellie Austin-Williams, the London-based author of Money Talks: A Lifestyle Guide for Financial Wellbeing, says it is best to bring it up straight away. “Have the conversation at the start: do you want to do a round, or shall we pay our own way?”
Isn’t that a bit embarrassing, though? “People feel it’s too awkward, but it’s better to say: ‘I’ll buy my own, I’m not drinking today.’ People really do respect that.” Conversely, if you’ve all agreed upfront to do rounds, it’s harder for someone to shirk their turn.
Matt Altmix, who is based in Atlanta, Georgia, and co-hosts the podcast How to Money, suggests budgeting for pub trips. If you’re happy with how much you’ve decided to spend that night, you don’t need to obsess about what everyone else is doing. “That way, you’re actually having a good time,” says Altmix. Warning: this may mean going to the pub less often. “Skipping out sometimes is totally acceptable,” he says. “Then, when you do show up, make it count.”
Alex Holder is the author of Open Up: Why Talking About Money Will Change Your Life. She rejects rounds culture altogether. “It’s presuming we’re all going to drink the same amount. Not everyone wants to drink five drinks,” she says. “Rather than noticing that someone gets a cheap drink when they’re paying and feeling enraged, exit the culture.”
Going out for dinner with friends is fraught with financial pitfalls. Do you simply divide the bill by the number of people? That’s a rough deal for the teetotal vegetarian with a small appetite, who ends up subsidising someone else’s steak, sides and wine. Do you pay only for what you ordered? That can seem petty – and somehow there’s always a shortfall.
Joel Larsgaard, Altmix’s best friend and co-host, says: “Typically, the things that add up are the drinks, the appetisers and the dessert. You can still go out and enjoy a nice dinner without overspending if you avoid those big culprits. But you don’t get the savings in the same way if you split a bill with somebody and they’re like: ‘Yeah, I got three cocktails and the fancy tiramisu.’”
Altmix suggests bringing it up in a lighthearted way. “‘Man, Sam’s over there just throwing down the steak, am I right?!’ There’s a way you can have those conversations without it feeling judgmental. Crack some jokes, be light about it and hopefully it leads to some healthy conversation.”
Of course, this approach won’t go down well with everyone. “To some, it’s normal to split the bill,” says Holder. “Not to is an attack on what they ordered.”
Austin-Williams would rather discuss money matters before dinner. “Try to bring it into the conversation when you’re planning. If friends want to go to a fancy restaurant, say: ‘Can we just get a burger? I’m on a budget.’”
Alternatively, raise it before ordering, she says. For example: “‘I’ve got a maximum of €30, so I’m just going to have a main, but you have what you want.’” Failing that, speak up when the bill arrives. You could say: “‘I didn’t have as much and I’m trying to watch my spending this month – is it okay if we pay per item this time?’” She says people worry about looking cheap and not being part of the group, but often others will be relieved that someone has spoken up.
“I believe we should tip because, unfortunately, that is the way that hospitality staff are paid properly. It’s a really hard job with low wages,” says Holder. She understands why some people may dislike the tipping system. “These things feel emotionally fraught: you feel deceived, that the establishment is out to get you.” However, like everyone else I speak to, she feels tipping is non-negotiable.
Larsgaard advises factoring in the tip when budgeting to eat out. “You cannot let your financial situation dictate how much you tip. If you can’t afford it, that is just a sign that you should be eating at home,” he says. “If you don’t want to tip, that’s not frugal, it’s cheap. That’s how we make a distinction: you’re being cheap when your attempts to save money are coming at someone else’s expense.”
[ Raising money-smart kids: How you can teach them from aged three to teens Opens in new window ]
Austin-Williams prefers to take charge, saying something like: “‘Can everyone add €2 for the tip?’” But Holder says: “You can’t make friends tip; everyone has different money rules. Work out your own relationship with tipping.”
If Larsgaard were to notice a friend hadn’t tipped, “that would probably make me mad enough to either leave more on my tip or have a conversation. ‘Did you see how hard she was working? Do you know how much she gets paid?’ I think sometimes people don’t understand the economics of being a server.”
Some people insist on being in the front row; others are happiest in the cheap seats. Often, these preferences have no correlation to bank balances. “Some things can be triggers for certain people, such as spending on theatre tickets or taxis,” says Holder. “Others find it easier to spend on experiences than things.” So what do you do if you’re misaligned with a friend?
Austin-Williams would try to compromise with a high spender. “Say: ‘I’d really like to go, but €80 seats are a bit out of budget at the moment. If you really want to go front row, count me out this time. If not, €35 tickets are fine,’” she says. “Give them the option – they’d probably rather go with you.” You can do similar with a low spender, saying, for example, that you struggled to see from the €20 seats last time, so would prefer to spend a little more if possible.
Larsgaard has other ways to compromise. “Maybe you take one for the team. You’re front row at this one because you both love this artist, then you either skip the next concert or sit in the cheap seats at that one. Or hang out before the show, go together, but sit in different spots.”
No one likes to be a letdown, but sometimes you have to decline an invitation. “One of my friends was just in Europe and went to see Harry Styles at Wembley,” says Larsgaard. “I was like: ‘No, sorry, I can’t afford that right now. Let’s put the record on at my house. If you can afford it, man, go and have an awesome time. I will be a little bit jealous, but also psyched for you.’”
“If you are a type A person who likes to plan everything,” says Altmix, this can happen. Friends may have every intention of getting the tickets next time, but just don’t get the chance. “If you kick back a little bit, that gives them an opportunity to, right? People work at different speeds and have different things going on in their lives and maybe they’re just in a really busy season.”
Austin-Williams says: “If you’re noticing a bit of a pattern, stop offering. Next time, say: ‘I’ll get mine,’ or: ‘Let’s just get our own.’ If your friendship is in danger, raise it. ‘I picked up the bill the last couple of times, would you mind getting it this time?’ Often, people just haven’t been paying attention.”
“Don’t presume that everyone has a collective relationship with money,” says Holder. “Some people find paying money back really difficult; they almost have a block.” She says most people will appreciate it if you are “very straight up” and text with your bank details.
If that doesn’t work, you’ll have to talk to them. “Have a really frank conversation,” says Austin-Williams. “Things happen – your car breaks down, you lose your job. It’s important to understand if your friend is struggling.”
Express concern, rather than making accusations, says Larsgaard. “‘Hey, I noticed you said you were going to pay and you didn’t. Is everything okay?’” They may simply apologise for forgetting, or they may open up about money worries. “It’s very easy to be a jerk, but they’re your friend. Asking a question about what’s going on gives you a chance for deeper connection and understanding.”
When you’re popping to the shops, some friends think nothing of placing an order, even if you haven’t offered. It might only be a couple of quid here and there, but even low-level freeloading can be annoying over time. What should you do?
“You’re thinking, I would never do that,” says Holder. But everyone is different; it has probably never crossed your friend’s mind that you might begrudge them a Diet Coke. “You can a) have a conversation, b) continue to be bothered or c) get over it,” she says. Unless money is really tight, getting over it seems the best option here.
It may feel as though you’re always the one paying for the taxi or doing the driving and that your friends are taking advantage. It’s probably not that calculated, says Holder. “Someone might think: ‘You’re always getting an Uber; I’ll get in it as I’m going that way.’ Accept that their norm about money may not be yours,” she says. “Rather than getting mad with friends, take responsibility for your own spending. For example, if you often give a friend a lift, either ask them for petrol money or don’t agree to drive them places.”
[ Our biggest worries: money, health and relationships Opens in new window ]
What if they said they’d contribute, but haven’t? “Always assume it’s unintentional,” says Austin-Williams. “Give them a nudge: ‘Just doing my budget and wondered if you could send that Uber fare over?’ Most friends just need that nudge.”
Ideally, says Holder, “holiday with people who are willing to spend a similar amount to you. Don’t holiday with really rich people or accept it’s really going to bug you.”
Altmix will only travel with someone he knows well. “You’ve got to pay for everything when you’re travelling, right? Everything costs money. You wake up, you’re paying for something – you’ve got to get some coffee, you’ve got to get some breakfast. There are all these money decisions throughout the day. And if you haven’t established an understanding of how much you like to spend and the type of travelling that you like to do, I think you could be in a world of hurt financially and from a relational standpoint.”
Be clear about your expectations at the planning stage, says Austin-Williams. “Be specific. ‘This is my budget for the whole trip; this is my budget for the accommodation. Who’s going to pay? What’s the repayment schedule?’ There’s a chance you won’t be able to align.”
Larsgaard says: “It comes down to honesty and having those conversations up front. ‘Yeah, I’d like to go to Spain, but how do you feel about a hotel versus a B&B? Can we save on this part of the trip and accentuate that part of the trip?” Is the holiday doomed if your friend wants to go for a five-star all-inclusive, and you want to go for budget self-catering, or vice versa? “I think people feel, if one of their friends suggests this fancy trip, they either have to be ‘I’m in or I’m out’. I don’t think that it’s a dichotomy like that. You can come to a happy medium. If you really don’t have the money, you can say: ‘Spain’s off for now, but maybe I can start saving up for next year. What do you think about a camping trip instead?’”
If you’re renting a shared house or a villa, do you pay per head, per room – or another way? What if some people are staying longer than others? It comes down to communication, says Austin-Williams. “Say if you’d like a bigger room and you’re happy to pay more rather than assuming everything is split equally. People feel resentful if they don’t get an en suite and they’re paying the same. There’s no right or wrong, but if you’ve had the conversation, no one can say it’s unfair.”
Olly Green, a Leeds-based content editor at the price comparison website TravelSupermarket, says: “Work out what each room would typically cost if booked on its own, then split the bill according to that. This way, a single traveller staying in a single room should pay less than a couple in a double room. Likewise, a family with children will pay more for a bigger room with extras such as additional beds or an en suite.”
Too complicated? Holder says this is one of the few occasions when she would recommend using AI: “You can outline the scenario and it will do the maths for you.” Failing that, “organise separate accommodation near each other”.
You budgeted for the travel and accommodation and thought you had plenty for food and activities, but now your friends want to eat at fancy restaurants and go on expensive excursions. Do you have to miss out?
“You could just sit back and not be a part of it and it’s going to seem like you’re a wet blanket,” says Altmix. “Or you catch the first whiff of that and you jump into the fray.” Make sure you’ve researched some better-value alternatives. “You say: ‘What if we are able to save some money by doing XYZ? It’s going to be a ton of fun. And then I heard about this thing over here that’s a great deal. We could have an absolute blast.’ Don’t retreat and be absent from the conversation, but steer it.” Chances are, others will appreciate some affordable options, too.
Groups have different ways of sharing holiday costs: some take it in turns to pay, some pay into a kitty, others keep a spreadsheet or use apps such as Splitwise. “There is no single ‘best’ way to share costs on holiday,” says Green. “The key thing is to be honest about how you’d prefer to do it before the holiday starts. Leaving it until it comes to paying the first bill can lead to awkward situations.”
[ Is it really possible to retire early? Look at how you are spending your money Opens in new window ]
Holder isn’t a fan of a shared pot: “Kitties can be difficult, as people have different spending habits.” She tells me about a group holiday where one friend was looking for the cheapest brand of grapes to buy while another was ordering fresh oysters to be delivered to the villa – both out of the kitty. “Often, everyone thinks they’re the reasonable person,” she says.
Nor is she a huge fan of technological solutions. “Apps can help, but some people forget to add their costs, while some people add every little thing,” she says. “It’s better if everyone has a night when they’re catering.”
Austin-Williams thinks these send-offs “have got a bit out of hand” and are one of the most difficult situations to handle with friends. “If you don’t want to go to an expensive hen do abroad, honesty is the best policy,” she says. “A really good friend doesn’t want you to rack up debts. Say that you can’t afford to go and offer an alternative: ‘I would love to take you out for lunch or spend a day with you instead.’ Try to present a positive angle.”
“You don’t have to go! You’re not held to ransom,” says Holder. “I believe very strongly that you can’t let yourself get into debt for someone else’s wedding.”
However, “if it’s a really close friend, you find ways to afford it”, says Altmix. “That doesn’t mean putting it on a credit card. It means cutting back in other areas.” Larsgaard mentions a friend who declined a wedding he could afford because he was prioritising saving, and later regretted not going. “Don’t be so cheap as to miss out on important life memories. Be there for your friends,” Larsgaard says.
If you genuinely can’t afford to attend, make an effort to be part of the day, says Altmix: “You could put together a cool video of you as friends over the years and include a nice, heartfelt note.”
You are not duty-bound to say yes, says Holder: “You don’t have to feel mugged or go into debt for a donkey sanctuary.” So what should you say to your friend, who may have been training hard for a cause close to their heart? “Say you’d love to support, but you give to specific charities regularly,” says Austin-Williams. “If that isn’t the case, be honest about your financial capacity and say that you have allocated all your budget.”
But every little helps – maybe you could consider making a small donation. “I’d always encourage people to factor giving into a budget where they can, as it’s such a key part of a healthy financial mindset,” says Austin-Williams. And if you can give a little something, says Holder, “you get to feel good twice – for being a supportive friend and for being charitable.”
Holder thinks it’s worth questioning your approach to gift-gifting: “What is the gift serving? Is it a true act of love or an awkward routine? Is a friendship going to fail because you didn’t buy them a gift?” She has noticed that “we buy our richest friends the most expensive gifts. Who are you doing it for? You can just stop.”
Austin-Williams would rather give friends a heads-up. “Say: ‘I’m changing my approach to gifting. I’m trying to reduce how much I’m consuming.’” She suggests buying books (“They can be from a charity shop”) or sharing an experience, such as a day trip.
It’s the thought that counts, says Larsgaard. “With a friend, so much of what they’re after is your thoughtfulness; it’s not how much the gift costs. If a friend saw something you were going through and wrote you a handwritten note, that would mean more to you than a fancy necklace. Just because you ditch expensive presents, it doesn’t mean you have to ditch the thoughtfulness behind gift-giving.”
Is it okay to ask a friend for a loan? This really depends on you and your friends. For Holder, it’s a hard no: “I would never ask to borrow money from a friend.” Austin-Williams, on the other hand, says: “If you’ve got a strong friendship, there’s no reason you shouldn’t be able to ask. Friends are meant to help you out in good and bad times.” To avoid potential difficulties, she says: “Be really clear about the amount and the payment terms. Don’t accept ‘pay me back whenever’. Push them to have a date in the diary.”
“I would be happy to lend to a friend if they were struggling and were clear about repayment,” says Austin-Williams. “I would not hesitate – and I hope my close friends would do the same for me.”
Only give money to a friend if you don’t expect to be paid back, says Larsgaard. “That’s the hard and fast rule: it has to be seen as a gift. If you’re haranguing them about it – ‘Hey, when are you going to give me that 150 bucks I lent you?’ – you’re going to do damage to your friendship.”
Even then, there can be negative consequences, he says: “Oftentimes, giving that gift or accepting a gift is a recipe for uncomfortable feelings and potential friendship harm. You have to be really careful before you wade into that territory.”
“Often, we meet new friends in a neutral environment where our circumstances are similar on the surface – at school, university or work,” says Austin-Williams. “As you notice differences, that can be uncomfortable. For example, you and your colleague have the same career path, but they were bought their flat and you’re struggling to pay your rent.”
She recommends talking about it openly. “Some people have been brought up in a ‘money is taboo’ family. But most people, if asked directly, will answer: ‘Mum and Dad gave me the deposit.’ It allows you to join the dots. The more you can talk about it, the more your friendship can thrive.” She even asks her friends how much they earn. “There’s a lot of shame attached to financial circumstances – not having money, or having it. But if the friendship can’t survive honesty, is it really that good?”
It’s a case of acknowledging that we’re all different, she continues. “Just because their finances are better, it doesn’t mean their life is rosy. Money feels all-consuming, but it doesn’t have to be a make-or-break in your friendship. A bit of jealousy is fine, but recognise it and try not to let it get in the way of your friendship.”
[ Cash is all but dead: How to navigate the complex world of virtual money Opens in new window ]
Holder says: “Friendships are all about bridging so many disparities: health, time, family. Wages are just one of these. Often, what gets in the way of friendships isn’t disparity in earnings, but different expectations and judgments of the ‘correct’ way to spend and save and share money. Our relationship with money is like our relationship with sex – there is no definitively ‘good’ way to be with money. I’ve seen overgenerosity annoy a friendship group as much as the person who never pays their share of petrol.”
What if you can’t afford to do the things your better-off friends suggest? “It’s quite sad when the only time you can socialise is through expensive experiences,” Holder says. “Acknowledge if it’s always costing money and suggest a different way to spend time together, such as coming round to yours for pasta.”
If you think a friend is struggling financially, should you broach the topic with them? “I’d definitely approach them with sensitivity,” says Austin-Williams. “I’d say: ‘I’ve noticed XYZ. You can always talk to me.’ You don’t have to be specific about money. Give them the opportunity: ‘I’m here to talk about anything if you’re struggling.’”
Larsgaard says: “Most people feel uncomfortable talking about money; it feels like another language. But if your friend is struggling and you have even just a little bit of knowledge and can point them to some resources, that’s what friends are for.”
Altmix adds: “You don’t have to have a specialised knowledge of the topic in order to be a good friend. A lot of times, folks just need someone to walk alongside them.” – Guardian

title: Willie Mullins snaps up Ryan Moore for Kentucky Downs raid with Ethical Diamond
description: Moore also rides Aidan O’Brien’s Causeway in $3m Nashville Derby while Ben Curtis teams up with Joseph O’Brien in same race
content:
Breeders’ Cup champion Ethical Diamond is back in the US this weekend where he will be a first runner at the Kentucky Downs track for Willie Mullins .
Jump racing’s dominant trainer has engaged Ryan Moore to ride Ethical Diamond in the Group Two Kentucky Turf Cup over a mile and a half. The race is worth $2 million, although non-Kentucky breds, such as last year’s shock Breeders’ Cup Turf winner, will compete for half that.
The only all-turf course in the US is located near the Tennessee border, and it won’t be entirely unfamiliar territory for Mullins.
He accompanied his father Paddy to the site in 1990 when it was first opened and was known as the Dueling Grounds. Grabel won an International Hurdle on that occasion when ridden by Tony Mullins.
That was the richest jumps race in America at the time and Mullins is again in pursuit of big bucks with his former hurdler in a race likely to contain 10 runners in all. Likely opposition includes the German Group One winner Tiffany, trained by Mark Prescott.
“They have described the track to me as being like Bath,” the Newmarket trainer commented.
Dylan Browne McMonagle memorably guided Ethical Diamond to victory at Del Mar last November. He is on the sidelines after a fall at Bellewstown last week, although Moore was in the saddle when Ethical Diamond narrowly landed last month’s Ballyroan Stakes at Leopardstown.
The English jockey is making his own first appearance at Kentucky Downs and will also team up with his Coolmore bosses in the Grade Two Nashville Derby, where Causeway flies the flag for Ballydoyle.
He is one of a dozen hopefuls still in the mix for a race run over just shy of 10 furlongs and won last year by the Frankie Dettori-ridden Wimbledon Hawkeye.
With a massive $3 million prize fund it is the second richest race for three-year-olds in the US, behind only the Kentucky Derby.
Causeway is on a retrieval mission having finished last on his previous start in July’s Grand Prix de Paris at Longchamp. Prior to that he’d won his four previous races, including Royal Ascot’s King Edward VII Stakes.
Causeway will be joined in Saturday’s lucrative contest by another Irish hope, Nil Bua Gan Dua. Joseph O’Brien’s hope – whose name roughly translates from Irish as no victory without hardship – will be ridden by US-based Irish rider Ben Curtis.
O’Brien has already tasted success at Kentucky Downs, winning a $500,000 race there in 2022 with Reckoning Force. Nil Bua Gan Dua won a Listed race at Gowran in July on his previous start.
In 2010 O’Brien and Curtis, along with Gary Carroll, were part of a three-way tie for the apprentice jockeys’ title in Ireland.
Saturday’s Kentucky Downs meeting is the latest at the course located about an hour north of Nashville and which offers a massive $37 million in prize money over a number of weeks. Casino revenue has financially propelled it into the top echelon of racetracks in terms of purse money.
The start of September accelerates focus on international racing generally and attention in Australia is already on Joseph O’Brien’s potential grip on November’s Aus$10 million Melbourne Cup.
O’Brien has twice won the race that famously stops a nation through Rekindling (2017) and Twilight Payment three years later. On Tuesday, a total of 101 initial entries were announced for the world-famous handicap, and O’Brien has 11 of them.
They include one of the 12-1 joint-favourites, Defiantly, last year’s runner-up Goodie Two Shoes and James J Braddock, who ran third in June’s Epsom Derby. The Derby winner, Christmas Day, is one of five entries made by Aidan O’Brien, who has yet to win the Melbourne Cup.
It’s an astonishing show of strength from O’Brien jnr in a race where six runners form a single trainer is the most in the history of the race.
James J Braddock’s owner, Ozzie Kheir, told media in Australia recently: “I spoke to him [O’Brien] last night and was joking to him that he’ll probably have half the field!”
The other Irish trainer still in the Melbourne Cup mix is Emmet Mullins, who has left in Winday. Among the long-range English entries is the former Champion Hurdle winner Constitution Hill. He is set to have the third start of his emerging flat career at Kempton on Saturday in the September Stakes, where he will need to finish in the first three to meet conditions of the Flemington contest.
The 2023 Champion Hurdle winner has been made a 20-1 in some lists to pull off an unlikely global double.

title: Ikea cuts Irish prices by up to 25% amid slumping consumer confidence
description: About 1,500 products in 20 European countries will be cheaper as furniture retailer battles cost-of-living crisis
content:
Ikea is cutting prices by €1.2 billion in Europe, including in Ireland, this year on some of its most popular products such as Billy bookshelves and Kallax storage units,. The move is an attempt by the flat-pack furniture retailer to counter the cost-of-living crisis by taking a hit to its profits.
The world’s largest furniture retailer said on Tuesday that it would cut costs of about 1,500 products by 15 to 25 per cent in more than 20 European countries as consumer confidence continues to remain depressed.
“Ikea likes to reduce the price of the umbrella when it’s raining. And it’s raining for many customers, because the cost of living is increasing. So this is exactly the right thing for Ikea to do,” Juvencio Maeztu, chief executive of the leading Ikea retailer Ingka, told the FT.
European consumer confidence remains at its lowest level in three years despite a recent uptick, taking a sharp hit after the Iran war began in February amid concerns about inflation and higher energy prices.
Ikea, which is privately owned by twin charitable foundations, did something similar in 2023 to offset large price rises due to rising logistic costs after the Covid-19 pandemic. That led to its first drop in revenues in a decade and a halving in profits.
The price reductions vary subtly from country to country but include 27 per cent off a Besta TV shelf in Germany, 28 per cent off Billy bookshelves in the UK and up to 29 per cent off Kallax storage systems in Italy.
Jakub Jankowski, chief executive of Inter Ikea, the owner of the brand and concept, said: “I strongly believe this is not a one-off. We will continue to do it. It’s a long-term commitment.”
He added that Ikea’s integrated supply chain meant it was easier to cut prices in Europe, but that the retailer would use €70 million to reduce them in the Americas and Asia as well.
Maeztu refused to comment on exactly how it would affect results, other than to acknowledge it would hurt profitability. Ikea is about to report full-year revenue figures as its financial year runs to the end of August, with the effect of the price cuts set to appear in next year’s figures.
“Our entry point is to accept that it will lower results, because it’s a time to side with the many people,” Maeztu added.
Ikea has historically cut the prices of its products slowly over the years by tweaking their design and assembly to reduce their size. But after decades of modest inflation in Europe and the US, it has been forced to take more radical action in recent years as it seeks to offer affordable furniture to customers even as the cost of raw materials and logistics has risen sharply. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Man ‘catastrophically’ injured in Leopardstown brawl dies in hospital
description: Two men accused of violent disorder following Saturday incident denied bail at Dún Laoghaire District Court
content:
A 24-year-old man who sustained “catastrophic injuries” in a large-scale violent confrontation in Leopardstown , Dublin, at the weekend has died.
Kevin Rostas (21) of Harrington Street, Dublin 8, and Cristian Demian (23) of Howth Road, Raheny, appeared before Judge Conor Fottrell in connection with the incident on Tuesday.
Dún Laoghaire District Court heard they were accused of violent disorder at the South County Business Park in Sandyford on Saturday evening.
Demian has an additional charge for assault causing harm to Siminic Rostas. Bail was denied, and more serious charges are anticipated.
The judge heard at 12.59pm – just as a bail hearing for Demian was beginning – that Siminic Rostas’ life support had been switched off and he had died at Beaumont Hospital’s intensive care unit.
Det Garda David Buckley and Det Garda Michael Doheny objected to bail.
They told the court at 8.25pm on Saturday that officers received a report of a large-scale disturbance involving several males engaged in violence at an abandoned premises.
Gardaí found three males – including Siminic Rostas – who were seriously injured and all of whom required hospitalisation.
The court heard initial inquiries established that about 15 members of the Roma community had resided at the abandoned premises for several months.
It was claimed the accused and three others called, stating they were there to collect personal property from someone at the premises.
The detectives said there was a verbal dispute that escalated suddenly to violence, the subject of which remains the subject of the Garda investigation.
The judge heard a sustained physical confrontation involving the defendant and three males against four other males who were occupants of the premises followed.
CCTV footage captured significant portions of the incident and has shown lethal weapons and implements were used during the fight, including poles, sticks and shovels.
Kevin Rostas and Demian were clearly visible on CCTV actively participating in the physical confrontation, the court heard, and Demian identified himself in the footage.
The detective stated Kevin Rostas could be seen striking other males on a number of occasions. He maintained he acted in self-defence.
Det Garda Doheny said Demian struck the severely injured man twice with a shovel, “rendering him unconscious and inflicting catastrophic injuries”. The court heard the now deceased man was also struck after he was unconscious.
The court also heard gardaí were concerned the incident had escalated rapidly into a confrontation involving multiple individuals with weapons.
It was alleged one of the hospitalised men has received several threatening messages on his phone, stating that there would be “retribution”, with the phrases “this is not the end of it” and “your brother is next”.
Violent disorder and assault causing harm carry a maximum sentence of 10 years, and the detective referred to the seriousness of the injuries.
Kevin Rostas was not represented due to the ongoing solicitors’ strike, which has seen solicitors withdraw their services in District Court legal aid cases over payment reforms.
Det Garda Buckley said Rostas had connections to Romania and travelled there annually.
Both men had separate bail hearings and were assisted by an interpreter.
Rostas was adamant he would not leave Ireland, and said he has been living in Ireland for 12 years. His reply to his charge was: “I didn’t threaten.”
The judge held that gardaí had established flight-risk grounds that the pair were likely to evade justice.
They were remanded in custody to appear at Cloverhill District Court on September 8th.
A third man, Augustin Rostas, has appeared in court faced with the same charge and allegations. The 22-year-old, with addresses at Convent Place, Hatch Street Lower, and Kevin Street, Dublin 2, was granted conditional bail.
He was remanded in custody pending a €1,000 lodgement and an address check. On taking up bail he must have no contact with witnesses. He will appear again on Friday.

title: Danny Gilligan lands another successful appeal against whip ban
description: Prolific dual Galway festival winner Timurshah aiming to translate hurdles form to the flat in Navan
